items.h: פְּתִיחָה

The theme: The whole work hangs on the Gemara’s seven statements in praise of teshuvah (Yoma 86). Teshuvah is drawn from the binah of the heart — which is why the Men of the Great Assembly fixed it after “binah” in the blessings. The seven praises correspond to the seven lower sefiros, the stages by which anything passes from the heart’s understanding into completed act; hence seven simanim, one per praise.

p: בְּיוֹמָא [פו.] ״גְּדוֹלָה תְּשׁוּבָה״ כו׳, עַיֵּין שָׁם שֶׁבַע מֵימְרוֹת בִּגְדֻלַּת וּמַעֲלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה

In Yoma [86a–b], “Great is teshuvah,” etc. — see there seven statements on the greatness and elevation of teshuvah.1Yoma 86a–b: Seven statements in praise of teshuvah: (a) “Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world”; (b) “Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory”; (c) “Great is teshuvah, for it overrides a Torah prohibition”; (d) “Great is teshuvah, for it hastens the redemption”; (e) “Great is teshuvah, for it turns willful sins into inadvertent ones — or into merits”; (f) “Great is teshuvah, for it lengthens a person’s days and years”; (g) “Great is teshuvah, for one individual who repents, he and the whole world are forgiven.” R’ Tzadok reads the seven as corresponding to the seven lower sefiros, and structures the work’s seven simanim accordingly.2Cf. Pesachim 54a (and Nedarim 39b): teshuvah is among the seven things created before the world — “Torah, teshuvah, Gan Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Beis HaMikdash, and the name of Mashiach.” The list itself traces this work’s arc: teshuvah (rooted in Binah) that reaches the Throne of Glory (Siman 2) and culminates in the name of Mashiach (Siman 4).3R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §100): “Teshuvah means that one returns the very thing to Hashem — that is, he recognizes that Hashem effects everything, and that His power was present even in the thought before it was formed in a man’s heart (Bereishis Rabbah 9); it emerges that Hashem gave him the strength even within the sin, and through this, after complete teshuvah, he merits that willful sins become merits, for this too was Hashem’s will.” This is the inner engine of the “seven greatnesses” the preamble sets out: teshuvah is no mere remorse but the restoring of the strayed thing to its Source — and because the very power spent on the sin was God-given, that power, turned back, becomes the ladder by which teshuvah “reaches the Throne.”
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
And it is known that teshuvah is drawn from the binah [understanding] of the heart —
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וּלְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב״, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרִינַן ״תְּשׁוּבָה״ אַחַר ״בִּינָה״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה [יז:]

as it says, “and his heart shall understand and he shall return” (Yeshayah 6:10)4Yeshayah 6:10: part of Yeshayah’s inaugural vision (ch. 6). After Israel has persisted in sin, the prophet is charged: “הַשְׁמֵן לֵב הָעָם הַזֶּה וְאָזְנָיו הַכְבֵּד וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע, פֶּן יִרְאֶה בְעֵינָיו וּבְאָזְנָיו יִשְׁמָע וּלְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ” — “Make the heart of this people fat, and their ears heavy, and seal their eyes, lest they see with their eyes and hear with their ears and their heart understand, and they return and be healed.” Rashi explains “hashmen” as a continuous hardening (of the form “hachbed es libo,” Shemos 8:11), and that “lest they see with their eyes and their heart understand and return, and it be their healing” describes the very outcome the people had closed their hearts against. R’ Tzadok draws on the order of the verse — first “their heart shall understand [yavin],” then “and return [va-shav]” — that teshuvah is drawn from the binah of the heart; this is why the Men of the Great Assembly set the blessing of teshuvah after binah in the Amidah (Megillah 17b), and why the “healing [ve-rafa lo]” that follows is the healing of forgiveness.; therefore we say [the blessing of] “teshuvah” after “binah” [in the Amidah], as they said in Megillah [17b].5Megillah 17b: “Why did [the Men of the Great Assembly] see fit to place teshuvah after binah [in the Amidah]? Because it is written, ‘and his heart shall understand and return and be healed’ (Yeshayah 6:10).” The Gemara then distinguishes the “healing” of forgiveness (which follows teshuvah directly) from bodily healing (which follows forgiveness): “that is not the healing of ailments but the healing of forgiveness.”

וְנוֹדַע דְּשֶׁבַע מַדְרֵגוֹת הֵם בִּיצִיאַת דָּבָר לַפּוֹעֵל מִבִּינַת הַלֵּב עַד גְּמַר הַפְּעֻלָּה, שֶׁהֵם סוֹד שֶׁבַע סְפִירוֹת חג“ת נהי”מ, וְנֶגְדָּם הוּא כָּל מִסְפַּר שֶׁבַע כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְכֵן שֶׁבַע גְּדוֹלוֹת אֵלּוּ דִּתְשׁוּבָה

And it is known that there are seven stages in a thing’s emergence into act, from the understanding of the heart until the completion of the deed — these being the secret of the seven sefiros Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferes, Netzach, Hod, Yesod, Malchus — and against them is every “seven,” as is known; so too these seven “greatnesses” of teshuvah.6R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §159): “An individual who repents is forgiven, and the whole world with him (Yoma 86b) — and how is such forgiveness possible? Only that he arouses in their hearts too the stirrings of teshuvah; and not everyone who wishes to make himself such an ‘individual’ can do so, for it has not yet been — only Mashiach ben David will be so, for his soul must include all souls, since otherwise his own thoughts of teshuvah could not generate thoughts of teshuvah in one who has none.” This marks the outermost reach of the “greatness of teshuvah” that heads the work: from the very same Yoma 86 sugya, a single true penitent can draw a whole world after him — the summit toward which the seven rungs ascend.

sections.en: Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world

items.h: גדולה תשובה שמביאה רפואה לעולם.
“Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world” (the first of the seven — corresponding to Chesed).

The theme: The “healing” of this first rung is the healing of forgiveness, not bodily healing — a rectification going forward only. The moment a person’s heart stirs to return he is already called a complete tzaddik, before he has performed any labor upon the past. But a trace remains, as with a healed baal mum, or a convert whose earlier state is not wholly uprooted.

p: [א] ״שֶׁמְּבִיאָה רְפוּאָה לָעוֹלָם״, וְנִרְאֶה לִי דְּהַיְינוּ רְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה כְּלִישָּׁנֵיהּ דִּקְרָא ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם״

“That it brings healing to the world” — and it appears to me that this means the healing of forgiveness, in the language of the verse “I will heal their backsliding” (Hoshea 14:5)7Hoshea 14:5: the climactic verse of the prophet’s call to teshuvah (ch. 14, “Shuvah Yisrael,” read as the haftarah of Shabbos Shuvah): “אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם, אֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה, כִּי שָׁב אַפִּי מִמֶּנּוּ” — “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely, for My anger has turned away from him.” Rashi (from Tanchuma, Ekev): “once they say [the words of teshuvah] before Me, I will heal their backsliding [meshuvah] and love them with a generous spirit — though they are not worthy of the love, I will freely bestow it — for My anger has turned from them.” R’ Tzadok adduces this as the source that the “healing” of which the Gemara speaks (Yoma 86a, “great is teshuvah, for it brings healing”) is the healing of forgiveness: “meshuvah” means backsliding [sin], and it is precisely this that is “healed.” Chassidic parallels — the verse itself becomes a map of the first movement of teshuvah. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Prophets, Hoshea 14:1, reads the whole passage beginning "Ashur lo yoshienu" as Israel's surrender of every claim to spiritual self-sufficiency. Good deeds, zerizus, yirah, and even fiery ahavah are not things in which a person can finally boast; the decisive point is the "kol demamah dakah," the quiet Divine seal in the heart that the present movement truly accords with Hashem's will. The Divine response is then precisely, "ארפא משובתם אוהבם נדבה כי שב אפי ממנו" — "I will heal their backsliding... for My anger has turned from him," which the Mei HaShiloach explains as the removal of Divine anger from Israel. This fits R' Tzadok's insistence that the first refuah is the refuah of selichah: before the past has been transformed, the relationship has already been reopened and the anger has turned away. Sefas Emes, Rosh HaShanah 25:4, develops the next words, "אוהבם נדבה." There is an ahavah dependent upon conduct, which can be obscured when conduct fails, and there is the essential love of Israel because "chelek Hashem amo," an ahavah she-einah teluyah badavar. Sin can conceal the soul's revelation, but teshuvah reawakens it; hence "ארפא משובתם" is followed by "אוהבם נדבה." In the language of the Sefas Emes, the healing is not merely the cancellation of a punishment but the re-emergence of the neshama-level bond that the aveirah had hidden. This supplies a Chassidic basis for R' Tzadok's distinction between a wound that has been healed and the deeper root that was never destroyed. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 39 (39:19 in Sefaria's segmentation), explicitly invokes the same ma'amar, "teshuvah brings healing to the world," in a strikingly concrete way: Torah learned with an ulterior motive can be held temporarily in exile within kelipas nogah, "עד אשר יעשה תשובה שמביאה רפואה לעולם, שבשובו אל ה' גם תורתו שבה עמו" — until he does teshuvah, which brings healing to the world; when he returns to Hashem, his Torah returns with him. The "world" healed by teshuvah thus includes the person's own earlier Torah and avodah: acts that were spiritually displaced are drawn back with the returning person. This is already a bridge from the first rung — healing from now on — toward the later rungs in which the past itself is recovered.,8Yoma 86a: “R’ Chama b’Rabbi Chanina said: Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world, as it says, ‘I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely’ (Hoshea 14:5).” He further contrasts “Return, backsliding children” (implying they were always wayward — teshuvah from love, which makes the very origin as innocent) with “I will heal your backslidings” (implying, as Rashi explains, one healed like a cured baal mum of whom “a trace of his name remains” — teshuvah from fear).
דִּמְבֹאָר דְּקָאֵי אַמְּשׁוּבָה, וּדְלֹא כַּמָּהַרְשָׁ"א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת

which clearly refers to backsliding [sin], and not as the Maharsha [held] in Chiddushei Aggados.9Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados, Yoma 86a: questions why the Gemara did not prove that teshuvah brings healing “to the world” from “and he shall return and be healed to him” (Yeshayah 6:10), and suggests the verse speaks of literal healing, implying the sinner is not yet forgiven. R’ Tzadok rejects this: the Gemara in Megillah makes explicit that the “healing” here is forgiveness itself, which comes immediately upon teshuvah — the sinner is at once forgiven.

וְהָא דְּלָא מַיְיתֵי ״וְשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ״, דְּשָׁם כְּתִיב ״לוֹ״ לְשׁוֹן יָחִיד, וְהָכִי דָּיֵיק ״לָעוֹלָם״ מִדְּפָתַח בִּלְשׁוֹן רַבִּים וְסִיֵּים בִּלְשׁוֹן יָחִיד כִּדְדָיֵיק רִי"ף בְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב

And the reason [the Gemara] does not adduce “and he shall return and be healed” (Yeshayah 6:10) is that there it is written “to him” in the singular; and thus [R’ Chama] derives “to the world” from the fact that [the verse in Hoshea] opens in the plural and closes in the singular, as the Rif derives in Ein Yaakov.
וּבְנֻסְחַת גְּמָרָא שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ אִיתָא ״רְפוּאוֹת״ לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים, וְאִם הוּא נֻסְחָא דַּוְוקָנִית יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּתַרְתֵּי קָאָמַר — רְפוּאַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ וּרְפוּאַת הַגּוּף, דְּהָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָא

And in our text of the Gemara it reads “healings [refu’os]” in the plural; if that is the precise text, one may say it states two — the healing of the soul and the healing of the body — for the one depends on the other,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״הַסֹּלֵחַ לְכָל עֲוֺנֵכִי הָרֹפֵא לְכָל תַּחֲלוּאָיְכִי״, וְכִדְאִיתָא בִּמְגִילָּה שָׁם

as it says, “Who forgives all your iniquity, Who heals all your diseases” (Tehillim 103:3)10Tehillim 103:3: “הַסֹּלֵחַ לְכָל עֲוֺנֵכִי, הָרֹפֵא לְכָל תַּחֲלֻאָיְכִי” — “Who forgives all your iniquity, who heals all your diseases” — from David’s psalm blessing Hashem for His benefactions to the soul. The two clauses run parallel — forgiveness of sin and healing of affliction — and the Gemara (Megillah 17b) derives from their order that the “healing” follows upon the “forgiveness”: first the iniquity is pardoned, then the ailments are healed. R’ Tzadok draws on this to explain the plural “refu’os [healings]” in the Gemara’s text as two — the healing of the soul (forgiveness) and the healing of the body — “for the one depends on the other,” the bodily ailments of Israel corresponding exactly to the ailments of the soul., and as is brought in Megillah there [17b].

דְּכָל חֳלָיֵי הַגּוּף שֶׁל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם בְּמִקְרֶה כְּלָל, רַק מַקְבִּילִים מַמָּשׁ לְחֳלָיֵי הַנֶּפֶשׁ, כַּמְפֹרָשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים; וּמִיָּד שֶׁמִּתְרַפֵּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ גַּם הַגּוּף מִתְרַפֵּא

For all the bodily ailments of the Children of Israel are in no way happenstance, but correspond exactly to the ailments of the soul, as the Torah states many times; and the moment the soul is healed, the body too is healed.11R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Eruvin §4): “As it says in the first chapter of Kiddushin (40a), that a good thought the Holy One joins to the deed — even if he [merely] thought [to do a mitzvah] and was prevented by circumstance, Scripture reckons it for him as though he did it; but an evil thought is not joined to the deed, for the transgression is only in the deed, and it is bounded, like this world, the world of action, whereas thought has no bound or limit at all.” The se’if’s point precisely: the mere thought of teshuvah makes one “a complete tzaddik” at once — for thought reaches beyond the bounded world of deed.
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מָהַרְשָׁ"א דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא נִסְלַח — לֵיתָא, דִּמְפֹרָשׁ בִּמְגִילָּה שָׁם דִּרְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה הוּא תֵּיכֶף אַחַר תְּשׁוּבָה, וּרְפוּאָה דְּתַחֲלוּאִים הוּא אַחַר הַסְּלִיחָה

And what the Maharsha wrote — that [at this stage] he has not yet been forgiven — is not so; for it is explicit in Megillah there that the “healing of forgiveness” comes immediately after teshuvah, while the “healing of ailments” comes after the forgiveness, not before it at all.

וְהוּא מַדְרֵגָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה דִּתְשׁוּבָה — לִרְפוּאָה מִכָּאן וְאֵילָךְ עַל כָּל פָּנִים; וְזֶה בָּא מִיָּד, דִּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב״ — עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלִבּוֹ נִקְרָא תֵּיכֶף ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּקִדּוּשִׁין [מט:], אַף דְּלֹא עָשָׂה עֲדַיִין כָּל תִּיקּוּנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה

And this is the first rung of teshuvah — healing from here on, at least; and it comes at once, for “his heart understands and returns” — through the mere thought of teshuvah in his heart he is immediately called a “complete tzaddik,” as they said in Kiddushin [49b], even though he has not yet performed any of the labors of teshuvah.12Kiddushin 49b: “[If a man betroths a woman] ‘on condition that I am a righteous man’ — even a completely wicked man — she is betrothed, for perhaps he had a thought of teshuvah in his mind.” R’ Tzadok adduces this as proof that a mere thought of teshuvah instantly renders one a “complete tzaddik,” even before any of the labors of rectification. Tanya and Izhbitz on the instantaneous halachic force of hirhur teshuvah. Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1 (1:7 in Sefaria's segmentation), defines the Torah's core mitzvah of teshuvah as "עזיבת החטא בלבד" — abandoning the sin — meaning that one "יגמור בלבו בלב שלם לבל ישוב עוד לכסלה," resolves wholeheartedly in his heart not to return to rebellion against His kingship. That formulation is especially apt here: Kiddushin 49b does not require that the man's biography already be visibly rewritten; the relevant question is whether, at that moment, the heart has truly turned. R' Tzadok's "complete tzaddik immediately" therefore accords with the Alter Rebbe's definition of the essential act of teshuvah as a present, inward resolution, while the further avodos of remorse, confession, fasting, and rectification address other dimensions of kapparah and purification. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Talmud, Berachos 4a:2, uses this very Kiddushin passage to describe the radical openness of human bechirah from one moment to the next. A person has, as it were, two open doors: "ברגע אחד יכול להשתנות ולהטיב דרכיו" — in a single moment he can change and improve his ways — and there is likewise an opening in the opposite direction. The Izhbitzer cites both halves of Kiddushin: "al menas she'ani tzaddik," perhaps he had a thought of teshuvah; and "al menas she'ani rasha," perhaps a dark thought entered him. The point is not to minimize deeds but to insist that the living point of choice is never frozen by yesterday's identity. This sharpens R' Tzadok's first rung of refuah: the past may still bear a scar, but the person's present spiritual status can turn immediately because the inner point of bechirah is alive now.13R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §145): “for the good, a good thought the Holy One joins to the deed” (Kiddushin 40a) — since “the soul You gave me is pure,” a good intent is reckoned as an act; “and in teshuvah, which takes all the [sinful] thoughts and returns them to their root, the deeds automatically remain a dead body without vitality.” This illuminates why a mere thought of teshuvah already makes one a “complete tzaddik”: for the good, thought itself counts as deed, and teshuvah’s thought withdraws the vitality the sins had drawn — leaving them lifeless — even before the labors of rectifying the past.

רַק הוּא כְּבַעַל מוּם שֶׁמִּתְרַפֵּא שֶׁמִּקְצָת שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו — הַיְינוּ לְמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֵר הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת, יָדַע שֶׁהָיָה בַּעַל מוּם, רַק דְּנִתְרַפֵּא עַתָּה, וְהוּא כַּגֵּר שֶׁמִּתְגַּיֵּיר, דְּאַף שֶׁהוּא כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין נֶעֱקַר הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי לִהְיוֹת כְּאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

only that he is like a baal mum [a blemished one] who has been healed, of whom “a trace of his name remains” — that is, one who recalls the earlier things knows he was a baal mum, only that he is now healed; and he is like a convert who converts, that although he is “a newborn” from here on, nonetheless the earlier [state] is not wholly uprooted to make him like a native-born Israelite.14R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §12): teshuvah has two aspects — the future and the rectification of the past — and correspondingly two “healings.” “It is established that atonement does not hold [teshuvah] back: for teshuvah, even if he [only] contemplated in his heart, he is a complete tzaddik” — yet this suffices only “for terumah, [that which is] lifted from the fully profane, to be at least within the class of a tzaddik; but for kodshim — one who wishes to sanctify himself and to be holy — he must also heal the past.” R’ Tzadok there anchors this in the Rambam’s “change of name” (one no longer stands in the very time and state of his defilement) and in “were the Holy One not to help him [he could not prevail].” This illuminates the se’if’s first rung: a stir of teshuvah instantly yields the “tzaddik” of forgiveness-going-forward, while the healed baal mum, of whom “a trace of his name remains,” still awaits the further healing of the past.

items.h: The theme: That lingering “trace” is the deficiency for which converts are said to be afflicted: their souls stood at Sinai, yet they did not enter at birth, only later. This root-lack is never fully healed in them. Hence the Torah’s repeated warning against ona’as ha’ger — a true word about a real deficiency works upon a person and can change his very essence.

p: [ב] וּבִיבָמוֹת [מח:] ״מִפְּנֵי מָה גֵּרִים מְעֻנִּין״ כו׳ ״מִפְּנֵי שֶׁשָּׁהוּ״ כו׳

And in Yevamos [48b]: “Why are converts afflicted?” — “because they delayed” [entering under the wings of the Shechinah].15Yevamos 48b: “R’ Yosei says: A convert who converts is like a newborn child [and is not punished for what preceded]. Then why are converts afflicted? Others say: because they delayed coming under the wings of the Shechinah.” R’ Tzadok reconciles the views: for practical punishment the convert is a “newborn,” but with regard to the inner judgments of Heaven the “delay” marks a root-deficiency.16R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §246): the souls of converts and [Canaanite] servants, too, “were at Har Sinai — their mazal was there” (Shabbos 146a); “only there was a difference in the hearing — for the erev rav of that generation stood outside the pillar of cloud, and therefore ‘their inclination is evil’ (Bava Metzia 59b) and they are unrestrained… for their hearing [at Sinai] was through a screen.” This deepens the se’if: the convert’s root-deficiency — that his soul stood at Sinai only at a remove, never entering “under the wings” at birth — is a lack in the very root, which “is never healed in them.”

וְזֶה לָא פְּלִיג אַדְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי שָׁם דְּהוּא כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד וְאֵין לְהַעֲנִישׁ עֲבֵירוֹת הַקּוֹדְמִים, וְגַם לֹא יוֹעִיל זֶה אֲגַר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּיֽר בְּבֵית דִּין בְּקַטְנוּתוֹ [וְכֵן קָשֶׁה אַתַּנָּא קַמָּא שָׁם], אֲבָל לְעִנְיַן דִּינֵי שָׁמַיִם הַכַּוָּונָה עַל שָׁרְשׁוֹ

And this does not disagree with R’ Yosei there [who holds] that he is “a newborn” and is not punished for the earlier transgressions — and this [status of a newborn] does not avail even regarding one who converted in beis din in his childhood [and so too it is difficult according to the first Tanna there] — but with regard to the [inner] judgments of Heaven, the intent is upon his root.
דְּאַף דְּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם נַפְשׁוֹת הַגֵּרִים הָיוּ בְּמַעֲמַד הַר סִינַי, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת [קמו רע"א] ״מַזָּלַיְיהוּ הֲווֹ״, וּמַזָּל הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָאָדָם

For although in truth the souls of converts, too, were present at the standing at Har Sinai — as they said in Shabbos [146a], “their mazal was there” — and the mazal is the root of a person17Shabbos 146a: the souls of future converts, too, were present at Sinai — “though they themselves were not there, their mazal [guiding root] was there.” R’ Tzadok: the mazal is a person’s root, so the convert’s soul was at Sinai; yet because he did not enter “at birth,” a residual deficiency of “delay” remains.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִכְנְסוּ תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה מִיָּד בְּלֵידָה רַק אַחַר כָּךְ, וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם חִסָּרוֹן זֶה בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁשִּׁהוּ, וְזֶה הַחִסָּרוֹן לֹא נִתְרַפֵּא בָּם כְּלָל

nonetheless they did not enter under the wings of the Shechinah immediately at birth, but only afterward; and they have this deficiency in the root — that they “delayed” — and this deficiency is never healed in them at all.18R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §41): “A convert who converts is like a newborn (Yevamos 22a), and it effects that the past is forgotten and as though it is not; but they cannot rectify [it so] that the past too be good — for the root of the nations has no good in it, and the [only] good in it is that it transforms to be called by the name ‘Israel,’ and the name of the [former] nations is submerged from him. But the name ‘Israel’ is called upon even the most wicked in the world.” Exactly the se’if’s distinction: the convert’s “delay” is a root-deficiency that is never truly healed, for the past cannot be made good — unlike a born Jew, whose root is good. Further Chassidic background to "ger shenisgayer ke-katan shenolad." Kedushas Levi, Lech Lecha §37, takes the halachic principle with great literalness in explaining Avraham's break with Terach: the convert's former genealogical life no longer defines his spiritual identity; he is reborn into a new relation to Hashem. Sefas Emes, Vayera 12:3, similarly says that after the milah Avraham became "בריה חדשה כענין גר שנתגייר כקטן שנולד" — a new creature, like a convert who is as a newborn — and reads the new appearance of Hashem at the tent as the opening of an entirely new derech. Beis Yaakov on Torah, Chayei Sarah 24:1, adds an Ishbitz-Radzin nuance especially relevant to R' Tzadok's language of changing the former state. After the Akeidah, milah, and the ten nisyonos, Avraham was "נשתנה מהיפך להיפך, כענין גר שנתגייר" — changed from one opposite to the other, like a convert who must overturn an ingrained former way. Rebirth is therefore not only a juridical severance from the old past but the revelation of a newly ordered personality. At the same time, these sources help preserve R' Tzadok's distinction here. A ger can truly become a new person from this point onward, yet R' Tzadok asks a different, more radical question: can the earlier reality itself become good? Resisei Layla §41 answers that for the ger the former world can be forgotten and submerged, but not transformed into a good Jewish root that was already present there. Shem MiShmuel, Shabbos Shuvah 3:12, compares the highest teshuvah to total immersion: when all the powers of the soul are swallowed into teshuvah one becomes "כקטן שנולד"; this is precisely why the analogy is so powerful for R' Tzadok — ordinary rebirth means a new beginning, whereas the higher Jewish power of teshuvah can ultimately go beyond beginning anew and recast the past itself.
וְעַל כֵּן הִזְהִירָה תּוֹרָה עַל אוֹנָאַת הַגֵּר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים, שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמַר ״פֶּה שֶׁאָכַל נְבֵילוֹת״ כו׳, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא [נח:]

And therefore the Torah warned against wronging the convert many times — that one not say to him, “a mouth that ate carcasses [now comes to learn Torah],” as they said in Bava Metzia [58b].19Bava Metzia 58b: the Mishnah (Bava Metzia 4:10) teaches — “Just as there is ona’ah [wronging] in buying and selling, so is there ona’ah in words. If one is a baal teshuvah, one may not say to him, ‘Remember your earlier deeds’; and if he is the child of converts, one may not say to him, ‘Remember the deeds of your ancestors’ — as it is said, ‘And a convert you shall not wrong, nor oppress him’ (Shemos 22:20).” The Gemara adds: “If he was a convert who came to study Torah, one may not say to him, ‘Shall a mouth that ate carcasses and tereifos, abominations and creeping things, come to study the Torah that was uttered from the mouth of the Almighty?’” This is the source R’ Tzadok cites for the Torah’s repeated warning against ona’as ha-ger.20R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §77): “even a very great person, if there is a blemish in his family, one should not attach oneself to him — for [even] if [it is tolerated] on account of his own greatness, it will yet harm his offspring,” as in “even were he like Yehoshua bin Nun, I would not give him [my daughter]” (Yevamos 45a); “yet from the side of the crown of Torah one need not be concerned about lineage, for the crown of Torah is set out for all… and the foundation of the Oral Torah is R’ Akiva, who was of a family of converts.” This illumines the se’if from the other side: the convert’s root-blemish is real and reaches his seed, yet the crown of Torah wholly transcends it — a “mouth that ate carcasses” can become the very wellspring of the Oral Torah.
וּמֵהוֹצֶרֶךְ לְהַזְהִיר מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא דָּבָר שֶׁנִּיתָּן לֵיאָמֵר, דְּיֵשׁ בּוֹ מִשּׁוּם אוֹנָאָה; דְּמַה שֶּׁאֵינוֹ כְּלָל לֹא אִיכְפַּת לָאָדָם אִם יֹאמְרוּ עָלָיו

And from the very need to warn, it is implied that this is a thing that can be said — that there is in it [substance for] “wronging”; for that which is not [true] at all does not trouble a person if it is said of him,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא אִיכְפַּת לְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ אָח עֵשָׂו, וּלְאַבְרָהָם שֶׁיָּצָא מִתֶּרַח, כֵּיוָן דְּאֵין לוֹ שׁוּם שַׁיָּיכוּת עוֹד לָזֶה
just as it did not trouble Yaakov that he had a brother Esav, nor Avraham that he issued from Terach, since he has no connection to it any longer.

וְאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא [נט:] ״מִפְּנֵי מָה הִזְהִירָה תּוֹרָה עַל הַגֵּרִים — שֶׁטּוֹחֵן רַע״, רָצָה לוֹמַר שָׁרְשָׁן וִיסוֹדָן בֶּאֱמֶת רַע; עַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ הַזְהָרָה עַל אוֹנָאָתוֹ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים גְּדוֹלָה, דְּעִיקָּרָהּ הוּא כַּאֲשֶׁר אוֹמֵר דְּבַר אֱמֶת שֶׁבּוֹ

And they said in Bava Metzia [59b], “Why did the Torah warn about converts — because their inclination is evil,” meaning their root and foundation are in truth [susceptible to] evil; therefore a warning against wronging him is needed, for there is in it a great verbal wronging — its essence being precisely when one speaks a true thing about him,21Bava Metzia 59b: “It is taught — R’ Eliezer the Great says: For what reason did the Torah warn in thirty-six places, and some say in forty-six places, concerning the convert? Because his inclination is evil (mipnei she-soro ra)” [R’ Tzadok’s text reads she-tochen ra]. The Gemara continues (R’ Nassan): “‘And a convert you shall not wrong, nor oppress him, for you were strangers in the land of Egypt’ — a blemish that is in you, do not ascribe to your fellow (mum she-becha al tomar la-chavercha).” This is precisely R’ Tzadok’s point here: verbal wronging “works upon” a person only because it names a real deficiency in his root.
אָז פּוֹעֵל בּוֹ הַרְבֵּה, עַד שֶׁיּוּכַל לִפְעֹל בּוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה שִׁינּוּי בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁמַּזְכִּיר הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת כֵּן בְּעֶצֶם
for then it works upon him greatly, to the point that it can effect in him a change in his very essence, through mentioning the deficiency that is in truth so in essence.

items.h: The theme: The same caution extends to the baal teshuvah: “do not say to him, remember your former deeds.” At teshuvah’s beginning the past is not yet visibly rectified, so the reminder still stings. David, who raised up the yoke of teshuvah, was pained by it — and that his sin had been rectified retroactively was not made known in his own lifetime.

p: [ג] וַחֲזַ"ל הוֹסִיפוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה [שָׁם נח:] גַּם לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה ״[לֹא יֹאמַר] זְכֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ [הָרִאשׁוֹנִים]״

And the Sages added in the Mishnah [Bava Metzia 58b] [this warning] also regarding a baal teshuvah: “[one may not say to him,] remember your former deeds,”22Bava Metzia 58b: the Mishnah (Bava Metzia 4:10), having taught that “just as there is ona’ah [wronging] in buying and selling, so is there ona’ah in words,” rules: “if one is a baal teshuvah, one may not say to him, ‘remember your former deeds.’” R’ Tzadok notes that this clause — unlike the warning against wronging the convert — is not the Torah’s own prohibition (for from the side of absolute truth a Jew’s sin is not of his essence, and no true “wronging” applies); the Sages added it, because at the beginning of teshuvah the rectification of the past is not yet manifest. The same daf continues (Bava Metzia 58b–59a): “whoever whitens the face of his fellow in public is as though he sheds blood” — Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak observing, “we see that the red departs [azil sumka] and pallor comes.” This is R’ Tzadok’s source for reading the “whitening of the face” as the departing of the red, i.e. of the blood — “the blood is the soul,” the animal soul that is the seat of sin — so that at the mention of an as-yet-unrectified sin the penitent’s blood is “swallowed within him.”
אַף דַּחֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינָם בְּעֶצֶם, וְסוֹף הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן לִהְיוֹת כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא כְּלָל

even though the sins of Israel are not of their essence, and the end of teshuvah is to rectify the past as well, so as to be as if he had never sinned at all.23R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §158): “Through mesirus nefesh unto death in one’s very thought, in complete truth — that he consents in his heart that if it be God’s will and better for him to die, he desires it willingly — he is saved from the decree of death… for his thought and his acceptance upon himself is reckoned as the deed itself, and it is thereafter as though he had come in a second gilgul to this world, knowing what he had spoiled in the first, and able to rectify it; and there is no sin [that cannot thus be mended].” This is the very mechanism of §1-3’s higher rung — “the root of Israel that can change even the past”: the wholehearted giving-over of the nefesh (the “blood” that is the nefesh) sets a man, as it were, in a new life over against his old, from which he can reach back and heal what was.

וְעַל כֵּן אֵין בָּזֶה הָאַזְהָרָה בַּתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהִיא מִצַּד הָאֱמֶת הַגָּמוּר — לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים זוֹ כְּלָל; רַק חֲכָמִים הוֹסִיפוּהוּ, כִּי גַּם בְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה תְּחִלַּת מַדְרֵגַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה אֵינוֹ נִגְלֶה עֲדַיִין תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם

And therefore this warning is not in the Torah [itself] — for from the side of the utter truth this “verbal wronging” does not apply at all; only the Sages added it, since even in a baal teshuvah, at the beginning of the rung of teshuvah, the rectification of the past is not yet revealed.24Cf. R’ Tzadok’s fuller treatment of David as “the one who raised up the yoke of teshuvah” in Takanas HaShavin 11 and Pri Tzaddik (Pinchas §15; Vayeilech / Shabbos Shuvah §21): David “was not fit for that deed” and acted only “to teach teshuvah,” and Mashiach will be the individual whose teshuvah draws forgiveness upon the whole world.25R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §164): “In the reckoning of people the baal teshuvah is not [seen] as a complete tzaddik… because teshuvah is called ‘alma de-iskasya’ [the concealed world], and its preciousness and beauty are not revealed to people” — even though the Sages taught, “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand [the wholly righteous cannot stand]” (Berachos 34b). He likens it to Leah, who “was hated” and wept — the hidden secret of teshuvah — against Rachel of “revealed beauty”; yet the essential offspring are from Leah, “for the essence of birth, the renewal of Torah and of souls by God’s will, is all through the rung of teshuvah.” This illuminates why David’s face was whitened at the mention of his sin, and why the higher rung — full rectification of the past, with no shame at all — “was not yet revealed in his lifetime”: teshuvah’s beauty belongs to the concealed world. Izhbitz-Radzin parallel to Leah as alma d'iskasya. Beis Yaakov on Torah, Vayetzei 63:1, explicitly describes the zivug of Yaakov and Leah as "עלמא דאתכסיא," above ordinary human grasp. Rachel's beauty and the stature of her children are visible on the surface; Leah and her children repeatedly require later birur. Yehudah and Tamar, Reuven and Bilhah, and other episodes can look compromised at the moment of occurrence while their inner place in the Divine plan emerges only later. That is exactly the phenomenology R' Tzadok assigns to teshuvah: its "yofi" is concealed because the present observer still sees the broken history, whereas the deeper birur by which that history becomes the vehicle of a higher birth is not yet visible. Beis Yaakov, Vayetzei 66:2, develops the same point through Leah's naming of Yehudah. On the surface she appears to have received Yehudah without the same visible struggle as the earlier children, yet "אין הקב"ה נותן בחנם רק על ידי יגיעה"; her hidden labor in the first three births is gathered into the fourth. Therefore she says "הפעם אודה את ה'," and the Midrash's "Leah grasped hoda'ah, and her children opened with hoda'ah" becomes a principle: what appeared externally unearned or even unattractive is later disclosed as the fruit of hidden avodah. R' Tzadok's equation of Leah with teshuvah is thus thoroughly Ishbitzian: the baal teshuvah belongs to a world in which the truth of a life cannot be read from its first visible form. This also explains the David connection. David descends from Leah through Yehudah, and his own teshuvah remains an "alma d'iskasya" in his lifetime: forgiven, yet publicly shamed; inwardly rooted in the future Malchus, yet without the visible vindication that comes only through Shlomo. The concealed-world pattern of Leah becomes the historical pattern of Davidic teshuvah.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה שֶׁהָיָה ״הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה [ה.], אָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא [נט.] שֶׁהָיוּ מַלְבִּינִים פָּנָיו עַל יְדֵי הַזְכָּרַת הַחֵטְא עַד שֶׁאִם הָיוּ קוֹרְעִים בְּשָׂרוֹ כו׳

And David HaMelech, who was “the man who raised up the yoke of teshuvah,” as they said in Avodah Zarah [5a], of whom they said in Bava Metzia [59a] that they would “whiten his face” through mentioning the sin, to the point that “were they to tear his flesh [no blood would flow],” etc.26Avodah Zarah 5a: “‘The utterance of David son of Yishai, and the utterance of the man raised up on high [hukam al]’ (Shmuel II 23:1) — the man who raised up the yoke [ulah] of teshuvah.” Bava Metzia 59a: David said before the Holy One, “Master of the Universe, it is revealed before You that if they were to tear my flesh my blood would not flow to the ground [from shame], for even when they are engaged in [the laws of] leprous marks and tents they say to me: David, one who comes upon a married woman — his death is by what? And I say to them: his death is by strangulation, yet he has a share in the World to Come; but one who publicly shames his fellow has no share in the World to Come.”27Shmuel II 12:13: After the affair of Bas-Sheva and Uriah (Shmuel II ch. 11), the prophet Nathan came to David, told him the parable of the poor man’s ewe lamb, and declared, “You are the man!” (12:7), decreeing that “the sword shall never depart from your house” (12:10). David answered: “וַיֹּאמֶר דָּוִד אֶל־נָתָן: חָטָאתִי לַה׳. וַיֹּאמֶר נָתָן אֶל־דָּוִד: גַּם־ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ, לֹא תָמוּת” — “David said to Nathan: ‘I have sinned against Hashem.’ And Nathan said to David: ‘Hashem, too, has removed your sin; you shall not die’” (Shmuel II 12:13). Radak explains that “also (gam)” comes to include David’s confession — “as you confess, so too He has accepted your teshuvah”; and “you shall not die” means “not the death of the wicked, whose soul descends to Gehinnom — though you will still be punished in this world,” namely the death of the child, Avshalom’s rebellion, and “the sword shall not depart from your house.” It is upon this instantaneous exchange — a single word of confession met at once with “Hashem has removed your sin” — that Chazal call David “the man who raised up the yoke of teshuvah” (Avodah Zarah 5a); cf. Shabbos 56a, “whoever says David sinned is merely mistaken,” and Shabbos 30a, that the full manifestation of his atonement was withheld in his lifetime. Izhbitz on David's purification. Mei HaShiloach, Volume II, Writings, Tehillim 51:1, comments on David's plea "תחטאני באזוב ואטהר." He distinguishes a supernal purification in which Hashem illuminates the depth of the heart so that the person recognizes that he was bound to Him even in the hour of sin, from the more constricted purification of the ezov, given to the most distant forms of tumah. The latter requires extreme self-contraction, recognition of lowliness, and sweeping away every trace of ga'avah. David, the Mei HaShiloach says, longed so intensely for taharah that he was prepared for either path: like a man covered in filth who says to his friend, cleanse me with whatever broom you choose, only cleanse and purify me. "תחטאני באזוב" therefore expresses not self-justification but a willingness to undergo the deepest birur. That teaching is important for reading the Izhbitz-Radzin doctrine of yedi'ah and bechirah in connection with David. The higher disclosure — that even during the sin the deepest neshama had never ceased to be attached to Hashem — is a *result* of purification, not a permission granted beforehand to follow desire. Before the birur, David's avodah is confession, brokenness, and readiness for correction. Only after that can there be a revelation of a level on which the root-attachment was never severed. Shem MiShmuel repeatedly cites the Zohar on "גם ה' העביר חטאתך לא תמות" as referring to the removal of the destructive accuser generated by sin. In Nitzavim 2:15 and Sukkos 3:2-3, he explains that the sin itself creates a prosecuting force that closes the heart; through true vidui and teshuvah that force is "passed away" so the person can again turn toward Hashem. This fits R' Tzadok's exact wording of the first rung. "Hashem has removed your sin; you shall not die" is genuine and immediate healing — the death-bearing obstruction is removed — even though the later punishments in David's life show that the complete revelation of retroactive tikkun has not yet arrived.

דְּהַלְבָּנַת פָּנִים הוּא עַל יְדֵי דְּאָזֵיל סוּמָּקָא, שֶׁהוּא הַדָּם שֶׁמֵּחֲמָתוֹ הַחֵטְא; כִּי הַדָּם הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ כַּמְפֹרָשׁ בִּקְרָא וְקָאֵי אַבְּהֵמָה — כִּי הִיא נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית שֶׁבָּאָדָם שֶׁמִּמֶּנָּה הַחֵטְא, וְעָלֶיהָ הוּא פְּשָׁטֵיהּ דִּקְרָא ״נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא״

For the “whitening of the face” occurs through the departing of the red — that is, the blood, from which the sin comes; for “the blood is the soul,” as the verse states explicitly, and it refers to the animal [dimension] — for it is the animal soul within man, from which sin issues, and it is upon this soul that the plain sense of the verse “a soul that sins” [speaks].
וְכֵן אִיתָא בְּבָבָא בָּתְרָא [נח:] ״בְּרֵישׁ כֹּל מַרְעִין אֲנָא דָּם״, וְעַל כֵּן בְּהַזְכָּרַת הַחֵטְא כְּשֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם נִבְלַע דָּמוֹ בְּתוֹכוֹ

And so it is [stated] in Bava Basra [58b], “at the head of all illnesses am I, blood,” and therefore, at the mention of the sin — when the past is not yet rectified — his blood is “swallowed” within him.28Bava Basra 58b: “[Shmuel said:] at the head of all illnesses am I — blood”; Rashi: “all of a person’s ailments come on account of the blood.” R’ Tzadok links the “blood” (the seat of the animal soul and of sin) to the “whitening of the face” (the draining of red) that shame produces when an unrectified sin is recalled.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה הוּא הַתְחָלַת מַדְרֵגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁהוּא הָרְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא, דְּעַל זֶה נִתְבַּשֵּׂר ״גַּם ה’ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ לֹא תָמוּת״

And David HaMelech is the beginning of the rungs of teshuvah, which is the healing going forward, for regarding this he was assured, “the Lord has also removed your sin, you shall not die” (Shmuel II 12:13).29R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §28): “This is the rung of David, who ‘raised up the yoke of teshuvah’ — for although he went where he went and sank where he sank, he can return to his root and his place in holiness, at the highest rung; as is known to the seers of the Merkavah, that every light appears like the flash of lightning — to the place from which they go, from there they return, in the sense of ‘from there He will take you’ (Devarim 30:4): specifically ‘from there,’ from the very lowest, he draws wholly close to Hashem.” This is the se’if’s David — “the beginning of the rungs of teshuvah,” the healing that reaches even the one sunk lowest.

אֲבָל לִהְיוֹת נִתְקָן לְשֶׁעָבַר, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ בּוּשָׁה עוֹד בָּזֶה כְּלָל — דָּבָר זֶה לֹא יָדְעוּ עֲדַיִין בְּחַיָּיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת [ל.] ״בְּחַיֶּיךָ אֵינִי מוֹדִיעַ״ כו׳, כִּי אָז לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה עֲדַיִין מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה

But that the past be rectified — so that he have no shame in it at all any longer — this was not yet known in his lifetime, as they said in Shabbos [30a], “in your lifetime I will not make [it] known,” etc.; for then this [higher] rung of teshuvah had not yet been revealed.30Shabbos 30a: David asked for a sign that his sin was forgiven; God replied, “In your lifetime I will not make it known; in the lifetime of your son Shlomo I will make it known.” When Shlomo brought the Ark into the Holy of Holies and the gates would not open, he was answered only when he invoked “remember the kindnesses of David Your servant” — “at that moment the faces of all David’s enemies turned black, and all knew that God had forgiven him.” R’ Tzadok: the retroactive rectification (removing all shame) was not manifest in David’s own lifetime, for that higher rung had not yet been revealed.

items.h: The theme: David’s root runs back to Avraham, who began as “first of the converts” and only afterward revealed himself as father of the nation. Because Yitzchak was born to him, and the branch is contained in the root, the whole of Knesses Yisrael was folded into him. This is “the root of Israel” — a root cleaving to God with no dross at all, so that sins are incidental to it, thorns standing around a rose.

p: [ד] וִיסוֹד דַּרְגָּא דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה הוּא, שֶׁהָיָה תְּחִלָּה לַגֵּרִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּחֲגִיגָה [ג.]

And the foundation [yesod] of Avraham Avinu’s rung is this: that he was “first of the converts,” as they said in Chagigah [3a].31Chagigah 3a (and Bereishis Rabbah): Avraham is called “the father of converts” — the first to bring others “under the wings of the Shechinah.” R’ Tzadok: Avraham’s own starting-point was that of a ger, and only after fathering Yitzchak did he reveal his deeper root as native-born father of Israel. Avraham's transition from ger to root-father in Chassidus. Beis Yaakov, Chayei Sarah 24:1, portrays Avraham after milah, Akeidah, and the ten nisyonos as a person transformed "מהיפך להיפך" in the manner of a ger. Yet the very same transformation reveals, rather than manufactures, the depth for which he was created. This is close to R' Tzadok's paradox: Avraham begins historically as the first ger, but after Yitzchak is included in him the earlier stage itself can be read from the standpoint of his native root as father of Israel. Kedushas Levi, Lech Lecha §37, similarly refuses to define Avraham by Terach. Using "ger shenisgayer ke-katan shenolad," he argues that Avraham's true av is the Divine middah and mission from which he is spiritually hewn — the revelation of Hashem's Name through the future Jewish people. Thus the ger-principle becomes not simply erasure of ancestry but discovery of a deeper ancestry. R' Tzadok pushes this one step farther: once Yitzchak and Yaakov are understood as already latent in Avraham, the branch discloses what was hidden in the root, and the past can be reread accordingly.
רַק אַחַר כָּךְ מִשֶּׁנּוֹלַד יִצְחָק וְאִתַּכְלִיל בּוֹ, זָכָה לְשֵׁם ״אֵיתָן הָאֶזְרָחִי״ לִהְיוֹת כְּאֶזְרָח בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ הַשי"ת ״לְךָ טַל יַלְדוּתְךָ״

only afterward, once Yitzchak was born and was “enclothed” within him, did he merit the name “Eisan HaEzrachi” — to be like a native-born in Israel — for Hashem assured him, “yours is the dew of your youth” (Tehillim 110:3)32Tehillim 110:3: “עַמְּךָ נְדָבֹת בְּיוֹם חֵילֶךָ, בְּהַדְרֵי קֹדֶשׁ מֵרֶחֶם מִשְׁחָר, לְךָ טַל יַלְדֻתֶיךָ” — a verse whose plain meaning is famously difficult. Rashi reads the psalm as addressed to Avraham: “your people will volunteer on the day of your host” — when Avraham mustered his men to pursue the four kings (Bereishis 14), Aner, Eshkol, and Mamre going out with him of their own accord; “in the beauty of holiness, from the womb” — in the merit of the holiness that was in him from his mother’s womb, for “he recognized his Creator at the age of three” (Nedarim 32a); and “yours is the dew of your youth [lecha tal yaldusecha]” — “your youth shall be reckoned to you: the ways of uprightness by which you conducted yourself in your youth will be to you as pleasant as this dew.” R’ Tzadok links this to the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 39) that Avraham feared, “shall I say that there is sin in my hand?” and was reassured that he is “the beloved of the world [meruchamo shel olam]”: Avraham was in truth holy from the womb, so that his beginning as a convert — the “youth” preceding the revealing of his root — is itself like dew, pure and pleasant, and no taint.,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [פ’ לט] ״תֹּאמַר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּיָדִי עָוֹן״ כו’, וְדָרְשׁוּ ״מְרֻחָמוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם״

as they said in Bereishis Rabbah [39:8], “[Avraham feared:] shall I say that there is sin in my hand?” and they expounded “the beloved [or: the one shown mercy from creation] of the world.”33Bereishis Rabbah 39:8 (on Tehillim 110:3, “yours is the dew of your youth”): “Avraham feared and said: shall I say I have sin in my hand, that I served idols all these years? God said: ‘yours is the dew of your youth’ — just as dew evaporates, so your sins evaporate.” The Midrash reads merechem mishachar as “the one shown mercy from [the creation of] the world” — i.e. Avraham’s merit predates the world. R’ Tzadok: Avraham was in essence holy from the womb; the “convert” phase was only his beginning.

הַיְינוּ דְּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה הָיָה קָדוֹשׁ מֵרֶחֶם וּמִתְּחִלַּת בְּרִיָּיתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, וְרַק תְּחִלָּתוֹ הָיְתָה כְּגֵר; אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ זָכָה לְגַלּוֹת שָׁרְשׁוֹ שֶׁהוּא אַב הָעוֹלָם וְשֹׁרֶשׁ הָאֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית כֻּלָּהּ

That is, that in truth Avraham Avinu, too, was holy from the womb and from the very beginning of the world’s creation; only his beginning was as a convert, but afterward he merited to reveal his root — that he is the father of the world and the root of the entire Israelite nation
שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת יַחַס זֶה דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁיּוּכַל לְשַׁנּוֹת הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן

which is the beginning of this lineage of “the root of Israel,” which can change even the past.34R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §11): “Avraham Avinu, who is called ‘first of the converts’ (Chagigah 3a) — it is brought that he ‘bound the twenty-two letters of the Torah on his tongue,’ that he merited at first only the letters of speech, until he fathered Yitzchak, and after the tenth trial, when [Yitzchak] was ‘incorporated’ [within him] — and this was on Rosh Hashanah, as they said (Rosh Hashanah 10a) that Sarah was remembered, that is, in conception, from which time he is called ‘father.’” This is the se’if’s Avraham: he began as a ger, and only once he fathered Yitzchak did he reveal his root as father of the nation.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ זַ"ל [בר"ר סג, ב] דְּיַעֲקֹב פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם [מִכִּבְשַׁן הָאֵשׁ], רָצָה לוֹמַר שֹׁרֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב שֶׁהָיָה כָּלוּל בּוֹ, כִּי אֵין הַדָּבָר נוֹתֵן מַה שֶּׁאֵין בּוֹ, וּלְעוֹלָם הֶעָנָף כָּלוּל בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ וְהַבָּנִים גְּנוּזִים כֹּחָם בְּאָבוֹת

And therefore the Sages said [Bereishis Rabbah 63:2] that “Yaakov redeemed Avraham [from the fiery furnace]” — meaning the root of Yaakov that was contained within him; for a thing cannot give what is not in it, and the branch is always contained in the root, and the children’s power is stored within the fathers.35Bereishis Rabbah 63:2: “Yaakov redeemed Avraham” — the merit/root of Yaakov (whose “bed was whole,” with no unfit offspring) was already contained within Avraham and “redeemed” him. R’ Tzadok’s principle: the branch is contained in the root, so the whole future nation was folded into Avraham once he fathered Yitzchak, all the more so when the heh of the Name (Knesses Yisrael) was joined to him (Avram → Avraham).
וּכְשֶׁנִּתְוַסֵּף בּוֹ ה’, הוּא ה’ אַחֲרוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם הָרוֹמֶזֶת לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, נִכְלָל בּוֹ כָּל שֹׁרֶשׁ כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת

And when the heh was added to him [Avram → Avraham] — the final heh of the Divine Name, which alludes to Knesses Yisrael — there was included in him all the root of Knesses Yisrael of every generation.36R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §172): “Just as there is, in place, the even shesiyah [foundation stone] from which the world was founded — and it is the root of the whole world — so among souls there is one soul that includes the whole generation, which is the parnas ha-dor [leader of the generation]; and likewise one that includes all the generations; and so too in time there is a time that includes all the days, which is the day of Shabbos.” This illuminates Avraham’s rung in the se’if: as “father of the world and root of the entire Israelite nation,” he is the even shesiyah of Knesses Yisrael — the single root-soul in whom “all the root of Knesses Yisrael of every generation” is folded, so that “the branch is contained in the root” and even the past can be changed from within him.

וְשֹׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא דְּשָׁרְשָׁם דָּבוּק בהשי“ת וְאֵין שָׁם פְּסֹלֶת כְּלָל, כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע”ה שֶׁמִּטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה; וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים אֵינָם בְּעֶצֶם רַק בְּמִקְרֶה, כְּאָסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי הוּצֵי שֶׁהִמְשִׁילוֹ רז"ל בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין [מד.]

And “the root of Israel” is one whose root cleaves to Hashem with no dross at all — like Yaakov Avinu, “whose bed was whole”; and all the sins are not essential but incidental, “like a myrtle that stands among thorns,” the parable the Sages gave in Sanhedrin [44a],37Sanhedrin 44a: On “Israel has sinned” (Yehoshua 7:11), R’ Abba bar Zavda said: “Even though he sinned, he is [still] Israel.” R’ Abba added the folk-adage: “a myrtle [asa] that stands among thorns [chilfei] — its name is myrtle and they call it myrtle.” R’ Tzadok: Israel’s sins are “thorns around the rose,” incidental and severable, never the essence of the root, which cleaves wholly to God.
וְקוֹצִים הַסּוֹבְבִים אֶת הַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה, שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לַחְתֹּךְ הַקּוֹצִים וְהַהוּצֵי וְתִשָּׁאֵר הָאָסָא וְהַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה נְקִיָּה וּשְׁלֵימָה לְגַמְרֵי כַּאֲשֶׁר הִיא בְּעַצְמוּתָהּ

and [the sins are like] thorns surrounding the rose, which can be cut away — the thorns and reeds — leaving the myrtle and the rose wholly clean and whole, as it is in its own essence.38R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §131): “The root of the souls of all Israel is from the Source of life… and this matter was first revealed in full clarity through Bilaam, whose entire passage concerns this virtue of Israel — that even should they pile sins one upon another, the love of the Holy One is not severed from them by so much as a hair’s breadth” (and Bilaam, who had no share in the World to Come, was its unwilling herald). This is the very point of “the root of Israel” in the se’if: the root “cleaves to Hashem with no dross at all,” so that the sins are but incidental thorns encircling the rose — they can be cut away and the rose “left wholly clean and whole, as it is in its own essence.”

items.h: The theme: Rectifying the past is the higher rung; the beginning of teshuvah is Avraham’s — bringing healing to the world at least from now on. Rectification of the past belongs to Israel alone, whose root is truly good; the nations have only a forward-healing, and even that does not endure with them. This first rung, however, embraces the entire world.

p: [ה] וְזֶהוּ תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם, שֶׁיְּבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ; אֲבָל הַתְחָלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה אָב לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, לְהָבִיא רְפוּאָה לָעוֹלָם עַל כָּל פָּנִים מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא

And this [uprooting of the past] is the rectification of what came before — “the sin of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none” (Yirmeyah 50:20)39Yirmeyah 50:20: “בַּיָּמִים הָהֵם וּבָעֵת הַהִיא נְאֻם ה׳, יְבֻקַּשׁ אֶת עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ, וְאֶת חַטֹּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאינָה, כִּי אֶסְלַח לַאֲשֶׁר אַשְׁאִיר” — “In those days and at that time, says Hashem, the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none, and the sins of Judah and none shall be found; for I will pardon those I leave as a remnant.” The verse falls within Yirmeyah’s prophecy of the downfall of Bavel and the return of Israel (ch. 50): at that future time Israel’s sin is not merely forgiven but “sought and not found” — uprooted entirely. This is R’ Tzadok’s emblem for the highest rung of teshuvah, the rectification of the past itself. Radak explains that the verse must speak of the Messianic future — “for I will pardon” — since sinners still remained throughout the Second Temple and this present exile; and “to the remnant I leave” likewise points to that time, as in “he who remains in Zion and is left in Jerusalem shall be called holy” (Yeshayah 4:3) and “the remnant of Israel shall do no wrong” (Tzefaniah 3:13).; but the beginning of teshuvah is the rung of Avraham Avinu from his own side, who was father to the whole world, to bring healing to the world at least from here on.
דִּלְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ, שֶׁהָיוּ בְּיָמָיו גּוֹיִם, וְלֹא נִיתְּנָה תְּשׁוּבָה אֶלָּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּנִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה וְנִתְחַדְּשָׁה הִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה

For to rectify the past is impossible for the entire world, since in his days there were gentiles, and teshuvah was given only to Israel — for the Torah was given and the laws of teshuvah were newly instituted

[וּנְהִירְנָא דְּרָאִיתִי כֵּן להרמ“ע בַּעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת, ולהר”י אַבְּרַבַנְאֵל בְּנַחֲלַת אָבוֹת, וְעוֹד קַדְמוֹנִים; וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי מְפֹרָשׁ בְּתַנְחוּמָא [פ’ הַאֲזִינוּ] ״עוֹשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה נוֹשֵׂא לוֹ פָּנִים, יָכוֹל לַכֹּל — תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר אֵלֶיךָ, וְלֹא לְאֻמָּה אַחֶרֶת״]

[and I recall having seen thus in the Ramma in Asarah Ma’amaros, and in R’ Yitzchak Abarbanel in Nachalas Avos, and other early authorities; and I later found it explicit in Tanchuma (Ha’azinu): “one who does teshuvah, He shows him favor — one might think to all; therefore Scripture says ‘to you’ — and not to another nation”].40Yerushalmi Makkos 2:6: “They asked Wisdom: what is the sinner’s punishment? It said, ‘evil pursues sinners’ (Mishlei 13:21). They asked Prophecy: ‘the soul that sins shall die’ (Yechezkel 18:4). They asked the Holy One: ‘let him do teshuvah and it will atone for him.’” — Tanchuma, Ha’azinu: “One who does teshuvah, He shows him favor — one might think for all [nations]; Scripture says ‘to you’ — and not to another nation.” R’ Tzadok marshals these (with the Ramma and Abarbanel) that the Torah’s innovation of teshuvah-that-rectifies-the-past was given to Israel alone; the nations have only “healing going forward” (as at Nineveh). Chassidic explanation of why teshuvah belongs uniquely to the root of Israel. Shem MiShmuel, Ki Seitzei 2:17, writes that the effectiveness of teshuvah for Israel is bound to their essential connection to Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov. Jewish souls are "בעצם נפשות טהורות וטובות" — intrinsically pure and good — and aveiros are a contingent soiling. When a Jew returns, the inner point reconnects with the chain reaching the Avos and a new current of life can flow from the root. This is nearly the same metaphysical distinction R' Tzadok draws here between sin that is incidental to a good shoresh and sin that belongs to an essence lacking that root. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 2 (2:1), supplies the Chabad formulation of the same root claim: "ונפש השנית בישראל היא חלק אלוה ממעל ממש." The Divine soul of Israel is not merely an ethically improved personality but a soul whose deepest origin is Godly. On this account teshuvah can be more than behavioral correction: return is literally return to the soul's own source. R' Tzadok's language remains his own and should not be collapsed into Tanya's system, but the comparison clarifies why a Jewish past can ultimately be healed from within: the deepest subject of that past was never identical with the sin.41R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §54): “Whereas the nations of the world — even should they repent — ‘teshuvah was given only to Israel’ (Midrash Tanchuma Ha’azinu 4); but for them there is no atonement at all, for by them the sin is in its very essence [be-etzem].” This is the ground of §1-5’s ruling that among the nations “it is not an enduring healing, and in the end the wound is destined to reopen”: the Torah’s teshuvah was legislated for Israel alone — “whose root is truly good” — so their sins are but incidental thorns, whereas for the nations the sin cleaves to the essence itself, and even their “forward-healing” cannot hold. R’ Tzadok there rests the point, exactly as the se’if does, on the same Tanchuma: “to you — and not to another nation.”
לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁשָּׁרְשָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת טוֹב, וְעַל כֵּן נִיתְּנָה תּוֹרָה לָהֶם; וְלֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי, דְּאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ עִם הַתּוֹרָה

[given] to Israel, whose root is truly good, and therefore the Torah was given to them; and “He did not do so for any [other] nation,” for they have no connection in their root with the Torah.42R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §5): Amalek, “the first of the nations,” aims his whole grievance at the very distinction between Israel and the nations — “he wants, God forbid, that the house of Israel be like all the nations.” But “Amalek’s whole grasp is only upon the outward appearance [le-mar’is ha-ayin], for he has no connection or hold on the truth”; and the erev rav whom the cloud “spat out” had “some connection to the nations.” This illuminates the se’if: the nations’ forward-healing “is not an enduring healing,” for their hold — like Amalek’s — is merely external, with no grip on the inner truth, whereas Israel’s root is “truly good.”

וְרַק רְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא זֶה יֵשׁ גַּם בַּגּוֹיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתוּב בְּנִינְוֵה כְּשֶׁשָּׁבוּ מִדַּרְכָּם דְּנִתְבַּטֵּל הַפּוּרְעָנוּת הַנִּגְזָר, דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים הַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת לֹא חָטְאוּ, וּלְעוֹלָם עָוֹן עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ נִמְחָק כְּלָל גַּבַּיְיהוּ

And only “healing going forward” exists among the nations too, as it is written of Nineveh, that when they turned from their way the decreed punishment was annulled — for at any rate now they do not sin; but the sin itself is never erased with them at all.43R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §4): “All the creation of the world is for the sake of man, to serve in it and bring forth its abundance; [and] this too was blurred and spoiled through what people spoiled in their deeds. But ‘your people are all righteous — forever they shall inherit the land’ (Yeshayah 60:21): an eternal inheritance that has no cessation or spoiling — for they are called ‘the remnant of Yosef.’” This is the se’if’s contrast: Israel’s healing is enduring (“an inheritance with no cessation”), whereas the nations’ forward-healing is destined to reopen.
וְשֹׁרֶשׁ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה נִתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְרַפֵּא עַל כָּל פָּנִים לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ לְהַבָּא
And the root of Avraham Avinu was aroused through this to heal, at least going forward, the entire world.

אַף דִּלְעִנְיַן רְפוּאָה דִּלְהַבָּא גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ חִילּוּק בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, דְּאֶצְלָם אֵינָהּ רְפוּאָה הַמִּתְקַיֶּימֶת כְּלָל, וּבְבֵירוּר סוֹף הַמַּכָּה לַחֲזֹר וּלְהִתְגַּלּוֹת

though even regarding forward-healing there is a difference between Israel and the nations: for with them it is not an enduring healing at all, and it is clear that in the end the wound is destined to return and reappear;

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל ״עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״, וְנִקְרָא מִיָּד צַדִּיק גָּמוּר, לִהְיוֹת ״דֶּרֶךְ צַדִּיקִים כְּאוֹר נֹגַהּ הוֹלֵךְ וָאוֹר״, דְּהַתְחָלַת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בַּלֵּב פּוֹעֵל לִהְיוֹת מוֹסִיף וְהוֹלֵךְ

whereas Israel — “your people are all righteous” (Yeshayah 60:21)44Yeshayah 60:21: “וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים, לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ, נֵצֶר מַטָּעַי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי לְהִתְפָּאֵר” — “And your people, all of them righteous, shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which I take glory.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of the future redemption of Tzion (ch. 60). R’ Tzadok cites it to contrast Israel with the nations: because at their root “your people are all righteous,” a Jew is called a complete tzaddik the instant the stirring of teshuvah begins. Rashi (on lehispa’er): “that I shall take glory in them.” And the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a, Perek Chelek) makes this verse the prooftext that “all Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it is said, ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever.’” The phrase "ועמך כולם צדיקים" receives a striking Chassidic complement in Tanya ch. 2. If the neshama of Israel is "chelek Eloka mima'al mamash," then the prophetic designation "all of your people are righteous" can be read as a statement about root-identity rather than a denial of actual transgression. The revealed personality can become entangled in sin, while the second, Divine soul remains the inner source to which teshuvah returns. Sefas Emes, Rosh HaShanah 25:4, expresses the same distinction in terms of two loves. There is an ahavah awakened by mitzvos and good deeds, and there is the essential love of Israel rooted in "chelek Hashem amo," which is not dependent on a particular deed and cannot be extinguished by "many waters." Sin obscures the manifestation of the neshama; teshuvah causes it to awaken again. Thus R' Tzadok's use of "ועמך כולם צדיקים" is not sentimental: it is the ontological premise that allows teshuvah to uncover a righteousness deeper than the historical act. — one is at once called a complete tzaddik, so that “the path of the righteous is like the light of dawn, growing ever brighter” (Mishlei 4:18); for the initial stirring of a thought of teshuvah in the heart takes effect to go on increasing.
אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה הוּא מִצַּד מַדְרֵגוֹת הָעֲתִידוֹת; אֲבָל מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ דִּתְשׁוּבָה בִּרְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא עַל שֶׁעָבַר לְבַד, זֶה כּוֹלֵל כָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ
But that [ever-brightening] belongs to the future rungs; whereas this rung of teshuvah — healing-going-forward, for the past alone — this embraces the entire world.

items.h: The theme: This is the middah of Chesed, which is expansion — and it reaches forward only. Forgiveness from Chesed presupposes that a sin exists and is pardoned, so a residue of shame remains. To be as though one had never sinned is impossible from this side: Chesed is expansion without force, and the heart’s first stirring is broad but not yet strong.

p: [ו] וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד שֶׁהוּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת [וּמִדַּת ״וְרַב חֶסֶד״ הוּא רִיבּוּי יוֹתֵר, דְּנוֹשֵׂא עָוֹן גַּם בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה, עַיֵּין בְּהָרִי"ף פֶּרֶק קַמָּא דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה; וְגַם שָׁם מִכָּל מָקוֹם עָוֹן עַצְמוֹ אֵינוֹ נִמְחָק, דְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי ר’ יִשְׁמָעֵאל ״מַעֲבִיר רִאשׁוֹן רִאשׁוֹן״]

And this is the middah of Chesed, which is “expansion” [and the middah of “and abounding in kindness” is a yet greater abundance, that bears sin even without teshuvah — see the Rif, first chapter of Rosh Hashanah; yet there too the sin itself is not erased, for the school of R’ Yishmael [taught] “He passes over the first [sins], one by one”].45Rif, Rosh Hashanah (17a in the Rif; on the Thirteen Attributes): “‘Bearing iniquity and passing over transgression’ — the school of R’ Yishmael taught: He passes over the first [sins], one by one [and does not reckon them]; and such is His measure.” The Gemara adds (Rava): “but the sin itself is not erased — for if his sins are a majority, it is reckoned among them.” R’ Tzadok: even rav chesed, which bears sin without teshuvah, only “passes over” — it does not erase the sin’s essence.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְהַבָּא, כִּי הַסְּלִיחָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הַחֶסֶד הֲרֵי יֵשׁ עָוֹן, רַק שהקב"ה בְּרוֹב חֲסָדָיו הוּא מוֹחֵל וְסוֹלֵחַ
And nonetheless it is only going forward, for forgiveness that is from the side of Chesed [presumes that] there is a sin, only that the Holy One in His abundant kindness pardons and forgives —

וּכְמוֹ מִי שֶׁחָטָא נֶגֶד חֲבֵירוֹ וּמְבַקְּשׁוֹ לִמְחֹל, דְּאִם אֵינוֹ אַכְזָרִי מוֹחֵל מִיָּד; וְאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא [פז.] דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ יוֹתֵר מִשָּׁלוֹשׁ פְּעָמִים, כִּי יֵשׁ בָּזֶה כְּדֵי פִּיּוּס לְכָל אָדָם, וּלְאִישׁ טוֹב וְחֶסֶד וַדַּאי דַּי בְּפַעַם אַחַת

like one who sinned against his fellow and asks him to pardon, that if he is not cruel he pardons at once; and they said in Yoma [87a] that one need not ask more than three times, for in that there is enough appeasement for any person — and for a good and kind man, surely once suffices.46Yoma 87a: “One who seeks pardon from his fellow need not ask more than three times” (for that suffices as appeasement). R’ Tzadok: a fortiori before God, whose kindness is boundless — the slightest remorse and a light request (“forgive us”) bring immediate pardon; yet this Chesed-forgiveness still leaves residual “shame,” which only the higher, Gevurah-rooted teshuvah (the coming simanim) removes.

וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן חַסְדּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא לְאֵין שִׁיעוּר, וַדַּאי בַּחֲרָטָה כָּל דְּהוּ דַּי לְפָנָיו, וּבְבַקָּשָׁה קַלָּה דְּ״סְלַח לָנוּ״ דַּי שֶׁהוּא מוֹחֵל וְסוֹלֵחַ לְאַלְתַּר, וְהוּא כְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר

all the more so His boundless kindness: surely the slightest remorse suffices before Him, and a light request of “forgive us” suffices, that He pardons and forgives immediately, and he is as a complete tzaddik.

אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ בּוּשָׁה עֲדַיִין, וּכְמוֹ בִּבְנֵי אָדָם אַף שֶׁמָּחַל לוֹ, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁמַּזְכִּירִים לוֹ מִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מִזֶּה; וְדָבָר זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם, זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּשֶׁהַסְּלִיחָה מִצַּד מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד, וְכֵן כְּשֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה מִצַּד אוֹתָהּ מִידָּה

only that shame still remains — as with people, even though [one’s fellow] pardoned him, whenever they remind him of it he is ashamed by it; and this — that it be as if he had never sinned at all — is impossible when the forgiveness is from the side of the middah of Chesed, and likewise when the teshuvah is from that same middah.47R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §242): “Teshuvah is like the hataras chacham [a Sage’s release of a vow], which uproots the matter retroactively [le-mafrea], so that the evil angel formed from the sin is nullified entirely; whereas [teshuvah] from love, by which [sins] become as merits, means not that [the sin] is nullified but that it is transformed to good — and these are two rungs, le-is’hapcha [to transform] and le-ischafya [to subdue].” This lays bare precisely what §1-6’s Chesed-forgiveness lacks: Chesed only pardons a sin that still exists (hence “forward” only, and “shame remains”), whereas the higher, forceful rung uproots it from its origin — as though it had never been — which is why “to be as if he had never sinned at all is impossible when the forgiveness is from the side of Chesed.”

כִּי הֵם שְׁתֵּי מִדּוֹת — גְּדוֹלָה וּגְבוּרָה — שֶׁהֵם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים; וּ״גְדוֹלָה״ הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בְּגֹדֶל, אֲבָל אֵינוֹ בִּגְבוּרָה; וְהַתְחָלַת כָּל עִנְיָן הוּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת, וְאַחַר כָּךְ מַתְחִיל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר בּוֹ, וְאָז הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִצְטַמְצֵם עַל יְדֵי הַהִתְגַּבְּרוּת

For they are two middos — Gedulah [Chesed] and Gevurah — which are two opposites; and Gedulah is expansion in magnitude but not in force; and the beginning of every matter is in expansion, and afterward it begins to intensify, and then the expansion contracts through the intensification.48R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §4): “This is [Avraham’s] grip on the middah of Chesed — which is the perfection of all his desires in holiness, for the sake of Heaven, as they said, ‘a man’s desire is his chesed’; and therefore they said of him that he did not [even] neglect his marital obligation, for he had no other intent but the mitzvah.” The se’if’s Chesed is “expansion” — Avraham’s boundless outpouring; its very expansiveness is why, at teshuvah’s beginning, it heals “going forward” but has not yet the contracting force of Gevurah.

וְכֵן הַתְחָלַת הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלֵב אָדָם שֶׁאֵינוֹ עֲדַיִין בִּגְבוּרַת הַלֵּב בְּכֹחַ אַמִּיץ וְחָזָק שֶׁלֹּא יִנָּתֵק, אע"פ שֶׁהוּא בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת יוֹתֵר, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין כֹּחוֹ חָזָק כָּל כָּךְ, וְעַל כֵּן מֵבִיא רַק רְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא

So too the beginning of a thought of teshuvah in a person’s heart, which is not yet in the strength of the heart, in a firm, powerful force that will not snap — although it is more expansive, nonetheless its power is not yet so strong, and therefore it brings only forward-healing;
דְּמִזֶּה לֹא יִמָּלֵט אֲפִילּוּ תְּשׁוּבָה הַיּוֹתֵר קַלָּה, וּמִיָּד בְּהַתְחָלָתָהּ זֶה גְּדֻלָּתָהּ

for from this not even the lightest teshuvah is exempt, and immediately at its beginning — this is its “greatness.”49R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §40): “The essence of teshuvah is until Hashem enlightens his eyes, that the willful sins become as merits — that he recognize and grasp that all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem” (as in Berachos 31b, and the Arizal’s reconciling of foreknowledge and free choice, “both true, each in its own domain”); “and when he attains this immense light, then all his willful sins are turned [to merits].” This is the crown of the rung §1-6 opens toward: not the Chesed that pardons yet leaves shame, but the Gevurah-born light in which the past itself is re-read as Divine guidance — the “as if he had never sinned,” and beyond. Izhbitz-Radzin on yedi'ah and bechirah — and the boundary that prevents this doctrine from becoming an excuse for sin. Mei HaShiloach, Vayeilech 3, says that even though bechirah is given into human hands, one who sees deeply recognizes that human action is "רק דבר מועט כקליפת השום" relative to the encompassing Divine conduct. In Tazria 2 he can say simultaneously that a person's eventual attainment was prepared from the beginning of creation and, nevertheless, "מצד האדם יש לו בחירה." The two statements are intentionally held together: from the creature's lived standpoint, command, responsibility, restraint, and teshuvah are real; from the later Divine illumination, the person may discover a providential depth that was never visible at the moment of choice. This is the key to R' Tzadok's use of the Arizal's yedi'ah/bechirah resolution and his statement that, at the highest teshuvah, a person can recognize that "all he sinned was also by the will of Hashem." The recognition belongs to the *afterward* of teshuvah — "until Hashem enlightens his eyes" — not to the beforehand of temptation. Mei HaShiloach, Devarim 2, sometimes reads the Torah's naming of places of Israel's sins as teaching that circumstances and spiritual "place" can radically narrow a person's field of choice. But Beis Yaakov, Bereshis 69:1, supplies the essential guardrail through its reading of Cain. Cain's "השומר אחי אנכי" is understood as the claim that overwhelming anger had removed his bechirah and therefore he should not be liable. The Divine answer rejects the self-exculpation: "קול דמי אחיך צועקים" proves that the deficiency is attributed to Cain and that he had a point of responsibility by which he could have guarded himself. The Ishbitz doctrine therefore works in two directions at once. Before and during action, a Jew must regard himself as a baal bechirah, obey Torah, resist the yetzer, and never invoke hidden providence to legitimate a prohibited act. After a genuine teshuvah that has uprooted identification with the sin, Hashem may reveal a deeper yedi'ah: the fall itself can be integrated into a providential road by which the person came to a higher recognition. That latter illumination is what R' Tzadok associates with zedonos becoming zechuyos. It does not say the aveirah was permitted; it says that Divine omnipotence can reclaim even the prohibited past and make the *teshuvah born from it* part of the final good. This is the precise Izhbitz-Radzin frame in which the radical sentence of Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 should be read.

sections.en: Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory

items.h: גדולה תשובה שמגעת עד כסא הכבוד.
“Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory” (the second — corresponding to Gevurah).

The theme: “Reaching the Throne of Glory” is the healing of the past as well. The neshamah — the mind’s thought — stays essentially pure; the seat of sin is the heart. By persisting in teshuvah until the rectification reaches the mind, which is the person’s essence, the heart comes under his control, and only then is the past itself rectified.

p: [א] ״שֶׁמַּגַּעַת עַד כִּסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד״, הוּא רְפוּאַת הַקּוֹדֵם וּמַה שֶּׁעָבַר גַּם כֵּן

“That it reaches the Throne of Glory” — this is the healing of what came before, of the past as well.50Yoma 86a: “R’ Levi said: Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory, as it says, ‘Return, O Israel, unto [ad] Hashem your God’ (Hoshea 14:2).” R’ Tzadok: the word ad (“up to”) indicates a teshuvah that ascends to the very root of the soul at the Throne — i.e. the rectification of the past, not merely the future. Maharal on "until the Throne of Glory." Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah ch. 2 (§13 in Sefaria's segmentation), treats the Yoma statement itself: "גדולה תשובה שמגעת עד כסא הכבוד." Elsewhere in the same chapter (§16, §22), the Maharal explains that teshuvah removes the sinner from the material level in which sin took hold and returns him to a higher, separated level. Because teshuvah reaches the Kisei HaKavod and itself precedes the created world, it belongs to a plane above the ordinary causal order of sin and consequence. This gives conceptual force to R' Tzadok's distinction between simple forgiveness and tikkun ha-kodem: the Kisei is not merely a very high place to which the penitent climbs; it is the level from which the soul's created history can be re-grounded. The Maharal's formulation also dovetails with R' Tzadok's language of return to the shoresh. Teshuvah is a "return" because the person ceases to be fixed at the material level defined by the sin and is restored to the higher source from which his neshama proceeds. Hence Yoma's "ad kisei ha-kavod" is not rhetorical praise but a statement about the metaphysical reach of teshuvah.51Cf. Me’or Einayim (Lech Lecha, and Mattos on “Shuvah Yisrael ad Hashem Elokecha”): “Great is teshuvah, for it reaches the Throne of Glory” means teshuvah elevates a person until he himself becomes a Kisei haKavod — a chariot in which the Shechinah rests; cf. Likkutei Torah, Ki Teitzei.
כִּי נֶפֶשׁ רוּחַ נְשָׁמָה שֶׁבָּאָדָם הוּא מִג’ עוֹלָמוֹת — כִּסֵּא, מַלְאָכִים, וְגַלְגַּלִּים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתִיקּוּנֵי הַזֹּהַר [תִּיקּוּן מ"ג] שֶׁהֵם בי"ע

for the nefesh, ruach, and neshamah in a person are from three worlds — Throne, angels, and spheres — as they said in Tikkunei HaZohar [tikkun 43], which are Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah.52Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 43: the source R’ Tzadok cites for the teaching that the three levels of the soul — nefesh, ruach, and neshamah — are drawn from the three lower worlds: nefesh from Asiyah (the world of the spheres, galgalim), ruach from Yetzirah (the world of the angels), and neshamah from Beriah (the world of the Throne of Glory). Because Beriah, the world of the Throne, is “mostly good,” the neshamah — which corresponds to the thought of the mind — remains essentially pure, as we declare each morning, “the soul You placed within me is pure.” The corruption of sin therefore lodges not in the neshamah but in the heart, the seat of the yetzer.
וּבִבְרִיאָה רוּבּוֹ טוֹב כַּנּוֹדָע, לְכָךְ אוֹמְרִים ״נְשָׁמָה שֶׁנָּתַתָּ בִּי טְהוֹרָה הִיא״ גַּם עַתָּה, דְּאֵין הַקִּלְקוּל בְּחֵלֶק הַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ

And in Beriah the majority is good, as is known; therefore we say “the soul You placed in me is pure” — even now — for the corruption is not in the portion of the neshamah, which corresponds to the thought in the mind.53R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Eruvin §3): “There are five levels in the soul — nefesh, ruach, neshamah, chayah, yechidah; and nefesh, ruach, neshamah are deed, speech, and thought: the deed [corresponds] to the liver, which is full of blood, and ‘the blood is the soul’; speech to the heart — ‘and speaks truth in his heart’ — the seat of the ‘spirit of life’ (so Onkelos renders it ‘a speaking spirit,’ for speech is in the ruach); and the neshamah [is thought].” Exactly the se’if’s structure: the neshamah — the mind’s thought — is the highest, drawn from the “Throne,” above the reach of deed.
וְעִיקַּר הַחֵטְא מִן הַלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לֹא תָתוּרוּ אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם״, דְּשָׁם מִשְׁכַּן הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וְאָמְרוּ בְּרָכוֹת [סא.] דְּיוֹשֵׁב בֵּין שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב
