And through reaching, in his heart’s teshuvah, up to the root of the soul in the mind — which is up to the Throne of Glory — from there is drawn and spread the rectification also of the deeds’ emergence into act.233R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §1): “The ‘completion of the deed’ dwells in all the souls of Israel; and this is when his thought is bound day and night to the revealed [parts] of Torah and mitzvos, which is grasped by every Jew; and this ‘garment’ clothes also the ‘sealed thought’ that is above all — for all thoughts are only garments, except that this is more external and that more internal.” The se’if’s rectification: the heart’s teshuvah reaches up to the “sealed thought” — the root of the soul — and from there spreads down to the deeds.

וְטַעַם ״כִּשְׁגָגוֹת״ עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, הַיְינוּ דְּהָוֵי כְּ״נִתְכַּוֵּין לֶאֱכֹל בְּשַׂר חֲזִיר וְעָלָה בְּיָדוֹ בְּשַׂר טָלֶה״, דִּמְדַמֶּה [בְּנָזִיר כג.] לִשְׁגָגוֹת לְעִנְיַן סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה, דַּהֲרֵי הוּא מִיהָא לְאִיסּוּרָא אִיכַּוֵּין

And the reason [it becomes] “as inadvertent” is through teshuvah from fear: it is like “one who intended to eat pork and lamb came up in his hand” — which [the Gemara] likens [Nazir 23a] to inadvertent acts as regards pardon and atonement, since he did, at any rate, intend the forbidden.234Nazir 23a: “One who intended to eat pork [basar chazir] and lamb came up in his hand [basar taleh] — even so he requires atonement and pardon”; the Gemara treats him like an inadvertent sinner as regards atonement, since he intended the forbidden. R’ Tzadok: teshuvah from fear leaves the deed “as inadvertent” — the intent to sin still needs atonement, though the act is no longer “willful.”

וְאִם כֵּן אַף שֶׁנִּתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם לִהְיוֹת נַעֲשֶׂה הַכֹּל זְכֻיּוֹת, דְּהַכֹּל רְצוֹן השי"ת וְאֵין רַע כְּלָל ״כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי״ — מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם כְּשֶׁעָלָה בְּיָדוֹ זְכֻיּוֹת, אִם הוּא לְאִיסּוּרָא אִיכַּוֵּין נֶחְשָׁב שְׁגָגוֹת

And so, even though the past is rectified so that all becomes merits — for all is God’s will, and there is no evil at all, “You are with me” — nonetheless, even when it turned out to be merits, if he intended the forbidden it is reckoned “inadvertent.”235R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §27): “willful sins as inadvertent ones means [they become] like mis’asek [one who acts with no intent at all], like a labor not needed for its own purpose.” This is §5-1’s “as inadvertent ones” made precise: teshuvah from fear does not erase the deed, but drains it of the intent that made it willful — so that what was done with full will is reckoned only as an unintended, purposeless act, a shogeg, the residue left once the sinful will is withdrawn.

וְצָרִיךְ לְתַקֵּן כָּל כָּךְ לְמַפְרֵעַ עַד שֶׁיּוּכַל לַחְשֹׁב גַּם כַּוָּנָתוֹ שֶׁלְּמַפְרֵעַ שֶׁהָיְתָה לִזְכוּת וְלֹא לְאִיסּוּרָא כְּלָל, אַף שֶׁאָנוּ יוֹדְעִים שֶׁהוּא כִּיוֵּן אָז לְהֵזִיד וּלְהַרְשִׁיעַ

And [to reach “merits”] one must rectify so far retroactively that even his earlier intent can be reckoned as merit — that it was for good and not for the forbidden at all — though we know that he then intended to act willfully and wickedly.

וּקְרָא דְּ״שׁוּבָה״ שֶׁאָמַר בּוֹ ״עַד ה’ אֱלֹקֶיךָ״ — דְּהַיְינוּ עַד כִּסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד — מְסַיֵּים ״כִּי כָשַׁלְתָּ״, דְּהוּא רַק כִּשְׁגָגוֹת , אַף דְּהוּא עַתָּה מַגִּיעַ עַד כִּסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד דְּאֵין שֵׁם רַע כְּלָל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד כַּוָּנָתוֹ אָז נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ לְמִכְשׁוֹל עַל כָּל פָּנִים. רַק בִּקְרָא דְּ״וּבְשׁוּב״ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְעָשָׂה מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה״, מְסַיֵּים עֲלֵיהֶם ״הוּא יִחְיֶה״

And the verse “Return,” which said of it “up to Hashem your God” — that is, up to the Throne of Glory — concludes “for you have stumbled [in your iniquity],” which is only “as inadvertent” — for although he now reaches the Throne of Glory, where there is no evil at all, nonetheless from the side of his intent then it is still reckoned to him as a stumbling-block — whereas the verse “and when [the wicked] returns,” which said “and does justice and righteousness,” concludes about them “he shall live” [i.e. merits].
וְזֶהוּ הַחִילּוּק בֵּין ״מֵאַהֲבָה״ לְ״יִרְאָה״: כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּאַהֲבָה שֹׁרֶשׁ לְ״קוּם וַעֲשֵׂה״, וְיִרְאָה לְ״שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה״
And this is the difference between “from love” and “from fear”: as is known, love is the root of “arise and do,” and fear of “sit and do not.”

וְעַל יְדֵי יִרְאָה הוּא רַק שְׁבִיתַת לֵב וּמֹחַ מֵהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לָרַע, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מְתַקֵּן רַק מַעֲשֵׂה הָאִיסּוּר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְזָדוֹן, כִּי כָּל זְכֻיּוֹת שֶׁל הָעוֹשֶׂה מִיִּרְאָה הוּא רַק מִפְּנֵי שהשי"ת צִיוָּה לַעֲשׂוֹת כֵּן, וְיָרֵא לְהַמְרוֹת צִיווּיוֹ

And through fear there is only the stilling of the heart and mind from arousal to evil, and by this he rectifies only the deed of the forbidden, that it not be reckoned willful — for all the “merit” of one who acts from fear is only because Hashem commanded to do so, and he fears to defy His command.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי [פ"ט דִּבְרָכוֹת] ״עֲשֵׂה מִיִּרְאָה: שֶׁאִם בָּאתָ לִבְעֹט, דַּע שֶׁאַתָּה יָרֵא, וְאֵין יָרֵא בּוֹעֵט״

as they said in the Yerushalmi [Berachos 9], “act from fear: for if you come to kick [rebel], know that you are in fear, and one who fears does not kick.”236Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5: “עֲשֵׂה מֵאַהֲבָה וַעֲשֵׂה מִיִּרְאָה. עֲשֵׂה מֵאַהֲבָה — שֶׁאִם בָּאתָ לִשְׂנֹא, דַּע כִּי אַתָּה אוֹהֵב, וְאֵין אוֹהֵב שׂוֹנֵא. עֲשֵׂה מִיִּרְאָה — שֶׁאִם בָּאתָ לִבְעֹט, דַּע שֶׁאַתָּה יָרֵא, וְאֵין יָרֵא בּוֹעֵט” — “Serve from love and serve from fear. Serve from love — for if you come to hate, know that you are one who loves, and a lover does not hate. Serve from fear — for if you come to kick [rebel], know that you are one who fears, and one who fears does not kick.” This is the exact source (parallel in Yerushalmi Sotah 5:5): it stands in the sugya expounding “and you shall love Hashem your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your might” (on the Mishnah, “a person is obligated to bless over the bad as he blesses over the good”), the same passage that lists the “seven types of perushim” and crowns them with “the parush of love, like Avraham” (over against “the parush of fear, like Iyov”). Meforshim (Korban HaEidah, Pnei Moshe): fear is a real but lower rung — since fear restrains, one who genuinely fears will not “kick,” i.e. throw off the yoke. R’ Tzadok builds on this: fear can only still the heart from arousal to evil — “one who fears does not kick” — so it rectifies the deed (that the sin be reckoned only “as inadvertent,” not willful), but not the intent; the transformation of the past into outright merits belongs to love.

אֲבָל הָאוֹהֵב, כָּל חִשְׁקוֹ וְתַאֲוָתוֹ לְמַלֹּאות רְצוֹן אֲהוּבוֹ וְלַעֲשׂוֹת מַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן לְפָנָיו, בֵּין צִיוָּהוּ בֵּין לֹא צִיוָּהוּ; וְזֶה מִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה שֶׁקִּיֵּים כָּל הַתּוֹרָה עַד שֶׁלֹּא נִיתְּנָה [בְּיוֹמָא כח:], וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר ״אַבְרָהָם אוֹהֲבִי״

But the lover — his whole longing and desire is to fulfill his beloved’s will and to do whatever will be pleasing before Him, whether He commanded it or not; and this is the middah of Avraham, who kept the whole Torah before it was given [Yoma 28b], and therefore it says, “Avraham My beloved.”237Yoma 28b: “Rav said: Avraham Avinu kept the entire Torah before it was given, as it says, ‘because Avraham obeyed My voice and kept My charge, My commandments, My statutes, and My laws’ (Bereishis 26:5).” R’ Tzadok: this is the mark of love — Avraham “My beloved” (Yeshayah 41:8) sought to do God’s will even where no command yet bound him.

items.h: The theme: From the side of love a person can enter even an aveirah lishmah, as Yael did — a heter nowhere explicit in the Torah. Out of her longing to save Israel she disregarded both the transgression and the defilement it cast upon her, forfeiting even her own soul. Esther’s “and if I perish, I perish” and Shimshon’s “let my soul die with the Plishtim” are of the same order — a surrender possible only through the intensity of love for Him.

p: [ב] וּמִצַּד הָאַהֲבָה יוּכַל לְהַכְנִיס עַצְמוֹ לְעִנְיָן כָּזֶה, עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ״ דְּיָעֵל, וְלֹא מָצִינוּ בְּפֵירוּשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה מֻתָּר, רַק מֵהָתָם הוּא דְּיָלְפִינַן

And from the side of love one can enter into such a matter, by way of “a transgression for its own sake [aveirah lishmah],” as with Yael; and we do not find explicitly in the Torah that this is permitted — only from there [from Yael] do we derive it.238R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Zachor §12): “and R’ Akiva answered him,”and if in the place of our life we are afraid [how much more so…]" — because he sensed in himself that it was necessary that it come to his hand." Exactly the se’if: entering such a matter “from the side of love” is not recklessness but a sensing that this very thing has been placed in one’s hand — as with Yael, who forfeited even her own soul.

וְהִיא מֵרֹב חָשְׁקָהּ וְאַהֲבָתָהּ לְהַצָּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְבַעֵר צוֹרֵר וְאוֹיֵב ה’ כָּמֹהוּ מֵהָעוֹלָם, לֹא הִבִּיטָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה וְעַל הַזֻּהֲמָא שֶׁהֵטִיל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנָזִיר כג:] שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה רָעָה הוּא אֶצְלָהּ

And she, out of her great longing and love to save Israel and to remove such a foe and enemy of Hashem from the world, paid no heed to the transgression or the defilement he cast [upon her], which the Sages said [Nazir 23b] “was an evil to her,”

מִכָּל מָקוֹם הִפְקִירָה גַּם נַפְשָׁהּ בִּשְׁבִיל דָּבָר זֶה, שֶׁחִשְּׁבָה: אֲפִילּוּ אֵין שׁוּם הֶיתֵּר לְדָבָר זֶה וְהִיא תֵּעָנֵשׁ עָלָיו, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מוּטָב תֹּאבַד הִיא וִיאַבֵּד צוֹרֵר ה’ מֵהָעוֹלָם

yet she forfeited even her own soul for this, reasoning: even if there is no heter for this and I will be punished for it, still, better that I perish and God’s foe perish from the world.239R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §22): “a transgression for its own sake is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake (Nazir 23b)… and through this the sins become [white] — the crimson turned to snow; and the victory [over Sisera] was through Devorah the prophetess.” This is §5-2’s very setting: the war against Sisera, God’s foe, was won by the power of aveirah lishmah — the deed that, done wholly for Heaven, outweighs a lukewarm mitzvah — the same power by which “the willful become as merits,” the crimson sins made white.Izhbitz on exceptional action and the limits of bechirah. Mei HaShiloach I, Pinchas §2, is an unusually close — and deliberately dangerous — parallel to the category R’ Tzadok is discussing. The Izhbitzer distinguishes levels in which a person progressively exhausts his ability to escape a temptation, culminating in a case where, after genuine resistance, he understands the event as bound up with a hidden Divine will; he applies this to Zimri while simultaneously presenting Pinchas’s opposite judgment as valid and accepted by Heaven. The point is therefore not a prospective license to transgress. On the contrary, the passage dramatizes how little a person can know, before the fact, whether he has truly reached such a boundary of bechirah. This sharpens R’ Tzadok’s treatment of Yael, Esther, and Shimshon: an aveirah lishmah is not the ordinary suspension of halachah by subjective inspiration, but an extreme case of self-surrender in which personal benefit is absent and the actor is prepared even to bear punishment. The Izhbitz parallel is especially useful here because it places the question precisely at the fault-line between human choice and the hidden Divine ordering that can be recognized, if at all, only after the deed has been fully clarified.

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה עָשְׂתָה אֶסְתֵּר בַּמֶּה שֶׁאָמְרָה ״וְכַאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי אָבַדְתִּי״ — הַיְינוּ גַּם עַל אָבְדַן הַנֶּפֶשׁ ח"ו, עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁעָשְׂתָה עֲבֵירָה בְּרָצוֹן לְהַצָּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל
And in this manner Esther acted, in what she said, “and if I perish, I perish” — meaning even the perishing of the soul, God forbid, through the transgression she did willingly to save Israel.

וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר שִׁמְשׁוֹן ״תָּמוֹת נַפְשִׁי עִם פְּלִשְׁתִּים״ — לְשׁוֹן ״תָּמוּת נַפְשִׁי״ אֵינוֹ מוֹרֶה מִיתַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִיתַת גּוּף וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ תָּשׁוּב אֶל הָאֱלֹקִים, וּמִיתַת נֶפֶשׁ הַיְינוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And likewise Shimshon’s “let my soul die with the Plishtim” — the expression “let my nefesh die” indicates not merely the death of this world (which is the death of the body, while the soul returns to God), but the death of the soul, that is, in the World to Come.

וְשִׁמְשׁוֹן הֵמִית עַצְמוֹ לֹא לְהַצָּלַת נַפְשׁוֹ מֵעֲבֵירוֹת וְלֹא לְהַצָּלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק כְּדֵי לְהָמִית פְּלִשְׁתִּים הַרְבֵּה וְלִנְקֹם נִקְמָתוֹ, וְעַל זֶה הָיָה חוֹשֵׁב דְּאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ דִּין ״מְאַבֵּד עַצְמוֹ לְדַעַת״ דְּאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And Shimshon killed himself not to save his soul from transgressions, nor to save Israel, but only to slay many Plishtim and avenge himself; and regarding this he thought he might have the status of “one who takes his own life knowingly,” who has no share in the World to Come240Nazir 23b: “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Greater is a transgression for its own sake [aveirah lishmah] than a mitzvah not for its own sake” — proven from Yael (“blessed above women be Yael, the wife of Chever the Kenite; above women in the tent she is blessed,” Shoftim 5:24), who submitted to Sisera to destroy him (“all the good of the wicked is an evil to the righteous”). Gittin 57b: the four hundred boys and girls taken captive for immoral purposes who drowned themselves in the sea, deriving from “I will bring back from Bashan, I will bring back from the depths of the sea” (Tehillim 68:23) that they attain the World to Come. R’ Tzadok reads Yael, Esther (“if I perish, I perish”), and Shimshon (“let my soul die with the Plishtim”) as acts of aveirah lishmah born of overwhelming love — risking even the soul.

אֲבָל נִתְרַצָּה גַּם בָּזֶה כְּדֵי לְהָמִית הַרְבֵּה מֵאוֹיְבֵי ה’, דִּ״בְאִבּוּד רְשָׁעִים רִנָּה״, וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״תָּמוּת נַפְשִׁי עִם [פְּלִשְׁתִּים]״, כְּאִלּוּ חִלְּקוּ עִמָּהֶם יַחַד בְּמִיתַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם גַּם כֵּן, דְּלֹא חָשׁ לְכָל זֶה, כְּדֵי לִמְנֹעַ חִילּוּל שְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁתְּפָשׂוּהוּ, וּלְאַבֵּד אוֹיְבֵי ה’ וְיִשְׂרָאֵל; וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי תֹּקֶף הָאַהֲבָה לוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ

but he consented even to this, in order to slay many of God’s enemies, for “at the destruction of the wicked there is joyous song” — and therefore he said “let my soul die with [the Plishtim],”241Shimshon and the Plishtim — background: Shimshon (Shoftim chs. 13–16), of the tribe of Dan, was the last of the great Shoftim and a nazir from the womb (his mother so instructed by the angel), of whom it was foretold “he shall begin to save Israel from the hand of the Plishtim.” The Plishtim were Israel’s dominant oppressors in his day, and his superhuman strength was bound up with his uncut Nazirite hair. He judged Israel twenty years; Delilah, at the Plishtim chieftains’ bidding, drew out his secret; they seized him, put out his eyes, and bound him to grind in the prison-house at Azzah (Gaza). At the temple of their god Dagon, his hair regrown, he prayed “remember me and strengthen me only this once,” grasped the two central pillars, and cried “tamos nafshi im Plishtim — let my soul die with the Plishtim” (Shoftim 16:30), bringing the house down upon the assembled lords — “so that the dead he slew at his death were more than those he slew in his life.” On this the Sages (Sotah 9b–10a) expound his whole career, and rule that “Shimshon judged Israel like the Father in Heaven.” R’ Tzadok reads “tamos nafshi” at its depth: Shimshon feared he might be judged a me’abed atzmo la-da’as (one who knowingly takes his own life, who forfeits even his share in the World to Come) — for he died to avenge himself and slay God’s enemies, not to save his soul from sin or to save Israel — yet out of sheer love for God, to prevent the chillul Hashem of his capture, he consented even to that. as though he shared with them together in the death of the soul, God forbid, for he paid no regard to any of this — to prevent the desecration of His Name (which came about through their capturing him) and to destroy the enemies of God and Israel; and this is possible only through the intensity of love for Him.242R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §5): “…he considered this a matter of aveirah lishmah — to draw out the good root from him; for the defeat of any nation is [accomplished] by extracting its good root to holiness, as in Egypt through Basya, daughter of Pharaoh, [after which] all that remains of the nation goes to ruin.” This lays bare why §5-2’s love-driven transgression could destroy God’s foe: Yael’s aveirah lishmah, entered “through the intensity of love for Him,” was no mere killing but the drawing-out of the last good hidden in the enemy — and only then does the foe himself fall to nothing.

items.h: The theme: The mitzvah of love says “with all your soul” — plainly, to give over one’s life — and prefaces it with “with all your heart,” which the Sages read as “with your two inclinations.” Avraham made the yetzer hara good; David, whose middah is the intensity of fear, could not, and killed it outright. From the side of love the yetzer is not subdued but transformed, so that through it a person becomes “very good.”

p: [ג] וְעַל זֶה אָמַר בְּמִצְוַת הָאַהֲבָה ״בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״, דִּפְשׁוּטוֹ הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לִמְסֹר נַפְשׁוֹ וְנִשְׁמָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן בִּשְׁבִיל אַהֲבַת השי“ת; וְהִקְדִּים ״בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ״, שֶׁאָמְרוּ זַ”ל [בְּרָכוֹת נד.] ״בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרֶיךָ״, דְּזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן מִמִּדַּת הָאַהֲבָה

And regarding this the mitzvah of love says “with all your soul,” whose plain sense is, as they said, to give over one’s very life and soul for the love of Hashem; and it prefaced “with all your heart,” which the Sages expounded [Berachos 54a] “with your two inclinations” — for this too is of the middah of love.243Berachos 54a (Mishnah): “‘You shall love Hashem your God with all your heart’ — with your two inclinations, the good inclination and the evil inclination; ‘with all your soul’ — even if He takes your soul; ‘with all your might [me’odecha]’ — with all your money; another interpretation: with every measure [middah] He metes out to you, thank Him exceedingly.” R’ Tzadok: loving God “with both inclinations” is the transformative love that turns the yetzer itself into an instrument of service.244R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §16): “‘With all your heart’ — with your two inclinations: with the good inclination through ‘subduing’ and battle, and with the evil inclination, after one has conquered it, using its powers for the good; and this is the rung of Yosef and David — Yosef was in ‘overcoming’ and fencing off desire, while David, on the contrary, appeared a man of desire [yet served with it].” Exactly the se’if’s reading of “with all your heart” — serving God with both inclinations.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי ״אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע“ה עָשָׂה יֵצֶר רַע טוֹב, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ‘וּמָצָאתָ אֶת לְבָבוֹ נֶאֱמָן’״; וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע”ה לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לַעֲמֹד בּוֹ וַהֲרָגוֹ, כִּי מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת הוּא תֹּקֶף הַיִּרְאָה, ״מִשֶּׁכָּרַע אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף״ [בְּרָכוֹת לד:], וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה’״, וְהִיא מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה לִכְבֹּשׁ יִצְרוֹ וּלְאִכְפַּיָיא

And as they said in the Yerushalmi, “Avraham made the yetzer hara good, as it says, ‘and You found his heart faithful before You’ (Nechemyah 9:8)245Nechemyah 9:8: “וּמָצָאתָ אֶת לְבָבוֹ נֶאֱמָן לְפָנֶיךָ, וְכָרוֹת עִמּוֹ הַבְּרִית לָתֵת אֶת אֶרֶץ הַכְּנַעֲנִי […] לָתֵת לְזַרְעוֹ, וַתָּקֶם אֶת דְּבָרֶיךָ כִּי צַדִּיק אָתָּה” — “And You found his heart faithful before You, and made the covenant with him to give the land of the Canaanite… to give it to his seed; and You fulfilled Your words, for You are righteous.” The verse is from the great confession-prayer of the Leviim at the teshuvah-assembly of Ezra and Nechemyah’s generation (Nechemyah 9), which retells God’s kindnesses from creation onward — here, His choosing Avram, bringing him out of Ur Kasdim, renaming him Avraham, and “finding his heart faithful.” Meforshim: the “faithful heart” is Avraham’s steadfastness proven through his trials (the Ten Nisyonos). The Yerushalmi (Berachos 9:5 — see the note there) presses “u-matzasa es levavo ne’eman” one degree further: Avraham “made even his yetzer hara faithful [good],” so that his whole heart — both inclinations — was faithful before God; whereas of David it says “ve-libi chalal be-kirbi” (Tehillim 109:22), that he “slew” his yetzer within him. On this rests R’ Tzadok’s contrast: Avraham (love) transformed the yetzer; David (kingship / fear) could only kill it.”; but David HaMelech could not withstand it and killed it — for the middah of kingship is the intensity of fear, “once he bows he does not straighten up”246Berachos 34b: the sugya of bowing (keri’ah) in Shemoneh Esrei. The Mishnah teaches that a commoner bows at “Modim” and at “Baruch Atah Hashem” of the first berachah; the Gemara (34a–b) adds the gradations of rank: a Kohen Gadol bows at the end of every berachah, “and a king, once he has bowed, does not straighten up until he completes his entire prayer” (מֶלֶךְ כֵּיוָן שֶׁכָּרַע שׁוּב אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף עַד שֶׁגּוֹמֵר כָּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ). Rashi: the more exalted one’s station, the more constant the submission (hachna’ah) required of him before the King of kings. R’ Tzadok takes this as the emblem of kingship = the intensity of fear and submission: the king, once bowed, never straightens — unremitting hachna’ah. Hence David, whose middah is malchus / Gevurah, could not merely subdue the yetzer (which leaves it standing, ready to rise) but was compelled to kill it outright. [Berachos 34b], the rung of “a woman who fears Hashem” (Mishlei 31:30)247Mishlei 31:30: “שֶׁקֶר הַחֵן וְהֶבֶל הַיֹּפִי, אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא תִתְהַלָּל” — “Grace is false and beauty is vain; a woman who fears Hashem — she shall be praised.” This is the sealing verse of “Eishes Chayil” (Mishlei 31:10–31), the alphabetical hymn to the woman of valor with which Shlomo HaMelech closes the book. Meforshim: in its plain sense, outward charm and beauty are fleeting, and only yiras Hashem is the abiding ground of praise; the Midrash and meforshim also read Eishes Chayil allegorically (of the Torah, the soul, and the Shechinah). R’ Tzadok fastens on “isha yiras Hashem”: fear is the “feminine” principle — the nukva, the receiving-and-submitting side, malchus — and this is precisely David’s rung, “a woman who fears Hashem,” the middah of Gevurah that subdues the yetzer; over against Avraham’s “masculine” love that transforms it., which is the middah of Gevurah, to subdue the yetzer and to suppress it.248Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5 (“Avraham made the yetzer hara good,” from “You found his heart faithful,” Nechemyah 9:8; and “act from fear, for one who fears does not kick”); with Berachos 34b (“a king, once he bows, does not straighten up”). R’ Tzadok contrasts Avraham (love — transforming the yetzer) with David (the fear of kingship / Gevurah — who “killed” his yetzer, since it could not be merely subdued).249R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §101): “as they said [Bava Kama 46],”one who has a pain goes to the physician’s house“; and the Holy One arranges the unwitting one to the place of the willful one, and not the reverse — for there is no need to arrange [it otherwise].” Exactly the se’if: David could not transform his yetzer and had to kill it, for from the side of Gevurah the encounter is arranged as a judgment — the ailing one brought to the place of healing, not the healer to him.

וּלְפִיכָךְ מִצַּד מִדָּתוֹ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְאִכְפַּיָיא לְגַמְרֵי דֶּרֶךְ כְּבִישָׁה, כִּי עִיקַּר הַאֲחִיזָה בְּסִטְרָא דְּנֻקְבָּא כַּיָּדוּעַ, הֻכְרַח לְהָרְגוֹ לְגַמְרֵי וּלְהַאֲבִידוֹ מִמְּצִיאוּת. אֲבָל מִצַּד מִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה וְתֹקֶף הַחֵשֶׁק להשי"ת יוּכַל לְאַהְפְּכָא וְלַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ טוֹב

And therefore, from his middah, it is impossible to suppress it entirely by way of subduing — since the essence of its grip is on the side of the nukva, as is known — [so] he was compelled to kill it entirely and remove it from existence. But from the side of the middah of love and the intensity of longing for Hashem, one can transform it and make it good,

כַּיָּדוּעַ מִמְּשַׁל הַזּוֹנָה הַמּוּבָא בַּזֹּהַר, דְּעִיקַּר בְּרִיָּיתוֹ הָיָה בִּרְצוֹן השי"ת; וְכֵן בְּרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [ט, ז] ״‘טוֹב’ זֶה יֵצֶר טוֹב, ‘מְאֹד’ זֶה יֵצֶר רָע״, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת ״טוֹב מְאֹד״

as is known from the parable of the harlot brought in the Zohar — that its very creation was by God’s will; and so Bereishis Rabbah [9:7]: “‘good’ is the good inclination, ‘very’ is the evil inclination” — for through it one can become “very good.”250Zohar (the “parable of the harlot”): a king commands a harlot to seduce his son, precisely so the son will resist and prove his love — “she did the king’s command”; so the yetzer hara was created by God’s will, to be overcome (or transformed). R’ Tzadok invokes it to show the yetzer’s root is itself holy.251Bereishis Rabbah 9:7: “‘And behold it was very good’ (Bereishis 1:31) — ‘good’ is the good inclination, ‘very [me’od]’ is the evil inclination. Is the evil inclination ‘very good’?! — Yes, for were it not for the evil inclination a man would not build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in commerce.” R’ Tzadok: the lover of God does not merely suppress the yetzer but transforms it — finding in the desires of this world themselves a means of serving God (“very good”).252R’ Tzadok — parallel (Ohr Zarua LaTzadik §5): “R’ Akiva was, all his days, awaiting to give over his soul upon the sanctification of the Name — this is the matter of ‘holy flesh’ and a holy body; and this is the matter of the akeidah of Yitzchak.” This is §5-3’s “with all your soul” in the flesh: the love that “gives over one’s very life and soul” is no abstraction but R’ Akiva’s lifelong yearning to fulfill “be-chol nafshecha — even if He takes your soul” (Berachos 61b), the same bond first laid upon the altar in Yitzchak.

כִּי מִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ בּוֹעֵר בְּאַהֲבַת השי“ת, כָּל אֲהָבוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת בְּטֵלוֹת לְגַבָּהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָנוּ רוֹאִין בְּאַהֲבוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּמָמוֹן וְכַיּוֹצֵא, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁשָּׁקוּעַ וְשׁוֹקֵד לְמַלֹּאות אַהֲבָתוֹ וְתַאֲוָתוֹ בְּדָבָר זֶה — גַּם אִם יִמְצָא וְיִפְגַּע בַּאֲהָבוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת לֹא יִפֶן לָהֶם, וְאֵין חִילּוּק אֵלָיו בְּלֶכְתּוֹ לְהַרְוִיחַ מָמוֹן הַרְבֵּה אִם אוֹכֵל מַעֲדַנִּים אוֹ לֶחֶם צַר, וְלֹא יַטְרִיד עַצְמוֹ אֲפִילּוּ רֶגַע מוּעֶטֶת בִּשְׁבִיל אֲכִילַת מַעֲדַנֵּי עוֹלָם אִם יַפְסִיד עַל יְדֵי זֶה רְוַוח הֶעָצוּם שֶׁשּׁוֹקֵד לְהַרְוִיחַ; וְגַם כְּשֶׁאוֹכֵל אֵין לִבּוֹ פּוֹנֶה לְעִידּוּן הַמַּאֲכָל וּמִילּוּי תַּאֲוָה זוֹ כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁקוּעַ וּבוֹעֵר לְמַלְּאָהּ בְּתַאֲוָה אַחֶרֶת. וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּאַהֲבַת השי”ת, דִּמְעַט מֵהָאוֹר שֶׁמְּאִירִים עֵינָיו עַל יְדֵי זֶה דּוֹחֶה הַרְבֵּה מִן הַחוֹשֶׁךְ, וְכָל תַּאֲוַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מְאוּסִים בְּעֵינָיו לְגַמְרֵי; אֶלָּא שֶׁהָאוֹהֵב השי"ת וְכָל חִשְׁקוֹ לִמְצוֹא אֵיזֶה דָּבָר לַעֲשׂוֹת נַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנָיו, הִנֵּה הוּא מוֹצֵא גַּם בְּתַאֲוַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה לְנַחַת רוּחַ לְפָנָיו

For one whose heart burns with love of God, all other loves are nullified before it — as we see with worldly loves such as money and the like: one who is sunk and diligent in filling his love and desire for that thing pays no heed to other loves even if he meets them, and it makes no difference to him, as he goes to earn much money, whether he eats delicacies or meager bread, nor will he trouble himself even a brief moment over eating the world’s delicacies if he would thereby lose the immense profit he is intent on earning; and even when he eats, his heart does not turn to the pleasure of the food and the filling of that desire, so long as his heart is sunk and burning to fill another desire. And all the more so with the love of Hashem, for a little of the light that illumines his eyes thereby drives away much of the darkness, and all worldly desires become utterly repugnant in his eyes — only that the lover of God, whose whole longing is to find something to give Him a pleasure, finds even in the desires of this world what will be a pleasure before Him —
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהוּא יִתְבָּרֵךְ בָּרָא דָּבָר זֶה וְחֵשֶׁק זֶה בָּעוֹלָם, וַדַּאי יֵשׁ בּוֹ צֹרֶךְ וְתוֹעֶלֶת לִקְדֻשָּׁה, וְלִהְיוֹת לוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ גַּם כֵּן נַחַת רוּחַ מִזֶּה
for since He created this thing and this longing in the world, surely it has a need and benefit for holiness, and [the potential] to give Him a pleasure from it.

וְזֶה כָּל עֲבוֹדַת הָאוֹהֵב ה’ בְּעִנְיְנֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ לְהִתְאַמֵּץ לְאִכְפַּיָיא רַק לְאַהְפְּכָא, שֶׁיִּמָּצֵא בָּהֶם דַּרְכֵי עֲבוֹדַת ה’; וְזֶהוּ שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה טוֹב, וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״טוֹב מְאֹד״

And this is the whole service of the lover of God in worldly matters: he need not exert himself to subdue, only to transform, that the ways of God’s service be found within them; and this is what Avraham made “good,” and it is called “very good.”

items.h: The theme: “With all your heart” reaches even the desires of this world; “with all your soul,” even a matter of transgression; “with all your might,” one’s money. The essence of this world’s suffering is in money, and to love Him in distress is the ultimate clarification of love. These are the “sufferings of love” — brought only after a person has been clarified in the first two rungs, which is why “with all your might” is absent from the second paragraph of Shema.

p: [ד] וְזֶהוּ ״בְּכָל לְבָבְךָ״ — הַיְינוּ אֲפִילּוּ בַּאֲהָבוֹת וְתַאֲוַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה; ״וּבְכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״ הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּפֶרֶק הָרוֹאֶה] ״בְּכָל דְּרָכֶיךָ דָּעֵהוּ אֲפִילּוּ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה״, שֶׁהַכַּוָּונָה כְּעִנְיַן עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ הַנִּזְכָּר

And this is “with all your heart” — meaning even amid the loves and desires of this world; “and with all your soul” is in the manner brought [Berachos 63a], “‘in all your ways know Him’ — even in a matter of transgression,” the intent being like the aveirah lishmah mentioned.253Berachos 63a: “‘In all your ways know Him, and He will straighten your paths’ (Mishlei 3:6) — Rava said: even in a matter of transgression [davar aveirah].” R’ Tzadok ties this to aveirah lishmah — serving God “with all your soul” even along paths that appear forbidden, when done purely for His sake.254R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Eikev §19): "“though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, for You are with me” — the matter is according to what they said [Berachos 63a] on “in all your ways know Him,” and “He shall straighten your paths.”" Exactly the se’if: “in all your ways know Him — even in a matter of transgression” is the same verse by which one walks unafraid through the valley itself, because He is there too.

״וּבְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ״ דְּקָאֵי אַמָּמוֹן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת נד.]; וְהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן ״דָּבָר אַחֵר״ דְּשָׁם, ״בְּכָל מִדָּה שֶׁמּוֹדֵד לְךָ הֱוֵי מוֹדֶה לוֹ״, דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר אֲפִילּוּ בְּעָאקוֹ (בְּצַעַר) רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְּלַן

“And with all your might [me’odecha]” refers to money, as they said [Berachos 54a]255Berachos 54a (Mishnah Berachos 9:5): the same Mishnah continues: “‘and with all your might [me’odecha]’ — with all your money [mamoncha]; another interpretation: with every measure [middah] that He metes out to you, thank Him exceedingly [modeh lo me’od me’od].” Rashi: “me’odecha” is expounded “with all your money,” for there are people to whom their money is dearer than their body; and the “middah” reading — bless Him for the measure of bad as one blesses for the measure of good. (The Yerushalmi, ad loc., records both readings identically.) R’ Tzadok draws the §4 point from here: loving God “with all your might” means loving Him even in distress and loss of money — the ultimate proof of love, which is shown not when He “shows a pleasant face” but when one loves Him in his affliction; and these are the “sufferings of love.”; and this is also the “other interpretation” there, “with every measure He metes out to you, thank Him” — meaning even in one’s distress [b’aako], God forbid.256R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §7): “all the judgments of the Torah penetrate and descend into all the worlds and all matters — whether in the physical [gashmiyus] or in the spiritual.” This grounds §5-4’s “with all your might — [which] refers to money”: since the Torah’s service reaches down even into the material — a man’s possessions and dealings — the very me’odecha, one’s wealth, is drawn into the domain of Divine service; no corner of the physical, not even money, is left outside the love of “in all your ways know Him.”
וְעִיקַּר יִסּוּרִין דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּמָמוֹן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זַ"ל ״חֶסְרוֹן כִּיס קָשֶׁה מִכֻּלָּם״, וּמְפֹרָשׁ בְּאִיּוֹב ״כִּי כָל זֶה בָּחַרְתָּ מֵעֹנִי״

And the essence of this world’s sufferings is in money, as the Sages said, “the loss of purse is harder than all”; and it is explicit in Iyov, “for you chose this over affliction [poverty]” (Iyov 36:21)257Iyov 36:21: “הִשָּׁמֶר אַל תֵּפֶן אֶל אָוֶן, כִּי עַל זֶה בָּחַרְתָּ מֵעֹנִי” — from the speech of Elihu ben Barachel (chs. 32–37), who rebukes Iyov for justifying himself against God. The verse is famously difficult. In its plain sense (Rashi) Elihu warns: “beware, do not turn to iniquity [aven — sinful complaint], for this you have preferred to [accepting] affliction” — do not choose wrongful protest over bearing your suffering. R’ Tzadok invokes the reading that takes the mem of “me-oni” comparatively — “you chose all this [your afflictions] rather than poverty” — to establish that poverty and loss of money are the harshest of all sufferings: even Iyov, who bore the extremity of bodily affliction, would sooner have all his sufferings than be poor. Hence “with all your might” (money) is the crown of love’s trial — “the loss of purse is harder than all.”.

וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית בֵּירוּר הָאַהֲבָה: כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר השי"ת מַרְאֶה לוֹ פָּנִים מַסְבִּירוֹת אֵין הָאַהֲבָה רְבוּתָא כָּל כָּךְ, אֲבָל אִם הוּא אוֹהֵב גַּם בַּעֲאָקוֹ רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְּלַן, זֶהוּ בֵּירוּר עַל שְׁלֵימוֹת הָאַהֲבָה

And this is the ultimate clarification of love: for when Hashem shows him a pleasant face, the love is no great feat; but if he loves Him even in his distress, God forbid, this is the proof of the completeness of love —
וְאֵלּוּ הַיִּסּוּרִין הֵן הַנִּקְרָאִין ״יִסּוּרִין שֶׁל אַהֲבָה״, שֶׁגַּם השי"ת אֵין מְבִיאָן עַל הָאָדָם אֶלָּא מֵאַהֲבָתוֹ אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב [ה’] יוֹכִיחַ״

and these sufferings are those called “sufferings of love,” which even Hashem brings upon a person only out of His love for him, as it says, “whom Hashem loves, He chastises” (Mishlei 3:12)258Mishlei 3:12: “כִּי אֶת אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב ה׳ יוֹכִיחַ, וּכְאָב אֶת בֵּן יִרְצֶה” — “For whom Hashem loves He rebukes, as a father the son in whom he delights” — from Shlomo’s exhortation (Mishlei 3) not to despise the mussar of Hashem nor recoil from His reproof. Meforshim: God’s chastisements are the very mark of His love, as a father who loves his son corrects him. From this verse (with others) the Gemara (Berachos 5a) establishes the category of “yissurin shel ahavah,” sufferings of love. R’ Tzadok applies it precisely: the trials God brings upon the lover — the sufferings that clarify his love — are brought “only out of His love for him,” as it says, “whom Hashem loves, He rebukes.”.

וּבְהַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לְמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה אֵין השי“ת מֵבִיא עָלָיו נִסְיוֹנוֹת עֲדַיִין, רַק אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְבָּרֵר בִּשְׁתֵּי הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת דְּ״כָל לְבָבְךָ״ וְ״כָל נַפְשְׁךָ״, אָז השי”ת מְנַסֵּהוּ בְּיִסּוּרִין

And at the beginning of a person’s entry into the middah of love, Hashem does not yet bring trials upon him; only after he has been clarified in the two rungs of “with all your heart” and “with all your soul,” then Hashem tests him with sufferings.259R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §34): “‘in all your ways know Him,’ and they said (Berachos 63a) ‘even for a matter of transgression’… [meaning] that he gives himself over to Hashem — even to lose his entire portion in the World to Come, when Hashem’s will is so — as with the test of the akeidah.” This is §5-4’s “in all your ways know Him, even in a matter of transgression”: the love that serves God in every path, even one that looks like sin, is the love ready to surrender even its own eternal reward — the will bent wholly to His, keeping nothing of self back.

וְעַל כֵּן לָא כְּתִיב בְּפָרָשָׁה שְׁנִיָּה דִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמַע ״בְּכָל מְאֹדְכֶם״, כִּי אֵין הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת לַצִּבּוּר וְלִכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק לִיחִידִים הַיְּכוֹלִים לַעֲמֹד בְּנִסָּיוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [לב, ג] שֶׁ״אֵין מְנַסֶּה אֶלָּא קַנְקַנִּים חֲזָקִים״

And therefore “with all your might” is not written in the second paragraph of Kerias Shema, for the trials are not for the community and the whole of Israel, only for individuals able to withstand a trial, as they said in Bereishis Rabbah [32:3] that “one tests only strong vessels [kankanim].”260Bereishis Rabbah 32:3: “‘Hashem tests the righteous’ (Tehillim 11:5) — the potter does not test flawed vessels, which he could not strike once without breaking; rather he tests strong vessels [kankanim], which he strikes many times and they do not break. So the Holy One tests the righteous.” R’ Tzadok: the “sufferings of love” (the highest trial, “with all your might”) are given only to the “strong vessels” — the individuals who can withstand them — not to the community, hence “b’chol me’odchem” is absent from the second paragraph of Shema.

items.h: The theme: Avraham is the first of those tested, the first to clarify the middah of love until he became a Chariot for it. Trials of worldly suffering are no great feat from the side of fear; it is loving Him in distress that proves love complete. The whole length of the exile hangs on this: God wills that the arousal come first from below — “Return to Me” — though we ask that His arousal precede ours.

p: [ה] וְאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה הוּא הָרִאשׁוֹן לַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת, כִּי הוּא הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁבֵּירֵר מִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה בְּכָל תֹּקֶף, עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה כַּנּוֹדָע

And Avraham Avinu is the first of the trials, for he is the first who clarified the middah of love in all its force, until he became a Chariot for the middah of love, as is known.261R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek, Likutim §3): “These are the ten trials with which Avraham Avinu was tested, and he was found whole in all of them, that they did not move him even a hair’s breadth — and then he merited the name ‘Eisan,’ and at once also the title ‘HaEzrachi’; and this is the trial of the Akeidah, and it is known in the Zohar that then Avraham and Yitzchak were ‘incorporated’ one in the other.” The se’if’s Avraham: through the ten trials, culminating in the Akeidah, he “became a Chariot for the middah of love.”

דְּכָל נִסְיוֹנוֹת מִצַּד יִסּוּרֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּרוֹב נִסְיוֹנוֹת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע“ה, מִצַּד הַיִּרְאָה אֵינוֹ רְבוּתָא — דְּאַדְּרַבָּא יוֹתֵר יִרְאָה יֵשׁ עַל הָאָדָם כַּאֲשֶׁר רוֹאֶה מִדַּת הַדִּין ח”ו מְתוּחָה, שֶׁהִיא הַמְּטִילָה יִרְאָה עַל הָאָדָם; וּמִדַּת חֲסָדָיו יִתְבָּרֵךְ מְבִיאָה אַהֲבָה לִבְנֵי אָדָם

For all trials from the side of this-worldly sufferings, like most of Avraham’s trials, are — from the side of fear — no great feat; for, on the contrary, greater fear is upon a person when he sees the Attribute of Justice, God forbid, stretched out, which casts fear upon a person; while His kindness brings love to people.262R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §5): “with respect to Israel, who are the essence of the form of ‘adam’ that is in the merkavah, all the nations too are not in the category of ‘adam’ but like a beast in the form of a man.” This is the ground of §5-5’s “[Avraham] became a Chariot for the middah of love”: Avraham, the first who clarified love and the root of Israel, is the very “form of adam” borne upon the Chariot — the avos hen hen ha-merkavah — so that the love he embodied became the enduring shape of the Chariot itself.

אֲבָל אִם הוּא אוֹהֵב גַּם בַּעֲאָקוֹ רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְּלַן, זֶהוּ בֵּירוּר עַל שְׁלֵימוֹת הָאַהֲבָה; וְאֵלּוּ הַיִּסּוּרִין הֵן הַנִּקְרָאִין ״יִסּוּרִין שֶׁל אַהֲבָה״, שֶׁגַּם השי"ת אֵין מְבִיאָן עַל הָאָדָם אֶלָּא מֵאַהֲבָתוֹ אוֹתוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲשֶׁר יֶאֱהַב״ וְגוֹ‘, וְנֶאֱמַר ״ה’ חָפֵץ [דַּכְּאוֹ]״ וְדָרְשׁוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת ה.] ״מִי שֶׁחָפֵץ בּוֹ״

But if he loves even in his distress, God forbid, this is the proof of the completeness of love; and these sufferings are called “sufferings of love,” which even Hashem brings only out of His love for him, as it says, “whom He loves He rebukes,” and “Hashem desired to crush him,” which they expounded [Berachos 5a], “whomever He desires.”263Berachos 5a: “If a person sees that sufferings come upon him, let him examine his deeds; if he examined and found nothing [to attribute them to], let him know they are sufferings of love, as it says, ‘whom Hashem loves He chastises’ (Mishlei 3:12). Rav Sechora said in the name of Rav Huna: Whomever the Holy One desires, He crushes with sufferings, as it says, ‘and Hashem desired to crush him’ (Yeshayah 53:10).” R’ Tzadok: such sufferings are themselves an expression of love (the “water reflecting a face”), and withstanding them is the proof of love’s completeness.264R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §14): “‘what does Hashem [ask of you] but to fear,’ and ‘the end of the matter… fear God, for this is the whole of man’ — and therefore this mitzvah is set on Rosh Hashanah, to bring the fear into the heart for all the days of the year.” This is precisely the rung §5-5 measures Avraham against: fear is “the whole of man,” the baseline every person can reach — so enduring the world’s sufferings “is no great feat from the side of fear.” Avraham’s greatness lay elsewhere — in the love that a fear-trial can never disclose.

כַּיָּדוּעַ דִּ״כְמַיִם הַפָּנִים״ וְגוֹ’, וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא וְדִלְעֵילָּא מְעוֹרְרִים זֶה אֶת זֶה; רַק שֶׁאָנוּ אוֹמְרִים ״מָשְׁכֵנִי265Shir HaShirim 1:4: “מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה, הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו” — “Draw me, we will run after You; the King has brought me into His chambers.” Shir HaShirim is read as the allegory of the love of the Holy One and Knesses Yisrael — “all the Writings are holy, but Shir HaShirim is the Holy of Holies” (Mishnah Yadayim 3:5; Rashi). Meforshim: “mashcheni” — Israel asks God to draw her, for the first arousal must come from Him. R’ Tzadok’s use: “mashcheni acharecha narutza” (and, in prayer, “hashiveinu Hashem eilecha ve-nashuvah,” Eichah 5:21) express that love and return depend on the drawing from Above; a person’s “running” follows only after God draws — it is not in his power to awaken love by his own striving. [אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה]״ וַ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא קוֹדֶמֶת לְעוֹרְרֵנוּ, וְאָנוּ נִמְשׁוֹךְ וְנָרוּץ אַחֲרָיו

As is known, “as water [reflects] a face,” and the arousal from below and from Above rouse one another; only that we say “draw me [after You we will run]” and “return us,” that the arousal from Above precede to rouse us, and we will be drawn and run after Him.

והשי“ת אוֹמֵר בְּהֵיפֶךְ ״שׁוּבוּ [אֵלַי וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם]״, וְעַל זֶה הוּא כָּל אֹרֶךְ הַגָּלוּת — שהשי”ת רוֹצֶה שֶׁנְּעוֹרֵר אֲנַחְנוּ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא, וְאִם יִשְׂרָאֵל עוֹשִׂים תְּשׁוּבָה מִיָּד נִגְאָלִים

But Hashem says the reverse, “Return to Me [and I will return to you],” and upon this hangs the whole length of the exile — for Hashem wills that we arouse, with an arousal from below, and “if Israel do teshuvah they are immediately redeemed.”

אֲבָל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין לוֹ להקב"ה בְּעוֹלָמוֹ אֶלָּא אוֹצָר שֶׁל יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם בִּלְבַד — הַיִּרְאָה הִיא הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא כַּיָּדוּעַ, דְּעָלֶיהָ נֶאֱמַר ״זֶה הַשַּׁעַר [לַה’]״, דְּהִיא ״תַּרְעָא לְאַעֲלָא גּוֹ מְהֵימָנוּתָא״

But in this world the Holy One has in His world only the treasury of yiras shamayim alone — fear being the arousal from below, as is known, of which it says “this is the gate [to Hashem],” which is “the gate to enter into faith.”

דְּבִתְחִילַּת כְּנִיסַת הָאָדָם לַעֲבוֹדַת השי“ת הוּא עַל יְדֵי יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם, שֶׁהִיא ״רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה״ — הַתְחָלַת הַכָּרַת הָאָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְצִיאוּת השי”ת — מִיָּד יַגִּיעַ אֵלָיו הַיִּרְאָה וְהַהַכְנָעָה כו’, כִּלְשׁוֹן רמ״א [בְּרֵישׁ שֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ אוֹרַח חַיִּים] — וְנֶאֱמַר ״מָה ה’ אֱלֹקֶיךָ שֹׁאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה״, דְּאֵין הַמְבֻקָּשׁ מֵהָאָדָם רַק מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה

For a person’s initial entry into God’s service is through yiras shamayim, which is “the beginning of wisdom” — the beginning of a person’s recognition that Hashem exists — whereupon fear and submission immediately reach him, etc., in the language of the Rema (at the beginning of Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim)266Rema (R’ Moshe Isserles, c. 1530–1572), in his gloss at the very opening of Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chayim 1:1, teaches on the verse “I have set Hashem before me always” (Tehillim 16:8) that “this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God”; for a person’s sitting, movements, and dealings when he is alone in his house are not like his sitting, movements, and dealings when he stands before a great king. And when a person takes to heart that the great King, the Holy One, blessed is He, whose glory fills the whole earth, stands over him and sees his deeds, “immediately the awe and the submission in the fear of Him reach him” (the Rema there citing Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim III:52). R’ Tzadok invokes this to show that the very recognition that God exists draws down yirah of itself. — and it says, “what does Hashem your God ask of you but to fear” — for what is asked of a person [at first] is only the middah of fear.

items.h: The theme: Love cannot be reached by a person’s own effort, for “there is no love except between equals” — how shall the axe boast over the one who hews with it? It is God who confers the equality, calling Knesses Yisrael “My twin.” Hence from the side of Israel’s service fear comes first, but from the side of His own middos love precedes — as Chesed precedes Gevurah, and Avraham begot Yitzchak.

p: [ו] אֲבָל הָאַהֲבָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם, כִּי ״אֵין אַהֲבָה אֶלָּא בֵּין הַדּוֹמִים״, וְאֵיךְ יִתְפָּאֵר הַגַּרְזֶן עַל הַחוֹצֵב לוֹמַר שֶׁאוֹהֲבוֹ

But love cannot be reached by a person’s effort, for “there is no love except between equals” — and how shall the axe boast over the one who hews with it, to say that it loves him?267R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Seitzei §8): "“just as a dove, from the hour she recognizes her mate, does not exchange him for another — so Israel”; and as they said [Eruvin 100b], “had the Torah not been given we would have learned [modesty from the dove].”" Exactly the se’if: love holds between a pair that answer one another — which is why He calls Knesses Yisrael “My twin,” a like recognizing its like and never exchanging it.

רַק השי“ת בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו קוֹרֵא לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל ״אֲחוֹתִי, תַּמָּתִי, תְּאוֹמָתִי״, וְאוֹמֵר ״אָהַבְתִּי אֶתְכֶם268Malachi 1:2: “אָהַבְתִּי אֶתְכֶם אָמַר ה׳, וַאֲמַרְתֶּם בַּמָּה אֲהַבְתָּנוּ, הֲלוֹא אָח עֵשָׂו לְיַעֲקֹב נְאֻם ה׳, וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב” — “‘I have loved you,’ says Hashem; yet you say, ‘How have You loved us?’ — Was not Esav a brother to Yaakov, declares Hashem, yet I loved Yaakov.” The opening of Malachi, last of the prophets. Rashi/Radak: God’s love for Israel is unconditional and rooted in the Avos, shown by His choosing Yaakov over his very brother Esav. R’ Tzadok’s use: this love applies uniquely to Israel — “I have loved you, says Hashem” — for Israel alone is called, as it were, God’s “twin,” and love (unlike fear) obtains only between equals; God’s love (the arousal from Above) precedes and evokes Israel’s love in return.״ וְגוֹ’; וּכשהשי”ת אוֹהֵב הָאָדָם מִמֵּילָא הָאָדָם אוֹהֲבוֹ גַּם כֵּן, וְהָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא קוֹדֶמֶת בָּזֶה לְעוֹלָם

Only God, in His abounding mercy and kindness, calls Knesses Yisrael “My sister, My perfect one, My twin,” and says “I have loved you,” etc.; and when God loves a person, of itself the person loves Him too, and here the arousal from Above always precedes.

וּלְכָךְ מִצַּד עַבְדוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהוּא בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא, הַיִּרְאָה קוֹדֶמֶת; אֲבָל מִצַּד מִדּוֹתָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ, יָדוּעַ דְּאַהֲבָה קוֹדֶמֶת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לְךָ ה’ הַגְּדֻלָּה וְהַגְּבוּרָה269Divrei HaYamim I 29:11: “לְךָ ה׳ הַגְּדֻלָּה וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהַתִּפְאֶרֶת וְהַנֵּצַח וְהַהוֹד, כִּי כֹל בַּשָּׁמַיִם וּבָאָרֶץ, לְךָ ה׳ הַמַּמְלָכָה” — “Yours, Hashem, is the greatness and the might and the splendor and the eternity and the majesty…” — from David HaMelech’s public blessing of Hashem before the whole assembly at the gathering for the building of the Beis HaMikdash. This is the classic scriptural enumeration of the seven lower middos/sefiros (Gedulah = Chesed, Gevurah, Tiferes, Netzach, Hod, “ki chol” = Yesod, and ha-mamlachah = Malchus). R’ Tzadok reads the order: “ha-gedulah [Chesed] ve-ha-gevurah” — Chesed (love) named before Gevurah (fear) — as showing that from God’s side love precedes fear; and correspondingly among the Avos, who “are the Merkavah [Chariot]” (Bereishis Rabbah 47:6, 82:6), “Avraham begot Yitzchak” (Bereishis 25:19) — Avraham (Chesed) before Yitzchak (Gevurah).״, גְּדוֹלָה קוֹדֶמֶת; וְכֵן בְּאָבוֹת שֶׁהֵן הַמֶּרְכָּבָה, ״אַבְרָהָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִצְחָק״

Therefore, from the side of Israel’s servitude, which is the arousal from below, fear comes first; but from the side of His middos, it is known that love precedes, as it says, “Yours, Hashem, is the greatness [gedulah] and the might [gevurah]” — greatness first; and so among the Avos, who are the Chariot, “Avraham begot Yitzchak.”270R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Bo §4): “For there is no love except between equals; and the form of Yaakov is engraved on the Throne of Glory, and the Avos are ‘the Chariot,’ and we are called ‘children to Hashem’ from this side — that we are children of the Avos, who are the Chariot — whereas the nations have no connection to this.” Exactly the se’if: love is only “between equals,” so it is God who “calls” Knesses Yisrael — the children of the Avos, His Chariot — into love.

דֶּרֶךְ בַּעֲבוֹדַת פְּרָטֵי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת אַחַר מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ קִנְיָין להשי"ת, שׁוֹאֵל מֵהֶם לְיִרְאָה וּלְהָעִיר בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא; אֲבָל הָאָבוֹת, שֶׁהֵם בִּנְיַן כְּלַל הַכְּנֵסִיָּה וְשָׁרְשָׁהּ וּמְקוֹרָהּ, וַדַּאי בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא לְבַד — כְּמוֹ תְּחִלַּת בְּרִיַּית הָעוֹלָם שֶׁהָיָה רַק בְּמַאֲמָרוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ ״יְהִי אוֹר״

In the service of individual souls after matan Torah — who became an “acquisition” for Hashem — He asks of them fear, to arouse with an arousal from below; but the Avos, who are the building of the whole community, its root and source, [were roused] surely by an arousal from Above alone — like the beginning of the world’s creation, which was only by His utterance, “let there be light,”
דְּאָדָם אֵין לַעֲבֹד בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא; וְכֵן זְרִיחַת אוֹרוֹ דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע“ה מִתּוֹךְ הַחוֹשֶׁךְ נֶאֱמַר ״מִי הֵעִיר מִמִּזְרָח״ וְגוֹ’, שהשי”ת הֵעִירוֹ וְעוֹרְרוֹ לָזֶה

[when] there was no man to serve with an arousal from below; and so, of the shining-forth of Avraham’s light out of the darkness, it says, “who aroused one from the east” (Yeshayah 41:2)271Yeshayah 41:2: “מִי הֵעִיר מִמִּזְרָח, צֶדֶק יִקְרָאֵהוּ לְרַגְלוֹ, יִתֵּן לְפָנָיו גּוֹיִם וּמְלָכִים יַרְדְּ, יִתֵּן כֶּעָפָר חַרְבּוֹ כְּקַשׁ נִדָּף קַשְׁתּוֹ” — “Who roused one from the east, calling righteousness to his feet? He delivers up nations before him and makes him tread down kings; his sword makes them as dust, his bow as driven chaff.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of consolation (ch. 41), in which God summons the nations to judgment and asks “who aroused [he’ir]” the victor from the east. Rashi and the Sages apply “mi he’ir mimizrach” to Avraham — whom God “roused” from the east (Ur Kasdim / Aram), “calling righteousness to his feet,” and before whom He delivered up the four kings (Bereishis 14). R’ Tzadok reads the verb “he’ir” as the point: it was God who first aroused Avraham — Avraham’s light shining “out of the darkness” came not by his own initiative but by God’s love preceding him, the “arousal from Above” (is’aruta di-le’eila) that always precedes love. (The received text reads Yeshayah 41:2.) — that Hashem aroused and stirred him to this.

וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד מִדַּת אַהֲבָתוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ, שֶׁמַּטְבֵּעַ הַטּוֹב וְאִישׁ הַחֶסֶד לְהֵטִיב חַסְדּוֹ מִבְּלִי שֶׁיִּקְדְּמֶנּוּ הַלָּה לְבַקְּשׁוֹ עַל זֶה כְּלָל; וְכָל אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת הִיא הַמְּעוֹרֶרֶת מִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה, כִּי הָאַהֲבָה מְעוֹרֶרֶת אַהֲבָה, שֶׁהָאַהֲבָה הוּא בִּדְבָרִים הַדּוֹמִים

And this is from the side of the middah of His love — that the nature of the Good and the man of kindness is to do his kindness before the other has asked him at all; and every preceding arousal from Above is what rouses the middah of love — for love rouses love, love being between like things.272R’ Tzadok — parallel (Sichas Shedim §1): “when a person is made whole [in the middah of Yaakov], the Holy One calls him ‘My twin [te’omasi]’ — that both are equal; and ‘He did not budge from cherishing her until He called her My mother’ — as though she were even greater than He, generating, as it were, the beginning-of-thought that is His.” This is §5-6’s astonishing claim exactly: love needs equals, and God Himself confers the equality — calling Knesses Yisrael “My twin,” then raising her past even that, to “My mother,” so that the love has its “like” on both sides.

items.h: The theme: Fear is not between equals: this one fears, and the Other casts and gives the dread. So even when Gevurah is aroused above and begets fear below, this is not called an arousal from Above preceding one from below, for the two are not one matter. Love, which begets love, is therefore Israel’s alone; fear reaches the nations too, but only as dread of punishment, never drawn after it in clear truth.

p: [ז] מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַיִּרְאָה, מִמִּי שֶׁהוּא מִתְיָירֵא — עַל כָּרְחָךְ אֵינָם דּוֹמִים, וְאֵין הַמִּדָּה שָׁוָה בִּשְׁנֵיהֶם, שֶׁזֶּה מִתְיָירֵא וְזֶה מֵטִיל וְנוֹתֵן הַמּוֹרָא

Not so fear — [fear] of the one whom one fears: perforce they are not equals, and the middah is not the same in both — for this one fears, and that one casts and gives the dread.273R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §24): “One [greets] his fellow out of love and joining; but fear is from the side of ‘derech eretz’ toward a man who is great and separate from him. And by Hashem, both are together, and one without the other does not suffice — for fear alone brings folly (‘is not your fear your folly?’), and joy alone brings frivolity.” The se’if’s point: fear, unlike love, is not between equals — it is toward “one great and separate,” who “casts and gives the dread.”

וּלְכָךְ בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה מוֹלִיד הַיִּרְאָה בְּלֵבַב הָאָדָם — כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא ״כשהקב"ה עוֹשֶׂה דִּין בָּרְשָׁעִים הוּא יָראוּי״ כו’ — אֵין זֶה נִקְרָא ״אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת לְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא״, שֶׁאֵין שְׁנֵיהֶם עִנְיָן אֶחָד

And therefore, at the arousal of the middah of Gevurah above — through which it begets fear in a person’s heart (as it is brought, “when the Holy One executes judgment on the wicked He is feared,” etc.)274“When He does judgment on the wicked He is feared”: R’ Tzadok cites in brief the established teaching that God’s awe is made manifest through judgment. Its scriptural anchor is “nora Elokim mi-mikdashecha” (Tehillim 68:36), which the Sages expound, “read not mi-mikdashecha (from Your sanctuary) but mi-mekudashecha (through those You sanctify [in executing judgment])” (Zevachim 115b; and cf. the Zohar, that when the Holy One performs judgment “He is exalted and held in awe”). R’ Tzadok’s use: the arousal of Gevurah above (the doing of din) is precisely what begets fear in the human heart; yet, unlike love, “the middah is not the same in both” — the One feared and the one who fears are not equals — so this is not called “an arousal from Above that precedes an arousal from below.” — this is not called “an arousal from Above preceding an arousal from below,” for the two are not one matter.275R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §25): “[one kindles the lamp] before Shabbos — but on Shabbos there is no longer a time to arouse the fear, for it is entirely love and deveikus in God.” This sharpens §5-7’s contrast of the two middos: fear belongs to the striving of the weekday, a thing a person can rouse in himself by his own effort; love, like the Shabbos, is a gift already given — not “aroused” but received — which is why love “cannot be reached by a person’s effort,” while fear can.

וּלְכָךְ אַף דְּגַם הַיִּרְאָה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד הָאָדָם, וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר ״מִי הִקְדִּימַנִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּם״ — דְּגַם בָּזֶה השי"ת הַמַּקְדִּים לְהָבִיא אֵלָיו דָּבָר הַמְּעוֹרֵר הַיִּרְאָה — מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא שֶׁבָּא בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא, כֵּיוָן שֶׁאֵין אוֹתוֹ דָּבָר מְעוֹרֵר בְּפֹעַל בָּרוּר כְּמוֹ אַהֲבָה הַמּוֹלִיד אַהֲבָה

And therefore, although fear too is not [purely] from the person’s side — and so it says, “who has preceded Me that I should repay?” (Iyov 41:3)276Iyov 41:3: “מִי הִקְדִּימַנִי וַאֲשַׁלֵּם, תַּחַת כָּל הַשָּׁמַיִם לִי הוּא” — “Who has preceded Me, that I should repay him? Whatever is under the whole heaven is Mine.” From God’s answer to Iyov out of the whirlwind (the Livyasan passage, ch. 41), asserting His absolute sovereignty. Rashi: who has come before Me [with a gift or a merit] that I should owe him repayment — for everything under the heavens is already Mine. The Sages apply “mi hikdimani va-ashalem” to the mitzvos: none can “precede” God and put Him in his debt, since He Himself first provides the very means of the mitzvah (a house before its mezuzah, a garment before its tzitzis — Vayikra Rabbah 27:2, and the like). R’ Tzadok’s use: even fear is not purely from the person’s own side — “who has preceded Me?” — for God Himself precedes to bring him the thing that rouses fear; yet it is still called “an arousal from below,” since (unlike love) that thing does not rouse “in clear act.”, [for] in this too Hashem precedes to bring to him the thing that rouses fear — nonetheless it is called coming “with an arousal from below,” since that thing does not rouse in clear act like love, which begets love,

וּכְטַעַם ״מָשְׁכֵנִי [אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה]״ וַ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״; וְעַל כֵּן זֶה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ רַק בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּ״אָהַבְתִּי אֶתְכֶם יֹאמַר ה’״, מִצַּד שֶׁהֵם קְרוּיִים ״תְּאוֹמָתִי״ כִּבְיָכוֹל וְשַׁיָּיךְ אַהֲבָה בְּגַבַּיְיהוּ

like “draw me [after You we will run]” and “return us”; and therefore this [love] applies only in Israel, “I have loved you, says Hashem,” in that they are called “My twin,” as it were, and love applies with them.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה הוּא גַּם בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, רַק שֶׁהִיא יִרְאָה תַּתָּאָה בְּיוֹתֵר, שֶׁיְּרֵאִים מֵעֳנָשָׁיו יִתְבָּרֵךְ; כִּי עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת גְּבוּרָה מוֹלִיד יִרְאָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם אֵינָהּ נִמְשֶׁכֶת אַחֲרֶיהָ בְּבֵירוּר

whereas the middah of fear is also among the nations, only that it is a much lower fear — that they fear His punishments; for at all events, when the middah of Gevurah is aroused it begets fear, only that with them it is not drawn after it in clear [truth].

שֶׁהֲרֵי בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם נֶאֱמַר ״וְהָיָה כִי יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף וְקִלֵּל [בְּמַלְכּוֹ וּבֵאלֹהָיו]״, שֶׁהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה וְזַעַם, אִם מוֹלִיד בְּלִבּוֹ, אַדְּרַבָּא חָפֵץ לְהִתְגַּבֵּר וְלִזְעֹם וּלְהִתְקַצֵּף וְלִמְרוֹד כִּבְיָכוֹל בהשי"ת

for of the nations it says, “and it shall be when he is hungry, he grows furious and curses his king and his god” (Yeshayah 8:21)277Yeshayah 8:21: “וְעָבַר בָּהּ נִקְשֶׁה וְרָעֵב, וְהָיָה כִי יִרְעַב וְהִתְקַצַּף וְקִלֵּל בְּמַלְכּוֹ וּבֵאלֹהָיו וּפָנָה לְמָעְלָה” — “And he shall pass through it hard-pressed and hungry; and it shall be, when he is hungry, that he grows furious and curses his king and his god, and turns his face upward.” From Yeshayah’s prophecy of the darkness overtaking those who will not heed “to Torah and to testimony” (ch. 8). Rashi: the one in distress, rather than turning to God, “curses his king” (his ruler) “and his god” (his idol) and rails upward. R’ Tzadok’s use: this typifies the lower fear of the nations — when the middah of Gevurah and wrath is aroused in them, it does not draw them to submission but to the reverse: they “strengthen themselves” and rebel (the dross of Gevurah) — as against those in Israel who “desire to fear His Name” and “search like buried treasures” for the fear of God. — that the arousal of the middah of Gevurah and wrath, if it begets [anything] in his heart, on the contrary makes him wish to strengthen himself, and to rage and be furious and rebel, as it were, against Hashem.

רַק אוֹתָם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בָּהֶם ״הַחֲפֵצִים לְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמֶךָ״ וְ״הַמְחַפְּשִׂים כַּמַּטְמוֹנִים לְהָבִין יִרְאַת ה’״ — הֵם יִמְצָאוּהָ, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא״; וְזֶה כָּל עִנְיַן הַתּוֹרָה, דְּמִסִּטְרָא דִּגְבוּרָה נָפְקָא, הַמְצַוָּוה וּמַזְהֶרֶת לָאָדָם לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל לִבְחֹר בַּטּוֹב בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּילֵיהּ

Only those of whom it says, “who desire to fear Your Name” (Nechemyah 1:11)278Nechemyah 1:11: “אָנָּא אֲדֹנָי, תְּהִי נָא אָזְנְךָ קַשֶּׁבֶת אֶל תְּפִלַּת עַבְדְּךָ וְאֶל תְּפִלַּת עֲבָדֶיךָ הַחֲפֵצִים לְיִרְאָה אֶת שְׁמֶךָ […] וְאֲנִי הָיִיתִי מַשְׁקֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ” — “Please, O Lord, let Your ear be attentive to the prayer of Your servant and the prayer of Your servants who desire to fear Your Name…” The verse closes Nechemyah’s opening prayer (ch. 1), as he steels himself to approach the Persian king; he characterizes the faithful as “ha-chafeitzim le-yirah es shemecha” — those whose very desire is to attain the fear of God. R’ Tzadok’s use: fear, though roused from Above through Gevurah, is called “an arousal from below” because it takes hold only in those who seek it — “who desire to fear Your Name” — and who “search” for it; only they find it. and “who search like buried treasures to understand the fear of Hashem” (Mishlei 2:4–5)279Mishlei 2:4–5: “אִם תְּבַקְשֶׁנָּה כַכָּסֶף, וְכַמַּטְמוֹנִים תַּחְפְּשֶׂנָּה. אָז תָּבִין יִרְאַת ה׳, וְדַעַת אֱלֹקִים תִּמְצָא” — “If you seek it like silver and search it out like buried treasures, then you will understand the fear of Hashem and find the knowledge of God.” From Shlomo’s exhortation (Mishlei 2) that wisdom and the fear of God are won only by strenuous search. Meforshim: yiras Hashem is not given passively — one must “dig” for it as for hidden treasure. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because fear must be sought out — “search like buried treasures” — it is “an arousal from below,” the striving of the person; and this is the whole matter of the Torah, which issues from the side of Gevurah, commanding a person to labor to choose the good. — they will find it; and therefore it is called “an arousal from below”; and this is the whole matter of the Torah, which issues from the side of Gevurah, commanding and warning a person to strive to choose the good, by an arousal of his own.280R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §13): “the beginning of the Ten Days of Teshuvah — and especially the very beginning — is to arouse the fear in the heart; and it is known that Rosh Hashanah is called ‘the second day,’ that is, the middah of Gevurah and fear.” This is §5-7’s point that fear, unlike love, lies within a person’s reach: because “the middah of Gevurah above is aroused… [and] begets fear in a person’s heart,” a man can arouse that fear himself — the very labor with which the Days of Awe open — needing no equality with the One he fears.

items.h: The theme: After the tenth trial, the Akeidah, it says “now I know that you fear God” — for Avraham was then included in the middah of Yitzchak. This is love’s completion: he added his own vigor and striving upon the arousal from Above that had preceded him, until he could be called its author. Hence they said of him, “they chose him but did not bring him near — rather he brought himself near.”

p: [ח] וְאַחַר שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה בְּאַהֲבָה הַגְּמוּרָה בַּנִּסָּיוֹן הָעֲשִׂירִי דַּעֲקֵידָה, שֶׁהָיָה לְגַבָּיו תַּכְלִית תֹּקֶף דִּ״בְכָל מְאֹדֶךָ״, נֶאֱמַר ״עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יְרֵא אֱלֹקִים אַתָּה״, דְּאִתְכַּלֵּיל אָז בְּמִדַּת יִצְחָק

And after Avraham Avinu was clarified in complete love in the tenth trial, the Akeidah — which for him was the ultimate force of “with all your might” — it says, “now I know that you fear God” — for he was then included in the middah of Yitzchak [fear].281R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §186): “Then Avraham and Yitzchak were united together, as it says ‘now I know that you fear God’ — and this is like ‘R’ Chisda and R’ Sheshes’ (Eruvin 67a), two opposites, R’ Chisda ‘sharp’ and R’ Sheshes ‘Sinai,’ each ‘trembling’ before the other — that is the fear; and through the ‘sharpening,’ the God-fearing ones spoke and were joined and included [one in the other].” Exactly the se’if: after the Akeidah, Avraham was “included in the middah of Yitzchak” — fear.

כִּי זֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוֹת הָאַהֲבָה דְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה, שֶׁהָיָה מִדָּתוֹ אַהֲבָה לְבַד, שֶׁהִיא מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא, רַק שֶׁהוּא הוֹסִיף אֹמֶץ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת מְרֻבָּה עַל יְדֵי דְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא שֶׁקְּדָמַתּוּ, עַד שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת נִקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ כְּאִלּוּ הוּא הַמְעוֹרֵר, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת הַיִּרְאָה

For this is the completion of Avraham’s love, whose middah was love alone (which is from an arousal from Above); only that he added great vigor and striving upon the arousal from Above that preceded him, until he merits to be “called by his name,” as if he is the arouser — and this is the middah of fear.

וְהָאַהֲבָה הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה נֶחְשָׁב שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּילֵיהּ, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי שֶׁהוּא נִתְעוֹרֵר לְיִרְאָה, עַל יְדֵי זֶה ״רוּחַ אַמְשֵׁיךְ רוּחַ״ אַהֲבָה לְעֵילָּא, וְנִתְעוֹרֵר אַחַר כָּךְ לְאַהֲבָה

And the love that comes by way of fear is reckoned as coming through his own arousal: for because he aroused himself to fear, thereby “a spirit draws down a spirit” of love from above, and he is afterward aroused to love.282R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §10): “the [modes of] service are love, fear, and deveikus; love and fear are the two wings and the two arms of the world — and they are the two Avos, Avraham and Yitzchak; and deveikus is ‘the one who grasps the body of the King,’ the form of Yaakov engraved on the Throne.” This is the structure behind §5-8’s “now I know that you fear God”: love and fear are the two wings on which one rises, and neither flies alone — so Avraham’s love reached its height only when, at the Akeidah, it was joined to Yitzchak’s fear, the two wings become one.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּאַבְרָהָם שֶׁ״בָּחֲרוּ אֲבָל לֹא קֵרְבוּ, רַק הוּא קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ״ [בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה ג, ב] — פֵּירוּשׁ, תְּחִלַּת הָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא שֶׁהָיָה עָלָיו וְנִבְחַר הוּא מִכָּל הָעוֹלָם כֻּלּוֹ לְעוֹרְרוֹ לְאַהֲבַת השי"ת — זֶהוּ מֵה’ שֶׁבָּחַר בְּאַבְרָם וְהוֹצִיאוֹ כו’ — אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ נִתְנַסָּה בַּנִּסְיוֹנוֹת

And this is what is brought regarding Avraham, that “they chose him but did not bring him near — rather he brought himself near” [Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2] — meaning, the beginning, the arousal from Above that was upon him (that he was chosen of the whole world to be roused to God’s love) — this stems from Hashem, who ‘chose Avram and brought him out,’ etc. — but afterward he was tested in the trials.283Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2 (on “happy is the one You choose and bring near,” Tehillim 65:5): “Happy is he whom the Holy One chose, even if He did not bring him near; and happy is he whom He brought near, even if He did not choose him. Whom did He choose [but not bring near]? Avraham, of whom it says ‘You are Hashem the God who chose Avram’ (Nechemyah 9:7) — but He did not bring him near; rather he brought himself near. So too Yaakov and Moshe. And whom did He bring near but not choose? Yisro and Rachav the harlot. And who is ‘happy’ doubly? — one whom He chose and brought near: Aharon and Levi.” R’ Tzadok makes this the frame of the whole se’if: the Avos “brought themselves near” by striving (the way of Torah/this world), while Aharon was “brought near” without striving.284R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §21): “Avraham and Yitzchak are love and fear: love is the root of the positive commandments — the distancing from envy, through the chesed of Avraham, by actively doing good; and fear is the foundation of the negative commandments — the distancing from desire.” This is §5-8 exactly: Avraham’s love was made whole only when it was “included in the middah of Yitzchak,” for love and fear are the two roots of all avodah — the “doing good” of Avraham and the “turning from evil” of Yitzchak — and the complete servant, like Avraham at the Akeidah, holds both.

וְיָדוּעַ דְּמִסְפַּר עֶשֶׂר הוּא מִסְפָּר כּוֹלֵל וּמִדַּת קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁתַּכְלִית כָּל עִנְיַן הַנִּסְיוֹנוֹת שֶׁיֵּשׁ בִּמְצִיאוּת הֵבִיא עָלָיו; וְכָל עִנְיַן הַנִּסָּיוֹן, יָדוּעַ דְּהַיְינוּ שהשי"ת מַרְאֶה עַצְמוֹ מְרֻחָק מִמֶּנּוּ בְּתַכְלִית, וְהוּא צָרִיךְ בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לְקָרֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ אֵלָיו

And it is known that “ten” is an all-inclusive number, a “complete stature” — meaning that God brought upon him the ultimate of every trial that exists; and the whole matter of a trial, it is known, is that Hashem shows Himself utterly distant from him, and he must, by his striving, bring himself near to Him.
כִּי זֶה יְסוֹד אֻמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית — לָתֵת מָקוֹם לַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא הַמֻּזְהֶרֶת בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם, וּמֵאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע"ה הִתְחִיל ״שְׁנֵי אֲלָפִים תּוֹרָה״

For this is the foundation of the Israelite nation — to make room for the Torah, which is [the wisdom] that warns [one to labor] through a person’s striving; and from Avraham the “two thousand years of Torah” began.

וּשְׁלֵימוּתָהּ עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ, שֶׁיְּתֻקַּן כָּל הַקּוֹדֵם — גַּם חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן — דְּיִתְהַפֵּךְ הַכֹּל לִזְכִיּוֹת; זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר רַק עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקֵּירוּב הַגָּמוּר מִמֶּנּוּ יִתְבָּרַךְ וַהֲסָרַת הַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לְגַמְרֵי, כִּי יִתְבָּרֵר דְּ״גַם כָּל מַחְשְׁבוֹתֵינוּ וּמַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָנוּ״, וְהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ יִתְבָּרֵךְ

And its completion is through Mashiach — that all the past be rectified, even the sin of Adam, so that all turns to merits; this is possible only through the revelation of complete nearness from Him and the utter removal of “striving,” when it will be clarified that “You have wrought all our deeds for us” (Yeshayah 26:12)285Yeshayah 26:12: “ה׳ תִּשְׁפֹּת שָׁלוֹם לָנוּ, כִּי גַּם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ” — “Hashem, You will establish peace for us, for You have also wrought all our deeds for us.” From the “song” of the future redemption sung in the land of Yehudah (Yeshayah 26). Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): all that we have accomplished, You have wrought for us — every good deed of ours is ultimately God’s own doing. R’ Tzadok’s use: the ultimate rectification (through Mashiach) requires the removal of “striving” and the revelation that “gam kol ma’aseinu pa’alta lanu” — all is from Him; and then even the past sins turn to merits, for the “distancings” themselves were, in truth, His drawings-near.Izhbitz-Radzin and Ger on the future revelation that “all our deeds You wrought for us.” Mei HaShiloach II, Zechariah 4:1, reads “לא בחיל ולא בכח כי אם ברוחי” as the future state in which the powers of human action are progressively effaced and the inheritance of Yaakov is revealed: Yaakov describes himself as one who does nothing, even in the smallest matter, until God “takes him by the hand and leads him like sheep after the shepherd.” That is a striking complement to R’ Tzadok’s use of Yeshayah 26:12 here: the final repair comes when the very framework of self-authored hishtadlus is removed and it is disclosed that “all is from Him.” Chiddushei HaRim, Vayigash §2, states the same point retrospectively: at the complete redemption it will be seen “למפרע שכל עניני הגלות היה לטובתינו,” and every detail of the exile will be clarified as part of the good; he therefore describes the descent itself as carrying its ascent within it, “אנכי ארד עמך… אעלך גם עלה.” These are not denials of the Torah’s present demand for bechirah; they describe the eschatological disclosure R’ Tzadok is speaking about — what becomes visible only when the work of human striving has reached its end., and all is from Him.

כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [פד, יז] בַּאֲחֵי יוֹסֵף ״כְּשֶׁרָצִיתָ נָתַתָּ בְּלִבָּם לֶאֱהֹב, וּכְשֶׁרָצִיתָ״ כו’, וְכָךְ רָצָה יִתְבָּרֵךְ לָתֵת בְּלֵב הָאָדָם לִשְׂנֹא — וְגַם זֶה מֵאִתּוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ שֶׁרָצָה לְקָרְבוֹ עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה, וְהָרִיחוּקִים הַכֹּל הֵם קֵירוּבִים, כְּעִנְיַן ״יִסּוּרִים שֶׁל אַהֲבָה״

As it is brought in Bereishis Rabbah [84:17] regarding Yosef’s brothers, “when You willed, You placed in their hearts to love, and when You willed [to hate],” etc.; so God willed to place in a person’s heart to hate — and even this is from Him, who willed to bring him near in this way — and the distancings are all drawings-near, like “sufferings of love.”286Bereishis Rabbah 84:17: on the brothers’ hatred of Yosef, “when You [God] willed, You placed in their hearts to love [Yosef’s father], and when You willed, You placed in their hearts to hate him.” R’ Tzadok: even the “distancing” (the brothers’ hatred, and all a person’s sins that lead him to teshuvah) is itself from God and is, at root, a drawing-near — like “sufferings of love.”

שֶׁהֲרֵי הַיִּסּוּר הוּא רִיחוּק וְהֵיפֶךְ הָאַהֲבָה, וּבִשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה כִּסְבוּרִים אָנוּ שֶׁהוּא רִיחוּק, וּבֶאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא קֵירוּב וְתֹקֶף אַהֲבָה; וְכֵן כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ הָאָדָם לָשׁוּב וְלִזְכּוֹת לְמַדְרֵיגַת בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה — הֲרֵי הָרִיחוּק הוּא סִבַּת קֵירוּב

For the suffering is a distancing, the opposite of love, and at the time of the deed we suppose it a distancing, but in truth it is only a nearness and the intensity of love; and so too all the transgressions that brought a person to return and merit the rank of baal teshuvah — the distancing is the cause of the drawing-near.

items.h: The theme: This rung comes through teshuvah from love, in which the nearness that follows distance is the greater — as the Sages explained the impurity of niddah, “so that she be beloved to him anew.” The willful sins themselves become merits, being the very cause of the drawing-near. Even David returned from complete love, yet was told “in your lifetime I will not make it known” — for love’s hour must come from Above.

p: [ט] וּמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ הוּא עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּהָאַהֲבָה יוֹתֵר בְּקֵירוּב שֶׁאַחַר הָרִיחוּק, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זַ"ל [נִדָּה לא:] בְּטַעַם טֻמְאַת נִדָּה ״כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא חֲבִיבָה עָלָיו״

And this rung is through teshuvah from love, for it is known that love is greater in the nearness that comes after distance, in the manner the Sages said [Niddah 31b] of the reason for the impurity of niddah, “so that she be beloved to him.”287Niddah 31b: “Why did the Torah say [a niddah is impure] seven days? Because [a husband] becomes habituated to his wife and repelled by her; therefore the Torah said she is impure seven days, so that she be beloved to him as on the day of her wedding.” R’ Tzadok: love renewed after distance is greater — so teshuvah from love makes the very sins (the “distance”) the cause of a greater nearness, i.e. “merits.”Maharal — distance itself can generate a stronger return. Maharal, Nesiv HaTeshuvah 2:17–19, gives a conceptual analogue to R’ Tzadok’s use of the niddah interval: the one who comes to God “from afar” can reveal a more forceful attachment than one who was never distant, just as fire far below moves upward toward its natural place with greater force. Maharal therefore says that the sin, which was itself the distance, becomes a merit when that very distance is what reveals the depth of the return. R’ Tzadok develops the same principle here in relational language: the separation makes the renewed nearness more beloved, and so the z’donos themselves become the causes of kiruv.288R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §70): “like Yaakov’s flight to Chutz la-Aretz — which is in distance from the face-to-face recognition of Yitzchak — and this is what clarifies his wholeness; for his wholeness (‘his bed was whole,’ his own cleaving to Hashem) is not [shown] complete except when, even in distance of place, [he holds fast].” This is §5-9’s “the greater love, in the nearness that comes after distance”: the bond is not fully revealed in unbroken closeness — it is the cleaving that survives a gulf that discloses love in its full force, so that the willful sins themselves become merits.

וְנִמְצְאוּ הַזְּדוֹנוֹת גַּם כֵּן כִּזְכִיּוֹת, שֶׁהֵם הַגּוֹרְמִים הַקֵּירוּב, וְיֵשׁ לוֹ זְכִיּוֹת הַרְבֵּה אֲלֻמּוֹת אֲלֻמּוֹת, מַה שֶּׁאֵין לַצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים; וּלְעָתִיד עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ יְתֻקַּן כֵּן בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֺן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, וְגַם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נַעֲשָׂה מִקְצָתוֹ לְהַשָּׁבִים מֵאַהֲבָה

And the willful sins are thus found to be as merits, being what cause the drawing-near, and he has merits “heaped up, sheaf upon sheaf,” which the completely righteous do not; and in the future, through Mashiach, this will be so for all Israel — of which it says “the sin of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none” — and in this world too, a portion of it is realized for those who return from love.289R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §53): “for fear is from near — when one stands before the King he fears Him… and as it says,”with great awe" — this is the revelation [of the Shechinah]." Exactly the se’if: fear operates in nearness, and therefore love is what is disclosed across distance — which is why the love of the returner, after estrangement, is the greater.

וְאַף דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע"ה וַדַּאי שָׁב מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּמוּרָה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נֶאֱמַר לוֹ ״בְּחַיֶּיךָ אֵינִי מוֹדִיעַ״ [שַׁבָּת ל.], דְּעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר ״אִם תָּעִירוּ290Shir HaShirim 2:7: “הִשְׁבַּעְתִּי אֶתְכֶם בְּנוֹת יְרוּשָׁלַ͏ִם […] אִם תָּעִירוּ וְאִם תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ” — “I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem… do not stir up or awaken the love until it desires” (repeated at 3:5 and 8:4). In its plain love-allegory sense it warns against forcing love before its time; the Sages also read the adjurations as the “three oaths” of exile (Kesuvos 111a). R’ Tzadok’s use: the influx of love descends only “when it desires” — a time set from Above — and it is not in a person’s power to awaken it by his striving; hence even David, who returned from complete love, was told “in your lifetime I will not make [it] known,” the time not yet having “desired.” וְאִם תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ״, דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ זְמַן שֶׁתֶּחְפֹּץ
