And even David surely returned from complete love, yet he was told “in your lifetime I will not make [it] known” [Shabbos 30a]291Shabbos 30a: the Gemara recounts that David said before the Holy One, “mechol li al oso avon — pardon me for that sin,” and He answered, “machul lach — it is pardoned you.” David then asked, “asei imi os be-chayai — make a sign [of the pardon] in my lifetime,” and He replied, “be-chayecha eini modia — in your lifetime I will not make it known; be-chayei Shlomo bincha ani modia — in the lifetime of Shlomo your son I will make it known.” (This was borne out when the Temple gates clung shut until Shlomo invoked “zochrah le-chasdei David avdecha,” whereupon all knew the Holy One had pardoned him.) R’ Tzadok’s use: even David, who returned from complete love, was told “in your lifetime I will not make known” — for “do not awaken love until it desires”: the influx of love descends only when its time has “desired,” and it is not in a person’s power to compel it by striving; yet David, by his very request, “brought himself near.”, for of him it says “do not stir up or awaken love until it desires” — that the time when it would “desire” had not yet come.

כִּי הָאַהֲבָה עִיקָּרָהּ מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא, וְצָרִיךְ לָזֶה זְמַן שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ לֵירֵד שֶׁפַע הָאַהֲבָה, וְאֵינוֹ בְּיַד הָאָדָם לְעוֹרֵר אַהֲבָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת וְאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא

For love’s essence is from an arousal from Above, and it requires a time when the influx of love “desires” to descend, and it is not in a person’s hand to arouse love by striving and an arousal from below.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע“ה נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן ״דְּלָא קֵרְבוּ, וְהוּא קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ״, וְאָמַר ״בְּחָנֵנִי וְנַסֵּנִי״, אַף שֶׁלֹּא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ לְמַרְאִית עַיִן — עַל הָאֱמֶת עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי זֶהוּ שֶׁהֱבִיאוֹ לְהָקִים עוֹלָה שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר הִתְעַלּוּת מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ מֵ״הֵ”א תַּתָּאָה״ — מִדַּת מַלְכוּת — לַעֲשׂוֹתָהּ ״הֵ"א עִלָּאָה״ הָרוֹמֶזֶת לִתְשׁוּבָה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ

And David too is called “not brought near — he brought himself near,” and said “examine me and test me” (Tehillim 26:2)292Tehillim 26:2: “בְּחָנֵנִי ה׳ וְנַסֵּנִי, צָרְפָה כִלְיוֹתַי וְלִבִּי” — “Examine me, Hashem, and test me; refine my kidneys and my heart” — David HaMelech’s request that God prove and refine him. The Sages (Sanhedrin 107a) relate that David asked to be tested: “why do we say ‘God of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov’ but not ‘God of David’? — because they were tested and you were not; if so, examine me and test me” — the trial in which he then stumbled. R’ Tzadok’s use: David “brought himself near” by requesting the nisayon; though “to the eye” it did not succeed (he fell), “in truth it did succeed,” for it is what brought him to raise the “yoke of teshuvah” — the ascent of malchus (the lower heh) into teshuvah (the upper heh).; though it did not succeed in his hand to the eye, in truth it did succeed — for this is what brought him to raise the “yoke of teshuvah,” which is the essential ascent of his rung from the lower heh (the middah of malchus) to make it the upper heh (which alludes to teshuvah) — and by this he brought himself near.293R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §2): “these are the days of smallness and distance — as in ‘from afar Hashem appeared to me’; therefore they are the ‘eyes’ that see from afar, as in ‘My eyes and My heart are there all the days’ — even in the days of distance (Berachos 62b).” This is the inner mood of §5-9: the very seasons of distance become the vantage from which the Beloved is seen and longed for — “from afar Hashem appears” — and the love kindled across that distance is the deeper love of the return, “so that she be beloved to him anew.”

items.h: The theme: “Happy is Aharon doubly — that he was chosen and brought near”: he did not bring himself near by striving. Such a thing does not otherwise exist in this world, which is the time of labor; Yisro and Rachav were brought near but not chosen. Aharon alone was both — and he merited it through the making of the Calf, which is why he stood ashamed, until he was told, “for this you were chosen.”

p: [י] וְ״אַשְׁרֵי אַהֲרֹן בְּכִפְלַיִם, שֶׁנִּבְחַר וְנִקְרָב״ — שֶׁהוּא לֹא קֵירֵב אֶת עַצְמוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדָה וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת, רַק השי"ת קֵירְבוֹ לַעֲבוֹדָה זוֹ; וְדָבָר זֶה לֹא הָיָה עֲדַיִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הָעֲבוֹדָה וְהַהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת ״וְהַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם״, וּמִי שֶׁנִּתְקָרֵב הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת

And “happy is Aharon doubly — that he was chosen and brought near” — for he did not bring himself near to the service by striving; rather Hashem brought him near to this service; and such a thing did not yet exist in this world (which is the time of labor and striving, “and the day to do them”) — and one who is “brought near” is one who needs no striving.294R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §6): “ruach ha-kodesh of this kind comes through an arousal from Above without an arousal from below [isarusa di-l’eila be-lo isarusa di-l’tata]; and so the first of the rungs of R’ Pinchas ben Yair — he did not name ‘learning’ or ‘engaging in Torah’ or human effort, [such as] zehirus and zerizus.” This is §5-10’s Aharon exactly: he “did not bring himself near to the service by striving; rather God brought him near” — the rung that comes purely by arousal from Above, without the labor of arousal-from-below, which “did not yet exist in this world,” the time of striving.

וְזֶה הָיָה רַק בְּיִתְרוֹ וְרָחָב שֶׁ״קֵרְבוּ אֲבָל לֹא בָּחֲרוּ״, וְהַקֵּירוּב שֶׁלָּהֶם הָיָה שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ לְהִתְגַּיֵּיר וְלִיטַּפֵּל לְאֻמָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית, שֶׁזֶּה לֹא הָיָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם כְּלָל — רַק יִתְרוֹ עַל פִּי סִבָּה שֶׁהָיָה חוֹתֵן מֹשֶׁה, וְרָחָב בְּסִבַּת הַמְרַגְּלִים שֶׁהָיוּ בְּבֵיתָהּ

And this was only with Yisro and Rachav, who were “brought near but not chosen”; and their nearness was that they came to convert and attach to the Israelite nation, which was in no way through their striving — Yisro by the circumstance that he was Moshe’s father-in-law, and Rachav by the circumstance of the spies who were in her house.

וְזֶה קֵירוּב מֵה’ בְּלֹא הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם, וְיֶשְׁנוֹ בְּגֵרִים: עַל תְּחִלַּת הַהִתְגַּיְּירוּת שַׁיָּיךְ קֵירוּב, וְאַחַר כָּךְ צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לִהְיוֹת בְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתָּכְנָהּ, כֵּיוָן דְּלָא נִבְחַר כְּלָל; אֲבָל מִי שֶׁהוּא נִבְחַר וְנִתְקָרֵב — אִם כֵּן אֵין צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת — זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק גַּבֵּי אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן שֶׁנִּבְחַר לַעֲבוֹדָה

This is a “nearness from God” without their striving, and it exists with converts: at the start of conversion “nearness” applies, but afterward striving is needed to become truly of Israel, since they were not chosen at all; but one who is chosen and brought near — needing no striving — this is impossible in this world, except with Aharon the Priest, who was chosen for the service.295R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh §3): “It is because the Holy One chose him and sanctified him, as [expounded] on ‘happy is Aharon, whom [God] chose and drew near’; and therefore ‘the lips of a kohen guard knowledge’ — for the crown [of kehunah] is external, but inwardly ‘knowledge fills his place.’” Exactly the se’if: Aharon was “chosen and brought near” — he did not bring himself near by striving.Sefas Emes on Aharon’s shame — “for this you were chosen.” Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, directly interprets Rashi’s “קרב אל המזבח — למה אתה בוש? לכך נבחרת” through the same axis as this se’if. He distinguishes בחירה, the standing of the complete tzaddik, from קריבה, the drawing-near of the baal teshuvah, and writes that Aharon certainly returned from love, so that even deliberate sins become merits — all the more an inadvertent participation in the Calf. He goes further: it is close to say that Aharon’s very connection to that sin was arranged so that he could elevate the teshuvah of Klal Yisrael into teshuvah from love; thus “לכך נבחרת” means that precisely through repairing the fall into zechus, his kiruv itself becomes a form of bechirah. This is almost a direct Chassidic commentary on R’ Tzadok’s paradox here: what appeared to disqualify Aharon from avodah became the very ground of his being chosen and brought near.

וְזָכָה לוֹ עַל יְדֵי עֲשִׂיַּית הָעֵגֶל, שֶׁהוּא אַדְּרַבָּא עֲבֵירָה, וְעַל כֵּן הָיָה בּוֹשׁ, דְּיָדַע בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁאֵינוֹ כְּדַאי וְהָגוּן, עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״לָמָּה אַתָּה בּוֹשׁ? לְכָךְ נִבְחַרְתָּ״

And he merited it through the making of the Calf — which is, on the contrary, a transgression — and therefore he was ashamed, knowing of himself that he was not fit and worthy, until [Moshe] said to him, “why are you ashamed? For this you were chosen.”

וְרָאִיתִי הַפֵּירוּשׁ דְּבִשְׁבִיל זֶה עַצְמוֹ שֶׁאַתָּה בּוֹשׁ בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה נִבְחַרְתָּ, הַיְינוּ דְּלַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ אֵין הקב"ה מִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ אֶלָּא בְּכֵלִים שְׁבוּרִים, וּמִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ שָׁבוּר וְדוֹאֵג בְּקִרְבּוֹ

And I have seen the explanation: that for this very [reason] — that you are ashamed — you were chosen; meaning that for His service the Holy One uses only broken vessels, and one whose heart is broken and anxious within him.296Yisro, Rachav, and Aharon — background: the se’if turns on two Talmudic categories (from Bamidbar Rabbah 3:2, cited in §8): “kervu aval lo bacharu” (brought near but not chosen) and “bacharu ve-kervu” (chosen and brought near). Yisro (Shemos 18) was the Midyanite priest and Moshe’s father-in-law; hearing of the splitting of the sea and the war with Amalek, he came to the wilderness, converted, and gave the counsel for the system of judges — his “nearness” arising by circumstance (being Moshe’s father-in-law), not by his own striving. Rachav (Yehoshua 2) was the innkeeper of Yericho who sheltered the two spies, declared “Hashem your God is God in the heavens above and on the earth below,” was spared at the city’s fall, and converted; the Sages (Megillah 14b) say she married Yehoshua and became ancestress of prophets and priests — her “nearness,” too, came by circumstance (the spies who lodged in her house). Both are “brought near but not chosen”: converts, whose initial drawing-near is God’s doing, though afterward striving is needed. Aharon alone, in this world, is “chosen and brought near” — chosen for the avodah without striving; and R’ Tzadok’s paradox is that he merited it through the shame of the Golden Calf, “for the Holy One uses only broken vessels”: as the Midrash (Toras Kohanim / Vayikra Rabbah, Shemini) records, Moshe said to the abashed Aharon, “lamah atah bosh? le-kach nivcharta — why are you ashamed? for this you were chosen.”297R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §15): “the rectification of envy is through lowliness to the ground, that one not seek what belongs to his fellow.” This lights up §5-10’s “his heart is broken and anxious within him”: Aharon, drawn near without his own striving, holds the service not as a prize he won but as a gift — and the fitting posture of one so favored, beyond all he labored for, is the lowliness of a broken heart, laid to the ground rather than laying claim.

items.h: The theme: This is “willful sins as merits” as attained in this world, not as it will be revealed in the future. Here it is not yet clear to the eye: since he intended the forbidden he does not leave the category of “inadvertent,” much as an aveirah lishmah still requires atonement. Therefore shame remains, and one may not remind a baal teshuvah of his former deeds — even one who returned from love.

p: [יא] וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵיגַת ״זְדוֹנוֹת וּזְכֻיּוֹת״ שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, לֹא כִּלְעַתִיד דְּ״יְבֻקַּשׁ הֶעָוֹן וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, כִּי יִהְיֶה גָּלוּי לַכֹּל אֵיךְ הוּא זְכוּת וְאֵינוֹ עָוֹן כְּלָל וְאֵין בּוֹשׁ כְּלָל

And this is the rung of “willful sins and merits” in this world — not like the future, when “the sin shall be sought and be no more,” for then it will be revealed to all how it is a merit and no sin at all, and there is no shame at all.298R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §19): “‘though your sins be as scarlet, they shall become white as snow’ (Shabbos 89b) — and they are transformed into merits, since it was the will of Hashem, from the six days of creation, that it be so; and it emerges that the essence of the holiness [in them] is only that it was Hashem’s will.” This is §5-11’s “revealed to all how it is a merit and no sin at all”: at the end the willful sins turn white and are seen to have been, all along, His will — merits, with “no shame at all.”
אֲבָל בְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין זֶה גָּלוּי וּמְבֹרָר לָעַיִן אֵיךְ הוּא כֵן, שאע"פ שֶׁחָשַׁב לְאִיסּוּר וְכַוָּנָתוֹ מִיהַת לְאִיסּוּרָא, לֹא יָצָא מִכְּלַל שׁוֹגֵג כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּנִקְרָא חֵטְא

But in this world it is not revealed and clarified to the eye how it is so: although he thought [it] forbidden and his intent, at least, was to the forbidden, he does not leave the category of “inadvertent,” as mentioned above (which is called a sin).

וּמַה שֶּׁמֵּבִיא לִידֵי זְכִיּוֹת אַחַר כָּךְ הָוֵי כְּמוֹ ״עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ״, דְּנָמֵי צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה עַל הָעֲבֵירָה — וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאֲפָרֵשׁ לְקַמָּן [סִימָן י’] מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת נָזִיר [כ.] וְתַעֲנִית [יא.] גַּבֵּי ״נָזִיר חוֹטֵא״, אַף דְּמִצְוָה רַבָּה עַל הַחֵטְא וְנִקְרָא ״נָאֶה״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן ״חוֹטֵא״

And what brings him to merits afterward is like aveirah lishmah, which also requires pardon and atonement for the transgression — as I will explain further [Siman 10] from the words of Tosafos in Nazir [20b] and Taanis [11a] regarding the “sinning nazirite”: though the mitzvah outweighs the sin and he is called “fitting,” nonetheless he is also called a “sinner.”299Nazir 3a / Taanis 11a; Tosafos, Nazir 19b–20b: R’ Elazar HaKappar holds a nazirite is a “sinner” (for afflicting himself from wine — “and he shall atone for him, for he sinned against the soul,” Bamidbar 6:11), and a fortiori one who afflicts himself by fasting; yet Scripture also calls the nazirite “fitting [na’eh].” Tosafos reconciles: he is both — the mitzvah outweighs the sin (so “fitting”), yet a trace of “sin” remains (so atonement is needed). R’ Tzadok: so too the baal teshuvah’s past — a merit that yet leaves residual “shame,” until the future reveals it as pure merit. (Developed further in Siman 10.)

וּלְכָךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה יֵשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מִזֶּה עֲדַיִין, וְאָסוּר לוֹמַר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה ״זְכֹר מַעֲשֶׂיךָ הָרִאשׁוֹנִים״ — אֲפִילּוּ לְמִי שֶׁשָּׁב מֵאַהֲבָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מֵעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁקָּדְמוּ, דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים בִּשְׁעַת הָעֲבֵירָה הָיָה מְרֻחָק, אַף דְּבֶאֱמֶת רִיחוּק זֶה קֵירוּב הוּא

Therefore in this world he still has shame from it, and it is forbidden to say to a baal teshuvah, “remember your former deeds” — even to one who returned from love, he still has shame from the earlier transgressions, for at any rate at the time of the transgression he was distant, though in truth that distance is a nearness.300R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §34): “in truth it is hidden and concealed — ‘the sin of Israel shall be sought and be no more, for I shall forgive’ — this is [so] only in Israel, whose sins are ‘like the [scarlet] threads’ set in order [from the six days of creation]… and they have a good fragrance from afar.” This is §5-11 precisely: in this world the merit hidden within the sin is “not revealed and clear to the eye,” concealed like a fragrance sensed only “from afar” — but at the end “the sin shall be sought and be no more,” disclosed to all as no sin at all.Izhbitz-Radzin on what is visible only after complete teshuvah. Sod Yesharim, Parashas Parah 2:1–2, draws a precise distinction between the sinner’s responsibility before teshuvah and the Divine disclosure afterward. From the human side, repentance clarifies that at the hour of sin his דעת was absent — like a body severed from its head — and he must attribute the deficiency to himself. But after complete teshuvah, when z’donos become zechuyos, Hashem can illuminate that the very act which had appeared dark was never outside the supernal will: “אותו הפעולה בעצמה… היתה נמי גם אז מלא אור.” The work insists on the sequence: first the person owns the failure and returns; only afterward is the deeper Divine connection disclosed. This maps closely onto R’ Tzadok’s distinction here between this world, where the former act still carries shame and cannot yet be seen with complete clarity, and the future, when it will be revealed that the apparent distance itself was a form of nearness. Beis Yaakov, Vayigash 11:1–3, develops the same point through the image of Torah as “living words”: after a person returns with his whole heart, he can see retroactively that what he passed through was encompassed within divrei Elokim chayim, and the earlier meaning of his history is “healed.” Again, this is a retrospective illumination granted by teshuvah, not a heter to define a prohibited act in advance as God’s will.

וּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה זֶה בְּבֵירוּר, שֶׁגַּם בִּשְׁעַת הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲבֵירָה הָיָה מְקֹרָב, וְזֶהוּ ״כִּזְכֻיּוֹת״ לְגַמְרֵי; בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין זֶה נִגְלֶה עֲדַיִין רַק בִּשְׁעַת ״עֲבוֹדָה״ דְּקָרְבָּנוֹת אוֹ ״עֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב זוֹ תְּפִלָּה״, דהקב"ה קָרוֹב יוֹתֵר לְמִי שֶׁלִּבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג בְּקִרְבּוֹ

In the future this will be revealed clearly — that even at the time of the distance and the transgression he was near — and this is “as merits” entirely; in this world it is not yet revealed except at the time of avodah — of sacrifices, or “the service of the heart, which is prayer” — for the Holy One is nearer to one whose heart is anxious within him.

וְכַאֲשֶׁר השי“ת קָרוֹב אֵלָיו, הֲרֵי הוּא מִתְקָרֵב להשי”ת גַּם כֵּן, כִּי זֶהוּ הָעֲבוֹדָה, שֶׁהוּא כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא בֶּן בַּיִת אֵצֶל הַמֶּלֶךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת לד:] בְּרַבִּי חֲנִינָא בֶּן דּוֹסָא ״אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ״, וְעַל כֵּן יָכוֹל לִפְעֹל בִּתְפִלָּה יוֹתֵר

And when Hashem is near to him, he too draws near to Hashem — for this is the “service”: that he is like a servant before the King, an intimate of the King’s house, as they said [Berachos 34b] of R’ Chanina ben Dosa, “he is like a servant before the King” [who enters at will] — and therefore he can accomplish more with prayer.301Berachos 34b: When R’ Chanina ben Dosa prayed for R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai’s sick son and he recovered, R’ Yochanan said, “Had ben Zakkai stuck his head between his knees all day, they would not have heeded him.” His wife asked, “Is Chanina greater than you?” He answered, “No — but he is like a servant before the King [who may enter at any time], while I am like a minister before the King [admitted only at set times].” R’ Tzadok: the “service” (prayer, “standing before the King”) is itself the nearness in which one sees that all is merit — and God is nearest to the broken, anxious heart.

דִּתְפִלָּה הוּא כְּעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְהוּא לְשׁוֹן דִּיבּוּק וְחִבּוּר; וְאָז בְּעֵת הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ וּמְקֹרָב אֵלָיו, וּמֵאִיר לְעֵינָיו אוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים הָאֲמִיתִּיִּים שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם מָוֶת וְרַע כְּלָל, אָז מִתְגַּלֶּה נֹכַח עֵינָיו אֵיךְ הַכֹּל זְכִיּוֹת גְּמוּרוֹת

for prayer is like standing before the King, and it is a term of cleaving and joining; and then, at the time of the service, standing before the King and drawn near to Him, the light of the King’s face shines to his eyes — the true life, in which there is no death and no evil at all — and then it is revealed before his eyes how all is complete merits.302R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §17): “After the teshuvah and rectification, that willful sins become merits — behold the people of Shushan, who ‘added’ in the sin of the [second] feast (which was in Shushan alone), and so there was added to them the merit of vengeance from their enemies one more day; and such is the measure: after they rectified their sin, judgment reached to slay those nations, where there had been a chillul Hashem.” The se’if’s “willful sins and merits” attained in this world — as with the people of Shushan.Mei HaShiloach — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher. Mei HaShiloach II, Berachos 34b, reconciles the opposing statements about tzaddikim and baalei teshuvah by separating body from soul: the complete tzaddik possesses the more purified body, but the baal teshuvah’s nefesh is hewn from a higher place. He explains that in the future, when deliberate sins become merits, Hashem will show the baal teshuvah that through his cry of teshuvah he touched an “עומק עמוק מכל דעת שהאדם יכול להשיג.” This is an especially close complement to R’ Tzadok’s language here: in this world the merit concealed in the old sin is not yet fully visible; the future disclosure is not that sin ceased to have been sin from the human standpoint, but that the baal teshuvah’s broken-hearted return reaches a depth that the earlier, unbroken state could not reveal.

items.h: The theme: This is Aharon’s rung — chosen and brought near without striving, the shame of the Calf being, to the eye, a striving toward the very opposite. In truth that distancing was itself the nearness through which he was drawn close. It answers to the middah of Hod, the radiance that spreads from Gevurah — a contracted glory, which is why they feared to approach Moshe’s rays.

p: [יב] וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּאַהֲרֹן שֶׁ״בָּחֲרוּ וְקֵרְבוֹ״ בְּעֵסֶק הָעֲבוֹדָה, דְּלֹא עָשָׂה שׁוּם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ, רַק הַבּוּשָׁה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל, שֶׁהָיָה לְמַרְאִית עַיִן הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת לְהֵיפֶךְ

And this is the rung of Aharon, who was “chosen and brought near” in the service — for he did no striving to reach this rung; only the shame he had from the making of the Calf, which to the eye was striving to the opposite.303R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §30): “Hashem said to Moshe, ‘Go down,’ at the making of the Calf — for [Aharon] was distanced and removed, so that he too would need this salvation of drawing-near; and through it he drew all Israel near with him.” This is §5-12’s paradox exactly: the very sin of the Calf, “which to the eye was a striving toward the opposite” — that should have pushed Aharon away from the service — was what made him need to be brought near, and so it became the doorway by which he, and all Israel with him, were drawn close.

שֶׁהָיָה רָאוּי לְהִתְרַחֵק מֵחֲמָתוֹ מֵעֲבוֹדַת השי"ת, כְּכֹהֲנִים שֶׁשִּׁימְּשׁוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּנִפְסְלוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה אַף שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה — וְהַיְינוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל לִהְיוֹת זְכֻיּוֹת לְגַמְרֵי מַמָּשׁ; וְאֵצֶל אַהֲרֹן הָיָה לְהֵיפֶךְ, דְּבֶאֱמֶת רִיחוּק זֶה קֵירוּב הוּא, דְּעַל יָדוֹ נִתְקָרֵב

For he should fittingly have been distanced on its account from God’s service, like priests who served idolatry, who are disqualified from the service even though they repented — that being teshuvah in this world, which does not avail to make [the past] literally complete merit; but with Aharon it was the reverse, for in truth that distancing is a nearness, through which he was drawn near —

וְרַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן וּמִצַּד הָאָדָם אָז הָיָה רִיחוּק. וְקֵירוּב זֶה הוּא לְעִנְיַן הָעֲבוֹדָה, דִּבְעֵת הָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁעוֹמֵד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ שַׁפִּיר שַׁיָּיךְ הַקֵּירוּב הַגָּמוּר גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

and only to the eye, from the human side, was it then a distancing. And this nearness is with respect to the service — for at the time of the service, standing before the King, the complete nearness fittingly applies even in this world.304R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §61): “The kohanim are called ‘holy,’ as it says ‘and Aharon was set apart, to sanctify him,’ and ‘you shall sanctify him.’ And in all his seed after him this rung exists, only that they differ between less and more — up to Aharon, who is the ultimate rung of holiness; therefore the [Temple] service is [given] to the kohanim.” The se’if’s Aharon, “chosen and brought near,” set apart as the very summit of holiness.

וְזֶהוּ נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַהוֹד, אֲשֶׁר הוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה: דִּבְמִדָּה זוֹ הקב“ה ״יָראוּי וּמְאֻיָּים״, וְכֵן בְּמִדַּת הַהוֹד — שֶׁהֲרֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע”ה שֶׁזָּכָה לְ״קַרְנֵי הוֹד״, יִירְאוּ מִגֶּשֶׁת אֵלָיו

And this is over-against the middah of Hod, which is the spreading-out of the middah of Gevurah: for in this middah the Holy One is “feared and dreaded,” and so too in the middah of Hod — for Moshe, who merited “rays of Hod,” they feared to approach him.

רַק שֶׁהַגְּבוּרָה הוּא מִדָּה עַצְמִית, וְהַהוֹד עִנְיָנוֹ זִיו הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט מִן הָעַצְמִיּוּת, וְהוּא מִתְפַּשֵּׁט מִצַּד מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁהִיא הַמְּצַמְצֶמֶת כְּבוֹד הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כְּמִדַּת הַחֶסֶד, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּלֶּה הַהוֹד וְהַזִּיו לְבַד

only that Gevurah is an essential middah, while Hod’s matter is the radiance that spreads from the essence; and it spreads from the side of the middah of Gevurah, which contracts the King’s glory so that it not be in [free] expansion like the middah of Chesed — and thereby the Hod and radiance alone are revealed.

וְעַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה מִתְפַּשֵּׁט הַיִּרְאָה, וּבְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הַהוֹד וְזִיו מֶלֶךְ מִתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת מִדַּת הַבּוּשָׁה, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן עֲנַף הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים כ.] ״לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם — זוֹ הַבּוּשָׁה״, שֶׁהִיא יִרְאָה שֶׁעַל הַפָּנִים הַמְכַסֶּה אֶת הַפָּנִים

And through the arousal of the middah of Gevurah, fear spreads; and through the arousal of the middah of Hod and the radiance of the King, the middah of shame spreads, which is also a branch of fear, as they said [Nedarim 20a], “‘that His fear be upon your faces’ — this is shame,” which is a fear that is upon the face, covering the face.305Nedarim 20a: “‘in order that His fear be upon your faces, that you sin not’ (Shemos 20:17) — Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai says: this is shame [bushah], for shame leads to fear of sin; from here they said, it is a good sign in a person that he is shamefaced.” R’ Tzadok: shame is the “fear upon the face,” the branch of yirah that answers to the middah of Hod (the radiance that veils the face), as fear answers to Gevurah.

וְהוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ מֵהוֹד, שֶׁהַזִּיו מְכַסֶּה הַפָּנִים; וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַיִּרְאָה הֵיפֶךְ מִגְּבוּרָה, שֶׁהַגִּבּוֹר אֵינוֹ מִתְיָירֵא רַק זֶה יָרֵא מִפְּנֵי הַגִּבּוֹר, כֵּן הַבּוּשָׁה הוּא מִפְּנֵי זִיו הַמֶּלֶךְ, שֶׁמַּכִּיר שֶׁזֶּהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּ״שִׁוִּיתִי306Tehillim 16:8: “שִׁוִּיתִי ה׳ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד, כִּי מִימִינִי בַּל אֶמּוֹט” — “I have set Hashem before me always; because He is at my right hand I shall not falter.” The Rema opens the Shulchan Aruch (Orach Chaim 1:1) by citing this verse: “‘I have set Hashem before me always’ — this is a great principle in the Torah and among the virtues of the righteous who walk before God,” for one who is ever mindful of standing before the King is filled with humility and awe. R’ Tzadok’s use: this “before me always” is the constant “face-to-face” of the radiance (Hod) — the rung that induces bushah (shame) before the King’s presence at every moment, the branch of fear that spreads from Hod. [ה’ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד]״ הַמֻּזְכָּר בַּהַגָּ"ה [דְּרֵישׁ ש“ע או”ח] שֶׁמֵּבִיא בָּשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד

And it is the reverse of Hod, [where] the radiance covers the face; and just as fear is the reverse of Gevurah — the mighty one does not fear, rather this one fears before the mighty one — so shame is before the radiance of the King, in that one recognizes this to be the rung of “I have set [Hashem before me always]” (mentioned in the gloss at the start of the Shulchan Aruch), which brings his shame before Him always.307The sefiros — background: Kabbalah counts ten sefiros (divine “attributes” or channels): Keser, Chochmah, Binah; then the seven “lower” sefiros — Chesed (loving-kindness / expansion), Gevurah (might / din / contraction), Tiferes (harmony); Netzach (eternity / victory), Hod (splendor / radiance), Yesod (foundation); and Malchus (kingship / the nukva, the receiving side). R’ Tzadok maps the rungs of teshuvah onto these middos, this fifth rung standing over-against Hod. He defines Hod as the ziv (radiance) that spreads from the essence of Gevurah: Gevurah “contracts” the King’s glory (so that it is not in free expansion like Chesed), and from that contraction only the radiance — Hod — is revealed. Thus as fear (yirah) spreads from Gevurah, so shame (bushah) — “a branch of fear” — spreads from Hod. (In the standard scheme Netzach and Hod are the “two thighs” from which the prophets are nourished — Moshe corresponding to Netzach and Aharon to Hod, as the next se’if develops.) A parallel development in R’ Tzadok’s own writings — on Hod, bushah, and the “whitening of the face” — is given in the corpus note on this se’if.308R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §28): “‘whoever is ashamed does not quickly sin’ (Nedarim 20a)” — shame is the guard set over the heart. This lights up §5-12’s “he brings his shame before Him always”: Aharon, drawn near not by striving but through the shame of his fall, keeps that shame ever before him — so the very shame that might have distanced him becomes his abiding safeguard, the trembling nearness of one who never forgets from where he was raised.

items.h: The theme: The clear “face-to-face” recognition is the rung of Yitzchak, and it cannot be sustained — which is why blessings open in the present and close in the hidden. The face-to-face of the radiance, however, can be held constantly, and this is the priests’ service in the Temple. Aharon merited it through shame, the concealment of the inner radiance of Hod — the same middah by which “all the honor of the king’s daughter is within.”

p: [יג] וְדָבָר זֶה דְּהַכָּרַת הַנּוֹכֵחַ בְּבֵירוּר הוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק אָבִינוּ ע“ה, דְּ״מֶחֱזֵי לְהוּ הקב”ה בְּעֵינַיְיהוּ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת פט:]; וְזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת בִּתְמִידוּת, דְּעַל כֵּן כָּל הַבְּרָכוֹת מַתְחִילִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נוֹכֵחַ וּמְסַיְּימִין בִּלְשׁוֹן נִסְתָּר, דְּמִיָּד נֶעְלַם הַנּוֹכֵחַ דִּפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ

And this “clear face-to-face recognition” is the rung of Yitzchak Avinu, of whom “the Holy One shows Himself to their eyes,” as they said [Shabbos 89b]; and this cannot be constant — therefore all blessings begin in the language of “You” [present] and conclude in the language of “He” [hidden], for the “face-to-face” of the King’s presence is at once concealed.309Shabbos 89b (see fuller citation on Siman 2): “Yitzchak showed them the Holy One with their own eyes.” R’ Tzadok: the clear, present vision (“You”) is Yitzchak’s rung but cannot be constant — hence blessings shift from “You” (nochach) to “He” (nistar); the enduring “before me always” is the vision of the radiance (Hod), the priests’ service.310R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §17): “the unification that will be as though set forth before the eye — that all is from Hashem, as before the creation of the world — and this is the attainment of Hashem in the aspect of truth.” Exactly the se’if: “face-to-face recognition” is a seeing in which nothing intervenes — and precisely for that reason it cannot remain open in this world, and closes at once into concealment.

אֲבָל הַנּוֹכֵחַ דְּזִיו אֶפְשָׁר לְקַיֵּים בּוֹ ״לְנֶגְדִּי תָּמִיד״, וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דַּעֲבוֹדָה דְּכֹהֲנִים בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ שֶׁשָּׁם נִיכָּר זִיו שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ תָּמִיד; וְהִתְקָרְבוּת זֶה דְּזִיו הוֹדוֹ זָכָה לוֹ אַהֲרֹן עַל יְדֵי הַבּוּשָׁה, שֶׁהוּא הֶעְלֵם זִיו הַהוֹד שֶׁבִּפְנִים, דְּפָנָיו מַלְבִּינוֹת

But the “face-to-face” of the radiance one can sustain, “before me always” — and this is the rung of the priests’ service in the Temple, where the radiance of His Presence is recognized constantly; and this drawing-near to the radiance of His Hod, Aharon merited through the shame, which is the concealment of the inner radiance of Hod, [for] his face “whitens” —

דְּעַל כֵּן הוּא כִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים [ב"מ נח:], כִּי פָּנָיו כִּפְנֵי הַמֵּת שֶׁמִּשְׁתַּנֶּה זִיו הַפָּנִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי [סוֹף יְבָמוֹת] וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ. [וּכְעִנְיָן שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּבֵלְשַׁצַּר ״זִיו אַפּוֹהִי אִשְׁתַּנִּי״ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁלָּבַשׁ בִּגְדֵי כְּהֻנָּה וְנִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בִּכְלֵי הַקֹּדֶשׁ, שֶׁהֵם זִיו וְהוֹד פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ יִתְבָּרֵךְ]

therefore it is “like bloodshed” [Bava Metzia 58b]311Bava Metzia 58b: in the sugya of ona’as devarim (wronging with words), the Gemara teaches that “one who whitens the face of his fellow in public [ha-malbin penei chaveiro ba-rabbim] — it is as though he sheds blood [shefichus damim],” for one observes that the shamed man’s redness drains away and his face whitens, like the pallor of the slain. R’ Tzadok draws on this: the whitening of the face in shame is the concealment of the inner Hod-radiance — “his face is like the face of the dead, whose facial radiance is altered” — and this is the very mark of bushah, the branch of Hod., for his face is like the face of the dead, whose facial radiance is altered — as they said in the Yerushalmi [end of Yevamos] and in the Midrash. [And like what is said of Belshatzar, “the radiance of his face was changed” (Daniel 5:6)312Daniel 5:6: “אֱדַיִן מַלְכָּא זִיוֺהִי שְׁנוֹהִי, וְרַעְיֹנֹהִי יְבַהֲלוּנֵּהּ, וְקִטְרֵי חַרְצֵהּ מִשְׁתָּרַיִן, וְאַרְכֻבָּתֵהּ דָּא לְדָא נָקְשָׁן” — “then the king’s radiance was changed, and his thoughts alarmed him; the joints of his loins were loosened, and his knees knocked one against the other.” The scene is Belshatzar’s feast (Daniel 5): the Babylonian king drank from the sacred vessels plundered from the Beis HaMikdash, whereupon a hand wrote upon the wall “mene mene tekel u-farsin,” and his face blanched in terror. R’ Tzadok draws on “ziv apohi ishtani” — the changing (blanching) of his face-radiance through his misusing the holy vessels, “which are the radiance and Hod of the King’s face” — as the image of the whitening of the face, the concealment of the inner Hod-radiance, which is the essence of bushah (shame): the kohen’s face, too, “whitens.”, through his donning priestly garments and using the holy vessels, which are the radiance and Hod of the King’s face.]313Bava Metzia 58b: “One who whitens his fellow’s face in public [malbin penei chaveiro] — it is as though he sheds blood, for the red departs and whiteness comes”; the shamed face is “like the face of the dead,” whose radiance is altered (cf. Yerushalmi Yevamos; and Daniel 5:6, Belshatzar’s face “changed” when he profaned the Temple vessels). R’ Tzadok: shame is the veiling of the inner radiance of Hod — the very concealment that is Knesses Yisrael’s true glory.

וְזֶהוּ מִדָּה טוֹבָה שֶׁבַּנָּשִׁים, שֶׁכְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כָּל כְּבוּדָּה314Tehillim 45:14: “כָּל כְּבוּדָּה בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה, מִמִּשְׁבְּצוֹת זָהָב לְבוּשָׁהּ” — “all the honor of the king’s daughter is within; her raiment is of golden settings.” Meforshim: a woman’s true honor and beauty are inward and concealed; the Sages derive from here the value of tzniyus (modesty) — that a woman’s dignity lies in her inwardness (cf. Shevuos 30a, Yevamos 77a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this “inwardness” is the middah of Hod from the side of the nukva — Knesses Yisrael, the eishes chayil, conceals the radiance of her face; and this very concealing of the radiance is her splendor, appearing outwardly as shame. בַת מֶלֶךְ פְּנִימָה״ וְאֵין מַגָּלִית זִיו פָּנֶיהָ; וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַהוֹד מִסִּטְרָא דְּנֻקְבָּא, וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהִיא ״אֵשֶׁת חַיִל״ לְהַעֲלִים זִיוָהּ, וּבוּשָׁה לִתְבֹּעַ בַּפֶּה

And this is the good middah among women — as it says, “all the honor of the king’s daughter is within” (Tehillim 45:14), and she does not reveal the radiance of her face; and this is the middah of Hod from the side of the nukva, and Knesses Yisrael, who is an “eishes chayil,” conceals her radiance and is ashamed to demand with the mouth.315R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §6): “‘[I who] sanctify them and give holiness in you’ — and this is in the language of nochach [present, ‘in you’]; and afterward, when it says in the language of nistar [hidden], ‘and they shall keep… between Me and Bnei Yisrael,’ it speaks of the Shabbos of the Holy One Himself.” This is §5-13’s law of the blessings exactly: the recognition opens face-to-face, in nochach (“in you,” the present), and because that clarity cannot stay fixed it closes in nistar (“between Me and Israel,” the hidden) — the very present-then-hidden turn R’ Tzadok hears in the covenant of Shabbos.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה הֶעָזָה פָנֶיהָ וְתֹאמַר וְגוֹ’, וְנֶאֱמַר ״מֵצַח אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה הָיָה לָךְ, מֵאַנְתְּ הִכָּלֵם״, וְנֶאֱמַר ״אֵשֶׁת כְּסִילוּת הוֹמִיָּה״; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵשֶׁת חַיִל עִיקַּר מִדָּתָהּ הַצְּנִיעוּת, וְהוּא מִדַּת רָחֵל בִּשְׁתִיקָה

Unlike a harlot, who is brazen-faced, and speaks; as it says, “you had a harlot’s forehead, you refused to be ashamed” (Yirmeyah 3:3)316Yirmeyah 3:3: “וַיִּמָּנְעוּ רְבִבִים וּמַלְקוֹשׁ לוֹא הָיָה, וּמֵצַח אִשָּׁה זוֹנָה הָיָה לָךְ, מֵאַנְתְּ הִכָּלֵם” — “the showers were withheld and the latter rain did not come; yet you had a harlot’s forehead, you refused to be ashamed.” From Yirmeyahu’s rebuke of Israel’s faithlessness (ch. 3), likening her to a wanton wife. Rashi: the “harlot’s forehead” is brazenness — the unblushing face of one who refuses to be shamed. R’ Tzadok’s use: the harlot is az panim (brazen-faced), the very opposite of the eishes chayil, whose middah is modesty and bushah; Knesses Yisrael’s true splendor is her shame, the concealed Hod., and “the woman of folly is boisterous” (Mishlei 9:13)317Mishlei 9:13: “אֵשֶׁת כְּסִילוּת הֹמִיָּה, פְּתַיּוּת וּבַל יָדְעָה מָּה” — “the woman of folly is boisterous [homiyah]; she is naive [simplicity itself] and knows nothing.” In Mishlei 9, Shlomo sets Lady Wisdom (who builds her house and invites the wayfarer to understanding) against Lady Folly — “eishes kesilus” — who sits brazenly at her door calling to passersby. Meforshim: homiyah (clamorous, noisy) marks folly’s brazen loudness. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “boisterous” woman of folly is the brazen harlot, the antithesis of the silent, modest eishes chayil (the middah of Rachel, “in silence”).; whereas the eishes chayil’s essential middah is modesty, which is the middah of Rachel, in silence.318R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §25): “through the tzimtzum [contraction] of desire, which is the middah of Yitzchak our father — ‘dwelling in the land of the Negev,’ dried of all the desire and craving of this world.” This uncovers why Yitzchak’s clear, face-to-face recognition in §5-13 can never be constant: Yitzchak’s very middah is tzimtzum, self-contraction, so the vision that opens wide must draw itself in — the blessing that begins in the present (nochach) contracting into the hidden (nistar).

וּמִדַּת לֵאָה כְּנֶגְדָּהּ בְּהוֹדָיָה: כָּל הִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁלָּהּ הָיָה רַק לְהוֹדוֹת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם וְלִידָּבֵק בְּמִדַּת הַהוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ, וְתָבְעָה בְּפֶה לְהַרְבּוֹת בָּנִים שִׁבְטֵי הוי"ה וְהוּא מִלֵּיֽדַת יְהוּדָה וְיִשָּׂשכָר, וְזֶה אֶחָד לֵידַת לֵוִי שֶׁאָמְרָה ״הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה [אִישִׁי אֵלַי]״, דְּזָכְתָה לְמִדַּת הַדְּבֵיקִים לְגַמְרֵי וְלִהְיוֹת מֶרְכָּבָה לְמִדַּת הַהוֹד שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה

And the middah of Leah is over-against it, in thanksgiving: all her revealing was only to give thanks before God and to cleave to His middah of Hod, and she demanded with the mouth to increase children, “the tribes of Havayah” — and this was from the birth of Yehudah and Yissachar — and one is the birth of Levi, of whom she said “this time my husband will accompany me” (Bereishis 29:34)319Bereishis 29:34: “וַתַּהַר עוֹד וַתֵּלֶד בֵּן, וַתֹּאמֶר עַתָּה הַפַּעַם יִלָּוֶה אִישִׁי אֵלַי כִּי יָלַדְתִּי לוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה בָנִים, עַל כֵּן קָרָא שְׁמוֹ לֵוִי” — at the birth of her third son Leah says, “now this time my husband will accompany [yilaveh] me, for I have borne him three sons; therefore he called his name Levi.” Rashi: the Avos were to raise up twelve tribes from four wives, and each matriarch, on bearing her portion, hoped her husband would now cleave to her; Leah’s word “yilaveh” (accompany / attach) gave Levi his name — the tribe of liwuy (attachment). Kabbalah (which R’ Tzadok develops here): Leah is the middah of hoda’ah (thanksgiving) and Hod — all her “revealing” and “demanding with the mouth” was to give thanks before God and to cleave to His middah of Hod; from her issued Levi and Aharon, who are “attached [nilveh] to Him like a servant before the King,” a Chariot for the supernal Hod — over-against Rachel, the middah of modesty and silence (the corpus note on this se’if brings R’ Tzadok’s parallel on Leah / Rachel and Hod). — for she merited the middah of those who cleave entirely, to be a Chariot for the supernal middah of Hod.

שֶׁכֵּן יָצָא מִמֶּנָּה אַהֲרֹן הַכֹּהֵן שֶׁהוּא נִלְוֶה אֵלָיו יִתְבָּרֵךְ כְּעֶבֶד לִפְנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וְזָכָה לְמִדַּת הַהוֹד עַל יְדֵי שְׁלֵימוּתוֹ בְּמִדָּה זוֹ מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהוּא בִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל — דְּהַיְינוּ הַעֲלָמַת הַזִּיו שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּבוּשָׁה; וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶה עִיקַּר זִיוָון וְהוֹדָן שֶׁל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהֵן ״בַּיְישָׁנִים״, שֶׁהוּא מִשְּׁלֹשָׁה סִימָנִים דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵשֶׁת חַיִל

for so Aharon the Priest issued from her, who is “attached [nilveh]” to Him like a servant before the King — and he merited the middah of Hod through his perfection in this middah, from the aspect of his being within Knesses Yisrael (that is, the concealing of the radiance, which appears as shame) — and in truth this is the essential radiance and Hod of the Children of Israel, who are “shamefaced [bayshanim],” which is one of the three signs of Knesses Yisrael, the eishes chayil.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת יב:] ״הָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה וּמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ [עַל כָּל עֲוֺנוֹתָיו]״, וּלְמָדוֹ מִשָּׁאוּל דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ עִמִּי בִּמְחִיצָתִי״

And therefore they said [Berachos 12b], “one who transgresses and is ashamed — they forgive him [all his sins],” and they derived it from Shaul, to whom [Shmuel] said, “you and your sons will be with me in my precinct” (Shmuel I 28:19)320Shmuel I 28:19: “וְיִתֵּן ה׳ גַּם אֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל עִמְּךָ בְּיַד פְּלִשְׁתִּים, וּמָחָר אַתָּה וּבָנֶיךָ עִמִּי, גַּם אֶת מַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל יִתֵּן ה׳ בְּיַד פְּלִשְׁתִּים” — on the eve of his death, having consulted the necromancer at Ein Dor, Shaul hears Shmuel’s raised spirit foretell: “Hashem will give Israel also with you into the hand of the Plishtim, and tomorrow you and your sons [shall be] with me [imi].” The Sages (Berachos 12b; and Vayikra Rabbah) expound “with me” as “in my precinct [bi-mechitzasi]” — with the righteous in Gan Eden; and from Shaul, who “transgressed and was ashamed” (accepting the decree in submission), they derive that “one who transgresses and is ashamed, they forgive him all his sins.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “with me, in my precinct” is the precinct of Hod — Shmuel’s rung, “weighed as Moshe and Aharon” — which one merits precisely through the shame..321Berachos 12b: “Anyone who commits a transgression and is ashamed of it — all his sins are forgiven, as it says [of Shaul], ‘and tomorrow you and your sons will be with me’ (Shmuel I 28:19) — with me, in my precinct [bi-mechitzasi].” R’ Tzadok: the penitent’s shame — the middah of Hod/bushah — itself wins full forgiveness; Shaul, ashamed, is placed “in the precinct” of Shmuel (the prophetic Hod).

וְיָדוּעַ דַּרְגָּא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל הַשָּׁקוּל כְּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן, שֶׁהֵם מִדַּת נֶצַח וְהוֹד, דְּמִשָּׁם יְנִיקַת הַנְּבִיאִים, וּשְׁמוּאֵל רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים, שֶׁהוּא בָּא וְהוֹרִיד הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַנְּבוּאָה בָּעוֹלָם, וְעִמּוֹ בִּמְחִיצָּתוֹ הַיְינוּ בִּמְחִיצַּת הַהוֹד שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לָהּ עַל יְדֵי הַכְּבוּשָׁה

And it is known that the rung of Shmuel is “weighed as Moshe and Aharon” (the middos of Netzach and Hod), from where the prophets draw their nourishment, and Shmuel is “the master of all the prophets,” who came and brought down the spreading of prophecy into the world — and “with me, in my precinct” means in the precinct of Hod, which he merits through the shame.322Berachos 31b; Rosh Hashanah 25b; Taanis 5b: “Shmuel is weighed against Moshe and Aharon [shakul ke-Moshe ve-Aharon], as it says, ‘Moshe and Aharon among His priests, and Shmuel among those who call His Name’ (Tehillim 99:6)”; and Shmuel is “the master [teacher] of the prophets.” R’ Tzadok maps Moshe and Aharon to Netzach and Hod (the source of prophecy), so Shaul’s placement “in Shmuel’s precinct” is the precinct of Hod, attained through shame.

items.h: The theme: The “willful sins as merits” that baalei teshuvah from love attain belongs to this middah of Hod — Aharon’s, “who loves the creatures and draws them near to Torah.” He drew them near by showing love, until a man grew ashamed of what was in his hand and forsook it. All the more so the love God Himself shows a person; and since the drawing-near comes through the sins, the distance works like the niddah that endears.

p: [יד] וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת ״זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת״ שֶׁזּוֹכִין בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה — הוּא מִצַּד מִדָּה זוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת אַהֲרֹן ״אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת323Avos 1:12: “הִלֵּל אוֹמֵר: הֱוֵי מִתַּלְמִידָיו שֶׁל אַהֲרֹן — אוֹהֵב שָׁלוֹם וְרוֹדֵף שָׁלוֹם, אוֹהֵב אֶת הַבְּרִיּוֹת וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה” — “Hillel says: be of the disciples of Aharon — loving peace and pursuing peace, loving the creatures and drawing them near to Torah.” Avos de-Rabbi Nasan (ch. 12) explains how he drew them near: Aharon would befriend even a known sinner and show him love and friendship, so that the man became ashamed of the transgressions in his hand and forsook them. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the engine of teshuvah from love — the love shown to a person (all the more, the love God shows him) begets shame over his sins, and through that shame he draws near to the avodah; and since the drawing-near comes through the sins, “by them he shall live,” and willful sins become as merits.Aharon’s love as the engine of teshuvah. Sefas Emes, Shemini 7:3, connects Aharon’s own teshuvah from love with the elevation of the entire people’s return, invoking “על כל פשעים תכסה אהבה.” Read beside Avos’ “אוהב את הבריות ומקרבן לתורה,” the two teachings illuminate one another: Aharon’s mode of kiruv is itself the logic of teshuvah me-ahavah. Love precedes the sinner’s shame; the shame then makes him abandon the sin; and the very path by which he had been distant becomes the cause of a deeper return. This fits R’ Tzadok’s point that in Aharon’s middah the z’donos become zechuyos specifically because the Divine or human love shown to the sinner is what produces the new nearness. וּמְקָרְבָן לַתּוֹרָה״ [אָבוֹת א, יב]

And this “willful sins as merits” that baalei teshuvah from love attain in this world is from the side of this middah — which is the middah of Aharon, “who loves the creatures and draws them near to Torah” [Avos 1:12].324Avos 1:12: “Hillel says: Be of the disciples of Aharon — loving peace and pursuing peace, loving the creatures and drawing them near to Torah.” R’ Tzadok (with the tradition that Aharon would befriend a sinner until the sinner grew ashamed and mended his ways): the love shown to a person begets a shame that turns him — a fortiori God’s own love, which is the middah of Hod/bushah by which “willful sins become merits.”325R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §4): “The crown of kehunah — Aharon merited it and took it, and ‘the non-kohen who approaches [shall die]’ — only kohanim of [pure] lineage; and it is called ‘Mount Moriah’ for the ‘myrrh [mor],’ the chief of all the spices (Megillah 10b), a thing of worth, ‘not ownerless to all.’ So too the ‘service of the heart.’” The se’if’s middah of Hod is Aharon’s: the “crown of kehunah” and the service of the heart, of him “who loves the creatures and draws them near to Torah.”
וְאָמְרוּ זַ"ל דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה מְקָרְבָן — עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהָיָה מִתְחַבֵּר וּמַרְאֶה אַהֲבָתוֹ לוֹ, וְהָיָה הַלָּה בּוֹשׁ מֵעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבְּיָדוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה וְעוֹזְבָן

And the Sages said that it was through this that he brought them near — for by joining with a person and showing him his love, the other became ashamed of the transgressions in his hand and forsook them.

וְאִם זֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבַת אָדָם כְּאַהֲרֹן, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה שֶׁמַּרְאֶה לוֹ השי"ת, שֶׁהוּא מוֹלִיד בּוּשָׁה גְּדוֹלָה בְּקִרְבּוֹ עַל עֲוֺנוֹתָיו; וְעַל כֵּן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הוּא תֹּקֶף הַכְּבוּשָׁה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְקָרֵב לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ וּמִתְפַּלֵּל וְנַעֲנֶה

And if this is through the love of a man like Aharon, all the more through the love that Hashem shows him, which begets a great shame within him over his sins; and therefore, through teshuvah from love, there is the intensity of shame, and thereby he draws near to His service and prays and is answered.

וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהִתְקָרְבוּת זֶה, שֶׁהוּא הַדְּבֵיקוּת בֶּאֱלֹקִים חַיִּים, הוּא עַל יְדֵי הָעֲוֺנוֹת, הֲרֵי ״עֲלֵיהֶם״ וְעַל יָדָם ״חַיֹּה יִחְיֶה״, וְנַעֲשָׂה אוֹתוֹ רִיחוּק דַּעֲבֵירָה דֻּגְמַת נִידּוֹת דְּאִשָּׁה הַנִּזְכָּר שֶׁהוּא לְחַבְּבָהּ עַל בַּעְלָהּ

And since this drawing-near — the cleaving to the living God — is through the sins, then “by them” and through them “he shall surely live,” and that distancing of transgression becomes like the niddah of a woman (mentioned), which is to endear her to her husband.326R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §7): “the middah of Aharon the Kohen, whose middah is to love the creatures and draw them near to the Torah (Avos 1) — to bring all creatures under the wings of the Shechinah, that all be blessed; and his service is ‘blessings and thanksgivings [hoda’os] to His name.’” This is the positive face of §5-14’s Hod: hoda’ah is the flowering of Hod, and Aharon draws the whole world near not by force but by love — “loving the creatures and drawing them near” — so that the drawing-close of §5-14 is achieved through love, the reverse of harsh distancing.
וְעַל יְדֵי כֵּן ״כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוֶה״, וְנוֹדַע דְּרוֹמֵז לְאֶלֶף הַחֲמִישִׁי, שֶׁאוֹתוֹ יוֹם כֻּלּוֹ בַּגָּלוּת, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד הַהוֹד דִּבְהִיפּוּךְ אַתְוָון ״דָּוֶה״

And thereby “all the day she is daveh [languishing]” (Eichah 1:13)327Eichah 1:13: “מִמָּרוֹם שָׁלַח אֵשׁ בְּעַצְמֹתַי וַיִּרְדֶּנָּה […] נְתָנַנִי שֹׁמֵמָה, כָּל הַיּוֹם דָּוָה” — “from on high He sent fire into my bones and it prevailed; […] He has made me desolate and faint [daveh] all the day.” From the first kinah of Eichah, Yirmeyahu’s lament over the Churban, in the voice of stricken Jerusalem. Meforshim: “daveh” is languishing, sick — the faintness likened to the davah of niddah. R’ Tzadok’s use: “kol ha-yom daveh” alludes to the fifth millennium, the “day” wholly given over to exile, which corresponds to Hod — for in reverse of letters “Hod” (ה־ו־ד) is “Daveh” (ד־ו־ה); the languishing distance of exile is, like the niddah of a wife, a distancing that is ultimately for a drawing-near of love., and it is known that this alludes to the fifth millennium (that “day” being wholly in exile), which is over-against Hod, [for] in reverse of letters “Hod” [is] “Daveh.”328R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tavo §17): “the middah of Hod, that Aharon the Kohen is a merkavah [chariot] for it; and in the fifth millennium, which corresponds to the middah of Hod, was the essence of the servitude and the yoke of exiles… ‘all the day daveh [faint]’ — for Hod was overturned into daveh.” This is the very axis of §5-14: Aharon bears Hod, and when Hod is not revealed it is overturned, letter-for-letter, into daveh — precisely the se’if’s “when it is not revealed it is called daveh, the reverse of Hod.” Aharon’s whole avodah is to keep Hod turned right-side-up.

וְהַיְינוּ כְּאִשָּׁה דָּוֶה, שֶׁהָרִיחוּק הוּא לְקֵירוּב אַהֲבָה — שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדַּת הַקֵּירוּב שֶׁל מִדַּת הַהוֹד, לֹא אַהֲבָה מְפֹרֶשֶׁת הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה גְּלוּיָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד, רַק אַהֲבָה הַבָּאָה מִכֹּחַ רִיחוּק

And this is like the languishing woman, whose distance is for a drawing-near of love — this being the middah of drawing-near of the middah of Hod: not an explicit love that comes through revealed love (as will be in the future), but a love that comes from the power of distance.
כִּי הוּא מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד הָאַהֲבָה, רַק שֶׁהִיא הַמְּבִיאָה לְאַהֲבָה; וּבִשְׁעַת הָרִיחוּק, טֶרֶם נִתְגַּלָּה הָאַהֲבָה, נִקְרָא ״דָּוֶה״ שֶׁהוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵהוֹד

For it is from the spreading-out of the middah of Gevurah, which is over-against love, only that it brings to love; and at the time of the distance, before the love is revealed, it is called “daveh,” which is the reverse of Hod.

items.h: The theme: Daniel’s “my Hod was turned within me to ruin” marks the kingdoms that caused Hod to become daveh. Rome, the seed of Esav, is the dross of that spreading-out — the reverse of Aharon who loved peace, yet making itself appear otherwise. Every nation seeks to resemble Knesses Yisrael precisely in what it most inverts, “like an ape that walks after a man.”

p: [טו] וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר בְּדָנִיֵּאל ״וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית״ כְּשֶׁבָּא אֵלָיו הַמַּלְאָךְ לְהַגִּיד מִמַּלְכוּת יָוָן וְרוֹמִי; וְהָרוֹמִים הֵם שֶׁגָּרְמוּ הִיפּוּךְ הַהוֹד לְדָוֶה, שֶׁהֵם זֶרַע עֵשָׂו שֶׁהָיָה פְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרָה, וְהֵם הַפְּסֹלֶת דְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁהוּא פְּסֹלֶת הַהוֹד דְּאַהֲרֹן שֶׁהָיָה ״אוֹהֵב שָׁלוֹם וְרוֹדֵף שָׁלוֹם״

Of this it says in Daniel, “and my Hod was turned within me to ruin” (Daniel 10:8)329Daniel 10:8: “וַאֲנִי נִשְׁאַרְתִּי לְבַדִּי, וָאֶרְאֶה אֶת הַמַּרְאָה הַגְּדֹלָה הַזֹּאת, וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר בִּי כֹּחַ, וְהוֹדִי נֶהְפַּךְ עָלַי לְמַשְׁחִית, וְלֹא עָצַרְתִּי כֹּחַ” — “and I alone was left, and I saw this great vision, and no strength remained in me; my Hod was turned within me to ruin, and I retained no strength.” From Daniel’s final vision (ch. 10) by the river Chidekel, where an angel comes to reveal “what shall befall your people in the end of days” — the succession of kingdoms, Yavan (Greece) and Edom (Rome) among them. Meforshim (Rashi, Ibn Ezra): overwhelmed by the vision, Daniel’s bodily hod — the fresh glow of the face — drained away to “ruin.” R’ Tzadok reads “ve-hodi nehpach alai le-mashchis” of the middah of Hod: the very turning of Hod into daveh foretold by the vision — the ruin of the Hod and radiance of Knesses Yisrael through the exiles of Greece and Rome (“Hod” reversed being “Daveh”)., when the angel came to tell him of the kingdoms of Greece and Rome; and the Romans are the ones who caused the turning of Hod to daveh — for they are the seed of Esav, who was the dross of Gevurah, and they are the dross of the spreading-out, which is the dross of the Hod of Aharon, who “loved peace and pursued peace.”

וְהֵם בְּהֵיפֶךְ — וְרֹעֶה דְּעֵשָׂו דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״עַל חַרְבְּךָ תִּחְיֶה״, רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן הָיוּ מְדַמִּים עַצְמָם גַּם הֵם כֵּן; וְכַנּוֹדָע מִדִּבְרֵי אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע טִיטוּס הַכָּתוּב בְּסֵפֶר יוֹסִיפוֹן, אֵיךְ בִּדְבָרָיו הָיָה מְבַקֵּשׁ רַק שָׁלוֹם, אַף שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת כַּוָּנָתוֹ הָיְתָה רַק לְהָרַע

And they are the reverse — the shepherd Esav, of whom it is written “by your sword you shall live” (Bereishis 27:40)330Bereishis 27:40: “וְעַל חַרְבְּךָ תִחְיֶה וְאֶת אָחִיךָ תַּעֲבֹד, וְהָיָה כַּאֲשֶׁר תָּרִיד וּפָרַקְתָּ עֻלּוֹ מֵעַל צַוָּארֶךָ” — “and by your sword you shall live, and you shall serve your brother; but it shall be, when you are aggrieved [tarid], that you will break his yoke from off your neck.” This is the blessing Yitzchak gave Esav, after Yaakov had received the primary blessing (ch. 27). Rashi: “al charbecha — by your sword you shall live”; Esav’s portion is the way of the sword and plunder; and “when you are aggrieved” — when Israel transgresses the Torah, Esav is given license to cast off his subjugation and dominate. R’ Tzadok’s use: “by your sword you shall live” brands Esav (and his seed, Rome) as the dross of Gevurah — the way of the sword — the very reverse of Aharon’s Hod, “who loved peace and pursued peace.”; only that to the eye they too made themselves seem so; as is known from the words of that wicked Titus, recorded in Sefer Yosippon — how in his speech he sought only “peace,” though in truth his intent was only to do evil,

כָּתַב כֵּן דֶּרֶךְ ״אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים הֶחְפִּיצָה לְהִתְתַּקֵּן בְּתִיקּוּנְתָּא בְּרָזָא דְּאֵשֶׁת חַיִל״; וּלְעוֹלָם כָּל אֻמָּה בְּאוֹתוֹ רַע שֶׁהֵם שְׁקוּעִים, שֶׁבָּהֶם הֵם הַהֵיפֶךְ מִכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֵם חֲפֵצִים בּוֹ דַּוְקָא לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, כַּנּוֹדָע בַּזֹּהַר שֶׁהוּא כְּגַוְנָא דְּקוֹפָא דְּאָזֵיל בָּתַר בַּר נַשׁ

writing thus in the way of “a woman of harlotry that wished to bedeck herself in the adornments, in the secret, of the eishes chayil”; and always, every nation, in the evil in which it is sunk — wherein they are the reverse of Knesses Yisrael — precisely in that they desire to resemble Knesses Yisrael, as is known in the Zohar, that it is “like an ape that walks after a man.”331R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §65): “there is still in this the dross of love and the dross of Gevurah, which is utterly evil; and they too call themselves ‘the seed of Avraham’ and ‘the seed of Yitzchak,’ though in truth it is not so… yet they press the claim, and therefore ‘the waters rose over us.’” This is §5-15’s rule that every nation, in the very evil in which it is the reverse of Knesses Yisrael, “precisely there desires to resemble her”: Esav, the dross of Gevurah (as the se’if names him), lays false claim to the fathers’ name — feigning the identity whose inward truth he wholly lacks.

וְהוּא בְּזֶרַע דְּעֵשָׂו בְּיִחוּד, שֶׁנִּמְשַׁל לַחֲזִיר שֶׁפּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ [וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה יג, ה]; וּבֶאֱמֶת בָּזֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵרָזָא דְּאֵשֶׁת חַיִל, שֶׁכָּל הוֹדָהּ וְזִיוָהּ וּכְבוֹדָהּ פְּנִימָה בְּהֶעְלֵם וּצְנִיעוּת, וּבְגִילּוּי הוּא אַדְּרַבָּא מִדַּת בּוּשָׁה שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ הַזִּיו

And this is especially in the seed of Esav, likened to the swine that “stretches out its hooves,” as they said in the Midrash [Vayikra Rabbah 13:5]; and in truth this itself is the reverse of the secret of the eishes chayil, whose whole Hod, radiance, and honor is within, in concealment and modesty, and in revelation it is, on the contrary, the middah of shame, which is the opposite of the radiance.332Vayikra Rabbah 13:5: “Why is [Rome/Edom] likened to a swine [chazir]? Because when the swine lies down it stretches out its hooves [poshet telafav] as if to say, ‘see, I am pure [split-hooved]’ — so the wicked kingdom robs and extorts while making a show of justice, as though it ‘sets up the platform [bimah].’” R’ Tzadok: Edom’s hypocrisy — evil within, a show of good without — is the exact inverse of Knesses Yisrael, the eishes chayil, whose radiance is within and whose outward face is shame.333R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §24): “and so did Esav — he stretches out his hooves like the swine (which has one kosher sign in its hooves, of the two signs that hint to deed and thought — the hooves to the deed).” This lays bare §5-15’s image exactly: the swine shows only the outer sign, the deed, and lacks the inner — so the nations “desire to show themselves good in revelation and to stretch out the hooves,” all their evil hidden within, the precise reverse of the eishes chayil whose radiance is within and whose revelation is shame.

כִּי הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲבֵירוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם רַק לְמַרְאִית עַיִן וּכְפִי הַנִּגְלֶה, אֲבָל בִּפְנִימִיּוּת מַעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבָם וּרְצוֹנָם הוּא רַק לְטוֹב; וְהֵם בְּהֵיפֶךְ — כָּל הָרַע שֶׁלָּהֶם פְּנִימָה, וּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת חֶפְצָם לְהַרְאוֹת עַצְמָם טוֹבִים וְלִפְשׁוֹט טְלָפַיִם, וְזֶהוּ מַמָּשׁ הַהֵיפֶךְ מִמִּדַּת הוֹד דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל

For the distance and transgressions of the Children of Israel are only to the eye, according to the revealed, but in the inwardness of the depths of their heart and will they are only for good; and [the nations] are the reverse — all their evil is within, and in revelation they desire to show themselves good and to “stretch out the hooves” — and this is exactly the reverse of the middah of Hod of Knesses Yisrael.334R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §57): “Matisyahu ‘repaired the Hod,’ which beforehand was ‘my Hod was turned within me to ruin’ [and this verse is said in Daniel 10, when the officer of Greece came]; therefore they fixed ‘for the miracles’ in the [blessing of] thanksgiving [Hoda’ah]; and therefore they are eight days, for Hod is the eighth sefirah, and they draw it down through the kindling [of the lights].” Exactly the se’if: “my Hod was turned to ruin” (Daniel) — the kelipah of the fourth kingdom caused the turning of Hod.

וְגַם מַלְכוּת יָוָן הוּא הַשְׁחָתַת הוֹד וְזִיו דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַבּוּשָׁה, וְהֵם כָּל כֹּחָם בְּעַזּוּת פָּנִים, דְּעַל כֵּן נִמְשְׁלוּ בְּנָמֵר, וְשָׁנִינוּ [אָבוֹת ה, כ] ״הֱוֵי עַז כַּנָּמֵר״

And also the kingdom of Greece is the ruining of the Hod and radiance of Knesses Yisrael, which is the middah of shame; and all their strength is in brazenness of face — therefore they are likened to a leopard, and we learned [Avos 5:20] “be bold as a leopard.”335Avos 5:20: “Yehudah ben Teima says: Be bold as a leopard [az ka-namer], light as an eagle, swift as a deer, and mighty as a lion, to do the will of your Father in Heaven.” R’ Tzadok (with the Rashbatz, Magen Avos, that the leopard is a cross-bred “mamzer,” and mamzerim are brazen-faced): Greece — whose founder Alexander was reputed a mamzer — is brazenness, the klipah opposite to Israel’s Hod/shame.

וְעַיֵּין רַשְׁבָּ"ץ בְּסֵפֶר מָגֵן אָבוֹת כִּי הוּא מַמְזֵר, וּמַמְזֵרִים עַזֵּי פָּנִים; וְכֵן אֲלֶכְּסַנְדֶּר מוֹקְדוֹן, רֹאשׁ וְשֹׁרֶשׁ מֶמְשֶׁלֶת יָוָן, הָיָה מַמְזֵר, וּמִדָּתוֹ הֵיפֶךְ הַבּוּשָׁה, וְרָצוּ לְהַכְנִיס קְלִיפָּה זוֹ בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

And see the Rashbatz in Sefer Magen Avos, that it [the leopard] is a mamzer, and mamzerim are brazen-faced; and so Alexander of Macedon, the head and root of the Greek empire, was a mamzer, whose middah is the reverse of shame — and they wished to bring this klipah into the Children of Israel.

items.h: The theme: Matisyahu repaired the Hod — hence “for the miracles” is fixed in the blessing of Hoda’ah. His seed took the kingship and were punished for it, since monarchy belongs to Yehudah, who “grasped the spindle of Hoda’ah.” For kingship is nothing but an apportioning of honor — the radiance of the King’s Hod spreading from its bearer; and the crown of the Sages is a kingship without a ruler’s scepter.

p: [טז] וּמַתִּתְיָהוּ דְּנִצְּחָם, יָדוּעַ בְּסֵפֶר פְּרִי עֵץ חַיִּים שֶׁ״תִּיקֵּן הַהוֹד״, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרִינַן ״עַל הַנִּסִּים״ בְּהוֹדָאָה; וְהוּא כֹּהֵן, וְזָכוּ זַרְעוֹ לַמַּלְכוּת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנֶּעֶנְשׁוּ עַל זֶה — לְפִי שֶׁהֵם כֹּהֲנִים וְנָטְלוּ מְלוּכָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ"ן [פָּרָשַׁת וַיְחִי] עַל פָּסוּק ״לֹא יָסוּר שֵׁבֶט״

And Matisyahu, who overcame them, it is known in Sefer Pri Etz Chaim that he repaired the Hod — therefore we say “for the miracles” in the blessing of thanksgiving [Hoda’ah]; and he was a priest, and his seed merited the kingship, even though they were punished for it — because they were priests and took the monarchy, as the Ramban wrote [Parashas Vayechi] on the verse “the scepter shall not depart [from Yehudah].”336Pri Etz Chaim, Shaar HaChanukah (ch. 4): the eight days of Chanukah correspond to the sefirah of Hod: normally Malchus (Rachel) receives the light of Hod only via Netzach (since “Hod was turned to ruin,” Daniel 10:8, while “Netzach Yisrael does not lie,” Shmuel I 15:29); but “Matisyahu ben Yochanan the High Priest repaired the Hod” in these eight days, so Malchus receives directly from Hod — “therefore we say ‘for the miracles’ in the blessing of Modim [thanksgiving], which corresponds to Hod.”337Ramban, Bereishis 49:10 (“the scepter shall not depart from Yehudah”): “This was the punishment of the Chashmona’im who reigned in the Second Temple — they were pious men of the Most High, and but for them Torah and mitzvos would have been forgotten from Israel, yet they were punished greatly — because they reigned though not of the seed of Yehudah and the House of David; and measure for measure, the Holy One set their own servants [Hordos] over them, and [these] cut them off.” R’ Tzadok: kingship is an “apportioning of the King’s Hod,” fit for the House of David (Yehudah) or, without a “scepter,” for the “kings of the Rabbis.”338R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §51): “kingship is drawn from His kingship, as we bless ‘shechalak mikevodo’ [who apportioned of His honor]; and to the nations of the world it is only ‘to His creatures,’ since they do not recognize this — only perforce, ‘the heart of kings is in the hand of Hashem, like an axe in the hand of the hewer.’” This is §5-16’s very definition of monarchy: the honor “is not from the essence of the person, but from the radiance of the King’s Hod that spreads from him” — apportioned, shechalak mikevodo; and Israel’s kings recognize the Source, while the nations are but “His creatures,” drawn after Him against their will.

וְהַיְינוּ דְּעִנְיַן הַמַּלְכוּת אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא ״חֲלוּקַת כָּבוֹד״, שֶׁכֵּן מְבָרְכִין עָלָיו ״שֶׁחָלַק מִכְּבוֹדוֹ״, וְאֵין הַכָּבוֹד מִפְּאַת עַצְמוּתוֹ רַק מִפְּאַת זִיו הוֹד מֶלֶךְ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט מִמֶּנּוּ

And this is [because] the matter of monarchy is nothing but an apportioning of honor — as one blesses over him “who apportioned of His honor” — and the honor is not from the essence of the person, but from the radiance of the King’s Hod that spreads from him.

וְעַל כֵּן זָכָה יְהוּדָה, שֶׁתָּפַס בְּפֶלֶךְ הוֹדָיָה, מִדַּת הוֹד לַמַּלְכוּת — וְהַיְינוּ ״שֵׁבֶט מוֹשְׁלִים״ שֶׁהוּא הוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְזֶהוּ מַלְכוּת דָּוִד וּשְׁלֹמֹה שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ ״וַיֵּשֶׁב עַל כִּסֵּא ה’״; וּמִדַּת הוֹד דְּאַהֲרֹן הוּא הוֹד דְּנֻקְבָּא — מִדַּת הַבּוּשָׁה כַּנִּזְכָּר

And therefore Yehudah, who grasped “the spindle of Hoda’ah,” merited the middah of Hod for the monarchy — the “scepter of rulers,” which is the Hod of His kingship; and this is the monarchy of David and Shlomo, of whom it says “he sat on the Throne of Hashem”; and the middah of Hod of Aharon is the Hod of the nukva — the middah of shame, as mentioned.

וְנֶאֱמַר ״הֵן יוֹרוּ מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ לְיַעֲקֹב״, וְגַם הוּא הוֹד מַלְכוּת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּגִיטִּין סב.] ״מַאן מַלְכֵי? רַבָּנָן״, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כָּבוֹד חֲכָמִים יִנְחָלוּ״ — אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא מַלְכוּת בְּלֹא ״שֵׁבֶט מוֹשְׁלִים״, שֶׁאֵין הַמֶּמְשָׁלָה אֶלָּא לְאִישׁ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְהוּא יִמְשֹׁל״

And it says, “they shall teach Your ordinances to Yaakov” (Devarim 33:10)339Devarim 33:10: “יוֹרוּ מִשְׁפָּטֶיךָ לְיַעֲקֹב וְתוֹרָתְךָ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, יָשִׂימוּ קְטוֹרָה בְּאַפֶּךָ וְכָלִיל עַל מִזְבְּחֶךָ” — “they shall teach Your ordinances to Yaakov and Your Torah to Israel; they shall place incense before You and whole-offerings on Your altar.” From Moshe’s blessing of the tribe of Levi (Vezos HaBerachah). Rashi: to Levi and the kohanim are given both the teaching of Torah and the avodah of the altar. R’ Tzadok’s use: “yoru mishpatecha le-Yaakov” shows that the priestly line, too, bears a Hod of kingship — the majesty of Torah instruction — which is the “kingship of the Rabbis,” a rule by Torah authority rather than by the “scepter of rulers.”, and this too is a Hod of kingship, as they said [Gittin 62a]340Gittin 62a: the Gemara teaches, “man malkei? Rabbanan — who are [called] kings? The Rabbis,” derived from “bi melachim yimlochu” (Mishlei 8:15) — that Torah scholars are crowned with a form of kingship. Rashi: the sages “rule” through the authority of the Torah. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “kings of the Rabbis” bear a Hod of kingship — the majesty of Torah instruction (“they shall teach Your ordinances to Yaakov”) — but a monarchy without a “scepter of rulers” (actual dominion), which belongs only to the Davidic king of the tribe of Yehudah., “who are the kings? The Rabbis,” and it says “the wise shall inherit honor” (Mishlei 3:35)341Mishlei 3:35: “כָּבוֹד חֲכָמִים יִנְחָלוּ, וּכְסִילִים מֵרִים קָלוֹן” — “the wise shall inherit honor, but fools carry off shame.” From the close of Mishlei ch. 3, contrasting the destinies of the wise and the foolish. Meforshim: kavod (honor) is the enduring inheritance of the wise, whereas the fool’s “elevation” is only disgrace. R’ Tzadok’s use: “kavod chachamim yinchalu” is the Hod — the honor and majesty — that the Torah-sages inherit, the “kings of the Rabbis,” over-against the fool who “raises up kalon (shame),” the counterfeit of the true bushah. — only that it is a monarchy without a “scepter of rulers,” for rulership belongs [only] to a man [of Yehudah], of whom it says “and he shall rule.”

וְגַם בִּיהוּדָה נֶאֱמַר ״וּמְחוֹקֵק מִבֵּין רַגְלָיו״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רז"ל [סַנְהֶדְרִין ה.] עַל נְשִׂיאֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהֵם מִנֻּקְבְּתָא דְּבֵית דָּוִד, דְּאֵין לָהֶם ״שֵׁבֶט״ לִרְדּוֹת בְּמַקֵּל, רַק הֵם מַלְכֵי דְּרַבָּנָן — דְּזֶהוּ עִיקָּר בְּכֹהֲנִים כַּמְפֹרָשׁ בִּקְרָא

And of Yehudah too it says “and a lawgiver from between his feet,” which the Sages expounded [Sanhedrin 5a] of the Nesi’im of Eretz Yisrael, who are of the female [line] of the House of David, who have no “scepter” to rule with the rod — rather they are the “kings of the Rabbis,” which is the essential [kingship] in priests, as is explicit in Scripture.342Sanhedrin 5a: “‘The scepter [shevet] shall not depart from Yehudah’ — these are the Exilarchs [Reish Galusa] of Bavel, who rule Israel with the rod [shevet]; ‘and a lawgiver [mechokek] from between his feet’ — these are the Nesi’im of Eretz Yisrael, who teach Torah in public.” R’ Tzadok: the Nesi’im (of the “female” Davidic line) hold a kingship of Torah — “the kings of the Rabbis” (Gittin 62a) — without the ruling “scepter.”

וְהַחַשְׁמוֹנָאִים שֶׁתִּיקְּנוּ מִדַּת הַהוֹד זָכוּ לַמַּלְכוּת, רַק לְפִי שֶׁהֵם לְקָחוּהָ בְּ״שֵׁבֶט מוֹשְׁלִים״ נֶעֶנְשׁוּ. וּבֶאֱמֶת בִּימֵי בַּיִת שֵׁנִי, שֶׁהָיָה ״פְּקִידָה בְּעָלְמָא״, לֹא הָיָה רָאוּי מַלְכוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא מָלַךְ מֶלֶךְ מִבֵּית דָּוִד

And the Chashmona’im, who repaired the middah of Hod, merited the monarchy — only that, since they took it with a “scepter of rulers,” they were punished; and in truth, in the days of the Second Temple, which was but a “remembrance,” monarchy was not fitting for Israel — and therefore no king of the House of David reigned.

וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֵם לָקְחוּ מַלְכוּת דְּמֶמְשָׁלָה לְעַצְמָם וְלֹא עַל פִּי נָבִיא, נֶעֶנְשׁוּ עַל יְדֵי הוֹרְדּוֹס שֶׁהֶאֱבִיד כָּל זֵכֶר לָמוֹ, וּבָא הַמַּלְכוּת לַעֲבָדִים שֶׁאֵין רְאוּיִים לַמַּלְכוּת כְּלָל; וְאָז נִבְחַר הִלֵּל, שֶׁהוּא מִנֻּקְבְּתָא דְּבֵית דָּוִד, לְנָשִׂיא

And because they took the ruling monarchy for themselves and not through a prophet, they were punished by Hordos, who destroyed all their memory, and the monarchy came to slaves not fit for it at all; and then Hillel — who is of the female [line] of the House of David — was chosen as Nasi.343R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §14): “it is the will of Hashem that He be their king — ‘who are the kings? the Rabbis’ — that they need no teacher and no guide, not even Moshe Rabbeinu, for Hashem is called ‘the One who teaches Torah to His people Israel.’” This is §5-16’s malchei d’rabbanan, “the wise shall inherit honor”: a kingship without a “scepter of rulers,” for the Rabbis reign by Torah alone, their crown drawn straight from the King who teaches them — the Hod of kingship borne without the rod.

וְהֵם מִמַּלְכֵי דְּרַבָּנָן, כִּי הִלֵּל רֹאשׁ לְחַכְמֵי הַמִּשְׁנָה, וְאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין יא.] דְּהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁתִּשְׁרֶה עָלָיו שְׁכִינָה כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּנוּ ע"ה; וּשְׁנֵיהֶם, עֶזְרָא וְהִלֵּל, יָסְדוּ תּוֹרָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל אַחַר שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּכְּחָה [סֻכָּה כ.]

And they are of the “kings of the Rabbis,” for Hillel is the head of the Sages of the Mishnah, and they said [Sanhedrin 11a] that he was worthy that the Shechinah rest upon him like Moshe Rabbeinu; and both, Ezra and Hillel, founded Torah in Eretz Yisrael after it had been forgotten [Sukkah 20a].344Asarah Ma’amaros (R’ Menachem Azaryah of Fano): since there is, in principle, no inheritance of the office of Torah-leadership (rabbanus), the fact that Hillel’s descendants inherited the Nesi’us “as by the law of kingship” shows that, after the Chashmona’i servants and Hordos usurped an unfit monarchy, the court instituted that “the crown of Torah complete the crown of kingship,” seating the son on his father’s throne — with Divine approval (Hillel’s line being of great pedigree).345Sanhedrin 11a: “After the last prophets — Chaggai, Zecharyah, Malachi — died, the ruach hakodesh departed from Israel, yet they still made use of a bas kol. Once [the Sages were reclining in the upper story of the house of Guria in Yericho], a bas kol went out: ‘There is one here worthy that the Shechinah rest upon him like Moshe Rabbeinu, but his generation is not fit for it’ — and the Sages set their eyes on Hillel the Elder; and when he died they said of him, ‘Alas, the pious one, alas, the humble one, disciple of Ezra.’” (Sukkah 20a: “When the Torah was forgotten from Israel, Ezra came up from Bavel and re-established it; [it was again forgotten, and] Hillel the Babylonian came up and re-established it.”) R’ Tzadok: Ezra founded the Written Torah anew (hence “worthy that the Torah be given through him,” Sanhedrin 21b), Hillel the Oral Torah (hence “worthy that the Shechinah rest upon him”).

וְעֶזְרָא הָיָה עִם נְחֶמְיָה יַחַד רָאשֵׁי הַדּוֹר, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם רָאשֵׁי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה וְרָאשֵׁי מְבִיאֵי גְּאֻלָּה דְּבַיִת שֵׁנִי, שֶׁהוּא אִתְעָרוּתָא דִלְתַתָּא דְּהוֹפָעַת אוֹר הַגְּאֻלָּה [לְעֵיל סִימָן ד’]

And Ezra was, with Nechemyah, the heads of the generation, and both were heads of the Men of the Great Assembly and heads of “those who brought the redemption” of the Second Temple, which is the arousal from below of the shining of the light of redemption [above, Siman 4].346R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §37): “[The days of Chanukah] were fixed [as festival days] upon the miracles that were done for Israel through them; and this is like ‘you have distinguished Hashem, and Hashem has distinguished you’ — for the exaltation of Hashem in this world is only through the Children of Israel who sanctify His name, for without them He would not be known in the world.” The se’if’s Chanukah: “for the miracles,” fixed in the blessing of Hoda’ah — the Hod repaired through Israel who sanctify His name.

items.h: The theme: Hillel was the reverse of Ezra and the Men of the Great Assembly, who diligently multiplied safeguards: he did not want a multitude of them, and Beis Hillel rule leniently throughout. Each acted according to his generation — Ezra’s needed those fences, and in that lay his piety and his humility. Once Matisyahu had repaired the Hod, Hillel, of David’s seed, could arouse the rectification of that middah instead.

p: [יז] וְהִנֵּה הִלֵּל הֵיפֶךְ עֶזְרָא וְאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁשָּׁקְדוּ לְהוֹסִיף סְיָיגוֹת וְהִזְהִירוּ עַל זֶה [כַּנַ"ל סִימָן ד’]; אֲבָל הִלֵּל לֹא הָיָה רוֹצֶה בְּרִיבּוּי הַסְּיָיגוֹת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְעִנְיַן שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה דָּבָר [שַׁבָּת יז.]

Now Hillel was the reverse of Ezra and the Men of the Great Assembly, who diligently added safeguards and warned of it [as above, Siman 4]; but Hillel did not want a multitude of safeguards, as they said regarding the “eighteen matters” [Shabbos 17a]347Shabbos 17a: the Gemara (on Mishnah Shabbos 1:4) recounts the “eighteen matters [shemoneh esrei davar]” enacted in the attic of Chananyah ben Chizkiyah ben Garon, on the day the vote went to Beis Shammai when they outnumbered Beis Hillel — a day the Gemara treats gravely (“as hard for Israel as the day the Calf was made”). Tosafos (with the Tosefta and Yerushalmi Shabbos 1:4) records the dispute of R’ Eliezer and R’ Yehoshua whether that day was for good — that “they heaped up the measure” of Torah — or for ill — that “they wiped away the measure” through an excess of stringencies. R’ Tzadok’s use: Hillel and his house did not favor a multitude of safeguards (Beis Hillel rule leniently); once Matisyahu “repaired the Hod” and the rung that rectifies the past shone forth, a proliferation of fences-going-forward was no longer needed..

וְעַיֵּין [שָׁם קנג:] וּבְרַשִׁ"י דִּפְלוּגְתָּא רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ לְעִנְיַן שְׁמוֹנֶה עֶשְׂרֵה דָּבָר: רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר — ״שַׁמּוּתִי״ מִתַּלְמִידֵי בֵּית שַׁמַּאי — אָמַר עַל זֶה לְשֶׁבַח [״גָּדְשׁוּ סְאָה״], אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מִבֵּית הִלֵּל אָמַר לִגְנַאי [״מָחֲקוּ סְאָה״ עַל יְדֵי רִיבּוּי סְיָיגוֹת], וְכֵן בְּכָל מָקוֹם בֵּית הִלֵּל לְקֻלָּא

And see [Shabbos 153b] and Rashi on the dispute of R’ Eliezer and R’ Yehoshua about the eighteen matters: R’ Eliezer — “Shammuti,” of the disciples of Beis Shammai — spoke of it in praise [“they heaped up the measure”], but R’ Yehoshua, of Beis Hillel, spoke of it in blame [“they wiped away the measure,” through a multitude of safeguards]; and so in every place Beis Hillel [rule] leniently.348Shabbos 153b (and 17a): “R’ Eliezer says: On that day [when the eighteen decrees were enacted in the upper chamber of Chananyah ben Chizkiyah] they heaped up the measure [gadshu se’ah — praise]; R’ Yehoshua says: On that day they wiped away the measure [machaku se’ah — blame].” Rashi: over-decreeing produces fences the community cannot bear, leading them to transgress. R’ Tzadok: R’ Eliezer (“Shammuti,” of Beis Shammai) praised the multiplication of fences; R’ Yehoshua (Beis Hillel) blamed it — for once Hod was repaired, the emphasis shifts from forward-guarding fences to the teshuvah that rectifies the past.349R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §32): “‘in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the perfectly righteous cannot stand’ — for the constant yoke of [His] lordship the tzaddik gamur cannot [bear], only the baal teshuvah; this is his place, from the abundance of his bitterness over what preceded; and this is the rung of the chasid who deals lovingly with his Maker.” This is §5-17 precisely: Ezra’s generation heaped up fences — the tzaddik’s guarding-going-forward — but Hillel, described there with chasidus and anavah, stands on the higher rung of the baal teshuvah, whose healed past needs no multitude of fences.

ואע"פ שֶׁהוּא נִקְרָא ״תַּלְמִידוֹ שֶׁל עֶזְרָא״, וְלֹא לָמַד לְפָנָיו, רַק שֶׁהָיָה הוֹלֵךְ בְּעִקְבוֹתָיו — וְהַיְינוּ בְּעִנְיַן הָעֲנָוָה וְהַחֲסִידוּת שֶׁתְּאָרוּהוּ שָׁם; וְכָל אֶחָד לְפִי דּוֹרוֹ: בְּדוֹר עֶזְרָא הָיוּ צְרִיכִים לְהַרְבּוֹת סְיָיגוֹת, וּבָזֶה הָיָה חֲסִידוּתוֹ גַּם עַנְוְותוֹ — שֶׁאֵין מַסְפִּיק לְפִי שִׁפְלוּתָם מִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה לְבַד, וְזֶהוּ תִּיקּוּן הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה דִּלְהַבָּא

And though he is called “the disciple of Ezra,” he did not learn before him, only that he followed in his footsteps — namely in the matter of humility and piety with which they described him; and each one [acted] according to his generation: in the generation of Ezra they needed to multiply safeguards, and in this lay his piety and also his humility — that the mitzvos of the Torah alone did not suffice for their lowliness — and this is the rectification of the baal teshuvah going forward.350R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §72): “the rung of David HaMelech, who raised up the yoke of teshuvah — and he is the Mashiach who gathers in and completes the assurance ‘for I will not forsake you’ through teshuvah, as in Perek Chelek.” This is §5-17’s “Hillel of the seed of David, who raised up the yoke of teshuvah, and aroused the rectification of the middah of teshuvah”: the very Davidic power that opens teshuvah as a public highway is what Hillel carried — drawing the light of the repaired Hod into the world, so that the past itself is healed.
