אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁמַּתִּתְיָהוּ תִּיקֵּן הַהוֹד, וְאַחֲרָיו בָּא הִלֵּל מִזַּרְעָא דְּדָוִד שֶׁהֵקִים עֻלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, וְעוֹרֵר תִּיקּוּן מִדַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִצַּד תִּיקּוּן הַהוֹד וְהַזִּיו הַמֵּאִיר בָּהּ — שֶׁהוּא הַתִּיקּוּן דִּלְשֶׁעָבַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת — אֵין צָרִיךְ עוֹד לְרִיבּוּי סְיָיגוֹת מֵעַתָּה לִשְׁמִירָה דִּלְהַבָּא

But afterward, once Matisyahu repaired the Hod, and after him came Hillel of the seed of David, “who raised up the yoke of teshuvah,” and aroused the rectification of the middah of teshuvah from the side of the repaired Hod and radiance that shines within it — which is the rectification of the past, that willful sins become as merits — there is no longer need for a multitude of safeguards for guarding-going-forward,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁגַּם הַזְּדוֹנוֹת שֶׁבּוֹ זְכִיּוֹת וְנִתְקַן לְשֶׁעָבַר גַּם כֵּן; וְעַל כֵּן בְּהוֹפָעַת אוֹר הַזֶּה עַל יָדוֹ אָז לֹא הֻצְרַךְ עוֹד לְרִיבּוּי סְיָיגִים

since even the willful sins in him are merits, and the past too is rectified; and therefore, in the shining of this light through him, there was no longer need for a multitude of fences.351R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chayei Sarah §9): "“coming with days” — that they had already come to be clarified in the supernal days; and Binah too is the World to Come, as it says in the Zohar; and Chochmah and Binah are likewise called “days.”" Exactly the se’if: Hillel’s “blessed is Hashem day by day” is a rung in which each day is itself already clarified — which is why he needed no multitude of safeguards.

וְנִמְשְׁכוּ תַּלְמִידֵי הִלֵּל הַנִּקְרָאִים ״בֵּית הִלֵּל״, שֶׁהֵם כְּ״אַנְשֵׁי בֵּיתוֹ״ הַנִּמְשָׁכִים אַחֲרָיו, עַד הַחֻרְבָּן — שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי הַקָּטָן שֶׁבְּתַלְמִידָיו עֲדַיִין קַיָּים וְנָשִׂיא אַחַר כָּךְ; וְנִמְצָא כָּל הָאַרְבַּע דּוֹרוֹת עַד רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הַנֶּהֱרָג , שֶׁהָיוּ נְשִׂיאִים עַד הַחֻוֽרְבָּן, כֻּלָּם עַל שֵׁם הִלֵּל יִקְרְאוּ, כִּי עֲדַיִין בֵּיתוֹ קַיָּים

And the disciples of Hillel, called “Beis Hillel,” who are like the “men of his house” drawn after him, continued until the Destruction — for R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai, the youngest of his disciples, was still alive and became Nasi afterward; and thus all the four generations — down to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel who was slain — who were Nesi’im until the Destruction, are all called by the name of Hillel, for his “house” still endured.

items.h: The theme: This light was revealed down to the Ten Martyrs, who clarified that there is death without sin — rather “so it arose in thought” before Him. R’ Akiva himself desired it, asking when “with all your soul” would come to his hand that he might fulfill it. And since the yetzer hara is itself the Angel of Death, the same holds for the deed of transgression: where it belongs to the kivshei d’Rachmana, the deed is His will, and therefore merits.

p: [יח] וְהֵם גִּילּוּ אוֹר זֶה עַד רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל וַחֲבֵרָיו ״עֲשָׂרָה הֲרוּגֵי מְלוּכָה״ מִגְּדוֹלֵי הַתַּנָּאִים, שֶׁבֵּירְרוּ ״דְּיֵשׁ מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא, רַק כָּךְ עָלָה בְּמַחְשָׁבָה לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרֵךְ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְנָחוֹת כט:] בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא

And they revealed this light down to Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and his colleagues, the “Ten Martyrs of the kingdom,” of the greatest of the Tannaim — who clarified that “there is death without sin, but rather so it arose in [His] thought before Him,” as they said [Menachos 29b] of R’ Akiva,

שֶׁהוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ רָצָה בְּכָךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת סא:] ״מָתַי יָבוֹא [לְיָדִי וַאֲקַיְּימֶנּוּ]״ כו’; וְהַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁרָצָה לְבָרֵר תֹּקֶף אַהֲבָתוֹ לוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ בְּ״כָל נֶפֶשׁ״, והשי"ת מִלֵּא רְצוֹנוֹ

who himself desired it, as they said [Berachos 61b], “when will [this verse] come [to my hand, that I may fulfill it]?”; and this is what he wished — to clarify the intensity of his love for Him “with all his soul” — and Hashem fulfilled his will.352Menachos 29b: Moshe saw R’ Akiva expounding “heaps of laws” from the crowns of the letters, then saw R’ Akiva’s flesh “weighed out in the market” [his martyrdom]. “He said: Master of the Universe, this is Torah and this is its reward? He said: Be silent — so it arose in [My] thought [kach alah be-machashavah lefanai].” Berachos 61b: as they raked R’ Akiva’s flesh with iron combs at the hour of Kerias Shema, he accepted the yoke of Heaven, saying, “All my days I was troubled by this verse, ‘with all your soul’ — even if He takes your soul — I said, when will it come to my hand that I may fulfill it? And now that it has come, shall I not fulfill it?” He prolonged “Echad” until his soul departed. R’ Tzadok: the martyrs clarified that death can be “without sin” — a merit or a kivshei d’Rachmana — and, since “the yetzer hara is the Angel of Death” (Bava Basra 16a), so too a sin can be, at root, God’s own will — hence “merits.”353R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §39): “the truth is only amid the kivshei d’Rachmana [the hidden counsels of the Merciful One] — why [seek further]?… and they did not rule [for others]; they acted [only] for themselves.” This is §5-18’s hinge: R’ Akiva’s death, and the willful sin that is “of the kivshei d’Rachmana, that so it arose in His will,” belong to the hidden divine counsel beyond the revealed reasons — and precisely because the deed is God’s own will, it is reckoned as merits.

וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים הֲרֵי מָצִינוּ מִיתָה לֹא לְעֹנֶשׁ, רַק לִזְכוּת אוֹ מִכְּבָשַׂי דְּרַחֲמָנָא; וַהֲרֵי ״הוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּבָבָא בָּתְרָא [טז.], אִם כֵּן כָּךְ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה וְהַזָּדוֹן שֶׁל יֵצֶר הָרָע: יֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא כָּךְ, אוֹ שֶׁהוּא מִכְּבָשַׂי דְּרַחֲמָנָא שֶׁכָּךְ עָלָה בִּרְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרֵךְ

And at all events, we have found death that is not for punishment but for a merit, or of the kivshei d’Rachmana; and behold, “the yetzer hara is the Angel of Death,” as they said in Bava Basra [16a]354Bava Basra 16a: Reish Lakish taught, “He is the Satan, he is the yetzer hara, he is the Angel of Death” — one and the same adversary under three names: he entices to sin (as the yetzer / Satan), ascends to accuse, and then descends to take the soul (as the Angel of Death). Rashi: the single power that seduces a person to sin is the very one that brings his death. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “the yetzer hara is the Angel of Death,” then just as the Sages found death without sin — “so it arose in [His] thought,” a matter of the kivshei d’Rachmana rather than punishment — so too the deed of the yetzer’s transgression may be of the kivshei d’Rachmana, “so it arose in His will”; and since the deed accords with God’s will, it is merits (only that the intent to the forbidden reckons it “as inadvertent,” or love transforms it to merit). — if so, so too with the deed of transgression and willfulness of the yetzer hara: there is [a case] that it is so [a death-like judgment], or that it is of the kivshei d’Rachmana, that so it arose in His will.355R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §9): “As they said (Menachos 29b) regarding R’ Akiva, ‘so it arose in thought,’ and on this it says ‘exceedingly deep are Your thoughts’ — that there are in it ‘depths of good,’ called ‘very good.’ And all of man’s deeds are the deeds of Hashem, as it says ‘You have also wrought all our deeds for us’ — and this certainly is ‘how great they are,’ like ‘willful sins become merits.’” The se’if’s Ten Martyrs and “death without sin”: “so it arose in thought” — the depths of good hidden within what appears to be loss.

וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהַמַּעֲשֶׂה כִּרְצוֹן ה’ הוּא זְכִיּוֹת — אֶלָּא דְּכַוָּנָתוֹ לְאִיסּוּר עוֹשֵׂהוּ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, אוֹ שֶׁמִּתֹּקֶף אַהֲבָה הוֹפְכוֹ לִזְכִיּוֹת, שֶׁהַחֵטְא הָיָה לְבֵירוּר תֹּקֶף אַהֲבָתוֹ

And since the deed is according to God’s will, it is merits — only that his intent to the forbidden makes it “as inadvertent,” or, from the intensity of love, [that love] turns it to merits, the sin having been for the clarification of the intensity of his love —

[וּכְמוֹ הַמִּיתָה לְבָרֵר ״בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, כֵּן הַחֵטְא שֶׁהוּא אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן כַּ״עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ״ — דְּהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן ״בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל] שֶׁהוּא גּוֹבֶרֶת יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁאַחַר הַחֵטְא כַּנִּזְכָּר

[and just as death clarifies “with all your soul” in its plain sense, so the sin that comes after the rectification, as an aveirah lishmah — which is likewise “with all your soul,” as mentioned above] — which prevails the more through the teshuvah that comes after the sin, as mentioned.356R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §5): “‘if the sins be as scarlet [ka-shanim]’ — which are ordered and come from the six days of creation — ‘like snow they shall whiten,’ and there is no sin here at all; and the root of all the sins is ‘if you walk with Me b’keri,’ that you reckon everything as happenstance.” This is §5-18’s “so it arose in thought before Him”: the willful sins were set within God’s primordial ordering from the six days, so they whiten to “no sin at all” — merits; while the true root of sin is the reverse, treating the world as mikreh rather than His will.

[וְגַם עַל יְדֵי תֹּקֶף הָאַהֲבָה הַמְּעוֹרֶרֶת כֹּחַ הַתְּנוּעָה בַּמּוֹחַ וָלֵב לְהֵיטִיב — דְּהַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לִפְעֹל טוֹב בָּא עַל יְדֵי אַהֲבָה שֶׁהִיא שֹׁרֶשׁ לְ״קוּם וַעֲשֵׂה״ — עַל יְדֵי זֶה מְתַקֵּן גַּם כַּוָּנַת מוֹחַ וָלֵב הַקּוֹדֶמֶת, לִהְיוֹת מִתְמַתֶּקֶת וּמִתְהַפֶּכֶת וּמִתְבַּטֶּלֶת, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁאֵינָהּ לְרָע]

[And also through the intensity of the love that arouses the power of motion in the mind and heart toward good — for the arousal to act for the good comes through love, which is the root of “arise and do” — thereby he rectifies even the earlier intent of mind and heart, so that it is sweetened and transformed and nullified; and all the more that it is not to evil.]

sections.en: Great is teshuvah, for it lengthens a person's years

items.h: גדולה תשובה שמאחדת שנותיו של אדם.

Hebrew text established from the printed editions and cross-checked against Sefaria. Round parentheses ( ) are the editor’s inserted source-references; square brackets [ ] within the Hebrew are the author’s own additions. Full vocalization (nikkud) has been supplied editorially. Footnotes give the sources cited by the author, with the מקור text and a working translation.
The theme: Teshuvah lengthens a person’s life by drawing down the deathless level of Yaakov Avinu — the root-soul of every Jewish generation.

p: [א] שֶׁמַּאֲרֶכֶת שְׁנוֹתָיו שֶׁל אָדָם

that [teshuvah] lengthens a person’s years. The author opens with the closing phrase of the Sages’ teaching, “Great is teshuvah, for it lengthens a person’s years”357Yoma 86b: R’ Shmuel bar Nachmani said: Great is teshuvah, for it lengthens a person’s years (per the Bach’s reading: “his days and his years”), as it says (Yechezkel 18), “and when a wicked man turns back from his wickedness — he shall live.” — and proceeds to explain how repentance can extend the very span of a life.
הוּא עַל יְדֵי הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מַדְרֵגַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה

it is through the spreading-forth of the level of Yaakov Avinu, of blessed memory, of whom the Sages said, “Yaakov Avinu did not die.” The capacity of teshuvah to add years is a drawing-down of that same deathless vitality which Yaakov embodies.
שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ חִזְקִיָּה בַּהֲאָרָכַת חַיִּים דְּ״וְהוֹסַפְתִּי עַל יָמֶיךָ״ וְגוֹמֵר

which Chizkiyahu [HaMelech] merited, in the lengthening of life [expressed in], “and I will add onto your days,” etc. (Yeshayahu 38:5)358Yeshayahu 38:5: “הָלוֹךְ וְאָמַרְתָּ אֶל חִזְקִיָּהוּ, כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ אֱלֹקֵי דָּוִד אָבִיךָ: שָׁמַעְתִּי אֶת תְּפִלָּתֶךָ, רָאִיתִי אֶת דִּמְעָתֶךָ, הִנְנִי יוֹסִף עַל יָמֶיךָ חֲמֵשׁ עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה” — “Go and say to Chizkiyahu: Thus says Hashem, the God of David your father: I have heard your prayer, I have seen your tears; behold, I am adding onto your days fifteen years.” Context: Chizkiyahu HaMelech, mortally ill, “turned his face to the wall” and prayed; Yeshayahu — who had told him “you shall die and not live” (a sealed decree; cf. Berachos 10a) — is sent back with this reprieve. Rashi: the fifteen years granted after his prayer. R’ Tzadok’s use: Chizkiyahu’s teshuvah, awakened “with such force as to burst through all the fences, decrees, and boundaries set upon his life,” drew down the deathless vitality of Yaakov — the very model of how teshuvah “lengthens a person’s years.” — the fifteen years granted him after his prayer of repentance —
עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ בְּתֹקֶף כָּל כָּךְ
through the awakening of his teshuvah with such force,
לִפְרֹץ כָּל הַגְּדֵרִים וְהַגְּזֵרוֹת וְהַגְּבוּלִים לְחַיָּיו
as to burst through all the fences, decrees, and boundaries [set] upon his life — that is, the fixed limit of
״עַד פֹּה תָבוֹא״

“until here you shall come [and no further]” (cf. Iyov 38:11)359Iyov 38:11: “וָאֹמַר עַד פֹּה תָבוֹא וְלֹא תֹסִיף, וּפֹא יָשִׁית בִּגְאוֹן גַּלֶּיךָ” — “and I said: until here you shall come and no further; and here shall your proud waves be stayed.” From God’s answer to Iyov out of the whirlwind, of the sea whose bounds He fixed at creation. Meforshim (Rashi): God set a limit (gevul) upon the sea, that it not overflow the dry land. R’ Tzadok’s use: “ad po tavo ve-lo tosif” is the archetype of the fixed boundary — the limit the Creator set upon every created thing, including the span of a man’s life; and teshuvah of the rung of Yaakov reaches “the inheritance of Yaakov without straits [bli metzarim],” beyond all such bounds, so that “death has no relevance to him.” —
רַק בְּנַחֲלַת יַעֲקֹב בְּלֹא מֵצָרִים

[dwelling] rather within the inheritance of Yaakov, which is without straits — “an inheritance without boundaries” (Shabbos 118a)360Shabbos 118a: “Rav Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Whoever delights in the Shabbos is given a boundless inheritance [nachalah bli metzarim], as it says (Yeshayahu 58:14), ‘Then you shall delight upon Hashem, [and I will cause you to ride upon the high places of the earth,] and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father’ — not the inheritance of Avraham, of whom it is written ‘arise, walk the land, to its length and to its breadth’ [a bounded measure], nor of Yitzchak, of whom it is written ‘for to you and to your seed I will give all these lands,’ but the inheritance of Yaakov, of whom it is written (Bereishis 28:14), ‘and you shall spread forth to the west and to the east, to the north and to the south’ [without limit].” (Yaakov’s inheritance alone is ‘without straits’ — the boundlessness the se’if identifies with his deathlessness.)361R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi §6): "“but Yisrael shall be your name” — and this name is called so because he defeated Samael, the minister of Esav, who is the Satan and the yetzer hara, as is known." Exactly the se’if: the name Yaakov bears is the one won over the very power whose whole instrument is death — which is why “death has no relevance to him.” —
דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא מֵת
and it is for this reason that he does not die.
כִּי הַמִּיתָה הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַגְּבוּל שֶׁשָּׂם הַבּוֹרֵא לְחַיֵּי הָאָדָם
For death comes about only by means of the boundary that the Creator set upon the life of man;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כְּשֶׁהוּא בְּלֹא מֵצָרִים
whereas when one stands without straits,
לֹא שַׁיָּךְ מִיתָה
death has no relevance to him.
וּמִיתָתוֹ הָיָה רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן
And [Yaakov’s] “death” was only in this world, to the perception of the eye,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתַעֲנִית ה:] ״מִקְרָא אֲנִי דּוֹרֵשׁ״ כו׳, ״מַקִּישׁ הוּא לְזַרְעוֹ״ כו׳

as they said [in Taanis 5b], “I am expounding a verse; he is likened to his offspring”362Taanis 5b: R’ Yochanan said: Yaakov Avinu did not die. [Rav Nachman] objected, “was it for nothing that the eulogizers eulogized, the embalmers embalmed, and the buriers buried him?!” He replied, “I am expounding a verse — as it says (Yirmeyah 30), ‘and you, fear not, My servant Yaakov, says Hashem — for behold I save you from afar and your offspring from the land of their captivity’ — Scripture likens him to his offspring: just as his offspring are alive, so too is he alive.”
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר
That is to say: you (Rav Nachman) bring me what was witnessed tangibly in this world — the eulogizing, embalming, and burial —
אֲבָל אֲנִי דּוֹרֵשׁ הַמִּקְרָא
but I expound the verse.
שֶׁהַדְּרָשׁ הוּא הַשָּׂגַת הָעֹמֶק הַנֶּעְלָם מֵהַפְּשָׁט
For the derashah is the apprehension of the hidden depth [that lies] beyond the plain sense;
וִידִיעַת הַדָּבָר לַאֲמִתּוֹ
and the knowledge of a matter as it truly is — which is concealed within this world —
הוּא הַדְּרָשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם תּוֹךְ הַכְּתָב שֶׁהוּא הַנִּגְלֶה לַכֹּל
is [precisely] the hidden derashah [contained] within the written text, which is [itself] revealed to all.
וְעִנְיַן חִיּוּתוֹ הוּא ״מַקִּישׁ הוּא לְזַרְעוֹ״ כו׳
And the matter of his vitality is [captured in], “he is likened to his offspring,” etc.:
פְּשׁוּטוֹ הַכַּוָּנָה דְּחִיּוּת שֶׁבְּזַרְעוֹ הַיְינוּ חִיּוּתוֹ
its plain intent is that the vitality present in his offspring is his own vitality,
דְּשֹׁרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל דּוֹר וָדוֹר בִּכְלָל הוּא נֶפֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה

for the root of the souls of each and every generation, collectively, is the soul of Yaakov Avinu, of blessed memory.363R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer §3): “[Yaakov] did not die, but was only as one asleep — as it is written, ‘Awake and sing, you who dwell in the dust’ (Yeshayah 26:19); and as expounded in the Gemara (Taanis 5b), ‘He likens him to his offspring — just as his offspring are alive, so is he alive.’ And since ‘there is no partial analogy,’ He likewise likens his offspring to him: that all the seed of Yaakov will [in the end] be clarified to stand in the level of ‘Yaakov did not die.’ And when [each one] is roused from his sleep, he will remember all the words of Torah; and concerning this we plead, ‘let us not be forgotten by You — neither in this world nor in the World to Come.’”364R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §40): “and they said (Taanis) ‘Yaakov Avinu did not die — he is likened to his offspring’; and this is ‘Yaakov who redeemed Avraham’ (Yeshayah 29:22) — for from the levels of Avraham and Yitzchak alone, which are the seeking of the love of Hashem and His fear in the ultimate clarification, salvation [from death] would not have been compelled.” This is §6-1’s own verse (Taanis 5b, makish hu l’zaro): Yaakov “does not die” because his life is the life of his offspring — and his rung so surpasses even Avraham and Yitzchak that he “redeems” them, the deathless root of every generation.Chassidic parallel - Sefat Emet, Vayechi 22:3 and 4:3: Sefat Emet gives an especially close Chassidic formulation of the life of Yaakov that R. Tzadok is invoking here. On "Yaakov Avinu lo meis," he explains that Yaakov "left all of his power within Klal Yisrael," so that his force can be awakened in Israel in every generation; elsewhere in Vayechi he explains that Yaakov drew the hidden vitality of Torah even into Egypt, and that through the middah of emes one can find life within the concealment of galus itself. This complements R. Tzadok's use of Taanis 5b: the "lengthening of years" produced by teshuvah is not merely an extension of biological time. Teshuvah reconnects the individual to the undying root of Yaakov, whose life persists in his descendants and can be reawakened within them. In that sense, the penitent's renewed life is a participation in a life that was never severed by death in the first place. The Sefat Emet also helps explain why R. Tzadok immediately moves from Yaakov himself to his seed: Yaakov's immortality is revealed precisely through the continuity of the souls and avodah of Israel.

items.h: The theme: Yosef is Yaakov’s essential “offspring” — the guarding of the bris — which is why even the poshei Yisrael are called “kulam tzaddikim.” The root of every Jewish soul is holy, so any apparent “dross” is only external; Yaakov’s “bed was whole.”

p: [ב] וְהִנֵּה תּוֹלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר תּוֹלְדוֹתָיו

And behold, “the offspring of Yaakov [is] Yosef” (Bereishis 37:2)365Bereishis 37:2: “אֵלֶּה תֹּלְדוֹת יַעֲקֹב: יוֹסֵף בֶּן שְׁבַע עֶשְׂרֵה שָׁנָה הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת אֶחָיו בַּצֹּאן” — “these are the offspring of Yaakov: Yosef…” The opening of the Yosef narrative (Vayeishev). Rashi: Scripture reckons the whole line of Yaakov’s toldos through Yosef — because Yaakov served Lavan only for [Rachel] Yosef’s mother, because Yosef’s features resembled his, and because all that befell Yaakov befell Yosef. R’ Tzadok takes “toldos Yaakov Yosef” to mean that Yosef is Yaakov’s essential offspring — the shomer ha-bris (guardian of the covenant) — so that Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef,” the holy root-soul of Yaakov borne onward through him. — [meaning] that he is his essential offspring.
וְאָמְרוּ ז״ל דְּזִיו אִיקוֹנִין דּוֹמֶה לוֹ

and the Sages said (Bereishis Rabbah 84:8)366Bereishis Rabbah 84:8: “‘And Yisrael loved Yosef’ (Bereishis 37:3) — R’ Yehuda and R’ Nechemya [expound it]: R’ Yehuda says, because the radiance of [Yosef’s] countenance [ziv ikonin] resembled his [Yaakov’s]; R’ Nechemya said, [because] all the halachos that Shem and Ever had transmitted to Yaakov, he transmitted to him [Yosef].” (Both readings underlie the se’if: Yosef is Yaakov’s ‘essential offspring’ — mirroring his father’s very form and his Torah.) that the radiance of [Yosef’s] countenance resembled his [father’s].
וְנוֹדָע דְּכָל זֶה אֵינוֹ בָּאִיקוֹנִין דְּגוּף
and it is known that all this is not [a resemblance] in the countenance of the body, which belongs to this world and is a fleeting thing,
רַק בָּאִיקוֹנִין דְּנֶפֶשׁ וְצֶלֶם אֱלֹקִים
but rather in the countenance of the soul and the “image of God” of the nishmas chayim,
שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר הַקַּיָּם לָעַד
which is an everlasting thing — and in that [inner form] Yosef resembled him.
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרְאוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל שְׁמוֹ ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״

And therefore Israel is called by his name, “the remnant of Yosef” (Amos 5:15)367Amos 5:15: “שִׂנְאוּ רָע וְאֶהֱבוּ טוֹב וְהַצִּיגוּ בַשַּׁעַר מִשְׁפָּט, אוּלַי יֶחֱנַן ה׳ אֱלֹקֵי צְבָאוֹת שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף” — “hate evil and love good, and establish justice in the gate; perhaps Hashem, God of Hosts, will be gracious to the remnant of Yosef.” From Amos’s call to repentance. Meforshim: “she’eris Yosef” is the remnant of Israel, called by Yosef’s name. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef” because Yosef, the guardian of the covenant, “comprises the souls of Israel in every generation” — and therefore even the transgressors of Israel are included in “the remnant of Yosef — all of them tzaddikim.”,
כִּי גַּם הוּא כּוֹלֵל נַפְשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל דּוֹר
for he too comprises the souls of Israel in every generation.
וְנֶאֱמַר ״וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״

and it says, “and your people are all tzaddikim” (Yeshayahu 60:21)368Yeshayahu 60:21: “וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים, לְעוֹלָם יִירְשׁוּ אָרֶץ, נֵצֶר מַטָּעַי מַעֲשֵׂה יָדַי לְהִתְפָּאֵר” — “and your people are all tzaddikim; they shall inherit the land forever; the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory.” From Yeshaya’s prophecy of Zion’s future glory. Meforshim: in the future all Israel will be found righteous (the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 90a, opens “all Israel have a share in the World to Come” from this verse). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the middah of all Israel — “kulam,” even the transgressors and the wholly wicked — for the essential meaning of “tzaddik” is a guardian of the covenant like Yosef; every Jew’s root is holy, whatever appears to the eye. — this being the middah of all Israel;
״כֻּלָּם״ הַיְינוּ אֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּרְשָׁעִים גְּמוּרִים
“all of them” — meaning even the transgressors of Israel and the wholly wicked,
דְּעִיקַּר שֵׁם ״צַדִּיק״ — שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית כְּיוֹסֵף

for the essential meaning of the title “tzaddik” is a guardian of the covenant, like Yosef.369R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §4): “‘your people are all tzaddikim’ — guardians of the covenant; and therefore, from the revelation of the illumination of yesod abba, comes the rectification of the bris and the fulfillment of milah, the sign of the holy covenant in every Jew.” This is §6-2 precisely: the essential title tzaddik is the shomer habris like Yosef, and it is this guarded covenant that makes “all Israel tzaddikim” — the holy root that no outward “orlah” can reach.
וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים דְּאֵין הָעׇרְלָה נִקְרֵאת אֶלָּא עַל שֵׁם אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

And indeed they said in Nedarim (31a)370Nedarim 31a (Mishnah): “One who vows [not to benefit] ‘from the arelim [the uncircumcised]’ is permitted [to benefit] from the uncircumcised of Israel and forbidden from the circumcised of the nations — for ‘orlah’ [uncircumcision] is called only after the name of the nations, as it says (Yirmeyah 9:25), ‘for all the nations are uncircumcised, and all the House of Israel are uncircumcised of heart.’” (Hence even an ‘uncircumcised’ Jew is essentially ‘circumcised’: orlah is, in its root, a name belonging to the nations alone.) that “orlah” (foreskin) is applied as a name only to the nations of the world,
וַאֲפִילּוּ עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים ״מוּלִים״
and even the “uncircumcised” of Israel are [essentially] called “circumcised.”
וּבְפֶרֶק עוֹשִׂין פַּסִּין

And in the chapter Osin Passin (Eruvin 19a)371Eruvin 19a: Reish Lakish taught that the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the transgressors of Israel, and that Avraham Avinu raises them up [by the sign of the covenant] — “except for a Jew who cohabited with a gentile woman, for his foreskin is drawn [moshech orlaso] and he is not recognized.” (As the se’if explains, this means only that the sign is not outwardly recognizable — not that he is truly ‘arel’; a mashuch is not really uncircumcised.) they said that one who cohabits with a gentile woman — “his foreskin is drawn” and “it is not recognized upon him” —
הַיְינוּ דְּאֵינוֹ מַכִּיר לְבַד, לֹא שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת עָרֵל

meaning [only] that it is not outwardly recognizable, not that he is truly “arel,” for the mashuch (one whose circumcision has been drawn over) is not truly uncircumcised — only Rabbinically, for appearance’s sake, must he repair it.
לְפִי רְאוּת הָעַיִן וְהַנִּגְלֶה דְּקִלְקֵל הַבְּרִית הֵיפֶךְ יוֹסֵף
[It is] according to the sight of the eye and the revealed [level] that he has corrupted the covenant — the opposite of Yosef.
שֶׁבָּזֶה עִיקַּר נִסָּיוֹן שְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית
For herein lies the essential trial of guarding the covenant — that of “subduing” (le-achpaya) at the level of tzaddik, in tzimtzum —
הוּא בַּאֲרַמִּית דְּאֵין לָהּ שַׁיָּיכוּת עִם זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל
it is [tested precisely] with a gentile woman, who has no connection to the seed of Israel.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן נִסָּיוֹן דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה בְּיִשְׂרְאֵלִית לֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדוֹ
whereas the trial of David HaMelech with a Jewish woman did not succeed for him,
שֶׁדַּם הַנִּסָּיוֹן הָיָה לְאַהְפְּכָא לֹא לְכַפְיָיא
for the “blood” of that trial was for “transforming,” not for “subduing,”
דְּבֶאֱמֶת רְאוּיָה הִיא לוֹ וְאֵין זֶה דַּרְגָּא דְּיוֹסֵף
since in truth she was fitting for him, and this is not the level of Yosef.
וְעִיקַּר הַהַבְדָּלָה בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים הוּא בְּאוֹת הַבְּרִית
And the essential distinction between Israel and the nations is in the sign of the covenant — which is why “orlah” is named for the nations.
וְרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בִּקְדֻשַּׁת שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתּוֹלָדָה
And he means [the distinction lies] in the holiness of the root of one’s generation,
כִּי בְּמַעֲשֶׂה אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם דָּוִים
for in [outward] deed it is possible that the two are alike [in fault],
רַק זֶה שָׁרְשׁוֹ טוֹב
but this one’s root is good;
וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְלַל ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים
and therefore even the transgressors of Israel are included in “the remnant of Yosef — all of them tzaddikim.”
וַאֲפִילּוּ חֲסִידֵי אֻמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת לָזֶה
And even the pious of the nations have no share in this,
כִּי הַמְשָׁכַת מְקוֹר חִיּוּתָם מִמְּקוֹם טֻמְאָה וְעׇרְלָה
for the drawing of the source of their vitality is from a place of impurity and “orlah”;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֹׁרֶשׁ חִיּוּתָם מִיַּעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה
whereas the Children of Israel — the root of their vitality is from Yaakov Avinu, of blessed memory.
דְּכָל עִנְיַן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה ״מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה״

For the whole matter of Yaakov Avinu, “his bed was whole” (Pesachim 56a; Vayikra Rabbah 36:5)372Pesachim 56a (and Vayikra Rabbah 36:5) — “mittaso shleimah”: the Gemara relates that as Yaakov lay dying he feared there might be a blemish in his “bed” (as Avraham had produced Yishmael, and Yitzchak, Esav); his sons declared, “Shema Yisrael, Hashem Elokeinu Hashem echad — just as in your heart there is [but] One, so in ours,” whereupon Yaakov responded “Baruch shem kevod malchuso le-olam va’ed.” The Sages conclude that Yaakov’s bed was whole [mittaso shleimah] — all his offspring were worthy, none cast off (so too Vayikra Rabbah 36:5). R’ Tzadok’s use: “mittaso shleimah” means all his offspring were [conceived] in holiness, for Yaakov completed the rectification of Adam’s sin (which was rooted in desire); hence no true “dross” issues from him — and the same holds of all Israel, his seed.,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁכָּל הוֹלְדוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה
means that all his offspring were [conceived] in holiness,
כִּי הוּא שְׁלֵימוּת תִּיקּוּן חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהָיָה בְּתַאֲוָה
for he is the completion of the rectification of Adam’s sin, which was [rooted] in desire.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ עַל יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ

And therefore they said of Yishai that he died “through the counsel of the serpent”373Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 (on “behold, in iniquity was I fashioned,” Tehillim 51:7): R’ Acha said: even the most pious of the pious cannot be wholly free of some trace of iniquity. David said before the Holy One, “Master of the worlds — did my father Yishai intend to bring me into being? He intended only his own pleasure” And this is [the meaning of] what they said in Shabbos 55b: “Four died [solely] through the counsel of the serpent [i.e., without personal sin]: Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David.” —
הַיְינוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָתַת הַנָּחָשׁ בְּחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן

that is, the root of the serpent’s incitement in Adam’s sin — for “in a full transgression, even the most pious of the pious,” since there was in him some root of self-interested intent.374R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §258): “‘More precious than wisdom and honor is a little folly’ (Koheles 10:1) — for there must be in every person at least a small measure of folly, and this [very thing] is [the mark of] wholeness; only that it is good for a man that this folly be as minimal as possible — and the two [evil] inclinations are desire, and the murderous [inclination of] anger, which stem from Adam and Chavah through the serpent’s incitement, and from Kayin. And this is [why] ‘the counsel of the serpent’ [etyo shel nachash] is in every person — as the Sages said (Yoma 69b), ‘the world has need of it’ [the inclination] and it cannot be nullified. This is the indispensable ‘little folly,’ [needed] in any case for the world’s continuance.” (Thus even a tzaddik like Yishai bears “the counsel of the serpent” not as a personal sin but as the residual, world-sustaining root of desire.)375R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §18): “as they said (Shabbos 55b) that [Yishai] died through the counsel of the serpent — and from yesod comes malchus… the beginning of the [royal] choice was in one of the sons of Yishai, for the father earns [merit] for his son.” This lights up §6-2’s “they said of Yishai that he died b’etyo shel nachash — the root of the serpent’s incitement in Adam’s sin”: even flawless Yishai tasted death only from that primordial counsel, yet from his guarded yesod issued the malchus of David — “dross” that is, in truth, no dross at all.
וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ הַבּוּשָׁה לְאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ אַחַר הַחֵטְא
And from this was drawn the shame of Adam and his wife after the sin, when they recognized that they were naked —
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁוּ בַּהֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית
because they felt bodily pleasure;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִקּוֹדֶם נֶאֱמַר ״וְלֹא יִתְבּוֹשָׁשׁוּ״

whereas beforehand it says, “and they were not ashamed” (Bereishis 2:25)376Bereishis 2:25: “וַיִּהְיוּ שְׁנֵיהֶם עֲרוּמִּים, הָאָדָם וְאִשְׁתּוֹ, וְלֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ” — “and the two of them were naked, the man and his wife, and they were not ashamed.” The state of Adam and Chavah before the sin. Rashi: they did not yet know the way of modesty, to distinguish good from evil — before the sin no yetzer hara stirred bodily desire, so there was no shame. R’ Tzadok’s use: shame entered only after the sin, when “they felt bodily pleasure”; Yaakov, by contrast, “felt no bodily pleasure whatever,” intending solely to establish offspring — hence “his bed was whole,” free of the shame that Adam’s sin drew into the world..
וְכֵן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה אָמַר ״הָבָה אֶת [אִשְׁתִּי]״ וְגוֹמֵר

And likewise Yaakov Avinu said, “Give [me] my wife”377Bereishis Rabbah 74:18: “And Yaakov said to Lavan, ‘give me my wife’” (Bereishis 29:21). R’ Aivu said: even a licentious man does not speak in such [blunt] language! Rather Yaakov said: the Holy One told me I would raise up twelve tribes; now I am about eighty-four years old — if I do not raise them up now, when? — therefore, “give me my wife.” [His blunt words were not from desire but from an urgent, holy intent to establish the tribes.] — a phrasing that even the coarsest of the coarse would not use, on account of the shame that came after Adam’s sin —
רַק הוּא דְּלֹא הִרְגִּישׁ בְּשׁוּם הֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית
but he felt no bodily pleasure whatever,
רַק לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלָדוֹת לְבַד נִתְכַּוֵּון
intending solely to establish offspring.
וּכְמוֹ לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא — ״לֵב בָּשָׂר״

And [it is] as in the Future to Come, of which the Sages expounded the verse “a heart of flesh” (Yechezkel 36:26)378Yechezkel 36:26: “וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב חָדָשׁ וְרוּחַ חֲדָשָׁה אֶתֵּן בְּקִרְבְּכֶם, וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר” — “and I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit will I put within you; and I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh.” From Yechezkel’s prophecy of Israel’s future purification. Meforshim: the stubborn “heart of stone” will be replaced by a responsive heart. R’ Tzadok reads “lev basar” at its depth — a heart that removes [the pull of] flesh — so that in the Future the marital act will be, like Yaakov’s, “as the donning of tefillin,” a pure mitzvah to which no shame applies. — a heart that removes [the pull of] flesh —
הֲרֵי זֶה אֶצְלוֹ כַּהֲנָחַת תְּפִילִּין
so that [the marital act] is to him like the donning of tefillin and all the mitzvos of the Torah, and no shame applies.
וְעַל כֵּן ״מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה״, דְּשׁוֹמֵר מִצְוָה לֹא יֵדַע דָּבָר רָע

And therefore “his bed was whole,” for “one who guards a mitzvah knows no evil thing” (Koheles 8:5)379Koheles 8:5: “שׁוֹמֵר מִצְוָה לֹא יֵדַע דָּבָר רָע, וְעֵת וּמִשְׁפָּט יֵדַע לֵב חָכָם” — “one who guards a mitzvah will know no evil thing; and a wise heart knows time and judgment.” From Shlomo’s counsel (Koheles 8). Meforshim: one engaged in a mitzvah is shielded from harm (cf. “those on a mission of mitzvah are not harmed,” Pesachim 8b). R’ Tzadok’s use: “shomer mitzvah lo yeda davar ra” proves that “his bed was whole” — it is entirely impossible that a sin or evil thing should issue from a mitzvah; the “dross” that appears in one’s offspring comes only through the admixture of bodily pleasures drawn from “the counsel of the serpent,” never from the mitzvah itself.,
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר כְּלָל שֶׁיָּבוֹא מִמִּצְוָה עֲבֵירָה וְדָבָר רָע ח״ו
and it is entirely impossible that a sin or evil thing should issue from a mitzvah, Heaven forbid.
רַק יְצִיאַת הַפְּסֹלֶת הוּא עַל יְדֵי עִירְבּוּב הֲנָאוֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת

Rather, the emergence of “dross” [in one’s offspring] comes about [only] through the admixture of bodily pleasures drawn from “the counsel of the serpent,” which became intermingled through Adam’s sin into all his seed.
וְהָאָבוֹת הֵם שֶׁבָּאוּ לְתַקֵּן זֶה, וּגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן הָיָה בְּיַעֲקֹב
And the Avos are those who came to rectify this, and the completion of the rectification was in Yaakov,
דְּאָמְרִי עֲלֵיהּ ״אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם״

of whom they expound, “[Yaakov,] who redeemed Avraham” (Yeshayahu 29:22; cf. Sanhedrin 19b)380Yeshayahu 29:22 (with Sanhedrin 19b): “לָכֵן כֹּה אָמַר ה׳ אֶל בֵּית יַעֲקֹב אֲשֶׁר פָּדָה אֶת אַבְרָהָם: לֹא עַתָּה יֵבוֹשׁ יַעֲקֹב, וְלֹא עַתָּה פָּנָיו יֶחֱוָרוּ” — “therefore thus says Hashem to the House of Yaakov, who redeemed Avraham: not now shall Yaakov be ashamed, nor now shall his face pale.” The phrase “who redeemed Avraham” is difficult (where do we find that Yaakov redeemed Avraham?). The Gemara (Sanhedrin 19b) resolves: Yaakov redeemed Avraham from the anguish of raising children [tza’ar giddul banim] — Avraham was spared distress over his descendants once Yaakov came, all of whose children were worthy. R’ Tzadok’s use: the completion of the rectification of Adam’s sin was in Yaakov — so that Avraham and Yitzchak too were “clarified” and, retroactively, “called Yaakov”; only Yaakov is, in the fullest sense, “the seed” of the Avos, and their “beds” too are reckoned whole, the “dross” (Yishmael, Esav) being no true part of their seed..
וְגַם אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק נִקְרְאוּ ״יַעֲקֹב״
And Avraham and Yitzchak too are [retroactively] “called Yaakov,”
הַיְינוּ אַחַר שֶׁבָּא הוּא לָעוֹלָם נִתְבָּרְרוּ גַּם הֵם
meaning that once he came into the world, they too were “clarified,”
דְּאֵין נִקְרָאוּ זַרְעוֹ שֶׁל אָבוֹת אֶלָּא יַעֲקֹב בִּלְבַד כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּנְדָרִים
for [in the fullest sense] only Yaakov is called “the seed” of the Avos, as they said in Nedarim.
וְנִמְצָא גַּם מִטָּתָם הָיְתָה שְׁלֵימָה
It follows that their “beds,” too, were whole,
שֶׁהֲרֵי הַפְּסֹלֶת אֵינוֹ זַרְעָם כְּלָל
for the “dross” (Yishmael, Esav) is not their [true] seed at all,
כִּי לֹא הָיָה זֶה מִצִּדָּם
since it did not come from their side.
וּכְמוֹ דְּאֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב — אַף שֶׁנִּרְאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ אֵיזֶה פְּסֹלֶת לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בֶּאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ פְּסֹלֶת כְּלָל
And just as by Yaakov — although it appears to the eye that there is some dross, in truth it is no dross at all —
כֵּן אֶצְלָם
so too by them.
דְּזֶה כָּל כֹּחַ יַעֲקֹב — ״נַחֲלָה בְּלִי מְצָרִים״

For this is the entire power of Yaakov — “an inheritance without boundaries” (Shabbos 118a)381Shabbos 118a — “nachalah bli metzarim”: R’ Yochanan said in the name of R’ Yosi, whoever delights in the Shabbos is granted “a boundless inheritance [nachalah bli metzarim],” as it says (Yeshaya 58:14), “then you shall delight in Hashem… and I will feed you the inheritance of Yaakov your father” — not the bounded inheritance promised to Avraham (“arise, walk the length and breadth of the land”) or to Yitzchak, but the unbounded inheritance of Yaakov, of whom it says “u-faratzta — you shall spread out to the west and east, north and south” (Bereishis 28:14). R’ Tzadok’s use (recurring from §1): the whole “power of Yaakov” is this “inheritance without boundaries”; the “boundaries” of this world exist only “according to the revealed appearance to the eye,” but in the inward truth the seed of Yaakov is beyond all straits — so that any apparent “dross” among the poshei Yisrael is only external.Izhbitz-Radzin and Sefat Emet parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Anthology, Collectanea, Siddur 1; Sefat Emet, Vayera 30:3: The Izhbitz-Radzin tradition sharply supports the distinction in this se'if between the holy root of the Jewish soul and the external corruption produced by sin. Mei HaShiloach teaches on "Neshamah shenasata bi tehorah hi" that the neshamah itself is never reached by cheit or pegam; nefesh remains joined to the body, while ruach signifies the faculty of bechirah through which a person chooses good and rejects evil. Thus sin is terribly real at the level of choice and embodied life, but it does not rewrite the deepest origin of the neshamah. Sefat Emet, Vayera 30:3, develops the complementary side: Israel are "zera emes" because their souls extend from beginning to end, and the bris is meant to bring the body itself into correspondence with the holy neshamah. This illuminates R. Tzadok's insistence that even poshei Yisrael retain the name and root of tzaddikim. The dross can cover, distort, and damage the vessel, but it is not the essential identity of the soul. Teshuvah therefore does not manufacture a new Jewish essence; it uncovers and re-aligns the embodied person with the holy root that remained intact beneath the concealment.:
הַיְינוּ גְּבוּלֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא כְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן
that is, the boundaries of this world, which exist [only] according to the revealed appearance to the eye — that is where the “boundaries” lie.
וְזֶהוּ דְּחִיַּית לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה
And this is the “pushing-aside of a negative commandment” of the Torah, mentioned [in Se’if 3],
שֶׁזּוֹכִין לָהּ בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה בְּעוֹמֶק תְּשׁוּבָתָם
which the baalei teshuvah merit in the depth of their teshuvah.
וְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר הוּא בְּהִיפּוּךְ מִזֶּה
The perfect tzaddik is the reverse of this:
שֶׁנִּשְׁמָר שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲבֹר עַל שׁוּם דָּבָר מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה
he guards himself from transgressing anything of the words of Torah —
וְהוּא זִיו אִיקוֹנִין שֶׁל יוֹסֵף, שֶׁהוּא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת מִדַּת יַעֲקֹב ע״ה בְּזַרְעוֹ שֶׁבַּחַיִּים בְּכָל דּוֹר
and he is the “radiance of the countenance of Yosef,” which is the spreading-forth of the middah of Yaakov Avinu among his living offspring in every generation.

items.h: The theme: Yaakov’s own deathlessness is not yet revealed in this world; here it appears as “Yosef” — addition through offspring. Chizkiyahu’s extra years were only the lower rung (the decree pushed off), not true length-of-life; the deeper rung comes through the depth of teshuvah. And the “addition”/tzaddik level carries a danger of haughtiness.

p: [ג] וּמִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה עַצְמוֹ דְּלֹא מֵת כְּלָל
And [as for] the measure of Yaakov Avinu himself, that he did not die at all — the deathless level in its own right, not merely its extension through descendants —
זֶה לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה עֲדַיִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַד שֶׁיְּבֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת

this has not yet been revealed in this world, until death shall be swallowed up [forever] (Yeshayahu 25:8)382Yeshayahu 25:8: “בִּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח, וּמָחָה אֲדֹנָי ה׳ דִּמְעָה מֵעַל כָּל פָּנִים” — “He will swallow up death forever, and the Lord God will wipe away tears from every face.” From Yeshaya’s prophecy of the end of days (ch. 25). Meforshim (Rashi; and the Sages, Kesuvos 111b) take “bila ha-maves la-netzach” to mean that death — decreed on mankind through Adam’s sin — is abolished in the World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s use here: the measure of Yaakov Avinu himself, “that he did not die at all,” cannot yet be revealed in this world until death is swallowed up — a world still ruled by death cannot contain an openly deathless man; therefore “him too the buriers buried and the embalmers embalmed,” the outward “death” that this world’s concealment requires. (The verse is treated also at Siman 3 §5.); for a world still ruled by death cannot yet contain an openly deathless man.
אֲבָל לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן גַּם אוֹתוֹ קָבְרוּ קַבְרַיָּא וַחֲנָטוּ כו׳
but to the eye’s perception, him too “the buriers buried and the embalmers embalmed,” etc. — the outward “death” that this world’s concealment requires.
רַק הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּחִיּוּת זַרְעוֹ
Rather, the [present] spreading-forth in this world is [only] in the vitality of his offspring — his deathless life shows itself here not as his own continued life but as the living-on of his seed;
וְזֶה נִקְרָא יוֹסֵף לְשׁוֹן הוֹסָפָה

and this is called “Yosef,” a term of “addition,”383Bereishis 30:24 (the name Yosef): “וַתִּקְרָא אֶת שְׁמוֹ יוֹסֵף לֵאמֹר, יֹסֵף ה׳ לִי בֵּן אַחֵר” — “and she called his name Yosef, saying, ‘May Hashem add [yosef] to me another son.’” Rachel, upon bearing Yosef (Vayeitzei). Rashi: the name is from the root y-s-f, “to add” — her prayer for an additional son. R’ Tzadok’s use: the name itself — “Yosef, a term of addition [hosafah]” — expresses the very mode by which Yaakov’s deathless vitality persists in this world: not as his own continued life, but as the adding of ever more souls of the seed of Israel in each generation. the name itself (from asaf/yosef, “to add”) pointing to this mode of survival-through-increase,
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתּוֹסְפוּ נְפָשׁוֹת רַבּוֹת דְּזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר
for through it many souls of the seed of Israel are added in each and every generation.

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [ע״ז ה.]384Avodah Zarah 5a: Reish Lakish: “come, let us be grateful to our ancestors — for had they not sinned, we would not have come into the world.” The Gemara concludes that had Israel not sinned they would not have died; and R’ Yosi taught, “Israel accepted the Torah only so that the Angel of Death should not rule over them,” as it says “I said, you are angelic beings, sons of the Most High, all of you — [yet] you corrupted your deeds, therefore you shall die like Adam” (Tehillim 82:6–7). אִלְמָלֵא אֲבוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁחָטְאוּ אָנוּ לֹא בָאנוּ, אוֹ כְּמִי שֶׁלֹּא בָּאנוּ

And along the lines of what they said [in Avodah Zarah 5a]: “Had our ancestors not sinned, we would not have come [into the world],” or “we would be as those who never came,” — a striking teaching: it is precisely the sin and its consequent mortality that made room for each later soul to be born as its own person;
שֶׁהָיִינוּ כְּלוּלִים בָּהֶם וְלֹא הָיָה מָקוֹם לְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ

for we would have been subsumed within them, and there would have been no place for [each soul] to spread forth as an entity of its own — all later generations remaining folded, undifferentiated, within the first.
וְהִנֵּה הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת זֶה הוּא גוֹרֵם הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת וְהִתְרַבּוּת נַחֲלַת וְנֶפֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה עַצְמוֹ
And behold, this very spreading-forth is what causes the spreading and increase of the portion and soul of Yaakov Avinu himself,
שֶׁהוּא עֶצֶם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
for he is the very essence of the souls of Israel — so that every soul added below is, at root, more of him.
וְנִמְצָא הָעוֹלָם חִיּוּתוֹ, שֶׁכִּסְבוּרִין אָנוּ שֶׁהוּא מִיעוּט חִיּוּת, אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא רִיבּוּי וְהוֹסָפַת חִיּוּת

It emerges that [what looks like his descent into] the world is [really] his vitality: what we imagine to be a diminishment of vitality is in fact a multiplication and addition of vitality — the “coming-down” into this world being not a loss but a widening of his life,
שֶׁנִּתְרַחֵב וְנִתּוֹסֵף בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר
which has broadened and increased through [this] spreading-forth all the more.
וְזֶה גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן הוֹסָפַת יָמִים עַל יָמָיו דְּחִזְקִיָּה אַחַר שֶׁקִּיבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ דְּלִינְסַב וְיוֹלִיד זֶרַע

And this too is the matter of the addition of days to the days of Chizkiyahu, after he accepted upon himself to marry and beget offspring (cf. Berachos 10a)385Berachos 10a: When Yeshayahu told Chizkiyahu “you shall die and not live” (Yeshayahu 38:1) — because “you did not engage in the mitzvah of procreation” — Chizkiyahu answered that he had seen by ru’ach ha-kodesh that unworthy children would issue from him. Yeshayahu replied: “What have you to do with the secrets of the Merciful One? What you are commanded, you are obligated to do.” Chizkiyahu said: “Then give me your daughter — perhaps my merit together with yours will cause worthy children to issue from me.” (Only after he accepted to marry and beget were his years lengthened.),
שֶׁיִּהְיוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת חִיּוּתוֹ לְדוֹרוֹת
so that his vitality would spread forth into future generations.
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּכָל הַצֶּאֱצָאִים גְּנוּזִים בַּאֲבוֹתָם
As is known, all offspring are stored away within their forebears,
וּבַהוֹלָדָה הֵם יוֹצְאִים מֵהֶעְלֵם לְגִילּוּי וּמֵהַצִּמְצוּם לְהִתְרַחֲבוּת
and in birth they emerge from concealment to revelation, from contraction to expansion;
וְזֶה גּוֹרֵם גַּם כֵּן הִתְרַחֲבוּת וְהוֹסָפָה בְּחִיּוּתוֹ וְיָמָיו, עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁאַחַר הַחֵטְא בָּזֶה
and this too brings about expansion and addition in his vitality and days, through the teshuvah that follows the sin.
וְהוּא הָיָה מִצַּד הַתְחָלַת מַדְרֵגָה זוֹ, דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה, שֶׁהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
But he [Chizkiyahu] was [only] at the beginning of this level — the rung of Yaakov Avinu — which [as yet] is concealed in this world.
וְעַל כֵּן אִיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר [יְבָמוֹת נ.] דְּרַק הִשְׁלִימוּ לוֹ וּמִשֶּׁלּוֹ נָתְנוּ לוֹ

Therefore there is an opinion [in Yevamos 50a] that they merely “completed” his [allotted years] and “gave him from his own,”386Yevamos 50a: It was taught: “‘the number of your days I will fill’ (Shemos 23) — these are the years preordained to a person at birth. If he merits, they complete [the full span] for him; if he does not merit, they reduce it — the words of R’ Akiva. And the Sages say: if he merits, they add to him; if not, they reduce.” They said to R’ Akiva: does it not say (II Melachim 20), “I will add to your days fifteen years” [to Chizkiyahu]? He answered: they added to him “from his own” [preordained allotment]. [R’ Akiva holds that merit “completes” one’s years rather than truly “adds” to them.]
וְאֵין כָּאן עֲדַיִין הָאֲרָכָה גְּמוּרָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and there is here as yet no true lengthening [of life] in this world.
וְגַם לְמַאן דְּאָמַר הוֹסִיפוּ לוֹ, לֹא הֶאֱרִיךְ יָמִים יוֹתֵר מִשְּׁאָר בְּנֵי הַדּוֹר
And even according to the one who holds that they “added” to him, he did not live longer than the rest of his generation,
וְאֵין כָּאן עֲדַיִין מַדְרֵגַת מַאֲרֶכֶת יָמָיו, רַק מַה שֶּׁנִּדְחָה הַגְּזֵרָה וְהַגְּבוּל מִיָּמָיו

and there is here as yet no level of “lengthening his years,” only that the decree and the boundary were pushed off from his days.387R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §13): “and "joy" applies only to an addition of good — as they said,”do not hold [it] a favor, for it is for this that you were created."" Exactly the se’if: Chizkiyahu’s extra years are precisely an addition — a rung of tosefes, a good added on — and not the unbroken length of life that belongs to Yaakov himself.
וְזֶהוּ רַק כִּדְחִיַּית לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וּגְזֵרַת הַתּוֹרָה
And this is only like the “pushing-aside” of a negative precept, a decree of the Torah;
אֲבָל כַּאֲשֶׁר יַעֲמִיק יוֹתֵר בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ וּבִדְבֵיקוּתוֹ בֵּאלֹקִים חַיִּים
but when a person delves deeper in his teshuvah and in his cleaving to the living God,
יִזְכֶּה לְחַיִּים וְהָאֲרָכַת יָמִים, עַל יְדֵי שׁוּבוֹ מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ — עַל יְדֵי זֶה יִחְיֶה

he will merit life and length of days; through his return from his wickedness — “through this he shall live.”388Yechezkel 18:27 (and 33:19): the phrase “through his return from his wickedness — he shall live” draws on the teshuvah-prophecy of Yechezkel: “וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה, וַיַּעַשׂ מִשְׁפָּט וּצְדָקָה — הוּא אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ יְחַיֶּה” (18:27), and “וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ… עֲלֵיהֶם הוּא יִחְיֶה” (33:19) — “when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, he keeps his soul alive.” Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): the penitent who turns from evil thereby lives. R’ Tzadok’s use: it is precisely by delving deeper in teshuvah and cleaving to the living God that one merits not merely the pushing-off of the decree (Chizkiyahu’s lower rung) but true life and length of days — “through this he shall live.”
כִּי יוֹסֵף שֶׁהָיָה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר, וְהוּא עִיקַּר דַּרְגָּא דְּהוֹסָפָה
For Yosef, who was a perfect tzaddik and is the essential rung of “addition,”
אָמְרוּ ז״ל (סוֹטָה יג:) דְּאַדְּרַבָּא נִפְחֲתוּ לוֹ עֶשֶׂר שָׁנִים בִּשְׁבִיל חֵטְא דְּשָׁמַע ״חֵטְא עַבְדְּךָ אָבִינוּ״

the Sages said (Sotah 13b)389Sotah 13b: “Why did Yosef die before his brothers? Because he conducted himself with lordship [hinhig atzmo b’rabbanus].” (Though Yosef is the very rung of “addition,” years were, on the contrary, diminished from him — he died at 110, before his elder brothers.) that, on the contrary, ten years were subtracted from his life on account of the “sin” of hearing [his brothers say] “your servant our father” [ten times, without protesting] — so that the very embodiment of “addition” was himself diminished, teaching that this rung is precarious.
הָעִנְיַן דְּהוֹסָפָה הֲרֵי נִרְאֶה כְּמוֹסִיף וּמַעֲדִיף עַל הָעִיקַּר
The matter is that “addition” appears as though it adds and exceeds beyond the essential root — and whatever seems to stand “above” its source invites the illusion of independent worth,
וְצָרִיךְ בָּזֶה שְׁמִירָה יְתֵירָה שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹא לְהִתְגָּאוֹת וְלַחְשֹׁב שֶׁהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת טוֹב יוֹתֵר
and this requires extra guarding, lest one come to haughtiness and think that he is truly better.
וְעַל זֶה הוּזְהֲרוּ ״אַל תֹּאמַר בְּצִדְקָתְךָ וּבְיֹשֶׁר לְבָבְךָ״ וְגוֹמֵר

Regarding this they were warned: “Do not say — ‘through my righteousness and the uprightness of my heart’ [Hashem has brought me in],’ etc.” (Devarim 9:4–5)390Devarim 9:4–5: “אַל תֹּאמַר בִּלְבָבְךָ… בְּצִדְקָתִי הֱבִיאַנִי ה׳ לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת הָאָרֶץ הַזֹּאת… לֹא בְצִדְקָתְךָ וּבְיֹשֶׁר לְבָבְךָ אַתָּה בָא לָרֶשֶׁת אֶת אַרְצָם, כִּי בְּרִשְׁעַת הַגּוֹיִם הָאֵלֶּה ה׳ אֱלֹקֶיךָ מוֹרִישָׁם מִפָּנֶיךָ” — “Do not say in your heart [when Hashem drives them out], ‘in my righteousness Hashem has brought me to possess this land’… not through your righteousness or the uprightness of your heart do you come to possess their land, but through the wickedness of these nations…” Moshe’s warning to Israel on the threshold of the Land. Rashi: they inherit it through the wickedness of the nations and the merit of the Avos — not their own righteousness. R’ Tzadok’s use: this admonition is addressed precisely to the perfect tzaddik — the “addition” / Yosef rung — who is liable to the illusion that he is “better than his Cause and his Root,” failing to recognize that “the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him.”,
וְאַזְהָרָה זוֹ הוּא לְמִי שֶׁהוּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
and this warning is [addressed precisely] to one who is a perfect tzaddik,
וְזֶה עָלוּל לִטְעוֹת, וּבָזֶה יוּכַל לְהַחְשִׁיב עַצְמוֹ טוֹב יוֹתֵר מֵעִילָּתוֹ וְשָׁרְשׁוֹ
for such a one is liable to err, and might come to consider himself better than his Cause and his Root,
וְאֵין מַכִּיר שֶׁעִיקַּר מַה שֶּׁהוּא טוֹב הוּא רַק מִמֶּנּוּ

not recognizing that the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him.391R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §36): “‘I am a shield [Magen] to you’ — as they said, ‘were it not that the Holy One helps him, [a person could not withstand the yetzer]’ (Sukkah 52b); ‘and I will guard them, lest they stumble in the yetzer hara with no recovery.’” This is the ground of §6-3’s warning to the perfect tzaddik not to say “through my righteousness”: even the tzaddik stands only because “the Holy One helps him” — the good is never his own doing, so the “addition” that seems to exceed its Root is, in truth, wholly a gift.392R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Korach §6): “he was not aware of this at all, and held no credit to himself — he looked only to Hashem who chose him, and not to his own power at all, as it says, ‘and what is Aharon [that you murmur against him]?’” This is §6-3’s tzaddik who does not stumble into the pride the se’if warns of: the rung of “addition” tempts one to “think he is truly better,” but Aharon — the very embodiment of drawing-near — took no credit, seeing all his good as flowing from the One who chose him.Chassidic parallel - Chiddushei HaRim on Torah, Chayei Sara 1; Sefat Emet, Vayechi 4:3: Chiddushei HaRim makes the relation between teshuvah and "length of days" unusually explicit. Commenting on Sarah's years, he notes the Zoharic principle that through teshuvah "in one hour and in one moment" a person can repair days that have already passed as though those days had been filled with mitzvos and good deeds; this is the deeper meaning of willful sins becoming merits. The point closely complements R. Tzadok's distinction here between merely postponing a decree of death and true arichus yamim. A penitent does not only receive additional days at the end of life; teshuvah can restore content and holiness to days already spent. Sefat Emet, Vayechi 4:3, adds that Yaakov drew a hidden current of life even into Egypt and that "Yaakov Avinu did not die" can be found by seeking the concealed Torah-life within exile. Read together, these sources sharpen R. Tzadok's claim: genuine lengthening of life reaches backward as well as forward. It is the recovery of the life concealed in apparently lost time, rooted in Yaakov's deathless emes rather than simply an extension of the calendar.

items.h: The theme: The three roots of tumah — kinah, taavah, kavod (envy, desire, honor) — stand opposite the three Avos. Gaavah (haughtiness) opposes Yaakov’s middah of emes/anavah; man’s greatness and lowliness are joined in the “form of Yaakov” engraved on the Throne, and Torah-pride is the yetzer’s opening — as in the story of R. Elazar b’R. Shimon and the “ugly man.”

p: [ד] וְיָדוּעַ דִּשְׁלֹשֶׁת שָׁרְשֵׁי הַטּוּמְאָה דְּיֵצֶר רָע, זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה לִשְׁלֹשֶׁת אֲבָהָן
And it is known that the three roots of impurity of the evil inclination correspond, “this-opposite-that,” to the three Avos:
הֵם קִנְאָה וְתַאֲוָה וְכָבוֹד

they are envy, desire, and honor (cf. Avos 4:21)393Avos 4:21: “R’ Elazar HaKappar says: Envy, desire, and honor [ha-kin’ah, ve-ha-taavah, ve-ha-kavod] remove a person from the world.” (These are the three roots of the evil inclination, standing over against the three Avos.).
שֶׁהוּא כַּעַס הַבָּא מִפְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרָה דְּיִצְחָק
[Envy] is the anger that comes from the “dross” of the Gevurah of Yitzchak — for envy and anger are Gevurah soured, the constrictive force turned destructive;
וְתַאֲוָה מִפְּסֹלֶת הַחֶסֶד דְּאַבְרָהָם
and desire [comes] from the dross of the Chesed of Avraham — the outflowing love of Chesed debased into craving —
שֶׁהֵם שָׁרְשֵׁי הָרָע שֶׁבָּאֻמּוֹת, אֱדוֹם וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל — בִּרְצִיחָה וְנִיאוּף

these being the roots of evil among the nations, Edom and Yishmael — in bloodshed and immorality [respectively].394R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §206): “All the imaginings and stray musings in a person are fixed in three roots — envy, desire, and honor [kinah, taavah, kavod] — which are the roots of the evil traits; and the root of [these] roots is haughtiness [gaavah], as is known, for the root of evil is from the World of Tohu and the ‘shattering of the vessels,’ which came about through the thought ‘I shall reign’ [ana emloch]. And from this the evil inclination [yetzer] is born — for ‘yetzer’ means a [stray] thought and musing in the heart, for there is the beginning of evil in the heart, as they said (Berachos 61a), ‘[the evil inclination] sits at the two entrances of the heart.’”
וְגַאֲוָה הוּא נֶגֶד מִדַּת אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב שֶׁמִּדָּתוֹ עֲנָוָה

And haughtiness stands opposite the middah of “Truth to Yaakov” (Michah 7:20)395Michah 7:20: “תִּתֵּן אֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב, חֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם, אֲשֶׁר נִשְׁבַּעְתָּ לַאֲבֹתֵינוּ מִימֵי קֶדֶם” — “You will grant truth to Yaakov, kindness to Avraham, which You swore to our fathers from days of old” — the sealing verse of Michah’s prophecy of pardon. Rashi: God will fulfill the oath of emes toward Yaakov and chesed toward Avraham. The Sages pair each Patriarch with a middah — Avraham = Chesed, Yitzchak = Gevurah/Pachad, Yaakov = Emes/Tiferes. R’ Tzadok’s use: “emes le-Yaakov” — truth is Yaakov’s middah, and its lived trait is anavah (humility), the opposite of gaavah (haughtiness, which is itself falsehood); therefore haughtiness stands “this-opposite-that” to Yaakov, the third of the three roots of impurity (envy, desire, honor) over against the three Avos., whose trait is humility —
[דַּרְגָּא דִּנְחֹשֶׁת נֶגֶד כֶּסֶף וְזָהָב]
[the rung of copper, as against silver and gold] —
שֶׁהֵם רוֹמְזִים לִשְׁלֹשָׁה ״אָבָן״ כַּיָּדוּעַ
which [three metals] allude to the three [Avos, hinted in the word] even (father-and-son), as is known.
כִּי הַגֵּיאוּת הוּא שֶׁקֶר
For haughtiness is falsehood;
דַּאֲפִילּוּ אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶאֱמַר ״גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ״ רַק דֶּרֶךְ לְבוּשׁ

for even regarding Hashem it says, “He has clothed Himself in majesty” (Tehillim 93:1)396Tehillim 93:1: “ה׳ מָלָךְ גֵּאוּת לָבֵשׁ, לָבֵשׁ ה׳ עֹז הִתְאַזָּר, אַף תִּכּוֹן תֵּבֵל בַּל תִּמּוֹט” — “Hashem reigns, He has clothed Himself in majesty [ge’us]; Hashem has clothed Himself, girded Himself with strength…” (the Shir shel Yom of Erev Shabbos). Meforshim: “majesty/loftiness” is ascribed to God as a garment — outward adornment, not essence. R’ Tzadok’s use: gaavah is falsehood — for even of Hashem “majesty” is spoken only “as a garment”; “He shows Himself lofty over the lofty, but to the lowly He gives grace and honor” (cf. Mishlei 3:34, “to the humble He gives grace”), and “in the place of His greatness, there you find His humility” (Megillah 31a). True greatness is thus inseparable from humility — the middah of Yaakov. — [majesty is His] only as a “garment,”
וּמִתְגָּאֶה עַל גֵּיוְתָנָא
and He “shows Himself lofty over the lofty,”
אֲבָל לַעֲנִיִּים יִתֵּן חֵן וְכָבוֹד
but to the lowly He grants grace and honor,
וּבִמְקוֹם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ אַתָּה מוֹצֵא עַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ

and “in the place of His greatness, there you find His humility” (Megillah 31a)397Megillah 31a: “R’ Yochanan said: Wherever you find the might [gevuraso] of the Holy One, blessed be He, there you find His humility [anvesanuso]. This is written in the Torah, repeated in the Prophets, and stated a third time in the Writings.” (The very “greatness” of Hashem is where His self-lowering is found.).
וְזֶהוּ צוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁחֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד

And this is the “form of Yaakov Avinu” that is engraved upon the Throne of Glory (Chullin 91b)398Chullin 91b: On “and behold, angels of God ascending and descending on it” (Bereishis 28:12): the angels “were ascending on high and gazing at his image [deyokno], and descending below and finding him sleeping” — for the features [ikonin] of Yaakov are engraved upon the Throne of Glory.399R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis §8): “‘and the likeness of Havayah he beholds’ — for the form of Yaakov is engraved on the Throne; Yaakov was like Adam before the corruption, and ‘the beauty of Yaakov was of the beauty of Adam ha-Rishon’ (Bava Basra 58a).” This deepens §6-4’s “form of Yaakov engraved on the Throne”: Yaakov’s engraved image is the restored image of Adam before the fall — man in his true stature, “I dwell on high, yet with the crushed and lowly” — so that his anavah is not smallness but the very form in which greatness and lowliness are one.,
דְּ״אֲנִי מָרוֹם אֶשְׁכּוֹן וְאֶת דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ״

[embodying] “I dwell on high — yet with the crushed and lowly of spirit” (Yeshayahu 57:15)400Yeshayahu 57:15: “כִּי כֹה אָמַר רָם וְנִשָּׂא שֹׁכֵן עַד וְקָדוֹשׁ שְׁמוֹ, מָרוֹם וְקָדוֹשׁ אֶשְׁכּוֹן, וְאֶת דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ, לְהַחֲיוֹת רוּחַ שְׁפָלִים וּלְהַחֲיוֹת לֵב נִדְכָּאִים” — “For thus says the High and Exalted One who dwells forever, whose Name is Holy: I dwell on high and holy — yet [am I] with the crushed and lowly of spirit, to revive the spirit of the lowly and the heart of the crushed.” Rashi: though God dwells on high, He rests His Presence upon the humble and contrite. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is precisely the “form of Yaakov engraved on the Throne of Glory” (Chullin 91b) — the joining of “marom eshkon” (greatness) with “es daka u-shfal ruach” (humility); the very union of loftiness and lowliness that is Yaakov’s middah.:
וְהָיוּ הַמַּלְאָכִים מַבִּיטִים לְמַעְלָה וְרוֹאִים צוּרָתוֹ, וְכֵן לְמַטָּה, דְּהָיוּ עוֹלִים וְיוֹרְדִים בּוֹ

the angels would gaze upward and behold his form, and likewise below, “ascending and descending upon him” (Bereishis 28:12)401Bereishis 28:12: “וַיַּחֲלֹם וְהִנֵּה סֻלָּם מֻצָּב אַרְצָה וְרֹאשׁוֹ מַגִּיעַ הַשָּׁמָיְמָה, וְהִנֵּה מַלְאֲכֵי אֱלֹקִים עֹלִים וְיֹרְדִים בּוֹ” — “and he dreamed, and behold, a ladder set on the earth whose top reached heaven; and behold, the angels of God ascending and descending upon him.” Yaakov’s dream at Beis-El (Vayeitzei). Meforshim (Bereishis Rabbah 68:12; Chullin 91b): “bo” is read “upon him [Yaakov]” — the angels ascended to gaze at his form engraved on the Throne and descended to behold that same form in the sleeping Yaakov below. R’ Tzadok’s use: this “ascending and descending upon him” is the joining of Yaakov’s greatness (his image on high) with his humility (his lowly form below) — “the place of his greatness is the place of his humility.” —
דְּהַיְינוּ מְקוֹם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ וְעַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ
which is [precisely] the joining of his greatness and his humility.
וְכֵן הוּא צוּרַת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם
And so is the form of man in the world:
שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (חֲגִיגָה יג:) דְּ״גָאֶה בְּכֻלָּם״ — אָדָם שֶׁמִּתְגָּאֶה עַל הַכֹּל

the Sages said (Chagigah 13b)402Chagigah 13b: Concerning the four faces of the chayah of the Merkavah — “the face of a man, the face of a lion, the face of an ox, and the face of an eagle” (Yechezkel 1:10) — the face of the man is the “great face” [appei ravrevei], the chief of them all. (So too the form of man is the highest of forms in the world.) that “the proudest of them all” [among the four faces of the Merkavah] is [the face of] man, who exalts himself over all,
וְעִיקַּר הַשֵּׁם מוֹרֶה פְּחִיתוּת
yet the very name [adam] indicates lowliness,

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹטָה ה.]403Sotah 5a: R’ Yochanan: “adam [man is a hint to] efer (ash), dam (blood), marah (bile)” — the theme of the sugya being the condemnation of arrogance (gassus ha-ruach) and the worth of a humble, lowly spirit. דְּ״מוֹרֶה״ — אֵפֶר, דָּם, מָרָה
as they said [in Sotah 5a]: it “instructs” [moreh] — efer (ash), dam (blood), marah (bile).
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת מֻרְכָּב מִנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֲצוּבָה מֵעוֹלַם הַכִּסֵּא לְמַעְלָה מִמַּלְאָכִים
This is because man is truly composed of a soul hewn from the world of the Throne, above the angels,
וְגוּף עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַשִּׁפְלוּת
and a body of dust from the earth, which is the utmost lowliness.
וְנֶפֶשׁ הוּא חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ מִמַּעַל, וּמִצִּידָהּ הוּא הַדְּבֵיקוּת בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

The soul is “a portion of God from above” (Iyov 31:2)404Iyov 31:2: “וּמֶה חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ מִמָּעַל, וְנַחֲלַת שַׁדַּי מִמְּרֹמִים” — “and what is the portion of God from above, and the heritage of Shakai from on high?” From Iyov’s closing avowal (ch. 31). This half-verse became the classic proof-text (in the Zohar and the mussar tradition) that the neshamah is “a portion of God from above” — a Divine portion within man. R’ Tzadok’s use: man is composed of this exalted soul — “hewn from the world of the Throne, above the angels” — together with a body of dust, the utmost lowliness; and from the soul’s side comes the cleaving to Hashem, so that the very height of the soul is what makes man liable to the yetzer of pride., and from its side comes the cleaving to Hashem;
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר בִּיהוֹשָׁפָט ״וַיִּגְבַּהּ לִבּוֹ בְּדַרְכֵי ה׳״

and regarding this it says of Yehoshafat, “and his heart was elevated in the ways of Hashem” (Divrei HaYamim II 17:6)405Divrei HaYamim II 17:6: “וַיִּגְבַּהּ לִבּוֹ בְּדַרְכֵי ה׳, וְעוֹד הֵסִיר אֶת הַבָּמוֹת וְאֶת הָאֲשֵׁרִים מִיהוּדָה” — “and his heart was elevated in the ways of Hashem, and he further removed the high places and the Asherim from Yehudah” — of the righteous King Yehoshafat. Meforshim (Rashi, Metzudos): his heart was raised up — emboldened and exalted — in the service of God, a praiseworthy “loftiness of heart” (as opposed to sinful pride). R’ Tzadok’s use: there is a legitimate elevation of heart, from the side of the soul (the “portion of God from above”), which is the true cleaving to Hashem — yet “through this very loftiness the yetzer can insinuate coarseness of spirit,” turning genuine spiritual height into self-importance (as befell R. Elazar b’R. Shimon with his Torah).406R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §29): “one needs elevation of heart [gavhus ha-lev] — for perhaps ‘it is for this you were fashioned,’ to subdue [the yetzer]; as (Bava Basra 16a) ‘You created tzaddikim [and You created reshaim]’… only ‘the opening is from the side.’” This is §6-4’s knife-edge exactly: the soul’s God-given loftiness (“his heart was elevated in the ways of Hashem”) is needed — one must know he is “a portion of God” fit to overcome — yet that very height is where “the yetzer can insinuate coarseness of spirit,” the opening it takes “from the side.”.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְהַכְנִיס בּוֹ יֵצֶר רָע גַּסּוּת הָרוּחַ

But through this [very loftiness] the evil inclination can insinuate into him coarseness of spirit — precisely the height of the soul becomes the yetzer’s foothold, turning genuine spiritual elevation into self-importance;
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּתַעֲנִית בְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן שֶׁלָּמַד תּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה וְזָחָה דַעְתּוֹ, וְנִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ הָאָדָם מְכוֹעָר

along the lines of what is brought in Taanis, of R. Elazar b’R. Shimon, who had learned much Torah and grew conceited, whereupon there happened upon him the “ugly man”407Taanis 20a: R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon, returning from his teacher’s house riding on a donkey by a riverbank, was in high spirits and conceited over how much Torah he had learned. A strikingly ugly man greeted him, “peace upon you, Rebbi,” but he did not return the greeting, saying, “Empty one! how ugly is that man — are all the people of your town as ugly as you?” The man replied, “I do not know; but go and tell the Craftsman who made me, ‘how ugly is this vessel You have made!’” Realizing he had sinned, he dismounted and prostrated himself before him [in apology]. — the encounter engineered to puncture exactly that Torah-born pride.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהַיֹּפִי וְהַכִּיעוּר בַּתּוֹרָה וּבְדִבְרֵי רַז״ל הַכֹּל בְּעִנְיָנֵי הַנַּפְשִׁיִּים
And it is known that “beauty” and “ugliness” in the Torah and the words of the Sages all refer to matters of the soul;
וְגִילָּה לוֹ דָּבָר זֶה דְּהַכֹּל מֵהָאוּמָן שֶׁעֲשָׂאַנִי
and [the ugly man] revealed to him this very point: that everything is from “the Craftsman who made me,”
וְאִם לָמַדְתָּ תּוֹרָה הַרְבֵּה אַל תַּחְזִיק טוֹבָה לְעַצְמְךָ כְּאִלּוּ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתְךָ גָּרְמָה

and if you have learned much Torah, do not hold the credit to yourself, as though your own effort brought it about (Avos 2:8)408Avos 2:8: “Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai [said]: If you have learned much Torah, do not hold the credit to yourself [al tachzik tovah le-atzmecha], for it was for this that you were created.” (Whatever good one has is only from Him.),
רַק כִּי לְכָךְ נוֹצַרְתָּ
but rather “it is for this that you were fashioned”;
וּבֶאֱמֶת נֶאֱמַר ״בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ״

for in truth it says, “Before I formed you in the belly I knew you” (Yirmeyah 1:5)409Yirmeyah 1:5: “בְּטֶרֶם אֶצָּרְךָ בַבֶּטֶן יְדַעְתִּיךָ, וּבְטֶרֶם תֵּצֵא מֵרֶחֶם הִקְדַּשְׁתִּיךָ, נָבִיא לַגּוֹיִם נְתַתִּיךָ” — “Before I formed you in the belly I knew you, and before you emerged from the womb I sanctified you; a prophet to the nations I appointed you” — God’s word to Yirmeyahu at his calling. Rashi: he was designated for prophecy from before his birth. R’ Tzadok’s use: this seals the lesson of the “ugly man” and of Avos 2:8 — “if you have learned much Torah, do not hold the credit to yourself… for it is for this that you were fashioned [notzarta]”: whatever a person is and attains is “from the Craftsman who made him,” fixed already “before I formed you in the belly,” so the tzaddik must not suppose that his own striving is the cause — “the essence of whatever good he has is only from Him.”Maharal parallel - Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2 and 7:2: Maharal's analysis of ga'avah clarifies why R. Tzadok places kavod and self-importance among the root forces opposed to Yaakov. In Netiv HaAnavah 3, Maharal describes pride as an improper "addition" to the person and compares the baal ga'avah to an asherah that grows upward as a foreign, idolatrous excrescence; ga'avah is thus bound to avodah zarah because the person gives independent weight and elevation to the self. In ch. 7 he adds a subtler warning: Torah itself is genuinely elevated, and a talmid chacham may therefore be exposed to a refined residue of pride precisely because of the objective greatness of Torah. The corrective is to be "soft like a reed": the higher the reed grows, the more it bends. This complements R. Tzadok's pairing of Yaakov's emes with anavah. Yaakov's greatness is not self-negation born of worthlessness, but the refusal to treat any excellence as self-generated. The more truth a person receives, the less room remains for autonomous self-glorification..

items.h: The theme: Though all is in one’s free choice, “in truth all is from Hashem” — the secret of yedi’ah and bechirah (Divine knowledge and free will). Where there is [Divine] knowledge there is no [creaturely] choice, and where there is choice there is no grasp of His knowledge; true humility is a person’s real greatness — recognizing that Hashem is with him and all is from Him. This is Israel’s superiority over converts.

p: [ה] וְאַף דְּהַכֹּל בִּבְחִירָה
And even though everything is [given over] to [man’s] free choice,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן בְּבָבָא בַתְרָא ״בָּרָאתָ צַדִּיקִים בָּרָאתָ רְשָׁעִים״

nonetheless they also said in Bava Basra, “You created the righteous, You created the wicked”410Bava Basra 16a: Rava said: Iyov sought to exempt the whole world from judgment. He said before Him, “Master of the world — You created the ox with cloven hooves and the donkey with closed hooves; You created Gan Eden and You created Gehinnom; You created the righteous and You created the wicked [the latter by way of the evil inclination] — who can stop You?” [i.e., since God made the yetzer hara, the sinner is as though compelled — an argument the Gemara rejects, though it reflects that “all is from Him.”] —
וְכֵן בְּבִרְכַּת רַבִּי נְחוּנְיָא בֶּן הַקָּנָה עַל ״שֶׁשָּׂם חֶלְקִי מִיּוֹשְׁבֵי בֵּית הַמִּדְרָשׁ״

and likewise in the blessing of R. Nechunya ben HaKanah, [thanking Hashem] “that He set my portion among those who sit in the beis midrash” (Berachos 28b)411Berachos 28b: “R’ Nechunia ben Hakanah would pray upon his exit from the beis midrash: ‘I give thanks before You, Hashem my God, that You have set my portion among those who sit in the beis midrash, and did not set my portion among those who sit on [street] corners.’” —
דְּעַל הָאֱמֶת הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
[showing] that in truth everything is from Hashem.
וְכַיָּדוּעַ מִסּוֹד הַיְדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה שֶׁנִּתְקַשָּׁה בּוֹ הָרַמְבַּ״ם

And as is known from the secret of [Divine fore-]knowledge and [human] free-choice, with which the Rambam grappled (Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5)412Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5: the Rambam confronts the classic difficulty — if the Holy One foreknows whether a person will be righteous or wicked, how can his choice be free? He answers that God and His knowledge are one (His knowing is not something added to His essence), and therefore “it is not within the power of the human mind to grasp this matter clearly”; His manner of knowing is utterly unlike ours (“ein yedi’aseinu ki-yedi’aso”) — yet, he insists, “without doubt a person’s deeds are in his own hand,” and free choice is a firm foundation of the Torah. R’ Tzadok’s use: the Rambam’s very acknowledgment that he had “no [full] resolution” — for our knowing is not like His — is itself the true resolution: [Divine] knowledge and [human] choice occupy different “places,” and both are real.,
וְגִילָּה שָׁם תַּכְלִית יְדִיעָתוֹ בְּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יָדַע תֵּירוּץ עַל זֶה
and there revealed the very summit of his knowledge in saying that he had no [full] resolution for it,
כִּי אֵין יְדִיעָתֵנוּ כִּידִיעָתוֹ
“for our knowing is not like His knowing” —
וְהוּא הַתֵּירוּץ הָאֲמִיתִּי עַל קֻשְׁיָא זוֹ
and that [very admission] is the true resolution of this difficulty,
וְלֹא כְּהָרַאֲבַ״ד שֶׁכָּתַב שֶׁהִנִּיחָהּ בְּקֻשְׁיָא

and not as the Ra’avad [charged], that he “left it as a difficulty.”413Hasagos HaRa’avad (ad loc.): R’ Avraham ben David objected that the Rambam “did not act in the manner of the wise — one should not begin a matter he cannot bring to completion; he opened with questions and difficulties and left the matter in a difficulty.” R’ Tzadok defends the Rambam against the charge: far from leaving it unresolved, the Rambam disclosed “the very summit of his knowledge” in recognizing that the human intellect cannot apprehend how God’s foreknowledge and man’s free choice cohere — and that recognition is the answer itself, “for our knowing is not like His knowing.”
וְסוֹדוֹ יָדוּעַ בְּתִיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר חָדָשׁ וּבְסֵפֶר ״אַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת שֶׁקֶל כֶּסֶף״ מֵהָאֲרִ״י ז״ל

Its secret is known [as expounded] in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and in the sefer Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef of the Arizal.414Tikkunei Zohar Chadash and Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: the “secret” of yedi’ah (Divine knowledge) and bechirah (free choice) is expounded in the Kabbalah — in Tikkunei Zohar Chadash, and in Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef, a work of the Arizal’s Kabbalah (its title drawn from “four hundred silver shekels,” Bereishis 23:16). There the two are set on different planes of the supernal roots: from the side of God’s knowledge (the higher unity) there is no independent “choice,” while free choice belongs to the “place” of this lower world — so that the two do not contradict. R’ Tzadok points to these as the mystical ground of the principle that “in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge.”415R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §47): “One must ascend to Hashem through an inquiry that is above the grasp of the intellect. For with the human intellect it is impossible to grasp the truth of this matter fully, as is known — as the Rambam wrote concerning the difficulty of [Divine] foreknowledge and [human] free choice. Only the Children of Israel, upon whom the light of Torah — ‘in which truth is written’ — has shone, grasp this: the Torah-scholars, called by the name ‘Israel,’ grasp it by way of chochmah — and this is what the name ‘Israel’ denotes, from ‘for you have striven [with the Divine and with men and have prevailed]’ (Bereishis 32:29), that he became a ‘prince’ over the angels — and this is from the complete cleaving to the ultimate truth.” And Tzidkas HaTzaddik (os 40) puts it most pointedly — citing the very same source adduced here, the Arizal at the end of Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: “The essence of teshuvah is that Hashem so illumine a person’s eyes that the willful sins become as merits — that is, that he recognize and understand that all he sinned was, too, by the will of Hashem… and this is the matter of yedi’ah and bechirah that the Arizal explained at the end of Arba Me’os Shekel Kesef: that both are true, each in its own place — in the place of choice there is no place for [His] knowledge, and in the place of [His] knowledge there is in truth no place for choice.
