And when one attains this tremendous light, then all his willful sins are [seen] never to have departed from the depth of Hashem’s knowledge — He, His knowing, and His will being all One; and since Hashem willed it so, all is indeed merits, and one attains the complete atonement of Yom Kippur.”416R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §11): “it returns to the question of yedi’ah u’bechirah; and what the Rambam wrote (Hilchos Teshuvah 5) — which is the prophet’s ‘for My thoughts are not your thoughts’ — intends what Zohar Chadash says: that in the place where there is [Divine] knowledge there is no choice at all, and there is a place that Hashem created where choice is handed over to man.” This is §6-5’s gist almost word for word — “in the place of knowledge there is no choice, and in the place of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge” — and, like the se’if, it reads the Rambam’s “our knowing is not like His knowing” not as an unsolved difficulty but as the answer itself.
וְתֹרֶף הָעִנְיַן דְּבִמְקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה אֵין בְּחִירָה, וּבִמְקוֹם הַבְּחִירָה אֵין הַשָּׂגָה לִידִיעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
And the gist of the matter is: in the “place” of [His] knowledge there is no [creaturely] choice, and in the “place” of choice there is no grasp of His knowledge.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּהַבְּחִירָה הוּא רַק מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
That is, free choice exists only from the vantage of this world,
וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁעֲדַיִין דָּבוּק בְּחוּמְרִיּוּת וְאֵינוֹ דָּבוּק לְגַמְרֵי בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
and so long as one is still attached to physicality and not wholly cleaving to Him,
וְאָז אֵינוֹ בְּתַכְלִית שְׁלֵימוּת הַבְּחִירָה עֲדַיִין
he is not yet at the ultimate perfection of “choice” —
שֶׁהוּא לִידָּבֵק בֵּאלֹקִים חַיִּים לְגַמְרֵי
which is to cleave utterly to the living God;
דְּאָז כְּשֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ מַשִּׂיג הָאֱמֶת שֶׁאֵין בְּחִירָה
for when one reaches that level he grasps the truth that there is no [independent] choice,
וְאֵינוֹ בְּצִדְקָתוֹ וּבְיֹשֶׁר לְבָבוֹ
and that [what he attained] is not [owing] to his own righteousness and the uprightness of his heart.
וְהַגֵּיאוּת הוּא מִצַּד הַשִּׁפְלוּת וְהַחוֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ
And haughtiness comes [precisely] from the lowly, material side within him,
וְאָז גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְרוֹמָם מִמֶּנּוּ
and then Hashem, too, is “removed on high” from him;
שֶׁאִלּוּ הָיָה מַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עִמּוֹ וְשֶׁהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ אֵין מָקוֹם לְגֵיאוּת
for were he to recognize that Hashem is with him and that all is from Him, there would be no place for haughtiness at all,
דְּאָז הוּא בִּמְקוֹם גְּדֻלָּתוֹ וְשָׁם עַנְוְתָנוּתוֹ
for then he stands “in the place of His greatness,” and there [is] His humility.
וְנִמְצָא הָעֲנָוָה הוּא הַגַּדְלוּת דְּאָדָם, כַּאֲשֶׁר נַפְשׁוֹ דְּבוּקָה בִּמְקוֹרָהּ

It emerges that humility is [in fact] a person’s greatness — when his soul cleaves to its Source — the paradox being that the nearer one draws to the Source of all, the less room remains to imagine any attainment as his own doing.
וְהַגֵּיאוּת הוּא מִצַּד הַגּוּף הַמְרוּחָק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמִּצִּידוֹ הַבְּחִירָה
Haughtiness comes from the body, distant from Hashem, from whose side [comes] “choice”;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא הַגֵּיאוּת כְּאִלּוּ הוּא הַמִּשְׁתַּדֵּל וּבוֹחֵר בַּטּוֹב
and through this comes haughtiness, as if it were he who exerts himself and chooses the good.
וְכָל בַּקָּשַׁת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה הָיָה ״אִם יִהְיֶה אֱלֹהִים עִמָּדִי (וּשְׁמָרַנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ הַזֶּה)״ וְגוֹמֵר, אָז ״וְהָיָה ה׳ לִי לֵאלֹהִים״

And Yaakov Avinu’s entire request was, “If God will be with me (and guard me on this way),” [and only] then “Hashem will be a God to me” (Bereishis 28:20–21)417Bereishis 28:20–21: “וַיִּדַּר יַעֲקֹב נֶדֶר לֵאמֹר: אִם יִהְיֶה אֱלֹקִים עִמָּדִי וּשְׁמָרַנִי בַּדֶּרֶךְ הַזֶּה אֲשֶׁר אָנֹכִי הוֹלֵךְ […] וְשַׁבְתִּי בְשָׁלוֹם אֶל בֵּית אָבִי, וְהָיָה ה׳ לִי לֵאלֹקִים” — “and Yaakov vowed a vow, saying: If God will be with me and guard me on this way that I go… then Hashem will be a God to me.” Yaakov’s vow as he set out for Charan (Vayeitzei). Meforshim (Rashi, Ramban): Yaakov made his service depend on God’s help and protection. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yaakov’s whole request was “im yihyeh Elokim imadi” — for he knew that “were the Holy One not to help him, he could not prevail” (Sukkah 52b); all attainment hinges on God’s being “with him,” and only then can he serve — the recognition that “all is from Him,” which is the very antithesis of haughtiness. —
דְּיָדַע שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ אֵין יָכוֹל לוֹ

for he knew that “were the Holy One not to help him, he could not prevail” (Sukkah 52b)418Sukkah 52b: “R’ Shimon ben Lakish said: A person’s [evil] inclination overpowers him every day and seeks to kill him — ‘the wicked one watches for the righteous and seeks to slay him’ (Tehillim 37:32) — and were it not that the Holy One, blessed be He, helps him, he could not prevail against it, as it says (Tehillim 37:33), ‘Hashem will not abandon him in his hand.’”,
רַק אִם הוּא יִהְיֶה עִמָּדִי וְיִשְׁמְרֵנִי אָז יִהְיֶה
but only if He be with me and guard me, then will it be;
וְהַמַּצֵּבָה (יִהְיֶה בֵּית אֱלֹהִים) שֶׁאוּכַל לְעָבְדוֹ
and the pillar [“will be a house of God”] — that I may [be able to] serve Him.
וְזֶה מִידָה יְתֵירָה שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מִבַּגֵּרִים

And this is a superior quality that Israel has over converts,419R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §3): “from an arousal-from-Above entirely, in the sense of ‘draw me after You, we will run,’ and like the coercion of the mountain as a barrel at Sinai — that Hashem forced them, to show that they are rooted in the very essence of their root in holiness, and cannot detach themselves from the holiness of Israel.” This is §6-5’s “superior quality Israel has over converts”: for Israel “Hashem is a God to them first, and only then ‘and they’” — He draws them after Him (“draw me after You”), for their root is in Him; the convert, lacking that, must let his own effort come first.
שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּפֶרֶק עֲשָׂרָה יוֹחֲסִין] דְּמִקּוֹדֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָהֶם לֵאלֹקִים, וַהֲדַר ״וְהֵם״ כו׳

as is brought [in the chapter Asarah Yuchsin, Kiddushin 70b]: that regarding Israel [Scripture places] Hashem “as a God to them” first, and only afterward “and they [shall be a people to Me],” etc.420Kiddushin 70b: Rabbah bar Rav Huna said: this is the added distinction between Israel and converts — for of Israel it is written (Yechezkel 37), “and I will be their God and they shall be My people” [Rashi: since I draw them near, they become My people], whereas of converts it is written (Yirmeyah 30), “who is this that has pledged his heart to draw near to Me, says Hashem — and you shall be My people and I will be your God” [they are not drawn near from Heaven; rather they draw themselves near first]. —
הוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה״

this being along the lines of “Draw me after You, we will run” (Shir HaShirim 1:4)421Shir HaShirim 1:4: “מָשְׁכֵנִי אַחֲרֶיךָ נָּרוּצָה” — “Draw me after You, we will run” (treated more fully at Siman 5 §5). In the love-allegory of the Holy One and Knesses Yisrael, Israel asks God to draw her first, and only then does she “run” after Him — the initial arousal must come from Above. R’ Tzadok’s use here: this is Israel’s superiority over converts — for Israel, Scripture places Hashem “as a God to them” first and “they [a people to Me]” only afterward (Kiddushin 70b); Israel apprehends that God alone directs “every detail of a person’s thoughts,” so the drawing precedes — whereas the convert reckons that his own effort came first.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Korach 2; Beit Yaakov on Torah, Bereshit 69:1: This se'if's yedi'ah-bechirah tension is central to Izhbitz, and the school itself supplies an important boundary against misunderstanding it. Mei HaShiloach, Korach 2, explains Korach's claim that at the deepest level "everything is in the hands of Heaven, even fear of Heaven." The teaching then says that Hashem specifically conceals this depth in olam ha-zeh so that human beings experience themselves as baalei bechirah and avodah can exist; if Divine direction were fully transparent, no meaningful human service would grow. Beit Yaakov, Bereshit 69:1, develops the same point through Kayin. Kayin argues "hashomer achi anochi" as though the overwhelming anger that led to Hevel's death proved that he had no choice. Hashem rejects that defense: the crying blood demonstrates that the deficiency lay in Kayin and that he did possess bechirah. These sources are a precise complement to R. Tzadok. "In truth all is from Hashem" is a truth disclosed from the deeper Divine perspective and, ultimately, after the avodah and teshuvah; it is not a practical heter before the act. Within the lived world of Torah, a person must treat the choice before him as real, binding, and his responsibility..
כִּי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַשִּׂיגִים כֵּן דְּרַק הוּא הַמַּנְהִיג בְּכָל פְּרָטֵי מַחְשְׁבוֹת אָדָם וְתַחְבּוּלוֹתָיו, וְשֶׁהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ
For Israel apprehend that it is He alone who directs every detail of a person’s thoughts and stratagems, and that all is from Him,
וּמִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְנַהֵג עִמּוֹ כֵּן
and measure-for-measure Hashem conducts Himself with him accordingly.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַגֵּרִים חוֹשְׁבִים הַדָּבָר בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם שֶׁבָּחֲרוּ בַּטּוֹב
whereas the converts reckon the matter [as achieved] by their own effort, that they chose the good —
עַל כֵּן הֵם צְרִיכִים הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם קוֹדֶם
and therefore their [own] effort must come first.

items.h: The theme: Yaakov’s whole endeavor was to clarify that “all is from Him.” Rachel is the revealed world (alma d’isgalya) — the perfected tzaddikim, comely in deed; Leah is the concealed world (alma d’iskasya) — Binah, the rung of the baal teshuvah, higher than the perfect tzaddik. Leah and her offspring “grasped the domain of hoda’ah” — the essence of teshuvah (Reuven, and Hoshea from his line).

p: [ו] וְכָל עִנְיַן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה הָיָה לְבָרֵר דָּבָר זֶה, כִּי הַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ

And the entire endeavor of Yaakov Avinu was to clarify this matter: that everything is from Him, and “there is nothing else besides Him” (Devarim 4:35)422Devarim 4:35: “אַתָּה הָרְאֵתָ לָדַעַת כִּי ה׳ הוּא הָאֱלֹקִים, אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ” — “You have been shown, to know, that Hashem is the God; there is nothing else besides Him.” From Moshe’s recollection of the Revelation (Devarim 4). Rashi: at Sinai the Holy One opened the seven heavens to show Israel that He alone is God. The Kabbalists take “ein od milvado” at its ultimate depth — that there is no true existence apart from Him. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yaakov’s whole endeavor was to clarify “that all is from Him, and there is nothing else besides Him” — this is his middah, the trait of deveikus (cleaving), the recognition that leaves no room for the illusion of independent choice or self-attainment.,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִדָּתוֹ, כַּדְּבֵיקוּת

for this [recognition] is his trait — [the trait of] deveikus, cleaving [to Hashem].423R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §14): “Outside of Him there is no iniquity or sin at all, since everything is from the truth of His will, and ‘there is none besides Him’ (Devarim 4:35). And this too is [the secret of] the wholeness of the Throne — [namely] the souls of Israel, which ‘are hewn from beneath the Throne of Glory’; and ‘the heavens are His throne’ is the soul[-root] above.” (Yaakov’s clarification that “all is from Him” is the very “recognition” that is the throne-rooted essence of the Jewish soul.)
וְעִיקַּר גִּלְגּוּלוֹ לְבֵית לָבָן הָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל רָחֵל שֶׁהִיא עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת — בֵּית יִשְׂרָאֵל

And the essential purpose of his journeying to the house of Lavan was for Rachel, who is the “mainstay of the house” (akeres ha-bayis) — the house of Israel (cf. Tehillim 113:9)424Tehillim 113:9: “מוֹשִׁיבִי עֲקֶרֶת הַבַּיִת אֵם הַבָּנִים שְׂמֵחָה, הַלְלוּיָהּ” — “He settles the akeres ha-bayis in the home, a joyful mother of children — Halleluyah” (from Hallel). Meforshim read “akeres ha-bayis” both as the once-barren woman [akarah] and, homiletically, as the mainstay of the house [ikar ha-bayis]; and the Sages apply the barren-turned-joyful mother to the Matriarchs, Rachel foremost (Bereishis Rabbah 71:2). R’ Tzadok’s use: Rachel is the “akeres ha-bayis” — the mainstay of the house of Israel — and Yaakov’s journeying to Lavan was essentially for her, since she and her offspring are the “revealed world” of perfect tzaddikim. —
כִּי הִיא יְפַת תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה, הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵאָדָם מְכוֹעָר

for she was “of beautiful form and beautiful appearance” (Bereishis 29:17)425Bereishis 29:17: “וְעֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת, וְרָחֵל הָיְתָה יְפַת תֹּאַר וִיפַת מַרְאֶה” — “and Leah’s eyes were tender, but Rachel was of beautiful form and beautiful appearance.” Yaakov’s arrival at Lavan’s house (Vayeitzei). Rashi: Leah’s eyes were tender from weeping [lest she fall to Esav’s lot]; Rachel was beautiful in form and appearance. R’ Tzadok’s use: Rachel’s beauty is read as the beauty of the soul — “the Craftsman fashioned her in beauty,” the reverse of the “ugly man” of §4 — and correspondingly her offspring are perfect tzaddikim, comely in their deeds: this is the “revealed world” (alma d’isgalya). — the opposite of the “ugly man” [of se’if 4] —
דְּהַיְינוּ בְּיֹפִי הַנֶּפֶשׁ, דְּהָאוּמָן עֲשָׂאָהּ בְּיֹפִי, וְכֵן זַרְעָהּ צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים
meaning in the beauty of the soul, for “the Craftsman fashioned her” in beauty; and likewise her offspring are perfect tzaddikim.
וְזֶהוּ עָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא
And this is the “revealed world” (alma d’isgalya),
שֶׁהֵם בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נָאִים בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם בְּכָל מִינֵי יֹפִי, כְּטַעַם ״יוֹסֵף יְפֵה תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה״

that they are, in their manifestation in this world, comely in their deeds with every kind of beauty — in the sense of “Yosef was of beautiful form and beautiful appearance” (Bereishis 39:6)426Bereishis 39:6: “…וַיְהִי יוֹסֵף יְפֵה תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה” — “and Yosef was of beautiful form and beautiful appearance.” Yosef in the house of Potifar (Vayeishev). Rashi: once Yosef saw himself a ruler he began to primp — whereupon the trial with Potifar’s wife befell him; and the Sages note that his beauty matched Rachel’s (the identical phrase of Bereishis 29:17). R’ Tzadok’s use: this shared “beauty of form and appearance” marks Yosef as Rachel’s true offspring — the revealed beauty of the soul, the tzaddik comely in his deeds, of the “revealed world.”.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָחֲזָה פֶּלֶךְ הַשְּׁתִיקָה
And this is [why Rachel] “grasped the distaff of silence,”
הַיְינוּ הַהַגְדָּרָה שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַגּוּף
that is, the [self-]bounding that comes from the side of the body,
כְּטַעַם ״לֹא מָצָאתִי לַגּוּף טוֹב אֶלָּא שְׁתִיקָה״

in the sense of “I found nothing better for the body than silence” (Avos 1:17)427Avos 1:17: “Shimon [ben Gamliel] says: All my days I grew up among the Sages, and I found nothing better for the body than silence [shesikah].” —
הַיְינוּ ״שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה״ בְּלֹא הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֶׁהוּא הַדִּבּוּר
that is, “sit and do not act,” without the “spreading-forth” that is speech,
כִּי ״בְּרֹב דְּבָרִים לֹא יֶחְדַּל (פֶּשַׁע)״

for “in a multitude of words, transgression does not cease” (Mishlei 10:19)428Mishlei 10:19: “בְּרֹב דְּבָרִים לֹא יֶחְדַּל פָּשַׁע, וְחוֹשֵׂךְ שְׂפָתָיו מַשְׂכִּיל” — “in a multitude of words, transgression does not cease; but one who restrains his lips is wise.” Meforshim: an abundance of speech inevitably leads to sin, and restraint of the tongue is wisdom (cf. Avos 1:17, “I found nothing better for the body than silence”). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why Rachel “grasped the distaff of silence” — the self-bounding of the body, “sit and do not act,” without the “spreading-forth” that is speech; “for in a multitude of words, transgression does not cease.”.
וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַמְכֻוָּן דְּבֵית יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כֵּן בְּפֹעַל גָּלוּי לַכֹּל
And this is the essential intent regarding the house of Israel — “your people are all tzaddikim” — that they be so in actual, revealed deed, [visible] to all,
וְעַל זֶה כָּל אַזְהָרוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
and it is to this end that all the admonitions of the Torah [are directed].
וְזֶה כָּל חֵפֶץ יַעֲקֹב לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלְדוֹת צַדִּיקִים הַמְקַיְּימִים דֶּרֶךְ ה׳
And this was Yaakov’s whole desire — to raise up offspring who are tzaddikim, upholding the way of Hashem,
שֶׁזֶּה כָּל עִנְיַן הָאָבוֹת לְהַעֲמִיד אוּמָה שְׁלֵימָה עוֹשֵׂי רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
for this is the entire matter of the Avos: to establish a whole nation that does the will of Hashem.
וְלֹא רָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּמִטָּתוֹ פְּסֹלֶת כְּלָל, וְעַל כֵּן אָהַב אֶת רָחֵל
He did not want there to be any “dross” in his bed at all, and therefore he loved Rachel,
רְצֹה לוֹמַר חָשַׁק בְּהוֹלָדָה כָּזוֹ דְּצַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים
that is, he yearned for offspring of this kind — perfect tzaddikim.
וְלֵאָה הָיְתָה בְּהֵיפֶךְ, כִּי הִיא סוֹד עָלְמָא דְּאִתְכַּסְיָא

And Leah was the reverse, for she is the secret of the “concealed world”429R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §74): “as the Sages said of Leah — and she is alma d’iskasya, for the intensity of the recognition is [precisely] the concealment: from the side of tzimtzum and the hiding of the light comes the revelation and the grasp above… and silence is the tzimtzum and bounding, while hoda’ah is from the side of revelation.” This unfolds §6-6’s Leah = “concealed world”: her “good is stored away within her,” for the deepest recognition lives in concealment — the reason the baal teshuvah, whose return is hidden, stands above the openly-comely tzaddik; and it even sounds the se’if’s own notes of silence (Rachel’s “distaff”) and hoda’ah. (alma d’iskasya),
הַיְינוּ דְּטוֹבִיָּה שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת צַדִּיק, אָמְרוּ ״צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב״, גָּנִיז בְּגַוֵּיהּ

meaning that her “good” — the trait of tzaddik, of which they said “[say of the] tzaddik that he is good” (Yeshayahu 3:10)430Yeshayahu 3:10: “אִמְרוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב, כִּי פְרִי מַעַלְלֵיהֶם יֹאכֵלוּ” — “Say of the tzaddik that he is good, for they shall eat the fruit of their deeds.” Rashi: declare the righteous fortunate, for they will enjoy the fruit of their good deeds. R’ Tzadok’s use: “tzaddik ki tov” — the very trait of tzaddik is “good”; and Leah’s “good” (the tzaddik-trait) is stored away within her — the “concealed world” (alma d’iskasya), outwardly unmanifest — over against Rachel’s revealed beauty. — is “stored away within her,”
וְהַהִתְגַּלּוּת לֹא כֵן
while the outward manifestation is not so.
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַבִּינָה דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב״, דַּרְגָּא דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מִצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים

And this is the trait of Binah — “and his heart shall understand, and he shall repent” (Yeshayahu 6:10) — the rung of the baal teshuvah, which stands higher than the perfect tzaddikim (cf. Berachos 34b)431Berachos 34b: “R’ Abbahu said: In the place where baalei teshuvah stand, even the wholly righteous [tzaddikim gemurim] do not stand, as it says (Yeshayahu 57:19), ‘Peace, peace, to the far and to the near’ — to the far first, and [only] afterward to the near.”432R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §10): “this is from the side of the Binah in the heart — ‘his heart shall understand and he shall repent’ — it is the portion of the clarifying of the eight rungs [of teshuvah].” This is §6-6’s Leah exactly — “the trait of Binah, ‘his heart shall understand and repent,’ the rung of the baal teshuvah, which stands higher than the perfect tzaddikim”: the return that reaches, through Binah, into a hidden depth that the never-fallen tzaddik, for all his perfection, never has cause to touch. — for the return from sin reaches into a hidden depth that the never-fallen tzaddik, for all his perfection, never has cause to touch.
וְהִיא וְכָל זַרְעָהּ תָּפְסוּ פֶּלֶךְ הַהוֹדָאָה
And she and all her offspring grasped the “distaff of hoda’ah” (thanksgiving / confession),
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּ״מוֹדֶה וְעוֹזֵב יְרוּחָם״

for this is the essence of teshuvah: “one who confesses and forsakes shall be granted mercy” (Mishlei 28:13)433Mishlei 28:13: “מְכַסֶּה פְשָׁעָיו לֹא יַצְלִיחַ, וּמוֹדֶה וְעֹזֵב יְרֻחָם” — “one who conceals his transgressions shall not succeed, but one who confesses and forsakes shall be granted mercy.” Meforshim: the essence of teshuvah is viduy (confession) joined to the abandonment of the sin. R’ Tzadok’s use: Leah and all her offspring “grasped the distaff of hoda’ah” (thanksgiving / confession) — “for this is the essence of teshuvah: one who confesses and forsakes shall be granted mercy”; hers is the rung of Binah, the baal teshuvah, higher than the perfect tzaddik — and from her line came Reuven, “the first to open with teshuvah,” and Hoshea..
וּרְאוּבֵן בְּכוֹרָהּ פָּתַח בִּתְשׁוּבָה תְּחִלָּה
Reuven, her firstborn, “was the first to open with teshuvah,”
וְכֵן הוֹשֵׁעַ מִזַּרְעוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל

and likewise Hoshea [who proclaimed “Return, O Israel”] was of his descendants, as the Sages said434Zohar, Vayeitzei (on “and Hashem saw that Leah was hated”): the editor adduces this passage for the importance of the matter — why was she hated? surely the children of a hated wife are not worthy children, yet we see that all the good sons issued from Leah! Rather, Leah corresponds to the concealed upper world (the Yovel / Binah / the world of teshuvah), all of whose matters are hidden; therefore her doings were hidden from Yaakov. Rachel corresponds to the revealed lower world (Malchus), the beginning of the ascent through the rungs. Yaakov cleaved by his outward will to the revealed (Rachel), in the secret of “and he shall cleave to his wife” — yet the “good sons” issue from the hidden root (Leah); for Yaakov corresponds to Zeir Anpin, son of Imma Ila’ah (Binah), and Rachel to the Nukva of Zeir Anpin (Malchus), called “daughter” to the supernal Abba and Imma. (Bereishis Rabbah 84:19)435Bereishis Rabbah 84:19: On “וַיָּשָׁב רְאוּבֵן אֶל הַבּוֹר” (Bereishis 37:29), the Midrash asks where Reuven had been, and answers that he was occupied “בְּשַׂקּוֹ וּבְתַעֲנִיתוֹ” — in his sackcloth and fasting, doing teshuvah for the matter of Bilhah (Bereishis 35:22). The Holy One said to him: “מֵעוֹלָם לֹא חָטָא אָדָם לְפָנַי וְעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, וְאַתָּה פָּתַחְתָּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה תְּחִלָּה — never has a person sinned before Me and repented, and you are the first to open with teshuvah; by your life, a descendant of yours will arise and be the first to open with teshuvah” — and who is that? Hoshea, as it says, “שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל עַד ה׳ אֱלֹקֶיךָ” (Hoshea 14:2). The Yefe To’ar notes that Hoshea would be the first to teach teshuvah me-ahavah — repentance from love, whereby willful sins become as merits. R’ Tzadok’s use: Leah’s firstborn Reuven, and Hoshea of his line, are those who “grasp the distaff of hoda’ah / teshuvah” — the rung of Binah, the baal teshuvah who stands higher than the perfect tzaddik.Izhbitz-Radzin parallel - Shem MiShmuel, Vayetzei 9:15; Sha'ar HaEmunah VeYesod HaChasidut, Entrance to the Gate of Beit Yaakov 24:3-4: Shem MiShmuel explicitly identifies Rachel with alma d'isgalya and Leah with alma d'iskasya, and explains that their differing modes of avodah correspond to revealed and concealed spiritual attainment: Rachel's side is more readily expressed through revealed "aseh tov," while Leah's hidden heights are reached through the inward work of "sur mera." This closely fits R. Tzadok's contrast between the externally beautiful, revealed tzaddik-rung of Rachel and Leah's Binah/teshuvah, whose beauty is initially hidden. Sha'ar HaEmunah deepens the identification of teshuvah with Binah: complete teshuvah returns a person to the place of Binah and thereby reaches "above time," where past, present, and future are not divided in the ordinary way and the past can be healed. The work explicitly links this to "u-miBnei Yissachar yodei binah la'itim" - those who know how to heal the time. The hidden world is therefore not merely less visible than Rachel's world; it is the level from which a person's apparently fixed history can be reread and repaired..

items.h: The theme: “Hashem saw that Leah was hated” — not that Yaakov hated her, but that the deeds of Esav were hateful in her eyes. Anger is the root of idolatry; Amalek is the root-“dross” of Gevurah and of all avodah zarah (declaring a power independent of Hashem). Leah’s superiority: her rejection of evil is at the root, in the heart — the trait of Yehudah, who “denies idolatry.”

p: [ז] וְזֶהוּ ״וַיַּרְא ה׳ כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה וַיִּפְתַּח אֶת רַחְמָהּ״

And this is [the meaning of] “And Hashem saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb” (Bereishis 29:31)436Bereishis 29:31: “וַיַּרְא ה׳ כִּי שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה, וַיִּפְתַּח אֶת רַחְמָהּ, וְרָחֵל עֲקָרָה” — “And Hashem saw that Leah was hated, and He opened her womb, while Rachel was barren” (Vayeitzei). Rashi: “hated” cannot mean Yaakov literally hated her — rather, He saw that the deeds of Esav were hateful to her (she had wept and prayed lest she fall to Esav’s lot), and rewarded her with children first. This verse is the axis of the whole se’if: the “hatred” is not Yaakov’s toward Leah — which would violate “lo sisna” (Vayikra 19:17) — but Leah’s inward loathing of Esav’s evil; and yet the plain sense stands too (“ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto”). —
דְּחָלִילָה שֶׁיַּעֲבֹר יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה עַל ״לֹא תִשְׂנָא אֶת אָחִיךָ בִּלְבָבֶךָ״ וְעַל לֹא דָבָר

for God forbid that Yaakov Avinu should transgress “You shall not hate your brother in your heart” (Vayikra 19:17)437Vayikra 19:17: “לֹא תִשְׂנָא אֶת אָחִיךָ בִּלְבָבֶךָ, הוֹכֵחַ תּוֹכִיחַ אֶת עֲמִיתֶךָ, וְלֹא תִשָּׂא עָלָיו חֵטְא” — “You shall not hate your brother in your heart; you shall surely reprove your fellow, and bear no sin because of him.” Rashi (from Sifra): the Torah forbids specifically hatred in the heart — concealed enmity — which is worse than open rebuke. Rambam (Hilchos De’os 6:5) counts it as a discrete prohibition. R’ Tzadok’s use: it is unthinkable (“God forbid”) that Yaakov Avinu transgressed “lo sisna es achicha bilvavecha” — and “over nothing,” toward his own wife no less — so “senuah Leah” cannot mean that he hated her. — and over nothing, no less —
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בִּהְיוֹתָהּ אִשְׁתּוֹ, וְיִהְיֶה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם ״בְּנֵי שְׂנוּאָה״

and all the more so as she was his wife, [such that] her children would be, Heaven forbid, “the children of a hated one.”438Devarim 21:15–17: “כִּי תִהְיֶיןָ לְאִישׁ שְׁתֵּי נָשִׁים, הָאַחַת אֲהוּבָה וְהָאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה… וְהָיָה הַבֵּן הַבְּכוֹר לַשְּׂנִיאָה” — the law of the “beloved” and the “hated” wife: the double portion of the firstborn goes to the bechor even when he is the son of the senuah (the less-loved wife). Meforshim (Rashi, Ramban): “senuah” here means less-beloved, not despised. R’ Tzadok’s use: were Leah truly Yaakov’s “hated” wife, her sons would be “bnei senuah” in this technical sense — yet her firstborn Reuven holds the bechorah’s “opening” (as in §6); the resolution is that the “hatred” was never Yaakov’s, but Leah’s own repudiation of Esav’s deeds.
וְעַל כֵּן דָּרְשׁוּ רַז״ל [ב״ב קכ״ג.] שֶׁשְּׂנוּאִים מַעֲשֵׂה עֵשָׂו בְּעֵינֶיהָ

Therefore the Sages expounded [in Bava Basra 123a] that “the deeds of Esav were hateful in her eyes”439Bava Basra 123a: “‘And Leah’s eyes were tender’ (Bereishis 29) — Rav said: literally tender, and this is no disgrace to her but her praise. For she would hear at the crossroads people saying, ‘Rivkah has two sons and Lavan two daughters — the elder [daughter] for the elder [son], the younger for the younger.’ She would sit at the crossroads and ask, ‘the elder — what are his deeds?’ ‘A wicked man, a highway robber.’ ‘The younger — what are his deeds?’ ‘A wholesome man, dwelling in tents.’ And she wept until her eyelashes fell out. And this is what is written, ‘and He saw that Leah was hated’ — what is ‘hated’? — Rather, the Holy One saw that the deeds of Esav were hateful to her, [and so] ‘He opened her womb.’” —
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין מִקְרָא יוֹצֵא מִידֵי פְּשׁוּטוֹ גַּם כֵּן

and yet “a verse never departs from its plain meaning,” either.440Shabbos 63a (and Yevamos 24a): “אֵין מִקְרָא יוֹצֵא מִידֵי פְּשׁוּטוֹ” — “a verse never departs from its plain meaning.” The principle that even where Chazal expound a verse midrashically (derash), its peshat is not thereby annulled but remains in force alongside the derash. R’ Tzadok invokes it for balance here: though the Sages expound “senuah” as the deeds of Esav were hateful to her (Bava Basra 123a), the plain sense — that Leah experienced herself as the less-loved wife — also holds, “ein mikra yotzei midei peshuto gam ken.”
כִּי מַעֲשֵׂה עֵשָׂו בִּרְצִיחָה, וְיִצְרָא דְּכַעַס הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ מִיִּצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁאִיבְּדוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה

For the deeds of Esav lie in bloodshed, and the inclination of anger is the root of the inclination toward idolatry, which the Men of the Great Assembly abolished (Yoma 69b)441Yoma 69b: The Men of the Great Assembly prayed against the inclination for idolatry: “they cried out [against it]” and it was handed into their power, and they neutralized it (casting a leaden seal into its mouth) — so that the “inclination toward idolatry” was abolished from Israel.,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (זֹהַר ח״א כז:) כָּל הַכּוֹעֵס כְּאִלּוּ עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
as they said (Zohar I 27b; cf. Shabbos 105b): “whoever is angry, it is as though he worships idols.”
כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּשֵׁם ״אֱלֹקִים״ הוּא לְשׁוֹן ״אֵיל״, כֹּחַ וּגְבוּרָה, שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל הַכֹּחוֹת כּוּלָּם

As is known, the Name Elokim is a term of “ayil” — power and might — [denoting] the “Master of all the forces”;442The Name Elokim as a term of “power/might”: the grammarians and the Kuzari derive Elokim / E-l from the root of “ayil” — strength, ram, mighty one (cf. “אֵילֵי הָאָרֶץ,” Yechezkel 17:13, “the mighty of the land”). Ibn Ezra and Radak (Sefer HaShorashim, root אול/איל) explain E-l as denoting power; the Kuzari (IV:1–3) treats Elokim as “the Master of all the forces” — the Governor of all the powers of nature. R’ Tzadok’s use: because Elokim is the “baal ha-kochos,” it is the Name of Gevurah — holy might, the conquering of the yetzer (Avos 4:1); and when a single “power” is “severed off” from Him and declared independent, that same term becomes “Elohim acheirim,” the root of idolatry and of the evil Gevurah of anger and bloodshed.
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יֵצֶר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (אָבוֹת ד, א)

and this is the trait of Gevurah — “the mighty one is he who conquers his inclination,” as they said (Avos 4:1)443Avos 4:1: “Ben Zoma says: Who is mighty [gibor]? He who conquers his inclination [ha-kovesh es yitzro], as it says (Mishlei 16:32), ‘one slow to anger is better than a mighty man, and one who rules his spirit than one who conquers a city.’”;
וּמִמֶּנּוּ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת ד״אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים״ בְּזֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה ״אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה אֱלֹקִים״

and from it [when fallen] spreads the “other gods,” in the “this-opposite-that” of “[God has made one opposite the other,] which God has made” (Koheles 7:14)444Koheles 7:14: “בְּיוֹם טוֹבָה הֱיֵה בְטוֹב, וּבְיוֹם רָעָה רְאֵה, גַּם אֶת זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה עָשָׂה הָאֱלֹקִים” — “In a day of good, be in good; and in a day of adversity, consider: God has made the one opposite the other [zeh l’umas zeh].” Rashi: God set good and its counterpart facing one another. The Sages (Chagigah 15a) derive from “zeh l’umas zeh” that for every holy potency the Holy One made a corresponding force in the sitra achra. R’ Tzadok’s use: the holy Gevurah — the Name Elokim, “asher asah ha-Elokim” — has its opposite “this-against-that”: the “Elohim acheirim” of idolatry, the counterfeit “power” that spreads out into anger and bloodshed.,
וּמֵהֶם מִתְפַּשֶּׁטֶת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה הָרָעָה בְּכַעַס וּרְצִיחָה
and from them spreads the evil [aspect of] Gevurah, in anger and bloodshed.
וְעַל כֵּן ״רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם עֲמָלֵק״ שֶׁהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ מִכָּל מִינֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁל כָּל שִׁבְעִים אוּמּוֹת

Therefore “Amalek is the first of the nations” (Bamidbar 24:20)445Bamidbar 24:20: “וַיַּרְא אֶת עֲמָלֵק וַיִּשָּׂא מְשָׁלוֹ וַיֹּאמַר: רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם עֲמָלֵק, וְאַחֲרִיתוֹ עֲדֵי אֹבֵד” — “He saw Amalek and took up his parable and said: ‘Amalek is the first of the nations, but his end is to perish forever’” (Bilaam’s oration). Rashi: Amalek was the first of the nations to make war on Israel. R’ Tzadok reads “reishis goyim” as root of the nations’ idolatry: Amalek is the “first” and source of all avodah zarah — the “dross” of Gevurah, the archetype of “severing off a power” and boasting “kochi ve-otzem yadi” (Devarim 8:17). — the root of every kind of idolatry of all seventy nations;446R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §20): “‘Reishis goyim Amalek’ is bloodshed — this is the first and the source of all the seven [evil] middos, and it is kinah [envy], which is the very opposite of ingathering and union.” This is §6-7’s Amalek exactly — “the root of every kind of idolatry… the root of the dross of Gevurah”: the first and source of all the evil traits, whose essence is envy and anger, the shattering of union — which is why “whoever is angry is as one who serves idols.”
דְּכָל אוּמָּה יֵשׁ לָהּ כֹּחַ מְיוּחָד שֶׁבּוֹ מִתְפָּאֲרִים ״כֹּחַם וְעֹצֶם יָדַם עָשָׂה זֶה״

for each nation has a particular “power” by which it boasts, “our strength and the might of our hand has wrought this,”447Devarim 8:17: “וְאָמַרְתָּ בִּלְבָבֶךָ: כֹּחִי וְעֹצֶם יָדִי עָשָׂה לִי אֶת הַחַיִל הַזֶּה” — “and you will say in your heart, ‘My strength and the might of my hand has wrought me this wealth’” — Moshe’s warning against the conceit that one’s own power produced one’s success (the next verse: “but you shall remember Hashem your God, for it is He who gives you strength to make wealth”). R’ Tzadok’s use: this “kochi ve-otzem yadi” is the essence of idolatry — crediting one’s own “power” with what is truly Hashem’s; each nation’s boasted “particular power” is its avodah zarah, and Amalek is the root of them all.
וְזֶהוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁלָּהֶם
and this is their idolatry.
דְּכָל עִנְיַן עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הַיְינוּ שֶׁמַּפְרִיד אֵיזֶה כֹּחַ מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאוֹמֵר שֶׁהוּא שַׁלִּיט וּבַעַל כֹּחַ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ
For the whole matter of idolatry is that one “severs off” some power from Hashem and declares it a ruler, a force in its own right.
וַעֲמָלֵק הוּא הָרֵאשִׁית וְהַמָּקוֹר שֶׁבְּכוּלָּם, כִּי הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ פְּסֹלֶת מִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה, דַּרְגָּא דֶּ״אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים״
And Amalek is the first and the source of them all, for he is the root of the “dross” of Gevurah, the rung of “other gods.”
וְאֵינוֹ נוֹפֵל אֶלָּא בְּיַד זַרְעָהּ שֶׁל רָחֵל

And he falls only by the hand of Rachel’s offspring (cf. Bava Basra 123b)448Bava Basra 123b: “The seed of Esav is delivered only into the hand of the seed of Rachel [ein zar’o shel Esav nimsar ela b’yad zar’o shel Rachel].” (Hence Esav ‘falls only by the hand of Rachel’s offspring.’) —
שֶׁהֵם הָאוֹחֲזִים בְּמִדַּת הַגְּבוּרָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה לִכְבֹּשׁ אֶת יִצְרָם
who grasp the trait of holy Gevurah, to conquer their inclination;
וְיָבוֹא מִי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ ״אֶת הָאֱלֹקִים אֲנִי יָרֵא״ דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק, וְיִפָּרַע מִמִּי שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בּוֹ ״וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים״

let the one of whom it is said “I fear God” (Yosef — the rung of Yitzchak) come and exact payment from the one of whom it is said “and he feared not God” (Amalek; Devarim 25:18)449“Let him of whom ‘I fear God’ is said come and exact payment from him of whom ‘he feared not God’ is said”: R’ Tzadok pairs two verses that share the phrase yarei Elokim. Of Yosef it is said “אֶת הָאֱלֹקִים אֲנִי יָרֵא” — “I fear God” (Bereishis 42:18); of Amalek it is said “וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים” — “and he feared not God” (Devarim 25:18). Yosef — of Rachel’s seed, bearing “the rung of Yitzchak” (holy Gevurah, the fear of Heaven) — is the one fit to overthrow Amalek, the God-denier: middah k’neged middah. The idiom “yavo… ve-yipara” (“let him come and exact payment”) is the Sages’ standard formula for such fitting retribution. (On Amalek falling only to Rachel’s seed, see Bava Basra 123b, cited just above.).
דְּאַף דְּזֶה נֶאֱמַר עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַיְינוּ דַּעֲמָלֵק פָּגַע בָּהֶם בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה, כִּי הוּא שָׁרְשׁוֹ מִצַּד אוֹתוֹ פְּסֹלֶת דְּיִצְחָק
And even though this [phrase] is said [in a context] concerning Israel, the meaning is that Amalek assailed them on this account, for his root is from that “dross” side of Yitzchak;
וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁרוֹאֶה גַּם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַרְאִית עַיִן כֵּן, יֵשׁ לוֹ טַעֲנָה לְקַטְרֵג חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עֲלֵיהֶם
and therefore, when he sees Israel too [stumble] to the eye’s perception, he has a “claim” to accuse them, Heaven forbid.
וְהַבְּרִיּוֹת הָיוּ אוֹמְרִים ״הַגְּדוֹלָה לַגָּדוֹל״
And people used to say, “the elder [daughter, Leah] for the elder [son, Esav],”
דְּמִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת הָיָה נִרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם דּוֹמֶה אֵלָיו, אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת שְׂנוּאִים מַעֲשֵׂה דְּעֵשָׂו בְּעֵינֶיהָ
for from the side of manifestation it appeared as if, Heaven forbid, she resembled him — but in truth the deeds of Esav were hateful in her eyes.
וּבָזֶה נִתְעַלֵּית הִיא עַל רָחֵל
And in this [respect] she [Leah] is elevated above Rachel:
דְּזַרְעָהּ הֵם רַק שְׂטָנוֹ שֶׁל עֵשָׂו, הַיְינוּ מְקַטְרְגִים בִּהְיוֹת הֵם טוֹבִים וְהוּא רַע
for [Rachel’s] offspring are only “the adversary of Esav” — accusers [of him] as long as they are good and he is evil;
אֲבָל אִם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יֶחְטָא הָאָדָם, הֲרֵי חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִרְאֶה דּוֹמֶה לוֹ
but if, Heaven forbid, a person sins, then he appears, Heaven forbid, to resemble him.
אוּלָם הִיא, שֹׁרֶשׁ מַעֲשָׂיו שְׂנוּאִים אֶצְלָהּ
She [Leah], however — the very root of his deeds is hateful to her,
וְהַשִּׂנְאָה הִיא בַּלֵּב שֶׁמְּמָאֵס הַדָּבָר
and this “hatred” is in the heart, which utterly rejects the thing;
וְאַף אִם בְּפֹעַל אֵינוֹ כֵן רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בְּאִתְגַּלְיָא, אֲבָל הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁבַּלֵּב אֵינוֹ כֵן
and even if in [outward] deed it is not so — only to the eye, in the revealed realm — the root in the heart is not so at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ בִּמְגִילָּה (יג.) ״הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי״

Therefore they said in Megillah (13a): “whoever denies idolatry is called a Yehudi,”450Megillah 13a: “כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי” — “whoever repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi.” The Gemara asks why Mordechai, a Binyaminite, is called “אִישׁ יְהוּדִי” (Esther 2:5), and answers that anyone who denies avodah zarah is called by the name Yehudi (after Yehudah). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the very root of Yehudah, son of Leah — the inward denial, “in the heart,” of every “power” set up against Hashem; Leah’s whole superiority lies in this root-level repudiation of idolatry, deeper than and prior to any outward deed.
דְּזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ יְהוּדָה מִזַּרְעָא דְּלֵאָה, דְּאֵין לוֹ אֱמוּנָה בַּלֵּב בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְשׁוּם כֹּחַ נֶגֶד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

for this is the root of Yehudah, of the seed of Leah: that he holds no belief in his heart in idolatry, nor in any “power” [set up] against Hashem — Leah’s whole superiority thus lies in this inward repudiation of every false power, deeper than, and prior to, any outward deed.451R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chag HaPesach §14): “(Shabbos 105b) ‘the el zar in a person’s body — this is the yetzer hara,’ that is, it is a foreign power — this is ‘a foreign god’; and the matter of the erasure of Amalek is to empty the evil from the heart.” This is the flip side of §6-7’s “denier of idolatry is called a Yehudi”: Amalek is the “foreign god” lodged within man, and Leah’s root — the heart that “utterly rejects the thing” — is the erasing of that foreign power, the inward Yehudah who holds “no belief in any power against Hashem.”Tanya and Maharal parallel - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25; Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2: Tanya's treatment of anger gives a strong conceptual parallel to R. Tzadok's association here of anger, avodah zarah, and the failure to recognize Divine rule. Iggeret HaKodesh 25 explains the dictum that one who becomes angry is "as though he serves idolatry": in ordinary worldly matters, anger arises when a person loses sight of the fact that the event confronting him has come through Divine providence. At the same time, Tanya carefully preserves the realm of yiras Shamayim and the obligation to prevent issur; the recognition of providence does not erase Torah responsibility. Maharal similarly describes ga'avah as an idolatrous growth, an asherah-like elevation of the self. Together they illuminate R. Tzadok's Leah-Esav contrast. Leah's hatred of "ma'aseh Esav" is rejection of the inner posture that grants independent ultimacy to force, rage, or self. Her teshuvah-root is therefore the opposite of avodah zarah: it acknowledges both the reality of human responsibility and the deeper truth that no power, including one's own anger or strength, possesses independent being before Hashem.

items.h: The theme: David’s rung is “va-ani tefillah” — all is received from Hashem. Yerovam (of Yosef’s line) introduced avodah zarah out of kavod — “whoever is haughty is as one who serves idols.” The two root-inclinations (avodah zarah, arayos) come from the “dross” of Esav and Yishmael; within Israel they split between Rachel’s and Leah’s seed. Leah is the root of Knesses Yisrael’s teshuvah — whose sins are “but thorns around the myrtle.”

p: [ח] וְזֶה שֹׁרֶשׁ דַּרְגָּא דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה ״וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה״

And this is the root of the rung of David HaMelech — “and I am [wholly] prayer” (Tehillim 109:4)452Tehillim 109:4: “תַּחַת אַהֲבָתִי יִשְׂטְנוּנִי, וַאֲנִי תְפִלָּה” — “In return for my love they accuse me, but I am [all] prayer.” Rashi: “I — my whole being is prayer to You.” Radak / Metzudos: even as they persecute him, David turns himself wholly to prayer. The Sages take “va-ani tefillah” as David’s very rung — he made himself into prayer, the paradigm of one who knows “he has nothing except what he receives from Hashem.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the exact antithesis of Yerovam’s haughtiness — David’s recognition that “all is from Hashem,” the rung of the King Mashiach (see the Resisei Layla parallel that follows). —
לְהַכִּיר שֶׁהַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵין לוֹ אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁמְּקַבֵּל מִמֶּנּוּ בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ

to recognize that all is from Hashem, and that a person has nothing except what he receives from Him through his prayer.453R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §36): “It is the recognition by a person that all is from Hashem — and therefore we open [the Amidah], ‘O Lord, open my lips,’ for one recognizes that even the prayer is from Hashem. And this recognition is the rung of the King Mashiach, as is known from what David HaMelech said of himself, ‘and I am prayer’ (Tehillim 109:4). For this is the entire distinction between this world — which is ‘a world of falsehood,’ in which the truth that all is from Hashem is not revealed — and the Future, when this will be revealed.”
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף, דְּעָמַד יָרָבְעָם שֶׁחִידֵּשׁ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

Not so from the seed of Yosef, from which arose Yerovam, who introduced idolatry into Israel.454Melachim I 12:28–30: After the kingdom split, Yerovam ben Nevat feared that pilgrimage to the Beis HaMikdash would draw Israel back to the house of David; “so the king took counsel and made two calves of gold, and said… ‘Behold your gods, O Israel, who brought you up from the land of Egypt,’” setting one in Beis-El and one in Dan — “and this thing became a sin.” Meforshim (Rashi, Radak): Yerovam did not truly believe in the calves; his aim was political — to secure his throne. R’ Tzadok’s use: Yerovam “introduced avodah zarah into Israel,” yet “in truth he too did not believe in idolatry”; his root was gaavah and kavod, not conviction — “whoever is haughty is as one who serves idols.”
וּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם הוּא לֹא הֶאֱמִין בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
And in truth he too did not [really] believe in idolatry,
כִּי גַּם כָּל בֵּית יוֹסֵף נִקְרָאִים יְהוּדִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁגַּם כָּל בֵּית יְהוּדָה נִקְרָאִים ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״
for the whole house of Yosef, too, is called “Yehudim,” just as the whole house of Yehudah is called “the remnant of Yosef,”
דְּכָל הַשְּׁבָטִים כְּלוּלִים זֶה בָּזֶה בְּמַעֲלוֹתֵיהֶם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל דְּהֶחְזִיר וּכְלָלָן בְּבִרְכוֹתֵיהֶם

for all the tribes are included one within another in their virtues, as the Sages said, that [Yaakov] “went back and included them [each within the others]” in their blessings.455Rashi, Bereishis 49:28 (from Bereishis Rabbah 99:12; Tanchuma Vayechi 16): on “אִישׁ אֲשֶׁר כְּבִרְכָתוֹ בֵּרַךְ אֹתָם” — “[Yaakov] went back and included them all together [chazar u-chelalan], [giving] each the blessings of the others, so that every tribe would be comprised of them all.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why “all the tribes are included one within another in their virtues” — so that the house of Yosef, too, is called “Yehudim,” and the house of Yehudah “the remnant of Yosef” (Amos 5:15); no tribe stands wholly apart from the merits of the rest.
וְעִיקַּר כַּוָּנָתוֹ הָיָה מִצַּד הַגֵּיאוּת וְהַכָּבוֹד
And his essential motive was from the side of haughtiness and honor —
כְּשֶׁיִּרְאוּ רְחַבְעָם יוֹשֵׁב וְהוּא עוֹמֵד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל [בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק]

[unable to bear] that people would see Rechavam sitting while he stood, as the Sages said [in Perek Chelek].456Sanhedrin 101b–102a: Rav Nachman said: the arrogance in Yerovam drove him from the world. For he reasoned (I Melachim 12), “now the kingdom will return to the house of David: if this people go up to offer sacrifices in the House of Hashem in Jerusalem [and see Rechavam seated while I stand, since only Davidic kings may sit in the Temple courtyard], they will say ‘this is the king and that is the servant,’ and they will kill me” — so at once “he took counsel and made two golden calves.” And (102a): “‘after this matter Yerovam did not turn back from his evil way’ (I Melachim 13) — what is ‘after’? R’ Abba said: after the Holy One grasped Yerovam by his garment and said, ‘repent, and I and you and the son of Yishai will stroll together in Gan Eden.’ He asked, ‘who will be at the head?’ ‘The son of Yishai at the head.’ [Yerovam] said, ‘if so, I do not want it.’”
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ דְּלֹא רָצָה לָשׁוּב בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״בֶּן יִשַׁי בָּרֹאשׁ״
And likewise they said that he refused to repent because he was told, “the son of Yishai [will be] at the head”;
וְזֶה הֱבִיאוֹ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, כִּי כָּל הַמִּתְגָּאֶה כְּאִלּוּ עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

and this brought him to idolatry, for “whoever is haughty is as though he worships idols” (Sotah 4b)457Sotah 4b: “R’ Yochanan said in the name of R’ Shimon ben Yochai: Whoever has haughtiness of spirit [gasus ha-ruach] is as though he worships idolatry — it is written here (Mishlei 16:5), ‘everyone haughty of heart is an abomination to Hashem,’ and it is written there (Devarim 7:26), ‘and you shall not bring an abomination into your house.’”458R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayishlach §9): “(Sanhedrin 101b) the coarseness of spirit [gasus ha-ruach] that was in Yerovam expelled him from the world.” This is §6-8’s Yerovam precisely — “his essential motive was from the side of haughtiness and honor… whoever is haughty is as one who serves idols”: the very gaavah that made him unable to bear Rechavam sitting while he stood is what drove him to idolatry and cast him from the World to Come..
וְהַיְינוּ דְּרַז״ל חָשְׁבוּ רַק שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים, דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וּדְעֲרָיוֹת

And this is why the Sages reckoned only two [root] inclinations — that of idolatry and that of illicit relations459The two “root” inclinations — idolatry and arayos: the Men of the Great Assembly first captured and blinded the yetzer of avodah zarah, and then prayed that the yetzer of arayos (illicit relations) be delivered into their hands as well (Yoma 69b; cf. Sanhedrin 63b–64a). These are the two “great” inclinations that Chazal single out. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely two — “for it was only from Avraham and Yitzchak that the ‘dross’ emerged” (Yishmael, the root of arayos; Esav, the root of avodah zarah, whose branches are anger and haughtiness); from Yaakov, the third Patriarch, no such “dross” issued. —
כִּי רַק מֵאַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק יָצְאוּ פְּסֹלֶת דְּעֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל
for it was only from Avraham and Yitzchak that the “dross” of Esav and Yishmael emerged.
וְעֵשָׂו הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר, דְּכַעַס וְגַאֲוָה הֵם עַנְפֵי יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
and Esav is the root of idolatry, as mentioned, for anger and haughtiness are the branches of the inclination to idolatry.
[וְשָׁמַעְתִּי עַל פָּסוּק ״וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ צְרוּעָה״, דְּעִנְיַן טוּמְאַת צָרַעַת בָּא מִמִּדַּת הַכַּעַס

[And I heard, regarding the verse460The Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach). Throughout Takanas HaShavin, R’ Tzadok’s “v’shamati” (“I heard”) and “v’kibalti” (“I have received”) denote teachings received from his rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef Leiner of Izhbitz, the Mei HaShiloach. Some appear verbatim in the printed Mei HaShiloach (see the Zimri teaching cited at §31, Parashas Balak / Pinchas); others — like the present one, that tzaraas stems from the trait of anger, bound up with the root of Yeravam — were transmitted from him orally. “and his mother’s name was Tzeruah” (Melachim I 11:26)461Melachim I 11:26: “וְיָרׇבְעָם בֶּן נְבָט אֶפְרָתִי מִן הַצְּרֵדָה, וְשֵׁם אִמּוֹ צְרוּעָה אִשָּׁה אַלְמָנָה” — “And Yerovam son of Nevat, an Efratite of Tzeredah — his mother’s name was Tzeru’ah, a widow.” The name Tzeru’ah echoes tzaraas / metzora, and the meforshim read such names as hinting at trait and destiny. R’ Tzadok’s received teaching: since tzaraas stems from anger (Arachin 16a), Yerovam’s blemish — traced “by way of his mother [Tzeru’ah — ‘the stricken one’]” — was the trait of anger, from which his fatal haughtiness was drawn., that the matter of the impurity of tzaraas comes from the trait of anger (cf. Arachin 16a)462Arachin 16a: “עַל שִׁבְעָה דְבָרִים נְגָעִים בָּאִין” — the plagues of tzaraas come upon a person for seven things: lashon hara, bloodshed, a vain oath, gilui arayos, gassus ha-ruach (haughtiness of spirit), robbery, and stinginess. R’ Tzadok links tzaraas here to anger — bound up with the gassus ha-ruach of this list — as the root of Yerovam’s flaw (hinted by his mother’s name Tzeru’ah): “for haughtiness is drawn from anger and the evil [side of] Gevurah, which craves to overpower all.”,
וְשׇׁרְשׁוֹ דְּיָרָבְעָם אַגַּב אִימֵּיהּ הָיָה מִמִּדַּת הַכַּעַס, דְּבָזֶה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁלּוֹ
and Yerovam’s root, by way of his mother [Tzeru’ah — “the stricken one”], was from the trait of anger, and therein lay his flaw.
וְהוּא נָכוֹן גַּם כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּהַגֵּאוּת נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַכַּעַס וּגְבוּרָה דְּרַע, שֶׁחָפֵץ לְהִתְגַּבֵּר עַל הַכֹּל]
and this accords, too, with what I wrote — that haughtiness is drawn from anger and the evil [side of] Gevurah, which craves to overpower all.]
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן חֲלוּקִים שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים אֵלּוּ בְּזַרְעָא דְּרָחֵל וְזַרְעָא דְּלֵאָה
And within Israel, correspondingly, these two inclinations are divided between the seed of Rachel and the seed of Leah;
וּלְכָךְ שִׂנְאַת מַעֲשֵׂה עֵשָׂו הוּא רַק אֵצֶל לֵאָה, שֶׁהִיא הַהֵיפֶךְ מִמֶּנּוּ מַמָּשׁ, וְלֹא שְׂטָנוֹ
and therefore the hatred of Esav’s deeds is [rooted] specifically by Leah, who is his very opposite — not [merely] his “adversary.”
וּבְאִתְגַּלְיָא הָיוּ הַבְּרִיּוֹת אוֹמְרִים דִּרְאוּיָה לוֹ
In the revealed [realm], people said she was “fitting for him” [Esav]:
הַיְינוּ דְּיָדוּעַ דְּהַשְּׁנֵי יְצָרִים הֵם זָכָר וּנְקֵבָה
that is, it is known that the two inclinations are “male and female”;
וְעֵשָׂו הָיָה דְּכוּרָא בְּיִצְרָא דְּכַעַס וַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
Esav was the “male” of the inclination of anger and idolatry,
וְחָשְׁבוּ כְּאִלּוּ הִיא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נוּקְבָא בְּיִצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת לְעֵשָׂו, שֶׁהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ דְּרַע
and they imagined that she, Heaven forbid, was the “female” of the inclination of arayos, [matched] to Esav, who is the root of evil —
וַדַּאי זִוּוּגוֹ הָרָאוּי לוֹ הוּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִיא גַּם כֵּן שֹׁרֶשׁ דְּרַע וּמִיִּצְרָא דַּעֲרָיוֹת
[reasoning that] his fitting mate would surely be one who is also a root of evil, of the inclination of arayos —
וְהִיא מָחֲלַת בַּת יִשְׁמָעֵאל

but that [true counterpart] is Machalas the daughter of Yishmael463Bereishis 28:9: “וַיֵּלֶךְ עֵשָׂו אֶל יִשְׁמָעֵאל, וַיִּקַּח אֶת מָחֲלַת בַּת יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אַבְרָהָם אֲחוֹת נְבָיוֹת עַל נָשָׁיו לוֹ לְאִשָּׁה” — “And Esav went to Yishmael and took Machalas the daughter of Yishmael… in addition to his [other] wives, as a wife.” (Bereishis Rabbah 67:13 reads Machalas as “nimchalu — his sins were pardoned” on his wedding day.) R’ Tzadok’s use: Esav’s truly fitting mate — the “female” of the inclination of arayos, matching his “male” of anger and idolatry — was Machalas, of Yishmael’s line (the root of arayos), not Leah; the crowd’s saying “the elder [Leah] for the elder [Esav]” mistook Leah’s inward loathing of evil for kinship with it. [whom Esav in fact married].
אֲבָל לֵאָה הִיא שֹׁרֶשׁ קְדֻשָּׁה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִצַּד מִדַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה
But Leah is the root of the supernal holiness of Knesses Yisrael, from the side of the trait of teshuvah —
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יֶחְטְאוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם וְיַגְדִּילוּ עֲוֹנוֹת, עִם כָּל זֶה שׇׁרְשָׁם דָּבוּק בֵּאלֹקִים
that even should they sin, Heaven forbid, and multiply iniquities, nonetheless their root remains bound to God,
שֶׁשְּׂנוּאִים מַעֲשֵׂה עֵשָׂו בְּעֵינֵיהֶם וְכוֹפְרִים בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
for the deeds of Esav are hateful in their eyes and they deny idolatry;
וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים רַק כְּהוֹצִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לְאָסָא

and all their sins are but “like the thorns that encircle the myrtle464R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §4): “‘the sins are like the thorn that surrounds the lettuce — and not in the root’; and this is from the side that our root is from Yitzchak… and thereby [Israel] becomes an actual merkavah, ‘children of the living God.’” This is §6-8’s Leah, “the root of the supernal holiness of Knesses Yisrael”: even should they “multiply iniquities,” the sins are only “thorns that encircle the myrtle” — peripheral, never the root — so that their inmost heart stays bound to God, and they remain “children of the living God.””465Sanhedrin 44a: “אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא — יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא” — “even though he has sinned, he remains Yisrael.” R’ Abba explained it by the folk-saying: “a myrtle that stands among thorns [hizmei] — its name is still ‘myrtle,’ and people [still] call it a myrtle.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s sins are “but like thorns that encircle the myrtle” — the hotzim surround and prick the surface but never reach the fragrant myrtle-essence within, whose root “stays bound to God”; this is Leah’s trait of teshuvah, whereby even multiplied iniquities cannot sever the root that loathes Esav’s deeds and denies idolatry. (The same Gemara is cited at Siman 1.) — surrounding it, pricking at its surface, yet never reaching the fragrant myrtle-essence within, which stays bound to God.
רַק לְפִי שֶׁהַגּוֹיִם אֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת לִתְשׁוּבָה, עַל כֵּן לֹא יָדְעוּ מִזֶּה
Only, since the nations have no connection to teshuvah, they did not know of this;
דְּבֶאֱמֶת הַכִּיעוּר שֶׁבְּלֵאָה, דְּ״עֵינֵי לֵאָה רַכּוֹת״, דְּזֶהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁדִּיבֵּר בִּגְנוּתָהּ
for in truth the “ugliness” [attributed] to Leah — “and Leah’s eyes were tender” — which only seemingly speaks in her disparagement —
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, אֲפִילּוּ בִּגְנוּת בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה לֹא דִיבֵּר הַכָּתוּב, אֶלָּא שֶׁהָיְתָה בּוֹכָה כו׳

[is really her praise], as the Sages said in Bereishis Rabbah: Scripture did not [even] speak disparagingly of an impure animal — rather, [her eyes were tender because] she was weeping [lest she fall to Esav’s lot], etc.466the editor notes: R. Tzadok’s wording indicates the Gemara Bava Basra 123a (cited in fn. 10), and that the matter is brought in brief in Bereishis Rabbah 70:16. The underlying principle — that Scripture will not utter a disparaging word even of an impure animal (cf. Bereishis 7:8) — is stated in Pesachim 3a.Maharal and Tanya parallel - Maharal, Netivot Olam, Netiv HaAnavah 3:2; Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25: R. Tzadok's contrast between David's "va-ani tefillah" and Yeravam's fall through kavod is sharpened by Maharal and Tanya. Maharal writes that the baal ga'avah is comparable to an asherah: pride is an alien growth because it treats the self as possessing an independent height. This is why Chazal can compare ga'avah itself to avodah zarah. Tanya makes the related point with anger: when a person experiences the human cause in front of him as an autonomous power, he forgets the Divine source of the event and enters the logic of idolatry. David's "I am prayer" represents the reverse posture. Tefillah is the admission that life, kingship, success, and even the power to serve are received rather than possessed. The more a king knows that his authority is a shefa entrusted to him, the more his malchus becomes a vessel for Malchus Shamayim; the more he claims the honor as his own, the more kingship becomes an idol of self. Thus R. Tzadok's two root-inclinations are opposite answers to the question: from where does one's power come?

items.h: The theme: The “eyes” are the essence of a woman’s beauty — the eye sees and the heart desires. True beauty is kevishas ha-taavah (mastering desire). Leah’s “tender eyes” seem a disgrace, but after teshuvah the very flawed limb becomes praiseworthy — “zdonos become zechuyos.” Re’iyah (seeing) is the letters of yirah; “all is in Heaven’s hands except the fear of Heaven.”

p: [ט] וְעִנְיַן הַגְּנוּת דְּעֵינַיִם הוּא עִיקָּר בָּאִשָּׁה
And the matter of the “disgrace” of the eyes is the essential [point] in a woman,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק ״מִבַּעַד לְצַמָּתֵךְ״] כָּל כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה

as they said [in Shir HaShirim Rabbah on “from behind your veil”]: any bride whose eyes are beautiful — her whole body needs no examination.467Shir HaShirim Rabbah 4:1 (on “עֵינַיִךְ יוֹנִים מִבַּעַד לְצַמָּתֵךְ” — “your eyes are doves from behind your veil”): “כָּל כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת — אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה; וְשֶׁעֵינֶיהָ טְרוּטוֹת — כָּל גּוּפָהּ צְרִיכָה בְּדִיקָה” — “any bride whose eyes are beautiful, her whole body needs no examination [she is surely fit]; but one whose eyes are bleared, her whole body requires examination.” (The Midrash applies the “eyes” to the Sanhedrin — the seeing “eyes” of the congregation.) R’ Tzadok’s use: the eyes are “the essential [point] in a woman,” for they disclose the inner state — hence the whole se’if turns on the meaning of Leah’s “tender eyes.”
וְהוּא כְּעִנְיַן ״הָסֵבִּי עֵינַיִךְ״ וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁ״הֵם הִרְהִיבֻנִי״

This is like “Turn away your eyes — for they have overwhelmed me” (Shir HaShirim 6:5)468Shir HaShirim 6:5: “הָסֵבִּי עֵינַיִךְ מִנֶּגְדִּי שֶׁהֵם הִרְהִיבֻנִי” — “Turn your eyes away from Me, for they have overwhelmed Me.” In the love-song of the Holy One and Knesses Yisrael, God, as it were, says that her gazing “overwhelms” Him. Rashi: “hirhivuni” — they have emboldened Me, stirred a rush of feeling within Me. R’ Tzadok reads “hirhivuni” as “they brought into Me [an aspect of] greatness and loftiness [gadlus ve-geius]” — the “eye” being the wellspring of both desire and pride, which is why He says “hasebi” (turn them away). —
וְאָמַר ״הָסֵבִּי״ שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה בְּכָךְ, לְפִי שֶׁהֵם ״הִרְהִיבֻנִי״ הִכְנִיסוּ בִּי גַּדְלוּת וְגֵיאוּת
and He says “turn away,” that He does not want [it] so, because “they have overwhelmed Me,” they have brought into Me, as it were, [an aspect of] greatness and loftiness.
כַּיָּדוּעַ עַיִן רוֹאָה וְלֵב חוֹמֵד שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ הַתְחָלַת הַתַּאֲוָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְתַאֲוָה הִיא לָעֵינַיִם״

As is known, “the eye sees and the heart covets” (Yerushalmi Berachos 1:5)469Yerushalmi Berachos 1:5: The eye and the heart are the “two agents of sin,” as it says (Bamidbar 15:39), “and you shall not go about after your heart and after your eyes” — the eye sees, the heart covets, and the instruments of action carry out [the sin].470R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §35): “‘the eye sees and the heart covets,’ and it says ‘the eye of the adulterer’; but the good eye is from the middos of Avraham, as [taught] in Avos.” This is §6-9’s “the eye sees and the heart covets, from which desire begins”: the eye is the gateway of taavah, and its rectification — the “good eye” — is Avraham’s chesed, so that the true beauty §6-9 speaks of is the mastered eye that no longer covets., from which the onset of desire [comes], as it says, “and a delight it was to the eyes” (Bereishis 3:6)471Bereishis 3:6: “וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה כִּי טוֹב הָעֵץ לְמַאֲכָל וְכִי תַאֲוָה הוּא לָעֵינַיִם, וְנֶחְמָד הָעֵץ לְהַשְׂכִּיל” — “and the woman saw that the tree was good for food and that it was a delight to the eyes…” The primordial sin begins with seeing: the eye beholds, the heart covets, and desire is born (as the Yerushalmi teaches, “the eye sees and the heart covets,” cited just above). R’ Tzadok’s use: the eye is “the onset of desire” — so mastery of the eye (Yosef, “alei ayin”) is the mastery of taavah itself..
וְעַל כֵּן בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף נֶאֱמַר ״עֲלֵי עָיִן״, וּמִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה אֵין הָעַיִן שׁוֹלֵט בָּהֶם

Therefore of Yosef’s seed it says “[a fruitful son] above the eye [ayin]” (Bereishis 49:22) — and measure-for-measure, the [evil] eye has no dominion over them (Berachos 20a)472Berachos 20a: “R’ Yochanan said: I am from the seed of Yosef, over whom the [evil] eye has no dominion [d’la shalta bei eina bisha], as it says (Bereishis 49:22), ‘Yosef is a fruitful son alei ayin [a fruitful son above the eye]’ — read it ‘olei ayin,’ [those who] rise above the [evil] eye.”.
וְעִיקַּר הַיֹּפִי הוּא בִּכְבִישַׁת הַתַּאֲוָה
And the essence of [true] beauty lies in the mastering of desire,
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים כ:] ״מִפְּנֵי מָה בָּנַיִךְ יְפֵיפִין״ בִּשְׁבִיל הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּלֵידָתָם

and regarding this they said [in Nedarim 20b], “Why are your children so beautiful?” — because of the holiness [observed] at their conception.473Nedarim 20b: They asked Imma Shalom, wife of R’ Eliezer, “why are your children so exceedingly beautiful?” She answered, “he does not converse with me at the beginning of the night nor at its end, but only at midnight; and when he converses, he uncovers a handbreadth and covers a handbreadth, and appears as one compelled by a demon. And when I asked him why, he said, ‘so that I not set my thoughts on another woman, and the children come to be as though mamzerim.’” [The children’s beauty flows from the sanctity and restraint of the parents.]474R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev §3): “for in sleep a person requires guarding, and Hashem guards him with an encompassing light — and He is”the Supporter of all the fallen."" Exactly the se’if: what is at issue is a beauty and wholeness that a man cannot maintain by his own vigilance — it is held for him from without, which is why it survives his lapses.
וּמִי שֶׁהוּא גִּבּוֹר הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ בְּתַאֲוָה אֵין כָּל גּוּפוֹ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה
And one who is a “mighty one” mastering his inclination in [the domain of] desire — his whole body needs no examination.
דְּזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּיִרְאַת ה׳, ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא תִתְהַלָּל״
For this is the rung of the fear of Hashem: “a woman who fears Hashem — she shall be praised” (Mishlei 31:30),
וְהוּא תַּרְעָא לְאַעֲלָא גּוֹ מְהֵימְנוּתָא

and it [fear] is “the gate through which to enter into faith” (Zohar I 11b)475Zohar I 11b: “Yirah [fear/awe] is the gate through which to enter within faith [yirah ihi tar’a l’aala go mehemnusa].” (Fear is the very portal of emunah.),
וּ״מָה ה׳ שׁוֹאֵל כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה״
and “what does Hashem ask of you, but to fear [Him]” (Devarim 10:12).
אֲבָל מִי שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ כְּעוּרוֹת כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה
But one whose eyes are “ugly” — her whole body requires examination;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּבְדִיקָה מִיתָה מְהַנֵּי שֶׁאֵין לְהַשְׁגִּיחַ עוֹד בִּגְנוּת הָעֵינַיִם
yet even so, upon [the proper] examination the [prior] flaw is negated, so that one need no longer regard the “disgrace” of the eyes.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי יֵשׁ שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּעֶצֶם
This is because [such disgrace] is sometimes not essential;
וּבְלֵאָה הָיָה אַדְּרַבָּא לְשֶׁבַח לְפִי שֶׁהָיְתָה בּוֹכָה כו׳
and by Leah it was, on the contrary, to her praise, for she was weeping [lest she fall to Esav], etc.
כִּי אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתִּיקּוּן, בְּאוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר שֶׁבּוֹ הַקִּלְקוּל נַעֲשֶׂה אַדְּרַבָּא אוֹתוֹ אֵבֶר מְשׁוּבָּח יוֹתֵר
For after teshuvah and rectification, that very limb through which the “spoiling” occurred becomes, on the contrary, the more praised;
וְהַגְּנַאי עַצְמוֹ שָׁב לִהְיוֹת שֶׁבַח כְּטַעַם ״זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכִיּוֹת״

and the disgrace itself turns into praise, in the sense of “[teshuvah from love turns] willful sins into merits” (Yoma 86b)476Yoma 86b: “Reish Lakish said: Great is teshuvah, for [through it] willful sins become for a person like merits [zedonos na’asu lo k’zchuyos], as it says (Yechezkel 33:19), ‘and when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness — upon them he shall live.’” (This is teshuvah from love; teshuvah from fear [merely] turns willful sins into inadvertent ones.)477R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shabbos Teshuvah (Vayeilech) §13): “he makes, against [the sins], bundles of mitzvos, and in the very limb through which he sinned he rectifies by the mitzvah he performs with it — implying that this too is ‘the same place.’” This is §6-9’s astonishing turn — “after teshuvah, that very limb through which the spoiling occurred becomes the more praised, the disgrace itself turning into praise, ‘willful sins into merits’”: the eye that saw and coveted becomes, once rectified, the very organ of praise. — the very wound, once healed, becoming the crown of the healing, so that the flawed “eye” is now her chief praise.
וּבְשִׁבְחָהּ דִּיבֵּר הַכָּתוּב לֹא בִּגְנוּתָהּ
[So here,] Scripture spoke in her praise, not her disgrace,
דְּמַה שֶּׁעֵינֶיהָ רַכּוֹת הָיָה מִצַּד שֶׁשְּׂנוּאִים מַעֲשֵׂה עֵשָׂו בְּעֵינֶיהָ, דְּיָדוּעַ דְּכַעַס וְתַאֲוָה הֵם שְׁנֵי הֲפָכִים
for her eyes’ being “tender” was on account of the deeds of Esav being hateful in her eyes — and it is known that anger and desire are two opposites.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן כְּפִי הַנִּגְלֶה בִּפְשַׁט הַכָּתוּב נִרְאֶה כִּגְנוּת וְכִיעוּר
Nonetheless, to the eye’s view — according to the revealed, plain sense of the verse — it appears as disgrace and ugliness;
וְכֵן כְּפִי פְּשַׁט לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״שְׂנוּאָה לֵאָה״ מוּסָב עָלֶיהָ
and likewise, by the plain wording, “Leah was hated” refers to her,
דְּעַל יְדֵי שֶׁשְּׂנוּאִים מַעֲשֵׂה כו׳ עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִגְרַם לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּהִיא שְׂנוּאָה
[in that] because “the deeds [of Esav] were hateful” [to her], this caused it to appear, to the eye, that she was hated —
רְצֹה לוֹמַר שְׂנוּאָה בְּמַעֲשֶׂיהָ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (קִדּוּשִׁין סח.) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְאַחַת שְׂנוּאָה״

that is, hated on account of her deeds, Heaven forbid — as the Sages said (Kiddushin 68a)478Kiddushin 68a: On “the one beloved and the one hated” (Devarim 21:15): “Is there a ‘beloved’ before the Omnipresent and a ‘hated’ before the Omnipresent? Rather, ‘beloved’ [means] beloved in her marriage, and ‘hated’ [means] hated in her marriage” — a union that Heaven ‘rejects.’ (So Leah’s being “hated” is read as hated on account of [the appearance of] her deeds.) on the verse “and the one [wife] hated.”
וְהוּא מִצַּד הָרְאִיָּה דְּ״וַיַּרְא ה׳״, כְּטַעַם ״וַיְהִי עֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״

And this is from the side of “seeing” — “and Hashem saw” — in the sense of “and Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem” (Bereishis 38:7)479Bereishis 38:7: “וַיְהִי עֵר בְּכוֹר יְהוּדָה רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳, וַיְמִתֵהוּ ה׳” — “And Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem, and Hashem put him to death.” Rashi (from Yevamos 34b): his “evil” was hashchasas zera — corruption of the seed, so that Tamar not conceive and lose her beauty. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the corruption of the bris is the ‘ugliness of the eyes’” — just as Er was “ra b’einei Hashem,” the pgam of the bris causes, as it were, an “evil in the eyes of Hashem” in the “matter Above”; the shared phrase “b’einei Hashem” binds the sin of the eye/desire to the sin of the covenant..
כִּי קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית הוּא כִּיעוּר הָעֵינַיִם
For the corruption of the bris is the “ugliness of the eyes,”
וְגוֹרֵם גַּם כֵּן בָּעִנְיָן דִּלְמַעְלָה כִּבְיָכוֹל לִהְיוֹת ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״
and it causes, as it were, in the “matter Above,” a “being evil in the eyes of Hashem.”
וְיִרְאַת ה׳ שִׂנְאַת רָע, שֶׁזֶּהוּ דַּרְגָּא דִּ״ירֵא ה׳״ הַכּוֹבֵשׁ יִצְרוֹ לִהְיוֹת שׂוֹנֵא רָע

And “the fear of Hashem is to hate evil” (Mishlei 8:13)480Mishlei 8:13: “יִרְאַת ה׳ שְׂנֹאת רָע, גֵּאָה וְגָאוֹן וְדֶרֶךְ רָע וּפִי תַהְפֻּכוֹת שָׂנֵאתִי” — “The fear of Hashem is to hate evil; pride, arrogance, an evil way, and a mouth of perversities do I hate.” Meforshim (Rashi, Metzudos): the very definition of yiras Hashem is the hatred of evil. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is “the rung of the God-fearing one who masters his inclination, becoming a hater of evil” — precisely Leah’s trait (the deeds of Esav hateful in her eyes); “fear of Hashem” and “hatred of evil” are one and the same, the antithesis of the corrupter of the bris. — this is the rung of the “God-fearing one” who masters his inclination, becoming a “hater of evil” —
שֶׁהוּא מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית כַּיָּדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר מִקְרָא דְּעֵר

[the opposite being] one who does not guard the bris, as is known in the Zohar from the verse concerning Er.481Zohar, Vayeishev (I 188a; cf. I 71b): on “וַיְהִי עֵר… רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳” (Bereishis 38:7), the Zohar teaches that Er’s sin was hashchasas ha-bris — he “spilled outward” (so that Tamar not conceive), and this “spilling” is the “ra” that blemishes the supernal bris / Yesod, the channel of holiness. R’ Tzadok invokes this — “as is known in the Zohar from the verse concerning Er”: the corruption of the covenant is the true “ugliness of the eyes,” while its opposite — guarding the bris — is the “God-fearing one” who “hates evil,” over whom the [evil] eye has no dominion (the rung of Yosef).
וּ״רְאִיָּה״ אוֹתִיּוֹת ״יִרְאָה״
And [the letters of] re’iyah (seeing) are the [very] letters of yirah (fear),
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד רְאִיַּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַיְינוּ הִסְתַּכְּלוּתוֹ בְּעָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא
this being from the side of Hashem’s “seeing” — His gazing into the revealed world;
דְּהַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם

for “all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven” (Berachos 33b)482Berachos 33b: “R’ Chanina said: Everything is in the hands of Heaven except for the fear of Heaven [ha-kol biydei shamayim chutz mi-yiras shamayim], as it says (Devarim 10:12), ‘and now, Israel, what does Hashem your God ask of you, but to fear [Him].’”Sefat Emet parallel - Eikev 24:3: Sefat Emet offers a striking parallel to R. Tzadok's equation of sight, fear, and the rectification of the eyes. On "mah Hashem Elokecha sho'el me'imach ki im le-yirah," he writes that the inward bond with Hashem is already planted in the souls of Israel, but materiality covers it; yirah opens that hidden interior. He then states explicitly, "yirah otiyot re'iyah": fear and seeing are composed of the same letters, because through yirah a person becomes able to see truth, and the Divine power concealed in the Jewish soul is revealed. He connects this to the opening of both moach and lev. This beautifully complements R. Tzadok's use of "the eye sees and the heart desires." The problem of sight is not solved merely by closing the eyes; it is rectified by transforming seeing itself. Unrectified re'iyah awakens taavah and draws the heart outward. Holy re'iyah, born of yirah, pierces the material covering and allows the heart to perceive Divine reality within what it sees. Leah's "tender eyes" can therefore become not a defect but the very place in which a higher seeing is formed through tears, fear, and teshuvah.,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עֵסֶק הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלַם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
which is [precisely] the [work] task of man in this world, which is the world of deed.

items.h: The theme: Leah’s holiness is in purity of thought (cleaving to the Divine “thought”). Every “birth” and increase of souls in Israel comes only through the teshuvah that follows sin — which bursts one’s allotted boundary and turns zdonos into zechuyos. Hence Rachel and Yehoshua bin Nun (perfect-tzaddik line) were barren; the deepest souls come through Leah — ima ila’ah, “the mother of the children.”

p: [י] וְכָל עֵסֶק קְדֻשַּׁת לֵאָה וְזַרְעָהּ הוּא בְּטָהֳרַת הַמַּחְשָׁבָה
And the entire “work” of the holiness of Leah and her offspring is in the purity of thought,
וְשֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁגִּיחַ בַּמַּעֲשֶׂה אִם לֹא כֵן
and in not fixating on the [outward] deed even when it is not [yet] so;
וְהוּא הַדְּבֵיקוּת בְּמַחְשַׁבְתּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּטַעַם ״יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלוּ בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה״

and this is the cleaving to His thought, in the sense of “Israel arose in [the Divine] thought” (Bereishis Rabbah 1:4)483Bereishis Rabbah 1:4: “Six things preceded the creation of the world; some were [actually] created and some arose in thought to be created — and the thought of [creating] Israel preceded all of them [machshavtan shel Yisrael kadmah l’chol davar].”.
וְאוּכְמָא הוּא לְגַבֵּי מַדְרֵיגוֹת שֶׁלְּמַטָּה הֵימֶנּוּ, וְשָׂנוּא לְגַבֵּי מַדְרֵיגַת הָרְאִיָּה
And [this hidden root] is “dark” relative to the levels beneath it, and “hated” relative to the level of [revealed] “seeing”;
אֲבָל זֶה גָּרַם לִפְתִיחַת הָרֶחֶם שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּלֹא דָּם וְטוּמְאָה דְּלֵידָה
but this [very “being hated”] is what brought about the “opening of the womb,” which does not come about without the blood and impurity of birth.
כִּי כָּל לֵידָה וְהוֹסָפַת קְדֻשָּׁה יְתֵירָה וְרִיבּוּי בִּנְפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַבָּאָה אַחַר הַחֵטְא וְהָרִיחוּק
For every birth, and every addition of extra holiness and multiplication of souls in Israel, comes about only through the teshuvah that follows sin and estrangement;
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְגַּדֵּל וְנִתְרַבָּה מַעֲלָתוֹ וְנִתְרַחֵב חֶלְקוֹ וְגוֹרָלוֹ שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהִתְרַבּוֹת הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר מִכְּפִי גְּבוּלוֹ הַנִּקְצָב
for through it one’s stature grows and multiplies, and his portion and lot expand, so that he can increase far beyond his allotted bound.
דְּזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה לִפְרֹץ מֵיצָרִים וּגְבוּלִים וְלַעֲשׂוֹת זְכִיּוֹת חֲדָשׁוֹת מִזְּדוֹנוֹת
For this is the trait of teshuvah — to burst through straits and boundaries, and to make new merits out of willful sins.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּדֶרֶךְ הַתּוֹרָה הַקָּצוּב וְהַמּוּגְבָּל וְאֵין בּוֹ הוֹסָפָה
Not so the perfect tzaddik, who is only upon the fixed, bounded path of the Torah, in which there is no “addition”;
וְעַל כֵּן רָחֵל עֲקָרָה, וְכֵן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן הַגָּדוֹל מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף לֹא הֲוִי לֵיהּ בְּנִין

and therefore Rachel was barren, and likewise Yehoshua bin Nun — the greatest of Yosef’s seed — had no children — for the perfectly-guarded life, never having broken its bounds, lacks the very mechanism of boundary-bursting increase that only teshuvah supplies.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר (דָּוִד) ״בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי״ וְגוֹמֵר
And therefore David said, “In iniquity was I fashioned, and in sin did my mother conceive me” (Tehillim 51:7);
וְעִיקַּר הַהוֹלָדָה מִנְּפָשׁוֹת יְקָרוֹת וּמְשׁוּבָּחוֹת כְּשִׁבְטֵי יָּהּ וְהַדּוֹמֶה

for the essential “bearing” of precious and exalted souls, such as “the tribes of Kah” and the like484Tehillim 122:4: “שֶׁשָּׁם עָלוּ שְׁבָטִים, שִׁבְטֵי יָהּ, עֵדוּת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, לְהֹדוֹת לְשֵׁם ה׳” — “for there the tribes went up, the tribes of Kah, a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the Name of Hashem.” Rashi: they are called “shivtei Kah” because the Divine Name is affixed to them, testifying to their legitimacy (cf. Bereishis Rabbah 82:11). R’ Tzadok’s use: the “precious and exalted souls, such as the tribes of Kah,” are the deep souls that come only through the rung of teshuvah (Leah / ima ila’ah) — not the “ordinary children of the world.” —
אוֹתָן שֶׁצַּדִּיקִים כְּרָחֵל וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ בִּן נוּן מִתְאַוִּים לָהֶם, לֹא כְּבָנִים דְּעָלְמָא
those souls that even tzaddikim like Rachel and Yehoshua bin Nun yearn for — not like ordinary “children of the world” —
אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי דַּרְגָּא דִּתְשׁוּבָה שֶׁהִיא אִימָא עִילָּאָה — ״אֵם הַבָּנִים״

[comes about] only through the rung of teshuvah, which is ima ila’ah (the supernal mother) — “the mother of the children” (Tehillim 113:9).485Cross-reference: the editor refers back to note 9 in this siman (the Zohar on Leah as ima ila’ah / the concealed upper world — Binah and the world of teshuvah).
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן רָחֵל, מִדַּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הַנִּקְרֵאת ״בְּרַתָּא״ וּבַת, ״שִׁמְעִי בַת וּרְאִי״

Not so Rachel — the trait of Knesses Yisrael that is called “berata” and “bas” (daughter): “Hearken, O daughter, and see” (Tehillim 45:11)486Tehillim 45:11: “שִׁמְעִי בַת וּרְאִי וְהַטִּי אָזְנֵךְ, וְשִׁכְחִי עַמֵּךְ וּבֵית אָבִיךְ” — “Hearken, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear; forget your people and your father’s house.” Rashi / Midrash: the “daughter [bas]” is Knesses Yisrael, addressed by the Holy One as a bride. R’ Tzadok’s use: Rachel is “the trait of Knesses Yisrael called berata / bas (daughter)” — the revealed world, summoned by “shim’i bas u-r’i” (hearken and see); she is ima tata’ah (the lower mother), over against Leah’s concealed ima ila’ah.;
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק בֶּן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה] ״בֵּן״ וְלֹא הָרָאוּי לִיקָּרֵא אָב

and they said [at the start of Perek Ben Sorer u-Moreh, Sanhedrin 68b]487Sanhedrin 68b (opening of Perek Ben Sorer u-Moreh): the Torah’s “ben sorer u-moreh” (Devarim 21:18) is expounded to require a “ben” in the strictest sense — “a son, and not one [already] fit to be [called] a father” (only a boy in the brief window after maturity, before he could himself beget a child). R’ Tzadok’s parallel: just as “ben” excludes one ripe to be a father, so Rachel, called “bas (daughter),” is “not one fit to be called a mother” — ima tata’ah only, the lower and revealed motherhood, as against Leah’s supernal motherhood of teshuvah.: “a ben (son)” — and not one [already] fit to be called a father;
הָכִי נַמִי ״בַּת״ וְלֹא הָרְאוּיָה לִיקָּרֵא אֵם
so too, “a bas (daughter)” — and not one fit to be called a mother.
וְנִקְרֵאת רַק אִימָא תַּתָּאָה
[Rachel] is called only ima tata’ah (the lower mother),
רְצֹה לוֹמַר מִצַּד הַתַּחְתּוֹנִים וְעָלְמָא דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא גַּם זֶה נִקְרָא אֵם
meaning, from the side of the lower [worlds] and the revealed world, this too is called “mother.”
כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אַדְּרַבָּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר חָשׁוּב יוֹתֵר מִבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה
For in this world, on the contrary, the perfect tzaddik is more esteemed than the baal teshuvah,
כִּי ״הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם״ מִי שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת

for “man looks to the eyes” (Shmuel I 16:7)488Shmuel I 16:7: “כִּי לֹא אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה הָאָדָם, כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם, וַה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב” — “for [God does] not [see] as man sees: for man looks to the eyes, but Hashem looks to the heart.” Spoken to Shmuel at David’s anointing, as he was about to judge by Eliav’s imposing appearance. Rashi / Radak: man judges by the outward, God by the inward.
