וְזֶהוּ הָ״א״ הָרוֹמֶזֶת לְמִדַּת הַחָכְמָה, שֶׁהוּא חֲסָדִים הַנֶּעֱלָמִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, הַמִּתְחַבְּרוֹת לְאוֹתִיּוֹת ״דִּי״ן״
And this is the alef that alludes to Chochmah — the “hidden chasadim” in this world — joining to the letters “din”;
וּבִתְחִלָּתוֹ הַיְינוּ כְּפִי דֶּרֶךְ יְרִידָתָם מִלְּמַעְלָה שֶׁזֶּהוּ נֶגֶד מִדַּת יוֹם
and [the alef] at its beginning [A-D-N-Y] is according to their [the chasadim’s] descent from Above — corresponding to “day”;
וְ״א״ בַּסּוֹף [דִּינָ״א] הוּא מִדַּת לַיְלָה, שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הַסּוֹף
and the alef at the end [D-Y-N-A] is the trait of “night,” the apprehension of Knesses Yisrael, the “end.”
וְהָאַחֲרִית מִזֶּה יִהְיֶה לְטוֹב, וּלְהַשָּׂגַת פְּלָאוֹת הַחָכְמָה דִּימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ וְעוֹלָם הַבָּא
And the “end” of this will be for good — [leading] to the apprehension of the wonders of Chochmah of the days of Mashiach and the World to Come.
וְעַל כֵּן יְצִירַת הַחוֹדֶשׁ בְּאוֹת הָ״ט״ דְּ״טוֹבִיָּה גָּנוּז בְּגַוֵּיהּ״, וּמַזָּלוֹ אַרְיֵה
And therefore the “formation” of the month is with the letter tes — of “its good [tuvia] is hidden within it” — and its constellation is Aryeh [Leo].
וְנִרְאֶה לִי שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד שֵׁבֶט דָּן
And it seems to me that it corresponds to the tribe of Dan.
[וְאַף שֶׁכְּפִי מַה שֶּׁקִּיבַּלְתִּי סִדְרָן שֶׁל שְׁבָטִים נֶגֶד חָדְשֵׁי הַשָּׁנָה אֵינוֹ כֵן, בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ כַּמָּה נוּסְחָאוֹת שׁוֹנוֹת בָּזֶה, עַיֵּין מְפָרְשֵׁי סֵפֶר יְצִירָה

[And although, according to what I received, the order of the tribes vis-à-vis the months738From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): R’ Tzadok’s “I have received” here — on the true order of the tribes vis-à-vis the twelve months — is a teaching of his rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see the note at §8 above). is not so, in truth there are several different versions — see the commentators on Sefer Yetzirah;
וּלְדַעְתִּי ״אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים״, כִּי יֵשׁ בֶּאֱמֶת סְדָרִים שׁוֹנִים בָּזֶה וְכוּלָּם אֱמֶת מִצַּד זוּלַת צַד
and in my view “these and those are the words of the living God,” for there truly are different orderings, all true, each from a different aspect;
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ לֹא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה עַצְמוֹ סֵדֶר הַשְּׁבָטִים לְי״ב פְּשׁוּטוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן מְקוֹם בֵּיאוּר זֶה]
and perforce the order of the tribes for the twelve “simple letters” is not [explicitly] stated in Sefer Yetzirah itself; and this is not the place to elaborate.]
״גּוּר אַרְיֵה״ שֶׁהוּא הַיְהוּדָה שֶׁבַּשְּׁבָטִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל

“A lion’s whelp [gur aryeh]” (Bereishis 49:9)739Bereishis 49:9: “גּוּר אַרְיֵה יְהוּדָה, מִטֶּרֶף בְּנִי עָלִיתָ, כָּרַע רָבַץ כְּאַרְיֵה וּכְלָבִיא מִי יְקִימֶנּוּ” — “Yehudah is a lion’s whelp; from the prey, my son, you have risen; he crouches, lies down like a lion, and like a lioness — who shall rouse him?” Background: Yaakov’s blessing to Yehudah, the royal tribe, likened to a lion. R’ Tzadok’s use: the lion (aryeh) is Yehudah, the kingly “singular of the tribes”; and Dan, too, is called “aryeh” — the “tail of the lion” — everywhere joined to Yehudah, so that beginning and end meet as one. — [Yehudah, the “Yehudah” par excellence] among the tribes, as the Sages said;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא ״אַרְיֵה״ כִּיהוּדָה, וּבְכָל מָקוֹם מְחוּבָּר לִיהוּדָה
and nonetheless [Dan] is called “Aryeh” like Yehudah, and everywhere is joined to Yehudah,
כַּנּוֹדָע בִּמְלֶאכֶת הַמִּשְׁכָּן וְהַמִּקְדָּשׁ [בְּצַלְאֵל מִיהוּדָה וְאָהֳלִיאָב מִדָּן], וְגַם לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר
as is known in the work of the Mishkan and the Mikdash [Betzalel of Yehudah and Oholiav of Dan], and also for the days of Mashiach, as they said in the Zohar.
וְהוּא מִצַּד מִדַּת הָעִגּוּלִים דְּהָרֹאשׁ וְהַסּוֹף מְחוּבָּר יַחַד
And this is from the trait of “circles,” in which the beginning and the end are joined together;
וְגַם ״זַנְבָא דְּאַרְיֵה הוּא, וְדָן יָדִין עַמּוֹ כְּאֶחָד״ וְגוֹמֵר — מְיוּחָד שֶׁבַּשְּׁבָטִים, זֶה יְהוּדָה

and also “he is the ‘tail of the lion,’ and ‘Dan shall judge his people as one740Bereishis 49:16: “דָּן יָדִין עַמּוֹ, כְּאַחַד שִׁבְטֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל” — “Dan shall judge his people, as one of the tribes of Israel.” Background: Yaakov’s blessing to Dan. Meforshim: Rashi reads “k’echad” as “like the singular [k’meyuchad] of the tribes” — i.e., Dan’s judge (Shimshon) will be like David, of Yehudah. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why Dan, though the “tail” and rearmost of the camp, is bound to Yehudah the “head” — as in the Mishkan (Betzalel of Yehudah, Oholiav of Dan) — the “circle” in which beginning and end are joined as one.’” — [as] the “singular of the tribes,” namely Yehudah. — even Dan, the “tail,” the very rear of the camp, is a lion bound to Yehudah the head, so that beginning and end meet as one.

items.h: The theme: Shimshon and Shlomo married “foreign women” whom, per the Rambam, they converted — aiming to subdue the nations and draw them beneath the wings of the Shechinah, which is the future work of Mashiach. This is Malchus Tata’ah, the lowest rung, where “her feet descend to death” and evil is consumed. But Malchus judges only outward: the essence of the King is full of mercy, and Israel’s sufferings are a father chastening a son for his good.

p: [לו] וְשִׁמְשׁוֹן וּשְׁלֹמֹה שְׁנֵיהֶם נָשְׂאוּ נָשִׁים נָכְרִיּוֹת, וְעַיֵּין בָּרַמְבָּ״ם [הִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה (פי״ג יד—טז)] שֶׁגִּיְּירוּם עַיֵּין שָׁם

Both Shimshon and Shlomo married “foreign women” — and see the Rambam [Hilchos Issurei Biah 13:14–16], that they converted them741Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 13:14–16: the Rambam cautions, “Let it not enter your mind that Shimshon the savior of Israel, or Shlomo king of Israel who was called ‘beloved of Hashem,’ married gentile women in their gentile state” — rather, these women were converted (13:16: “Shlomo converted women and married them, and so too Shimshon converted and married”). Background: the Rambam (13:14–15) explains that a beis din did not accept converts throughout the days of David and Shlomo — suspecting ulterior motives — yet many converted before laymen, and the great court “neither pushed them away nor drew them close, until their end be seen.” R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because these wives were converts, Shimshon’s and Shlomo’s whole intent was to “subdue” the nations and bring them into holiness — a foretaste of the work of Mashiach, who “will come to teach Torah and mitzvos to the nations,” while Israel will need no teacher.Be’er Mayim Chaim — drawing the distant good into kedushah: Be’er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis 1:2:7, explains Chazal’s statement that Israel were exiled among the nations in order that converts be added to them as a process of birur: holy sparks situated in foreign environments are themselves in exile, and when Israel reaches those places the concealed holiness is drawn toward its own kind — ‘מצא מין את מינו וניעור.’ He reads ‘עת אשר שלט האדם באדם לרע לו’ in the familiar Lurianic sense that the apparent dominion of the other side ultimately becomes ‘to its own detriment,’ because Israel departs carrying out the vitality that had been trapped there. This supplies an illuminating conceptual background to R’ Tzadok’s reading of Shimshon and Shlomo. Their aim, as he has grounded it in the Rambam’s insistence that the women were converted, was not to blur Israel’s boundary but to draw what could genuinely enter beneath the wings of the Shechinah. The Be’er Mayim Chaim makes the direction of the movement decisive: holiness may descend into a distant place in order to extract what belongs to it, but it must return with the spark rather than become absorbed by the shell. That distinction is exactly what keeps R’ Tzadok’s account from becoming a license for assimilation. The future conquest of evil by Malchus is not a sanctification of foreignness as foreignness; it is the disclosure and ingathering of whatever can truly be converted into service of Hashem., see there.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּכָל כַּוָּונָתָם הָיָה לְהַכְנִיעָם עַל יְדֵי זֶה וּלְהַכְנִיסָם לִקְדֻשָּׁה
That is, their whole intent was to subdue them thereby, and to bring them into holiness,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל דְּמָשִׁיחַ יָבוֹא לְלַמֵּד תּוֹרָה וּמִצְווֹת לְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יִצְטָרְכוּ לוֹ דְּיִלְמְדוּ מִפִּי הַגְּבוּרָה, ״וְאָנוּ אֵין לָנוּ מֶלֶךְ אֶלָּא אָתָּה״

as the Sages said, that Mashiach will come to teach Torah and mitzvos to the nations of the world; but Israel will not need him, for they will learn from the mouth of the Almighty, “and we have no king but You.”
וְכָל מַלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מַלְכוּתָם עַל הָאוּמּוֹת וּמַה שֶּׁיַּכְנִיסוּם גַּם כֵּן לִמְקוֹם הַגֵּרִים תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה

And the whole “kingship of Israel” is their rule over the nations, and their bringing them, too, into the “place of converts,” beneath the wings of the Shechinah.742R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §20): “This is the whole matter of Shlomo HaMelech in marrying foreign women: he wished that all should recognize the power of Your kingship, as it will be in the Future. And this is the reason for his prayer — that the nations too should come to recognize the holiness of the Mikdash, that they turn to pray toward it, until, by force of that recognition, they too should have some power in prayer, that they be answered.” (Precisely the se’if’s account of Shimshon and Shlomo: the marriages to ‘foreign women’ were an effort to draw the nations under the wings of the Shechinah — the future work of Mashiach’s Malchus.)
וְזֶהוּ מִצַּד מַדְרֵיגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה שֶׁבְּמִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהִיא ״מַלְכוּתָא תַּתָּאָה״
And this is from the lowest rung within the trait of Malchus, which is “Malchusa Tata’ah” [the lower kingship],
וְהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּאַרְיֵה מֶלֶךְ בַּחַיּוֹת — הֵם אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַנִּמְשָׁלִים לְ״חַיְתוֹ יָעַר״, שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם צוּרַת אָדָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (יְבָמוֹת סג:) דְּאֵין קְרוּיִים ״אָדָם״

and it is the rung of the “lion, king of the beasts” — [ruling over] the nations of the world, likened to the “beasts of the forest,” who have no “form of man,” as the Sages said (Yevamos 63b)743Yevamos 61a (the base cites Yevamos 63b): “‘And you, My flock, the flock of My pasture, are man [adam]’ (Yechezkel 34:31) — you [Israel] are called ‘Adam,’ but the nations of the world are not called ‘Adam.’” that they are not called “Adam.”
וּלְפִי שֶׁ״רַגְלֶיהָ יוֹרְדוֹת מָוֶת״ כַּנּוֹדָע, וְכָל שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּלִיַּעַל הוּא רַק בְּרַגְלִין וּמַדְרֵגָה תַּחְתּוֹנָה, שָׁם הוּא מִתְהַפֵּךְ לְרַע לוֹ
And since “her feet descend to death” (Mishlei 5:5), and all the dominion of the “base man” is only in the “feet,” the lowest rung — there it “turns to his own detriment,”
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִכְלֶה הָרַע וּמְעַט הַנִּשְׁאָר יִתְהַפֵּךְ לְטוֹב

for through this the evil is consumed, and the little that remains “turns over” to good.744R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §244): “as for desire, it cannot be killed, for it is needed for the world’s continuance… but in the days of Shlomo HaMelech, "peace shall be mine" — in the sense of "then I shall turn to the peoples [a clear tongue]" — to transform evil into [good].” Exactly the se’if: Shlomo’s engagement with the nations was not concession but the messianic labor of ithapcha — turning the lowest rung over to good rather than destroying it.
וּמָשִׁיחַ יִהְיֶה הַסּוֹף הָרַגְלִין דְּהוּא מַלְכוּת שֶׁבְּמַלְכוּת
And Mashiach will be the “end,” the “feet,” which is Malchus of Malchus;
וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה יְסוֹד שֶׁבְּמַלְכוּת, וְהוּא ״זַנְבָא דְּאַרְיֵה״ מִצַּד מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁבָּאֲרִי

and Shlomo HaMelech was Yesod of Malchus, and he is the “tail of the lion” — from the aspect of the trait of Malchus within the “lion.”745R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §18): “and therefore the victory then belonged to Edom, which is the source of envy and murder… and his downfall is at the hand of the seed of [Rachel].” The se’if’s Malchus Tata’ah precisely: at the lowest rung the evil is not argued with but consumed from within, and the little that survives “turns over” to good.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ״מֶּלֶךְ בְּמִשְׁפָּט יַעֲמִיד אָרֶץ״, וְכָל מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הִיא מִדַּת הַדִּין וְדִינָא דְּמַלְכוּתָא לִשְׁפּוֹט תֵּבֵל בְּצֶדֶק

And although “a king establishes the land through justice” (Mishlei 29:4)746Mishlei 29:4: “מֶלֶךְ בְּמִשְׁפָּט יַעֲמִיד אָרֶץ, וְאִישׁ תְּרוּמוֹת יֶהֶרְסֶנָּה” — “a king establishes the land through justice, but a man of exactions tears it down.” Background: kingship rightly exercised — through mishpat — gives a land its stability. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the “trait of Malchus,” which is Din — “the law of the kingdom, to judge the world with righteousness”; yet, he stresses, this judging function is only the outward “conduct of the kingdom,” not the essence of the King, who is “on the contrary, full of mercy.”, and every trait of Malchus is the trait of Din and “the law of kingship,” to judge the world with righteousness,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ רַק לְהַעֲמָדַת אָרֶץ וְהַנְהָגַת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא מִדַּת מַלְכוּת, אֲבָל עֶצֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ אַדְּרַבָּה מָלֵא רַחֲמִים

nonetheless this is only for the “establishing of the land” and the conduct of the kingdom — which is what is called the “trait of Malchus”; but the essence of the King is, on the contrary, full of mercy.
וְעַל כֵּן מַלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מִשֵּׁבֶט יְהוּדָה דְּנִקְרָא כּוּלּוֹ עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה שֶׁהוּא עֶצֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ וְהוּא מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים
And therefore the kingship of Israel is from the tribe of Yehudah — [a name] entirely called upon the Name of the Holy One, the Name Havayah, which is the essence of the King, the trait of mercy;
וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל״ כִּי אָנוּ בָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ
and He is called “King of Israel,” for we are His children.
וְהַמֶּלֶךְ בְּבֵיתוֹ אֵין שַׁיָּיךְ הַנְהָגַת הַמְּלוּכָה, דְּכָל אִישׁ שׂוֹרֵר בְּבֵיתוֹ, וְהַנְהָגַת מַלְכוּת הוּא רַק עַל זוּלָתוֹ

And [with] a king in his own home there is no “conduct of kingship” — for “every man rules in his own house747Esther 1:22: Achashverosh’s decree, sent to every province, that “…לִהְיוֹת כָּל אִישׁ שֹׂרֵר בְּבֵיתוֹ וּמְדַבֵּר כִּלְשׁוֹן עַמּוֹ” — “…that every man should rule in his own house and speak the tongue of his people.” Background: the edict issued after Vashti’s fall (the Sages, Megillah 12b, note how petty it seemed). R’ Tzadok’s use: he draws on the verse’s plain phrase — that “every man rules in his own house” — to explain that a king exercises “kingship” (the conduct of Din) only over others; within his own home he is merely a father, and there his children “cleave to the very essence of the King,” untouched by the ruling-rod of Malchus.,” and the conduct of kingship is only over others;
אֲבָל בְּבֵיתוֹ הוּא כְּכָל אָב לְבָנָיו וּדְבוּקִם בְּעֶצֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ
but in his home he is like any father to his sons, and they cleave to the very essence of the King.
אֲבָל מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁהוּא הַנְהָגַת הַמְּלוּכָה מִתְפַּשֵּׁט בִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִהְיוֹת מוֹשֵׁל בַּגּוֹיִם וְלִשְׁפּוֹךְ חֲמָתוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם, ״חֲמַת מֶלֶךְ מַלְאֲכֵי מָוֶת״

But the “trait of Malchus,” which is the conduct of the kingdom, “spreads out” in Knesses Yisrael to rule over the nations and to “pour out His wrath” upon them — “the wrath of a king is angels of death” (Mishlei 16:14)748Mishlei 16:14: “חֲמַת מֶלֶךְ מַלְאֲכֵי מָוֶת, וְאִישׁ חָכָם יְכַפְּרֶנָּה” — “the wrath of a king is angels of death, but a wise man will appease it.” Background: Mishlei warns of the deadly power of a king’s anger. R’ Tzadok’s use: this “wrath” is the face that Malchus turns outward, toward the nations — “to rule over them and pour out His wrath upon them.” Toward His own children, by contrast, the very same King is no destroyer but a father, whose “sufferings are only as a father chastening his son.”.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּהַיִּסּוּרִין רַק כְּאָב הַמְיַסֵּר אֶת בְּנוֹ לְהַחֲיוֹתוֹ וּלְהֵטִיב אַחֲרִיתוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה

which is not so with the Children of Israel, where the sufferings are only “as a father chastens his son” (Devarim 8:5)749Devarim 8:5: “וְיָדַעְתָּ עִם לְבָבֶךָ, כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר יְיַסֵּר אִישׁ אֶת בְּנוֹ, ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ מְיַסְּרֶךָּ” — “and you shall know in your heart, that just as a man chastens his son, so Hashem your God chastens you.” Background: Moshe frames the wilderness trials as a father’s loving discipline, not punishment. Meforshim: these are yissurin shel ahavah — “sufferings of love” (cf. Berachos 5a). R’ Tzadok’s use: here is the whole distinction between the nations and Israel — over the nations Malchus pours out lethal wrath, but Israel’s sufferings “are only as a father chastening his son, to give him life and to better his end thereby.” — to give him life and to better his end thereby. — toward the nations Malchus turns its face of judgment, but toward His own children the very same King is only a father, chastening for their good.

items.h: The theme: David — root of Malchus — asked to be “flogged,” accepting yissurin as the price of life; he is the dalet of Yehudah, Knesses Yisrael “poor and lowly,” who owns nothing of herself. Suffering earns Olam Haba (the “three good gifts” via yissurin). The soul, pure in itself, is bound to evil through the body — the parable of the chiger (soul, “lame,” no feet here) riding the suma (body, “blind,” mere instrument). Even holy “sight” can be pressed into the coveting of evil through the body’s dominion.

p: [לז] וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֹׁרֶשׁ מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת
And David HaMelech is the root of the trait of Malchus.
אָמְרוּ ז״ל דְּאָמַר ״לָמָּה הָרְצוּעָה תְּלוּיָה — הַלְקֵנִי״

The Sages said that he said, “Why does the strap hang [idle]? — Flog me750Sanhedrin 107a: in the same sugya, after the episode of Bas Sheva, when David pleaded to be wholly forgiven, “the Holy One said to him: Accept sufferings upon yourself — and he accepted them upon himself” (kabel alecha yissurin — kibel alav); and Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav that “for six months David was afflicted with tzara’as, the Shechinah departed from him, and the Sanhedrin withdrew from him.” Background: the daf opens with the warning that “a person should never bring himself to a test,” for David had asked, “Examine me, O Hashem, and test me” (Tehillim 26:2), and stumbled. R’ Tzadok renders David’s acceptance in fuller aggadic dress — “why does the strap hang idle? Flog me!” — reading it as David’s willing embrace of yissurin as the very price of “life”: for as the root of Malchus — Knesses Yisrael “poor and lowly,” who owns nothing of herself — his own “side” is to receive suffering and thereby merit the World to Come.!”
דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אָמַר לוֹ ״חַיִּים אַתָּה מְבַקֵּשׁ — צַפֵּה לְיִסּוּרִין״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ סִטְרָא דִּידֵיהּ

for the Holy One had said to him, “Life you seek? — Anticipate sufferings” — for this is his [own] “side.”751R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §44): “even though it is a blow, since its purpose is healing — and this is what they said in the first chapter of Bava Basra, "Rus had a good end," and it is not harder than Iyov… for with Iyov the blows do not bring about the good, and so they are [simply] evil.” Exactly the se’if’s David: he asked to be flogged — accepting sufferings whose whole character is that they are the price and the instrument of life, not a bare affliction.
וְהוּא הָ״ד״ שֶׁבִּיהוּדָה הָרוֹמֵז לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הָעֲנִיָּה וְהַדַּלָּה
And it is the dalet within [the name] Yehudah, alluding to Knesses Yisrael, “poor and lowly [dalah],”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל דְּכָל מָקוֹם ״ד׳ וְכוּ׳״ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם כְּלוּם מִצַּד עַצְמָם

as the Sages said, that wherever “dal” [and the like] appears, Scripture speaks of Israel — that they have nothing of their own.752R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayechi §10): "“all my days I was distressed over this verse, ‘with all your soul’ — and now that it has come to my hand, shall I not fulfill it?” He prolonged the echad until his soul departed at echad." Exactly the se’if: one who accepts yissurin is the one who tastes Olam Haba in his own lifetime — for he owns nothing of himself, and gives back at the word “One” what was never his.
וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית יִסּוּרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כָּל זֶה בָּחַרְתִּי מֵעֹנִי״ שֶׁהוּא תּוֹקֶף יִסּוּרֵי אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And this is the “purpose of sufferings,” as it says, “all this I have chosen [rather] than affliction [oni]” — the intensest of a person’s sufferings in this world;
דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ ״יָאֵי עֲנִיּוּתָא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל״, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכִין לְעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁנִּיתָּן רַק עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ה.]

concerning which they said, “poverty is becoming to Israel,” for through it they merit the World to Come, which is given only through sufferings, as they said [Berachos 5a],753Chagigah 9b: Eliyahu said to Bar Hei Hei: what is [the meaning of] “behold, I have refined you, but not with silver; I have chosen you in the crucible of affliction” (Yeshayah 48)? It teaches that the Holy One went through all the good traits to give to Israel, and found none [as fitting] as poverty — as people say, “poverty befits Israel like a red trapping on a white horse.” Berachos 5a: It was taught, R’ Shimon ben Yochai says: three good gifts did the Holy One give Israel, and all of them He gave only through afflictions — these are: the Torah, the Land of Israel, and the World to Come.
עַל שָׁלֹשׁ מַתָּנוֹת טוֹבוֹת שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד שְׁלוֹשֶׁת עַלְמִין בי״ע (בְּרִיאָה יְצִירָה עֲשִׂיָּה)
concerning the three good gifts [Torah, Eretz Yisrael, and the World to Come], which correspond to the three worlds BY"A (Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah).
דְּשָׁם יֵשׁ מְצִיאוּת לְרַע, וְ״אִמָּא מְקַנְּנָא בִּבְרִיאָה״ הוּא עוֹלָם הַבָּא
For there [in BY"A] there is “existence” for evil; and “Ima [Binah] nests in Beriah” — which is the “World to Come”;
״קֵן שֶׁלָּהּ״ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּנִשְׁמָתָן דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הַחֲצוּבִים מִכּוּרְסַיָּיא
and “her nest” in this world is in the souls of Israel, hewn from the “Throne.”
וְאַף דְּנְשָׁמָה מִצַּד עַצְמָהּ טְהוֹרָה הִיא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ בָּהּ גַּם כֵּן חִיבּוּר לְרַע מִצַּד חִיבּוּר לְגוּף כְּמָשָׁל חִיגֵּר וְסוּמָא

And although the soul, in itself, is pure, nonetheless it too has a “bond to evil” by virtue of its bond to the body — as in the parable of the lame man [chiger] and the blind man [suma].754Sanhedrin 91a–b: Antoninus said to Rebbi that body and soul could each escape judgment — the body pleading, “the soul sinned, for from the day it left me I lie still as a stone,” and the soul, “the body sinned, for from the day I left it I fly in the air like a bird.” Rebbi answered with a parable: a king set two watchmen over his orchard, one lame and one blind. The lame said, “I see fine figs — carry me and we will bring them”; the lame rode upon the blind, and they brought and ate. When the owner demanded the figs, the lame said, “have I legs?” and the blind, “have I eyes?” — so he set the lame upon the blind and judged them as one. So too the Holy One brings the soul, casts it into the body, and judges them together.Mei HaShiloach — the neshamah remains pure, while bechirah operates in the embodied person: Mei HaShiloach, Anthology, Collectanea, Siddur §1, explains the daily declaration ‘נשמה שנתת בי טהורה היא’ by distinguishing nefesh, ruach, and neshamah. ‘לנשמה אין שום חטא ופגם מגיע’ — no sin or blemish reaches the neshamah itself; nefesh remains bound to the body, while ruach signifies the human power of bechirah, through which one can choose good and reject evil. This is a precise Izhbitz complement to R’ Tzadok’s use of the blind-and-lame parable. The purity of the soul does not acquit the person, because the moral subject in this world is the joined human being: the soul supplies life and vision, the body supplies the instruments of action, and ruach is the arena in which choice is exercised. Thus R’ Tzadok can simultaneously maintain that the deepest Jewish soul is intrinsically pure and that the embodied person is fully answerable for what he does. The distinction is especially important in this siman, where retrospective descriptions of an unblemished root could otherwise be misunderstood as denying responsibility. Izhbitz itself preserves both truths: the neshamah is never transformed into evil, but the person’s bechirah remains real precisely in the level through which that holy life is translated into action. Yissurin can therefore refine the embodied partnership without implying that the essential soul had ceased to be holy.
כִּי הַנְּשָׁמָה חִיגֶּרֶת, דְּאֵין לָהּ רַגְלִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּרַגְלֶיהָ יוֹרְדוֹת מָוֶת
For the soul is “lame,” having no “feet” in this world — [whereas the body’s] “feet descend to death”;
וְשָׁם שְׁלִיטַת הָרַע בַּגּוּף שֶׁהוּא רַגְלִין דִּילָהּ, וְרוֹכֵב עַל הַגּוּף שֶׁהוּא סוּמָא
and there the dominion of evil is in the body, which is “her feet,” and [the soul] “rides upon” the body, which is “blind,”
כִּי הוּא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּלִי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הַגּוֹמְרִים

for it [the body] is nothing but the instrument that “completes the deed.”755R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Erev Yom Kippur §4): “and further it is brought in the Zohar on "es your souls" — that the word "es" is everywhere expounded to include what is subordinate, to include the whole body together with the soul.” Exactly the se’if’s parable of the lame man and the blind man: neither body nor soul is judged alone, for the deed was possible only through their partnership.
אֲבָל הָעַיִן רוֹאָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה הַלֵּב חוֹמֵד — הוּא כֹּחוֹת נְפָשִׁים הַנִּמְשָׁכִים מֵהַנְּשָׁמָה
But “the eye sees,” so that through it “the heart covets” — [and] these are soul-powers drawn from the neshamah.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעִיקַּר רְאִיַּית הַנְּשָׁמָה הוּא בְּטָהֳרָה וּקְדֻשַּׁת הָרְאִיָּה לִהְיוֹת רוֹאֶה רַק ״מַרְאוֹת אֱלֹקִים״ גַּם בְּכָל דָּבָר גַּשְׁמִי שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And even though the essential “seeing” of the soul is in purity and holiness of sight — to see only “visions of God” even in every physical thing of this world,
וְזֶה הָרְאִיָּה הַנִּמְשֶׁכֶת מֵהַיִּרְאָה דַּרְגָּא דְּאַרְיֵה [״אַתְוָון דְּדִין כְּאַתְוָון דְּדִין״] שֹׁרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא קְבִיצַת נִשְׁמוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל
this “sight” being drawn from “fear [yirah],” the rung of “Aryeh” [whose “letters are the letters of yirah”], the root of the holiness of Knesses Yisrael, the “gathering” of the souls of Israel —

מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַהִתְחַבְּרוּת הַגּוּף הַחוּמְרִי, שֶׁהוּא הָרַגְלִין דְּעַל יְדֵי שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בָּאָדָם, שׁוֹלֵט גַּם בְּמִדַּת הָרְאִיָּה לִהְיוֹתָהּ מְשַׁמֶּשֶׁת אֶל חֶמְדַּת הָרָעוֹת לְהַכְנִיסָם לַלֵּב

nonetheless, by virtue of the bond of the material body — which is the “feet,” through which “man rules over man to his detriment” — [the evil] rules also over the faculty of “sight,” making it serve the coveting of evils, to bring them into the heart. — the soul is thus never the sinner in its own right; it is drawn into evil only through its yoking to the body, as the lame man is carried by the blind.

items.h: The theme: The rectification of sight comes through oni, affliction — “Hashem saw my affliction.” David, “goodly to look upon,” called himself poor and accepted yissurin. This poverty is not material lack but the recognition that one owns nothing of himself: “poverty befits Israel like a red trapping on a white horse.” The nations say “my strength made this wealth”; the God-fearing man knows that all is in Heaven’s hands.

p: [לח] וְהִתְעַלּוּת קְדֻשַּׁת הָרְאִיָּה נֶאֱמַר בַּכָּתוּב בְּלֵידַת רְאוּבֵן ״כִּי רָאָה ה׳ בְּעׇנְיִי״ עַל יְדֵי מִדַּת הָעֹנִי

And the elevation of the holiness of sight is stated in Scripture at the birth of Reuven: “for Hashem has seen my affliction [b’onyi]” (Bereishis 29:32) — [attained] through the trait of oni [affliction];
כִּי לְתַקֵּן שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְחָלַת הַחֵטְא וְהַתְחָלַת שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּלִיַּעַל שֶׁהוּא בָּרְאִיָּה, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה תָּשׁוּב הַנְּשָׁמָה טְהוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיְתָה — הִיא בָּעֹנִי
for to rectify the root of the “beginning of the sin” and the “beginning of the base man’s dominion” — which is in sight — [the means] whereby the soul returns pure as it was, is through oni.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה ״טוֹב רֳאִי״ קָרָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ ״עָנִי״ בְּרָזָא דְּ״תְפִלָּה לְעָנִי״

And David HaMelech, who was “goodly to look upon” (I Shmuel 16:12), called himself “poor [ani],” in the secret of “a prayer of the poor man” (Tehillim 102:1)756Tehillim 102:1: “תְּפִלָּה לְעָנִי כִי יַעֲטֹף, וְלִפְנֵי ה׳ יִשְׁפֹּךְ שִׂיחוֹ” — “a prayer of the poor man [ani] when he faints, and pours out his plea before Hashem.” Background: the superscription of the psalm — the archetypal prayer of the “poor man.” R’ Tzadok’s use: David HaMelech, though a wealthy king, “called himself ani,” in the secret of “a prayer of the poor man” — the inner poverty of one who knows he owns nothing of his own, and therefore “pours out his plea” before God.Yismach Moshe — David’s poverty is the consciousness that everything is received: Yismach Moshe, Re’eh 16:1, asks how a person should understand giving tzedakah and answers that no one should imagine that he gives from property that is independently ‘his.’ Every human being enters the world empty-handed, and the Creator sustains all creatures through His tzedakah; the wealthy person is therefore a messenger through whom what Hashem has already designated reaches the recipient. He then explains David’s repeated self-description as ‘עני ואביון’: David could say this even as a king because he understood himself as one who only receives a greater measure of the Divine gift. This is almost a prose commentary on R’ Tzadok’s definition of oni in this se’if. The poverty that rectifies sight is not necessarily absence of possessions. It is the collapse of the illusion of autonomous ownership — the inner opposite of ‘כחי ועוצם ידי עשה לי את החיל הזה.’ A person may possess wealth, power, vision, or kingship, yet remain an ani when he sees all of it as entrusted rather than self-generated. In that state the eye no longer converts Divine gifts into grounds for self-expansion. It looks upward to the Giver. David’s poverty therefore belongs intrinsically to Malchus: the king who holds everything can still know that nothing is ‘from himself,’ and this recognition is itself the tikkun of the faculty that otherwise covets and claims.,
כְּשֶׁרָאָה רְשָׁעִים יוֹצְאִין מִמֶּנּוּ שֶׁפָּגְמוּ מִדָּתוֹ
when he saw wicked ones issuing from him who “blemished his trait”;
וְאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״הֲכִינוֹתִי בְעׇנְיִי״, כִּי הוּא קִיבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ יִסּוּרִין דְּעָנִי

and he said of himself, “in my affliction I prepared” (I Divrei HaYamim 22:14)757I Divrei HaYamim 22:14: “וְהִנֵּה בְעָנְיִי הֲכִינוֹתִי לְבֵית ה׳…” — “and behold, in my affliction [b’onyi] I have prepared for the House of Hashem…” — David’s words as he readied the gold, silver, and materials for the Temple that Shlomo would build. Meforshim: the commentators ask how David, of vast wealth, could speak of “my affliction,” and explain “onyi” as travail and toil, or (as here) an inner “poverty.” R’ Tzadok’s use: David “took upon himself the sufferings of the poor man,” calling even his Temple-preparations “b’onyi” — the affliction of the soul that recognizes it has nothing of its own., for he took upon himself the sufferings of the “poor man.”758R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §15): “"three are brazen — Israel among the nations"; therefore poverty befits Israel, to weaken the force of their brazenness — but they said, Torah [likewise] weakens the force of their brazenness; and this is "had not Your Torah been my delight, I would then have perished in my affliction."” Exactly the se’if: “poverty befits Israel” is not deprivation but the tempering of an inborn strength — the same work Torah does, from the other side.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה עָשִׁיר גָּדוֹל וּמֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ עֲנִיּוּת בִּמְקוֹם עֲשִׁירוּת, אֵין הַכַּוָּונָה עַל עֲנִיּוּת בְּפוֹעַל גּוּפָנִי
And although he was very wealthy and king of Israel — where “poverty” is inapplicable amid riches — the intent is not [physical] poverty in bodily fact,
דִּכְבָר אָמְרוּ ז״ל (אָבוֹת ד, א) ״אֵיזֶהוּ עָשִׁיר — הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ״

for the Sages already said (Avos 4:1)759Avos 4:1: “Ben Zoma says: Who is rich? He who rejoices in his portion [ha-sameach b’chelko], as it says (Tehillim 128:2), ‘when you eat the labor of your hands, you are praiseworthy and it is well with you.’”, “Who is wealthy? — He who rejoices in his portion.”
וְיֵשׁ עָנִי הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ וּמִתְעַנֵּג בְּכָךְ וְאֵין חָסֵר כְּלוּם, וְזֶהוּ מִדָּתָן שֶׁל חֲסִידֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ גַּבַּיְיהוּ עֲנִיּוּת אֶפֶס כְּלָל

And there is a “poor man” who rejoices in his portion and delights in it, lacking nothing — and this is the trait of the pious of Israel, like David HaMelech, to whom “poverty” is not applicable at all.760R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §175): “As the Sages said of David HaMelech, ‘your hands are sharp and decisive, to rule with them over His world’; and it says of him ‘admoni’ (ruddy) — like Esav — ‘but with beautiful eyes’ [yefeh einayim]: [he shed blood] only by the ruling of the Sanhedrin (Bereishis Rabbah 63); and therefore he merited kingship. And Shaul was removed because he became ‘merciful to the cruel’ — for the trait of Malchus is [that of] stern judgment.” (This is the se’if’s David: ‘ruddy’ like Esav yet ‘of beautiful eyes’ — his sight is rectified, seeing not by his own craving but by the da’as of the Sanhedrin, which is why ‘poverty’ of the eye does not apply to him.)
וְעִיקַּר עֲנִיּוּת הוּא כַּאֲשֶׁר ״לָרָשׁ אֵין כֹּל״ וְחָסֵר הַכֹּל, וְעוֹנִי גּוּפָנִי הוּא מִדָּה רָעָה

And the essence of poverty is when “the pauper has nothing” (II Shmuel 12:3)761II Shmuel 12:3: in Nathan the prophet’s parable, “וְלָרָשׁ אֵין כֹּל, כִּי אִם כִּבְשָׂה אַחַת קְטַנָּה” — “but the poor man had nothing, save one little ewe lamb.” Background: Nathan’s rebuke of David after the episode of Bas Sheva — the rich man who seizes the pauper’s single lamb. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the essence of poverty is when ‘the pauper has nothing’ and lacks everything” — real, bodily destitution, which is “a bad trait” — as opposed to Israel’s spiritual “poverty,” which lacks nothing but knows that all it has is from the King. and lacks everything — and bodily poverty is a bad trait;
וְהָרְשָׁעִים אַף שֶׁהֵם עֲשִׁירִים אֵינָם בְּשַׁלְוָה, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ מָנֶה רוֹצֶה מָאתַיִם וְהֵם עֲנִיִּים גְּדוֹלִים, וְזֶהוּ עֲנִיּוּתָא דְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
and the wicked, though wealthy, are not at peace — “he who has one hundred wants two hundred” — and they are “great paupers”: this is the “poverty of the nations of the world.”
אֲבָל עֲנִיּוּתָא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא כְּבַרְזָא סוּמְקָא לְסוּסְיָא חִיוָּרָא, שֶׁהוּא יוֹפִי הֵיפֶךְ הָעֲנִיּוּת שֶׁהוּא נִיוּוּל
But the “poverty of Israel” is “like a red trapping on a white horse” — a beauty, the opposite of [ordinary] poverty, which is a disgrace,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״בְּנוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל נָאוֹת, אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲנִיּוּת מְנַוַּולְתָּן״

as they said, “the daughters of Israel are comely, but poverty disfigures them762Nedarim 66a: a man vowed against benefiting from his unattractive niece; they brought her into R’ Yishmael’s house and beautified her, and R’ Yishmael — seeing the vow thereby void — “wept and said: the daughters of Israel are comely, only that poverty disfigures them” (banos Yisrael na’os hen, ela she-ha-aniyus menavaltan). Background: the Gemara’s poignant teaching that the true beauty of Israel’s daughters is merely masked by want. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel’s poverty is no true blemish but “like a red trapping on a white horse” — a beauty; the “disfigurement” is only the outward want, while inwardly “the daughters of Israel are comely.”.”
כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּנֵי מְלָכִים, וְכוּלָּם חָסֵר מִבֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ
For in truth all Israel are “children of kings,” and [whatever] they lack is [only] “from the King’s house”;
וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב שֶׁאָמַר ״יֶשׁ לִי כֹל״ דְּאֵין חָסֵר כְּלוּם, לֹא כְּעֵשָׂו שֶׁאָמַר ״יֶשׁ לִי רָב״ וְלֹא ״כֹל״ דַּעֲדַיִין חָסֵר, דְּ״בֶטֶן רְשָׁעִים תֶּחְסָר״

and this is the rung of Yaakov, who said “I have all [kol]”763Bereishis 33:11, 33:9: Yaakov pressed his gift upon Esav, saying “כִּי חַנַּנִי אֱלֹהִים וְכִי יֶשׁ לִי כֹל” — “for God has favored me, and because I have everything [kol]” (33:11) — whereas Esav had said only “יֶשׁ לִי רָב,” “I have much [rav]” (33:9). Meforshim: Rashi contrasts them — Yaakov says “all my need,” the tzaddik content with his portion, while Esav’s “much” is the boast of one still lacking. R’ Tzadok’s use: “yesh li kol” is the rung of Yaakov, who lacks nothing; Esav’s “rav” betrays that he “still lacks” — “and the belly of the wicked shall want” (Mishlei 13:25) — for the righteous are satisfied with their portion, but the wicked, however rich, are “great paupers.” — lacking nothing — unlike Esav, who said “I have much [rav],” but not “all” — [meaning] he still lacks, for “the belly of the wicked shall want” (Mishlei 13:25).
אֲבָל צַדִּיקִים שְׂמֵחִים בְּחֶלְקָם וּשְׂבֵעִים וְאֵין חָסֵר לָהֶם כְּלוּם

But the righteous rejoice in their portion, are satisfied, and lack nothing.764R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar §6): “there is no satiety, as it is written, "one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver," and it is brought, "a person does not leave the world with half his desire in his hand"; but "satisfied with favor" means that Hashem bestows ratzon [contentment] within him, and through this he is [satisfied].” Exactly the se’if’s “poverty”: the lack that matters is never material, and its remedy is not acquisition but a God-given contentment — “who rejoices in his portion.”

וְזֶהוּ ״סוּסְיָא חִיוָּרָא״, שֶׁהַסּוּס הוּא הַגּוּף שֶׁעָלָיו רוֹכֶבֶת הַנְּשָׁמָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתִיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר] עַל פָּסוּק ״עֲבָדִים רוֹכְבִים עַל סוּסִים״, וּכְשֶׁהוּא לָבָן הַיְינוּ נָקִי וּמָלֵא חֲסָדִים

And this is the “white horse”: the horse is the body, upon which the soul rides — as they said [in Tikkunei Zohar] on the verse “servants riding upon horses” (Koheles 10:7)765Koheles 10:7: “רָאִיתִי עֲבָדִים עַל סוּסִים, וְשָׂרִים הֹלְכִים כַּעֲבָדִים עַל הָאָרֶץ” — “I have seen servants upon horses, and princes walking like servants on the ground.” Background: Koheles’ lament at an overturned order. R’ Tzadok’s use: following the Tikkunei Zohar on this verse, the “horse” is the body upon which the soul “rides”; a “white horse” is a body “clean and full of chasadim” — yet even the finest horse needs the “rod and strap,” the “red” of Din, which upon the white horse becomes a grace and a beauty. — and when it is white, that is, clean and full of chasadim.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הַטּוֹב שֶׁבַּסּוּסִים צָרִיךְ לְשֵׁבֶט וּרְצוּעָה לְאַלְקָאָה וְהִיא סוּמְקָא וּמִדַּת הַדִּין
Yet even the best of horses requires a “rod and strap” for flogging — which is “red [sumka],” the trait of Din;
וּכְשֶׁהִיא יוֹרֶדֶת עַל הַסּוּס יֵשׁ בָּהּ נוֹי וְיוֹפִי לְפִי שֶׁהִיא רְצוּעָה אֲדוּמָּה
and when it comes down upon the horse it has grace and beauty, since it is a “red strap.”
וְאֵינוֹ כְּשׁוֹט לְסוּס הַנִּמְשָׁל לְ״שֵׁבֶט לְגֵו כְּסִילִים״, דְּהַשּׁוֹט עָשׂוּי לְהַכּוֹת לְבַד

And it is not like “a whip for the horse” (Mishlei 26:3)766Mishlei 26:3: “שׁוֹט לַסּוּס, מֶתֶג לַחֲמוֹר, וְשֵׁבֶט לְגֵו כְּסִילִים” — “a whip for the horse, a bridle for the donkey, and a rod for the back of fools.” Background: Mishlei’s image of the instruments of discipline. R’ Tzadok’s use: he distinguishes the whip — “made only to strike,” a bare blow (the “rod for the back of fools”) — from the leather strap, “which is also made for adornment”; Israel’s chastening is the beautifying red strap, not the fool’s whip., likened to “a rod for the back of fools” — for the whip is made only to strike;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הָרְצוּעָה שֶׁל עוֹר עֲשׂוּיָה לְנוֹי גַּם כֵּן, וּכְשֶׁמּוּנַּחַת עַל הַגּוּף יֵשׁ בָּהּ נוֹי לְמַרְאִית עֵינֵי אֲחֵרִים
whereas the leather strap is also made for adornment, and when it rests on the body it has grace to the eyes of others,
רַק הַסּוּס עַצְמוֹ לְבַדּוֹ הוּא שֶׁמַּרְגִּישׁ הַהַכָּאָה שֶׁהִיא רְצוּעָה לְאַלְקָאָה
only the horse itself alone feels the blow — that it is a “strap for flogging.”
וְכֵן עֲנִיּוּתָא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֵינוֹ חִסָּרוֹן גּוּפָנִי הַנִּרְאֶה לַכֹּל שֶׁהוֹמֶה וּמְהַמֶּה אַחַר חִסְרוֹנוֹ, רַק חִסָּרוֹן נַפְשִׁי, דְּרַק הַלֵּב יוֹדֵעַ מָרַת נַפְשׁוֹ
So too the “poverty of Israel” is not a bodily lack, visible to all, over which one moans and murmurs — but an inner lack, for “only the heart knows the bitterness of its soul” (Mishlei 14:10);
וְהוּא עוֹנִי רוּחָנִי דְּנֶפֶשׁ שֶׁמַּכִּיר בְּחִסְרוֹנוֹ דְּלֵית לֵיהּ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם
it is a spiritual affliction of the soul, which recognizes its own lack — that “it has nothing of its own.”
וּבָזֶה אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם עֲשִׁירִים, דִּמְדַמִּים בְּנַפְשָׁם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם כֹּחַ וְעֶצֶם יָד לַעֲשׂוֹת חַיִל
And in this the nations are “wealthy,” for they imagine that they have “power and strength of hand to make valor”;
וְעַל כֵּן הֵם מִתְפָּאֲרִים בְּעׇשְׁרָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּהָמָן שֶׁסִּיפֵּר ״כְּבוֹד עׇשְׁרוֹ״, וְהַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי שֶׁאָמַר דִּבְכֹחוֹ אָסַף לוֹ עוֹשֶׁר רַב כָּזֶה

and therefore they boast of their wealth, as it says of Haman, who “recounted the glory of his riches767Esther 5:11: “וַיְסַפֵּר לָהֶם הָמָן אֶת כְּבוֹד עָשְׁרוֹ וְרֹב בָּנָיו…” — “and Haman recounted to them the glory of his riches and the multitude of his sons…” Background: Haman boasting to his friends and wife at the summit of his fortune — just before his fall. R’ Tzadok’s use: Haman typifies the nations’ “wealth” — the conceit that “my strength and the might of my hand made this valor,” boasting of riches as self-made — whereas in truth “all is in the hands of Heaven,” decreed before one is even formed.” (Esther 5:11) — [boasting] that by his own power he amassed such great wealth.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כְּפִי הָאֱמֶת דְּהַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם, וְנִגְזַר קֹדֶם יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד, ״אַל יִתְהַלֵּל [חָכָם בְּחָכְמָתוֹ]״ וְגוֹמֵר
Which is not so in truth, where “all is in the hands of Heaven,” and [one’s lot] is decreed before the child’s formation; “let not [the wise man] glory [in his wisdom]” (Yirmeyah 9:22).
כִּי ״אִם בְּזֹאת [יִתְהַלֵּל הַמִּתְהַלֵּל]״ וְגוֹמֵר הוּא דַּרְגָּא דִּירֵא שָׁמַיִם הָרָמוּז בְּמִלַּת ״זֹאת״, דְּזֶהוּ בִּידֵי אָדָם
For “but in this [let the boaster boast]” (ibid. 9:23) is the rung of the God-fearing man, alluded to in the word “zos [this]” — for this [alone] is “in man’s hands”;
וְהוּא ״הַשְׂכֵּל וְיָדֹעַ אוֹתִי״ לְהַכִּיר אֶת קוֹנוֹ דְּהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהַחָכְמָה וְהַגְּבוּרָה וְהָעֹשֶׁר מִמֶּנּוּ
and it is “understanding and knowing Me” (ibid.) — to recognize his Maker, that all is from Him, and the wisdom and the might and the wealth are from Him.
וַאֲפִילּוּ יֵשׁ לוֹ אוֹצְרוֹת מְלָכִים מַכִּיר דְּאֵין לוֹ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ כְּלוּם, וְאִם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא יִרְצֶה שֶׁיֵּהָנֶה מֵהֶם הוּא כְּאִלּוּ אֵין לוֹ כְּלוּם
And even if he has the treasuries of kings, he recognizes that he has nothing of his own; and if Hashem does not will that he benefit from them, it is as though he has nothing.
וְרַק מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יִתֵּן לוֹ הוּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ, וְהוּא אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם כֹּחַ וְשׁוּם סִבָּה מִגַּרְמֵיהּ לַעֲשׂוֹת חַיִל כְּלָל
And only what Hashem gives him is what he “has,” while he has no power and no “cause” of his own to make valor at all;
וְאַל יַאֲמִין בְּעַצְמוֹ עַד יוֹם מוֹתוֹ, דְּכָל יְמֵי חַיָּיו הוּא בָּעֹנִי זֶה כִּי לֹא יֵדַע מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם

and “let him not trust in himself until the day of his death” (Avos 2:4)768Avos 2:4: “Hillel says: Do not trust in yourself until the day of your death [al taamin b’atzmecha ad yom mos’cha].”, for all the days of his life he is in this “affliction,” since “he knows not what a day may bring forth” (Mishlei 27:1)769Mishlei 27:1: “אַל תִּתְהַלֵּל בְּיוֹם מָחָר, כִּי לֹא תֵדַע מַה יֵּלֶד יוֹם” — “do not boast about tomorrow, for you know not what a day may bring forth.” Background: Mishlei’s caution against presuming upon the future. R’ Tzadok’s use: joined to “let a person not trust in himself until the day of his death” (Avos 2:4), this seals the point — the God-fearing man lives “all the days of his life in this affliction [oni],” owning nothing and presuming nothing, “for he knows not what a day may bring forth.”. — Israel’s “poverty,” then, is not a lack but a spiritual clarity: the red strap’s beauty upon the white horse, the felt knowledge that one owns nothing but what the King grants.

items.h: The theme: The purpose of yissurin is the reward of Olam Haba — “the righteous sit with their crowns,” delighting in the Shechinah’s radiance as companions that never part. This is the dalet of Yehudah: lowliness, eyes lifted on high, owning nothing but what is received from Above. After salvation the dalet becomes a hei; and “David” is a dalet at either end with a vav between — the king who knows his own lowliness.

p: [לט] וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁזּוֹכֶה עַל יָדָם לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַבָּא

And this is the purpose of the sufferings, that through them one merits the life of the World to Come,770R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Noach §2): "“only you have I known [therefore I shall visit upon you]” — His beloved He exacts from little by little; and also to arouse for the future, as it says, “he who withholds [the rod hates his son], and he who loves him seeks him with chastisement.”" Exactly the se’if: sufferings are the price and preparation of Olam Haba — exacted “little by little” precisely from the beloved, which is why even the covenant of milah is a “suffering of love.”
שֶׁהוּא קַבָּלַת הַשָּׂכָר דְּ״צַדִּיקִים יוֹשְׁבִין וְעַטְרוֹתֵיהֶם בְּרָאשֵׁיהֶם וְנֶהֱנִים״ כו׳, שֶׁאֵין חֲסֵרִים כְּלוּם

which is the receiving of reward, where “the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and delight” (Berachos 17a)771Berachos 17a: “A pearl [teaching] in the mouth of Rav: The World to Come is not like this world. In the World to Come there is no eating and no drinking, no envy and no hatred and no competition; rather, the righteous sit with their crowns upon their heads and delight in the radiance of the Shechinah [neheninnin mi-ziv ha-Shechinah].” — lacking nothing —
עַל יְדֵי הֲנָאַת זִיו הַשְּׁכִינָה הַגָּלוּי לְעֵינֵיהֶם בִּקְבִיעוּת וִישִׁיבָה בְּלִי שׁוּם הִילּוּךְ וְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת
through the delight of the radiance of the Shechinah, revealed to their eyes constantly, in “sitting” [settled repose], without any “walking” or striving;
שֶׁהוּא דַּרְגָּא דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּפְעָמִים נִגְלֶה וּפְעָמִים נֶעֱלָם, רַק רֵעִין דְּלָא מִתְפָּרְשִׁין

[unlike] the rung of this world, which is at times revealed and at times hidden — [there they are] only “companions that never part.”772R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §7): “"Shabbos is one sixtieth of the World to Come"… and the World to Come is the absence of doing — for "today to do them" [is this world] — only that the righteous… derive pleasure from the radiance of the Shechinah.” Exactly the se’if: the reward is not a further act but the cessation of acting — a state in which the soul only receives, and therefore nothing can part it from the light.
וְזֶהוּ הָ״ד״ דִּיהוּדָה הָרוֹמֶזֶת לְדַלּוּת זוֹ שֶׁדָּלוּ עֵינָיו לַמָּרוֹם, וְלֵית לֵיהּ מִגַּרְמֵיהּ רַק מַה שֶּׁמְּקַבֵּל מִשֵּׁם הֲוָיָ״ה ית״ש

And this is the dalet of Yehudah, alluding to this “lowliness [dalus]” — that “his eyes are lifted [dalu] on high,” and he has nothing of his own but what he receives from the Name Havayah.773R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §17): “death is called "lodging", as they said on the verse "when you lie down it shall watch over you" — in the grave — "and when you awake [it shall converse with you]."” The se’if’s “crowns” precisely: what looks like an ending is only a night’s lodging, and the Torah a man acquired keeps watch over him through it until the waking.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק עַרְבֵי פְּסָחִים] ״אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁדַּלּוֹתִי, לִי נָאֶה לְהוֹשִׁיעַ״
And concerning this they said [in Perek Arvei Pesachim, Pesachim 118b], “even though I am lowly [dalosi], deliverance befits me,”
עַל יְדֵי זֶה גּוּפֵיהּ דְּבְדַלּוּתֵנוּ עֵינֵינוּ צוֹפוֹת לַשָּׁמַיִם
through this very [lowliness], for in our lowliness our eyes are turned to Heaven.
וְאַחַר הַיְשׁוּעָה נַעֲשֶׂה מִ״ד״ ״ה״, שֶׁהוּא בָּתַר דְּקַבִּילַת עוֹבְּרָהּ שֶׁהוּא הַיְשׁוּעָה וּמִילּוּי הַחִסָּרוֹן
And after the salvation, the dalet becomes a hei — which is “after she has conceived,” which is the salvation and the “filling of the lack.”
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן רָזָא דְּדָוִד — ״ד״ תְּחִלָּה וָסוֹף וְ״ו״ בָּאֶמְצַע
And this too is the secret of “David”
[דוד]
a dalet at the beginning and end, and a vav in the middle —
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִיקַּר מַלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל לִהְיוֹת מַכִּיר דַּלּוּתוֹ וְחִסְרוֹנוֹ לְבִלְתִּי יָרוּם לְבָבוֹ מֵאֶחָיו

for this is the essence of the kingship of Israel: to recognize one’s lowliness and lack, “that his heart not be raised above his brothers774Devarim 17:20: among the laws of the king — “לְבִלְתִּי רוּם לְבָבוֹ מֵאֶחָיו, וּלְבִלְתִּי סוּר מִן הַמִּצְוָה יָמִין וּשְׂמֹאול” — “that his heart not be raised above his brothers, and that he not turn aside from the commandment, right or left.” Background: the Torah’s charge to the king, who writes and carries a Sefer Torah “to learn to fear Hashem” and remain humble despite his power. Meforshim: the Sifrei and Rashi stress that even a king may not lord himself over “his brothers.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is “the essence of the kingship of Israel” and “the perfection of the king” — the mitzvah unique to a king is precisely the guard against “raising of the heart”; hence David, root of Malchus, is the dalet of lowliness, who “recognizes his lowliness and lack.”” (Devarim 17:20).

וְזֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הַמֶּלֶךְ כְּשֶׁיִּשְׁמוֹר מִצְווֹת הַמְיוּחָדוֹת לַמֶּלֶךְ, דְּעִיקָּרָם הַזְּהִירוּת מֵרוּם הַלֵּב וְהַרְגָּשַׁת נִגְעֵי לְבָבוֹ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מְתוֹם מֵרֵאשִׁית הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה וְעַד סוֹף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה

And this is the perfection of the king, when he keeps the mitzvos unique to a king — whose essence is the caution against “raising of the heart,” and the sensing of “the afflictions of his heart,” that “there is no soundness in it” from the first thought to the final deed.
רַק הָ״ו״ בָּאֶמְצַע אוֹת אֱמֶת מַבְרִיחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה — דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב ע״ה

Only the vav in the middle [of David’s name] is the “letter of truth,” “reaching from end to end” — the rung of Yaakov775Shemos 26:28: of the Mishkan’s wall-boards — “וְהַבְּרִיחַ הַתִּיכֹן בְּתוֹךְ הַקְּרָשִׁים, מַבְרִחַ מִן הַקָּצֶה אֶל הַקָּצֶה” — “and the middle bar, within the boards, shall reach from end to end.” Background: the central crossbar running the full length of the Mishkan’s wall, binding all the boards together (per the Midrash, miraculously bending around all three sides). Meforshim: in Kabbalah this “middle bar” that “reaches from end to end” is Tiferes — the trait of Yaakov, “truth,” which mediates and joins the extremes. R’ Tzadok’s use: the vav in the middle of “David” is this “letter of truth” that “reaches from end to end” — the rung of Yaakov, “whose form is engraved on the Throne of Glory,” through whom the trait of Malchus is drawn only by cleaving to the very essence of the King.Sod Yesharim — the two dalets of David enclose the vav of connection: Sod Yesharim, Hoshana Rabbah 13:2, gives an unusually direct parallel to R’ Tzadok’s letter-symbolism. The name דוד, he writes, begins with a dalet because David knew ‘דלית ליה מגרמיה כלום’ — he possessed nothing from himself. The vav signifies the explicit connection Hashem then illuminates to the one who recognizes that dependence; precisely because David knows he has no independent power, Hashem shows him the bond through which all blessing reaches him. Yet after all his victories and revelations David still says ‘כי עני ואביון אנכי’ and ‘ה׳ לא גבה לבי ולא רמו עיני’; this continued self-nullification is the second dalet. The Sod Yesharim thus sharpens R’ Tzadok’s point that the vav of emes stands between two dalets. The first lowliness is not merely the condition before receiving Divine abundance, to be discarded once a person succeeds. The second dalet proves that even after the vav — after connection, strength, kingship, and salvation — the recipient has not converted the gift into self-possession. That is why Davidic Malchus can receive endlessly without becoming a rival sovereignty. Its greatness is real, but its truth is the knowledge that every greatness flowing through it remains the King’s. The structure of the name itself becomes a discipline of teshuvah: lack, connection, and then renewed lack even after illumination.,
שֶׁצּוּרָתוֹ חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד וְדָבוּק כּוּלּוֹ בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבְעֶצֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ
whose “form is engraved on the Throne of Glory,” entirely cleaving to Him and to the very essence of the King;
וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת רַק עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת בְּעֶצֶם הַמֶּלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא הַמַּנְהִיג הַמְּלוּכָה

and from this the trait of Malchus is drawn only through cleaving to the very essence of the King, who “conducts the kingship.” — the very shape of David’s name — a lowly dalet at either end, Yaakov’s vav of truth between — spells out the king who reigns only by knowing he owns nothing of himself.

items.h: The theme: Dan is the “tail” of the collective lion and the root of Din — so Shimshon was a judge and not a king, and is likened to a serpent, whose venom does not befit kingship. From anger comes coarseness, the branches of the drive for idolatry; hence Yerovam set a calf in Dan. Even Israel’s idolaters keep faith at their root — only Michah was so material that his spiritual soul barely connected to him at all.

p: [מ] וְדָן הוּא ״זַנְבָא״ דִּכְלָלוּת הָאַרְיֵה, וְהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ מִדַּת הַדִּין כִּשְׁמוֹ
And Dan is the “tail” of the collective “lion,” and he is the root of the trait of Din, as his name [Dan = “judged”] implies;
וְעַל כֵּן שִׁמְשׁוֹן הָיָה ״שׁוֹפֵט״ ״וְיָדִין עַמּוֹ״ לֹא מֶלֶךְ
and therefore Shimshon was a “judge” — “he shall judge his people” (Bereishis 49:16) — not a king;
וְעַל כֵּן בְּבִרְכַּת יַעֲקֹב נִמְשַׁל לְנָחָשׁ לֹא לְאַרְיֵה

and therefore in Yaakov’s blessing [Dan] is likened to a serpent, not to a lion.776R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim §4): “and among the tribes too we find [Shemos Rabbah 40], "you have none greater than the tribe of Yehudah, and none lower than [the tribe of] Dan."” Exactly the se’if: Dan is the collective’s “tail” — the extreme opposite pole to Yehudah, which is why kingship belongs to the one and judgeship alone to the other.
וְנוֹדָע דְּכַעַס הָאֲרִי מְעוֹרָב בְּרַחְמָנוּת גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַטִּבְעִיִּים, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן חֲמַת ״זוֹחֲלֵי עָפָר״ וּנְחָשִׁים, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נָאֶה לוֹ הַמְּלוּכָה

And it is known that the “wrath of the lion” is mingled with mercy as well, as the naturalists said — unlike the venom of “crawlers of the dust777Devarim 32:24: in Ha’azinu — “וְשֶׁן בְּהֵמֹת אֲשַׁלַּח בָּם, עִם חֲמַת זֹחֲלֵי עָפָר” — “and the teeth of beasts I will send against them, with the venom of crawlers of the dust.” Background: among the punishments Moshe foretells — the “crawlers of the dust” are serpents. R’ Tzadok’s use: he contrasts the “wrath of the lion,” which “the naturalists said” is mingled with mercy (and so befits kingship), with the pure venom of the serpent, the “crawler of the dust” — and since Dan is likened in Yaakov’s blessing to a serpent, “kingship does not befit him,” only judgeship.” (Devarim 32:24) and serpents; and therefore kingship does not befit him.778R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §21): "“[my property] to Toviah” — and two Tovyahs came; that “the discretion of the judges” [shuda d’dayanei], per Rashi, is to estimate the mind of the deceased." Exactly the se’if: Dan is the root of Din, and his is the “judging” power that must estimate what cannot be read off the words — the serpent’s discernment, which is not the open authority of kingship.
כִּי מֵהַכַּעַס בָּא לְגַסּוּת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל דִּשְׁנֵיהֶם חַד, וְהֵם עַנְפֵי יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
For from anger one comes to “coarseness [gassus],” as I wrote above, that the two are one — and they are “branches of the drive for idolatry”;
דְּעַל כֵּן שָׂם יָרׇבְעָם הָאֶחָד בְּדָן, וְשָׁם הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ לִמְצִיאוּת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
and therefore Yerovam placed the one [calf] in Dan, and there is the “root” of the existence of idolatry in Israel,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסִפְרֵי] עַל פָּסוּק ״פֶּן יֵשׁ בָּכֶם מִשְׁפָּחָה אוֹ שֵׁבֶט [אֲשֶׁר לְבָבוֹ פֹנֶה]״ — זֶה שֵׁבֶט דָּן

as they said [in the Sifri] on the verse “lest there be among you a family or a tribe [whose heart turns away]” (Devarim 29:17) — this is the tribe of Dan779Sifrei, on Devarim 29:17: the Torah warns, “פֶּן יֵשׁ בָּכֶם… מִשְׁפָּחָה אוֹ שֵׁבֶט אֲשֶׁר לְבָבוֹ פֹנֶה הַיּוֹם מֵעִם ה׳” — “lest there be among you… a family or a tribe whose heart turns away this day from Hashem” — and the Sifrei comments, “this is the tribe of Dan.” Background: the Danite associations with idolatry — the graven image of Michah (whose Levite served within Dan’s domain) and, later, one of Yerovam’s golden calves set in Dan. R’ Tzadok’s use: Dan, as the “root of Din,” is likewise the “root of the existence of idolatry in Israel” — for “from anger one comes to coarseness,” and the two are “branches of the drive for idolatry.”Tanya — anger becomes a form of avodah zarah when it attributes independent power to the event: Tanya, Iggeres HaKodesh §25, returns explicitly to Chazal’s statement that anger is ‘as though one worshipped idolatry.’ The Alter Rebbe explains that in ordinary worldly matters the root error of anger is failure to recognize that ‘הכל בידי שמים חוץ מיראת שמים’: the circumstance that provoked the person did not acquire an independent sovereignty outside Divine providence. He carefully limits this principle, noting that in matters of Heaven one may indeed protest wrongdoing in order to separate someone from an issur, as Moshe himself became angry. This distinction complements R’ Tzadok’s movement from Dan’s Din to anger, coarseness, and avodah zarah. Anger becomes spiritually related to idolatry when it experiences the offending person or event as an autonomous force that has displaced Hashem from the field. The issue is not that all forcefulness is forbidden; Din itself is holy, and zeal for Torah can be required. The corruption begins when gevurah ceases to be an instrument of yiras Shamayim and becomes the assertion of a separate center of power. This also explains why R’ Tzadok can trace idolatry to a distortion of Din rather than to an intellectual doctrine alone: the emotional act of rage can already enact the same metaphysical falsehood — treating a created force as though it stood on its own..
וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק חֵלֶק] ״פֶּסֶל מִיכָה עָבַר בַּיָּם״
And this is as they said [in Perek Chelek, Sanhedrin 103b], “the idol of Michah passed through the sea [with Israel].”
וּבְתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ דְּמִיכָה ״בָּעַט בְּאָנֹכִי״, וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
And in Tana d’Vei Eliyahu, that Michah “kicked at Anochi” [the first commandment] — and this [Anochi] is the root of the “Jewishness” of Israel;
דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא אָמַר ״אָנֹכִי״ בִּלְשׁוֹן צִיווּי, כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל ״מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים״

for therefore “Anochi” was not stated in the imperative, since the root of Israel is “believers, children of believers,”780R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §17): “"and after your eyes" — and they said, "after your eyes" — this is a sinful thought; only that the eye should be "lift up your eyes on high and see Who created these."” The se’if’s “branches of the drive” precisely: the same faculty that runs after the eye’s desire is the one that, lifted, becomes the organ of recognition.
וְגַם עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְלַל זֶה, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּבַעֲטִים בְּ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״ מִכָּל מָקוֹם שֹׁרֶשׁ לְבָבָם נִקְשָׁר בֶּאֱמוּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
and even the idolaters of Israel are included in this: though they “kick” at “You shall have no [other gods],” nonetheless the root of their heart is bound to faith in Hashem.
רַק מִיכָה שֶׁנִּתְמַכְמֵךְ בַּבִּנְיָן
Only Michah, who “was pressed into the building” [made into mortar in Egypt] —
כִּי אוֹתָם שֶׁשָּׂמוּ בִּמְקוֹם לְבֵנִים בַּבִּנְיָן הוּא כְּאִלּוּ אֵין בָּהֶם אֶלָּא חוֹמֶר הֶעָפָרִי לְבַד
for those set in place of bricks in the building, it is as though there is in them nothing but the “earthy matter” alone;

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב יֵשׁ בָּהֶם ״חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ מִמַּעַל״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְעוֹצֶם הַהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּמִצְרַיִם יֵשׁ שֶׁהָיָה גּוּפָם חוּמְרִיִּי כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ הִתְחַבְּרוּת כְּלָל עִם נַפְשׁוֹ הָרוּחָנִית

and although all the seed of Yaakov have in them “a portion of God from above” (Iyov 31:2), nonetheless, through the intensity of the “sinking” into Egypt, there were those whose body was so material that it had no connection at all with its spiritual soul,
עַד שֶׁגַּם בְּחַיָּיו הָיָה כְּאִלּוּ נִפְרָד מִמֶּנּוּ וְעוֹמֵד עֲלֵיהֶם בְּסוֹד מַקִּיף לְבַד
so that even in his lifetime [the soul] was as though separated from him, standing over them only “in the secret of an encompassing [light].”
וְזֶה טַעַם ״וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר״, שֶׁהוּא לְמַטָּה מִכָּל הַקּוֹמָה

And this is the meaning of “and beneath His feet was like the work of a sapphire brick781Shemos 24:10: at the vision of the elders at Sinai — “וַיִּרְאוּ אֵת אֱלֹהֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְתַחַת רַגְלָיו כְּמַעֲשֵׂה לִבְנַת הַסַּפִּיר, וּכְעֶצֶם הַשָּׁמַיִם לָטֹהַר” — “and they saw the God of Israel, and beneath His feet was like the work of a sapphire brick [livnas ha-sapir], and like the very heavens in purity.” Meforshim: Rashi (from the Midrash) explains that this “brick” recalled the bricks of Israel’s Egyptian bondage — set before Him throughout the enslavement as a remembrance of their affliction. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “brick,” “beneath His feet,” is “below the entire stature” — the lowest, most material rung (Michah, “pressed into the building”); yet “in the secret of an encompassing light” it is refined until it becomes “sapphirine,” translucent.” (Shemos 24:10) — [the “brick,”] which is below the entire “stature”;
אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם בְּסוֹד מַקִּיף הָיָה מְזַכְּכָם עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשׂוּ סַפִּירִיִּים

except that nonetheless, “in the secret of an encompassing [light],” He was refining them until they became “sapphirine” [translucent]. — so material was such a soul’s grip that it hovered over the body only from without, an encompassing light slowly rendering the brick-like matter translucent from outside.

items.h: The theme: Moshe longed for a complete tikkun in his own days, and therefore accepted the erev rav. He was told to raise Michah from the Nile mud, since Michah was connected to him. Michah’s error was corporealizing Hashem: he believed in the Name, but imagined it rested upon his idol — “kicking at Anochi” rather than at “you shall have no other gods.” Believers in corporeality are mistaken rather than wicked, yet he was close to deliberate.

p: [מא] וּלְפִי שֶׁחֵשֶׁק מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הָיָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר בְּיָמָיו
And since Moshe Rabbeinu’s desire was that the complete rectification be in his days,
כִּי לֹא חָשַׁב שֶׁיִּתְקַלְקֵל עַל יְדֵי הָעֵגֶל
for he did not think it would be spoiled by the [golden] calf,
דְּעַל כֵּן קִיבֵּל הַגֵּרִים דְּעֵרֶב רַב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד ״גֵּרִים גְּרוּרִים״ אַף דְּאֵין מְקַבְּלִים גֵּרִים בִּימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ

therefore he accepted the converts of the erev rav — as there will be in the Future “self-attached converts [gerim gerurim],” even though we do not accept converts in the days of Mashiach782Yevamos 24b: “the Sages taught: we do not accept converts in the days of the Mashiach — just as they accepted no converts in the days of David or of Shlomo.” Background: formal conversion is suspended in eras where ulterior motive is suspected. R’ Tzadok’s use: yet in the Future there will be “self-attached converts [gerim gerurim],” who join of their own accord; Moshe, longing for a complete tikkun already in his own days, “accepted the converts of the erev rav” in that very spirit — reaching to rectify even them. —
וְכֵן רָצָה לְתַקֵּן גַּם אֵלּוּ, וְכָל מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר לָבוֹא בַּסּוֹף לִידֵי תִּיקּוּן חָשַׁב שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵן בְּיָמָיו

and so he wished to rectify even these; whatever could ultimately come to rectification, he thought would be so in his days.783R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §44): “Moshe Rabbeinu taught Torah to Israel — and even the erev rav and the converts from the nations, once they had converted, are ‘established’ in the name of Israel. But Avraham Avinu taught the nations of the world; for of all the converts he made and ‘the souls they made [in Charan],’ none remained [reckoned] among Israel — since there was not yet a ‘name of Israel’ such that ‘a convert who converts is like a newborn child’ into Jewishness.” (This is why, as the se’if says, Moshe could take in the erev rav: through Moshe the Torah ‘establishes’ even the attached converts within Israel — the very work Moshe hoped would bring a complete tikkun in his days.)
וְצִיוָּהוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהוֹצִיא מִיכָה לְפִי שֶׁאֵלָיו הָיָה לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת
And Hashem commanded him to “bring out Michah” [from the Nile mud], because he had a “connection” to him,
שֶׁהֲרֵי נִתְחַבֵּר אֵלָיו יְהוֹנָתָן מִזַּרְעוֹ

for Yehonasan, of his [Moshe’s] seed784Shoftim 18:30: of Michah’s idol among the Danites — “וִיהוֹנָתָן בֶּן גֵּרְשֹׁם בֶּן מְנַשֶּׁה, הוּא וּבָנָיו הָיוּ כֹהֲנִים לְשֵׁבֶט הַדָּנִי” — “and Yehonasan son of Gershom son of Menasheh, he and his sons were priests to the tribe of Dan.” Meforshim: the nun of “Menasheh [מנשה]” is written suspended (nun teluyah), and the Sages (Bava Basra 109b) read the name as “Moshe” — Yehonasan was in truth the grandson of Moshe, the nun inserted only to shield Moshe’s honor. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is Moshe’s “connection” to Michah — since Yehonasan, of Moshe’s own seed, later served as Michah’s priest — which is why Hashem bade Moshe “bring out Michah” from the Nile mud., later attached himself to him [as Michah’s priest],
וְעַל יָדוֹ נִתְבָּרֵר שֹׁרֶשׁ טָעוּתוֹ כְּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה׳ לִי״ וְגוֹמֵר

and through him the “root of his error” was clarified, as he said, “now I know that Hashem will do me good785Shoftim 17:13: Michah’s words when a wandering Levite became his priest — “עַתָּה יָדַעְתִּי כִּי יֵיטִיב ה׳ לִי, כִּי הָיָה לִי הַלֵּוִי לְכֹהֵן” — “now I know that Hashem will do me good, for the Levite has become my priest.” Background: Michah’s private idol-shrine gains a Levite officiant. R’ Tzadok’s use: from this very verse the Sages learned that Michah “kicked at Anochi,” not at “no other gods” — for he said “Hashem [Havayah] will do me good,” a Name never applied to idolatry; he did believe in Havayah, only he “corporealized” Him upon his idol.Tanya — the basic error is imagining a created thing as possessing existence apart from the Divine power within it: Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah ch. 2, describes the ‘root of the error’ of those who deny continuous Divine providence as the comparison of creation to a human artisan. Once a craftsman finishes a vessel, the vessel can remain after his hands leave it; but creation ex nihilo is entirely different. Were the Creator’s power to withdraw for an instant, the created being would return to absolute nothingness. Therefore ‘כח הפועל בנפעל תמיד’ — the creative force must continuously be present within the creature to sustain it. This provides a useful conceptual complement to R’ Tzadok’s diagnosis of Michah. Michah did not simply erase the Name of Hashem; he could still say ‘ייטיב ה׳ לי.’ His corruption lay in fastening Divine presence to a separate corporeal object, as though the physical form could be a self-standing bearer or localization of God. The Tanya’s account explains why such corporealization is so profound a mistake: the creature has no independent ontological platform upon which God could later ‘rest’ as an added presence. Its entire being at every moment is only the effect of the Divine word sustaining it. Thus even when the language of faith remains on the lips, treating a created thing as an autonomous locus of power already fractures yichud. R’ Tzadok’s category of Michah as gravely mistaken rather than simply atheistic becomes more intelligible against this distinction.” (Shoftim 17:13).
דְּנִרְאֶה לִי דְּמִכָּתוּב זֶה לָמְדוּ שֶׁבָּעַט בְּאָנֹכִי וְלֹא בְּ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״, מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״יֵיטִיב ה׳״ — שֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה
And it seems to me that from this verse they learned that he “kicked at Anochi” and not at “You shall have no [other gods]” — [for] he said “Hashem will do me good” — the Name Havayah,
וְלֹא נִמְצָא כֵן בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּשׁוּם מָקוֹם כַּיָּדוּעַ, דְּעַל שֵׁם זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״וּכְבוֹדִי לְאַחֵר לֹא אֶתֵּן״

and [this Name] is not found [applied] to idolatry anywhere, as is known, for concerning this Name it says, “and My glory I will not give to another786Yeshayah 42:8: “אֲנִי ה׳ הוּא שְׁמִי, וּכְבוֹדִי לְאַחֵר לֹא אֶתֵּן, וּתְהִלָּתִי לַפְּסִילִים” — “I am Hashem, that is My Name, and My glory I will not give to another, nor My praise to idols.” Background: God declares that the honor of His Name belongs to Him alone, never to idols. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because the Name Havayah is never “given to another” — never found applied to idolatry anywhere — Michah’s applying it to his own idol was not the “invention of other gods” but the corporealizing of the true God: a “kicking at Anochi.”” (Yeshayah 42:8).
אֲבָל זֶה מוֹרֶה עַל גַּסּוּת חוּמְרוֹ שֶׁהָיָה מְרוּחָק לְגַמְרֵי מֵרוּחָנִיּוּת וְלֹא הֵבִין עִנְיַן הָרוּחָנִית כְּלָל

But this indicates the “coarseness of his matter” — that he was utterly distant from spirituality and did not comprehend the spiritual matter at all.787R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kedushas Shabbos §1): “even the wicked of Israel in their bodies — "the skull that never wore tefillin" — and the other greatest wicked of Israel, in whom there is no moisture of a mitzvah at all — nonetheless they too are full of the mitzvos of charity and kindness, which is found in all the seed of Israel.” Exactly the se’if’s reasoning: Moshe could accept even the erev rav, because no Jewish root is ever wholly without a living channel.
וְאַף הוּא הָיָה מִכָּל הַמַּאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים וְהֶאֱמִין בַּה׳, אֲבָל דּוֹמֶה שֶׁעַל הַפֶּסֶל שֶׁלּוֹ גַּם כֵּן חָל שֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה
He too was of “the believers, children of believers,” and believed in Hashem — but it seemed to him that the Name Havayah rested upon his idol as well.
וְזֶהוּ הַבְּעִיטָה בְּאָנֹכִי, דְּלֹא עָבַד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לְהַמְצִיא אֱלֹהִים אֲחֵרִים כְּלָל דְּהֶאֱמִין בַּהֲוָיָ״ה רַק שֶׁהִגְשִׁים כְּפִי חוּמְרִיּוּתוֹ
And this is the “kicking at Anochi”: he did not serve idolatry to “invent other gods” at all, for he believed in Havayah — only that he “corporealized” [Him] according to his materiality,
וַהֲרֵי כָּפַר בַּאֲמִיתּוּת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וּבָעַט בְּאָנֹכִי בְּ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״
and thereby he denied the truth of Hashem, and “kicked at Anochi” [rather than] at “You shall have no [other gods].”
וְכָל מַאֲמִינֵי הַהַגְשָׁמָה כֵּן, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָרַמְבָּ״ם [בְּהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה] קְרָאָם ״גְּדוֹלִים וְטוֹבִים״, הַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁהָיוּ שׁוֹגְגִים בָּזֶה
And all who believe in “corporeality [hagshamah]” are thus; and although the Rambam [in Hilchos Teshuvah 3:7] called them “great and good,” that is [only] because they were “inadvertent” in this,
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם מוֹדֶה דְּשָׁגְגוּ בָּזֶה

but nonetheless he concedes that they “erred” in it.788R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §12): “and the nations tasted from their flesh the taste of the mon… only that the taste absorbed in their flesh was no longer able to turn over [into every taste].” The se’if’s Michah exactly: the outsider can receive the substance and still not receive the power of transformation — he grasps the physical and “did not comprehend the spiritual matter at all.”
וְאַף דְּגַם הַשּׁוֹגֵג צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִקְרָא רָשָׁע כְּלָל אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא הִכִּיר כָּל יָמָיו בְּשִׁגְגָתוֹ וְלֹא שָׁב מִמֶּנָּה
And though even the inadvertent [sinner] requires atonement, nonetheless he is not called “wicked” at all — even though he never recognized his error all his days, nor repented of it.
וְאַף מִיכָה וַדַּאי מוּטְעֶה הָיָה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נִקְרָא ״בָּעַט״ לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לִלְמוֹד וְלֹא לָמַד
And Michah, too, was certainly “mistaken,” yet he is called one who “kicked” [deliberately], because “he ought to have learned, and did not learn,”
וְהָיָה קָרוֹב לְמֵזִיד בָּזֶה
and he was “close to intentional” in this —
עַל יְדֵי שֶׁעָבַר תְּחִלָּה עַל שְׁתֵּי דִּבְּרוֹת ״לֹא תִגְנוֹב״ וְ״לֹא תִשָּׂא״, שֶׁשָּׁמַע אֵלֶּה וְקִיבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ וְלֹא הוֹדָה, וְעַל ״כִּיבּוּד אֵם״

through having first transgressed two of the [other] commandments — “you shall not steal” and “you shall not bear [a false oath]” (having “heard an oath [alah],” and taken it upon himself, yet not confessing), and [the command of] “honoring [one’s] mother” —
וּבִתְלָתָא הֲוֵי חֲזָקָה שֶׁבָּא לְטַמֵּא לִהְיוֹת ״פּוֹתְחִין״ [לוֹ]

and “with three [times] there is a chazakah” [an established pattern], for “one who comes to defile himself, they open [the way] for him” (Yoma 38b)789Yoma 38b: “One who comes to purify himself is assisted [from Heaven]; and one who comes to defile himself, they open [the way] for him [ha-ba litamei, poschin lo].”. — sincere error in picturing the Divine is “mistaken,” not “wicked”; Michah crossed into culpability only by refusing to learn what he could readily have learned.

items.h: The theme: Michah was of Yosef’s seed, yet his idol “rolled” to the children of Dan — the first emergence of Rachel’s line, through Bilhah. Rachel named him Dan, sensing in this child the drive for idolatry and anger whose beginning lay in her own line. “The greater the man, the greater his drive”: Dan, lowest of the tribes, has a lesser though real one, while Yosef’s root has no connection to idolatry at all.

p: [מב] וְהוּא הָיָה מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף וְנִתְגַּלְגֵּל פִּסְלוֹ לִבְנֵי דָן
And he [Michah] was of the seed of Yosef, yet his idol “rolled” to the children of Dan —
שֶׁהֵם הַתְחָלַת גִּילּוּי זַרְעָא דְּרָחֵל עַל יְדֵי בִּלְהָה שִׁפְחָתָהּ שֶׁרָצְתָה לְהִבָּנוֹת מִמֶּנָּה בְּעוֹד שֶׁהָיָה עֲדַיִין מִדַּת הַדִּין נוֹתֶנֶת שֶׁלֹּא תִּפָּקֵד רָחֵל

who are the “beginning of the emergence” of Rachel’s seed, through Bilhah her handmaid — [Rachel] wishing to “be built up” through her while Din still decreed that Rachel not be remembered [with children].
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרָה ״דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹקִים״, רְצֹה לוֹמַר עַל שֶׁמַּגַּע הַהוֹלָדָה מִמֶּנָּה הִצְדִּיקָה הַדִּין, וְגַם ״שָׁמַע בְּקוֹלִי״ לְהִבָּנוֹת מִשִּׁפְחָתָהּ

Therefore she said “God has judged me [Danani]” (Bereishis 30:6)790Bereishis 30:6: at the birth of Bilhah’s first son — “וַתֹּאמֶר רָחֵל, דָּנַנִּי אֱלֹהִים וְגַם שָׁמַע בְּקֹלִי וַיִּתֶּן לִי בֵּן, עַל כֵּן קָרְאָה שְׁמוֹ דָּן” — “and Rachel said: God has judged me [danani], and He has also heard my voice and given me a son; therefore she called his name Dan.” Meforshim: Rashi — “He judged me [and] found me innocent,” acquitting her. R’ Tzadok’s use: Rachel named him for “the trait of Din in her” — sensing at his birth (as the Imahos could) the “drive for idolatry and anger” whose beginning lay in her own line (Yosef’s), and thereby “justifying the judgment” that had kept her barren; yet “He heard my voice,” for through this very child the power of that drive was weakened.Be’er Mayim Chaim — ‘Dan’ itself is remembered by Chazal as a point where avodah zarah obstructs holy advance: Be’er Mayim Chaim, Bereishis 12:8:6, comments on Chazal’s reading of ‘וירדוף עד דן’ — Avraham’s pursuit stopped at Dan because he prophetically saw the idolatry that would one day stand there. The Be’er Mayim Chaim stresses the strange spiritual force of that sin: avodah zarah ‘strikes before and behind,’ and Avraham therefore built an altar and sought to interpose holiness against the future blemish. This does not supply R’ Tzadok’s specific genealogy from Rachel through Bilhah, but it gives a striking Chassidic echo to the very association on which he builds: the name and place of Dan stand in Chazal as a frontier at which the power of avodah zarah becomes capable of arresting even Avraham’s forward movement. R’ Tzadok’s contribution is to locate that danger within the inner structure of the shevatim and to explain why it appears specifically at the ‘lowest’ end of Rachel’s extension. The Be’er Mayim Chaim helps frame the severity of the point without making Dan himself synonymous with evil. Avraham’s response is to build a mizbe’ach — to establish an opposing orientation toward Hashem. So too in R’ Tzadok, the very force that can descend into Din and anger is not discarded; it must be weakened, redirected, and ultimately restored to the service of the one God. — that is, over the “reach” of bearing through her she “justified the judgment,” and also “He heard my voice” to be built up through her handmaid791Bereishis 30:3: Rachel, still barren, gave her handmaid Bilhah to Yaakov — “הִנֵּה אֲמָתִי בִלְהָה בֹּא אֵלֶיהָ… וְאִבָּנֶה גַם אָנֹכִי מִמֶּנָּה” — “behold my handmaid Bilhah, come to her… and I too shall be built up through her.” Background: as Sarah had done with Hagar, Rachel seeks to be “built up” through her maidservant’s children. R’ Tzadok’s use: Bilhah’s sons are “the beginning of the emergence of Rachel’s seed” — Rachel “wishing to be built up” through her handmaid while Din still decreed that she herself not yet bear; and indeed “He heard her voice,” for the harsh drive was thereby drawn off and weakened..
וּקְרָאַתּוּ דָּן עַל שֵׁם מִדַּת הַדִּין בָּהּ, כִּי עַל יָדוֹ נִתְגַּלָּה לָהּ שֶׁהַשֵּׂכֶל בַּדִּין
And she called him “Dan,” for the trait of Din [judgment] in her — for through him it was “revealed to her intellect [that lay] in the judgment”;
כִּי בְּלֵידַת כָּל שֵׁבֶט וִיצִיאָתוֹ לַאֲוִיר הָעוֹלָם נִתְגַּלָּה אוֹרוֹ בָּעוֹלָם, וְנוֹדָע לְמְבִינֵי מַדָּע כָּאָבוֹת וְאִמָּהוֹת כָּל מַעֲלוֹת וְחִסְרוֹנוֹת שֶׁבּוֹ

for at the birth of each tribe and his “coming into the air of the world,” his light was revealed in the world, and to “those who understand knowledge,” like the Avos and Imahos, all his qualities and deficiencies became known.792R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §2): “and what one opinion said in Vayikra Rabbah and in the Yerushalmi — "he is a holy man" — that he did not gaze at her.” Exactly the se’if’s point: the “weakening of that drive” is measured not by what a person refrains from doing but by where his eye does not go at all.
וְהִרְגִּישָׁה בְּיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְכַעַס הַנִּמְצָא בּוֹ וְהַתְחָלָתָם בְּזַרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף, וְהֵבִינָה מִזֶּה הַצְדָּקַת דִּינָהּ
And she sensed the “drive for idolatry” and the anger found in him — and their “beginning” [was] in the seed of Yosef — and she understood from this the “justification of her judgment.”
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁמַע בְּקוֹלָהּ גַּם כֵּן דְּתוּכַל לְהִבָּנוֹת עַל יְדֵי זֶה, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה נֶחֱלַשׁ כֹּחַ אוֹתוֹ יֵצֶר
