He then cites the Yerushalmi's 'it is enough that I and your Creator know your power' and interprets it literally: no person fully knew Rashbi's power except Hashem and R' Akiva, the root of Torah shebe'al peh. The passage fits this se'if's theme of concealed strength in two ways. First, Rashbi's greatness is not measured by what was publicly ranked during his lifetime; it becomes established in Israel through the inward transmission of Torah. Second, the very medium associated with him - Torah shebe'al peh and its deepest secrets - is knowledge that lives in the mouths and hearts of Israel rather than in a simple visible monument. R' Tzadok's suggestion about the stock name 'Yosef ben Shimon' should therefore be read within that larger pattern: Shimon's power can be hidden in ordinary language, names, and conventions until the inner Torah discloses why those seemingly incidental forms were chosen.”;
דְּגַם הוּא שְׁמוֹ שִׁמְעוֹן, וְדָרְשִׁינַן שֵׁמוֹת כִּי זֶה הָיָה כֹּחוֹ וְשֹׁרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתוֹ

for he too, his name was “Shimon,” and “we expound names,” for this was “his power and the root of his soul.”924R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §20): “three names are called upon a person: one his father and mother called him at birth; and one that he called himself — righteous or wicked — and one that is written in the book of his generations.” Exactly the se’if’s reasoning from the name: a name is not a label but a record of a root, and therefore the name Shimon borne by R’ Shimon bar Yochai testifies to where his power came from.
וְכֵן קִיבַּלְתִּי כִּי הוּא הָיָה מִשֵּׁבֶט שִׁמְעוֹן, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה תּוֹקֶף כֹּחוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And so I have received, that “he was from the tribe of Shimon925From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): R’ Tzadok’s “I have received” — the tradition that R’ Shimon bar Yochai stemmed from the tribe of Shimon (whence his name and his fierce “power”) — is a teaching of his rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see §8 above).,” and therefore “the intensity of his power was not revealed in this world.”926R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §23): “but in the combination of the two together it prevails all the more, God forbid.” The se’if’s “enough that I and your Creator know your power” exactly: a power that is not disclosed is not thereby diminished — it is precisely in the joining of the hidden to the revealed that its full force appears.
וּבַתַּלְמוּד הַנִּגְלֶה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁגַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ מִמֶּנּוּ בְּהַפְלָגוֹת מַעֲלָתוֹ [בְּסוּכָּה] מַה שֶּׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ, וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [לה] וְעוֹד בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי

And in the “revealed Talmud,” even though there is [something] of it too — in the “extollings of his elevation” [in Sukkah], what he said of himself, and in Bereishis Rabbah [35] and several other places927Sukkah 45b: R’ Yirmeyah said in the name of R’ Shimon bar Yochai, “I am able to exempt the whole world from judgment from the day I was created until now — I have seen the ‘men of ascent’ and they are few; if they are a thousand, I and my son are among them; if a hundred, I and my son are among them; if two, they are I and my son.” A like statement appears in Bereishis Rabbah 35:2 (“if there is but one tzaddik in the world, it is he”). —
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּנִגְלוֹת הַתַּלְמוּד לֹא נִגְלָה מַעֲלָתוֹ נֶגֶד חֲבֵירָיו כְּלָל
nonetheless, “in the revealed [surface] of the Talmud, his elevation over his colleagues is not revealed at all”;
וְרַק בּוֹרְאוֹ וְכֵן רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בְּרוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ שֶׁבּוֹ לְהַכִּיר הַנֶּעֱלָמוֹת יָדַע כֹּחוֹ
and “only his Creator, and likewise Rabbi Akiva, through the ruach hakodesh in him to recognize hidden things, knew his power.”
וְאַף הַסּוֹדוֹת שֶׁגִּילָּה לֹא יִתְגַּלֶּה סוֹדָם לְעֵין הַכֹּל אֶלָּא בְּסוֹף יוֹמַיָּא
And even “the secrets that he revealed [in the Zohar], their [inner] secret will not be revealed to the eyes of all except at the ‘end of days.’”
וְנִרְאֶה לִי דְּזֶה סוֹד מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק גֵּט פָּשׁוּט] ״שְׁנֵי יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״, וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי דְּנָקַט ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״

And it seems to me that this is the “secret” of what they said [in Perek Get Pashut], “two [people named] Yosef ben Shimon,” and likewise in several places where [the Gemara] “takes ‘Yosef ben Shimon’” [as its example].
וְהָיָה לוֹ לִינְקַט לְמָשָׁל ״רְאוּבֵן בֶּן יַעֲקֹב״ כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּפֶרֶק הַמְגָרֵשׁ] ״רְאוּבֵן בֶּן יַעֲקֹב״ עֵד, שֶׁהוּא הַשֵּׁבֶט הָרִאשׁוֹן וְהַבֵּן הָרִאשׁוֹן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And it “should have taken, as its example, ‘Reuven ben Yaakov,’” in the manner stated [in Perek HaMegaresh], “‘Reuven ben Yaakov’ [as] witness” — for he is “the first tribe and the first son in Israel”;
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת ״רְאוּבֵן וְשִׁמְעוֹן״, ״רְאוּבֵן שֶׁלָּקַח שָׂדֶה מִשִּׁמְעוֹן״ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, טוֹבֵי שֶׁהֵם רִאשׁוֹנֵי הַשְּׁבָטִים
and in the manner stated in many places, “Reuven and Shimon,” “Reuven who bought a field from Shimon,” and the like — [taking as examples] preferentially those who are “the first of the tribes,”
וְכֵן בִּיבָמוֹת [צד:] ״רְאוּבֵן וְשִׁמְעוֹן וְלֵוִי״ וְכֵן בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי

and likewise in Yevamos [94b], “Reuven and Shimon and Levi928Yevamos 94b: the sugya of a man told his wife had died, who then married her sister — the status of the children (mamzer / not), and R’ Akiva’s ruling that even “a brother’s wife and a wife’s sister” require a bill of divorce, since each could yet become permitted (by yibum, or after the wife’s death). Background: such fraternal and co-wife cases are, by long learning-convention, set out with the first tribal names — Reuven, Shimon, and Levi. R’ Tzadok adduces Yevamos 94b (citing it as “Reuven and Shimon and Levi”) as one more place where the Talmud’s illustrative persons are drawn from “the first of the tribes” — the very foil to the anomalous, non-Scriptural “Yosef ben Shimon” that is his subject in this se’if.,” and in several places.
וַאֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקוֹם אִיסּוּר נָקְטוּ [יבמות י.] ״יַעֲקֹב אָנַס כַּלָּתוֹ וּמֵת רְאוּבֵן״ כו׳

And “even in a case of prohibition” they “took” [Yevamos 10a], “Yaakov violated his daughter-in-law and Reuven died929Yevamos 10a: in the sugya clarifying whether “his mother” — a woman his father took by force (anusas aviv) — can exempt her co-wife, Rav Ashi builds a placeholder case for Rav Kahana: “Yaakov forced his daughter-in-law and begot a son from her, and Reuven [the husband] died childless, and she fell before his [Yaakov’s] son [for yibum]; and since she herself is forbidden [to that son], her co-wife too is forbidden.” Meforshim: Rashi — the case is constructed only to probe the rule, and the Gemara answers that the mishnah “speaks of a permitted sisterhood, not a forbidden one.” R’ Tzadok’s point: note that “even in a case of prohibition [issur/arayos]” the Sages reached for the dignified names of the patriarch Yaakov and the firstborn Reuven — making it the more striking that for the “two men of one name” example they chose the un-Scriptural “Yosef ben Shimon.”” —
וּמָה עִנְיָן לִתְפּוֹס לְמָשָׁל ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״ שֶׁלֹּא נִמְצָא דּוּגְמָתוֹ בַּכָּתוּב כְּלָל
so what is the “reason to grasp, as an example, ‘Yosef ben Shimon,’” whose “likeness is not found in Scripture at all”?

וְכָל דִּבְרֵי חֲז״ל לֹא בָּאוּ בְּמִקְרֶה וְשֶׁלֹּא בְּדִקְדּוּק, וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁנָּקְטוּ לְמָשָׁל הַמּוּרְגָּל יֵשׁ בּוֹ טַעַם נֶעֱלָם גַּם כֵּן, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁנָּקְטוּ מָשָׁל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מוּרְגָּל

And “all the words of the Sages do not come by chance or without precision”; and “even where they take a customary example, there is a concealed reason in it too” — and all the more so “where they take an unusual example.”
וְרָחוֹק לוֹמַר כִּי הָיָה מָצוּי בֵּינֵיהֶם ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״ הַרְבֵּה
And it is “far-fetched to say that ‘Yosef ben Shimon’ was common among them.”
וְכִמְדוּמֶה כִּי הַשֵּׁם ״שִׁמְעוֹן״ מָצוּי בֵּין הַתַּנָּאִים וְאָמוֹרָאֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן לָקִישׁ וּבֶן פָּזִי וּבַר אַבָּא וְכַיּוֹצֵא, טוֹבֵי הַכֹּל מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל

And it seems that “the name Shimon is common among the Tannaim and the Amoraim of Eretz Yisrael” — like Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish, and ben Pazi, and bar Abba, and the like — mostly all from Eretz Yisrael.
אֲבָל בֵּין אָמוֹרָאֵי בָּבֶל לֹא נִמְצְאוּ כִמְדוּמֶה ״רַב שִׁמְעוֹן״ [דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא נִסְמַךְ, דְּאֵין סְמִיכָה בְּבָבֶל רַק ״רַבִּי״ שֶׁהוּא מֵאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל]
But “among the Amoraim of Bavel, it seems there is no ‘Rav Shimon’” [that is, one not ordained — for “there is no ordination in Bavel,” only ‘Rabbi,’ which is from Eretz Yisrael];
נִרְאֶה דְּהַשֵּׁם שִׁמְעוֹן לֹא הָיָה מָצוּי כָּל כָּךְ שָׁם
it appears “the name Shimon was not so common there.”
וְהַשֵּׁם ״יוֹסֵף״ מָצוּי בְּאָמוֹרָאֵי בָּבֶל וְלֹא בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק ״יוֹסֵי״, לֹא בַּתַּנָּאִים וְלֹא בְּאָמוֹרָאֵי אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל
And “the name Yosef is common among the Amoraim of Bavel, and not in Eretz Yisrael” — [where they say] only “Yosi,” not among the Tannaim nor the Amoraim of Eretz Yisrael.
כִּמְדוּמֶה אַף ״רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בֶּן יוֹסֵף״ וְכַיּוֹצֵא אֵין מָצוּי כָּל כָּךְ, כִּי שָׁם הָיוּ קוֹרִין לְיוֹסֵף ״יוֹסִי״
It seems that even “Rabbi Akiva ben Yosef” and the like is not so common — for “there they would call Yosef ‘Yosi.’”
וְאִם כָּךְ אַדְּרַבָּא אֵין ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״ מָצוּי כָּל כָּךְ, וְגַם זֶה לֹא בְּמִקְרֶה

And if so, “on the contrary, ‘Yosef ben Shimon’ is not so common” [either] — and “this too is not by chance.” — R’ Tzadok reads the Sages’ unusual placeholder as a quiet signature: the hidden “Shimon” power, like the man R’ Akiva praised, is known to its Creator alone, and surfaces only in oblique hints.

items.h: The theme: The sons “clarify” the fathers: what lay hidden in the father’s depths is revealed in the son. Every clarification works through its opposite — so Avraham begot Yitzchak, whose contraction and dread proved that Avraham’s revealed Chesed had been purely for Heaven. The nations are sunk in a single trait and cannot change; Avraham held the opposite trait in his depths, and wielded it when needed, as at the Akeidah.

p: [סה] אֲבָל נוֹדַע כִּי הַבָּנִים מְבָרְרִים הָאָבוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁשָּׁמַעְתִּי כִּי בַּבָּנִים נִגְלֶה מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב הָאָבוֹת וְהַנֶּעֱלָמוֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם

But it is known that “the sons clarify the fathers,” and as I heard, that930From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): “the sons clarify the fathers” — that in the sons the hidden depths of the fathers’ hearts are revealed — is a foundational teaching of R’ Tzadok’s rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz, which R’ Tzadok reports here as “I heard” (see §8 above).Izhbitz-Radzin development - Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayechi 83:1: Beit Yaakov supplies a useful framework for R' Tzadok's statement that clarification comes through an opposite. He describes the tribes as 'gevulei alachson' - diagonal boundaries whose lights are not replicas of one another. A trait that would be a major deficiency for Yosef can, in Yehudah's root, become a virtue: Yosef's holiness is built through restraint and therefore he must be one who 'passes over his measures,' whereas Yehudah's task can require a force that externally resembles the opposite. The point is not moral relativism, but that each holy root reveals a different facet of the Divine will and therefore must be clarified by what tests its particular danger. The same principle helps explain Avraham and Yitzchak in this se'if. If Avraham's Chesed were merely an unbounded temperament, it would collapse into its Yishmaelite counterfeit. The birth of Yitzchak - contraction, pachad, and finally the Akeidah - reveals that Avraham contains the opposite power and can surrender even the object of his greatest love when Hashem commands it. The 'son clarifies the father' because the later generation makes visible what had been latent in the earlier one. Beit Yaakov's tribal examples also preserve R' Tzadok's important qualification: what is a holy opposite in one root is not a license for another person to imitate its outer form. The clarification must arise from the actual Divine task of that soul, not from the appearance alone. “in the sons is revealed the depths of the fathers’ hearts and the hidden things in them.”
וְנוֹדַע דְּכָל בֵּירוּר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת בְּהֶפְכּוֹ

And it is known that “every clarification must be [effected] through its opposite”;931R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §42): "“bring me the book of genealogies, as my sons bring” — for he knew that they would sin; and as they said [Shabbos 89], “half upon me and half upon you.”" Exactly the se’if: the sons clarify the fathers — the father’s portion and the son’s are reckoned together, so that what lay hidden in the one is disclosed and answered in the other.
וְעַל כֵּן אַבְרָהָם הוֹלִיד אֶת יִצְחָק שֶׁהָיָה חֶפְצוֹ לְבָרֵר דְּהַחֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם הָיָה רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם

and therefore “Avraham begot Yitzchak” — for his desire was “to clarify that the Chesed of Avraham was only for the sake of Heaven.”932R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §39): “"and your name shall be Avraham" — after the circumcision, which is the complete removal of the desires… for this is the clarification of the cleanness of the love and longing of Avraham our father.” Exactly the se’if: Avraham’s Chesed required clarifying, and the clarification came by the very act that constrained it — which is why the son who follows is Yitzchak.
וְהַפְּסֹלֶת דְּיִשְׁמָעֵאל שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ לֹא נִקְרָא זַרְעוֹ, נִתְבָּרֵר עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהוֹלִיד יִצְחָק שֶׁנִּקְרָא זַרְעוֹ, שֶׁבּוֹ גִּילּוּי מַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ

And “the dross of Yishmael, who issued from him, is not called his seed933Bereishis 21:12: when Sarah demands that Yishmael be sent away, God reassures Avraham — “כִּי בְיִצְחָק יִקָּרֵא לְךָ זָרַע” — “for through Yitzchak shall seed be called for you.” Meforshim: Rashi — “b’Yitzchak” [through Yitzchak] “but not all of Yitzchak,” which excludes Esav; and the Sages (Nedarim 31a) expound that Yitzchak alone is “called your seed,” and not Yishmael. R’ Tzadok’s use: “the dross of Yishmael, who issued from Avraham, is not called his seed” — and this was “clarified through his begetting Yitzchak, who is called his seed,” in whom “the depths of Avraham’s heart were revealed”: that even his revealed trait of Chesed was purely for the sake of Heaven, held together with its very opposite — Yitzchak’s pachad and contraction — as at the Akeidah.” — [this] was clarified “through his begetting Yitzchak, who is called his seed,” in whom is “the revelation of the depths of his heart”;
וְהוּא אַדְּרַבָּא מִדָּתוֹ בְּצִמְצוּם וּפַחַד לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
and he [Yitzchak], on the contrary, “his trait is in contraction and fear [pachad], for the sake of Heaven” —
בָּזֶה נִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם הַחֶסֶד שֶׁהָיָה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת דְּמִדַּת אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
and by this it was “clarified that even the Chesed, which was the revealed trait of Avraham, was likewise only for the sake of Heaven.”
וְלֹא כְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁשְּׁקוּעִים בְּמִדָּה אַחַת וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לְשַׁנּוֹתָהּ, אֲבָל הוּא הֲרֵי הָיָה בְּמַעֲמַקָּיו גַּם מִדָּה הַהֲפֻכִּית

And not like the nations of the world, who are “sunk in one trait and cannot change it”; but he — “in his depths there was also the opposite trait,”934R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §47): “and from the side of Avraham’s thought regarding Yishmael, there was some joining of true love with an alien love — therefore there was room for Yishmael’s claim to say, "I am [the son]."” Exactly the se’if: every clarification works through its opposite, and it is the son who discloses which love in the father’s depths was genuinely for Heaven.
וְאִם הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְשַׁמֵּשׁ בָּהּ הָיָה גַּם כֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בָּעֲקֵידָה

and if it were “necessary, for the sake of Heaven, to use it, he would” [do so] as well — as was [the case] at the Akeidah.935R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §215): R’ Tzadok teaches that the integration of love (Avraham’s Chesed) and fear (Yitzchak’s tzimtzum and pachad) is the trait of Yaakov — “the form of man upon the Merkavah, the ultimate completion.” “And Avraham was not completed except after the tenth trial, at the Akeidah, when he became included in the trait of Yitzchak (as in the Zohar I:119b), as it says, ‘now I know that you fear [God]’ (Bereishis 22:12).” On this he reads Yeshayah 29:22 — “[the house of] Yaakov, who redeemed Avraham”: “from the side of the trait of Yaakov — the integration [of the opposites], which was itself also latent within Avraham — he was saved [nitzol].” The classical ground R’ Tzadok draws upon: the Gemara (Sanhedrin 19b) expounds the verse to mean that Yaakov redeemed Avraham from the fiery furnace, and the Midrash (Bereishis Rabbah 63:2) that Avraham was saved in the merit of Yaakov and the tribes destined to issue from him. This is exactly §65’s teaching that “the sons clarify the fathers”: Avraham’s revealed Chesed is shown to have been wholly for Heaven only because it held its own opposite within — proven through Yitzchak’s pachad at the Akeidah, and perfected in the integrating trait of Yaakov, through whose merit the father himself was redeemed. — a trait is proven pure only by its opposite: Yitzchak’s severity, issuing from Avraham, revealed that Avraham’s love was never self-serving, for one who can summon the reverse of his nature holds his nature for Heaven alone.

items.h: The theme: Rabban Gamliel was deposed for not honoring R’ Yehoshua, who exceeded him in wisdom — an act that looked like haughtiness and drew punishment here, though his intent was truly for Heaven. This world punishes by what is revealed, until the depths are clarified; so too David, who did not really sin and yet bore punishment measure for measure. Since the “sin” was in honor, the punishment was the removal of honor — and through a court, whose penalty atones at once.

p: [סו] וְכֵן מָצִינוּ בְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל שֶׁהָיָה ״מִתַּקִּיפֵי קַמָּאֵי״, וְהֶעֱבִירוּהוּ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא נָהַג כָּבוֹד בַּחֲכָמִים הַגְּדוֹלִים מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [פֶּרֶק תְּפִלַּת הַשַּׁחַר]

And so we find with Rabban Gamliel, who was “among the mighty of the early [Sages],” and “they deposed him” because “he did not conduct himself with honor toward the Sages greater than he,” as they said [Perek Tefillas HaShachar, Berachos 27b–28a] —
כִּי ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ הָיָה גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר בְּעַצְמוֹ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה] ״רַבִּי בְּחָכְמָה״

for R’ Yehoshua was greater than he, as he [Rabban Gamliel] himself said [in Rosh Hashanah 25a], “my master in wisdom.”936Berachos 27b–28a: A student cited to Rabban Gamliel that in R’ Yehoshua’s view the evening prayer is optional. Rabban Gamliel had R’ Yehoshua stand and challenged him publicly, forcing him to remain standing while Rabban Gamliel sat and lectured — until the assembly cried out for the meturgeman (Chutzpis) to stop, saying, “how long will he keep tormenting R’ Yehoshua? — at Rosh Hashanah he tormented him, in the Bechoros affair of R’ Tzadok he tormented him, here too — come, let us depose him”; and they removed Rabban Gamliel from the nesius. Rosh Hashanah 25a: Rabban Gamliel had accepted witnesses on the new moon whom R’ Dosa ben Horkinas and R’ Yehoshua deemed false, and decreed that R’ Yehoshua come to him “with your staff and your money on the day that is Yom Kippur by your reckoning.” R’ Akiva and R’ Dosa persuaded R’ Yehoshua that Rabban Gamliel’s court is authoritative; he came, and Rabban Gamliel rose, kissed him on the head, and said, “come in peace, my master and my student — my master in wisdom, and my student in that you accepted my words.”
וְזֶה נִרְאֶה כְּגַסּוּת הָרוּחַ וְשָׁקְלֵיהּ לְמַטְרַפְסֵיהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרֵר כַּוָּונָתוֹ דְּלֹא הָיָה מִפְּנֵי גַּסּוּת רוּחוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כְּלָל

And this “appears as haughtiness,” and “he received his due punishment [shakleih l’matrafseih]” in this world — as long as it was not clarified that his intent “was not from haughtiness at all,” God forbid;937R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayera §3): "“from where was the Holy One revealed to him?” — since he was then reckoned of his seed, there was an impediment from the side of Yishmael, that he could not merit this rung." Exactly the se’if: what looked like haughtiness in Rabban Gamliel was conduct directed from above — for a man’s standing at a given hour is set by impediments and openings not visible to those watching.
כִּי כָּךְ הוּא הַמִּדָּה לְהַעֲנִישׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּפִי הַנִּגְלֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרְרוּ וְנִגְלוּ הַמַּעֲמַקִּים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

for “such is the way, to punish in this world according to the revealed” — “as long as the depths have not been clarified and revealed” in this world.938R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §73): “Moshe knew that the wood-gatherer was liable to death… "the Torah covered him and you uncovered him" — for he held that he intended for the sake of Heaven.” Exactly the se’if: an act whose inner intent was truly for Heaven can still carry an outward face that invites judgment — and it is the outward face that draws the punishment in this world.

וּכְדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק בַּמֶּה בְּהֵמָה (נו.)]939Shabbos 56a: “R’ Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of R’ Yonasan: whoever says David sinned is simply mistaken — What, then, do I make of ‘why did you despise the word of Hashem, to do evil’ (II Shmuel 12:9)? — that he sought to do [evil] but did not do it.” Rav adds that Rebbi, who descended from David, “would expound in David’s favor.” דְּלֹא חָטָא בֶּאֱמֶת
As we find with David HaMelech: even though they said [in Perek Bameh Beheimah, Shabbos 56a] “that he did not [really] sin,”
וּבְחַיֵּי שְׁלֹמֹה בְּנוֹ הוֹדִיעַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּנִמְחַק הֶעָוֹן לְגַמְרֵי כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת לֹא חָטָא כְּלָל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן [בְּהַקְדָּמַת הַזּוֹהַר]
and in the lifetime of his son Shlomo, Hashem “made known that the iniquity was entirely erased,” for “in truth he did not sin at all,” as they also said [in the Introduction to the Zohar] —
מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן דְּבְחַיָּיו לֹא הוֹדִיעַ, עֲדַיִין הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְקַבֵּל עוֹנֶשׁ בְּחַיָּיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל זֶה, וְהָעוֹנֶשׁ מִדָּה כְּנֶגֶד מִדָּה

nonetheless, since “during his lifetime He did not make it known,” he “still had to receive punishment in his lifetime for it” — and the punishment [was] “measure for measure.”940R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §43): “"once a person transgressed and repeated" — as Rebbi [taught] — it becomes to him as though permitted; for the yetzer hara no longer needs to entice him.” The se’if’s “measure for measure” precisely: what looks like haughtiness must be answered at once, because an unchallenged appearance hardens into a settled standing.
וְרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל שֶׁחֶטְאוֹ בְּכָבוֹד נֶעֱנַשׁ בַּהֲסָרַת הַכָּבוֹד, וְלֹא מִמֵּילָא בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם בְּאֵיזֶה סִיבָּה רַק עַל יְדֵי הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין
And Rabban Gamliel, whose “sin was in [the matter of] honor,” was “punished by the removal of honor” — and “not automatically, by Heaven’s hand,” but “through the Sanhedrin”;
דְּבָזֶה הַכַּפָּרָה מִיָּד כְּמוֹ כָּל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין וְהַנֶּעֱנָשִׁים בְּבֵית דִּין דְּנִתְכַּפְּרִים מִיָּד, וַעֲדִיפִין מִנֶּעֱנָשִׁים בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם

for in this “the atonement is immediate,” like all “liable to court-imposed death penalties” and those “punished by a court, who are atoned for immediately” — and they are “preferable to those punished by Heaven’s hand.”
וְהַיְינוּ דְּבָזֶה מַכִּירִים הַחֵטְא מִיָּד, כִּי הַבֵּית דִּין מוֹדִיעִים לָהֶם חֶטְאָם וְשָׁבִים בִּתְשׁוּבָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין] כָּל הַמּוּמָתִים מִתְוַדִּים

that is, in this they “recognize the sin immediately,” for “the court makes known to them their sin,” and they “return in teshuvah,” as they said [in Sanhedrin 43b], “all those put to death confess941Sanhedrin 43b: the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 6:2) teaches that when the condemned man is “about ten cubits from the place of stoning, they say to him: Confess — for so is the way of all who are put to death to confess [she-ken derech kol ha-mumasin misvadin]; and whoever confesses has a portion in the World to Come.” The proof is Achan, whom Yehoshua urged, “My son, give glory to Hashem, God of Israel, and make confession to Him” (Yehoshua 7:19), and whose confession atoned — “on this day of your judgment you are troubled, but you will not be troubled in the World to Come.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Rambam (Hilchos Sanhedrin 13) — even one executed by the court is granted, through his confession, a share in the World to Come; and R’ Yehoshua ben Levi (opening this very amud) — one who “slaughters his [evil] inclination and confesses” is credited “as though he honored the Holy One in two worlds, this world and the next.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why court-imposed punishment is “preferable to those punished by Heaven’s hand” — for the court “makes known to them their sin,” rousing “the stirrings of teshuvah in his heart, to return and confess,” so that the sentence itself becomes “unto life.”.”
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״כָּל״ כו׳ הַיְינוּ לֹא עַל פִּי צִיווּי בֵּית דִּין בִּלְבַד, דְּמִי לֵיכָּא פָּרוּץ הַמַּמְרֶה פִּי בֵּית דִּין, רַק מֵעַצְמוֹ וּמִמֵּילָא הָיָה כֵן
And that they said “all” — that is, “not [merely] by command of the court alone” (for is there no “brazen one who defies the court”?) — but “of himself, automatically it was so”;
כִּי עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירַת הַבֵּית דִּין עָלָיו הָעוֹנֶשׁ וְהוֹלִיכוּ לְקַיֵּים בּוֹ הַמִּשְׁפָּט הָיָה מִתְעוֹרֵר הַהִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלִבּוֹ לָשׁוּב וּלְהִתְוַדּוֹת
for through the “court’s decree of punishment upon him,” and their “leading him to carry out the sentence,” there was “aroused the stirrings of teshuvah in his heart, to return and confess.”
וְרַק בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם אָמְרוּ [עֵירוּבִין יט.] דַּאֲפִילּוּ עַל פִּתְחוֹ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם אֵין חוֹזְרִים כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

And “only of the nations of the world” did they say [Eruvin 19a] that “even at the entrance of Gehinnom they do not repent942Eruvin 19a (Reish Lakish): distinct from the teaching that “Avraham raises up” Israel’s sinners from the fire of Gehinnom, Reish Lakish here says that “the wicked do not repent, even at the entrance of Gehinnom [afilu al pischo shel Gehinnom einan chozrin bi-teshuvah]” — expounding “and they shall go forth and look upon the carcasses of the men who rebel against Me” (Yeshayah 66:24): “it does not say ‘who rebelled,’ but ‘who rebel’ — they go on rebelling forever.” Meforshim: Rashi — ha-pordim, they perpetually part from Him; and the Gemara’s own resolution restricts this non-repentance to “the rebels among the nations of the world [poshei umos ha’olam],” never to the sinners of Israel (who do accept the judgment). R’ Tzadok’s use: “only of the nations of the world did they say” they cannot return — “for their sin is in the essence of their soul; such is their very being”; whereas in Israel sin “is not in the essence,” so that even “the wicked and those who commit severe transgressions” can always return.,” as is stated there —
כִּי חֶטְאָם הוּא בְּעֶצֶם נַפְשָׁם כִּי כָּךְ עַצְמִיּוּתָם, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לַחֲזוֹר
for “their sin is in the essence of their soul,” for “such is their very being,” and “it is impossible for them to return.”
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּאֵינוֹ בְּעֶצֶם, וְזֶהוּ גַּם בָּרְשָׁעִים וּבַעֲלֵי עֲבֵירוֹת חֲמוּרוֹת
Which is not so with the Children of Israel, in whom “it is not in the essence” — and this [is true] even “with the wicked and those who commit severe transgressions.”

וּבְצַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים שֶׁאֵין חוֹטְאִים כְּלָל בֶּאֱמֶת, רַק מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְדַקְדֵּק עִמָּהֶם כְּחוּט הַשַּׂעֲרָה, זֶה לֹא נִמְסַר כְּלָל לְבֵית דִּין, כִּי דִּקְדּוּק זֶה הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ

And with “complete tzaddikim, who do not [really] sin at all” — only that “the Holy One is exacting with them to a hair’s breadth” — “this is not handed to a court at all,” for “this exactitude is only through Hashem Himself.”

אֲבָל הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין אִם יְדַקְדְּקוּ בְּחוּט הַשַּׂעֲרָה גַּם בָּהֶם עַצְמָם יִמְצְאוּ כֵן, כִּי ״אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״וְקַשֵּׁט עַצְמְךָ״, וְלֹא נִיתַּן דָּבָר זֶה לַסַּנְהֶדְרִין כְּלָל

But the Sanhedrin, “if they would be exacting to a hair’s breadth, in themselves too they would find [the same],” for “there is no righteous man on earth [who does only good and never sins]” (Koheles 7:20)943Koheles 7:20: “כִּי אָדָם אֵין צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ, אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא” — “for there is no righteous man on earth who does [only] good and never sins.” Meforshim: Rashi and Ibn Ezra — no mortal is so perfectly righteous as to be wholly free of any lapse; and the Sages invoke the verse to teach that even the greatest can be found wanting under exacting measure. R’ Tzadok’s use: the “hair’s-breadth exactitude” that Hashem applies to complete tzaddikim “was not handed to a court at all” — for were the Sanhedrin to judge themselves so precisely, “in themselves too they would find the same,” since “there is no righteous man on earth who never sins”; such judgment “is only through Hashem Himself.”, and “adorn yourself944“Adorn yourself first” (keshot atzmecha v’achar kach keshot acheirim, Bava Metzia 107b; Bava Basra 60b): the dictum that one must “adorn [correct] yourself, and afterward adorn [correct] others,” derived (Bava Metzia 107b) from “הִתְקוֹשְׁשׁוּ וָקוֹשּׁוּ” (Tzefaniah 2:1) — read as “adorn yourselves [first], then adorn others.” Meforshim: Rashi — a person must first perfect his own conduct before he sets out to reprove his fellow. R’ Tzadok’s use: paired with “there is no righteous man on earth” (Koheles 7:20), the demand of hairsbreadth exactitude belongs to Hashem alone — for a court that would exact it of others “must first adorn itself,” and would then discover the identical lack within its own members; therefore “this matter was not given to the Sanhedrin at all.” [first]” — and “this matter was not given to the Sanhedrin at all.”
רַק שָׁם בַּהֲסָרַת הַהִתְפָּאֲרוּת עֲלֵיהֶם וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לָהֶם, זֶה שַׁפִּיר הָיָה בְּיָדָם לִטְעוֹן דְּמַאי אוּלְמֵיהּ, מִיתָה מִינַּיְיהוּ

Only there, in the “removal of the [presumption of] preeminence over them,” and “that he be equal to them” — this it was “properly in their power” to claim, “for what makes him greater” — [is he immune from] death, more than they?

וְדָבָר זֶה גַּם כֵּן הָיָה לִזְכוּתוֹ, וּבִשְׁבִיל שֶׁכַּוָּונָתוֹ הָאֲמִיתִּית הָיָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל כֵּן עָנְשׁוֹ הָיָה עַל יְדֵי גְּדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל [וְעַיֵּין זֹהַר שְׁמִינִי לו:]945Zohar, Shemini 36b: R’ Tzadok directs the reader here (an ayein — “see” — reference) in connection with the theme that David’s punishment came about through the great ones of Israel.Chassidic context - Sefat Emet, Lech Lecha 5:5: The Sefas Emes gives a precise framework for the tension here between inward humility and outward honor. He explains the maxim that one who flees honor is pursued by honor: honor is, in truth, the garment of the King - Hashem is the Melech HaKavod - and the servant must therefore flee the temptation to clothe himself in it as a private possession. But when a person returns every honor he receives to Hashem, the honor may actually pursue him, because the more he is honored while refusing to appropriate that honor to himself, the more kavod Shamayim is increased. He reads Avraham's promised public greatness in exactly this way: once Hashem found his heart faithful, Avraham could be made great in the world without that greatness becoming self-reference. This closely complements R' Tzadok's account of Rabban Gamliel. The revealed form of his conduct could be judged as ga'avah and therefore required the removal of kavod in the revealed world; yet that punishment does not establish that his inward motive was a pursuit of honor. On the contrary, once the inner intention is clarified as l'Shem Shamayim, nesius itself can return and become a vehicle of the King's honor. The se'if's measure-for-measure punishment thus concerns the garment through which the act appeared in this world, while the deeper clarification concerns to Whom that garment ultimately belonged.
And this matter too was “to his credit”; and because “his true intent was for the sake of Heaven,” therefore “his punishment came through the great ones of Israel” [see Zohar Shemini 36b],
דְּבָזֶה יֵשׁ טוֹבָה גְּדוֹלָה וִיתֵירָה בִּהְיוֹת כַּוָּונַת הַמְּרִיעִים גַּם כֵּן לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
for in this there is “a great and superior good” — in that “the intent of those who inflict [the punishment] is also for the sake of Heaven.”
וּמִלְּבַד מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי מֵהַמִּתְוַדִּין, דְּזֶה בָּא גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁכַּוָּונָתָם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
And apart from what I wrote about the “confessors” — for this too comes “through their intent being for the sake of Heaven” —
שֶׁהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ עֵץ שֶׁנִּתְלָה וְאֶבֶן שֶׁנִּסְקַל עָתִיד לִיתֵּן הַדִּין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתדב״א]
for even “the tree on which [a criminal] is hanged and the stone with which he is stoned will [one day] give a judgment,” as they said [in Tanna d’Vei Eliyahu];
וְעַל כֵּן הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין הִתְעַנּוּ אוֹתוֹ הַיּוֹם לְכַפֵּר עַל עַצְמָם וּלְבָרֵר עַצְמָם שֶׁכַּוָּונָתָם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
and therefore “the Sanhedrin fasted on that day, to atone for themselves and to clarify themselves that their intent was for the sake of Heaven.”
וְהַבֵּירוּר הָיָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִתְוַדָּה הַמּוּמָת, כִּי מִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה וְכָל דָּבָר קְדֻשָּׁה וּמַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁלְּשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם מוֹלִיד קְדֻשָּׁה בָּעוֹלָם
And the clarification was “through the one put to death confessing,” for “a mitzvah draws a mitzvah,” and “every holy matter and deed done for the sake of Heaven begets holiness in the world”;
וְאִם נִתְעוֹרֵר בּוֹ פֶּתַח תְּשׁוּבָה לְהִתְוַדּוֹת הֲרֵי פְּעוּלָתָם הָיָה לְחַיִּים בֶּאֱמֶת, חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְלֹא לְמָוֶת
and if “an opening of teshuvah was aroused in him, to confess,” then “their action was truly unto life” — “eternal life, and not unto death”;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְבָּרֵר דִּפְעוּלָתָם רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְשׁוּם שִׂנְאָה וְעִנְיַן עוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and through this it was “clarified that their action was only for the sake of Heaven,” and “not for any hatred or matter of this world.”
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה דְּעַל יָדוֹ נִטְרַד דּוֹאֵג הָאֲדוֹמִי בְּעוֹנֶשׁ בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם לָמוּת בַּחֲצִי יָמָיו, וְלֹא שָׁב בִּתְשׁוּבָה דְּאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, קִיבֵּל יִסּוּרִין עַל זֶה

And David HaMelech — through whom “Doeg the Edomite was banished,” by “a punishment from Heaven, to die in half his days,” and who “did not repent,” [so that] “he has no share in the World to Come” — “received sufferings for this”;

דְּכָל שֶׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל יָדוֹ אֵין מַכְנִיסִין [אוֹתוֹ בִּמְחִיצָתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, שַׁבָּת קמט:]946Shabbos 149b: “R’ Yaakov the son of the daughter of Yaakov said: anyone through whom his fellow is punished is not brought within the partition of the Holy One” — learned from the fate of those on whose account others were punished., אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן גָּרַם לוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁיָּשׁוּב בִּתְשׁוּבָה

for “anyone through whom his fellow is punished, they do not admit [him] into the [innermost] circle of the Holy One” (Shabbos 149b)947Shabbos 149b: “Anyone through whom his fellow is punished [on his account] is not brought into the [innermost] partition [mechitza] of the Holy One, blessed be He.” — “unless he caused him thereby to return in teshuvah.”
וְעַל כֵּן הַנִּידוֹנִין בַּסַּנְהֶדְרִין שֶׁהֵם דָּנִין עַל פִּי צִיווּי ה׳ וּמְחוּיָּבִים לְבַעֵר הָרַע, הָיוּ מְעוֹרְרִים תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלֵב הַנִּידוֹן

And therefore “those judged by the Sanhedrin” — who “judge by the command of Hashem” and are “obligated to root out the evil” — would “arouse teshuvah in the heart of the one judged.” — this world can only judge by appearances, so even a Rabban Gamliel, or a David who never truly sinned, must bear a measure-for-measure penalty until the depths are cleared; a court’s sentence is itself a mercy, for it atones at once and stirs the confession that turns punishment into life.

items.h: The theme: There is even a praise in this — “one killed by a king is more honored” than one killed by a slave. Since R’ Gamliel’s intent was truly for Heaven and he did not pursue honor, his punishment came by way of honor. To the outward eye, deposition by Israel’s own Sages looks more disgraceful than removal by chance; but to one who knows that all chance is from Hashem, it is the greater honor to be dealt with directly.

p: [סז] עוֹד זֹאת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה שֶׁבַח, עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּשַׁבָּת קח ע״א] ״זֶה שֶׁהֲרָגוֹ מֶלֶךְ מְשׁוּבָּח״ (מִזֶּה שֶׁנֶּהֱרַג עַל יְדֵי עֶבֶד), וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה כָּבוֹד

Furthermore, there is in this a “praise,” in the manner it is stated [in Shabbos 108a], “the one whom a king killed is [more] praiseworthy948Shabbos 108a: R’ Yehoshua HaGarsi answered a Baytusi who challenged why tefillin may be written on the hides of neveilos u-tereifos (kosher-species animals that died improperly) yet not on the hides of non-kosher animals, with a parable: “[it is comparable] to two men who were sentenced to death by the government [malchus] — one the king himself killed, and one the executioner [ispaklator] killed; which of them is more praiseworthy? Say: the one whom the king killed.” That is: to be put to death by the king’s own hand is the greater dignity. Meforshim: Rashi — the kosher species, even fallen to neveilah, keeps its fitness (its “honor”) because it is of the class “permitted in your mouth,” like the one dispatched by the king himself; the non-kosher animal is like the one killed by the lowly executioner. R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads the mashal straight into Rabban Gamliel’s deposition — to be “put to death” (removed) by the King’s own agents, “the Sages of Israel,” is “the one whom the king killed,” a far greater honor than removal by mere chance or by “the executioner [ispaklator]” — the very word he draws from this Gemara.” (than one killed by a slave) — and there is honor in this.949R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §41): “Kohanim in their service — their deeds; and Levi’im on their platform — speech, for the essence of song is with the mouth; and Israel at their station — thought… through a threefold [Torah], three gifts were given.” Exactly the se’if’s “honor”: rank is a matter of which faculty a man stands in, so a deposition administered by the Sages is itself a placement within the order, not an expulsion from it.
וּלְפִי שֶׁנֶּעֱנַשׁ [רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל] בַּהֲסָרַת כָּבוֹד וְהוּא בֶּאֱמֶת הָיָה לְשָׁמַיִם וְלֹא רָדַף חַס וְשָׁלוֹם אַחַר הַכָּבוֹד, עַל כֵּן הָיָה עָנְשׁוֹ דֶּרֶךְ כָּבוֹד
And since [Rabban Gamliel] was “punished by removal of honor,” while in truth his intent was for Heaven and he “did not pursue honor,” God forbid — therefore his punishment was “by way of honor.”

וְאַף שֶׁלְּעֵינֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא לְהֵיפֶךְ, אִלּוּ הוּעֲבַר דֶּרֶךְ מִקְרֶה עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירַת מֶלֶךְ אוֹ כַּיּוֹצֵא לֹא הָיָה בִּזָּיוֹן כָּל כָּךְ כְּמוֹ כְּשֶׁהֶעֱבִירוּהוּ חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַצְמָם

And even though, “to the eyes of people in this world, it is the opposite” — had he been deposed “by chance,” through a “king’s decree” or the like, “it would not have been so great a disgrace” as when “the Sages of Israel themselves deposed him” —
עַל הָאֱמֶת לְמַכִּירֵי הָאֱמֶת שֶׁגַּם כָּל הַמִּקְרִים הוּא מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְלֹא עָבֵיד קוּבָּ״ה בְּלָא דִּינָא
[yet] “in truth, to those who recognize the truth” — that “all ‘chance’ events too are from Hashem,” and “the Holy One does no [act] without judgment” —

אַדְּרַבָּא זֶה כָּבוֹד יוֹתֵר כְּשֶׁלֹּא נִמְסַר לַמִּקְרִים וְלָאִסְפַּקְלָטוֹר בְּעַד חֶטְאוֹ, אֶלָּא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ עַל יְדֵי עֲבָדָיו שְׁלוּחֵי דְּרַחֲמָנָא הָעוֹשִׂים לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם

on the contrary, “this is greater honor” — when he is “not handed over to chance and to the executioner for his sin,” but [rather to] “Hashem Himself, through His servants, the agents of the Merciful One, who act for the sake of Heaven” —
שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ הָעוֹשֶׂה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה גַּם כֵּן אֵין רַע כְּלָל, דְּמִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

[so] that it is “as though Hashem Himself does [it]”; and through this, too, “there is no evil at all,” for “from the mouth of the Most High evil does not go forth” (Eichah 3:38)950Eichah 3:38: in the heart of Yirmeyah’s lament — “מִפִּי עֶלְיוֹן לֹא תֵצֵא הָרָעוֹת וְהַטּוֹב” — “from the mouth of the Most High does there not go forth [both] evil and good?” Background: the sufferer accepts that all that befalls him, calamity as well as bounty, issues by God’s decree. Meforshim: Rashi — why should a living man complain? the “evil” comes only as the deserved consequence of sin, not as gratuitous evil from Above; and the Sages (Rashi citing the Midrash) read it that “evil” does not descend as evil directly “from the mouth of the Most High” — it comes about of itself, through a person’s own sin, while from Him only good goes forth. R’ Tzadok’s use: since Rabban Gamliel’s punishment issued directly “from the mouth of the Most High,” through His faithful agents acting for Heaven, “there is no evil in it at all” — what wears the face of disgrace is, at its source, unmixed good., God forbid.

וְעַל זֶה בִּיקֵּשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה ״מִלְּפָנֶיךָ מִשְׁפָּטִי יֵצֵא, עֵינֶיךָ תֶּחֱזֶינָה מֵישָׁרִים״, כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹאֶה לַלֵּבָב וְהָעוֹנֶשׁ רַק לְרֶגַע כְּפִי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד

And concerning this David HaMelech requested, “let my judgment come forth from before You; let Your eyes behold uprightness” (Tehillim 17:2)951Tehillim 17:2: in David’s “Tefillah” — “מִלְּפָנֶיךָ מִשְׁפָּטִי יֵצֵא, עֵינֶיךָ תֶּחֱזֶינָה מֵישָׁרִים” — “let my judgment come forth from before You; let Your eyes behold uprightness.” Background: David asks that his case be adjudicated by God directly, not by human eyes that see only the surface. Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — “from before You let my sentence issue,” not from flesh and blood, for You alone “behold uprightness,” seeing the heart’s true intent. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is precisely what David sought — that his judgment come “from before You,” from Hashem who “sees the heart,” so that the punishment is “only for a moment,” reckoned to this world alone; and so too Rabban Gamliel, once his inner intent for Heaven was clarified, was in the end reinstated. — for “Hashem sees the heart,” and the punishment is “only for a moment,” according to this world alone.952R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §8): “and it is in cleaving to the Torah, a threefold Torah… for the hidden things, which are the thought in the mind, are "to Hashem our God"; and the revealed things, in deed, are "to us" — and the will that is in the heart stands between.” Exactly the se’if: R’ Gamliel’s true intent belonged to “the hidden things,” which are God’s — so what was answerable here was only the revealed act, and that “only for a moment.”
וְעַל כֵּן גַּם שָׁם הוּחְזַר, וְהוּא חָזַר לְפַיֵּיס אֶת ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ וְהִכִּיר שֶׁלֹּא עָשָׂה כַּהוֹגֶן

And therefore “there too he was reinstated” — and he [Rabban Gamliel] “went back to appease R’ Yehoshua,” and “recognized that he had not acted properly.”953Berachos 28a: After Rabban Gamliel was deposed, he “did not absent himself from the study hall even for a moment,” and when a dispute over an Ammonite convert was decided in R’ Yehoshua’s favor, “Rabban Gamliel said: since this is so, I will go and appease R’ Yehoshua.” He came to R’ Yehoshua’s house, saw its walls “blackened,” and remarked, “from the walls of your house it is apparent that you are a charcoal-maker.” R’ Yehoshua replied, “woe to the generation whose leader you are, for you do not know the hardship of Torah scholars, how they sustain themselves.” Rabban Gamliel said, “I have wronged you — forgive me,” but R’ Yehoshua paid him no heed — until he said, “do it for the honor of my father [Abba],” and R’ Yehoshua was appeased. R’ Akiva then said, “R’ Yehoshua has been appeased; we [deposed him] only for your honor — tomorrow you and I will go early to his door [to restore him].”Chabad parallel - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25:30: The Alter Rebbe's discussion of hashgachah supplies a useful conceptual background to R' Tzadok's distinction between an event that appears to occur 'by chance' and one visibly carried out by the servants of Hashem. Tanya explains that anger over ordinary worldly injury contains a trace of avodah zarah precisely because 'hakol bidei Shamayim chutz mi-yiras Shamayim': the human agent who caused the loss is not an independent power outside Divine governance. At the same time, the Alter Rebbe explicitly limits this reasoning in matters of avodas Hashem - where there is an obligation to separate another from prohibition - thereby preserving human responsibility and the full force of Torah. That double point fits the present se'if. Rabban Gamliel's removal could have come through what people call mikreh, but to 'those who recognize the truth' the royal decree, political event, and decision of the Sages are all within hashgachah. What changes is not whether Hashem is acting, but the garment through which His judgment becomes visible. Hence R' Tzadok can call deposition through the chachmei Yisrael themselves a greater kavod: the judgment is mediated by servants consciously doing the will of Heaven rather than being hidden behind an apparently accidental worldly chain. The Tanya parallel also keeps the point disciplined - providence does not erase the bechirah or accountability of the actors; it denies only that the worldly agent is an autonomous source of power.

וּמַה שֶּׁתְּחִלָּה לֹא נִתְפַּיֵּיס ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, לֹא שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לִמְחוֹל עַל כְּבוֹדוֹ, דְּהֲרֵי גַּם תְּחִלָּה לֹא ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ עַצְמוֹ תָּבַע כְּבוֹדוֹ כְּלָל, וְגַם חֲלִילָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַכְזָרִי מִלִּמְחוֹל

And that “at first R’ Yehoshua was not appeased” — [this was] not that “he did not wish to forgo his honor,” for indeed “at the outset R’ Yehoshua himself did not claim his honor at all,” and God forbid that he “be cruel [and refuse] to forgive.”
רַק עִנְיַן פִּיּוּסוֹ הָיָה שֶׁיַּחְזְרוּ לְהַמְנוֹתוֹ נָשִׂיא, וְזֶה הָיָה בְּעֵינָיו זָחֲלָה כְּרוֹדֵף אַחַר הַכָּבוֹד, כַּאֲשֶׁר חֲשָׁבוּהוּ תְּחִלָּה כֵּן

Only, the [meaning of] “his appeasement” was that “they reinstate him as Nasi” — and “this, in his [R’ Yehoshua’s] eyes, was ‘crawling,’ like one who pursues honor,” just as “they had thought of him at first”;
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נִתְפַּיֵּיס עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״עֲשֵׂה בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד אַבָּא״, כִּי אֵין מִתְכַּוֵּין לִכְבוֹד עַצְמוֹ

and therefore “he was not appeased until [Rabban Gamliel] said to him, ‘do it for the honor of my father [Abba]’” — for “he does not intend for his own honor.” — to be brought low by God’s own faithful agents is, to one who sees truly, a greater honor than any accident of fate; and R’ Yehoshua held out not from wounded pride but lest restoring the Nasi look like chasing honor.

items.h: The theme: R’ Gamliel’s inner truth was clarified through his son, Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — one of the three truly humble, who humbled himself before R’ Shimon bar Yochai, whose greatness his generation did not recognize. That is real humility: being humble toward one truly greater, not toward one lesser. He also enacted the Nasi’s honor; and when R’ Meir and R’ Nasan plotted to depose him they failed, for his humility was revealed and not only in the depths.

p: [סח] וּבֵירוּרוֹ הָיָה בִּבְנוֹ רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, שֶׁהוּא מִשְּׁלוֹשָׁה עַנְוְותָנִין, וְהוּא הָעִיקָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק הַפּוֹעֲלִים]

And his “clarification” was through his son Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, who is “of the three humble ones,” and he is the “principal one,” as they said [in Perek HaPo’alim, Bava Metzia 84b–85a]954Bava Metzia 84b–85a: When Rabbi saw that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon was much sharper than his own son, “Rabbi’s spirit weakened.” R’ Shimon [the father] said, “my son, let it not grieve you — he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.” Hence Rebbi’s teaching: “three humble ones: Abba [RaShbaG, Rebbi’s father], the sons of Beseira, and Yehonasan ben Shaul.” The sons of Beseira “seated Hillel at the head and appointed him Nasi” when they saw he was greater; Yehonasan ben Shaul said to David, “you shall be king over Israel, and I shall be second to you” (I Shmuel 23:17). The Gemara concludes that only RaShbaG is certainly [singled out for] humility. —
שֶׁהֶרְאָה עַנְוְותָנוּתוֹ נֶגֶד ר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי, שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ יוֹדְעִין כֹּחוֹ בְּדוֹרוֹ כָּל כָּךְ, רַק הוּא הִכִּיר הָאֱמֶת
for he “showed his humility” toward R’ Shimon bar Yochai, whose power “they did not so recognize in his generation” — only he [RaShbaG] “recognized the truth.”
וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הָעַנְוְותָנוּת, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא חָשְׁבוּ שָׁם הִלֵּל שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן עָנָיו, וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהֵעִידָה תּוֹרָה עַל עַנְוְותָנוּתוֹ מִכָּל הָאָדָם

And this is “the essence of humility” — for therefore “they did not count there Hillel,” who was also humble, nor Moshe Rabbeinu, of whose humility “the Torah testified” [that he was humble] “of all men.”955Bamidbar 12:3: “וְהָאִישׁ מֹשֶׁה עָנָיו מְאֹד, מִכֹּל הָאָדָם אֲשֶׁר עַל פְּנֵי הָאֲדָמָה” — “and the man Moshe was exceedingly humble, more than any person on the face of the earth.” Background: the Torah interjects this testimony in the midst of Miriam and Aharon’s speaking about Moshe — he bore their words in silence, never defending himself. Meforshim: Rashi — anav means “lowly and forbearing [shefal v’savlan]”; the Sifrei and Ibn Ezra dwell on his humility despite his unrivalled greatness. R’ Tzadok’s use: precisely because Moshe was “truly greater than all men,” his humility — like Hillel’s — “is not so great a wonder”; the wonder, and “the essence of humility,” is RaShbaG’s lowering himself before one truly greater than he (Rashbi), whom his generation did not recognize — which is why the Gemara’s list of “the three humble ones” passes over even Moshe and Hillel.
אֲבָל מִי שֶׁהוּא גָּדוֹל בֶּאֱמֶת מִכָּל אָדָם וְהוּא עָנָיו נֶגֶד הַקָּטָן מִמֶּנּוּ אֵין זֶה רַבּוּתָא כָּל כָּךְ, וְהָרַבּוּתָא הוּא כְּשֶׁהוּא עָנָיו נֶגֶד מִי שֶׁהוּא גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ בֶּאֱמֶת

But “one who is truly greater than all men, and is humble toward one lesser than he — this is not so great a wonder”; and “the wonder is when he is humble toward one who is truly greater than he.”956R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayakhel §5): “but the crown of the Holy One Himself, as it were, one does not merit — only one who makes himself as leftovers, to be as nothing; through this he merits to attain the light of the supernal Keser, which is called "ayin" [nothing].” Exactly the se’if’s “sign of complete humility”: the rung is reached only by one who has made himself nothing — and it is therefore invisible precisely to a generation that measures by something.

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה לוֹ [לְרַשְׁבַּ״ג] כָּבוֹד יוֹתֵר, וּמַכִּיר הָאֱמֶת לְהַשְׁפִּיל עַצְמוֹ נֶגֶד מִי שֶׁהוּא שָׁפָל בֶּאֱמֶת נֶגְדּוֹ, וְלֹא לְפָנִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד, זֶהוּ סִימָן הָעַנְוָות הַגָּמוּר

And nonetheless “in this world he [RaShbaG] had more honor”; and to “recognize the truth, [and] lower himself before one who is [regarded as] lowly, [though] truly [greater] than he” — and “not [merely] outwardly in this world” — “this is the sign of complete humility.”957R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Parshas Shekalim §7): “and then, once he became lowly in his own eyes, to be as dust and ashes, he had already merited the aspect of Atika.” Exactly the se’if: RaShbaG’s humbling of himself before one his generation did not recognize is not self-diminishment but the acquisition of the highest rung.
וְכָל הָנֵי שְׁלוֹשָׁה דְּחָשִׁיב שָׁם — יְהוֹנָתָן וּבֶן בְּתֵירָה וְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הָיוּ כֵן
And all these three counted there — Yehonasan [ben Shaul], and Ben Beseira, and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — were so.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הוּא דָּרַשׁ וְהִתְקִין בִּכְבוֹד הַנָּשִׂיא נֶגֶד הֶחָכָם וְאַב בֵּית דִּין כִּדְאִיתָא [סוֹף הוֹרָיוֹת]

And nonetheless he too “expounded and enacted” concerning the “honor of the Nasi” vis-à-vis the “Chacham” and the “Av Beis Din,” as is stated [end of Horayos 13b].958Horayos 13b: A baraisa taught the honors due the Nasi, Av Beis Din, and Chacham; R’ Yochanan said it was taught in the days of RaShbaG (Nasi), R’ Meir (Chacham), and R’ Nasan (Av Beis Din) — when RaShbaG enacted that the [full standing] honor be shown only to the Nasi. R’ Meir and R’ Nasan, feeling slighted, plotted to ask RaShbaG to expound Uktzin (which he did not know) and thereby depose him. R’ Yaakov ben Karshi overheard and, fearing RaShbaG’s disgrace, sat outside his chamber reviewing the tractate aloud until RaShbaG “gave his attention and learned it.” Next day RaShbaG expounded it, then said, “had I not learned it, you would have shamed me,” and had them removed from the study hall. When R’ Yosi protested, “shall the Torah be outside and we within?”, RaShbaG readmitted them but penalized them that teachings not be cited in their names (R’ Meir → “Acheirim,” R’ Nasan → “Yesh Omrim”). Later they were told in a dream to appease him; R’ Nasan went, R’ Meir did not.
וְר׳ מֵאִיר וְר׳ נָתָן חֲשָׁדוּהוּ גַּם כֵּן לִמְבַקֵּשׁ כְּבוֹדוֹ וּבִיקְשׁוּ לְהַעֲבִירוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשׂוּ לְאָבִיו, וְלֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָם
And R’ Meir and R’ Nasan “suspected him too of seeking his [own] honor,” and “sought to depose him, as they did to his father” — but “it did not succeed in their hand,”
כִּי הוּא לֹא הָיָה עַנְוְותָן בַּמַּעֲמַקִּים לְבַד רַק גָּלוּי לָעַיִן וּמְפוֹרָשׁ בָּעִנְיָן שֶׁאֵין מָקוֹם לְחָשְׁדוֹ בְּכָךְ
for he was “not humble in the depths alone,” but “revealed to the eye and explicit in the matter,” so that “there was no room to suspect him of this.”

וְהֵם שֶׁחֲשָׁדוּהוּ הָיָה מִצַּד חִסָּרוֹן קְצָת שֶׁהָיָה בָּהֶם בָּזֶה, כַּיָּדוּעַ דְּכָל הַפּוֹסֵל בְּמוּמוֹ פּוֹסֵל, וְאַף בִּגְדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל ״אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ״ כו׳ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן כָּל שֶׁהוּא

And their suspecting him was from “some slight deficiency that was in them in this,” as is known, that “one who disqualifies [others] disqualifies with his own blemish” — and even among the great ones of Israel, “there is no righteous man on earth” who has not “some deficiency, however slight.”
וּלְפִי שֶׁהֵם אָמְרוּ ״נַעֲבֵד כִּי לְדִידַן״ כו׳, ״וְנֶהֱוֵי אֲנָא אַב בֵּית דִּין וְאַתְּ נָשִׂיא״, דְּנִרְאֶה שֶׁכִּיוְּונוּ לְגַרְמַיְיהוּ, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא עָלְתָה בְּיָדָם

And since they said, “let us enact [a distinction] for ourselves too,” “and I will be Av Beis Din and you Nasi” — [so that] “it appears they intended for themselves,” therefore “it did not succeed in their hand.”
עַל יְדֵי זֶה חָשְׁדוּ בָּזֶה לְרַשְׁבַּ״ג
[And] on account of this [their own motive] they suspected RaShbaG of it.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הֵם חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁכִּיוְּונוּ לְגַרְמַיְיהוּ בֶּאֱמֶת
Yet, God forbid [to say] that they too “truly intended for themselves”;
וְר׳ מֵאִיר שֶׁהָיָה הַמְעוֹרֵר רָצָה לְהוֹשִׁיב לְר׳ נָתָן בָּרֹאשׁ
for R’ Meir, who was “the initiator,” “wished to seat R’ Nasan at the head.”
וְאַף דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהָיָה מִשּׁוּם ״קָמְרָא קַמָּא דַּאֲבוּהּ״, שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן רֹאשׁ גָּלוּת וּמִבֵּית דָּוִד, וְר׳ מֵאִיר בֶּן גֵּרִים
And though one might say it was because of “the ‘girdle’ of his father” — that [R’ Nasan] “was the son of the Exilarch, from the house of David,” while R’ Meir was “descended from converts” —
מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּשֶׁהֶעֱבִירוּ רַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל בִּיקְשׁוּ לְמַנּוֹת ר׳ עֲקִיבָא אַף דְּגַם כֵּן הָיָה בֶּן גֵּרִים
nonetheless, “when they deposed Rabban Gamliel [the father], they sought to appoint R’ Akiva,” even though he too was “descended from converts” —
רַק מִשּׁוּם דְּלֵית לֵיהּ זְכוּת אָבוֹת דִּילְמָא עָנֵישׁ לֵיהּ, וְר׳ מֵאִיר מַשְׁמַע דְּלֹא חָשׁ לָזֶה
only [they refrained] because “he has no ancestral merit,” lest [Rabban Gamliel] “punish him” [by Heaven] — and it is implied that “R’ Meir was not concerned about this.”
וְאַף ר׳ עֲקִיבָא נִרְאֶה דְּהוּא לֹא הָיָה חוֹשֵׁשׁ לָזֶה, וְכִדְאִיתָא [בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי] דְּנִצְטַעֵר עַל זֶה שֶׁלֹּא זֶה מִינּוּהוּ

And even R’ Akiva, it appears, “was not concerned about this,” as is stated [in the Yerushalmi] that “he was distressed that they had not appointed him.”959Berachos 27b: After deposing Rabban Gamliel, [the Sages asked] “whom shall we appoint? R’ Yehoshua? — he is a party to the matter. R’ Akiva? — perhaps [Rabban Gamliel] will punish him [by Heaven], for he has no ancestral merit. Rather, R’ Elazar ben Azariah — wise, wealthy, and tenth in descent from Ezra.” They asked him; he said, “let me consult my household.” His wife warned, “perhaps they will [later] depose you”; he replied, “let a man use a precious cup one day, and let it break tomorrow.” Yerushalmi Berachos 4:1: R’ Akiva “sat distressed,” saying, “not that he is more a master of Torah than I, but he is of greater lineage — fortunate the man whose ancestors have gained merit for him.”
וְהֲרֵי ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן עֲזַרְיָה אָמַר ״לִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ יוֹמָא חֲדָא״ כו׳, אַף דְּהָדַר לִתְבַר

And indeed R’ Elazar ben Azariah said, “let [a man] use [a precious cup] for one day,” even though “it will later break”;960Berachos 28a: when R’ Elazar ben Azariah was offered the office of Nasi after Rabban Gamliel’s removal, his wife warned, “perhaps they will depose you, just as they deposed Rabban Gamliel”; he answered with the folk-saying, “let a person use a precious goblet [kasa d’mokra] one day, and tomorrow let it break” — seize the honor of the hour, though it not endure. Meforshim: Rashi — the “precious cup” is that day’s greatness; better to have served one day than never. R’ Tzadok’s use: on this he says R’ Akiva and R’ Meir “certainly desired” the office “even if they should be punished and it break” — the honor of the moment, done for Heaven, is worth the cost; the Sages held back from appointing them only because “they wished to appoint a Nasi who would endure.”Chassidic context - Tiferet Shlomo, Sh'lach 1: The Tiferes Shlomo reads the Torah's description of the spies as 'ish echad... kol nasi vahem' as a warning built into the very office of leadership. The greatness of a tzaddik, he says, rests in anavah and shiflus; the more truly 'low' he is in humility, the more he can be raised as a rosh. He therefore reads 'lamateh avosav tishlachu kol nasi vahem' homiletically as a charge to the princes to strip themselves of the inward claim of nesius even while carrying its public function. Their later failure began when that office became hisnas'us within the heart. This sharply complements R' Tzadok's description of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel. His humility is not proved by surrendering the Nasi's institutional honor - he himself established the order of honor due the Nasi, Chacham and Av Beis Din - but by knowing the truth about himself in relation to one who was genuinely greater, even where the public hierarchy gave him more visible kavod. Humility and nesius are therefore not opposites. The test is whether office is borne as a shelichus or converted into a private measure of self. That is why R' Tzadok can see RaShbaG's enacted honor and his humility as mutually clarifying rather than contradictory: the outward structure remains, while the inward 'nasi' has been stripped of self-importance.
וְאִם כֵּן גַּם ר׳ עֲקִיבָא וְר׳ מֵאִיר וַדַּאי רָצוּ בָּזֶה וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם יֵעָנְשׁוּ וְיִתְבַר
and if so, “R’ Akiva and R’ Meir too certainly desired this,” even if “they should be punished and it break.”
אֶלָּא שֶׁהַחֲכָמִים שָׁם לֹא רָצוּ לְמַנּוֹתוֹ מֵהַאי טַעְמָא, דְּהֵם רָצוּ לְהַמְנוֹת נָשִׂיא שֶׁיִּתְקַיֵּים
Except that “the Sages there did not wish to appoint him [R’ Akiva] for this reason” — for “they wished to appoint a Nasi who would endure.”
וּכְמוֹ דְּשָׁם לֹא רָצוּ לְהַמְנוֹת ר׳ יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהָיָה ״בַּעַל דָּבָר״, וְכַאן ר׳ מֵאִיר וְר׳ נָתָן גַּם כֵּן ״בַּעֲלֵי דָּבָר״
And just as “there they did not wish to appoint R’ Yehoshua because he was ‘a party [to the dispute]’” — so here, R’ Meir and R’ Nasan too were “parties to the matter.”
וְהֵם לֹא חָשׁוּ לָזֶה, וְחָשְׁבוּ דְּהַחֲכָמִים יַסְכִּימוּ לְפִי שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלִים בַּתּוֹרָה מִכּוּלָּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ר׳ יוֹסֵי שָׁם ״תּוֹרָה מִבַּחוּץ״
But “they were not concerned about this,” and “thought the Sages would agree,” since “they were the greatest in Torah of all,” as R’ Yosi said there, “[shall] the Torah [be] outside [and we within]?”
וְר׳ מֵאִיר הָיָה גָּדוֹל הַרְבֵּה בְּחָכְמָה מֵר׳ נָתָן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [פ״ק דְּעֵירוּבִין] דְּאֵין בְּדוֹרוֹ כְּמוֹתוֹ

And R’ Meir was “much greater in wisdom than R’ Nasan,” as they said [in the first chapter of Eruvin], “that there was none in his generation like him”;961Eruvin 13b: R’ Acha bar Chanina taught, “it is revealed and known before the One who spoke and the world came into being that in the generation of R’ Meir there was none his equal [she-ein b’doro shel R’ Meir kamoso]; and why did they not fix the halachah according to him? Because his colleagues could not fathom the depth of his opinion” — for he could “declare the impure pure and adduce a justification, and the pure impure and adduce a justification.” (On the same amud: his true name was R’ Nehorai, “because he illumines [meir] the eyes of the Sages in halachah” — see §54.) R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the ground for “R’ Meir was much greater in wisdom than R’ Nasan, for there was none in his generation like him”; yet, as “the initiator” of the move against RaShbaG, R’ Meir deliberately stepped back — “so as not to be like one biased, seeking his own honor” — asking only to be Av Beis Din and not Nasi.

אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁהוּא הָיָה הַמְעוֹרֵר רָצָה לְהַרְחִיק עַצְמוּתוֹ מִן הַכִּיעוּר, וּלְגַבֵּי נַפְשֵׁיהּ גַּם כֵּן לְבַל יִהְיֶה כְּנוֹגֵעַ וְדוֹרֵשׁ לִכְבוֹד עַצְמוֹ, לֹא רָצָה לִהְיוֹת נָשִׂיא רַק אַב בֵּית דִּין

but since he was “the initiator,” he “wished to distance himself from [any] unseemliness,” and, for himself too, “so as not to be like one biased, seeking his own honor,” he “did not wish to be Nasi, but [only] Av Beis Din.”

וְהֵם יָדְעוּ כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת הֵם גְּדוֹלִים מֵרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם לְמַרְאִית עַיִן כְּפִי הַלָּשׁוֹן הַנִּזְכָּר כַּוָּונָתָם לְגַרְמַיְיהוּ, וְעַל כֵּן יִקָּנְסוּ עוֹד לְשָׁעָה בְּהוֹרָדַת כָּבוֹד הַקּוֹדֵם

And they knew that “in truth they were greater than Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel”; but nonetheless, “to the outward eye, according to the aforementioned wording, their intent [appeared] for themselves” — and therefore “they were penalized, for a time, by the removal of their former honor.”
וּמִכְּבוֹד רַשְׁבַּ״ג לֹא נִגְרַע מְאוּמָה, כִּי אֶצְלוֹ הָיָה כְּבָר מְבוֹרָר שֶׁאֵינֶנּוּ רוֹדֵף אַחַר הַכָּבוֹד כְּלָל

And from the honor of RaShbaG “nothing was diminished,” for with him “it was already clarified that he does not pursue honor at all.” — true humility is measured not by bowing to lesser men but by bowing to a greater one whom the world does not yet recognize; that is why RaShbaG, not the far greater Hillel or Moshe, heads the list.

items.h: The theme: Rebbi, his grandson, held fast to the same humility — “when Rebbi died, humility ceased” — yet told his son to conduct his office with authority, since his humility was already established and all knew his firmness was for Heaven. Through Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel the depths of Rabban Gamliel’s own heart were clarified. So his line’s nesius endured, and his deposition was “only for a moment.”

p: [סט] וְכֵן רַבִּי בְּנוֹ בֶּן דְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל הֶחֱזִיק בָּעֲנָוָה
And likewise Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi], his son, the son of Rabban [Shimon ben] Gamliel, “held fast to humility,”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [סוֹף סוֹטָה] דְּמִשֶּׁמֵּת בָּטְלָה עֲנָוָה, וּבְסוֹף הוֹרָיוֹת ״אֲפִילּוּ רַבִּי דַּעֲנוּתָנָא״ כו׳, מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא הָיָה עָנָיו יוֹתֵר מֵאָבִיו

as they said [end of Sotah 49a], “when Rebbi died, humility ceased,”962Sotah 49a: the closing Mishnah of the tractate catalogues what “ceased” with the passing of the great ones — “when R’ Meir died, the composers of parables ceased… when Rabban Gamliel the Elder died, the honor of the Torah ceased… and when Rabbi [Yehudah HaNasi] died, humility and fear of sin ceased [batlah anavah v’yiras chet].” Meforshim: Rashi and the Bartenura — with Rebbi’s death there was none who so embodied humility; and the Gemara (Sotah 49b) relates that when the tanna taught this, Rav Yosef said, “do not teach that humility ceased — for I am here,” and Rav Nachman, “do not teach that fear of sin ceased — for I am here.” R’ Tzadok’s use: Rebbi, grandson of Rabban Gamliel, “held fast to humility” so completely that humility itself was bound up with him — proof that the family’s inner trait was true humility, which clarifies in retrospect that Rabban Gamliel’s firmness, too, was never for his own honor. and at the end of Horayos [14a], “even Rabbi, who is humble”963Horayos 14a: on the last page of the tractate, Rebbi’s son asked why they cite rulings of the Sages “whose water we drink but whose names we do not mention” — namely R’ Meir and R’ Nasan, who had sought to depose Rebbi’s father RaShbaG; and Rebbi taught the ruling as “they said in the name of R’ Meir,” not “R’ Meir said.” Rava observed: “even Rabbi, who is humble [afilu Rabbi da’anavtan hu], [only] taught ‘they said in the name of R’ Meir,’ but did not say ‘R’ Meir said’” — even the humble Rebbi withheld the fuller honor of naming him outright, on account of the affront once aimed at his father’s house. Meforshim: Rashi — the force of the statement is the measure of Rebbi’s humility, that Rava designates him “the humble one.” R’ Tzadok’s use: this proves Rebbi was “even more humble than his father”; hence, when he too “conducted his office of Nasi with authority,” all knew it was for Heaven and none suspected self-seeking. — implying that “he was more humble than his father.”964R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §78): “over three things Korach disputed: the nesius of Elitzafan, the kingship of Moshe, and the priesthood of Aharon.” Exactly the se’if: office is a real appointment and not a private possession — which is why Rebbi, for all his humility, had to instruct his son to conduct the nesius with authority.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הוּא הִזְהִיר לִבְנוֹ [בְּפֶרֶק הַנּוֹשֵׂא] ״נְהוֹג נְשִׂיאוּתְךָ בְּרָמִים״
And nonetheless he too “warned his son” [in Perek HaNosei, Kesubos 103b], “conduct your office of Nasi with authority [b’ramus]”;
וּלְפִי שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְבָּרֵר בָּעֲנָוָה יָדְעוּ הַכֹּל כִּי אֵין כַּוָּונָתוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד עַצְמוֹ כְּלָל רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא חַיְישִׁי לָהּ

and since he was “already clarified in humility,” “all knew his intent was not for his own honor at all, but for Heaven,” and “they were not concerned about it.”965R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §28): “[Rebbi] commanded his son (Kesubos 103b), ‘conduct your office of Nasi with authority [nheg nesiuscha b’ramus] and cast fear upon the students.’ And Moshe Rabbeinu, the humblest of all men — Dasan and Aviram said to him, ‘will you make yourself a prince over us?’ (Shemos 2:14); and surely they did not speak mere falsehood, and all the more that such a thing would not be written in the Torah — but they sensed in him, to the outward eye, some measure of ‘exercising authority.’” (Exactly the se’if’s paradox: the very man of whom ‘when Rebbi died, humility ceased’ bids his son rule with authority — because inner humility and an outward bearing of authority, like Moshe’s, are no contradiction.)
וְעַל יְדֵי רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל נִתְבָּרְרוּ גַּם מַעֲמַקֵּי לֵב דְּרַבָּן גַּמְלִיאֵל כִּי הָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת מָלֵא עֲנָוָה וְלֹא כִּיוֵּן לִכְבוֹדוֹ כְּלָל

And through Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, “the depths of the heart of Rabban Gamliel [the father] were also clarified” — that “he was truly full of humility and did not intend for his honor at all,”966R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §99): “and regarding all of them it is written "nasi" — except for Yehudah, Shimon and Binyamin.” The se’if’s distinction exactly: the title of office and the inward standing are two different things, and Scripture itself withholds the title precisely where the standing is deepest.Izhbitz parallel - Mei HaShiloach, Volume I, Shmini 7: The Ishbitzer warns that there is such a thing as anavah pesulah. He interprets those who left manna overnight as having regarded themselves as especially humble - perhaps, they thought, they were not worthy that Hashem should provide for them again tomorrow. Yet by singling themselves out as less worthy than Klal Yisrael they had actually left the place Hashem assigned them; what appeared to human eyes as modesty was not the humility Hashem desired. He contrasts this with David's 've'anochi tola'as,' a lowliness that did find favor before Hashem. This is an unusually close complement to R' Tzadok's 'nehog nesi'uscha beramim.' Once genuine humility has been clarified, refusing the responsibility and dignity attached to a Divine office can itself become a distorted humility. Rebbi could be 'anav' and still instruct his son to conduct the nesius with force, because anavah does not mean denying the truth of the role Hashem has given. It means that the role does not become a claim about one's independent self. The Ishbitzer's distinction also explains why outward appearances are insufficient: a deferential posture may conceal self-consciousness, while firm leadership may arise from complete bittul to the task. Thus the son can reveal the father's inward truth precisely by joining two qualities that look contradictory in this world - deep humility and unapologetic exercise of nesius - and showing that both can flow from one l'Shem Shamayim center.
וְעַד שֶׁאָמְרוּ [פ״ק דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין] ״תָּא חֲזֵי מַה בֵּין תַּקִּיפֵי קַדְמָאֵי לְעִינוְתָנֵי בַּתְרָאֵי״, שֶׁהָיָה עָנָיו עוֹד יוֹתֵר מִבְּנוֹ

until they said [first chapter of Sanhedrin 11a], “come and see the difference between the mighty former ones and the humble latter ones” — [Rebbi] being even more humble than his [own] son.967Sanhedrin 11a: The Gemara relates that Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel dictated letters intercalating the year, signing them with characteristic humility (concluding, “and it seemed proper to me and to my colleagues”). Comparing his manner to that of his son Rebbi, the Gemara exclaims, “come and see the difference between the mighty former ones [Rabban Gamliel] and the humble latter ones [Rebbi]” — Rebbi being still more self-effacing.
וְעַל כֵּן נִשְׁאַר שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת נְשִׂיאוּתוֹ לְזַרְעוֹ עַד שֶׁבָּטְלָה הַנְּשִׂיאוּת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וּמַה שֶּׁהֶעֱבִירוּהוּ הָיָה רַק עַד אַרְגִּיעָה
And therefore the “chain of his [line’s] nesius remained to his seed” until the nesius ceased from Israel; and his deposition was “only for a moment.”
וְכֵן כָּל הַבֵּירוּרִים הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַבָּנִים, כַּאֲשֶׁר הֵם הַתַּכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת בְּאוֹתוֹ עִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן בָּאָב

And so “all the clarifications are through the sons” — when they are “the ultimate perfection” in that very matter in which “there was the deficiency in the father.” — the son is the father’s vindication: precisely where the father’s inner intent lay hidden and suspect, the son brings it fully to light.

items.h: The theme: Shimon’s deficiency looks the severest in the souls of Israel, yet is truly the lightest — which is why it is unwritten in the Torah, since in truth it cannot exist in a Jewish soul at all. Hence its penalty comes not from a court but from a zealot, who does not deliberate in order to acquit. The complete clarification is “Yosef ben Shimon” — the son revealing his father’s depths precisely by being his opposite.

p: [ע] וְהִנֵּה שֹׁרֶשׁ הַחִסָּרוֹן הַיּוֹתֵר עָצוּם לְמַרְאִית עַיִן שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא הַחִסָּרוֹן דְּשִׁמְעוֹן
Now, the “root of the most severe deficiency, to the outward eye, in the souls of Israel,” is “the deficiency of Shimon”;
וְעַל הָאֱמֶת הוּא הַחִסָּרוֹן הַיּוֹתֵר קַל, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא נִכְתַּב בַּתּוֹרָה, כִּי עַל הָאֱמֶת אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חִסָּרוֹן בָּזֶה בְּנַפְשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל
but “in truth it is the lightest deficiency” — therefore “it was not written in the Torah,” for “in truth it is impossible for there to be [such] a deficiency in the souls of Israel at all,”
אֶלָּא שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ לְבֵירוּרִים גְּדוֹלִים

only that “this matter requires great clarifications.”968R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §19): “there is a bounding-in that comes from a desire that is not good, as they said [Sanhedrin 65], "this is one who starves himself so that a spirit of impurity should rest upon him."” Exactly the se’if: the same outward restraint can issue from opposite roots — which is why Shimon’s matter “requires great clarifications” before it can be judged at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אֵין מִיתָתוֹ בְּבֵית דִּין אֶלָּא מִקַּנָּאִי הַפּוֹגֵעַ בּוֹ
And therefore “his death is not [administered] by a court,” but by “a zealot who strikes him”;
וְהַקַּנָּאִי הוּא שֶׁזָּרִיז וּמָהִיר לִנְקוֹם וְאֵין מָתוּן בַּדָּבָר וּמְצַדֵּד לִזְכוּת וּלְהַצִּיל כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ עוֹשִׂין הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין

and the zealot is “quick and swift to take vengeance,” and “not deliberate in the matter,” [not] “seeking to acquit and to save,” as the Sanhedrin would do.969R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §96): “three good gifts corresponding to three transgressions they had to be wary of in the wilderness: idolatry — from Peor; Gan Eden — from Nachal Shittim, which was of harlotry; and [the third] — for they had not yet crossed the Jordan, and there is a raging heart.” Exactly the se’if’s Shittim: the very place named for that deficiency is met by an answering gift — which is why the matter is in truth the lightest and not the severest.

וְהַבֵּירוּר הַשָּׁלֵם הוּא כַּאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״, שֶׁהַבֵּן יְגַלֶּה הַמַּעֲמַקִּים שֶׁבָּאָב, כַּאֲשֶׁר יִהְיֶה הַבֵּן הֵיפֶךְ לוֹ מַמָּשׁ שֶׁזֶּהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ יוֹסֵף שֶׁהוּא מוּגְדָּר בָּזֶה בְּתַכְלִית

And “the complete clarification” is when there is “Yosef ben Shimon” — [when] “the son reveals the depths in the father,” [precisely] when “the son is his very opposite” — which is the root of Yosef, “utterly bounded-in” in this [separateness].
וְעַל כֵּן סְתָם בֵּן הַמְבָרֵר אָבִיו יֵשׁ לִקְרוֹתוֹ עַל דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״
And therefore, any “son who clarifies his father” may be called, by way of example, “Yosef ben Shimon”;
כִּי בֵּירוּר זֶה הוּא בָּרוּר בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהֲרֵי חִסָּרוֹן זֶה אֵינוֹ בְּעֶצֶם בְּמִי שֶׁהוּא מִשָּׁרְשָׁא וְגִזְעָא קַדִּישָׁא דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
for this clarification is “certain in all Israel,” since “this deficiency is not in the essence of one who is of the holy root and stock of Israel.”

וְלָכֵן נָקְטוּ לְמָשָׁל הַשֵּׁם ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״ כְּשֶׁדִּבְּרוּ מִשְּׁנֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם הַשָּׁוִין בַּשֵּׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה [ב״ב קעב.] וּבַגְּמָרָא שָׁם [קסז:] וּבְכוֹרוֹת [מח.]970Bava Basra 172a (Mishnah; the Gemara there 167b; and Bechoros 48a): the Mishnah and Gemara treat the case of two men in one town who bear the same name [and the safeguards required for their documents] — the source for the point that distinct people may share an identical name.

And therefore they “took, as an example, the name ‘Yosef ben Shimon’” when they spoke of “two people identical in name,” as they said in the Mishnah [Bava Basra 172a], in the Gemara there [167b], and in Bechoros [48a].
דְּנִרְאֶה דְּהוּא שֵׁם הַמָּצוּי, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין זֶה עַצְמוֹ שֵׁם מָצוּי בְּפוֹעַל, הֵם נָקְטוּ לְמָשָׁל מַה שֶּׁהוּא רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בַּשֹּׁרֶשׁ
[so] that “it appears to be a common name” — and even though “this is not itself a common name in fact,” they “took, as an example, what is fitting to be [so] in the root.”

וּכְפִי דַּרְכָּם לִתְפּוֹס לְמָשָׁל שְׁמוֹת הַשְּׁבָטִים שֶׁהֵם רָאשֵׁי הָאוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת שֵׁם בֵּן וְאָב, רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בֵּן הַמְבָרֵר הָאָב שֶׁעַל זֶה הוּא עִיקַּר עִנְיַן הַבָּנִים, הַמָּצוּי הַרְבֵּה ״יוֹסֵף בֶּן שִׁמְעוֹן״

And per their way of “taking, as examples, the names of the tribes,” the “heads of the Israelite nation” — it is “fitting to be a name of son and father,” meaning “the son who clarifies the father” (the essential matter of the sons); and the most common [instance] is “Yosef ben Shimon,”
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר הַשֵּׁמוֹת יוֹסֵף וְשִׁמְעוֹן שֶׁל הַשְּׁבָטִים יִהְיֶה זֶה בֵּן לָזֶה וּמְבָרֵר אֶת זֶה
meaning: [in the root,] “the names Yosef and Shimon of the tribes” — this one [Yosef] would be a son to that one [Shimon], and “clarify him.”
וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּפוֹעַל לְדוֹרוֹת שְׁמוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם כֵּן, דְּלֹא כָּל שִׁמְעוֹן וְיוֹסֵף שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הֵם דּוּגְמַת הַשְּׁבָטִים
And not that “in fact, in the generations, people’s names [must be] so” — for “not every Shimon and Yosef in the world is like the [respective] tribes”;
וּפוּק חֲזֵי כַּמָּה ״יוֹסֵף״ אִיכָּא בַּשּׁוּק שֶׁאֵין גְּדוּרִים בַּעֲרָיוֹת כְּיוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק
“go out and see how many [people named] ‘Yosef’ there are in the market” who are “not fenced-in from immorality like Yosef HaTzaddik.”
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם וַדַּאי ״שְׁמָא גָּרִים״ לִהְיוֹת לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת מָה לְשֹׁרֶשׁ שְׁמוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין הַבֵּירוּר בַּשֵּׁמוֹת יוֹסֵף וְשִׁמְעוֹן בְּעָלְמָא

And even though, certainly, “the name has an effect [shema garim]971Berachos 7b (“shema garim”): amid the Gemara’s expositions of names as portents (Reuven, Ruth, Yehudah), it asks, “from where that the name has an effect [shema garim]? R’ Eliezer said: the verse states, ‘go, see the works of Hashem, who has set desolations [שַׁמּוֹת] in the earth’ (Tehillim 46:9) — do not read שַׁמּוֹת [shamos, desolations] but שֵׁמוֹת [sheimos, names]” — a person’s name is among “the works of Hashem in the earth.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Maharsha — the name (given, as the Arizal teaches, with a trace of ruach hakodesh) draws down and shapes the bearer’s nature and path; and R’ Meir “would scrutinize names” (Yoma 83b) — distrusting the innkeeper “Kidor” from “ki dor tahpuchos heimah” (Devarim 32:20), and proven right. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “the name is the essence of the soul and the vitality,” the Sages’ stock pair “Yosef ben Shimon” is chosen not for its frequency in the market but for its root meaning — the tribal names Yosef and Shimon fitted, at their source, to model “the son who clarifies the father”; hence “not every Yosef and Shimon in the world is like the tribes,” yet the name still “has an effect,” bearing “some connection to the root of his name.”R' Tzadok - close parallel (Pri Tzadik, Korach 8:4): In Pri Tzadik R' Tzadok returns explicitly to Chazal's stock expression 'Yosef ben Shimon' and gives essentially the same root-level reading developed here. All Israel, he explains, can be called by Yosef's name - 'she'eiris Yosef' - because 've'ameich kulam tzaddikim,' and the Zohar associates bris with the title tzaddik. He then makes the striking point that this remains true even of Shimon, although the majority of the twenty-four thousand who died at Baal Peor came from Shimon and their sin appears to be the very opposite of Yosef's defining shemiras habris. That is why 'Yosef ben Shimon' is so expressive: at the level of the revealed episode, Shimon and Yosef appear opposed; at the root, Shimon too is included in Yosef's name of tzaddik. This cross-reference strengthens the present se'if's claim that the defect is not part of Shimon's essential shoresh. It also guards against a superficial reading.
