The reason he gives is structural: in forbidden unions the vitality becomes bound in a form of kelipah from which ordinary teshuvah cannot simply lift it, whereas in wasted seed the vitality is clothed and held differently and therefore remains capable of ascent. R' Tzadok's formulation is not identical to Tanya's kabbalistic mechanics, but the convergence is extraordinary. Both notice the same absence from the Torah's explicit list of arayos, both refuse to infer leniency from that absence, and both understand the absence as pointing to a different relation between the fallen spark and its possible return. Tanya thereby gives an important control on R' Tzadok's provocative language: the point is certainly not that the act is permitted - the Alter Rebbe calls it severe - but that severity and metaphysical irretrievability are not synonyms. The Torah's silence can therefore coexist with grave culpability while still intimating that the spark is not, in ultimate truth, an eternal nidach.

וְזֶהוּ ״דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים״, שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתדבא״ר רפ״א] ״דֶּרֶךְ זוֹ דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ״, דְּמִי שֶׁהוּא בְּ״דֶרֶךְ אֶרֶץ״ בִּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית כָּרָאוּי יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְעֵץ הַחַיִּים שֶׁיִּחְיֶה לְעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לֶעָתִיד

And this is “the way [to] the Tree of Life” — of which they said [in Tana d’Vei Eliyahu Rabbah 1], “‘the way’ [in ‘to guard the way to the Tree of Life’] — this is derech eretz” — for “one who is in ‘derech eretz,’ in guarding the bris as befits, can reach the Tree of Life, to live forever,” as will be in the Future.

אֲבָל לֹא זָכָה לָזֶה עֲדַיִין אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה זוּלַת אֵלִיָּהוּ דְּנִקְרָא ״מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית״, וְאָמְרוּ [בַּזוֹהַר] דְּהָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת מַלְאָךְ מִתְּחִלָּתוֹ וְנִשְׁלַח לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְזָכָה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בּוֹ יִצְרָא דְּתַאֲוָה כְּלָל

But “no person in this world has yet merited this, except Eliyahu,” called “the angel of the bris” — and they said [in the Zohar] that “he was truly an angel from his origin,” “sent to this world,” and “merited that there was in him no yetzer of desire at all.”
אֲבָל שְׁאָר כָּל אָדָם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה, וַאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים כו׳, כִּי יֵשׁ ״כְּרוּבִים וְלַהַט הַחֶרֶב״ לִשְׁמוֹר אֶת ״דֶּרֶךְ״ וְגוֹמֵר

But “every other person cannot reach this — even the most pious of the pious” — for there are “the Keruvim and the flame of the [ever-turning] sword to guard the way [to the Tree of Life]” (Bereishis 3:24).

וְיָדוּעַ פֵּירוּשׁ רַז״ל עַל ״כְּרוּב״ — ״כְּרַבְיָא״, וְכַאן רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן ״חַטַּאת נְעוּרִים״, כִּי ״יֵצֶר לֵב הָאָדָם רַע מִנְּעוּרָיו״, וּבְיַלְדוּתוֹ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי מִתַּאֲוֹת

And the known interpretation of the Sages, that “keruv” [means] “keravya [like a child]”1053Sukkah 5b: discussing the faces of the Keruvim, the Gemara asks — “what is [the face of] a cherub [keruv]? R’ Abahu said: like [that of] a child [ke-ravya], for in Babylonia they call a child ‘ravya’.” Meforshim: Rashi — the cherubs bore the faces of children; and the Gemara resolves the verse “the face of the keruv… the face of a man” (Yechezkel 10:14) as the small face of a child versus the large face of an adult. R’ Tzadok’s use: since “keruv” denotes a child, the “Keruvim and the ever-turning flaming sword to guard the way to the Tree of Life” (Bereishis 3:24) allude to the “sin of youth [chatas ne’urim]” — for “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Bereishis 8:21), and in childhood no one, save Eliyahu (an angel from his very origin), is wholly clean of desire. — and here [is] “the sin of youth,” God spare us, for “the inclination of man’s heart is evil from his youth” (Bereishis 8:21), and “in his childhood it is impossible to be entirely clean of desires.” — the Torah left this un-prohibited precisely because, in ultimate truth, no spark is ever finally lost; only to this-worldly eyes does the wasted seed seem an irredeemable outcast, and guarding the bris is nothing less than the path back to the Tree of Life.

items.h: The theme: Even one born wholly clean of desire has, set against it, a deficiency of anger — the two opposite inclinations in man, “the flame of the ever-turning sword,” at times life and at times death. There is an anger of the Sages that is good on every side, the Torah making a man seethe. Yet even he will not escape some deficiency of anger — for otherwise he would live forever, and Hashem created the yetzer “to guard the way to the Tree of Life.”

p: [פד] וְגַם אִם יִמָּצֵא הַנָּקִי לְגַמְרֵי גַּם מִיַּלְדוּתוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ עַל כָּרְחָךְ מִי שֶׁבְּטֶבַע תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ אֵין בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן זֶה דְּתַאֲוָה, יֵשׁ לְעוּמָּתוֹ בּוֹ הַחִסָּרוֹן בְּכַעַס, דְּהֵם תְּרֵין יִצְרִין הַהֲפוּכִים שֶׁבָּאָדָם

And even if one is found “entirely clean, even from his childhood” — which is, perforce, one whose “nature by birth” has not this “deficiency of desire” — there is, “over against it, in him, the deficiency of anger” — for these are “two opposite inclinations in man.”1054R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §17): “for the sun dries and desiccates all the moisture of the water, which is the desiring power — and this is the assurance to Noach and his sons, for the nations reckon by the sun, and immediately after the Flood the nations arose and fenced themselves from [immorality].” Exactly the se’if: the two edges of the ever-turning sword are the two opposite inclinations — the drying force set against the moist force of desire, each checking the other.1055R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §5): “the keruvim are love, and "the flame of the ever-turning sword" is fear — and therefore they said [to recite] Kerias Shema upon one’s bed (the acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, and fear)… holding a two-edged sword.” Exactly the se’if: the “ever-turning sword” is not simply a menace but the second of the two opposite inclinations — the fear set over against love, turning between them.
וְזֶהוּ ״לַהַט הַחֶרֶב הַמִּתְהַפֶּכֶת״, וְאָמְרוּ [בְּזוֹהַר וְתִיקּוּנִים] דְּמִתְהַפֶּכֶת ״לִזְמַנִּין חַיֵּי לִזְמַנִּין מוֹתָא״

And this is “the flame of the ever-turning sword” — and they said [in the Zohar and Tikkunim] that “it turns [mishapechet]: at times [it is] life, at times death.”1056R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §63): “and therefore it was said to him at the time of the famine, which indicates lack — and that he is still in this world — "dwell [in this land]"… and "gur" is also an expression of fear and dread.” Exactly the se’if’s “at times life, at times death”: the very word of the promise carries dwelling and dread together, because in this world the two inclinations are never separated.
הַיְינוּ דְּמִי שֶׁנָּקִי לְגַמְרֵי מִתַּאֲוֹת אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ שֹׁרֶשׁ כַּעַס, אֶלָּא דְּיֵשׁ ״רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן״ דְּאִיהוּ טַב בְּכָל סִטְרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בַּזוֹהַר]

That is, one who is “entirely clean of desires,” it is “impossible that there not be in him a root of anger” — except that there is “the anger of the Sages [rugza d’rabbanan],” which is “good in all its sides,” as it is stated [in the Zohar];
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (תַּעֲנִית ד.) דְּ״אוֹרַיְיתָא מַרְתְּחָא לֵיהּ״, דְּהִנֵּה ״כֹּה דְבָרַי כָּאֵשׁ״, וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים וְיֵשׁ בָּזֶה חַיִּים וְתוֹסֶפֶת חִיּוּת

as the Sages said (Taanis 4a)1057Taanis 4a: “Rava said: If a young Torah scholar [tzurva mei-rabbanan] grows hot-tempered, it is the Torah within him that makes him seethe [Oraisa hi de-ka marsecha lei], as it says (Yirmeyah 23:29), ‘is not My word like fire?’” Chabad clarification - Tanya, Iggeret HaKodesh 25:30: The Alter Rebbe draws almost the exact distinction needed for R' Tzadok's discussion of anger. He returns to Chazal's statement that anger is 'like serving avodah zarah' and explains that this applies to ordinary worldly matters: 'hakol bidei Shamayim chutz miyiras Shamayim,' so rage at the human agent treats that agent as though he possessed autonomous power outside Divine providence. But he then explicitly limits the rule: in 'mili diShmaya,' where one must separate another from prohibition, this reasoning does not apply, and he cites the very Torah expression 'vayiktzof Moshe.' Thus the Tanya does not flatten every manifestation of anger into one category. There is an anger born of wounded selfhood and denial of hashgachah, and there can be a forceful response whose entire content is responsibility to the revealed will of Hashem. This sharpens the present se'if's use of 'Oraisa ka-martecha lei.' The fire of Torah can make the scholar seethe, but that does not sanctify personal irritability; it means that the same faculty of gevurah can be requisitioned by Torah when the situation truly calls for it. R' Tzadok's reading of Moshe then becomes even more precise: Moshe's anger was not wrong merely because anger is always evil. Its defect lay in the fact that at Mei Merivah the force did not match the particular Divine revelation of that moment. The prospective test is therefore exacting: holy anger is not whatever the righteous person feels intensely, but anger subordinated to the command and measure of Heaven. that “the Torah makes him ‘seethe’ [martecha lei]” — for “‘behold, My word is like fire’ (Yirmeyah 23:29),” and these are “the words of the living God,” and in this there is “life and an increase of vitality.”
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַנָּקִי מִתַּאֲוֹת לֹא יִמָּלֵט שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חִסָּרוֹן בְּכַעַס, דְּלוּלֵי כֵן הָיָה חַי לְעוֹלָם
But nonetheless, “one clean of desires will not escape having some deficiency of anger” — for “were it not so, he would live forever”;
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא רָצָה בָּזֶה עַד עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיְּבוּלַע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח, וּבָרָא יֵצֶר הָרַע ״לִשְׁמוֹר דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים״
and Hashem “did not will this until the End of Days, when death will be swallowed up forever,” and He “created the evil inclination ‘to guard the way to the Tree of Life.’”
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה רַבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל יוֹכִיחַ, דְּנִקְבַּר מוּל פְּעוֹר הָרוֹמֵז לְתַאֲוֹת שֶׁהָיָה נֶגֶד זֶה לְגַמְרֵי
And Moshe Rabbeinu, “the master of Israel,” proves [it] — for he “was buried opposite Pe’or,” which “alludes to desires,” to which he was “entirely opposed”;

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ ז״ל (שַׁבָּת נה:) ״אַף הוּא בְּחֶטְאוֹ מֵת״, מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמּוֹרִים״ וְהַכָּאַת הַסֶּלַע, שֶׁהָיָה מִכְּלַל כַּעַס וְרוּגְזָא שֶׁלֹּא בִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַנִּגְלֶה

and nonetheless the Sages said (Shabbos 55b)1058Shabbos 55b: “Rav Ami said: There is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity [ein misah b’lo chet ve-ein yissurin b’lo avon].” (Cited here on the same daf as “whoever says Reuven sinned is mistaken.”) that “he too died through his [own] ‘sin’” — [in] what he said, “listen now, O rebels” (Bamidbar 20:10)1059Bamidbar 20:10: at the waters of Merivah — “וַיֹּאמֶר לָהֶם שִׁמְעוּ נָא הַמֹּרִים, הֲמִן הַסֶּלַע הַזֶּה נוֹצִיא לָכֶם מָיִם” — “and he said to them, ‘listen now, O rebels; shall we bring forth water for you from this rock?’” Meforshim: Rashi — “ha-morim” means fools / rebels (some render it “those who would instruct their teachers”); the commentators dispute what precisely Moshe’s sin was — Rashi holds it was striking the rock instead of speaking to it, while the Rambam (Shemonah Perakim, ch. 4) holds it was the anger betrayed in “shimu na ha-morim.” R’ Tzadok’s use: he follows the anger-reading — “shimu na ha-morim” and the striking of the rock “were part of anger and wrath, not according to Hashem’s revealed will”; and so even Moshe, buried opposite Pe’or as the utter opposite of desire, “died through his [own] sin” (Shabbos 55b) — the flash of that anger — proof that no one born clean of desire escapes some deficiency of anger., and the striking of the rock, which were “part of anger and wrath, not according to Hashem’s revealed will.” — even the man born wholly free of desire cannot escape a root of anger, the ever-turning sword that is life on one edge and death on the other; Moshe himself, buried facing Pe’or as its complete opposite, still met death through a single flash of that wrath.

items.h: The theme: Even for the view that death comes only “through the serpent’s counsel,” that counsel is the inborn deficiency of desire — the guarding of the way to the Tree of Life. So the Zohar’s “teshuvah does not avail” means only that it cannot avail completely, turning sins into merits; for then the guard would be removed. Yet nothing stands before teshuvah: the teshuvah of the bris redeems death into length of days.

p: [פה] וְאַף לְמַאן דְּאָמַר יֵשׁ מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא אֶלָּא בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ

And even according to the one who says “there is death without sin,” but [only] “through the counsel of the serpent”1060Shabbos 55a–b: Rav Ami said, “there is no death without sin, and no suffering without iniquity,” bringing proofs from Scripture (“the soul that sins — it shall die”). The Gemara challenges: it was taught that “four died [only] through the counsel of the serpent [b’etyo shel nachash], without sin of their own — Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David” — proving that there is death without sin and suffering without iniquity, and refuting Rav Ami.1061R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §93): “as against what He said to him, that he would die — and he knew that the one who brings [Israel] into Eretz Yisrael must be of those who left Egypt, and they had all died… therefore he said "God of the spirits" — for He can also give life.” Exactly the se’if: even where death is decreed as a general order, it is not the last word — the same Name that decrees it is the One who revives. —
עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ הַיְינוּ חִסְרוֹן הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בַּתּוֹלָדָה מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל

“the counsel of the serpent” is the “deficiency of desire that there is in [human] birth, from the counsel of the serpent,” as I wrote above.1062R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §13): “the reward of a mitzvah that one performs from obligation [is one thing]; but what he does beyond the line of the law, the Holy One repays him in his lifetime, as Rashi explained on "up to a third from his own, beyond that from the Holy One."” Exactly the se’if: what belongs to the ordinary decreed order is settled elsewhere — but what a man does beyond the line reaches him here, which is why “teshuvah does not avail” cannot be the whole account.
וְזֶהוּ הַשְּׁמִירָה לְ״דֶרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים״, וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בַּזוֹהַר] דְּאֵין מוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה

And this is the “guarding of the way to the Tree of Life”; and therefore they said [in the Zohar] that “teshuvah does not avail”1063R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis §3): “[Shabbos 89b]”if your sins be like shanim [scarlet/years] — which are ordered and come from the six days of Creation — they shall whiten like snow“; and this is that through teshuvah from love [the willful sins become as merits].” Exactly the se’if’s exception: only the comprehensive teshuvah from love reaches the inborn deficiency — turning the very lack white, and the willful sins into merits. —

הַיְינוּ שֶׁיּוֹעִיל לְגַמְרֵי כְּמִשְׁפַּט הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה דִּזְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכִיּוֹת, שֶׁמְּתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי וְעַד שֶׁיֵּשֵׁב עוֹד לִזְכוּת, וְעָדִיף מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר דְּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה כו׳

meaning, [it does not] “avail entirely, as [in] the law of complete teshuvah — in which ‘deliberate sins become like merits,’ which ‘rectifies the past entirely,’ until it is ‘reckoned still further to [his] merit,’ and is ‘preferable to a complete tzaddik,’ [as] ‘in the place where masters of teshuvah [stand]’”
דְּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר בְּעָוֹן זֶה, דְּאִם כֵּן הָיָה מִסְתַּלֵּק מִמֶּנּוּ הַשְּׁמִירָה מִדֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים וְהָיָה יָכוֹל אוֹכֵל וְחַי לְעוֹלָם
for “this is impossible with this iniquity” — for [if] so, “the guarding of the way to the Tree of Life would be removed from him,” and “he would be able to eat and live forever”;

וְאֵין רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בָּזֶה, וְשָׁם שׁוֹמְרִים שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן כָּל כָּךְ וְלָשׁוּב לְגַמְרֵי עַד שֶׁיּוּכַל לִחְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם

and “it is not Hashem’s will, in this world, [for] this”; and “there they guard, that he not be able to reach this” — meaning, “that he not be able to rectify so [completely] and return entirely, to the point of being able to live forever.”
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם ״אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה״, וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבְּמִדַּת הַיְסוֹד בְּרִית קוֹדֶשׁ זוֹכֶה [מִ]מִּיתָה לְהַאֲרָכַת יָמָיו וּשְׁנוֹתָיו
But nonetheless “there is nothing that stands before teshuvah” — and the teshuvah in the trait of Yesod, the “holy bris,” “merits, from [what would be] death, a lengthening of his days and years.”
וְכָל הַבְטָחוֹת הַתּוֹרָה הוּא עַל הַאֲרָכַת יָמִים, וְכֵן נֶאֱמַר בַּתּוֹרָה ״אֹרֶךְ יָמִים בִּימִינָהּ״, וְדָבָר אָרוֹךְ יֵשׁ לוֹ סוֹף עֲדַיִין אֶלָּא שֶׁאָרוֹךְ

And all the “promises of the Torah” are [in terms of] “lengthening of days,” as it says, “length of days is in her right hand” (Mishlei 3:16)1064Mishlei 3:16: of Wisdom (the Torah) — “אֹרֶךְ יָמִים בִּימִינָהּ, בִּשְׂמֹאולָהּ עֹשֶׁר וְכָבוֹד” — “length of days is in her right hand; in her left, riches and honor.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Gemara (Shabbos 63a) — to those who engage the Torah for its own sake [lishmah] she grants “length of days” (her “right”), and even to those who do not, “riches and honor” (her “left”). R’ Tzadok’s use: “all the promises of the Torah are [couched as] length of days” — for the teshuvah of Yesod (the bris) redeems what would be death into “a lengthening of his days and years”; yet “a long thing still has an end, only that it is long” — unlike Yaakov, whose inheritance is “without bounds [bli meitzarim],” and who therefore “did not die at all.” — and “a long thing still has an end, only that it is long.”
וְזֶה לֹא כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁנַּחֲלָתוֹ בְּלֹא מֵצָרִים, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא מֵת כְּלָל
And this is unlike Yaakov Avinu, “whose inheritance is ‘without bounds [meitzarim]’” — and therefore he “did not die at all.”
וּבֶאֱמֶת הַתּוֹרָה נִקְרָא ״חַיֵּי עוֹלָם שֶׁנָּטַע בְּתוֹכֵנוּ״, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ ״עֵץ הַחַיִּים זוֹ תּוֹרָה״ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״עֵץ חַיִּים הִיא לַמַּחֲזִיקִים בָּהּ״ וְאוֹכְלֶיהָ חַיִּים לְעוֹלָם

And in truth the Torah is called “eternal life which He planted within us”; and so they said, “‘the Tree of Life’ — this is the Torah,” as it says, “she is a Tree of Life to those who hold fast to her” (Mishlei 3:18) — and “those who eat of her live forever.”
וְכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ הַתּוֹרָה עַל הַר סִינַי ״אֲחִידִין בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא״, וְעַל כֵּן כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּהַיְינוּ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם
And all the souls of Israel who “received the Torah at Sinai are ‘grasped in the Torah’” — and therefore “all Israel have a share in the World to Come,” which is “eternal life.”
אַךְ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּנִקְרָא ״עַלְמָא דְּשִׁקְרָא״, שֶׁאֵין הָאֱמֶת לְיַעֲקֹב נִגְלֶה, אֵין דָּבָר זֶה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת
But in this world, called “the world of falsehood,” where “the truth of Yaakov is not revealed,” this matter is “not in revelation.”

וְכֵן קִיבַּלְתִּי בְּפֵירוּשׁ לְשׁוֹן [הַתִּיקּוּנֵי זוֹהַר] גַּבֵּי ״אַבְנֵי שַׁיִשׁ טָהוֹר״, דְּלֶעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה דְּלֹא הָיָה מִיתָה כְּלָל בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב, וְהַמִּיתָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא רַק מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְלֹא כְּשֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ

And so I have received, in the interpretation of the language1065From the Ishbitzer (Mei HaShiloach): R’ Tzadok’s “I have received” — the interpretation of the language of the Tikkunei Zohar cited here — is a teaching of his rebbe, R’ Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz (see §8 above). Direct Izhbitz source - Mei HaShiloach I, Bereshit 6: The source from R' Mordechai Yosef of Izhbitz is exceptionally close to R' Tzadok's language here. Commenting on the trees and rivers of Gan Eden, Mei HaShiloach identifies 'Etz HaChaim' with 'teshuvah amitis shemerape'os es hakodem' - true teshuvah that heals what came before. He returns to the point a second time: the river Peras corresponds to baalei teshuvah because 'teshuvah merape'es es hakodem,' and Peras reaches back to the first source; complete return therefore means arriving again at one's primordial shoresh. This sheds light on why R' Tzadok can put the Tree of Life, the bris and the repair of the past into one conceptual chain. Ordinary moral improvement moves forward from the present. Etz HaChaim-teshuvah reaches to the source from which the damaged history emerged and heals the prior deficiency at that root. At the same time, R' Tzadok is carefully distinguishing the measure in which that truth can be disclosed in this world: the full revelation of life without death is guarded, while teshuvah can already convert what would have produced death into arichus yamim. Mei HaShiloach therefore supplies the inner meaning of the 'Tree of Life' without requiring an overstatement about present experience. The baal teshuvah reaches the original river, while this-worldly revelation may still show mortality and temporal limits. This is also a fitting expansion of R' Tzadok's explicit 'kibalti' from his rebbe in the footnote: the Ishbitz teaching is not merely a biographical source but a direct conceptual gloss on his claim that true teshuvah is a healing of the earlier root. [of the Tikkunei Zohar] regarding “stones of pure marble,” that “in the Future it will be revealed that there was no death at all in the root of the seed of Yaakov” — and “death in this world is only from the side of the revealed [order] of this world,” and not [as it will be] “when the absolute truth is revealed.”
וְעַל כֵּן בַּקְּרָא כְּתִיב ״וּבְשׁוּב רָשָׁע [מֵרִשְׁעָתוֹ] הוּא יִחְיֶה״, סְתָם חַיִּים הַיְינוּ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם, וְרַז״ל לָמְדוּ מִזֶּה דְּמַאֲרֶכֶת שְׁנוֹתָיו

And therefore in Scripture it is written, “and when a wicked man returns [from his wickedness] — he shall live” (Yechezkel 18:27) — [where] “‘live’ [unqualified] means eternal life”; and the Sages learned from this that “it lengthens his years.”
כִּי עִיקַּר הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב בְּנַפְשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּ״לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִיא״
For the essence of the Oral Torah is “the revelation of the Written Torah in the souls of the Children of Israel in this world,” of which “‘it is not in heaven’” (Devarim 30:12).

וְהַכְּתָב הוּא דִּבְרֵי הַנָּבִיא מִפִּי ה׳ מְגַלֶּה הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא נֶעֱלָם וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָדַעַת כְּלוּם מִתּוֹךְ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב רַק עַל יְדֵי פֵּירוּשָׁהּ שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא גִּילּוּי מַה שֶּׁבִּכְתָב

And the “Written [Torah]” is “the words of the prophet, from the mouth of Hashem, revealing the absolute truth”; except that “in this world it is concealed,” and “it is impossible to know anything from the Written Torah except through its Oral interpretation,” which is “the revelation of what is in writing.”

וּכְפִי הַגִּילּוּי דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא רַק הַאֲרָכַת שָׁנִים, כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִתְגַּלּוּת יוֹתֵר, שֶׁהֲרֵי אַף יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה דְּלֹא מֵת כְּפִי הַנִּגְלֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֲרֵי ״קְבָרוּ קָבְרַיָּא וְחָנְטוּ חָנְטַיָּא״

And according to the “revelation of this world,” it is only a “lengthening of years” — for “in this world greater revelation is impossible,” for indeed even Yaakov, “who did not die,” according to the revealed [order] of this world “the buriers buried [him] and the embalmers embalmed [him]” (Taanis 5b). — the Torah is the Tree of Life whose eaters “live forever,” and every Jewish soul, grasped in it at Sinai, already holds eternal life; this world of falsehood can only disclose that gift as “lengthened years,” while the deeper truth — that in Yaakov’s root there is no death at all — waits to break through only at the End.

items.h: The theme: Rebbi, of whom the Sages say he “came home after his death,” was a spark of Yaakov, who did not die — but once it became known he came no more, full revelation being impossible in this world. Of the line of David, Hillel and RaShbaG, he rectified teshuvah down to its Yesod — hence “Kadosh,” attained through the fence against immorality. Holiness surpasses piety: it brings holiness into physical pleasure itself.

p: [פו] וְרַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עָלָיו [כְּתוּבּוֹת קג.] דְּבָא לְאַחַר מִיתָתוֹ לְבֵיתוֹ

And Rabbeinu HaKadosh [Rebbi], of whom they said [in Kesubos 103a] that “he came, after his death, to his house”1066Kesubos 103a: At the time of Rebbi’s passing he charged his sons, “be careful with your mother’s honor; a lamp shall be lit in its place, the table set in its place, the bed made in its place.” Why? — for “every Sabbath eve he would come to his house.” One Sabbath eve a neighbor came and called at the door; the maidservant said, “be silent, for Rebbi is sitting [here].” When he heard that it had become known, “he came no more — so as not to cast aspersion on the earlier righteous ones.”1067R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Korach §4): “that the beginning of the Torah is with an aleph — "Anochi" — the aleph being the letters of "pele" [wonder], which is the hidden intellect; for the Torah is the revelation of the first light, unlike the order of creation, which begins with beis.” Exactly the se’if: a rung that reaches back past death belongs to the hidden aleph, and once it becomes known it can no longer operate in the open order of beis. —
כָּתְבוּ גּוּרֵי הָאֲרִ״י ז״ל דְּהָיָה נִיצוֹץ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה דְּלֹא מֵת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסֵפֶר יַיִן הַמְשׁוּמָּר וְזוּלָתָן]
the disciples of the Arizal wrote that “he was a spark of Yaakov Avinu, who did not die,” as they said [in the Sefer Yayin HaMeshumar and elsewhere].
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא הָיָה קְצָת בְּגָלוּי יוֹתֵר, דְּבָא לְבֵיתוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּמִשֶּׁנּוֹדַע לִשְׁבָבְתֵּי לֹא בָּא עוֹד, כִּי בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר

And even though [with Rebbi] it was “somewhat more revealed” — that “he came to his house” — nonetheless they said there that “once it became known to the neighbors, he came no more,” for “in [full] revelation, in this world, it is impossible.”1068R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §67): “"he prays two [prayers]: one on entering and one on leaving" — the Rambam explained in his Commentary on the Mishnah that the one on leaving is thanksgiving.” Exactly the se’if’s coming and no longer coming: the entering and the leaving are two distinct acts each requiring its own word — and once the leaving was disclosed, the entering could not simply continue.
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן מִזַּרְעָא דְּדָוִד וְזֶרַע הִלֵּל וְרַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל, וְתִיקֵּן מִדַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה עַד הַיְסוֹד בָּהּ
And he too was “of the seed of David,” and the seed of Hillel and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel — and he “rectified the trait of teshuvah down to the Yesod within it”;

דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי ״גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת קיח:]1069Shabbos 118b: Among the pious sayings there: “Rebbi had another matter [of exceptional modesty] — that he never placed his hand beneath his belt”; and Rebbi himself said, when asked why he was called “Rabbeinu HaKadosh [our holy teacher]”: “in all my days I never looked at my own circumcision” — expressions of his guarding of the bris. דְּלֹא הִנִּיחַ יָדוֹ לְמַטָּה מֵאַבְנֵטוֹ, וְהוּא לִשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית

for therefore he is called “Kadosh [Holy],” which is [attained] through “a fence against immorality,” as they said [in Shabbos 118b] that “he did not place his hand below his belt” — which is [an expression] of the “guarding of the bris.”
וְכֵן אָמַר שָׁם לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ דְּלֹא נֶהֱנָה מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּאֶצְבַּע קְטַנָּה, וּפֵירְשׁוּ קַמָּאֵי דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (פְּסָחִים קיב:) ״לֹא כָּל הָאֶצְבָּעוֹת שָׁווֹת״

And so he said, there, before his death, that “he did not derive benefit from this world [even] with his little finger1070Kesubos 104a: it is related that at Rebbi’s passing “he raised his ten fingers toward Heaven and said: Master of the Universe, it is revealed and known before You that I toiled with my ten fingers in the Torah, and I derived no benefit from this world even with my small finger; may it be Your will that there be peace in my repose” — whereupon a Divine Voice proclaimed, “he enters in peace” (Yeshayah 57:2). Meforshim: Rashi — despite all his wealth and honor, Rebbi took no personal pleasure from this world; and the earlier commentators note the precision of “even with my little finger” (compare Pesachim 112b, “not all the fingers are alike”). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the mark of the rung of holiness, which stands above mere piety — Rebbi did not merely restrain pleasure but sanctified it, so that even within his enjoyment “he derived no benefit from this world”; and he was the one who clarified, in this world, the hidden holiness that belongs to all Israel. Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim, ch. 7: Tanya's treatment of kelipas nogah helps define the kind of kedushah R' Tzadok attributes to Rebbi. The Alter Rebbe distinguishes a permitted physical act performed merely to satisfy the body's appetite from the same physical vitality used 'lehar'chiv da'ato laHashem uleSoraso' or for the mitzvah of Oneg Shabbos and Yom Tov. In the latter case the vitality of the food and wine is itself clarified and rises to Hashem 'ke'olah u'chekorban.' Even an ordinary word of humor can be elevated when its purpose is to open the mind and gladden the heart for Torah and avodah. This is more than abstinence. The physical thing, precisely because it belongs to the mixed and permitted realm, can become a carrier of holiness. That distinction closely complements R' Tzadok's assertion that kedushah is higher than chassidus. Rebbi's statement that he benefited from this world 'not even with the small finger' cannot mean that his wealthy table or bodily life literally did not exist; R' Tzadok reads it to mean that the enjoyment was not appropriated as an independent worldly end. In Tanya's terms, the vitality itself can be taken up into avodah. Thus the fence of the bris and the sanctification of permissible enjoyment are two sides of the same Yesod: first the power is guarded from prohibited dispersion, and then the permitted physical life is joined to its Divine purpose. Rebbi's holiness is therefore not a flight from embodiment but the clarification of embodiment until even pleasure no longer stands opposite avodas Hashem.” — and the earlier [commentators] explained that he meant [it] in the manner it is stated (Pesachim 112b)1071Pesachim 112b: “For not all the fingers are alike [she-ein kol etzba’os shavos]” — concluding [the teaching] that not all people, or all cases, are equal., “not all the fingers are alike” [a hint of the deepest degree].

וְאַף דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים כו׳, מַדְרֵגַת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הוּא לְמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגַת הַחֲסִידוּת, שֶׁמַּכְנִיס קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם בַּהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ עַד שֶׁאֵין בָּזֶה נֶהֱנֶה מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And although “even the most pious of the pious [cannot remove the pleasure]” — [nonetheless] “the rung of holiness is above the rung of piety,” in that it “brings holiness even into one’s own [physical] pleasure,” to the point that “in this he derives no benefit from this world” [at all].
וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאוּ ״קְדוֹשִׁים״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל, אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵינוֹ מְבוֹרָר, וְהוּא הָיָה הַמְבָרֵר דָּבָר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And all Israel are called “holy,” as I wrote above — only that in this world it is “not clarified”; and he [Rebbi] was “the one who clarified this in this world.”
וְעַל כֵּן אַף דְּאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק הַפּוֹעֲלִים] דְּשָׁלְחָה לוֹ אֵשֶׁת ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בְּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן דְּ״נִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ כְּלִי שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ [בּוֹ] קֹדֶשׁ״ כו׳

And therefore, even though they said [in Perek HaPo’alim, Bava Metzia 84b] that “the wife of R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon sent [to Rebbi, who sought to marry her], ‘shall a vessel that was used for holiness [now] be used for the mundane?’”1072Bava Metzia 84b: Rebbi sent [a proposal of marriage] to the widow of R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon; she replied, “a vessel that was used for holiness [my late husband], shall it now be used for the mundane?” — and [the proverb], “in the place where the master of the house hangs his weapons, shall the lowly shepherd hang his satchel?” He sent to her, “granted he was greater than I in Torah — but in good deeds, who is greater than I?” She replied, “in Torah I do not know whether he was greater; in [his] deeds I do know, for he accepted sufferings upon himself” —
וּמִדְּהוּבָא בַּגְּמָרָא דְּבָרֶיהָ מַשְׁמַע דְּלֹא דִּבְּרָה דִּבְרֵי רִיק, וְגַם מַשְׁמַע שָׁם דְּרַבִּי הוֹדָה לָהּ
and since her words were “brought in the Gemara,” it implies that “she did not speak empty words,” and it also implies there that “Rebbi conceded to her” —
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ סְתָם בֵּין כָּל הַתַּנָּאִים, לֹא ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בְּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן
nonetheless he [Rebbi] is called “Kadosh” [par excellence] among all the Tannaim, [and] not R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon —
הַיְינוּ דְּהוּא מִשֵּׁבֶט שִׁמְעוֹן כְּפִי קַבָּלָתִי הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, עַל כֵּן הָיְתָה קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ נֶעֱלֶמֶת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהַגִּילּוּי הָיָה רַבִּי

that is, [R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon] “was of the tribe of Shimon,” per my received tradition mentioned above — therefore “his holiness was concealed in this world,” and “the revelation was [through] Rebbi.” — holiness stands a rung above piety: it does not merely restrain pleasure but sanctifies it, so that a man draws no benefit from this world even within his enjoyment of it — and Rebbi, a spark of the Yaakov who never died, was the one who made that hidden holiness of all Israel visible here below.

items.h: The theme: Rebbi was “akin to Mashiach” — “if he is among the living, it is one such as Rabbeinu HaKadosh” — an extension of Chizkiyah, whom too Hashem sought to make Mashiach. In both their generations Torah and greatness reached their peak; but Chizkiyah was not preeminent throughout, whereas Rebbi, once appointed Nasi, had all subordinate to him. The generations advance toward ever-greater revelation; in Rebbi it was the ultimate revelation in potential.

p: [פז] וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צח:]1073Sanhedrin 98b: In the discussion of the Mashiach’s identity: “Rav said: if he is from among the living, it is one such as Rabbeinu HaKadosh [Rebbi]; if from among the dead, it is one such as Daniel, the treasured man.” Chabad parallel - Tanya, Likkutei Amarim 2:5: R' Tzadok's description of the Nasi as the 'head' who contains the full stature of his generation has a direct parallel in Tanya. The Alter Rebbe writes that although Jewish souls occupy innumerable levels, in every generation there are 'rashei alfei Yisrael' whose souls are literally the aspect of 'head and brain' in relation to the souls of the multitude, just as later generations can stand to earlier ones as heel to head. The metaphor is organic rather than merely administrative: one national body can contain radically different limbs while the head serves as the integrating consciousness of the whole. This makes R' Tzadok's inference from Rebbi's personal kedushah to the latent holiness of the generation much easier to follow. If the Nasi were only an unusually pious individual, his achievement would testify only about himself. If his neshamah is the rosh of the generational komah, a revelation concentrated in him can disclose what exists in potential throughout the body even before every limb has actualized it. The same structure explains the transition from Rebbi to Mashiach in this se'if. Rebbi represents 'tachlis hagilui bekoach': the head already carries the form of the whole and his Mishnah holds the later Oral Torah in seed. Mashiach is the stage at which that latent form spreads through the whole body 'bepo'al.' Tanya thus gives a close Chassidic analogue for the collective anthropology behind R' Tzadok's language, without implying that the moral state of every individual was already equal to Rebbi's; head and heel are not identical, but they belong to one living stature. ״אִי מִן חַיָּיא הוּא״ (אִם מִן הַחַיִּים הַמָּשִׁיחַ) ״כְּגוֹן רַבֵּינוּ הַקָּדוֹשׁ״

And therefore they said [in Sanhedrin 98b], “if [the Mashiach] is from among the living, it is one such as Rabbeinu HaKadosh [Rebbi]”1074R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §82): "“you brought out and you watered — all of it yourself” — and the blessing rests upon this; and therefore the Name of Heaven was sanctified through him, as with the mon, which they had to gather each day." Exactly the se’if: Rebbi is “akin to Mashiach” in that the sanctification of the Name rested on his own daily bearing — a spark of Yaakov, sustaining his generation as the mon was gathered.1075Sanhedrin 98b: “Rav said: If [the Mashiach] is among the living, it is one such as Rabbeinu HaKadosh [Rebbi]; and if among the dead, it is one such as Daniel, the man of delights.” —

וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ [אֵיכָה] וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי [דְּשַׁבָּת] אָמְרוּ עָלָיו קְרָא דְּ״רוּחַ אַפֵּינוּ מְשִׁיחַ ה׳״, שֶׁהוּא הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּחִזְקִיָּה דְּגַם כֵּן בִּקֵּשׁ [הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא] לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ מָשִׁיחַ

and in the Midrash [Eichah] and the Yerushalmi [Shabbos] they applied to him the verse “the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of Hashem” (Eichah 4:20)1076Eichah 4:20: “רוּחַ אַפֵּינוּ מְשִׁיחַ ה’, נִלְכַּד בִּשְׁחִיתוֹתָם, אֲשֶׁר אָמַרְנוּ בְּצִלּוֹ נִחְיֶה בַגּוֹיִם” — “the breath of our nostrils, the anointed of Hashem, was caught in their pits — he of whom we said, ‘in his shadow we shall live among the nations’.” Meforshim: the plain sense (Rashi and the Radak) refers to the captured Davidic king (Yoshiyahu or Tzidkiyahu); the Midrash (Eichah Rabbah) and the Yerushalmi apply the verse to the Mashiach — and to Rebbi. R’ Tzadok’s use: the Sages read this verse of Rebbi, “akin to Mashiach,” an extension of Chizkiyah whom too the Holy One sought to make the Mashiach. — for he is “an extension of Chizkiyah,” [of] whom too “[the Holy One] sought to make him the Mashiach.”1077R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §73): “and as they said [Eruvin 65], "one who is appeased in his wine" — meaning, as it says in Avos, that his fear of sin precedes his wisdom, and he expounds well and fulfills well — this one reaches the rung of having in him something of the knowledge of his Maker.” Exactly the se’if: what made Rebbi “akin to Mashiach” is precisely this — a wisdom preceded by fear and matched by deed, which is the nearest a man in this world comes to that rung.
וּבְדוֹרוֹ הָיָה הַרְבָּצַת הַתּוֹרָה בְּיוֹתֵר בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כַּיָּדוּעַ בְּדִבְרֵי רַז״ל כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים, וְכֵן בְּדוֹר רַבִּי

And in his [Chizkiyah’s] generation there was the greatest dissemination of Torah in Israel, as is known in the words of the Sages many times — and so [too] in Rebbi’s generation.1078R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Hashanah §13): “for the essence of the exiles among the nations is in order to bring out their swallowed [prey] from their mouth.” Exactly the se’if: the one who is “akin to Mashiach” appears within the exile and not after it, because the exile itself is the working — and every generation has its candidate for that labor.
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין] דְּמִימוֹת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה עַד רַבִּי לֹא הָיְתָה תּוֹרָה וּגְדֻלָּה בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד

And they said [in Sanhedrin, and Gittin 59a] that “from the days of Moshe Rabbeinu until Rebbi, Torah and greatness were not [found] in one place1079Gittin 59a (and Sanhedrin 36a): “from the days of Moshe [Rabbeinu] until Rebbi we do not find Torah and greatness in one place.” Meforshim: Rashi — Rebbi united consummate mastery of Torah with the wealth and worldly eminence of the Nasi, a pairing unseen since Moshe. R’ Tzadok’s use: once appointed Nasi, Rebbi “was the greatest of all, for all were subordinate to him” — the head of the generation, whose complete “stature” bears the whole generation as its branches..”
וְחִזְקִיָּה לֹא הָיָה כּוּלֵּי שְׁנֵי, דַּהֲוָה שֶׁבְנָא שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה כָּפוּף לוֹ
And Chizkiyah “was not [preeminent] all [his] years,” for there was Shevna, who “was not subordinate to him”;
וְרַבִּי מִשֶּׁנִּתְפַּרְסֵם וְנִתְגַּלָּה קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּתְמַנָּה נָשִׂיא, הָיָה הוּא הַיּוֹתֵר גָּדוֹל דְּהַכֹּל כְּפוּפִים לוֹ
but Rebbi, once his holiness became famous and revealed in Israel, in that he was appointed Nasi, was the greatest [of all], for “all were subordinate to him.”
כִּי כֵן הַדּוֹרוֹת הוֹלְכִים בְּגִילּוּי יוֹתֵר עַד מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תַּכְלִית הַגִּילּוּי בְּפֹעַל, וְאֵצֶל רַבִּי הָיָה גַּם כֵּן תַּכְלִית הַגִּילּוּי בְּכֹחַ

For thus the generations proceed with ever-greater revelation, until the Mashiach, when there will be “the ultimate revelation in actuality”; and by Rebbi there was, too, “the ultimate revelation in potential.”
הַיְינוּ כִּי יָדוּעַ דְּנֶפֶשׁ הַפַּרְנָס וְרֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר הוּא הַכּוֹלֵל כָּל הַדּוֹר, כִּי לְעוֹלָם כָּל דּוֹר הוּא קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה, וְהָרֹאשׁ הוּא הָעִיקָּר וְכוּלָּם עֲנָפָיו

That is, it is known that “the soul of the leader [parnas] and the head of the generation is the one who includes the entire generation” — for “every generation is [always] a complete stature,” and “the head is the essence, and all [the rest] are its branches.”

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּעֵרָכִין] ״פַּרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר וְהַדּוֹר לְפִי הַפַּרְנָס״, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת1080Erchin 17a: On the verse “this is the generation of those who seek Him, who seek Your face — Yaakov, selah” (Tehillim 24:6), R’ Yehudah Nesi’ah and the Rabbanan disagreed: one said “the generation [is] according to the leader [parnas],” and one said “the leader according to his generation.” The Gemara challenges [that this cannot concern their relative worthiness] — for there was Tzidkiyah, who was worthy though his generation was not, and Yehoyakim, who was not worthy though his generation was; “rather,” it concludes, “we speak with regard to tukfa (severity) and nichusa (mildness).”
And therefore they said [in Erchin 17a], “the leader according to the generation, and the generation according to the leader” — “and both are true.”
אַף עַל גַּב דְּמַקְשֶׁה הָתָם מִצִּדְקִיָּה וִיהוֹיָקִים, הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיַן הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בְּפֹעַל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם ״תּוּקְפָּא וְנִיחוּתָא״ הַיְינוּ כֹּחוֹת הַלֵּב

even though it challenges there from Tzidkiyah and Yehoyakim — [the resolution is that] this [distinction is] “with regard to the revelation in actuality in this world”; and what they said there, “tukfa [severity] and nichusa [mildness],” refers to “the powers of the heart.”
וּבְדוֹר רַבִּי הָיָה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בּוֹ, הַמְּעִידָה גַּם כֵּן עַל קְדֻשַּׁת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל ״קְדוֹשִׁים״ שֶׁהֵם עֲנָפָיו
And in Rebbi’s generation there was “the revelation of holiness in him,” which attests as well to “the holiness of all Israel, [who are called] ‘holy,’” who are “his branches.”

וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה הִיא הַמַּדְרֵגָה אַחֲרוֹנָה בַּמַּדְרֵגוֹת דְּר׳ פִּנְחָס בֶּן יָאִיר [בְּסוֹף סוֹטָה] [כְּפִי גִּירְסָא דִּילָן בַּגְּמָרָא וְהִיא הָעִיקָּר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בָּזֶה בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר]

And “holiness” is “the last rung among the rungs of R’ Pinchas ben Yair1081Sotah 49b (the closing Mishnah of the tractate; also as a baraisa, Avodah Zarah 20b): R’ Pinchas ben Yair’s ladder of ascent — a graded sequence of traits, from care and alacrity up through kedushah (holiness), “and holiness leads to [the higher rungs, culminating in] ruach hakodesh, and ruach hakodesh to the resurrection of the dead, and the resurrection of the dead comes through Eliyahu.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Maharsha trace the progressive self-refinement that opens onto the highest attainments. R’ Tzadok’s use: in his girsa (which he holds to be the primary one) kedushah is “the last of the [human] rungs” — the summit of a person’s own effort, which then brings him to ruach hakodesh, the coming of Eliyahu, and the resurrection; and Rebbi, “the holy one,” embodied this rung.” [at the end of Sotah] [per our version in the Gemara, which is the primary one, as I have written on this elsewhere] —
בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת הָאָדָם הַמְּבִיאָה לִידֵי רוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ וּבִיאַת אֵלִיָּהוּ וּתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים
[attained] “through man’s effort, which brings [him] to ruach hakodesh, and the coming of Eliyahu, and the resurrection of the dead.”
עַל כֵּן הָיָה מֵעֵין מָשִׁיחַ, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בְּפֹעַל בְּכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבַּדּוֹר עַד שֶׁתָּשׁוּב הַנְּבוּאָה וְרוּחַ הַקּוֹדֶשׁ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
Therefore he was “akin to Mashiach” — except that “the revelation was not in actuality in all the souls of Israel of that generation,” until “prophecy and ruach hakodesh return to Israel,”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לֶעָתִיד ״אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת רוּחִי עַל כָּל בָּשָׂר״ וְיִזְכּוּ לִתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים

as it says of the Future, “I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh” (Yoel 3:1)1082Yoel 3:1: of the Future — “וְהָיָה אַחֲרֵי כֵן אֶשְׁפּוֹךְ אֶת רוּחִי עַל כָּל בָּשָׂר, וְנִבְּאוּ בְּנֵיכֶם וּבְנֹתֵיכֶם” — “and it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and daughters shall prophesy.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — in the Messianic era prophecy will be restored, universally, to Israel. R’ Tzadok’s use: Rebbi was “akin to Mashiach,” yet the revelation was not yet “in actuality in all the souls of the generation” — that awaits the Future, when “I will pour out My spirit upon all flesh” and all merit ruach hakodesh and the resurrection of the dead., “and they will merit the resurrection of the dead.”
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא זָכָה לְעַצְמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא מֵת, וְזָכָה לְחַבֵּר הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת חִבּוּר הַכּוֹלֵל כָּל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עַד זְמַנּוֹ
And nonetheless he himself merited “that he did not die,” and merited “to compose the Mishnayos — a compilation encompassing all the Oral Torah — which had not existed until his time.”
וְהַתְחָלַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא מִדָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֶׁהִתְחִיל לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת אוֹר מַלְכוּת, ״פֶּה תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה קָרֵין לָהּ״
And “the beginning of the Oral Torah is from David HaMelech,” in whom “the light of Malchus began to be revealed” — “‘the mouth’ [Malchus] — they call the Oral Torah.”
וְתַכְלִיתוֹ בְּמָשִׁיחַ, שֶׁאָז יִהְיֶה שְׁלֵימוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא הַחָכְמָה הַמִּתְגַּלֵּית עַל יְדֵי חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And its culmination is in the Mashiach, when there will be “the completeness of the Oral Torah,” which is “the wisdom revealed through the Sages of Israel in this world”;
דְּעַד זְמַנּוֹ יִתְגַּלֶּה כָּל מַה שֶּׁמּוּכָן לְתַלְמִיד וָתִיק לְהִתְחַדֵּשׁ וּלְהִתְגַּלּוֹת
for “by his [Mashiach’s] time there will be revealed all that is destined for a ‘worthy disciple’ to innovate and to reveal.”

וּבִימֵי רַבִּי הִתְחִיל שְׁלֵימוּת זֶה בְּחִבּוּר הַמִּשְׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא הַכּוֹלֵל כָּל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וְגַם כָּל מַה שֶּׁתַּלְמִיד וָתִיק עָתִיד לְחַדֵּשׁ נִכְלָל בָּהּ, אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲדַיִין הַכֹּל בְּכֹחַ לֹא בְּפֹעַל

And in Rebbi’s days this completeness began, in the composition of the Mishnah, which “encompasses all the Oral Torah” — and also “all that a worthy disciple is destined to innovate is included in it” — except that “as yet it is all in potential, not in actuality.” — Rebbi was Mashiach “in potential” as Mashiach will be “in actuality”: the head of a generation bears its whole stature, so his revealed holiness testifies to the latent holiness of all Israel, his branches — and his Mishnah already encloses, in seed, every word the Sages will ever draw out.

items.h: The theme: At the very close of the Talmud: “whoever studies halachos every day is assured a share in the World to Come” — for “halachos” means the Mishnah, and through it one merits eternal life. The grasp of Torah comes only by way of the Oral Torah, which is the revelation of the Written Torah to Israel’s hearts; the Written cannot be grasped except through it. Had they not sinned, the Chumash and the Book of Yehoshua would have sufficed.

p: [פח] וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹף נִדָּה] — שֶׁהוּא סִיּוּם הַשַּׁ״ס — ״כָּל הַשּׁוֹנֶה הֲלָכוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם מוּבְטָח לוֹ שֶׁהוּא בֶּן עוֹלָם הַבָּא״

And therefore they said [at the end of Niddah — which is the conclusion of the Talmud], “whoever studies halachos every day is assured that he is a member of the World to Come1083Niddah 73a (the closing words of the entire Talmud): “the school of Eliyahu taught: whoever studies halachos every day is assured that he is destined for the World to Come, as it is stated, ‘his ways [halichos] are eternal’ (Chavakuk 3:6) — read not halichos [ways] but halachos.” Meforshim: Rashi — “halachos” denotes the fixed traditions (the Mishnah and baraisos); one who reviews them daily attains eternal life. R’ Tzadok’s use: “halachos” means the Mishnah (called “halachos”/“hilcheta” throughout Shas) — the Oral Torah, in which the Written Torah is grasped by Israel’s souls — and through it one merits “eternal life”; fittingly the Talmud seals itself with this very promise. Chassidic context - Tiferet Shlomo, Birkat HaTorah 8: The Tiferes Shlomo comments on the exact closing ma'amar of Shas, 'kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom muvtach lo shehu ben Olam Haba,' and reads 'hashoneh' dynamically. A person should 'change' the halachah each day by reaching a deeper and newer apprehension even in the very halachah he studied yesterday. He then joins the derashah 'al tikrei halichos ela halachos' back to its literal wording: through living halachah the student changes the 'halichos olam,' drawing new good flow into the world's conduct. 'Ben Olam Haba' consequently does not refer only to a reward postponed until death; Torah draws something of Olam Haba into the present day, renewing the world through fresh apprehension. This is a strong complement to R' Tzadok's use of the same passage. R' Tzadok stresses Mishnah as the form in which Torah Shebe'al Peh makes the Written Torah graspable to Jewish hearts and thereby opens chayei olam. Tiferes Shlomo adds the experiential mechanism: Oral Torah is not a static archive. The learner revisits fixed halachah and brings latent meaning into new actual apprehension, so that 'halachos' are literally 'halichos' - movement. That sits especially well with the se'if's description of the light hidden after the sin and recovered through toil in Torah Shebe'al Peh. The text is fixed, yet its stored light can be newly disclosed each day. The assurance of Olam Haba therefore belongs precisely to repeated study: what is eternal is not inert repetition but the unending capacity of Torah to yield new life from the same Divine source..”
דַּ״הֲלָכוֹת״ רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר מִשְׁנָה, דְּקָרוּ לֵיהּ ״הֲלָכוֹת״ וְ״הִלְכְתָא״ בְּכָל הַשַּׁ״ס וּמִדְרָשׁוֹת, שֶׁבָּזֶה זוֹכֶה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם

for “halachos” means the Mishnah — which throughout the Talmud and Midrashim is called “halachos” and “hilcheta” — [and] through this “one merits eternal life.”1084R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Lag BaOmer §3): “a son of the World to Come — and death will be for him only as sleep, and he remembers his students and all that passed over him… and about this he asked, "is there in this market a son of the World to Come?"” Exactly the se’if’s closing of the Talmud: the assurance of “a share in the World to Come” is not a distant promise but a present standing, in which death itself is reduced to sleep.
דְּהָאֲחִיזָה בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁבָּהּ הוּא הַגִּילּוּי דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הַמּוּשָּׂג לַלְּבָבוֹת וְנַפְשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
for “the grasp of the Torah is only through the Oral Torah,” in which is “the revelation of the Written Torah, [made] graspable to the hearts and souls of the Children of Israel”;
שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה

“for it is impossible to grasp the Written Torah except through the Oral [Torah].”1085R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Kuntres Shvisas Shabbos §2): “and at any rate we learned from what [is said] there, that "Zachor" of Shabbos is not [expounded] of Kiddush alone, but of the shinun [repeated study] of Torah [that belongs to] the mitzvos of Shabbos in the Written Torah.” Exactly the se’if: “shoneh halachos” is the language of shinun — the daily repetition of the Mishnah — and it is this, not a one-time hearing, that the promise is attached to.
כִּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא הוֹפָעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אוֹרוֹ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּשְׁעַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּנַעֲשׂוּ עַל יְדֵי זֶה ״חֵרוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע״
For the Written Torah is “the shining-forth of Hashem’s light to Israel at the Giving of the Torah,” by which they became “free of the evil inclination”;
וְאָז הָיָה דַּי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְבַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים] דְּאִלְמָלֵא חָטְאוּ לֹא נִיתְּנָה לָהֶם אֶלָּא הַתּוֹרָה וְסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ — עֶרְכָּהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל

and then the Written Torah alone would have sufficed, as they said [in Nedarim 22b] that “had they not sinned, there would have been given to them only the [Five Books of the] Torah and the Book of Yehoshua” — [the latter being] “the apportionment of the Land of Israel.”1086Nedarim 22b: Rav Adda b’Rabbi Chanina taught, “had Israel not sinned, there would have been given to them only the Five Books of the Torah and the Book of Yehoshua alone — for it [Yehoshua] is the apportionment of Eretz Yisrael.” Meforshim: the Ran and the commentators — before the sin, the light of the Written Torah alone would have disclosed everything; only the Torah (the way of life) and the settling of the Land (Yehoshua) would have been required. R’ Tzadok’s use: at Sinai the Written Torah by itself would have sufficed — “the Torah is from the side of time and the soul, given in the wilderness, while the fixing of place is set out in the Book of Yehoshua” — but the sin concealed that light (like the primordial light stored away in the Torah), and its recovery is the whole work of the Oral Torah.
דְּהַתּוֹרָה הוּא מִצַּד הַזְּמַן וְהַנֶּפֶשׁ וְנִיתְּנָה בַּמִּדְבָּר, דִּקְבִיעוּת הַמָּקוֹם הוּא נִתְפָּרֵשׁ בְּסֵפֶר יְהוֹשֻׁעַ, וּבֵיאַרְתִּי זֶה בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר
for “the Torah is from the side of time and the soul,” and “was given in the wilderness” — whereas “the fixing of place is set out in the Book of Yehoshua”; and I have explained this elsewhere.
וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת מוּבָן הַכֹּל מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְבַד, כִּי הָיָה גָּלוּי אוֹר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתּוֹרָה הַמֵּאִיר וּמְגַלֶּה כָּל נֶעֱלָם
In any case, it would have sufficed for them “that all be understood from the Written Torah alone,” for “the light of Hashem was revealed in the Torah, illumining and disclosing every hidden thing.”
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא נֶעֱלַם זֶה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּעֱלַם הָאוֹר דְּשֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית שֶׁנִּגְנַז לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, שֶׁאָמְרוּ שֶׁנִּגְנַז בַּתּוֹרָה

But through the sin this became hidden — just as “the light of the six days of Creation was hidden,” “stored away for the righteous in the Future,” of which they said that “it was hidden away in the Torah.”
וְהַהִתְגַּלּוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שֶׁהוּא תִּיקּוּן הַחֵטְא, כִּי ״הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע״
And “the [re]revelation is through the Oral Torah,” which is “the rectification of the sin” — for “the Torah is the antidote [tavlin] to the evil inclination” —
וְלֹא עַל לְהַבָּא לְבַד, רַק גַּם עַל מַה שֶּׁעָבַר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל בְּתִיקּוּן הָעֲבֵירוֹת ״לְהוֹסִיף בְּלִימּוּד״, וּבָזֶה נִתְבַּטֵּל הַיֵּצֶר

and “not [only] for the future, but also for what is past” — as the Sages said, [that] for “the rectification of transgressions” one should “add in [Torah] study,” and thereby “the [evil] inclination is nullified.”
וּכְפִי הָהַעֲמָקָה בְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה כָּךְ יוּכַל לְהַשִּׂיג מֵעִמְקֵי מַדְרֵיגַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם
And “according to the depth [of one’s] delving in words of Torah, so can he attain, from the depths [of Torah], the rung of teshuvah, to rectify the past”;

כִּי עַל יְדֵי הַיְגִיעָה בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה לְהַשִּׂיג מֵעִמְקֵי הַתּוֹרָה, עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְגַּלֶּה לוֹ כָּל אוֹרוֹת הַתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת מְאִירִים לוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא נִדְחֶה כָּל מִינֵי חֲשֵׁכוֹת
for “through toil in the Oral Torah, to attain the depths of Torah, thereby all the lights of Torah become revealed to him and shine for him, and of themselves all kinds of darkness are repelled.”
וְעַל כֵּן בִּשְׁלֵימוּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִשְׁלַם כָּל תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם, וְנִתְגַּלָּה אוֹר הַבָּהִיר שֶׁבִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּאֲחִידָא בְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וּבְעֵץ הַחַיִּים

And therefore, “in the completeness of the Oral Torah, all the rectification of the past is completed,” and “the radiant light within the Children of Israel — who are ‘grasped in the Torah and in the Tree of Life’ — is revealed.” — the Written Torah is the light Hashem shone at Sinai, hidden again by the sin; the Oral Torah is its recovery, and toil in it rectifies even the past — so that the daily study of “halachos” reopens that stored light and secures the eternal life it carries.

items.h: The theme: The awakening of this revelation began in Rebbi’s days with the composition of the Mishnah — hence “by the merit of the Mishnayos the exiles are gathered in.” Rebbi gathered the outcasts: the scattered sparks of Israel’s souls. So studying Mishnayos, it appears to R’ Tzadok, is itself a rectification for damage to the bris, gathering those outcasts back to holiness — for the Torah and Israel are one.

p: [פט] וְהִתְחִיל הִתְעוֹרְרוּת גִּילּוּי אוֹר זֶה בִּימֵי רַבִּי בְּחִבּוּר הַמִּשְׁנָה

And the awakening of the revelation of this light began in Rebbi’s days, in the composition of the Mishnah;1087R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §64): “a rung that one is able to walk to, and no further; and as it says [Berachos 17a],”the righteous sit" — meaning and do not walk to a rung [beyond]." Exactly the se’if: the Mishnah is the one text in which every Jewish soul has its own fixed portion — each standing where his rung sets him, which is why its merit gathers all of them in together. Chassidic context - Arvei Nachal, Vayeshev 1:5: The Arvei Nachal supplies a strikingly direct explanation for R' Tzadok's claim that the roots of Jewish souls and the Oral Torah belong together. He writes that every Jew has a particular achizah and deveikus of his neshamah in Torah; one soul's portion cannot be supplied by another, even by someone greater. This is why, at times, a lesser talmid chacham can say a Torah insight that a greater sage cannot: 'bekartelisa de'anya tishkach marganisa' - a pearl can be found in the poor man's basket - because that point is his own portion. The nitzotzos a person releases through Torah chiddush are therefore joined specifically to his soul. He connects this idea to the same promise, 'kol hashoneh halachos bechol yom muvtach lo shehu ben Olam Haba.' This makes a particularly organic addition to the present se'if. When R' Tzadok says the Mishnah includes the root of the souls and that later generations unfold Oral Torah according to their own souls, he is not merely saying that everyone studies a common book. The common corpus contains differentiated points waiting for the corresponding souls to draw them into actuality. The Mishnah can consequently be a gathering-place without erasing individuality: precisely because every soul has a non-interchangeable Torah point, the totality of those points forms one Torah Shebe'al Peh. The ingathering effected by Mishnah study is thus both communal and personal - no Jewish spark is superfluous, because no other soul can reveal exactly the same facet of the Divine Torah.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה] דְּבִזְכוּת הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת הַגָּלֻיּוֹת מִתְקַבְּצִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כִּי יִתְנוּ בַגּוֹיִם [עַתָּה אֲקַבְּצֵם]״

and therefore they said [in Vayikra Rabbah] that “by the merit of the Mishnayos the exiles are gathered in,” as it says, “though they recount [yisnu — expounded as shonim, ‘repeat/study’] among the nations, now I will gather them” (Hoshea 8:10).
וְהוּא קִיבֵּץ הַנִּדָּחִים שֶׁל כָּל הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַמְּפוּזָּרוֹת, שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי עֲוֹן קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

And he [Rebbi] “gathered the outcasts” of all the “scattered sparks of the Children of Israel” — [the scattering of] which is through “the iniquity of damaging the bris,” as mentioned above.1088R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §71): “and this is the allusion of the joining of the two stones and their being made whole — meaning, it alludes to the Creator and the created, which is unified; and through this is the building of the House.” Exactly the se’if: the composition of the Mishnah is a building — a joining of what was scattered — and this is why its merit is precisely the gathering of the scattered.
וְעַל כֵּן לִימּוּד הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת נִרְאֶה לִי דְּהוּא תִּיקּוּן לַעֲוֹן קֶרִי וְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, וּמוֹעִיל לְקַבֵּץ הַנִּדָּחִים וּלְהַחֲזִירָם לִקְדֻשָּׁה

And therefore the study of Mishnayos, it appears to me, “is a rectification for the iniquity of keri and wasting seed,” and “avails to gather the outcasts and restore them to holiness.”1089Vayikra Rabbah 7:3: “R’ Huna said: all these exiles are gathered in only by the merit of the Mishnayos [bizchus mishnayos], as it says (Hoshea 8:10), ‘though they recount among the nations, now I will gather them.’”
כִּי כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שָׁרְשָׁם בַּתּוֹרָה, דְּ״אוֹרַיְיתָא וְיִשְׂרָאֵל חַד״

For all the souls of the Children of Israel “are rooted in the Torah,” for “the Torah and Israel are one.”1090R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §196): “there are three loves: the love of the Holy One, and of the Torah, and of Israel — and all of them are one, as is known in the Zohar, for one without the other does not suffice.” Exactly the se’if’s reason: the Mishnah gathers the exiles because “the Torah and Israel are one” — so a renewal in the one is necessarily an ingathering of the other.
בְּסוֹד נֶפֶשׁ דְּדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, דּוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מֹשֶׁה שֶׁקִּיבְּלוּ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, שׁוֹרְשָׁם בְּאוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב כַּיָּדוּעַ
In the secret of the soul of “the generation of the wilderness” — Moshe’s generation, who received the Written Torah — “their root is in the letters of the Written Torah,” as is known.
וּשְׁאָר הַדּוֹרוֹת שֶׁהֵם הָעֲנָפִים הַמִּתְפַּשְּׁטִים מֵאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר, נִרְאֶה לִי דְּשָׁרְשָׁם בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב
And the rest of the generations — which are “the branches spreading forth from that generation” — it appears to me “their root is in the Oral Torah,” which is “the expansion of the Written Torah.”
וְלֵיכָּא מִידִי דְּלָא רְמִיזֵי בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב, אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא שָׁם בְּרֶמֶז וְהֶעְלֵם

And “there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Written Torah1091Taanis 9a: R’ Yochanan, pondering a verse in Mishlei, wondered aloud, “is there anything written in the Writings [Kesuvim] that is not alluded to in the Torah?” — whereupon the young son of Reish Lakish showed him the allusion (in “their heart failed them… what is this that God has done to us,” Bereishis 42:28); the principle emerging is that everything in the later Scriptures is already hinted at in the Chumash. Meforshim: Rashi — R’ Yochanan sought, and was shown, that nothing in Nach lacks a root in the Five Books. R’ Tzadok’s use: he extends this — “there is nothing that is not hinted at in the Written Torah, only that it is there by allusion and concealment”; hence all the souls of the later generations (whose root is the Oral Torah, the expansion of the Written) lay “stored and concealed” within the wilderness generation, who received the Written Torah, “for from them they came forth.”” — only that it is there “by allusion and concealment.”
וְכָךְ הָיוּ נַפְשׁוֹת שְׁאָר כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת גְּנוּזוֹת וּכְלוּלוֹת בְּהֶעְלֵם בְּדוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר, שֶׁהֲרֵי מֵהֶם יָצָאוּ
And so the souls of all the other generations “were stored and included, in concealment, in the generation of the wilderness” — for indeed “from them they came forth.”
וּכְפִי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הַמִּתְחַדֶּשֶׁת בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר, כֵּן הֵם הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר

And “according to the Oral Torah that renews itself in each and every generation, so are the souls of the Children of Israel of that generation.” — Israel and the Torah are one: the wilderness generation is rooted in the letters of the Written Torah, and every later generation in the Oral Torah that expands it — so Rebbi’s Mishnah, gathering the scattered sparks, is itself the ingathering of Israel’s scattered souls.

items.h: The theme: Through the Tree of Knowledge, even the Torah as grasped in this world is from that Tree’s side, and many words of Torah were “handed over to the outer forces” to be extracted from them. Hence the Written Torah contains passages of terror, and the words of Lavan, Esav, Pharaoh, Bilaam and Balak. At Sinai all of it returned to holiness and the whole Torah came forth from its sheath — had they merited then, it would have been the final End.

p: [צ] וְיָדוּעַ דְּעַל יְדֵי עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע, דְּגַם תּוֹרָה שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמּוּשֶּׂגֶת עַתָּה הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּתִּיקּוּנִים], נִמְסְרוּ הַרְבֵּה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה לַחִיצוֹנִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהוֹצִיא מֵהֶם

And it is known that, through the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil — for even the Torah in this world, as grasped now, is “from the side of the Tree of Knowledge,” as they said [in the Tikkunim] — “many words of Torah were handed over to the outer [forces],” which must be “extracted from them.”1092R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §46): “In the Zohar (I 27a) they said that the Oral Torah is from the side of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil — ‘valid and invalid,’ etc.; that is, the Tree of Knowledge is the human intellect, which has variations this way and that; but the Tree of Life is ‘in the midst of the garden,’ at the central point, which does not incline to the extremes — and that is the Written Torah.” (Precisely the se’if’s teaching: the Torah as it is grasped now, in this world, is ‘from the side of the Tree of Knowledge’ — its light dispersed toward the extremes, some of it needing to be ‘extracted’ back from the outer forces.) Chassidic parallel - Sefat Emet, Bo 18:2: The Sefas Emes reads the Egyptian exile itself as a preparation for Torah and explicitly distinguishes a written and an oral dimension within that process. The Divine 'signs' placed in Pharaoh correspond to what is given from Above, while 'lema'an tesaper' points to the human articulation and expansion of Torah Shebe'al Peh. He then states the governing principle: 'kol galus hu lehotzi nitzotzos kedoshos shenis'arvu bahem' - every exile exists to draw out holy sparks that became mixed among the nations. During exile those sparks are concealed and the wicked mistake the borrowed vitality for their own power; at redemption Israel remove the hidden illuminations for whose sake they were sent there, and it becomes clear that 'Ani Hashem' was the truth throughout. This is exceptionally close to R' Tzadok's image of Torah-words being handed to the chitzonim and later reclaimed. The frightening passages and even the words placed in the mouths of Lavan, Pharaoh, Bilaam and Balak become Torah not because their speakers were independent teachers of holiness, but because a Divine spark can be clothed in an alien voice and later gathered into the Torah of Israel. Sefas Emes also clarifies why extraction and redemption are one motion: once the good hidden in the foreign garment has been taken out, the apparent autonomous power of that garment collapses. R' Tzadok extends the same dynamic from the written record of the early exiles to the continuing development of Torah Shebe'al Peh; Sefas Emes gives the Chassidic language of nitzotz and geulah that makes that continuity explicit.

כְּמוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הַרְבֵּה פָּרְשִׁיּוֹת מֵאֵימוֹת וְדִבְרֵי לָבָן וְעֵשָׂו וּפַרְעֹה וְכַיּוֹצֵא וּפָרְשַׁת בִּלְעָם וּבָלָק וְכַדּוֹמֶה, וְהֵם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁנִּמְסְרוּ מֵחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן לַמָּקוֹם שֶׁנִּמְסְרוּ

just as there are in the Written Torah many passages “of terrors” and the words of Lavan, Esav, and Pharaoh and the like, and the portion of Bilaam and Balak and so forth — and these are “words of Torah that were handed over, from the sin of Adam HaRishon, to the place to which they were handed.”1093Avodah Zarah 2b: In the Future the nations will claim before the Holy One that they built marketplaces, made bathhouses, and amassed silver and gold “only so that Israel might engage in the Torah”; and the Holy One will reply, “all that you did, you did for your own needs.”
וּבִשְׁעַת מַתַּן תּוֹרָה חָזְרוּ הַכֹּל לִקְדֻשָּׁה וְיָצְתָה כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ מִנַּרְתֵּקָהּ לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת לְנַפְשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּשְׁלֵימוּתָהּ
And at the Giving of the Torah “all returned to holiness,” and “the entire Torah came forth from its sheath” to be revealed to the souls of Israel “in its completeness”;
עַד שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא זָכוּ אָז הָיָה עֵת קֵץ הַגָּמוּר לִהְיוֹת חֵרוּת מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת וְיֵצֶר הָרָע וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת, אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא

to the point that “had they merited then, it would have been the complete End of Days — to be free of the Angel of Death, the evil inclination, and the subjugation of the kingdoms” — except that “the sin caused [otherwise].”1094R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Nisan §2): “"the word of Hashem" — this is halachah; it is called "dibbur" [speech]. And here it said "in sichah" and not "in dibbur" — for we have said that words of Torah are called dibbur, unlike sichah [conversation].” Exactly the se’if’s distinction: what was handed to the outer forces went out as sichah, and the labor is to draw it back into dibbur.

וְאַף דְּהַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא כְּבָר בִּשְׁלֵימוּתָהּ לִבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַד ״וְלֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ בָּהּ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְהוֹצִיא מֵהַחִיצוֹנִים

And although the Written Torah is already “in its completeness” for Israel alone — “and He did not do so for any [other] nation” (Tehillim 147:20) — nonetheless, “from the side of the expansion of the Oral Torah, there still remains in it what must be extracted from the outer [forces]” —
רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁנִּמְסַר עַל יְדֵי הַחֲטָאִים דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְיִחוּד עֲוֹן דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
meaning, “that was handed over through the sins of the Children of Israel, and especially the iniquity of wasting seed.”
אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה אֵינוֹ אֶצְלָם דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה גְּלוּיִים בְּפֹעַל כְּמוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב שֶׁמִּדִּבְרֵיהֶם וְשִׂיחָתָם מַמָּשׁ נַעֲשֶׂה דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה

Except that “this is not, by them [the nations], words of Torah revealed in actuality,” as in the Written Torah, where “from their very speech and conversation words of Torah are made.”1095R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro §3): “"and your ears shall hear a word from behind you" — which is expounded, that a bas kol is made use of; and in the Yerushalmi they learned [a halachah] from a woman who said [something in passing].” Exactly the se’if: words of Torah are indeed made out of ordinary speech and conversation — the Torah handed over to the “outer” is extracted precisely from there.

כִּי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב הוּא מַחֲשֶׁבֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דְּעַל כֵּן הוּא דְּפוּס שֶׁל מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פ״א] שֶׁהִיא הַדִּפְתְּרָאוֹת וּפִנְקְסָאוֹת שֶׁל צִיּוּר כָּל הָעוֹלָמוֹת הַנּוֹצָרִים וְנִבְרָאִים

For the Written Torah is “the thought of Hashem in the creation of the world” — therefore it is “the mold of the Work of Creation,” as they said [in Bereishis Rabbah, ch. 1] that “she is the ‘ledgers and account-books’ of the design of all the worlds formed and created.”

וְגַם הָאוּמּוֹת מִכְּלַל בְּרִיאָתוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם, וְיֵשׁ גַּם בָּהֶם אוֹתִיּוֹת דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה, שֶׁמִּזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ הַנִּיצוֹץ הַמְּחַיֶּה אוֹתָם, דְּלוּלֵי כֵן לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם שׁוּם מְצִיאוּת כְּלָל

And the nations too are “part of the creation of the world,” and there are “even in them letters of words of Torah, whence flows the spark that enlivens them” — for “were it not so, they would have no existence at all.”
וְעַל כֵּן הֶחֱזִיר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הַתּוֹרָה עַל כָּל אוּמָּה וְלָשׁוֹן לְקַבְּלָהּ, כִּי הָיָה לוֹ גַּם כֵּן צַד שַׁיָּיכוּת מַה אֵלֶיהָ כְּפִי הַדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And therefore the Holy One “took the Torah round to every nation and tongue1096Avodah Zarah 2b (R’ Yochanan): expounding “Hashem came from Sinai, and shone forth from Seir upon them, appeared from Mount Paran” (Devarim 33:2; cf. Chavakuk 3:3), the Gemara asks what God “sought in Seir and in Paran,” and answers — “this teaches that the Holy One took the Torah round to every nation and tongue [Edom in Seir, Yishmael in Paran, and the rest], but they did not accept it, until He came to Israel, and they accepted it.” Meforshim: Rashi — each nation, offered the Torah, refused when a commandment clashed with its ancestral trait (Esav balked at “you shall not murder,” Yishmael at “you shall not steal”). R’ Tzadok’s use: the Holy One offered the Torah to every nation because “it too had some aspect of connection to it” — there are, within the nations, letters of Torah, “the spark that enlivens them”; but their root being in evil they refused, and those Torah-letters “were taken from them and given to Israel,” “the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov” — so that “a gentile who engages in the Torah is liable to death.”” to accept it, for “it too had some aspect of connection to it, according to the semblance of this world.”
אַךְ כְּפִי הָאֱמֶת דְּשָׁרְשָׁם בָּרָע, כָּל מְצִיאוּתָם הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְצָרְכָּם
But in truth, since “their root is in evil,” “their whole existence is for the sake of Israel and their needs”;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהֵם בְּעַצְמָם עֲתִידִים לוֹמַר לֶעָתִיד כְּשֶׁיַּכִּירוּ הָאֱמֶת, דְּהַרְבֵּה כְּרַכִּים וּגְשָׁרִים וּמֶרְחֲצָאוֹת וְכו׳ הַכֹּל בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֵישׁ ע״ז]1097Avodah Zarah 2b: In the Future the Holy One will bring a Torah scroll, place it in His bosom, and say, “let whoever occupied himself with it come and take his reward.” The nations gather in confusion; He asks the kingdom of Rome first, “with what did you occupy yourselves?” They answer, “Master of the world — we established many marketplaces, built many bathhouses, amassed much silver and gold — and we did it all only for Israel, that they might occupy themselves with the Torah.” He replies, “fools of the world — all that you did, you did for your own needs: you set up marketplaces to place harlots in them, bathhouses to indulge yourselves; and the silver and gold are Mine, as it says, ‘Mine is the silver and Mine the gold’ (Chaggai 2:8). Is there any among you who declares this? — and ‘this’ is nothing but the Torah.” They depart crestfallen; the kingdom of Persia enters after them — and so with every kingdom.

as “they themselves are destined to say, in the Future, when they recognize the truth” — that “the many cities and bridges and bathhouses, etc., [were made] entirely for the sake of Israel,” as they said [at the beginning of Avodah Zarah, 2b].
וְהַיְינוּ דְּבֶאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ הָיָה הַכֹּל בִּשְׁבִיל יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק שֶׁהֵם לֹא כִּיוְּנוּ לָזֶה
And that is: “in absolute truth it was all for the sake of Israel — only that they did not intend it so.”
וְעַל כֵּן כָּל הָאוֹתִיּוֹת דְּדִבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁהָיָה בָּהֶם מִצַּד הַשְׁפָּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה, נִיטַּל מֵהֶם וְנִיתַּן לְיִשְׂרָאֵל ״מוֹרָשָׁה קְהִילַּת יַעֲקֹב״

And therefore “all the letters of words of Torah that were in them” — from Hashem’s outpouring [upon them] in Creation — “were taken from them and given to Israel,” “the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov” (Devarim 33:4) —
״וְגוֹי הָעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה״

and [therefore] “a gentile who engages in the Torah is liable to death” (Sanhedrin 59a)1098Sanhedrin 59a: “R’ Yochanan said: A gentile who engages in [the study of] the Torah is liable to death, as it says (Devarim 33:4), ‘Moshe commanded us the Torah, an inheritance [morasha] of the congregation of Yaakov’ — an inheritance for us, and not for them.”. — even the Torah-letters that give the nations their very life are, in truth, Israel’s alone — taken up and restored to “the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov” — so that the nations exist only for Israel’s sake, and a gentile who seizes the Torah as his own trespasses on what was never his.

items.h: The theme: But the Oral Torah is what Israel’s sages draw from their own heart, and this alone is in Israel’s hand. “Whoever says there is Torah among the nations, do not believe” — there is chochmah among them, but no words of Torah are made from it. The Sages foresaw by ruach ha-kodesh the later philosophizers who would call Greek wisdom “the secrets of the Torah,” and warned us not to believe it.

p: [צא] אֲבָל תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הוּא מַה שֶּׁחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹצְאִים מִלִּבָּם, דָּבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּיַד בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

But the Oral Torah is “what the sages of Israel find from their heart” — this thing “is only in the hand of the Children of Israel.”1099R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §26): “In truth they said (Midrash Rabbah, Eichah [2:9]): ‘there is Torah among the nations of the world — do not believe,’ for it is ‘the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov’ alone. And in the manner they said (Tanchuma, Ki Sisa 34), that ‘in the Future the nations will say, we are Israel,’ etc. — [the Torah is] ‘My mystery.’ And this is [the meaning of] the resting of the Shechinah: that they will not attain the wisdom of the Oral Torah.” (Exactly the se’if’s distinction: the Oral Torah is ‘the inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov’ alone — ‘whoever says there is Torah among the nations, do not believe’ — for it is drawn from Israel’s own heart and is in Israel’s hand alone.) Chabad context - Likkutei Torah, Pinchas 4:11: Likkutei Torah gives a precise reason that Torah Shebe'al Peh cannot be reduced to human wisdom. 'Malchus peh Torah Shebe'al Peh karinan lah': the mouth/Malchus is called Oral Torah, and although Malchus 'leis lah migarmah klum,' it is the revelation of the innermost Divine will. Torah and mitzvos, the Alter Rebbe explains, are the pnimiyus ratzono, and that inner will descends all the way into the most physical details of the six orders of Mishnah in order to lift the lower world into its Source. Thus the human mouth and the concrete halachic case are not alternatives to revelation; they are the vessels through which the inner will becomes articulated below. This complements R' Tzadok's distinction between chochmah among the nations and Torah found in the heart of Israel. A philosopher can reach a true intellectual proposition and it remains chochmah. Torah Shebe'al Peh is a different category because its claim is not simply that the conclusion is clever or correct, but that the inward Divine ratzon is being disclosed through the covenantal mouth of Knesses Yisrael. This is also why its apparently mundane discussions do not make it less 'mistorin': the very descent into physical particulars is the form in which pnimiyus ratzon reaches the earthly realm.
