Meforshim: the Radak — some hold this is David HaMelech himself, revived to reign; others, a scion of his house called by his name; and the Gemara (Sanhedrin 98b, cited earlier in this volume) likewise weighs whether the Mashiach is “of the living” or “of the dead, like David.” R’ Tzadok’s use: on the deeper plane Mashiach is David, one soul — David being “the beginning of the effort, from the side of the ‘end of the deed,’” and Mashiach “the culmination of the perfection of the stature, as it is in ‘thought first’”; so Adam, had he not sinned, would himself have been David, and could then have risen to the rung of Mashiach — the two souls hinted in his name (Adam-David-Mashiach). — except that David was the beginning of the effort, from the side of the “end of the deed,” and Mashiach is the culmination of the perfection of the stature, as it is in “thought first.”1149R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §6): “and in the word”Bereishis" is alluded “he shall fear the Shabbos,” as it says in Tikunei Zohar; **and this is because Israel are called, through the guarding of Shabbos, “those who fear My Name,” and they accept the yoke of His kingship." Exactly the se’if: the “thought first” that Mashiach completes is already hidden in the world’s first word — so the end is not an addition to the beginning but its disclosure.
וְהַהַגָּעָה לְשֹׁרֶשׁ הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה תְּחִלָּה עַצְמוֹ זֶהוּ עוֹלָם הַבָּא
And the reaching of the root of “thought first” itself — that is Olam Haba;
וִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ הֵם קוֹדֶם עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהוּא סוֹף הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ יַגִּיעוּ לְעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְתַכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת הָאֶפְשָׁרִי לָאָדָם לְהַגִּיעַ אֵלָיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

and the days of Mashiach are before Olam Haba — [they are] the end of this world, from which they reach Olam Haba, and the ultimate perfection possible for a person to reach in this world.1150R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shelach §13): “and this verse was written in the Torah after the sin of the spies, and He said to him”and now" — and “and now” is nothing but teshuvah — for certainly they would do teshuvah." Exactly the se’if: the completion is not deferred to another order of time — “and now” is itself the language of teshuvah, and the days of Mashiach are reached from within the present effort.
וְ״הָאֱלֹקִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר״, וְאִלְמָלֵא חָטָא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן הָיָה הוּא דָּוִד בְּעַצְמוֹ סוֹף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה דִּבְרִיאָה

And “God made man upright” — and had Adam HaRishon not sinned, he himself would have been David, the “end of the deed” of Creation;1151R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §51): “It is known that Adam is the acronym of Adam–David–Mashiach, for all is one — since the world is like a sphere (as it says in the Yerushalmi, Avodah Zarah), and in a sphere the beginning and the end are one point; so too Adam and Mashiach, that is, David — all is one.” The “end of the deed” (David) and the “thought that was first” meet: Adam, David, and Mashiach are one root-soul, the beginning embedded in the end.Early Chassidic parallel - Me'or Einayim, Pinchas 13: The Me'or Einayim gives an exceptionally close Chassidic account of the Adam-David-Mashiach structure used here. Citing the teaching of the Baal Shem Tov, he writes that every Jew must 'repair and prepare the portion of the stature of Mashiach that belongs to his soul.' Adam is read as the roshei teivos Adam-David-Mashiach. Adam HaRishon's original stature extended from one end of the world to the other because all the souls of Israel were included within him; after the sin that stature was diminished. Mashiach will once again be 'komah sheleimah mikol nishmos Yisrael,' a complete stature composed of the entirety of Jewish souls, corresponding to Adam before the sin. Consequently, the building of Mashiach is not external to the avodah of ordinary souls: each person must prepare his own chelek until the entire stature is repaired and a permanent universal yichud becomes possible. This sheds unusually direct light on R' Tzadok's statement that Mashiach is David himself at the level of root, while David is the beginning of the effort from 'sof ma'aseh' and Mashiach is its completed form as it stands in 'machshavah techilah.' The continuity is not merely genealogical. Adam, David and Mashiach are names for successive states of one collective human-Jewish komah: primordial inclusion, historical repair through teshuvah, and final reintegration. Me'or Einayim also prevents the doctrine from becoming passive: because every soul constitutes a limb of that future stature, each individual's present avodah literally belongs to the construction of the completed Mashiach.
וּבְהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ לְהַגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית שְׁלֵימוּתוֹ הָאֶפְשָׁרִי לוֹ הָיָה יָכוֹל לוֹ לְהַגִּיעַ גַּם כֵּן אַחַר כָּךְ לְמַדְרֵיגַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ
and by his striving to reach the perfection possible for him, he could also, afterward, have reached the rung of Mashiach —
וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּהוּא כּוֹלֵל שְׁתֵּי נְפָשׁוֹת אֵלּוּ הָרְמוּזִים בְּרָאשֵׁי תֵּיבוֹת שְׁמוֹ
as is known, that he [Adam] includes these two souls, hinted in the initials of his name

(אדם — אדם, דוד, משיח).1152אדם (Adam) — an acronym: the classic teaching that the name אדם is an acronym of אדם — דוד — משיח (Adam, David, Mashiach): the same root-soul passes through Adam, is repaired in David, and is completed in Mashiach — the three “stations” of the single stature R’ Tzadok has been describing.

items.h: The theme: The sin caused what it caused — twenty generations until Avraham, who began to build Knesses Yisrael as a nation distinct from all peoples, in whom Heaven’s glory would be revealed below. The other nations are the dross drawn from the evil side of Adam’s sin. His seed, and Moshe and Aharon after them, completed the building, and through them all were rectified.

p: [ו] אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא וְיָצָא מַה שֶּׁיָּצָא עֶשְׂרִים דּוֹר עַד אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה, שֶׁהִתְחִיל לְתַקֵּן וְלִבְנוֹת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל אוּמָּה מְיוּחֶדֶת מִכָּל הָעַמִּים

But the sin caused [otherwise], and there emerged what emerged — twenty generations until Avraham Avinu1153Pirkei Avos 5:2: “עֲשָׂרָה דוֹרוֹת מֵאָדָם וְעַד נֹחַ… עֲשָׂרָה דוֹרוֹת מִנֹּחַ וְעַד אַבְרָהָם… עַד שֶׁבָּא אַבְרָהָם וְקִבֵּל עָלָיו שְׂכַר כֻּלָּם” — “ten generations from Adam to Noach… ten generations from Noach to Avraham… until Avraham came and received the reward of them all.” Meforshim: the Bartenura — the Mishnah counts these twenty generations of provocation to make known God’s great patience, until Avraham arose and began the world’s rectification, “receiving the reward of them all.” R’ Tzadok’s use: “the sin caused what it caused — twenty generations until Avraham Avinu, who began to rectify and to build Knesses Yisrael, a nation distinguished from all the peoples”; the other nations remain “the dross drawn from the evil side of Adam’s sin,” while Avraham inaugurates the holy line destined to become the stature of Malchus., who began to rectify and to build Knesses Yisrael, a nation distinguished from all the peoples,
שֶׁבָּהֶם בְּיִחוּד יִהְיֶה הִתְגַּלּוּת כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים, וּשְׁאָר אוּמּוֹת הֵם הַפְּסֹלֶת הַנִּמְשָׁכִים מִצַּד הָרַע דְּחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן

in whom especially the glory of Heaven would be revealed below; and the other nations are the “dross” drawn from the evil side of the sin of Adam HaRishon.1154R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §56): “and Yitzchak, from the side of his material too, is blessed — unlike Eliezer, who from the side of his material is cursed… for the materials are not alike.” Exactly the se’if: Avraham began a nation distinct from all peoples at the level of material and not merely of conduct — which is why the other nations remain the “dross” of Adam’s sin.
וְאַחֲרָיו זַרְעוֹ יִצְחָק וְיַעֲקֹב וְיוֹסֵף עִם שְׁאָר שִׁבְטֵי יָ-הּ, וּמֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן הִשְׁלִימוּ קוֹמַת הַשֵּׁשׁ קְצָווֹת, עַד שֶׁיָּצָא לְפֹעַל אוּמָּה שְׁלֵימָה

And after him his seed — Yitzchak, Yaakov, and Yosef with the rest of the tribes of God; and Moshe and Aharon completed the stature of the six extremities, until a complete nation emerged into actuality —
כְּנֵסִיָּה שֶׁהוּא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, מוּכָנִים לְקַבֵּל תּוֹרָה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהִיא מִדָּה אַחֲרוֹנָה

an assembly that is “for the sake of Heaven” (cf. Avos 4:11)1155Pirkei Avos 4:11 (R’ Yochanan HaSandlar): “כָּל כְּנֵסִיָּה שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם; וְשֶׁאֵינָהּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, אֵין סוֹפָהּ לְהִתְקַיֵּם” — “every assembly [kenisiyah] that is for the sake of Heaven will in the end endure; and one that is not for the sake of Heaven will not, in the end, endure.” Meforshim: the Bartenura — the enduring assembly is one bound together by truth alone; and the classic example of the assembly “not for the sake of Heaven” that did not endure is the assembly of Korach. R’ Tzadok’s use: Israel, forged by the Avos, Moshe, and Aharon into “a complete nation,” is precisely “an assembly for the sake of Heaven,” prepared to receive the Torah — the “last middah”; Korach’s counter-assembly was the “not for the sake of Heaven” that could not stand., prepared to receive the Torah from Hashem, which is the last middah.
וּכְשֶׁטָּעֲנוּ עֲדַת קֹרַח ״כָּל הָעֵדָה כּוּלָּם קְדוֹשִׁים וּבְתוֹכָם ה׳״, וְלֹא הָיָה דְּבַר שֶׁקֶר חָלִילָה, דְּלֹא הָיָה נִכְתָּב בַּתּוֹרָה

And when Korach’s assembly claimed, “the whole congregation are all holy, and Hashem is among them” (Bamidbar 16:3)1156Bamidbar 16:3 (Korach’s claim): “וַיִּקָּהֲלוּ עַל מֹשֶׁה וְעַל אַהֲרֹן… רַב לָכֶם, כִּי כָל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים וּבְתוֹכָם ה’, וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ עַל קְהַל ה’” — “they assembled against Moshe and against Aharon, and said to them: You take too much upon yourselves! For the whole congregation are all holy, and Hashem is among them; why then do you exalt yourselves over the assembly of Hashem?” Meforshim: Rashi — the premise was sound (all Israel “heard the words at Sinai from the mouth of the Almighty”), but Korach’s inference — that therefore no leader was needed — was his rebellion and his ruin. R’ Tzadok’s use: the claim “was no word of falsehood, God forbid, for otherwise it would not have been written in the Torah” — “the Shechinah rested then within all the souls of Israel of that generation”; had they merited, this would have been the ultimate perfection, the whole nation as the stature of Malchus of holiness, “like David.” — this was no word of falsehood, God forbid, [for] otherwise it would not have been written in the Torah;
דְּכֵן הָאֱמֶת, שֶׁהָיָה הַשְׁרָאַת הַשְּׁכִינָה אָז בְּתוֹךְ כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר

for so was the truth: the Shechinah rested then within all the souls of the Children of Israel of that generation.1157R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §18): “As Korach’s assembly claimed, that ‘the whole congregation are all holy’ and worthy of the high priesthood — and Moshe Rabbeinu showed them that it is not so in actuality in this world, [where] the revelation of their holiness [is not yet manifest]; and only ‘the one whom Hashem chooses’ is holy in actuality among the souls. So too with the days [of the year]; and the World to Come is called (end of Tamid) ‘a day that is wholly Shabbos,’ for [then] there is no division of times, since all is holy.” Korach’s claim was true at the root — the Shechinah did rest in all — but its full manifestation awaits the Future, when the whole nation stands “like David.”Direct Izhbitz source - Mei HaShiloach I, Korach 3: R. Mordechai Yosef addresses Korach's exact claim and makes the temporal distinction that R' Tzadok develops here. Korach argued that there should be no superiority of one Jew over another because 'betocham Hashem' - Hashem dwells within all of them equally. Mei HaShiloach says that this describes the Future, when Hashem will make a machol, a circle, for the tzaddikim: in a circle there is no point intrinsically closer to the center than another. Korach's error was to insist 'she'atah gam kein hu kach' - that the future equality was already the operative order of the present. The Izhbitzer then turns Korach's own history against him: when the crown and distinction of Levi were given to him, he did not protest that Israel admits no hierarchy. This is an extraordinarily precise complement to R' Tzadok's reading. 'Kulam kedoshim' is not dismissed as false; it is a truth of shoresh and destiny. Yet the world of avodah before final birur still contains differentiated offices, chosen vessels and unequal degrees of revealed kedushah. To collapse the future root into the present state is itself a distortion of that root. R' Tzadok can therefore say both that the claim was true enough to be written in Torah and that Moshe's distinction remained necessary. The completed seventh rung of teshuvah is what finally allows the circular truth to become manifest without destroying the ordered avodah through which that completion is reached.
וְאִלְמָלֵא זָכוּ הָיָה אָז תַּכְלִית הַשְּׁלֵימוּת, שֶׁהָיוּ הֵם כּוּלָּם קוֹמַת מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה
And had they merited, it would then have been the ultimate perfection — that they all be the stature of the middah of Malchus of holiness —
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לֶעָתִיד ״וְהָיָה הַנִּכְשָׁל בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא כְּדָוִד״, כִּי דָּוִד הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת כַּנּוֹדָע

in the manner of what is said of the Future, “and the stumbler on that day shall be like David” (Zechariah 12:8),1158Zechariah 12:8: “On that day Hashem will shield the inhabitants of Jerusalem, and the stumbler [nichshal] among them on that day shall be like David” — a Future promise that even the fallen attain David’s rung, which R’ Tzadok reads as the universal ascent of Knesses Yisrael to the holiness of Malchus. for David is the root of the holiness of Knesses Yisrael, the middah of Malchus, as is known.
וְאָז שֶׁיִּשְׁלְמוּ כָּל נְפָשׁוֹת דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל יִהְיוּ כּוּלָּם בַּשְּׁלֵימוּת הַהוּא, אֶלָּא שֶׁבֵּית דָּוִד יִהְיוּ אָז בְּמַעֲלָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה
And then, when all the souls of Knesses Yisrael are perfected, they will all be in that [same] perfection — except that the House of David will then be at a still greater elevation,
דִּכְבָר זָכָה דָּוִד בְּכֶתֶר הַמַּלְכוּת וּנְטָלוֹ לִהְיוֹת הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהַלֵּב דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְעַל יָדוֹ הוּא שֶׁנִּבְנוּ וְנִתְקְנוּ כּוּלָּם

for David already merited the crown of kingship and took it, to be himself the root of Knesses Yisrael and the “heart” of the Children of Israel — and through him it is that they were all built and rectified.1159R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shemos §10): “as they said [Gittin 57a],”come and see what is between the sinners of Israel and the prophets of the nations of the world" — it comes to teach us that even such a sinner of Israel is superior to Bilaam, who was a prophet of the nations of the world." Exactly the se’if: the other nations are the “dross” of Adam’s sin, so that the lowest of Israel stands above the highest of theirs — the difference is of root, not of attainment.

אֲבָל אִלְמָלֵא אֲבוֹתֵינוּ שֶׁחָטְאוּ הָיָה אָז בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן בִּשְׁלֵימוּת, חֵירוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע, וְהַדּוֹר הַמִּדְבָּר לֹא הָיוּ צְרִיכִים לְמֶלֶךְ כְּלָל, רַק ״מַאן מַלְכֵי — רַבָּנָן״

But had our fathers not sinned, there would then, at the Giving of the Torah, have been the complete finish of the rectification — freedom from the evil inclination — and the wilderness generation would have needed no king at all, only “who are kings? — the Rabbis” (Gittin 62a).1160Gittin 62a: When Geneiva passed Rav Huna and Rav Chisda, he greeted them, “Peace upon you, kings!” They asked, “From where [do you know] that the Rabbis are called kings?” He answered, “As it is written, ‘By me kings reign’ (Mishlei 8:15)” — i.e., through the Torah. Hence “who are kings? — the Rabbis”: the wilderness generation would have needed no king but the Torah-authority of its Sages.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הוּא הָיָה (אָז) מֶלֶךְ הַמָּשִׁיחַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בַּזוֹהַר] דְּהוּא יִהְיֶה מָשִׁיחַ
And Moshe Rabbeinu — he would (then) have been the King Mashiach, and as it is stated [in the Zohar] that he “will be Mashiach”;
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כָּלוּל נַפְשׁוֹ מִשְּׁנֵיהֶם, שֶׁכֵּן ״דָּוִד מֹשֶׁה״ בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא ״מָשִׁיחַ״ עִם הַכּוֹלֵל

that is, that his soul would be composed of both — for “David Moshe” equals, in gematria, “Mashiach,” with the kollel.1161The gematria: דוד (David) = 14, משה (Moshe) = 345, together 359; משיח (Mashiach) = 358, and with the kollel (adding one for the whole) = 359. Hence “David Moshe” equals “Mashiach” — expressing that Mashiach’s soul unites the powers of both.
אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא וְהוּצְרְכוּ לַהֲקָמַת עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה עַל יְדֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה לְתַקֵּן הַחֲטָאִים הַקּוֹדְמִים
Except that the sin caused [otherwise], and they required the “raising up of the yoke of teshuvah” through David HaMelech, to rectify the earlier sins.
וְהַכֹּל לְטוֹבָה, לְהַגִּיעַ עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְמַדְרֵגָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה, מְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין

And all is for the good — to reach thereby a greater rung, “the place where masters of teshuvah stand” [where the wholly righteous cannot stand].1162Berachos 34b: “In the place where masters of teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand.” The very fall and return reach a depth the never-fallen tzaddik never touches — so that the sin, once rectified, becomes the ladder to a higher rung, which is R’ Tzadok’s “all is for the good.”

items.h: The theme: In everything there are seven rungs — three “fathers,” three “offspring” like them, and a seventh that brings the six extremities into actuality and perfects them all. This is the seventh elevation of teshuvah, which we still await: the individual of David’s seed who will repent, and thereby forgive the whole world entire, the living and the dead.

p: [ז] וּבְכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ שֶׁבַע מַדְרֵגוֹת: שְׁלוֹשָׁה אָבוֹת, וְשָׁלוֹשׁ תּוֹלָדוֹת כַּיּוֹצֵא בָּהֶן, וְהַשְּׁבִיעִית הַמּוֹצִיאָה שֵׁשׁ קְצָווֹת אֵלּוּ לְפֹעַל וְלִהְיוֹת שְׁלֵימוּת כָּל הַמַּדְרֵגוֹת

And in everything there are seven rungs: three “fathers,” and three “offspring” like them, and the seventh, which brings these six extremities into actuality and [effects] the perfection of all the rungs.1163R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §14): “and Eliyahu is the last Kohen, who will teach all the secrets of the Oral Torah to Israel before the coming of the World to Come; and afterward there will be the two Mashiachs — Mashiach ben Yosef [and Mashiach ben David].” Exactly the se’if’s seventh elevation: the final rung is not a solitary act but an ordered sequence — a last teacher, then the two anointed ones who bring the six extremities into actuality.
וְזֶהוּ הַמַּעֲלָה הַשְּׁבִיעִית שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁאָנוּ מְחַכִּים לָהּ בִּמְהֵרָה בְּיָמֵינוּ

And this is the seventh elevation of teshuvah, for which we wait, speedily in our days:1164Cf. R’ Tzadok’s own framing in Takanas HaShavin, Siman 1, where the seven statements in praise of teshuvah (Yoma 86a) are aligned with the seven lower sefiros (Chesed through Malchus) — the seventh, Malchus (David), being the rung that brings the six “extremities” into actuality, as here.
שֶׁיָּבוֹא הַיָּחִיד מִזֶּרַע דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֶׁשָּׁב בְּתַכְלִית הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל מַדְרֵיגוֹתֶיהָ
that the individual from the seed of David HaMelech will come, who repents in the ultimate expansion of the power of teshuvah in all its rungs —
עַד שֶׁיִּמָּשְׁכוּ מִמֶּנּוּ, בִּהְיוֹתוֹ הַלֵּב דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים לְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר וּבְכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת כּוּלָּם
until there are drawn from him — he being the “heart” of all Israel — the wellsprings of life to all the hearts of the Children of Israel, in that generation and in all the generations,
עַד שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה יִמְחֲלוּ לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, הַחַיִּים וְהַמֵּתִים

until, through this, they forgive the whole world entire — the living and the dead.1165R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §23): “and so in the Future the two Mashiachs will come — Mashiach ben Yosef, who will clarify all Israel” Exactly the se’if: the seventh rung that “forgives the whole world entire” is a work of clarification performed upon all Israel together, not a pardon granted to each separately.Izhbitz-Radzin culmination - Tiferet Yosef, Hoshana Rabba 4: Tiferet Yosef describes David's distinctive middah in language that almost states the conclusion of this siman. David refuses to take personal spiritual force even from his own mesirus nefesh; he returns the power of avodah itself to Hashem and recognizes that 'all his strength and all the strength of his service is entirely from Hashem.' From that radical bittul, R. Yosef explains, a new capacity emerges: one who does not appropriate even his own righteousness can 'give a place to the whole creation' and can find a defense even for those whose deeds appeared until now to be without light. If another did not serve as he should have, the fully surrendered Davidic consciousness can see the question of the power and illumination that Heaven gave him, without thereby calling darkness light. He connects this to the aravah, which has neither taste nor fragrance yet is destined to give fragrance, and finally to Mashiach's title 'bar nafli': why call him the son of falling rather than the son of rising? Because 'through his falling, by nullifying himself to Hashem, he raises the whole creation.' This is an exceptionally close Izhbitz-Radzin parallel to R' Tzadok's seventh greatness of teshuvah. The single Davidic soul does not save the world by becoming the most self-assertive spiritual individual; precisely through complete bittul it becomes capacious enough to carry the whole komah. The forgiveness of all is therefore the expansion of teshuvah to its Malchus-form: no private possession remains, even of one's own avodah, and the returning individual becomes a vessel through which the entire creation can be stood again before Hashem.
וּבָזֶה יִהְיֶה נִבְלַע הַמָּוֶת לְגַמְרֵי וְיִכְלֶה הַיֵּצֶר מִן הָעוֹלָם

And with this, death will be wholly swallowed up, and the [evil] inclination will cease from the world1166Sukkah 52a (“God will slaughter the evil inclination”): “R’ Yehuda expounded: In the Future, the Holy One will bring the evil inclination and slaughter it in the presence of the righteous and in the presence of the wicked. To the righteous it appears as a high mountain, and to the wicked as a strand of hair; these weep and those weep — the righteous weep and say, ‘How were we able to overcome so high a mountain?’, and the wicked weep and say, ‘How were we unable to overcome this strand of hair?’” Meforshim: Rashi — with the yetzer’s slaughter, evil is abolished from the world; its true measure is unmasked at last — a mountain to those who conquered it, a mere thread to those it enslaved. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is the seventh and final elevation of teshuvah — when the individual of David’s seed repents in the fullest expansion of teshuvah’s power, “death will be wholly swallowed up” (Yeshayah 25:8) and “the evil inclination will cease from the world,” and it is the day of which is said, “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none” (Yirmeyah 50:20).;1167R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Lag BaOmer §8): “the conclusion of Shas, with the teaching of Tanna d’Bei Eliyahu, "whoever studies… is assured that he is a son of the World to Come"; and we have said that the meaning of "assured that he is a son of the World to Come," and not "designated for the World to Come," is that he merits to taste in his lifetime a foretaste of the World to Come — that in his very lifetime he is a son of the World to Come.” Exactly the se’if’s seventh elevation: the final rung is not only awaited but tasted here, which is why it can be borne by an individual of David’s seed within this world.Chassidic synthesis - Tiferet Shlomo, Shabbat HaGadol 4: The Tiferet Shlomo identifies Mashiach with the completion of the very stature that R' Tzadok has traced from Adam through David. He notes the familiar remez Adam-David-Mashiach and calls Mashiach 'gemar hatikkun bechol komas Adam HaRishon' - the completion of the rectification of the entire stature of Adam HaRishon. The significance of this formulation is that the final redemption is not simply the arrival of an extraordinary righteous person alongside an otherwise unchanged humanity. The stature itself is what reaches tikkun. That language helps gather the preceding se'ifim of this siman into one point: all souls were included in Adam; David becomes the heart of teshuvah within the fractured historical body; Mashiach is the completed Adamic stature in which the dispersed limbs have reached their intended relation and the original life can flow without the obstruction of sin and death. It also explains why the seventh greatness of teshuvah necessarily has a universal horizon. If Mashiach were only a private tzaddik, his perfection would remain one local excellence among many. If he is the 'gemar hatikkun' of Adam's whole komah, then his Davidic teshuvah belongs by definition to the structure in which the lives of all Israel are included. R' Tzadok's conclusion - the disappearance of the yetzer and death and the inability to find Israel's sin - is therefore not an additional miracle after teshuvah; it is what the complete repair of the collective Adam means when the final limb of the historical stature has returned to its root.
וְהוּא הַיּוֹם אֲשֶׁר ״יְבוּקַּשׁ אֶת עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ וְאֶת חַטֹּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה״ וְגוֹמֵר

and it is the day of which [it is said,] “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none, and the sins of Yehudah, and they shall not be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant” (Yirmeyah 50:20). — Thus the seven rungs of Siman 6 culminate here in the seventh: a teshuvah so complete that, welling up from the one who is the nation’s heart, it heals the entire shared “stature” at once, and with it undoes death itself.

sections.en: Great is teshuvah, for it tears up an evil decree

items.h: גדולה תשובה שמקרעת גזר דין.

The theme: There is yet an eighth greatness of teshuvah, not listed in Yoma but taught in Rosh Hashanah: teshuvah “tears up a person’s sealed verdict.” R’ Tzadok reads the wordings closely — “and he shall be healed” implies a healing of the past, that he is already healed, and of itself. This is a different matter from “I will heal their backsliding.”

p: [א] וְעוֹד יֵשׁ מַעֲלָה שְׁמִינִית בְּמַה שֶּׁגְּדוֹלָה תְּשׁוּבָה, וְלֹא נִזְכַּר בְּיוֹמָא, רַק [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז:] אִיתָא ״גְּדוֹלָה תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמְּקָרַעַת גְּזַר דִּינוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם״, וְדָיֵּיק מִ״לְּבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב וְרָפָא [לוֹ]״

And there is yet an eighth elevation in “how great is teshuvah,” which is not mentioned in [tractate] Yoma; rather, [in Rosh Hashanah 17b] it is taught, “great is teshuvah, for it tears up a person’s verdict” — and [R’ Yochanan] derived it from “and his heart shall understand, and he shall repent, and it shall be healed for him” (Yeshayah 6:10).1168R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II §1): “the Holy One said to him: I have no sleep before Me… and you said there is sleep before Me — by your life, from within "sleep" I rouse Myself over that man and destroy him, as it says,”and Hashem awoke as one asleep."" Exactly the se’if: what looks like a sealed and settled state is not settled at all — the very image of “sleep” is the one Scripture uses for a verdict that can still be roused and undone.1169Rosh Hashanah 17b: “R’ Yochanan said: Great is teshuvah, for it tears up a person’s [sealed] verdict, as it says (Yeshayah 6:10), ‘and his heart shall understand, and he shall repent, and it shall be healed for him.’ Rav Pappa said to Abbaye: perhaps [this is only] before the verdict [is sealed]? He answered: ‘and it shall be healed for him’ is written — what is a thing that requires healing? — say, that is a [sealed] verdict.”Shelah — direct kabbalistic background (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Rosh HaShanah, Torah Ohr §19): The Shelah identifies precisely the level that R' Tzadok places behind the phrase 'levavo yavin vashav.' The kelipos, he writes, obtain their hold around the sevenfold 'building' of the middos, but at Binah — the root from which that building issues — 'there is no touch of the outsider'; it is the secret of Olam Haba. 'Binah is called teshuvah, for there the emanation of the building returns.' When a person confesses, abandons the sin, repairs the damage and 'returns with all his heart,' he awakens that root of the building, 'and everything is purified, and the accuser departs, because there he has no hold.' This is an unusually exact background to the eighth rung described here. R' Tzadok's point is not merely that repentance persuades Heaven to cancel an externally imposed punishment. The heart's Binah reaches the root from which the lower structure and its dinim emerged; at that root the prosecuting hold is absent. Thus 've-rafa' can be described as a healing that has already taken place at the level of the heart itself, even before the full sevenfold actualization of teshuvah has been completed. The Shelah also helps explain why Rosh Hashanah is the natural setting for this teaching: the shofar awakens the lower person toward that root of Binah, while Yom Kippur completes and brings into actuality what was awakened in potential. R' Tzadok's grammatical distinction between 'erpa' and 've-rafa' therefore reflects two levels of one process — Divine completion from above, and a prior return of the damaged structure to the root in which its healing is already latent.1170Cf. Rosh Hashanah 16b: “Four things tear up a person’s [evil] decree: charity, crying out, change of name, and change of deed” — change of deed (shinuy maaseh) being teshuvah. This is the halachic root of the “tearing of the verdict” that R’ Tzadok analyzes throughout this siman (individual vs. community, before vs. after the sealing).
וּבְיוֹמָא, אֵם מֵבִיא רְפוּאָה מַיְיתֵי מִ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם״ וְלֹא מֵהַאי
whereas in Yoma, when [it says] teshuvah “brings healing,” it brings [its proof] from “I will heal their backsliding” (Hoshea 14:5), and not from this [verse].
וְאִי מִשּׁוּם דְּהַהוּא רְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְגִילָּה יז:] גַּם ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם״ אֵימָא כֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי [לְעֵיל סִימָן א] בֶּאֱמֶת כֵּן

And if [one would say] it is because that healing is [merely] one of pardon — [then] one could say the same of “I will heal their backsliding,” as they said [in Megillah 17b]1171Megillah 17b: In deriving the order of the Shemoneh Esrei — “Why did they see fit to say teshuvah after binah? — because it is written, ‘and his heart shall understand and return, and it shall be healed [ve-rafa lo]’ (Yeshayah 6:10)” — the Gemara concludes that this “healing” is “not the healing of illnesses, but the healing of pardon [refuah di-selicha].” This is the distinction R’ Tzadok draws on: “ve-rafa” denotes a healing that is [only] pardon.; and as I wrote [above, Siman 1], indeed it is so.
רַק דְּ״אֶרְפָּא״ מַשְׁמַע לְהַבָּא, וְכִדְדָיֵּיק גְּמָרָא שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ לְפֵירוּשׁ א׳ דְּרַשִׁ״י

Only that “I will heal [erpa]” implies [something] for the future, as the Gemara itself derives there afterward, according to the first explanation of Rashi;1172Yoma 86a / Rashi: On “I will heal their backsliding, I will love them freely” (Hoshea 14:5) — Rashi’s first explanation is that “I will heal” refers to a future healing, “like one blemished who was cured, upon whom part of his [former] name still rests.” R’ Tzadok leans on the grammar: erpa (“I will heal”) is a future act of God, whereas ve-rafa (“and he shall be healed”) is a completed, self-effected healing of the past.
אֲבָל ״וְרָפָא״ הַיְינוּ לְשֶׁעָבַר, שֶׁכְּבָר נִרְפָּא

but “and he shall be healed [ve-rafa]” refers to the past — that he is already healed.1173R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §113): “but when he was assured that he would return, and he thought so at once — therefore he ran in order to return immediately.” Exactly the se’if’s “ve-rafa”: the healing spoken of is of what is already past — the assurance is given first, and the running follows from it rather than earning it.
וְעוֹד, ״אֶרְפָּא״ מַשְׁמַע מִפְּעוּלַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אֲבָל ״וְרָפָא״ מַשְׁמַע מֵעַצְמוֹ
And further: “I will heal” implies [healing] from the action of Hashem, whereas “and he shall be healed” implies [healing] of itself.
וְזֶה דָּבָר מוּפְלָא, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִרְפָּא מֵעַצְמוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, וַהֲרֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״יָדוֹ פְּתוּחָה לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים״, מַשְׁמַע דְּצָרִיךְ לְקַבָּלָתוֹ

And this is a wondrous thing — that one should be healed of himself through teshuvah — for [we say that] Hashem’s “hand is outstretched to receive the penitent,”1174“Your right hand is outstretched to receive the penitent” (the Ne’ilah liturgy of Yom Kippur): in the closing service we declare, “You give a hand to transgressors, and Your right hand is outstretched to receive penitents” (yeminecha peshutah lekabel shavim) — that the sinner’s return is consummated when God, in His mercy, reaches out to receive him. Meforshim: the phrase distills the Sages’ portrayal of teshuvah’s welcome — the gates of return ever open, and the Holy One Himself drawing the penitent near. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is exactly the difficulty he presses — if teshuvah’s healing “requires His acceptance,” how can Scripture say “and he shall be healed [ve-rafa],” of itself? His answer: at its root (Rosh Hashanah — Binah in the heart) teshuvah already heals of itself, while its full actualization (Yom Kippur) is “what Hashem completes on his behalf and accepts.” which implies that [the healing] requires His acceptance.
אֲבָל בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מַיְירֵי בְּעִנְיַן הַכַּפָּרָה שֶׁל הַתְּשׁוּבָה, לְהַבָּא וּלְשֶׁעָבַר, וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא הוֹצָאַת עִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְפֹעַל
But on Yom Kippur [the Gemara] deals with the matter of the atonement of teshuvah — for the future and the past — and this is the bringing of the matter of teshuvah into actuality.
וְכָל דָּבָר הַיּוֹצֵא לְפֹעַל יֵשׁ בּוֹ שָׁלוֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת הַמּוֹלִידוֹת דָּבָר הַהוּא בְּכֹחַ, שֶׁמֵּהֶם נִמְשָׁכוֹת שֶׁבַע תַּחְתּוֹנוֹת מִדּוֹת הַבִּנְיָן שֶׁל הַהוֹצָאָה לְפֹעַל

And everything that comes into actuality has within it three “first” [powers] that give birth to that thing in potential, from which are drawn the seven lower [ones], the “building” middos of the actualization.
כִּי כָּל דָּבָר מוּגְבָּל עַל כָּרְחֲךָ נֶחְלָק לְשָׁלוֹשׁ חֲלוּקוֹת וְהַגְבָּלוֹת: רֹאשׁ, תּוֹךְ, סוֹף, וְהֵם הַשָּׁלוֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת
for anything bounded is perforce divided into three divisions and delimitations — beginning, middle, end — and these are the three “first” [powers];

[וּמֵהֶם נִבְנִים הַיְצִיאָה לְפֹעַל בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַמָּקוֹם: שָׁלוֹשׁ הַגְבָּלוֹת דְּאֹרֶךְ וְרֹחַב וְגֹבַהּ אוֹ עֹמֶק, שֶׁבָּהֶם הַשֵּׁשׁ קְצָווֹת דְּכָל דָּבָר, וְהַשֶּׁבַע הוּא כְּלָלוּת הַשֶּׁטַח כַּיָּדוּעַ]

[and from them is built the actualization, in the expansion of “place”: the three delimitations of length, breadth, and height (or depth), in which are the “six extremities” of anything, and the seventh is the totality of the surface, as is known].
וּמִזֶּה מַיְירֵי [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה], דְּזֶהוּ ״וּלְבָבוֹ יָבִין״ — הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה בִּהְיוֹתָהּ עֲדַיִין בְּכֹחַ בַּבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב לְבַד
And of this [Rosh Hashanah] speaks: for this is “and his heart shall understand” — the root of teshuvah, while it is still in potential, in the Binah that is in the heart alone.
וַעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְשׁוּבָה הֵם עֶשֶׂר מִדּוֹת הַקּוֹמָה, וּבְרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה הוּא הַהַתְחָלָה וְשָׁלוֹשׁ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת, וּבְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא הַגְּמָר וְהַסִּיּוּם
And the Ten Days of Teshuvah are the ten middos of the “stature”: on Rosh Hashanah is the beginning and the three “firsts,” and on Yom Kippur is the finish and the conclusion —
וְכַדֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאוֹמְרִים ״בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יִכָּתֵבוּן וּבְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים יֵחָתֵמוּן״
as we say, “on Rosh Hashanah they are inscribed and on Yom Kippur they are sealed.”

וְעַל כֵּן בְּמַסֶּכֶת רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה בֵּיאֲרוּ מַעֲלָה זוֹ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד עֶצֶם מִדָּתָהּ, שֶׁהִיא מִדָּה הַשְּׁמִינִית מִתַּתָּא לְעֵילָּא, כַּנּוֹדָע דְּבִינָה תַּמָּן שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ אֶלָּא בַּלֵּב

And therefore in tractate Rosh Hashanah they set out this elevation of teshuvah [as it is] from the side of its very middah — the eighth middah counting from below upward — as is known, that Binah is there [the eighth], the root of teshuvah, which is only in the heart.1175R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Rosh Chodesh Adar §8): “the labor of this month is that even in sleep Israel are kuf — holy, since they are bound at the root in Hashem — and this accords with "I sleep [from the mitzvos] but my heart is awake [to do them]."” Exactly the se’if’s “ve-rafa”: the healing spoken of reaches a bond that never lapsed — the sleeping man was holy throughout, and therefore what is healed is genuinely the past.Izhbitz parallel — Mei HaShiloach I, Bereshit §6: The Mei HaShiloach calls the Etz HaChaim 'teshuvah amitiyos she-merape'os es ha-kodem' — true teshuvah that heals what came before — and then repeats the point with the river Peras: it waters the Tree of Life because it corresponds to baalei teshuvah, 'u-teshuvah merapei es ha-kodem,' healing even the deficiency that has accompanied a person from his earliest beginning and returning him to his first source. This makes R' Tzadok's close reading of 've-rafa' especially sharp. The Izhbitzer does not define teshuvah only as a new direction from now onward; its deepest form reaches the prior reality and changes the meaning of what preceded. That is exactly why R' Tzadok distinguishes the future-oriented 'erpa meshubasam' from 've-rafa' — already healed. Yet Mei HaShiloach also places the doctrine inside the image of the Tree of Life: the healing comes through return to the source of life, not through declaring the breach unreal while remaining where the breach occurred. The stronger the claim of retroactive healing, the stronger the implied demand of actual return. In the language of this se'if, the root-healing exists in the Binah of the heart, while the complete emergence of that healing into the seven lower middos still requires the Divine help and acceptance that carry the person's inward return into a finished life.
וְהַיְצִיאָה לְפֹעַל הוּא מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ גּוֹמֵר בַּעֲדוֹ וּמְקַבְּלָהּ, וְאָז יֵשׁ לָהּ שֶׁבַע מַדְרֵיגוֹת וּמַעֲלוֹת דְּיוֹמָא
And the emergence into actuality is what Hashem “completes on his behalf” and accepts — and then it has the seven rungs and elevations of Yoma.

items.h: The theme: They also taught that an individual’s sealed verdict is not torn — “I, Hashem, have not changed.” R’ Tzadok resolves it from the wordings themselves: “torn,” “teshuvah tears,” “healed of itself” all mean that teshuvah is what does the tearing and the healing, not a change in Him. When it is truly within a person, the “book” of the verdict is torn.

p: [ב] וְאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה] שָׁם ״גְּזַר דִּין דְּיָחִיד אֵינוֹ נִקְרָע״, וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲנִי ה׳ לֹא שָׁנִיתִי״

And they said [in Rosh Hashanah 17b] there that “an individual’s verdict is not torn up” — and this is as it says, “I, Hashem, have not changed” (Malachi 3:6).1176R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §87): "“He has not looked [with a fixed gaze]” — “iniquity in Yaakov”; a multitude in whom transgressions are frequent requires a fixed gaze in order to punish them — “and He has not seen,” with a mere glance, in Israel." Exactly the se’if: “I, Hashem, have not changed” describes His looking, not His mercy — the individual’s verdict stands because it was fixed by a gaze, and it is teshuvah itself that must do the tearing.1177Rosh Hashanah 17b–18a: After R’ Yochanan’s teaching that teshuvah tears up a verdict, the Gemara raises an objection and answers by distinguishing the individual from the community — an individual’s sealed verdict is not [automatically] torn, corresponding to “I, Hashem, have not changed” (Malachi 3:6), whereas a community’s is.Izhbitz on an apparently irrevocable Divine word — Mei HaShiloach II, Yonah 4:1: R. Mordechai Yosef gives a striking model for R' Tzadok's paradox of a verdict that is true and yet whose destructive effect can be removed without implying any change in God. Once a prophecy and Divine utterance has gone forth, the Mei HaShiloach says, 'it must necessarily accomplish something'; even if the people repent, 'this utterance does not return empty.' After Yonah had prophesied the overturning of Nineveh and Nineveh repented, Yonah still feared that some houses or streets would have to fall, because the prophetic word could not simply be false. Hashem therefore showed him the breadth of redemption: the entire operative force of the prophecy was discharged upon Yonah's kikayon. The word remained true, but its destructive application to the repentant city did not. This is an exceptionally useful Izhbitz complement to 'Ani Hashem lo shanisi.' Teshuvah is not a claim that Divine truth becomes untrue or that a sealed word is casually rescinded. Rather, return creates a new relation to the truth of that word, so that the person or community need no longer stand in the place upon which the din was written. R' Tzadok expresses this inwardly: the letters of the decree are formed from the sin and written in the heart; when the heart itself breaks and returns, the 'book' on which the decree was written is torn. The Izhbitzer expresses the same non-change from the side of prophecy: the word is not emptied, but mercy can redirect how its truth becomes actual. Neither teaching licenses presumption before the fact; both describe what becomes possible only when genuine teshuvah has changed the spiritual reality to which the decree had attached.
כִּי הִנֵּה לְשׁוֹן ״נִקְרָע״, וְכֵן ״תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמְּקָרַעַת״, וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״וְרָפָא״ — מֵעַצְמוֹ, הַיְינוּ דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵעַצְמָהּ הִיא הַקּוֹרַעַת וּמְרַפֵּאת

For behold, the term “torn,” and likewise “teshuvah that tears,” and likewise the wording of the verse “and he shall be healed” — [all imply] of itself: that is, teshuvah of itself is what tears and heals.
כְּמוֹ דֶּרֶךְ מָשָׁל שֶׁנָּפַל מַיִם עַל נְיָיר כָּתוּב וְנִמְחֲקוּ הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, כִּי אוֹתִיּוֹת הַגְּזַר דִּין הוּא מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ, כִּי ״חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה״

Like, by way of example, water that falls on written paper and the letters are erased — for the “letters” of the verdict come from the deed of the transgression itself, since “evil pursues sinners” (Mishlei 13:21);1178Mishlei 13:21: “Evil pursues sinners [chataim tirdof ra’ah], but the righteous is rewarded with good.” R’ Tzadok reads the verse literally as a principle of Creation — the punishment is not an external decree but the transgression’s own consequence “pursuing” the sinner — the recurring motif of this siman.
וּמִזֶּה נַעֲשָׂה נְיָיר שֶׁל הַגְּזַר דִּין, דְּהַיְינוּ ״סִפְרָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים״

and from this is made the “paper” of the verdict — that is, “the book of the wicked.”1179R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §41): “the expression of "laughter" indicates a thing that cannot be believed, and nonetheless it is so… but one who does not believe at all is not called "laughing" but "scoffing."” Exactly the se’if: “I, Hashem, have not changed” and yet the verdict is torn — a thing that cannot be believed and is nonetheless so, because it is teshuvah itself, and not a change in Him, that does the tearing.

דְּיָדוּעַ שֶׁהַסֵּפֶר שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים וְשֶׁל רְשָׁעִים וְשֶׁל בֵּינוֹנִים הוּא לֵב הָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ, וּכְשֶׁשָּׁב לִבּוֹ וְעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה וְנִשְׁבַּר לִבּוֹ בְּקִרְבּוֹ, הֲרֵי נִקְרָע הַסֵּפֶר שֶׁל גְּזַר דִּין

for it is known that the “book” of the righteous, of the wicked, and of the intermediate is the heart of the person himself — and when his heart repents and he does teshuvah, and his heart is broken within him, then the “book” of the verdict is torn.1180R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Chanukah §7): “because their Torah and mitzvos were not accepted before Him, and it is like one who pours a jug [of water] over his face; and through this they became embittered, and the longing in their hearts to occupy themselves with Torah in secret grew great.” Exactly the se’if: when the “book of the wicked” is what stands, the response is not an appeal from outside but a deepening within — and it is that inward turn that tears the writing.

רַק מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ עֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַשְׁלִים כָּל מַדְרֵיגוֹת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בִּשְׁלֵימוּת וְלֹא יִמְנָעֵהוּ יִצְרוֹ הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר בְּכָל יוֹם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [סוּכָּה נב:] דְּאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ אֵין יָכוֹל לוֹ

Only, nonetheless, he needs Hashem’s help to be able to complete all the rungs of teshuvah in [full] perfection, so that his inclination — which strengthens against him each day — not prevent him, as they said [Sukkah 52b], “were the Holy One not to help him, he could not prevail against it”;1181Sukkah 52b: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: a person’s [evil] inclination renews itself against him each day [and seeks to overpower him], and were the Holy One not to help him, he could not prevail against it, as it says (Tehillim 37:33), ‘God will not abandon him into his hand.’”
וְזֶהוּ לְעִנְיַן לְהַבָּא, דְּעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״אֶרְפָּא״
and this is with regard to the future — of which it is said, “I will heal.”
וּמִטַּעַם זֶה אֵין תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לִפְטוֹר מֵעוֹנְשֵׁי בֵּית דִּין, שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי עֲקִירַת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לְמַפְרֵעַ
And for this reason teshuvah does not avail to exempt [one] from the punishments of the [earthly] court — which [would work] by uprooting the deed retroactively —
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא, וְהַזְּדוֹנוֹת כִּשְׁגָגוֹת אוֹ זְכֻיּוֹת, וְלָמָּה יֵעָנֵשׁ
for through teshuvah it is “as if he did not sin,” and the willful sins become as unwitting ones, or as merits — so why should he be punished?
אֲבָל כָּל תִּיקּוּנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַכֹּל בַּלֵּב, אַךְ בַּיְצִיאָה לְפֹעַל שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁמְּקַבְּלוֹ — ״אֲנִי ה׳ לֹא שָׁנִיתִי״

But all the rectifications of teshuvah are entirely in the heart; [it is only] in the emergence into actuality — which is from the side of Hashem, who accepts it — [that] “I, Hashem, have not changed” [applies].
וּמֵאַחַר דִּגְזַר דִּין כָּתוּב בַּתּוֹרָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְשַׁנּוֹתוֹ, דְּתוֹרָה נִקְרָא ״אֱמֶת״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ה רע״ב], וֶאֱמֶת הוּא מַה שֶּׁיִּכּוֹן לָעַד וְלֹא יִשְׁתַּנֶּה לְעוֹלָם

And since a [sealed] verdict is “written in the Torah,” it cannot be changed — for the Torah is called “truth,” as they said [Berachos 5b]1182Berachos 5b: In the exposition of “with mercy and truth [emes] iniquity is expiated” (Mishlei 16:6), the Gemara identifies “emes — this is Torah, as it says, ‘buy truth and do not sell it’ (Mishlei 23:23).” Hence the Torah is “truth” — that which endures unchanged forever — so that a verdict “written in the Torah” cannot be altered. — and “truth” is that which endures forever and never changes;
וְכֵן חוֹתָמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא אֱמֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [יוֹמָא סט:]

and likewise “the seal of the Holy One is truth,” as they said [Yoma 69b].1183Yoma 69b (also Shabbos 55a; Sanhedrin 64a): “The seal [chosam] of the Holy One is truth [emes].” R’ Tzadok pairs this with the Torah’s being “truth”: what bears God’s seal, like truth itself, is fixed and unchanging — the ground for a sealed verdict’s permanence.
וְעַל כֵּן גְּזַר דִּין — דְּהַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁנֶּחְתַּם, כִּדְמַשְׁמַע [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה טז.] — אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִשְׁתַּנּוֹת
And therefore a verdict — that is, when it has been sealed, as is implied [Rosh Hashanah 16a] — cannot be changed.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יז.] בְּמִינוּת וּזְנוּת שֶׁאִם יָשׁוּבוּ לֹא יַשִּׂיגוּ אָרְחוֹת חַיִּים, דְּעַל זֶה לֹא יוֹעִיל הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דּוּגְמַת לִפְטוֹר מִמִּיתַת בֵּית דִּין

And therefore they said [Avodah Zarah 17a] regarding heresy and licentiousness, that if they repent “they will not attain the paths of life” — for regarding this, teshuvah will not avail — analogous to [its not availing] to exempt from death at the hands of the court;1184Avodah Zarah 17a: Concerning “none who come to her return, nor attain the paths of life” (Mishlei 2:19) — the Gemara applies it to minus (heresy) [and, in context, licentiousness], indicating that one so “gripped” does not easily return to the paths of life; R’ Tzadok reads this as a “sealed” verdict in this world, though never as a final bar before the true power of teshuvah.
דְּמֵאַחַר דְּאָדוּק בְּהוּ, זֶה מִקְרֵי דְּנֶחְתַּם גְּזַר דִּין
for since he is “gripped” by them, this is called a “sealed” verdict.
כִּמְבוֹאָר [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.] דְּזֶהוּ מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר ״נִכְתָּם עֲוֹנֵךְ״, רְצֹה לוֹמַר כְּכֶתֶם הַנִּכְנָס בַּבֶּגֶד בְּחוֹזֶק, שֶׁאַף שֶׁיַּעֲבִירוּ כָּל שֶׁבַע סַמָּנִין אֵין עוֹבֵר

As is explained [Rosh Hashanah 18a], this is what is said, “your iniquity is stained [nichtam]” (Yirmeyah 2:22)1185Rosh Hashanah 18a: “From where that a community’s verdict is never [permanently] sealed? — though it be sealed, it is [yet] torn, as it says, ‘as Hashem our God whenever we call upon Him’ (Devarim 4:7).” The objection from “your iniquity is stained [nichtam] before Me” (Yirmeyah 2:22) is resolved by distinguishing a verdict sealed with an oath (untearable — the house of Eli, I Shmuel 3:14) from one sealed without an oath. R’ Tzadok reads the indelible “stain” as the sin sunk into the depths of the heart. — meaning, like a stain that has entered a garment firmly, which, even if they pass over it all “seven cleansing agents,”1186The seven cleansing agents (Mishnah Niddah 9:6; Niddah 61b): “Seven substances remove a stain [kesem]: insipid saliva, bean-water, urine, natron [neser], borit, kimonia, and eshleg” — the fixed series by which the Sages test a suspected bloodstain. Meforshim: these are the most powerful launderers known to the Mishnah; and Rosh Hashanah 18a invokes two of them in expounding “though you wash with natron and use much borit, your iniquity is stained [nichtam] before Me” (Yirmeyah 2:22) — the stain of sin that no scouring removes. R’ Tzadok’s use: so too one “sunk in iniquity in all the depths of his heart” is like the “impure stain” that will not launder out “even if they pass over it all seven cleansing agents” — and this is the “sealing” of a verdict that cannot be torn, of which is said “none who come to her return” (Mishlei 2:19). does not pass;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ סִימַן הַכֶּתֶם הַמְּטַמֵּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנִדָּה] שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִתְכַּבֵּס וְעוֹבֵר כְּלָל
which is the mark of the impure stain, as they said [in Niddah] — that it does not launder out and pass at all;
כָּךְ הַשָּׁקוּעַ בְּעָוֹן וּבָרַע בְּכָל מַעֲמַקֵּי לְבָבוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לְהִתְכַּבֵּס, וְזֶהוּ חֲתִימַת גְּזַר דִּין שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִקְרָע, דְּ״כָּל בָּאֶיהָ [לֹא יְשׁוּבוּן]״ וְגוֹמֵר

so [too] one sunk in iniquity and evil in all the depths of his heart, who cannot be laundered [clean] — and this is the “sealing” of a verdict that is not torn, [of which it is said,] “none who come to her return, nor do they attain the paths of life” (Mishlei 2:19).

וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּ״אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּעִנְיַן הַיְצִיאָה לְפֹעַל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, הֲרֵי יֵשׁ ״אַרְבָּעָה חִלּוּקֵי כַפָּרָה״ הַנִּזְכָּר [בְּיוֹמָא], דְּצָרִיךְ לְיִסּוּרִין, וּמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת

And even though “there is nothing that stands before teshuvah,” nonetheless with regard to the emergence into actuality, in deed, there are the “four divisions of atonement” mentioned [in Yoma 86a] — that [some sins] require sufferings, and [for some] death scours [them away].1187Yoma 86a: The “four divisions of atonement” of R’ Yishmael — for a positive commandment, teshuvah alone atones; for a negative, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for [sins bearing] kareis or court-death, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend and sufferings scour; and for one who profanes the Divine Name, only death, together with the others, scours. Hence in this world some sins still require suffering or death to complete the atonement.
וְהַיְינוּ כָּל יְמֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ לִשְׁלֵימוּת מַדְרֵיגָתָהּ, שֶׁיַּגִּיעוּ לֶעָתִיד דְּיִבּוּלַע הַמָּוֶת וְיִכְלוּ הַיִּסּוּרִין מִן הָעוֹלָם

And this [applies] all the days of this world, when [teshuvah] has not yet reached the perfection of its rung — [a perfection] they will reach in the Future, when “death is swallowed up” and sufferings cease from the world —
כִּי יַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת ״מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ״, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ
for [then teshuvah] will reach the rung of “they forgive him and the whole world with him,” when there will be an awakening of teshuvah in the whole world entire.

items.h: The theme: For a community, however, the verdict is torn — for then it is an “hour of favor,” and favor is the opposite of wrath and judgment. When the community rouses such an hour, of itself there is no room for judgment. And this is no change in God at all: it is the revelation of the middah of His favor and goodness, which is always to do good.

p: [ג] וּבְצִבּוּר נִקְרָע, דְּאָז הוּא ״עֵת רָצוֹן״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ח.] ״אֵימָתַי עֵת רָצוֹן [בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁהַצִּבּוּר מִתְפַּלְּלִין]״ כו׳

And for a community, [the verdict] is torn — for then it is an “hour of favor,” as they said [Berachos 8a], “when is an ‘hour of favor’? — when the community prays.”1188R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis §13): "“and as for me, my prayer is to You, Hashem, [at] a time of favor” — David HaMelech taught us what to pray for when we pray at a time of favor: that the prayer be “God, in the abundance of Your kindness” — since we can effect abundant kindness at a time of favor." Exactly the se’if: an “hour of favor” is not merely a suspension of judgment but a positive opening — and Scripture instructs what to ask for precisely because the opening is real.1189Berachos 8a: “What is [the meaning of] ‘and as for me, my prayer is to You, Hashem, [at] an hour of favor’ (Tehillim 69:14)? When is an hour of favor? — when the community prays.” Communal prayer is inherently accepted, so it constitutes an “hour of favor” in which judgment gives way.Sefas Emes — the community itself generates the 'hour of favor' (Chukas 4:5): On 'va'ani sefilasi lecha Hashem es ratzon,' the Sefas Emes makes explicit the mechanism that R' Tzadok is deriving here. 'Bnei Yisrael awaken through their prayer an es ratzon,' he writes, citing the very teaching of Chazal, 'when is an hour of favor? when the community prays.' He reads the verse not merely as prayer taking advantage of a preexisting favorable moment, but as 'ha-tefillah goremes ha-ratzon' — the prayer causes the favor. There are, he adds, times when Hashem desires precisely that Israel should themselves bring forth this ratzon; the deepest Shabbos hour, ra'ava de-ra'avin, is a desire from above that Israel awaken desire from below. This maps almost exactly onto R' Tzadok's formulation that when the tzibbur awakens an es ratzon, there is automatically no place for din. The judgment need not be imagined as a decree that God first wills and then changes His mind about. A different Divine middah becomes the operative light because Knesses Yisrael, acting as a collective, has entered the relationship of ratzon. The Sefas Emes further says that on Shabbos Hashem has nachas from Creation through Israel's testimony to the Creator, and that this ratzon becomes the vitality of the coming week. R' Tzadok's phrase that Hashem is 'merutzeh be-olamo u-motzei naycha mi-beriyosav' is therefore not rhetorical ornament: Chassidic teaching treats the communal awakening of ratzon as a real source of renewed chiyus. The torn decree is the negative face of a positive event — the world has entered a state animated by favor rather than prosecution.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יח.] דְּבַיָּחִיד נִקְרָא ״בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ״ בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְשׁוּבָה, וּבַצִּבּוּר ״בְּכָל קָרְאֵנוּ [אֵלָיו]״, וַאֲפִילּוּ לְאַחַר גְּזַר דִּין, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and as they said [Rosh Hashanah 18a] that for the individual it is called “[seek Him] when He is found” — [namely] in the Ten Days of Teshuvah — while for the community, “[Hashem is near] in all our calling upon Him,” even after a verdict — see there.1190Rosh Hashanah 18a: “Seek Hashem when He is found” (Yeshayah 55:6) — for the individual, “when He is found” refers to the Ten Days of Teshuvah between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur; whereas of the community it says “as Hashem our God is [near us] in all our calling upon Him” (Devarim 4:7) — at any time.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּ״רָצוֹן״ הוּא הַהֵיפֶךְ מֵרוֹגֶז וְדִין, וְכֵיוָן דְּהַצִּבּוּר מְעוֹרְרִים ״עֵת רָצוֹן״, מִמֵּילָא אֵין מָקוֹם לְדִין

And this is: “favor” is the opposite of wrath and judgment; and since the community rouses an “hour of favor,” of itself there is no room for judgment.1191R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §4): “and therefore the Midrash opened this portion with the verse”when you cry out, let your gatherings save you"" Exactly the se’if: it is the community’s cry — the “gatherings” — that rouses the hour of favor, which is why for a community the verdict is torn.
וְאֵין כַּאן שִׁינּוּי, שֶׁהַדִּין לֹא נִשְׁתַּנָּה, רַק שֶׁנִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר חָדָשׁ בָּעוֹלָם, שֶׁהוּא אוֹר רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא לְעוֹלָם לְהֵטִיב

And there is no “change” here: the judgment is not altered; rather, a new light is revealed in the world — the light of His will, which is always to do good.1192R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §11): “‘And as for me, my prayer [is to You, Hashem,] at an eis ratzon [a time of favor]’ — meaning: an eis ratzon is when Hashem desires that they pray before Him, as in ‘if my prayer is fluent in my mouth’ (Berachos 34b); for without Hashem it would be impossible for a person to pray before Him at all.” The “hour of favor” is not a change in God but the revelation of His will — that He desires their return — which is itself the light “always to do good.”
וּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת ״עֵת רָצוֹן״ זֶה, שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְרוּצֶה בְּעוֹלָמוֹ וּמוֹצֵא נַיְיחָא מִבְּרִיּוֹתָיו עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וְאוֹבַנְתָּא דְּלִבָּא

And in the revelation of this “hour of favor” — when the Holy One is pleased with His world and finds contentment from His creatures, through the teshuvah of the heart and “the understanding of the heart” —

אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִגְמַר הַיְצִיאָה לְפֹעַל עַל יְדֵי עֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַד עֵת קֵץ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כְּבָר ״וְרָפָא״ מֵעַצְמוֹ, וּמִמֵּילָא נִקְרָע גְּזַר דִּין עַל יְדֵי גִּילּוּי מִדַּת רְצוֹנוֹ וְטוּבוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

even though the emergence into actuality is not yet completed — [which comes only] through Hashem’s help, at the End of Days — nonetheless “he is already healed of himself,” and of itself the verdict is torn, through the revelation of the middah of His favor and goodness.

items.h: The theme: The Tannaim differ over an individual’s verdict too. R’ Yitzchak holds that “a cry avails a person both before and after the verdict,” and we rule like him — which is why we pray even for the gravely ill after a verdict has been sealed. But that operates by prayer and mercy, not by the tearing that teshuvah itself accomplishes.

p: [ד] וְעַיֵּין [שָׁם יח.] פְּלִיגֵי תַּנָּאֵי גַּם בִּגְזַר דִּין דְּיָחִיד

And see [there, Rosh Hashanah 18a] that Tannaim differ also regarding an individual’s verdict.1193R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayeishev §3): “it is of the order of”a prayer of the poor man," who has nothing of his own — “I am with the crushed”; and this is what is said, “when you cry out, let your gatherings save you.”" Exactly the se’if: the cry that avails “both before and after the verdict” is the cry of one who claims nothing — which is why it operates by prayer and mercy rather than by right.R' Tzadok's later Chassidic development — Pri Tzadik, Shemos 8:1: Pri Tzadik develops the power of tze'akah in a way that clarifies why this se'if separates prayer and crying from teshuvah alone. On Israel's cry in Egypt, he cites the Zohar that 'tze'akah is greater than all of them, for tze'akah is in the heart,' and then: 'great is tze'akah, for it rules in this world and in the World to Come; through tze'akah a person inherits this world and the World to Come.' He identifies the two worlds with Malchus and Binah and returns to the same verse used throughout Takanas HaShavin: when fear penetrates to the depths of the heart, 'levavo yavin vashav' — Binah in the heart — becomes teshuvah ila'ah. The cry therefore reaches both the revealed order in which a decree operates and the higher root from which repair can flow. This is precisely why R' Tzadok here can preserve a real distinction between teshuvah and tze'akah without diminishing teshuvah. Teshuvah is the inward return of the heart; prayer and cry are the act by which that heart, stripped of self-sufficiency, turns directly to Hashem for rachamim. A sealed individual decree may remain fixed within the ordinary legal order, yet the cry can appeal from that order to the Source that encompasses both worlds. Pri Tzadik even applies this to those who appear spiritually lost or enclosed by kelipah, teaching that the 'great shofar' can awaken the root of return in the hidden heart. Thus 'yafah tze'akah bein kodem gezar din bein le'achar gezar din' is not an alternate technical loophole. It is a distinct mode of relation: instead of the sinner arguing that his inner change should itself erase the judgment, the broken heart cries to the One before whom both the judgment and the possibility of its merciful transcendence are present.
וּלְאִיבָּעֵית אֵימָא [שָׁם טז.] הָא דִּמְצַלֵּינַן אַקְּצִירֵי וּמָרִיעֵי — דְּקַיְימָא לָן כְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק דְּגַם לְאַחַר גְּזַר דִּין יָפָה צְעָקָה, וּדְקָרְעָה

And according to the “if you wish, say” [answer, there, 16a], that which we pray over the [dangerously] ill [is] because we hold like R’ Yitzchak, that even after a verdict “an outcry avails,” and that it tears [the verdict].1194R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §32): “were there two opposites in one subject — if Reuven judged it beautiful and Shimon repulsive… this would be a difficulty only if the beautiful and the repulsive were each an independent reality.” Exactly the se’if’s dispute: whether an individual’s verdict can be torn is not a contradiction in God but a question of which reality the verdict belongs to — and the answer settles which remedy applies.1195Rosh Hashanah 16a & 18a: “Rabbi Yitzchak said: a cry avails a person both before the verdict and after the verdict.” On this basis the Gemara explains why “we pray over the [dangerously] ill” — even after a decree, outcry and prayer can tear it. The Tannaitic dispute (18a) is whether an individual’s verdict can be torn at all; the halachah follows R’ Yitzchak that an outcry helps.
אַךְ מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ דְּמוֹעִיל תְּפִלָּה וּצְעָקָה, אֲבָל הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְבַדָּהּ לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל אֵין מוֹעִילָה
But in any case they said that prayer and outcry avail; teshuvah alone, by all opinions, does not avail [to tear an individual’s sealed verdict].
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא מוֹקֵי הָא דְּרַבִּי יִצְחָק גַּם בִּגְזַר דִּין דְּיָחִיד כִּסְתִימוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן וּכְמַאן דְּאָמַר הָכִי, כֵּיוָן דְּקַיְימָא לָן כְּוָותֵיהּ

And therefore [the Gemara] does not establish R’ Yitzchak’s statement [as applying] even to an individual’s verdict — as the plain wording [would suggest], and as the one who so holds — since we rule like him;
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד דִּיבֵּר, וּבָזֶה לֵיכָּא לְמַאן דְּאָמַר
and perforce [this is] because R’ Yochanan spoke of teshuvah alone — and regarding that, there is no one who holds [that it tears an individual’s verdict].
וְהוּא מוּכְרָח גַּם כֵּן מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּלֹא מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה לְמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין

And this is also forced by what I wrote, that teshuvah does not avail [to exempt] from death at the hands of the court.1196R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §67): “for the blessings are in this world, and from the side of the Attribute of Justice there is no place for Yaakov to receive good in this world, for there are many claims against him… and the counsel for this is "with the shofar I will entreat him" [on the Day of Judgment].” Exactly the se’if: where strict judgment leaves no opening, what avails is entreaty — the cry, which operates by prayer and mercy rather than by right.
[וּבְנוֹדָע בִּיהוּדָה קַמָּא סִימָן ל״ה כָּתַב דְּאִם כֵּן בִּטַּלְתָּ כָּל עוֹנְשֵׁי תוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

[And in the Noda BiYehudah, first edition, §35, he wrote that if so [i.e., if teshuvah exempted from the court], “you would nullify all the Torah’s penalties” — see there;1197Noda BiYehudah (Mahadura Kama, Orach Chaim §35): Ruling on a man who had sinned gravely and later did great teshuvah, R’ Yechezkel Landau writes that a court still administers capital penalties despite the sinner’s repentance — “for otherwise you would nullify all the Torah’s penalties in general, and no one would ever be executed by the court, for [each] would say ‘I have sinned and behold I repent’”; hence it is a decree of Scripture that teshuvah does not save one from the court. R’ Tzadok accepts the conclusion but rejects the “deterrence” reasoning, since court executions are in fact rare (requiring witnesses and forewarning), grounding the rule instead in the intrinsic order of Creation.
וְאֵין זֶה מַסְפִּיק, לַעֲשׂוֹת דִּינָא בְּלֹא דִּינָא, וְאֵין אַחֲרָיוּת עוֹנָשִׁין עָלֵינוּ
but this is not sufficient [reason] — to render “judgment without [true] judgment”; the responsibility for [administering] the penalties is not [ours to force by such logic].

וּמַה שֶּׁחָשַׁב שֶׁהָעוֹנָשִׁין כְּדֵי לִמְנוֹעַ הָעוֹבְרִין — אֵינוֹ כֵּן, דְּאֵין עוֹנֶשׁ בֵּית דִּין אֶלָּא בְּעֵדִים וְהַתְרָאָה, וְאֵין זֶה מָצוּי כָּל כָּךְ, וְסַנְהֶדְרִין הַהוֹרֶגֶת אַחַת לְשֶׁבַע שָׁנִים נִקְרֵאת ״חַבְלָנִית״

And that which he supposed — that the punishments are [meant] to deter transgressors — is not so: for court-punishment [applies] only with witnesses and forewarning, which is not so common; and a Sanhedrin that executes once in seven years is called “destructive” (Makkos 7a).1198Makkos 7a (Mishnah): “A Sanhedrin that executes [once] in seven years is called destructive [chovlanit]. Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah says: once in seventy years. Rabbi Tarfon and Rabbi Akiva say: had we been on the Sanhedrin, no one would ever have been executed.” Capital cases were subjected to such exacting scrutiny that convictions were exceedingly rare — R’ Tzadok’s proof that the Torah’s penalties do not function as ordinary deterrents.
וְאִם יִהְיֶה הַדּוֹר פָּרוּץ וְהוּא צוֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה, דָּבָר זֶה נִמְסַר לְבֵית דִּין לַעֲנוֹשׁ גַּם שֶׁלֹּא מִן הַתּוֹרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּיבָמוֹת צ׳ ב

And if the generation is unrestrained and it is a “need of the hour,” this [power] is handed to the court, to punish even not [strictly] according to the Torah, as they said in Yevamos 90b1199Yevamos 90b: “R’ Elazar ben Yaakov said: I heard that the court flogs and punishes not according to the Torah — not to transgress the words of Torah, but to make a fence for the Torah. There was an incident with a man who rode a horse on Shabbos in the days of the Greeks, and they brought him to court and stoned him — not because he was fit for it, but because the hour required it.” This is the source for the court’s power to punish “as a need of the hour,” which R’ Tzadok invokes here.;
וְאֵין ״עוֹנְשִׁין״ הַתּוֹרָה מִי״ג מִדּוֹת וְצוֹרֶךְ שָׁעָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּךְ קָצַב הָעוֹנֶשׁ הַמַּגִּיעַ לְאוֹתוֹ עָוֹן

and [thus] the Torah’s punishments are not [merely] from the “thirteen hermeneutical principles” or [ad hoc] “need of the hour” — rather, so is the [Divinely] apportioned punishment that befits that iniquity.
וּכְשֶׁקִּיבֵּל עוֹנְשׁוֹ נִתְכַּפֵּר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״כֵּיוָן שֶׁלָּקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ״

And once he has received his punishment he is atoned, as they said, “once he has been flogged, he is [again] like your brother” (Makkos 23a).1200Makkos 23a (Mishnah): “Once he has been flogged, he is [again] like your brother [ki’achicha]” — after receiving his court-imposed punishment the transgressor is fully restored, the penalty itself effecting atonement (derived from “and your brother be dishonored before your eyes,” Devarim 25:3: once flogged, he is again “your brother”).
וְנָהִינָא דְּרָאִיתִי בְּאֵיזֶה סֵפֶר, וּבְסֵפֶר הָרַב חִיד״א בְּשֵׁם אַחֲרוֹנִים, כָּתְבוּ הַטַּעַם דְּשֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁב בְּכָל לֵב, רַק אִיעֲרוֹמֵי מְעָרֵים מִפְּנֵי פַּחַד הָעוֹנֶשׁ

And I recall having seen in some sefer — and in a sefer of the Rav Chida, in the name of Acharonim — that they wrote the reason [teshuvah does not exempt from the court is] that perhaps he has not repented wholeheartedly, but is merely dissembling out of fear of the punishment.
וְגַם זֶה אֵין מַסְפִּיק לַהֲמִיתוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַסָּפֵק, כֵּיוָן דְּאִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת פָּטוּר, סְפֵק נְפָשׁוֹת לְהָקֵל, וְאֵין לַהֲמִיתוֹ מִסָּפֵק שֶׁמָּא מְעָרֵים

But this too is insufficient [reason] to put him to death on account of a doubt — for if he repented in truth he is exempt, and “in capital doubts we are lenient”; one may not put him to death on the doubt that perhaps he is dissembling.
וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם כֵּן לוֹמַר בָּזֶה ״אֵין סָפֵק [תְּשׁוּבָה] מוֹצִיא מִידֵי וַדַּאי [חֵטְא]״ לְהוֹצִיא הַלָּה לְמִיתָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה
Nor does it apply here to say “a doubt [of teshuvah] does not override a certainty [of sin]” so as to bring this one out to death thereby —
דַּהֲרֵי לְקוּלָּא יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא אָמְרִינַן כֵּן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת פְּסָחִים ט׳ א׳ ד״ה ״כְּדֵי״, וּבְחוּלִּין וּבְנִדָּה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

for leniently one may say we do not say so, as Tosafos wrote (Pesachim 9a, s.v. “kedei,” and in Chullin and Niddah)1201“A doubt does not override a certainty” (ein safek motzi midei vadai; Pesachim 9a-b): in the laws of searching for chametz — the marten that may have dragged off the bread, and the case of the “nine shops” — the Gemara sets out the principle that an uncertainty does not displace an established certainty. Meforshim: Tosafos (Pesachim 9a, s.v. “kedei”; and in Chullin and Niddah) qualify that the rule does not hold universally — in certain cases, leniently, we do not apply it. R’ Tzadok’s use: one might argue that the doubt whether the penitent has truly repented cannot override the certainty of his sin, so he should still be executed; R’ Tzadok answers that even this maxim is “not a clear-cut matter” (per those Tosafos) — all the more so in capital law, where “in capital doubts we are lenient” — and so it cannot send to his death a man who “cries out, ‘I truly repent!’” — see there —
הֲרֵי דְּלָאו מִילְּתָא פְּסִיקָא הוּא גַּם בְּאִיסּוּרִין, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בְּדִינֵי נְפָשׁוֹת, וְהַלָּה צֹוֵחַ ״אֲנִי שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת״]
so it is not a clear-cut matter even in ritual prohibitions, all the more so in capital law — and this one cries out, “I truly repent!”]

וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמּוֹעִילָה, הַיְינוּ רַק מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיָּדוֹ פְּתוּחָה לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים, אֲבָל מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה — ״הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחוֹטֵאת תָּמוּת״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי דְּמַכּוֹת]

And perforce, teshuvah — though it avails — [avails] only from the side of Hashem, whose “hand is outstretched to receive the penitent”; but from the side of [strict] wisdom, “the soul that sins shall die,” as they said [in the Yerushalmi of Makkos].1202Yerushalmi, Makkos: When Wisdom, Prophecy, and the Holy One were each “asked” what the sinner’s punishment should be — Wisdom answered, “evil pursues sinners”; Prophecy, “the soul that sins, it shall die”; and the Holy One, “let him do teshuvah and it shall be atoned.” R’ Tzadok’s point: from the side of chochmah (strict order), the sinning soul’s death is intrinsic — teshuvah’s saving power comes only from the higher side of Hashem Himself.

items.h: The theme: Were the Torah’s mitzvos merely a king’s decree, and its penalties merely for transgressing the royal will, reason would demand that repentance and a plea for pardon should help — for even a flesh-and-blood king ought not be cruel. It is his honor to pardon sinners who ask. That the matter is not so simple shows that the mitzvos are of another order entirely.

p: [ה] וְהַיְינוּ דְּוַדַּאי אִלּוּ הָיָה מִצְוַת הַתּוֹרָה רַק גְּזֵירַת מֶלֶךְ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ, וְכָל חֲטָאֵי הָעוֹבֵר וְהָעוֹנָשִׁין הַבָּאִין עָלָיו רַק מִפְּנֵי שֶׁעָבַר מִצְוַת הַמֶּלֶךְ

And this is: were the mitzvos of the Torah merely a “decree of a king,” [given] to do His will — and all the transgressor’s “sins,” and the punishments that come upon him, only because he transgressed the king’s command —
אִם כֵּן הָיָה בַּדִּין, לִכְשֶׁיָּשׁוּב וִיבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה וְכַפָּרָה, שֶׁיּוֹעִיל

then it would be just, when he repents and asks pardon and atonement, that it avail.1203R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach §8): "“I shall sing to Hashem, for He is exceedingly exalted” indicates this aspect too, for this expression always indicates greatness and loftiness and exaltation with respect to Hashem — that He is without measure, above the grasp of human beings." Exactly the se’if: were the mitzvos a king’s decree, reason alone would settle the matter — but what is at issue is beyond measure and beyond the grasp that reason brings to bear.
שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ בָּשָׂר וָדָם צָרִיךְ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה אַכְזָרִי מִלִּמְחוֹל כְּשֶׁמְּבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
For even a mortal must not be cruel [and refuse] to pardon when [one] asks pardon — all the more the King of the kings of kings, the Holy One,
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּפִי גְּדוּלָּתוֹ הַמְרָאַת רְצוֹנוֹ חֵטְא גָּדוֹל וְעָצוּם מְאוֹד, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מֶלֶךְ מָלֵא רַחֲמִים, וּכְבוֹדוֹ לִמְחוֹל לְחוֹטְאִים הַמְבַקְּשִׁים מְחִילָה

for although, in keeping with His greatness, defying His will is an exceedingly great and grave sin, nonetheless He is “a King full of mercy,” and it is His honor to pardon sinners who ask pardon.1204R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Tu BiShvat §2): "“his eye [saw]” — this is Ra and his companions — things that were not revealed to Ra and his companions… and this was after the spoiling, when it became necessary to rectify the abundance of anger." Exactly the se’if: the Torah’s penalties are not the anger of an offended king; the very things hidden from the outward eye are what determine why a plea for pardon should or should not avail.

וּבַדִּין הוּא כָּךְ לְמֶלֶךְ רַחְמָן כְּמוֹתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהוּא מְקוֹר הָרַחֲמִים שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם, שֶׁגַּם הַיּוֹתֵר רַחְמָנִי שֶׁבִּבְנֵי אָדָם אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם שַׁיָּיכוּת וְעֵרֶךְ לְרַחְמָנוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַנִּבְרָאִים
And by right so it is for a merciful King like Him — the source of all the mercy in the world, [such] that even the most merciful of men bears no relation or measure to His mercy upon His creatures —

וְלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל הַדַּעַת שֶׁיִּתְאַכְזֵר וְלֹא יִמְחוֹל לְמִתְחָרֵט וּמְבַקֵּשׁ מְחִילָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁכְּבָר הִבְטִיחַ עַל הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְשֶׁהוּא חָפֵץ בִּתְשׁוּבַת רְשָׁעִים וּמַרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ

and it is inconceivable that He would be cruel and not pardon one who regrets and asks pardon — all the more so as He has already promised regarding teshuvah, and that He “desires the repentance of the wicked” and “abundantly pardons” (Yeshayah 55:7).
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא בִּטְרוּנְיָא עִם בְּרִיּוֹתָיו, לְהָטִיל עֲלֵיהֶם גְּזֵירוֹת כְּדֵי לְהַעֲנִישָׁם אִם יַעַבְרוּ
But in truth the Holy One does not “come with a grievance” against His creatures, to impose upon them decrees in order to punish them if they transgress.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בַּמִּדְרָשׁ] שֶׁ״אַל תֹּאמַר לְרָעַתְכֶם נָתַתִּי הַתּוֹרָה, לֹא נִיתְּנָה אֶלָּא לְטוֹבַתְכֶם״

And of this they said [in the Midrash]: “Do not say, ‘I gave you the Torah for your harm’ — it was given only for your good.”1205R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vaeschanan §3): “"and I entreated Hashem"… at the opening of the portion it says how Moshe prayed and was not answered; and after this it says, "and now, Israel, hearken to the statutes" — and this seems to require explanation: what has one to do with the other?” Exactly the se’if’s question: if the mitzvos were a mere royal decree, a plea should have availed — and Scripture’s own juxtaposition of unanswered prayer with the chukim is where the answer must be sought.1206The Midrash (in the spirit of Devarim Rabbah and parallels): “Do not say, ‘I gave you the Torah for your harm’; I gave it only for your good” — the mitzvos are not arbitrary decrees but the very conditions of life, “the things a man shall do and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5).
וְאֵין רְצוֹנֵנוּ לוֹמַר ״לְרָעַתְכֶם״ מַמָּשׁ, דְּזֶה לֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל הַדַּעַת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, רַק רְצֹה לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵינוֹ גְּזֵירָה בְּעָלְמָא
And we do not mean “for your harm” literally — that is inconceivable, God forbid — rather it means that it is not a mere “decree”;
דְּאִם כֵּן רָעָה הוּא לְגַבֵּי הָעוֹבְרִים שֶׁהֵם הָרוֹב, וְ״אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ״ כו׳, וּבְבָבָא בַתְרָא ״רוּבָּן [בְּגֶזֶל וּמִיעוּטָן בַּעֲרָיוֹת וְהַכֹּל בַּאֲבַק לָשׁוֹן הָרָע]״

for if [it were a mere decree], it would be a “harm” with respect to the transgressors — who are the majority (for “there is no righteous man on earth” etc., and in Bava Basra 165a, “most [fail] in [some shade of] theft, a minority in immorality, and all in the ‘dust’ of evil speech”)1207Bava Basra 165a: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: the majority [succumb] to [some shade of] robbery, a minority to sexual sin, and all to the ‘dust’ of evil speech [avak lashon hara].” R’ Tzadok cites this to show that transgressors are the majority — so the Torah’s penalties cannot be a mere royal “decree,” for then the Torah would be a net “harm” to most. —
וּמוּטָב הָיָה שֶׁלֹּא יִגְזוֹר וְלֹא יֵעָנְשׁוּ
and it would have been better that He not decree at all, so that they not be punished.
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הַתּוֹרָה הוּא דְּפוּס מַעֲשֵׂה בְרֵאשִׁית כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה א], וּכְפִי חוּקֵי הַבְּרִיאָה הַהֶכְרֵחַ הוּא לִשְׁמוֹר חוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה כְּדֵי לְקַיֵּים הָעוֹלָם

But in truth the Torah is the “blueprint of the Work of Creation,” as they said [Bereishis Rabbah 1]1208Bereishis Rabbah 1:1: “‘And I was beside Him as an amon’ (Mishlei 8:30) — read uman [craftsman]: the Torah says, ‘I was the tool of craft [kli umanuso] of the Holy One.’ Just as a builder works from plans and tablets, so ‘the Holy One looked into the Torah and created the world.’” This is R’ Tzadok’s “blueprint of the Work of Creation”: since the world was made by means of the Torah, keeping its laws is what sustains the world.Izhbitz-Radzin — Torah is not an external code but the anatomy of life (Tiferet Yosef, Talmud Anthology, Chagigah §2): Tiferet Yosef develops the Zoharic principle 'Kudsha Berich Hu looked into the Torah and created the world' into exactly the ontology R' Tzadok requires in this se'if. The Torah, he explains, corresponds to the organs and joints of the human being; the 248 positive commandments and 365 prohibitions correspond to the limbs and sinews.
