A person whose desire is to remove concealment and see the Divine purpose within things can therefore discover Torah in his own created being — 'u-mi-besari echezeh Eloka' — because the world itself was formed through Torah. This is why Chazal compare Torah to the goad that directs an animal's furrow 'to bring life into the world': Torah directs its learners 'from the ways of death to the ways of life.' Tiferet Yosef then makes the consequence explicit. One who truly perceives the Torah within his own spiritual anatomy knows that severing himself from even one positive command or transgressing a prohibition is not merely disobeying an arbitrary order; it is a real disconnection from life. This is almost a Chassidic gloss on R' Tzadok's words that, were mitzvos only royal decrees, pardon should suffice, whereas in truth Torah is the 'blueprint of Creation' and the aveirah itself pursues the sinner. The punishment is not fundamentally retaliation added from outside; the Torah has disclosed which movements accord with the organism of Creation and which tear at it. Yet Tiferet Yosef also points toward teshuvah: the purpose of the struggle is to remove hester and come back to Divrei Torah, at which point even the road by which one reached them can be gathered into the Divine teaching. That final point preserves R' Tzadok's broader thesis: the objective structure of Torah is real, but return can reach a root deep enough to restore life to what had been severed. — and by the laws of Creation it is a necessity to keep the laws of the Torah in order to sustain the world;
וְ״חַטָּאִים תְּרַדֵּף רָעָה״ — הִיא הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ רוֹדֶפֶת אוֹתָם, וְאֵין לוֹ לְהִתְאוֹנֵן עַל חַי עוֹלָמִים, רַק עַל עַצְמוֹ
and “evil pursues sinners” — the transgression itself pursues them; and he has no [ground] to complain against the Life of the worlds, only against himself.

וְטוֹבָה גְּדוֹלָה עָשָׂה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוֹדִיעָנוּ הַדְּבָרִים אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה הָאָדָם וָחַי, וְהִזְהִיר כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים עַל הַבְּחִירָה בַּחַיִּים, כִּי הֵם חַיֵּינוּ מִצַּד עַצְמָם

And Hashem did a great kindness at the Giving of the Torah, in making known to us “the things that a man shall do and live [by them],” and warning many times to “choose life” — for they are our life1209“A man shall do them and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5); “choose life” (Devarim 30:19): “You shall keep My statutes and My ordinances, which a man shall do and live by them” (Vayikra 18:5); and “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse; therefore choose life, that you may live” (Devarim 30:19). Meforshim: Rashi, citing the Sifra — “and live by them” means in the World to Come, “for should you say [it refers to] this world, does he not ultimately die?” — the mitzvos being the wellspring of enduring life. R’ Tzadok’s use: these verses show that the mitzvos “are our life, of themselves” — not an arbitrary royal decree whose breach merely offends the King, but the very “vitality of the limbs of the soul,” so that the sinner “wounds or severs a limb” of his own being, and “evil pursues sinners” by the built-in law of Creation., of themselves.
וְאִם כֵּן מַה מָּקוֹם לִתְשׁוּבָה וּבַקָּשַׁת מְחִילָה, אִם גּוּף הַדָּבָר מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ רַע וּמַר וּמֵבִיא הָעוֹנֶשׁ
And if so, what room is there for teshuvah and asking pardon — if the thing itself, of itself, is evil and bitter and brings the punishment?
הָא לְמָה הַדָּבָר דּוֹמֶה, לְאָדָם שֶׁפָּצַע בְּעַצְמוֹ, וְיוֹעִיל מַה שֶּׁיִּתְחָרֵט אַחַר כָּךְ, וְעַל כָּרְחוֹ לָשׂוּם רְטִיּוֹת וְסַמָּנִים מְרַפְּאִים; וְאִם קָטַע יָדוֹ אֵין לוֹ תַּקָּנָה עוֹד

To what may this be compared? To a man who wounded himself: his later regret helps, and perforce [he must] apply plasters and healing remedies — but if he has severed his hand, he has no repair anymore.
וּמִצְוַת הַתּוֹרָה הֵם חַיּוּת אֵבְרֵי הַנֶּפֶשׁ, וְהַחוֹטֵא הוּא כְּפוֹצֵעַ אוֹ קוֹטֵעַ אֵבֶר כְּפִי גּוֹדֶל הַחֵטְא
And the mitzvos of the Torah are the vitality of the limbs of the soul, and the sinner is like one who wounds or severs a limb, according to the magnitude of the sin;
וּלְפִיכָךְ מִצַּד הַחָכְמָה אֵין מָקוֹם לְתוֹעֶלֶת הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְהַצָּלַת הַמִּיתָה הָרְאוּיָה לַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחוֹטֵאת
and therefore, from the side of [strict] wisdom, there is no room for teshuvah to avail to save [from] the death that befits the sinning soul.

items.h: The theme: All of that holds only from the side of the “laws” Hashem inscribed in His world — the middos and utterances by which it was made in the seven days, which give bound and measure to everything, and by which the Torah fences in man, who mirrors the world. There are gates above all the gates of the world’s governance, and the sins of “exiting the laws” do not reach there.

p: [ו] אֶלָּא שֶׁכָּל זֶה מִצַּד חוּקִים שֶׁחָקַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעוֹלָמוֹ, וְהַמִּדּוֹת וְהַמַּאֲמָרוֹת שֶׁבָּהֶם נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם בְּשֶׁבַע יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, הַנּוֹתְנִים גְּבוּל וְקִצְבָה לְכָל דָּבָר

Except that all this is [only] from the side of the “laws” [chukim] that Hashem inscribed in His world — the middos and “utterances” by which the world was created in the seven days1210“By ten utterances the world was created” (Avos 5:1): “By ten utterances the world was created. And what does this teach — could it not have been created by a single utterance? Rather, to exact punishment from the wicked, who destroy the world created by ten utterances, and to give good reward to the righteous, who sustain the world created by ten utterances.” Meforshim: the Bartenura — the ten are the nine “and God said”s of Creation together with “In the beginning” (itself reckoned an utterance); the world is literally built by them, so that keeping or violating its order sustains or ruins it. R’ Tzadok’s use: “all this is only from the side of the laws Hashem inscribed in His world — the middos and utterances by which the world was made in the seven days” — by which the Torah’s laws “fence in” man; teshuvah, by contrast, “was created before the world,” standing above those very laws.Maharal — teshuvah as a pre-world foundation, not an exception to Creation (Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah 4:13): The Maharal writes that teshuvah is not a contingent remedy introduced only after sin appeared: 'ha-teshuvah hi mi-yesodei ha-olam' — teshuvah is one of the foundations of the world. He proves this from Chazal's teaching that teshuvah was among the things created before the world, and adds a characteristic Maharalian principle: 'a thing that was created cannot fail to come into actuality, for otherwise its creation would be in vain.' This gives conceptual precision to R' Tzadok's insistence that the gates of teshuvah stand above the gates of the world's ordinary governance. If teshuvah were simply one more mechanism inside the created legal order, it would remain subject to that order's finalities — a broken law would generate its result and an irrevocable din would remain irrevocable. By placing teshuvah before the world, Chazal identify it as a principle by which the created order itself was founded with a path of return already built into its deepest design. The Maharal's formulation also prevents a common misunderstanding of 'above the laws.' Teshuvah is not lawlessness; it is itself a yesod established by Hashem prior to the differentiated world. Its transcendence of the world's boundaries is therefore part of Divine order at a more primordial level. This fits R' Tzadok's language exactly: the Torah's chukim correspond to the bounded middos and utterances of Creation, while the sinner who reaches the root of teshuvah reaches a prior level at which the breach of those boundaries does not define the whole of his being. The gates open because the possibility of return preceded the gate-system itself. of Creation — which give bound and measure to everything;
וּכְפִיהֶם הֵם חוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַמַּגְדֶּרֶת הָאָדָם שֶׁהוּא דּוּגְמַת הָעוֹלָם

and in accordance with them are the laws of the Torah, which “fence in” man, who is a “likeness of the world” [a microcosm]1211Man, “a likeness of the world” (Midrash Tanchuma, Pekudei 3): the Midrash teaches that “the Tabernacle was equal to all the world and to the human embryo — which is a world in miniature,” for “the formation of the embryo is like the formation of the world.” Meforshim: this is the classic teaching that man is an olam katan — a microcosm — whatever the Holy One set in the great world He set, in small, in man. R’ Tzadok’s use: because man is “a likeness of the world,” the Torah’s laws — patterned on “the middos and utterances by which the world was created” — “fence in” man exactly as those laws bound and measure the world; so a sin is a breach of the very order of Creation, and “evil pursues sinners” of itself..
אֲבָל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא הַתְּשׁוּבָה קוֹדֶם לָעוֹלָם, וְקָדְמָה לַתּוֹרָה גַּם כֵּן

But Hashem created teshuvah before the world, and it preceded the Torah as well;1212Pesachim 54a / Nedarim 39b: Teshuvah is among the things “created before the world.” R’ Tzadok takes this to mean that teshuvah stands above the ordered structure of Creation and its “laws,” so that one who reaches it has risen beyond the reach of the “sins of exiting the laws.”1213Cf. Pesachim 54a (and Nedarim 39b): teshuvah is among the seven things “created before the world” — “Torah, teshuvah, Gan Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Beis HaMikdash, and the name of Mashiach.” This is precisely R’ Tzadok’s point here: teshuvah stands “above the bound of the world and its laws,” so the sins of “exiting the laws” do not reach it.
כִּי יֵשׁ מַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה יוֹתֵר, שֶׁכְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לְשָׁם כְּבָר עָבַר לְמַעְלָה מִגְּבוּל הָעוֹלָם וְחוּקָּיו, וְאֵין חֲטָאֵי יְצִיאַת הַחוּקִּים מַגִּיעִים לְשָׁם

for there is a higher rung — [such] that when one reaches there, he has already passed above the bound of the world and its laws, and the sins of “exiting the laws” do not reach there.1214R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Shelach §9): "“but every man whose spirit moves him… and he removes from his neck the yoke of the many calculations — behold, this one is sanctified a holy of holies, and Hashem shall be his portion and his inheritance.”" Exactly the se’if: there are gates above all the gates of the world’s governance, and one who removes the yoke of the world’s “calculations” stands there — where the sins of “exiting the laws” do not reach.
וְזֶהוּ פְּתִיחַת הַשַּׁעַר לְדוֹפְקֵי בִּתְשׁוּבָה — הֵם ״שַׁעֲרֵי תְשׁוּבָה״ דִּלְמַעְלָה מִכָּל הַשְּׁעָרִים שֶׁל הַנְהָגוֹת הָעוֹלָם

And this is the “opening of the gate to those who knock in teshuvah” — [these are] the “gates of teshuvah,” which are above all the gates of the world’s governance.1215R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Balak §14): “and Yishmael corresponds to wine, the aspect of the wine of the Oral Torah — for which the yetzer and the longing were created, to be "the desire of Torah, the joy of the teaching."” Exactly the se’if: the “laws” that bound and measure are the very ones that give the yetzer its place — the fence and the longing belong to one order.
וְהֵם גַּם כֵּן הַשְּׁעָרִים הַנִּפְתָּחִים בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, דְּעַל יְדֵי כֵן יוּכַל הַכֹּהֵן הַגָּדוֹל לִיכָּנֵס אָז לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים, מַה שֶּׁאֵין יָכוֹל לִיכָּנֵס כָּל הַשָּׁנָה
And they are also the gates opened on Yom Kippur — through which the Kohen Gadol may then enter the Holy of Holies, which he cannot enter all [the rest of] the year.
וְיָדוּעַ בַּזוֹהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [שְׁלַח קסא:] דְּבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים הוּא ״לִבָּא דְּכָל אַרְעָא וְעָלְמָא״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And it is known in the holy Zohar [Shelach 161b] that the Holy of Holies is “the heart of all the earth and the world” — see there.1216R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §75): “the names indicate the revealed material… and "earth" alludes in many places to the deed, and "heaven" to thought, which are man and woman, as it says, "as the rain descends from heaven… and waters the earth"; and they said, "this rain is the husband of the earth" — and these are the drops of wisdom that descend.” Exactly the se’if: the “laws” by which the world was made are precisely what give bound and measure below — and the gates above them are of another order entirely.1217Zohar, Shelach 161b: Just as the Holy One set the heart at the center of the body — the source of the whole body’s vitality, itself bound to the brain in the head — so He set Jerusalem at the center of the settled world, the Temple Mount within it, the courts within that, the Chamber of Hewn Stone, the altar, the Sanctuary, and innermost the Holy of Holies, “where the Shechinah, the Kapores, the Keruvim, and the Ark rest — and here is the heart of all the earth and the world,” from which all places are nourished.Earlier kabbalistic background — Sha'arei Orah, Gates Three–Four, §83: R. Yosef Gikatilla connects Binah, teshuvah, and the cancellation of a sealed decree with remarkable directness. Expounding 'es Mi no'atz va-yevineqhu,' he identifies the Divine name 'Mi' with Binah and calls it 'the place of teshuvah'; he then states: 'therefore, even though a verdict has been sealed above, Israel can annul it through the power of teshuvah that is called Mi.' This is valuable background to the entire movement of Siman 8 and especially to R' Tzadok's placement of the Holy of Holies, the heart, Binah and the gates of teshuvah in one structure. The ordinary verdict belongs to the articulated order of governance; Binah is the womb/root from which that articulation proceeds. To return there is not to overpower Divine judgment from outside but to reach the source at which judgment can be reconfigured within a higher unity. R' Tzadok's image of the Kodesh HaKodashim as 'liba de-kol ar'a ve-alma' adds an anthropological dimension to the same map: the person carries a corresponding hidden sanctuary in the depth of the heart, and 'levavo yavin vashav' is the inward movement toward that place. Sha'arei Orah thus supplies an older kabbalistic precedent for the very claim that might otherwise sound paradoxical: a sealed decree can remain genuinely sealed in the lower order while teshuvah, by ascending to Binah, reaches a level from which the decree can be undone. The cancellation is not a denial of the lower judgment but an appeal to its root.
וְתַמָּן הַלֵּב מֵבִין רָזָא דְּבִינָה עִילָּאָה, שֶׁהוּא ״עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי״ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת שֵׁשׁ קְצָווֹת דְּעָלְמָא דֵּין
And there the heart grasps the secret of the supernal Binah — which is “the World to Come,” above the expansion of the six extremities of this world.

items.h: The theme: “Days were fashioned, and one among them is His” — this is Yom Kippur, a day of a higher rung than the seven “building” days, as Shabbos too is “a taste of Olam Haba.” It is called “Shabbos Shabbason,” and it completes the count of ten, which is a complete stature. Hence it is then a time of teshuvah for all — “his heart understands and repents.”

p: [ז] ״יָמִים יוּצָּרוּ וְלוֹ אֶחָד בָּהֶם״ — זֶה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתָנָא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה פ״א]

“Days were fashioned, and ‘one’ [echad] among them is His” (Tehillim 139:16) — this is Yom Kippur, as they said [in Tana d’Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 1]:1218Tana d’Vei Eliyahu Rabbah, ch. 1: Expounding “days were fashioned, and one of them is His” (Tehillim 139:16), the Midrash identifies the “one” singular day as Yom Kippur (and speaks likewise of Shabbos as “a taste of Olam Haba”) — a day drawn from a rung higher than the seven “building” days of the week.

שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קָבַע בַּשָּׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא דּוּגְמַת הָעוֹלָם [כִּי הוּא הַמְשַׁמֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם שֶׁתַּחַת הַזְּמַן], יוֹם אֶחָד שֶׁהוּא מִמַּדְרֵגָה עֶלְיוֹנָה מִשְּׁאָר יָמִים שֶׁהֵם שֶׁבַע יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן

that Hashem fixed within the year — which is a “likeness of the world” [being what “serves” in the world subject to time] — one day that is of a higher rung than the other days, which are the seven “building” days.1219R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Yisro §1): “a beis din is needed to accept him — for even if he circumcises and accepts upon himself the yoke of the mitzvos, he is not a convert until they immerse him before three; and Aharon and the elders of Israel brought holiness into him so that he could eat in holiness.” Exactly the se’if: Yom Kippur is “Shabbos Shabbason” — a rung above the seven building days — and a rung above is entered only by an act of acceptance, never by mere continuation from below.
וְגַם עַל שַׁבָּת נִדְרָשׁ שָׁם, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן ״מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא״

And [this] is expounded there of Shabbos too, which is likewise “a taste of Olam Haba.”1220R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §18): “but an eclipse of the sun is an evil sign for the nations of the world, whose recompense for their deeds is in the World to Come, and the evil that reaches [them] in this world is according to the array — and they are not [judged so].” Exactly the se’if: the day of the higher rung is Israel’s alone, for only they are governed from above the array — which is why the “one among them that is His” is a day of teshuvah for all of them.

וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים נִקְרָא ״שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן״, כִּי שַׁבָּת הוּא סוֹד ה׳ הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה הַיּוֹנֶקֶת מֵה׳ עֶלְיוֹנָה, וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים סוֹד ה׳ עֶלְיוֹנָה עַצְמָהּ, וְעַל כֵּן אָז זְמַן תְּשׁוּבָה לַכֹּל

And Yom Kippur is called “Shabbos Shabbason”: for Shabbos is the secret of the lower heh, which nurses from the upper heh, while Yom Kippur is the secret of the upper heh itself — and therefore it is then a time of teshuvah for all.1221R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §57): “for in every thing there are two extremes and a middle… and behold, the right itself is likewise divided into these three, as with everything bounded.” Exactly the se’if: the seven “building” days are an order of bounded things, each subdividing further — and Yom Kippur, “Shabbos Shabbason,” stands as the day that is not one of them.Tanya — the two heh's and the two levels of teshuvah (Iggeres HaTeshuvah, ch. 4): The Alter Rebbe opens his deeper explanation of teshuvah with the Zohar's reading of the word itself: 'tashuv hei' — the lower heh gives teshuvah tata'ah and the upper heh gives teshuvah ila'ah. He then maps the Divine Name in the same order used here by R' Tzadok: yud as the concealed point of Chochmah; the first heh as the expansion and revelation of Binah; vav as the downward extension through the six holy middos; and the final heh as Malchus and revealed speech. In the human soul, the same structure appears as concealed intellect, Binah and contemplation in the heart, the love and fear born from that understanding, and their final expression in Torah and mitzvos through speech and deed. This makes R' Tzadok's statement that Shabbos corresponds to the lower heh while Yom Kippur is the upper heh itself much more than a symbolic equivalence. The two heh's mark two locations of return within the same Divine-human structure. Teshuvah tata'ah restores the final, revealed level; teshuvah ila'ah returns the inner life toward the Binah from which the middos and their expression are born. It also explains why the Ten Days culminate on Yom Kippur. The tenth day is not merely the last date in a sequence but the disclosure of the upper root that can gather the differentiated lower levels back into one complete komah. R' Tzadok's 'Shabbos Shabbason' is therefore the Sabbath of the Sabbath: not only rest within the created order, but return of the created order toward its supernal mother-source.
וּמוֹשֶׁכֶת עִמָּהּ כָּל עֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְשׁוּבָה, כִּי כָּל הַדְּבָרִים כְּלוּלִים בְּעֶשֶׂר שֶׁהֵם קוֹמָה שְׁלֵימָה כַּנּוֹדָע
And it draws with it all the Ten Days of Teshuvah, for all things are included in “ten,” which are a complete “stature,” as is known.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים בַּשָּׁנָה הוּא דּוּגְמַת קָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים בָּעוֹלָם, וְלֵב בַּנֶּפֶשׁ, וְשָׁם עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וָשָׁב״
And Yom Kippur in the year is a “likeness” of the Holy of Holies in the world, and of the heart in the soul — and there is the essence of teshuvah, “his heart understands and repents.”
וְהוּא אַחַת מִמִּצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁגַּם זֶה אַחַת מֵחוּקֵי הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁיּוֹעִיל תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁגַּם זֶה מֵחוּקֵי הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁחָקַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעוֹלָמוֹ
And it [teshuvah] is one of the mitzvos of the Torah — for this too is one of the Torah’s “laws,” that teshuvah avails, and this too is one of the laws of Creation that Hashem inscribed in His world.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם בְּהַאי עָלְמָא כְּמוֹ קָדְשֵׁי קֳדָשִׁים בָּעוֹלָם
Except that it is concealed in this world, like the Holy of Holies in the world;

דְּבִזְמַן קְדוּשָּׁתוֹ שֶׁהָיָה שָׁם לֵב הָעוֹלָם הָיָה בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם, דְּ״כָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד״, וַאֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם (מַלְאָכִים) שֶׁדְּמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם כו׳, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי דְּיוֹמָא]

for in the time of its holiness, when the “heart of the world” was there, it was in the ultimate concealment — for “no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting” (Vayikra 16:17)1222Vayikra 16:17: “וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד בְּבֹאוֹ לְכַפֵּר בַּקֹּדֶשׁ עַד צֵאתוֹ” — “and no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting when he enters to make atonement in the Sanctuary, until he comes out.” Meforshim: Rashi, from the Sifra — “no man” excludes even those [angelic beings] “the likeness of whose face was a human face” (cf. Yechezkel 1:10); while the Kohen Gadol makes atonement within, no other being may be present — a place of utter concealment. R’ Tzadok’s use: the Holy of Holies, “the heart of the world,” stood “in the ultimate concealment”; so too teshuvah — though a genuine law of Creation — is hidden in this world, like the unfathomable heart into which only “Hashem searches.”Shelah on Yom Kippur as return of the branches to Binah (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Aseret HaDibrot, Yoma, Torah Ohr §27): The Shelah gives an almost point-for-point parallel to the close of this siman. The first heh of the Divine Name is the supernal mother, he writes, and sin separates the mother from the children; 'great is teshuvah, for the mother returns upon her children — em ha-banim semechah.' 'There in Binah is the root of teshuvah,' and Binah is the secret of Olam Haba. The six upper days/middos are the children: they branch out from Binah and 'el ha-Binah shavim' — to Binah they return. For that reason a person must engage in teshuvah through the days of action and even on Shabbos, so that 'the branches return to their root.' This is precisely R' Tzadok's architecture of seven building days, a higher day, the upper heh, and a complete tenfold stature. The deepest function of Yom Kippur is therefore gathering: scattered acts, middos and days are not merely pardoned one by one; they are returned to the maternal root from which their life originally came. That also clarifies why the Kodesh HaKodashim and the heart are the matching coordinates in olam and nefesh. Both are hidden centers rather than exterior surfaces. The public world sees deeds after they have branched outward; Hashem 'searches the heart,' the concealed point in which their root can be understood and redirected. When R' Tzadok calls teshuvah itself one of the laws of Creation but says that it remains hidden in this world, the Shelah explains the paradox: it is indeed a law, but it is the law of the hidden root — Binah/Olam Haba — from which the visible sevenfold world continually issues and to which it is capable of returning., and even those (angel-like Keruvim) “whose faces resembled [those of men],” etc. [were hidden], as they said [in the Yerushalmi of Yoma].
וְכֵן הַלֵּב בָּאָדָם — ״עָקֹב הַלֵּב מִכֹּל וְעָמוֹק, מִי יֵדָעֶנּוּ״, רַק ״אֲנִי ה׳ חוֹקֵר לֵב״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְנֶאֱמַר ״ה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב״

And likewise the heart in man: “the heart is the most deceitful [and] deep [of all] — who can know it?” (Yirmeyah 17:9), only “I, Hashem, search the heart” (ibid. 10); and it says, “Hashem sees to the heart” (I Shmuel 16:7).
וְכֵן בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְדַּמִּים בּוֹ לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת, שֶׁמִּתְרַחֲקִים מִכָּל תַּאֲוַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַגּוּפָנִי, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הֶעְלֵם הַגּוּפָנִיּוּת

And likewise on Yom Kippur Israel resemble the ministering angels, withdrawing from every desire1223Pirkei d’Rabbi Eliezer 46 (Israel like the ministering angels): expounding Yom Kippur, the Midrash has the accuser Sammael concede before God — “You have one people like the ministering angels of heaven: just as the ministering angels have neither food nor drink, so Israel have neither food nor drink on the Day of Atonement; just as the ministering angels are barefoot, so Israel are barefoot; just as the ministering angels are innocent of all sin, so Israel are innocent of all sin on the Day of Atonement.” Meforshim: the classic reading — Israel’s fast and withdrawal from bodily need make them, for that day, like the angels who neither eat nor sin. R’ Tzadok’s use: “on Yom Kippur Israel resemble the ministering angels, withdrawing from every desire of this physical world” — the “concealment of physicality,” for “from the side of the body there is no access to the holiness of this day,” which is concealed in this world. of this physical world — which is the “concealment of physicality” —
כִּי מִצַּד הַגּוּפָנִיּוּת אֵין שַׁיָּיכוּת לִקְדוּשַּׁת יוֹם הַזֶּה, כִּי הוּא נֶעֱלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

for from the side of physicality there is no access to the holiness of this day, since it is concealed in this world. — And so, whichever way we turn, the eighth greatness of teshuvah proves to be its ascent above the ordered world entirely: it is the heart’s own hidden gate, opened where the six extremities end and the upper heh begins.

sections.en: The essence of teshuvah is in the heart's contemplation

items.h: עיקר התשובה בהרהור הלב.
(The source pages supplied cover the opening se’ifim of Siman 9; the sefer continues beyond them.)

The theme: The essence of teshuvah lies in the heart’s contemplation alone: a person is called a “complete tzaddik” even if a moment before he was wholly wicked. Even verbal viduy, though a Torah mitzvah, is a separate mitzvah and does not hold the teshuvah back. What is required is the resolve not to return to his folly — not that others see an act of teshuvah from him.

p: [א] וְעִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא בְּהִרְהוּר הַלֵּב בִּלְבָד, שֶׁהֲרֵי נִקְרָא בְּכָךְ ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ אֲפִילּוּ הָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם רָשָׁע גָּמוּר, כִּמְבוֹאָר [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:]

And the essence of teshuvah is in the contemplation of the heart alone — for by it one is called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he was, beforehand, wholly wicked, as is explained [in Kiddushin 49b].1224R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Nasso §5): “in Ra’aya Mehemna:”teshuvah — tashuv heh to the vav; that the letter heh is the confession of words… and it is the breath that issues and enters in the mouth."" Exactly the se’if: viduy is a real and distinct mitzvah with its own standing — the heh of the Name — and precisely therefore it is not the thing that makes the teshuvah of the heart valid.Izhbitz-Radzin — the hidden heart and the public act (Beit Yaakov on Torah, Vayigash 1:2): Beit Yaakov distinguishes with unusual precision between a sin that has remained in thought and a sin that has emerged into public action. While the fault remains inward, he writes, it is easier to return and repair, because the matter has not yet become externally fixed; and since what occurred in thought is known only to Hashem, 'teshuvah ba-lev' is sufficient, 'she-ikar ha-teshuvah hu ba-lev' — the essence of teshuvah is in the heart. Once the sin has gone out into deed, however, an additional problem arises: the sinful act is visible to people, while the inward return is hidden from them, 'she-ein adam yode'a mah be-libbo shel chaveiro.' Beit Yaakov is not denying the efficacy of inward teshuvah before Heaven. Rather, he is separating two planes that R' Tzadok also separates throughout this se'if: the inner status known to the Knower of hearts, and the public/legal status that human beings can judge only through revealed conduct. This is an especially close Izhbitz parallel to R' Tzadok's explanation of why a man can become a 'tzaddik gamur' through a genuine thought of teshuvah even though the world may still require observable acts before restoring his credibility. The stronger claim is therefore also the more disciplined one: teshuvah is not made real by public performance, but neither does hidden inward change automatically erase the evidentiary consequences of a deed already visible in the world. The heart is decisive before Hashem; human institutions must still work with the revealed. That distinction preserves both the immediacy of teshuvah and the integrity of halachic judgment.1225Kiddushin 49b: One who betroths a woman “on condition that I am a [complete] tzaddik” — even if he is [known to be] wholly wicked, she is betrothed [from doubt], for perhaps he contemplated teshuvah in his mind [at that moment]. This is R’ Tzadok’s proof that the heart’s contemplation alone can, in an instant, confer the status of a complete tzaddik.Tanya — the heart can turn in an instant, yet the heart has many depths (Likkutei Amarim, ch. 29 §13): The Alter Rebbe writes, 'af she-kevar asah teshuvah nechonah, harei ikar ha-teshuvah ba-lev' — even after one has already made a proper teshuvah, the essence of teshuvah is in the heart — and immediately adds that the heart contains 'many aspects and levels,' varying according to the person, the time and the place. This is a useful complement to R' Tzadok's apparently radical use of Kiddushin 49b. The halachic status can indeed turn in one inward moment: if at this moment the man truly regrets and resolves not to return to his folly, Heaven knows that truth and he is no longer the same rasha he was a moment before. Yet the Tanya prevents us from flattening that moment into a claim that all subsequent avodah has become unnecessary. Precisely because the heart itself has many depths, a real teshuvah can be both complete in the sense relevant to the present moment and still capable of further deepening afterward. R' Tzadok's distinction between the essence of teshuvah and the additional fences required of a baal teshuvah fits this structure well. The resolve of the heart creates the present turn; the continuing work exposes and repairs deeper strata of that same heart so that the turn can remain stable when circumstances change. This also explains why a later relapse need not prove that the earlier teshuvah was false. A genuine inward level may have been reached and then later overwhelmed at another level. The Torah can therefore recognize the truth of the first moment without pretending that the yetzer has ceased to exist.1226Cf. Avodah Zarah 17a: Elazar ben Durdaya, utterly sunk in sin, “placed his head between his knees and wept until his soul departed; and a bas kol went out and said, ‘Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya is destined for the life of the World to Come.’” Rebbi wept: “there is one who acquires his World in many years, and one who acquires his World in a single hour” — the very power of the heart’s teshuvah described here, in which one wholehearted moment of return makes a “complete tzaddik.”
וַאֲפִילּוּ הַוִּידּוּי דְּבָרִים, אַף עַל גַּב דְּהוּא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מִן הַתּוֹרָה, ״וְהִתְוַדּוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר — זֶהוּ מִצְוָה בִּפְנֵי עַצְמָהּ, וְאֵינוֹ מְעַכֵּב הַתְּשׁוּבָה

And even the verbal confession — though it is a positive Torah commandment, “and they shall confess” (Bamidbar 5:7)1227Bamidbar 5:7 (the mitzvah of confession): “וְהִתְוַדּוּ אֶת חַטָּאתָם אֲשֶׁר עָשׂוּ, וְהֵשִׁיב אֶת אֲשָׁמוֹ בְּרֹאשׁוֹ, וַחֲמִישִׁתוֹ יֹסֵף עָלָיו, וְנָתַן לַאֲשֶׁר אָשַׁם לוֹ” — “and they shall confess their sin that they did, and he shall restore his guilt in its principal, add its fifth to it, and give it to the one against whom he was guilty.” Meforshim: the Rambam (Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1) takes this verse as the Torah’s source for the mitzvah of viduy — verbal confession before Hashem. R’ Tzadok’s use: the verbal confession, “though a positive Torah commandment… is a mitzvah in its own right, and does not hold up the teshuvah, whose essence is in the heart alone”; note, too, that the verse itself joins confession to “restoring the theft” — the very case of the thief that the se’if goes on to treat. — that is a mitzvah in its own right, and it does not hold up the teshuvah,
שֶׁעִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב לְבַד, שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט עַל הֶעָבָר וּמַסְכִּים בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לָשׁוּב עוֹד לְכִסְלָה וְשֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד

whose essence is in the heart alone: that he regrets the past, and resolves in his heart not to return again to [his] folly, and not to sin again.1228R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis §12): “for in holiness they correspond to the four legs of the Chariot, which are the three Avos and David HaMelech, who is the fourth leg of the Chariot, as it says in the Zohar.” Exactly the se’if: what makes a man a “complete tzaddik” in an instant is his standing in the Chariot’s own structure — a matter of the heart’s place, not of an act performed.1229Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1: מצות התשובה מן התורה היא עזיבת החטא בלבד… שיגמור בלבו בלב שלם לבל ישוב עוד לכסלה… ולא כדעת ההמון שהתשובה היא התענית… ולכן לא הזכירו הרמב“ם והסמ”ג שום תענית כלל במצות התשובה, רק הוידוי ובקשת מחילה Exactly the se’if’s position, in nearly the same words: the Torah’s mitzvah of teshuvah is the heart’s abandoning of the sin alone — “not as the multitude suppose, that teshuvah is fasting” — and the Rambam records only viduy, never affliction.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא נִגְלָה לְשׁוּם אָדָם וַאֲפִילּוּ לְמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת שֶׁאֵין יוֹדְעִים מַה שֶּׁבַּלֵּב, ״קַמֵּי שְׁמַיָּא גַּלְיָא״
And although it is not revealed to any person — nor even to the ministering angels, who do not know what is in the heart — “before Heaven it is revealed”;
וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ בֶּאֱמֶת, אֲפִילּוּ הִגְדִּיל עֲבֵירוֹת עַד לְמַעְלָה, דִּ״בְכָל רָשָׁע גָּמוּר״ אֲמָרוּהוּ שָׁם, וַאֲפִילּוּ עָבַר עַל כָּל תּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ

and he is truly called a “complete tzaddik,” even if he multiplied transgressions to the utmost — for they said it there [of] “any wholly wicked man,” even one who transgressed the entire Torah.1230R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Toldos §1): “and it appears that he expounded”righteous" of Yaakov, who is the plain “righteous one” — for since a person transgresses a transgression, even a rabbinic one, he is thereafter called wicked, as it says [in Yevamos]." Exactly the se’if: the titles “wicked” and “complete tzaddik” attach instantly and by a hair’s breadth — which is exactly why the heart’s turn alone can move a man from one to the other in a moment.
וּבְבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל וְחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק [בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן לח] כָּתְבוּ דַּאֲפִילּוּ גָּזַל וְלֹא הֶחֱזִיר הַגְּזֵילָה, רַק שֶׁקִּיבֵּל בְּלִבּוֹ לְהַחֲזִיר, מְהַנֵּי

And in the Beis Shmuel and Chelkas Mechokek [Even HaEzer §38] they wrote that even one who stole and did not return the theft — only that he accepted in his heart to return it — it avails [to make him a “tzaddik”];1231Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 38:31: “‘On condition that I am a tzaddik’ — even a wholly wicked man — she is betrothed [from doubt], lest he contemplated teshuvah.” Chelkas Mechokek (there): even though we still see the theft in his hand, and he is not [yet] called a baal teshuvah until he “casts the vermin from his hand” [returns it], nonetheless, since he resolved in his mind to return it, he is also called a “tzaddik,” and out of the doubt of betrothal she is not released [without a get]. Beis Shmuel cites the dispute whether contemplation helps for a robber before he has returned the theft, concluding that if he states he is contemplating teshuvah he is believed.Shelah — inward bittul is the essence, while speech and deed complete the cleansing (Shenei Luchot HaBerit, Bo, Derekh Chayim §4): The Shelah uses bedikas chametz as an extended map of teshuvah. Each limb must be searched in the place where 'chametz' can enter — the mouth for harmful speech and forbidden food, the eyes for improper sight, the heart for evil thought, the head for haughtiness, and so forth — but he then states the governing point: 've-ikar ha-bittul ba-lev, she-ya'aseh teshuvah be-khol libbo' — the essential nullification is in the heart, that he repent with his whole heart, with 'a broken and crushed heart.' He immediately adds that Chazal also instituted verbal bittul, so that the purification should extend through 'speech, thought and deed.' This is exactly the balance required by R' Tzadok's se'if. The heart is not merely one component among three; it is the root-act that makes the return teshuvah. Yet because the human being is a whole embodied person, a heart that has truly turned seeks expression through the mouth and limbs. Viduy and altered conduct therefore do not manufacture an otherwise nonexistent teshuvah, but reveal and carry outward what has already occurred at the root. The Shelah's chametz image also clarifies why R' Tzadok allows a man to be genuinely righteous at the moment of inward return while still requiring special safeguards afterward. One may have performed the essential bittul in the heart and nevertheless still need to search the many rooms through which old habits can re-enter. The root has changed; the house must now be brought into conformity with its new master.
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע [בִּבְרָכוֹת ה:] בְּעוֹבָדָא דְּאַרְבַּע מֵאוֹת דַּנֵּי דְּחַמְרָא, דְּסַגֵּי בְּהָכִי

and so it is implied [in Berachos 5b] in the case of the four hundred jars of wine [of Rav Huna], that this [acceptance] suffices.1232Berachos 5b: Four hundred jars of Rav Huna’s wine turned to vinegar. The Sages hinted that he had withheld from his sharecropper the [customary] share of vine-cuttings; Rav Huna accepted upon himself to give it — whereupon (say some) the vinegar turned back to wine, or (say others) the price of vinegar rose to that of wine. This shows that the acceptance to make restitution already effects the turnaround, before any deed.Chassidic parallel — the difference between inner teshuvah and merely imitating a tzaddik's practices (Maor VaShemesh, Ki Teitzei §13): The Maor VaShemesh attacks the assumption that fasting, self-denial, or copied devotional practices are themselves the essence of repentance. Teshuvah, he argues, is among the realities that preceded the created world; it therefore cannot be identified with an external act belonging only to the world of action. 'Ela bevadai she-ikar ha-teshuvah be-lev nishbar ve-nidkeh' — rather, certainly the essence of teshuvah is in a broken and crushed heart — 'be-chochmah u-ve-binah,' through understanding the greatness of the Creator and breaking the heart before Him. The fasts and disciplines are, in his words, secondary instruments that may help a person arrive at such a heart. He adds an important criterion: when the return is made through 'binas ha-lev,' it has endurance; when one merely copies what a tzaddik did without the tzaddik's daas and inwardness, the practice can disappear as soon as the spiritual weather changes. This complements R' Tzadok's distinction between the immediate reality of teshuvah and the later disciplines of the baal teshuvah. An inward turn is not 'less real' because it precedes visible action; it is more fundamental. But the authenticity of that inward turn is not measured by theatrical severity either. It is measured by whether the person's will has actually changed. Thus the Maor VaShemesh gives a Chassidic language for R' Tzadok's halachic insistence: teshuvah can occur in the heart alone, while the lasting transformation of habit and circumstance remains a subsequent task.

וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כה:] בַּחֲזָרָתָן שֶׁל בַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ לְעִנְיַן נֶאֱמָנוּתוֹ לְעָלְמָא, דְּחוֹשְׁשִׁין שֶׁמָּא לֹא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת וּמְרַמֶּה הַבְּרִיּוֹת, וְצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּרְאוּ בְּנֵי אָדָם מִמֶּנּוּ מַעֲשֵׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בְּפֹעַל

And what they said [in Sanhedrin 25b] regarding the “return” of penitents [breaking their dice and the like] is with respect to his credibility to the public — for we are concerned lest he has not truly repented and is deceiving people, and [so] people need to see from him an actual act of teshuvah.1233Sanhedrin 25b: Those disqualified as witnesses — dice-players, usurers, pigeon-racers, and traders in Sabbatical produce — and “when is their return [accepted]? When they break their dice and retract entirely; when [the usurer] tears up his bonds and would not lend on interest even to a gentile; when [the pigeon-racer] would not do it even in the desert [where there is no fraud].” R’ Tzadok reads these stringencies as pertaining to public credibility, not to the inner teshuvah itself.
וְהַהַגְדָּרוֹת בַּמּוּתָּר שֶׁהִזְכִּירוּ שָׁם הֵם עֵצוֹת טוֹבוֹת לַשָּׁב, שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקְפֵהוּ יִצְרוֹ לְהַבָּא עוֹד
And the “fences in the permitted” that they mentioned there are good counsels for the penitent, that his inclination not overpower him again in the future;

וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לִגְזוֹר עַצְמוֹ גַּם בַּמּוּתָּר, כְּדֵי לְהַרְחִיקוֹ מֵהָאִיסּוּר שֶׁכְּבָר נִכְשַׁל בּוֹ, וּבְנָקֵל יוּכַל הַיֵּצֶר — אֲשֶׁר כְּבָר קָנָה לוֹ קֵן בְּלִבּוֹ וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת — לְהַכְשִׁילוֹ, וְלָכֵן צָרִיךְ לְהַגְדָּרוֹת יְתֵירוֹת

and therefore he must fence himself even in the permitted, so as to distance himself from the prohibition in which he already stumbled — for the inclination, having already made itself a “nest” in his heart and become “master of the house,”1234Sukkah 52b (the yetzer becomes “master of the house”): “Rava said: At first Scripture calls the evil inclination a ‘traveler’; then it calls it a ‘guest’; and finally it calls it ‘man’ — for it has become the master of the house,” as in Nathan’s parable of the poor man’s lamb (“and there came a traveler to the rich man,” II Shmuel 12:4). Meforshim: Rashi — the yetzer enters as a passing wayfarer, is welcomed as a guest, and ends as the resident householder who commands. R’ Tzadok’s use: this is why the penitent “needs extra fences even in the permitted” — for the inclination, “having already made itself a nest in his heart and become master of the house, can easily trip him” again. can easily trip him, and so he needs extra fences.
אֲבָל אֵין זֶה עִיכּוּב לְהַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּשַׁעְתָּהּ, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יַחֲזוֹר וְיַרְשִׁיעַ מַשְׁמַע מֵהַהִיא דְּקִידּוּשִׁין דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָוֵי קִידּוּשִׁין
But this is no impediment to the teshuvah at its moment — for even if he returns and becomes wicked [again], it is implied from that [ruling] in Kiddushin that the betrothal nonetheless holds,
וְאָמְרִינַן דְּנִקְרָא ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבְּלִבּוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה בֶּאֱמֶת, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא שֶׁתְּקָפוֹ יִצְרוֹ
and we say that he is called a “complete tzaddik” through the heart’s contemplation of teshuvah at that moment, truly — and [only] afterward did his inclination overpower him.
וְכֵן בְּדִבְרֵי בֵּית שְׁמוּאֵל וְחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק הַנִּזְכָּר בְּגָזֵל, אֲפִילּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ לֹא הֶחֱזִיר הַגְּזֵילָה וְלֹא הוֹעִיל לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם — הַיְינוּ לִהְיוֹת נִמְחָל לְגַמְרֵי

And likewise in the words of the Beis Shmuel and Chelkas Mechokek mentioned, regarding theft: even if afterward he did not return the theft and did not succeed in rectifying the past — that [failure bears] only on being entirely forgiven;
אֲבָל בִּשְׁעַת הַהִרְהוּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁהָיָה בְּדַעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת לְהַחֲזִיר, הֲרֵי זֶה ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הוּא דְּאִתְרַע, וּכְ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ שֶׁהִרְשִׁיעַ

but at the moment of the contemplation of teshuvah, when it was truly in his mind to return it, he is a “complete tzaddik” at that moment — and afterward it “went bad,” like a complete tzaddik who [then] became wicked.
וְעַיֵּין בִּתְרוּמַת הַדֶּשֶׁן [סִימָן שמ״ט] דְּרַק כְּשֶׁלֹּא הָיָה הוֹכָחָה בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁשָּׁב, אָמְרִינַן ״הוֹכִיחַ סוֹפוֹ עַל תְּחִלָּתוֹ״ דְּלֹא שָׁב כְּלָל בֵּינְתַיִם

And see the Terumas HaDeshen [§349]1235Terumas HaDeshen (Pesakim u-Ketavim §349): where a person’s conduct was wicked both before and after, with no indication at the time of the act that he had repented in between, we apply “his end proves about his beginning” — that he did not repent at all; but where there is indication that he genuinely repented, the momentary teshuvah stands. R’ Tzadok uses this to establish that a later relapse does not retroactively erase a genuine interim teshuvah. that only when there was no proof at the time of the deed that he repented do we say “his end proves about his beginning” — that he did not repent at all in the interim —
כֵּיוָן דִּתְחִלָּתוֹ וְסוֹפוֹ בְּרִשְׁעוּת; אֲבָל אִם הָיָה הוֹכָחָה, דְּנִרְאֶה שֶׁהָאֱמֶת שֶׁשָּׁב, מְהַנֵּי
since his beginning and his end are in wickedness; but if there was proof that it is true that he repented, it avails.

items.h: The theme: The Rambam’s phrase — “the Knower of secrets will testify about him that he will never return to this sin” — cannot be a condition of teshuvah. As Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh explain, he takes Hashem as witness to the truth of his present resolve: that his mind is genuinely not to return. Regret without any thought of abandoning the sin is not teshuvah at all.

p: [ב] וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם [פ״ב מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה ה״ב] ״וְיָעִיד עָלָיו יוֹדֵעַ תַּעֲלוּמוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב לָזֶה הַחֵטְא לְעוֹלָם״ — עַל כָּרְחָךְ כַּוָּונָתוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ בְּכֶסֶף מִשְׁנֶה וְלֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם, דְּיִקַּח לוֹ אֶת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְעֵדוּת

And that which the Rambam wrote [Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2], “and the Knower of secrets will testify about him that he will never return to this sin” — perforce his intent is as the Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh explained there: that he takes Hashem as a witness [upon himself],1236Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: teshuvah is that the sinner abandon his sin, remove it from his thoughts, and resolve in his heart never to repeat it, and regret the past; “and the Knower of secrets will testify about him that he will never return to this sin.” Kesef Mishneh and Lechem Mishneh explain that the Rambam does not mean God literally guarantees the future (which would negate free choice), but that the penitent takes God as witness to the sincerity of his present resolve; R’ Tzadok adopts this and shows their attendant difficulties dissolve.
וְהַיְינוּ לְבָרֵר אֲמִיתּוּת רְצוֹנוֹ אָז, בְּרֶגַע הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּדַעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב

that is, to clarify the truth of his will then, at the moment of teshuvah — that his mind is genuinely not to return.1237R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §2): “Yehudah [offered] this prayer, and he regretted with a broken heart that he had caused this, and returned and said that he was confident that he would be a servant to my lord, that he would not be spoiled in Egypt; and certainly, since this was written in the Torah, the truth is so — that he was confident.” Exactly the se’if: “the Knower of secrets will testify” is not a condition imposed from outside but the confidence of a genuinely broken heart — a present certainty, which Scripture itself is willing to record as true.
וְהַגַּם דְּקוּשְׁיַת לֶחֶם מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם לֹא קָשֶׁה מִידֵי, דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַיְדִיעָה וּבְחִירָה שְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, וּכְשֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת לֹא יֶחֱטָא הֲרֵי יָעִיד עָלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אָז

And although the difficulty of the Lechem Mishneh there is really no difficulty — for [Divine] knowledge and [human] choice are both true, and when he genuinely will not sin, Hashem indeed “testifies” about him then;

וְגַם קוּשְׁיַת כֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם לֹא קָשֶׁה, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר פֵּירוּשׁ ״וְלֹא נֹאמַר [אֱלֹקֵינוּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ]״ וְגוֹמֵר, הַיְינוּ דָּבָר בָּרוּר שֶׁלֹּא נֶאֱמַר עוֹד וְלֹא נַעֲשֶׂה זֶה, וְזֶהוּ כַּוָּונַת לְשׁוֹן ״וְיָעִיד״ כו׳, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּבֵירוּר שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב

and the difficulty of the Kesef Mishneh there is also no difficulty, for one can explain “and we will no longer say [our god to the work of our hands]” (Hoshea 14:4)1238Hoshea 14:4: “אַשּׁוּר לֹא יוֹשִׁיעֵנוּ, עַל סוּס לֹא נִרְכָּב, וְלֹא נֹאמַר עוֹד אֱלֹהֵינוּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה יָדֵינוּ, אֲשֶׁר בְּךָ יְרֻחַם יָתוֹם” — “Assyria shall not save us, we will not ride upon horses, nor will we say any more ‘our god’ to the work of our hands — for in You the orphan finds mercy.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — part of the prophet’s teshuvah-charge (Hoshea 14, “Return, O Israel”): Israel renounce their false supports and their idols. R’ Tzadok’s use: he reads “we will no longer say” as a clarified certainty — that this will not again be said or done; and this is the sense of the Rambam’s “and the Knower of secrets will testify” — not a precondition of the teshuvah, but that the sincerity of the present resolve be made clear.Chassidic clarification of Rambam's knowledge/free-will problem — Be'er Mayim Chaim, Bereshit 3:5:3: The Be'er Mayim Chaim states the paradox in almost the same terms as this se'if: 'vadai sheneihem emes' — both are certainly true. Hashem sees to the end of all generations and knows which road a person will choose, yet 'ein ha-yedi'ah zo machrachat ha-adam' — that knowledge does not compel the person — and human choice remains free. He applies the point to Adam and Chavah in a way that is especially relevant to R' Tzadok's discussion of the Rambam. The serpent's sophistry was to reason from the truth of free choice that they could safely expose themselves to a forbidden test: since Divine foreknowledge does not force them, they could choose well even after eating. The Be'er Mayim Chaim rejects that move sharply. The compatibility of yedi'ah and bechirah never gives a person license to override a revealed command or to rely upon his own future strength; Shlomo's 'I will multiply [wives] and my heart will not turn' is his parallel example of the same mistake. For R' Tzadok this supplies an important boundary around 'the Knower of secrets will testify.' Divine knowledge can truthfully know that a present resolve is genuine without converting the future into coercion. The penitent's obligation remains located in his present choice: at the moment of teshuvah he must abandon the sin without reserving an intention to return to it. What happens later belongs again to the arena of bechirah. Thus 'yedi'ah u-vechirah sheneihem emes' supports R' Tzadok's reading precisely because it refuses both errors — neither making Divine knowledge fictitious nor making human responsibility unreal. to mean a “clear thing” — that this will not again be said or done — and this is the intent of the wording “and He will testify,” that is, that it be clarified that he will not return.1239R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Beshalach §7): “the time for [rectifying] the blemish of the bris is on Shabbos… and they can rectify the blemish — and if all Israel should merit this, they are immediately redeemed; and the essence of the rectification is when he contemplates teshuvah” Exactly the se’if: what is being testified to is the state of the mind at this moment — “the essence of the rectification is when he contemplates” — and not a guarantee about a future that has not occurred.Izhbitz on the narrow human share of choice — without weakening present responsibility (Mei HaShiloach I, Vayeilech §3): The Mei HaShiloach writes that David HaMelech knew deeply that, although bechirah is given into human hands, the portion of independent human action is 'davar mu'at ke-klippas ha-shum' — a small thing, like the skin of garlic — while in the deeper truth 'kol asher chafetz Hashem asah ba-shamayim u-va'aretz.' He connects this awareness to Shabbos and Shemittah: periods in which man is made to stop acting remind him that even when weekday labor resumes he may not say 'kochi ve-otzem yadi.' This is a fitting Izhbitz background to R' Tzadok's insistence that Divine knowledge and human choice are simultaneously true. The Izhbitzer is not using the hidden Divine perspective as a prospective excuse for sin. On the contrary, the whole teaching is designed to break self-attribution after action and to restore the person to dependence upon Hashem. In the present se'if the same distinction is crucial. Before and during the choice, a person must own the small but decisive point that is actually his: he must not keep an intention to sin again. Only after a choice has genuinely been made can the larger Divine frame be contemplated. Read this way, 'ke-klippas ha-shum' does not shrink responsibility; it identifies where responsibility truly sits. The human point may be narrow, but it is exactly the point at which teshuvah begins. Once that point turns, the whole person can be assisted and redirected from Above.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה מִתְּנַאי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, וְרַק כְּשֶׁבְּדַעְתּוֹ גַּם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה לַחֲזוֹר וְלַחֲטוֹא, הֲרֵי לֹא שָׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ כְּלָל

In any case, it is impossible that this be a condition of the teshuvah; rather, [the rule is] only that when it is in his mind, even at the time of the act, to return and to sin [again], then he has not repented wholeheartedly at all.
וְזֶהוּ מִדָּתָן שֶׁל ״פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַמְּלֵאִים חֲרָטָה״, הַיְינוּ חֲרָטָה לְבַד בְּלֹא עֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא

And this is the trait of “the sinners of Israel who are full of regret” (cf. Eruvin 19a) — that is, regret alone, without abandoning the sin;1240Eruvin 19a (and parallels) speaks of “the sinners of Israel who are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate.” R’ Tzadok invokes the type of the penitent who is “full of regret” — sorrow for a spent pleasure — to contrast it with true teshuvah, which requires azivas ha-cheit, the resolve to forsake the sin going forward.
כִּי רַק עַל הֶעָבָר שֶׁכְּבָר חָלְפָה הֲנָאָתוֹ וְאֵינָהּ עוֹד מִתְחָרֵט, אֲבָל אֵין דַּעְתּוֹ לַעֲזוֹב לְהַבָּא הֲנָאָה זוֹ אִם יִזְדַּמֵּן לְפָנָיו אֲפִילּוּ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע

for only over the past — whose pleasure has already passed and is no more — does he regret; but he has no intent to abandon this pleasure in the future, should it present itself before him, even at that [very] moment.
וְזֶה אֵין עָלֶיהָ שֵׁם תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל, רַק חֲרָטָה לְבַד, שֶׁאַחַר הַחֵטְא שֶׁעָבְרָה הֲנָאָתוֹ מִתְחָרֵט חֲרָטָה בְּעָלְמָא בְּלֹא מַחְשֶׁבֶת עֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא
And this bears no name of “teshuvah” at all, only regret: that after the sin, its pleasure having passed, he regrets a mere regret, without any thought of abandoning the sin.
וְהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב הַמּוֹעִיל, הַיְינוּ בַּעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא ״שֶׁשָּׁב לַה׳״

And the heart’s contemplation of teshuvah that avails is [the one] with abandoning the sin — for that is what is called “returning to Hashem.”1241R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §152): “There should be, from the depths of his heart, a complete arousal of azivas hacheit [the abandonment of the sin] — to forsake all matters of this world even for a single moment; that suffices.” This is the se’if’s dividing line: regret alone is not teshuvah; the heart’s contemplation avails only when it is joined to abandoning the sin — which is “returning to Hashem.”

items.h: The theme: This concerns the talmid chacham “who commits a sin at night” — night being the time of desire’s sins, and the hour before sleep being fitting for teshuvah, when one tastes a sixtieth of death. What is asked is not regret alone but complete teshuvah. And at its own moment his teshuvah was genuine, even if he afterward returned to his wont.

p: [ג] וּמִדָּתָן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים, דְּעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה בַּלַּיְלָה

And the trait of the talmidei chachamim, [of one] “who commits a sin at night”1242R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomot §11): “they pass by way of the passage of the kelipos of that nation and are clothed in the garment of those kelipos; and only when they come to Eretz Yisrael do they strip it off from themselves.” Exactly the se’if: the talmid chacham who “commits a sin at night” is not disclosing his essence but a garment picked up in passage — which is why it can be stripped, and why the hour before sleep is its time. —
[שֶׁאָז הוּא זְמַן עֲבֵירוֹת דְּתַאֲוֹת בִּזְנוּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״בְּנֶשֶׁף בְּעֶרֶב יוֹם״ וְגוֹמֵר, דְּאֵין רוֹאֶה; וּבְשַׁבָּת (פט:) אִיתָא ״דַּל פַּלְגָא דְּלֵילָא״ דְּאָז אֵין חֲטָאִין

[for that is the time of the sins of desire, in immorality, as it says, “in the twilight, in the evening of day” (Mishlei 7:9), when none sees; and in Shabbos 89b it is stated “subtract half the night,” for then there is no sinning;1243Shabbos 89b (“subtract half the night”) and Mishlei 7:9 (“in the twilight, in the evening of day”) mark night as the time of concealed sins of desire. Megillah 28a: before sleep [Mar Zutra] would say, “may his Master forgive everyone who has troubled me.” Shabbos 153a: “Repent one day before your death” — i.e., every day, since one never knows. Sleep being “one-sixtieth of death,” nightfall is the fitting hour of nightly reckoning and return.
וּבַזוֹהַר הַגִּירְסָא אִיפְּכָא: תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁעָבַר עֲבֵירָה בַּיּוֹם אַל תְּהַרְהֵר בַּלַּיְלָה, וְנִרְאֶה דְּדֶרֶךְ לָשׁוּב בַּלַּיְלָה לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁינָה
and in the Zohar the version is reversed: a talmid chacham who transgressed by day — do not suspect [him] at night; and it appears that the way is to repent at night, before sleep,

כְּדוֹן שֶׁאִיתָא (מְגִילָּה כח.) כִּי סָלֵיק לְפוּרְיֵיהּ אָמַר ״שְׁרֵי לֵיהּ מָארֵיהּ לְכָל מַאן דְּצַעֲרַן״, כִּי אָז טָעֵים טַעְמָא דְּמוֹתָא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזוֹהַר, וּבַהוֹרָאָה דְּהוּא אַחַת מִשִּׁשִּׁים בַּמִּיתָה

as it is stated (Megillah 28a) that when he would go up to his bed he would say, “may his Master forgive everyone who has troubled me” — for then one “tastes a taste of death,” as they said in the Zohar, and by the ruling [that sleep] is one-sixtieth of death,1244R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Tetzaveh §2): “"lest they become sunk in evil" — but in truth you shall have greater elevation when you know of good and evil, and afterward return to the good — and you shall have added praise; and this is what is said, "for on the day you eat… and you shall be as God, knowing good and evil."” Exactly the se’if: the sin at night is not the end of the matter — the return that follows it yields “added praise,” which is why complete teshuvah, and not regret alone, is what is asked.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא (שַׁבָּת קנג.) ״שׁוּב יוֹם אֶחָד לִפְנֵי מִיתָתְךָ״, וְאָז שְׁעַת הַחֶשְׁבּוֹן לְמָארֵי דְּחוּשְׁבְּנָא עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם]
and this is in the manner of “repent one day before your death” (Shabbos 153a) — and then is the hour of reckoning, for the “master of the reckoning,” over all that he did on that day] —
אַל תְּהַרְהֵר אַחֲרָיו בַּיּוֹם, וַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת יט.], לֹא בַּחֲרָטָה לְבַד, רַק בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְמוּרָה

[the rule is:] do not suspect him afterward, by day — he has surely done teshuvah, as they said [Berachos 19a] — and not with regret alone, but with complete teshuvah.1245R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Ki Tavo §15): “that although David HaMelech was lowly in his own eyes, and called himself "poor and destitute, a worm and not a man" — nonetheless he called himself a chassid.” Exactly the se’if: the talmid chacham who sinned at night truly repented at its moment, and the lowliness he feels does not cancel the standing he genuinely holds.1246Berachos 19a: “If you see a talmid chacham transgress by night, do not think ill of him by day, for he has surely repented.” R’ Tzadok stresses this means a complete teshuvah in the interim, not mere regret — and probes the limiting case of a scholar who is seen to relapse.Me'or Einayim — 'one who comes to purify is helped' means added daas is drawn after the initial arousal (Toldos §32): The Me'or Einayim explains 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in lo' through the structure of daas. A person first makes an awakening from below; then, precisely because he has come to purify himself, Heaven draws to him an added daas 'me-olam ha-ta'anug' so that he will be strengthened in his avodah. The help is therefore not a substitute for the first movement of the person but a response to it. This matches R' Tzadok's answer to the apparent difficulty in this se'if. If a talmid chacham later falls again, one cannot reason backward that no help was given and therefore the prior teshuvah must have been false. The maxim describes a living sequence: first a real human turn, then assistance that expands the person's capacity; later, new concealment or a new trial can still occur and require a renewed awakening. The Me'or Einayim even describes daas as sometimes being withdrawn so that it can later return in greater measure. That Chassidic pattern gives conceptual room for what R' Tzadok is defending halachically — a genuine spiritual state at one time need not be invalidated by a different state at another time. The truth of the earlier return is judged at the moment in which the heart actually turned.
וַאֲפִילּוּ רוֹאֵהוּ חוֹזֵר וְשׁוֹנֶה אַחַר כָּךְ בְּחֶטְאוֹ
And even [if] you see him returning and repeating his sin afterward —

[וּמִיהוּ אֶפְשָׁר דְּהָךְ ״אַל תְּהַרְהֵר״ הַיְינוּ קוֹדֶם שֶׁרוֹאֵהוּ שׁוֹנֶה בְּחֵטְא, דְּמַחֲזִיקִין שֶׁשָּׁב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד; אֲבָל כְּשֶׁרוֹאֵהוּ שׁוֹנֶה וּתְחִלָּתוֹ וְסוֹפוֹ בְּחֵטְא, אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם לֹא מַחֲזִיקִין שֶׁשָּׁב בִּדְלֵיכָּא הוֹכָחָה

[though it is possible that this “do not suspect” is [only] before you see him repeating the sin — [when] we presume he repented and will not sin again; but when you see him repeating, his beginning and end in sin, it is possible that even of a talmid chacham we do not presume that he repented, absent proof;
אוֹ עַל כָּל פָּנִים אַחַר פַּעַם שְׁנִיָּה שֶׁשָּׁנָה בְּחֵטְא רַשַּׁאי לְהַרְהֵר אַחֲרָיו, דַּהֲרֵי ״עָבַר וְשָׁנָה נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ כְּהֶיתֵּר״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא פו:)

or at least, after the second time he repeated the sin, one may suspect him, for “[once] he transgressed and repeated, it becomes to him as though permitted,” as they said (Yoma 86b);1247Yoma 86b: “Once a person has transgressed and repeated the transgression, it becomes to him as though permitted [na’aseh lo k’heter]” — he no longer senses it as a sin. R’ Tzadok weighs this in deciding whether, after a visible relapse, one may still presume that a scholar (or penitent) had truly repented in the interim.

אֶלָּא דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר אִם שָׁב בֵּינְתַיִם בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְמוּרָה, דְּהָוֵי לֵיהּ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״, כְּשֶׁחוֹזֵר וְחוֹטֵא אֵין עָלָיו דִּין ״עָבַר וְשָׁנָה״ רַק כִּתְחִלַּת חֵטְא, דְּהָרִאשׁוֹנָה כְּבָר נִמְחֲקָה בַּתְּשׁוּבָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שֶׁבֵּינְתַיִם

except that one can say: if he repented in the interim with complete teshuvah — being at that moment a “complete tzaddik” — then when he returns and sins, the law of “transgressed and repeated” does not apply to him, but [it is] only as a beginning of sin, for the first was already erased by the prior teshuvah in between;
וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ הַמַּתְחִיל בְּחֵטְא, וְגַם כֵּן ״אַל תְּהַרְהֵר״, דְּגַם אַחַר כָּךְ יָשׁוּב, וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן]
and this is like a “complete tzaddik” who begins to sin, of whom too “do not suspect,” for afterward too he will repent — and this requires further study] —
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּשַׁעְתּוֹ שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת
nonetheless, at its moment he truly repented.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁ״הַבָּא לִיטָּהֵר מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא לח סע״ב], אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר: מִדְּלֹא סִיְּיעוּהוּ עַל כָּרְחָךְ לֹא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת

And even though “one who comes to purify [himself] is helped,” as they said [Yoma 38b], one might say: since they did not help him, perforce he did not truly repent —1248Yoma 38b: “One who comes to purify himself is helped [from Heaven].” R’ Tzadok resolves the apparent objection: the “help” is granted at the very instant of coming to purify; a later relapse (permitted by Heaven as a test) does not retroactively cancel the genuine teshuvah of that instant.Izhbitz — human effort in the revealed area, Divine help in the hidden area (Mei HaShiloach II, Nitzavim §3): On 'ha-nistaros la-Hashem Elokeinu ve-ha-niglos lanu u-levaneinu,' the Mei HaShiloach warns a person not to declare himself already clarified merely because he can blame the atmosphere around him for what he feels. Instead, 'yishtadel ha-adam leva'er ha-ra mi-kirbo ve-livdok ad makom she-yado maga'as ba-niglos' — a person must strive to remove the evil from within himself and examine as far as his hand reaches in the revealed matters — 've-Hashem yitbarach ya'azor lo ba-nistaros' — and Hashem will help him in the hidden matters. This is perhaps the cleanest Izhbitz formulation of 'ha-ba le-taher mesay'in oso' for the present discussion. The person is not asked to control every hidden layer of psyche and circumstance before his teshuvah can count. He is asked to do honestly what lies within the reach of his revealed choice. Once he turns there, the hidden work is not abandoned; it becomes the arena of Divine assistance. That makes R' Tzadok's position both demanding and merciful. The thought of teshuvah is sufficient when it is true because the human being is judged on the point genuinely in his hand; but sincerity requires that he actually use that point rather than invoke hidden causes as an excuse. The later assistance belongs to Hashem, and a later test does not retroactively erase the earlier human act of turning.

וְהָךְ ״מְסַיְּיעִין״ הַיְינוּ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע שֶׁבָּא לִיטָּהֵר, וְאִלְמָלֵא בָּא לְיָדוֹ אָז בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה — אֵין הָכִי נָמֵי שֶׁהָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזְרוֹ וְיָכוֹל לוֹ

[but the answer is:] this “helping” is at that very instant that he comes to purify; and had a matter of transgression come to his hand then, at that instant — indeed the Holy One would have helped him, and he would have prevailed.
וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּגַם בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע לֹא יָכוֹל, אִם הוּא גָּמַר בְּלִבּוֹ לְהִתְקוֹמֵם נֶגֶד יִצְרוֹ בְּכָל כֹּחוֹ
And even if you say that even at that instant he could not [prevail] — if he resolved in his heart to stand against his inclination with all his strength,

אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁוַּדַּאי אִלּוּ הָיָה בֶּאֱמֶת בְּכָל כֹּחוֹ הָיָה יָכוֹל לוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם אַחַר כָּךְ יִצְרוֹ אַלְבְּשֵׁיהּ וַהֲסִיתוֹ לִדְבַר עֲבֵירָה, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא נִדְחָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שֶׁהָיְתָה בֶּאֱמֶת

though certainly, had it truly been “with all his strength,” he would have prevailed — nonetheless, if afterward his inclination “clothed” [overpowered] him and enticed him to a transgression, one may say that his earlier teshuvah, which was genuine, is not thereby nullified;
דְּגַם בְּהַהִיא דְּקִידּוּשִׁין לֹא חִילְּקוּ, אֲפִילּוּ רוֹאֵהוּ תֵּיכֶף בְּרֶגַע אַחַר הַקִּידּוּשִׁין חוֹטֵא וּמַרְשִׁיעַ כְּדַרְכּוֹ
for even in that [ruling] of Kiddushin they did not distinguish — even [if] you see him, immediately, a moment after the betrothal, sinning and acting wickedly as [is] his wont.

וּמַה דְּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם לֹא סִיְּיעוּהוּ אַחַר שֶׁהֵחֵל לִיטָּהֵר בְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב עַד שֶׁיֵּשׁ עָלָיו שֵׁם ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ — הַרְבֵּה תְּשׁוּבוֹת לַמָּקוֹם, שֶׁהָיָה הַמִּשְׁפָּט לְנַסּוֹתוֹ וְשֶׁלֹּא לְסַיְּיעוֹ

And that Heaven did not help him after he began to purify himself with the heart’s contemplation of teshuvah — [to the point] that the name “complete tzaddik” [already] rests upon him — [to this] there are many answers with the Omnipresent: that the judgment was to test him and not to help him;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִדְחָה מִשֵּׁם ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע דְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה
and nonetheless he is not removed from [the status of] “complete tzaddik” at that moment of the heart’s contemplation of teshuvah.

items.h: The theme: “Who is the true baal teshuvah?” By our text, the same sin must present itself twice and he refrain — for two times establish a chazakah that he will not stumble again. The Rif, Rosh and Rambam lack “a first and a second time.” Once the trial has been withstood, the name of the thing becomes fixed and enduring in him.

p: [ד] וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה״ כו׳, עַיֵּין שָׁם [בְּיוֹמָא פו:] — כְּפִי גִּירְסָא שֶׁלָּנוּ צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּזְדַּמֵּן שְׁנֵי פְּעָמִים וְיִנָּצֵל, דִּבְתְרֵי הָוֵי חֲזָקָה שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל עוֹד

And what they said, “who is [the true] baal teshuvah?” etc., see there [Yoma 86b]: by our text, [the sin] must present itself twice and he be saved — for with two [times] it is a chazakah that he will not stumble again.1249R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §114): "“and behold, three flocks of sheep” — he thought perhaps it is chance that this one wishes to sell his flock and gathered them; but in three times it is a chazakah — that is, that in three times it is impossible that it be chance." Exactly the se’if’s reasoning: a chazakah is precisely the exclusion of chance — which is why the repetition of the same trial, and not a single refraining, is what establishes that he will not stumble again.1250Yoma 86b: “Who is a [true] baal teshuvah? Rav Yehudah said: one to whose hand a matter of transgression comes a first time and a second time, and he is saved from it” — Rav Yehudah demonstrated: “the same woman, the same season, the same place.” Our text has “a first and a second time,” establishing a chazakah; the Rif, Rosh, and Rambam read that one occasion suffices.
וְרִי״ף וְרֹא״שׁ וְרַמְבַּ״ם לֹא גָּרְסֵי ״פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹנָה וּשְׁנִיָּה״, וּבְפַעַם אַחַת סַגֵּי, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּזְדַּמֵּן לְיָדוֹ וְיִנָּצֵל

And the Rif, Rosh, and Rambam do not have the reading “a first and a second time,” and once suffices — yet in any case [the sin] must come to his hand and he be saved.1251R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Bereishis §11): "“[the Holy One does not join His Name] to a person in this world, but only to one who has repented of his sin”" Exactly the se’if: the title “baal teshuvah” is a name that becomes fixed and enduring in a man — and it is only upon the one who has actually turned that the Name is joined.

כְּבָר יִישְּׁבָהּ רַמְבַּ״ם [בְּרֵישׁ פ״ב מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה] דְּזֶהוּ לְעִנְיַן תְּשׁוּבָה גְמוּרָה וּמִן הַמּוּבְחָר, וְכָתַב ״וְאִם כו׳ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה מְעוּלָּה מוֹעֶלֶת הִיא״

The Rambam already resolved [Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1] that this is with respect to complete and choicest teshuvah, and he wrote, “and if [he repented only in old age, when he can no longer do what he once did], though it is not the choicest teshuvah, it avails.”1252Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1: “What is complete teshuvah? One who has the opportunity to repeat a sin he committed, and it is within his power to do it, yet he refrains and does not — out of teshuvah, not fear or incapacity. And even if he repented only in his old age, when he can no longer do what he once did — though it is not the choicest teshuvah, it avails, and he is a baal teshuvah.”
וְאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא בְּשֵׁם זֶה ״בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה״
And one can also say that what they said, “who is a baal teshuvah,” means [when] he is called by this name, “baal teshuvah”;
וּקְרִיאַת הַשֵּׁם הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עַצְמוּתוֹ כָּךְ, דְּאָז נַעֲשָׂה לוֹ שֵׁם הָעֶצֶם קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּים
and “being called a name” means that his very essence becomes so — that then the name of the essence becomes fixed and enduring in him.

וְכָל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלְּשַׁעְתּוֹ הוּא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת וְהוּא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה לְשָׁעָה, כֵּיוָן דְּאֵינוֹ בָּטוּחַ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקַלְקֵל וְיַחֲזוֹר לְסוּרוֹ, אֵינוֹ נִקְבָּע לוֹ לְשֵׁם עַצְמוֹ

And every baal teshuvah — though for his moment he truly repents and is a baal teshuvah for the hour — since he is not secure that he will not spoil and return to his ways, [the name] is not fixed to him as his essential name,
עַד שֶׁיָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה פַּעַם אַחַת וּשְׁנִיָּה כְּגִירְסָא דִּילָן, דְּבָזֶה בָּטוּחַ דְּלֹא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
until a matter of transgression comes to his hand a first and a second time, per our text — for by this he is secure that he will not sin again.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא לח:] מִקְּרָא דְּ״רַגְלֵי חֲסִידָיו יִשְׁמוֹר״, דְּ״חָסִיד״ נִקְרָא כְּשֶׁמִּתְגַּבֵּר יוֹתֵר מִצַּדִּיק

And as they said [Yoma 38b] from the verse “the feet of His pious ones He guards” (I Shmuel 2:9)1253I Shmuel 2:9: “רַגְלֵי חֲסִידָיו יִשְׁמֹר, וּרְשָׁעִים בַּחֹשֶׁךְ יִדָּמּוּ, כִּי לֹא בְכֹחַ יִגְבַּר אִישׁ” — “He guards the feet of His pious ones, and the wicked are silenced in darkness; for not by [his own] strength does a man prevail” (from Chana’s prayer). Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak — God protects the steps of the devout, while the wicked perish; a man triumphs not by his own power but by Hashem’s help. R’ Tzadok’s use: from “the feet of His pious ones [chasidav] He guards” the Sages derive that one is called a “chassid” when he strengthens himself beyond a mere tzaddik; and the verse’s close, “not by strength does a man prevail,” is why the one saved from sin is called “mighty of strength” (Kiddushin 40a) — his victory is by God’s help. — for one is called a “chassid” when he strengthens [himself] more than a [mere] tzaddik.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּאוֹתִיּוֹת דְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא] עַל פָּסוּק ״וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ״ ״אֵלּוּ רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעֲתִידִים כו׳״, כִּי יוֹתֵר תּוֹקֶף גְּבוּרָה בְּנִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר צָרִיךְ הָרָשָׁע כְּשֶׁשָּׁב

And therefore they said [in Osios d’Rabbi Akiva] on the verse “and Your pious ones shall sing” (Tehillim 132:9)1254Tehillim 132:9 (and 132:16): “כֹּהֲנֶיךָ יִלְבְּשׁוּ צֶדֶק, וַחֲסִידֶיךָ יְרַנֵּנוּ” — “Your priests shall clothe themselves in righteousness, and Your pious ones shall sing.” Meforshim: Rashi and the Radak read it of the Temple — its priests and its devout rejoicing before Hashem. R’ Tzadok’s use: he cites the derashah [Osios d’Rabbi Akiva] that “and Your pious ones shall sing” refers to “the wicked of Israel who are destined [to be counted among the pious]” — for the returning wicked, needing greater might to subdue the yetzer, becomes God’s “chasid,” His exceedingly pious one, “the pious of Hashem” like “the cedars of Hashem.” — “these are the wicked of Israel who are destined [to be called ‘pious’]” — for the wicked man, when he repents, needs greater might in conquering the inclination;
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״חֲסִידֶיךָ״, פֵּירוּשׁ ״חֲסִידֵי ה׳״ הַיְינוּ מוּפְלְגֵי הַחֲסִידוּת, כְּמוֹ ״עֲצֵי ה׳״ ״אַרְזֵי ה׳״, וּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁמַּסְמִיךְ אֶל ה׳ לְהַפְלָגַת הַדָּבָר בְּיוֹתֵר

and therefore he is called “Your pious ones” — meaning “the pious of Hashem,” that is, the exceedingly pious, like “the trees of Hashem,” “the cedars of Hashem,” and everywhere that [Scripture] attaches [a thing] to Hashem to [express] the superlative of the matter.

וּמִי שֶׁבָּא דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל נִקְרָא [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מ רע״א] ״גִּבּוֹרֵי כֹחַ״, וּבָזֶה מוּבְטָח לְהִשָּׁמֵר מֵעַתָּה, עַד שֶׁקָּנָה לוֹ שֵׁם עַצְמוֹ שֶׁל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה

And one to whom a matter of transgression came and who was saved is called [Kiddushin 40a] “mighty of strength”1255Kiddushin 40a: “Anyone to whom a matter of forbidden intercourse presented itself and who was saved from it — a miracle is performed for him, as it says, ‘mighty of strength, who do His word’ (Tehillim 103:20) — such as Rabbi Tzadok and his colleagues” (whose accounts of withstanding temptation follow there). Hence one who faces the trial and is saved is a “mighty one of strength,” secured against relapse.Kedushas Levi — why the baal teshuvah can stand higher without manufacturing a new test (Kedushat Levi, Bereshit §24): R. Levi Yitzchak explains the superiority of the baal teshuvah through the work of transforming darkness itself: the fallen sparks are raised through Torah and mitzvos, and when they return to their root their light is intensified, 'ke-yisron ha-or min ha-choshech.' He therefore invokes Chazal's teaching that 'in the place where baalei teshuvah stand' the completely righteous cannot stand, comparing it to a son who wandered far from his father and whose return produces an added delight. This sharpens R. Tzadok's use here of the person who actually withstood the recurring temptation. The advantage is not that sin or exposure to sin is intrinsically valuable; the advantage lies in the transformation of a darkness that already existed. A baal teshuvah has confronted an energy that once carried him away and has now redirected that same life toward Hashem. The 'gevurah' praised in Kiddushin is therefore the strength of conversion and return, not the pursuit of danger. In the language of this se'if, repeated resistance can establish the enduring name 'baal teshuvah' because it shows that the earlier force no longer governs him; Kedushas Levi supplies the inner mechanism — the very distance becomes material for a stronger attachment once it has genuinely been brought back to its source. — and by this he is assured to be guarded from now on, until, through this, he has acquired for himself the essential name of “baal teshuvah.”1256R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §115): “"and He will give me bread to eat and a garment to wear" — this Yaakov added to what Hashem had said to him… for Yaakov was in doubt about himself, whether he was a completely righteous man.” Exactly the se’if: the whole question of the chazakah is whether a man may be secure about himself — and even Yaakov withheld that security until it had been established.

items.h: The theme: The essential reading: when they said “such as” — the same woman, the same place, the same circumstance — they meant that his teshuvah should be of that quality, such that were the trial to present itself he would refrain. It need not actually befall him in fact. On this reading the Rambam’s words stand, and all of it is “the choicest teshuvah.”

p: [ה] וְהָעִיקָּר נִרְאֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״כְּגוֹן״ כו׳ — פֵּירוּשׁ ״כְּגוֹן זֶה״, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ בַּלֵּב כְּגוֹן וְאוֹפֶן הַזֶּה שֶׁל מִי שֶׁבָּא כו׳

And the essential [reading] appears [to be]: what they said, “such as [k’gon]” etc. — meaning “such as this” — that his teshuvah of the heart be of the manner and mode of one who came [to the sin and was saved],
שֶׁכָּל כָּךְ מִתְחָרֵט וְשָׁב מִן הַדָּבָר עַד שֶׁאִם הָיָה מִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ אוֹתָהּ כו׳ הָיָה נִמְנָע — אֲבָל אֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לוֹ כֵּן בְּפֹעַל דַּוְקָא

[such] that he so regrets and turns from the matter, that were “that [same woman, place, circumstance]” to present itself to him he would refrain — but it need not [actually] befall him so, in fact.1257R’ Tzadok — parallel (Pri Tzaddik, Vayigash §14): "“or heard” — and to understand this, for it is written “indeed God heard, He hearkened to the voice of my prayer”… but the intent is not upon the sound heard by a person’s ear, only the cry that issues from the innermost point [of the heart]." Exactly the se’if: the teshuvah must be “of that quality” — measured at the innermost point — and therefore need not actually be tested by an outward recurrence at all.
וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה בָּאַחֲרוֹנָה וּבְיוֹם מוֹתוֹ, וְלֹא נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ כְּלָל דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִם הָיְתָה בְּכָל לִבּוֹ
And therefore, even if he did teshuvah at the last, on the day of his death, and no matter of transgression presented itself to him at all — nonetheless, if it was with all his heart —

וַאֲפִילּוּ נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ וְלֹא עָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן, אִם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה הָיְתָה בְּכָל לִבּוֹ וְאִלּוּ נִזְדַּמֵּן לוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע לֹא הָיָה חוֹטֵא — הֲרֵי זֶה בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה, וְאֵין צוֹרֶךְ לְדִבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם בָּזֶה, וְהַכֹּל תְּשׁוּבָה מְעוּלָּה
