and even if [the trial] presented itself afterward and he did not withstand it — if at the time [of teshuvah] it was with all his heart, and had it presented itself at that moment he would not have sinned — he is a complete baal teshuvah at that time, and there is no need for the Rambam’s words here, and it is all “choicest teshuvah.”1258R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah II §9): “Eretz Yisrael, which is the foundation of the world, as it says”from Zion, the perfection of beauty“… and therefore it is said several times in the Torah that the conquest of the Land depends on the worthiness of the deeds.” Exactly the se’if: what is required is a quality of readiness, not the occurrence of a particular event — the standing is measured by worthiness, and the trial is its index rather than its cause.

וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה יט.] ״אַשְׁרֵי שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה תְשׁוּבָה כְּשֶׁהוּא אִישׁ״, הַיְינוּ דִּבְזִקְנוּתוֹ אֵין לוֹ כֹּחַ בִּמְזִמּוֹת לְבָבוֹ לְהִתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ לָשׁוּב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת

And what they said [Avodah Zarah 19a], “fortunate is he who does teshuvah while he is a man [i.e., young and vigorous]”1259Avodah Zarah 19a: On “fortunate is the man who fears Hashem” (Tehillim 112:1): “‘fortunate is the man’ — and not the woman? Rav Amram said in the name of Rav: fortunate is one who does teshuvah while he is [still] a man [ish] — [in his vigor, before old age]. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: fortunate is one who overcomes his inclination like a man.” R’ Tzadok invokes the first reading: youthful strength is needed for wholehearted teshuvah. — [means] that in his old age he lacks the strength, in the schemes of his heart, to overcome his inclination [so as] to repent with all his heart, truly.

וּבִפְרָט שֶׁנִּשְׁתָּרֵשׁ בַּחֵטְא, וְכָתַב [בְּלִיקּוּטֵי מַהֲרִי״ל] דַּעֲבֵירָה שֶׁעָבְרוּ עָלָיו רוֹב שְׁנוֹתָיו מְלַפַּפְתּוֹ וְהוֹלֶכֶת, וְעַיֵּין בְּשַׁעֲרֵי תְשׁוּבָה [סוֹף שַׁעַר ב] ט׳ טְעָמִים בָּזֶה

And especially [when] he has become rooted in the sin — and it is written [in Likutei Maharil] that a transgression which most of his years have “passed over him [in]” wraps around him and goes [with him] — and see the Shaarei Teshuvah [end of Shaar 2], nine reasons in this [matter].1260Shaarei Teshuvah (Rabbeinu Yonah), end of Shaar 2: nine reasons not to defer teshuvah to old age — e.g., worldly distractions never cease; desire is never sated; one’s time steadily shortens; delay itself becomes an added sin; the yetzer grows stronger with time; one may die first; old sins are forgotten; teshuvah from a weakened desire earns less reward; and in old age one lacks the vigor to renew wholehearted resolve. Likutei Maharil: a sin that has “passed over” most of one’s years clings and follows.
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁשָּׁב, תְּשׁוּבָה מְעוּלָּה הוּא, וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לֵיהּ גַּבֵּיהּ בְּאוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק
But when he does repent, it is “choicest teshuvah,” even though you cannot find it with him “in that circumstance” [that a trial actually recurred].

וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר בְּפֹעַל מַמָּשׁ, דְּהֵיכִי מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לָהּ, וּבִשְׁעַת עֲבֵירָה בַּתְּחִלָּה נִתְיַיחֵד עִמָּהּ וְאַחַר כָּךְ שְׁאָר הִתְקָרְבוּת, וַהֲרֵי אָסוּר לְהִתְיַיחֵד

And perforce one must say that [Yoma 86b] does not mean “in fact” literally — for how could you find it? At the time of the [original] transgression he first secluded himself with her and thereafter [came] the rest of the intimacy — and behold, it is [now] forbidden to seclude!1261The prohibition of yichud [seclusion] (Kiddushin 80b): the Mishnah and Gemara forbid a man to be secluded with a woman forbidden to him — and with men “steeped in immorality” a woman may “not be secluded even with ten.” Meforshim: yichud with the arayos is a Torah prohibition, derived (Avodah Zarah 36b) from “your brother, the son of your mother [may entice you]” (Devarim 13:7) — [implying] a son may be secluded with his mother, but no other man with any of the forbidden relations; and yichud with an unmarried woman was decreed by David’s court after the affair of Amnon and Tamar (Sanhedrin 21a). R’ Tzadok’s use: this is his proof that Yoma 86b’s “k’gon” — “one who came to the same woman, place, and circumstance [and refrained]” — cannot describe a literal recurrence, “for would it enter your mind that the prohibition of seclusion was permitted for a baal teshuvah?!” Hence it means a teshuvah of that quality, not an actual repeated trial.
וְכִי סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דְּהוּתַּר אִיסּוּר יִחוּד לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, וְלֹא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לָהּ ״בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם״
Would it enter your mind that the prohibition of seclusion was permitted for a baal teshuvah?! — and [so] you cannot find it “in that [same] place.”
וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם אֵירַע שֶׁהָיְתָה עִמּוֹ בְּיִחוּד, צָרִיךְ לִבְרוֹחַ מִיָּד, וְדָבָר זֶה חוֹבָה עַל כָּל אָדָם, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן עַל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִגְדּוֹר עַצְמוֹ בְּיוֹתֵר
And even if it happened that she was with him in seclusion, he must flee at once — and this is an obligation upon every person, all the more upon a baal teshuvah, who must fence himself the more.
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין [קז רע״א] דְּלְעוֹלָם לֹא יָבִיא אָדָם עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּשֵׁל, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה

And in Sanhedrin [107a]: a person should never bring himself to a test, lest he stumble1262Sanhedrin 107a: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: a person should never bring himself to a test [nisayon], for David king of Israel brought himself to a test and stumbled.” David had asked why we say “God of Abraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov” but not “God of David,” and was told, “they were tested by Me, and you have not been”; he asked to be tested — and fell in the matter of Bathsheba. This is the proof-text against a penitent’s courting temptation.Izhbitz-Radzin safeguard against courting a test — Sod Yesharim, Shabbos HaGadol 3:1: Sod Yesharim gives a remarkably explicit formulation of the distinction R' Tzadok is laboring to preserve here. A nisayon can indeed raise a person: 'mi-sibas nisayon nis'aleh madreigas ha-adam,' because through the concealment of the test one who stands in it can discover that Hashem was present even within the hester. Yet the sefer immediately insists that this truth is only retrospective. 'Ha-adam mi-tzido eino rashai le-hachnis atzmo be-nisayon' — from his own side a person is not permitted to place himself into a test — and this remains so 'even in a case where he would stand in the test.' That is why we pray 'al tevi'einu lo lidei nisayon': a person is not authorized to desire a spiritual ascent purchased by deliberately entering danger. Only 'after Hashem has brought a person into some test without his knowledge' should he understand that the trial can be for his elevation and refuse to rebel against it. This is an exceptionally exact Radzin complement to R' Tzadok's rejection of a literal requirement that the baal teshuvah recreate the scene of his sin. The same hidden-Providence doctrine that can reveal holiness within a test also forbids turning that doctrine into a prospective heter. The trial may be read as Divine after it has arrived from Above; it may not be manufactured below in order to prove one's righteousness. Thus the deepest Izhbitz language of hashgachah itself becomes the strongest protection of ordinary halachic responsibility. — all the more a baal teshuvah.
וְכֵן הוּא בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים [סִימָן קס״ז] דְּלֹא יֹאמַר אָדָם ״הֲרֵי אֲנִי בְּאוֹתָהּ כו׳, אֲקַיֵּים זֶה״, דְּשֶׁמָּא תִּתְרַצֶּה, וְלֹא אָמְרוּ שֶׁיָּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְעָוֹן, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And so it is in the Sefer Chassidim [§167]: a person should not say, “here I am with that [same woman, place, circumstance] — I will fulfill this [test],” lest she consent [and he sin]; and they did not say that one should bring himself to iniquity — see there.1263Sefer Chassidim §167: a person should not say, “since [the Sages spoke of] ‘the same woman, the same place, the same season,’ I will place myself in that very situation [to prove my teshuvah]” — lest the woman consent and he come to sin; they never said one should bring himself to iniquity.
וְעַל כָּרְחָךְ דְּהַכַּוָּונָה רַק שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה יִהְיֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִבּוֹ בָּטוּחַ שֶׁיִּצְרוֹ בְּיָדוֹ לִכְפּוֹתוֹ, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא יִבְטַח עַל עַצְמוֹ בְּפֹעַל

And perforce the intent is only that the teshuvah be of this manner — that his heart be confident that his inclination is in his hand, to subdue it — but nonetheless he should not rely on himself in fact.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהַהִתְרַחֲקוּת לְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא מַכִּיר בְּיִצְרוֹ, וּמִי שֶׁבּוֹטֵחַ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ אֵין צָרִיךְ כָּל כָּךְ הַרְחָקָה
And although the [degree of] distancing [required] is for each one according to what he recognizes of his own inclination — and one who [truly] trusts himself does not need so much distancing —
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרִיטְבָ״א [בְּסוֹף קִידּוּשִׁין] מֵהָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן יָתֵיב אַשַּׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה, וְעוֹד טוּבֵי, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּאֲרִיכוּת

as the Ritva wrote [end of Kiddushin] from [the case] that R’ Yochanan would sit at the gates of [the women’s] immersion [-place], and many other [such cases] — see there at length —1264Ritva, end of Kiddushin: one who truly recognizes that his inclination is subdued and stirs no improper thought is permitted [certain leniencies of proximity] — as R’ Yochanan would sit at the gates of the immersion place without concern — but this is only for a great, self-knowing individual, and “not all may trust their inclinations,” as the very cases in the sugya show. So too Tosafos, Shabbos 13a (s.v. “u-fliga”) and Niddah 13a. R’ Tzadok stresses these are fences for the never-fallen, never license for a penitent to court a test.
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ בְּתוֹסָפוֹת [שַׁבָּת יג סע״א] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וּפְלִיגָא״, וְכֵן בְּנִדָּה [יג סע״א], עַיֵּין שָׁם
and similarly in Tosafos [Shabbos 13a, s.v. “u-fliga”], and likewise in Niddah [13a] — see there —
זֶהוּ בְּהַרְחָקָה בְּעָלְמָא, מִשּׁוּם גֶּדֶר וּסְיָיג, וְלֹא לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן, דְּזֶה אָסוּר, דְּאָז הַיֵּצֶר גּוֹבֵר
this is [only] as a mere distancing, for a fence and a hedge — and not to bring oneself to a test, which is forbidden, for then the inclination overpowers —
וְאָנוּ מְבַקְּשִׁין בְּכָל יוֹם ״אַל תְּבִיאֵנוּ לִידֵי [נִסָּיוֹן]״ כו׳

and we ask each day, “do not bring us to [a test],” etc.1265R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Soferim §33): “[Once] they have given him a taste of Olam Haba, he comes to a test — for the Holy One tests only ‘whole vessels’ [kankanim sheleimim] (Bereishis Rabbah 32); and the King of the world is the ‘form of man upon the throne,’ the likeness of Yaakov Avinu — that is, the hidden root of all the souls of Israel in every generation.” The se’if’s caution: a person may not bring himself to a test; God Himself “tests only whole vessels” — and never the baal teshuvah, who has tasted sin and dares not trust himself.

וְגַם זֶה בְּ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם, וְלֹא בְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא; וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁכְּבָר שָׁב בְּכָל לִבּוֹ, וַדַּאי אֵין לוֹ לִבְטוֹחַ בְּעַצְמוֹ כְּלָל

And even this [leniency of a fence] is for a “complete tzaddik” who never sinned — and not for a baal teshuvah, who has already tasted the taste of sin; and although it seems to him that he has already repented with all his heart, he certainly must not trust himself at all.

items.h: The theme: A personal aside: R’ Tzadok recalls a sefer of Rav Yeiva citing the Baal Shem Tov, in the name of the Heavenly Academy, permitting a baal teshuvah to bring himself to such a test — and likewise the Kli Yakar. He notes that ordinary people may not bring themselves to a test, unlike the baal teshuvah; and that in any case this cannot be said as a practical ruling.

p: [ו] [וְאִיבְּרָא נְהִירְנָא זֶה זְמַן רַב שֶׁהָיָה בְּיָדִי סֵפֶר רַב יֵיבָא, וְרָאִיתִי שָׁם בִּתְהִלִּים עַל פָּסוּק ״הֶחֱלִיק אֵלָיו בְּעֵינָיו״, מֵבִיא מֵהַבַּעַל שֵׁם טוֹב בְּשֵׁם ״מְתִיבְתָּא דִּרְקִיעַ״ לְהַתִּיר לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה לִידֵי כָּךְ

[And indeed I recall — this [was] long ago — that I had in hand a sefer of Rav Yeiva, and I saw there, on Tehillim, on the verse “he flatters himself in his own eyes” (Tehillim 36:3), that he brings from the Baal Shem Tov, in the name of “the Heavenly Academy,” to permit a baal teshuvah to bring himself to such [a test].1266R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §33): “the difference between a pesi [simple one] and a fool and his other names: that pesi is from the root”enticed," who believes everything; and therefore it is called “simpleness,” which is only a matter of faith." Exactly the se’if: bringing oneself to a test is a matter of what one may rely on — and the whole question is whether such reliance is faith or mere credulity, which is why it “cannot be said as practical ruling.”

וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי דְּגַם בְּסֵפֶר כְּלִי יָקָר [רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת חוּקַת] כָּתַב כֵּן, וּפֵירֵשׁ בְּשֵׁם ״יֵשׁ מְפָרְשִׁים״ בָּזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין אֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמוֹד״

And I later saw that in the sefer Kli Yakar [start of Parashas Chukas] he wrote so too, and explained thereby, in the name of “some interpreters,” what they said: “in the place where masters of teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand” —1267Kli Yakar, Chukas: the baal teshuvah’s might must be shown “in the very place he sinned”; and “some interpret” thereby “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand” — for the penitent must return to the place and circumstance of his sin, which is forbidden to a complete tzaddik (to whom seclusion and self-testing are barred). R’ Tzadok records this but declines to rule it as practical halachah.Baal Shem Tov — a safer explanation of 'where baalei teshuvah stand' (Baal Shem Tov, Nitzavim §6:1): A teaching recorded in the name of the Baal Shem Tov explains the higher standing of the baal teshuvah without requiring him to recreate the scene of sin. The baal teshuvah, it says, has already known the 'heat and enthusiasm' of transgression; when he returns and turns to Torah and mitzvos, he can perform them with an unusually intense warmth and desire because he already knows what powerful yearning feels like. The tzaddik who never entered that terrain does not possess that same experiential transformation. This provides an important contextual counterweight to the striking report R. Tzadok records here from Rav Yeiva and the Kli Yakar. The special power of the baal teshuvah can be understood as the redirection of an already-experienced force, not as permission to create a forbidden encounter in order to prove himself. That reading also fits R. Tzadok's own hesitation — 'tzarich iyun me'od ve-lo nitan le-iamer klal' as a practical rule — and his later move to David's use of permitted desire to break the yetzer. The Chassidic advantage of teshuvah is thus preserved in its strongest form while ordinary halachic responsibility remains intact: one transforms the fire one has already known; one does not light a new forbidden fire for the sake of extinguishing it.1268Cf. Sanhedrin 107a: David said before the Holy One, “examine me, Hashem, and test me” (Tehillim 26:2) — and did not withstand the trial [of Bas-Sheva], conceding afterward that he had not prevailed. This is R’ Tzadok’s caution here: even the greatest should not bring themselves to a test — as we pray daily, “do not bring us into the hands of a trial” (Berachos 60b).
הַיְינוּ דְּהֵם אֲסוּרִים לְהִתְיַיחֵד וּלְהָבִיא עַצְמָם לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

that is, that they [the wholly righteous] are forbidden to seclude and to bring themselves to a test, unlike the baal teshuvah — see there.1269R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMinchah I §51): “only that she exerts herself to subdue her inclination, until they said,”[four] things require strengthening“… and in the Midrash, the three times that one pushes away a convert.” Exactly the se’if: the baal teshuvah is like the convert who is pushed away and returns — the pushing is not a rejection but the established way such a standing is proved.
וְאֵין כָּעֵת הַסֵּפֶר אִתִּי לָדַעַת בּוּרְיָין שֶׁל דְּבָרִים וּבֵירוּרָן, וּבְעִיקַּר דָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ לְעִיּוּן מְאוֹד וְלֹא נִיתַּן לֵיאָמֵר כְּלָל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

And the sefer is not with me now, to know the clear and settled [reading] of the matters; and in the essence of this matter, it requires great study, and “cannot be said [as practical ruling] at all,” as I wrote.

וְאִם הוּתַּר, הַיְינוּ רַק בְּעִנְיָנֵי הֶיתֵּר, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה [בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי פ״ב דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין הל״ג] בְּעֶשֶׂר פִּלַגְשִׁים שֶׁהָיָה מְקַלְּעָן וּמְקַשְּׁטָן (וּמַכְנִיסָן לְפָנָיו בְּכָל יוֹם)

And if it was permitted, it is only in permitted matters — in the manner it is stated of David HaMelech [Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin, ch. 2, halachah 3] regarding the ten concubines, whom he would have braided and adorned (and brought before him each day),1270Yerushalmi, Sanhedrin 2:3: [in the aggadic discussion of David] David would have his ten concubines braided and adorned and brought before him daily, and would say to his evil inclination, “you desired a thing forbidden to you — by your life, I will [instead] desire with you a thing permitted to you” — mastering the yetzer through the permitted, not the forbidden.
וְאָמַר לְיִצְרוֹ הָרָע (תָּאַבְתָּ דָּבָר הָאָסוּר לְךָ — חַיֶּיךָ) ״אֲנִי מִתְאַבֶּךָ דָּבָר הַמּוּתָּר לְךָ״

and he would say to his evil inclination, “[you] craved a thing forbidden to you — by your life, I will crave [with you] a thing permitted to you.”1271R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §73): “when a person rectifies what he sinned, Hashem arranges for him that same season and that same place, so that it should be a teshuvah of the [exact] measure — for there are certainly things a person is forbidden to bring himself to, as in [the case of] that woman.” Exactly the se’if’s question: the recurrence of the trial is arranged from Above rather than engineered by the person — which is precisely why the leniency “cannot be said as practical ruling.”

וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, לִגְדּוֹר עַצְמוֹ בַּמּוּתָּר, וּבָזֶה יָכוֹל לְהָבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְנִסָּיוֹן — וְלֹא בְּדָבָר הָאָסוּר כְּלָל וּ״בְאוֹתָהּ״ כו׳; וְאוּלַי גַּם הוּא רָצָה לוֹמַר כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא, בְּדָבָר הַמּוּתָּר

And this is the trait of a baal teshuvah — to fence himself in the permitted — and in this he may bring himself to a test; but not in a forbidden matter at all, nor “with that [same woman]” etc.; and perhaps [the Kli Yakar] too meant [only] in such a manner, in a permitted matter.

וְהִנֵּה גַּם דָּבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ בֵּירוּר גָּמוּר, כִּי הַיֵּצֶר חוֹשֵׁק וְגוֹבֵר רַק בְּדָבָר הָאָסוּר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין עה.] דְּלָא מְיַיתְּבָא דַּעְתֵּיהּ בְּהֶיתֵּר, אֶלָּא בְּ״מַיִם גְּנוּבִים״

And behold, even this is no complete clarification — for the inclination craves and overpowers only in the forbidden, as they said [Sanhedrin 75a] that “his mind is not settled” by the permitted, but [only] by “stolen waters [that are sweet]” (Mishlei 9:17);1272Sanhedrin 75a: a man’s mind is “not settled” [satisfied] by what is permitted him, but craves specifically what is forbidden — as “stolen waters are sweet” (Mishlei 9:17). Hence, R’ Tzadok notes, David’s parading of the permitted concubines was not a genuine “test” of his yetzer (which craves only the forbidden), but a way to provoke and break the evil inclination through the good.
וְלֹא עָשָׂה זֶה לְבֵירוּר תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ וּלְנִסָּיוֹן, רַק לְהַרְגִּיז יֵצֶר טוֹב עַל יֵצֶר הָרָע וְלִשְׁבּוֹר אוֹתוֹ]

and [David] did this not to clarify his teshuvah or as a test, but [only] “to enrage the good inclination against the evil inclination,” and to break it1273Berachos 5a (“rouse the good inclination against the evil”): “Reish Lakish said: One should always rouse [enrage] his good inclination against his evil inclination, as it says, ‘Tremble and do not sin’ (Tehillim 4:5); if he subdues it — good, and if not, let him engage in Torah… recite the Shema… remember the day of death.” Meforshim: Rashi — one wages war upon the yetzer by rousing the good inclination against it, with Torah, the Shema, and the thought of death as its weapons. R’ Tzadok’s use: David’s parading the ten concubines before him was “not to clarify his teshuvah or as a test, but to enrage the good inclination against the evil inclination, and to break it” — the roused good yetzer shatters the evil one, which craves only the forbidden..] — With this personal, unresolved note the section as given closes: the deepest reaches of the penitent’s self-testing R’ Tzadok deliberately leaves b’iyun, as a matter too fine to legislate.

sections.en: Teshuvah from love transforms sin into merits

items.h: תשובה מאהבה מתקנת את החטא והופכתו לזכויות.

Opening statement of the siman: שְׁלוֹשָׁה מִינֵי תְשׁוּבָה הֵם (מֵאַהֲבָה, מִיִּרְאָה, וּמִיִּסּוּרִין), כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁבֵּיאֲרוּ לָנוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה [בְּיוֹמָא פו סע״א] — There are three kinds of teshuvah — [teshuvah] from love, from fear, and through sufferings — as the Sages of blessed memory explained to us [in Yoma 86a]. [1: Yoma 86a–b: R’ Chama b’Rabbi Chanina raised a contradiction: it is written “Return, O wayward [shovavim] sons” (Yirmeyah 3:22) — implying you were wayward from the outset — yet it is written “I will heal your backslidings” (Hoshea 14:5), implying the sin is still remembered. He resolved: “No difficulty — here [all forgiven as if never sinned] from love; there [the sin still remembered] from fear.” Rav Yehudah likewise contrasted “Return, wayward sons, I will heal your backslidings” (repentance open to all) with “for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family” (Yirmeyah 3:14, only select individuals): “No difficulty — here, through suffering [available to all]; there, from love or from fear [attained by few].” Rashi (s.v. me’ikara shovavim): “when you repent I reckon it upon you as if the beginning of the sin was through youthfulness and folly and waywardness”; (s.v. from love): “one who repents from love — his sin is uprooted from its very beginning.” And earlier (86b): “Reish Lakish said: Great is teshuvah, for willful sins become for a person like merits” — this being teshuvah from love.]

The theme: The first — teshuvah from love — rectifies the past, for through it “willful sins become like merits.” R’ Tzadok’s key move: teshuvah from love reveals retroactively that even at the moment of the sin the person did not act “from his heart” but through a mere “spirit of folly” (Sotah 3a). For every Jew’s heart is truly “to Heaven” (the Holy One is “the heart of Israel”), and his sins are only the thorns encircling the rose, never touching its fragrant core.

p: הָרִאשׁוֹן: תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, וּבָזֶה מְתַקֵּן אֶת הַקּוֹדֵם, וְעַיֵּין [שָׁם:] דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

The first: teshuvah from love — and by it he rectifies the past; and see [there, Yoma 86b] that with teshuvah from love, “willful sins become like merits.”2Yoma 86b: “Reish Lakish said: Great is teshuvah, for [through it] willful sins [zedonos] become for a person like merits [zechuyos], as it says, ‘and when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, upon them [aleihem] he shall live’ (Yechezkel 33:19).” The Gemara resolves that this is teshuvah from love; teshuvah from fear renders the willful sins [only] like unwitting errors. This is the foundational source of the entire siman.
וְאִם כֵּן פֵּירַשׁ״י שֶׁכָּתַב בְּד״ה ״דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא״ דְּ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ — כְּאִלּוּ תְּחִלַּת חֵטְא עַל יְדֵי נַעֲרוּת כו׳, צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן לִכְאוֹרָה
If so, Rashi’s comment (s.v. “d’me’ikara”) — that “shovavim” [means it is reckoned] “as if the beginning of the sin was through youthfulness,” etc. — requires study, at first glance.
[וִיעוּיַּן מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְקַמָּן רֵישׁ סִימָן י״א לְפָרֵשׁ בְּעִנְיָן אַחֵר, וְדִבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י צָרִיךְ יִישּׁוּב]
[And see what I wrote below, start of Siman 11, to explain [it] in another way; and Rashi’s words require settling.]

וְנִרְאֶה דְּ״מֵעִיקָּרָא שׁוֹבָבִים״ הַכַּוָּנָה קוֹדֶם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּעַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה נִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם שְׁעַת הַחֵטְא שֶׁקּוֹדֶם הַתְּשׁוּבָה לֹא עֲשָׂאוֹ מִלִּבּוֹ כְּלָל, רַק מַעֲשֵׂה נַעֲרוּת וּשְׁטוּת בְּעָלְמָא

And it appears that “me’ikara shovavim” means before the teshuvah: that through teshuvah from love it is clarified that even the moment of the sin3R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §107): “They said in Sotah (3a), ‘a person does not transgress unless a spirit of folly [ruach shtus] has entered him’ — and that is ‘a strange god,’ of which the Zohar (II 103a) says ‘it is castrated and bears no fruit,’ and the Arizal explained that it has no da’as. Therefore Moshe Rabbeinu, who is the secret of da’as, is its rectification.” Exactly the se’if’s move: the sin is never the act of the true self but of a passing “folly”; the fragrant “rose” of the Jewish heart is untouched., before the teshuvah, he did not do “from his heart” at all — only an act of “youthfulness and mere folly” —
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹטָה ג.] דְּאֵין אָדָם עוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן נִכְנָס [בּוֹ] רוּחַ שְׁטוּת

as they said [in Sotah 3a], “a person does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly [ruach shtus] has entered him.”4Sotah 3a: “Reish Lakish said: a man does not commit a transgression unless a spirit of folly [ruach shtus] enters him, as it says, ‘if any man’s wife goes aside [tisteh]’ (Bamidbar 5:12)” — read tishteh, from shtus, folly. R’ Tzadok takes this as a general truth of every Jew: the sin is never from the true self but from a passing “folly” overlaying a heart that is essentially “to Heaven.”

וְשָׁם אֲמָרוּהוּ דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל עַל כָּל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, לְפִי שֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לִבָּן לַשָּׁמַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשהש״ר] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְלִבִּי עֵר״ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל

And there they said it as a general rule of every Jew — for in truth “the heart of all Israel is to Heaven,” as they said [in Shir HaShirim Rabbah] on the verse “and my heart is awake” (Shir HaShirim 5:2), that “the Holy One is the heart of Israel.”5Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2; Tehillim 73:26; Resisei Layla §44; Machshavos Charutz §4 — “the Holy One is the heart of Israel”: The Midrash reads “I am asleep, but my heart is awake” as Knesses Yisrael’s confession that even when she is “asleep” from particular mitzvos or from the final redemption, an inner heart remains awake; R’ Chiya bar Abba identifies that heart with Hashem from “the Rock of my heart and my portion.” Rav Tzadok develops this into a doctrine of the Jewish root: Resisei Layla states that even deeply sinful Jews remain attached to Hashem in the depths of the heart, and Machshavos Charutz explains that the “sleep” of imagination does not reach that innermost point. The Midrash itself does not say that sinful acts are innocent; the claim that they do not define the deepest self is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis and is precisely what makes teshuvah possible.
וּבִבְרָכוֹת [יז.] ״גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ (לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ), וּמִי מְעַכֵּב — שְׂאוֹר (שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת)״, וְהוּא הָרוּחַ שְׁטוּת

And in Berachos [17a], “it is revealed and known [before You] that our will is to do Your will — and what prevents [it]? — the ‘leaven in the dough’ [and the subjugation to the kingdoms]” — and that [leaven] is the “spirit of folly.”6Berachos 17a; Rambam, Hilchos Gerushin 2:20; Resisei Layla §44 — the essential will beneath the “leaven”: The prayer in Berachos distinguishes Israel’s underlying will — “our will is to do Your will” — from the forces that obstruct it, the leaven in the dough and political subjugation. The Rambam applies a related principle in halachah: when a Jew who must perform a mitzvah is compelled until he says “I want,” the coercion subdues the yetzer that had overpowered his true will to be part of Israel and observe the mitzvos. Resisei Layla explicitly joins the Rambam’s formulation to Berachos and to Rav Tzadok’s teaching about the depths of the Jewish heart. This does not excuse wrongdoing or remove responsibility; it explains why the obstructing layer can be overcome and why sincere teshuvah can reveal a will that was concealed rather than create an entirely foreign identity.7Berachos 17a: “It is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will; and what prevents [it]? — the leaven in the dough [se’or she-ba’isah] and the subjugation to the kingdoms.” R’ Tzadok identifies this “leaven” — the yetzer working from outside the true self — with the “spirit of folly” of Sotah 3a.

וְעַל כָּךְ אָמַר [סַנְהֶדְרִין מד.] דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא — יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא, מָשָׁל לַאֲסָא דְּקָאֵי בֵּינֵי חִילְפֵי, שֶׁמֵּעַצְמוּת לֵב אִישׁ הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִי לְעוֹלָם מֵרִיחַ רֵיחַ טוֹב כַּאֲסָא

And concerning this they said [Sanhedrin 44a], “even though he has sinned, he is [still] a Jew” — a parable to “a myrtle standing among thorns [chilfei]” — for from the very essence of the heart of a Jewish man there always wafts a good fragrance, like a myrtle.8Sanhedrin 44a: On Achan — “‘Israel has sinned’ (Yehoshua 7:11): R’ Abba bar Zavda said, even though [the people] sinned, [they are still called] ‘Israel.’ Rabbi Abba said: this is as people say, ‘a myrtle [asa], though it stands among thorns [chilfei], is [still] called a myrtle.’” The Jew’s essence, like the myrtle’s fragrance, is untouched by the surrounding thorns of sin.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בב״ר וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין לז.] עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיָּרַח אֶת רֵיחַ בְּגָדָיו״ — ״רֵיחַ בּוֹגְדָיו״, וְהַחֲטָאִים הֵם רַק דֻּגְמַת חוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים אֶת הַשּׁוֹשַׁנָּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כְּשׁוֹשַׁנָּה (בֵּין הַחוֹחִים)״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְהַחוֹחַ עוֹקְצָהּ לְפִי שָׁעָה

and as they said [in Bereishis Rabbah and Sanhedrin 37a] on the verse “and he smelled the fragrance of his garments [begadav]” — [read] “the fragrance of his traitors [bogdav]”9Sanhedrin 37a (and Bereishis Rabbah 65): On “and he smelled the fragrance of his garments [begadav] and blessed him” (Bereishis 27:27) — “do not read begadav [his garments], but bogdav [his traitors]” — [teaching] that even the “traitors” among Israel are full of good deeds. R’ Tzadok: the “good fragrance” of the Jewish soul is never lost; the sins are only “thorns” around the rose. — and the sins are only like the thorns that surround the rose, as it says, “like a rose [among the thorns]” (Shir HaShirim 2:2), the thorn pricking it [only] for a moment.10Sanhedrin 44a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1; Resisei Layla §44 — the myrtle remains a myrtle: “Even though he sinned, he is Israel” preserves covenantal identity; it does not pronounce the sin permitted or already forgiven. Peri Tzadik reads this as part of the redemption’s promise: even a wicked child born into Israel cannot remove himself from the sanctity of Israel, and ultimately “none shall be cast away” without rectification. Resisei Layla similarly explains that the myrtle’s name and inner fragrance remain because the deepest heart is still rooted in Hashem. These parallels clarify Rav Tzadok’s image of thorns surrounding the rose: sin can wound, obscure, and require judgment and teshuvah, yet it does not become the essential definition of the Jewish soul.
וְלֶעָתִיד יְבוֹרַר זֶה בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁ״יְּבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, כִּי ״כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ״ שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַלֹּבֶן וְהַבְּהִירוּת

And in the Future this will be clarified in all Israel — that “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none” (Yirmeyah 50:20) — for “though [your sins be as scarlet] they shall become white as snow” (Yeshayah 1:18), which is the ultimate of whiteness and radiance, —
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
meaning, that they become like merits.

וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה זוֹכֶה לָזֶה, דְּנִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם מִקּוֹדֶם בִּשְׁעַת הַחֵטְא הָיָה רַק שׁוֹבָבוּת וּמַעֲשֵׂה נַעֲרוּת, וְלֹא זָדוֹן גָּמוּר, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה נַעֲשָׂה עוֹד כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And in this world, one who merits to repent from love merits this — for it is clarified that even beforehand, at the moment of the sin, it was only “waywardness and an act of youth,” and not full willful sin; and through this, after the teshuvah, it becomes further “like merits.”11Yirmeyahu 50:20; Yeshayahu 1:18; Yoma 86b; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40; Machshavos Charutz §4 — future clarification and sins becoming merits: The prophets promise that Israel’s iniquity will ultimately be sought and not found and that scarlet sins can become white as snow; Yoma distinguishes teshuvah from love, through which willful sins become merits, from teshuvah from fear, through which they become unwitting errors. Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 describes the deepest teshuvah as illumination that discloses how the entire history of the fall lay within divine knowledge, while Machshavos Charutz §4 says that in the future Israel’s sins will be clarified as having been ordered from Creation and transformed like an aveirah lishmah. This is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic synthesis, not the literal wording of the verses or Gemara. At the level of human choice the act remains forbidden and accountable; only through actual teshuvah can its place in the larger divine purpose be disclosed and redirected into merit.
וּמַהֲרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת [שָׁם:] תָּמַהּ עַל זֶה אֵיךְ חוֹטֵא נִשְׂכָּר, וְנִדְחַק דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁמּוֹסִיף זְכֻיּוֹת

And the Maharsha, in Chiddushei Aggados [there, Yoma 86b], wondered at this — “how is a sinner rewarded?” — and forced [an answer], that it means [only] “that he adds merits.”12Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados (Yoma 86b): On “willful sins become like merits,” the Maharsha raises the difficulty — how can a sinner be rewarded [for his sin]? — and answers, [with some difficulty,] that it means the penitent thereby “adds merits.” R’ Tzadok proposes a further reason: the power of the baal teshuvah, who has tasted sin and returned, is greater, for he must overcome the yetzer more — so the sin itself is retroactively the very impetus of his higher rung.

וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁכֹּחַ הַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא וְשָׁב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר [שֶׁצָּרִיךְ הִתְגַּבְּרוּת נֶגֶד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בְּיוֹתֵר], וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם [פ״ז מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה ה״ד]

But he could also have said [it is] because the power of the baal teshuvah — who has already tasted the taste of sin and returned to Hashem — is greater [for he needs a greater overcoming against the evil inclination], as the Rambam wrote [Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4].13Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4: “Let not a baal teshuvah imagine that he is distant from the level of the righteous because of the sins and transgressions he committed. It is not so — rather, he is beloved and dear before the Creator as if he had never sinned. Moreover, his reward is great, for he has tasted the taste of sin and separated from it and conquered his inclination. The Sages said: ‘In the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand’ — their level is greater than those who never sinned, for they subdue their inclination more than they.”
וְזֶה טַעַם מַאן דְּאָמַר [בִּבְרָכוֹת לד:] דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּדוֹל מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר, וְעַיֵּין בְּסֵפֶר הַיָּשָׁר הַמְיוּחָס לְרַבֵּינוּ תָּם [שַׁעַר י׳] עַיֵּין שָׁם

And this is the reasoning of the one who says [Berachos 34b] that “a baal teshuvah is greater than a complete tzaddik”; and see the Sefer HaYashar attributed to Rabbeinu Tam [Shaar 10] — see there.14Sefer HaYashar (attributed to Rabbeinu Tam), Shaar 10: complete teshuvah purifies the wicked of all his sins, making him “like a day-old infant.” On “in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand” (Berachos 34b), it offers several readings — including that the true one is that a baal teshuvah whose heart is now as firm as a tzaddik’s, having been upright, strayed, and returned, has “doubled his righteousness” and is “more honored than the tzaddik who never sinned.”

items.h: The theme: The Gemara’s wording is precise: the willful sins themselves become merits. For a sin done “for its own sake” (aveirah lishmah) is reckoned a mitzvah, on the model of “a mitzvah not for its own sake, from which one comes to its own sake.” Had the person intended it so, it would have been a mitzvah from the outset (“a time to act for Hashem”).

p: [ב] אֲבָל לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מְבוֹאָר דְּהַזְּדוֹנוֹת עַצְמָן נַעֲשִׂין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וּכְפֵירַשׁ״י דַּ״עֲלֵיהֶם״ מַשְׁמַע עַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה אַף עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת

But the language of the Gemara is explicit that the willful sins themselves become “like merits” — and as Rashi explained, “aleihem” [“merits” is stated upon them] implies [it is reckoned] upon everything he did, even upon the transgressions.15Yoma 86b; Yechezkel 33:19; Rashi on Yoma 86b — “upon them” includes the former transgressions: The Gemara derives sins becoming merits from “when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, upon them he shall live.” Rashi explains “upon them” to mean upon everything he did, “even upon the transgressions.” The primary source therefore supports more than the addition of new merits: under teshuvah from love, the former acts themselves enter the transformed accounting. Rav Tzadok’s further claim — that their hidden role in the person’s ascent is revealed retroactively — is an interpretation of this wording, not a statement that the acts were permissible when committed.

כִּי נֶחְשָׁב עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ דַּחֲשִׁיבָא מִצְוָה [בְּנָזִיר כג:], וּכְמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לִשְׁמָהּ, הָכִי נָמֵי מִתּוֹךְ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ בָּא לְמִצְוָה לִשְׁמָהּ

For it is reckoned “a transgression for its own sake [aveirah lishmah],” which is considered a mitzvah [Nazir 23b]: and just as “a mitzvah not for its own sake — for out of [doing it] not for its own sake one comes to its own sake,” so too “out of a transgression for its own sake one comes to a mitzvah for its own sake.”16Nazir 23b: “Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak said: Greater is a transgression for its own sake [aveirah lishmah] than a mitzvah not for its own sake” — and the Gemara emends it to “equivalent to a mitzvah not for its own sake.” It is proven from Yael: “Blessed above women shall Yael be, the wife of Chever the Kenite; above the women in the tent shall she be blessed” (Shoftim 5:24) — “the women in the tent” are the Matriarchs; she gave herself to Sisera for Heaven’s sake. And as “from [performing] a mitzvah not for its own sake one comes to [performing it] for its own sake,” so — R’ Tzadok adds — from an aveirah lishmah one comes to a mitzvah for its own sake.

וְעַל כֵּן הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ חֲשׁוּבָה מִצְוָה וּזְכוּת, דְּאִלּוּ כִּוֵּן תְּחִלָּה לְכָךְ הֲרֵי הָיָה מִצְוָה לְכַתְּחִלָּה גַּם כֵּן, בְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, ״עֵת לַעֲשׂוֹת לַה׳ הֵפֵרוּ תּוֹרָתֶךָ״, וְאֵלִיָּהוּ בְּהַר הַכַּרְמֶל

And therefore the transgression itself is considered a mitzvah and a merit — for had he intended it so from the outset, it would have been a mitzvah even initially, as in every “transgression for its own sake”: “it is a time to act for Hashem — they have voided Your Torah” (Tehillim 119:126), and [as with] Eliyahu on Mount Carmel [who offered on a private altar].17Eliyahu on Mount Carmel (I Melachim 18): he offered a sacrifice on a “private altar [bamah]” at a time when such offerings were forbidden — a paradigm of “a time to act for Hashem” (Tehillim 119:126; Berachos 63a), a deliberate transgression of the Torah’s letter done, by prophetic word, wholly for God’s sake.
וְאַף דִּבְנָבִיא יֵשׁ גְּבוּל, דְּבַכֹּל אִם יֹאמַר לַעֲבֹר עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שְׁמַע לוֹ חוּץ מֵעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה — זֶהוּ רַק עַל פִּי נָבִיא

And though for a prophet there is a limit — that “in everything, if he says to transgress the words of Torah, listen to him, except for idolatry” — that [license] is only “by [the word of] a prophet”;18Yevamos 90b; Devarim 18:15; Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 9:3 — the limits of a prophet’s temporary suspension: “To him you shall listen” authorizes obedience to an established prophet who temporarily directs violation of a Torah command, as Eliyahu did by offering outside the Temple in order to defeat the prophets of Baal. The Rambam stresses three limits: the instruction must be temporary, it cannot permanently uproot a mitzvah, and it never permits idolatry. Thus the Mount Carmel precedent is a formal hora’as sha’ah by prophecy; it is not a general license for a person to redefine a prohibited act as an aveirah lishmah on his own initiative.

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם לְחֵטְא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ תִּקּוּן לִהְיוֹת נֶחְשָׁב אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה כַּעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, דְּמָצִינוּ דֻּגְמָא גַּם בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז.] עַל פָּסוּק ״עַד הָרֹאשׁ״, שֶׁבִּיקֵּשׁ דָּוִד כו׳ עַיֵּין שָׁם

but nonetheless, even for a Jew’s sin of idolatry there is a rectification, to be reckoned after teshuvah as “a transgression for its own sake” — for we find an example even in idolatry of “a transgression for its own sake” [Sanhedrin 107a] on the verse “unto the top [rosh]” (II Shmuel 15:32), that “David sought [to serve idolatry]” — see there.19Sanhedrin 107a: “Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: David sought to worship idolatry, as it says, ‘and David came to the top [rosh] where he would bow to God’ (II Shmuel 15:32), and ‘rosh’ means only idolatry (Daniel 2:32).” Chushai the Archite met him and argued, “shall they say, a king like you will serve idols?” David reasoned that it was better he alone profane the Name than that the public say a righteous king was killed by his son. Rashi: his aim was to prevent a public desecration of God’s Name — i.e., even this “idolatry” was, in intent, for Heaven’s sake.

וּמֵאַחַר דְּאַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר, מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, וְהֶעֱבִירָהּ הוּא שֶׁהֱבִיאַתּוּ לָזֶה, אִם כֵּן אִגַּלַּאי מִילְּתָא לְמַפְרֵעַ דַּהֲפָרַת הַתּוֹרָה בַּעֲבֵירָה הָיָה לְטוֹב וְלַעֲשׂוֹת לַה׳

And since after the teshuvah he merits, through the sin, a greater rung — “the place where masters of teshuvah stand” — and the transgression is what brought him to it, then the matter is “revealed retroactively” that the “voiding of the Torah” through the transgression was “for good, and to act for Hashem.”20Berachos 34b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4; Peri Tzadik, Pesach Sheni 3:2 — the fall as the route to a higher return: The higher standing of the baal teshuvah is explained by the Rambam as the reward of one who tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered the inclination more forcefully. Peri Tzadik describes Pesach Sheni as a root-level rectification in which distance itself, when it awakens brokenhearted return, is transformed until willful sins become merits. These sources illuminate Rav Tzadok’s “revealed retroactively”: the transgression becomes the occasion and material of ascent only through the later teshuvah. The doctrine cannot be invoked prospectively to choose sin in order to attain a higher level.

וְאַף דְּהוּא לֹא כִּוֵּן לְכָךְ בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה, הַכֹּל הָיָה מְסֻדָּר וּבָא מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּבְּרִיאָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שַׁבָּת פט:] עַל פָּסוּק ״חֲטָאֵיכֶם כַּשָּׁנִים״

And though he did not intend so at the time of the act, all was “arranged and came from the six days of Creation, from Hashem’s will in creation,” as they said [Shabbos 89b] on the verse “though your sins be like scarlet [ka-shanim]” (Yeshayah 1:18).21Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1–5; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — divine ordering and human responsibility: The Rambam establishes free choice as a foundation of Torah, reward, punishment, and teshuvah, while acknowledging that divine knowledge is beyond ordinary human comprehension. Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 explicitly holds both perspectives together: in the realm of choice, the act is fully the person’s responsibility; in the higher realm of divine knowledge, nothing lies outside Hashem’s knowledge and will. Rav Tzadok’s language that the course was arranged from Creation belongs to that second perspective and becomes spiritually accessible through complete teshuvah; it does not erase culpability at the moment of choice.22Shabbos 89b: On “though your sins be like scarlet [ka-shanim]” (Yeshayah 1:18) — the Sages read shanim, “years,” teaching that the pattern was “arranged” from long before. R’ Tzadok takes this as: the whole course of a person’s sin-and-return was ordered from the six days of Creation by God’s will.
וְכֵן [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם] ״רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה בַּת שֶׁבַע לְדָוִד מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּאת לוֹ בְּמַכְאוֹב״, שֶׁהֻצְרַךְ לִסְבּוֹל אַחַר זֶה יִסּוּרִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And so [in Sanhedrin 107a], “Bas Sheva was fit for David from the six days of Creation — only that she came to him through pain” — for he had to bear, after this, sufferings in this world.
וְזֶהוּ הַאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה, שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ טַעַם כָּל כָּךְ לִפְנֵי זְמַנּוֹ, דְּלֹא הָיָה הַקְּדֻשָּׁה מֻרְגֶּשֶׁת עֲדַיִן בְּפֹעַל בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְעֵין כֹּל
And this is “the eating of unripe fruit [pagah],” which has “not much taste before its time” — for the holiness was “not yet felt in actuality at that time, to every eye”;

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּלֵב דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה, וְלֹא כִּוֵּן לְחֵטְא כְּלָל, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״פַּגָּה״, שֶׁהוּא הַפְּרִי הַחֲשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ, רַק שֶׁלֹּא נִגְמְרָה עֲדַיִן לִהְיוֹת חֲשִׁיבוּתָהּ בְּפֹעַל

but nonetheless, in the heart of David HaMelech it was “full of holiness even at that time,” and he “did not intend to sin at all” — therefore it is called “pagah,” which is “the important fruit itself,” only that it “was not yet completed to have its importance in actuality.”23Sanhedrin 107a; Peri Tzadik, Vayeishev 12:1 — Bas Sheva as “unripe fruit”: The Gemara says that Bas Sheva was destined for David from Creation but “came to him through pain,” and the school of Rabbi Yishmael calls the act eating unripe fruit — taking what was destined before its permitted time. Peri Tzadik uses the related episode of Avigail to show that the yetzer can cloak temptation in a plausible claim of destined spiritual connection, while divine protection preserves the saint from acting on that premature claim. Rav Tzadok’s description of hidden holiness develops the Gemara’s metaphor, but the metaphor itself condemns timing that had not yet ripened into lawful actuality.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם] דְּאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ דְּהָיָה יָכוֹל לִכְפּוֹת לְיִצְרוֹ אִם רָצָה, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד:] דְּלִבּוֹ הָיָה חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ, וְלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, רַק לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה

And as they said [in Sanhedrin 107a] that he said of himself “he could have subdued his inclination had he wished,” and as they said [in Avodah Zarah 4b] that “his heart was hollow within him24R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §4): “In truth we find that ‘an aveirah lishmah is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake’ (Nazir 23b); and such a one too is called a ‘tzaddik,’ for all his deeds are for the sake of Heaven, even ‘as to a matter of transgression.’ And in the Future it will be so clarified regarding all the sins of the Children of Israel — as they said in Shabbos (89b) on the verse ‘though your sins be like scarlet’ — that they are ‘ordered and come from the six days of Creation.’” The se’if’s principle exactly: the aveirah lishmah is reckoned a mitzvah, all arranged by God’s will from Creation.,” and “he was not fit for that deed — only to teach teshuvah.”25Sanhedrin 107a; Avodah Zarah 4b–5a: Rava expounded on “Against You alone have I sinned, and done what is evil in Your eyes, so that You are just when You speak” (Tehillim 51:6): David said before the Holy One, “It is revealed and known before You that had I wished to subdue my inclination I could have subdued it; but I said [I will sin], lest they say a servant prevailed over his master.” And (Avodah Zarah 4b–5a): “R’ Yochanan said in the name of R’ Shimon bar Yochai: David was not fit for that deed [with Bat-Sheva], and Israel were not fit for that deed [of the Golden Calf]. David was not fit, as it is written, ‘and my heart is hollow within me’ (Tehillim 109:22); Israel were not fit, as it is written, ‘would that this heart of theirs would remain, to fear Me’ (Devarim 5:26). Then why did they do it? — to tell you that if an individual sinned [and despairs of repentance] he is told, ‘Go to the individual [David, and learn from him]’; and if a community sinned, they are told, ‘Go to the community.’” That is, the deed was to teach the power of teshuvah — staged, not intrinsic to David, precisely to model repentance for all.

items.h: The theme: Every sin of a generation must leave a trace even in the head of the generation — for all Israel are one “stature,” and the leader includes them all. So Moshe broke the tablets at the sin of the calf (himself performing a “sin of that kind,” yet for Heaven’s sake). And when God said “yishar kochacha that you broke them,” he thereby won atonement for Israel too, its sin being revealed as an aveirah lishmah.

p: [ג] וְכָל חֵטְא הַדּוֹר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת גַּם בְּרֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר שֶׁמֶץ מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל קוֹמָה שְׁלֵמָה, וְרֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַדּוֹר, ״פַּרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר״ כַּיָּדוּעַ

And every sin of the generation must have, even in the head of the generation, a “trace” of it — for all Israel are one “complete stature,” and the head of the generation includes the whole generation, “a leader according to the generation,” as is known.26Arakhin 17a; Machshavos Charutz §17:5 — the leader and generation as one organic stature: Arakhin states that “the generation follows the leader” or “the leader follows his generation,” but the Gemara limits that dispute to harshness and gentleness, explicitly noting that a righteous leader may stand over an unworthy generation and conversely. Machshavos Charutz describes Israel as one complete stature whose spiritual “head,” “eyes,” and “heart” transmit life to the whole body. Rav Tzadok’s claim that a trace of the generation’s sin appears in its head is therefore his organic-mystical synthesis of collective soulhood; it is broader than the literal scope of the Arakhin passage and does not erase each person’s individual responsibility.

וּכְשֶׁשִּׁיבֵּר מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הַלּוּחוֹת בְּחֵטְא יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעֵגֶל — שֶׁזֶּה גַּם כֵּן חֵטְא מֵעֵין דֻּגְמָא, אֲבָל הוּא כִּוֵּן לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם — וּכְשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ ״יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ שֶׁשִּׁבַּרְתָּ״, אָז פָּעַל סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה גַּם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי נִתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם חֶטְאָם הָיָה כְּעֵין עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And when Moshe Rabbeinu broke the tablets at Israel’s sin of the calf — which is also a “sin of that kind,” but he intended it “for the sake of Heaven” — and when [Hashem] said to him afterward, “yishar kochacha that you broke [them]” (Shabbos 87a), then he effected “forgiveness and atonement for Israel too,” for it was clarified that “their sin too was like a transgression for its own sake.”27Shabbos 87a; Menachos 99b; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushas Shabbos 7:7 — divine assent to breaking the Tablets: Shabbos records Moshe’s kal vachomer: if an apostate may not eat the single mitzvah of the Pesach offering, Israel after the calf could not receive the Torah as a whole; “asher shibarta” is then read as “yishar kochacha that you broke them.” Menachos formulates the principle that an apparent nullification of Torah can become its foundation, because the breaking led to the second Tablets. Peri Tzadik explains that loss and renewed toil can disclose a deeper power of Torah. Rav Tzadok’s further conclusion here — that Moshe’s parallel act drew atonement and revealed an inner likeness to aveirah lishmah in Israel’s sin — is his own interpretive extension, not the Gemara’s explicit wording.28Shabbos 87a: On Moshe’s breaking of the tablets — the Holy One’s assent, “yishar kochacha that you broke [them]” — R’ Tzadok reads as the paradigm of a leader who performs, for Heaven’s sake, an act mirroring his generation’s sin, thereby drawing atonement to them and revealing their sin, too, as an aveirah lishmah.29R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §154): “In all the sins of Israel, Moshe too ‘sinned,’ for he is their totality — as with the calf, Moshe’s ‘sin’ was in the breaking of the Tablets. And in truth it is an astonishing and very strange thing: even to tear, in one’s anger, a Torah scroll written by an ordinary human scribe and cast it to the ground [would be grave] — all the more the Tablets, ‘the writing of God’! And it is literally the sin of the calf. And when he was told, ‘yishar kochacha that you broke [them],’ he knew that so too it was with the Children of Israel; and [Hashem] desires and receives contentment [nachas ruach] from the good portion within them.” This is the se’if’s very point: Moshe’s breaking the Tablets was a “sin of that kind” done wholly for Heaven, and the “yishar kochacha” revealed that Israel’s sin too was arranged by God’s will — an aveirah lishmah.

וְכֵן בְּדוֹר אֵלִיָּהוּ הֻצְרַךְ הוּא לְהַקְרִיב בַּחוּץ, שֶׁזֶּה נִקְרָא ״כַּגּוֹיִם״ וּכְדֶרֶךְ עוֹבְדֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, אֲבָל הוּא עָשָׂה מְפוֹרָשׁ בִּדְבַר ה׳ וּלְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מָצָא מָקוֹם לִטְעוֹן גַּם בְּעַד יִשְׂרָאֵל ״וְאַתָּה הֲסִבּוֹתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית״

And so in Eliyahu’s generation he had to offer “outside” [on a private altar] — which is called “like the nations” and the way of idolaters — but he did it “explicitly by the word of Hashem and for the sake of Heaven”; and through this he “found room to plead for Israel too”: “and You turned their heart backward” (I Melachim 18:37)30I Melachim 18:37; Berachos 31b–32a; Rashi ad loc.; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — “You turned their heart backward”: Berachos calls Eliyahu’s words a bold plea directed Heavenward and says that God ultimately conceded the claim through “those whom I have caused to act wickedly” (Michah 4:6). Rashi explains that Heaven had allowed room for their turning away and could have prepared their hearts. The Rambam, however, reads the verse as punitive hardening after repeated voluntary sin: they first chose evil, and only afterward were prevented from easy return. Tzidkas HaTzadik employs this verse at the level of divine knowledge to explain how complete teshuvah can uncover that nothing lies outside Hashem’s will. Rav Tzadok’s synthesis thus mitigates despair and opens teshuvah; it does not mean that the original worshippers of Baal were free of culpability. —

שֶׁגַּם חֶטְאָם הוּא עַל יָדְךָ וְאַתָּה רָצִיתָ שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ כֵּן, וְעַל כָּרְחָם הָיָה שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ כִּרְצוֹנְךָ, דְּלָא יֹאמְרוּ ״עַבְדָּא דְּזָכֵי לְמָרֵיהּ״, וּפָעַל לְעוֹרֵר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּקֶרֶב כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל

that “their sin too is by Your hand, and You willed that they do so,” and “against their will it was that they did Your will,” lest they say “a servant who prevailed over his Master” — and he effected the “arousal of teshuvah among all Israel.”

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִפְטְרוּ מִן הָעֹנֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל חֲטָאִים הַגְּדוֹלִים הָהֵם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְהָיָה הַנִּמְלָט מֵחֶרֶב חֲזָאֵל (יָמִית יֵהוּא)״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְהִשְׁאַרְתִּי (בְיִשְׂרָאֵל שִׁבְעַת אֲלָפִים כָּל) הַבִּרְכַּיִם אֲשֶׁר לֹא (כָרְעוּ לַבַּעַל)״

And nonetheless they were not exempted from punishment in this world for those great sins, as it says, “and it shall be, whoever escapes the sword of Chazael, Yehu shall slay” and “I will leave [in Israel seven thousand, all] the knees that have not [bowed to the Baal]” (I Melachim 19:17–18).

וְכָל הַחוֹטְאִים נֶעֶנְשׁוּ, וּכְמוֹ בָּעֵגֶל ״וּבְיוֹם פָּקְדִי וּפָקַדְתִּי״, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בִּתְשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵמָה מֵאַהֲבָה דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה כְּכָל עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And all the sinners were punished — as with the calf, “and on the day of My reckoning I will reckon [their sin upon them]” (Shemos 32:34) — [and] even though they repented with complete teshuvah from love, which “becomes like merits,” nonetheless it requires atonement, like every “transgression for its own sake.”31Shemos 32:34; Yoma 86a; Takanas HaShavin 10:6–7 — transformed merit does not always complete temporal atonement: “On the day of My reckoning I will reckon” preserves a later accounting for the calf. Yoma distinguishes forgiveness and inner return from the completion of kapparah: for grave prohibitions, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend judgment while suffering may complete the cleansing, and chillul Hashem requires an even longer process. Rav Tzadok later returns to Esther and Yael to explain that an aveirah lishmah can yield immeasurable merit while still exacting a price in this world. The se’if therefore distinguishes the retroactive spiritual transformation of the act from the remaining process by which its damage and public consequences are purified.
וְעַל כֵּן הֻצְרְכָה יָעֵל לִבְרָכָה, דְּמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר ״תְּבֹרַךְ מִנָּשִׁים״ וְגוֹמֵר הוּא לְהָגֵן עָלֶיהָ מִיִּסּוּרִים

And therefore Yael needed a “blessing” — for what is said, “blessed above women [shall Yael be]” (Shoftim 5:24) is “to shield her from sufferings.”32Shoftim 5:24; Nazir 23b; Rashi ad loc.; Takanas HaShavin 10:6–7 — Yael’s blessing and the cost of aveirah lishmah: Nazir first states that an aveirah lishmah is greater than a mitzvah shelo lishmah, then qualifies the formulation to say that they are equivalent. Yael is praised as “blessed above women in the tent,” and Rashi explains that she is blessed for undertaking the transgression for Heaven’s sake in order to weaken Sisera and kill him. The Gemara itself presents the blessing as praise for her saving act. Rav Tzadok adds that the blessing also shielded her from the suffering naturally attached to such an act; that protective function is his interpretive synthesis, not an explicit statement of Nazir.

וְאֵין לְךָ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ גְּדוֹלָה מֵאֶסְתֵּר, וְנִכְתַּב בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרָה עַל עַצְמָהּ ״כַּאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי אָבָדְתִּי״, דְּמִסְּתָמָא יֵשׁ בָּזֶה שֵׁם ״אֲבֵדָה״ בֶּאֱמֶת, מִצַּד עֲבֵירָה כָּזוֹ דְּנִבְעֶלֶת לַגּוֹי

And you have no “transgression for its own sake” greater than Esther’s; and it was written by ruach hakodesh what she said of herself, “and as I am lost, I am lost” (Esther 4:16) — for presumably there is in this a name of “loss” in truth, from such a transgression as “being bedded by a gentile,”
שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַטִּמּוּעַ בֵּין הָעַמִּים שֶׁנִּקְרָאִים ״אוֹבְדִים״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וּבָאוּ הָאֹבְדִים בְּאֶרֶץ אַשּׁוּר״ עַל אוֹתָם שֶׁנִּטְמְעוּ בֵּין הָעַמִּים

which is the ultimate of “assimilation among the peoples,” who are called “the lost ones,” as it says, “and the lost ones shall come [from] the land of Ashur” (Yeshayah 27:13) — [said] of those who were “assimilated among the peoples.”33Esther 4:16; Megillah 15a; Yeshayahu 27:13 with Rashi; Machshavos Charutz 20:14–15; Takanas HaShavin 10:6 — Esther’s “loss” and descent among the nations: Megillah explains “as I am lost, I am lost” precisely: until then Esther’s relations with Achashverosh were coerced, but her voluntary approach for Israel’s rescue would render her forbidden to Mordechai — “as I was lost from my father’s house, so I shall be lost to you.” Yeshayahu’s “lost in the land of Assyria” refers, in Rashi, to exiles scattered beyond the Sambatyon, not explicitly to intermarriage. Rav Tzadok expands both images into the spiritual peril of immersion among the nations. Machshavos Charutz treats Esther’s descent as an aveirah lishmah that repaired an earlier mingling of holy and profane, while later in this siman Rav Tzadok stresses that she risked not only her body but the felt integrity of her soul in order to recreate Israel through salvation. — The section thus opens the siman’s governing theme: that even the gravest descent, when its inner intent is wholly to God, is an aveirah lishmah whose sin the future reveals as merit — though in this world it still exacts its price.

items.h: The theme: God’s way is to “sweeten the bitter with the bitter” — as at Marah, where a bitter branch was cast in to sweeten the bitter water. So Esther added “as I am lost,” taking the decree of “loss” hanging over all Israel upon herself. This is illustrated by R’ Yishmael (“I am Israel’s atonement”), Mashiach bearing Israel’s poverty, and Moshe rebuked “for Israel’s sake,” since the head of the generation is the generation.

p: [ד] וְכָךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמְתִּיק הַמַּר בְּמַר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיַּשְׁלֵךְ [עֵץ]״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַיִּמְתְּקוּ הַמַּיִם״, שֶׁהָיָה עֵץ הַרְדּוּפְנִי מַר, רַק שֶׁהָיָה בְּצִיּוּרַיָּיא וּבִרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבָזֶה נִמְתַּק הַמְּרִירוּת הַזֶּה וְהַקּוֹדֵם

And so is the way of Hashem — to “sweeten the bitter with the bitter”: as the Sages said on the verse “and he cast [a tree] and the waters were sweetened” (Shemos 15:25), that it was a bitter oleander branch — only that it was “by [Divine] design and by the will of Hashem” — and by this the [present] bitterness and the earlier [bitterness] were sweetened.34Shemos 15:25; Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayassa 1; Chovos HaLevavos, Sha’ar HaBitachon 4; Peri Tzadik, Purim 8:1 — healing bitterness through bitterness: The Mekhilta records several identifications of the tree at Marah — willow, olive, oleander, cedar, and, homiletically, Torah — and Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel formulates the governing principle: human beings heal bitter with sweet, whereas the Holy One may heal bitter with bitter, placing a harmful substance into what is already damaged so that the miracle itself becomes manifest. Chovos HaLevavos cites Marah, Elisha’s salt, and Yeshayahu’s fig-cake as examples of cure through an ordinarily harmful agent. Peri Tzadik reads Esther’s voluntary approach to Achashverosh and the birth of Daryavesh, who enabled the Temple’s rebuilding, as the same paradoxical pattern. Rav Tzadok’s application to Esther is therefore an interpretive synthesis of the Mekhilta’s principle, not the literal subject of the Midrash.
וְהִיא הוֹסִיפָה עוֹד בַּאֲמִירַת ״כַּאֲשֶׁר אָבַדְתִּי״, לְקַבֵּל עָלֶיהָ עֹנֶשׁ הָאֲבַדּוֹן הַנִּגְזָר עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל
And she [Esther] added further, in saying “as I am lost,” to take upon herself the punishment of “loss” that was decreed upon all Israel.
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל [בְּרֵישׁ פ״ב דִּנְגָעִים] ״כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲנִי כַּפָּרָתָן״, שֶׁרָצָה לְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ הָעֹנֶשׁ דִּנְגָעִים בַּעֲבוּרָן, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּהָרַע״ב וְתוֹי״ט

in the way that R’ Yishmael said [Negaim 2:1], “all Israel — I am their atonement,” wishing to take upon himself the punishment of nega’im on their behalf — see there in the Bartenura and Tosafos Yom Tov.35Negaim 2:1: “R’ Yishmael says: the children of Israel — I am their atonement [ani kaparasan] — they are [in color] like boxwood, neither black nor white but intermediate.” Bartenura: out of his love for them he would say “I am their atonement,” meaning “all the punishment fit to come upon them I take upon myself to atone for them”; and R’ Yishmael holds “by that which purifies one of them, all are purified, and by that which defiles one, all are defiled.” Tosafos Yom Tov (citing the Maharam): he adopted this phrasing because he wished to mention the affliction of tzaraas in Israel — “may no evil befall them, and I am their atonement.”

וּכְמוֹ מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁסּוֹבֵל עֲנִיּוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכֵן בִּיחֶזְקֵאל בִּשְׁעַת הַחֻרְבָּן, וְכֵן מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״לֵךְ רֵד״, דְּאָמְרוּ ז״ל שֶׁנִּתְנַזֵּף בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה, הוּא לְכַפָּרַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּלְקַבֵּל הָעֹנֶשׁ שֶׁעֲלֵיהֶם, כִּי רֹאשׁ הַדּוֹר הוּא הַדּוֹר

And like Mashiach, who “bears the poverty of Israel,” and likewise Yechezkel at the time of the Destruction, and likewise Moshe Rabbeinu, to whom [God] said “go down” (Shemos 32:7) — of which the Sages said [that his being] rebuked in the Heavenly court was “for the atonement of Israel and to receive the punishment that was upon them” — for “the head of the generation is the generation.”36Berachos 32a; Arachin 17a; Yechezkel 4:4–6; Sanhedrin 98b; Machshavos Charutz 17:5 — the head shares the generation’s burden: Berachos explains “Go, descend” as Moshe’s descent from greatness because his greatness was granted for Israel; when they fell, his standing was affected, and that very dependence moved him to plead for them. Arachin states that the disposition of a generation and its leader correspond, though it does not claim that every righteous leader personally committed the generation’s sin. Yechezkel is commanded symbolically to bear Israel’s iniquity, and Sanhedrin applies “our illnesses he bore” to Mashiach. Machshavos Charutz describes Israel as one complete organism whose leaders are its head and vital organs. Rav Tzadok combines these sources into the stronger idea that the head can accept the generation’s suffering for its repair; this is his synthesis, not a mechanical transfer of legal guilt.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרָה (אֶסְתֵּר) לְהַצִּיל בָּזֶה כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל מֵעֹנֶשׁ הַגְּזֵרָה דִּלְאַבֵּד, כִּי כְּבָר נִתְקַיֵּים בָּהּ, דַּאֲבַדּוֹנָהּ מִגּוּף קָדוֹשׁ דְּמָרְדְּכַי — אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר נֶאֶבְדָה מֵעַמָּהּ וּמוֹלַדְתָּהּ — נֶחְשָׁב אֲבַדּוֹן גָּמוּר לָהּ

And therefore (Esther) intended thereby to save all Israel from the punishment of the decree of “loss” — for it was already fulfilled in her: her “loss” from the holy body of Mordechai — after she had already been “lost” from her people and her birthplace — is reckoned a “complete loss” for her.

וְגַם דְּאִלּוּ לֹא נֶאֶסְרָה לְמָרְדְּכַי, אֶפְשָׁר הָיְתָה מוֹלִידָה מִמֶּנּוּ וְהָיָה הַוָּלָד טָהוֹר מֵאִמּוֹ וּמֵאָבִיו, וְאָז וַדַּאי ״זְרוֹק חוּטְרָא אַעִקָּרֵיהּ קָאֵי״, וְהָיָה נִשְׁאַר מִמֶּנָּה זֶרַע בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And moreover, had she not become forbidden to Mordechai, she might have borne from him, and the child would have been “pure from its mother and its father,” and then certainly “throw a stick and it lands on its root” [i.e., it reverts to its origin], and seed of hers would have remained in Israel.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁהוֹלִידָה דָּרְיָוֶשׁ מֵאֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, אַף שֶׁהָיָה טָהוֹר מֵאִמּוֹ וְהָיָה מֶלֶךְ כָּשֵׁר וּבָנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה מִכְּלַל הַגּוֹיִם וְנִטְמַע בֵּינֵיהֶם, וְנִתְקַיֵּים הָאֲבַדּוֹן בְּזַרְעָהּ

Not so afterward, when she bore Daryavesh to Achashverosh — for although he was “pure from his mother,” and was a “fit king” who built the Beis HaMikdash, nonetheless he was of the category of the nations and was assimilated among them, and the “loss” was fulfilled in her offspring.37Esther Rabbah 8:3; Vayikra Rabbah 13:5; Rashi to Ezra 1:1 and 4:24; Peri Tzadik, Purim 8:1 — Daryavesh as Esther’s son and the rebuilding of the Temple: The Midrash identifies the later Daryavesh as Esther’s son, “pure from his mother and impure from his father.” Rashi likewise identifies the Persian Daryavesh who renewed the Second Temple’s construction as the son of Achashverosh and Esther. Peri Tzadik makes this tradition central to Esther’s hidden achievement: her entry “not according to the law,” undertaken for Israel, became the concealed preparation for the Temple’s rebuilding through the child born from that union. This parentage is a rabbinic and medieval chronological tradition rather than an explicit statement in Megillas Esther or Ezra; Rav Tzadok uses it to show how the bitter act itself generated the historical remedy.
וְזֶהוּ אִבּוּדָהּ מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כָּבוּ לַהֹלֵךְ כִּי לֹא יָשׁוּב וְרָאָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ [בב״ב קטו.] עַל מִי שֶׁלֹּא הִנִּיחַ בֵּן

And this is her “loss” from this world, as it says, “weep for the one who goes, for he shall not return and see [his birthplace]” (Yirmeyah 22:10), which they expounded [Bava Basra 115a] of one who “left no son.”38Bava Basra 115a: On “weep not for the dead, nor bemoan him; weep sorely for him that goes [away]” (Yirmeyah 22:10) — “‘him that goes’ [ha-holech]: this is one who departs [this world] without leaving a son [to succeed him].” R’ Tzadok reads Esther’s fate — bearing Daryavesh, assimilated among the nations — as this “loss” of leaving no enduring Jewish seed.

וְעַל בִּיאַת גּוֹי מַגִּיעַ עֹנֶשׁ זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין פב.] בְּבִיאַת אֲרַמִּית — אִם לֹא פָּגְעוּ קַנָּאִין — ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ עֵר וְעוֹנֶה״ וְכֵן ״מַגִּישׁ״ וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי זֶהוּ עִיקַּר חִלּוּל הַבְּרִית

And for the union with a gentile this punishment comes, as they said [Sanhedrin 82a] regarding one who “beds an Aramean woman” — if the zealous do not strike him — “may he have no ‘awakener [er] and answerer [oneh]’” and “‘one who brings near [an offering]’” (Malachi 2:12) — for this is the essence of the “profaning of the bris.”39Sanhedrin 82a: “One who cohabits with an Aramean woman — the zealous strike him [kana’im pog’in bo].” And on the verse “Yehudah has dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel and in Jerusalem; for Yehudah has profaned the holiness of Hashem which he loved, and has cohabited with the daughter of a foreign god” (Malachi 2:11), the Gemara adduces the next verse: “May Hashem cut off, to the man who does this, one awake [er] and one answering [oneh] from the tents of Yaakov, and one presenting a meal-offering to Hashem of Hosts” (Malachi 2:12) — “if he is a Torah scholar, may he have none awake among the Sages nor answering among the disciples; if a priest, may he have no son to present a meal-offering,” i.e., that he leave no offspring. This, for R’ Tzadok, is the essence of the profaning of the bris.
וְנֶאֱמַר [תְּהִלִּים נה] ״אֲשֶׁר אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ וְלֹא יָרְאוּ אֱלֹקִים״, וְדָרְשׁוּ [בב״ב שָׁם] ״אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת״ עַל בָּנִים הַמְמַלְּאִים מְקוֹמוֹ

And it says (Tehillim 55:20), “who have no ‘changes [chalifos],’ and fear not God,” which they expounded [Bava Basra 116a] — “no changes” [refers to] sons who fill his place.40Bava Basra 116a: On “who have no changes [chalifos], and fear not God” (Tehillim 55:20) — “R’ Yochanan and R’ Yehoshua ben Levi [differed]: one said, [it refers to] anyone who does not leave a son [to succeed him]; and one said, anyone who does not leave a disciple.” R’ Tzadok reads “no changes” as the lack of “sons who fill one’s place,” bound up with the verse’s “fear not God” — for the power to beget “seed after its kind” depends on gevurah, which is fear of Heaven.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְלֹא יָרְאוּ אֱלֹקִים״, כִּי ״אִישׁ יָרֵא אֶת ה׳״ — ״גִּבּוֹר בָּאָרֶץ יִהְיֶה זַרְעוֹ״, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כָּל יְרֵא ה׳״ — ״אֶשְׁתְּךָ כְּגֶפֶן פֹּרִיָּה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״כִּי כֵן יְבֹרַךְ גָּבֶר יְרֵא ה׳״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וּרְאֵה בָנִים לְבָנֶיךָ״

And this is why it says “and fear not God” — for [of] “a man who fears Hashem,” [it is said,] “his seed shall be mighty in the land” (Tehillim 112:2); and it says, “everyone who fears Hashem — your wife shall be as a fruitful vine [in the recesses of your house, your children like olive shoots around your table]; behold, for so shall the man who fears Hashem be blessed. [May Hashem bless you from Zion, and may you see the good of Jerusalem;] and see children to your children” (Tehillim 128).
כִּי הַיִּרְאָה הִיא הַגְּבוּרָה כַּיָּדוּעַ, וְכֵן הֵם בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא שָׁוֶה, כִּי הַיָּרֵא הוּא הַמִּתְגַּבֵּר עַל יִצְרוֹ, וְהַגִּבּוֹר מִתְיָרְאִין מִמֶּנּוּ

For “fear [yirah] is gevurah,” as is known, and they are equal in gematria — for the God-fearing one is “the one who overpowers his inclination,” and the mighty one is feared.41Avos 4:1; Mishlei 31:30; Peri Tzadik, Masei 9:1 and Metzora 6:1 — yirah as gevurah: Avos defines the gibbor as one who conquers his inclination, while Mishlei crowns the “woman who fears Hashem” with praise. Peri Tzadik repeatedly connects fear of Heaven with the inner strength by which a person masters desire, locating that strength in the heart rather than in outward force. Rav Tzadok’s further equation of yirah and gevurah through their equal numerical value is his own interpretive association; it is not the wording of the Mishnah. In this se’if the association explains why guarding the bris and transmitting holy seed depend upon disciplined awe and self-mastery rather than physical power alone.

וְכֵן כָּל מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם שֵׁם ה׳ נִקְרָא עָלָיו, וּמִתְקַיֵּים בּוֹ ״וְיִרְאוּ מִמְּךָ״ כַּיָּדוּעַ. וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ גַּבְרָא לְהַזְרִיעַ זֶרַע לְמִינֵהוּ, דְּתָלוּי בִּגְבוּרָה

And likewise, whoever has fear of Heaven, “the Name of Hashem is called upon him,” and there is fulfilled in him “and they shall fear you” (Devarim 28:10). And through this he has the “power of a man” to sow “seed after its kind,” which depends on gevurah,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״כְּחִצִּים בְּיַד גִּבּוֹר כֵּן בְּנֵי הַנְּעוּרִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנִדָּה] ״כֹּל שֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹרֶה כַּחֵץ״ כו׳

as it says, “like arrows in the hand of a mighty one, so are the children of youth” (Tehillim 127:4), and as they said [in Niddah 43a], “anyone who does not shoot [his seed] like an arrow”42Niddah 43a: “Anyone [whose seed] does not shoot like an arrow [yoreh ka-chetz] cannot fertilize [eino maz’ria].” R’ Tzadok links the “arrow” to “like arrows in the hand of a mighty one, so are the children of youth” (Tehillim 127:4) — the “power of a man” to beget, which “depends on gevurah,” the fear of Heaven that guards the holy seed.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁלֹּא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים — ״אֵין חֲלִיפוֹת לָמוֹ״
Not so one who fears not God — “they have no ‘changes.’”
וּבַעֲמָלֵק דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״וְלֹא יָרֵא אֱלֹקִים״, וְנִצְטַוּוּ בִּמְחִיַּת כָּל זָכָר לוֹ, כִּי הוּא נִקְרָא ״רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ [דְּ]גוֹיִם שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים

And of Amalek it is written, “and he feared not God” (Devarim 25:18), and they were commanded to blot out his every male — for he is called “the first of the nations” (Bamidbar 24:20), the root of the nations who have no fear of God.

וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא הָעָרְלָה עַל שֵׁם אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים לא:] מִקְּרָא דְּ״כָל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים״, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּימּוֹל, וְהוּא חִלּוּל הַבְּרִית שֶׁהוּא לָהֶם מִצַּד שֶׁרָשַׁם, עַל יְדֵי הֶעְדֵּר יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם הַגּוֹרֵם שִׁיקּוּעַ בְּתַאֲוָה

And therefore the “orlah” is named for the nations, as they said [Nedarim 31b] from the verse “for all the nations are uncircumcised [arelim]” (Yirmeyah 9:25) — even one who is circumcised — and this is the “profaning of the bris” that is theirs by their root: through the absence of fear of Heaven, which causes immersion in desire.43Nedarim 31b: “R’ Elazar ben Azaryah says: repulsive is the orlah, for the wicked are disgraced by it, as it says, ‘for all the nations are uncircumcised [arelim]’ (Yirmeyah 9:25).” R’ Tzadok takes “orlah” as the emblem of the nations’ root-defect — the absence of yiras shamayim — such that even a circumcised gentile is “uncircumcised,” while even an arel of Israel is essentially “circumcised.”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַהֲרָגוּנִי עַל דְּבַר אִשְׁתִּי״
as [Avraham] said, “only there is no fear of God [in this place], and they will slay me over my wife” (Bereishis 20:11).
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה יז.] דְּפוֹשְׁעֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם בְּגוּפָן הוּא בַּעֲרָיוֹת, שֶׁהֵם מְשׁוּקָּעִים בָּזֶה

Therefore they said [Rosh Hashanah 17a] that “the sinners of the nations, in their body,” is in [the domain of] immorality, for they are “sunk” in it.44Rosh Hashanah 17a: In distinguishing categories of sinners — “the sinners of Israel with their body and the sinners of the nations with their body descend to Gehinnom, and are judged there.” The Gemara identifies “the sinners of Israel with their body” as “the skull that never donned tefillin [karkafta d’lo manach tefillin],” whereas the nations’ bodily sin is centered in immorality — the contrast on which R’ Tzadok builds: Israel’s lapse is a mere absence of the sign, not, like the nations’, an essence “sunk” in desire.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דַּאֲפִילּוּ הָעֲרֵלִים נִקְרָאִים ״מוּלִים״, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ הַחוֹטֵא אֵינוֹ מְשׁוּקָּע, כִּי שָׁרְשׁוֹ מֵרָזָא דְּ״אֵשֶׁת חַיִל״ — ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳״

Not so in Israel — for even the “arelim” [among them] are called “mulim [circumcised],” for even the sinner is “not sunk,” since his root is from the secret of “a woman of valor” — “a woman who fears Hashem.”45Nedarim 31b; Sanhedrin 44a; Resisei Layla 44; Peri Tzadik, Shemos 1:1; Machshavos Charutz 8:12 and 14:5 — Israel’s covenantal root beneath outward failure: The Mishnah rules that a vow concerning “the uncircumcised” includes circumcised gentiles but not uncircumcised Jews, because Scripture uses orlah as a national designation for the nations; this is a legal classification of covenantal identity. Sanhedrin adds that “Israel, although he sinned, remains Israel.” Rav Tzadok’s parallel passages develop the metaphysical implication: circumcision marks an inherited root prior to conscious achievement, so even a Jew whose conduct appears uncircumcised remains “circumcised” in root and is not essentially submerged in desire. Resisei Layla similarly speaks of the enduring inner trace of Israel’s bond. These sources do not excuse the outward sin; they explain Rav Tzadok’s distinction between severe culpable failure and a root that has not been severed.
לֹא נִקְרְאוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן אֶלָּא ״קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין״, שֶׁהוּא הֶעְדֵּר שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם בִּקְרִיאַת שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו

“The sinners of Israel in their body” are called only “the skull that never donned tefillin” — which is [merely] the absence of the root of fear of Heaven in the “calling of the Name of Heaven upon him,”

כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְגִלָּה] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְרָאוּ [כָּל עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ] כִּי שֵׁם ה׳ נִקְרָא עָלֶיךָ״ — ״אֵלּוּ תְּפִלִּין שֶׁבָּרֹאשׁ״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאוֹת שֶׁמְּיוּחָד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, לְקַבֵּל עֹל מַלְכוּתוֹ כְּעֶבֶד הַנּוֹשֵׂא עָלָיו חוֹתַם רַבּוֹ וְסִימָנוֹ

as they said [Megillah 16b] on the verse “and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of Hashem is called upon you” (Devarim 28:10) — “these are the tefillin of the head” — which is “the sign dedicated to Hashem,” to accept the yoke of His kingship like a servant who bears upon himself his master’s seal and mark.46Megillah 16b: On “and all the peoples of the earth shall see that the Name of Hashem is called upon you, and they shall fear you” (Devarim 28:10) — “R’ Eliezer the Great says: these are the tefillin of the head.” The tefillin are the outward “sign” of God’s Name resting on a Jew, “like a servant bearing his master’s seal.”

items.h: The theme: This is the “precious honor [yekar]” (expounded as tefillin) that Israel merited through Esther’s miracle. Though “defiled” by Achashverosh — seemingly an “adulterous wife,” God forbid — she was then the inclusive gathering of Israel, who “donned ruach hakodesh,” the middah of Malchus, the secret of “a woman of valor.” For “great is an aveirah lishmah,” and it signals no true profaning of the bris — on the contrary, it clarifies that even those who appear to profane it are, in root, “circumcised.”

p: [ה] וְזֶהוּ הַ״יְּקָר״ שֶׁדָּרְשׁוּ שָׁם ״זֶה תְּפִלִּין״, שֶׁזָּכוּ עַל יְדֵי הַנֵּס דְּאֶסְתֵּר
