And this is the “yekar [precious honor]” (Esther 8:16) that they expounded there [means] “this is tefillin” — which [Israel] merited through the miracle of Esther.47Megillah 16b; Devarim 28:10; Peri Tzadik, Purim 7:1 — “yekar” as tefillin and revealed rootedness: The Gemara expounds the four gifts restored after Haman’s fall: “light” as Torah, “gladness” as Yom Tov, “joy” as circumcision, and “honor [yekar]” as tefillin. For tefillin it cites “the Name of Hashem is called upon you,” which Rabbi Eliezer identifies with the tefillin of the head. Peri Tzadik distinguishes the levels represented by these gifts: Torah reflects Israel’s avodah, circumcision reveals inherited holiness from the Avos, and tefillin disclose holiness bestowed by Hashem and Israel’s attachment to its supernal root. Rav Tzadok therefore reads Esther’s miracle not merely as permission to resume wearing tefillin, but as the public revelation of a bond that Haman’s decree could not sever.
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִיא נִטְמְאָה עַל יְדֵי אֲחַשְׁוֵרוֹשׁ, שֶׁזֶּה נִרְאֶה כְּ״אֵשֶׁת זְנוּנִים״ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם — וְהִיא הָיְתָה אָז בִּשְׁעַת נֵס זֶה כּוֹלֵל [כְּנֶסֶת] יִשְׂרָאֵל

For although she was defiled by Achashverosh — which appears, God forbid, like “an adulterous wife” — she was then, at the time of this miracle, the “inclusive [gathering] of Israel”48Megillah 15a; Resisei Layla 52:5, 8–9 — Esther as Knesses Yisrael and Malchus: Megillah states that “Esther donned royalty” means that she donned ruach hakodesh; the Gemara itself does not explicitly identify Esther with Knesses Yisrael. Resisei Layla develops that identification: Esther represents the Shechinah and Knesses Yisrael in exile, while her eventual rule reveals that her subjection to Achashverosh never became an inner acquisition or defilement. Rav Tzadok emphasizes that she remained righteous from beginning to end and received ruach hakodesh precisely as she entered the impure royal house. Thus the equation of Esther, Malchus, and the collective soul of Israel is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis built upon the Gemara’s statement.;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [בִּמְגִלָּה] עַל פָּסוּק ״וַתִּלְבַּשׁ אֶסְתֵּר מַלְכוּת״ שֶׁלָּבְשָׁתָּהּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, הַיְינוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּת הַיָּדוּעַ, שֶׁהִיא רָזָא דְּ״אֵשֶׁת חַיִל״

and as they said [Megillah 15a] on the verse “and Esther donned royalty [malchus]” (Esther 5:1), that “she donned ruach hakodesh” — namely, the known middah of Malchus, which is the secret of “a woman of valor.”49Megillah 15a: On “and it came to pass on the third day, and Esther donned royalty [malchus]” (Esther 5:1) — “R’ Elazar said in the name of R’ Chanina: this teaches that she donned ruach hakodesh.” R’ Tzadok identifies this “royalty” with the middah of Malchus — the “woman of valor” — under whose aspect Esther’s act was an aveirah lishmah.

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת גְּדוֹלָה עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, וְאֵין זֶה מוֹרֶה חִילּוּל הַבְּרִית חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, אֶלָּא אַדְּרַבָּא עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְבָּרֵר דַּאֲפִילּוּ הַנִּרְאִים מְחַלְּלֵי הַבְּרִית בֶּאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כֵּן

For in truth “great is a transgression for its own sake,” and this indicates no “profaning of the bris” in Israel, God forbid — rather, on the contrary, through it it is clarified that even those who appear to profane the bris are, in truth, not so.
וַאֲפִילּוּ בּוֹעֵל אֲרַמִּית, שֶׁזֶּהוּ תַּכְלִית הַחִילּוּל, שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּעֵירוּבִין יט.] דְּמִמַּשְׁכָא עׇרְלָתוֹ — הַיְינוּ רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, שֶׁאֵין נִיכָּר

And even one who “beds an Aramean woman,” which is the ultimate profanation, of whom they said [Eruvin 19a] that “his foreskin is drawn [mimashcha]” — that is only “to the outward eye,” that it is not discernible;50Eruvin 19a: In the aggadah on Gehinnom — even Israel’s transgressors are “full of mitzvos as a pomegranate,” and Avraham “raises up” from Gehinnom all but the one “whose foreskin is drawn [mimashcha lei orlasei].” R’ Tzadok reads even that “drawing” of the foreskin as only an outward semblance, the inner root of yiras shamayim remaining intact.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת] מִשֶּׁמּוֹשֵׁךְ צָרִיךְ לַחֲזוֹר וּלְמוּלוֹ רַק מִדְּרַבָּנָן מִטַּעַם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן, אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם זֶה מָהוּל, כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ הַיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם קָבוּעַ בְּלִבָּם מִצַּד הִתְקַשְּׁרוּת שָׁרְשָׁם בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

and as they said [in Yevamos] that one whose [foreskin] is drawn must be re-circumcised — but only rabbinically, for the sake of appearance — yet in truth he too is “circumcised,” for the root of the fear of Heaven is fixed in their heart by the binding of their root to Hashem.51Yevamos 72a; Eruvin 19a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:6; Takanas HaShavin 15:46 — a drawn foreskin changes appearance, not Torah status: Yevamos rules that one whose circumcised flesh was drawn forward remains circumcised by Torah law and is required to be circumcised again only by rabbinic decree because he appears uncircumcised. Eruvin describes the man who cohabits with a gentile woman as one whose foreskin is drawn and whom Avraham does not recognize at the entrance to Gehinnom. Yisrael Kedoshim joins the two teachings: human sight sees the outward orlah, whereas Hashem sees the heart and the Jewish root that remains attached to Him. The halachic sugya establishes legal status and appearance; Rav Tzadok’s claim about the unaltered inner root is his theological interpretation and does not diminish the gravity of the sin.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַמַּרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁצָּרִיךְ תִּיקּוּן לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן, הוּא צָרִיךְ עֹנֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְכַפָּרָה

And nonetheless, from the side of “the outward appearance” of this world, which requires rectification “to the eye,” he requires punishment in this world for atonement.52Yoma 86a; Tzidkas HaTzadik 40; Takanas HaShavin 10:3 — transformed sin and the remaining process of atonement: Yoma distinguishes forgiveness through teshuvah from the completion of kapparah: depending on the transgression, Yom Kippur, suffering, or death may still complete the cleansing. Tzidkas HaTzadik explains the highest teshuvah as an illumination in which deliberate sins can be understood as merits within Divine knowledge, while the earlier discussion in this siman nevertheless retains worldly punishment for grave acts. Rav Tzadok is therefore distinguishing two planes: the act’s inner meaning and covenantal root may be transformed, while its visible damage in this world may still require purification. The Gemara states the stages of atonement; this root-versus-appearance formulation is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
וְהָאוּמּוֹת שֶׁהֵם בְּשָׁרְשָׁן כֵּן, לָכֵן יִהְיֶה הָעֹנֶשׁ כֵּן בְּשָׁרְשָׁן לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְלִהֵט אוֹתָם״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲזֹב לָהֶם שֹׁרֶשׁ וְעָנָף״

And the nations, whose root is [evil] so, therefore their punishment will be so, in their root, forever — as it says, “and it shall consume them, [the coming day,] that shall leave them neither root nor branch” (Malachi 3:19).

וּפְשָׁטֵיהּ בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קָאֵי; וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין [קי סע״ב] דְּדָרֵישׁ לֵיהּ אַרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — הַיְינוּ מִכָּל עוֹשֵׂי רִשְׁעָה, וְעַל זֶה פְּלִיג רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, אֲבָל בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם מוֹדִים

And its plain sense refers to the nations; and in Sanhedrin [110b], where it is expounded of the wicked of Israel [re their young children], that is [of] “any evildoer,” and on this R’ Akiva disputes — but regarding the nations, [all] agree,53Sanhedrin 110b: A Tannaitic dispute — “the young children of the wicked of Israel do not enter the World to Come — the words of Rabban Gamliel; R’ Akiva says: they do enter.” As to the young children of the nations, all agree they do not, derived (per Rabban Gamliel) from “and You destroyed their every remembrance” (Yeshayah 26:14). R’ Tzadok: for Israel every punishment is only “to the eye,” their souls enduring; the total “root and branch” destruction is the nations’ alone.
כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם מִ״וַתְּאַבֵּד כָּל זֵכֶר לָמוֹ״
as it is there, from “and You destroyed their every remembrance” (Yeshayah 26:14).

אֲבָל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּהֵפֶךְ: כָּל עֹנֶשׁ הוּא רַק לְמַרְאִית עַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כִּילּוּי בָּנִים — הַיְינוּ רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲבָל נַפְשָׁם צְרוּרוֹת בַּה׳ וְקָמִים לִתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים וּלְעוֹלָם הַבָּא

But in Israel it is the reverse: every punishment is only “to the outward eye,” in this world; and even one upon whom, God forbid, “cutting off of children” was decreed — that is only in this world, but their souls are “bound in the bond of life” and rise for the resurrection of the dead and for Olam Haba.54I Shmuel 25:29; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1; Sanhedrin 44a; Machshavos Charutz 14:5; Resisei Layla 52:9 — the soul remains bound to Israel’s covenantal root: Avigayil describes David’s soul as “bound in the bond of life with Hashem,” and the Mishnah opens with the rule that all Israel have a share in the World to Come before listing defined exceptions. Sanhedrin’s principle, “Israel, although he sinned, is Israel,” preserves national identity despite transgression. Machshavos Charutz and Resisei Layla apply these foundations to Purim and circumcision: outward sin and punishment can be “only for appearance,” while the hidden heart remains attached to Hashem. These sources establish enduring identity, not a blanket exemption from judgment; Rav Tzadok applies that enduring root here to souls and progeny whose manifestation is absent in this world.

וַאֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁלֹּא הוֹלִיד כְּלָל — הַיְינוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה; אֲבָל אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר כְּתָב יָד [הֱבִיאוֹ הָרַב חִידָ״א בְּחַסְדֵּי אָבוֹת פ״ו מ״א] עַל פָּסוּק ״מִי יָלַד לִי אֶת אֵלֶּה״, שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם טִיפָּה שֶׁאֵינָהּ בְּאִיסּוּר הוֹלֵךְ לְאִיבּוּד, וּגְנוּזוֹת בְּהֵיכְלָא חַד, וְלֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ בָּנִים וּבָנוֹת רַבִּים, וְיַכִּיר כָּל אֶחָד אָבִיו — עַיֵּין שָׁם

And even one who did not beget at all — that is [only] in this world; but they said in the Zohar (in manuscript, cited by the Rav Chida in Chasdei Avos 6:1) on the verse “who bore me these?” (Yeshayah 49:21), that “no drop [of seed] that is not [emitted] in prohibition goes to loss,” and they are “stored in one chamber,” and in the Future he will have “many sons and daughters, and each will recognize his father” — see there.55Zohar (in manuscript), cited by the Chida, Chasdei Avos 6:1: On “who bore me these?” (Yeshayah 49:21) — R’ Shimon taught that one should fulfill the mitzvah of conjugal union with his wife for Heaven’s sake even if she is barren or aged, for no [licit] “drop” is ever lost; all such holy drops are “stored in one chamber of the King,” and in the Future each will be given a body — “many sons and daughters, and each will recognize his father.” (The Chida adduces this so that even one who “did not beget” loses nothing eternally.)

items.h: The theme: Certainly the principle of aveirah lishmah applies to women as well, as shown by Yael and Esther. The Sages say that R’ Akiva’s soul was drawn out from the kelipah through Yael, and R’ Tzadok suggests a similar process in Esther’s case. Because these women acted improperly only on the outward level, their punishment in this world was likewise only outward.

p: [ו] וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם בְּאִשָּׁה בַּעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כְּיָעֵל וְאֶסְתֵּר כֵּן, וְכַיָּדוּעַ מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בְּיָעֵל דְּאָז קָלְטָה נֶפֶשׁ רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא מִמֶּנּוּ, וְהָיְתָה אָז תְּחִלַּת יְצִיאָתוֹ מֵהַקְּלִיפָּה, וּמִסְּתָמָא גַּם בְּאֶסְתֵּר כֵּן

And certainly in a woman too, with a “transgression for its own sake” like Yael and Esther, it is so; and it is known what they said of Yael, that the soul of R’ Akiva was then “absorbed” from her [i.e., from that union], and it was then the beginning of its emergence from the kelipah — and presumably so with Esther too.56Gittin 57b; Megalleh Amukos, Va’eschanan §88; Resisei Layla §46; Petach Einayim to Gittin 57b — R’ Akiva and the sparks of Sisera: The Bavli states only that descendants of Sisera taught Torah in Jerusalem; it does not identify them by name. Megalleh Amukos and Rav Tzadok identify R’ Akiva with the holy power extracted from Sisera through Yael, and Resisei Layla describes those relations as the beginning of that power’s emergence from the kelipah. The Chida, however, records more than one kabbalistic formulation: one tradition connects R’ Akiva’s emergence to the union itself, while another, attributed to the Ari, places the extraction of the sparks in Yael’s driving the tent peg through Sisera’s head. Rav Tzadok’s statement is therefore a kabbalistic identification built upon, but not stated explicitly by, the Gemara.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהֵם לֹא עָשׂוּ אֶלָּא לִפְנִים, כָּךְ הָיָה הָעֹנֶשׁ רַק לְפָנִים וּלְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְבַד

And just as they [the penitents] acted only “outwardly,” so the punishment was only outward and “to the eye,” in this world alone.57Megillah 12a; Eichah 3:33; Resisei Layla §52 — “outwardly” answered “outwardly”: When asked why Israel was saved after bowing to Nevuchadnetzar’s image, Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai answers: “They acted only outwardly; likewise the Holy One acted with them only outwardly,” citing “He does not afflict from His heart.” The Gemara refers to the threatened annihilation in the Purim story. Rav Tzadok extends the same pattern to the temporal punishment associated with Yael and Esther: an act whose deepest intent was not separation from Hashem produces a punishment that remains on the plane of this-worldly appearance. That extension is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis; the Bavli itself does not formulate a general rule that every such punishment is confined to this world.

וְגַם בְּפֹעַל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק ״וְאֵלֶּה בְּנֵי בִּתְיָה״ דְּכָל הַמְגַדֵּל בֶּן חֲבֵירוֹ (מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ יְלָדוֹ, סַנְהֶדְרִין יט:), וְכֵן מִקְּרָא דְּ״אֵלֶּה תּוֹלְדוֹת מֹשֶׁה וְאַהֲרֹן״ עַל הַמְלַמֵּד בֶּן חֲבֵירוֹ תּוֹרָה

And even in actuality in this world: they said on the verse “and these are the sons of Bisya” (I Divrei HaYamim 4:18) that “whoever raises the child of his fellow, Scripture reckons it as if he bore him” (Sanhedrin 19b), and likewise from the verse “these are the offspring of Moshe and Aharon” (Bamidbar 3:1) — [said] of one who teaches his fellow’s son Torah.58Sanhedrin 19b: “R’ Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of R’ Yonatan: whoever raises an orphan in his home, Scripture reckons it as though he bore him” — derived from “and these are the sons of Bisya [daughter of Pharaoh], whom she raised” (I Divrei HaYamim 4:18), Bisya having raised Moshe. And “these are the offspring of Moshe and Aharon” — and it then lists, “these are the sons of Aharon” (Bamidbar 3:1) — yet only Aharon’s sons are listed — “to teach that whoever teaches his fellow’s son Torah, Scripture reckons it as though he bore him.”
וְאָמְרוּ גַּם בְּנֶפֶשׁ יְחִידָה, דְּכָל הַמְקַיֵּים נֶפֶשׁ אַחַת כִּמְקַיֵּים עוֹלָם מָלֵא, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן הַמְקַיֵּים עוֹלָם מָלֵא וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל

And they said even of a single soul, that “whoever sustains one soul is as one who sustains a whole world” (Sanhedrin 37a)59Sanhedrin 37a (Mishnah): “Whoever destroys a single soul [of Israel], Scripture reckons it as though he destroyed a whole world; and whoever sustains a single soul [of Israel], Scripture reckons it as though he sustained a whole world.” R’ Tzadok applies the latter to Esther — who “sustained” all Israel, and so is as one who “bore a whole world.” — all the more one who sustained a “whole world” and all Israel;
וְ״לַיְּהוּדִים הָיְתָה אוֹרָה״ — זוֹ תּוֹרָה, דַּהֲדַר קִבְּלוּהָ אָז מֵאַהֲבָה, וְהַכֹּל הָיָה עַל יָדָהּ, דַּהֲרֵי הוּא כְּהוֹלִידָהּ עוֹלָם מָלֵא וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל

and “the Jews had light [orah]” — “this is Torah” (Megillah 16b)60Megillah 16b: “‘The Jews had light [orah] and gladness and joy and honor’ (Esther 8:16) — R’ Yehudah said: ‘orah — this is Torah, as it says, “for the mitzvah is a lamp and the Torah is light.”’” R’ Tzadok: in Esther’s days Israel “re-accepted the Torah from love,” and so — saved from the decree — they were “like a new creation.”, which they then “re-accepted from love,”61Shabbos 88a; Rashi ad loc.; Resisei Layla §43; Peri Tzadik, Purim §2 — renewed acceptance from love: Rava teaches that in the days of Achashverosh Israel “again accepted” the Torah willingly, fulfilling what had previously been accepted under the coercion of the mountain. Rashi explains that this renewed acceptance came “from love of the miracle.” Rav Tzadok develops the point further: Purim marks an awakening from below and the flowering of Torah Shebe’al Peh, especially through the downfall of Haman and Israel’s voluntary love of Torah. Thus the phrase “re-accepted from love” combines the Gemara’s renewed acceptance, Rashi’s explanation of its motive, and Rav Tzadok’s account of its special relation to the Oral Torah. and all was through her — for it is as if she “bore” a whole world and all Israel,
דְּאַחַר שֶׁנִּגְזַר עֲלֵיהֶם לְהַשְׁמִיד וְנִיצּוֹלוּ, הֲרֵי הֵם כִּבְרִיָּה חֲדָשָׁה, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (ויק״ר ל, ג) עַל פָּסוּק ״וְעַם נִבְרָא״ וְגוֹמֵר

for after it was decreed upon them to be destroyed and they were saved, they are “like a new creation,” in the manner the Sages said (Vayikra Rabbah 30:3) on the verse “and a people yet to be created [shall praise God]” (Tehillim 102:19).62Tehillim 102:19; Vayikra Rabbah 30:3 — Mordechai’s generation as a “new creation”: The Midrash first derives from “a people yet to be created shall praise Hashem” that penitents are created anew, and then applies the same verse specifically to the generation of Mordechai, who had stood on the verge of death and were recreated after their deliverance. Rav Tzadok’s language here is therefore nearly literal Midrash: the rescued nation was not merely spared but received the standing of a newly created people. His further conclusion—that Esther is consequently as one who bore all Israel—joins this Midrash to the preceding rabbinic principles concerning raising, teaching, and sustaining another.

וְגַם זָכְתָה לְ״יָד וְשֵׁם טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּבָנוֹת״, שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צג:] ״זֶה סֵפֶר דָּנִיֵּאל שֶׁנִּקְרָא עַל שְׁמוֹ״, וְכֵן הוּא מְגִילַּת אֶסְתֵּר נִקְרֵאת עַל שְׁמָהּ, וְזֶה נִקְרָא ״טוֹב מִבָּנִים וּבָנוֹת״

And she also merited “a memorial [yad va-shem] better than sons and daughters” (Yeshayah 56:5) — for they said [Sanhedrin 93b] “this is the book of Daniel, called by his name” — and likewise Megillas Esther is called by her name, and this is “better than sons and daughters.”63Sanhedrin 93b: On the fate of Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah — “and where did they go? [the Gemara gives several answers]. As for the book of Daniel, [it is] called by his name [al shemo].” R’ Tzadok extends the principle to Esther: a work of Scripture bearing one’s name is “a memorial better than sons and daughters” (Yeshayah 56:5).64Yeshayah 56:5; Megillah 7a; Resisei Layla §52 — Esther’s memorial “better than sons and daughters”: Yeshayah promises the faithful “a hand and a name better than sons and daughters.” Sanhedrin applies the phrase to Daniel’s book, as noted in the preceding footnote. Megillah records Esther’s requests, “Establish me for generations” and “Write me for generations,” and the Sages’ eventual inclusion of the Megillah within the scriptural memorial of Amalek. Resisei Layla reads this enduring institution as Esther’s service to the Shechinah and as an “eternal sign” of Israel’s hidden bond with Hashem. Rav Tzadok accordingly treats the Megillah bearing her name as a lasting spiritual progeny that exceeds ordinary biological continuity.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקִּיבְּלָה עֹנֶשׁ עַל עַצְמָהּ בְּעַד הָעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ, וְכֵן עַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל — אַחַר שֶׁשָּׁבוּ דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכוּיוֹת מֵעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ — זָכְתָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְשָׂכָר הַטּוֹב מֵהָעֹנֶשׁ, וְכָל הָעֹנֶשׁ הוּא רַק בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְהַשָּׂכָר לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

And even though she received punishment upon herself for the “transgression for its own sake,” and likewise for all Israel — after they repented, so that it became “like merits” from a “transgression for its own sake” — she merited through this the good reward [that emerged] out of the punishment; and all the punishment is only in this world, while the reward is forever.

items.h: The theme: A mitzvah not for its own sake works the same way: an early authority (Responsa of Maharach Or Zarua) holds that all “not for its own sake” is one category and is, in a sense, “a transgression.” But that transgression was permitted whose end is to come to a mitzvah. And Nazir likens it to the deed of Yael.

p: [ז] וְגַם מִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ הוּא כֵּן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב קַדְמוֹן אֶחָד בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת מהר״ח אוֹר זָרוּעַ הַנִּדְפָּס מֵחָדָשׁ [סוֹף סִימָן קס״ג], דְּכָל שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ חַד הוּא וְכוּלָּם ״עֲבֵירָה״, אַךְ אוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה הוּתְּרָה שֶׁסּוֹפָהּ לָבוֹא לִידֵי מִצְוָה כו׳

And a mitzvah not for its own sake is also so; as one early authority wrote in the Responsa of Maharach Or Zarua (newly printed, end of §163), that “everything ‘not for its own sake’ is one [category], and they are all [in a sense]65Berachos 17a; Pesachim 50b; Tosafos to Berachos 17a — two uses of “not for its own sake”: Berachos condemns one who acts “not for its own sake” as one for whom it would have been preferable not to have been created, while Pesachim and Nazir direct a person to engage in Torah and mitzvos even not for their own sake because this leads to lishmah. Tosafos distinguishes one who studies in order to provoke or defeat others, which is condemned, from one who studies for honor, which may become a path to lishmah. The approach cited here from Maharach Or Zarua is more sweeping: every ulterior intention contains a defective element, yet the act may still be permitted and rewarded because it becomes the route to a later mitzvah lishmah. ‘a transgression’66Peri Tzadik, Shoftim 1:1 — punishment for the defect and reward for the Torah: Rav Tzadok explicitly cites Rabbeinu Chaim Or Zarua as reconciling the opposing statements: a person may be punished for having learned shelo lishmah and nevertheless receive reward for the learning because it brings him to lishmah. He compares this to a mitzvah accompanied by a real fault, such as fasting on Shabbos for a troubling dream: the mitzvah accomplishes its good while the improper element still requires atonement. Thus calling shelo lishmah an “aveirah” identifies the impurity of motive; it does not erase the mitzvah-content of the deed. — but that transgression was permitted whose end is to come to a mitzvah,67Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 10:5 — a deliberately transitional form of service: The Rambam defines serving for reward or from fear of punishment as shelo lishmah, yet rules that beginners should be trained in precisely this way until their understanding expands and they are gradually brought to service from love. This is the practical meaning of a defect “permitted because its end is to come to a mitzvah”: the ulterior motive is tolerated only as a stage ordered toward lishmah, not as an ideal in which one may remain.” etc.68Tzidkas HaTzadik §59; Resisei Layla §6 — the act introduces holiness before the intention is perfected: Rav Tzadok writes that Torah learned shelo lishmah does not yet disclose the inner “light” that fully guides and returns a person to the good. Nevertheless, speaking words of Torah remains a mitzvah that places holiness in the heart; elsewhere he adds that a mitzvah protects even when performed shelo lishmah, although only lishmah produces its complete transforming opposite. The deed is therefore deficient but not empty: its holiness can open the way to the later moment of lishmah.
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע [בְּנָזִיר] שֶׁמְּדַמֶּה אוֹתָהּ לְמַעֲשֵׂה דְּיָעֵל כו׳ עַיֵּין שָׁם

And so it is implied [in Nazir 23b] that [the Gemara] compares it [a mitzvah not for its own sake] to the deed of Yael, etc. — see there.69Responsa Maharach Or Zarua §163: an early authority holds that everything done “not for its own sake” is of one category and is, in a measure, a “transgression” — yet the Sages permitted precisely that “transgression” whose end is to lead to a mitzvah (as with “a mitzvah not for its own sake,” from which one comes to its own sake). Nazir 23b implicitly compares this to Yael’s deed — an aveirah lishmah — the two being the poles of the one principle R’ Tzadok is developing.70Nazir 23b — Yael and the Gemara’s final formulation: The Gemara first states that an aveirah lishmah is greater than a mitzvah shelo lishmah, but challenges this from the rule that shelo lishmah leads to lishmah and revises the conclusion: an aveirah lishmah is “like” a mitzvah shelo lishmah. Yael is then compared to Sarah, Rivkah, Rachel, and Leah, the “women in the tent.” The comparison explains the spiritual valuation of Yael’s exceptional act after the fact; it is not a general authorization to choose a prohibition in the hope of producing a mitzvah. — With this the siman’s foundational block closes: the single principle of aveirah / shelo lishmah — an act outwardly a breach but inwardly wholly to God — that reframes David, Esther, Yael, and the wayward of Israel alike.

items.h: The theme: The distinction between a mitzvah shelo lishmah and an aveirah lishmah applies only as an ideal at the outset. A revealed act of holiness, even when done with an imperfect motive, can draw a person toward serving God for its own sake. A transgression normally pulls toward further sin, which is why one who plans to sin and then repent is not granted the opportunity.

p: [ח] וְהַחִילּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם רַק לְעִנְיַן לְכַתְּחִלָּה, דְּבָזֶה אָמְרוּ ״לְעוֹלָם יַעֲסֹק (אָדָם בַּתּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ)״ כו׳, שֶׁהַמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ יֵשׁ בָּהּ מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה גְּלוּיָה הַמַּכְנֶסֶת קְדֻשָּׁה בַּלֵּב, שֶׁבְּהֶכְרֵחַ וּבְבֵירוּר בָּא מִכֹּחָהּ וְעַל יָדָהּ לִשְׁמָהּ

And the distinction between them is only regarding l’chatchilah — for concerning [a mitzvah not-lishmah] they said, “let a person always occupy himself [with Torah and mitzvos, even not for their own sake],” for a mitzvah not-lishmah has in it a revealed act of mitzvah that “brings holiness into the heart,” so that necessarily and certainly, by its power and through it, one comes to lishmah.71Avos 4:2; Tzidkas HaTzadik §59; Resisei Layla §6 — opposite chains begun by the deed itself: Ben Azzai pairs “a mitzvah draws another mitzvah” with “a transgression draws another transgression.” Rav Tzadok explains that Torah learned shelo lishmah has not yet disclosed its inner light, but the words and act remain a mitzvah that place holiness in the heart; elsewhere he writes that a mitzvah protects even when done shelo lishmah, although only lishmah produces its full transforming effect. This grounds the l’chatchilah asymmetry here: the revealed mitzvah-act already points toward holiness, while the prohibited act habituates the heart in the opposite direction.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הָעֲבֵירָה, אַדְּרַבָּא גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה הַמַּכְנֶסֶת טוּמְאָה בַּלֵּב וְהֵיפֶךְ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וְהָאוֹמֵר ״אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב״ אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין (בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה, יוֹמָא פה:)

Not so a transgression — on the contrary, it “drags along [another] transgression,” bringing impurity into the heart, the opposite of holiness; and “one who says ‘I will sin and repent’ is not given [the opportunity] (to do teshuvah)” (Yoma 85b).72Yoma 85b: “One who says, ‘I will sin and repent, I will sin and repent’ — he is not given the opportunity to repent; [one who says] ‘I will sin and Yom Kippur will atone’ — Yom Kippur does not atone.” R’ Tzadok limits this to one for whom the sin is “reckoned as nothing,” who therefore can never reach the shattered remorse of true teshuvah — not to the genuine penitent whose returned-from sin becomes a merit.
וְלֹא דִּיבְּרוּ חֲכָמִים בְּשׁוֹפְטָנֵי — שׁוֹטִים וּרְשָׁעִים הַחוֹטְאִים לְמַלֹּאות תַּאֲוַת יִצְרָם וִידַמּוּ שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ אַחַר שֶׁיִּמְלְאוּ תַּאֲוָתָם — דְּזֶה שְׁטוּת גָּדוֹל

And the Sages did not speak of “fools” — the foolish and wicked who sin to fill the desire of their inclination and imagine that they will repent after they sate their desire — for that is great folly:
כִּי אִם בִּתְחִלַּת כְּנִיסַת הַיֵּצֶר לְלִבּוֹ לֹא יָכוֹל לְנַצְּחוֹ, עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אִישׁ וּבַעַל הַבַּיִת וְחֵטְא בְּפֹעַל — אֵיךְ יְחַכֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ לְנַצְּחוֹ

for if at the very entry of the inclination into his heart he could not overcome it, then once it has become a “man” and a “master of the house” and a sin in actuality — how will he then hope to overcome it?73Sukkah 52b; Yoma 86b; Resisei Layla §38 — from passerby to guest to master of the house: Sukkah describes the yetzer first as a passing traveler, then as a welcomed guest, and finally as an “ish,” a man of established standing; it likewise begins by misleading from outside and ends “within them.” Yoma adds that after a person repeats a sin it becomes to him “as though permitted.” Rav Tzadok explicitly joins these images: the initial encounter is incidental, but repetition turns the impulse into the resident “man and master of the house.” The se’if’s warning is therefore psychological as well as juridical: postponing resistance strengthens the very power one imagines he will later defeat.
אֲבָל הַכַּוָּונָה עַל הַטּוֹעִים הַחוֹשְׁבִים לַחֲטוֹא כְּדֵי לָשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
Rather, the intent is regarding the erring ones who think to sin in order to repent afterward and reach the rung of baalei teshuvah —
וְגַם זֶה בַּהֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע: לְמִי שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לְהַסִּיתוֹ לְחֵטְא גָּמוּר לַעֲבוֹר עַל רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, מְסִיתוֹ שֶׁזֶּהוּ כְּמוֹ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

and this too is by the enticement of the evil inclination: one whom it cannot entice to an outright sin, to transgress Hashem’s will, it entices [by suggesting] “this is like a transgression for its own sake.”

וְעַל זֶה הֵעִידוּ חֲכָמִים דְּאֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ, כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת זֶה הַחוֹטֵא לְכַתְּחִלָּה עַל מְנָת לָשׁוּב אֵין הַחֵטְא נֶחְשָׁב בְּעֵינָיו לִכְלוּם, וְאֵיךְ יִזְכֶּה לִתְשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה שֶׁהִיא הַהִתְמַרְמְרוּת וְהַחֲרָטָה הַגְּמוּרָה בַּלֵּב עַל מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה

And of this the Sages testified that “he is not given [the chance]” — for in truth, this one who sins l’chatchilah “on condition to repent,” the sin is reckoned as nothing in his eyes; and how will he merit the complete teshuvah, which is the [bitter] embittering and complete regret of the heart over what he did?74Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2; 4:1, 4:6 — withheld assistance, not a permanently locked gate: The Rambam lists “I will sin and then repent” among the grave acts for which Heaven does not grant the sinner the usual opportunity to repent because of the seriousness of his choice. Yet he concludes that these matters impede teshuvah but do not prevent it absolutely: if such a person truly repents, he is a baal teshuvah. Complete teshuvah requires abandoning the sin, removing it from thought, resolving never to return, and regretting the past. Rav Tzadok’s point is that treating the sin in advance as a tool empties it of the very regret needed for that return, without denying that sincere teshuvah remains possible.

וּלְעִנְיַן לְכַתְּחִלָּה בְּוַדַּאי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְדַמּוֹתָם כְּלָל, שֶׁזֶּה מִצְוָה גְּמוּרָה וְזוֹ עֲבֵירָה גְּמוּרָה. אֲבָל אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עֲזָרוֹ שֶׁשָּׁב לַה׳ בְּכָל לְבָבוֹ וּבְכָל נַפְשׁוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת, שַׁפִּיר עַל הָעֲבֵירוֹת עַצְמָן ״חָיֹה יִחְיֶה״, דְּיַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And regarding l’chatchilah, certainly they cannot be likened at all — this being a complete mitzvah and that a complete transgression. But after he has sinned, and Hashem helped him so that he returned to Hashem with all his heart and all his soul in truth — well then, upon the transgressions themselves “he shall surely live,” that they become like merits,75Yoma 86b; Yechezkel 33:19 — sins become merits only after teshuvah from love: Reish Lakish distinguishes two levels: repentance from fear reduces intentional sins to unwitting failures, whereas repentance from love transforms them into merits, derived from “when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, upon them he shall live.” The transformation is retrospective and follows an authentic return with the whole heart. It therefore supports Rav Tzadok’s boundary: after the fall, teshuvah can convert its history into merit; before the act, that future possibility cannot authorize creating the sin.

וְכַמִּצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ דַּחֲשִׁיבִי כְּמוֹ לִשְׁמָהּ גָּמוּר, וְכַמְבוֹאָר [בַּעֲרָכִין טז:] גַּבֵּי עֲנָוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ ״מִי לָא מוֹדֵית דְּלִשְׁמָהּ עֲדִיפָא״, הָכִי נָמֵי שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

like a mitzvah not-for-its-own-sake which is reckoned like complete lishmah; and as is explained [Arachin 16b] regarding “humility not-for-its-own-sake” — “do you not concede that for-its-own-sake is preferable?” — so too “not-for-its-own-sake” [is good] — see there.76Arachin 16b: R’ Yehudah b’Rabbi Shimon asked, “reproof for its own sake, or humility not for its own sake — which is preferable?” [R’ Yehudah HaNasi] answered, “do you not concede that humility for its own sake is preferable? — for the Master said, ‘humility is greatest of all’; [and so] even humility not for its own sake [is preferable], for Rav Yehudah said in the name of Rav: let a person always occupy himself with Torah and mitzvos even not for their own sake, for from not-for-its-own-sake one comes to its own sake.”

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ד.] דִּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל ״הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״ [דְּהָא דְּ״מִתּוֹךְ״ כו׳ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּאָנוּ מְבָרְכִין ״אֲשֶׁר קִדְּשָׁנוּ בְּמִצְוֹתָיו וְצִוָּנוּ״, שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוָה גַּם שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ מַמְשֶׁכֶת קְדֻשָּׁה לַלֵּב לְהָבִיא לִשְׁמָהּ, ״וְלֹא עָשָׂה כֵן לְכָל גּוֹי״]

And so they said [Rosh Hashanah 4a] that in Israel [one who gives charity so that his sons live or that he merit the World to Come] “is a complete tzaddik” [for “from not-lishmah one comes to lishmah” applies only in Israel — for we bless “who sanctified us with His mitzvos and commanded us,” so that the mitzvah-act, even not-lishmah, draws holiness to the heart to bring [him] to lishmah — “and He did not do so for any [other] nation”].77Rosh Hashanah 4a: “But it was taught: one who says, ‘this sela is for charity so that my sons may live,’ or ‘so that I may merit the World to Come’ — he is a complete tzaddik! No difficulty: here [it refers] to a Jew, there to a gentile.” Rashi: “here to a Jew” — whose heart is [ultimately] to Heaven, and who, if afflicted, does not complain but attributes the sufferings to his sin. R’ Tzadok: only in Israel does a mitzvah-act, even not-lishmah, draw holiness to the heart and lead to lishmah — “and He did not do so for any [other] nation.”
וְזֶהוּ בַּקָּשַׁת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה ״[הֶרֶב] כַּבְּסֵנִי מֵעֲוֹנִי וּמֵחַטָּאתִי טַהֲרֵנִי״, שֶׁמֵּהַחֵטְא וְהֶעָוֹן עַצְמוֹ יִהְיֶה הַכִּיבּוּס וְהַטָּהֳרָה

And this is the request of David HaMelech, “wash me thoroughly from my iniquity78R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §174): “As they said, ‘in the place where baalei teshuvah stand [the wholly righteous cannot stand]’ — although, God forbid, [one may not] say ‘I will sin and repent’ and act so by his [free] choice, since ‘they do not give him the chance’ — nevertheless, of itself it comes about [that he falls and returns], for ‘there is no wholly righteous man on earth,’ even Yosef HaTzaddik.” The se’if’s distinction: the deliberate ploy “I will sin and repent” is denied Heaven’s help, yet the true, unplanned fall — once repented from the depths — is what raises the penitent above the tzaddik., and cleanse me from my sin” (Tehillim 51:4) — that from the sin and the iniquity itself will come the washing and the purification;

שֶׁכָּךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, בַּמֶּה שֶׁהוּא מַכֶּה בּוֹ מְרַפֵּא, וּבְדָבָר שֶׁקִּלְקְלוּ בּוֹ נִתַּקְּנוּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין עא רע״ב] וּמַמְתִּיק הַמַּר בְּמַר; וְאֵין הַכִּיבּוּס וְהַטָּהֳרָה לְחֵטְא בְּדָבָר אַחֵר, רַק בְּהַחֵטְא עַצְמוֹ, דְּאַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא עַצְמוֹ הַגּוֹרֵם הַטָּהֳרָה

for such is the way of the Holy One: “with what He strikes, He heals,” and “with the thing they spoiled, they are rectified,” as they said [Sanhedrin 71b], “and He sweetens the bitter with the bitter”; and the washing and purification of a sin is not through some other thing, but through the sin itself — for after the teshuvah, it itself is what causes the purification.79Shemos Rabbah 50:3; Tanchuma Buber, Beshalach 18:2; Resisei Layla §38 — healing through the very blow: The Midrash contrasts a human physician, who wounds with one instrument and heals with another, with the Holy One, Who heals through the very means of the blow. At Marah, a bitter substance sweetened the bitter water — “the bitter heals the bitter.” Rav Tzadok applies this pattern to Esther and Purim: the apparent wound itself becomes the vehicle of repair, as sins transformed by teshuvah become merits. Here the same structure explains David’s prayer: after teshuvah, the sin itself becomes the occasion and material of purification; it was not healing while chosen as sin.

items.h: The theme: In the story of Reish Lakish (Bava Metzia 84a), his cry to R’ Yochanan — “what benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi’!” — is astonishing after his teshuvah. R’ Tzadok’s reading: Reish Lakish spoke something great. A man of his stature merited teshuvah from love, whereby his willful sins literally shine as merits. So that his former “chief of the bandits” was reckoned an elevation, truly like his present eminence among the Sages.

p: [ט] וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא [פד.] בְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דְּאָמַר לֵיהּ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית לִי, הָתָם רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי [וְהָכָא רַבִּי קָרוּ לִי]״ כו׳, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י

And in Bava Metzia [84a], concerning Reish Lakish, who said to him [R’ Yochanan], “what benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi’!” — see there in Rashi.80Bava Metzia 84a: R’ Yochanan, bathing in the Jordan, was leapt upon by the brigand Reish Lakish; R’ Yochanan said, “your strength for Torah!” and offered him his sister [in marriage] if he would repent. Reish Lakish repented and became a great Sage. Later, in a study-hall dispute over when metal vessels become susceptible to impurity, R’ Yochanan said, “a brigand knows his brigandry” [i.e., you know weapons]. Reish Lakish was pained: “what benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi.’” R’ Yochanan was pained that Reish Lakish did not feel benefited — and both suffered grievously thereafter. Rashi: “‘Rebbi they called me’ — I was chief of the bandits.” Tosafos: cite Rabbeinu Tam that Reish Lakish had originally been a scholar who cast off the yoke of Torah. R’ Tzadok reads Reish Lakish’s cry as a profound claim: through teshuvah from love, his former “chief of bandits” itself shines as an elevation.
וְלִכְאוֹרָה תָּמוּהַּ מְאוֹד, דְּאַחַר שֶׁשָּׁב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֵיךְ יֹאמַר ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית״ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי בֵּין הַלִּיסְטִים
And at first glance this is very astonishing: after Reish Lakish repented, how could he say “what benefit,” on account of his having been “chief among the bandits”?

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּדָבָר גָּדוֹל דִּיבֵּר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בָּזֶה: כִּי בְּוַדַּאי אָדָם גָּדוֹל כְּמוֹתוֹ זָכָה לִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵאַהֲבָה, שֶׁכָּל זְדוֹנוֹתָיו נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת לִהְיוֹת מְאִירִים וּמַזְהִירִים מַמָּשׁ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And perforce Reish Lakish spoke a great matter here: for certainly a great man like him merited complete teshuvah from love, [such] that all his willful sins became like merits — literally shining and radiant like merits —81Yoma 86b; Yechezkel 33:19; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — teshuvah from love transforms the willful past: Reish Lakish distinguishes repentance from fear, in which intentional sins are counted as unwitting failures, from repentance from love, in which they become merits. Rav Tzadok describes the highest teshuvah as an illumination through which the sinner recognizes that even the fallen history never lay outside Divine knowledge, and its energy is returned to holiness. This transformation is retrospective: it follows sincere teshuvah and does not authorize sin beforehand or erase human responsibility for the original choice.
וּמַה שֶּׁהָיָה קוֹדֶם ״רַבִּי בֵּין הַלִּיסְטִים״ נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ לִגְדֻלָּה וּמַעֲלָה מַמָּשׁ כְּמוֹ עַכְשָׁיו שֶׁהוּא רַב בֵּין הַחֲכָמִים
and what he was before — “Rebbi among the bandits” — was reckoned to him as greatness and elevation, literally like now, when he is a master among the Sages.
כִּי כָּךְ הוּא יְשׁוּעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה, שֶׁמֵּאִיר אֶת עֵינָיו לְהַשִּׂיג זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵיךְ הָעֲוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת מַמָּשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם קְדֻשָּׁה
For such is Hashem’s salvation to one who merits: that He illumines his eyes to attain, in this world, how the iniquities are literally like merits that have holiness in them.

דְּעַל כֵּן נִכְתְּבוּ כָּל חֲטָאֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּתּוֹרָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה הַקַּיֶּימֶת לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד; וַהֲרֵי לֶעָתִיד נֶאֱמַר דִּיבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ וְחַטַּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה — וְאֵיךְ נִכְתְּבוּ בַּתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת לְמַזְכֶּרֶת עָוֹן לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

Therefore all the sins of Israel were written in the holy Torah, which endures forever — yet of the Future it is said, “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and be no more, and the sins of Yehudah, and they shall not be found”; so how were they written in the Torah to be “a remembrancer of iniquity” forever?

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר שֶׁהַכֹּל נַעֲשֶׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְיָאִיר זֶה לְעֵינֵי הַכֹּל אֵיךְ הֵם זְכֻיּוֹת, אֵין כָּאן גְּנוּת וּמַזְכֶּרֶת עָוֹן, אֶלָּא שֶׁבַח וּמַזְכֶּרֶת זְכוּת

And perforce, after the complete rectification, when everything becomes like merits, and this shines to all eyes how they are merits — there is here no disgrace or “remembrancer of iniquity,” but praise and a “remembrancer of merit.”82Yirmiyahu 50:20; Sanhedrin 107a; Yoma 86b — an enduring record after the iniquity is no longer found: Yirmiyahu promises that in the final restoration Israel’s iniquity will be sought and not found. Yet Sanhedrin teaches that David’s entire episode, once fit to be written in Scripture, could not be omitted even at his request. Rav Tzadok joins these teachings with the principle that teshuvah from love turns sins into merits: the event remains eternally recorded, but after complete rectification its meaning is no longer a memorial of guilt; it testifies to the greatness of teshuvah and becomes a memorial of merit.

וְלֹא לְחִנָּם לָמְדוּ [בע״ז נב.] עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה מִמִּזְבֵּחַ, ״מָה מִזְבֵּחַ טָעוּן (גְּנִיזָה אַף אֲשֵׁרָה טְעוּנָה גְּנִיזָה)״, כִּי כְּבָר הִבְטִיחָנוּ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּ״לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח״, וְהַכֹּל יְתוּקַּן לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא בְּתַכְלִית הַתִּיקּוּן, וַאֲפִילּוּ חָטָא עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

And not for nothing did they learn [Avodah Zarah 52a] that Israel’s idolatry “requires genizah [burial]” from [the law of] the altar — “just as the altar requires [burial, so the asheirah requires burial]” — for Hashem already assured us “that no outcast shall be cast away from Him” (II Shmuel 14:14), and all will be rectified in the Future in the ultimate rectification, even the sin of idolatry.83Avodah Zarah 52a: Israelite idolatry (e.g., an asheirah) “requires genizah” — derived from the altar of the calf, which was buried rather than destroyed. R’ Tzadok reads the requirement to store away rather than annihilate as a sign that even the gravest Israelite sin is not finally “cast off,” but destined for rectification in the Future.84II Shmuel 14:14; Sanhedrin 44a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:5 — no soul finally cast away: The phrase “He devises means that the banished one not be cast away from Him” appears in the woman of Tekoa’s appeal to David. The Bavli supplies the covenantal principle that even after sin a Jew remains “Israel,” and the Rambam states that the Torah has promised that Israel will ultimately repent at the end of exile and immediately be redeemed. These sources support Rav Tzadok’s confidence in final rectification, while still preserving the need for actual teshuvah and accountability in the present.

דְּיִהְיוּ ״כַּשָּׁנִים״ הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, דְּהַכֹּל מְסֻדָּר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְּחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה, וּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הָיָה לְכָךְ, דְּ״גַם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ פָּעַלְתָּ לָּנוּ״, ״וְאַתָּה הֲסִבּוֹתָ אֶת לִבָּם אֲחֹרַנִּית״, וְהוּכְרְחוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת כִּרְצוֹנְךָ ״לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק בְּדָבְרֶךָ תִּזְכֶּה בְשָׁפְטֶךָ״

for they will be like these “shanim [scarlet/years],” arranged and coming from the six days of Creation — for all is arranged by Hashem from the beginning of Creation, and Hashem’s will was so:85Yeshayah 1:18; Shabbos 89b; Resisei Layla §34 — “scarlet” read as the ordered years from Creation: On “though your sins be ka-shanim,” the Gemara asks why the plural form is used and reads it as “like these years that have proceeded in order from the six days of Creation until now”; even sins as numerous as those years can become white as snow. Rav Tzadok elsewhere cites this derashah together with the future disappearance of Israel’s iniquity and the hidden fragrance of Israel’s apparent betrayals. Here he extends the phrase from the promise of cleansing to the providential ordering of history; that extension is his theological reading, not the Gemara’s explicit conclusion. “also all our deeds You have wrought for us” (Yeshayah 26:12), “and You turned their heart backward,” and they were compelled to do Your will, “so that You be justified when You speak, and be right when You judge” (Tehillim 51:6).

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק זֶה בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה [סַנְהֶדְרִין קז.] דְּ״לָא לֵימְרוּ עַבְדָּא דְּזָכֵי לְמָרֵיהּ״, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יָכוֹל לָנֶצַח יִצְרוֹ לֹא הָיָה רַשַּׁאי, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ יַחֲשִׁיבוּ לְחֵטְא וְיֵעָנְשׁוּ עַל זֶה, כֵּיוָן דִּרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ

in the manner they said on this verse regarding David [Sanhedrin 107a] — “lest they say, a servant who prevailed over his Master” — that even though he could have conquered his inclination, he was not permitted [to], and even though he knew Hashem would reckon it a sin and they would be punished for it, since Hashem’s will was so.86Berachos 31b–32a; Sanhedrin 107a; Avodah Zarah 4b–5a; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — Divine causation, human failure, and the paradigm of teshuvah: Elijah pleaded, “You turned their heart backward,” and the Gemara cites verses showing that Heaven’s shaping of the human heart tempers judgment. Sanhedrin places in David’s mouth the claim that he could have subdued his inclination but did not, so that “a servant should not be said to have prevailed over his Master”; Avodah Zarah adds that David was not naturally fit for that failure, but became the model proving that an individual can repent. Rav Tzadok synthesizes these aggados through the paradox of Divine knowledge and human choice. They are not a practical license to sin: Sanhedrin opens by warning never to invite a test, and David still required repentance, suffering, and atonement.

items.h: The theme: This is the service of “with all your soul,” which David merited (the Zohar: “‘my soul’ — this is David”). The aim is to surrender even the soul to God: knowing he thereby “sins against the soul,” yet if God’s will were to destroy his soul he would consent, never to deviate from God’s will. He is “the man who raised the yoke of teshuvah” for all Israel — the individual whose repentance is forgiven “him and the whole world” — arousing teshuvah in the whole stature of Knesses Yisrael.

p: [י] וְזֶהוּ עֲבוֹדַת ״בְּכָל נַפְשְׁךָ״ שֶׁזָּכָה לָזֶה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה [לְתַקֵּן דַּרְגָּא דִּידֵיהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ (לֵךְ פד.) ״מַאן נַפְשִׁי — דָּא דָוִד״, וּבְפָרָשַׁת וַיִּגַּשׁ ״נֶפֶשׁ — דָּא נֶפֶשׁ דָּוִד״ עַיֵּין שָׁם ר״ו א] — לִמְסוֹר גַּם הַנֶּפֶשׁ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

And this is the service of “with all your soul,” which David87R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek §1): “As the Zohar says (Va’era 27a) on ‘with all your soul’ — ‘this is David.’ But the wicked man, in [mere] deed, has no ‘soul’ — which is the perfection of deed, the rung of David HaMelech — from which flow true longing, thirst, and hunger [for God], from which comes joy, as it says, ‘the heart of those who seek Hashem shall rejoice,’ though he still seeks and has not yet found.” The se’if’s service of “with all your soul,” which David alone fully merited — surrendering the very soul to God’s will. HaMelech merited [to rectify his own rung — as they said in the holy Zohar (Lech Lecha 84a), “who is ‘my soul’? — this is David,” and in Parashas Vayigash, “‘nefesh’ — this is the nefesh of David,” see there 206a] — to surrender even the soul to Hashem:
שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ שֶׁחוֹטֵא עַל הַנֶּפֶשׁ בָּזֶה, אִם רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְאַבֵּד אֶת נַפְשׁוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִתְרַצָּה גַּם לָזֶה, שֶׁלֹּא לִנְטוֹת מֵרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

that even though he knows he “sins against the soul” in this, if Hashem’s will were to destroy his soul, God forbid, he consents even to this — not to deviate from Hashem’s will.88Berachos 61b; Devarim 6:5 — “with all your soul,” even if He takes your soul: Rabbi Akiva interprets “with all your soul” as fidelity to Hashem even when He takes one’s life, and he fulfilled the verse while accepting the yoke of Heaven at his execution. Rav Tzadok extends that total surrender from bodily martyrdom to David’s willingness not to make even the preservation of his own spiritual standing the final criterion when the Divine will is known. This describes an extraordinary rung of David; it is not permission to identify a Torah prohibition as God’s will without an explicit command or an authoritative prophetic mandate.

וְהוּא הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּ״יָחִיד שֶׁשָּׁב מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ וּלְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ״, שֶׁמְּעוֹרֵר הִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל קוֹמַת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּבְכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And he is “the man who raised the yoke of teshuvah” for all Israel — “an individual who repents, they forgive him and the whole world with him” — who arouses stirrings of teshuvah in the whole stature of Knesses Yisrael and in all the souls of Israel.89Avodah Zarah 4b–5a; Yoma 86b — David opens teshuvah for the individual and, through him, for the world: The Gemara says that David was not naturally suited to that failure, but his episode established a “claim” for penitents: if an individual sins, he is directed to David, “the man who raised the yoke of teshuvah.” Yoma adds that because one individual repents, the entire world is forgiven. Rav Tzadok joins these teachings by locating David’s soul within the collective stature of Knesses Yisrael, so that his return awakens return throughout Israel. That collective, kabbalistic extension is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis of the two sugyos.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִגְלֶה אֶצְלָם בְּפֹעַל, הֲרֵי גַּם מִשֶּׁהִרְהֵר תְּשׁוּבָה בְּלִבּוֹ הֲרֵי זֶה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר, וּמִמֵּילָא יִהְיֶה הַתִּיקּוּן לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, דִּיבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן (יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ) כו׳, דְּלֵיכָּא עָוֹן עוֹד, כִּי הַכֹּל זְכוּת מֵאַחַר שֶׁהָיָה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ

And even though it is not revealed among them in actuality, behold, even from when he contemplated teshuvah in his heart, he is a complete tzaddik, and of itself the rectification will be for the whole world — “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and be no more” — for there is no iniquity anymore, since all is merit, once Hashem’s will was so.90Kiddushin 49b; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5 — a thought of teshuvah can immediately alter one’s standing: If a man betroths a woman on condition that he is righteous, even though he had been completely wicked, the Gemara is concerned that he may have contemplated teshuvah in his heart. The Rambam therefore rules that she is doubtfully betrothed. This is the halachic basis for Rav Tzadok’s statement that from the moment of an inward turning he is already called a complete tzaddik. It concerns the change of direction and identity effected by teshuvah; it does not mean that restitution, confession, suffering, or other stages of atonement required for particular sins have automatically been completed.

וַהֲרֵי הָיָה בָּזֶה עוֹבֵד לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וַאֲפִילּוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הַחֲמוּרָה, הֲרֵי זֶה כְּעֵין הַשָּׂעִיר לַעֲזָאזֵל, שֶׁאִלּוּ עָשִׂינוּ מֵעַצְמֵנוּ כְּמוֹ זֶה הָיָה נֶחְשָׁב הַקְרָבָה לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
And indeed he was, in this, “serving Hashem”; and even in grave idolatry, it is like the sa’ir la-Azazel: had we done such of our own accord, it would be reckoned an offering to idolatry, God forbid,
אֲבָל מֵאַחַר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ צִיוָּה כָּךְ, הֲרֵי אָנוּ עוֹבְדִין בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁאָמַר וְנַעֲשָׂה רְצוֹנוֹ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אוֹתוֹ הַשָּׂעִיר נוֹשֵׂא כָּל עֲוֹנֹתָם

but since Hashem commanded so, we are thereby also “serving Hashem,” who spoke and His will is done — and through this that goat “bears all their iniquities.”91Ramban to Vayikra 16:8; Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 46; Tzidkas HaTzadik §40 — the sa’ir is service only because Hashem commanded it: The Ramban insists that the goat is not an offering from Israel to Azazel, Heaven forbid: both goats are first placed before Hashem, the lot is disposed by Him, and the emissary merely fulfills the Master’s command. Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer describes the accuser’s “portion” as ultimately causing him to testify to Israel’s purity on Yom Kippur. Rav Tzadok uses this as the paradigm of an act that, if initiated independently, would be idolatrous, but through an explicit Divine command is wholly service of Hashem and becomes an instrument of atonement. The explicit command is therefore the indispensable boundary of the comparison.

כִּי כֵן הֵם כָּל עֲוֹנֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל — אֵין יוֹצְאִים מֵאֲמִיתּוּת רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְכָל חֲטָאֵי הַצִּבּוּר וְהַיְּחִידִים מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁנִּכְתְּבוּ בַּתַּנַ״ךְ וּבְתַלְמוּד הַמְקוּדָּשׁ הַקַּיָּם לָעַד, וַדַּאי לֹא לְשֵׁם גְּנוּת נִכְתַּב, דַּאֲפִילּוּ בִּגְנוּת בְּהֵמָה טְמֵאָה לֹא דִּיבֵּר הַכָּתוּב

For so are all the iniquities of the Children of Israel — they do not depart from the truth of Hashem’s will; and all the sins of the community and the individuals of Israel written in Tanach and in the sanctified, eternal Talmud were certainly not written for disgrace, for “Scripture did not speak even in the disgrace of an impure animal” (Pesachim 3a).92Pesachim 3a: “A person should never let a coarse word leave his mouth — for Scripture ‘circumvented’ [by using] eight [extra] letters rather than let a coarse word leave [it],” writing of the animals “that are not clean” (Bereishis 7:8) rather than “impure.” R’ Tzadok: if Scripture guards its speech even about an impure animal, all the more does it record a great man’s deeds only “for praise.”

וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא שֶׁהָיָה זֶה מִכְּלַל עוֹנְשֵׁי הַחֵטְא, שֶׁיִּתְפַּרְסֵם הַגְּנוּת לְכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת — מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר גְּנוּת קַיָּם לָעַד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּלָא נִכְתַּב אֶלָּא לְשִׁבְחָן

And even if you say it was part of the punishment of the sin, that the disgrace be publicized to all generations — nonetheless, it is impossible that a disgrace remain forever, as I wrote; and perforce it was written only for their praise.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהַחֲטָאִים הָהֵם הָיוּ גְּדוֹלִים בִּשְׁעַת הַחֵטְא בְּעִנְיַן חֶטְאָם, כָּךְ הֵם גְּדוֹלִים אַחַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּעִנְיַן הַזְּכוּת הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מֵהֶם, כִּי ״שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם לְרַע לוֹ״: כְּפִי תֹּקֶף הַשְּׁלִיטָה בְּרֶגַע הַשְּׁלִיטָה, כָּךְ הוּא תֹּקֶף הָרַע הַנִּמְשָׁךְ לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ מִזֶּה, כְּשֶׁמּוֹצִיאִין ״בָּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו״

And just as those sins were great at the time of the sin in the matter of their sin, so they are great after the rectification in the matter of the merit made from them — for “man ruled over man to his [own] harm” (Koheles 8:9): as the intensity of the [evil] rule at the moment of ruling, so is the intensity of the good afterward drawn from it, when they extract it — “swallowed back from its mouth” (Iyov 20:15).93Koheles 8:9; Zohar, Mishpatim 3:27; Iyov 20:15; Divrei Chalomot §22 — temporary domination becomes harm to the dominator: On “a man ruled over a man to his harm,” the Zohar reads the final words as harm ultimately returning upon the one who rules. Iyov’s “he swallowed wealth and vomited it; God drew it from his belly” became the image of forcing the outer forces to surrender the holy vitality they had absorbed. Rav Tzadok states in Divrei Chalomot that the “man of Belial” rules the holy man only for a time, because the end is to “extract what he swallowed from his mouth.” Se’if 10 applies that law of birur to teshuvah: the greater the temporary seizure, the greater the recovered good after rectification. This does not praise the sin while it is being committed; it describes the later reversal accomplished through teshuvah.

items.h: The theme: Moshe asked that his “misdeed” be written; David asked that his not be — each according to his rung. Moshe is the root of the Written Torah, “revealed to all,” the middah of day/sun, “whose secrets are revealed”; how could such a one truly “sin”? His body was already refined like an angel’s, and “the fear of God upon his face” makes sin impossible — so the very existence of his “sin” is “from the hidden things of the Merciful,” “awesome in deed,” who “places tehillah in His angels.”

p: [יא] וּבְיוֹמָא [פו סע״ב] דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה אָמַר ״אַל יִכְתּוֹב״ — הַיְינוּ כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ

And in Yoma [86b], that Moshe Rabbeinu asked that his “misdeed [surchan]” be written, while David HaMelech said “let it not be written” — that is, each according to his rung.94Yoma 86b: “Two good leaders [parnasim] arose for Israel — Moshe and David. Moshe said, ‘let my misdeed [surchan] be written,’ as it says, ‘because you did not believe in Me, to sanctify Me’ (Bamidbar 20:12); David said, ‘let my misdeed not be written,’ as it says, ‘happy is he whose transgression is forgiven, whose sin is covered’ (Tehillim 32:1).” The Gemara illustrates with two women flogged by the court — one for licentiousness and one for eating unripe Sabbatical fruit — the latter asking that the reason be proclaimed, lest people equate the two.

כִּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב דִּכְתִיבָא וּמַנְּחָא גָּלוּי לְכָל אֶחָד, וְהוּא מִדַּת ״יוֹם״ וְנֶגֶד הַחַמָּה בָּעוֹלָם, וּ״מַאן דִּבְחַמָּה — רוּזִין גַּלְיִין״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שַׁבָּת קנו.]

For Moshe is the root of the Written Torah, “written and set, revealed to each one,” and he is the middah of “day” and corresponds to the sun in the world — and “one who is [born] under the sun — his secrets are revealed,” as they said [Shabbos 156a].95Shabbos 156a: In the astrological aggadah — “one who is [born] under the sun [chama] will be a person whose secrets are revealed [ruzin galyin],” a self-made man; whereas “one under the moon [levanah]” will be one “whose secrets are hidden.” R’ Tzadok maps Moshe (Written Torah, “day”/sun) to the revealed, and David (Oral Torah, “night”/moon) to the concealed.96Bava Basra 75a; Likkutei Ma’amarim, on Yehoshua §23 — Moshe’s face as the sun and the Written Torah as day: The elders described “the face of Moshe as the face of the sun” and the face of Yehoshua as the moon. Elsewhere Rav Tzadok explains this symbolism directly: the first illumination was the Written Torah, the middah of day shining from Moshe’s sun-like face, while Yehoshua begins the moon-like, nocturnal mode associated with Torah Shebe’al Peh. Se’if 11 combines that parallel with Shabbos 156a, where one born under the sun has “revealed secrets.” The Bavli itself states the sun comparison; its identification with Written Torah and revealed inward light is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
וְלָכֵן אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטְאוּ — סוֹד גָּדוֹל וְכָמוּס, כִּי אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר לְשֶׁכְּמוֹתוֹ שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא כְּלָל, וּכְבָר נִזְדַּכֵּךְ גּוּפוֹ כְּמַלְאֲכֵי מָרוֹם שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם חֵטְא
And therefore, that “they sinned” is a great and hidden secret — for how is it possible for one like him to sin at all, his body already refined like the angels on high, who have no sin?

וְגַם מִקְרָא מְפוֹרָשׁ ״לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ עַל פְּנֵיכֶם לְבִלְתִּי תֶחֱטָאוּ״, שֶׁמִּי שֶׁיִּרְאַת ה׳ עַל פָּנָיו אֵינוֹ חוֹטֵא כְּלָל, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא אָדָם אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁנִּסְתַּלֵּק יִרְאַת ה׳ מֵעַל פָּנָיו בְּאוֹתָהּ רֶגַע, וַהֲרֵי אָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת לג סע״ב] דְּ״יִרְאָה — לְגַבֵּי מֹשֶׁה מִילְּתָא זוּטַרְתִּי״

And an explicit verse: “so that His fear be upon your faces, that you not sin” (Shemos 20:17) — for one upon whose face is the fear of Hashem does not sin at all, and it is impossible for a person to sin except when the fear of Hashem departs from his face at that moment; and they said [Berachos 33b] that “fear — regarding Moshe — is a small matter.”97Berachos 33b: “Is fear of Heaven a small matter? — Yes, for Moshe it is a small matter [milsa zutrasi]” — for one of Moshe’s stature, attaining the fear of Heaven is easy. R’ Tzadok infers that one so wholly possessed of yiras Hashem cannot truly “sin” except by a Divinely-staged “departure” of that fear for a moment.

וּבְוַדַּאי מְצִיאוּת עִנְיַן חֵטְא אֶצְלוֹ הוּא ״מִכְּבָשַׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא״, שֶׁהוּא ״נוֹרָא עֲלִילָה עַל בְּנֵי אָדָם״, ״וּבְמַלְאָכָיו יָשִׂים תְּהִלָּה״, וְקָאֵי עַל מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״מַלְאָךְ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַיִּשְׁלַח מַלְאָךְ וַיּוֹצִיאֵנוּ מִמִּצְרָיִם״

And certainly the very existence of the matter of “sin” by him is “from the hidden things of the Merciful,”98Berachos 10a; Takanas HaShavin 3:9 — “the hidden counsels of the Merciful”: When Chizkiyahu withheld from procreation because he foresaw wicked descendants, Yeshayah answered: “Why involve yourself with the hidden counsels of the Merciful? What you were commanded, you must do; what pleases the Holy One, let Him do.” Rav Tzadok elsewhere uses this sugya to distinguish the revealed order of Torah, by which man must judge and act, from a Divine secret whose full arrangement is known only to Hashem. Here he applies that distinction to Moshe: the visible lapse and its judgment remain real within the revealed order, while the ultimate reason that such a lapse could occur belongs to the concealed Divine design. This is a theological explanation after the fact, never a license to disregard a command. who is “awesome in deed over the sons of man” (Tehillim 66:5), [and]99Tehillim 66:5; Midrash Tanchuma, Vayeshev §4; Tzidkas HaTzadik §100 — “awesome in His dealings” and Mei Merivah: The Tanchuma explicitly applies “nora alilah al benei adam” to Moshe. It reads earlier verses as already intimating that he would not enter the Land, and says that when he later declared “Hear now, rebels,” the decree was attached to the Mei Merivah episode. Rav Tzadok repeatedly cites this Midrash to describe a failure whose occasion is woven into a larger Divine plan and whose meaning is disclosed through teshuvah. The Midrash does not erase Moshe’s accountability or the decree of death; it supplies the concealed frame within which Rav Tzadok reads the event. “in His angels He places tehillah” (Iyov 4:18) — referring to Moshe, called an “angel,” as it says, “and He sent an angel and brought us out of Egypt” (Bamidbar 20:16).

וּבְמִלַּת ״תְּהִלָּה״ שְׁתֵּי מַשְׁמָעוּת — לְשׁוֹן גְּנוּת וְחֶרְפָּה, וּלְשׁוֹן אוֹר וְנֹגַהּ — וּשְׁנֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּצַּד מַרְאִית הָעַיִן לְשָׁעָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה בָּזֶה גְּנוּת וְנִגְזַר עָלָיו מִיתָה, בֶּאֱמֶת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה נַחַת רוּחַ גָּדוֹל

And in the word “tehillah” are two meanings — a term of disgrace and reproach, and a term of light and radiance — and both are true: for although, from the side of outward appearance, for a moment in this world, there was in it disgrace and a decree of death upon him, in truth there is in it great “contentment of spirit.”100Iyov 4:18; Rashi — two resonances of “tehillah”: In Iyov the form תָּהֳלָה is understood by Rashi from הוללות, “folly” or reproach: even His servants are not absolutely trusted, and among His angels He detects deficiency. The ordinary word תְּהִלָּה, however, means praise or glory. Rav Tzadok deliberately hears both resonances in the nearly identical word: outwardly there is blame and a death-decree; inwardly there is praise, which he describes as light and radiance. The second, luminous reading is a homiletical development of Rav Tzadok, not the plain lexical meaning of Iyov’s verse.

וְזֶהוּ הָרָז הַגָּנוּז בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, שֶׁעַל זֶה בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁיִּכָּתֵב סוּרְחָנוֹ, דְּ״רָזוֹהִי גַּלְיִין״, שֶׁמִּצַּד מִדָּתוֹ מִדַּת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב גַּם הָאוֹר וְהָרָז שֶׁבְּדָבָר זֶה נִתְגַּלָּה לְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, לְהַמְשִׁיךְ אוֹר הַנֶּעְלָם לִלְבָבָם עַל יְדֵי זֶה

And this is the secret hidden in that deed, over which he asked that his “misdeed” be written — for “his secrets are revealed” — that from the side of his middah, the middah of the Written Torah, even the light and the secret in this matter was revealed to all the hearts of Israel, to draw the hidden light to their hearts thereby.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר ״הֵמָּה מֵי מְרִיבָה״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וַיִּקָּדֵשׁ בָּם״, שֶׁנִּמְשַׁךְ הִתְגַּלּוּת קְדֻשַּׁת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּעוֹלָם וּבִלְבָבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר זֶה, כְּמוֹ עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה גְּדוֹלָה

And this is the meaning of “these are the waters of Merivah, [where Israel quarreled with Hashem,] and He was sanctified through them” (Bamidbar 20:13) — that the revelation of Hashem’s holiness was drawn into the world and into the hearts of Israel through this matter, as through the act of a great mitzvah.101Bamidbar 20:13; Rashi; Vayikra 10:3; Zevachim 115b — “He was sanctified through them”: Rashi explains that Hashem was sanctified at Mei Merivah through the deaths of Moshe and Aharon: when judgment is executed upon those holy to Him, people fear and sanctify His name. He compares this to “through those near to Me I will be sanctified,” which Zevachim applies to Nadav and Avihu, whose deaths revealed how exacting Divine judgment is with the most honored. Rav Tzadok moves beyond that public reverence to an inward effect: because Moshe belongs to the revealed Written Torah, the hidden holiness within the episode itself is drawn into Israel’s hearts. That further claim — that the event operates like a great mitzvah after its secret is revealed — is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive extension of the classical sources.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה — מִדַּת מַלְכוּת ״פֶּה״, תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״מִסְטוֹרִין שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתַנְחוּמָא פָּרָשַׁת תִּשָּׂא] עַל פָּסוּק ״כְּתָב לְךָ״ — ״מִי שֶׁמִּסְטוֹרִין שֶׁלּוֹ בְּיָדוֹ — אֵלּוּ בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״

And David HaMelech — the middah of Malchus, “the mouth [peh],” the Oral Torah, which is called “the mysteries of the Holy One102R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §2): “In the time of exile, which is the intensity of night’s darkness, the Written Torah is the middah of day, from the side of Hashem, who wishes to illumine man to grasp the truth revealed plainly to the eye — ‘God made man upright, but they sought many reckonings,’ for this world is full of errors and the darknesses of the yetzer hara.” The se’if’s polarity: Moshe/Written Torah is the “day whose secrets are revealed”; David/Oral Torah is the “night whose secrets are hidden.”,” as they said [in Tanchuma, Parashas Tisa] on “write for yourself [these words]” (Shemos 34:27) — “the one whose mysteries are in his hand — these are Israel.”103Tanchuma, Ki Sisa: On “write for yourself these words” (Shemos 34:27) — the Holy One wished to give the Mishnah [Oral Torah] in writing too, but foresaw the nations translating the Written Torah and claiming “we are Israel”; therefore the Oral Torah was kept unwritten, “the mysteries of the Holy One” — “the one whose mysteries are in his hand, these are My children, Israel.” R’ Tzadok links this “hidden” Torah to David and the middah of Malchus/night.

וְהוּא מִדַּת ״לַיְלָה״ שֶׁהִיא בְּהֶעְלֵם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתַרְגּוּם שה״ש] דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב לְמֵדִין בַּיּוֹם וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה בַּלַּיְלָה, וְכֵן אִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ גַּבֵּי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה; וּ״מַאן דִּבִלְבָנָה — רוּזִין כַּסְיִין״

And it is the middah of “night,” which is in concealment, as they said [in the Targum of Shir HaShirim] that the Written Torah is learned by day and the Oral Torah by night — and so it is in the Midrash regarding Moshe; and “one who is [born] under the moon — his secrets are hidden.”
וְעַל כֵּן בִּיקֵּשׁ שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, וְאָמַר לוֹ דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר, ״וּמַה יוֹ״ד שֶׁנָּטַלְתִּי מִשָּׂרַי״ כו׳, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז סע״א]

And therefore he asked that his “misdeed” not be written; and [God] told him that it is impossible: “and what of the yud that I took from Sarai,” as they said [Sanhedrin 107a].104Sanhedrin 107a: When David begged that “his transgression not be written,” he was answered that it is impossible: “the yud that I removed from Sarai [when her name became Sarah] stood and cried out for [many] generations until Yehoshua came and I added it to his name” (Bamidbar 13:16) — all the more that a whole Torah-portion, fit to be written, cannot be withheld. R’ Tzadok turns the proof around: the yud cried because it was demoted; the Bathsheba portion, were it mere disgrace, the letters would gladly go unwritten — so its being written must be for praise.

וּמִזֶּה גַּם כֵּן דְּנִכְתְּבָה הַפָּרָשָׁה לְשִׁבְחָן, דְּאִי לִגְנוּתוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ, מָה רְאָיָה מִיּוֹ״ד דְּשָׁרֵי, דְּזָכָה שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁמָהּ שֶׁל אוֹתָהּ צַדֶּקֶת, וּבַדִּין הוּא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה עוֹמֵד וְצוֹוֵחַ עַל מַה שֶּׁהוֹרִידוּהוּ מִמַּעֲלָתוֹ לִינָּטֵל מִשָּׁם

And from this too [we learn] that the portion was written for their praise — for if it were for his disgrace, God forbid, in its plain sense, what proof is there from the yud that “cried out”? For [the yud] merited to be in the name of that righteous woman [Sarah], and it is right that it stand and cry over being lowered from its elevation, taken from there;

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אוֹתָהּ פָּרָשָׁה דַּהֲרֵי הִיא מְדַבֶּרֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בִּגְנוּת אוֹתוֹ הַצַּדִּיק — אַדְּרַבָּא שֶׁבַח וְנוֹחַ הָיָה לְאוֹתָן אוֹתִיּוֹת שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתְּבוּ; אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת רְאוּיָה הִיא לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

not so that [Bathsheba] portion, which speaks, God forbid, in disgrace of that tzaddik — [where] on the contrary it would be praise and satisfaction for those letters not to be written! But in truth it is fitting for him from the six days of Creation, as it is [explained] there. — And so the two greatest “parnasim,” Moshe and David, embody the two Torahs: the one whose lapse is written as revealed light, the other whose is hidden — yet both, at root, “fitting from the six days of Creation,” praise and not disgrace.

items.h: The theme: The royal line of David and the awaited Mashiach descends from Bas Sheva through Shlomo, a destiny David perceived through ruach hakodesh. This explains why David fasted and prayed that his first child with Bas Sheva should live. Had their union retained a true trace of sin, the child’s death would have relieved rather than distressed him.

p: [יב] וְתֵדַע דַּהֲרֵי כָּל שַׁלְשֶׁלֶת מַלְכוּת בֵּית דָּוִד וְהַמָּשִׁיחַ הַמְקוּוֶה בִּמְהֵרָה בְּיָמֵינוּ הוּא מִמֶּנָּה, מִשְּׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה; וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה רָאָה זֶה בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְהִבְטִיחָהּ דְּזַרְעָהּ יִמְלֹךְ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל

And know: the whole chain of the kingship of the House of David and the Mashiach we await, speedily in our days, is from her [Bas Sheva], from Shlomo HaMelech; and David HaMelech saw this by ruach hakodesh, and assured her that “her seed would reign,” as the Sages said.105I Melachim 1:13, 17, 30 — David’s oath that Shlomo would reign: Nasan instructs Bas Sheva to remind David of his oath that “Shlomo your son shall reign after me, and he shall sit upon my throne”; Bas Sheva repeats the oath, and David then confirms that he will fulfill it that very day. These verses establish the promised royal succession specifically through Bas Sheva and Shlomo. The verses themselves do not state that David knew this by ruach hakodesh; that further explanation is Rav Tzadok’s reading of the promise.
וְעַל זֶה צָם וְהִרְבָּה בִּתְפִלָּה שֶׁיִּחְיֶה אוֹתוֹ יֶלֶד, וְאִלּוּ הָיָה שֶׁמֶץ חֵטְא אַדְּרַבָּא הָיָה לוֹ לִשְׂמוֹחַ כְּשֶׁמֵּת, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ כְּמַזְכִּיר עָוֹן

And over this he fasted and prayed much that the child would live — and had there been [even] a trace of sin, on the contrary he should have rejoiced when it died, so that it not be for him “a reminder of iniquity.”106II Shmuel 12:14–23 — David fasts and pleads for the first child while he still lives: After Nasan declares that “also the child born to you shall surely die,” the child becomes gravely ill. David seeks Hashem on the child’s behalf, fasts, and lies on the ground; after the child dies he explains that while the child was alive he fasted because perhaps Hashem would be gracious and the child would live. This narrative directly underlies Rav Tzadok’s argument that David positively desired the child’s survival. The further inference — that this desire reflects the child’s hidden messianic potential rather than merely paternal hope — is Rav Tzadok’s chiddush.

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת, אִלּוּ הָיָה אוֹתוֹ יֶלֶד חַי וְהָיָה הוּא הַמֶּלֶךְ אַחֲרָיו וְהַבּוֹנֶה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, נִמְצָא לֹא הָיָה אוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֵׂה אֲכִילַת פַּגָּה גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, שֶׁהֲרֵי בְּהֶכְרֵחַ הָיָה אוֹתוֹ וָלָד לְהִיוָּלֵד אָז

But in truth, had that child lived and been king after him and the builder of the Beis HaMikdash, then that act of “eating unripe fruit” would not have been [a lapse] even in this world — for that child necessarily had to be born then;107Sanhedrin 107a — Bas Sheva was destined for David, but he “ate her unripe”: Rava teaches that Bas Sheva was designated as fitting for David from the six days of Creation, but came to him through pain; the school of Rabbi Yishmael states more sharply that she was fit for David, “ela she’achalah pagah” — he partook of her before the appointed time. The image therefore does not mean that the destined union itself was intrinsically alien to him; it marks the attempt to realize what was destined before its proper time and permitted form.

וְהָיָה בָּזֶה תִּיקּוּן גָּמוּר לְחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן בַּאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהָיָה גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן וְעֵת קֵץ, וְאוֹתוֹ וָלָד הָיָה מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד, וְהַבַּיִת שֶׁהָיָה נִבְנֶה עַל יָדוֹ הָיָה קַיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

and there would have been in it a complete rectification of the sin of Adam HaRishon — which too was an “eating of unripe fruit,” as is known — and it would have been the finish of the rectification and the End of Days; and that child would have been Mashiach ben David, and the House built by him would have stood forever.108Berachos 40a; Akeidas Yitzchak, Shaar 60 — Adam’s sin as the earlier “unripe fruit” pattern: Berachos records Rabbi Nechemiah’s view that the Tree of Knowledge was a fig tree, because with the very thing through which Adam and Chavah were corrupted they were afterward repaired, as shown by the fig leaves. Akeidas Yitzchak develops the timing motif explicitly, contrasting the one who guards the fig until its fruit may properly be enjoyed with Adam, who ate it “unripe.” This supplies an early interpretive bridge for Rav Tzadok’s comparison: in both Adam and David, the problem is framed as taking a destined good before its ripening and appointed time.
וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹתוֹ וָלָד נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ וּמוּכָן לָזֶה, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַקֵּץ עֲדַיִן

And certainly that child bore the soul of Mashiach and was ready for it — only that the End had not yet arrived.109Divrei Soferim §28 — Rav Tzadok’s direct parallel: the first child as the soul of Mashiach: Rav Tzadok returns to David’s ordeal and cites both the teaching that David did not sin in the ordinary sense and Sanhedrin’s statement that Bas Sheva was destined for him but was taken “unripe.” He then states that the first child was the neshamas Mashiach; because this “pagah” preceded the ketz, the child could not endure. He explains that even in the place where David appeared to act from desire, his deeper aim was toward what had been destined for him and toward bringing the soul of Mashiach into the world. This is a close parallel to the present se’if and strongly confirms its messianic reading.

וְזֶהוּ הָאֲכִילָה פַּגָּה טֶרֶם הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן וְהַקֵּץ, שֶׁהוּא הָיָה עָסוּק בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה לִבְרוֹא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בברא״ר ר״פ פה] בְּעִנְיַן יְהוּדָה ״וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הָיָה עוֹסֵק בּוֹרֵא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם; אֶלָּא שֶׁחָשַׁב לְמַהֲרוֹ לִפְנֵי זְמַנּוֹ

And this is “the eating of unripe fruit before the time and the End came” — for he was engaged in that act to “create the light of Mashiach,” as they said [Bereishis Rabbah 85:1] regarding Yehudah, “and the Holy One was engaged in creating the light of Mashiach,” see there — only that he thought to hasten it before its time.110Bereishis Rabbah 85:1: On “and it was at that time, that Yehudah went down [from his brothers]” (Bereishis 38:1) — “the tribes were occupied with selling Yosef, Yosef with his sackcloth and fasting, Reuven with his sackcloth and fasting, Yaakov with his [sackcloth and fasting], and Yehudah was occupied taking a wife — and the Holy One was occupied creating the light of Mashiach”; “before the first oppressor [Egypt] was born, the final redeemer was born.” R’ Tzadok applies this to David’s union with Bas Sheva: he was, in that act, “creating the light of Mashiach,” reaching for the End before its time.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר [תְּהִלִּים נא] ״מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד בְּבוֹא [אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא] כַּאֲשֶׁר בָּא [אֶל בַּת שֶׁבַע]״, דִּכְמוֹ אָז הָיָה עָסוּק בְּבוֹרֵא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ, כֵּן ״בְּבוֹא״ כו׳ לֹא חָשׁ לְעַצְמוֹ וּלְאַבְּדָן נַפְשׁוֹ בַּחֲשַׁאי, רַק כָּל מְגַמָּתוֹ לְהַצָּלַת כְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲלַמְּדָה פוֹשְׁעִים [דְּרָכֶיךָ]״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְסִיֵּים ״בִּישׁוּעַת צִיּוֹן, הֵיטִיבָה [בִרְצוֹנְךָ אֶת צִיּוֹן, תִּבְנֶה] חוֹמוֹת יְרוּשָׁלִָם״

And therefore he said [Tehillim 51], “A psalm of David, when [Nathan the prophet came to him], as he came [to Bas Sheva]” — for just as then he was engaged in “creating the light of Mashiach,” so “as he came, [so shall he go],” he did not care for himself and the loss of his own soul in secret, but his whole aim was the salvation of all Israel, as it says, “I will teach transgressors Your ways, [and sinners shall return to You],” and he concluded, “in the salvation of Zion” — “do good in Your favor to Zion, build the walls of Jerusalem.”

וְזֶה שֶׁאָמַר ״מִזְמוֹר לְדָוִד״, שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ לְעוֹרֵר רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ עָלָיו עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁירָה וְהַזֶּמֶר, וְכִדְאִיתָא [פְּסָחִים קיז.] — הַיְינוּ לְפִי שֶׁאָז נִסְתַּלְּקָה מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר ״הָשִׁיבָה לִּי שְׂשׂוֹן יִשְׁעֶךָ״ וְכִדְאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם]
