And this is why it says “Mizmor l’David” [rather than “l’David Mizmor”] — that he had to rouse the ruach hakodesh upon himself through song and melody, as it is stated [Pesachim 117a] — because then the ruach hakodesh had departed from him, and of this he said, “restore to me the joy of Your salvation,” as it is stated [in Sanhedrin 107a].111Pesachim 117a: “‘L’David Mizmor’ teaches that the Shechinah rested upon him and then he uttered song; ‘Mizmor L’David’ teaches that he uttered song and then the Shechinah rested upon him — teaching that the Shechinah rests neither through sloth nor through sadness [but through the joy of a mitzvah].” And Sanhedrin 107a: “For six months David was stricken with tzaraas and the Shechinah departed from him — as it is written, ‘restore to me the joy of Your salvation’ (Tehillim 51:14).” R’ Tzadok: the departure came through the sadness of the [seeming] sin, and had to be undone by the joy of the mitzvah of teshuvah.

וְהוּא עַל יְדֵי הָעַצְבוּת מֵהַחֵטְא, כִּי עֶצֶם הַחֵטְא לֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל, רַק אַדְּרַבָּא קְדֻשָּׁה גְּדוֹלָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה כּוּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳, וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר אֶצְלוֹ מִלְּבַד [ה׳] חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

And it [the departure] was through the sadness from the sin — for the essence of the sin was no sin at all, but on the contrary great holiness, since David HaMelech was wholly “holy to Hashem,” and there was nothing by him “besides [Hashem],” God forbid.

אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁלְּמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה חֵטְא, וְהָיָה חִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם בְּפִי הַבְּרִיּוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַנָּבִיא [ש״ב יב] ״אֶפֶס כִּי נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״גַּם הַבֵּן הַיִּלּוֹד לְךָ מוֹת יָמוּת״

But because, to the outward eye in this world, it was a sin and a “profaning of the Name” in people’s mouths — as the prophet said to him [II Shmuel 12], “only, because you have utterly scorned [the enemies of Hashem by this deed], also [gam] the child born to you shall surely die” —

וּלְשׁוֹן ״גַּם״ מְבוֹאָר דְּבָא לְהוֹסִיף וְלוֹמַר שֶׁכְּמוֹ שֶׁעָשִׂיתָ כֵּן יִהְיֶה לְךָ גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד זֶה דָּבָר זֶה; כִּי מֵאַחַר דְּרָזוֹהִי [כַּסְיָין], וְאֵין הִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עֲדַיִן מֵאוֹר הַבָּהִיר שֶׁלְּךָ, בְּהֶכְרֵחַ אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹר הַוָּלָד הַזֶּה, דְּאִם כֵּן אֵינוֹ אֲכִילַת פַּגָּה וְלֹא הָיָה כָּאן חֵטְא בְּעֵינֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת גַּם כֵּן

and the word “gam [also]” is precise — coming to add: that as you did, so shall correspondingly be [done] to you in this matter — for since “his secrets are [hidden],” and there is not yet, in this world, a revelation of your “radiant light,” necessarily the light of this child cannot be revealed; for if it were [revealed], it would not be “eating unripe fruit,” and there would have been no sin in people’s eyes either.

וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לוֹ הָעַצְבוּת אַחַר כָּךְ בְּבִיאַת הַנָּבִיא לוֹ לְהַגִּיד שֶׁלֹּא עָלָה בְּיָדוֹ, כִּי נֶחְשָׁב חֵטְא וְצָרִיךְ לְעֹנֶשׁ, וּבָזֶה נִסְתַּלֵּק מִמֶּנּוּ רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ לְעוֹרְרוֹ בְּשִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה — הַיְינוּ מִצְוַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לָהּ עַל יְדֵי חֵטְא זֶה, לִהְיוֹת מֵקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, ״וַאֲלַמְּדָה [פוֹשְׁעִים דְּרָכֶיךָ]״

And through this the sadness came to him afterward, at the prophet’s coming to tell him that “it did not succeed in his hand” — for it is reckoned a sin and requires punishment; and thereby the ruach hakodesh departed from him, until he had to rouse it through “the joy of a mitzvah” — namely, the mitzvah of teshuvah that he merits through this sin, to be “the raiser of the yoke of teshuvah,” “and I will teach [transgressors Your ways].”

items.h: The theme: So is God’s way in creating the world — “first darkness, then light”; He “created worlds and destroyed them” (the worlds of tohu) until the world of tikkun emerged. And precisely through those “destructions” was the world of rectification built, by raising the lights of the “broken vessels.” Mashiach comes to rectify the root of evil in Creation. Hence the sin of the Flood-generation and of Er and Onan: opposite the arousal of holiness rises “this-against-that,” the intensified power of evil — “evil in the eyes of Hashem.”

p: [יג] וְכָךְ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דִּבְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא; וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בברא״ר] דְּהָיָה בּוֹרֵא עוֹלָמוֹת וּמַחֲרִיבָן כו׳ — וְהֵן עוֹלָמוֹת הַתֹּהוּ עַד שֶׁיָּצָא עוֹלָם הַתִּיקּוּן כַּנּוֹדָע

And so is the way of Hashem in the creation of the world — “first darkness, and then light”112Shabbos 77b — “first darkness, then light” is the pattern of Creation: Rav Yehuda explains that the order of goats before sheep mirrors the creation of the world: “at first darkness, and afterward light.” Rav Tzadok takes this aggadic sequence as a general spiritual pattern: concealment precedes disclosure, so an apparent descent or destruction can become the preparation from which later tikkun emerges.; and so they said [in Bereishis Rabbah] that “He was creating worlds and destroying them,” these being the worlds of tohu, until the world of tikkun113R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §206): “The root of the roots [of evil] is arrogance — for the root of evil is from the world of tohu and the breaking of the vessels [sheviras hakelim], which came about through the thought ‘I will reign [ana emloch]’; and from this the yetzer was born — for ‘yetzer’ means the thought and stirring in the heart, where evil begins, as it says (Berachos 61a), ‘it sits at the two entrances of the heart.’” The se’if’s cosmology: the “worlds created and destroyed” are tohu, and precisely from raising the lights of the “broken vessels” is the world of rectification built. came forth, as is known.114Bereishis Rabbah 3:7 & 9:2: “The Holy One was creating worlds and destroying them” until He made this one and said, “this pleases Me.” R’ Tzadok reads these as the kabbalistic “worlds of tohu” whose “shattered vessels” are raised in the “world of tikkun” — the very pattern of sin-and-rectification, and of Mashiach’s work at the root of Creation.

וְכֵן הוּא בְּכָל דָּבָר; וְכָל גִּלְגּוּלֵי הַמָּשִׁיחַ שֶׁהָיוּ כְּבָר בָּעוֹלָם הֵם דֻּגְמַת ״בּוֹרֵא עוֹלָמוֹת וּמַחֲרִיבָן״, וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹתָן חוּרְבָּנוֹת דַּוְקָא הָיָה בִּנְיַן עוֹלָם הַתִּיקּוּן, בְּהַעֲלָאַת אוֹתָן אוֹרוֹת דְּשִׁבְרֵי כֵלִים כַּנּוֹדָע; וּמָשִׁיחַ הוּא הַבָּא לְתַקֵּן שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע שֶׁבִּבְרִיאָה

And so it is in everything; and all the “reincarnations of Mashiach” that were already in the world are a “likeness” of “creating worlds and destroying them” — and through those very destructions was the building of the world of tikkun, by the raising of those “lights of the broken vessels,” as is known; and Mashiach is the one who comes to rectify the root of the evil in Creation.
וְזֶהוּ חֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל וְחֵטְא עֵר וְאוֹנָן, שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם הִתְעוֹרְרוּת אוֹר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הוּא כְּנֶגְדּוֹ הִתְגַּבְּרוּת כֹּחַ הָרַע, דְּ״זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה״

And this is the sin of the generation of the Flood and the sin of Er and Onan: that in the place of the arousal of the light of holiness there is, opposite it, the intensification of the power of evil — “this-against-that.”115Koheles 7:14 — “this opposite that God made”: The verse sets the day of good and the day of adversity “this opposite that,” both within Divine making. Here Rav Tzadok applies the formula structurally: an arousal of holiness can call forth a corresponding intensification on the side of evil. The verse supplies the “zeh le’umas zeh” principle; its application to opposed forces of kedushah and ra is the se’if’s interpretive development.

וְהוּא נִקְרָא ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן בְּאוֹנָן נֶאֱמַר ״וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן אוֹמֵר עַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה [ש״ב יא] ״וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר״ וְגוֹמֵר ״בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְכֵן אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ [תְּהִלִּים נא] ״וְהָרַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ עָשִׂיתִי״

And it is called “evil in the eyes of Hashem”; and so of Onan it says, “and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem” (Bereishis 38:10), and so it says of David [II Shmuel 11], “and the thing was evil in the eyes of Hashem,” and so he said of himself [Tehillim 51], “and I did the evil in Your eyes.”

וְהָעִנְיָן כְּמוֹ דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין נִקְרָאִים ״עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה״ בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁמְּדַבֵּר מֵהַשְׁגָּחָתָם עַל הָעֵדָה, כִּי הָעַיִן הוּא הַמַּשְׁגִּיחַ; וְכֵן אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״דֵּעוֹת ה׳״, ״עֵינֵי ה׳ הֵמָּה מְשׁוֹטְטוֹת״, וְכֵן הוּא אוֹמֵר [תְּהִלִּים לג] ״עֵין ה׳ אֶל יְרֵאָיו״

And the matter is like the Sanhedrin being called “the eyes of the congregation”116Bamidbar 15:24; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:12:1 — the Sanhedrin as “the eyes of the congregation”: The Torah speaks of error arising “from the eyes of the congregation,” and the Midrash identifies these “eyes” with the Sanhedrin, adding that just as the body’s limbs follow the eyes, Israel follows its Sanhedrin. This supports Rav Tzadok’s semantic move from “eye” to guidance and oversight, and from there to the Divine “eye” as the language of revealed hashgachah. where it speaks of their oversight [hashgachah] over the congregation — for “the eye is the overseer”; and so with Hashem, as it says, “a God of knowledge,” “the eyes of Hashem range [over the earth]” (Zechariah 4:10), and it says [Tehillim 33], “the eye of Hashem is to those who fear Him.”117Bava Basra 16a: “Rava said: Iyov sought to acquit the whole world of judgment — he said, ‘Master of the world, You created the ox with cloven hooves and the donkey with closed hooves; You created Gan Eden and Gehinnom, You created the righteous and You created the wicked [by way of the evil inclination] — who can stop You?’” R’ Tzadok invokes this “all is from His hand” motif in reading sin, too, as within the compass of the Divine “eye”/providence that oversees all.

וּבַזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [בְּרֵאשִׁית נז רע״א] ״רַע״ לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא ״מַאן דִּמְחַבֵּל אוֹרְחֵיהּ [זַרְעוֹ]״ כו׳ ״וְיָהֵיב חֵילָא״ כו׳, ״דִּבְהַאי אִסְתְּלִיק שְׁכִינְתָּא מֵעָלְמָא״ כו׳, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And in the holy Zohar [Bereishis 57a], “evil [ra]” is said only of “one who corrupts his way [his seed]” — “and gives power [to the spirit of impurity],” “through which the Shechinah departs from the world” — see there.118Zohar, Bereishis 57a: R’ Yosi asked whether “ra [evil]” is not the same as “rasha [wicked].” The answer: a “rasha” is even one who merely raised his hand against his fellow; but “ra” is said only of “one who corrupts his way [mechabbel orchei — wastes his seed] and defiles himself and the land, and gives strength to the spirit of impurity called ‘ra,’ and does not enter the Sanctuary of Hashem nor behold the face of the Shechinah, for through this sin the Shechinah departs from the world.” R’ Tzadok reads this “departure” as the withdrawal of revealed providence, which makes evil seem mere “chance.”

הַיְינוּ סִילּוּק הַהַשְׁגָּחָה הַפְּרָטִית הַגְּלוּיָה עַל יְדֵי שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים, שֶׁכָּל כֹּחַ הִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּרַע בָּעוֹלָם הוּא מִצַּד הִתְעַלְּמוּת הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּמַרְאִים כְּאִלּוּ הַכֹּל בְּמִקְרֶה

that is, the removal of the revealed particular providence through His Shechinah among the lower ones — for all the power of the spread of evil in the world is from the concealment of His providence, [which] makes it appear as if all is “by chance [mikreh].”119Resisei Layla §18; Peri Tzadik, Emor §13 — Amalek’s “chance” is concealment of providence: Rav Tzadok elsewhere makes the same identification explicitly. Resisei Layla says Amalek is rooted in “mikreh”: because “asher karcha” presents itself as chance, Amalek attributes everything to chance, whereas its defeat comes from recognizing that even apparent mikreh is from Hashem. Peri Tzadik sharpens the point: Amalek seeks that Divine hashgachah be withdrawn from Israel so that they be left to “mikreh.” This is a direct parallel to the present se’if’s equation of evil with the concealment of revealed providence.

וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע וְכָל כֹּחַ עֲמָלֵק שֶׁהוּא ״רֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם״, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״אֲשֶׁר קָרְךָ״, שֶׁרָצָה לְהַכְנִיס בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל דָּבָר זֶה; ורז״ל דְּרָשׁוּהוּ לְשׁוֹן ״קֶרִי״, כִּי גַּם זֶה נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״מִקְרֵה לַיְלָה״

And this is the root of evil and the whole power of Amalek, “the first of the nations,” of whom it is written, “who happened upon you [asher karcha]” (Devarim 25:18) — who wished to introduce this thing into Israel; and the Sages expounded it as a term of “keri [emission],” for this too is called, in the language of Scripture, “a nocturnal happening [mikreh laylah]”120Rashi to Devarim 25:18 — “asher karcha” joins chance, keri, and cooling: Rashi gives three readings of “karcha”: a mikreh, a chance encounter; keri and tumah; and cooling Israel’s former heat before the nations. The first two readings are especially important here: the same word links the ideology of happenstance with sexual impurity, allowing Rav Tzadok to move from Amalek’s “chance” to the Torah’s “mikreh laylah” and to the concealment of the Divine eye. —

שֶׁכַּאֲשֶׁר אֵינוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וּלְשֵׁם מִצְוָה, רַק עַל יְדֵי הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּקְרָא ״רַע״, נֶחְשָׁב לְ״מִקְרֶה״, שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה כִּבְיָכוֹל עַיִן שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה כְּאִלּוּ אֵינוֹ רוֹאֶה, שֶׁעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְמֵית עֵינוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע, אָמַר ״מִי שֶׁהוּא קָדוֹשׁ וְטָהוֹר״ כו׳ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנִדָּה לא סע״א]

for when it is not in holiness and for the sake of a mitzvah, but through the inclination called “evil,” it is reckoned a “chance-happening” — making, as it were, “the eye above” as if it does not see; over which matter the eye of that wicked one [Bilaam] was blinded, [who] said, “shall He who is holy and pure [gaze at this]?” — as they said [Niddah 31a].121Niddah 31a: R’ Abbahu expounded “who has counted the dust of Yaakov, and the number [rova] of Israel” (Bamidbar 23:10) — “the Holy One sits and counts the revi’iyos of Israel, [awaiting] the drop from which a righteous one will be formed; and over this matter the eye of the wicked Bilaam was blinded, [who] said, ‘shall He who is pure and holy, whose ministers are pure and holy, gaze at this?!’ — immediately his eye was blinded, as it says, ‘the utterance of the man whose eye is blocked’ (Bamidbar 24:3).”

items.h: The theme: In truth God is “pure of eyes, [too pure] to look on evil” — but this act is the very foundation of Creation (“He did not create it tohu”) and the first positive commandment. How could it hold evil or impurity? As Adam was made upright, “they were not ashamed,” for there was no bodily desire in it. This is illustrated by Yaakov, who felt no shame saying “give me my wife, that I may come to her,” knowing no intent but to raise offspring.

p: [יד] וּבֶאֱמֶת הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״טְהוֹר עֵינַיִם מֵרְאוֹת בְּרָע״; אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁהוּא כְּלַל בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דְּ״לֹא תֹהוּ בְרָאָהּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, וּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁצִּיוָּה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְמִין הָאָדָם — אֵיךְ אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ רַע וְטוּמְאָה

And in truth the Holy One is “pure of eyes, [too pure] to look upon evil” (Chavakuk 1:13); but this thing, which is the general foundation of the creation of the world — “He did not create it tohu [but formed it to be inhabited]” (Yeshayah 45:18) — and the first positive commandment Hashem commanded to the human species [be fruitful and multiply] — how is it possible that there be in it evil and impurity?122Bereishis 1:28; Yeshayah 45:18; Gittin 41b — procreation as a purpose of Creation: The Torah’s first command to humanity is “be fruitful and multiply,” while Yeshayah says that Hashem “did not create [the world] tohu; He formed it to be inhabited.” The Gemara invokes that verse to state that the world was created for procreation. This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s opening question: an act placed within the created purpose of the world and commanded as a mitzvah cannot be intrinsically impure; the impurity belongs to the admixture of fallen desire, not to the generative act as such.
אֲבָל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁעָשָׂה הָאָדָם יָשָׁר נֶאֱמַר ״וְלֹא יִתְבּוֹשָׁשׁוּ״, כִּי לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית שֶׁמִּזֶּה הוּא הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבּוֹ, עַל כֵּן לֹא הִרְגִּישׁ בּוּשָׁה

Rather, according to how “God made man upright,” it says “and they were not ashamed” (Bereishis 2:25) — for there was in it no bodily desire, from which is the impurity in it; therefore he felt no shame,123Rashi to Bereishis 2:25 — shame appears only after the yetzer hara enters: On “they were not ashamed,” Rashi explains that Adam and Chavah had not yet acquired the mode of modesty that distinguishes good from evil; although Adam already possessed da’as, the yetzer hara did not enter him until after eating from the tree. Rav Tzadok develops this distinction specifically in the bodily sphere: before the mixture of the yetzer, the generative faculty could be known without lust, and therefore without the shame attached to post-sin desire.

רַק כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁלֹּא בּוֹשׁ לוֹמַר ״הָבָה [אֶת אִשְׁתִּי]״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְאָבוֹאָה [אֵלֶיהָ]״, מַה שֶּׁקַּל שֶׁבַּקַּלִּים אֵין אוֹמֵר כֵּן, רַק שֶׁהוּא לֹא יָדַע מִכַּוָּנָה אַחֶרֶת אֶלָּא לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלָדוֹת, וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בָּזֶה בּוּשָׁה

like Yaakov Avinu, who was not ashamed to say, “give me my wife, that I may come to her” (Bereishis 29:21) — which the lightest of the light would not say — only that he knew no other intent than to raise up offspring, and shame does not apply to that.124Rashi to Bereishis 29:21; Bereishis Rabbah 70:18 — Yaakov’s words were solely for offspring: Rashi asks how Yaakov could say so directly, “that I may come to her,” when even an ordinary coarse person would not speak that way. The answer is that Yaakov spoke with his mind fixed on establishing the twelve tribes — “to beget offspring.” This is the exact Chazal-source for Rav Tzadok’s example: the absence of embarrassment reflects not looseness, but the absence of an ulterior sensual intention.

אֶלָּא אַחַר הַטָּלַת הַזּוּהֲמָא דְּנָחָשׁ, שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע שֶׁנִּבְרָא בָּעוֹלָם, וְזֶהוּ ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בשוח״ט (ויק״ר יד, ה)] עַל פָּסוּק ״בְּעָוֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי״ ״אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים [אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ צַד אֶחָד מֵעָוֹן]״, ״אִישִׁי אֲבִי דָוִד שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת נה:]

[This shame arises] only after the injection of the “filth [zuhama] of the serpent,” which is the root of the evil created in the world — and this is “the counsel of the serpent,” as they said [in Shocher Tov / Vayikra Rabbah 14:5] on the verse “in iniquity I was fashioned” (Tehillim 51:7), “even the most pious of the pious [cannot be entirely without some trace of iniquity]”; “my father Yishai, who died [only] through the counsel of the serpent,” as they said [in Shabbos 55b].125Shabbos 55b: “Four died [only] through the counsel of the serpent [b’etyo shel nachash], with no sin of their own: Binyamin son of Yaakov, Amram father of Moshe, Yishai father of David, and Kilav son of David.” And Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 (on “in iniquity I was fashioned,” Tehillim 51:7): even the most pious cannot be wholly free of some trace of “iniquity” — the residue of the serpent’s “filth” in ordinary human generation.

וְזֶהוּ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי שֶׁפָּסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם קמו רע״א], וְלֵיכָּא רַק ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״; אֲבָל בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא הַהִיא שֶׁלֹּא פָּסְקָה כְּלָל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּהֵם מְזוֹהָמִים

And this is [the case] with Israel who stood at Har Sinai, whose “filth ceased,” as they said [Shabbos 146a] — leaving only “the counsel of the serpent”; but in the nations it is the root of that filth, which never ceased at all, and as they said there that they are “filthy.”126Shabbos 146a: “When the serpent came upon Chavah he cast filth [zuhama] into her; [when] Israel stood at Sinai their filth ceased; the nations, who did not stand at Sinai — their filth did not cease.” R’ Tzadok: in Israel only “the counsel of the serpent” (a mere residue) remains, while the nations retain the root of that filth unbroken.

וּבִלְעָם וַעֲמָלֵק מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ אֶחָד כַּנּוֹדָע וּמוּבָא [בְּלִיקּוּטִים שֶׁבְּסוֹף סֵפֶר דָּן יָדִין] וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דִּבְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם קָם [נָבִיא כְּמֹשֶׁה], וּמַנּוּ — בִּלְעָם, שֶׁהָיָה דֻּגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

And Bilaam and Amalek are of one root, as is known, and as they said that “among the nations there arose [a prophet like Moshe]” — and who was he? Bilaam — who was the “likeness” of Moshe Rabbeinu in holiness [in the realm of the kelipah].

שֶׁהוּא [מֹשֶׁה] שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָרַת הַזּוּהֲמָא מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּהוֹרָדַת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא הַתַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁבִּבְרִיאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (קִידּוּשִׁין ל:) ״בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע בָּרָאתִי תּוֹרָה [תַּבְלִין]״; וְזֶהוּ כֹּחַ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהוֹרִיד לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דָּבָר זֶה שֶׁל נִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה וּבִבְרִיאָה

For he [Moshe] is the root of “removing the filth from Israel,” by bringing down the Torah, which is “the seasoning for the evil inclination” [created] in Creation, as they said (Kiddushin 30b), “I created the evil inclination, I created the Torah as its antidote”; and this is the power of Moshe, that he brought down to this world this matter of conquering the inclination that is in [human] birth and in Creation.127Kiddushin 30b: “The Holy One said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its antidote [tavlin]; if you occupy yourselves with Torah you will not be handed into its power.” R’ Tzadok casts Moshe — who brought down the Torah — as the root of “removing the filth” and conquering the inborn inclination, with Bilaam his kelipah-counterpart, who spreads it.

וְכֹחַ בִּלְעָם זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה מִצַּד הָרַע, לְהַמְשִׁיךְ וּלְפַשֵּׁט יוֹתֵר כֹּחַ הָרַע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה, כִּי בּוֹ הָיָה שֹׁרֶשׁ זוּהֲמָא זוֹ דְּנָחָשׁ, דְּעַל כֵּן פָּרַץ גָּדֵר שֶׁל עֲרָיוֹת שֶׁנִּגְדַּר מִימוֹת הַמַּבּוּל

And Bilaam’s power is “this-against-that,” from the side of evil — to draw out and spread further the power of evil in [human] birth, for in him was the root of that “filth of the serpent”; therefore he “breached the fence of immorality” that had been fenced off since the days of the Flood.128Sifrei Devarim 357:40; Peri Tzadik, Bo 12 — Bilaam as Moshe’s counterpart and the failure to grasp holiness in this act: Sifrei expounds “no prophet arose in Israel like Moshe” to mean: in Israel none arose, but among the nations one did — Bilaam — while still sharply distinguishing their prophetic character. Rav Tzadok returns to this contrast in Peri Tzadik: Bilaam, aligned with the kelipah of Amalek, could not understand that holiness can reside in this bodily sphere, and this is why Chazal place the blinding of his eye precisely here. The parallel supports the present se’if’s “this-against-that” construction of Moshe and Bilaam.
וּמִי שֶׁהוּא מָלֵא זוּהֲמָא אֵין יָכוֹל לְהַאֲמִין כְּלָל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּזֶה קְדֻשָּׁה
And one who is full of filth cannot believe at all that there is holiness in this [act].

[וְכֵן אִיתָא [בבר״ר] עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיִּשַּׁק יַעֲקֹב לְרָחֵל״, דְּהָרוֹעִים אָמְרוּ עָלָיו שֶׁבָּא לִפְרוֹץ גָּדֵר עֲרָיוֹת, וְלֹא הֶעֱלוּ עַל לִבָּם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נְשִׁיקָה שֶׁל קוּרְבָה בְּלִי שׁוּם מַחְשָׁבָה לְתַאֲוָה כְּלָל]

[And so it is [in Bereishis Rabbah] on the verse “and Yaakov kissed Rachel” (Bereishis 29:11), that the shepherds said of him that he came “to breach the fence of immorality,” and it did not enter their hearts that it could be a kiss of kinship, with no thought of desire at all.]
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר עֲמָלֵק ״טוֹל מַה שֶּׁבָּחַרְתָּ״, כִּי אוֹת בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ שֶׁבִּבְשָׂרָם הוּא הַמֵּעִיד שֶׁגַּם תַּשְׁמִישׁ אֵבֶר זֶה אֵצֶל זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא רַק לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וּבִקְדֻשָּׁה

And therefore Amalek said, “take what you chose” — for the sign of the holy bris in their flesh is what testifies that even the use of this organ, by the seed of Israel, is only for the sake of Heaven and in holiness.129Midrash Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 9; Machshavos Charutz §16; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos §6 — Amalek attacks the bris because it testifies to bodily holiness: Tanchuma records Amalek cutting the circumcisions of Israel and casting them heavenward with the taunt, “take what You chose.” Rav Tzadok explains the same image in Machshavos Charutz: Hashem placed His covenantal seal on this organ to testify that Israel is filled with kedushah, a truth the nations cannot comprehend; he there again joins Bilaam and Amalek as one root of evil. In Peri Tzadik he likewise reads Amalek’s taunt as a denial of Israel’s inner purity and Bilaam’s blinded eye as the same inability to perceive holiness beneath the bodily appearance. This is a direct parallel to the conclusion of the se’if.

items.h: The theme: This is what divides Israel from the nations: “all the nations are arelim,” unable to be truly “circumcised” (save by conversion, when they are “as a newborn”). Amalek cannot believe holiness could inhere in this act, and so must strip all providence from the world, reducing everything to “chance [mikreh].” Amalek is the “keser of the kelipah,” root of all evil’s spread, of Esav’s seed (“a Jewish apostate”).

p: [טו] וְזֶהוּ הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים, דְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים, שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לִהְיוֹת נִימּוֹלִים כְּלָל [אִם לֹא שֶׁיִּתְגַּיְּירוּ, דְּאָז הֵם כְּקָטָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד וּבְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יְכַנֶּנּוּ]

And this is what “distinguishes between Israel and the peoples” — that “all the nations are arelim,” who cannot be “circumcised” at all [unless they convert, when they are “like a newborn,” and “by the name of Israel he calls himself” (Yeshayah 44:5)].130Nedarim 31b; Yevamos 48b — “arelim” and “mulim” as covenantal identity, and conversion as a new birth: The Mishnah rules that one who vows not to benefit from “arelim” may nevertheless benefit from uncircumcised Jews, while he may not benefit from circumcised members of the nations; conversely, a vow concerning “mulim” includes even an uncircumcised Jew and excludes a circumcised non-Jew. It explains that the Torah’s language calls the nations “arelim.” Yevamos states the complementary rule that “a convert who converts is like a newborn child.” These sources supply the precise halachic language behind Rav Tzadok’s opening distinction: the terms here mark covenantal identity, not merely physical condition. This does not exempt an uncircumcised Jew from the mitzvah of milah; it explains why he nevertheless remains within the covenantal category called “mul.”
וַעֲמָלֵק לֹא יָכוֹל לְהַאֲמִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן קְדֻשָּׁה בְּדָבָר זֶה כְּלָל, כִּי הַגּוֹיִם לֹא יוּכְלוּ לְהָבִין שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְצִיאוּת קְדֻשָּׁה כְּלָל בָּזֶה
And Amalek could not believe that there is, by Israel too, holiness in this matter at all — for the nations cannot grasp that there could be any existence of holiness in it.

וּמִזֶּה בְּהֶכְרֵחַ לָהֶם לְסַלֵּק הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְגַמְרֵי, דְּאֶפְשָׁר מִי שֶׁהוּא וְכו’, וּמִמֵּילָא כֵּיוָן שֶׁעִיקַּר הַהִתְהַוּוּת מִקְרֶה, הֲרֵי הַכֹּל מִקְרֶה, וְזֶהוּ הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ וְהָרֵאשִׁית גּוֹיִם בְּכֹחַ עֲמָלֵק וּבִלְעָם

And from this it is necessary for them to remove His providence from this world entirely — [holding] that perhaps someone [else brought it about], etc. — and of itself, since the essence of “coming-into-being is chance,” then all is “chance” — and this is the root and “the first of the nations” in the power of Amalek and Bilaam.131Tanchuma, Ki Seitzei 9: “What would the house of Amalek do? They would cut off the circumcised organs [milos] of Israel and toss them heavenward, saying, ‘is this what You chose? — take for Yourself what You chose!’” R’ Tzadok reads Amalek’s taunt as the denial that holiness could inhere in Israel’s guarded seed — the root of the nations’ reduction of all to “chance.”132Cf. Devarim 25:18, “who chanced upon you on the way [asher karcha ba-derech]” — the Sages read Amalek as the power of “chance” (mikreh / keri), cooling the recognition of providence; and Shemos 17:16, “Hashem has a war with Amalek from generation to generation” — Amalek being, as here, the root that would reduce all existence to happenstance.

וַעֲמָלֵק הָיָה מֶלֶךְ, כִּי הוּא הַכֶּתֶר דִּקְלִיפָּה, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״רֵאשִׁית״, וְהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִכָּל קוֹמַת הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת דְּרַע, שֶׁבָּא מִזֶּרַע עֵשָׂו הַנִּקְרָא ״יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר״ [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין יח.]

And Amalek was “a king,” for he is “the keser of the kelipah,” and therefore is called “first,” and he is the root above the whole stature of the spread of evil — coming from the seed of Esav, who is called “a Jewish apostate [Yisrael mumar]” [Kiddushin 18a].133Bamidbar 24:20; Machshavos Charutz §16:2; Resisei Layla §52:7 — Amalek as the keser and Bilaam as the da’as of the kelipah: The Torah calls Amalek “the first of the nations.” Rav Tzadok makes the present structure explicit elsewhere: in Machshavos Charutz he writes that Amalek is “the beginning and the keser of the kelipah,” while Bilaam, who says “knower of the knowledge of the Most High,” corresponds to the da’as of the kelipah; keser and da’as are one root, outwardly and inwardly. Resisei Layla similarly states that Amalek, who arose in Moshe’s generation, stood opposite him in the kelipah and is one with Bilaam: Bilaam is the inward da’as of evil, while Amalek is its outward “first of the nations.” This is a direct Rav Tzadok parallel to the architecture of this se’if.134Kiddushin 18a: In discussing an apostate’s rights of inheritance, the Gemara considers “a Jewish apostate [Yisrael mumar]” — one still bound, at root, to Israel yet who has “exchanged” his way. R’ Tzadok applies the term to Esav (Yitzchak’s son): still holding the ancestral root of holiness, and so able to uproot himself — unlike Yaakov’s seed, from whom the name “Israel” can never be uprooted.

וּבִלְעָם שֶׁהִתְפָּאֵר דְּ״יוֹדֵעַ דַּעַת עֶלְיוֹן״ [שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה בְּסוֹד הַדַּעַת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה] הוּא כֹּחַ הַדַּעַת דִּקְלִיפָּה כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהוּא הַמְחַבֵּר חׇכְמָה וּבִינָה, שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ כֹּחַ הָעַיִן שֶׁמִּתְיַיחֵס לַלֵּב וְלַמּוֹחַ

And Bilaam, who boasted “he knows the knowledge of the Most High” (Bamidbar 24:16) [which is over-against Moshe, who was in the secret of holy Da’as], is the power of the Da’as of the kelipah, as is known — the one “joining Chochmah and Binah,” whence comes the power of the eye, which relates to the heart and the brain,

כְּעִנְיַן ״וְלִבִּי רָאָה הַרְבֵּה חׇכְמָה״; וּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה [כח:] ״שׁוּרְיָינָא דְּעֵינָא בְּאוּבַנְתָּא דְּלִבָּא תָּלֵי״, הַיְינוּ בִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּקוֹמוֹ בָּרֹאשׁ נֶגֶד הַמּוֹחַ, כִּי הוּא מֵחִיבּוּר שְׁנֵיהֶם

as in “and my heart saw much wisdom” (Koheles 1:16); and in Avodah Zarah [28b], “the sinew of the eye hangs on the understanding of the heart [ubanta d’liba]” — namely the Binah of the heart, and though its place is in the head opposite the brain, [it is so] because it is from the joining of the two.135Avodah Zarah 28b: In a medical passage — “the sinew of the eye hangs on [is bound up with] the understanding of the heart [shuryana d’eina b’ubanta d’liba tali].” R’ Tzadok reads it kabbalistically: the eye’s power derives from Binah “in the heart,” the faculty joining Chochmah and Binah (the “Da’as”), which Bilaam possessed on the side of the kelipah.

וּלְפִיכָךְ כָּל הַשָּׂגַת בִּלְעָם הָיָה מִצַּד הַקְּדֻשָּׁה, שֶׁהֲרֵי דְּבָרָיו נֶאֶמְרוּ בַּתּוֹרָה הַקְּדוֹשָׁה, וְהוּא נְבוּאַת אֱמֶת, וְכָל נְבוּאָתוֹ עַל מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁהִכִּיר הָאֱמֶת וּבִיקֵּשׁ עַל נַפְשׁוֹ ״תָּמֹת נַפְשִׁי מוֹת יְשָׁרִים וּתְהִי [אַחֲרִיתִי כָּמֹהוּ]״

And therefore all of Bilaam’s apprehension was from the side of holiness — for his words were said in the holy Torah, and it is “true prophecy,” and all his prophecy was about the greatness of Israel; for he recognized the truth and begged for his own soul, “let my soul die the death of the upright, and let my end be like his” (Bamidbar 23:10).136Bava Basra 14b; Sifrei Devarim 357 — Bilaam’s prophecy enters Torah specifically through Moshe: The baraisa states, “Moshe wrote his book, the portion of Bilaam, and Iyov.” Sifrei, on “no prophet arose again in Israel like Moshe,” expounds: in Israel none arose, but among the nations one did — Bilaam — and then sharply distinguishes the character of their prophecy. Together these sources provide the textual framework for Rav Tzadok’s claim: Bilaam is the prophetic counterpart on the side of the nations, yet what is true in his apprehension is preserved inside Torah through Moshe. The Gemara’s separate mention of “the portion of Bilaam,” even after saying that Moshe wrote his book, is especially apt for Rav Tzadok’s emphasis on this absorption into Torah.

וּבָנָיו יַנִּיס וְיַמְבְּרוּס יָצְאוּ עִם יִשְׂרָאֵל מִמִּצְרַיִם, דְּהֵם הָעֵרֶב רַב שֶׁעָשׂוּ הָעֵגֶל כַּיָּדוּעַ בַּזֹּהַר, וְהִכִּירוּ מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד שֶׁרָשׁוּם בְּרַע וְזוּהֲמָא לֹא יָכְלוּ לְהַפְרִיד עַצְמָם מִמֶּנָּה

And his sons, Yannis and Yambrus, went out with Israel from Egypt — they are the “mixed multitude [erev rav]” who made the calf, as is known in the Zohar — and they recognized Israel’s greatness, only that, being rooted in evil and filth, they could not separate themselves from it.137Zohar, Ki Sisa 11:61; Zohar, Balak 13:174 — Yonnos and Yimbrus, the Erev Rav, the calf, and Bilaam: The Zohar asks why the group is called “Erev Rav” and answers that they were the Egyptian sorcerers, headed by Yonnos and Yimbrus. In Balak, the Zohar identifies Yonnos and Yomberos as Bilaam’s two sons and explicitly refers to them as those who made the calf. These passages are the direct source for Rav Tzadok’s compressed chain here: Bilaam’s sons belonged to the Egyptian magical elite that joined the mixed multitude, recognized the power surrounding Israel sufficiently to attach themselves to it, yet remained rooted in the side that produced the calf.

וְעַל כֵּן עַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְמֵית עֵינוֹ, כִּי כָּל כֹּחַ עֵינוֹ וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ הוּא מִצַּד שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ אֲחִיזָה מַה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁיֵּשׁ מְצִיאוּת רַע בָּעוֹלָם, וְ״אַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כּוּלָּם״ כְּתִיב כַּנּוֹדָע

And therefore over this matter his eye was blinded — for all the power of his eye and apprehension was from the side that he had some grasp in holiness, through the [fact] that there is an existence of evil in the world, and “You give life to them all” (Nechemiah 9:6) is written, as is known.

וְהוּא הָיָה נֶגֶד הָעַיִן דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, כְּמוֹ מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה רֹאשׁ לְכָל הַסַּנְהֶדְרָאוֹת שֶׁבְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת, דְּעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בּוֹ ״לֹא כָהֲתָה עֵינוֹ״ — כָּךְ הוּא זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, הִתְפָּאֵר ״אֲשֶׁר מַחֲזֵה [שַׁ-דַּי יֶחֱזֶה]״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וּגְלוּי עֵינָיִם״

And he [Bilaam] was over-against “the eye of holiness” — like Moshe, who was “head of all the Sanhedrins of all generations,” of whom it says “his eye did not dim” (Devarim 34:7); so is this one, “this-against-that,” who boasted, “who sees the vision of Sha-dai, [falling, yet] open of eyes” (Bamidbar 24:4).138Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6; Devarim 34:7; Bamidbar 24:4 — Moshe over the seventy elders and the undimmed “eye of holiness”: The Mishnah derives the seventy-one-member Great Sanhedrin from “gather Me seventy men” together with “Moshe over them,” placing Moshe at the head of the foundational court. The Torah then closes his life with “his eye had not dimmed.” Bilaam, by contrast, boasts of himself as one who sees the vision of Sha-dai, “falling, yet open of eyes.” Rav Tzadok joins these verses typologically: Moshe’s undimmed eye represents the governing eye of holy da’as, while Bilaam is its opposing imitation. The phrase “head of all the Sanhedrins of all generations” is Rav Tzadok’s extension of the Mosaic model; the Mishnah itself speaks directly of Moshe standing over the original seventy elders.

items.h: The theme: All that was revealed to Bilaam was only for Israel’s sake — hence written in the Torah by Moshe, who “drew the swallowed prey from his mouth,” ending the resting of prophecy on the nations. Once the holy sparks were absorbed from him, Bilaam reverted to mere sorcery (the kelipah-counterpart of Moshe, master of the prophets). His essence is “blind of eye” — no grasp of the “eye of holiness.”

p: [טז] אֲבָל כָּל מַה שֶּׁנִּתְגַּלָּה לוֹ הָיָה רַק לְצֹרֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְעַל כֵּן נִכְתַּב בַּתּוֹרָה עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהוֹצִיא ״בָּלְעוֹ מִפִּיו״, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה פָּעַל שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁרֶה עוֹד שְׁכִינָה עַל אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

But all that was revealed to him was only for the sake of Israel; therefore it was written in the Torah through Moshe Rabbeinu, who “brought forth the swallowed [prey] from his mouth” (cf. Iyov 20:15) — and through this he effected that the Shechinah would no longer rest upon the nations.139Berachos 7a; Bava Basra 15b; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos 7:32 — Moshe’s request that prophecy cease from the nations, and Bilaam’s revelation only for Israel: Berachos records that Moshe asked that the Shechinah not rest upon the nations, and that his request was granted from “and we shall be distinguished, I and Your people” (Shemos 33:16). Bava Basra therefore reasons that after Moshe’s death the Shechinah no longer rested upon a prophet of the nations. Rav Tzadok supplies the inner complement: in Peri Tzadik he writes that Bilaam, “head of the sages of the nations,” attained the truth of Israel’s greatness, but the nations apprehend only what Hashem reveals to them “for the sake of Israel.” This closely parallels the opening of the present se’if: Bilaam’s true prophetic content was extracted into Israel’s Torah, while the independent channel of gentile prophecy was closed.

וְאַף בִּלְעָם, אַחַר שֶׁנִּקְלַט מִמֶּנּוּ הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת, חָזַר לִהְיוֹת קוֹסֵם [וְהוּא רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַקּוֹסְמִים וְהַמְכַשְּׁפִים, שֶׁכּוּלָּם מְקַבְּלִים מִבִּלְעָם וּמִמְּקוֹם קִבְרוֹ וְעַצְמוֹתָיו כִּדְאִיתָא בַּזֹּהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ, וְדֻגְמַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, רַבָּן שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים, וְכוּלָּן מְקַבְּלִין נְבוּאָתָן מִמֹּשֶׁה, וְנִרְמְזוּ בִּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא (נְדָרִים לח.) ״וְכוּלָּן מִמֹּשֶׁה״ וְכַנּוֹדָע]

And Bilaam, too, after the holy sparks were absorbed from him, reverted to being a diviner [and he is the master of all diviners and sorcerers, who all “receive” from Bilaam and from the place of his grave and bones, as it is stated in the holy Zohar — the “likeness” of Moshe in holiness, master of all the prophets, all of whom “receive” their prophecy from Moshe, alluded to in the Gemara’s phrase (Nedarim 38a), “and all from Moshe,” as is known].140Yehoshua 13:22; Sanhedrin 106a; Bamidbar Rabbah 20:19 — “at first a prophet, and at the end a diviner”: Yehoshua calls him “Bilaam son of Beor, the diviner.” The Gemara asks the obvious question — “a diviner? he was a prophet!” — and R’ Yochanan answers: “at first a prophet, and at the end a diviner.” Bamidbar Rabbah states the same descent even more explicitly: Bilaam attained ruach hakodesh and then “returned to being a diviner as at first.” These are the direct Chazal sources for Rav Tzadok’s wording that once the holy sparks had been absorbed from Bilaam, he reverted to the lower status of kosem.141Nedarim 38a: “R’ Yochanan said: the Holy One rests His Presence only upon one who is mighty, wealthy, wise, and humble — all [learned] from Moshe.” R’ Tzadok takes the phrase “all from Moshe” as alluding that all prophets “receive” from Moshe, the master of the prophets — with Bilaam his exact counterpart in the realm of impurity, master of all diviners.
וְעַצְמוּתוֹ הָיָה ״שְׁתוּם הָעַיִן״, כִּי אֵין לוֹ הַשָּׂגָה בְּעַיִן דִּקְדֻשָּׁה כְּלָל
And his essence was “blind of eye [shesum ha’ayin],” for he has no apprehension in the “eye of holiness” at all.
וּבֶאֱמֶת לְגַבֵּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נֶאֱמַר ״כָּל חֹשֶׁךְ לֹא יַחְשִׁיךְ [מִמֶּךָּ]״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְנֶאֱמַר ״אֲנִי ה׳ הַשּׁוֹכֵן אִתָּם בְּתוֹךְ טוּמְאֹתָם״

And in truth, regarding Hashem it says, “even darkness is not dark [to You], and night shines as the day” (Tehillim 139:12), and it says, “I am Hashem who dwells with them amid their impurity” (Vayikra 16:16).142Tehillim 139:12; Yoma 56b; Sichas Malachei HaShareis §4 — holiness remains present even inside impurity: The psalm declares, “even darkness is not dark to You.” Yoma expounds “Who dwells with them amid their impurity” (Vayikra 16:16): “even when they are impure, the Shechinah is with them.” Rav Tzadok makes this inward and personal in Sichas Malachei HaShareis: “the Shechinah … dwells within their impurity,” meaning that Hashem is hidden in the heart of every Jew even when he is at the farthest distance. This supports the se’if’s distinction between the apparent displacement of holiness in the revealed world and its non-displacement at the root.

שֶׁאַף דְּהַטּוּמְאָה הוּא הֵפֶךְ דְּטָהֳרָה וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה, וּמִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִרְאֶה שֶׁהַטּוּמְאָה מְסַלֶּקֶת קְדֻשָּׁה — זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַאי עָלְמָא דְּשִׁקְרָא; אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל זֶרַע אֱמֶת מַכִּירִים הָאֱמֶת, דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר מְצִיאוּת שׁוּם דָּבָר בְּלֹא כֹּחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמְּחַיֵּיהוּ

For although impurity is the opposite of purity and holiness, and from the side of revelation in this world it appears that impurity “removes” holiness — that is [only] from the side of this “world of falsehood”; but Israel, “seed of truth,” recognize the truth: that it is impossible for anything to exist without the power of Hashem that enlivens it.

וַאֲפִילּוּ הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם וּמְשׁוּקָּע בְּמָקוֹם שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּקַּע, וְגַם ״כִּי אֵלֵךְ בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת״, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַחוֹשֶׁךְ דְּ״אַחְשֵׁךְ אַנְפֵּי בִּרְיָיתָא״, ״לֹא אִירָא רָע״ — שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע הַנּוֹתֵן כֹּחַ לְטוּמְאָה וְצַלְמָוֶת וּמְסַלֵּק הַשְּׁכִינָה — לֹא אִירָא מִזֶּה, ״כִּי אַתָּה עִמָּדִי״ גַּם שָׁם

And even if it is in the ultimate concealment, sunk in the place where it sank, and even “though I walk in the valley of the shadow of death” — which is the ultimate darkness that “darkened the face of Creation” — “I will fear no evil”: [no fear of] the root of evil that gives power to impurity and death-shadow and removes the Shechinah — “I will fear” it not, “for You are with me” even there.143Tehillim 23:4; Divrei Soferim §32; Machshavos Charutz §9 — “You are with me” within the very place of concealment: Rav Tzadok develops this verse elsewhere almost word for word. Divrei Soferim distinguishes two salvations: sometimes Hashem removes a person entirely from darkness, and sometimes He illuminates for him, while he is still in the “valley of the shadow of death,” that “You are with me”; this itself is already a great salvation, because he no longer fears the evil. Machshavos Charutz similarly teaches that the root of emunah is to know that even while one is sunk in darkness, Hashem is with him; by that recognition one can emerge from the impurity, because where Hashem is present the apparent evil has no independent existence. This is the direct conceptual parallel to the present passage.

וּמִמֵּילָא כְּשֶׁמַּאֲמִין וּמַכִּיר זֶה נִסְתַּלֵּק הָרַע, דְּ״לֹא יְגוּרְךָ רָע״; וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים ״מוּלִים״, דַּאֲפִילּוּ חֵטְא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא [רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן]

And of itself, when one believes and recognizes this, the evil departs — for “evil shall not sojourn with You” (Tehillim 5:5); and therefore even the “arelim of Israel” are called “mulim,” for even a sin of Israel is [only outward].144Yirmiyahu 2:21; Machshavos Charutz §14:6 — Israel as “all seed of truth” even when outwardly deficient: Yirmiyahu describes Israel at its planting as “a choice vine, all of it seed of truth.” Rav Tzadok explains in Machshavos Charutz that Hashem alone is absolute truth, and Israel, because they are attached to Him, are “seed of truth”; even when they are poor in mitzvos, their deepest root remains directed toward Him. The present conclusion applies that essential identity to sin itself: the outward state can obscure the covenantal truth without uprooting it. The earlier halachic rule that even uncircumcised Jews are called “mulim” is thus used here as a model for the deeper claim that Israel’s essential bond survives the visible defect.

items.h: The theme: This matter, in this world “resembling night,” is in ultimate concealment — hence in the Saba d’Mishpatim it is “a beautiful maiden who has no eyes,” for though beauty’s essence is in the eyes, here they are hidden. This was the serpent’s enticement: “your eyes will be opened, and you shall be like God, knowing good and evil.” For God “knows good and evil equally,” gazing on both in a single glance, His providence over all, “there is none besides Him” even amid impurity.

p: [יז] אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא בְּסָבָא דְּמִשְׁפָּטִים [צה.] ״עוּלֶמְתָּא שַׁפִּירְתָּא דְּלֵית לָהּ עַיְינִין״ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעִיקַּר הַיֹּפִי בָּעֵינַיִם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״כָּל כַּלָּה שֶׁעֵינֶיהָ יָפוֹת [אֵין כָּל גּוּפָהּ צָרִיךְ בְּדִיקָה]״ כו׳, אֲבָל הֵם בְּהֶעְלֵם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

But this thing, in this world “resembling night,” is in the ultimate concealment; therefore it is called, in the Saba d’Mishpatim [Zohar II 95a], “a beautiful maiden who has no eyes” — although the essence of beauty is in the eyes, and as they said, “any bride whose eyes are beautiful [her whole body needs no examination]”145Taanis 24a; Resisei Layla §52 — “beautiful eyes” and the condition of the whole person: Taanis expounds “if it was hidden from the eyes of the congregation” (Bamidbar 15:24) with the parable: when a bride’s eyes are beautiful, her whole body requires no examination; when her eyes are bleary, the whole body requires examination. Rav Tzadok elsewhere explains the inner logic: the sages are the “eyes of the congregation”; where a person’s thought is directed, the person is drawn after it, the eye fixes the thought, the thought enters the heart, and from there it reaches the limbs. In this se’if he develops the same image further: the “eyes” signify revealed apprehension, and the beauty is real even when those eyes are concealed in this world. — but they [the eyes] are in concealment in this world.146Zohar, Saba d’Mishpatim (II 95a–b): the famous parable of the Torah as “a beautiful maiden without eyes [ulemta shappirta d’leis lah einin],” hidden in her palace, who reveals herself only gradually to her lover. R’ Tzadok turns the image to this world, “resembling night,” where the “eyes” (the revealed apprehension of holiness within the physical act) are, for now, concealed.

וְזֶה שֹׁרֶשׁ הֲסָתַת הַנָּחָשׁ ״וְנִפְקְחוּ עֵינֵיכֶם וִהְיִיתֶם [כֵּאלֹקִים יֹדְעֵי טוֹב וָרָע]״ — הַיְינוּ שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא יוֹדֵעַ טוֹב וָרַע בְּשָׁוֶה, דְּיוּכַל לְהִסְתַּכֵּל עַל שְׁנֵיהֶם יַחַד, וְכוּלָּן בִּסְקִירָה אַחַת, כִּי הַשְׁגָּחָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל הַכֹּל, דְּהוּא מְחַיֶּה אֶת הַכֹּל וְאֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ, וַאֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקוֹם טוּמְאָה

And this is the root of the serpent’s enticement: “and your eyes shall be opened, and you shall be like God, knowing good and evil” (Bereishis 3:5) — that is, Hashem “knows good and evil equally,” able to gaze upon both together, all in a single glance,147Rosh Hashanah 18a; Tehillim 33:15 — “all are scanned in a single glance”: R’ Yochanan teaches that although all created beings pass in judgment individually, “all are scanned in a single scan,” and the Gemara grounds this in “He Who fashions their hearts together, Who understands all their deeds.” Rav Tzadok borrows that formulation to describe the Divine apprehension of good and evil together: multiplicity and opposition do not divide the Creator’s knowledge or providence. The next paragraph is therefore essential to his argument: this simultaneous Divine gaze cannot be copied by a human being, whose holiness is creaturely and limited. for His providence is over all, for He enlivens all and “there is none besides Him,” even in a place of impurity.148Devarim 4:35; Sanhedrin 67b — “there is none besides Him,” even with respect to sorcery: On “there is none besides Him,” R’ Chanina says: “even with respect to a matter of sorcery.” The sugya uses the verse to deny any genuinely independent power outside Hashem. This is a particularly close classical support for Rav Tzadok’s statement that Divine vitality and providence extend even into a place identified with impurity. His use of the principle is metaphysical, not permissive: the following paragraph immediately insists that a human being may not infer that he can expose himself to impurity and remain untouched as only Divine holiness can.

אֲבָל עַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״קְדוֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ, יָכוֹל כָּמוֹנִי? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר [כִּי קָדוֹשׁ אֲנִי — קְדֻשָּׁתִי לְמַעְלָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁתְכֶם]״ (ויק״ר כה, ט) — הַיְינוּ דְּלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל דַּעַת אָדָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם כֵּן קָדוֹשׁ כִּבְיָכוֹל כָּמוֹהוּ, שֶׁכָּל טוּמְאָה לֹא תְּטַמְּאֶנּוּ, דְּזֶהוּ רַק קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

But regarding this it says, “you shall be holy” — could it mean “like Me”? — Scripture teaches [otherwise: “for I am holy” — My holiness is above your holiness] (Vayikra Rabbah 24:9) — meaning, let it not enter a person’s mind that he could be holy, as it were, like Him, whom no impurity defiles, for that is His holiness alone.149Vayikra Rabbah 24:9: On “you shall be holy, for I am holy” (Vayikra 19:2) — “could it be [holy] like Me? Scripture teaches, ‘for I am holy’ — My holiness is above your holiness.” R’ Tzadok: no created being may be “holy like God,” whom no impurity can touch; a person still sunk in evil cannot even see the good, whereas one wholly cleaving to good (Adam before the sin) cannot see the evil — hence Adam’s shamelessness.

אֲבָל הָאָדָם הַמְשׁוּקָּע בְּרַע כְּאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע אֵין יָכוֹל לִרְאוֹת וּלְהַשִּׂיג הַטּוֹב; וּמִי שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ דָּבוּק בַּטּוֹב כְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, אֵינוֹ רוֹאֶה וּמַשִּׂיג הָרַע, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ בּוּשָׁה, כִּי לֹא הִשִּׂיגוּ צַד רַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה כְּלָל

But the person “sunk in evil,” like that wicked one, cannot see and attain the good; and one wholly cleaving to the good, like Avraham Avinu and Adam before the sin, does not see or apprehend the evil — and therefore he had no shame, for they apprehended no “evil side” in this at all.150Bereishis 2:25; Rashi — Adam’s lack of shame before the sin: On “they were both naked … and were not ashamed,” Rashi explains that Adam and Chavah did not yet know the mode of modesty that distinguishes good from evil. Adam certainly possessed intellect — he had already named the creatures — but the yetzer hara had not entered him until he ate from the tree; only then did experiential knowledge of good and evil enter. This closely matches Rav Tzadok’s formulation: before the sin Adam could not “see” the evil side in the bodily reality, and therefore nakedness did not yet produce shame.

וְהַנָּחָשׁ הִסִּיתָם שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְדַּמּוֹת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהֵם בִּקְדֻשָּׁה כָּזוֹ שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לִהְיוֹת פִּקּוּחֵי עֵינַיִם כֵּאלֹקִים, לָדַעַת וּלְהַשִּׂיג טוֹב וָרַע יַחַד, וְכָל טִינּוֹפֶת לֹא תְּטַנְּפֵם

And the serpent enticed them that they could liken themselves to Hashem — that they are in such holiness that they could be “open of eyes like God,” to know and apprehend good and evil together, and no filth would soil them.

אֲבָל תֵּיכֶף מִשֶּׁנִּפְקְחוּ עֵינֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם לְהִסְתַּכֵּל בְּרַע, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּאוּ לִידֵי בּוּשָׁה, בִּיקְּשׁוּ לְסַמּוֹת רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן ״עֵינוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם״, שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ כִּבְיָכוֹל עַיִן שֶׁל מַעְלָה כְּאִינוֹ רוֹאֶה, שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ לְהִתְחַבֵּא מִמֶּנּוּ — וְזֶהוּ שֹׁרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא וְהָרַע שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם

But immediately when the eyes of both were opened to gaze on evil — through which they came to shame — they sought to blind, God spare us, “the eye of the world,” for they thought, as it were, that “the eye above” does not see, that they could hide from it — and this is the root of the filth and the evil in the world.151Bereishis 3:7–10; Tehillim 139:7–12 — opened eyes, shame, and the attempt to hide: The Torah itself places the stages in immediate sequence: “the eyes of both were opened,” they knew they were naked and made coverings; they then heard Hashem in the garden and “the man and his wife hid,” with Adam explaining, “I was afraid because I was naked, so I hid.” Tehillim states the opposite theological truth: there is nowhere to flee from His presence, and even darkness is not dark before Him. Rav Tzadok reads the narrative sequence homiletically as the first attempt to behave as though the “eye above” could be screened from human conduct; that deeper characterization is his interpretation of the Torah’s juxtaposition.

וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי [דִּבְרָכוֹת] ״עַיִן וָלֵב שְׁנֵי סַרְסוּרֵי [דַּעֲבֵירָה]״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לֹא תָתוּרוּ [אַחֲרֵי לְבַבְכֶם וְאַחֲרֵי עֵינֵיכֶם]״, וְהַהַתְחָלָה הוּא מֵהָעַיִן רוֹאָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ לֵב חוֹמֵד, וּכְלִי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה גּוֹמְרִים

And in the Yerushalmi [Berachos 1:5], “the eye and the heart are the two agents of transgression,”152Yerushalmi, Berachos 1:5 (and Bamidbar Rabbah 10:6): On “and you shall not go astray after your heart and after your eyes” (Bamidbar 15:39) — “the eye and the heart are the two agents [brokers] of transgression [shenei sarsurei aveirah]”: the eye sees, the heart covets, and the instruments of action complete the deed. This underlies the se’if’s account of the eye and the heart as sin’s two agents. as it says, “you shall not go astray [after your heart and after your eyes]” (Bamidbar 15:39) — and the beginning is from the eye seeing, then the heart coveting, and the instruments of action complete [it].

וְכֵן הָיָה חֵטְא הָרִאשׁוֹן עַל יְדֵי הָעַיִן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וַתֵּרֶא הָאִשָּׁה״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְכִי תַאֲוָה הוּא לָעֵינַיִם״; וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל בָּאוּ לַלֵּב הַחוֹמֵד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְכָל יֵצֶר מַחְשְׁבֹת לִבּוֹ רַק [רַע]״ וְגוֹמֵר

And so the first sin was through the eye, as it says, “and the woman saw [that the tree was good for food] and that it was a delight to the eyes” (Bereishis 3:6); and afterward, in the generation of the Flood, they came to “the coveting heart,” as it says, “and every inclination of the thoughts of his heart was only [evil]” (Bereishis 6:5).

items.h: The theme: Knesses Yisrael boasts “I am asleep, but my heart is awake.” Expounded of the Holy One (“the Rock of my heart”): though Israel “sleep” from the mitzvos and have “no eyes,” the soul’s root is “a portion of God,” and the depths of the heart cleave to Him. So even the sleeper’s imaginings cleave to God, and in the deepest sinking there remains the power to awaken to Him.

p: [יח] וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִתְפָּאֶרֶת ״אֲנִי יְשֵׁנָה וְלִבִּי עֵר״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רז״ל [בשהש״ר] ״זֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא״, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״צוּר לְבָבִי״ וְגוֹמֵר

And Knesses Yisrael boasts, “I am asleep, but my heart is awake” (Shir HaShirim 5:2), which the Sages expounded [in Shir HaShirim Rabbah], “‘my heart’ — this is the Holy One,” as it says, “the Rock of my heart [and my portion is God forever]” (Tehillim 73:26).153Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2: On “I am asleep, but my heart is awake” — “‘I am asleep’ [from the mitzvos], ‘but my heart is awake’ [to do acts of kindness]; ‘I sleep’ — from the mitzvos; ‘my heart is awake’ — this is the Holy One,” as it says, “the Rock [tzur] of my heart and my portion is God forever” (Tehillim 73:26). R’ Tzadok: the depths of the Jewish heart, cleaving to God, never truly “sleep,” even amid exile and sin.

דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיְּשֵׁנִים מִן הַמִּצְוֹת וְלֵית לְהוּ עַיְנִין, כִּבְעֵת הַשֵּׁינָה דְּהָעַיְנִין סְתוּמִים וְהַלֵּב מְשׁוּקָּע בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מֵאַחַר שֶׁשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַנֶּפֶשׁ ״חֵלֶק אֱלוֹקַּ״, וּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, הֲרֵי גַּם כָּל הַדִּמְיוֹנוֹת דָּבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

For although they “sleep from the mitzvos” and “have no eyes” — as in the time of sleep, when the eyes are shut and the heart is sunk in imaginings — nonetheless, since the root of the soul is “a portion of God,” and the depths of the heart cleave to Hashem, then even all the imaginings cleave to Hashem.154Iyov 31:2; Resisei Layla §40 — “a portion of God” and the inextinguishable point in the heart: The phrase “chelek Eloka mima’al” appears in Iyov 31:2. Rav Tzadok elsewhere gives the conceptual formulation used here: the root-depth of the Jewish heart is attached to Hashem even among sinners; no Jewish soul stands outside the complete stature of Israel, and each contains a “portion of God above.” He describes a fixed point of Divine vitality in the heart through which Israel can recognize and feel the living God, and explicitly connects this to “I am asleep, but my heart is awake.” The biblical phrase itself is from Iyov; its use as a description of the soul’s ineradicable root is Rav Tzadok’s theological reading.

וְאַף בְּעֵת תַּכְלִית הַהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת בְּדִמְיוֹנוֹת הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַמַּעֲלִימִים הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ, יֵשׁ בּוֹ כֹּחַ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִצַּד דְּבֵיקוּת הַלֵּב בֵּאלֹקִים חַיִּים

And even in the moment of the ultimate sinking in the imaginings of this world, which conceal the absolute truth, there is in him a power of “awakening” to Hashem, from the side of the cleaving of the heart to the living God.
וְזֶה טַעַם קְרִיאַת יְהוּדָה שֵׁם בְּנוֹ ״עֵר״ עַל שֵׁם ״וְלִבִּי עֵר״
And this is the reason Yehudah named his son “Er,” after “and my heart is awake [er].”

דְּאַחַר מְכִירַת יוֹסֵף שֶׁהוֹרִידוּהוּ מִגְּדֻלָּתוֹ — דִּלְעוֹלָם אַחַר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וּבִפְרָט צַדִּיקִים כְּמוֹהֶם, הִרְגִּישׁוּ הָאֱמֶת — דְּיוֹסֵף הָיָה קְדֻשַּׁת הַיְסוֹד בְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ שֶׁבְּקוֹמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה וּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל

For after the sale of Yosef, who was “brought down from his greatness” — for always, after the deed, and especially tzaddikim like them, they felt the truth — that Yosef was the holiness of Yesod, the holy bris, in the stature of Yaakov Avinu and Knesses Yisrael.

דְּעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״כִּי אֵרֵד [אֶל בְּנִי אָבֵל שְׁאֹלָה]״, שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁחָזַר הַקִּלְקוּל לִמְקוֹמוֹ, וְשֶׁ״חַיָּה רָעָה אֲכָלָתְהוּ״ — לְאֵבֶר הַבְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ הַמַּבְדִּיל בֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים — כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם עַל יְדֵי הַמְּכִירָה, שֶׁהָיָה חַס וְשָׁלוֹם נִטְמַע בֵּין הָעַמִּים אִלְמָלֵא דְּמוּת דְּיוֹקְנוֹ [שֶׁל אָבִיו]

Therefore [Yaakov] said, “for I will go down to my son, mourning, to She’ol” (Bereishis 37:35) — for he thought the corruption had returned to its place, and that “an evil beast devoured him” — [devoured] the limb of the holy bris that distinguishes Israel from the nations — as it would have been, God forbid, through the sale: that [Yosef] would have been assimilated among the nations, were it not for “the image of his [father’s] likeness [dmus dyokno]” [that appeared to him].155Sotah 36b — Yosef’s test and the image of Yaakov: In the account of Yosef and Potiphar’s wife, one opinion says that Yosef entered the house intending to satisfy his desire. At that moment “the likeness of his father appeared to him in the window” and warned him that the names of his brothers were destined to be engraved on the stones of the Ephod: did he wish his own name erased from among them? The Gemara then reads “his bow remained firm” as Yosef recovering his restraint. This is the direct source for Rav Tzadok’s reference to the dmus dyokno that prevented Yosef from being swallowed into the nations and preserved the holiness of the bris.

דְּעֵשָׂו נִקְרָא ״יִשְׂרָאֵל מוּמָר״, שֶׁהָיָה בְּיָדוֹ עֲדַיִן לְהָמִיר וְלַעֲקוֹר עַצְמוֹ מִשֹּׁרֶשׁ הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב, אֲפִילּוּ יַגְדִּיל עֲוֹנוֹת זוֹ לְמַעְלָה מִזּוֹ וְיִיטָּמַע בָּעַמִּים, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲקוֹר מִמֶּנּוּ שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל

For Esav is called “a Jewish apostate” — it was still in his power to apostatize and uproot himself from the root of holiness he had from his fathers; not so the seed of Yaakov — even if he magnify iniquities one above another and be assimilated among the peoples, it is impossible to uproot from him the name “Israel” at all.156Kiddushin 18a; Sanhedrin 44a — Esav as a possible “apostate Israelite” and the enduring name Israel: Kiddushin rejects a proof from Esav’s inheritance by asking whether Esav may be different because he was a “Yisrael meshummad,” an apostate Israelite; this is the Talmudic phrase Rav Tzadok adopts when describing Esav. By contrast, Sanhedrin states of Achan, “even though he sinned, he is Israel.” Rav Tzadok combines these sugyos into a developmental distinction: before the completed emergence of Yaakov’s seed, Esav could still sever himself from the inherited holy root, whereas a descendant of Yaakov cannot lose the essential name Israel. That final historical-metaphysical contrast is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis, not a verbatim conclusion of either sugya.

וְאָז בְּהַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיָה עֲדַיִין דָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ לְבֵירוּרִים, וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרֵר בְּיוֹסֵף שֶׁעָמַד בַּנִּסָּיוֹן — שֶׁעַל שְׁמוֹ נִקְרָא כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל ״שְׁאֵרִית יוֹסֵף״ — לֹא יָדְעוּ זֶה עֲדַיִין

And then, at the beginning of the building of Knesses Yisrael, this matter still required clarifications; and until it was clarified through Yosef, who “withstood the test” — for whom all Israel is called “the remnant of Yosef” (Amos 5:15) — they did not yet know this.

וּלְפִיכָךְ חָשְׁבוּ הַשְּׁבָטִים שֶׁמִּמֵּילָא יֵשׁ הוֹרָדָה גַּם כֵּן לִגְדֻלַּת יְהוּדָה, שֶׁהוּא הַמֶּלֶךְ בָּעָם — שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם הַלֵּב בַּגּוּף כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֵפֶר יְצִירָה — וְאֵין מֶלֶךְ בְּלֹא עָם וְלֹא לֵב בְּלִי גּוּף

And therefore the tribes thought that, consequently, there is a “lowering” also to Yehudah’s greatness — he being “the king among the people,” who is “in the place of the heart in the body,” as they said in Sefer Yetzirah157Sefer Yetzirah 6:3: which sets the heart at the center of the body’s organs and concludes: “and EL, the faithful King, rules over them all — one over three, three over seven, seven over twelve, and all of them fastened this one to that one.” R’ Tzadok reads the heart as the “king” among the limbs: just as “there is no king without a people,” so there is no heart without a body — ruler and ruled each requiring the other. — and “there is no king without a people,” nor a heart without a body;
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁחָשְׁבוּ שֶׁנִּתְקַלְקֵל חַס וְשָׁלוֹם כָּל בִּנְיַן קוֹמַת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְהָעָם אֶחָד, מִמֵּילָא אֵין מָקוֹם וּמְצִיאוּת לְמַלְכוּתוֹ גַּם כֵּן
and since they thought that the whole building of the stature of Knesses Yisrael and “the one people” was corrupted, God forbid, then of itself there is no place or existence for his kingship either.

וִיהוּדָה, דְּיָדַע בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ דִּלְבָבוֹ דָּבוּק בֶּאֱמֶת בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ — דְּעַל כֵּן כּוּלּוֹ נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְכֵן ״כָּל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל (מְגִילָּה יג.) — יָרַד מֵאֵת אֶחָיו לְתַקֵּן זֶה בְּעַצְמוֹ

And Yehudah, who knew in himself that his heart truly cleaves to Hashem — for which reason he is wholly “called by the Name of Hashem,”158Sotah 36b — Yehudah’s entire name bears the Divine Name: R’ Chana bar Bizna in the name of R’ Shimon Chasida contrasts Yosef and Yehudah: Yosef sanctified the Divine Name in private and therefore one letter of Hashem’s Name was added to his own, while Yehudah sanctified the Divine Name publicly and “was called entirely by the Name of the Holy One.” This is the direct rabbinic basis for Rav Tzadok’s phrase that Yehudah is wholly “called by the Name of Hashem”; he then connects that name to the heart’s undivided cleaving to God. and likewise “whoever denies idolatry is called a Yehudi,” as the Sages said (Megillah 13a) — “went down from his brothers” to rectify this in himself.159Sotah 13b; Bereishis 38:1 — Yehudah was lowered from greatness after Yosef’s sale: R’ Elazar teaches that one who begins a mitzvah but does not complete it can be lowered from his greatness, citing “at that time Yehudah went down from his brothers.” The sugya explains the verse as Yehudah’s brothers demoting him after he began Yosef’s rescue but did not carry it through. Rav Tzadok retains that classical reading of Yehudah’s descent and adds an inward dimension: Yehudah accepts the brothers’ judgment and enters his own process of rectification because he knows that, beneath the damaged outer stature, the heart remains awake to Hashem.160Megillah 13a: “Why was Mordechai called ‘Yehudi’ though he was of the tribe of Binyamin? — because he denied idolatry; for anyone who denies idolatry is called a Yehudi, as it says, ‘there are Yehudi men — [Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego] — who do not serve your gods’ (Daniel 3:12).” R’ Tzadok links this to Yehudah, whose heart cleaves wholly to God — the “awake heart” that no descent can sever.
דְּחָשַׁב שֶׁאֶחָיו וַדַּאי כַּדִּין הוֹרִידוּהוּ, דְּהֵם הִרְגִּישׁוּ קִלְקוּל בְּנַפְשָׁם מִזֶּה, אֲבָל הַקִּלְקוּל לֹא נָגַע עֲדַיִין עַד הַלֵּב וְלֹא הִגִּיעַ לוֹ
for he thought his brothers had certainly rightly brought him down, since they felt a corruption in their soul from this — but the corruption did not yet reach the heart and did not touch it;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּל קוֹמַת הַגּוּף הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם וְהַסְתֵּר פָּנִים מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, עֲדַיִין ״לִבִּי עֵר״ וְדָבוּק בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְזֶה הָיָה הַמְשָׁכַת נֶפֶשׁ ״עֵר״ בָּעוֹלָם

and although the whole “stature of the body” is in concealment and “hiding of the face” from Hashem, still “my heart is awake” and cleaves to Hashem — and this was the drawing-down of the soul of “Er” into the world. — And so the “sleep” of exile and sin never touches the heart of Israel, whose depths remain awake and bound to God — the root, in Yehudah’s very son, of the name and the kingship that no descent can uproot.

items.h: The theme: Scripture records Er and Onan in the genealogies (Vayigash, Pinchas, I Divrei HaYamim) though they died childless. Teaching that their “name endures forever,” for the light of every soul that entered this world remains inscribed. Yehudah was occupied in rectifying these two souls, thinking the holy bris had been wholly lost among the nations, with hope only from the heart’s cleaving to God.

p: [יט] וְלֹא לְחִנָּם בְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּכְתַּב תּוֹלְדוֹתֵיהֶם הִזְכִּיר גַּם עֵר וְאוֹנָן [בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיִּגַּשׁ וּבְפָרָשַׁת פִּנְחָס וּבִדְהֵ״א ב], אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֵם כְּבָר מֵתוּ וְלֹא הֶעֱמִידוּ תּוֹלָדוֹת, וּמַאי נָפְקָא מִינַהּ בְּזִכְרוֹנָם

And not for nothing does [Scripture], wherever their genealogies are written, mention Er and Onan too [in Vayigash, in Pinchas, and in I Divrei HaYamim 2] — even though they had already died and raised no offspring; and what difference does their remembrance make?161Bereishis 46:12; Bamidbar 26:19; I Divrei HaYamim 2:3 — Er and Onan remain in Israel’s genealogical record: All three genealogical passages explicitly retain Er and Onan even while recording that they died in Canaan; I Divrei HaYamim again lists them among Yehudah’s sons before noting Er’s death. Scripture itself does not state why childless sons are repeatedly retained. Rav Tzadok reads the repetition as evidence that entry of a soul into this world leaves an enduring spiritual imprint, so that their names are not erased from the developing stature of Knesses Yisrael.

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דִּשְׁמָם נִשְׁאַר קַיָּים לָעַד, דְּעִנְיַן הַתּוֹלָדָה שֶׁמּוֹלִיד וּמֵבִיא נֶפֶשׁ כָּזוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאוֹר שֶׁל כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אַף שֶׁנִּסְתַּלְּקוּ, נִרְשַׁם הָאוֹר, וְכַיָּדוּעַ בְּהָנֵי דְּשָׁבַק חַיִּים

And perforce their name “remains forever” — for the matter of offspring, that one begets and brings such a soul into this world, and the light of all the souls that were in this world, even after they departed, “the light is inscribed,” as is known regarding “those who left life [behind].”162Resisei Layla §53:4; Machshavos Charutz §17:5 — departure does not erase the spiritual life already impressed below: Rav Tzadok elsewhere formulates the principle directly: an illumination that has appeared in this world may withdraw from open revelation, but it does not disappear; it remains hidden and “engraved in the depths of the hearts of Israel,” in the sense of “shavak chayei lechol chai,” leaving its life behind. In Machshavos Charutz he similarly explains that when a tzaddik dies, the life he generated through his service remains fixed in Israel. Se’if 19 extends this principle from the enduring influence of tzaddikim to the very fact that a soul once entered the world: its light leaves a lasting reshimah.

וְכֵן אֵלּוּ שְׁתֵּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן, שֶׁהָיָה יְהוּדָה עָסוּק בָּהֶם לְתַקֵּן קִלְקוּל הַקּוֹדֵם; אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא חָשַׁב שֶׁהַבְּרִית קֹדֶשׁ כְּבָר נִתְקַלְקֵל וְנִטְמַע בֵּין הָעַמִּים לְגַמְרֵי, וּדְאֶפְשָׁר עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ תִּקְוָה מִצַּד דְּבֵיקוּת הַלֵּב בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

And so these two souls of Er and Onan, with whom Yehudah was occupied, to rectify the earlier corruption — only that he thought the holy bris had already been corrupted and wholly assimilated among the nations, and that there might still be hope from the side of the heart’s cleaving to Hashem.

דְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן נֶגֶד שְׁנֵי מַפְתְּחוֹת הַלֵּב: ״עֵר״ הוּא נֶגֶד ״לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ״, שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ; וְהַשְּׂמֹאל הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּנוּקְבָּא, שֶׁשָּׁם הַתְחָלַת הָרַע

For Er and Onan are over-against the two “chambers of the heart”: “Er” corresponds to “the heart of the wise is to his right” (Koheles 10:2), where is the essence of the arousal to Hashem; and the left is from “the side of the Nukva,” where is the beginning of evil.163Berachos 61a; Koheles 10:2; Peri Tzadik, Shavuos §6 — the two entrances of the heart, right and left: Rav teaches that the yetzer hara sits “between the two entrances of the heart”; the same sugya associates the right with counsel toward good and the left with counsel toward evil, citing “the heart of the wise is to his right, but the heart of the fool to his left.” Rav Tzadok elsewhere makes this mapping explicit: the right chamber, “lev chacham limino,” receives the positive Divine word, while the left chamber, “lev kesil lismolo,” is the place from which evil must be emptied. Se’if 19 applies that established anatomy-symbolism to Er and Onan as the two heart-aspects.

וְעַל כֵּן הִיא קָרְאָה שְׁמוֹ מִסִּטְרָא דִּידַהּ ״אוֹנָן״ לְשׁוֹן אֲנִינוּת, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ז״ל [סַנְהֶדְרִין קט סע״ב] עַל ״אוֹן בֶּן פֶּלֶת״ דְּנִקְרָא כֵּן שֶׁיָּשַׁב כָּל יוֹם בַּאֲנִינוּת, וְהוּא הַחֲרָטָה וְהַתְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הָרַע הַקּוֹדֵם

And therefore she named him, from her side, “Onan,” a term of aninus [mourning], in the way the Sages said [Sanhedrin 109b] of “On ben Peles” — who was so called because “he sat every day in mourning” — and this is the regret and teshuvah to rectify the earlier evil.164Sanhedrin 109b: On “On ben Peles” (Bamidbar 16:1), who appears in Korach’s rebellion but then vanishes from the account — the Gemara relates that his wife saved him from Korach’s fate; the name “On” is linked to his “sitting in aninus [mourning].” R’ Tzadok uses the association of “Onan” with aninus to cast Onan’s very name as the “left-side,” mourning-and-regret aspect of teshuvah.

וּבֶאֱמֶת אִלּוּ הָיָה כֵּן [שֶׁנֶּאֱבַד יוֹסֵף לְגַמְרֵי] לֹא הָיָה תִּיקּוּן בִּמְצִיאוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אָז כְּלָל, דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״ דַּוְקָא — דַּרְגָּא דְּצַדִּיק הֵם דְּיָרְשׁוּ אֶרֶץ; וּלְפִיכָךְ גַּם הֵם [עֵר וְאוֹנָן] חָטְאוּ בַּבְּרִית

And in truth, had it been so [that Yosef was wholly lost], there would have been no rectification in reality in this world then at all — for “your people are all tzaddikim” specifically: it is the rung of tzaddik [Yesod] that “inherited the land”; and therefore they too [Er and Onan] “sinned in the bris.”
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתִּיקֵּן הַלֵּב, לֹא תִּיקֵּן עֲדַיִין הָעֵינַיִם שֶׁהוּא עִיקַּר הַהַתְחָלָה, וּלְפִיכָךְ הָיוּ ״רָעִים בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״

And even though he rectified the heart, he did not yet rectify the eyes, which are “the essential beginning”; and therefore they were “evil in the eyes of Hashem.”165Bereishis 38:7–10; Rashi to 38:7; Yevamos 34b — Er and Onan’s shared blemish of the bris: The Torah calls Er “evil in the eyes of Hashem” and describes Onan as destroying his seed to the ground. Rashi, citing the sugya in Yevamos, explains that Er committed the same act as Onan and reads “He put him to death also” as linking their deaths to the same transgression. Rav Tzadok takes this classical identification of their sin and places it within his larger structure: if the Yesod represented by Yosef were truly lost, the attempted heart-level repair alone could not yet restore the bris.

וּבְעִנְיַן תָּמָר שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי הָרְאִיָּה — ״וַיִּרְאֶהָ יְהוּדָה״ וְגוֹמֵר — הִתְחִיל לְתַקֵּן הָעֵינַיִם, וְכַיָּדוּעַ דְּהֵם נִתְגַּלְגְּלוּ וְנִתַּקְּנוּ בְּפֶרֶץ וְזֶרַח, וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בָּהּ ״וַתֵּשֶׁב בְּפֶתַח עֵינַיִם״ — הוּא הַכְּנִיסָה לְתִיקּוּן הָעֵינַיִם

And in the matter of Tamar, which was through seeing — “and Yehudah saw her [and took her for a harlot]” (Bereishis 38:15) — he began to rectify the eyes; and it is known that they [Er and Onan] were reincarnated and rectified in Peretz and Zerach; and therefore it says of her, “and she sat at the opening of the eyes [pesach einayim]” (Bereishis 38:14) — this is the entry to the rectification of the eyes.166Sha’ar HaGilgulim 36:69; Bereishis 38:14–15; Sotah 10a — Er and Onan in Peretz and Zerach, and “pesach einayim” as Rav Tzadok’s eye-tikkun: Sha’ar HaGilgulim states explicitly that Er and Onan themselves were reincarnated in Peretz and Zerach. The Torah says Tamar sat at “pesach einayim” and that Yehudah “saw her.” Sotah 10a reads pesach einayim as Avraham’s entrance, a place named Einayim, or Tamar “giving eyes” to her words. Rav Tzadok adds a further homiletical layer: since the encounter begins through seeing and culminates in the souls’ repair, pesach einayim becomes the entrance to eye-tikkun. This is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis, not the Gemara’s plain interpretation.

items.h: The theme: The completion of the rectification is in David — “of beautiful eyes and goodly to look upon.” Had the generation been worthy, this would have been the final tikkun and David would have been Mashiach (“high and lifted up [and exalted], very lofty,” higher than the Avos and Moshe). Hence he sought to have God’s Name unified upon him as upon the Avos (“why do they not say ‘God of David’?”).

p: [כ] וּגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּדָוִד, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ [ש״א טז] ״יְפֵה עֵינַיִם וְטוֹב רֹאִי״; וְאִלּוּ הָיָה הַדּוֹר רָאוּי הָיָה אָז גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה הוּא מָשִׁיחַ, דִּכְתִיב בֵּיהּ ״יָרוּם וְנִשָּׂא וְגָבֹהַּ מְאֹד״, וְדָרְשׁוּ רז״ל מֵאָבוֹת וּמִמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה

And the completion of the rectification is in David, of whom it is written [I Shmuel 16:12], “of beautiful eyes and goodly to look upon”; and had the generation been worthy, it would then have been the completion of the rectification, and that he be Mashiach, of whom it is written, “he shall be high and lifted up and very lofty” (Yeshayah 52:13), which the Sages expounded [to be higher] than the Avos and than Moshe Rabbeinu.167I Shmuel 16:12; Yeshayah 52:13; Midrash Tanchuma, Toldos §14 — David’s “beautiful eyes” and the exalted rung of Mashiach: Shmuel describes David as “admoni, with beautiful eyes and goodly appearance.” Tanchuma identifies the “great mountain” with Mashiach ben David and expounds “he shall be high and lifted up and very lofty” as a stature above the Avos, above Moshe, and above the ministering angels. Rav Tzadok joins these two strands: David’s perfected seeing is the point from which, had the generation been worthy, his kingship could have opened into the final messianic tikkun.

וּלְפִיכָךְ בִּיקֵּשׁ לְיַחֵד שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו כְּמוֹ עַל הָאָבוֹת, וְכִדְאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם] דְּאָמַר ״מִפְּנֵי מָה אֵין אוֹמְרִים אֱלֹקֵי דָּוִד״, כִּי הִכִּיר שֶׁהוּא הַמְתַקֵּן הַכֹּל, וְיִיחוּד שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עָלָיו הוּא יוֹתֵר מִכּוּלָּם

And therefore he sought to have the Name of Heaven unified upon him as upon the Avos, as it is stated [Sanhedrin 107a], that he said, “why do they not say ‘God of David’?” — for he recognized that he is the rectifier of all, and the unification of the Name of Heaven upon him is greater than [upon] them all.168Sanhedrin 107a — “Why do they not say: God of David?” and the ordeal that leads directly to the rooftop: David asks why prayer says “God of Avraham, God of Yitzchak, and God of Yaakov,” but not “God of David.” Hashem answers that the Avos were tested, whereupon David asks to be tested; the Gemara then introduces the test of ervah and immediately proceeds to “he walked upon the roof of the king’s house” and the sight of Bas Sheva. Rav Tzadok reads this narrative sequence structurally: David reached for the patriarchal unification before its appointed time. The specific symbolism of the “roof” as a place above his present rung is Rav Tzadok’s own derash.

וְזֶהוּ ״וַיִּתְהַלֵּךְ עַל גַּג בֵּית הַמֶּלֶךְ״: הַ״בַּיִת״ הוּא הַמָּקוֹם לְקוֹמַת הָאָדָם כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ, וּ״בֵית הַמֶּלֶךְ״ מְתוּקָּן לְמִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת, וְהַ״גַּג״ הוּא הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמְּקוֹם מַדְרֵגָתוֹ

And this is “and he walked upon the roof of the king’s house” (II Shmuel 11:2): the “house” is the “place” for a person’s stature according to his rung; “the king’s house” is fitted to the middah of Malchus; and the “roof” is the place above the place of his rung.

כִּי כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בַּמַּלְכוּת שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ דּוֹר, ״דְּפַרְנָס לְפִי הַדּוֹר״, הָיָה בַּקָּשַׁת דָּבָר זֶה דָּבָר שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמַּדְרֵגָתוֹ, כִּי עֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיּוּכַל לָבוֹא לִגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן בְּפֹעַל גָּלוּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

For according to his rung in this world, in the kingship of that generation (“a leader according to the generation”), the request of this thing was something above his rung — for the End had not yet come, that he could reach the completion of the rectification in revealed actuality in this world.169Arachin 17a; Likkutei Ma’amarim, on Yehoshua §10 — “a leader according to the generation” and the comprehensive soul of the parnas: The Gemara records the paired formulations “a generation according to its leader” and “a leader according to his generation.” Rav Tzadok explains that the soul of the parnas encompasses the souls of his generation, just as the king is the collective form of the nation and can therefore lead it. This gives a direct parallel to the present se’if: David’s revealed royal rung was bound to what his generation could contain, so seeking the openly realized final tikkun before the ketz meant reaching above the level then available in Malchus.

וְזֶה גָּרַם קְצָת קִלְקוּל בִּרְאִיָּה, דְּ״וַיַּרְא אִשָּׁה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״ — חָזַר הַקִּלְקוּל בָּעֵינַיִן עַל יְדֵי הָרַע דִּפְגַם הַבְּרִית, שֶׁהָיָה לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּאוֹיְבֵי ה׳ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And this caused a slight corruption in “seeing” — “and he saw a woman,” “and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem”170Cf. Shabbos 56a (“whoever says David sinned is merely erring”) and Avodah Zarah 4b–5a (“David was not fit for that deed” — it was so decreed only “to teach the power of teshuvah”) — the frame in which R’ Tzadok reads David’s “seeing” as the rectification of the eye rather than a lapse. — the corruption returned to the eyes through the evil of the blemish of the bris, which was [only] to the outward eye of “the enemies of Hashem” in this world.
