וְהוּא (דָּוִד) שֶׁיָּדַע דִּרְאוּיָה לוֹ, וְרָאָה כָּל הַשַּׁלְשֶׁלֶת שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנָּה, לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ דָּבָר רַע כְּלָל; רַק כְּשֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ שֶׁהַדָּבָר בָּא מֵהֲסָתַת הַיֵּצֶר וְגָרַם סִילּוּק שְׁכִינָה, וְהוּא יָדַע דְּ״לִבּוֹ חָלָל בְּקִרְבּוֹ״ רַק שֶׁרְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ — עַל יְדֵי זֶה הִכְנִיס שִׂמְחָה שֶׁל מִצְוָה בְּלִבּוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי עוֹשֶׂה בָּזֶה רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דִּ״לְמַעַן תִּצְדַּק״ וְגוֹמֵר, וַעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ

And he (David), who knew that she was fit for him, and saw the whole chain that would issue from her, no evil thing arose in his heart at all; only when he sensed that the matter came from the yetzer’s enticement and caused the removal of the Shechinah — and he knew that “his heart was hollow within him,” only that Hashem’s will was so — through this he introduced “the joy of a mitzvah” into his heart, for he is thereby doing Hashem’s will, “so that You be justified [when You speak],” and a “transgression for its own sake” is like a mitzvah not-for-its-own-sake.171Nazir 23b; Horayos 10b; Tzidkas HaTzadik §100 — aveirah lishmah and David’s “lemaan titzdak”: Chazal compare an aveirah lishmah with a mitzvah shelo lishmah, with Yael as the classic case; Horayos places the statement alongside Tamar, whose act produced kings and prophets. Rav Tzadok, in Tzidkas HaTzadik, explains complete teshuvah as returning the entire event to Hashem and cites David’s “lemaan titzdak” to describe a withdrawal of Divine assistance that itself belonged to the providential order. That parallel illuminates the present language of acting wholly for Heaven and finding “simchah shel mitzvah” within the ordeal. It is a retrospective theological reading of David’s unique case, not a general halachic permission to choose transgression.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה חָזַר לוֹ גַּם אָז רוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מַמָּשׁ, בִּנְבוּאַת נָתָן הַנָּבִיא לוֹ וּבִשְׁעַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
And through this the ruach hakodesh literally returned to him even then, in the prophecy of Nathan the prophet to him, and at the time of his teshuvah.

כִּי בֶּאֱמֶת מִצִּידּוֹ הָיָה מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה גַּם בִּשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה וְלֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל, וּלְפִיכָךְ הוּא לֹא הִתְעוֹרֵר לִתְשׁוּבָה כְּלָל עַל זֶה מֵעַצְמוֹ, כִּי לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁיַּחְשׁוֹב לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עָוֹן בְּדָבָר זֶה, שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ כָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם

For in truth, from his side he was “full of holiness” even at the time of the act, and there was no sin at all; therefore he was not aroused to teshuvah at all of himself over this, for it did not enter his heart that Hashem would reckon it an iniquity, since he knew his whole intent was for the sake of Heaven —

עַד שֶׁהוּצְרַךְ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִשְׁלֹחַ אֵלָיו נָתָן הַנָּבִיא לְהַגְדִּיל הֶעָוֹן וְשֶׁהוּא צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה, שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה כָּל הַכַּוָּונָה: לִיתֵּן פִּתְחוֹן פֶּה לַשָּׁבִים וּלְהָקִים עוֹלָהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בע״ז ה רע״א] עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת ד״ה ״וּצְרִיכָא״, פֵּירוּשׁ לִכְתּוֹב חֶטְאָם וְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתָם

until Hashem had to send him Nathan the prophet, to “magnify the iniquity” and [teach] that he needs teshuvah — for this was the whole intent: to give an “opening of the mouth” to penitents and to raise the yoke of teshuvah, as they said [Avodah Zarah 5a] — see there in Tosafos, s.v. “u-tzricha” — meaning, to write their sin and the acceptance of their teshuvah.172Peri Tzadik, Va’eschanan §2 — Nathan’s “atah ha-ish,” the hollow heart, and the creation of a new heart: Rav Tzadok elsewhere describes Nathan’s rebuke as the moment David grasped the terrible distance opened by the episode despite all his prior labor, “until his heart was hollow within him,” which Chazal associate with having subdued the yetzer. Precisely from that paradox came David’s cry, “Create for me a pure heart, O God,” a plea for a new creation that Divine mercy granted. This is a close parallel to Se’if 20’s movement from David’s certainty that his intent was for Heaven to the prophetic rebuke that compelled the full form of teshuvah.173Avodah Zarah 5a (and Tosafos s.v. “u-tzricha”): the Gemara teaches that “David was not fit for that deed — [it was so decreed] only in order to teach the power of teshuvah — that if an individual sins, he is told, ‘go to David [as a model]’; and if a community sins, they are told, ‘go to the generation of the wilderness.’” Tosafos explains why both cases are “necessary.” R’ Tzadok: the whole point was to have “written” both the sin and the accepted teshuvah, as an open gateway for all penitents.

וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא הוֹעִיל בְּבַקָּשָׁתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִכְתּוֹב סוּרְחָנוֹ, כִּי בַּכָּתוּב נֶאֱמַר שֶׁחָטָא, וְשֶׁהוּא הוֹדָה וְאָמַר ״חָטָאתִי לַה׳״, רַק שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הִזְכִּיר חַטָּאתוֹ עַל יְדֵי [מַעֲשֵׂה] יָדָיו וּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ

And therefore his request that his misdeed not be written did not avail — for in Scripture it says that he sinned, and that he confessed and said “I have sinned to Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:13) — only that Hashem “mentioned his sin” together with [the deed of] his hands and his teshuvah.

items.h: The theme: The Sages revealed it: “whoever says David sinned is merely erring” (Shabbos 56a) — phrased so, to say it is unthinkable that such a man sinned; only one “confused in mind” could say it. David effected this by his prayer “that the Rabbis not speak of it” — that they not magnify the sin to teach teshuvah. “Let them not rule over me [al yimshelu bi]” — Rashi reads mashal: “let them not expound [my sin].”

p: [כא] ורז״ל גִּילּוּ הַדָּבָר שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שַׁבָּת נו.] דְּהָאוֹמֵר ״דָּוִד חָטָא״ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה; וְאָמְרוּ בְּלָשׁוֹן זֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין לְהַעֲלוֹתוֹ עַל הַדַּעַת כְּלָל שֶׁאִישׁ כְּמוֹתוֹ יֶחֱטָא, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיֹּאמַר כֵּן אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁהוּא טוֹעֶה וּמְשׁוּבָּשׁ בְּדַעְתּוֹ

And the Sages revealed the matter, saying [Shabbos 56a] that “whoever says David sinned is merely erring”; and they said it in this language to convey that it is a thing that cannot be entertained at all — that a man like him should sin — and it is impossible to say so except one who is “erring and confused in his mind.”174Shabbos 56a: “Rabbi Shmuel bar Nachmani said in the name of Rabbi Yonatan: whoever says David sinned is merely erring [eino ela to’eh] — for it is impossible that sin came to his hand,” the Gemara reinterpreting the affair of Bathsheba in David’s favor (Uriah had given her a conditional divorce, etc.). R’ Tzadok reads this as the Oral Torah’s revelation of the inner truth — that David did not, in essence, sin — over against the Written account that “reckons it as if he sinned” to teach teshuvah.
וְדָבָר זֶה פָּעַל בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ, ״דְּלָא לִשְׁתָּעֵי בֵּיהּ רַבָּנָן״ — שֶׁלֹּא יִרְצוּ אַדְּרַבָּא לְהַגְדִּיל הַחֵטְא כְּדֵי לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה אֲפִילּוּ לְחֵטְא גָּדוֹל
And this thing he effected by his prayer, “that the Rabbis not speak of it” — that they not wish, on the contrary, to magnify the sin, in order to teach teshuvah even for a great sin.
וְזֶהוּ ״אַל יִמְשְׁלוּ בִי״, דְּפֵירַשׁ״י שָׁם לְשׁוֹן ״מָשָׁל״, אַל יִדְרְשׁוּ [בְּחַטָּאתִי חַכְמֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת]; וְלֹא פֵּירֵשׁ לָמָּה קָרֵי לִדְרָשָׁתָם בִּלְשׁוֹן ״מָשָׁל״

And this is “let them not rule over me [al yimshelu bi]” (Tehillim 19:14), which Rashi there interprets as a term of “mashal [parable]”: “let them not expound [my sin, the sages of the generations]”; and he did not explain why he calls their expounding by a term of “mashal.175Sanhedrin 107a; Rashi ad loc. — “al yimshelu bi” as “do not make me a mashal”: The Gemara reads David’s request as “that the Rabbis not speak of me.” Rashi makes the wordplay explicit: “al yimshelu” is from mashal — “let the sages of the generations not expound my sin.” Rav Tzadok makes this the se’if’s key: David wants the paradigm to be the efficacy of teshuvah, not an enlarged portrayal of the aveirah.”

אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁעִיקַּר הַכַּוָּונָה בְּחֶטְאוֹ וּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מָשָׁל וְדֻגְמָא לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁיִּלְמְדוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה, עַל זֶה אָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יִמְשְׁלוּ בּוֹ בְּעִנְיַן הַחֵטְא, רַק בְּעִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד, וּדְהַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת, שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר אַחַר כָּךְ דְּלָא חָטָא, וְהָאוֹמֵר כו׳ טוֹעֶה

But because the essential intent in his sin and teshuvah was that it be “a mashal and example” for others, that they learn from him to do teshuvah — on this he said, that they not “use him as a mashal” in the matter of the sin, only in the matter of the teshuvah alone; and that the teshuvah avails, so that it be clarified afterward that he did not sin, and “whoever says [he sinned] is erring.”176Shabbos 30a; Sanhedrin 107b — David’s public vindication at the gates of the Mikdash: When Shlomo could not bring the Aron into the Kodesh HaKodashim, the gates opened only after he invoked “the kindnesses of David Your servant.” Chazal say David’s enemies were shamed and all Israel knew Hashem had forgiven him. Thus the episode remains in Scripture while David is publicly vindicated. Chazal here speak of forgiveness; Rav Tzadok’s stronger inner reading rests on Shabbos 56a and the Oral-Torah layer developed here.

אֲבָל זֶהוּ בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, שֶׁהוּא גִּילּוּי הַמִּסְתּוֹרִין; אֲבָל בַּכָּתוּב בַּנְּבִיאִים נֶאֱמַר שֶׁחָטָא, דְּמַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב כְּאִלּוּ חָטָא. וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהוּא כְּאִלּוּ חָטָא, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַכָּתוּב קְרָאוֹ ״חוֹטֵא״, הוּא צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה, וְיָלְפִינַן הוֹרָאַת תְּשׁוּבָה

But this is in the Oral Torah, which is the revelation of the mysteries;177Resisei Layla §51 — Torah Shebe’al Peh as the Divine “mistorin” that cannot be written: Rav Tzadok explains that what is “written and laid before all” is openly accessible, whereas Torah Shebe’al Peh is Hashem’s “mistorin,” what is in the Divine thought and “cannot be revealed in writing at all,” disclosed through the sages of Israel by their deveikus. This directly parallels the se’if’s distinction between the prophetic record and the hidden inner meaning disclosed by Chazal. whereas in the Written [Torah], in the Prophets, it says that he sinned — for “Scripture reckons it upon him as if he sinned.178Sanhedrin 107a; Yad Ramah — “that my fault not be written” is a distinct request: In the Bavli’s printed sequence, after David asks that the Rabbis not discuss his episode, he separately asks that his disgrace not be written; Hashem refuses and invokes the yud removed from Sarai. Yad Ramah explains that the episode had already “arisen in thought to be written and cannot be uprooted.” His alignment of the Psalm’s phrases differs from Rashi’s, but the distinction between rabbinic exposition and the fixed Scriptural record remains.” And since it is “as if he sinned” — for Scripture called him a “sinner” — he requires teshuvah, and we learn from it “the teaching of teshuvah.179Takanas HaShavin 10:11 — Moshe/Torah Shebiksav and David/Torah Shebe’al Peh: Earlier in this siman Rav Tzadok contrasts Moshe, root of Torah Shebiksav, day and sun — who asked that his failing be written — with David, “Malchus peh, Torah Shebe’al Peh,” night and moon, who asked that his failing not be written. If David’s parashah were mere disgrace, he argues, Hashem’s comparison to Sarai’s removed yud would be inverted; its inclusion must contain hidden praise and tikkun. Se’if 21 develops that distinction.”

וְהַכַּוָּונָה: דְּוַדַּאי אִם הָיָה בָּזֶה תּוֹעֶלֶת לְהָשִׁיב רַבִּים מֵעָוֹן עַל יְדֵי זֶה, וַדַּאי גַּם הוּא עַצְמוֹ הָיָה מַסְכִּים לָזֶה, וְהָיָה מְוַתֵּר כְּבוֹדוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם וְתִיקּוּן הָרַבִּים; אֲבָל תְּפִלָּתוֹ הָיָה שֶׁלְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה [יִהְיֶה הַלִּימּוּד]

And the intent: certainly, had there been benefit in turning many from iniquity through it, certainly he too would have consented, and would have forgone his honor for the honor of Heaven and the rectification of the many; but his prayer was that [the learning] be for the arousal of teshuvah [alone].

items.h: The theme: This is the perfect arousal of teshuvah at its highest rung. And the essential root of David, who is himself the soul of Mashiach: the root of rectifying the evil of [human] birth, nullifying the yetzer and “the counsel of the serpent,” and guarding the bris. As the Tikkunei Zohar says: “do not await the footstep of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in shining colors, or until the ‘sign’ [of the bris] is revealed.”

p: [כב] וְזֶהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ; וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר שֹׁרֶשׁ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁהוּא עַצְמוֹ נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ — הוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתִּיקּוּן דְּרַע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה, וּבִיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר וְעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, שַׁבְּתָאוּת, וּשְׁמִירַת הַבְּרִית

And this is the perfection of the arousal of teshuvah, and that it be at this rung; and this is the essential root of David HaMelech, who is himself the soul of Mashiach180Peri Tzadik, Pinchas §8 — Adam, David, and Mashiach as one soul-chain: Rav Tzadok writes that before David appeared, Adam HaRishon was “the soul of David,” citing the remez ADaM = Adam-David-Mashiach. David is the fourth leg of the Merkavah, corresponding to Malchus. This directly parallels the se’if’s identification of David as the soul-root of Mashiach and bearer of the final tikkun. — the root of rectifying the evil in [human] birth, and the nullification of the inclination and “the counsel of the serpent,” “Sabbateanism [shabtaus],” and the guarding of the bris.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתִיקּוּנֵי זֹהַר תִּיקּוּן לז] ״לָא תְּצַפֵּי לְרַגְלָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא עַד דְּתֶחֱזֵי קֶשֶׁת בִּגְוָונִין נְהִירִין, אוֹ עַד דְּאִתְגַּלְיָא אוֹת בְּעָלְמָא — מַאי אוֹת? — אוֹת בְּרִית״

And as they said [in Tikkunei Zohar, tikkun 37], “do not await the footstep of Mashiach until you see a rainbow in shining colors, or until the ‘sign’ is revealed in the world — what ‘sign’? — the sign of the bris.”181Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 37: “Do not expect the footstep of Mashiach until you see a rainbow [keshes] in shining colors [illumining the world], or until the sign [os] is revealed in the world — what is the ‘sign’? — the sign of the bris.” The rainbow (whose usual appearance signals a generation deserving of the Flood but protected by God’s oath) will then shine in radiant colors, and the guarded bris be manifest — the marks of the Redemption R’ Tzadok binds to David’s rectification.
וְיָדוּעַ הַקֶּשֶׁת הוּא גַּם כֵּן סִימַן תִּיקּוּן הַבְּרִית, שֶׁבָּזֶה הוּא הַהֲגָנָה מֵעֹנֶשׁ חֵטְא דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל

And it is known that the rainbow [keshes] is also a sign of the rectification of the bris, whereby is the protection from the punishment of the sin of the generation of the Flood.182Bereishis 9:12–17 — the rainbow is explicitly the “sign of the covenant”: After the Flood, Hashem calls the rainbow “os ha-bris” and says that on seeing it He will remember the everlasting covenant so that the waters will never again destroy all flesh by flood. This is the Scriptural basis for Rav Tzadok’s keshes as covenantal protection from the Flood-generation’s punishment.
רַק הַחִילּוּק, דְּקֶשֶׁת הוּא סִימָן שֶׁצְּרִיכִין הֲגָנָה מִצַּד הַבְטָחַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְלוּלֵי רֹב רַחֲמָיו הָיוּ חַיָּיבִים

Only the difference: that the rainbow is a sign that they require protection from the side of Hashem’s promise, and but for His abundant mercy they would be liable.183Zohar, Pinchas 9:35 — the rainbow protects when the generation lacks a protecting tzaddik: The Zohar says, “the rainbow comes to protect the world.” When a tzaddik is present, “he is the covenant” and protects; when no such tzaddik is present, the rainbow appears because the world stands in danger but is sustained by the covenantal sign. This directly supports Rav Tzadok’s distinction between revealed bris and rainbow-protection through mercy.
וְזֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [סַנְהֶדְרִין צח.] ״אֵין בֶּן דָּוִד בָּא אֶלָּא בְּדוֹר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ [זַכַּאי] כו׳ שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ חַיָּיב כו׳, לְמַעֲנִי אֶעֱשֶׂה״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And this is in the manner it is stated [Sanhedrin 98a], “the son of David comes only in a generation that is wholly [worthy] or wholly liable — ‘for My own sake I will do it’” — see there.184Sanhedrin 98a: “R’ Yochanan said: the son of David comes only in a generation that is wholly worthy or wholly liable — ‘wholly worthy,’ as it says, ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever’; ‘wholly liable,’ as it says, ‘and He saw that there was no man, and was astonished that there was none to intercede; therefore His own arm brought salvation’” — and “for My own sake, for My own sake, I will do it” (Yeshayah 48:11). R’ Tzadok reads the two conditions as the “rainbow in shining colors” (redemption “for His sake,” protecting even the liable) and the revealed “sign of the bris” (the wholly-worthy generation) — both included in David.

וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מֵאִיר וּמַרְאֶה לְעֵין כֹּל אֵיךְ הַכֹּל ״מִמֶּנּוּ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים״, וְשֶׁאֵין חֵטְא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל; וְזֶהוּ הַקֶּשֶׁת בְּגַוְונֵי נְהִירִין, הַיְינוּ הַהֶאָרָה גְּמוּרָה בַּהֲגָנַת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעֲנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ; אוֹ בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹת הַבְּרִית בָּעוֹלָם בְּפֹעַל, וְהַיְינוּ בְּדוֹר שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ זַכַּאי

And Hashem illumines and shows to every eye how “all issued from Me [as] suppressed [holy ones],”185Makkos 23b — “ממני יצאו כבושים” at Yehudah and Tamar: When Yehudah declared “tzadkah mimeni,” a bas kol confirmed, “Mimeni yatzu kevushim” — these hidden matters came from Me. This occurs at the union from which Peretz and Malchus Beis David descend. Rav Tzadok’s phrase therefore points back to David’s own root: after teshuvah, hidden Divine direction can be revealed within what appeared outwardly as failure. and that there is no sin in Israel186R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §49): “[Yael’s rescue] falls only into the hand of the seed of Yosef, who corresponds to the holy ‘sign of the covenant’ [os bris kodesh], and who is the guardian of the covenant — against whom there is no claim even to the outward eye. And it is known that the twelve months correspond to the twelve tribes, and Adar to Yosef — hence there are two Adars, as Yosef was divided in two — and in this month is the power of ‘be fruitful and multiply.’” The se’if’s David is “the guardian of the bris,” soul of Mashiach — the rainbow and the revealed “sign” both marking the covenant’s rectification. at all — and this is “the rainbow in shining colors,” namely the complete illumination in the protection of Israel “for His own sake”; or in the revelation of “the sign of the bris” in the world in actuality — namely, in “a generation that is wholly worthy.”187Kesubos 77b — in the days of a complete tzaddik, no rainbow was needed: Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai asked Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi whether a rainbow had appeared in his days. The Gemara concludes that none had appeared; his merit protected the generation, though he declined to credit himself. This concretizes the se’if’s contrast: a rainbow marks needed covenantal protection, while complete righteousness can itself stand as the protecting bris.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה כּוֹלֵל שְׁנֵיהֶם: דְּמִצַּד עַצְמוּתוֹ כּוּלּוֹ זַכַּאי, וּמִצַּד מַרְאִית הָעַיִן אֵצֶל אוֹיְבָיו הוּא לְהֵפֶךְ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״רַע לוֹ״ [שֶׁהוּא שֹׁרֶשׁ הָרַע חַס וְשָׁלוֹם], ״מָתַי יָמוּת וְאָבַד שְׁמוֹ״ וְגוֹמֵר

And David HaMelech includes both: from the side of his essence, “wholly worthy”; and from the side of the outward eye, by his enemies, the reverse — who said “evil to him” [that he is the root of evil, God forbid], “when will he die and his name perish” (Tehillim 41:6).
וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא [נט רע״א] דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, מִיתָתוֹ בַּמֶּה״

And in Bava Metzia [59a], where they said to him, “one who beds a married woman — by what [death] does he die?”188Bava Metzia 59a: among the torments David describes, “even at the time when they are engaged in [the laws of] the four court-imposed death penalties, they interrupt their study and say to me, ‘David, one who beds a married woman — by what [death] does he die?’” — publicly needling him over the Bathsheba affair. R’ Tzadok cites it as the “outward eye” of David’s enemies, who cast the very root of rectification as the emblem of sin. — With this the section reaches David’s paradox: the very one who is the root of the rectification and the soul of Mashiach is, to the world’s outward eye, made the emblem of the sin he came to heal.

items.h: The theme: David’s taunters raise “nega’im and ohalos” — which (Pesachim 50a) are “precious light [or yekaros], congealed for the World to Come.” Why these two? Because the Sages taught that God created two root inclinations — idolatry and licentiousness. And nega’im alludes to idolatry (the “filth of idolatry,” the utter denial of God, than which nothing is lower), while ohalos (corpse-impurity) alludes to desire, through which death and the body’s impurity came.

p: [כג] וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בִּנְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת, הַכַּוָּונָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּפְסָחִים נ רע״א] ״אוֹר יְקָרוֹת וְקִפָּאוֹן — אֵלּוּ נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת״, שֶׁ״יְּקָרִים״ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּ״קְפוּאִים״ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And what he said, “when they are engaged in nega’im and ohalos” — the intent is as they said [Pesachim 50a], “‘precious light [or yekaros] and congelation [kippaon]’ (Zechariah 14:6) — these are nega’im and ohalos,” which are “precious [yekarim]” in this world and “congealed [stored]” for the World to Come.189Pesachim 50a: On “and it shall be on that day, there shall not be light, but precious things [yekaros] shall congeal [vekippaon]” (Zechariah 14:6) — “R’ Elazar said: this refers to the [teachings] that are ‘precious’ [i.e., rare and difficult] in this world but ‘ready/stored’ in the World to Come — these are nega’im and ohalos.” R’ Tzadok takes these two, the hardest and most “precious” areas of Torah, as corresponding to the two root inclinations — idolatry (nega’im) and desire/death (ohalos) — whose conquest is the whole “precious” labor of this world.

וְהָעִנְיָן דְּקָרֵי לְהוּ ״אוֹר יָקָר״, אֲבָל כְּבָר אָמְרוּ [בשהש״ר] עַל פָּסוּק ״זֹאת קוֹמָתֵךְ״, שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים בָּרָא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּעוֹלָמוֹ: יֵצֶר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְיֵצֶר זְנוּת, וְכֵן נִזְכָּר שְׁנֵי יְצָרִים אֵלּוּ [בְּיוֹמָא סט:]

And the matter, that it calls them “precious light.” But they already said [in Shir HaShirim Rabbah] on the verse “this is your stature” (Shir HaShirim 7:8) that the Holy One created two [root] inclinations in His world: the inclination of idolatry and the inclination of licentiousness — and so these two inclinations are mentioned [Yoma 69b].190Yoma 69b — the two root inclinations and their unequal abolition: The Men of the Great Assembly first prayed against the yetzer of idolatry; it was delivered into their hands and sealed away. They then prayed against the yetzer of sexual transgression, but were warned that destroying it would end procreation, so they only diminished its force. This is the precise Talmudic structure behind Rav Tzadok’s pairing here: idolatry and licentious desire are the two root drives, but only the first could be wholly removed within history.

וּנְגָעִים רוֹמֵז לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה סו״פ יז] ״כְּנֶגַע נִרְאָה לִי בַּבָּיִת — זֶה טִינּוֹפֶת עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה״, שֶׁעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הִיא תַּכְלִית הָרַע שֶׁבְּכֹחַ הַיֵּצֶר, לְהָבִיא אֶת הָאָדָם ״הַיּוֹם עֲשֵׂה כָּךְ וּלְמָחָר״ [אוֹמֵר לוֹ] עַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר לוֹ ״לֵךְ עֲבוֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה״ (שַׁבָּת קה:), שֶׁזֶּהוּ סוֹף הַכְּפִירָה בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְגַמְרֵי

And nega’im alludes to idolatry, as they said [Vayikra Rabbah, end of ch. 17]191Vayikra Rabbah 17: On “and I shall put a plague of tzara’as in a house” and “like a plague it appeared to me in the house” (Vayikra 14:34–35) — the “house” is expounded as “the filth of idolatry.” So the nega’im correspond to the inclination of idolatry — the root R’ Tzadok assigns to them here (the Sages there list idolatry first among the sins for which nega’im come)., “‘like a plague it appeared to me in the house’ (Vayikra 14:35) — this is the filth of idolatry” — for idolatry is the ultimate of evil in the power of the inclination, to bring a person “today do this, and tomorrow [it says] do this,” until it says to him, “go serve idols” (Shabbos 105b)192Shabbos 105b: “Such is the craft of the evil inclination: today it says to a person ‘do this,’ and tomorrow it says to him ‘do that,’ until it says to him ‘go and serve idols,’ and he goes and serves.” This is the se’if’s picture of the yetzer’s incremental descent, culminating in idolatry — “the utter denial of God.” — which is the final, utter denial of Hashem, than which there is nothing lower in evil.
וְאֹהָלוֹת הוּא כְּטוּמְאַת מֵת שֶׁבָּא עַל יְדֵי יֵצֶר דְּתַאֲוָה, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִגְזַר הַמִּיתָה, וְעִיקַּר הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבְּגוּף הַמֵּת הוּא מִצַּד הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁבַּגּוּף שֶׁבּוֹ הַטּוּמְאָה

And ohalos [tent-impurity] is like the impurity of a corpse, which comes through the inclination of desire — for through it death was decreed, and the essence of the impurity in a corpse is from the side of the bodily desire, in which the impurity resides.
וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה ״אֹהָלִים״, וּמַעֲלִים אֶת הָאָדָם מִטּוּמְאָה לְטָהֳרָה וּמִכַּף חוֹבָה לְכַף זְכוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת טז רע״א]

And therefore words of Torah too are called “ohalim [tents],” and they raise a person from impurity to purity193R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §3): “[If this repulsive one meets you, drag it to the beis midrash — if it is a stone it will dissolve]: if [one can dismiss] the idle matters from his heart, good; and if not, let him occupy himself with Torah, which is a ‘seasoning’ [tavlin] to the yetzer — as the Rambam wrote at the end of Hilchos Issurei Biah, that lewd thoughts prevail only in ‘a heart empty of words of Torah,’ for when the heart is immersed in thoughts of Torah, no other thought can enter it at all.” The se’if’s teaching precisely: Torah is the tavlin that raises a person from impurity, the study of nega’im and ohalos being “precious light” for that very labor. and from the scale of guilt to the scale of merit, as they said [Berachos 16a].
וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [קִידּוּשִׁין ל:] ״אִם פָּגַע בְּךָ מְנוּוָּל זֶה — מָשְׁכֵהוּ לְבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ״, וּ״מְנוּוָּל״ הַיְינוּ יִצְרָא דַּעֲבֵירָה

And this is as they said [Kiddushin 30b], “if this vile one [menuval] meets you, drag him to the study hall” — and “vile” means the inclination of transgression.194Kiddushin 30b: “The Holy One said to Israel: My children, I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its antidote; if you occupy yourselves with Torah you will not be handed into its power; and, [as the Sages taught,] if this vile one [the yetzer] meets you, drag him to the study hall — if he is stone he will dissolve, if iron he will shatter.” R’ Tzadok identifies the “vile one” as the inclination of transgression, subdued by the “tent” of Torah.

וְעִיקַּר הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין הוּא לְיֵצֶר הָרָע זֶה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם [סוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִיאָה] דְּאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת מְצוּיוֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And the essence of the Torah is a “seasoning [tavlin]” for this inclination, as the Rambam wrote [end of Hilchos Issurei Biah] that “the desires are found only in a heart empty of words of Torah” — see there.195Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 22:21: “Greater than all [counsels]: let him turn himself and his thought to words of Torah and broaden his mind in wisdom — for a thought of immorality gathers strength only in a heart empty of wisdom.” R’ Tzadok makes this the practical face of “Torah as the antidote [tavlin] to the yetzer.”

וְעַל כֵּן דָּרְשׁוּ [בְּרָכוֹת סג:] מֵ״אָדָם כִּי יָמוּת בְּאֹהֶל״ — לְהָמִית עַצְמוֹ עַל דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה, כִּי זֶהוּ זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, נֶגֶד הַמִּיתָה בְּאֹהֶל שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי הַתַּאֲווֹת, וּבִיטּוּלָן עַל יְדֵי הַ״מִּיתָה בְּאֹהֶל״ עַל יְדֵי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה

And therefore they expounded [Berachos 63b] from “a man, when he dies in a tent [ohel]” (Bamidbar 19:14) — that one should “put himself to death over words of Torah” — for this is “this-against-that,” over-against the “death in a tent” that is through the desires, and their nullification by the “death in a tent” of words of Torah.

אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת אַדְּרַבָּא הִיא הַנּוֹתֶנֶת לוֹ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת י.], וְגַם חַיֵּי שָׁעָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם ל רע״ב] בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא [פו.] בְּרַבָּה בַּר נַחְמָנִי

But in truth, on the contrary, it [Torah] gives him eternal life, as they said [Shabbos 10a], and also temporal life, as they said [Shabbos 30b] regarding David, and in Bava Metzia [86a] regarding Rabbah bar Nachmani [whom the Angel of Death could not take while he was engaged in Torah].196Shabbos 30b; Bava Metzia 86a — Torah study itself holds the Angel of Death at bay: David studied continuously on the Shabbos of his death, and the Angel of Death could not overcome him until his learning was interrupted. Rabbah bar Nachmani is described in almost identical terms: the Angel of Death could not approach because his mouth did not cease from Torah — immediately after the Gemara identifies him as uniquely expert in nega’im and ohalos. Rav Tzadok therefore reads these narratives literally into the “life” generated by Torah.

וְיֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בב״ב טז.], וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמַּצִּיל מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע כֵּן מַצִּיל מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, וְכִבְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה שֶׁהָיוּ ״חֵירוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע״ וּמִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת

And the evil inclination is the Angel of Death, as they said [Bava Basra 16a];197Bava Basra 16a — Satan, the yetzer hara, and the Angel of Death are one: Reish Lakish states explicitly: “He is Satan, he is the evil inclination, he is the Angel of Death.” The same sugya adds that although Hashem created the yetzer, He created Torah as its antidote. This supplies the conceptual hinge of the se’if: Torah’s victory over the yetzer and its victory over death are not two unrelated effects, because Chazal identify the two adversaries as one power. and just as [Torah] saves from the evil inclination, so it saves from the Angel of Death — as at the Giving of the Torah, when they were “free of the evil inclination” and of the Angel of Death.198Shemos Rabbah 41:7; Vayikra Rabbah 18:3; Yisrael Kedoshim §8 — “charus” as freedom from death: Chazal read “charus al haluchos” as “cheirus,” freedom — including freedom from the Angel of Death. Rav Tzadok elsewhere describes the unrealized completeness of the Exodus/Sinai redemption as freedom from the yetzer hara, subjection to kingdoms, and the Angel of Death together. The Sinai comparison here is therefore exact: Torah at its full revelation attacks both the inward enslaver, the yetzer, and its outward terminus, death.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר רַבָּה בַּר נַחְמָנִי [שָׁם בב״מ] ״אֲנִי יָחִיד בִּנְגָעִים, אֲנִי יָחִיד בְּאֹהָלוֹת״, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הַתּוֹרָה הַמַּצֶּלֶת בִּשְׁנֵי יְצָרִים אֵלּוּ

And this is what Rabbah bar Nachmani said [there in Bava Metzia], “I am unique in nega’im, I am unique in ohalos” — which is the power of the Torah that saves in [the matter of] these two inclinations.

[וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּבִיטְּלוּ אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, יָדוּעַ דְּיִצְרָא דְּכַעַס עוֹמֵד בִּמְקוֹמוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּשַׁבָּת קה: ״הַמְקָרֵעַ כְּסוּתוֹ בַּחֲמָתוֹ כו׳ כְּעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה״, וְכֵן עִיקַּר הַמְּצֹרָע עַל כַּעַס וַעֲנָפָיו כַּיָּדוּעַ]

[And although the Men of the Great Assembly abolished the inclination of idolatry, it is known that the inclination of anger stands in its place, as they said in Shabbos 105b, “one who tears his garment in his anger [or scatters his money in his anger] is like one who serves idols”; and so the essence of the metzora is over anger and its branches, as is known.]

וּבַחֲגִיגָה [יד.] וְסַנְהֶדְרִין [סז סע״ב] דְּאָמַר לוֹ לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא ״כְּלָךְ אֵצֶל נְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת״ — גַּם כֵּן לְכַוָּונָה זוֹ; כְּמוֹ שֶׁקִּיבַּלְתִּי כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ נִשְׁמַת רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא [שֶׁהָיָה יְסוֹד תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה] הוּא מִדִּיבּוּר ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״, שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל מִינֵי בֵּירוּרִים וְהַפְרָדָה לְסִטְרָא דְּרַע

And in Chagigah [14a] and Sanhedrin [67b], where they said to R’ Akiva, “turn to [the study of] nega’im and ohalos” — [that] too [is] for this intent; as I have received, that the root of R’ Akiva’s soul [who was the foundation of the Oral Torah] is from the utterance “you shall have no [other gods]” — which includes all kinds of “clarifications” and the separation [of holiness] from the side of evil.199Mei HaShiloach, Bo §5 — the Izhbitz source for R’ Akiva and “לא יהיה לך”: Rav Tzadok’s teacher explicitly teaches that Moshe corresponds to “Anochi,” while R’ Akiva corresponds to “Lo yihyeh lecha.” R’ Akiva’s task is to cleanse the heart of evil and impurity, and his halachic fences — issur/heter, pasul/kasher, tamei/tahor — are all acts of separating evil from good. This closely explains Rav Tzadok’s phrase “as I received” and why nega’im and ohalos are especially identified with R’ Akiva’s soul-root.200Chagigah 14a (and Sanhedrin 67b): in a rebuke over esoteric speculation, R’ Yochanan ben Zakkai (or the Sages) said to R’ Elazar ben Arach — and elsewhere the phrase “turn [klach] to [the study of] nega’im and ohalos” is directed at a scholar, urging him from lofty mysteries to the demanding “precious” areas of law. R’ Tzadok links R’ Akiva — foundation of the Oral Torah, whose soul-root he receives as the second commandment (“you shall have no other gods”) — to the “clarifications” that separate holiness from evil.

items.h: The theme: The study of nega’im and ohalos is “precious light” in this world, for a person’s whole labor here is conquering the yetzer (which “appears to the righteous like a mountain”) — a great and precious attainment. In Olam Haba, with no yetzer, it is “nothing,” yielding no such light (as for the angels). Mashiach is the ultimate completion of conquering the yetzer — “he asked life of You, You gave it him” — so that death too is swallowed, “for this depends on that,” the yetzer being the Angel of Death.

p: [כד] וְזֶהוּ הַלִּימּוּד דִּנְגָעִים וְאֹהָלוֹת שֶׁהוּא ״אוֹר יְקָרוֹת״ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּכָל הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּנִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר, דְּ[לַ]צַּדִּיקִים דּוֹמֶה לְהַר, וּכְשֶׁזָּכוּ לְנַצְּחוֹ הוּא דָּבָר גָּדוֹל וְיָקָר, וּמַשִּׂיגִים מִזֶּה אוֹר גָּדוֹל

And this is the study of nega’im and ohalos, which is “precious light” in this world — for all a person’s labor in this world is in conquering the inclination, [which] “to the righteous appears like a mountain”; and when they merit to conquer it, it is a great and precious thing, and they attain from it a great light.201Sukkah 52a — the yetzer as a mountain and its final slaughter: R’ Yehudah teaches that in the future Hashem will bring the evil inclination and slaughter it before the righteous and the wicked. To the righteous it appears as a high mountain, and they weep: “How were we able to conquer so high a mountain?” This is the exact source for Rav Tzadok’s phrase here. Rav Tzadok adds the interpretive step: precisely because overcoming the yetzer is such a formidable achievement in this world, its conquest yields the “precious light” that will no longer arise once that struggle has ended.
וּבָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּלֹא יִהְיֶה יֵצֶר הָרָע, אֵינוֹ כְּלוּם, וְאֵין מוּשָּׂג שׁוּם אוֹר מִזֶּה, כְּמוֹ לַמַּלְאָכִים
And in Olam Haba, where there will be no evil inclination, it is nothing, and no light is attained from it — as [is the case] for the angels.

וְהַמָּשִׁיחַ הוּא תַּכְלִית הַשְׁלָמַת נִיצּוּחַ הַיֵּצֶר, עַד דְּ״חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּ לּוֹ״, שֶׁיְּבוּלַּע גַּם כֵּן הַמָּוֶת, עַל יְדֵי דְּהָא בְּהָא תַּלְיָא, וְהוּא יֵצֶר הָרָע הוּא מַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת

And Mashiach is the ultimate completion of the conquest of the inclination, until “he asked life of You, You gave it him” (Tehillim 21:5) — that death too be swallowed up, since “this depends on that,” and the evil inclination is [itself] the Angel of Death.202Sukkah 52a; Yeshayah 25:8 — Mashiach ben David asks for life and death is swallowed: In the same sugya, Mashiach ben David asks the Holy One for only one gift — life — and is answered that David had already prophesied of him, “He asked life of You; You gave it to him” (Tehillim 21:5). Yeshayah promises, “He will swallow death forever.” These sources directly ground Rav Tzadok’s eschatological sequence: the final victory over the yetzer culminates in Mashiach’s enduring life and the disappearance of death.

וְדָוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ וּמִצַּד עַצְמוּתָם — ״עַמֵּךְ כּוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, דְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא; וַאֲפִילּוּ הַבָּא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּמִיתָתוֹ בְּחֶנֶק יֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּנִקְרָא צַדִּיק

And David, king of Israel, in his essence and from the side of their essence — “your people are all tzaddikim [they shall inherit the land forever],” for “all Israel have a share in Olam Haba”203Cf. Sanhedrin 90a: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says, ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever’ (Yeshayah 60:21)” — the basis for R’ Tzadok’s point that Israel’s sins do not touch their essential righteousness (the thorns around the rose).; and even one who beds a married woman, whose death is by strangulation, has a share in Olam Haba — and perforce he is called a “tzaddik,”204Bava Metzia 59a — strangulation, yet still a share in Olam Haba: David reports that even while the Sages studied nega’im and ohalos they taunted him: “One who beds a married woman — by what death does he die?” He answered: “By strangulation, and he has a share in Olam Haba; but one who publicly whitens his fellow’s face has no share in Olam Haba.” The Gemara does not lessen the gravity or punishment of adultery. Rav Tzadok uses its explicit distinction to show that even a capital transgression does not by itself uproot Israel’s essential bond to Olam Haba.
דִּבְהָא תַּלְיָא עוֹלָם הַבָּא כְּפִי הַמִּשְׁנָה [דר״פ חֵלֶק], וּמִשּׁוּם דְּגַם עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים מוּלִים
for on this depends [the share in] Olam Haba, according to the Mishnah [start of Perek Chelek], and because even the “arelim of Israel” are called “mulim.”

וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זָכָה לְהוֹלִיד תֵּיכֶף אַחַר כָּךְ מִמֶּנָּה שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁכָּתוּב מִיָּד בְּלֵידָתוֹ ״וַה׳ אֲהֵבוֹ״, וְשָׁלַח לִקְרוֹא שְׁמוֹ ״יְדִידְיָהּ בַּעֲבוּר ה׳״, שֶׁהוּא יְדִידוֹ וְאוֹהֲבוֹ מִלֵּידָה וּבֶטֶן, אֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה אַחַר כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה

And through this he merited to beget, immediately afterward, Shlomo HaMelech from her, of whom it is written at once, at his birth, “and Hashem loved him,” and He sent to call his name “Yedidyah, for the sake of Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:24–25) — that he is His beloved and friend “from birth and womb,” whatever he might be afterward,
וְכַאֲשֶׁר הִבְטִיחוֹ גַּם כֵּן מִקּוֹדֶם עַל זַרְעוֹ [ש״ב ז] ״וְהוּא יִהְיֶה לִּי לְבֵן, אֲשֶׁר בְּהַעֲוֹתוֹ וְהוֹכַחְתִּיו״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְחַסְדִּי לֹא יָסוּר מִמֶּנּוּ״

as He assured him beforehand too regarding his seed [II Shmuel 7], “and he shall be to Me a son; when he sins, I will chastise him [with the rod of men and the afflictions of the sons of men], but My kindness shall not depart from him.”205II Shmuel 12:24–25; 7:12–15 — Yedidyah and a covenantal love that survives chastisement: At Shlomo’s birth Scripture states, “Hashem loved him,” and through Nasan the prophet names him Yedidyah, “for the sake of Hashem.” Earlier, Hashem had promised David concerning his seed: “I will be to him a father and he will be to Me a son; when he sins I will chastise him ... but My kindness shall not depart from him,” unlike Shaul. The verses therefore place discipline inside an enduring father-son covenant. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “whatever he might afterward become” is his theological reading of that combination.

וְהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכֵן חֶטְאוֹ הָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְכָל חֲטָאֵי כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בִּשְׁבִירַת הַלּוּחוֹת שֶׁהָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְחֵטְא הָעֵגֶל עַל יְדֵי שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״יִישַׁר כֹּחֲךָ״ עַל חֶטְאוֹ, וְזֶהוּ הַיִּצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

And he [David/Shlomo] includes all of Knesses Yisrael; and so his sin was a rectification for all the sins of Knesses Yisrael — as I wrote above, regarding the breaking of the tablets, which was a rectification for the sin of the calf, through the Holy One saying to him “yishar kochacha” over his sin — and this is [the rectification of] the inclination of idolatry.206Likkutei Ma’amarim, on Yehoshua §10 — Shlomo as the collective soul of Knesses Yisrael: Rav Tzadok writes elsewhere that Shlomo HaMelech, precisely as king, was “the totality of all Knesses Yisrael.” He explains more generally that the leader’s soul includes the souls of his generation, just as a king is the collective form of the nation. This is a direct parallel to the statement here that Shlomo “includes all Knesses Yisrael.” The further step — that his sin therefore participates in a rectification of Israel’s sins — is the present se’if’s application of that collective-soul principle.

items.h: The theme: Moshe did not fully uproot the inclination of idolatry, lacking “the merit of Eretz Yisrael.” It was completed by the Men of the Great Assembly — chiefly Ezra, “like Moshe” (worthy that the Torah be given through him). This was the intensity of Moshe’s prayers to enter the Land: there he would have uprooted idolatry, and Israel would never have been destroyed.

p: [כה] וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה לֹא פָּעַל לְעָקְרוֹ (לְיִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה) לְגַמְרֵי, מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ זְכוּת דְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּעֲרָכִין לב:]; וְנִגְמַר עַל יְדֵי אַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה, וְהָעִיקָּר עֶזְרָא כִּדְאִיתָא [שָׁם בַּעֲרָכִין], כִּי הוּא הָיָה כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כא:] דְּהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁתִּינָּתֵן תּוֹרָה עַל יָדוֹ

And Moshe Rabbeinu did not effect to uproot it (the inclination of idolatry) completely, because he did not have “the merit of Eretz Yisrael,” as they said [Arachin 32b]; and it was completed by the Men of the Great Assembly, chiefly Ezra, as it is there [in Arachin] — for he was “like Moshe,” in the manner it is stated [Sanhedrin 21b] that “he was worthy that the Torah be given through him.”207Arachin 32b: the Men of the Great Assembly “prayed for mercy” and abolished the inclination for idolatry; and the Gemara discusses why the “merit of Eretz Yisrael” of the returnees under Ezra availed for this where the wilderness generation’s did not — “Ezra should [by right] have had the Torah given through him, but Moshe preceded him.” R’ Tzadok: Moshe’s prayers to enter the Land were, at root, to uproot idolatry there — a task reserved for Ezra’s generation, “for everything has its time.”

וְזֶה הָיָה תֹּקֶף רִיבּוּי הַתְּפִלּוֹת דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה לִיכָּנֵס לָאָרֶץ, דְּאָז הָיָה עוֹקֵר יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְלֹא עָבְדוּ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וְלֹא כָּלוּ, וְהָיָה כִּיבּוּשׁ עוֹלָם, אֲבָל לֹא הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן עֲדַיִין, כִּי לַכֹּל זְמָן

And this was the intensity of Moshe Rabbeinu’s many prayers to enter the Land — for then he would have uprooted the inclination of idolatry, and they would not have served idolatry and would not have been destroyed, and it would have been a “conquest of the world”; but the time had not yet come, “for everything has its time.”208Sotah 14a — Moshe’s longing to enter Eretz Yisrael: R’ Simlai asks why Moshe desired to enter the Land: many mitzvos can be fulfilled only there, and he wanted them fulfilled through him. Rav Tzadok adds an inner communal dimension. Since Arachin places the final abolition of the idolatry-yetzer in Ezra’s return, Moshe’s wish becomes also a wish to complete in the Land the rectification his generation began. This expands Chazal’s stated reason rather than replacing it.

וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הַמְתַקֵּן לְיִצְרָא דִּזְנוּת — עַל יְדֵי שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר חֶטְאוֹ, מַה שֶּׁגַּם כֵּן מַעֲלֶה עָלָיו הַכָּתוּב חֵטְא גָּמוּר וְשֶׁ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, וְהוּא מָלֵא קְדֻשָּׁה בֶּאֱמֶת, דַּהֲרֵי רְאוּיָה לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית

And David HaMelech is the rectifier of the inclination of licentiousness — through his “sin” being clarified: that Scripture too reckons upon him a “complete sin,” and that “[he did] evil in the eyes of Hashem,” yet he was truly “full of holiness,” for she was fit for him from the six days of Creation;209Sanhedrin 107a — Bat Sheva was destined for David, but “he ate her unripe”: Rava says Bat Sheva was fit for David “from the six days of Creation,” but came to him through pain; the school of R’ Yishmael says she was fit for him, “but he ate her unripe.” The sugya thus holds both truths together: the zivug belonged to him at root, yet its premature realization was blameworthy. This is Rav Tzadok’s exact dialectic: root-level holiness does not erase Scripture’s “evil in the eyes of Hashem”; later clarification reveals a true destiny reached before its proper time.

וְכָךְ כָּל חֲטָאֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל סְדוּרִים וּבָאִים מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית, וְאָז ״כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ״, וְהַגּוֹמֵר יִהְיֶה מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד שֶׁבְּיָמָיו יְבוּלַּע הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי

and so all the sins of the Children of Israel are “arranged and come from the six days of Creation,” and then “they shall become white as snow”210Shabbos 89b; Tzidkas HaTzadik §228 — “sins arranged from the six days of Creation”: On Yeshayah 1:18, R’ Yitzchak reads “if your sins are kashanim” as “like these years, ordered and coming from the six days of Creation until now — they shall become white as snow.” Tzidkas HaTzadik §228 repeats this formulation: at Israel’s hidden root even the apparent nega is ultimately transformed into oneg. This is not a license to sin; within this-worldly choice the act remains sin. It describes the post-teshuvah clarification in which the prior fall itself is incorporated into rectification.; and the one who completes [it] will be Mashiach ben David, in whose days the inclination will be wholly swallowed up.

וְנִרְאֶה לִי דִּכְמוֹ דִּלְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן מִפְּנֵי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל, לְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁלֹּא גָּמַר הוּא עֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי, מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִבְנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ עֲדַיִין

And it appears to me that, just as for Moshe the deficiency was because he was not in Eretz Yisrael, for David the deficiency was that he did not complete the uprooting of the inclination entirely — in that the Beis HaMikdash was not yet built.

שֶׁאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל מְיוּחֶדֶת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״אֱלֹקֵי הָאָרֶץ״ וַ״אֲשֶׁר הוּא דּוֹרֵשׁ אֹתָהּ״, שֶׁהַשְׁרָאָתוֹ וֶאֱלֹקוּתוֹ נִיכָּר בָּהּ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּכְתוּבּוֹת קי סע״ב] שֶׁהַדָּר בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אֱלוֹהַּ, וְהַדָּר בְּחוּץ לָאָרֶץ כְּעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

For Eretz Yisrael is dedicated to Hashem — called “the God of the land,” “which He seeks out” — where His indwelling and Godliness are recognized; and as they said [Kesubos 110b], one who dwells in Eretz Yisrael is “like one who has a God,” and one who dwells outside the Land is “like one who serves idols” — see there.211Kesubos 110b: “The Sages taught: one should always dwell in Eretz Yisrael, even in a city that is mostly gentile, and not outside the Land even in a mostly-Jewish city — for whoever dwells in Eretz Yisrael is like one who has a God, and whoever dwells outside the Land is like one who has no God, and like one who serves idols; and so of David it says, ‘for they have driven me out this day from cleaving to the inheritance of Hashem [saying, go serve other gods]’ (I Shmuel 26:19).” Hence, for R’ Tzadok, the uprooting of idolatry belongs specifically to the Land.
וּלְכָךְ אִי אֶפְשָׁר עֲקִירַת יִצְרָא דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה אֶלָּא בְּאֶרֶץ יִשְׂרָאֵל; וּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הוּא מְקוֹם מִשְׁכַּן הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״מִקְדָּשׁ״

And therefore the uprooting of the inclination of idolatry is impossible except in Eretz Yisrael; and the Beis HaMikdash is the “place of the dwelling of holiness in the world,” and therefore called “Mikdash [Sanctuary].”
וְעִיקַּר הַקְּדֻשָּׁה הוּא בִּפְרִישׁוּת מִתַּאֲווֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁאַתָּה מוֹצֵא גֶּדֶר עֶרְוָה שָׁם אַתָּה מוֹצֵא קְדֻשָּׁה״

And the essence of holiness is “abstinence from the desires,” as they said, “wherever you find a fence against immorality, there you find holiness.”212Rashi to Vayikra 19:2; Gur Aryeh to Shemos 22:30 — separation from arayos as kedushah itself: Rashi defines “Kedoshim tihyu” as separation from arayos and transgression, because wherever the Torah fences sexual immorality it speaks of holiness. Maharal sharpens: “the separation from arayos itself is the holiness,” precisely because desire is strongly drawn there; abstention does not merely preserve holiness but produces it. This directly supports Rav Tzadok’s phrase that “the essence of holiness is abstinence from desires,” and his correspondence between the Mikdash as a makom of kedushah and the rectification of desire in the nefesh.

וְעַד שֶׁלֹּא נִבְנָה בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה דְּמָקוֹם בָּעוֹלָם, גַּם בַּנֶּפֶשׁ לֹא הָיְתָה הִתְגַּלּוּת הַקְּדֻשָּׁה בְּפֹעַל, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא יָכוֹל לְהָבִיא לְיָדוֹ גְּמַר דַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר דַּעֲרָיוֹת

And until the Beis HaMikdash was built, when there was no revelation of the holiness of “place” in the world, in the soul too there was no revelation of holiness in actuality; and therefore he could not bring to his hand the completion of the uprooting of the inclination of immorality.

וְזֶהוּ הִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה לְבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, וְאִלְמָלֵא זָכוּ שֶׁהוּא יִבְנֶנּוּ הָיָה עֵת קֵץ בַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְלֹא הָיָה נֶחֱרָב עוֹד, אֶלָּא שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַקֵּץ

213Tehillim 132:1–5; I Divrei HaYamim 22:7–10 — David’s consuming desire to build the Mikdash: Tehillim portrays David refusing home, bed, and sleep “until I find a place for Hashem.” Divrei HaYamim records him telling Shlomo, “it was with my heart to build a House for the name of Hashem my God,” while the building was assigned to his son, the man of menuchah. Rav Tzadok reads this thwarted longing metaphysically: David possessed the root of the rectification, but its historical time had not arrived, so completion passed to Shlomo. The claim that a Temple built by David would never have been destroyed is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis, not an explicit statement of these verses.And this is David’s yearning for the building of the Beis HaMikdash; and had they merited that he build it, it would have been the End of Days in the uprooting of the evil inclination, and it would never have been destroyed again — only that the End had not [yet] come.

items.h: The theme: Therefore the pardon of David’s iniquity was likewise not revealed to all — “a sign for good, that his enemies see and be ashamed.” Until the Beis HaMikdash was completed, when “they could not bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies” until David’s merit was invoked. This is the essence of the First Temple’s holiness — for the Second, lacking the Ark, lacked the Shechinah; and the Ark alludes to the Torah.

p: [כו] וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה גַּם כֵּן מְחִילַת אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן לְעֵין כֹּל עַל יְדֵי הָאוֹת לְטוֹבָה, שֶׁיִּרְאוּ שׂוֹנְאָיו וְיֵבוֹשׁוּ, עַד שֶׁנִּגְמַר בִּנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת ל.] דְּלֹא יָכְלוּ לְהַכְנִיס אָרוֹן לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים

And therefore the pardon of that iniquity was also not revealed to all eyes, through a “sign for good, that his enemies see and be ashamed” (cf. Tehillim 86:17), until the building of the Beis HaMikdash was completed — as they said [Shabbos 30a] that “they could not bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies” [until Shlomo invoked the merit of David].214Shabbos 30a: When Shlomo sought to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies, the gates clung shut and would not open until he prayed, “remember the chasdei [pious deeds] of David Your servant” (II Divrei HaYamim 6:42) — whereupon they opened, and “the faces of David’s enemies turned black [with shame], and all knew that the Holy One had forgiven him for that sin.” R’ Tzadok: only with the completed Sanctuary was David’s pardon revealed to all.
דְּזֶהוּ עִיקַּר קְדֻשַּׁת בַּיִת רִאשׁוֹן, דִּבְבַיִת שֵׁנִי דְּלָא הָיָה אָרוֹן לֹא הָיְתָה שְׁכִינָה גַּם כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא כא:], וְגַם דְּאָרוֹן רוֹמֵז לַתּוֹרָה

For this is the essence of the holiness of the First Temple — for in the Second, where there was no Ark, there was also no Shechinah, as they said [Yoma 21b];215Yoma 21b — Ark and Shechinah in the First Temple: The Gemara lists both the Ark and the Shechinah among the sanctities absent from the Second Temple, directly grounding Rav Tzadok’s contrast. and also, the Ark alludes to the Torah.216Bava Basra 14a — the Ark as the locus of Torah: The Luchos lay in the Ark, and Moshe’s Sefer Torah is placed in or alongside it; this is the classical basis for “the Ark alludes to the Torah.”217Kiddushin 30b — Torah as the yetzer’s antidote: “I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its antidote”; if it confronts a person, “draw him into the beis midrash.”

וְעַצְמוּתוֹ ״עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים״, וְיָדוּעַ דְּ״נַחַל הַשִּׁטִּים״ הוּא מַרְבֶּה זְנוּת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנְחוּמָא [סו״פ בָּלָק וּבְבַמִּדְבַּר רַבָּה כ] דְּמֵעֵין שִׁטִּים שֶׁל זְנוּת, וְלֶעָתִיד יִתְיַיבֵּשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וּמַעְיָן מִבֵּית ה׳ יֵצֵא וְהִשְׁקָה אֶת נַחַל הַשִּׁטִּים״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And its substance is “acacia wood [atzei shittim]218Sotah 3a; Machshavos Charutz §4; Peri Tzadik, Terumah §8 — Shittim transformed: Sotah links sin with ruach shtus; Rav Tzadok links Shittim with that shtus and the Ark’s atzei shittim with redirecting desire into Torah, until the future brook itself becomes “chamidu d’Oraisa.””; and it is known that “the brook of Shittim [nachal haShittim]” increases licentiousness, as they said in Tanchuma [end of Balak, and Bamidbar Rabbah 20] that [it is] “from the spring of Shittim of licentiousness”; and in the Future it will dry up, as it says, “and a spring shall come forth from the House of Hashem and water the brook of Shittim” (Yoel 4:18) — see there.219Tanchuma (Balak) & Bamidbar Rabbah 20: the “brook of Shittim” is associated with the sin of Baal Pe’or at Shittim — “a spring of licentiousness [zenus].” Yoel 4:18 promises, “a spring shall come forth from the House of Hashem and water the brook of Shittim” — which R’ Tzadok reads as the Future transformation of the very wellspring of desire into a wellspring of holiness (and the Ark’s “acacia [shittim] wood” as its rectified root).
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוֹתוֹ מֵעֵין שֶׁל קְדֻשָּׁה
meaning, that this very spring will [become] one of holiness — the wellspring of desire itself transformed, in the End, into a wellspring flowing from the Sanctuary.

items.h: The theme: This is the ultimate “sweetening” of the yetzer through the Torah’s “seasoning.” Of Moshe and David it is said that “enemies did not rule over the work of their hands” (Sotah 9a). For they began the complete uprooting of the yetzer from the heart (which brings, too, “freedom from the kingdoms,” since the “leaven in the dough” and the subjugation to kingdoms are interdependent). Though the time had not come for this in actuality in all Israel, their beginning was not nullified, only “stored away,” to be revealed in the Future — enduring forever.

p: [כז] וְזֶהוּ תַּכְלִית הַמְתָּקַת הַיֵּצֶר עַל יְדֵי תַּבְלִין דְּתוֹרָה. וּבְסוֹטָה [ט סע״א] דְּמֹשֶׁה וְדָוִד לֹא שָׁלְטוּ שׂוֹנְאִים בְּמַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיהֶם, כִּי הֵם הַמַּתְחִילִים בַּעֲקִירַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי מִלֵּב

And this is the ultimate sweetening of the inclination through the “seasoning” of Torah. And in Sotah [9a], that over “Moshe and David, enemies did not rule over the work of their hands” — for they are the ones who begin the complete uprooting of the inclination from the heart,220Sotah 9a: “R’ Chinena bar Pappa expounded: ‘sing, O righteous, in Hashem; for the upright praise is comely [navah]’ (Tehillim 33:1) — read not ‘navah [comely]’ but ‘naveh [dwelling] of praise’ — this is Moshe and David, over whose handiwork their enemies did not rule. David — as it is written, ‘her gates are sunk into the earth’ (Eichah 2:9) [the gates he made were hidden away, not seized by the Temple’s destroyers]. Moshe — as the Master said: when the First Temple was built, the Tent of Meeting was stored away — its boards, clasps, bars, pillars, and sockets — [these were stored away] beneath the tunnels of the Sanctuary.”
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא הַחֵירוּת מִמַּלְכֻיּוֹת גַּם כֵּן, דִּ״שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה״ וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכֻיּוֹת הָא בְּהָא תַּלְיִין

for through this is also “the freedom from the kingdoms,” since “the leaven in the dough” and the subjugation to the kingdoms are interdependent.221Berachos 17a; Likkutei Ma’amarim, Mo’adim §16 — leaven and exile are interdependent: R’ Alexandri prays that Israel’s true will is to do Hashem’s will, impeded by “the leaven in the dough and the subjugation to kingdoms.” Rav Tzadok elsewhere states explicitly, “they are all one … this depends on that,” and says Matan Torah brought freedom from both — an exact parallel to this se’if.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ הַזְּמַן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בְּפֹעַל כֵּן בְּכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵיהֶם וְהַהַתְחָלָה שֶׁלָּהֶם לֹא נִתְבַּטֵּל כְּלָל, רַק נִגְנַז, וּלְעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה דְּ״לֹא אָבַד סִבְרָן וּבָטֵל סִיכּוּיָן״, רַק הֵם קַיָּימִין לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד

And even though the time had not come for it to be so in actuality in all Israel, nonetheless the work of their hands and their beginning was not nullified at all — only “stored away [nignaz]” — and in the Future it will be revealed that “their hope did not perish and their expectation was not voided,” but they endure forever.

וְהַמִּשְׁכָּן — קְדֻשַּׁת שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּאֹהֶל אֲרַעַי — הָיָה עַל יְדֵי מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָיָה בַּמִּדְבָּר, דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא הָיָה לוֹ קְבִיעוּת מָקוֹם; וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הוּא שֶׁהִתְחִיל בְּבִנְיַן בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ

And the Mishkan — the holiness of His Shechinah in a “temporary tent” — was through Moshe, who was in the wilderness, when there was not yet a fixed place; and David HaMelech is the one who began the building of the Beis HaMikdash.222I Divrei HaYamim 21:22–22:5 — David acquired and prepared the Mikdash site: David buys Ornan’s threshing floor for full price, builds an altar, receives heavenly fire, and declares, “This is the House of Hashem.” He then prepares stone, iron, copper, and cedar before his death. This grounds Rav Tzadok’s attribution of the Mikdash’s beginning to David despite Shlomo’s completion.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא נִבְנָה עַל יָדוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא הָיָה הַמַּתְחִיל עַל יְדֵי הִשְׁתּוֹקְקוּתוֹ וְחִשְׁקוֹ וַהֲכָנָתוֹ, וְהַכֹּל לוֹ; גַּם קָנָה הַמָּקוֹם, וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַמָּקוֹם קִידְּשָׁהּ לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְקַיָּים לָעַד, וְעַל פִּי צִיוּוּיוֹ לִשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה נִבְנָה

And although it was not built by him, nonetheless he was the initiator, through his yearning and desire and preparation, and all is his; he also acquired the “place,” and the holiness of the place he sanctified for the Future — enduring forever — and by his command to Shlomo HaMelech it was built.223Rambam, Hilchos Beis HaBechirah 6:14–16 — enduring sanctity, with a halachic distinction: The Rambam rules that Shlomo’s first consecration sanctified Jerusalem and the Mikdash “for the Future,” because the Shechinah never ceases; even desolate sanctuaries retain holiness. Rav Tzadok’s attribution to David is thus conceptual — his purchase and preparation are the spiritual root — not the Rambam’s formal legal attribution.

וּלְפִיכָךְ הַשְּׁעָרִים — הַיְינוּ פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לִקְדֻשַּׁת הַמִּקְדָּשׁ — הֵם מַעֲשֵׂה יָדָיו; וְזֶה ״טָבַע בָּאָרֶץ״ וְנִגְנַז לִהְיוֹת קַיָּים לָעַד, וְלֹא יוּכְלוּ אוֹיְבִים לִשְׁלוֹט בָּהֶם וּלְהוֹצִיאָם לְחוּלִּין כְּלָל

And therefore the “gates” — that is, the entrance to the holiness of the Mikdash — are the work of his hands; and this “sank into the earth” (Eichah 2:9) and was “stored away” to endure forever, and enemies cannot rule over them or profane them at all —
דְּמִשֶּׁבָּאוּ פָּרִיצִים חִלְּלוּהוּ, לְפִי שֶׁ״דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּים״ וּקְדֻשָּׁתוֹ קַיֶּימֶת, וְלֹא אָבַד סִבְרוֹ, רַק שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם וּבִגְנִיזָה

[though] “when the destroyers came they profaned it” (cf. Yechezkel 7:22) — [that is only] because224Avodah Zarah 52b; Nedarim 62a — “marauders entered it and profaned it”: Chazal use Yechezkel 7:22 to explain how sacred Temple property seized by invaders could become chullin. Rav Tzadok’s contrast is precise: David’s gates were sunk away rather than captured, so his handiwork escaped the conqueror’s act of profanation. “David king of Israel lives and endures,” and his holiness endures, and his hope did not perish; only that in this world it is in concealment and storage.

וְעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁבָּא לְהַכְנִיס הָאָרוֹן לְבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים — דְּהָאָרוֹן רוֹמֵז לִקְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֲצֵי שִׁטִּים בָּאֶמְצַע הֵם מְצוּפִּים זָהָב מִבַּיִת וּמִחוּץ — וְעַל כֵּן מְקוֹמוֹ בְּבֵית קָדְשֵׁי הַקֳּדָשִׁים, שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַקְּדֻשָּׁה שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לָאָדָם לְהַשִּׂיג, שֶׁהוּא לְמַעְלָה מֵהַשָּׂגַת הַמַּלְאָכִים, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַמַּלְאָכִים אֵין יְכוֹלִים לִיכָּנֵס שָׁם

And therefore, when [Shlomo] came to bring the Ark into the Holy of Holies — for the Ark alludes to this holiness of David, [in] that although there is acacia wood in the middle, it is “overlaid with gold within and without” (Shemos 25:11) — and therefore its place is in the Holy of Holies, which is the ultimate holiness a person can attain, above the attainment of the angels, for the angels cannot enter there,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי [פ״ה דְּיוֹמָא] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְכָל אָדָם לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּאֹהֶל מוֹעֵד״ אֲפִילּוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁדְּמוּת פְּנֵיהֶם פְּנֵי אָדָם, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וּכְמוֹ לֶעָתִיד דִּמְחִיצַּת הַצַּדִּיקִים יִהְיֶה לִפְנִים מִמְּחִיצַת מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת

as they said in the Yerushalmi [Yoma, ch. 5] on “and no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting” (Vayikra 16:17) — even those “whose faces are the face of a man” [the angels], see there — and as in the Future the partition of the tzaddikim will be within the partition of the ministering angels.225Yerushalmi, Yoma ch. 5: On “and no man shall be in the Tent of Meeting” when the Kohen Gadol enters the Holy of Holies (Vayikra 16:17) — “even those [angels] ‘whose faces are the face of a man’ (Yechezkel 1:10) were not [permitted] there.” R’ Tzadok pairs this with the teaching that in the Future the tzaddikim’s partition will be within that of the ministering angels — the Holy of Holies being a holiness beyond even the angels’ reach.
וְדָבְקוּ הַשְּׁעָרִים שֶׁהֵם מַעֲשֵׂה יְדֵי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, דְּהוּא שַׁעַר הַכְּנִיסָה לִקְדֻשָּׁה הַקַּיֶּימֶת לָעַד
And the “gates,” which are the work of David’s hands — the gate of entry to the holiness that endures forever — clung shut.

וְזֶה לֹא הָיָה מַדְרֵיגַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה, דִּבְמַעֲשֵׂי יָדָיו שָׁלְטוּ אוֹיְבִים, וּלְפִיכָךְ לֹא יָכוֹל לִפְתּוֹחַ עַד שֶׁאָמַר ״זָכְרָה לְחַסְדֵי דָּוִד״, שֶׁהֵם הַנֶּאֱמָנִים וְקַיָּימִים לָעַד; וְיָדוּעַ דְּ״תַאֲוַת אָדָם חַסְדּוֹ״, וְאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה הַכֹּל מִצַּד הַחֶסֶד דִּקְדֻשָּׁה

And this was not the rung of Shlomo, over whose handiwork enemies did rule; therefore he could not open [them] until he said, “remember the pious deeds [chasdei] of David,” which are “faithful and enduring forever”; and it is known that “the desire of a man is his kindness [chesed]” (Mishlei 19:22), and by him all was from the side of the chesed of holiness.226Yeshayah 55:3; Mishlei 19:22 — David’s enduring chesed: Yeshayah calls the everlasting covenant “chasdei David ha-ne’emanim”; Mishlei says “ta’avas adam chasdo.” Rav Tzadok joins them: David’s longing for the Mikdash is itself chesed d’kedushah, hence enduring.

items.h: The theme: R’ Tzadok interprets the darkening of David’s enemies’ faces through the image of a pot’s blackened bottom. Rosh Hashanah applies that image to those who stretch out their hands against the zevul, the fixed and enduring Temple. David’s enemies opposed the sanctuary he longed to establish, while his own bond with enduring holiness continued even after death.

p: [כח] וְאָז נֶהְפְּכוּ פְּנֵי שׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד ״כְּשׁוּלֵי קְדֵרָה״, הַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [ר״ה יז.] עַל אוֹתָן שֶׁפָּשְׁטוּ יְדֵיהֶם בִּזְבוּל, דִּפְנֵיהֶם דּוֹמִין לְשׁוּלֵי קְדֵרָה, וְשׂוֹנְאֵי דָּוִד הֵן הֵן הֵם שֶׁפָּשְׁטוּ כו׳, כִּי כָּל חֵשֶׁק דָּוִד לִבְנוֹת בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ הַקָּבוּעַ וְקַיָּים לָעַד

And then the faces of David’s enemies turned “like the bottom of a pot [shulei kedeirah]” — that is, as they said [Rosh Hashanah 17a] of those “who stretched forth their hands against the zevul [Temple],” whose faces resemble the bottom of a pot; and David’s enemies are the very ones who “stretched forth [their hands]” — for David’s whole desire was to build the fixed, enduring Beis HaMikdash.227Rosh Hashanah 17a: among those who “descend to Gehinnom and are judged there for generations of generations, and their faces become black like the bottom of a pot [shulei kedeirah]” — including “those who stretched forth their hands against the zevul” (the Temple). R’ Tzadok identifies David’s slanderers with these, since they obstructed the fixed, enduring “zevul” that was his whole desire.

וְזֶהוּ הַנִּקְרָא ״זְבוּל״, וּכְמוֹ ״הַפַּעַם יִזְבְּלֵנִי אִישִׁי״, שֶׁעִיקַּר קְבִיעוּת דִּירָתוֹ אֶצְלָהּ לָעַד — דְּגַם בִּקְבוּרָה נִקְבַּר עִמָּהּ בִּמְעָרַת הַמַּכְפֵּלָה — וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב ״בֵּית זְבוּל לָךְ מָכוֹן לְשִׁבְתְּךָ עוֹלָמִים״

And this is called “zevul,” as in “this time my husband will dwell with me [yizbeleni]” (Bereishis 30:20) — that the essence of his fixed dwelling is with her forever (for even in burial he is buried with her, in Me’aras HaMachpelah) — and so the language of Scripture, “a house of zevul [lofty dwelling] for You, a place for Your dwelling forever” (I Melachim 8:13).228Rashi to Bereishis 30:20; I Melachim 8:13 — Zevul as a fixed dwelling-place: Rashi explains “yizbeleni” as “a term of beis zevul … a dwelling-house,” Leah meaning that from now on Yaakov’s primary residence would be with her. Shlomo calls the Mikdash “בית זבול לך מכון לשבתך עולמים,” a zevul prepared for God’s dwelling forever. Together they provide the lexical and biblical basis for Rav Tzadok’s use of zevul as permanent habitation; Rav Tzadok extends that language to the enduring quality of the Mikdash David desired.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנֶּחֱרַב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִכְתַּב דִּבְרֵי שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״בָּנִיתִי בַיִת״ וְגוֹמֵר, מִשּׁוּם דִּקְדֻשָּׁה רִאשׁוֹנָה קִידְּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא וְסוֹפוֹ לַחֲזוֹר וְלִבְנוֹת, וְהַבִּיטּוּל הָיָה רַק לְשָׁעָה

And even though it was destroyed, nonetheless Shlomo’s words were recorded, that he said of himself, “I have built a house [of habitation for You],” because the first holiness “sanctified for the Future,” and it is destined to return and be rebuilt, and the nullification was only for a time.229Mishnah Eduyos 8:6; Rambam, Hilchos Beis HaBechirah 6:15 — Sanctity enduring beyond destruction: The Mishnah teaches that offerings may be brought even without a standing Temple and sacred foods eaten in their proper areas because “the first sanctity sanctified for its time and sanctified for the Future”; the Rambam codifies this for the Mikdash and Jerusalem. This is the halachic basis for Rav Tzadok’s statement that the destruction was only a temporary bittul: the physical structure ceased, but the sanctity of the place did not. His further claim about the eternal “building” is his own homiletical-metaphysical development.

וְאִלּוּ בְּנָאוֹ דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה לֹא הָיָה נֶחֱרַב בֶּאֱמֶת, אֶלָּא שֶׁשּׂוֹנְאָיו שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ ״רַע לוֹ״ גָּרְמוּ דְּלֹא נִתְגַּלֵּית קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ בְּפֹעַל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּיָמָיו, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה לֹא זָכָה לִבְנוֹתוֹ

And had David built it, it truly would not have been destroyed;230Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:1:6; Yerushalmi Taanis 2:9; Sotah 9a; Machshavos Charutz §20 — David as foundation and enduring builder: Shir HaShirim Rabbah says that David “built the foundations” while Shlomo “built the superstructure”; the Yerushalmi has David say that through Israel’s census crisis God “gave me the Beis HaMikdash.” Sotah adds that enemies never ruled over David’s handiwork, citing his gates that “sank into the earth.” Rav Tzadok gathers these strands explicitly in Machshavos Charutz §20: Shlomo erected the visible structure, but David purchased and sanctified the mountain, that sanctity endured, and therefore the essential building that remains forever is attributed to David. The Midrash, Yerushalmi, and Gemara establish David’s foundational role and the endurance of his works; the identification of those facts with the Mikdash’s metaphysically eternal “building” is Rav Tzadok’s development. only that his enemies, who said “evil to him,” caused that his holiness was not revealed in actuality in this world in his days, and through this he did not merit to build it.231Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:134 — Had David built the Mikdash, it would not have been destroyed: Rav Tzadok states there directly that had David built the Beis HaMikdash it would not have been destroyed, and that he did not build it because his own level had not yet been fully clarified during his lifetime. This is an unusually close parallel to the present se’if: David’s enduring holiness is intrinsically fit for an indestructible Mikdash, while the lack of its full revelation in his lifetime prevented that possibility from becoming actual.

וּלְפִיכָךְ הֵם פָּשְׁטוּ יְדֵיהֶם בִּזְבוּל, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״אוֹיְבֵי ה׳״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ [אֶת] אוֹיְבֵי ה׳״, וְהַכַּוָּונָה עַל אוֹיְבָיו, רַק דְּהֵם נֶחְשָׁבִים לְאוֹיְבֵי ה׳ עַל יְדֵי זֶה; וְכֵן אוֹמֵר ״מְשַׂנְאֶיךָ ה׳ אֶשְׂנָא״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְהוּא הָיָה שׂוֹנֵא מִסְּתָמָא לְשׂוֹנְאָיו, דִּ״כְמַיִם הַפָּנִים לְפָנִים״

And therefore they “stretched forth their hands against the zevul,” and so they are called “the enemies of Hashem,” as it says, “you have utterly scorned the enemies of Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:14)232Rashi to II Shmuel 12:14 — David’s sin and the enemies’ opening: On “כי נאץ נאצת את אויבי ה׳,” Rashi, citing Targum Yonasan, explains: “you have opened the mouth of the enemies of the people of Hashem.” The verse and its targumic interpretation establish that David’s apparent sin supplied hostile observers with an opening to speak. Rav Tzadok reads this homiletically in the opposite direction as well: those who fasten upon that opening and obstruct the revelation of David’s holiness thereby become, in this se’if, “enemies of Hashem.” — the intent being upon his enemies, only that they are reckoned “enemies of Hashem” thereby; and so it says, “those who hate You, Hashem, I hate” (Tehillim 139:21), and he certainly hated his haters, “as water reflects face to face” (Mishlei 27:19).

items.h: The theme: It was then clarified that the “life” David asked for was granted — he is “alive and enduring forever.” And that iniquity pardoned, his “Shittim” being the one that “drinks from the spring going forth from the House of Hashem,” gold-overlaid within and without. So their sin was written as a “sign and token” for all Israel’s sins and their “act of spirit-of-folly,” after teshuvah.

p: [כט] וְנִתְבָּרֵר אָז דְּהַחַיִּים שֶׁשָּׁאַל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה נִיתַּן, כִּי הוּא בֶּאֱמֶת חַי וְקַיָּים לָעַד, וְשֶׁנִּמְחַל אוֹתוֹ עָוֹן, דְּנִתְבָּרֵר דְּ״שִׁטִּים״ דִּידֵיהּ הוּא הַשּׁוֹתֶה מִמַּעְיָן הַיּוֹצֵא מִבֵּית ה׳ וּמְצוּפֶּה זָהָב מִבַּיִת וּמִבַּחוּץ

And it was then clarified that the “life” David asked for was granted — for he is truly “alive and enduring forever”233Tehillim 21:5; Rosh Hashanah 25a; Sukkah 52a; Machshavos Charutz §7 — David’s requested life as enduring kingship: Tehillim says, “He asked life of You; You gave it to him — length of days forever and ever.” Rosh Hashanah uses “David, king of Israel, lives and endures” as the sign for sanctifying the new moon, while Sukkah reads the same verse of the promised life of Mashiach ben David. Rav Tzadok makes the connection explicit in Machshavos Charutz §7: “David, king of Israel, lives and endures” expresses the enduring life and kingship that may be hidden in this world but is never truly annulled. The Bavli establishes the Davidic language of enduring life; Rav Tzadok develops it into the metaphysical permanence asserted here. — and that that iniquity was pardoned, for it was clarified that “his Shittim” is the one that “drinks from the spring going forth from the House of Hashem,” overlaid with gold within and without.234Shemos 25:10–11; Yoel 4:18; Yoma 72b — “Shittim” overlaid within and without and watered from the Mikdash: The Ark is made of atzei shittim and “overlaid with pure gold, within and without”; Yoel foretells that “a spring shall go forth from the House of Hashem and water Nachal HaShittim.” Yoma derives from the Ark’s inner and outer gold that a Torah scholar must have an interior matching the exterior. Rav Tzadok fuses these distinct sources homiletically: David’s “shittim” — the element associated in this se’if with folly — is not discarded but disclosed as an inner substance wholly enveloped by holiness and nourished from the Mikdash. The verses and Gemara do not themselves apply this imagery to David’s sin; that synthesis is Rav Tzadok’s.
וּלְפִיכָךְ נִכְתַּב חֶטְאוֹ לִהְיוֹת ״אוֹת וְסִימָן״ לְכָל חֲטָאֵי בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וּמַעֲשֵׂה רוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁלָּהֶם אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתִּיקּוּן

And therefore his sin was written, to be a “sign and token” for all the sins of the Children of Israel and their “act of spirit-of-folly,” after the teshuvah and the rectification.235Sotah 3a; Avodah Zarah 4b–5a — David as the written paradigm for the “spirit of folly” and teshuvah: Sotah states that a person does not transgress unless a “spirit of folly” enters him. Avodah Zarah teaches that David was not intrinsically suited to the episode of Bas Sheva; rather, his fall and return were set forth so that an individual sinner could be directed to David as the paradigm of teshuvah. Rav Tzadok combines the two teachings into the present claim: after teshuvah and clarification, David’s recorded sin becomes an “אות וסימן” for the sins of Israel — a model showing how the deed can be exposed as a transient ruach shtus rather than the deepest identity of the sinner. The two sugyos establish the separate premises; their synthesis is Rav Tzadok’s.

בְּשׁוֹחֵר טוֹב [מִזְמוֹר לד] דְּאָמַר דָּוִד ״הֲשָׁטוֹת שֶׁבָּרָאתָ מַה הֲנָאָה יֵשׁ״ כו׳, אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״חַיֶּיךָ שֶׁתִּצְטָרֵךְ לוֹ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם — הַכַּוָּונָה עַל הָרוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁבִּבְרִיאַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע

In Shocher Tov [on Psalm 34], that David said, “the madness [shtus] You created — what benefit is there [in it]?” — the Holy One said to him, “by your life, you will [yet] need it” — see there — the intent [being] upon the “spirit of folly” in the creation of the evil inclination.236Midrash Shocher Tov (Tehillim 34): David questioned the value of the “madness [shtus]” God created — “what pleasure is there before You when a man tears his clothes in the market and children run after him?” — and was answered, “by your life, you will yet need it and pray for it,” as fulfilled when David feigned madness before Achish, king of Gath (I Shmuel 21:14), and was thereby saved. R’ Tzadok reads the “spirit of folly” as the raw material of the yetzer that, rightly turned, becomes an aveirah lishmah and even a “redemption.”
וּבֶאֱמֶת יֵשׁ בָּזֶה צֹרֶךְ וְתוֹעֶלֶת, וְ״יִתְרוֹן אֶרֶץ בַּכֹּל הוּא״, שֶׁלִּפְעָמִים צָרִיךְ לְשַׁנּוֹת אֶת טַעְמוֹ, וְהוּא כְּמוֹ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ

And in truth there is in this a need and a benefit, and “the profit of the earth is in everything” (Koheles 5:8) — that sometimes one needs to “change his reason [taste],” and it is like a “transgression for its own sake.”

וְסִיּוּם אוֹתוֹ מִזְמוֹר ״פּוֹדֶה ה׳ נֶפֶשׁ עֲבָדָיו״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְקִיבַּלְתִּי דְּנֶאֱמַר [עַל] פְּגַם הַבְּרִית, דְּלִפְנֵי זֶה שֶׁאָמַר ״וְשֹׂנְאֵי צַדִּיק יֶאְשָׁמוּ״ [וְכֵן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״פְּנֵי ה׳ בְּעֹשֵׂי רָע״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְאָמַר ״צָעֲקוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת, ״וְאֶת דַּכְּאֵי רוּחַ יוֹשִׁיעַ״, כִּי הַשָּׁב מִפְּגָם זֶה הוּא בִּשְׁבִירַת לֵב וְדִכְאוּת רוּחַ בְּיָדְעוֹ גּוֹדֶל הַפְּגָם הֵיכָן מַגִּיעַ]

And the conclusion of that psalm, “Hashem redeems the soul of His servants, and none who take refuge in Him shall be condemned” (Tehillim 34:23) — and I have received that it is said [regarding] the blemish of the bris; for before this he said, “and those who hate the tzaddik shall be condemned” [and likewise “the face of Hashem is against evildoers, [to cut off their memory from the earth],” and he said “they cried out [and Hashem heard],” that teshuvah avails, “and He saves the crushed of spirit” — for one who repents from this blemish is with a broken heart and crushed spirit, knowing the magnitude of the blemish, where it reaches].
אֲבָל ״עֲבָדָיו הַחוֹסִים בּוֹ״ לֹא יֶאְשָׁמוּ אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפְּגָמוֹ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, דְּיֵשׁ לָהֶם פִּדְיוֹן עַל זֶה
but “His servants who take refuge in Him” shall not be condemned, even though he blemished, God forbid — for they have a “redemption” for it.
וְקִיבַּלְתִּי דִּפְעָמִים ״מִקְרֶה״ שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לָאָדָם הוּא הַצָּלָה מִמִּיתָה רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו, וְהוּא לְפִדְיוֹן נַפְשׁוֹ, וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן שְׁטוּת שֶׁנִּבְרָא לְצֹרֶךְ

And I have received that sometimes a “mishap [mikreh]” that befalls a person is a salvation from a death, God spare us, that was decreed upon him, and it is for “the redemption of his soul” — and this too is a “folly created for a purpose.”237Tehillim 34:22–23; Tzidkas HaTzadik §243 — “Podeh Hashem” as redemption through an apparent mishap: The psalm contrasts “those who hate the tzaddik shall be condemned” with “Hashem redeems the soul of His servants, and none who take refuge in Him shall be condemned.” In Tzidkas HaTzadik §243 Rav Tzadok returns independently to this same psalm and to David’s “changing his reason”: he records a received teaching that an apparently shameful bodily mishap can serve as a pidyon and rescue from death, and reads the psalm’s closing “podeh” in that light. This is an exceptionally close parallel to the present se’if. Rav Tzadok expressly presents the application to the blemish of the bris and to such a pidyon as received teaching; it is not the plain meaning of the biblical verse.

וְכָל עֲסָקָיו שֶׁל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ ע״ה הָיָה בָּזֶה, לְבָרֵר וּלְתַקֵּן כָּל הַחֲטָאִים שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל; וְכֵן כָּל רָאשֵׁי הַדּוֹרוֹת שֶׁלְּאַחֲרָיו, דּוֹר דּוֹר עַד בִּיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, עִסְקָם בָּזֶה, לְתַקֵּן חֲטָאֵי הַדּוֹר שֶׁיִּהְיוּ זְדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, עַד עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר זֶה לְגַמְרֵי
