And all David’s occupations were with this — to clarify and rectify all the sins of all Israel; and so all the heads of the generations after him, generation by generation until the coming of Mashiach, are occupied with this — to rectify the sins of the generation, that willful sins become like merits, until the End of Days, when this will be wholly clarified.238Yisrael Kedoshim §5; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 10 — the head of the generation contains and rectifies the generation: In Yisrael Kedoshim §5 Rav Tzadok describes each generation as a complete spiritual body whose head and heart are bound to all the souls of that generation; the sanctity awakened in the head can therefore awaken the latent holiness of those below. Earlier in this siman he states the complementary principle explicitly: every sin of the generation has some trace in its head, because the head includes the generation, and the head’s rectification can become a channel of rectification for Israel. This supplies Rav Tzadok’s own conceptual background for the closing claim here that David and the heads after him labor to rectify the sins of their generations until the final clarification.

items.h: The theme: Reish Lakish, too — his having been “a bandit” means that through him was a rectification for all the bandits of Israel. Certainly, if he killed, he killed only those “lowered and not raised” (whose blood is permitted). And he was “clearing thorns from the vineyard of Hashem,” in the very manner of R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon (and later R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei), who caught thieves — which is why the Gemara juxtaposes the Reish Lakish narrative to theirs.

p: [ל] וְגַם רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ וַדַּאי מַה שֶּׁאָמַר שֶׁהָיָה לִיסְטִים — עַל יָדוֹ הָיָה תִּיקּוּן לְכָל הַלִּיסְטִים דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

And Reish Lakish too — certainly what he said, that “he was a bandit”239Bava Metzia 84a; Rashi — the basis for calling Reish Lakish a bandit: Bava Metzia later has R’ Yochanan say, “a bandit knows his banditry”; Rashi glosses the opening “Reish Lakish saw him” with “for he was a bandit.” Rav Tzadok is exact that the Bavli’s narrator does not independently state the biography; the identification comes through the dialogue and Rashi. His claim that the bandit period itself served rectification is his own interpretive extension. [means] that through him was a rectification for all the bandits of Israel.240Tosafos and Maharsha to Bava Metzia 84a — “return” implies an earlier Torah identity: Tosafos cites Rabbeinu Tam that Reish Lakish had learned Torah before casting off its yoke and taking up brigandry; “if you return” means returning to an earlier state. Maharsha likewise reads “there they called me Rabbi” as recalling prior learning. Neither source sanctifies the brigandry. Rav Tzadok goes further, reading the later teshuvah as clarifying even that fallen period as a power ultimately redirected toward rectification.

וּבְוַדַּאי אִם הוּא הָרַג אָדָם, לֹא הָרַג אֶלָּא מֵאוֹתָן הַ״מּוֹרִידִין וְלֹא מַעֲלִין״ שֶׁדָּמוֹ מוּתָּר [וּמָמוֹנוֹ מוּתָּר מִקַּל וָחֹמֶר, וְאַף לְמַאן דְּפָלֵיג בְּסוֹף בָּבָא קַמָּא וְאוֹסֵר, דְּהַיְינוּ לְאַבְּדוֹ, אֲבָל מוּתָּר לִיקַּח לְעַצְמוֹ]

And certainly, if he killed a person, he killed only from those “who are lowered [into a pit] and not raised out,” whose blood is permitted [and whose property is permitted a fortiori — and even according to the one who disputes at the end of Bava Kamma and forbids, that is [only] to destroy it, but it is permitted to take [it] for oneself].241Avodah Zarah 26b; Bava Kamma 119a; Rambam, Hilchos Rotzeach 4:10–11 — “moridin” and the property a fortiori: Avodah Zarah limits “moridin ve-lo ma’alin” to defined categories, and the Rambam distinguishes them from ordinary sinners. Bava Kamma disputes a moser’s property: one view permits destroying it because “his property should not be more stringent than his body”; another forbids this lest worthy descendants inherit. The Gemara addresses destruction, not personal taking; Rav Tzadok’s latter permission is his inference. His hypothetical therefore does not concern ordinary thieves.

וְקוֹצִים הָיָה מְכַלֶּה מִכֶּרֶם ה׳, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [שָׁם בב״מ פג:] אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן, וְכֵן אַחַר כָּךְ אַרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, וּבְוַדַּאי מִפְּנֵי זֶה סָמְכוּ עִנְיָן לוֹ [הַלִּיסְטִיּוּת דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֵצֶל מַעֲשֵׂה ר׳ אֶלְעָזָר]

And “he was clearing thorns from the vineyard of Hashem,”242Yeshayahu 5:7; 27:2–6; Bava Metzia 83b — Israel as Hashem’s vineyard and the thorns within it: Yeshayahu identifies “the vineyard of Hashem of Hosts” with Israel and later speaks of vineyard thorns. Bava Metzia gives R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon’s phrase, “clearing thorns from the vineyard.” Rav Tzadok distinguishes Israel, the vineyard, from destructive growth. The biblical imagery is classical; applying it to Reish Lakish is Rav Tzadok’s homiletical development. in the manner it is stated [there in Bava Metzia 83b] — R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon said [it], and likewise afterward regarding R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei [who caught thieves for the government] — and certainly for this reason they “juxtaposed the matter” [placing Reish Lakish’s banditry beside the deed of R’ Elazar].243Bava Metzia 83b: R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon was appointed by the government to catch thieves. R’ Yehoshua ben Korchah rebuked him, “vinegar son of wine [a wicked son of a righteous father] — how long will you hand over the people of our God to slaying?” He replied, “I am [merely] clearing thorns from the vineyard.” Said the other: “let the Owner of the vineyard come and clear His own thorns.” The same account continues with R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei. R’ Tzadok notes that the Gemara juxtaposes the story of Reish Lakish’s earlier banditry to these — hinting that the “bandit,” too, was, at root, “clearing thorns” for the rectification of Israel. — R’ Tzadok reads the Sages’ very placement of these accounts side by side as pointing to the shared secret: that the “bandit” and the thief-catcher alike were “clearing thorns” — an outward evil that was, in root, the rectification of Israel’s sins.

items.h: The theme: Though R’ Yochanan “prodded” Reish Lakish — “what benefit did I do you?” And, to disparage him, used the phrase “beneath the wings of the Shechinah” (which, per the Arizal, is the abode of converts’ souls — implying, needlingly, that Reish Lakish was a mere “returnee” lowered in status). Reish Lakish’s silence was itself a “winning answer,” which is why R’ Yochanan’s mind was pained.

p: [לא] וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הִשִּׂיכוֹ ״אַהֲנַאי [לָךְ]״ כו׳, וּלְגַנּוֹתוֹ אָמַר הַלָּשׁוֹן ״תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַשְּׁכִינָה״ — וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִיזָ״ל דְּשָׁם מִשְׁכַּן נַפְשׁוֹת הַגֵּרִים — וְשֶׁאָמַר לוֹ עַל נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן, דְּמוֹרִידוֹ לְמַטָּה, וְהוּא אָמַר עָלָיו כֵּן כְּאִלּוּ הָיָה כְּגֵר שֶׁנִּתְגַּיֵּיר, וּלְהַקְנִיטוֹ אָמַר זֶה

And although R’ Yochanan “prodded” him, “[what] benefit [did I do you],” etc., and, to disparage him, used the expression “beneath the wings of the Shechinah” — and it is known from the Arizal that there is “the abode of the souls of converts”244Shabbos 31a; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135 — “under the wings of the Shechinah” and converts: Shabbos 31a repeatedly uses this expression for converts brought near by Hillel. In the direct parallel Dover Tzedek 4:135, Rav Tzadok explicitly notes that the phrase is used in the Gemara of gerim and repeats the attribution to the Arizal that this is the locus of converts’ souls; he contrasts native Jewish souls and reads R’ Yochanan’s wording as a challenge to Reish Lakish’s spiritual root. The Bavli itself does not call the phrase derogatory; that lower-status implication here is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic reading. — and he said this of a soul of Israel, [meaning] that he lowers him [in status], saying it of him as though he were “like a convert who converted,” and to needle him he said this245Bava Metzia 84a: After R’ Yochanan drew Reish Lakish from banditry to Torah and gave him his sister in marriage, a study-hall dispute arose over when weapons become susceptible to impurity; R’ Yochanan said, “a brigand knows his brigandry.” Reish Lakish, pained, retorted, “what benefit did you do me? there they called me ‘Rebbi,’ and here they call me ‘Rebbi.’” R’ Yochanan replied, “I benefited you, that I brought you beneath the wings of the Shechinah.” R’ Yochanan’s mind was weakened; Reish Lakish fell ill and died, and R’ Yochanan, grief-stricken and unconsoled, lost his own mind and died. R’ Tzadok reads R’ Yochanan’s phrase as (needlingly) casting Reish Lakish as a “convert” (whose souls rest “beneath the wings of the Shechinah”). —
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא הֱשִׁיבוֹ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָז כְּלוּם, וְלָכֵן חָלַשׁ דַּעְתֵּיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, דְּהִרְגִּישׁ דִּתְשׁוּבָה נִיצַּחַת הֱשִׁיבוֹ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
and therefore Reish Lakish did not answer him anything then; and so R’ Yochanan’s mind was weakened, for he sensed that Reish Lakish had “answered him with a winning [decisive] response.”

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהֶעֱנִישׁ לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁהֶחְלִישׁ דַּעְתּוֹ וְהוּא הָיָה רַבּוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם סוֹף נֶעֱנַשׁ הוּא עַל יָדוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ, כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם סִיּוּם הַסִּיפּוּר; אֶלָּא שֶׁאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה זֶה מִתּוֹךְ צַעֲרוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ וַחֲרָטָתוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁחֲבֵירוֹ נֶעֱנַשׁ עַל יָדוֹ

And although he punished Reish Lakish for weakening his mind — and he was his teacher — nonetheless, in the end R’ Yochanan himself was punished through him afterward, as it is there [in the] conclusion of the story; only that with him [R’ Yochanan] this was out of his pain, in his teshuvah and regret over his fellow’s being punished through him.246Bava Metzia 84a; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:135 — illness, punishment, and R’ Yochanan’s grief: The Bavli states in sequence that R’ Yochanan’s mind was weakened, Reish Lakish became ill and died, and R’ Yochanan afterward grieved until his own mind departed. It does not explicitly say that R’ Yochanan intentionally caused or decreed the illness. Rav Tzadok reads the sequence as an onesh flowing from the teacher’s hurt and, in Dover Tzedek, as a heavenly consequence of the accusation awakened against Reish Lakish’s root; R’ Yochanan’s later anguish is then read as teshuvah and charatah.
וְהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בְּרַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַשִּׁי [קִידּוּשִׁין פא:] דְּכָל יָמָיו הִתְעַנָּה עַד שֶׁמֵּת בְּאוֹתָהּ מִיתָה, וּמִתְּחִלָּה רָצָה לְהָמִית אֶת עַצְמוֹ

And this is in the manner it is stated regarding R’ Chiya bar Ashi [Kiddushin 81b], who fasted all his days until he died by that [same] death; and at first he wished to put himself to death [thinking he had sinned with a married woman].247Kiddushin 81b: R’ Chiya bar Ashi, who used to fall on his face praying “may the Merciful save me from the evil inclination,” was tested — his own wife disguised herself as the harlot “Charuta”; when he learned the truth he was inconsolable and fasted until he died. R’ Tzadok cites his cry, “rejoice, my intestines!” — confident that no worm would rule his uncorrupted flesh — as the mark of a body wholly guarded and holy.248Kiddushin 81b — repentance for intended transgression: After R’ Chiya bar Ashi’s wife proved that she herself had been the disguised woman, he nevertheless answered, “I intended for a prohibition,” and fasted for the rest of his life until he died. The Gemara thus makes the inner intention, although no forbidden partner was actually involved, the object of repentance. Rav Tzadok invokes that model for remorse whose force lies in the penitent’s own moral reckoning, not merely in an externally completed offense.

הִנִּיחַ יָדוֹ עַל בְּנֵי מֵעָיו, אָמַר: ״שִׂישׂוּ בְּנֵי מֵעַי שִׂישׂוּ! וּמָה סְפֵקוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם כָּךְ, וַדָּאִיּוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה; מוּבְטָח אֲנִי בָּכֶם שֶׁאֵין רִימָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּכֶם״

he placed his hand upon his intestines and said, “rejoice, my intestines, rejoice! if your doubtful [sins] are [dealt with] thus, your certain ones all the more; I am confident of you that no worm or maggot rules over you.”

וַאֲפִילּוּ כָּךְ לֹא נִתְיַישְּׁבָה דַּעְתּוֹ, הִשְׁקוּהוּ סַם שֵׁינָה וֶהֱבִיאוּהוּ לְבֵיתָא דְּשֵׁישָׁא וּבִקְּעוּ אֶת כְּרֵיסוֹ וְהָיוּ מוֹצִיאִים מִמֶּנּוּ סַלִּים מְלֵאִים שׁוּמָּן — וְלֹא הִסְרִיחוּ — קָרָא עַל נַפְשׁוֹ ״אַף בְּשָׂרִי יִשְׁכּוֹן לָבֶטַח״

And even so his mind was not settled; they gave him a sleeping potion and brought him to a marble chamber and split open his belly and were extracting baskets full of fat (for he was very corpulent), and [they did] not rot — [and] he applied to himself, “even my flesh shall dwell secure” (Tehillim 16:9).249Bava Metzia 83b; Tehillim 16:9 — “rejoice, my innards” belongs to R’ Elazar b’R’ Shimon: The ensuing cry “rejoice, my innards,” the assurance that worm and maggot would not rule, the marble-chamber test, and “my flesh shall dwell secure” are the Bavli’s account of R’ Elazar b’R’ Shimon, immediately before the R’ Yishmael b’R’ Yosei episode. They are not part of Kiddushin’s story of R’ Chiya bar Ashi. Rav Tzadok places the episodes together as parallel forms of severe self-scrutiny after a morally troubling act.

וְאַף רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי הִגִּיעַ לְיָדוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה כָּזֶה לִתְפּוֹס גַּנָּבִים; פָּגַשׁ אוֹתוֹ אֵלִיָּהוּ, אָמַר לוֹ: ״עַד מָתַי אַתָּה מוֹסֵר עַמּוֹ שֶׁל אֱלֹקֵינוּ לַהֲרִיגָה?״ אָמַר לוֹ: ״מָה אֶעֱשֶׂה? פְּקוּדַּת הַמֶּלֶךְ הִיא״; אָמַר לוֹ: ״אָבִיךָ בָּרַח לְאָסְיָא, אַתָּה בְּרַח לְלוֹדְקְיָא״

And R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, too, had such a matter come to his hand — to catch thieves; Eliyahu met him [and] said, “how long will you hand over the people of our God to slaying?” He said, “what can I do? it is the king’s decree”; he said, “your father fled to Asya — you flee to Ludkya.”250Bava Metzia 84a — Eliyahu’s rebuke to R’ Yishmael b’R’ Yosei: When R’ Yishmael answered that catching thieves was a royal command, Eliyahu did not accept compulsion as sufficient: his father had fled to Asya, and he too should flee to Ludkya. The source therefore sharply qualifies the preceding “clearing thorns” rationale. Rav Tzadok’s citation preserves both sides: destructive conduct may be understood as removing thorns, yet handing Jews over to execution remains morally perilous even under state authority.

items.h: The theme: The Bava Metzia passage opens with R’ Yochanan’s “beauty [shufreih]” — “I remained from the beautiful ones of Jerusalem” — which is the beauty of the tzaddikim who guard the bris (like “Yosef, of beautiful form”). For the Torah does not mean the imagined bodily beauty of this world (which, truly seen, is “the ultimate ugliness, like the children of Kushites”). Real beauty is only in “the holy flesh of the seed of Israel” — the “nine kav of beauty that Jerusalem took” (Kiddushin 49b), beauty by way of truth.

p: [לב] וְשָׁם [בב״מ] הִתְחִילוּ בְּסִיפּוּר שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאִשְׁתַּיֵּיר מִשַּׁפִּירֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם, וְהוּא הַיֹּפִי לַצַּדִּיקִים שׁוֹמְרֵי הַבְּרִית, כְּעִנְיַן ״יוֹסֵף יְפֵה תֹאַר וִיפֵה מַרְאֶה״

And there [in Bava Metzia] they began with the account of the “beauty [shufreih]” of R’ Yochanan, who “remained from the beautiful ones of Jerusalem” — and this is the beauty [belonging] to the tzaddikim who guard the bris, in the manner of “Yosef, of beautiful form and beautiful appearance” (Bereishis 39:6).251Bava Metzia 84a: “R’ Yochanan said: I alone remain of the beautiful ones of Jerusalem. One who wishes to see R’ Yochanan’s beauty, let him bring a silver goblet fresh from the smith, fill it with red pomegranate seeds, wreathe its rim with red roses, and set it between sun and shade — that radiance is a semblance of R’ Yochanan’s beauty.” And R’ Yochanan would sit at the gates of the immersion-place, “so that when the daughters of Israel emerge from their mitzvah-immersion they meet me, and have children as beautiful as I and as learned in Torah as I” — fearing no evil eye, “for I am of the seed of Yosef, over whom the evil eye has no power” (“a fruitful son above the eye,” Bereishis 49:22).252Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim §12 — R’ Yochanan’s beauty as kedushas ha-bris: Rav Tzadok gives an unusually direct parallel to this se’if. He explains Yosef’s “beautiful form and beautiful appearance” as a clean, refined body rooted in kedushas ha-bris, and reads R’ Yochanan’s being among the “beautiful ones of Jerusalem” the same way. He joins this to R’ Yochanan’s statement that he came from Yosef, whose eye did not seek what was not his (Berachos 20a), and contrasts such beauty with the “Kushi” image of blemish. This is not merely a conceptual comparison: Peri Tzadik explicitly identifies the shufra of R’ Yochanan with perfection in guarding the bris.

כִּי לֹא דִּיבְּרָה תוֹרָה בַּמֵּתִים מְיוּפֵּי הַדִּמְיוֹן שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וּמִי שֶׁעֵינַיִם לוֹ יִרְאֶה שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַכִּיעוּר וְכִבְנֵי כּוּשִׁיִּים, וְאֵין יֹפִי בִּבְשַׂר הַגּוּף אֶלָּא בִּבְשַׂר קֹדֶשׁ זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל

For the Torah did not speak, regarding the dead, of the “imagined beauty” of this world — and one who has eyes will see that it is the ultimate ugliness, “like the children of Kushites” — and there is no beauty in the flesh of the body except in the “holy flesh” of the seed of Israel.253Rashi to Vayikra 19:2, citing Vayikra Rabbah — guarding arayos as holiness: On “You shall be holy,” Rashi explains that one must separate from forbidden sexual relations and sinful thoughts, adding that wherever the Torah places a fence around arayos it speaks of holiness. This supplies a classical basis for Rav Tzadok’s association of bodily holiness with restraint in the realm of the bris. The source itself does not define such restraint as physical beauty; Rav Tzadok develops the further claim that a body purified in this sphere is what Torah truly calls beautiful.
וְהֵם ״תִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין יֹפִי שֶׁנָּטְלָה יְרוּשָׁלַיִם״ מֵעֲשָׂרָה קַבִּין שֶׁיָּרַד לָעוֹלָם, כִּדְאִיתָא [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:], הַיְינוּ מַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא יֹפִי עַל דֶּרֶךְ הָאֱמֶת

And they are the “nine kav of beauty that Jerusalem took” of the ten kav that descended to the world, as it is stated [Kiddushin 49b] — namely, that which is called “beauty” by way of truth.254Kiddushin 49b: “Ten measures [kav] of beauty descended to the world — nine were taken by Jerusalem” (and likewise ten of wisdom — nine taken by Eretz Yisrael; ten of Torah — nine by Eretz Yisrael, etc.). R’ Tzadok reads the “nine kav” as the nine supernal rungs (down to Yesod) — “beauty by way of truth,” the holiness of the guarded bris.

וְזֶהוּ דְּיָתֵיב אַשַּׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה, ״דְּלֶהֱווֹ בְּנֵי שַׁפִּירֵי כְּוָותִי, גְּמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא כְּוָותִי״; וְאִם רָצָה לוֹמַר יֹפִי גּוּפָנִי לְבַד, לָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לֵישֵׁב מִשּׁוּם זֶה בְּשַׁעֲרֵי טְבִילָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לֵיהּ לְהַקְדִּים זֶה לִגְמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא

And this is [why] he “sat at the gates of immersion” — “that they have children beautiful like me, learned in Torah like me”; and had he meant [only] bodily beauty, he should not have sat, for that reason, at the gates of immersion, and all the more he should not have placed this [beauty] before “learned in Torah.”

וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּרוֹצֶה לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁנִּקְרָא אֵצֶל הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהַתּוֹרָה וְיִשְׂרָאֵל הַהוֹלְכִים בְּעִקְבוֹתָיו ״יֹפִי בַּגּוּף״; וְזֶה הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַיִּרְאָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״לְמַעַן תִּהְיֶה יִרְאָתוֹ״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כִּי אָמַרְתִּי רַק אֵין יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי יִרְאַת אֱלֹקִים מְבַטֶּלֶת תַּאֲווֹת רָעוֹת

And perforce, as I wrote, he means that which is called, by Hashem and the Torah and the Israel who walk in His footsteps, “beauty in the body”; and this is through the fear [of God], as it says, “so that His fear be [upon your faces]” (Shemos 20:17), and it says,255Nedarim 20a; Yevamos 79a — yirah upon the face as shame that prevents sin: Chazal read “so that His fear may be upon your faces, that you not sin” (Shemos 20:17) as referring to boshes, shame: shame leads to fear of sin, and one who is capable of shame does not quickly sin. Yevamos lists bashfulness among the three identifying traits of Israel and cites this same verse. Thus the verse itself links yirah to a disposition manifested “upon the face.” Rav Tzadok develops that visible moral refinement into his language of genuine bodily beauty. “for I said, only there is no fear of God [in this place]” (Bereishis 20:11) — for the fear of God nullifies evil desires.256Bereishis 20:11 — absence of yiras Elokim and unrestrained desire: Avraham explains why he concealed Sarah’s status: “Surely there is no fear of God in this place, and they will kill me because of my wife.” The verse itself therefore links the absence of yiras Elokim with the possibility of murder in pursuit of sexual possession. Rav Tzadok generalizes this biblical logic: yirah restrains the evil desires that otherwise seize the body, and is therefore the spiritual root of the purified “beauty in the body” described here.
וְזֶהוּ יִרְאָתוֹ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ, וְעַל כֵּן הִקְדִּימוּ לִגְמִירֵי אוֹרָיְיתָא

And this is [the] “fear” that must precede his wisdom, and therefore they placed it before “learned in Torah.”257Pirkei Avos 3:9; Rabbeinu Yonah — fear must precede wisdom: R’ Chanina ben Dosa teaches that when a person’s fear of sin precedes his wisdom, his wisdom endures; when wisdom precedes fear, it does not. Rabbeinu Yonah explains that one whose starting purpose is to guard himself from sin acquires wisdom in a form that reinforces that prior moral commitment. This is the direct classical basis for Rav Tzadok’s phrase “his fear must precede his wisdom.” Rav Tzadok then reads R’ Yochanan’s ordering — “beautiful like me” before “learned in Torah like me” — homiletically through that principle.

items.h: The theme: Earlier in that passage, the Sages recount that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon and R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei were “corpulent [ba’alei basar].” R’ Tzadok reads this too as making known the holiness of their bodily flesh — that even all their physicality was wholly “holy to Hashem.” For otherwise, why record of them that they were fleshy at all? — since an abundance of flesh, which becomes “worm and maggot,” is plainly only a disgrace (as the Mishnah in Avos teaches, “one who increases flesh increases worms”).

p: [לג] וְשָׁם מִקּוֹדֶם, בַּר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בַּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן וְר׳ יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּר׳ יוֹסֵי, סִיפְּרוּ מַה שֶּׁהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי בָּשָׂר — נִרְאֶה לִי גַּם כֵּן הַכַּוָּונָה לְהוֹדִיעַ מִקְּדֻשַּׁת בְּשַׂר גּוּפָם, שֶׁגַּם כָּל גּוּפָנִיּוּתָם הָיָה כּוּלּוֹ קֹדֶשׁ לַה׳

And there, earlier, regarding R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon and R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, they recounted that they were “corpulent [ba’alei basar]” — it appears to me the intent, too, is to make known the holiness of the flesh of their body: that all their physicality, too, was wholly “holy to Hashem.”258Bava Metzia 83b–84a: the Gemara relates that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon and R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei were so corpulent that, when they stood face to face, a yoke of oxen could pass beneath them without touching. A [gentile] noblewoman taunted that their children could not be theirs; they answered variously (including “love compresses the flesh”). R’ Tzadok reads the account not as mere anatomical lore but as testimony to the holiness of their flesh — otherwise mere obesity would be, as Avos teaches, only a disgrace.

דְּזוּלַת זֶה, מַה שַׁיָּיךְ לְהַזְכִּיר בָּהֶם דָּבָר זֶה, דְּהָיוּ בַּעֲלֵי בָּשָׂר כְּלָל? וְהָא וַדַּאי וּפָשׁוּט דְּרִיבּוּי בָּשָׂר הַנַּעֲשֶׂה רִימָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לִגְנַאי, וּכְדִתְנַן בְּאָבוֹת ״מַרְבֶּה בָשָׂר [מַרְבֶּה רִימָּה]״

For otherwise, what relevance is there to mention of them this matter — that they were corpulent at all?259Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev §7; Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:15 — “holy flesh” as sanctified physicality: Rav Tzadok elsewhere states that when the blemish of the bris is rectified, the body is in holiness and is called basar kodesh, so bodily enjoyment itself can be taken in holiness; in Likkutei Maamarim he likewise describes milah as the bodily distinction between “holy flesh” and “impure flesh.” These are direct conceptual parallels to the present se’if. Rav Tzadok is not praising corpulence as such; he is claiming that the tzaddik’s physical flesh can itself become a vessel and expression of kedushah. And it is certainly plain that an “abundance of flesh,” which becomes “worm and maggot,”260Tehillim 16:8–9; Bava Metzia 83b — R’ Elazar’s flesh as resistant to decay: Immediately before the corpulence passage, the Gemara recounts that R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon said of his innards that worm and maggot would not rule over them. Baskets of his fat were then placed in the summer sun and did not putrefy, despite red vessels that normally would; he applied to himself, “my flesh also shall dwell securely.” The biblical verse itself follows “I have set Hashem before me always.” Thus the sugya already presents his bodily flesh as unusually aligned with righteousness and preservation. Rav Tzadok develops that datum into the broader claim here about the holiness of the physicality of these Sages. is only to [one’s] disgrace, as we learned in Avos,261Avos 2:7; Rabbeinu Yonah and Derekh Chayyim ad loc. — ordinary flesh and the principle of decay: Rabbeinu Yonah explains “one who increases flesh increases worms” as the futility of bodily pampering before inevitable corruption. The Maharal broadens the point: “flesh” represents material embodiment itself, and materiality pursued as materiality carries he’eder — loss and decay — within it. This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s question. If ordinary excess flesh signifies precisely the perishable side of corporeality, the Gemara’s deliberate preservation of these Sages’ bodily dimensions invites an interpretation beyond mere physical bulk. “one who increases flesh increases worms” (Avos 2:7).262Midrash Shmuel on Avos 2:7; Be’er HaGolah, Be’er 5 §4 — the Bava Metzia episode as an exception, not a celebration of bulk: Midrash Shmuel explicitly points to R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon as an exception to “more flesh, more worms”: his fat did not decay, and the commentary distinguishes his natural corpulence from flesh cultivated through indulgence. Maharal, explaining the same Bava Metzia exchange “love compresses the flesh,” reads the marital union described there as empowered by a higher divine bond, not as merely animal physicality. Neither source states Rav Tzadok’s full thesis that their flesh was “wholly holy to Hashem,” but together they show a classical interpretive tradition that distinguishes their bodies from ordinary material excess and reads the surrounding sugya in spiritual terms.

items.h: The theme: Rather, the intent is to tell of the holiness of their bris: “wisdom of nine kav” is the holiness of the “nine rungs,” from the top of all the rungs down to the Yesod. The Sages denote the middos by “kav” (Kiddushin 49b, “ten kav”), meaning the ten middos of every “stature.” R’ Yochanan’s “five kav” (or “three”) is the span from Gevurah to Yesod (or Netzach-Hod-Yesod) — less than R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, whose clarification of holiness reached the root; and Rav Pappa’s, less still, for “the generations go and diminish.”

p: [לד] אֲבָל הַכַּוָּונָה לְסַפֵּר בִּקְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית שֶׁלָּהֶם, וְ״חׇכְמַת בַּת תִּשְׁעָה קַבִּין״ הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הַתִּשְׁעָה דַּרְגִּין שֶׁמֵּרֵישׁ כָּל דַּרְגִּין עַד הַיְסוֹד

But the intent is to tell of the holiness of their bris; and “wisdom of nine kav” is the holiness of the “nine rungs,” from the top of all the rungs down to the Yesod.263Bava Metzia 84a — the measured sequence Rav Tzadok interprets: Bava Metzia measures R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei’s organ as a vessel of nine kav; R’ Yochanan’s as five kav, or in another version three; and Rav Pappa himself by the baskets of Harpanya. The Bavli gives these physical measures without a mystical explanation. Rav Tzadok reads the descending sequence homiletically as degrees of kedushas ha-bris; that kabbalistic reading is his extension, not the sugya’s plain statement.

וְדַרְכָּן לְכַנּוֹת הַמִּדּוֹת בְּקַבִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּקִידּוּשִׁין מט:] ״עֲשָׂרָה קַבִּין״ עַל כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים, וְכַוָּונָתָם עַל עֶשֶׂר מִדּוֹת וּמַדְרֵיגוֹת שֶׁל כָּל קוֹמָה הַיְּדוּעִים

And their way is to denote the middos by “kav,” as they said [Kiddushin 49b], “ten kav,” regarding several things — their intent being upon the ten middos and rungs of every “stature,” as is known.264Kiddushin 49b; Peri Tzadik, Vayikra §5 — “kav” as a scale of the middos: Kiddushin repeatedly distributes “ten kav” of wisdom, beauty, wealth, and other qualities — nine to one place and one to the rest. More directly, Rav Tzadok elsewhere interprets Bava Metzia 38a’s “one kav of his own more than nine of his fellow” through the ten middos: nine are the upper measures of holiness, while the tenth, Malchus, is the person’s “own kav” acquired through service. This strongly parallels his method here; the specific identification of Bava Metzia 84a’s nine kav with the rungs through Yesod is the further application of this se’if.

וּבַת חֲמִשָּׁה קַבִּין אוֹ שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן, הַיְינוּ מֵהַגְּבוּרָה עַד הַיְסוֹד, אוֹ נֶגֶד נֶצַח הוֹד יְסוֹד; וְזֶהוּ פָּחוֹת מִדְּר׳ יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּר׳ יוֹסֵי שֶׁהִגִּיעַ בֵּירוּר קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ עַד הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ, וּדְרַב פַּפָּא בְּפָחוֹת עוֹד, כִּי הַדּוֹרוֹת הוֹלְכִין וּמִתְמַעֲטִין

And the “five kav” — or “three” — of R’ Yochanan is [the span] from Gevurah to Yesod, or corresponding to Netzach-Hod-Yesod; and this is less than R’ Yishmael b’Rabbi Yosei, whose clarification of holiness reached to the root; and Rav Pappa’s [was] less still, for the generations265Sefer Yetzirah 1:3–4; Rabbeinu Bahya to Bereishis 17:13 — ten sefirot and the bris of Yesod: Sefer Yetzirah establishes the tenfold sefirah structure — “ten and not nine, ten and not eleven” — and places a “singular covenant” in the bodily symbolism of the organ. Rabbeinu Bahya’s kabbalistic reading of bris milah identifies the eternal covenant with “tzaddik, yesod olam” and the covenantal organ with Yesod. These provide the classical basis for linking bris and Yesod within a tenfold structure; Rav Tzadok develops that framework into the specific “nine rungs” and varying kav-measures of this se’if. “go and diminish.”266Eruvin 53a; Shabbos 112b — “the generations go and diminish”: R’ Yochanan contrasts the “hearts of the early ones” with later Sages through progressively narrower Temple entrances; Shabbos similarly says that if the early generations were like angels, later ones are merely human — and if they were human, later ones are like donkeys. These are classical expressions of generational diminution. They concern Torah and spiritual stature broadly; Rav Tzadok applies the principle here specifically to descending degrees of clarified kedushas ha-bris.
וְכָל אֶחָד שֶׁהָיָה גַּם הוּא בְּעִנְיָן זֶה הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַבְחִין וּלְהַשִּׂיג מַדְרֵיגַת הַקּוֹדֵם לוֹ, שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן מֵעִנְיַן מַדְרֵגָתוֹ וְגָדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ קְצָת

And each one who was himself engaged in this matter [of guarding the bris] could discern and apprehend the rung of the one before him — who was also of the character of his rung, and somewhat greater than him.

[וְאׇמְנָם, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא [בְּשַׁבָּת קכד.] דְּ״דִּיקּוּלֵי דְּהַרְפַּנְיָא שְׁלוֹשָׁה מִקּוּפָּה״, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת [שָׁם קכו סע״ב] ד״ה ״מְפַנִּין״ מֵהַיְּרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּ״קוּפָּה שְׁלוֹשָׁה סְאִין״, אִם כֵּן דִּיקּוּלָא סְאָה — וּמְיַישֵּׁב עַל פִּי זֶה שִׁיעוּרֵי הַקַּבִּין הַנִּזְכָּרִים]

[And indeed, according to what is stated [Shabbos 124a] that “the baskets [dikulei] of Harpanya are a third of a kupah,” and Tosafos [there, 126b, s.v. “mefanin”] from the Yerushalmi that “a kupah is three se’ah” — if so, a dikula is a se’ah — and on this basis he reconciles the measures of the “kav” mentioned]. — Thus even the Sages’267Yerushalmi Shabbos 18:1; Bava Metzia 84a; Sefer HeArukh — the kupah/dikula calculation: The Yerushalmi derives that a kupah holds three se’ah. Bava Metzia 84a compares Rav Pappa to the “baskets of Harpanya,” and the Arukh explains dikurei/dikulei as baskets. Rav Tzadok’s parenthetical appears to combine these measurement traditions to reconcile the arithmetic of the kav-measures. The printed citation to Shabbos 124a is difficult to verify in the standard text; the Bavli discussion of the kupot is at Shabbos 126b–127a. This technical calculation is not an earlier source for his kabbalistic reading. “corpulence” and “beauty,” and their very measures, are read by R’ Tzadok as a coded testimony to the rungs of holiness each attained in guarding the bris — the higher the guarding, the “greater” the flesh that is wholly holy.

items.h: The theme: R’ Yochanan’s beauty stems from the holiness of the yesod [the guarded covenant] drawn from Gevurah — the rung of Yitzchak, “dwelling in the parched Negev,” dried of all desire. This is the beauty of Jerusalem, the level of perfected yirah. Because he was of the intense Gevuros, “he had no hadras panim [beard]” — the beard signifies the middos of Rachamim.

p: [לה] וְזֶהוּ שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, שֶׁקְּדֻשַּׁת הַיְסוֹד שֶׁלּוֹ נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַגְּבוּרָה, דַּרְגָּא דְּיִצְחָק ״יוֹשֵׁב בְּאֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב״ מְנוּגָּב מִכָּל תַּאֲוָה, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּתְמוּרָה טז.] עַל פָּסוּק ״אֶרֶץ הַנֶּגֶב נְתַתָּנִי״

And this is the “beauty” of R’ Yochanan — that the holiness of his yesod is drawn from Gevurah, the rung of Yitzchak, “dwelling in the parched Negev [eretz haNegev],” dried [menugav] of all desire, as it is brought [in Temurah 16a] on the verse “You have given me the Negev land.”268Temurah 16a: On Achsah’s plea “You have given me the Negev land [eretz haNegev]” (Yehoshua 15:19), the Gemara expounds: “a home dried out [menugav] of all goodness.” R’ Tzadok applies this to Yitzchak, the Gevurah, “dwelling in the Negev” — dried of all desire — as the root of R’ Yochanan’s beauty, which is the perfected yirah of Jerusalem.
וְזֶהוּ הַיֹּפִי דִּירוּשָׁלַיִם שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵגַת שְׁלֵימוּת הַיִּרְאָה כַּנּוֹדָע

And this is the beauty of Jerusalem, which is the level of the “perfection of fear [of Heaven],” as is known.269Bereishis Rabbah 56:10; Peri Tzadik, Pesach §44 — Yerushalayim as yirah shleimah: Bereishis Rabbah joins Avraham’s Yireh and Shem’s Shalem as Yerushalayim. Peri Tzadik, Pesach §44 reads the name as yirah shleimah and links it to maaser sheni’s “that you may learn to fear.” Rav Tzadok applies that perfected yirah here to R’ Yochanan’s beauty and Gevurah-rooted kedushas ha-yesod.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיָה מִתֹּקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת, עַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּ״הַדְרַת פָּנִים זָקָן״ לֹא הָיָה לוֹ, דְּהַדִּיקְנָא מוֹרֶה עַל מִדּוֹת הָרַחֲמִים כַּנּוֹדָע

And because he was of the intensity of the Gevuros, therefore it said that “the splendor of the face — a beard” he did not have; for the beard indicates the middos of Rachamim [mercy], as is known.270Bava Metzia 84a; Rashi ad loc.; Zohar, Idra Rabba; Sha’ar HaKavanot, Derushei Vaya’avor §5 — beauty, beard, and mercy: Bava Metzia calls R’ Yochanan a remnant of Jerusalem’s beauty but says he lacked hadras panim; Rashi: “a beard.” Kabbalistic sources treat the tikkunei dikna as channels of rachamim; Sha’ar HaKavanot links the thirteen middos ha-rachamim to the thirteen beard-tikkunim. The physical datum is Talmudic; its Gevurah-versus-Rachamim reading is Rav Tzadok’s.

וְאַף דְּהָיָה אֶצְלוֹ ״רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן״ דְּטַב מִכָּל סִטְרִין, לְפִי שֶׁזִּילְזֵל בְּרוּגְזֵיהּ דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שֶׁהָיָה גַּם כֵּן ״רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן״ — נִמְצָא פְּגָם בְּרוּגְזָא דִּילֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן

And though he possessed “the anger of the Sages,” which is “good from every side,”271Taanis 4a; Zohar II 182b; Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev §7 — rogza d’rabbanan: Taanis says a sharp Torah scholar’s heat is Torah boiling within him. The Zohar calls rogza d’rabbanan “good on every side”; Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Kislev §7 cites this as Torah-fire. Rav Tzadok adds that slighting Reish Lakish’s equally holy anger exposed a defect in R’ Yochanan’s own Gevurah. because he slighted the anger of Reish Lakish — which was also “the anger of the Sages” — a blemish was found in his own anger as well.272Rogza d’rabbanan (holy anger): on “the anger of the Sages, which is good from every side,” see above (this Siman, and note on Berachos/rogza). R’ Tzadok’s point: even holy anger belongs to the Gevuros, and R’ Yochanan’s slighting of Reish Lakish’s equally-holy anger left a “blemish” in his own — the single remaining trace that necessitated the episode of his death.

וּמִפְּנֵי שֶׁבָּא לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הֶעְדֵּר יְדִיעָתוֹ בְּמַעֲלַת וּמַדְרֵגַת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, שֶׁלֹּא הֶחֱזִיקוֹ בְּמַדְרֵגָה כָּל כָּךְ שֶׁתִּיקֵּן כָּל כָּךְ הַקּוֹדֵם, עַד דְּגַם הָתָם ״רַבִּי קָרוּ לֵיהּ״ — עַל כֵּן אַף מִדַּעְתּוֹ

And because it came to him through his lack of knowledge of Reish Lakish’s stature and rung — that he did not hold him to be at so high a level that he had rectified the past so thoroughly, until even there “Rebbi they called him” — therefore it was even unwitting on his part.273Vayikra 4; Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1 — shogeg still requires kapparah: Vayikra’s chatas and Rambam show that inadvertence removes deliberate status without necessarily removing kapparah: an unwitting actionable prohibition whose deliberate violation bears karet requires a chatas. Rav Tzadok uses that model aggadically here; he does not equate every inadvertent interpersonal wrong with that sacrificial law.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהַשּׁוֹגֵג צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה; וְכֵן רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ גַּם כֵּן לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה מִן ״הַנֶּעֱלָבִין וְאֵין עוֹלְבִין״

only that the inadvertent one, too, requires pardon and atonement; and likewise Reish Lakish [needed the same], since he was not of “those who are insulted and do not insult.”274Shabbos 88b; Yoma 23a — “those who are insulted and do not insult”: Chazal praise those insulted yet not insulting in return, who hear shame without answering and act from love. Rav Tzadok invokes this exceptional restraint as the refinement still lacking in Reish Lakish’s understandable but responsive hurt.

אֲבָל וַדַּאי גַּם רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן הֶחֱזִיקוֹ תְּחִלָּה כָּךְ, דְּגַם מַעֲשָׂיו הַקּוֹדְמִין נֶחְשָׁבִין כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְאֵין כָּאן גְּנוּת כְּלָל [וְעַיֵּין לְעֵיל סִימָן א׳], וְלֹא נִתְכַּוֵּון לְגַנּוֹתוֹ מִתְּחִלָּה

But certainly R’ Yochanan, too, at first held him thus — that his earlier deeds as well are reckoned as merits, and there is no disgrace here at all [see above, Siman 1] — and he did not intend to shame him at the outset.275Yoma 86b; Takanas HaShavin, opening of this siman — sins becoming merits: Reish Lakish teaches that teshuvah me’ahavah turns deliberate sins into merits. At the opening of this siman Rav Tzadok applies this directly to Reish Lakish: after complete repentance, even his former bandit life can become merit. That grounds R’ Yochanan’s initial view that mentioning the past carried no disgrace.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקְּרָאוֹ ״לִיסְטָאָה״, לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה בֵּין הַלִּיסְטִים, וְגַם דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הָיָה דּוֹמֶה לְלִיסְטִיּוּת
And even though he called him “bandit [listaa],” it was because he had been among the bandits, and also because the deed resembled banditry.

וּבִלְעָם הָרָשָׁע קָרְיֵיהּ לְפִינְחָס ״לִיסְטָאָה״, ורז״ל הֶעְתִּיקוּ הַלָּשׁוֹן [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קו רע״ב], וְהוּא עַל הֲרִיגָתוֹ לְזִמְרִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה בְּבֵית דִּין וְלֹא נִצְטַוָּוה עַל זֶה, דְּ״אִם בָּא לִשְׁאוֹל אֵין מוֹרִין לוֹ״, רַק שֶׁקִּינֵּא קִנְאַת ה׳

And wicked Bilaam called Pinchas “listaa,” and the Sages transmitted the phrasing [Sanhedrin 106b] — this being on account of his slaying of Zimri, who was not liable to court-death and about whom he had not been commanded (for “had he come to ask [beforehand], they would not have instructed him to do it”), only that “he was zealous with the zeal of the Lord.”276Sanhedrin 106b: A heretic tells R’ Chanina that Bilaam’s chronicle recorded, “Bilaam the lame was thirty-three years old when Pinchas the bandit [Pinchas listaa] killed him.” R’ Tzadok notes that the Sages preserved wicked Bilaam’s epithet “listaa” for Pinchas — because Pinchas slew Zimri, who bore no court-imposed death penalty and about whom Pinchas had not been commanded (“had he come to ask, they would not have ruled for him”); killing one not legally liable, purely for Heaven’s sake “to clear thorns,” is “banditry for the sake of Heaven.”
וְהַהוֹרֵג לְמִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ חַיָּיב מִיתָה מִן הַדִּין אֶלָּא שֶׁכַּוָּונָתוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם ״לְכַלּוֹת קוֹצִים״ וְכַיּוֹצֵא, זֶהוּ מַעֲשֵׂה לִסְטִיּוּת לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
And one who kills someone not liable to death by law, but whose intent is for Heaven, “to clear away thorns” and the like — this is “an act of banditry for the sake of Heaven.”

items.h: The theme: R’ Yochanan at first did not intend disgrace or ona’as devarim — he thought there was no disgrace in it. But Reish Lakish, who felt the shame (“what benefit [have I gained]”), supposed he did intend to shame him. So although Reish Lakish knew within himself that in truth all was reckoned to him as merits, this had not yet been revealed and clarified to every eye — hence he had not yet reached the utter completion of the rectification, manifest to all.

p: [לו] וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִתְּחִלָּה לֹא כִּיוֵּון לִגְנוּת וְאוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּמַעֲשָׂיו רִאשׁוֹנִים, רַק חָשַׁב דְּאֵין לוֹ גְּנוּת מִזֶּה
And R’ Yochanan at first did not intend disgrace or “verbal wronging,” God forbid, regarding his earlier deeds — he only thought that there is no disgrace to him from this.

אֲבָל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳ שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁ גְּנוּת, וְסָבוּר דְּכִיוֵּון לְגַנּוֹתוֹ — עַל כֵּן אַף עַל פִּי דְּיָדַע בְּנַפְשׁוֹ דְּבֶאֱמֶת הַכֹּל נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ לִזְכֻיּוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה וְנִתְבָּרֵר זֶה עֲדַיִין לְעֵין כֹּל וּלְעֵינֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם עֲדַיִין

But Reish Lakish, who said to him “what benefit,” etc. — who felt the disgrace, and supposed that he intended to shame him — therefore, even though he knew within himself that in truth all was reckoned to him as merits, nonetheless this was not yet revealed and clarified to every eye and to the eyes of people.
וּמִמֵּילָא דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא הִגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית גְּמַר הַתִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מְבוֹרָר לַכֹּל
And consequently he had not yet reached the ultimate completion of the perfect rectification that would be clear to all.

דְּגַם מַה שֶּׁבְּנֵי אָדָם חוֹשְׁדִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אִם אֵינוֹ מִצַּד אֵיבָה וְשִׂנְאָה, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מַה מִזֶּה עֲדַיִין בַּלֵּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא פָּסַק הַחֲשָׁד וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן יח:]

For even that which people suspect in this world — if it is not from enmity and hatred — perforce there is in him some faint trace of it still in the heart, at any rate, so long as the suspicion has not ceased, as they said [Moed Katan 18b].277Moed Katan 18b: the Gemara’s discussions of chashad — that suspicion, once it attaches, reflects and does not fully lift until the matter is truly cleared. R’ Tzadok reads this as: lingering human suspicion (when not born of hatred) testifies to some faint residue still in the heart, until the rectification is complete and “the sin of Israel is sought and is no more” (Yirmeyah 50:20).278Meiri on Moed Katan 18b — the gradations of suspicion and the exception of hatred: The Meiri spells out the sugya’s ladder: ordinarily suspicion implies the act, part of it, a thought of it, or pleasure in seeing it; he expressly excludes suspicion born of jealousy or hatred. This closely parallels Rav Tzadok’s qualification “if it is not from enmity and hatred.” The Gemara supplies the rule; Rav Tzadok turns it inward, treating lingering public suspicion as evidence that the final inner birur is not yet manifest.
וּבִגְמַר הַתִּיקּוּן דְּ״יְבוּקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״, יִפָּסֵק גַּם הַחֲשָׁד מִפִּי הַבְּרִיּוֹת

And at the completion of the rectification, when “the sin of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none,” the suspicion, too, will cease from the mouths of people.279Yirmeyahu 50:20 — “the sin of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none”: In context, Yirmeyahu describes Israel and Judah after Bavel’s fall: their iniquity will be sought but not found, “for I will pardon those whom I leave.” The verse speaks first of Divine pardon. Rav Tzadok extends it to earthly recognition: at the completed tikkun, even the social suspicion attached to sin disappears.

וּמִצַּד הַזֶּה בָּא לַחְשׁוֹד אֶת רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁבָּא לְאוֹנָאוֹתוֹ בִּדְבָרִים, דְּמִי שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ חִסָּרוֹן לֹא יָכוֹל לַחְשׁוֹד אֶת חֲבֵירוֹ גַּם כֵּן בְּחִסָּרוֹן, דְּאֵין מַרְגִּישׁ בִּמְצִיאוּת חִסָּרוֹן וְדָן הַכֹּל לְכַף זְכוּת

And from this side he came to suspect R’ Yochanan of coming to wrong him with words; for one who has in him no trace of a defect cannot suspect his fellow of a defect either — he does not sense the existence of a defect and judges everything favorably.280Pirkei Avos 1:6; Rambam ad loc.; Shabbos 97a, 127b — judging favorably and suspecting the righteous: Avos commands judging every person favorably. The Rambam requires a favorable reading even of an apparently bad act by a known tzaddik when a plausible good interpretation remains, citing the warning against suspecting the worthy; Shabbos adds that one who judges favorably is judged favorably. Rav Tzadok adds the inner claim that freedom from a defect itself limits one’s tendency to project that defect onto another.

וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ ז״ל ״כָּל הַפּוֹסֵל בְּמוּמוֹ פּוֹסֵל״, דְּאֵין אָדָם פּוֹסֵל לַחֲבֵירוֹ בְּמַה שֶּׁאֵין בּוֹ, אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מִזֶּה, וְאָז רוֹאֶה גַּם בַּחֲבֵירוֹ מֵאוֹתוֹ חִסָּרוֹן שֶׁבּוֹ, כִּי הַנְּפָשׁוֹת כְּמַרְאוֹת כַּנּוֹדָע

And therefore the Sages said, “whoever disqualifies, disqualifies with his own blemish” — a man does not disqualify his fellow with what is not in himself, unless there is in his own soul a trace of it, and then he sees in his fellow, too, that same defect that is in him; for souls are like mirrors, as is known.281Kiddushin 70a: “Whoever disqualifies [others], disqualifies with his own blemish [kol haposel — b’mumo posel].” R’ Tzadok: a person cannot perceive in another a defect he does not himself possess in some trace — “souls are like mirrors.” Reish Lakish’s very feeling of the sting thus marked the last faint trace still requiring clarification.282Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:90 — “souls are like mirrors” as Rav Tzadok’s general principle: Rav Tzadok states there almost the same rule as here: “souls are like mirrors” and “b’mumo posel,” because one’s perception of another follows what he himself is. He also reads “judge every person favorably” as a demand to become the kind of person whose own inner state enables favorable perception. The present metaphor is thus part of a broader Rav Tzadok principle.
וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ שְׁנֵיהֶם הָיוּ מִתֹּקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת הַקְּדוֹשׁוֹת, וְהָיוּ נְקִיִּים לְגַמְרֵי מִכָּל תַּאֲוָה וְחֶמְדָּה גּוּפָנִית דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish were both of the intensity of the holy Gevuros, and were completely clean of all desire and bodily craving of this world.
דְּעַל כֵּן נָסֵיב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לַאֲחָתֵיהּ, וְלֹא חָשׁ שֶׁיֹּאמְרוּ כו׳ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהִרְגִּישׁוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם [ד״ה ״אִי״], וְלֹא פֵּירְשׁוּ הַטַּעַם

which is why Reish Lakish married his [R’ Yochanan’s] sister, and did not worry “lest they say [it is permitted]” — a difficulty the Tosafos there felt [s.v. “iy”] but did not explain.283Tosafos, Bava Metzia 84a (s.v. “iy”): on Reish Lakish’s marrying R’ Yochanan’s sister, Tosafos raises — but leaves unexplained — why there was no concern “lest people say [it is permitted]” R’ Tzadok resolves it: such concern applies only where a sin of desire is at issue; Reish Lakish was universally known to be clean of bodily desire, so no suspicion could attach.

אֲבָל הוּא מְבוֹאָר דְּשָׁם הָיָה חֵטְא בְּתַאֲוָה שַׁיָּיךְ ״שֶׁמָּא יֹאמְרוּ״ כו׳, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אֵצֶל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא יָדְעֵי דְּהָיָה נָקִי מִזֶּה וְלֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ בְּכָךְ, כִּי לֹא הָיָה בְּלִבּוֹ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ מִדָּבָר זֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מָקוֹם לְחָשְׁדוֹ

But it is clear: where there is a sin of desire, “lest they say [it is permitted]” applies; whereas with Reish Lakish all the world knew he was clean of this and would not suspect him of it, for there was in his heart no trace of this matter that could give room to suspect him.
וְאֵין חוֹשְׁדִין לְאָדָם אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ שֶׁמֶץ מַה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וַהֲרֵי דְּהָיָה נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי בְּתַאֲוָה בְּלִי שׁוּם מַשֶּׁהוּ שֶׁמֶץ מַה בַּמַּעֲמַקִּים גַּם כֵּן

And one does not suspect a person unless there is in him some trace, as I wrote; and behold, [Reish Lakish] was completely clean of desire, without even the slightest trace in the depths as well.284Peri Tzadik, Miketz §6 — “b’mumo posel” and a suspected blemish in desire: In Miketz §6, Rav Tzadok says Yosef’s brothers knew themselves clean of the suspected sexual fault and therefore reasoned, by “b’mumo posel,” that Yosef must bear it. This parallels the present se’if: suspicion reveals something about the perceiver even when the suspicion is mistaken.

items.h: The theme: R’ Yochanan’s “beauty” — teacher of Reish Lakish and of R’ Abbahu (whose beauty was “a semblance of Yaakov Avinu’s,” which is the supernal “form of Adam”) — is the ultimate beauty of the human form after Adam’s sin. “A semblance of Adam’s beauty” means Adam before the sin, whose facial radiance was then taken. Yaakov rectified his portion fully (“he did not die”), yet in this world only a semblance remained — as Shabbos is “a semblance of Olam Haba” (one-sixtieth: the faintest still-perceptible trace).

p: [לז] וְכֵן שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן שֶׁהָיָה רַבּוֹ דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְכֵן הָיָה רַבּוֹ דְּר׳ אַבָּהוּ, שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּשֻׁפְרֵיהּ מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה, שֶׁהוּא צוּרַת אָדָם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה

And likewise the “beauty [shufreih]” of R’ Yochanan, who was the teacher of Reish Lakish, and also the teacher of R’ Abbahu — of whom they said there that “his beauty was a semblance [me’ein] of Yaakov Avinu’s,” which is the “supernal form of Adam.”285Bava Metzia 84a: “The beauty of R’ Abbahu is a semblance [me’ein] of the beauty of Yaakov Avinu; the beauty of Yaakov Avinu is a semblance of the beauty of Adam HaRishon.” When the Gemara asks why R’ Yochanan is not included, it answers: “R’ Yochanan is different, for he had no hadras panim [beard].” R’ Tzadok reads “a semblance of Adam” as Adam before the sin (whose facial radiance was later removed), and R’ Yochanan’s beardlessness as a mark of his belonging to the intense Gevuros.286Yisrael Kedoshim §10 — Yaakov and the supernal “form of Adam”: Rav Tzadok elsewhere says Yaakov’s form is engraved upon the Kisei HaKavod, from the “form of Adam upon the Throne,” linking this with Yaakov’s purified heart. Thus shufra here measures how fully earthly human form reveals its primordial, supernal tzelem.

וּבְוַדַּאי הוּא תַּכְלִית הַיֹּפִי דְּצוּרַת אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אַחַר חֵטְא דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן; וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״מֵעֵין שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּאָדָם״, הַיְינוּ קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ נִיטַּל מִמֶּנּוּ זִיו פָּנָיו, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בברא״ר פ׳ י״ב] מִקְּרָא דְּ״מְשַׁנֶּה פָנָיו וַתְּשַׁלְּחֵהוּ״

And certainly it is the ultimate beauty of the “form of man” in this world after the sin of Adam HaRishon; and what it said, “a semblance of Adam’s beauty,” means [Adam] before the sin — for afterward “the radiance of his face was taken from him,” as they said [Bereishis Rabbah, ch. 12] from the verse “You change his face and send him away” (Iyov 14:20).287Bereishis Rabbah 12:6 — Adam’s lost ziv and its future restoration: The Midrash lists six things taken from Adam after the sin; first is his ziv, citing Iyov 14:20, and it says these losses will return in the future. This directly grounds Rav Tzadok’s treatment of pre-sin facial radiance as a lost perfection awaiting restoration.

וְיַעֲקֹב תִּיקֵּן חֶטְאוֹ לְגַמְרֵי מִצַּד עַצְמוֹ, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [תַּעֲנִית ה:] דְּלֹא מֵת; אֶלָּא שֶׁכְּפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָיָה רַק ״מֵעֵין״, כְּמוֹ שַׁבָּת ״מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא״

And Yaakov rectified his sin completely, from his own side — therefore they said [Taanis 5b] that “he did not die”; only that, according to the revelation in this world, it was but a “semblance,” like Shabbos, [which is] “a semblance of Olam Haba.”288Taanis 5b: “R’ Yochanan said: Yaakov Avinu did not die — [I expound a verse:] just as his offspring are alive, so he is alive” (from Yirmeyah 30:10). R’ Tzadok: Yaakov rectified his portion completely — hence “did not die” — though in this world only a semblance of that perfection was manifest, like Shabbos to Olam Haba.

כִּי כָּל הַשָּׂגָה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, גַּם לְמִי שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג עוֹלָמוֹ בְּחַיָּיו כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה, אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא ״מֵעֵין״ דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הַיְינוּ בְּתַכְלִית קוֹטֶן הַהַרְגָּשָׁה הָאֶפְשָׁרִית

For all apprehension of this world — even for one who “attains his world in his lifetime,” like Yaakov Avinu — is only a “semblance” of Olam Haba: namely, at the ultimate smallness of possible perception.289Berachos 17a; Bava Basra 17a — “your world in your lifetime”: Berachos blesses, “May you see your world in your lifetime”; Bava Basra says Yaakov tasted Olam Haba. Rav Tzadok joins them: Yaakov attained his world while alive, but its earthly disclosure remained only a me’ein.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת נז:] ״שַׁבָּת אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא״, דְּיָדוּעַ הַפֵּירוּשׁ מִשּׁוּם דְּבִיטּוּל הַטַּעַם בְּשִׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד, וְשִׁשִּׁים וְאֶחָד אֵין עוֹד הֶרְגֵּשׁ; אֲבָל אֶחָד מִשִּׁשִּׁים, שֶׁהוּא רַק חֲמִשִּׁים וָתֵשַׁע פַּעַם כְּמוֹתוֹ, יֵשׁ הֶרְגֵּשׁ, וְהוּא הַיּוֹתֵר מוּעָט וְקָטָן, עַד שֶׁבְּפָחוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ אֵין עוֹד הֶרְגֵּשׁ נִיכָּר — זֶה נִקְרָא ״מֵעֵין״ הַדָּבָר

And as they said [Berachos 57b], “Shabbos is one-sixtieth of Olam Haba” — the known explanation being that the nullification of taste [occurs] at one-in-sixty-one, and at sixty-one there is no longer perception; but at one-sixtieth — which is only fifty-nine times its like — there is [still] perception, and it is the smallest and least, [such] that below it no perceptible sensation remains — [and] this is called “a semblance [me’ein]” of the thing.290Chullin 98a–b; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 98 — sixty and sixty-one: Chullin sets bittul at sixty: one prohibited unit plus sixty permitted is one of sixty-one total; one in sixty has only fifty-nine opposing. Rav Tzadok uses the arithmetic homiletically for the last faint trace before nullification.291Berachos 57b: “Shabbos is one-sixtieth of Olam Haba” (among several such “one-sixtieth” comparisons). R’ Tzadok explains “me’ein [a semblance]” via the halachic threshold of taste: a flavor is nullified at one part in sixty-one and beyond, but at one-in-sixty it is still faintly perceptible — the smallest possible “trace” of the thing.

וּדְרַבִּי אַבָּהוּ ״מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה״, שֶׁגַּם הוּא בְּתַכְלִית הַיֹּפִי, מֵעֵין דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, וְלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לָמוּת; וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ עָלָיו [בִּירוּשַׁלְמִי רפ״ג דע״ז] דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הֶרְאָה לוֹ מַתַּן שְׂכָרוֹ, וְנַפְשׁוֹ שְׂבֵעָה לוֹ וְיָשֵׁן עַיִן, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And R’ Abbahu’s [beauty was] “a semblance of Yaakov Avinu’s” — that he too is at the ultimate beauty, a semblance of Adam before the sin, and was not fit to die; and therefore they said of him [Yerushalmi, start of ch. 3 of Avodah Zarah] that the Holy One “showed him his reward, and his soul was sated, and [his] eye slept” — see there.292Yerushalmi, Avodah Zarah (start of ch. 3): at R’ Abbahu’s passing, the Holy One “showed him his reward,” and it is said of him that “his soul was sated” and his eye rested — a death of one “not fit to die” through sin, but taken in fullness. R’ Tzadok pairs this with his “semblance of Yaakov’s beauty.”

וְשֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן הָיָה בְּיוֹתֵר, שֶׁהֲרֵי אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״אֲנָא אִשְׁתַּיַּירִי״ [מִשַּׁפִּירֵי יְרוּשָׁלַיִם], מַשְׁמַע הוּא לְבַדּוֹ; וְר׳ אַבָּהוּ הָיָה תַּלְמִידוֹ וּבְדוֹרוֹ, אֲבָל שֻׁפְרֵיהּ יוֹתֵר מִמֶּנּוּ — וְלָא חֲשַׁבְיֵהּ [לְר׳ יוֹחָנָן ״מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב״] מִשּׁוּם דְּהַדְרַת [פָּנִים] כו׳, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל

And R’ Yochanan’s beauty was greater, for he said of himself, “I alone remain [of the beautiful ones of Jerusalem],” implying he alone; and R’ Abbahu was his student and in his generation, yet [Yaakov’s] beauty [surpassed] his — and [the Gemara] did not reckon [R’ Yochanan293Tosafos, Bava Metzia 84a; Maharsha, Berachos 5b — “I remain of Jerusalem’s beautiful ones”: Tosafos reads “I remain” as remaining from the families of Jerusalem’s beautiful ones; Maharsha links R’ Yochanan’s beauty to Jerusalem’s surviving remnant. Rav Tzadok adds that R’ Abbahu’s being his contemporary disciple makes the wording imply a higher shufra, despite R’ Yochanan’s lack of hadras panim. “a semblance of Yaakov”] because “the hadras panim [the splendor of a beard] he did not have,” as I wrote above.
כִּי הוּא הָיָה מִתּוֹקֶף הַגְּבוּרוֹת דִּקְדֻשָּׁה, וּבָזֶה הָיָה הַחִסָּרוֹן שֶׁלּוֹ, שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד מֵ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״, דְּ״אֵין אָדָם [צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ]״

For he was of the “intensity of the Gevuros of holiness,” and in this was his deficiency — for there is in each one [something] of “the counsel of the serpent,” [since] “there is no [wholly righteous] man [on earth].294Bava Basra 17a; Shabbos 55b; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:77 — “the counsel of the serpent” and residual defect: Bava Basra says four died only through the serpent’s counsel; Tosafos on Shabbos makes “there is no righteous man … who does not sin” the rule for most. Dover Tzedek 4:77 similarly says hidden root-deficiency generally remains in human birth. Rav Tzadok applies that doctrine here to R’ Yochanan’s final trace.”

items.h: The theme: “To see R’ Yochanan’s beauty in a silver goblet”: silver (kesef, “yearning”) alludes to desire, over against Avraham’s Chesed; “fresh from the smith” means new, at its full luster. But that white radiance reaches its peak of beauty only when the red glow of the pomegranate seeds strikes it. Yaakov’s middah, in which Gevuros are blended with Chasadim, leaving no room for the “dross” of evil desire to spread (unlike Avraham, from whom the dross of Yishmael issued and was then purged).

p: [לח] וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר [שָׁם בב״מ] ״לְמִחְזֵי שֻׁפְרֵיהּ דְּר׳ יוֹחָנָן״ בְּ״כָסָא דְּכַסְפָּא״ — יָדוּעַ דְּ״כֶסֶף״ רוֹמֵז לְתַאֲוָה, לְשׁוֹן ״כִּיסּוּפִין״, וְהוּא נֶגֶד הַחֶסֶד לְאַבְרָהָם

And this is what it said [there in Bava Metzia], “to see R’ Yochanan’s beauty in a silver goblet” — it is known that “silver [kesef]” alludes to desire, a term of “yearning [kisufin],” and it is over-against the Chesed [attributed] to Avraham.
וּפָשׁוּט דְּ״מִבֵּי סָלְקֵי״ הַיְינוּ מִבֵּית הָאוּמָּן שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ בּוֹ, וּבִהְיוֹתוֹ חָדָשׁ הוּא בְּתַכְלִית זִיווֹ וְזַהֲרוּרִיתוֹ
And it is plain that “from the smith’s [house]” means fresh from the craftsman, not yet used — and being new, it is at the ultimate of its luster and radiance.

אֲבָל אוֹתוֹ זַהֲרוּרִית לְבָנָה, וְעִיקַּר הַיֹּפִי בְּתָקְפּוֹ, הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַכָּאַת זִיו הָאֹדֶם בּוֹ — הַיְינוּ מִדָּתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁמְּמוּזָּג הַגְּבוּרוֹת בַּחֲסָדִים, וְאֵין מָקוֹם לִפְסֹלֶת דְּתַאֲווֹת רָעוֹת לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט

But that white radiance, and the essence of beauty in its full force, is [only] through the striking of the red glow upon it — that is, the middah of Yaakov Avinu, in whom the Gevuros are blended with the Chasadim, and there is no room for the “dross” of evil desires to spread

[כְּאַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁיָּצָא מִמֶּנּוּ פְּסֹלֶת דְּיִשְׁמָעֵאל; וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאַחַר שֶׁיָּצָא נִתְבָּרֵר גַּם הוּא וְנִשְׁאַר נָקִי, דְּיִשְׁמָעֵאל אֵין נִקְרָא עוֹד זַרְעוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּנְדָרִים לא]

[unlike Avraham Avinu, from whom the dross of Yishmael issued; and though after it issued he too was clarified and remained clean — for Yishmael is no longer called “his seed,” as it is stated in Nedarim 31].295Bava Metzia 84a; Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh §12; Nedarim 31a — Silver, Avraham, and Yaakov’s synthesis: Bava Metzia supplies the concrete image: a new silver goblet from the smithy, filled with red pomegranate seeds, crowned with red roses, and placed between sun and shade so that its radiance gives a semblance of R’ Yochanan’s beauty. The Gemara itself does not assign the colors to particular middos. Rav Tzadok does so elsewhere with striking explicitness: in Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh §12 he identifies silver with love and Chesed, the middah of Avraham; calls Yishmael the “dross of the silver,” namely foreign desires that issued from Avraham; and explains that Yaakov contains both love and fear in purified combination. Nedarim 31a supplies the legal-scriptural basis for the further statement that Yishmael is no longer termed Avraham’s “seed,” deriving it from “for in Yitzchak shall seed be called to you.” Thus the Bavli and Nedarim provide the image and exclusion, while the silver/Chesed, dross, and integrated-Yaakov reading is Rav Tzadok’s own sustained symbolic system.

וְזֶהוּ ״פַּרְצִידֵי דְּרוּמָּנָא סוּמָּקֵי״ — רִימּוֹן רוֹמֵז לְמִילֵּי דְּתוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת נז.]; וְכֵן ״כְּלִילָא דְּוַרְדָּא סוּמָּקָא״ — הַ״כֶּתֶר״ הוּא הָרֹאשׁ וְהַשֹּׁרֶשׁ שֶׁבִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַנִּמְשָׁל בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים לְשׁוֹשַׁנָּה

And this is the “red pomegranate seeds” — the pomegranate alludes to matters of Torah and mitzvos, as they said [Berachos 57a]296Berachos 57a: “One who sees a pomegranate in a dream — if a Torah scholar, let him anticipate [greatness in] Torah; and even the empty ones [reikanin] among Israel are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate.” R’ Tzadok reads the pomegranate — packed with seeds — as an allusion to one filled with “Torah and mitzvos.”; and likewise “the wreath of red roses” — the “Keser [crown]” is the head and the root in Knesses Yisrael, likened in Shir HaShirim to a “rose.297Zohar, Introduction 1:1; Peri Tzadik, Shushan Purim §1 — The rose as Knesses Yisrael, red and white: The Zohar opens by identifying the “rose among the thorns” with Knesses Yisrael and explaining that, just as a rose contains red and white, Knesses Yisrael contains din and rachamim; its thirteen petals correspond to the thirteen attributes of mercy that surround it. Rav Tzadok repeats this identification in Peri Tzadik, Shushan Purim §1, explicitly describing the shoshana as Knesses Yisrael and associating it with the thirteen measures of mercy. This is the close kabbalistic background to the “wreath of red roses” here. Rav Tzadok’s further step — reading the wreath as Keser, the head and root of Knesses Yisrael, and integrating that symbolism into the Gemara’s portrait of R’ Yochanan — is his own application of the Zoharic image.”

וְכָל הַמִּילּוּי שֶׁבִּפְנִים, שֶׁזֶּהוּ אוֹר פְּנִימִי, וְכָל הַהַמְשָׁכָה עַד הַכֶּתֶר, הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ מִצַּד הַגְּבוּרוֹת וְהָאֹדֶם, רַק הָאוֹר מַקִּיף הוּא דְּכֶסֶף; וּמִצַּד זֶה הָיָה אֶצְלוֹ תֹּקֶף הַיֹּפִי בְּהַגְדָּרַת [הַ]תַּאֲווֹת

And all the “filling” within — which is the “inner light” — and all the drawing up to the Keser, was, by him, from the side of the Gevuros and the red; only the “encircling light” was of “silver”; and from this side was, by him, the intensity of beauty in the fencing-in of desires.298Etz Chaim 1:2:2; Peri Tzadik, Vayigash §7 — Or penimi and or makif: Etz Chaim sets out the basic kabbalistic distinction between light received within a vessel and a surrounding or encompassing light, speaking explicitly of or penimi and or makif. Rav Tzadok uses the same vocabulary elsewhere; in Peri Tzadik, Vayigash §7 he describes garments as a form of or makif, invoking “He wraps Himself in light like a garment.” These sources establish the technical categories employed in this sentence. They do not, however, identify the inner “filling” of R’ Yochanan’s image with red/Gevuros or the surrounding radiance with silver/Chesed. That assignment is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive construction here, extending the earlier color-symbolism into the kabbalistic language of inner and surrounding light.
וּלְפִי שֶׁרָצָה לְסַפֵּר אַחַר כָּךְ דָּבָר שֶׁגָּרַם מוֹתוֹ, מַזְכִּיר מִקּוֹדֶם שִׁבְחוֹ, ״דְּבַאֲשֶׁר מִשְׁפָּטוֹ שָׁם פָּעֳלוֹ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת עח סע״ב]

And because it wished to recount afterward the thing that caused his death, it first mentions his praise — “for where his judgment is [decreed], there his deed [is stated],” as they said [Yevamos 78b].299Yevamos 78b with Rashi — “Where his judgment is, there his deed”: The phrase appears in the discussion of the famine in David’s reign and the wrong done by Shaul’s house to the Givonim. At the very moment the divine claim against Shaul is disclosed, the Gemara also says that Heaven demanded honor for him because he had not been eulogized properly. Rashi explains the principle: in the place where a person is judged, his righteous deeds are also mentioned. Rav Tzadok generalizes that narrative rule. When Scripture or the Talmud records the particular matter through which a great person’s death came about, the adjoining praise is not incidental biography; it identifies the person’s essential greatness alongside the one residual point still requiring judgment.

וּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּכָּתוּב, וְכֵן בַּתַּלְמוּד, מִיתָה מִפְּנֵי אֵיזֶה דָּבָר — לֹא הָיָה בּוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר וְחֵטְא אַחֵר זוּלַת זֶה, רַק זֶה לְבַדּוֹ נִשְׁאַר בּוֹ מֵ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ שֶׁבַּעֲבוּרוֹ הוּכְרַח לָמוּת, ״דְּאֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא״

And everywhere that a death “on account of some matter” is mentioned in Scripture, and likewise in the Talmud, there was in him no other matter or sin except this — only this alone remained in him of “the counsel of the serpent,” on account of which he had to die, for “there is no death without sin.300Shabbos 55a–b; Bava Basra 17a — “No death without sin” and the serpent’s counsel: Rav Ami states in Shabbos that “there is no death without sin,” but the sugya subsequently challenges him from the tradition that Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav died only “through the counsel of the serpent,” and concludes with a formal refutation; Bava Basra 17a preserves the same list. That qualification is especially important here. Rav Tzadok has already made “the counsel of the serpent” the name for the primordial residue that can remain even in the righteous. He is therefore not simply presenting Rav Ami’s formulation as the unqualified conclusion of the Bavli. Rather, within his own framework, even death attributed to the primordial serpent reflects a remaining root-level defect of mortality, while a death explicitly attached by Chazal to a particular event discloses the final individualized trace that still required clarification.”

וְאָמְרוּ [בתנדב״א] ״אִם יֹאמַר לְךָ אָדָם אִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא [אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן]״ כו׳ — הֲרֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא וְחַי לְעוֹלָם, וְהוּא ״מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית״; וּ״פִנְחָס זֶה אֵלִיָּהוּ״ שֶׁכָּל קִנְאָתוֹ הָיְתָה רַק ״קִנְאַת ה׳ צְבָאוֹת״ וְ״רוּגְזָא דְּרַבָּנָן״

And they said [in Tanna d’Vei Eliyahu], “if a man says to you, had [Adam] not sinned [he would have lived forever]” — behold Eliyahu, who did not sin and lives forever, and he is “the angel of the bris”; and “Pinchas is Eliyahu,” whose whole zeal was only “the zeal of the Lord of Hosts” and “the anger of the Sages.301Pesikta de-Rav Kahana 9:4; Yalkut Shimoni, Pinchas §771; Malachi 3:1, 23–24 — Eliyahu, Pinchas, and the covenant of life: A close parallel to the formulation cited here appears in Pesikta de-Rav Kahana: if one says that, had Adam not sinned, he would still be alive, the answer is Eliyahu, who did not sin and remains alive. Yalkut Shimoni transmits Reish Lakish’s statement “Pinchas is Eliyahu” and links Pinchas’s peacemaking zeal with Eliyahu’s future mission of restoring the bond between Israel and God. Malachi first speaks of the coming “angel of the covenant” and later names Eliyahu as the messenger sent before the great day of Hashem. These traditions supply the chain Eliyahu–Pinchas–bris–enduring life. Rav Tzadok’s added thesis is that this immortality expresses a perfected Gevurah: zeal stripped of personal anger and wholly subordinated to “the zeal of Hashem,” which becomes the paradigm for the Sages’ sanctity of the bris.”
וְהֵם זָכוּ לִקְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית דֻּגְמַת אֵלִיָּהוּ, וְהַחִסָּרוֹן מֵ״עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ״ שֶׁלָּהֶם הָיָה מִפְּסֹלֶת הַגְּבוּרוֹת
And they [these Sages] merited the holiness of the bris like Eliyahu, and the deficiency of their “counsel of the serpent” was from the “dross of the Gevuros.”

items.h: The theme: So too with R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish, whose cause of death was recorded through R’ Yochanan’s not speaking “in fully clean language.” Reish Lakish’s “what benefit?” meant: it was not R’ Yochanan’s returning him in teshuvah that rectified the past (for that would leave disgrace, the act having been a sin). Rather, at the very time of the act his intent was for Heaven, and “Rebbi they called him,” so R’ Yochanan “added nothing.”

p: [לט] וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן בַּר׳ יוֹחָנָן וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, שֶׁנִּכְתַּב בַּתַּלְמוּד סִיבַּת מִיתָתָם עַל יָדוֹ — אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁתְּחִלָּה לֹא נִתְכַּוֵּון לְבַזּוֹתוֹ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא דִּיבֵּר בְּלָשׁוֹן נְקִיָּה כָּל כָּךְ

And this too [applies] to R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish, whose cause of death was written in the Talmud through him — although at first he did not intend to shame him, as I wrote, nonetheless he did not speak “in fully clean language.”302Pesachim 3a; Bava Metzia 58b — Lashon nekiyah and the special sensitivity owed a baal teshuvah: Pesachim 3a teaches that a person should never bring a degrading expression from his mouth; Scripture itself lengthens its wording to avoid an unclean formulation, and Rashi explains that the language of the Sages should pursue refined and clean speech. Bava Metzia 58b supplies an even closer halachic background: verbal wronging includes telling a baal teshuvah, “remember your former deeds.” This does not by itself establish that R’ Yochanan’s first remark was a technical violation of ona’as devarim—the present se’if itself explains that he did not expect the word “bandit” to shame Reish Lakish. Rather, these sugyos explain Rav Tzadok’s exact standard: even where no insult was initially intended, recalling a penitent’s former identity can fall short of the fullest lashon nekiyah once that past becomes a source of pain. Rav Tzadok’s further linkage of this defect in speech to the recorded cause of death is his own interpretive thesis.

וְזֶה דְּשָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁהֵשִׁיב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ ״מַאי אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳ — דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ דְּלֹא עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁהֶחֱזִירוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה הוּא שֶׁתִּיקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם [דְּבָזֶה עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ גְּנַאי, כֹּל שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי, כֵּיוָן דְּבִשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה הָיָה חֵטְא, וְשֶׁהוּא הֶהֱנָהוּ שֶׁהֱבִיאוֹ לְכָךְ]

And this is [why], there afterward, when Reish Lakish answered “what benefit,” etc. — that is, he said to him that it was not through his having returned him in teshuvah that he rectified the past [for in that there would still be disgrace, insofar as it was not rectified completely, since at the time of the act there was a sin, and he “benefited” him by bringing him to it];

אֲבָל בַּתְּחִלָּה וּבִשְׁעַת מַעֲשֶׂה גַּם כֵּן הָיְתָה כַּוָּונָתוֹ לַשָּׁמַיִם בֶּאֱמֶת, וְ״רַבִּי קָרוּ לֵיהּ״, וְאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק בּוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁבְּכֹחוֹ וְעַל יָדוֹ הוּא שֶׁשָּׁב, כִּי הוּא לֹא הוֹסִיף לוֹ כְּלוּם

but from the start and at the time of the act, too, his intent was truly for Heaven, and “Rebbi they called him,” and [R’ Yochanan] has no share in it to say that by his power and through him he repented — for he added nothing to him.303Tosafos to Bava Metzia 84a — “There they called me Rebbi”: Reish Lakish’s earlier Torah stature: Rabbeinu Tam reads “if you return” to mean that Reish Lakish had already known much Torah before his period of banditry, later cast off the yoke of Torah, and then returned to what he had once been. On “there they called me Rebbi,” Tosafos therefore rejects Rashi’s explanation “master of the bandits” and understands the title literally: he had been called Rebbi before, but had forgotten his learning. This is an important classical foothold for Rav Tzadok’s insistence that the title “Rebbi” points to a Torah identity deeper than the external bandit-role. At the same time, Tosafos does not say that the acts of banditry themselves were already wholly l’shem Shamayim, and in fact says that Reish Lakish had forgotten his earlier Torah. Rav Tzadok’s stronger conclusion here—that the act itself was inwardly for Heaven and that R’ Yochanan “added nothing” to his essential root—is therefore a distinct and much more radical development.
הוֹסִיף ר׳ יוֹחָנָן לְזַלְזְלוֹ בְּפֵירוּשׁ וְאָמַר ״אַהֲנֵית״ כו׳, הַיְינוּ דְּהַשְׁתָּא דְּרוֹאֶה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ בּוּשָׁה מִזֶּה, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ לֹא תִּיקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי
R’ Yochanan went on to disparage him explicitly, saying “[what] benefit,” etc. — meaning, now that he sees Reish Lakish is ashamed of this, perforce he did not rectify it completely.

וְהוּא יָדַע עוֹצֶם הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ בַּתּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה, דְּהָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיְּתוּקַּן לְגַמְרֵי, דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא עָלָה בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוֹנָאַת דְּבָרִים וּבוּשָׁה לוֹ בַּאֲמִירַת ״לִיסְטָאָה״; וּכְשֶׁרָאָה דְּאֵינוֹ כֵן, חָשַׁב דְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ בּוֹ חִסָּרוֹן בָּזֶה מִתּוֹלָדָה שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְתַקְּנוֹ

And he knew the intensity of his [Reish Lakish’s] later effort in Torah and service, [such] that he was fit to be rectified completely; therefore it did not enter his mind that “verbal wronging [ona’as devarim]” and shame would come to him by saying “bandit”; and when he saw it was not so, he thought that certainly there is in him an inborn deficiency in this that cannot be rectified.
וְחִסָּרוֹן זֶה אֵינוֹ רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת בְּשֹׁרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל, כַּיָּדוּעַ דִּמְצוֹרָע מִשְׁתַּלֵּחַ חוּץ לְמַחֲנֵה יִשְׂרָאֵל, כִּי חִסָּרוֹן זֶה אֵין רָאוּי לְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל

And this deficiency is not fit to be in the root of Israel — as is known, that a metzora is “sent outside the camp of Israel,” for this deficiency is not fit for Israel at all.304Peri Tzadik, Nasso §1; Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Dover Tzedek, Berakhot ch. 3 — Metzora, jealousy, and anger as outside Israel’s root: Rav Tzadok states the principle almost verbatim elsewhere. In Peri Tzadik, Nasso §1 he explains that the metzora is sent outside all three camps because this impurity corresponds to jealousy and anger, “which have no portion at all in Israel.” In Kuntres Dover Tzedek on Berakhot, ch. 3, he adds that the seven causes of tzaraas listed by Chazal are branches of kinah and interpersonal evil; the metzora is therefore sent outside Machaneh Yisrael because this is not an essential Jewish trait, invoking the rabbinic characterization of Israel as merciful and bestowers of kindness. These are direct parallels to the present se’if. Rav Tzadok is not denying that Jews can actually become jealous or angry; his distinction is between what appears in conduct and what belongs to the shoresh and essential identity of Knesses Yisrael.
וְהַצָּרַעַת אֵינָהּ אֶלָּא פְּרִיחָה בְּעוֹר בָּשָׂר, וְלֹא בַּעֲצָמוֹת שֶׁהֵם עַצְמוֹת גּוּף הָאָדָם, וּמֵהֶם הוּא הָעֶצֶם הַקָּטָן שֶׁבַּשִּׁדְרָה הַקַּיָּים לָעַד

And tzaraas is only a “sprouting in the skin of the flesh,” and not in the bones, which are the bones of the body of man — and from them is the “small bone in the spine [the luz]” that endures forever.305Bereishis Rabbah 28:3; Zohar, Toldos 6:50–51 — The luz of the spine and the indestructible nucleus of resurrection: Bereishis Rabbah records the tradition that the Holy One will cause the human being to sprout again at the resurrection from the luz of the spine. When Hadrian demanded a demonstration, R’ Yehoshua ben Chananyah produced the bone: it could not be ground, burned, dissolved in water, or crushed on an anvil. The Zohar likewise describes a particular bone of the spine that remains in the grave when the other bones decay, and says that at techiyas hameisim the body will be rebuilt from this surviving root. These sources provide the precise aggadic and kabbalistic basis for Rav Tzadok’s “small bone in the spine that endures forever.” His use of the luz here is interpretive: it becomes the bodily analogue for an inner Israelite essence that remains untouched even when a surface-level blemish appears in the “skin of the flesh.”
וְ״רָקָב עֲצָמוֹת קִנְאָה״, שֶׁהוּא גּוֹרֵם כִּילָּיוֹן הָעֲצָמוֹת גַּם כֵּן; וּבְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהוּא בְּשָׁרְשָׁם כֵּן, נִגְלֶה הַכֹּל וְאֵין קָמִים בִּתְחִיַּית הַמֵּתִים

And “rot of the bones is jealousy [kinah]” (Mishlei 14:30), which causes the destruction of the bones too; and in the nations, whose root is [evil] so, all is revealed [in the bones], and they do not rise at the resurrection of the dead.306Mishlei 14:30; Shabbos 152b — “Rot of the bones is jealousy” as an actual principle of bodily decay: The verse contrasts “a tranquil heart” with “jealousy, the rot of the bones.” Shabbos 152b turns the phrase into a concrete rule in the story of R’ Achai bar Yoshiyah, whose body remained intact in the grave: one who has jealousy in his heart has bones that rot, while one who has no jealousy in his heart has bones that do not rot. Thus Rav Tzadok’s language that kinah can reach and destroy the bones is not merely a metaphor invented for this se’if; it rests on an explicit Talmudic reading of the verse. What Rav Tzadok adds is the larger symbolic architecture: “bones” stand for the enduring essence, and the contrast between Israel and the nations is read at the level of spiritual root and resurrection rather than as a simple biological rule about every individual.

אֲבָל אֵצֶל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל עִנְיְנֵי קִנְאָה וְכַעַס אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְעַצְמִיּוּתוֹ, רַק מִצַּד הַמַּלְבּוּשׁ דְּ״כָתְנוֹת עוֹר״ בָּשָׂר שֶׁעַל גַּבָּיו, שֶׁבּוֹ זוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ הָאַרְסִי, הַנּוֹשֵׁךְ וּמֵמִית בְּלֹא שׁוּם הֲנָאָה לְגַרְמֵיהּ, דְּכָל כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְהָרַע לְבַד מִצַּד הַקִּנְאָה שֶׁבּוֹ

But with the Children of Israel, all matters of jealousy and anger have no relation to their essence — only from the side of the “garment” of the “coats of skin/flesh” upon them, in which is the “filth of the poisonous serpent,” that bites and kills with no benefit to itself, its whole intent being only to harm, from the side of the jealousy in it.307Bereishis 3:21; Shabbos 146a; Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim §14; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:90; Taanis 8a — “Coats of skin,” serpent-contamination, and harm without benefit: After Adam’s sin, Scripture says that God made Adam and Chavah “coats of skin.” Shabbos 146a describes the serpent as having cast a zuhama into Chavah; Israel’s contamination ceased when they stood at Sinai, whereas the nations, who did not stand there, retained it. Rav Tzadok develops the imagery explicitly in Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim §14: the body is only a garment for the soul; before the sin there were “coats of light,” while afterward the “coats of skin” became the mishcha d’chivya, the serpent-skin. Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:90 elaborates the same distinction between the holy root of the Jewish soul and its bodily serpent-skin garment. Finally, Taanis 8a records Reish Lakish’s own teaching that the other animals ask the snake what pleasure it receives from biting, since unlike a lion or wolf it does not eat its victim; the snake answers by comparing itself to the destructive power of the tongue.
