That sugya is the exact classical background to Rav Tzadok’s final image here: jealousy and hostile speech belong to the serpent-layer because their defining impulse is to harm another even without personal gain. The synthesis of all these strands into a distinction between Israel’s essence and its external garment is Rav Tzadok’s characteristic construction.

items.h: The theme: Reish Lakish’s actual “banditry” is never told in the Talmud as a story in its own right — it was wholly erased, being no sin at all. Even his “selling himself to the Ludaei” (Gittin 47a) is, R’ Tzadok argues, no improper deed: not mere “self-disparagement” (Tosafos) but bordering on suicide (he could not know in advance he would be spared). Yet if he truly acted improperly, why would the Sages record his disgrace, “speaking ill of tzaddikim”?

p: [מ] וְגוּף הַלִּסְטִיּוּת דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לֹא נִזְכַּר כְּלָל בַּתַּלְמוּד בְּסִיפּוּר בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה כְּבָר נִמְחַק לְגַמְרֵי, כִּי לֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל
And the actual “banditry” of Reish Lakish is not mentioned at all in the Talmud as a story in its own right — for this was already wholly erased, since it was no sin at all.

וְנִרְאֶה לִי דְּגַם הָעוּבְדָּא דִּ״זְבַן נַפְשֵׁיהּ לְלוּדָאֵי״ [בְּגִיטִּין מז.] אֵינוֹ מִכְּלַל הַדָּבָר שֶׁעָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם דְּהָיָה קוֹדֶם שֶׁחָזַר לְמוּטָב, דְּלֹא הָיָה מְזַלְזֵל בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And it appears to me that also the incident that “he sold himself to the Ludaei” [Gittin 47a] is not of the category of a thing he “did improperly,” as Tosafos said there — that it was before he returned to good, that he would not “disparage himself” — see there.308Gittin 47a: “Reish Lakish sold himself to the Ludaei [gladiator-cannibals]”; taking a bundle and a stone (with a ruse to overpower them), he was ultimately saved. Tosafos explains that this was before he returned to Torah, when “he did not care about his own life.” R’ Tzadok argues that the deed borders on forbidden self-endangerment, and that the Sages would not record it as mere disgrace — rather, it reflects a penitent’s terror for his soul, testing himself.
וּבֶאֱמֶת לֹא זִלְזוּל לְבַד הוּא, אֶלָּא גַּם אִיסּוּר ״מְאַבֵּד עַצְמוֹ לְדַעַת״, כִּי לֹא יָדַע תְּחִלָּה שֶׁיִּתְרַצּוּ בְּהַהַכָּאוֹת וְשֶׁיִּנָּצֵל מִיָּדָם

And in truth it is not only “self-disparagement,” but also the prohibition of “one who takes his own life knowingly [suicide],” for he did not know at first that they would consent to the beatings [in his ruse] and that he would be saved from their hands.309Bava Kamma 91b; Rambam, Hilchos Rotzeach u’Shmiras HaNefesh 11:5 — Self-injury and deliberate danger: Bava Kamma 91b distinguishes the prohibition of taking one’s own life from the broader dispute about injuring oneself: the verse “but your blood of your souls I will demand” is cited as a source that a person is answerable even for his own blood, while the sugya separately discusses whether lesser self-injury is permitted. The Rambam codifies the practical principle more broadly: the Sages prohibited conduct that places life in danger, and one may not say, “I will endanger myself; what concern is it of others?” These sources supply the halachic background for Rav Tzadok’s sharp description of Reish Lakish’s sale to the Ludaei as approaching the category of me’abed atzmo lada’as rather than mere self-disparagement. They do not themselves classify the Gittin incident, nor do they create a general license to risk one’s life for teshuvah; that application is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive argument in this se’if.

וְאִם כְּפִי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת שֶׁלֹּא חָזַר לְמוּטָב, דְּמַשְׁמַע דְּבֶאֱמֶת עָשָׂה שֶׁלֹּא כַּהוֹגֶן — לָמָּה לָהֶם לרז״ל לְהַזְכִּיר גְּנוּתוֹ, וּלְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ הִזְכִּירוּ כְּלָל סִיפּוּר הַהוּא, שֶׁכְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה פְּשָׁטֵיהּ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא סִיפּוּר דְּבָרִים בְּעָלְמָא, לְסַפֵּר [אַחַר] מִיטָּתָן שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים וּלְדַבֵּר בִּגְנוּת דְּצַדִּיקִים

And if, per Tosafos’s words, [it was] that he had not returned to good — implying he truly acted improperly — why would the Sages mention his disgrace, and for what need did they mention that story at all, which, per its apparent plain sense, is merely a “recounting of matters,” to speak [ill] of Torah scholars and to speak in disgrace of tzaddikim?310Berachos 19a — Chazal’s presumption in favor of the honor and teshuvah of a talmid chacham: R’ Yehoshua ben Levi states that one who speaks disparagingly after the bier of Torah scholars “falls into Gehinnom,” and the same sugya teaches that if one saw a talmid chacham commit a bodily transgression at night, he should not continue to suspect him the next day: the Gemara strengthens “perhaps he repented” to “certainly he repented.” This gives real force to Rav Tzadok’s rhetorical question why Chazal would preserve an apparently purposeless story whose only function would be to disgrace Reish Lakish after the fact. The sugya does not establish a formal literary rule that every recorded fault of a sage must secretly be praise; Chazal do record failures when they are themselves instructive. Rav Tzadok’s inference is therefore narrower: where the Ludaei episode seems, on a superficial reading, to add nothing except posthumous disgrace, the rabbinic ethic of judging a talmid chacham through the lens of teshuvah supports looking for a l’shem Shamayim meaning within the story.

אֲבָל הַפָּשׁוּט בְּעֵינַי דְּהוּא עָשָׂה זֶה בְּכַוָּונָה גְּדוֹלָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבְּכָל לִסְטִיּוּתוֹ הָיָה רַק מְכַלֶּה קוֹצִים וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה יָרֵא לְנַפְשׁוֹ

But the plain [truth] in my eyes is that he did this with great intent for the sake of Heaven — for although in all his banditry he was only “clearing thorns,” as I wrote, nonetheless he feared for his own soul.311Bava Metzia 83b — “I am clearing thorns from the vineyard”: the source and its built-in protest: The image “I am clearing thorns from the vineyard” appears in the episode of R’ Elazar b’R’ Shimon’s work apprehending thieves for the government. When R’ Yehoshua ben Korcha rebuked him for handing Jews over to a gentile court, R’ Elazar answered, “I am eradicating thorns from the vineyard”; R’ Yehoshua immediately replied, “Let the Owner of the vineyard come and eradicate His own thorns.” The original sugya therefore preserves both the self-understanding of removing destructive elements and a powerful objection to acting upon that judgment. Rav Tzadok’s use of “clearing thorns” for Reish Lakish should be read against that tension. He is not simply citing a Talmudic endorsement of vigilantism; he is using the metaphor to describe what he believes was Reish Lakish’s inward intention, while the very uncertainty of such judgment explains why Reish Lakish could still fear for his own soul.

שֶׁהֲרֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ ע״ה שֶׁהָרַג אוּכְלוּסֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם הָיָה מִתְפַּחֵד, עַד שֶׁהִבְטִיחוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״אַל תִּירָא״ דְּכוּלָּם ״קוֹצִים כְּסוּחִים״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בברא״ר מד]

For behold, Avraham Avinu, who slew “the multitudes of the nations,” was afraid — until Hashem assured him “fear not” (Bereishis 15:1), for they are all “thorns cut down,” as they said [Bereishis Rabbah 44].312Bereishis Rabbah 44: After Avraham slew the kings and their multitudes (Bereishis 14), “he was afraid, [thinking] perhaps there was a righteous or God-fearing man among those I killed” — until God assured him, “fear not” (15:1), for they were all “thorns cut down [kotzim kesuchim].” R’ Tzadok applies this to Reish Lakish: even “clearing thorns,” a penitent still trembles for his soul.
וְכֵן בַּר׳ אֶלְעָזָר בַּר׳ שִׁמְעוֹן [בב״מ שָׁם פג:] אַף אַחַר שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ ״וּמַה סְפֵקוֹת שֶׁלָּכֶם״ כו׳, אֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי לָא מְיַתְּבָא דַּעְתּוֹ וְחוֹזֵר לְנַסּוֹת וּלְבָרֵר

And likewise with R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon [Bava Metzia 83b]: even after he said of himself, “if your doubtful [sins are dealt with thus, how much more the certain],” nonetheless his mind was not settled, and he returned to test and clarify [himself];

וְגַם אַחַר כָּךְ, אַחַר שֶׁקָּרָא עַל עַצְמוֹ ״אַף בְּשָׂרִי יִשְׁכּוֹן לָבֶטַח״, חָזַר לְהִסְתַּפֵּק בְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכֵי לָא סָמַךְ אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ וְקַבֵּיל עָלֵיהּ יִסּוּרִים; וְגַם רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לֹא סָמַךְ אַדַּעְתֵּיהּ

and even afterward, after he applied to himself “even my flesh shall dwell secure,” he returned to be in doubt about himself, and even so did not rely on himself but accepted sufferings upon himself; and Reish Lakish, too, did not rely on himself.313Bava Metzia 83b–84b; Avos 2:4; Peri Tzadik, Behar §2 — “He did not rely on himself” even after extraordinary signs of righteousness: The Bava Metzia narrative is deliberately cumulative. After the condemned laundryman was shown to be gravely wicked, R’ Elazar declared, “Rejoice, my innards,” yet “even so his mind was not settled”; he then subjected his body to a test, and even after his flesh and veins did not decay and he applied “my flesh too shall dwell secure” to himself, the Gemara returns: “even so, R’ Elazar b’R’ Shimon did not rely on his own opinion; he accepted sufferings upon himself.” This embodies Hillel’s rule, “Do not trust yourself until the day of your death.” Rav Tzadok develops the same principle explicitly in Peri Tzadik, Behar §2: even one who has attained an exalted, almost Olam-Haba-like spiritual state must still fear the yetzer so long as evil remains in the world and must not rely upon his own stature. That parallel explains his comparison here: Reish Lakish’s doubt is not evidence that his earlier acts were necessarily sinful; for Rav Tzadok, the refusal of a tzaddik to rely on himself can itself be a mark of spiritual greatness.

וּמָצִינוּ דְּמוּתָּר גַּם לְאַבֵּד נַפְשׁוֹ לִתְשׁוּבָה, וְלָא מִיבַּעְיָא לַעֲבֵירוֹת חֲמוּרוֹת בְּמֵזִיד שֶׁחַיָּיב עֲלֵיהֶם מִיתָה בְּבֵית דִּין, כְּיוֹיָקִים אִישׁ צְרוֹרוֹת [בברא״ר ס״פ סה, שֶׁחָזַר בִּתְשׁוּבָה וְקִיֵּים בְּעַצְמוֹ אַרְבַּע מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין], אֶלָּא גַּם בַּעֲבֵירוֹת קַלּוֹת כְּהַהוּא כּוֹבֵס [בִּכְתוּבּוֹת קג:]

And we find that it is permitted even to give one’s own life for teshuvah — and not only for grave sins committed deliberately, for which one is liable to death by the court, like Yehoyakim ish Tzeraros [Bereishis Rabbah, end of ch. 65, who repented and enacted upon himself the four court-death-penalties], but even for light sins, like that laundryman [in Kesubos 103b].314Bereishis Rabbah 65:22; Kesubos 103b; Maharal, Derekh Chaim 6:11 — Yekum Ish Tzerorot and the laundryman as extreme teshuvah narratives: Bereishis Rabbah names the first figure יקום איש צרורות, Yekum (or Yakum) Ish Tzerorot, the nephew of R’ Yosei ben Yoezer. Pierced by his uncle’s rebuke, he arranged that the four modes of court execution converge upon himself; R’ Yosei then saw his bier flying and exclaimed that in a short hour Yekum had preceded him to Gan Eden. The printed wording cited here, “Yoiyakim/Yehoyakim Ish Tzerorot,” is a variant form of that midrashic name, not a reference to King Yehoyakim. Kesubos 103b tells the second story: a laundryman who had regularly come before Rebbi missed Rebbi’s funeral, heard the heavenly proclamation concerning those who attended, went up to a roof, fell and died, and a second proclamation declared him destined for life in the World to Come. Maharal reads the laundryman’s death as a form of self-surrender born of profound grief and notes the atoning force of such suffering, while also distinguishing “destined for life in the World to Come” from a simplistic rule that one isolated act automatically erases every liability. Rav Tzadok adduces both aggados to show that total self-sacrifice can become part of a genuine teshuvah process; this is an aggadic-theological argument, not a practical halachic permission for self-harm.315Bereishis Rabbah, end of ch. 65: Yehoyakim (or, in the tradition, one who repented) is depicted as having “fulfilled upon himself the four court-imposed death penalties” in his teshuvah. Together with the account of the laundryman who died accepting his lot (Kesubos 103b), R’ Tzadok adduces that one may even give one’s life in the course of true teshuvah — for grave sins and even light ones.

items.h: The theme: The Gemara continues, “he went out, came, sat, ate and drank.” Rashi glosses “all his days [whatever he earned he did not save for tomorrow],” taking it as a matter in its own right. R’ Tzadok objects: read plainly, it is continuous with the rescue — Reish Lakish sat and ate in joy at having been saved from the Ludaei.

p: [מא] וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ ״נְפַק וַאֲתָא יָתֵיב אָכֵיל וְשָׁתֵי״, ורש״י פֵּירֵשׁ ״כָּל יָמָיו״ כו׳, מַשְׁמַע דִּמְפָרֵשׁ דְּהוּא עִנְיָן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, וְלֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן רַק דְּהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ לְהַקּוֹדֵם

And this is what it says there afterward, “he went out and came, sat, ate and drank”; and Rashi explained “all his days,” etc. — implying that he takes it as a matter in its own right; but it does not read so — rather, that it is continuous with the preceding.316Rashi, Gittin 47a (s.v. kol yamav): on “he sat, ate and drank,” Rashi glosses that all his days Reish Lakish would consume whatever he earned, saving nothing for the morrow — leading into “when he died, he left [only] a kav of saffron.” R’ Tzadok argues that the plain sense reads the phrase as continuous with the rescue (a meal of joy at deliverance), and that Rashi’s difficulty was only the seemingly purposeless mention of eating.
וְאִם רָצָה לוֹמַר דְּגַם סִיפּוּר הַקּוֹדֵם מַה דְּזָבַן נַפְשֵׁיהּ הָיָה בִּשְׁבִיל אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, אִם כֵּן הַכֹּל הוּא לְגַנּוֹתוֹ וְשֶׁהָיָה רַעַבְתָן חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
And if one wished to say that even the earlier account — that “he sold himself” — was for the sake of eating and drinking, then it is all to his disgrace, that he was a glutton, God forbid.
וְאֵיךְ אָמַר ״כָּל יָמָיו״ כו׳, וַהֲרֵי אַחַר כָּךְ חָזַר וְהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וּבְוַדַּאי כָּל אֲכִילָתוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

And how could it say “all his days,” when afterward he returned and became a Torah scholar, and certainly all his eating was in holiness?317Avos 2:12; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 3:2–3; Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat §2 — Eating itself as avodas Hashem: The Mishnah’s rule “all your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven” is applied by the Rambam specifically to bodily acts: a person should eat and drink not merely for pleasure, but so that the body remain a sound instrument for knowing and serving God; when this intention embraces one’s ordinary life, even eating and sleeping become service of the Omnipresent. Rav Tzadok develops the same idea in Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat §2. There he describes the task of “repairing the eating so that it be in holiness,” invokes Hillel’s treatment of the body as a guest whose needs are supplied without making bodily pleasure the goal, and cites striking cases of very abundant eating by righteous figures to show that quantity alone does not define gluttony when the eating is truly for Heaven. This is the conceptual background to Rav Tzadok’s certainty here that after Reish Lakish became a talmid chacham, “all his eating was in holiness.” The classical sources establish that permitted eating can itself become avodah through intention; Rav Tzadok’s stronger application to Reish Lakish’s entire post-teshuvah eating belongs to his own spiritual reading of the sage.
וְאֵיךְ הִסְמִיךְ זֶה לְהַקּוֹדֵם שֶׁמָּכַר עַצְמוֹ לְמִיתָה בִּשְׁבִיל אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, וְאֵין לְךָ ״זוֹלֵל וְסוֹבֵא״ גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה

And how could this be juxtaposed to the preceding — that he sold himself to death for the sake of eating and drinking — [for] you have no greater “glutton and drunkard” than this?318Sanhedrin 70a–71a; Rambam, Hilchos Mamrim 7:1–3 — “Zolel v’sovei” as a sharply delimited halachic category: The Torah’s “glutton and drunkard” is not a loose legal label for anyone who eats or drinks excessively. The Mishnah and Gemara require meat and wine in specified amounts and circumstances, and the Rambam codifies a long list of further conditions: the son must steal from his father, buy the meat and wine cheaply, eat outside his father’s domain with a base company, consume the meat only partially cooked “as thieves do,” and drink the wine in the characteristic manner specified by Chazal. Even a meal that is itself a mitzvah, or conversely involves another aveirah, falls outside the statutory case. Rav Tzadok therefore uses “you have no greater zolel v’sovei than this” rhetorically, not as a claim that Reish Lakish could have had the halachic status of a ben sorer u’moreh. His point is qualitative and literary: if the Ludaei episode meant that Reish Lakish exposed himself to death merely in order to eat and drink, it would portray a degree of appetite more extreme than the very biblical image of unrestrained consumption.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַכֹּל סִיפּוּר אֶחָד, דִּכְשֶׁיָּצָא מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה, יָתֵיב וְאָכַל וְשָׁתָה בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְשִׂמְחָתוֹ שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מֵהֶם

Perforce it is all one account: when he emerged from his plight, he sat and ate and drank at that very hour, in his joy at being saved from them.319Berachos 54b; Tehillim 107:10–22 — Deliverance from mortal danger and the obligation of thanksgiving: Chazal list one who was imprisoned and then released among the four who “must give thanks,” grounding the rule in Tehillim 107, where a person brought out of darkness and the shadow of death is commanded to acknowledge God’s kindness. The same psalm repeatedly moves from danger and deliverance to joy and thanksgiving, culminating in praise before the congregation. Reish Lakish’s escape from captors who intended to kill him is not presented in Gittin as a formal case of birkas hagomel, and the Gemara does not state that his subsequent eating and drinking constituted a prescribed seudas hoda’ah. Nevertheless, this rabbinic framework makes Rav Tzadok’s peshat psychologically and religiously natural: “he went out and came” from deadly danger, and the immediately following “he sat, ate and drank” can be heard as the bodily expression of relief and joy after salvation rather than as a lifetime program of indulgence.

וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה דְּהוּקְשָׁה לְרַשִׁ״י לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ יַזְכִּיר זֶה דְּאָכַל וְשָׁתָה כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נִזְכַּר שׁוּם סִיפּוּר וְהֶמְשֵׁךְ עִנְיָן עַל זֶה, וְעַל כֵּן מְפָרֵשׁ דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר כָּל יוֹם כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר כו׳, וְנִמְשָׁךְ לְמַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״כִּי נָח נַפְשֵׁיהּ״ כו׳

And apparently Rashi was troubled: for what purpose would it mention “he ate and drank,” since no incident or continuation is recorded upon it — and therefore he explains that it means “each day, all that he earned,” etc., continuing to what it says afterward, “when he passed away,” etc.320Beitzah 16a; Ramban to Shemos 20:8; Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat §2 — “Blessed is Hashem, day by day” and holy non-hoarding: Beitzah contrasts Shammai, who would reserve the best food he found for Shabbos, with Hillel, whose “different trait” was that all his deeds were for the sake of Heaven and who lived by “Blessed is Hashem, day by day.” Ramban explains Hillel’s practice as trust that the One who provided a worthy portion today would provide an even finer portion for Shabbos. Rav Tzadok returns to this very model in Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat §2: Hillel’s ordinary bodily maintenance is l’shem Shamayim, and properly rectified eating can itself be holy. This is an important qualification to the present argument. Rav Tzadok is not rejecting the spiritual possibility reflected in Rashi’s portrait of Reish Lakish as one who consumed what he earned rather than hoarding for tomorrow; elsewhere, the “day by day” mode can be a lofty expression of bitachon. His objection here is exegetical and chronological: he argues that those details are not actually stated in the words “he sat, ate and drank,” and therefore should not displace the more immediate narrative connection to Reish Lakish’s escape.
אֲבָל לְפִי זֶה הָעִיקָּר דְּאָכַל וְשָׁתָה כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר וְשֶׁלֹּא הִשְׁאִיר כְּלוּם חָסֵר מֵהַסֵּפֶר
But according to this, the main point — that he ate and drank all he earned, and left nothing over — is missing from the text.

items.h: The theme: On R’ Tzadok’s reading, the extra word “better” comes to teach, for the flow of the story, how ravenous bandits are. For example, in Pesachim 12b, “the second hour is the bandits’ mealtime,” ravenous like the Ludim who eat the instant they wake. The root of banditry is ravenousness — failing to draw one’s needs through faith, or casting oneself upon the community (so a ben sorer u’moreh “ends up robbing people,” Sanhedrin 72a).

p: [מב] וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי ״טוֹבִי״ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן לְהֶמְשֵׁךְ הַסִּיפּוּר כַּמָּה לִיסְטִים רַעַבְתָנִים הֵם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּפְסָחִים יב:] ״שָׁעָה שְׁנִיָּה מַאֲכַל לִיסְטִים״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּהֵם רַעַבְתָנִים כְּלוּדִים לֶאֱכוֹל מִיָּד שֶׁנֵּיעוֹרִים

And per what I wrote, “better” comes to teach us — for the continuation of the story — how ravenous bandits are, as they said [in Pesachim 12b], “the second hour is the bandits’ mealtime”; see Rashi there, that they are ravenous, like the Ludim, to eat the moment they wake.321Pesachim 12b: in fixing the hours of the day, “the second hour is the mealtime of bandits [listim]”; Rashi explains they are ravenous, like the Ludim, eating the moment they rise. R’ Tzadok: the root of banditry is ravenousness — not drawing one’s needs through faith — and Reish Lakish, having suspected his own hunger, needed the clarification that his eating was in fact holy.

וְעִיקַּר הַלִּסְטִיּוּת בָּא מֵרַעַבְתָנוּת שֶׁאֵין מוֹצִיא כָּל צָרְכּוֹ מֵאֱמוּנוֹת אוֹ לְהָטִיל עַצְמוֹ עַל הַצִּבּוּר, וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין עב רע״א] בְּבֶן סוֹרֵר וּמוֹרֶה ״סוֹפוֹ עוֹמֵד וּמְלַסְטֵם הַבְּרִיּוֹת״

And the root of banditry comes from ravenousness — of one who does not draw all his need through faith, or casts himself upon the community; and so they said [Sanhedrin 72a] of the ben sorer u’moreh, “his end is to stand and rob people.”322Avos 2:2; Bartenura; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:10; Shulchan Arukh, Yoreh De’ah 246:21 — Livelihood, dependence, and the road to banditry: The Mishnah teaches that Torah without derech eretz — work or a livelihood — ultimately becomes null and “causes sin.” Bartenura makes the mechanism concrete: because a person cannot live without food, one who lacks a livelihood may come to “rob people”; the Rambam ends his warning against deciding to study without working and live from charity with the same striking phrase, “in the end this person will rob people,” and Shulchan Arukh preserves that formulation. The Rema there also records important circumstances in which communal support of Torah scholars is permitted or appropriate. These sources therefore give a remarkably close classical and halachic background to Rav Tzadok’s causal language linking unmet material need with listiyut. His broader spiritual diagnosis — that ravenousness itself is the root of banditry — is his own formulation, and should not be read as a blanket condemnation of every form of communal support.

וְהוּא שֶׁחָשַׁד עַצְמוֹ לְלִיסְטִים גַּם אֲכִילָתוֹ חָשַׁב שֶׁהוּא רַעַבְתָנוּת בְּעָלְמָא כְּמַאֲכַל כָּל לִיסְטִים; וּלִכְשֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר דְּאֵינוֹ לִיסְטִים כִּי כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם לְבַעֵר הָרַע, מִמֵּילָא גַּם אֲכִילָתוֹ וּשְׁתִיָּיתוֹ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

And he who suspected himself a bandit thought his eating too was mere ravenousness, like every bandit’s meal; but once it was clarified that he is no bandit — for all his deeds are for Heaven’s sake, to burn out the evil — then, of itself, his eating and drinking too are in holiness.323Dover Tzedek, Likkutim §1; Peri Tzadik, Masei §12 — A talmid chacham’s bodily eating becomes Torah: Rav Tzadok gives an unusually close parallel in Dover Tzedek. Because a talmid chacham’s mind is immersed in Torah, he writes, even the scholar’s ordinary speech is Torah; likewise bodily eating and drinking become “Torah” and nourishment for the soul, the body itself becoming included in holiness, and precisely through that union comes ruach hakodesh. In Peri Tzadik, Masei §12, he similarly explains that meat and wine needed by a talmid chacham for clarity of mind can be eating and drinking “in holiness, for the sake of Heaven.” These passages supply Rav Tzadok’s own conceptual background for the present claim that once Reish Lakish’s deeds are clarified as l’shem Shamayim, his consumption is no longer mere ravenousness. The Gemara itself does not say this of Reish Lakish; it is Rav Tzadok’s spiritual reading of the sage.
וְגַם עִיקַּר קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דּוֹמֶה לַמִּזְבֵּחַ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [חֲגִיגָה כז רע״א] ״פָּתַח בְּמִזְבֵּחַ וְסִיֵּים בְּשֻׁלְחָן״ כו׳

And the essence of the holiness of eating is that it resemble the altar, as they said [Chagigah 27a], “[Scripture] began with the altar and ended with the table” — [now that the Temple is destroyed, a man’s table atones for him].324Chagigah 27a: “Why does the [Torah passage] begin with the altar and end with the table? — [while the Temple stood, the altar atoned;] now that the Temple is destroyed, a man’s table atones for him” (like the altar). R’ Tzadok builds on this that holy eating literally stands in for the sacrificial service — hence a body fit for it must be free of bloodshed.325Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat 1:2 — Human dependence on food as a field of kedushah: Rav Tzadok states there that God created the human being to require eating for the maintenance of life, that this life is “chiyus ha-kedushah,” and that “there was holiness in the eating.” He reads the Edenic permission “of every tree of the garden you shall surely eat” as the primordial model of rectified consumption, before desire distorted the act, and later describes the tzaddik as one who eats “to the satiety of his soul” rather than from taavah. This makes the present altar comparison part of a broader theology: bodily need was not created as an obstacle to avodah but as material capable of becoming avodah. The decisive distinction is not simply how much one eats, but whether necessity and pleasure are integrated into service of God or seized by appetite for its own sake.

וּבִפְרָט בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא עא סע״א] ״לְנַסֵּךְ עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ — יְמַלֵּא גְּרוֹנָם שֶׁל תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים״, וּבִכְתוּבּוֹת [קה סע״ב] ״הַמֵּבִיא דּוֹרוֹן לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם כְּמַקְרִיב בִּיכּוּרִים״, דְּכָל אֲכִילוֹתָיו וּשְׁתִיּוֹתָיו כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת

and especially with a Torah scholar, as they said [Yoma 71a], “to pour a libation upon the altar — [rather,] fill the throats of the Sages,” and in Kesubos [105b], “one who brings a gift to a Torah scholar is as one who offers first-fruits” — for all his eating and drinking are like korbanos.326Yoma 71a; Kesubos 105b; Magen Avos to Avos 4:5 — Feeding a talmid chacham as sacrificial avodah: The Yoma passage is more pointed than a loose comparison: R’ Berekhya interprets Mishlei 8:4, “to you, ishim, I call,” so that the word resonates with isheh, the altar-fire, and says that one who wishes to pour wine upon the altar should fill the throats of talmidei chachamim with wine. Kesubos derives from the man who brought Elisha “bread of the first fruits” that bringing a gift to a talmid chacham is as though offering bikkurim. Magen Avos explicitly explains that just as bikkurim and libations are avodah, honoring Torah in this way is avodah. Chazal thus establish a sacrificial analogy to sustaining the scholar; Rav Tzadok makes the further step that the talmid chacham’s own eating and drinking themselves are like korbanos.
וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּא [פָּרָשָׁה ס״ה] ״אִם לְקָרְבָּנְךָ הִמְצִיא כו׳ לְמַאֲכָלְךָ עַל אַחַת כַּמָּה וְכַמָּה״, מַשְׁמַע דְּחָשׁוּב טְפֵי מִקָּרְבָּנוֹת

And in Bereishis Rabbah [65]: “if for your offering [God] provided, then for your food how much more so” — implying it is reckoned even greater than korbanos.327Bereishis Rabbah 65:19 — “If for your offering He provided… for your food all the more so”: The Midrash comments on Yaakov’s answer to Yitzchak, “because Hashem your God arranged it before me” (Bereishis 27:20). R’ Yochanan and Reish Lakish dispute the comparison: one says that if the Holy One providentially supplied Avraham with the ram for his offering, then surely He will provide ordinary food; the other makes the same kal vachomer from the providential finding of Rivkah as a wife. The explicit Midrashic point is therefore hashgachah in provision. Rav Tzadok’s conclusion here — that the wording “implies it is reckoned even greater than korbanos” — is an interpretive development from the kal vachomer, not an explicit statement of the Midrash that ordinary food possesses greater sanctity than sacrifice.

וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁהַלִּיסְטִים מָמוֹנָן גֶּזֶל וְכָל אֲכִילָתָן מִגְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲמָסִים, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן וְהַקְּדֻשָּׁה, ״דַּאֲנִי ה׳ שׂוֹנֵא גָּזֵל בְּעוֹלָה״, וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּא [פָּרָשָׁה ג] ״הוֹפַק שֶׁמָּלֵא גְּזֵילוֹת וַחֲמָסִין אַל יִקְרַב לְגַבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ״

And since the bandits’ money is robbery, and all their eating is from robberies and extortions, it cannot be a favorable offering or holiness — for “I the Lord hate robbery in a burnt-offering,” and in Vayikra Rabbah [3], “one whose [hand] is full of robberies and extortions — let him not draw near the altar.”328Vayikra Rabbah 3 (and Yeshaya 1:11–15): God “hates robbery in a burnt-offering”; one whose hand is full of “robberies and extortions” may not approach the altar, and “your hands are full of blood.” R’ Tzadok: a bandit’s food, being robbery, cannot be a favorable “offering,” and a shedder of blood cannot have his table resemble the altar.
וְעוֹד דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְקָרְבָּן וְהוּא לִיסְטִים וְשׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים, הֲרֵי קְרָא צָוַוח ״לָמָּה לִּי רוֹב זִבְחֵיכֶם וְגוֹ׳ יְדֵיכֶם דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ״
And further, since he resembles a korban yet is a bandit and shedder of blood, the verse cries out: “Why to Me your many sacrifices” — “your hands are full of blood” (Yeshaya 1).
[וּבְאוֹר זָרוּעַ מַשְׁמַע דְּכֹהֵן רוֹצֵחַ בְּמֵזִיד וְלֹא שָׁב פָּסוּל לַעֲבוֹדָה וְלִנְשִׂיאַת כַּפַּיִם, וְכֵן לִהְיוֹת שְׁלִיחַ צִבּוּר; וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ בָּזֶה.]

[And from the Or Zarua it is implied that a kohen who murdered deliberately and did not repent is disqualified for the Temple service and for the priestly blessing, and likewise from serving as a shaliach tzibbur; and this is not the place to expand on it.]329Ohr Zarua I §112; Berachos 32b; Shulchan Arukh, Orach Chayim 128:35 — A kohen who killed: avodah, duchaning, and shaliach tzibbur: Berachos 32b states that a kohen who killed a person does not raise his hands, citing Yeshaya’s “your hands are full of blood.” Ohr Zarua I §112 addresses an accidental killer serving as shaliach tzibbur and distinguishes a deliberate murderer, whom the community must distance, while also bringing more lenient material regarding killing that was accidental or not habitual. The practical law of duchaning is itself disputed: Shulchan Arukh rules that even an accidental killer may not duchan even after teshuvah, whereas the Rema records the view that sincere teshuvah restores him and says the custom is to be lenient so as not to close the door before penitents. Rav Tzadok’s bracketed discussion is therefore deliberately tentative — “it is implied” — and he himself notes tension among avodah, nesias kapayim, and tefillah; it should not be read as stating a simple, uncontested halachic rule.
וּבְשַׁבָּת [לג.] ״דְּבַעֲוֹן שְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים בֵּית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ חָרֵב וּשְׁכִינָה מִסְתַּלֶּקֶת״, הֲרֵי דְּאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא רוֹצֶה בַּעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁל שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים

And in Shabbos [33a], “for the sin of bloodshed the Temple is destroyed and the Shechinah departs” — so the Holy One does not desire the service of a shedder of blood.330Shabbos 33a; Yoma 85a: “For the sin of bloodshed the Temple is destroyed and the Shechinah departs from Israel”; and even an individual’s bloodshed drives out the Shechinah. R’ Tzadok infers that God does not desire the “service” (or the sanctified eating) of a shedder of blood — the body must be fit for the Shechinah’s indwelling.
וּבְיוֹמָא [פה סע״א] אִיתָא גַּם אַשְּׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים דְּיָחִיד דְּגוֹרֵם לַשְּׁכִינָה שֶׁתִּסְתַּלֵּק מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
And in Yoma [85a] it is stated that even the bloodshed of an individual causes the Shechinah to depart from Israel.

וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְעִנְיַן קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, דְּצָרִיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גּוּפוֹ מוּכָן לְהַשְׁרָאַת שְׁכִינָה, דְּאָז יוּכַל לְדַמּוֹת לְקָרְבָּנוֹת דְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ

All the more so regarding the holiness of eating, that it be reckoned as korbanos — for one’s body must be ready for the indwelling of the Shechinah, and then it can resemble the korbanos of the Temple.

items.h: The theme: In Taanis 11a, “one should ever regard himself as though a holy one dwells within his innards” — and therefore he may not fast. Through this his eating is holy like korbanos, as though offering them on God’s altar. By contrast, a murderer, who drives out the Shechinah, surely has no “holy one” within.

p: [מג] וּבְתַעֲנִית [יא רע״ב] ״דְּיִרְאֶה כְּאִלּוּ קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּתוֹךְ מֵעָיו״, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה אָסוּר לְהִתְעַנּוֹת, וְהַיְינוּ דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה הוּא קְדֻשַּׁת הָאֲכִילָה כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת וְהוּא כְּמַקְרִיב קָרְבָּנוֹת עַל מִזְבַּח ה׳

And in Taanis [11a], “one should regard himself as though a holy one dwells within his innards,” and because of this it is forbidden to fast; that is, through this the holiness of eating is like korbanos, and he is as one offering korbanos upon the altar of the Lord.331Taanis 11a: “R’ Elazar said: A person should always regard himself as though a holy one dwells within his innards [kadosh sharui b’tocho],” as it says, “the Holy One is in your midst” — from which it is derived that one may not afflict (starve) himself. R’ Tzadok: this “holy one within” is precisely what makes eating a sacred, korban-like act.
וְהָרוֹצֵחַ שֶׁגּוֹרֵם לְסִילּוּק שְׁכִינָה מִכָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל כָּל שֶׁכֵּן שֶׁאֵין קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי תּוֹךְ מֵעָיו
And the murderer, who causes the departure of the Shechinah from all Israel, certainly has no “holy one dwelling within his innards.”

וְנִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בַּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן [בב״מ שָׁם פג:] ״שִׂישׂוּ בְּנֵי מֵעַי״ כו׳, כִּי כְּשֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֲוֹן דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים עַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לִהְיוֹת קָדוֹשׁ תּוֹךְ מֵעָיו וְכָל אֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, וּמִמֶּנּוּ הִתְהַוּוּ חֶלְבּוֹ וּבְשָׂרוֹ

And it appears that this is what R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon said [Bava Metzia 83b], “rejoice, my innards!” — for when it was clarified that there is in him no sin of bloodshed, through this a holy one can dwell within his innards, and all his eating is like korbanos, from which his fat and flesh were formed.332Bava Metzia 83b: R’ Elazar b’Rabbi Shimon, having accepted sufferings and tested his own righteousness, cried, “Rejoice, my innards, rejoice, my innards [sisu bnei me’ai]! — if [I am punished even] for my doubtful [sins], how much more [rewarded for the certain].” When he was confident his flesh bore no sin, he declared his flesh would “dwell secure” and not putrefy. R’ Tzadok ties this to the “holy one within,” whose flesh is formed from korban-like eating.333Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 9:2 — ‘A holy one dwells within his innards’ as sanctified eating: Rav Tzadok there returns explicitly to Taanis 11a and reads ‘bekirbecha kadosh’ through the realm of eating itself: the language of ‘within you’ points to what enters and rests within the innards. He connects ‘I will remove sickness from your midst’ with release from the yetzer hara that seizes upon eating, and explains that food received from God’s blessing can bring holiness into the heart rather than arouse the opposite force. This is a close parallel to the present step. The Gemara supplies the rule that one must preserve the body because a holy presence dwells within; Rav Tzadok develops it into a theology in which the digestive and nutritive life itself can become a dwelling for kedushah, so that eating is korban-like and the flesh formed from it is correspondingly holy.

וַהֲרֵי תְּנַן [בְּפֶרֶק ה׳ דְּאָבוֹת וְיוֹמָא יט.] דְּלֹא הִסְרִיחַ בְּשַׂר הַקֹּדֶשׁ מֵעוֹלָם, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בִּבְשַׂר הָאָדָם הַקָּדוֹשׁ, שֶׁמֵּעָיו בִּמְקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ וְגִידּוּל בְּשָׂרוֹ מֵאֲכִילָה קְדוֹשָׁה שֶׁכְּקָרְבָּן, דְּאֵין שַׁיָּיכוּת לְסֵירָחוֹן אֵלָיו כְּלָל

And we learned [in the fifth chapter of Avos, and Yoma 39a] that “the holy flesh never became putrid” — all the more the flesh of the holy man, whose innards are in the place of the altar, and the growth of whose flesh is from holy eating that is like a korban, to which no putrefaction pertains at all.334Yoma 39a / Avos 5:5; Bava Basra 17a: among the Temple miracles, “the holy flesh never became putrid”; and “seven whom the worm and maggot did not rule” (the Patriarchs, Moshe, Aharon, Miriam, Binyamin), for the worm comes only from the decay that follows death by “the drop of the Angel of Death” — not for those united with the Shechinah. R’ Tzadok: all the more, the holy man’s korban-flesh knows no putrefaction.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״מוּבְטַחְנִי״ כו׳, דִּבְשָׂרוֹ יִשְׁכּוֹן לָבֶטַח שֶׁלֹּא יַסְרִיחַ, וּמִמֵּילָא לֹא יִהְיֶה רִמָּה וְתוֹלֵעָה הַבָּאִים אַחַר הַסֵּירָחוֹן
And therefore he said “I am confident,” etc. — that his flesh shall “dwell secure,” that it will not putrefy, and consequently there will be no worm or maggot, which come only after putrefaction.

וְעַל כֵּן רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ כִּדְנָפַק מִלּוּדָאֵי, דַּה׳ עֲזָרוֹ שֶׁנִּיצוֹל מִיָּדָם, נִתְבָּרֵר לוֹ דְּאֵין בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁמֶץ עֲוֹן דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּמִים, דְּאָז לֹא הָיָה נִיצוֹל דְּלָא עָבֵיד קוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא נִיסָּא לְשִׁקְרָא, וְגַבְרָא מִיבַּדְקֵי בְּכָל מְקוֹם סַכָּנָה כִּדְאִיתָא [בְּשַׁבָּת לב.]

And so Reish Lakish, when he emerged from the Ludaei — since God helped him to be saved from their hand — it was clarified to him that he bears no trace of a bloodshed sin; for otherwise he would not have been saved, as “the Holy One performs no miracle for a falsehood,” and a man is examined at every place of danger, as it is stated [Shabbos 32a].335Shabbos 32a: “A man is examined [gavra mibadki] at every place of danger”; and “the Holy One performs no miracle for a falsehood.” R’ Tzadok: Reish Lakish’s very survival of the Ludaei was itself a heavenly examination that certified he bore no bloodshed sin — for a guilty man would not have been miraculously spared.
וּכְשֶׁנִּבְדַּק וְנִמְצָא נָקִי אָז הָלַךְ לֶאֱכוֹל בְּשִׂמְחָה לַחְמוֹ וְלִשְׁתּוֹת בְּלֵב טוֹב יֵינוֹ, כִּי כְּבָר רָצָה אֱלֹקִים אֶת מַעֲשָׂיו וְקָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּמֵעָיו

And when he was examined and found clean, he then went to eat his bread in joy and to drink his wine with a glad heart, for God had already favored his deeds, and a holy one dwells within his innards.336Koheles 9:7; Zohar, Vaera 138–139 — Joyful eating once one’s deeds are accepted: Koheles says, ‘Go, eat your bread with joy and drink your wine with a good heart, for God has already favored your deeds.’ The Zohar asks why Shlomo framed eating in these terms and explains that when a person walks in the ways of the Holy One and God draws him near, the bread and wine he eats and drinks are accompanied by gladness precisely because God desires his deeds. Rav Tzadok is therefore using the verse here as a spiritual diagnostic after Reish Lakish’s ordeal: the joyous meal is not evidence of indulgence but of divine acceptance. The Zohar supplies the classical mystical background connecting accepted deeds with sanctified enjoyment; identifying the escape from the Ludaei as the concrete test that authorized Reish Lakish’s joy is Rav Tzadok’s application.

וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״כְּרֵיסִי כָּרִי״, שֶׁחֶלְבּוֹ וּבְשָׂרוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לוֹ רַק כְּמוֹ כַּר וְכֶסֶת וְדָבָר שֶׁחוּץ מִמֶּנּוּ, כִּי עַצְמוּתוֹ עִנְיָן אַחֵר שֶׁהָיָה כּוּלּוֹ קָדוֹשׁ לַה׳ בְּהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַגַּשְׁמִיּוּת, וְהַגּוּף אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא בְּשַׂר אָדָם לְבוּשׁ לְעֶצֶם הָאָדָם שֶׁהוּא הַנַּעֲשֶׂה בְּצֶלֶם אֱלֹקִים

And this is what he said afterward, “my belly is my cushion”337Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:104 — Direct parallel: the Ludaei, korban-like eating, and ‘krisi kari’: Rav Tzadok elsewhere retells this Reish Lakish complex almost point for point. He explains that Reish Lakish’s surrender of himself to the Ludaei functioned as a genuine test of whether the hidden root of his former violence had been clarified; after he overcame them, that clarification allowed him to go out and eat and drink, because his eating was ‘from the side of holiness’ and ‘reckoned like a korban.’ He then turns immediately to ‘krisi kari,’ explaining that the belly that sustains bodily life is only a bedding or support for the person’s true life and essence. This is more than a thematic resemblance: it is a near-commentary on the present se’if and confirms Rav Tzadok’s sequence — existential clarification first, joyful sacred eating second, and then the demotion of the belly from ‘self’ to mere support for the self. — that his fat and flesh were reckoned by him only as a cushion and pillow, a thing outside himself; for his essence was another matter, wholly holy to the Lord in the stripping-away of physicality, and the body is but “the flesh of man,” a garment for the essence of man, which is the part made “in the image of God.”338Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim 14:1; Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2 — The body as garment and the soul as the true Adam: In Peri Tzadik Rav Tzadok explains the prophetic language of ‘garments’ as referring to the body, which clothes the soul; citing Zohar II 76a, he states that ‘the principal Adam is the soul, and the body is called only basar adam,’ and invokes Iyov’s ‘skin and flesh You clothed me’ to describe embodiment as clothing. In Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot he sharpens the same anthropology: the human body, taken by itself, shares the animal plane, while the nefesh nishmas chayim is the tzelem Elokim manifested through mastery of bodily forces. These parallels explain the present wording with unusual precision. Reish Lakish can call his fat and flesh a cushion because they are not his essence; the true Adam is the God-imaged spiritual self that governs the body rather than identifying itself with the body’s appetites.
וְלוֹמַר דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹכֵל וְשׁוֹתֶה לֹא הָיָה מַרְגִּישׁ מִזֶּה הֲנָאָה, כִּי לֹא הָיָה לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת עִם הֲנָאָה הַגּוּפָנִית כְּלָל —

to say that although he ate and drank, he felt no pleasure from it, for he had no connection to bodily pleasure at all.339Kesubos 104a; Avodah Zarah 11a, Tosafos; Yisrael Kedoshim §5 — Abundant eating without felt self-pleasure: On his deathbed Rebbi testified that he had labored in Torah with all ten fingers yet had not benefited from this world even with one little finger. Tosafos in Avodah Zarah notes the apparent tension with the report that radish, lettuce, and cucumbers never ceased from Rebbi’s table. Rav Tzadok addresses that tension directly in Yisrael Kedoshim §5: the delicacies could truly have been present and eaten, while Rebbi nevertheless ‘did not feel his own enjoyment’ because the eating itself was performed in complete kedushah and for the needs of the life entrusted to him; Rav Tzadok compares this to Hillel’s description of feeding the body as an act of kindness to a guest. That provides a precise precedent for the final claim here about Reish Lakish: the ideal is not necessarily abstention from food, but eating without appropriating the bodily pleasure as the self’s pleasure.

items.h: The theme: Tosafos there adduces from Zevachim 5a that Reish Lakish “would lie on his belly [rami a’me’ohi]” (and R’ Tzadok emends the printed “their way” to “his way” — this was Reish Lakish’s practice alone), asking why the Gemara mentions it. R’ Tzadok answers: he lay on his belly medicinally — it aids digestion (as in Sefer Otzar HaChaim and Rambam, Hilchos De’os). And since he ate a great deal (per Rashi, all that he earned), he required it as a remedy.

p: [מד] וְתוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם מַיְיתֵי מִזְּבָחִים [ה רע״א] ״רָמֵי אַמְּעוֹהִי״, וּמַקְשֶׁה דְּהָיָה דַּרְכּוֹ [וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ שָׁם ״דַּרְכָּן״ כו׳, טָעוּת סוֹפֵר, וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דַּרְכּוֹ, דְּרַק רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דַּרְכּוֹ כָּךְ וְלֹא מָצִינוּ כֵן בִּשְׁאָרֵי]

And Tosafos there brings from Zevachim [5a] “he lay upon his belly [rami a’me’ohi],” and asks that “it was his way” [and what they wrote there, “their way,” is a scribal error; it should read “his way,” for it was only Reish Lakish’s way thus, and we do not find so with others].340Zevachim 5a: “Reish Lakish would lie upon his belly [rami a’me’ohi] and raise a difficulty: If [offerings brought "not for their own sake"] are valid, let them satisfy [the owner’s obligation]; and if they do not, why are they brought?” R’ Tzadok emends Tosafos’s “their way” to “his way,” and explains that Reish Lakish’s belly-lying was a digestive aid (Rambam, Hilchos De’os) needed because he ate greatly — a sign not of gluttony but of korban-like, holy eating.341Niddah 13b; Chiddushei HaRa’ah to Berachos 13b; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 4:5 — What posture is ‘aparkid’?: The Gemara records that R’ Yehoshua ben Levi would censure one who sleeps aparkeid because of the danger of improper arousal, while allowing a slight turn to the side. Rashi understands the term as lying face-up; the Aruch, cited by Rishonim, understands it as lying face-down, and the Ra’ah notes that some authorities include both postures. The Rambam consequently rules that one should sleep neither on one’s face nor on one’s back, but on one’s side. This creates an important textual background to Reish Lakish’s ‘rami a’me’ohi’: if the Aruch’s face-down reading is adopted, his practice appears to press against the ordinary restriction. In the fuller text of this passage Rav Tzadok himself notices the problem and suggests either that Reish Lakish disagreed with that reading or that he knew himself to be free of its danger. The classical sources establish the posture issue; Rav Tzadok’s use of it as evidence for the holiness of Reish Lakish’s eating is his own homiletical development.

וְנִרְאֶה טַעַם שְׁכִיבָתוֹ עַל בִּטְנוֹ בְּפָשׁוּט הָיָה, לְפִי מַה שֶּׁרָאִיתִי בְּסֵפֶר אוֹצַר הַחַיִּים וּבְפֵירוּשׁ דִּבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ״ם [הִלְכוֹת דֵּיעוֹת] דְּהוּא עוֹזֵר וּמְסַיֵּיעַ הָעִיכּוּל

And it appears the reason for his lying upon his belly was simple: per what I saw in Sefer Otzar HaChaim and in the explanation of the Rambam’s words [Hilchos De’os], that it aids and assists digestion.342Rambam, Hilchos De’os 4:3–5; Chiddushei Mayim Chayim 4:5 — Digestion and reclining: a medical nuance: The Rambam’s health regimen does connect bodily posture with digestion: after eating one should remain seated or recline on the left side and avoid exertion until the food has been digested; he also advises against retiring immediately after a meal. A later commentary, Chiddushei Mayim Chayim, explains the left-side posture physiologically, as helping the digestive process. At the same time, the Rambam explicitly says not to sleep face-down or face-up. Rav Tzadok is therefore precise in writing that he saw this in ‘the explanation of the Rambam’s words,’ not that the Rambam himself prescribed prone lying. His conclusion that Reish Lakish lay on his belly specifically as a digestive remedy is an interpretive medical application drawn from this broader regimen, together with the Otzar HaChaim he cites.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהָיָה אוֹכֵל הַרְבֵּה, כַּנִּרְאֶה מִדִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י ״כָּל מַה שֶּׁהִרְוִיחַ״, הוּצְרַךְ לָזֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ הָרְפוּאָה
And because he ate a great deal — as appears from Rashi’s words, “all that he earned” — he required this by way of remedy.

וְזֶהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי שֶׁכָּל אֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת הַכֹּל בִּקְדֻשָּׁה וְלֹא לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, וְאֵינוֹ מִדַּת רַעַבְתָנוּת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, רַק כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בַּאֲכִילַת קָרְבָּנוֹת [בִּפְסָחִים נז סע״א] בְּיוֹחָנָן בֶּן נַרְבָּאי ״וְיֹאכַל בְּקָדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם״

And this is as I wrote, that all his eating is like korbanos, wholly in holiness and not for his own pleasure, and it is no trait of ravenousness, God forbid — only in the manner brought regarding the eating of korbanos [Pesachim 57a] concerning Yochanan ben Narbai, who “would fill his belly from the holies of Heaven.”343Pesachim 57a: among the “four cries of the Temple courtyard,” it was said of Yochanan ben Narbai (Nadvai), a priest, that “he would fill his belly from the holies of Heaven” — eating vast quantities of sacrificial portions — yet “in all his days no nosar [leftover sacrificial meat] was found in the Temple.” R’ Tzadok invokes him as the model of great but wholly sacred consumption, paralleling Reish Lakish.344Rambam, Hilchos Maaseh HaKorbanos 10:1 — Sacrificial eating is itself a mitzvah and part of atonement: The Rambam codifies the eating of the chatas and asham by the kohanim as a positive commandment, deriving it from ‘they shall eat those things through which atonement was effected,’ and formulates the principle: ‘the kohanim eat and the owners receive atonement.’ He adds that the eating of other sacred portions assigned to kohanim is likewise a mitzvah. This gives halachic depth to Rav Tzadok’s analogy between the talmid chacham’s sanctified eating and korbanos: sacrificial eating is not merely permitted consumption after the avodah but can itself belong to the mitzvah-process of the korban. Rav Tzadok then spiritualizes that structure, treating Reish Lakish’s bodily nourishment as an act whose very eating is avodah.

וְהִנֵּה כְּמוֹ כָּל הַזְּבָחִים שֶׁנִּזְבְּחוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָן כְּשֵׁרִין כִּדְתְנַן [רֵישׁ זְבָחִים], דִּלְשֵׁם חוּלִּין אֲפִילּוּ בְּחַטָּאת כְּשֵׁרָה, דְּלָא מִינָּהּ לָא מַחְרִיב בָּהּ כִּדְאִיתָא [שָׁם ג.]

And behold, just as all offerings slaughtered “not for their own sake” are valid, as we learned [beginning of Zevachim] — that even a chatas [slaughtered] “for the sake of unconsecrated meat” is valid, since [an intent] not of its own kind does not uproot it, as it is stated [there, 3a] —345Mishnah Zevachim 1:1; Rambam, Hilchos Pesulei HaMukdashin 15:1 — Validity without discharge of obligation: The Mishnah’s governing rule is that most offerings brought shelo lishman remain valid but do not discharge the owner’s obligation; the principal exceptions are the korban Pesach in its proper time and the chatas. The Rambam codifies the same distinction: the sacrificial service continues and the korban remains acceptable, yet the owner must still bring the offering required of him. Rav Tzadok’s comparison depends on precisely this two-level halachic structure. A passing intent of bodily enjoyment does not, in his analogy, turn holy eating into forbidden or spiritually void eating; rather, it represents an imperfection of lishmah within an act whose underlying sacred identity remains intact.346Zevachim 3a; Rashi as cited by Tosafos HaRid — ‘Not of its kind does not uproot it’: Zevachim distinguishes a chatas slaughtered for the sake of another korban from one slaughtered ‘for the sake of chullin.’ The latter remains valid because an alien designation that is not itself a sacrificial identity cannot seize the korban and uproot its existing name. Rashi explains the mechanism as the foreign name failing to take hold upon the offering so as to displace its consecrated identity. This sharpens Rav Tzadok’s metaphor. The occasional thought of physical pleasure is treated not as a rival sacred purpose that redefines the eating, but as something extraneous to the eater’s established kedushah; it therefore does not ‘destroy’ the korban-like character of the act. The Gemara and Rashi supply the technical rule; this psychological application is Rav Tzadok’s own analogy.

הָכִי נַמֵּי מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה דִּכְאִלּוּ קָדוֹשׁ שָׁרוּי בְּמֵעָיו דַּאֲכִילָתוֹ כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, אֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה לוֹ אֵיזֶה פַּעַם כַּוָּונַת הֲנָאָה — דְּלֹא הַכֹּל זוֹכִין לִהְיוֹת כְּרַבִּי שֶׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ [כְּתוּבּוֹת קד.] ״וְלֹא נֶהֱנֵיתִי״ כו׳ — אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָן כְּשֵׁרִין כְּקָרְבָּנוֹת

so too one who merits that “a holy one dwells within his innards,” whose eating is like korbanos: even if he should sometimes have an intent of pleasure — for not all merit to be like Rebbi, who said of himself [Kesubos 104a], “I did not benefit,” etc. — nonetheless, “not for their own sake” they are valid, like korbanos.347Zevachim 2a–3a: all offerings slaughtered “not for their own sake [shelo lishman]” are nonetheless valid (though they do not discharge the owner’s obligation); even a chatas slaughtered with intent “for unconsecrated meat” is valid, since an intent “not of its own kind does not uproot it.” R’ Tzadok’s analogy: the sanctified eater’s occasional thought of pleasure is like shelo lishmah — the “offering” of his eating remains valid and favorable.348Pesachim 50b; Tosafos ad loc. — Not every ‘shelo lishmah’ is the same: Chazal also teach that one should engage in Torah and mitzvos even shelo lishmah because one may thereby come to lishmah. Tosafos immediately limits that encouragement: the constructive form of shelo lishmah is not the malicious kind pursued in order to boast, provoke, or defeat another. The distinction is useful here because Rav Tzadok is not granting blanket sanctity to every self-interested motive. His case is much narrower: a person whose eating is fundamentally established as avodah may occasionally experience an intent of personal pleasure, and that residual admixture does not uproot the act’s holy identity. Thus the korban analogy should be read as describing an imperfect lishmah within a holy framework, not as erasing Chazal’s moral distinctions among different motives.
וְזֶהוּ ״דְּרָמֵי אַמְּעוֹהִי״, שֶׁזֶּה מוֹרֶה עַל קְדֻשַּׁת אֲכִילוֹתָיו, דִּמְעֵי כְּרֵיסוֹ הוּא קָדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם, וַאֲפִילּוּ שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ כְּשֵׁרִין
And this is “he lay upon his belly” — which indicates the holiness of his eating: that the innards of his belly are “the holies of Heaven,” and even “not for their own sake” they are valid.

items.h: The theme: “Upon this Reish Lakish said, ‘I will open an opening for myself [eftach ana pischa l’nafshai]’” (Zevachim 5a) — a phrase both needlessly long and awkward. Per R’ Tzadok’s reading — that the whole “rami a’me’ohi” question is “for his own soul’s sake,” wishing his eating to be favorable. The phrase fits perfectly: “I will open” an opening for his soul, which thirsts and craves this.

p: [מה] וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ עַל זֶה אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ ״אֶפְתַּח אֲנָא פִּתְחָא לְנַפְשַׁאי״, וּמִלְּבַד דְּאֵין מוּבָן צֹרֶךְ אֲרִיכוּת לָשׁוֹן זֶה הוּא מְגוּמְגָּם גַּם כֵּן

And this is what it says there afterward: upon this Reish Lakish said, “I will open an opening for myself” — and besides that the need for this lengthy wording is not understood, it is also awkward.349Zevachim 5a: “Reish Lakish said: I will open an opening for myself [eftach ana pischa l’nafshai]” — introducing his derivation about offerings brought shelo lishmah. R’ Tzadok reads the odd phrase homiletically: it is an “opening for his soul,” which thirsts to know that even his shelo-lishmah eating is holy and favorable to God — a nedavah, like a freewill-offering.

וּלְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּעִיקַּר קֻשְׁיָא דְּ״רָמֵי אַמְּעוֹהִי״ הַיְינוּ ״לְצֹרֶךְ נַפְשֵׁיהּ״, דְּהוּא רָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְרָצוֹן גַּם כֵּן, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר שַׁפִּיר לְשׁוֹן ״אֶפְתַּח״ כו׳ שֶׁזֶּה פֶּתַח לְנַפְשׁוֹ הַצְּמֵאָה וּתְאֵבָה לְדָבָר זֶה

And per what I wrote — that the essence of the “he lay upon his belly” question is “for his soul’s need,” that he wished it to be favorable as well — upon this he aptly said the term “I will open,” for this is an opening for his soul, which thirsts and craves this thing.

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא בִּמְגִילָּה [י: יא.] ״פָּתַח לָהּ פִּתְחָא לְהַאי פָּרָשְׁתָא״, דְּהַכַּוָּונָה שֶׁאוֹתוֹ מַאֲמָר הוּא פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ כָּל עִנְיַן פָּרָשַׁת הַמְּגִילָּה — וְכָךְ בֵּירוּר דָּבָר זֶה הוּא פֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לְשֹׁרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת נַפְשׁוֹ, בִּהְיוֹת גַּם הַשֶּׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ קָדוֹשׁ לֵאלֹקָיו וּמְרוּצֶּה גַּם כֵּן

In the manner brought in Megillah [10b], “he opened for her the opening to this passage” — the meaning being that that statement is an “open gateway” to the root of the whole matter of the Megillah’s account; so too the clarification of this matter is an open gateway to the root of his soul’s holiness, in that even the “not for its own sake” is holy and favorable to his God.350Megillah 10b–11a; Makkos 10b — ‘Opening an opening’ as a thematic gateway: The Bavli repeatedly uses the formula patach lah pischa l’hai parshata when an Amora introduces a biblical section through a verse that exposes its governing theme; the opening pages of Megillah preserve an extended series of such petichos. Reish Lakish himself uses the same formula in Makkos when introducing the parashah of the accidental killer. In those classical settings, the ‘opening’ is not merely a first citation but an interpretive gateway into the root-idea of the entire passage. Rav Tzadok deliberately internalizes that familiar derashah-form: Reish Lakish’s explanation of shelo lishmah becomes a petach not only to a sugya but to the shoresh of his own nefesh. The Bavli supplies the literary form; identifying that form with the inner structure of Reish Lakish’s soul is Rav Tzadok’s homiletical development.
וְהָא דְּלֹא עָלָה לְחוֹבָה הַיְינוּ רַק לָצֵאת יְדֵי נִדְרוֹ, אֲבָל נְדָבָה הָוֵי, וְהוּא כְּקָרְבַּן נְדָבָה שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳

And that it “did not count toward obligation” means only that it did not fulfill his vow; but it is a nedavah [freewill-offering], and it is like a korban nedavah, which too is favorable before the Lord.351Zevachim 5a; Mishnah Zevachim 1:1; Bartenura ad loc. — ‘Nedavah’ without discharge of the vow: Reish Lakish derives the rule from ‘what has crossed your lips you shall keep and perform, as you vowed … a freewill-offering’ (Devarim 23:24): if the korban was offered as vowed, the owner fulfills his neder; if it was brought shelo lishmah, it remains valid ‘as though he brought it as a nedavah,’ but he has not discharged the obligation and must still bring the korban of his vow. Bartenura spells out that ‘nedavah’ here describes the first korban’s continued validity and acceptability, not the fulfillment of the original neder. This is the exact halachic hinge of Rav Tzadok’s analogy: the imperfectly directed act is still ratzui and retains sacrificial standing, even though it does not accomplish the particular chovah for which full lishmah was required.

וְכֵן אֲכִילַת הַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁכְּקָרְבָּנוֹת, וְהַפֶּה הוּא פֶּתַח הַגּוּף, וְכֵן ״כָּל עֲמַל אָדָם לְפִיהוּ״, וְ״אָדָם לַעֲמַל פֶּה יוּלָּד״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צט רע״ב], וְהָעִיקָּר לַעֲמַל תּוֹרָה כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

And likewise the eating of the Torah scholar, which is like korbanos; and the mouth is the opening of the body, and so “all a man’s toil is for his mouth,” and “man is born for the toil of the mouth,” as they said [Sanhedrin 99b] — the essence being the toil of Torah, as it is stated there.352Sanhedrin 99b: “‘For man is born unto toil’ (Iyov 5:7) — [whether toil of the mouth or of labor? Scripture says, ‘for his mouth compels him’:] man was created for the toil of the mouth [amal peh]” — and the Gemara concludes, for the toil of Torah. R’ Tzadok: the mouth is the body’s “opening”; its highest toil is Torah, but the eating that passes through it must itself be sanctified.

אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ הַמּוּבָא בַּתּוֹסָפוֹת [כְּתוּבּוֹת קד רע״א] דְּעַד שֶׁמִּתְפַּלֵּל שֶׁיִּכָּנְסוּ דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה יִתְפַּלֵּל שֶׁלֹּא יִכָּנְסוּ מַעֲדַנִּים, דְּאַף דְּעִיקַּר הַכֹּל הוּא כְּנִיסַת הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה בַּלֵּב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צְרִיכָה לִהְיוֹת יִרְאָתוֹ קוֹדֶמֶת לְחָכְמָתוֹ הַמַּגְדִּירָתוֹ בְּסוּר מֵרָע

But nonetheless they said in the Midrash cited in Tosafos [Kesubos 104a] that before one prays that words of Torah should enter, he should pray that delicacies not enter — for although the main thing is the entry of the words of Torah into the heart, nonetheless his fear must precede his wisdom, fencing him in “turning from evil.353Tosafos to Kesubos 104a; Tanna Devei Eliyahu Rabbah 26; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:12 — Delicacies before Torah: Tosafos explains Rebbi’s declaration that he had not benefited from this world by citing the Midrash: before one prays that Torah enter his body, one should pray that delicacies not enter it. Tanna Devei Eliyahu gives the fuller ethical formulation: even one who has not yet merited to pray for Torah should at least pray that excessive eating and drinking not enter his innards, and it then records Rebbi’s testimony that his eating and drinking were only for sustaining life and Torah. The Rambam codifies the same educational direction, ruling that Torah does not endure in one who studies amid indulgence in food and drink. Rav Tzadok therefore reads restraint in appetite not as an independent ascetic ideal, but as the protective clearing through which Torah can truly enter and remain.”

דְּלוּלֵי זֶה ״לָמָּה זֶּה מְחִיר בְּיַד כְּסִיל״ כו׳; וְהָעִיקָּר בַּתַּאֲווֹת, וְהַהַתְחָלָה בַּאֲכִילָה שֶׁבָּזֶה הָיָה חֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, וְכָל אֲכִילָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ עֲבוֹדָה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לְכָל רַע, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת לב.] ״מְלֵי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ זָנֵי בִּישֵׁי״, וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בַּאֲכִילָה דִּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא פֶּתַח הַכְּנִיסָה לְכָל טוֹב

For without this, “why this price in the hand of a fool?”; and the essence is in the desires, and the beginning is in eating — wherein was the sin of Adam HaRishon — and every eating that is not holy service is the gateway of entry to all evil, as they said [Berachos 32a], “[when] he fills his belly [come] the evil kinds”; and the reverse — eating in holiness — is the gateway of entry to all good.354Pirkei Avos 3:9; Yoma 72b; Rashi ad loc.; Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim 3:1 — Yirah must precede wisdom: R’ Chanina ben Dosa teaches that when fear of sin precedes wisdom, the wisdom endures, whereas wisdom that precedes fear does not. Yoma applies ‘why is there a price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom when he has no heart?’ (Mishlei 17:16) to Torah scholars who possess learning without yiras Shamayim; Rashi explains that Torah is a gateway through which one enters fear of Heaven, so yirah must be established as the goal that precedes the learning. Rav Tzadok develops the same point in Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim §3: a person may possess Torah-learning and nevertheless be called a kesil when yiras Shamayim is absent, because Torah’s purpose is to direct the person in the way of Hashem. This supplies the classical and Rav-Tzadokian background to the present insistence that the fence of sur mera must precede the heart’s acquisition of Torah.355Berachos 32a: “‘When they were fed they became full, [their heart was exalted;] therefore they forgot Me’ — a lion does not roar over a basket of straw but over a basket of meat; [when] he fills his belly come all the evil kinds [mali karsei, zanei bishi].” R’ Tzadok: unsanctified eating is the gateway to every evil (as with Adam’s sin), while holy eating is the gateway to all good.356Peri Tzadik, Pesach 1:1; Kuntres Amalah shel Torah §3; Peri Tzadik, Tazria §3 — The first breach was eating, and its repair begins there: Rav Tzadok states repeatedly that the primordial corruption began when the serpent introduced bodily desire into eating. In Peri Tzadik, Pesach §1 he explains that the first mitzvah-food of the redeemed nation, korban Pesach and then matzah, repairs Adam HaRishon’s root defect in eating; in Kuntres Amalah shel Torah §3 he again calls taavas achilah the beginning of the world’s wound; and in Peri Tzadik, Tazria §3 he writes that kedushas hama’achalim embraces the entire Torah, because one whose eating is guarded in holiness is thereby protected across the mitzvos. These parallels make the final sentence here especially exact: eating is the ‘gateway’ because Rav Tzadok treats appetite as the first point at which the yetzer hara entered human experience, while sanctified eating reverses that entry at its root.

items.h: The theme: The very first mitzvah commanded at the Exodus — the beginning of entering Jewishness and building the Israelite nation. Was the mitzvah of eating the korban Pesach (whose essence is its eating, Pesachim 76b), and likewise the eating of matzah. The prohibition of eating chametz is the warning against eating from the side of the yetzer hara, called “the leaven in the dough” (Berachos 17a), which “raises the dough higher than it is” — the craving for excess beyond one’s portion.

p: [מו] וּמִצְוָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁנִּצְטַוּוּ בִּיצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם, שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת כְּנִיסַת הַיַּהֲדוּת וּבִנְיַן אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, הָיָה מִצְוַת אֲכִילָה דְּקָרְבַּן פֶּסַח דְּעִיקַּר מִצְוָתוֹ הוּא אֲכִילָתוֹ, וְכִדְתְנַן [פְּסָחִים עו סע״ב], וְכֵן אֲכִילַת מַצָּה

And the first mitzvah with which they were commanded at the Exodus from Egypt — which is the beginning of the entry into Jewishness and the building of the Israelite nation — was the mitzvah of eating the korban Pesach, whose essence of its mitzvah is its eating, as we learned [Pesachim 76b]; and likewise the eating of matzah.357Pesachim 76b (Mishnah/Gemara on the korban Pesach): the essence of the Pesach mitzvah is its eating (“its beginning [purpose] is for people, to eat”). R’ Tzadok stresses that Israel’s founding mitzvah is a mitzvah of eating — establishing sanctified consumption as the nation’s very foundation, over against the chametz of the yetzer hara.

וְאַזְהָרַת אֲכִילַת חָמֵץ הוּא אַזְהָרַת אֲכִילָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע הַנִּקְרָא [בִּבְרָכוֹת יז רע״א] ״שְׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה״, שֶׁהוּא הַמְרוֹמֵם הָעִיסָּה יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁהִיא, וְזֶהוּ בַּקָּשַׁת הַמּוֹתָרוֹת יוֹתֵר מֵהַשַּׁיָּיךְ לְחֶלְקוֹ

And the prohibition against eating chametz is the warning against eating from the side of the yetzer hara, called358R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek §3): “I heard that our Rabbis likened the yetzer to the ‘leaven in the dough’ (Berachos 17a) — and the leaven is [also] the ‘repair’ of the dough (and it says in Berachos 34a that of leaven, ‘its small amount is good’).” The se’if’s reading of chametz: the leaven is the yetzer’s craving for excess “beyond one’s portion,” while matzah is the holy eating for Heaven in which the leaven has no part. [in Berachos 17a] “the leaven in the dough,” which raises the dough higher than it [truly] is — and this is the seeking of excess, beyond what belongs to one’s portion.359Sotah 9a–9b; Maharal, Netivos Olam, Nesiv HaOsher 2 — Desire beyond one’s proper portion: Chazal formulate a general rule from the sotah and then from the primordial serpent: one who sets his eyes on what is not fitting for him does not receive what he seeks, and even what he already possesses is taken from him. The Maharal explains that every person has that which is specifically fitting to him; once desire reaches toward what is not his proper portion, the person leaves the condition in which his own portion could satisfy him and becomes marked by deficiency. This is a close classical parallel to Rav Tzadok’s definition of the se’or she-ba’isah here as bakashas ha-mosaros — craving for excess beyond what belongs to one’s chelek. The Gemara supplies the ethical structure; Rav Tzadok identifies that structure with the inflationary action of leaven in the dough.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מַצָּה הוּא הָאֲכִילָה בִּקְדֻשָּׁה שֶׁהִיא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, וְאֵין לַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה חֵלֶק בָּהּ; וְזֶהוּ הַפֶּתַח לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּפָתַח רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, דְּגַם הַנֶּפֶשׁ ״לֹא תִמָּלֵא״ בְּתַאֲווֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה

whereas matzah is the eating in holiness, which is for the sake of Heaven, and the “leaven in the dough” has no part in it; and this is the “opening for his soul” that Reish Lakish opened — that even the soul “shall not be filled” [the close of “the toil of man is for his mouth, and yet the soul is not filled,” Koheles 6:7] with the desires of this world.

וְכֵן בִּקְדֻשָּׁה ״אוֹהֵב מִצְוָה לֹא יִשְׂבַּע מִצְוָה״, וְ״צַדִּיק אוֹכֵל לְשׂוֹבַע נַפְשׁוֹ״, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹ שְׂבִיעָה בְּמַה דְּשַׁיָּיךְ לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ; מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן ״בֶּטֶן רְשָׁעִים״ דְּ״קֶבֶר פָּתוּחַ גְּרוֹנָם״ הוּא לְעוֹלָם חָסֵר דְּאֵין לוֹ מִילּוּי, וְהַשְּׂבִיעָה שֶׁלּוֹ אֵינוֹ שְׂבִיעָה אֶלָּא מִילּוּי הַכֶּרֶס לְבַד

And likewise in holiness, “one who loves a mitzvah is not sated with mitzvos,”360Devarim Rabbah 2:26 — Love of Torah and mitzvos is intrinsically unsated: On ‘one who loves silver will not be satisfied with silver’ (Koheles 5:9), the Midrash first reads the ‘silver’ as Torah: one who loves Torah is never sated with Torah. It then gives the parallel derashah that one who loves mitzvos is not sated with mitzvos, illustrating the point through David, who prepared for the Beis HaMikdash although he had been told that he would not build it, and Moshe, who designated the eastern cities of refuge although they would not yet function until the cities in Eretz Yisrael were designated. Rav Tzadok therefore invokes a well-established Midrashic paradox: holy desire is also ‘unsated,’ but unlike bodily craving it is not a deficit seeking to fill itself; it is the expansiveness of love for Torah and mitzvos that continually seeks another act of service. and “the tzaddik eats to the satisfaction of his soul”361Midrash Mishlei 13:5 — ‘The tzaddik eats to the satiety of his soul’ as spiritual filling: Midrash Mishlei reads ‘tzaddik ochel l’sova nafsho’ (Mishlei 13:25) as referring to one who fills his soul with words of Torah, while ‘the belly of the wicked is lacking’ describes one who is empty of Torah. A second reading says that one who learned in youth continues filling his soul with Torah throughout old age rather than abandoning what he acquired. Rav Tzadok preserves the verse’s language of eating while making the same decisive shift from the belly to the nefesh: true satiety belongs to what pertains to the soul. His point is therefore not merely moderation in food. The righteous person’s eating participates in a mode of life whose real receptacle is the nefesh, whereas the wicked person’s pursuit remains trapped at the level of the belly. — for he has satiety in what pertains to his soul; whereas “the belly of the wicked,” whose “throat is an open grave,” is forever lacking and has no filling, and his “satiety” is not satiety but a mere filling of the gut.362Maharal, Ohr Chadash to Esther 5:13; Netivos Olam, Nesiv HaOsher 2 — Nefesh, belly, and the structure of satiety: The Maharal explains the contrast in Mishlei 13:25 by taking its vocabulary with precision: the tzaddik has shleimus, and therefore ‘eats to the satiety of his nefesh’; the wicked person is described instead through the beten, the material belly, because matter is characterized by chesaron and consequently does not attain true satiety. In Nesiv HaOsher he develops the same principle with regard to the eye that is never satisfied with wealth: when a person’s desire is rooted in deficiency, every acquisition generates another lack rather than completion. Rav Tzadok’s distinction here between genuine sevi’ah and mere milui ha-keres closely tracks that metaphysical contrast. A stomach can be physically filled while the person remains existentially unsatisfied; satiety, in the stronger sense, belongs to a life ordered by the completed nefesh.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁמְּמַלֵּא כְּרֵיסוֹ מִקָּדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם הִיא אֲכִילָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ שְׂבִיעָה

whereas one who fills his belly from the holies of Heaven — that is an eating in which there is satiety.363Yoma 39a; Rashi and Ritva ad loc. — Holy food carrying an actual blessing of satiety: During the forty years of Shimon HaTzadik’s service, the Gemara says that blessing rested upon the Omer, the Two Loaves, and the Lechem HaPanim: a kohen who received a kezayis could eat it and be satisfied, and some even left over. After that period the blessing ceased, and the portions no longer satisfied; Rashi defines the later curse precisely as ‘it does not satiate him,’ while the Ritva emphasizes the contrast between the blessed portion that brought satiety and the later portion that did not. This supplies a striking Temple analogue to Rav Tzadok’s phrase that one who fills himself from kodshei Shamayim experiences an eating ‘in which there is satiety.’ Chazal literally portray sacred food as capable of carrying a quality of sevi’ah beyond its physical quantity; Rav Tzadok extends that model to the sanctified eating of the tzaddik.

וְזֶהוּ אֲכִילַת אוֹתוֹ צַדִּיק — רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, דִּכְפִי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י דְּאָכַל כָּל מַה שֶּׁמִּשְׁתַּכֵּר נִרְאֶה כְּמִלֵּי כְּרֵיסֵיהּ, אֲבָל הָיָה מִקָּדְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם, וְזֶהוּ הַפֶּתַח לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ דְּהַכֹּל לְרָצוֹן לִפְנֵי ה׳

And this is the eating of that tzaddik — Reish Lakish — for according to Rashi’s words that he ate all he earned, it appears as a “filling of his belly”; but it was from the holies of Heaven, and this is the “opening for his soul,” that all was favorable before the Lord.

וְעַל כֵּן לֹא רָצָה לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים יְגִיעוֹ, וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמַר רַב לְרַב הוּנָא [עֵירוּבִין נד רע״א] ״אִם יֵשׁ לְךָ הֵיטֵב לְךָ״ וְגוֹ׳, ״וְאִם תֹּאמַר אַנִּיחַ לְבָנַי״ כו׳ — כִּי מֵאַחַר דְּבָטוּחַ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁכָּל הֲנָאוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, לָמָּה לֵיהּ לְהַנִּיחַ לַאֲחֵרִים שֶׁאֵין יוֹדֵעַ מַה יִּהְיוּ

And therefore he did not wish to leave his toil to others, in the manner Rav said to Rav Huna [Eruvin 54a], “if you have, benefit yourself [for there is no enjoyment in the grave], and if you say, I will leave it for my children,” etc. — for since he is confident within himself that all his pleasures are in holiness, why should he leave for others, of whom one does not know what they will be —

וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [קֹהֶלֶת ב, יח–יט] ״וְשָׂנֵאתִי אֶת כָּל עֲמָלִי שֶׁאַנִּיחֶנּוּ לְאָדָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחֲרַי וּמִי יוֹדֵעַ הֶחָכָם יִהְיֶה אוֹ סָכָל״ וְגוֹ׳, וְאָמַר [שָׁם ג, כב] ״אֵין טוֹב מֵאֲשֶׁר יִשְׂמַח הָאָדָם בְּמַעֲשָׂיו כִּי הוּא חֶלְקוֹ״

as it says [Koheles 2:18–19], “And I hated all my toil, that I must leave it to the man who will be after me, and who knows whether he will be wise or foolish,” and it says [ibid. 3:22], “there is nothing better than that a man rejoice in his deeds, for that is his portion.”364Eruvin 54a: “Rav said to Rav Huna: “[my son,] if you have [means], do good for yourself — [for there is no enjoyment in the grave] — and if you say, ‘I will leave [it] for my children’ — who will tell you [what will be] in the grave?” — paired with Koheles 2:18–19, 3:22. R’ Tzadok: one whose every enjoyment is holy rightly benefits from his own toil rather than hoarding for uncertain heirs; Reish Lakish’s leaving even a kav he counted against himself.

items.h: The theme: But leaving an estate for one’s children is the way of the amei ha’aretz who occupy themselves with settling the land, or of one to whom God grants abundance and who is but a “channel” through whom God provides to others. For such a person, that is his portion, what is stored up for him above, and so too leaving his children their statute. A talmid chacham whose Torah is his craft, however, who works only for his sustenance and whose every pleasure is holy, need not stint himself to leave for his children.

p: [מז] אֲבָל זֶהוּ מִדַּת עַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ הָעוֹסְקִים בְּיִשּׁוּבָהּ שֶׁל אֶרֶץ, אוֹ מִי שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לוֹ הַרְבֵּה וְהוּא אֵין רַשַּׁאי לְהוֹצִיא בְּמוֹתָרוֹת וְרַק הוּא צִינּוֹר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ עַל יָדוֹ לַאֲחֵרִים — וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן חֶלְקוֹ מַה שֶּׁגְּנָזוֹ לוֹ לְמַעְלָה, וְכֵן לְהַנִּיחַ לְבָנָיו חוֹק

But this [leaving an estate] is the trait of the amei ha’aretz who occupy themselves with the settlement of the land, or of one to whom the Blessed Name grants abundance and who is not permitted to spend it on excess, but is only a “channel” through whom the Blessed Name provides to others — for him, too, that is his portion, what has been stored up for him above, and so too the leaving of a statute for his children.365Bava Basra 133b; Rambam, Hilchos Nachalos 6:11; Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 282:1 — Leaving heirs versus actively transferring their inheritance: Chazal say that one who gives his property to others and leaves his children without it has acted effectively, but ‘the spirit of the Sages is not pleased with him’; Shmuel even warns against participating in a transfer away from a rightful heir, and the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch codify that restraint. Rav Tzadok’s statement here is therefore narrower than a general rejection of inheritance. He distinguishes between the ordinary person, for whom leaving a portion to children belongs to the normal ordering of worldly life, and the talmid chacham who need not impoverish or constrict his own holy use of his earnings merely in order to accumulate an estate. The halachic sources concern actively diverting an inheritance from heirs; Rav Tzadok is discussing whether one must stint during life so that a surplus will remain.
אֲבָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁתּוֹרָתוֹ אוּמָּנוּתוֹ וְאֵין עוֹסֵק בִּמְלָאכָה אֶלָּא כְּדֵי פַּרְנָסָתוֹ וְכָל הֲנָאוֹתָיו בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, אֵין לוֹ לְצַמְצֵם עַצְמוֹ לְהַנִּיחַ לְבָנָיו

But a Torah scholar whose Torah is his craft, who occupies himself with labor only enough for his sustenance, and all of whose pleasures are in holiness — he need not stint himself in order to leave for his children.366Berachos 35b; Pirkei Avos 1:15; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:7 — Torah primary and labor secondary: Chazal contrast the earlier generations, who made Torah their fixed occupation and work secondary and succeeded in both, with later generations who reversed the priorities. Shammai’s ‘make your Torah fixed’ is explained by the Rishonim as making Torah the ikar and labor tafel, and the Rambam likewise instructs one not to postpone Torah until after accumulating wealth, but to make Torah fixed and one’s occupation temporary. This supplies the classical frame for Rav Tzadok’s phrase talmid chacham she-Toraso umanuso: he is not describing idleness, but a life in which work is undertaken only to the measure required for sustenance while Torah remains the defining vocation. Rav Tzadok then adds his own further premise here—that such a person’s permitted enjoyments themselves can be incorporated into kedushah.
וְקַבָּא דְּמוֹרִיקָא שֶׁהִנִּיחַ רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ קָרֵי אַנַּפְשֵׁיהּ ״וְעָזְבוּ לַאֲחֵרִים חֵילָם״, שֶׁחָשַׁב זֶה לְעֹנֶשׁ לוֹ שֶׁעָזַב יְגִיעוֹ לַאֲחֵרִים אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר מוּעָט

And the “kav of saffron” that Reish Lakish left over, he applied to himself, “and they leave their wealth to others” (Tehillim 49:11) — for he reckoned it a punishment to himself that he left his toil to others, even though it was a small thing.367Tehillim 49:11; Gittin 47a: “the fool and the boor perish together and leave their wealth to others [v’azvu la’acherim cheilam].” When Reish Lakish died leaving only “a kav of saffron,” he applied this verse to himself — treating the small unenjoyed remainder as the trace of his one light sin (for “there is no death without sin”), which alone kept him from benefiting from all his own toil.

כִּי מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַשְׁפִּיעַ לְאָדָם הוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיֵּהָנֶה הוּא בּוֹ, וּמַה שֶּׁלֹּא זָכָה לֵיהָנוֹת הוּא בִּשְׁבִיל אֵיזֶה חֵטְא; וְאוֹתוֹ חֵטְא קַל שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ מֵת, דְּאֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא, אוֹתוֹ הַחֵטְא גָּרַם גַּם כֵּן לְאוֹתוֹ דָּבָר מוּעָט שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לֵיהָנוֹת מִמֶּנּוּ בְּעַצְמוֹ
