For what the Blessed Name provides to a person is so that he himself should benefit from it, and what he did not merit to benefit from is on account of some sin; and that light sin for which he died — “for there is no death without sin” — that very sin also caused that small thing which he could not himself benefit from, and had to leave to others.368Koheles 5:17–18; 6:2; Rashi ad loc. — The Divine gift includes the ability to enjoy one’s own portion: Koheles calls it good for a person to eat, drink, and see good in the toil of the life God has given him, ‘for that is his portion’; it then calls God’s granting a person wealth together with the power to eat from it and rejoice in his toil a matnas Elokim. The contrasting tragedy is the man whom God gives wealth and honor but ‘does not empower him to eat from it,’ so that a stranger consumes it. Rashi explains the positive verse as the power to enjoy one’s possessions during life, and the negative verse as the failure to be happy in one’s portion and derive settled benefit from one’s wealth. These verses give a direct biblical background to Rav Tzadok’s claim that what Heaven provides a person is meant to become his own permitted benefit, while an unenjoyed remainder can signify that this gift of ‘power to eat from it’ was withheld. Rav Tzadok’s attribution of Reish Lakish’s particular remainder to a final light defect is his own reading of the episode.
וְנִמְצָא כָּל הַסִּיפּוּר דְּשָׁם בְּ״הַשּׁוֹלֵחַ״ כּוּלּוֹ לְשִׁבְחוֹ שֶׁל רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ, וְחָלִילָה לָהֶם לְהַזְכִּיר דָּבָר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גְּנוּת לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם

And thus the entire account there, in “HaSholeach,” is wholly to the praise of Reish Lakish, and far be it from them [the Sages] to mention a matter that carries disgrace for a Torah scholar.369Shabbos 55b–56a — Chazal’s pattern of rereading the apparent sins of great figures: A sustained sugya reexamines biblical descriptions of Reuven, the sons of Eli, the sons of Shmuel, David, and others, repeatedly formulating that ‘one who says that so-and-so sinned is mistaken’ and then defining more precisely what fault the verse does and does not attribute to the figure. This provides an important classical analogue to Rav Tzadok’s insistence that reports concerning great people cannot simply be read as ordinary disgrace. Yet the Gemara does not establish the sweeping rule Rav Tzadok states here: it analyzes particular figures and particular verses, and in several cases still identifies a real, though differently calibrated, fault. Rav Tzadok generalizes the pattern through his doctrine of complete teshuvah: once the failing has been rectified and transformed, its preservation in Torah or Chazal can itself become part of the person’s praise.

וְגַם לְפִי דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה הָיָה קוֹדֶם שֶׁחָזַר, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַה שֶּׁסִּיפְּרוּ זֶה עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאַחַר שֶׁחָזַר תִּיקֵּן גַּם מַעֲשֶׂה זוֹ עַד שֶׁגַּם זֶה נַעֲשֶׂה זְכֻיּוֹת וְיֵשׁ בָּהּ שֶׁבַח

And even according to the words of Tosafos — that the deed was before he returned [in teshuvah] — nonetheless, the very fact that they recounted it perforce shows that after he returned he rectified even this deed, until it too became merits and there is praise in it.370Tosafos to Gittin 47a, s.v. ‘Reish Lakish zabin nafshei l’Luda’ei’ — The episode before his return: Tosafos state explicitly that Reish Lakish’s selling himself to the Luda’ei occurred ‘before he returned for the better,’ reasoning that after his return he presumably would not have treated himself with such disregard. Rav Tzadok accepts that chronology as a possible reading but draws a striking inference from the Gemara’s decision to preserve the story next to the account of Reish Lakish’s later life and death: if the incident belonged to his pre-teshuvah past, its inclusion after his transformation means that the past itself had been repaired until even its retelling contained shevach. Tosafos establish the chronology; the claim that the narrated failure was retrospectively converted into praise is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive development.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּמַה דְּנִיצוֹל מִיָּדָם מוֹכִיחַ כִּי אֵין בּוֹ חֵטְא דִּשְׁפִיכוּת דָּם, וְהַמְּכִירָה הוּצְרְכָה לְבָרֵר זֶה, כִּי כְּפִי דַּעַת בְּנֵי אָדָם הָיָה רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת מִשְׁפָּטוֹ כֵּן לְהִמָּסֵר לַלּוּדִים שֶׁהֵם רָאשֵׁי הַשּׁוֹפְכִים דָּמִים

And as I wrote, that his being saved from their hand proves there is in him no sin of bloodshed, and the “selling” was needed to clarify this — for by human reckoning it would have been fitting for his sentence to be thus, to be handed over to the Ludim, who are the chief of the shedders of blood.

וְעִיקַּר אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכוּת דָּם שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לִבְנֵי נֹחַ נִסְמְכָה לְהֶתֵּר אֲכִילַת בְּשַׂר בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים, עַל זֶה אָמַר ״וְאַךְ אֶת דִּמְכֶם וְגוֹ׳ שֹׁפֵךְ דָּם וְגוֹ׳״, לְפִי שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ שֶׁהוּתַּר אֲכִילַת בָּשָׂר הוּתַּר גַּם כֵּן לְהָרְגוֹ לִשְׁאָר צָרְכֵי בְּנֵי אָדָם

And the essence of the prohibition of bloodshed said to the sons of Noach was juxtaposed to the permission to eat the flesh of living creatures; upon this it said, “But your blood, of your lives, I will require; whoever sheds man’s blood, by man shall his blood be shed” (Bereishis 9:5–6) — for since the eating of flesh was permitted, one might have thought killing [a man] too was permitted for other human needs.

וְאָמַר דְּאָדָם אֵין מָסוּר לְאָדָם אַחֵר לְהָרְגוֹ לְצָרְכּוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהוּתַּר אֲכִילַת בַּעֲלֵי חַיִּים, וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הָרְצִיחָה לְצֹרֶךְ אֲכִילָה וּבִכְלָלוֹ לִשְׁאָר הֲנָאוֹת, וְיוֹתֵר אַכְזָרִיּוּת הוּא גַּם כֵּן לִרְצוֹחַ לְאָכְלוֹ; וּלְפִיכָךְ הֵם רָאשֵׁי הָרוֹצְחִים, וְהוּא נִמְכַּר לָהֶם, וְנִתְכַּפֵּר בְּמַה שֶּׁנִּיצוֹל מִיָּדָם כִּי אֵין לוֹ מִשְׁפַּט מָוֶת

And it said that a man is not given over to another to kill him for his need, as the eating of animals was permitted; this is the essence of murder for the sake of eating — and included in it, for other pleasures — and it is even greater cruelty to murder in order to eat him. Therefore they [the Ludim] are the chief of murderers, and he was sold to them, and was atoned by his being saved from their hand — for he bears no death-sentence.

וְדָבָר זֶה כְּלָל גָּדוֹל בְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּזְכַּר בַּתַּלְמוּד כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ וּבִשְׁאָר מְקוֹמוֹת בְּדִבְרֵי רז״ל, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר בַּמִּקְרָאוֹת: מֵחֵטְא אָדָם גָּדוֹל הוּא מַה שֶּׁכְּבָר נִתְקַן עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שְׁלֵימָה מֵאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וְלֹא נִכְתַּב אֶלָּא לְשִׁבְחָן

And this matter is a great principle wherever the like is mentioned in the Talmud, and in other places in the words of the Sages, and needless to say in the verses of Scripture: regarding the sin of a great man, that which has already been rectified through complete teshuvah from love, until it became as merits, is recorded only to their praise.
וְזֶהוּ תֹּקֶף הַתְּשׁוּבָה בַּמַּדְרֵגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה הָרִאשׁוֹנָה, וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁגְּדוֹלִים בּוֹ מִצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים, כִּי הַזְּדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

And this is the force of teshuvah at the great, first rung371R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §9): “‘You have wrought all our deeds for us’ — and this is certainly [the sense of] ‘how great they are,’ like ‘willful sins become as merits’; and the thoughts of man and the hidden things, which are ‘brain and heart,’ are certainly ‘to Hashem our God’ — they are His thoughts, [and] ‘these are very deep.’” The volume’s closing principle: seen from the end, even the sins were God’s own working — so that a great man’s rectified sin is recorded only to his praise, and the penitent stands above the never-fallen tzaddik. — that in which [penitents] are greater than the wholly righteous — for the willful sins [become] as merits.372Yisrael Kedoshim §7; Berachos 34b — The higher reach of the baal teshuvah in Rav Tzadok’s system: Berachos records R’ Abbahu’s teaching that in the place where baalei teshuvah stand, wholly righteous people cannot stand. Rav Tzadok develops this in Yisrael Kedoshim §7 by contrasting Eliyahu, who ‘never sinned’ and became angelic, with ordinary humanity descending from Adam: man was created for the possibility of falling and repairing, and the baal teshuvah thereby reaches a level higher than the angels. He adds that baalei teshuvah possess a greater force precisely because they must draw themselves back from distance to nearness. This is an unusually close parallel to the close of the present se’if. The superiority is not a praise of the original sin; it belongs to the transformative avodah that returns the broken history to God and creates an attained level unavailable to one who never passed through that repair.373Yoma 86b: “Great is teshuvah, for [through repentance] from love, willful sins are accounted to a person as merits [zedonos na’asu lo k’zachuyos].” This is R’ Tzadok’s closing principle for the whole Siman: the great man’s rectified sin is recorded only to his praise, and the penitent at this first, highest rung stands above the wholly righteous.

sections.en: Teshuvah from fear turns willful sins into inadvertent ones

items.h: תשובה מיראה הופכת זדונות לשגגות.

The theme: Teshuvah from fear heals only “from here onward” and, reaching back, recasts willful sins (zedonos) as inadvertent ones (shegagos). Yet it leaves the penitent “like a healed baal mum, a trace of whose name remains” (Rashi). Complete healing — turning the sin itself into nedavah and merit — belongs to teshuvah from love, which the verse sets after the return from fear.

p: הַשֵּׁנִי: תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה מְרַפֵּא מִכָּאן וּלְהַבָּא, אֲבָל עַל הַקּוֹדֵם אֵין מְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי, רַק כְּבַעַל מוּם שֶׁנִּתְרַפֵּא שֶׁמִּקְצָת שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו

The second [mode of teshuvah]: teshuvah from fear heals from here onward, but it does not rectify the past completely — [the penitent remains] only like a baal mum [a blemished one] who has been healed, of whom "a trace of his name remains".
כֵּן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ"י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וּכְתִיב״ וּבַגְּמָרָא (יוֹמָא פו עַמּוּד ב) דְּמוֹעִיל עַל הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ כִּשְׁגָגוֹת

So it is in Rashi (s.v. "u’ksiv"), and in the Gemara [at the start of 86b], that [teshuvah from fear] avails for the past as well, to render it [as though it had been done] like inadvertent sins.374Yoma 86a-b and Rashi: R’ Chama bar Chanina contrasts “Return, backsliding children” (Yirmiyah 3:14) with “I will heal your backslidings” (3:22), and the sugya distinguishes teshuvah from love from teshuvah from fear. Rashi (s.v. u’ksiv erpa) explains “I will heal” as healing only from this point onward, “like a baal mum who was healed, a trace of whose name remains”; by contrast, love uproots the sin from its beginning. On 86b, Reish Lakish teaches that fear turns zedonos into shegagos, while love turns them into merits. Meforshim: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados to 86a, preserves the standard printed sequence and reads the voluntary “Return” as love and the threatened healing as fear of punishment. R’ Tzadok accepts Rashi’s hierarchy of partial versus complete healing, but uses the variants and Hoshea’s word ohavem to argue that complete healing belongs to love. Halachic background of the metaphor: a kohen with either a permanent or a passing blemish is disqualified from the avodah while the blemish is present (Vayikra 21:17-23; Rambam, Hilchos Bi’as HaMikdash 6:1-2). Rashi borrows this language as an image: the active pesul can be healed, yet the prior designation still leaves a remembered trace. R’ Tzadok makes that “trace” the residual shegagah left by teshuvah from fear.
וְלוּלֵי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ"י הָיָה נִרְאֶה לְפָרֵשׁ אִיפְּכָא, דְּ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ דְּמֵעִיקָּרָא שׁוֹבָבִים זֶהוּ מִיִּרְאָה שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, וְעַל יְדֵי שׁוֹבְבוּת הַיְינוּ כְּשׁוֹגֵג

Were it not for Rashi’s words, it would have seemed [right] to explain the reverse: that "backsliding — for from the outset they were backsliding [shovavim]" is [the trait] of fear, which makes [the sin] like inadvertent — for by way of "waywardness" [shovevus, childish folly] it becomes like a shogeg.

וְ״אֶרְפָּא״ דְּסִיֵּים ״אוֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה״ הַיְינוּ מֵאַהֲבָה, וּרְפוּאָה דְּ״מְשׁוּבָתָם״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה כְּמוֹ שׁוֹבָב גַּם כֵּן, רַק שֶׁמֵּאַהֲבָתָם יַחֲשִׁיב הֶעָוֹן לִנְדָבָה וּלְמִצְוָה וּזְכִיּוֹת

while "I will heal," which concludes "loving them freely [ohavem nedavah]," is [the trait] of love; and the "healing of their backsliding" means that he will no longer be like a shovav either — rather, out of their love He reckons the very sin as a free-will offering [nedavah], as a mitzvah, and as merits.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין הַסֵּדֶר כָּאן וְכוּלֵיהּ מְכֻוָּון לְסֵדֶר הַכְּתוּבִים שֶׁסִּידֵּר תְּחִלָּה בְּקוּשְׁיָא, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּבְמַה דְּסִיֵּים פָּתַח

And although the order here is not aligned with the order of the verses [as the Gemara] first arranged them in the question, one may say that he opened [his answer] with what he had concluded [in the question].

וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהַכְּתוּבִים נָקַט כְּסִדְרָן בִּנְבִיאִים וּכְתוּבִים, וּתְרֵי עָשָׂר מְאוּחָר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בָּתְרָא יד עַמּוּד ב), וּבַתֵּירוּץ הִקְדִּים ״מֵאַהֲבָה״ שֶׁהִיא הַמְעוּלָּה

And one may also say that he cited the verses in their order in Tanakh — and Trei Asar [the Twelve Prophets, i.e. Hoshea] comes later [in the canonical order], as they said [in Bava Basra 14b] — while in the resolution he gave precedence to "from love," which is the superior [mode].375Bava Basra 14b — order of Nevi’im: the baraisa lists Yirmiyah, Yechezkel, Yeshayah and then Trei Asar. It asks why Hoshea, who prophesied earlier, was not placed first, and answers that his short book was joined to the single scroll of the Twelve; if written separately it might be lost. Rashi notes that Chaggai, Zecharyah and Malachi were the last prophets, so Hoshea is counted with their collected scroll. R’ Tzadok therefore distinguishes historical chronology from canonical book-order: the Gemara’s question can cite Yirmiyah before Hoshea because that is their order in the received sequence, while its answer gives priority to love because love is the higher spiritual rung.

וְזֶהוּ כְּפִי הַגִּירְסָא שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב (שֶׁלִּפְנֵי דְּפוּס פִּירְדָּא) שָׁם (סִימָן ע"ג) ״וּכְתִיב אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבָתָם״, וְכֵן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ"י שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב שָׁם וְכֵן בַּיַּלְקוּט (יִרְמְיָה סוֹף סִימָן רס"ט), וְהַיְינוּ קְרָא דְּהוֹשֵׁעַ

And this accords with the reading in Ein Yaakov [in the editions before the Fürth printing] there (§73) — "and it is written, I will heal their backsliding" — and likewise in Rashi in Ein Yaakov there and in the Yalkut [Shimoni, Yirmiyah, end of §269] — [where the proof-verse] is the verse in Hoshea.376Ein Yaakov and Yalkut Shimoni — background and textual function: Ein Yaakov, compiled by R’ Yaakov ibn Chaviv and completed by his son R’ Levi ibn Chaviv, gathers the aggadic passages of the Bavli together with commentaries; its editions sometimes preserve readings different from the standard printed Shas. Yalkut Shimoni is a medieval midrashic anthology arranged along the books of Tanakh and is an independent witness to parallel rabbinic material. R’ Tzadok is therefore doing textual criticism: the reading “I will heal their backsliding” points to Hoshea 14:5, whose continuation “loving them freely” explicitly supplies the category of love. Important context: in the next se’if he reopens the Yalkut evidence and concludes that its placement under Yirmiyah makes that witness more complicated than it first appeared. Thus the variant is part of his argument, not a casual citation.

וּלְפִי גִּירְסָא זוֹ נִרְאֶה וַדַּאי הַפֵּירוּשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי מִדִּכְתִיב ״אוֹהֲבֵם״, וְגַם מִדְּלֹא מַקְשֶׁה מִסִּיּוּם לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב דְּיִרְמְיָה עַצְמוֹ, אֶלָּא דְּמַיְיתֵי הַאי מִשּׁוּם הַתֵּירוּץ דְּבֵיהּ מְפוֹרָשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ ״אוֹהֲבֵם״

And according to this reading the interpretation is certainly as I have written, since it is written "loving them" [ohavem, i.e. from love], and also because he does not raise a difficulty from the conclusion of the verse of Yirmiyah itself, but rather adduces this [verse from Hoshea] on account of the resolution, in which "loving them" is explicitly stated afterward.
וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּעִיקַּר הַקּוּשְׁיָא מֵהָא מִדִּכְתִיב ״אוֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה״, מַשְׁמַע דְּאֵינָם כְּשׁוֹבָבִים גַּם כֵּן רַק נֶחְשָׁב עוֹד לִנְדָבָה וְעַל כֵּן ״אוֹהֲבֵם״ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

And one may also say that the core of the difficulty is from this: since it is written "loving them freely [nedavah]," it implies that they are not treated as wayward either, but rather it is reckoned further as a freewill gift, and therefore He loves them, just as I wrote;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קְרָא דְּיִרְמְיָה דְּחַד קְרָא הוּא, לָא מַפְסְקִינַן לֵיהּ
whereas the verse of Yirmiyah is a single verse, which we do not split into parts.
וְגַם סֵיפֵיהּ דְּ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ קָאֵי אַמִּירְאָה וְאֵין רְפוּאָה גְּמוּרָה רַק מִקְצָת שְׁמוֹ עָלָיו, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן רְפוּאָה דְּהוֹשֵׁעַ הוּא לְגַמְרֵי

Moreover, the latter clause, "I will heal your backslidings" [in Yirmiyah, addressed in the second person], refers to [teshuvah] from fear — and there is no complete healing, only "a trace of his name remains"; whereas the healing [spoken of] in Hoshea ["I will heal their backsliding, loving them freely"] is complete.377R’ Tzadok — parallels and conceptual setting: Peri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah §8 asks the same controlling question: if teshuvah from fear has secured pardon, what remains in calling the former willful sins shegagos? His answer throughout these teachings is that fear removes the rebellious will but leaves the deed’s residual form; love reaches the root and transforms the past. Compare Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9, 11, 17, where the order in Hoshea is read as a spiritual process: Israel first says Shuvah through its own effort, then Hashem answers erpa by granting complete teshuvah from love; at that point even the former bad deeds produce a good “fragrance” and are turned to merits. Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah ch. 2, locates the baal teshuvah’s added stature in having tasted sin and then conquered the inclination; Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados to Yoma 86b, emphasizes the extra good deeds generated by the return. R’ Tzadok’s formulation is stronger: the avon itself, once absorbed into teshuvah from love, is reckoned as nedavah, mitzvah and merit.

וְנִרְאֶה סִיּוּעַ לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי מִמֵּימְרָא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת שָׁם דִּמְבִיאָה רְפוּאָה מִקְּרָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא״ וְגוֹמֵר ״נְדָבָה״ עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְאַמַּאי לָא מַיְיתֵי קְרָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ דְּיִרְמְיָה דִּקְדִים

And there seems to be a support for what I have written from the earlier statement there — "[Great is teshuvah] for it brings healing" — [which is derived] from the verse "I will heal [their backsliding], loving them freely" [of Hoshea, not from the Yirmiyah verse]; and why did he not adduce the verse "I will heal your backslidings" of Yirmiyah, which comes earlier?378Yoma 86a and Hoshea 14:2-5: “Great is teshuvah, for it brings healing to the world,” derived from “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” The prophetic context moves from Israel’s command, “Return, O Israel,” and its verbal confession (vv. 2-4), to Hashem’s answer of healing and renewed love (v. 5). Meforshei Tanakh: Radak explains that Hashem heals the rebellion committed until now and then loves Israel with a freely given love once His anger has turned away. Metzudas David sharpens the distinction: confession can remove enmity, but it cannot by itself produce love; the renewed love is a divine gift even when Israel is not yet worthy. Malbim likewise reads a sequence — first the wound of backsliding is healed, and afterward Hashem returns not merely to pardon but to love. R’ Tzadok’s distinctive move: he reads ohavem nedavah not only as undeserved divine love but as the sign that the past itself has been transvalued: the avon becomes a nedavah, mitzvah and merit. In Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9 and 11, he repeats the same order — human return, divine assistance toward complete love, and finally the former bad deeds yielding a pleasing fragrance. That parallel shows why this verse, rather than Yirmiyah’s more limited “healing,” bears the se’if’s idea of total retroactive repair.
אֲבָל לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא, דְּהָתָם שֶׁבָּא לְבָאֵר גְּדוּלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה, נָקַט הַאי קְרָא דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁמְּרַפֵּאת הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי

But according to what I have written it is well understood: for there, where it comes to explain the greatness of teshuvah, he took this verse of the great teshuvah from love, which heals the past completely.

וְעַיֵּין בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי הָרִי"ף שֶׁבְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב שָׁם דְּדִקְדֵּק בֶּאֱמֶת לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ"י לָמָּה נָקַט הָתָם מִמַּעֲלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה דְּאֵינָהּ כָּל כָּךְ גְּדוֹלָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וּלְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא

And see the Chiddushei HaRif in Ein Yaakov there, who indeed pressed, according to Rashi's interpretation, why he took there [as his proof] from the lesser virtue of teshuvah from fear — see there; and according to what I have written it is resolved.379Chiddushei HaRif on Ein Yaakov: this is the aggadic commentary Me’or Einayim of R’ Yoshiyahu Pinto (the “Rif” of Ein Yaakov), a leading Damascus sage and commentator on Aggadah — not R’ Yitzchak Alfasi, the halachic Rif. His difficulty is exact: according to Rashi, the verb “I will heal” signals the lesser teshuvah from fear, yet the verse used by the earlier teaching continues “I will love them freely,” which clearly sounds like love. The Rif must press the two clauses into Rashi’s arrangement. R’ Tzadok turns that difficulty into evidence for his own reading: Hoshea describes complete healing through love, whereas Yirmiyah’s “I will heal your backslidings” can describe the partial healing of fear. The note therefore links textual girsa, prophetic syntax and the conceptual hierarchy of the two teshuvos.

items.h: The theme: In the Yalkut, the proof-verse of the earlier statement really is the Yirmeyah verse, and there it cannot be emended. So the Rif’s difficulty (why “I will heal” — from fear — is paired with “loving them freely” — from love) actually confirms R’ Tzadok’s reading. The order of the verse mirrors the order of the penitent’s ascent: first “Return” — from fear, which depends on man’s own effort, “for all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven”; then “I will heal” — from love, which Heaven grants him.

p: אַךְ רָאִיתִי בַּיַּלְקוּט (יִרְמְיָה שָׁם) הַגִּירְסָא בֶּאֱמֶת בְּמֵימְרָא הַקּוֹדֶמֶת מִקְּרָא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ דְּיִרְמְיָה, וְשָׁם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיהַּ

However, I saw in the Yalkut [Shimoni, Yirmeyah there] that the textual reading in the preceding statement is truly from the verse “Return, [wayward children,] I will heal your backslidings” (Yirmeyah 3:22) of Yirmeyah, and there it is impossible to emend,
מִדְּמַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ לְהַךְ מֵימְרָא שָׁם בְּיִרְמְיָה אַמִּקְרָא זֶה וְלֹא בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּכָךְ הָיְתָה הַנּוּסְחָא לִפְנֵי הַמְחַבֵּר בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם
since he adduces that Talmudic statement there in Yirmeyah upon this verse and not in Hoshea; perforce such was the textual reading before the author in the Gemara there.
וְנוּסְחַת הַגְּמָרָא הוּא גַּם בְּהַךְ רוּמְיָא גַּם כֵּן ״וּכְתִיב אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״, וְהַיְינוּ סֵיפֵיהּ דְּאוֹתוֹ מִקְרָא דְּיִרְמְיָה
And the text of the Gemara is also in that contradiction: “and it is written, I will heal your backslidings,” which is the conclusion of that very verse in Yirmeyah.
כֵּן הוּא בְּהָרִי״ף בְּעֵין יַעֲקֹב, וְהוּא הִקְשָׁה מִקְּרָא דְּ״אוֹהֲבֵם נְדָבָה״ דְּמַשְׁמַע מֵאַהֲבָה וּכְתִיב גַּם כֵּן ״אֶרְפָּא״, וְהַיְינוּ לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י, וְנִדְחַק

So it is in the Rif in Ein Yaakov, and he raised a difficulty from the verse “loving them freely” (Hoshea 14:5), which implies from love, yet “I will heal” is written there as well — and this [difficulty] is according to Rashi’s interpretation, and he was pressed [into a strained resolution].
אֲבָל גַּם זֶה מוֹכִיחַ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּהַקּוּשְׁיָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ מַשְׁמַע דִּמְרַפֵּא גַּם הַשּׁוֹבָבוּת, וְזֶהוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
But this too proves as I wrote: for the difficulty is that “I will heal your backslidings” implies that He heals the waywardness as well, and this is [only possible] from love.
וְסֵדֶר הַכָּתוּב הוּא כְּפִי סֵדֶר הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת לָאָדָם הַשָּׁב, דִּתְחִלָּה הוּא מִיִּרְאָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ בָּא לְמֵאַהֲבָה
And the sequence of the verse follows the order of the rungs for the returning penitent: first it is from fear, and afterward he arrives at [teshuvah] from love.
וּמִיִּרְאָה אָמַר ״שׁוּבוּ״, תָּלָה בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם, דְּ״הַכֹּל בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם חוּץ מִיִּרְאַת שָׁמַיִם״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּבְרָכוֹת לג עַמּוּד ב) מִקְּרָא דְּ״כִּי אִם לְיִרְאָה״

And concerning [the return] from fear, it says “Return” — attributing it to human initiative, for “all is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven,” as they said (Berachos 33b) from the verse “except to fear”.380Berachos 33b — free choice, fear, and divine assistance: R’ Chanina teaches, “Everything is in the hands of Heaven except the fear of Heaven,” deriving it from Devarim 10:12. Rashi explains that a person’s natural circumstances — long or short life, poverty or wealth, wisdom or foolishness — are decreed, but whether one becomes righteous or wicked is entrusted to the person, before whom two paths are placed. Rambam, Shemoneh Perakim ch. 8, similarly limits “everything” to natural conditions and insists that mitzvah and aveirah remain matters of choice. Rashi to Megillah 25a adds the important nuance: Hashem can transform the heart, yet the initial preparation of the heart toward fear was handed to man. R’ Tzadok develops exactly this progression in Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Galus Mitzrayim 4:4-6: yirah is the arena of human choice and effort; ahavah can then enter the heart “of itself.” Human awakening from below is the gate, and afterward “the Holy One helps him.” Accordingly, “Return” is phrased as an imperative to man, while “I will heal” is Hashem’s answering gift.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ ״אֶרְפָּא״ תָּלָה בְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כִּי מַה שֶּׁזּוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הוּא מַה שֶּׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ
And afterward, “I will heal” He made dependent on the Blessed Name, for what he subsequently merits — teshuvah from love — is that which Heaven grants him as assistance.

וְכַיָּדוּעַ הַטַּעַם דִּלְאַהֲבָה אֵין צָרִיךְ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם כָּל כָּךְ, רַק בָּאָה מִמֵּילָא אַחַר הַיִּרְאָה שֶׁהִיא נוּקְבָא ״אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳״, וְאַהֲבָה בְּרָזָא דִּדְכוּרָא, וּדְדֶרֶךְ אִישׁ לַחֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵיהּ

And as is well known, the reason is that love does not require human initiative to such an extent, but rather comes of itself after fear — for fear is the feminine aspect, “a woman who fears Hashem” (Mishlei 31:30), while love is in the secret of the masculine, and “it is the way of a man to search [after a woman],” etc.381Yalkut Shimoni, the Rif on Ein Yaakov, and R’ Tzadok’s framework: Yalkut Shimoni is a medieval anthology arranged along the verses of Tanakh. In Yirmiyah, remez 269, it places the teaching upon “Return, wayward children; I will heal your backslidings” (Yirmiyah 3:22). Because the material is attached to that verse rather than to Hoshea, its location is textual evidence that the compiler’s Gemara read the Yirmiyah wording; R’ Tzadok therefore reopens and qualifies the variant discussed in the previous se’if. The “Rif” here is R’ Yoshiyahu Pinto’s aggadic commentary Me’or Einayim on Ein Yaakov, not R’ Yitzchak Alfasi. His difficulty is that Rashi associates “I will heal” with the lesser teshuvah from fear, while “I will love them freely” plainly denotes love. R’ Tzadok turns that strain into a sequence: the human call “Return” begins in fear, and the divine “I will heal” culminates in love. Compare Machshavos Charutz §7, where he describes lower and upper teshuvah as the two heh’s of the Divine Name. The lower return prepares the vessel; the upper return completes the healing. Se’if Beis thus joins textual criticism to R’ Tzadok’s recurring two-stage map of teshuvah.,382Zoharic background to fear as “female” and love as “male”: Mishlei 31:30 supplies the phrase “a woman who fears Hashem,” while Kiddushin 2b states that it is the way of the man to seek the woman. R’ Tzadok reads these as a spiritual metaphor. In the kabbalistic map, yirah aligns with restraint, gevurah and the receptive/feminine principle; ahavah aligns with chesed, the right side and the bestowing/masculine principle. Zohar II 216a gives the controlling order: after fear rests upon a person, love — identified there with the right side — is awakened, and through love the worshipper rises and cleaves above. The metaphor therefore describes movement from disciplined receptivity to an overflowing gift; it is not a claim about the relative spiritual worth of men and women. Compare Tzidkas HaTzadik §200: revealed yirah can be awakened through a person’s own self-rebuke, whereas revealed “great love” is a gift of Hashem and is not attained by effort in the same way. Together with Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Galus Mitzrayim 4:4, this is the closest parallel to the present se’if: fear is cultivated; love comes afterward from Heaven and completes the return.

וְכָךְ בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ פָּתַח ״שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל״ וְגוֹמֵר תָּלָה בְּדִידְהוּ, וְסִיֵּים עַל זֶה ״כִּי כָשַׁלְתָּ בַּעֲוֹנֶךָ״ דְּדָרְשִׁינַן מִזֶּה (שָׁם בְּיוֹמָא) דְּנַעֲשִׂין כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, וְהַיְינוּ מִיִּרְאָה

And so in Hoshea, it opened “Return, O Israel [unto Hashem your God],” etc. (Hoshea 14:2) — making it depend on them — and concluded upon this “for you have stumbled in your iniquity,” from which we expound (there in Yoma 86b) that willful sins become like inadvertent ones, and that is [the return] from fear.383Hoshea 14:2-5, Yoma 86b, and the meforshim: The prophecy begins with Israel’s own act — “Return, O Israel, to Hashem your God, for you have stumbled in your iniquity” — and proceeds through confession to Hashem’s response, “I will heal their backsliding; I will love them freely.” Yoma 86b reads “you have stumbled” as a willful sin reduced to a mere stumbling: teshuvah from fear turns zedonos into shegagos, while teshuvah from love turns them into merits; Rashi states this distinction directly. Radak explains that Hashem first heals the earlier rebellion and then loves Israel after His anger has turned away. Metzudas David notes that removal of enmity does not itself create love, so the renewed love is a divine gift. Malbim likewise reads a progression from healing to positive love. Maharsha to Yoma 86b emphasizes the added good generated by the penitent’s return. R’ Tzadok’s sharper reading is that the verse’s order maps the penitent’s ascent: human yirah first strips the sin of deliberate rebellion, and the divinely granted ahavah then heals and transforms the remaining deed. Compare Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §§9 and 11, where he repeats the sequence of human return, heavenly assistance, and the former bad deeds ultimately producing a pleasing fragrance.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר ״אֶרְפָּא״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ מִמֵּילָא אַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְאַהֲבָה וְלָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה עַד דִּירוּפָּא גַּם הַשּׁוֹבָבוּת

And afterward it said “I will heal [their backsliding],” etc. (Hoshea 14:5), so that they should spontaneously merit through this afterward to attain love and return from love, until even the waywardness itself is healed.

וְעִיקַּר לְשׁוֹן רְפוּאָה הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁנִּתְרַפֵּא לְגַמְרֵי, דְּאִם הוּא כִּשְׁגָגוֹת הֲרֵי גַּם הַשּׁוֹגֵג צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה וְכַפָּרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּנָזִיר כג עַמּוּד ב) וַעֲדַיִין הוּא צָרִיךְ רְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה

And the essential meaning of the term “healing” applies when one is healed completely; for if it remains like inadvertent sins, behold even an inadvertent sinner requires forgiveness and atonement, as they said (Nazir 23b), and he still requires the healing of forgiveness.384Nazir 23a-b and the halachic residue of an inadvertent sin: The passage begins on Nazir 23a in common Vilna pagination (the sefer cites 23b). A woman’s husband annulled her vow without her knowledge, yet when she acted against the vow the verse still says, “Hashem will forgive her.” R’ Akiva would weep: if one intended to eat pork but unknowingly ate permitted meat still requires forgiveness, how much more one whose intended sin was actually committed. Halachically, a shogeg is free of the willful punishment but is not spiritually neutral. Vayikra ch. 4 and Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, require a chatas for an inadvertent violation whose deliberate form carries kares; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, requires teshuvah and vidui even when a chatas or asham is brought. Ramban to Vayikra 4:2 explains the reason: every sin, even inadvertent, leaves a blemish in the soul, and the offering purifies it so it may again draw near to its Creator. R’ Tzadok uses that halachic-spiritual background precisely: teshuvah from fear removes the zadon — the rebellious will — but the residual deed remains a shegagah needing “the healing of forgiveness.” Love is complete healing because it does not merely excuse that residue; it transforms the deed itself. Compare Peri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah §8, which asks why sins are still called shegagos after pardon and answers through this distinction between removal of will and transformation of the deed.
וְעַל כֵּן מֵ״אֶרְפָּא״ גּוּפֵיהּ נַמֵּי דַּיֵּיק, דְּמַשְׁמַע דְּנִתְרַפֵּא לְגַמְרֵי וְאֵין צָרִיךְ עוֹד סְלִיחָה
And therefore from “I will heal” itself it is also precisely derived, which implies that he has been cured completely and requires no further pardon;

וְאִם הוּא מִשּׁוֹבְבוּת וּשְׁטוּת עַל יְדֵי רוּחַ שְׁטוּת דְּיֵצֶר הָרָע עֲדַיִין נֶחְשָׁב כְּשׁוֹגֵג וְצָרִיךְ עוֹד לִרְפוּאָה, וְ״אֶרְפָּא״ מַשְׁמַע רְפוּאָה שְׁלֵימָה שֶׁלֹּא צָרִיךְ עוֹד אַחַר כָּךְ לִרְפוּאָה שֵׁנִית

for if it stems from waywardness and folly through the spirit of folly of the evil inclination, it is still reckoned like an inadvertent deed and requires yet further healing, whereas “I will heal” implies a complete healing that does not require a second healing afterward.

items.h: The theme: Teshuvah from fear uproots the evil intention that accompanied the earlier act. The willful sin is therefore reclassified as inadvertent, leaving the deed without its former rebellious will. This is a genuine retroactive uprooting, as expressed in the promise that Israel’s iniquity will be sought and not found (Yirmeyah 50:20).

p: וְגַם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל (רֵישׁ סִימָן א׳) דִּרְפוּאָה מַשְׁמַע אַלְּהַבָּא, וְעַד הֵנָּה הָיָה וְלֹא שֶׁנֶּעֱקַר לְגַמְרֵי עַיֵּין שָׁם
And also according to what I wrote above (beginning of Siman 1), that "healing" implies from here onward, whereas up until now it existed, and not that it was uprooted entirely — see there;
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן דְּהוּא מְכֻוָּון לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּקָאֵי אַרְפוּאָה דִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הַבָּאָה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה
one may likewise say that it aligns with what I wrote, that it refers to the healing of teshuvah from love that comes following teshuvah from fear.
דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה נֶעֱקַר מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ הָרָעָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה נַעֲשָׂה מִזְּדוֹנוֹת שְׁגָגוֹת, שֶׁהוּא מַעֲשֶׂה בְּלֹא כַּוָּונָה וְרָצוֹן לְרַע
For through teshuvah from fear his prior evil thought is uprooted, whereby intentional sins [zedonos] become inadvertent ones [shegagos], leaving an act without intention or desire for evil;
וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא עֲקִירָה לְגַמְרֵי לְמַפְרֵעַ, דְּהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה שֶׁהָיָה לְרַע הוּא כְּמִי שֶׁאֵינָהּ
and this thing is a complete retroactive uprooting, for the thought that was directed toward evil is as though it never existed.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר ״בַּיּוֹם הַהוּא יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ וְחַטַּאת יְהוּדָה וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה״

And concerning this it is stated (Yirmeyah 50:20), “In those days and at that time... the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none; and the sins of Yehudah, and they shall not be found”:
דְּעָוֹן, דְּהַיְינוּ בְּמֵזִיד כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (יוֹמָא לו עַמּוּד ב), אֵינֶנּוּ כְּלָל, כֵּיוָן דְּנֶעֱקַר הָרָצוֹן דְּרַע לְגַמְרֵי לְמַפְרֵעַ

for avon [iniquity], meaning intentional transgression as they said (Yoma 36b), “there shall be none” at all, since the desire for evil has been completely uprooted retroactively;385Yirmiyah 50:20, Yoma 36b, and the language of confession: The prophecy announces the fall of Bavel and the restoration of both Israel and Yehudah: “The iniquity [avon] of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none, and the sins [chata’os] of Yehudah, and they shall not be found; for I will pardon those I leave.” Metzudas David explains that even if the guilt is searched for it will not be present, for the surviving remnant has been cleansed through the hardship of exile and forgiven. Malbim sharply differentiates the nouns: Israel’s avon is the intellectual distortion of idolatry and will cease to exist when the idolatrous inclination is abolished; Yehudah’s chatas is a sin of desire that may exist as an act, yet will not be found because Hashem forgives the remnant. Yoma 36b supplies the rabbinic lexicon. In the dispute over the order of vidui, the Sages define chata’os as inadvertent sins, avonos as intentional sins, and pesha’im as rebellious sins; they therefore require confession from the lighter to the graver — “chatasi, avisi, pashati.” The Gemara explains Moshe’s contrary verse-order as a plea that, after Israel repents, its deliberate and rebellious sins be treated before Hashem like inadvertent ones. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, codifies the Sages’ order in the standard formula of vidui. R’ Tzadok reads not only the nouns but also the verbs: avon “is not” because the evil will has truly been uprooted, while chatas “is not found” because the residual act has not vanished — teshuvah from love has changed its identity into merit. Compare Tzidkas HaTzadik §100, where complete teshuvah makes possible precisely this new reading of the past, and Peri Tzadik, Shmini §4, where he again uses Yoma’s terminology to describe the communal residue of the Calf as a shogeg requiring later kapparah.,386The sinner is not identical with the sin — Berachos 10a and Siman 15 §77: Beruriah corrected R’ Meir’s prayer against the violent men in his neighborhood by reading Tehillim 104:35 precisely: “Let sins [chata’im] cease,” not “sinners [chot’im].” He should pray that they return, whereupon “the wicked will be no more.” Maharsha asks how one person’s prayer can produce another’s teshuvah when fear of Heaven belongs to free choice; the question itself highlights that the prayer seeks heavenly assistance and opportunity, not coercion of the sinner’s will. Zohar, Balak §15, gives the same separation in mystical language: a person should not fix his identity as “wicked”; when he confesses, he detaches from the side of impurity and cleaves to the right hand extended to receive penitents. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6-7, likewise describes the baal teshuvah as no longer distant but beloved, close and joined to the Shechinah. In Siman 15 §77 R’ Tzadok joins Beruriah’s derashah to Yirmiyah 50:20: avon can be uprooted while the person remains, and the residual chatas can be healed and transformed. That later passage is therefore not merely a cross-reference; it confirms the anthropology underlying this se’if. Teshuvah does not erase the human being, nor must it erase the historical deed. It removes the evil identification and ultimately converts the deed into a source of merit. This is why the prosecutor can search for a “sin” and fail to find it, even though the life-event itself has not disappeared.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן חַטָּאת, דְּהוּא שׁוֹגֵג שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה מִקּוֹדֶם מֵהַמֵּזִיד עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת, שֶׁהוּא הַשְׁאָרַת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה הַגּוֹלֶמֶת בְּלֹא כַּוָּונָה

whereas chatas [sin], which is the inadvertent status produced earlier from the intentional sin through the preceding teshuvah from fear — being the residue of the raw physical deed devoid of intention —
זֶה נִתְרַפֵּא אַחַר כָּךְ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
this is healed afterward through teshuvah from love.
וְלֹא שֶׁנֶּעֱקַר לְמַפְרֵעַ כְּאִלּוּ לֹא הָיָה מֵעוֹלָם וְאֵינֶנּוּ, דְּאִם כֵּן מַה נַּעֲשָׂה כִּזְכִיּוֹת, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּהַמַּעֲשֶׂה אֵין נֶעֱקֶרֶת כְּלָל רַק נִתְרַפֵּאת

And it is not that it was uprooted retroactively as if it never existed at all and is gone, for if so, what then becomes transformed into merits? Perforce, the deed itself is not uprooted at all, but rather healed.
וְזֶהוּ ״דְּלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה״ — לֹא דְּאֵינָהּ, רַק דְּנִתְהַפְּכָה לִזְכוּת וְאֵין הַחַטָּאת נִמְצֵאת, שֶׁאִם הַמְקַטְרֵג יְחַפֵּשׂ אַחֲרֶיהָ לֹא יִמְצָא כֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּשְׁתַּנֵּית לִזְכוּת

And this is [the precision of] “they shall not be found” — not that it does not exist, but rather that it was transformed into a merit and the sin is no longer found; for if the accuser searches after it, he will not find it, since it has altered into a merit.

וְאָמַר תְּחִלָּה ״יִשְׂרָאֵל״, כִּי תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה נִתְעוֹרְרוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָזֶה בְּמַעֲשֵׂה דְּעֵגֶל, שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ רְאוּיִים לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד עַמּוּד ב)

And it mentioned “Israel” first, because to teshuvah from fear all of Israel were awakened in the incident of the Golden Calf, as they were not fitting for that deed except to teach the pathway of repentance, as they said (Avodah Zarah 4b);387Shemos 32:30-34 — pardon now, with a residue still awaiting repair: After the Golden Calf, Moshe calls the act a “great sin,” asks whether he can obtain atonement, and is told to continue leading the people; nevertheless Hashem adds, “On the day of My accounting, I will account their sin upon them” (32:34). Rashi explains that Hashem accepted Moshe’s plea not to destroy Israel at once, but dispersed a portion of the punishment into later reckonings; Sanhedrin 102a formulates this as a minute portion of the Calf entering subsequent punishments. Ramban reads the verse as a deferred visitation extending even after entry into the Land and into exile, while Sforno stresses that mercy has postponed rather than erased the liability should sin recur. The midrashic setting is Moshe’s sustained intercession: Shemos Rabbah 44:1 describes forty days and nights of pleading. Zohar, Vayakhel 1:11, likewise speaks of Israel’s light being darkened by the alien power and then of immediate divine forgiveness before Moshe reassembles the people. These sources distinguish acceptance and renewed covenant from the final purging of every effect. The halachic analogue appears in Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4: teshuvah begins the atonement process, yet the completion of kapparah varies with the gravity of the sin and may still require Yom Kippur or suffering. R’ Tzadok gives the distinction its inner structure: the nation’s immediate fear and regret remove the rebellious will, while the remaining deed is now a shegagah — a “guarded” chatas — awaiting the complete healing of love. Compare Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah §18, where he says that Moshe prayed at once because Israel had already entertained teshuvah, but the body of the deed still required the four divisions of atonement. Thus “u’veyom pokdi” is not a denial that their teshuvah was accepted; it identifies the untransformed residue that this se’if is explaining.,388R’ Tzadok’s distinction between the evil will and the physical deed: In Likkutei Maamarim §16, R’ Tzadok locates culpability primarily in the desire and will for the transgression. A deed lacking knowing, evil intent belongs to the lesser category of shegagah and still needs atonement, but it is not the same spiritual object as a deliberate rebellion. This supplies the conceptual bridge from Yoma 86b: teshuvah from fear does not pretend the event never occurred; rather, it retroactively removes the zadon from it, leaving a bare deed without the former will. His more radical parallel is Tzidkas HaTzadik §100: only after complete teshuvah does the penitent recognize how divine providence can disclose a holy purpose even through the past fall, and on that higher plane zedonos become zechuyos. The order is essential. Before teshuvah, Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1-3, insists that choice and responsibility are real; no one may attribute his sin to a decree and excuse himself. R’ Tzadok’s language therefore describes the retrospective revelation granted by complete teshuvah, not permission to sin and not a cancellation of free will. In the present se’if he is still describing the first stage: yirah uproots the guilty intention, while ahavah later heals and reinterprets the remaining act. This is also why Peri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah §8, asks why sins are still called shegagos after pardon: the will has been removed, but the deed has not yet been transformed into merit.,389Avodah Zarah 4b-5a — the Golden Calf as the communal opening for teshuvah: R’ Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that Israel made the Calf “to give an opening of speech to penitents,” and R’ Yochanan in the name of R’ Shimon bar Yochai pairs the community with David: if a community sins, it is told to learn from Israel; if an individual sins, from David. Rashi explains that Israel were then spiritually strong and masters of their inclination; the unusual empowerment of the yetzer was a divine decree so that a later sinner who despairs of acceptance can be shown that even the Calf was received in teshuvah. This aggadah cannot mean that the act was permitted or that responsibility disappeared. Rambam’s doctrine of free choice in Hilchos Teshuvah ch. 5 remains controlling, and Akeidas Yitzchak, Sha’ar 53, emphasizes that the fall reveals the instability of even a very high human state and the real possibility of return — not a license to manufacture sin for pedagogic purposes. The later ritual repair also matters. The Sifra on Vayikra 9 teaches that the calf-offering comes to atone for the Calf; Peri Tzadik, Shmini §4, develops this by calling Israel’s remaining communal defect a shogeg and distinguishing the chatas that atones from the olah that restores favor and straightens the heart. This is the closest parallel to the present se’if: Israel’s fear upon Moshe’s rebuke immediately removed deliberate rebellion, but a chatas-residue still required pardon, prayer and later repair. The Gemara establishes the Calf as proof that return is always open; R’ Tzadok explains why acceptance can be immediate while complete transformation still unfolds in stages.
וּתְשׁוּבָתָם הָיָה מִיִּרְאָה כְּשֶׁהִגִּיד לָהֶם מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם חֶטְאָם הַגָּדוֹל וְעָנְשָׁם
and their repentance was out of fear when Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, told them their great sin and their punishment.

וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר (שָׁם בְּפָרָשַׁת כִּי תִשָּׂא) ״וּבְיוֹם פָּקְדִי וּפָקַדְתִּי עֲלֵיהֶם חַטָּאתָם״ — ״חַטָּאת״ הַיְינוּ שׁוֹגֵג, לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי רַק נַעֲשָׂה כְּשׁוֹגֵג דְּצָרִיךְ עֲדַיִין סְלִיחָה וְעֹנֶשׁ לְכַפָּרָה

And therefore it is said (Shemos 32:34, in Parashas Ki Tisa), “Nevertheless in the day when I visit, I will visit their sin upon them” — “sin” [chatas] denotes an inadvertent transgression, because it was not pardoned completely, but only rendered like an inadvertent deed, which still requires forgiveness and suffering for atonement.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּתְפִלָּתוֹ פָּעַל סְלִיחָה לְאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה לְגַמְרֵי, וְעַל זֶה הָיָה כָּל תְּפִלּוֹתָיו לִסְלוֹחַ לְגַמְרֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב גַּם שׁוֹגֵג

And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, by his prayer effected complete forgiveness for that hour; and regarding this were all his prayers directed: to forgive completely so that it should not even be reckoned as an inadvertent sin.
דְּגוּף הַמְּחִילָה אַחַר שֶׁשָּׁבוּ אֵין צָרִיךְ לְהַרְבּוֹת בִּתְפִלָּה, דִּכְבָר יָדוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ פְּתוּחָה לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים וְהַשָּׁב וּמִתְוַודֶּה מוֹחֵל לוֹ

For the essential pardon itself once they repented does not require multiplying prayer, since His hand, may He be blessed, is already open to receive penitents, and whoever returns and confesses is granted forgiveness;

רַק לִהְיוֹת דַּעֲדַיִין נִשְׁאַר שׁוֹגֵג, וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״חָטְאוּ חֲטָאָה גְדֹלָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״בְּעַד חַטַּאתְכֶם״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״חָטָא הָעָם הַזֶּה חֲטָאָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״תִּשָּׂא חַטָּאתָם״ וְגוֹמֵר — הַכֹּל לְשׁוֹן חֵטְא שׁוֹגֵג

it was only because an inadvertent sin still remained, and therefore he said: “have sinned a great sin” (Shemos 32:31), “for your sin” (32:30), “this people have sinned a great sin” (32:31), “forgive their sin” (32:32) — all employing the language of inadvertent sin [chet / chatas].
דִּכְבָר שָׁבוּ וְנִתְחָרְטוּ בָּזֶה מִיָּד בְּבִיאַת מֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְדָבָר זֶה בְּדִידְהוּ תַּלְיָא
For they had already repented and felt regret immediately upon Moshe Rabbeinu's arrival, peace be upon him, and this matter is dependent on them [man’s own initiative].
וְהַתְּפִלָּה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא לְזַכּוֹתָם לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁהוּא בְּסִיּוּעַ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם, וְשֶׁיְּכֻפַּר לְגַמְרֵי שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה עוֹד חֵטְא וְשׁוֹגֵג גַּם כֵּן

And the prayer to Hashem, blessed be He, was to grant them the merit of teshuvah from love, which comes through divine assistance from Heaven, and that it be completely atoned so that there should remain neither sin nor inadvertence.
וְעַל זֶה לֹא הוּבְטַח לְגַמְרֵי, רַק ״בְּיוֹם פָּקְדִי״ וְגוֹמֵר, דַּעֲדַיִין נִשְׁאַר חֵטְא שׁוֹגֵג שָׁמוּר

And concerning this he was not fully reassured, but only told “in the day when I visit [I will visit their sin upon them]” (Shemos 32:34), showing that an inadvertent sin still remained preserved [for future cleansing].

items.h: The theme: David — “the man who raised up the yoke of teshuvah” (Avodah Zarah 5a) — attained complete rectification. This is malchus, which Yehudah merited by “prevailing over his brothers” in subduing the yetzer to confess after sinning — reckoned greater than Yosef’s mastery, who conquered without any sin and gained but one letter of the Divine Name, whereas Yehudah is called entirely by the Name (Sotah 10b). For Yehudah merited that his very sin become a great merit — the emergence of Mashiach’s light from that deed.

p: אֲבָל דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה לְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי
But David HaMelech, peace be upon him, raised up the yoke of complete teshuvah, to rectify entirely;
וְזֶהוּ מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת שֶׁזָּכָה יְהוּדָה אֲשֶׁר גָּבַר בְּאֶחָיו בִּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר לְהוֹדוֹת אַחַר הַחֵטְא

and this is the attribute of malchus [kingship] that Yehudah merited, who "prevailed over his brothers" (I Divrei HaYamim 5:2) through subduing the inclination so as to confess after the sin,390Expanded source note: Sources and meforshim: Avodah Zarah 5a expounds Shmuel II 23:1, 'the man raised up on high [hukam al],' as 'the man who raised up the yoke [ulah] of teshuvah' - David's history teaches the individual penitent not to despair. Divrei HaYamim I 5:2 states, 'Yehudah prevailed over his brothers, and the ruler came from him, though the birthright belonged to Yosef.' Rashi, Radak, and Metzudas David explain the peshat as a division of prerogatives: kingship passed to Yehudah, while Yosef retained the double portion; Malbim emphasizes that Yehudah 'prevailed' over Yosef specifically in leadership. R' Tzadok internalizes that political kingship as mastery after failure. The kabbalistic background appears in Zohar I 206a as explained by Ohr HaChammah: Yehudah is Nefesh David/Malchus, while Yosef is Yesod; their encounter joins two distinct modes of holiness.,391Expanded source note: R' Tzadok in context: Peri Tzadik, Pinchas §15 explains that Yosef represents the tzaddik who never damaged the covenant, a level that most of the community cannot sustain; the final communal repair therefore comes through Mashiach ben David, who awakens teshuvah in all Israel. Machshavot Charutz §7 likewise distinguishes Yosef's gevurah among the nations - mastery of the external powers of desire - from Yehudah's gevurah 'among his brothers,' the ability to master and repair the inborn deficiencies found within Israel. This is why R' Tzadok can rank Yehudah's post-sin confession above Yosef's pre-sin restraint without diminishing Yosef: each is a necessary rung, but Yehudah supplies the path for one who has already fallen. Cf. Siman 15 §105 in this volume, where David's teshuvah is joined to healing through Refael.
דְּזֶה נֶחְשָׁב יוֹתֵר מִכְּבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר דְּיוֹסֵף, שֶׁכָּבַשׁ בְּלֹא חֵטְא כְּלָל וְנוֹסַף לוֹ רַק אוֹת אֶחָד מִשְּׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא

for this is reckoned greater than the subduing of the yetzer by Yosef, who conquered with no sin at all and had only one letter from the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, added to him [the letter hei of "Yehosef", Tehillim 81:6],
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יְהוּדָה דְּנִקְרָא כּוּלּוֹ עַל שְׁמוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בְּסוֹטָה י עַמּוּד ב)

whereas Yehudah is called entirely by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He, as it is stated (Sotah 10b),392Expanded source note: Sotah 10b and 36b-37a: Sotah 10b reads Yehudah's admission, 'She is more righteous than I' (Bereishis 38:26), as a public sanctification of Heaven's Name. Yehudah therefore merited that all four letters of the Divine Name appear in Yehudah, with the additional dalet; Yosef, who sanctified the Name privately by resisting Potiphar's wife, received one added letter - the heh of Yehosef (Tehillim 81:6), not a yod. Sotah 36b-37a gives the parallel formulation at the Sea: Yosef's private sanctification is contrasted with Yehudah's public sanctification through Nachshon's descent. Rashi on Bereishis 38:26 adds the Midrashic background to mimmeni: a Heavenly voice declared, 'From Me' these hidden events came, because kings were destined to descend from Tamar. R' Tzadok fuses the two sugyos: public confession is itself Kiddush Hashem, and the tribe's leap into the Sea reveals that confession in national action.
כִּי הוּא זָכָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חֶטְאוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לִזְכוּת גָּדוֹל, בְּרִיאַת אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ שֶׁיָּצָא מֵאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, דְּאֵין זְכוּת גָּדוֹל מִזֶּה
for he merited that his sin be reckoned as a great merit — the creation of the light of Mashiach that would issue from that very deed [with Tamar] — than which there is no greater merit,
וְזֶהוּ גְּבוּרָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה גַּם הָרַע עַצְמוֹ נֶהְפָּךְ לְטוֹב מְאוֹד
and this is a greater spiritual might: that even the evil itself is turned into "very good".
וְיוֹסֵף כְּשֶׁנִּקְרָא ״יְהוֹסֵף״ עֲדַיִין חָסֵר לוֹ הֵ״א אַחֲרוֹנָה שֶׁבּוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּמְנָחוֹת כט עַמּוּד ב)
And Yosef, when called "Yehosef," still lacked the final hei [of the Tetragrammaton] with which this world was created, as they said (Menachos 29b),
שֶׁשָּׁם הַפֶּתַח פָּתוּחַ לָצֵאת, לַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא דְּפוֹתְחִין לוֹ, וּתְלִיָא כַּרְעֵיהּ לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה

where the lower opening is open to exit, for one who comes to defile himself, to whom "they open [the way]"; and its leg hangs suspended [leaving an upper opening] for the baal teshuvah to re-enter.393Expanded source note: Mashiach’s light and sins transformed into merits: Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 says that while Yaakov and his sons were occupied with the sale, Hashem was ‘creating the light of Mashiach’ through Yehudah and Tamar; Matnos Kehunah and Rashi to Bereishis 38:26 explain the royal line’s hidden Divine direction. Yoma 86b supplies the governing rule: teshuvah from fear makes deliberate sins like inadvertent ones, but teshuvah from love makes them merits. R’ Tzadok, Peri Tzadik, Shemos §3 and Bereishis §14, connects this to Zohar II 184a: ‘no light except from darkness, and no good except from evil.’ The deed is not good while unrepented; after genuine teshuvah uproots and redirects it, the former fall becomes the cause of deeper humility, longing, and closeness. Menachos 29b’s final heh, open below yet bearing a separate opening for return, gives the letter-symbolism behind this transformation and Yehudah’s higher gevurah.
וּכְבִישַׁת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי וְלִהְיוֹת צַדִּיק גָּמוּר לֹא כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה, וְ״אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ״
And to subdue the inclination entirely and be a complete tzaddik not every man merits, and "there is no righteous man on earth [who does good and sins not]" (Koheles 7:20),
וּמַה יַּעֲשֶׂה מִי שֶׁעָבַר וְחָטָא, וַהֲרֵי הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כּוּלּוֹ לְפִי זֶה מְרוּחָק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִצַּד הַחֲטָאִים שֶׁבּוֹ

so what shall one do who has transgressed and sinned, when according to this the entire physical world would be distanced from the Blessed Name on account of the sins within it?394Expanded source note: Providence, free choice, and the retrospective reading of sin: Koheles 7:20 teaches universal human frailty, not permission to sin; ‘there is none besides Him’ is Devarim 4:35. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1, rules that every person freely chooses righteousness or wickedness. Resisei Layla §52 warns that Bilaam’s claim that Israel’s evil was simply ‘from the truth of His will’ helped lead to Shittim; Peri Tzadik, Shelach §6 adds that one may never rely beforehand on the future transformation of sin, for ‘I will sin and repent’ is denied the ordinary assistance of teshuvah. R’ Tzadok’s statement here is therefore retrospective: only after confession and complete teshuvah may the distance be revealed as a cause of greater closeness. Takanas HaShavin 5:7 and Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud §13 describe this as Yehudah’s is’hapcha, transforming bitterness, beyond Yosef’s iskafya, subduing it before the act.

אֲבָל יְהוּדָה גָּבַר לְבָרֵר דְּ״אֵין עוֹד מִלְּבַדּוֹ״ וְהַכֹּל מֵאֲמִיתּוּת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּשֶׁמִּתְבָּרֵר אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּהַחֲטָאִים הֵם זְכִיּוֹת גְּדוֹלוֹת וַעֲשִׂיַּית רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ

But Yehudah prevailed to clarify that "there is none else beside Him" and all is from the truth of His Blessed will, as it becomes clear after teshuvah that the sins themselves are great merits and a fulfillment of the will of His Name, may It be blessed.

וּבָזֶה נִתְמַלֵּא הַשֵּׁם שָׁלֵם אֶצְלוֹ, שֶׁגַּם עִנְיָינָיו הָאַרְצִיִּים וְגַשְׁמִיִּים שֶׁלּוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁנִּרְאִים כְּרִיחוּק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, אַדְּרַבָּא הֵן הֵם תַּכְלִית הַקֵּירוּב

And through this the Divine Name became full and complete in him: that even his earthly, corporeal matters in this world, which appear as distance from the Blessed Name, are on the contrary the ultimate closeness.
וְהוּא הָיָה הַמַּתְחִיל בְּוִידּוּי וְהוֹדָאָה עַל חֵטְא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסוֹטָה י עַמּוּד ב) ״מִי גָּרַם לִרְאוּבֵן שֶׁיּוֹדֶה? יְהוּדָה״
And he was the first to begin with verbal confession and acknowledgment over sin, as they said (Sotah 10b): "Who caused Reuven to confess? Yehudah";
וְזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַוִּידּוּי דְּבָרִים, לְהִתְחָרֵט וּלְהִכָּלֵם עַל יְדֵי זֶה מֵעֲוֹנוֹ
and this is the essence of teshuvah: the confession in words, to regret and thereby become ashamed before Him of one's iniquity,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם כְּשֶׁאָמַר לְנָתָן ״חָטָאתִי לַה׳״, מִיַּד אָמַר לוֹ ״גַּם ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ״ וְגוֹמֵר

as it is said of David HaMelech, peace be upon him: when he said to Nasan, "I have sinned to Hashem," [Nasan] immediately said to him, "Hashem also has put away your sin; [you shall not die]" (II Shmuel 12:13).395Expanded source note: Vidui, shame, and Kiddush Hashem: Sotah 7b says, ‘Who caused Reuven to confess? Yehudah,’ with parallels at Bava Kamma 92a and Makkos 11b; Sotah 10b adds that Yehudah’s public admission sanctified Heaven’s Name. Shmuel II 12:13 records David’s ‘I have sinned to Hashem’ and Nasan’s immediate assurance of forgiveness. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1 and 2:2, defines teshuvah as abandoning the sin, regret, resolve, and verbal confession. Berachos 12b deepens R’ Tzadok’s phrase ‘to regret and be ashamed’: Rav teaches that one who sins and is ashamed is forgiven, first from Yechezkel 16:63 and then from Shaul, whose shame over Nov kept him from mentioning the Urim veTumim; ‘tomorrow you and your sons will be with me’ is read as his restoration among the righteous. Vidui therefore converts concealed failure into open submission: shame shows that the sinner no longer identifies with the act, and public confession can become Kiddush Hashem.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁקָּפַץ שִׁבְטוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה תְּחִלָּה לַיָּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם לז עַמּוּד א)

And this is why the tribe of Yehudah leapt first into the sea, as they said (there, Sotah 37a),396Expanded source note: R' Tzadok - map and parallels: Avodah Zarah 5a presents David as the model through whom an individual sinner learns that teshuvah remains possible. R' Tzadok develops that model in several complementary places. Tzidkat HaTzadik §254 links David's perpetual sense of incompletion to Malchus: instead of resting in achieved perfection, David remains in continuing longing and therefore 'raised the yoke of teshuvah.' Likkutei Maamarim, Upon Completion of Talmud §13 contrasts Yosef's iskafya - subduing the impulse before sin - with Yehudah's is'hapcha - transforming the bitter itself into sweetness after teshuvah. Peri Tzadik, Vayigash §10 adds that David, as the 'heart' of Israel, implants this power of teshuvah in every Jewish heart. Se'if 4 therefore treats David, Yehudah, Malchus, and Mashiach not as separate themes, but as one power: a fall is confessed, repaired, and ultimately redirected toward holiness.,397Expanded source note: Sea, covenant, and punishment: Sotah 36b-37a records a tannaitic dispute. R' Meir says Binyamin entered first; R' Yehudah says the tribes hesitated until Nachshon ben Aminadav and Yehudah descended, citing Hoshea 12:1 and Tehillim 69. R' Tzadok follows R' Yehudah's version. A second tradition in Midrash Tehillim 114:4 and Yalkut Shimoni §873 explains 'the sea saw and fled' (Tehillim 114:3): it saw Yosef's coffin and fled in reward for Yosef's own flight from temptation (Bereishis 39:12). Rabbeinu Bachya and Kli Yakar develop that link; Kli Yakar explicitly connects Yosef's sexual restraint, the Flood's sexual corruption, drowning as the providential analogue of strangulation, and the splitting of the Sea. The legal background is Mishnah Sanhedrin 11:1 and Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 1:6, which place ordinary adultery under chenek; Sanhedrin 37b says that after the courts ceased, one liable to strangulation may drown. R' Tzadok's contrast is exact: Yosef fled the test, while Yehudah, having sinned and confessed, entered the water and accepted judgment - teshuvah from love rather than fear of punishment.
דְּהַיָּם אֲרוֹנוֹ שֶׁל יוֹסֵף רָאָה וַיָּנָס, כִּי עֹנֶשׁ הַטְּבִיעָה בַּמַּיִם הוּא בַּעֲבוּר קִלְקוּל הַבְּרִית כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל

for the sea "saw the coffin of Yosef and fled" (Tehillim 114:3), because the punishment of drowning in water corresponds to the corruption of the covenant [bris], as we find in the generation of the Flood,
וְכֵן עֹנֶשׁ אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ בְּחֶנֶק וְדִינוֹ לִטְבּוֹעַ בַּנָּהָר כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין לז עַמּוּד ב)
and likewise the penalty for adultery with a married woman is strangulation [chenek], whose court-assigned equivalent is to drown in a river, as they said (Sanhedrin 37b),
וְיוֹסֵף דְּלָא חָטָא כְּלָל בָּרַח מִמֶּנּוּ
and Yosef, who did not sin at all in this, the water fled from him;
וִיהוּדָה שֶׁחָטָא וְשָׁב קָפַץ לְתוֹכוֹ קוֹדֶם שֶׁנִּקְרַע וְאַחַר כָּךְ נִקְרַע
while Yehudah, who sinned and repented, leapt into its midst before it split, and only afterward did it split,
וְהַקְּפִיצָה הָיָה דִּמְקַבֵּל עַל עַצְמוֹ עֹנֶשׁ שָׁמַיִם אִם הוּא מְחוּיָּיב בְּכָךְ
and this leap was an act of accepting upon himself the heavenly judgment, should he be liable to it.

items.h: The theme: Teshuvah from love is not from fear of punishment; on the contrary, one accepts the punishment willingly, if such is Hashem’s will. And through this Hashem removes even the inadvertent residue, and the penalty is wholly pardoned. Indeed he merits deliverance, and even malchus (Sotah 37a).

p: וְזֶהוּ הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁלֹּא מִיִּרְאַת עֹונֶשׁ, דְּאַדְּרַבָּא מְקַבֵּל עָלָיו הָעֹונֶשׁ בִּרְצוֹנוֹ אִם הוּא רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כָּךְ

And this is teshuvah from love — not from fear of punishment; on the contrary, he accepts the punishment upon himself willingly, if such is Hashem’s will;398Expanded source note: Yoma 86b:3 — the two stages of teshuvah: Reish Lakish derives from Hoshea 14:2 that deliberate avon becomes a 'stumbling,' i.e., an inadvertent sin; the Gemara then reconciles his second teaching, based on Yechezkel 33:19, that deliberate sins become merits: the first is teshuvah from fear, the second teshuvah from love. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, nevertheless requires abandonment of the sin, regret, firm resolve, and verbal confession; transformation into merit never makes the original deed permissible. R' Tzadok's point is that love changes the spiritual meaning drawn from the past: the fall becomes the occasion for deeper surrender, longing, and closeness. Thus the remaining shogeg is not merely erased; it is healed and incorporated into zechus.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִמֵּילָא גַּם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַעֲבִיר חֶטְאוֹ הַשּׁוֹגֵג גַּם כֵּן, וְנִמְחַל הָעֹונֶשׁ לְגַמְרֵי
and through this, of itself, Hashem too removes even his inadvertent sin, and the punishment is wholly pardoned,
וְאַדְּרַבָּא זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִישׁוּעָה וְנֵס וּלְהִנָּצֵל מֵאוֹתוֹ עֹונֶשׁ, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה גַּם כֵּן לַמַּלְכוּת כִּדְאִיתָא (בְּסוֹטָה שָׁם)

and, on the contrary, through this he merits salvation and a miracle, and to be saved from that very punishment; and thereby he merits malchus [kingship] as well, as is brought (in Sotah 37a).399Expanded source note: Sotah 36b–37a — Yehudah, the Sea, and kingship: R' Yehudah teaches that the tribes hesitated until Nachshon ben Aminadav and the tribe of Yehudah entered the Sea. Tehillim 69 is read as Nachshon's prayer while the waters reached him, and Hashem then told Moshe, 'Speak to the children of Israel that they travel' (Shemos 14:15). The Gemara concludes that for this reason Yehudah merited dominion in Israel, expounding Tehillim 114:2–3: 'Yehudah became His sanctuary; Israel His dominion; the sea saw and fled.' R' Tzadok reads the descent as willing acceptance of Heaven's judgment: precisely the submission that does not flee punishment becomes the act through which the decree is removed and malchus is revealed.,400Expanded source note: Gemara and meforshim on public sanctification and kingship: Sotah 36b:10 contrasts Yosef, who sanctified Heaven's Name privately and received one added letter in Yehosef, with Yehudah, who sanctified the Name publicly and bears the entire four-letter Name within Yehudah. Rashi there identifies Yehudah's public act with the descent into the Sea. Sotah 37a:6 then concludes that Yehudah merited dominion in Israel, expounding Tehillim 114:2, 'Yehudah became His sanctuary; Israel, His dominions.' Maharal, Netivos Olam, Netiv Ahavas Hashem 2:2, explains the contrast as one of spiritual form: Yosef's attachment is hidden, while Yehudah's blessing and Kiddush Hashem are revealed before all. Ben Yehoyada on Sotah 37a adds that the leap did not first create Yehudah's royal destiny; it secured the continuity of that kingship. R' Tzadok joins this national act to the personal act of teshuvah: willing entry into judgment becomes public Kiddush Hashem, and the same submission that accepts the decree becomes the source of rescue, miracle, and enduring malchus.

כִּי מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת הִיא הֵ״א אַחֲרוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי זֶהוּ מִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ אֲשֶׁר בַּכֹּל מָשָׁלָה, גַּם בַּמַּדְרֵגוֹת הַיּוֹתֵר תַּחְתּוֹנִים הַכֹּל הוּא מֵהַנְהָגָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר חוּץ לְמֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ וְהַנְהָגָתוֹ

For the attribute of malchus is the final hei of the Name [Havayah], as is known, for this is the attribute of His kingship, “whose rule is over all” (Tehillim 103:19): even in the lowest rungs, all is from His governance, and nothing is outside His dominion and providence.401Expanded source note: Zohar — the final heh as Malchus: Zohar, Tzav 56:1 identifies the yoke of the kingdom of Heaven with the final heh of the Divine Name, which is called Malchus. The standard sefirotic correspondence is yud–Chochmah, first heh–Binah, vav–the six middos, and final heh–Malchus (see Sulam on Zohar, Vayikra 285:1). Malchus receives the higher lights and reveals them below; therefore it is the letter associated with the lowest and most manifest realm. R' Tzadok uses this kabbalistic map as the architecture of teshuvah: the final heh reveals that Divine kingship reaches the very place that appeared most distant, so even a fall can become the site of renewed revelation.,402Expanded source note: Tehillim 103:19 and the reach of Malchus: The full verse reads, 'Hashem established His throne in the heavens, and His kingship rules over all.' In peshat, the heavenly throne is followed by universal sovereignty over every part of creation. Tikkunei Zohar 40b:2 says that no action among the lower realms occurs except through Malchus, applying this verse; Tikkunei Zohar 56b:10 identifies the Shechinah with the same kingship and describes it as ruling even over the realm of the Tree of Knowledge of good and evil. R' Tzadok therefore stresses the lowest levels: evil has no independent sovereignty, though human free choice and responsibility remain fully real. Teshuvah uncovers the deeper rule that was concealed within the apparent opposition.

וּמַלְכוּת יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא מַה שֶּׁחָלַק מִכְּבוֹדוֹ לְבָשָׂר וָדָם, וְזָכוּ לָהּ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁנֶּעֶשׂוּ גַּם הַזְּדוֹנוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת וְנִתְבָּרֵר דְּאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר נֶגֶד כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ

And the kingship of Israel is [that portion] which He apportioned of His glory to flesh and blood, and they merited it through teshuvah from love, whereby even the willful sins became like merits, and it was made clear that nothing stands against the honor of His kingship.403Expanded source note: Berachos 58a — earthly kingship as borrowed glory: The Gemara's exact blessing over a Jewish king is 'Who shared of His glory with those who fear Him,' while over a gentile king it is 'Who gave of His glory to flesh and blood.' The same passage teaches, 'earthly kingship is patterned after heavenly kingship,' and urges one to see kings so that the future distinction can be recognized. Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 224:8, codifies these blessings. R' Tzadok's phrase compresses the two Talmudic formulas; it is not presented as the verbatim text of the berachah. His point is that human sovereignty is never autonomous: Israel's malchus is a portion of Divine glory entrusted to human beings and is legitimate only insofar as it reveals Heaven's kingship.
וְאַדְּרַבָּא, עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא אַחַר שֶׁהוֹדָה בָּזֶה נִתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא, וְגָרַם בּוֹ קִידּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁפָּעַל יוֹסֵף בַּכְּבִישָׁה מֵחֵטְא

On the contrary: through the sin, once he confessed it, the Name of Heaven was sanctified in public, and he brought about thereby a sanctification of the Name of Heaven greater than what Yosef effected by his mastery [that kept him] from sin.404Expanded source note: Sotah 36b and 10b — private and public Kiddush Hashem: Sotah 36b contrasts Yosef, who sanctified Heaven's Name in private and received one added heh in Yehosef, with Yehudah, who sanctified the Name publicly and contains the entire four-letter Name within Yehudah. The Gemara there identifies the public act with Yehudah's descent into the Sea. Sotah 10b supplies the complementary personal model: Yehudah publicly admitted concerning Tamar, 'She is more righteous than I,' and a Heavenly voice affirmed his confession. R' Tzadok joins these two expressions of Yehudah: entering judgment publicly and confessing after failure reveal a greater Kiddush Hashem than hidden mastery alone, because the power of teshuvah itself becomes manifest before others.
וְזֶהוּ כָּל עִנְיַן הִתְגַּלּוּת כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה קִידּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בָּעוֹלָם, וּלְכָךְ נִתְיַיחֵס תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה לִיהוּדָה

And this is the whole purpose of the revelation of the honor of His kingship: that there be a sanctification of the Name of Heaven in the world; and therefore teshuvah from love is ascribed to Yehudah.405Expanded source note: Primary source, halachic framework, and R' Tzadok: Yoma 86b:3 resolves two statements of Reish Lakish: teshuvah from fear reduces deliberate sins to inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love transforms them into merits. Sforno on Shemos 34:7 reads venakeh in this light: complete cleansing belongs to those who return from love, whose sins are accounted as merits. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, defines the formal elements of teshuvah as abandoning the sin, removing it from one's thought, resolving never to repeat it, regretting the past, and verbal confession. R' Tzadok's willing acceptance of punishment is therefore not an additional judicial condition or a call to seek suffering; it describes the inner surrender of love, in which the penitent wants only Hashem's will. Resisei Layla section 38 explains 'with all your soul' (Devarim 6:5) as surrendering even one's spiritual self-interest and consenting to lose the soul itself for the Divine will. That parallel clarifies the se'if: the penitent accepts whatever Hashem wills, and precisely this bitul opens the change from shogeg residue to complete merit.

וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים עַל שֵׁם יְהוּדָה, דְּ״מִקֶּרֶב אַחֶיךָ תָּשִׂים עָלֶיךָ מֶלֶךְ״ כְּתִיב, דַּהֲקָמָתוֹ הוּא מִקֶּרֶב וּמֵהַפְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל, רַק שֶׁאֶצְלָם הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם וּבְקֶרֶב לִבָּם וְאֶצְלוֹ הוּא בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת וּבְפֹעַל

And all Israel are called by the name of Yehudah, for “from the midst of your brethren shall you set a king over you” (Devarim 17:15) is written, [teaching] that his elevation is from the midst and from the innermost core of all Israel, only that in them it is hidden, within their heart, while in him [the king] it is revealed and actualized.406Expanded source note: Peshat, halachah, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Devarim 17:15 commands, 'From among your brethren shall you set a king over yourself.' In its plain halachic use, 'from among' sets a boundary on appointment: Rambam, Hilchos Melachim 1:4, applies it to the king and other positions of authority. R' Tzadok then reads mikerev homiletically as 'from the inward core': the king actualizes a royal point hidden within the people. Berachos 58a, codified in Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 224:8, calls the blessing over a Jewish king 'Who apportioned of His glory to those who fear Him,' while the blessing over a gentile king says 'Who gave of His glory to flesh and blood.' The distinction supports R' Tzadok's point that Israel's kingship participates in Divine glory rather than standing as an autonomous power. The Zohar, Tzav 8:56, identifies the yoke of Heaven's kingship with the final heh; Zohar, Introduction 30:241, identifies Knesses Yisrael with that final heh as it receives and unites the higher powers. Machshavot Charutz 7:18 supplies R' Tzadok's parallel: every Jewish soul includes both Yosef and Yehudah, but Yehudah is Israel's primary name and the root of Knesses Yisrael because his power repairs deficiency and creates renewal after a fall.

וְעַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּתוֹ נִתְעוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן תְּשׁוּבָה בְּכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁגַּם כְּלַל הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל הִיא הָרְמוּזָה בְּהֵ״א אַחֲרוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם כַּאֲשֶׁר שָׁבִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת וּמִתְאַחֲדִים בְּמִדַּת מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

And through his arousal, repentance is likewise awakened in all the hearts of the Children of Israel, for the collective of Knesses Yisrael is also alluded to in the final hei of the Name when they return to the Blessed Name in truth and unite in the attribute of His kingship,407Expanded source note: Zohar, Introduction 30:241 — Knesses Yisrael and the final heh: The Zohar maps the four sections of Shema onto the four letters of the Divine Name. The fourth section, 'Vehayah im shamoa,' represents the two influences received by Knesses Yisrael, 'the lower gevurah,' and corresponds to the second/final heh, which receives the preceding letters and is included from them. This is the precise background to R' Tzadok's national reading. The king does not manufacture a foreign spiritual power; he actualizes openly the point of Malchus and return that is already hidden within the collective heart of Israel. His awakening can therefore stir teshuvah throughout Knesses Yisrael.

שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַכְּפִירָה בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, שֶׁאֵין שׁוּם כֹּחַ שְׁלִיטָה וּמֶמְשָׁלָה מִבַּלְעָדָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְ״כָל הַכּוֹפֵר בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה נִקְרָא יְהוּדִי״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּמְגִלָּה יג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א), שֶׁזֶּהוּ קְדֻשָּׁתוֹ שֶׁל יְהוּדָה שֶׁנִּקְרָא כּוּלּוֹ עַל שֵׁם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא

for this is the denial of idolatry: that there is no power of rule or dominion apart from Him, and “whoever denies idolatry is called a Yehudi,” as they said (Megillah 13a), which is the holiness of Yehudah, who is called entirely by the Name of the Holy One, blessed be He.408Expanded source note: Megillah 13a — why 'Yehudi' means rejection of idolatry: Mordechai belonged to Binyamin, yet Megillas Esther calls him a Yehudi. The Gemara answers that anyone who repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi, and cites Daniel 3:12, where Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah are called 'Jewish men' because they refused the royal idol. Maharal, Ohr Chadash 2:5, explains that the name marks exclusive allegiance to the One God against every competing power. R' Tzadok connects this to Yehudah's name, which contains the Divine Name: the holiness of Yehudah is the recognition that no rule exists independently of Hashem. In Yisrael Kedoshim he similarly treats Yehudi as Israel's name of self-surrender and Kiddush Hashem.,409Expanded source note: Gemara, halachah, prophecy, and R' Tzadok: Megillah 13a asks why Mordechai, a Benjaminite, is called Yehudi and answers that anyone who repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi, citing Daniel 3:12, where Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah are called 'Jewish men.' Maharal, Ohr Chadash 2:5:2, explains that Mordechai earned the name by affirming the Divine unity against the whole world; Yehudi thus signals both denial of alien rule and singular allegiance to Hashem. The halachic framework is Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:1 and 5:4: all Israel are commanded in Kiddush Hashem, and when the law requires one to die rather than transgress, doing so before ten Jews is public sanctification; the Rambam names Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah as models. Actual martyrdom follows the detailed limits of that halachah, not a blanket rule. The concluding verse is Yirmiyahu 50:20: 'The iniquity of Israel shall be sought and be absent, and the sins of Yehudah shall not be found.' Radak places it in the future complete purification; Malbim distinguishes Israel's avon of idolatrous error from Yehudah's chatas of desire. R' Tzadok goes further: when Yehudah's holiness is revealed through teshuvah from love, even that chatas is not found because it has become merit. Yisrael Kedoshim 8:16 makes the same association: all Israel are called Yehudim from Yehudah, whose root is self-sacrifice for Kiddush Hashem against idolatry.
