וְכֵן כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּמָסְרֵי נַפְשַׁיְיהוּ עַל קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם, לְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא, שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁגִּיחַ בְּמֶלֶךְ בָּשָׂר וָדָם נֶגֶד מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, כַּחֲנַנְיָה מִישָׁאֵל וַעֲזַרְיָה דְּנִקְרְאוּ ״גּוּבְרִין יְהוּדָאִין״ דְּמִזֶּה יָלְפִינַן לַהּ הָתָם

And so too all Israel who surrender their lives for the sanctification of the Name, to sanctify the Name of Heaven in public, paying no heed to a king of flesh and blood against His kingship, like Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah, who were called “Jewish men [guvrin Yehuda'in]” (Daniel 3:12), from which we derive it there [in Megillah 13a].410Expanded source note: Halachah of Kiddush Hashem: Vayikra 22:32 commands, 'I shall be sanctified among the children of Israel.' Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:1–4, defines when a Jew must surrender life rather than transgress: the three cardinal prohibitions, specified cases of public coercion before ten Jews, and a time of persecution, with the detailed distinctions set out there. He names Daniel, Chananyah, Mishael, and Azaryah among the scriptural models. Thus mesirus nefesh is governed by halachah and is not a general license to seek danger. R' Tzadok invokes its inner root: the Yehudah-point refuses to acknowledge an earthly power as independent of Divine kingship, and that absolute allegiance is the deepest source of public Kiddush Hashem.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״חַטַּאת יְהוּדָה (וְלֹא תִמָּצֶאנָה)״ וְגוֹמֵר, דִּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת קְדֻשָּׁה זוֹ הוּא הַסְּלִיחָה גְּמוּרָה, דְּגַם הַשּׁוֹגֵג לֹא נִמְצָא דְּנַעֲשָׂה זְכִיּוֹת

And therefore it said, “[and the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and there shall be none; and] the sins of Yehudah, and they shall not be found” (Yirmeyah 50:20), for in the revelation of this holiness lies complete forgiveness, wherein even the inadvertent sin is “not found,” having been turned into merits.411Expanded source note: Yirmiyahu 50:20 — 'the sin of Yehudah shall not be found': In the prophecy of Bavel's fall and Israel's restoration, the verse says, 'In those days…the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none, and the sins of Yehudah shall not be found, for I will pardon those whom I leave.' Metzudas David explains that even a search will uncover no guilt because the surviving remnant has been cleansed and forgiven. Malbim distinguishes the terms avon and chatas and the different histories of Israel and Yehudah. R' Tzadok reads the wording with further precision: 'not found' does not mean that the historical deed never occurred; through teshuvah from love its present spiritual identity has changed into merit. The accuser searches for a chatas and cannot find one in that form.

items.h: The theme: This is the rule and order for every penitent: even David, in his lifetime, was not informed of the complete pardon that turns sins into merits — because teshuvah, on man’s side, always begins from fear. Hence “my iniquity I declare, I worry over my sin” (Tehillim 38:19): once he confessed the willful avon, he no longer worried over it. It is surely forgiven from being deliberate, but he still worried over the chatas [the inadvertent residue] that remains, which needs Hashem’s assistance to return from love.

p: וְכֵן הוּא הַמִּדָּה וְהַסֵּדֶר לְעוֹלָם שֶׁל כָּל בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, דְּאַף דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּחַיָּיו לֹא הוֹדִיעוּהוּ מִמְּחִילָה הַגְּמוּרָה לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, דִּתְחִלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם לְעוֹלָם הוּא מִיִּרְאָה

And such is the rule and order, always, for all penitents: that even David HaMelech, peace be upon him, in his lifetime, was not informed of the complete pardon that renders [sins] into merits, for the beginning of teshuvah from man’s side is always from fear.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר (תְּהִלִּים ל״ח:י״ט) ״עֲוֹנִי אַגִּיד אֶדְאַג מֵחַטָּאתִי״
And therefore he said (Tehillim 38:19), “For I declare my iniquity; I worry over my sin”;
וְרֵישֵׁיהּ דִּקְרָא שָׁם ״לְצֶלַע נָכוֹן״ נִדְרַשׁ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז עַמּוּד א) אַמַּעֲשֵׂה דְּבַת שֶׁבַע
and the opening of the verse there, “for I am ready to halt,” is expounded (in Sanhedrin 107a) regarding the incident of Bas Sheva.
וּמִשֶּׁהִגִּיד עֲוֹנוֹ וְהִתְוַדָּה עָלָיו לֹא דָּאַג עוֹד עָלָיו, דְּוַדַּאי נִמְחַל עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב עוֹד לְעָוֹן מֵזִיד

And once he declared his iniquity and confessed over it, he no longer worried over it, for it was certainly pardoned through the teshuvah so that it would not be reckoned any longer as a willful iniquity;
אֲבָל דָּאַגְתִּי מֵהַחֵטְא שֶׁנִּשְׁאַר לִזְמַן, דִּלְזֶה צָרִיךְ עֵזֶר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה

“but I worried over the sin [chatas, the inadvertent residue] that remained for a time,” for to [rectify] this requires the assistance of the Blessed Name, to return from love.412Expanded source note: Verse, Gemara, and R' Tzadok's reading: Tehillim 38:19 says, 'For my iniquity I declare; I worry over my sin.' Sanhedrin 107a reads an earlier phrase in the psalm, 'for my loins are filled with burning' (38:8), against the background of David and Bat-Sheva; the psalm is therefore an appropriate scriptural setting for David's continuing teshuvah. The avon/chatas distinction in this note is R' Tzadok's close derash of the verse's changing nouns and verbs. 'I declare' means that the deliberate avon has been faced through vidui and is no longer reckoned as willful rebellion; 'I worry' describes the remaining chatas, the inadvertent status to which fear-based teshuvah has reduced it. This uses Reish Lakish's first ruling in Yoma 86b:3, that deliberate sins become inadvertent through fear, while reserving the second ruling, transformation into merits, for love. It does not mean that confession authorizes carelessness or that a forgiven sin should be forgotten. Rather, R' Tzadok distinguishes confidence in the efficacy of teshuvah from the penitent's honest awareness that the highest healing is a gift. The adjacent Tehillim 51:5, 'my transgressions I know, and my sin is before me always,' makes the same distinction sharper: knowledge of the past preserves humility, while the residue 'before me' continues to call for love and Divine help.
וְכֵן אָמַר (שָׁם נ״א:ה׳) ״פְּשָׁעַי אֲנִי אֵדָע וְחַטָּאתִי נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד״, דְּיָלְפִינַן מִינַּהּ (בְּיוֹמָא פו עַמּוּד ב) דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה

And so he said (Tehillim 51:5), “For I acknowledge my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me,” from which we derive (in Yoma 86b) that one repeatedly confesses [the same sin each Yom Kippur].413Expanded source note: Gemara, halachah, and the Maharsha dispute: Yoma 86b:12 records two views about confessing a sin already confessed on an earlier Yom Kippur. The first opinion invokes Mishlei 26:11, the dog returning to its vomit; R' Eliezer ben Yaakov calls renewed confession praiseworthy and cites Tehillim 51:5, 'my sin is before me always.' Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:8, rules that one may and should confess such earlier sins again, even while remaining firmly repentant. Sha'arei Teshuvah 4:21 records variant traditions about repeating them orally and reconciles the moral concerns: the penitent keeps the sin in mind, trusts Hashem's forgiveness, and continues to seek mercy without turning remembrance into despair. Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados on Yoma 86b:9, reads David's words to mean that the former pesha'im, now reduced by teshuvah to the status of shogeg/chatas, still require confession as inadvertent sins. R' Tzadok explicitly presses beyond that reading: the Gemara says that he confesses 'the first sins' again, and it makes no exception for one who has reached teshuvah from love. He therefore understands repeated vidui as naming the original deed truthfully, even after forgiveness or transformation. Its purpose is enduring knowledge and shame before Hashem, not denial of pardon; forgetting the fall would erase the humility and self-knowledge produced through it. This distinction is central throughout Takanat HaShavin: transformation into merit does not rewrite the historical act as permissible, but reveals how teshuvah can draw holiness from the penitent's response to that act.
וְאַפְּשָׁעִים דְּמֵזִיד אָמַר לְשׁוֹן ״אֵדָע״, דְּהַוִּידּוּי הוּא רַק אַיְדִיעָה שֶׁכְּבָר פָּשַׁע לְשֶׁעָבַר
And regarding willful transgressions [pesha'im] he used the term “I acknowledge” [eda], for the confession is merely an acknowledgment that he had already transgressed in the past;
וְאַף דִּכְבָר נִמְחַל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא יִשְׁכָּחֶנּוּ וְצָרִיךְ לֵידַע וְלִהְיוֹת נִכְלָם תָּמִיד מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל זֶה
and although it was already pardoned, nevertheless he must not forget it, but must know it and remain continually humbled and shamed before the Blessed Name over it.

אֲבָל ״חַטָּאתִי הוּא נֶגְדִּי תָמִיד״ — עוֹמֵד לְנֶגְדִּי מַמָּשׁ, כִּי לֹא נִמְחַל עֲדַיִין כְּלָל, דִּבְחַיָּיו לֹא הוֹדִיעוּהוּ עֲדַיִין דְּנֶחְשָׁב לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה וְלִהְיוֹת נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי

But “my sin [chatas] is ever before me” means that it literally stands before me, for it has not yet been pardoned at all [at the highest level], since during his lifetime they did not yet inform him that it was reckoned as teshuvah from love to be pardoned completely.
(וּמַהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שָׁם הִרְגִּישׁ קְצָת בָּזֶה, אֶלָּא שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ דְּמַה דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה הַיְינוּ עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג
(And the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados there sensed this slightly, but he explained that one’s repeated confession is only over the inadvertent sin;
וּלְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מַשְׁמַע דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה עַל הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת כְּמוֹ עַל אוֹתָן שֶׁשּׁוֹנֶה בְּאִוַּלְתּוֹ וּלְהַחֲשִׁיבָן עֲבֵירָה דְּמֵזִיד
yet the wording of the Gemara implies that one repeatedly confesses over the original sins just as over those repeated in his folly, accounting them deliberate transgressions;
וְגַם לְפִי דְּבָרָיו הַשָּׁב מֵאַהֲבָה אֵין חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה, וְלֹא חִילְּקוּ בָּזֶה
and also according to his words, one who repents from love would not repeatedly confess, yet [the Sages] made no such distinction.

וְנִרְאֶה עִיקָּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דִּלְעוֹלָם חוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה כְּבָרִאשׁוֹנָה מַמָּשׁ, דְּגַם ״אֲנִי אֵדָע״ הַיְינוּ דְּחוֹזֵר וּמִתְוַדֶּה, דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי הוּא נִשְׁכָּח מִלֵּב וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לְדַעְתָּם עוֹד)

And what appears primary is what I wrote: that one always returns and confesses exactly as at first, for “I acknowledge” also implies repeated confession, since otherwise it would be forgotten from the heart and there would be no need to retain knowledge of them any longer).
כִּי הָעֲבֵירָה שֶׁלּוֹ הָיְתָה בְּחִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר (שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ב:י״ד) ״אֶפֶס כִּי נִאֵץ נִאַצְתָּ״ וְגוֹמֵר
For his transgression involved a desecration of the Name, as it says (II Shmuel 12:14), “Howbeit, because by this deed you have given great occasion to the enemies of Hashem to blaspheme...”;
וְעַל חִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם אָמְרוּ (בְּיוֹמָא פו עַמּוּד א) דְּמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה גְּמַר מְחִילָתוֹ קוֹדֶם הַמִּיתָה

and regarding desecration of the Name they said (in Yoma 86a) that only death scours [and completes atonement], wherefore the culmination of his pardon was not revealed prior to death.414Expanded source note: Chilul Hashem and the four divisions of atonement: Shmuel II 12:14 describes the public consequence of David's deed. Radak explains that it gave the enemies of Israel an opening to speak disparagingly, so the desecration lies in the public meaning created by the act. Yoma 86a:8 teaches the classic gradation: for neglect of a positive command, teshuvah atones immediately; for an ordinary prohibition, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for kareis or judicial death, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend while suffering completes; for chilul Hashem, those three suspend and death completes the cleansing. Rambam codifies this in Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4. Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 5:11, also explains that for a prominent Torah figure, conduct that is not intrinsically sinful can become chilul Hashem when observers reasonably speak disparagingly because of it. That halachic category illuminates R' Tzadok's later claim that David's deed, at its hidden root, was merit although to human sight it appeared sinful and produced a public desecration. 'Death scours' here describes the structure and timing of complete kapparah; it is not counsel to seek death or suffering. R' Tzadok's innovation is that the eventual revelation reverses the public meaning itself: David's punishment, lifelong confession, and extraordinary teshuvah become a Kiddush Hashem, showing how exactingly Hashem deals with those nearest to Him and how completely teshuvah can heal.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נָתָן הִבְטִיחוֹ ״ה׳ הֶעֱבִיר חַטָּאתְךָ לֹא תָמוּת״, וְהַיְינוּ דְּ״דָוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּים״ בֶּאֱמֶת

Nonetheless, Nasan assured him (II Shmuel 12:13), “Hashem also has put away your sin; you shall not die,” which means that “David, king of Israel, lives and endures” in truth;415Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's order of teshuvah: Resisei Layla section 36 distinguishes two sounds of the shofar. The groan born of dread is teshuvah from fear, while the weeping of a child yearning for his father is teshuvah from love; the order is first groaning and afterward crying. This corrects a possible compression of the parallel: yearning is the higher stage of love, not the initial fear. The underlying Talmudic distinction is Yoma 86b:3: Reish Lakish teaches that deliberate sins become inadvertent sins through teshuvah from fear, but become merits through teshuvah from love. Thus the se'if's claim that teshuvah 'on man's side' begins with fear describes the ordinary human point of entry, not its final measure. Fear enables confession and removes the status of willful rebellion; the complete reversal into merit requires the Divine assistance that awakens love. Resisei Layla section 36 further associates the higher teshuvah with a level beyond ordinary time, where the future is repaired at its root. Takanat HaShavin, Siman 5, likewise explains that the deepest healing reaches the root beneath the manifested sin. David's lifetime uncertainty therefore serves R' Tzadok's broader architecture: pardon can be real before the penitent is shown the final, eschatological disclosure that the fall itself has been incorporated into merit.
אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִתְגַּלָּה זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַד בִּיאַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ מִזַּרְעוֹ, וְהוּא דָּוִד בְּעַצְמוֹ דְּ״חַיִּים שָׁאַל נָתַתָּ לּוֹ״

only that this was not yet revealed in this world until the advent of the Mashiach from his seed, who is David himself, concerning whom it is said (Tehillim 21:5), “He asked life of You, and You gave it him”,416Expanded source note: Nasan's assurance and David's enduring kingship: On Shmuel II 12:13, 'Hashem has removed your sin; you shall not die,' Radak explains that David's immediate confession is met by immediate acceptance. 'You shall not die' means that he will not suffer the death of the wicked or lose the World to Come, although temporal consequences announced by Nasan still follow. R' Tzadok reads the assurance at a still deeper level: David's essential life and kingship endure until their full vindication is manifest. The phrase 'David, king of Israel, lives and endures' appears in Rosh Hashanah 25a as the coded signal for the sanctification of the new moon. That lunar setting supplied later tradition with a natural symbol for the Davidic house: the moon wanes, disappears, and is renewed. Ramban on Bereishis 38:29 connects Peretz and the house of David with this pattern of lunar diminution and renewal. Zohar, Vayeshev 25:275, associates David's plea, 'renew a steadfast spirit within me' (Tehillim 51:12), with renewal of the moon and with 'David Melech Yisrael chai vekayam.' The Rema, Orach Chaim 426:2, records the phrase in Kiddush Levanah, where the renewal of Israel and the Davidic kingdom is enacted liturgically. R' Tzadok turns that symbol into a doctrine of teshuvah: David's apparent fall and death do not cancel his root; the concealed life reappears through Mashiach ben David, when the transformation of the sin into merit becomes publicly knowable.,417Expanded source note: The verse and R' Tzadok's internal map: Tehillim 21:5 says, 'Life he asked of You; You gave it to him, length of days forever and ever.' Radak reads the two clauses as long life in this world and enduring life in the World to Come. Metzudas David gives the verse an explicitly messianic setting: after seeing Mashiach ben Yosef killed, Mashiach ben David asks for life and is granted it. These readings supply the scriptural range within which R' Tzadok identifies David's promised life with the future Mashiach from his seed. The full conceptual parallel is developed later in this volume, Takanat HaShavin, Siman 15, sections 87, 90, and 101. There R' Tzadok associates the final vindication of David with Mashiach ben David, who is elevated beyond Moshe in attaining the hidden fiftieth gate, and with the complete healing in which sins become merits. The reference is therefore not merely genealogical: Mashiach reveals what David's lifetime could not yet display, namely that the apparent rupture itself belonged to the path of repair. 'Lives and endures' marks continuity at the root while history still presents concealment, punishment, and death. This eschatological identification is R' Tzadok's synthesis of the verse, the lunar saying of Rosh Hashanah 25a, and his theology of teshuvah; it should not be mistaken for the plain context of the Talmudic password by itself.
כִּי לֹא יִצְטָרֵךְ עוֹד לְמִיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת מֵאַחַר דְּנִתְגַּלָּה דְּהוּא כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
because he will no longer require a scouring death once it is revealed that [his former sins] are like merits.
וְאַדְּרַבָּא, הוּא קִידּוּשׁ הַשֵּׁם, שֶׁאַף בְּדָבָר זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ חֵטְא אֶלָּא זְכוּת, רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דִּבְנֵי אָדָם נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא, וְגַם עַל זֶה קִיבֵּל עֹונֶשׁ
On the contrary, it is a sanctification of the Name: that even in this matter — which is not a sin but a merit, only to the human eye is it reckoned a sin, and for which he even accepted punishment —
וְעִם כָּל זֶה הִרְבָּה כָּל כָּךְ בִּתְשׁוּבָה וְחַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד וּבוֹשׁ וְנִכְלָם לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
yet with all this he engaged so abundantly in teshuvah, his sin ever before him, ashamed and humbled before the Blessed Name.
וְזֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְקִידּוּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַרְאֶה דְּ״סְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד״

And this is reckoned a sanctification of the Name of Heaven, wherein the Blessed Name demonstrates that “round about Him it tempesteth greatly” (Tehillim 50:3) [i.e., He is exacting with the righteous to a hairsbreadth],
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק ״בִּקְרֹבַי אֶקָּדֵשׁ״ דִּשְׁמוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְקַדֵּשׁ כְּשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה דִּין בִּקְרוֹבָיו

and as the Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse “Through those near to Me I will be sanctified” (Vayikra 10:3), that His Blessed Name is sanctified when He executes judgment upon those near to Him,418Expanded source note: Those near to Hashem and Kiddush Hashem: Vayikra 10:3 records Moshe's words after the deaths of Nadav and Avihu: 'Through those near to Me I shall be sanctified, and before all the people I shall be honored,' followed by Aharon's silence. Rashi, drawing on Sifra, Zevachim 115b, and Vayikra Rabbah 12:2, explains that the Mishkan would be sanctified through Hashem's honored ones; Moshe tells Aharon that his sons have proved even greater than they, and Aharon receives reward for his silence. Ramban preserves that derash and adds a peshat dimension: when judgment is executed upon those closest to the Sanctuary, the people learn reverence for Hashem and His holy place; he also discusses whether vayidom means that Aharon ceased crying or became wholly silent. Chazal and the classical commentators propose several particular failings of Nadav and Avihu, including the unauthorized fire and other lapses proportionate to their stature. R' Tzadok is stressing that proportionality, not erasing every classical account of error: among the exceptionally near, even a slight deviation that would seem negligible in another person bears enormous public weight. He applies the same pattern to David. Divine exactitude toward the righteous creates awe 'before all the people,' while David's acceptance of judgment and lifelong teshuvah turn an apparent chilul Hashem into Kiddush Hashem. The analogy also explains the phrase 'around Him it storms exceedingly' (Tehillim 50:3, expounded by Chazal as exacting judgment with the righteous): nearness increases responsibility because the public reads Hashem's honor through the conduct and fate of those nearest to Him.
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה ״עַל פְּנֵי כָל הָעָם אֶכָּבֵד״, שֶׁמִּתְרַבֶּה כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם כְּשֶׁרוֹאִים עַד הֵיכָן צָרִיךְ לִירָא מִפָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ
for through this “before all the people I will be glorified,” as the honor of Heaven is magnified when people behold the dread degree to which one must revere His Blessed presence.
דִּמְקוֹרָבָיו כְּנָדָב וַאֲבִיהוּא לֹא חָטְאוּ כְּלָל, אֶלָּא בְּדָבָר קַל שֶׁאֵין רָאוּי לְהַחְשִׁיבוֹ חֵטְא כְּלָל, אֲבָל מִצַּד גְּדוּלַּת כְּבוֹד שָׁמַיִם נֶחְשָׁב גַּם זֶה לְחֵטְא

For those near to Him like Nadav and Avihu did not sin at all, except in a minute matter unworthy of being termed a sin at all, yet from the immense elevation of the honor of Heaven, even this was reckoned against them as a sin.

items.h: The theme: Since through David’s sufferings and his prodigious repentance the Name was sanctified, that very act is reckoned in truth a sanctification, not a desecration — so no scouring death is needed. On the contrary, he merits eternal life (for “from the negative you infer the positive”). A mere thought of teshuvah in the heart already sufficed to transform willful sins into inadvertent ones, yet the inadvertent residue (shogeg) remained, for human repentance begins from fear (teshuvah tata'ah). Through brokenheartedness he draws down divine assistance (teshuvah ila'ah), ascending higher than complete tzaddikim, until he rectifies even the ancestral root of desire in birth (etyo shel nachash).

p: וְכֵיוָן שֶׁבְּעָנְשֵׁי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּבְהַפְלָגַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ נִתְקַדֵּשׁ שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל יָדוֹ, הֲרֵי נֶחְשָׁב אוֹתוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה קִידּוּשׁ ה׳ בֶּאֱמֶת לֹא חִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם

And since through the punishments of David HaMelech, peace be upon him, and through the greatness of his repentance, the Name of Heaven was sanctified through him, that deed is reckoned in truth a sanctification of Hashem, not a desecration of the Name;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין צָרִיךְ לְמִיתָה הַמְּמָרֶקֶת, רַק אַדְּרַבָּא זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם
and therefore he does not require a scouring death, but on the contrary merits through this eternal life,
דְּמִכְּלַל לָאו אַתָּה שׁוֹמֵעַ הֵן בְּכָל מָקוֹם בַּתּוֹרָה
for “from the negative you infer the positive” everywhere in the Torah:
וְאִם חִילּוּל הַשֵּׁם צָרִיךְ מִיתָה לְכַפָּרָה, מִידָּה טוֹבָה מְרוּבָּה דְּקִידּוּשׁ ה׳ נוֹתֵן חַיִּים
and if desecration of the Name requires death for atonement, the measure of goodness being greater, sanctifying Hashem grants life.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם אָמַר ״חָטָאתִי לַה׳״, כִּי גַּם בְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בַּלֵּב דַּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי (לְעֵיל רֵישׁ סִימָן ט׳)
And David HaMelech, peace be upon him, said, “I have sinned to Hashem” (II Shmuel 12:13), for even a stirring of teshuvah in the heart suffices, as I wrote (above, start of Siman 9);
וּמִיַּד שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט בַּלֵּב וְשָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת, יָדַע וְהִרְגִּישׁ בְּלִבּוֹ דִּכְבָר נִמְחַל וְנַעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, אֶלָּא דְּהַשּׁוֹגֵג עֲדַיִין נִשְׁאַר

and as soon as he regretted in his heart and returned in truth, he knew and felt in his heart that it was already pardoned and transformed into inadvertent sins, only that the inadvertent residue still remained.
כִּי הַתְחָלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם לְעוֹלָם הוּא מִצַּד הַיִּרְאָה
For the beginning of teshuvah from man’s initiative is always from the side of fear,
דְּעַל כֵּן שַׁיָּיךְ גַּם כֵּן לַמֶּלֶךְ בְּיִחוּד, דְּבוֹ תּוֹקֶף הַיִּרְאָה דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁכָּרַע שׁוּב אֵינוֹ זוֹקֵף
wherefore it applies especially to a king, in whom is the ultimate intensity of fear, for “once he bows, he does not straighten again” (Berachos 34b).
וְזֶה הַתְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה שֶׁבְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם הַמַּקְדִּישׁ עַצְמוֹ מְעַט מִלְּמַטָּה, דְּ״שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי״
And this is the lower teshuvah [teshuvah tata'ah] through the initiative of man sanctifying himself a little from below, of “Return to Me” (Malachi 3:7);
וְאַחַר כָּךְ ״וְאָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם״ בִּתְשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַמַּקְדִּישׁ אוֹתוֹ הַרְבֵּה מִלְּמַעְלָה

and afterward “and I will return to you,” with the higher teshuvah [teshuvah ila'ah] that comes from the Blessed Name, Who sanctifies him abundantly from Above.419Expanded source note: Peshat, Midrash, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Malachi 3:7 says, 'Return to Me and I will return to you.' In the immediate prophetic context, the rebuke concerns neglected tithes; Malbim explains that Israel's return restores the rain and blessing withheld through that neglect. Chazal broaden the verse into a general structure of teshuvah. Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2:2 reads 'Open for Me' as Hashem's request that Israel make one opening of teshuvah like the eye of a needle, after which He opens gates wide enough for wagons. The same reciprocity appears in Yoma 38b and Shabbos 104a: one who comes to purify is assisted from Heaven. The Zohar's Ra'aya Mehemna, Naso 122a-123a, supplies the terminology of teshuvah tata'ah and teshuvah ila'ah, interpreting teshuvah mystically as tashuv heh, the restoration of the lower and upper heh of the Divine Name. R' Tzadok adapts that kabbalistic map to the moral sequence here: the lower return is the person's limited movement from below, rooted in yirah; the higher return is Hashem's answering nearness, which opens love and a degree the person could not produce alone. Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Elul 4:1, likewise connects the needle-opening to it'aruta de-letata, an awakening from below. The Midrash is therefore not a promise that effort or the halachic elements of teshuvah may be skipped. It explains the asymmetry of grace: a sincere human beginning is small but real, and the Divine assistance it elicits is vastly greater.
וְהוּא הַסִּיּוּעַ שֶׁמְּסַיְּיעִין לַבָּא לִיטַּהֵר בִּפְתִיחָה קְטַנָּה שֶׁבַּהֵ״א לְמַעְלָה שֶׁיּוּכַל לִיכָּנֵס בַּפֶּתַח הַגָּבוֹהַּ יוֹתֵר, דְּ״אֶת דַּכָּא וּשְׁפַל רוּחַ״

And this is the heavenly assistance granted to “one who comes to purify himself” (Yoma 38b), through the small opening in the upper part of the letter hei (Menachos 29b), enabling him to enter via the higher opening, as in “with the crushed and lowly of spirit” (Yeshayah 57:15).
וְהַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה לִבּוֹ נִשְׁבָּר, דָּכוּי וְשָׁפָל מִפְּנֵי עֲוֹנוֹתָיו, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְקָרֵב אֵלָיו הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּיוֹתֵר, דְּ״קָרוֹב ה׳ לְנִשְׁבְּרֵי לֵב״

And the penitent’s heart is broken, crushed, and humbled because of his iniquities, and through this the Blessed Name draws exceedingly near to him, for “Hashem is near to the brokenhearted” (Tehillim 34:19),
וְיוּכַל לִיכָּנֵס לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה בְּיוֹתֵר, וְהוּא הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין שֶׁאֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִין לַעֲמוֹד

and he is able to enter a higher rung, which is “the place where baalei teshuvah stand, [where] the wholly righteous cannot stand” (Berachos 34b).420Expanded source note: Pesukim, Gemara, meforshim, and halachah: Yeshayah 57:15 joins two apparent opposites: the One who dwells in the high and holy place also dwells with the crushed and lowly, in order to revive them. Malbim identifies the crushed person here with the baal teshuvah and reads the verse as answering objections to the very possibility of repentance: Divine transcendence does not prevent Hashem from drawing near to the contrite. Tehillim 34:19 similarly promises that Hashem is near to the broken-hearted and saves those crushed in spirit. Berachos 34b records a dispute about the resulting rank. R' Abahu says that complete tzaddikim cannot stand where baalei teshuvah stand, reading Yeshayah 57:19, 'peace, peace to the far and to the near,' with the formerly distant person first. R' Yochanan reads 'far' as one who was always far from sin and therefore places the complete tzaddik first. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, codifies the penitent's extraordinary closeness without turning the disagreement into a license to sin: a baal teshuvah must not imagine himself remote, for he is beloved and desirable before the Creator and has tasted sin yet separated from it and conquered his inclination. R' Tzadok follows R' Abahu's higher valuation in this se'if. The fall is not itself the advantage; the advantage is the broken-hearted return that converts distance into a deeper nearness. The phrases 'crushed' and 'broken' therefore describe humility and honest dependence on Hashem, not hopelessness or self-destruction. They provide the vessel through which the higher teshuvah, Hashem's answering return, can enter.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ ״גַּם ה׳״ וְגוֹמֵר, דִּכְמוֹ שֶׁאַתָּה שַׁבְתָּ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כֵּן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שָׁב אֵלֶיךָ וְנִתְקָרֵב לְךָ יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי כֵּן, וְהֶעֱבִיר גַּם הַשּׁוֹגֵג

And this is what [Nasan] said to him: “Hashem also [has put away your sin; you shall not die]” (II Shmuel 12:13), meaning: just as you returned to the Blessed Name, so the Blessed Name returned to you and drew nearer to you through this, removing even the inadvertent residue.
אַךְ ״אֶפֶס כִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְגַלּוֹתוֹ עֲדַיִין בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּחַיֶּיךָ שֶׁזָּכִיתָ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה הַגְּמוּרָה

“Howbeit, because [by this deed you have given great occasion to the enemies of Hashem to blaspheme]” (12:14), and it is impossible to reveal it yet in this world during your lifetime, that you merited complete teshuvah from love.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אָמַר מִזְמוֹר עַל זֶה, וְאָמַר שָׁם ״זִבְחֵי אֱלֹהִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַקָּרְבָּן הַמְכַפֵּר גַּם עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג

Yet nevertheless he uttered a song [mizmor] over this, saying there: “The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; [a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise]” (Tehillim 51:19), which is the offering that atones even for the inadvertent sin,
שֶׁמִּתְקָרֵב עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ עַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁבִירַת לֵב שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַחֵטְא כְּשֶׁשָּׁב, וְנִמְצָא הַיְּרִידָה צוֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה וְרָאוּי לְזַמֵּר

for he draws near through this to the Blessed Name by the heartbreak he experiences on account of the sin when he repents, so that the descent proves to be for the sake of ascent, and it is fitting to sing.421Expanded source note: Tanakh, halachah, and R' Tzadok's parallel: Shmuel II 12:13 places David's entire spoken response in two words, 'I have sinned to Hashem,' and Nasan immediately announces that Hashem has removed his sin. Radak explains the word gam reciprocally: just as David confessed, Hashem accepted his confession, although earthly consequences still remained. The power of an inward turn has a concrete halachic analogue in Kiddushin 49b: a thoroughly wicked man who betroths a woman on condition that he is righteous creates a doubtful kiddushin, lest he have entertained a thought of teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 38:31, codify that ruling. This does not erase the formal mitzvah of verbal confession in Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1; rather, the inward resolve can immediately change the person's direction and standing, while complete vidui and repair still follow. R' Tzadok also invokes Berachos 34b, codified in Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 5:10: a king, once he bows in the Amidah, does not raise his head until the prayer is finished. Kingship therefore demands an intensified yirah and submission precisely because of its public elevation. The se'if's inference that Kiddush Hashem grants life rests on the wider rule that the measure of good exceeds the measure of punishment (Sotah 11a; compare Ramban on Shemos 20:5). Kometz HaMincha II section 27 supplies R' Tzadok's own parallel: David raised the yoke of teshuvah, from which a well of living water produces new longing each day. Thus David's punishment, confession, and continued return transform the public meaning of the episode from desecration into sanctification and replace 'scouring death' with enduring spiritual life.,422Expanded source note: The broken heart as an inner korban: Tehillim 51 is David's penitential psalm after Nasan's rebuke. Immediately before the cited verse David says, 'You do not desire sacrifice, else I would give it' (51:18). Rashi explains that an animal chatas is not brought for a deliberate sin; Radak similarly says that the Torah prescribed such offerings for inadvertent sins, whereas for David's willful act Hashem desires a broken heart. On verse 19 Radak calls the broken spirit the sacrifice Hashem seeks even when no animal accompanies it. Sotah 5b makes the comparison explicit: R' Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that one of lowly spirit is credited as though he offered all the sacrifices, and his prayer is not despised. The halachic plane remains distinct: Vayikra 4 and Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, require the prescribed chatas when an inadvertent transgression and its Temple-era conditions apply, and Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, requires confession with the offering. R' Tzadok is describing the inner work of kapparah, not cancelling a korban obligation. Because fear-based teshuvah has reduced the deliberate act to a residual shogeg, the contrition generated by remembering the sin becomes its corresponding inward offering. That is the paradox of yeridah tzorech aliyah: the sin remains forbidden and regretted, yet the broken heart it produces draws the penitent nearer than before. The fall becomes a vehicle of ascent only through teshuvah, not by being reclassified as an act one was permitted to perform.

וְאַף דַּעֲדַיִין חַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה לִבּוֹ שָׁבוּר בְּיוֹתֵר וּמִתְקָרֵב בְּיוֹתֵר, וְכָל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְתַקֵּן גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי״ וְגוֹמֵר

And even though his sin is still before him, through this his heart is even more broken and he draws even closer, so much so that he merits to rectify even the root, as it is said (Tehillim 51:7): “Behold, I was shaped in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me”.423Expanded source note: Gemara, Midrash, meforshim, and R' Tzadok's root-language: Niddah 31b:2 cites Tehillim 51:7, 'Behold, in iniquity was I formed,' in its discussion of conception close to the anticipated menstrual period; Rashi explains avon as proximity to the prohibition of niddah. The classical commentators also read the verse more broadly as a statement about embodied human nature. Ibn Ezra says that desire is implanted in the heart from birth. Radak compares conception to a seed whose natural qualities continue in its fruit: sexual desire belongs to the constitution from which a person is formed, although the righteous person must master it. Malbim distinguishes avon, distortion of judgment rooted in material limitation, from chatas, the pull of desire inherited through embodied conception. Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 offers the Midrashic layer developed in the next se'if: even the most pious conception contains some trace of self-directed pleasure; David contrasts his parents' human intention with Hashem's gathering of every drop into life. R' Tzadok does not use the verse to accuse David's parents of an ordinary transgression. He identifies the 'root' as the primordial admixture of self-interest and the serpent's taint within otherwise permitted and even mitzvah-directed human life. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 147 develops the same account of Yishai and the residue of primordial shame. Se'if 7 states the endpoint before Se'if 8 explains it: David's broken-hearted teshuvah reaches backward from the visible deed to heal the inherited orientation from which desire arises, so that even the root becomes a source of nearness and truth.
וְיִיחֵס עָוֹן מֵזִיד עַל הָאָב יִשַׁי שֶׁמֵּת בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וְלֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם כְּלָל
And he attributed willful iniquity [avon] to his father Yishai, who died [only] through the counsel of the serpent (etyo shel nachash, Shabbos 55b) and never sinned at all,
רַק מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּעָוֹן מָלֵא דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד וְכוּלֵיהּ, מַה שֶׁכִּוֵּון לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ

save for that which the Sages of blessed memory expounded on “in full iniquity” (Vayikra Rabbah 14:5), that even the pious [cannot escape some trace of sin], namely that he intended for his own personal pleasure;
דְּזֶה בָּא עַל יְדֵי עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַמְגָרֶה תַּאֲוָה בַּלֵּב, לְכַוֵּון לַהֲנָאָתוֹ לֹא לְשֵׁם מִצְוָה לְבַד כְּהַנָּחַת תְּפִלִּין

for this comes through the counsel of the serpent and the root of the evil inclination existing in the world that incites bodily desire in the heart, to intend for one's own pleasure and not solely for the sake of the mitzvah, as when donning tefillin.424Expanded source note: Gemara, Midrash, and meforshim: Shabbos 55b lists Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav as four people who died solely because death had entered the world through Adam and the serpent. The Gemara finds a Scriptural allusion specifically for Yishai. II Shmuel 17:25 calls Avigayil 'the daughter of Nachash,' although I Divrei HaYamim 2:13-16 identifies her as Yishai's daughter; Nachash is therefore read as a title for Yishai, who died only through the serpent. Rashi on II Shmuel 17:25 records precisely this explanation. Vayikra Rabbah 14:5, a discourse on conception opening from 'When a woman conceives' (Vayikra 12:2), cites Tehillim 51:7 and R' Acha's teaching that even the most pious cannot be wholly without one subtle side of avon in the human process of conception. Ibn Ezra and Radak on Tehillim 51:7 explain more generally that desire accompanies embodied human formation; Malbim distinguishes the material distortion called avon from the appetitive pull called chet. R' Tzadok combines the Gemara and Midrash without contradicting either. In the ordinary juridical sense Yishai never sinned; in the scale of inner purity appropriate to one of David's stature, the faint turn toward personal gratification can still be named 'full avon.' The phrase does not stigmatize marital intimacy or David's conception. It measures how completely even a permitted and commanded act can be directed toward Hashem alone, while preserving the Gemara's unequivocal testimony to Yishai's righteousness.,425Expanded source note: Directing permitted enjoyment toward Heaven: Berachos 63a calls “In all your ways know Him” (Mishlei 3:6) a brief passage on which all the fundamentals of Torah depend, and Rava applies it even to situations bordering on transgression. Avos 2:12 states, “All your deeds should be for the sake of Heaven.” Rambam, Hilchos De'os 3:2-3, applies this principle specifically to eating, drinking, marital relations, and procreation: these acts are not to be pursued merely for pleasure, but as part of health, continuity, and the service of Hashem; he adds that one should hope to bring forth a child who will become wise and great in Israel. Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 231, codifies this all-embracing avodah. R' Tzadok's comparison to laying tefillin does not imply that bodily pleasure is intrinsically forbidden. It measures whether the self experiences the act as an isolated gratification or as a transparent fulfillment of the mitzvah. In Yishai's case the deed remained wholly a mitzvah; only the nearly imperceptible inward turn toward self-enjoyment is called avon relative to his extraordinary purity.

items.h: The theme: The inner blemish in procreation exists solely in thought and desire, not in the physical act itself, which is a great mitzvah bringing a precious soul into the world. Such an inward blemish is called avon [iniquity] written with a full vav (עָווֹן), the letter of truth, for in the supernal realm the longing of the bestower (mashpia) to the receiver (mushpa) is pure truth, likened in Shir HaShirim to the holy love between Hashem and Knesses Yisrael.

p: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא בַּלֵּב בִּלְבַד וְאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם דָּבָר בְּפֹעַל, דַּהֲרֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּפֹעַל לְהָבִיא נֶפֶשׁ יְקָרָה דְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם לָעוֹלָם הוּא מִצְוָה גְּדוֹלָה וְאֵין בָּהּ שׁוּם חֵטְא כְּלָל שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ תִּיקּוּן

And this matter exists in the heart alone, with nothing of it in physical action, for the actual deed of bringing the precious soul of David HaMelech, peace be upon him, into the world is a great mitzvah, bearing no sin whatsoever that would require rectification;
וְכַוָּונַת הַלֵּב לַהֲנָאָתוֹ אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה דְּנָחָשׁ הַקַּדְמוֹנִי שֶׁיּוֹשֵׁב עַל שְׁנֵי מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב

and the heart’s intention for personal pleasure stems solely from the “leaven in the dough” of the primordial serpent, which sits at the two entrances of the heart (Berachos 61a).426Expanded source note: The yetzer as leaven and as a force between the heart's entrances: Berachos 17a preserves the prayer of the Sages, 'Our will is to perform Your will; what prevents us? The leaven in the dough and subjection to the kingdoms.' Rashi identifies the leaven with the yetzer hara: as a small amount ferments and swells an entire dough, a subtle self-centered impulse can expand within an otherwise good act. Berachos 61a adds Rava's image that the yetzer hara resembles a fly sitting between the two entrances of the heart, alongside the verse 'A wise man's heart is to his right and a fool's heart to his left' (Koheles 10:2). Maharsha reads the imagery as describing an impulse with no independent substance, seeking entry and movement between the heart's powers. The later kabbalistic-mussar tradition maps the right chamber to the good inclination and the left to the animal or evil inclination; Tanya, chapter 9, is a classic formulation. R' Tzadok calls this same residue the primordial serpent because he is tracing it back to the loss of transparent, unashamed mitzvah-consciousness after Adam's sin. The point is subtler than labeling pleasure itself evil. The act may remain a complete mitzvah, while the 'fly' or 'leaven' introduces a private claim - that the self, rather than Hashem's will, is the act's center. David's rectification uncovers the holy root of desire and resubordinates its pleasure to the mitzvah, which is why the following paragraphs can call the act true from its beginning even while refining its intention.
וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא ״עָווֹן״ שֶׁיִּמָּחֶה לְגַמְרֵי וְאֵינֶנּוּ, וְלֹא נַעֲשָׂה מִמֶּנּוּ חֵטְא וְשׁוֹגֵג מִקּוֹדֶם
And this matter is termed an avon [iniquity] that is erased completely and is no more, from which no inadvertent sin was previously produced;
גַּם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכֻיּוֹת אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דַּהֲרֵי גַּם מִתְּחִלָּתוֹ זְכוּת הוּא
nor does it apply that it should turn into merits following repentance, for from its very inception it was already a merit.
וַאֲפִילּוּ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרְפָהּ לְמַעֲשֶׂה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה דְּאֵיזֶה חֵטְא כְּלָל

And even an evil thought the Holy One, blessed be He, does not combine with action in the case of an Israelite (Kiddushin 40a), how much more so in this case, which is not an evil thought of any sin at all;427Expanded source note: Thought and deed in the Gemara and halachic-moral tradition: Kiddushin 40a contrasts good and evil intention. Hashem joins a good thought to the deed - and, when circumstances prevent the intended mitzvah, credits the intention - but ordinarily does not join an evil thought to an act for punishment, based on Tehillim 66:18, 'Had I regarded iniquity in my heart, Hashem would not hear.' The sugya itself limits the rule: idolatrous thought is treated exceptionally, and a settled intention repeatedly pursued may be punished when it reveals a formed rebellious disposition. Thus the statement is not permission to cultivate improper fantasies; it distinguishes inward temptation from a completed transgression. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 4:4, accordingly includes sinful thoughts and separation from them among matters requiring teshuvah, while the juridical equation of thought and deed remains limited. R' Tzadok uses the kal vachomer carefully. Yishai's intent was not an evil plan at all: the marital act was permitted, life-giving, and a mitzvah, and the trace of personal enjoyment was stirred by the universal se'or she-ba-isah rather than chosen as rebellion. Therefore it never became a shogeg that must later be converted into merit. The mitzvah was merit from the outset; only a degree of inward opacity, measured against Yishai's extraordinary closeness, needed to be erased. This preserves both moral responsibility for chosen thought and the se'if's central distinction between an act's halachic status and the purity of its innermost motive.
רַק לְגַבֵּי סְבִיבָיו כְּיִשַׁי זֶה לְעָווֹן מָלֵא
it is only relative to those [exceedingly holy ones] around Him, like Yishai, that this is reckoned as a “full avon” [spelled plene with a vav,
עָווֹן]. וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִיזַ״ל דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנּוֹסַף אוֹת מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם הַהֲוָיָ״ה יֵשׁ בּוֹ תּוֹסֶפֶת מַעֲלָה וּקְדוּשָׁה
And it is known from the Arizal that wherever a letter of the Name Havayah is added, there is in it an augmentation of spiritual elevation and sanctity,
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אוֹת וָא״ו שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא (בַּזֹּהַר רֵישׁ וַיִּקְרָא)

and all the more so the letter vav, which is the sign of Truth, as stated (in the Zohar, start of Vayikra 2a).428Expanded source note: Textual and Zoharic clarification: The fuller spelling of avon contains an added vav. At the beginning of Zohar III, Vayikra 2a, the discussion of sacred letters expounds Yehoshua 2:12, 'Give me a sign of truth,' and states explicitly that vav is the ot emes, the 'letter of truth.' The next passage maps 'deepen the request' (Yeshayah 7:11) to the final heh of the Divine Name and 'raise it high' to yod, the head of the Name. Accordingly, the expected reading in R' Tzadok's phrase is vav - the letter added in the plene spelling and the letter the cited Zohar calls truth. A printed or OCR reading yod conflates two adjacent statements in the Zohar: vav is called the sign of truth, while yod is the highest, first letter of the Name. The Arizal's broader letter-symbolism treats the addition of a letter from the Divine Name as an elevation in identity; familiar Biblical precedents are the heh added to Avram and Sarai (Bereishis 17:5, 15) and the yod added to Hoshea to form Yehoshua (Sotah 34b; Rashi to Bamidbar 13:16). R' Tzadok is using that symbolism to read be-avon malei: what looks like an intensified avon secretly contains the vav of truth. The added letter does not turn a prohibited deed into holiness. It reveals that this particular act was already a mitzvah, and that the apparent defect lay only in a concealing admixture of self-interest. Once that covering is removed, the life-giving deed displays the Divine truth that was present within it all along.
וְזֶהוּ ״עָווֹן״ מָלֵא, דַּאֲפִילּוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ מִי שֶׁדָּבוּק בָּאֱמֶת לְגַמְרֵי
And this is [the meaning of] avon spelled fully: that even [a trace of bodily pleasure touches] one who cleaves to Truth completely;
וְזֶהוּ דַּרְגָּא דְּיַעֲקֹב דְּלָא מֵת, כִּי הַמִּיתָה הִיא מִצַּד הַשֶּׁקֶר שֶׁהוּא עַד אַרְגִּיעָה וְאֵין לוֹ קִיּוּם
and this is the rung of Yaakov, who “did not die” (Taanis 5b), for death stems from falsehood, which endures only for a moment and has no permanence (Mishlei 12:19),
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא כָּזָב, רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר דָּבָר הַפּוֹסֵק, וְהוּא הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁנִּקְרָאת לֶחֶם שֶׁקֶר

wherefore it is termed kazav [deceit], meaning a transient, ceasing thing, which is the desire called “bread of falsehood” (Mishlei 23:3);429Expanded source note: Kazav as something that fails and ceases: Mishlei 12:19 contrasts permanence and transience: “The lip of truth is established forever, but a lying tongue is only for a moment.” R' Tzadok gives the precise linguistic formulation in Pri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos 7:11: “Falsehood has no legs or endurance; the meaning of kazav is a thing that stops,” and he continues that the affairs of this world have only temporary existence unless they are joined to the enduring root. This supplies the background to the present sentence. Falsehood is not merely an inaccurate statement; it is an experience cut off from its source and therefore incapable of lasting. Yaakov, whose attribute is emes (Michah 7:20), represents the opposite movement: finite life and action become enduring when attached to Hashem's will. R' Tzadok therefore links “Yaakov did not die” with the permanence of truth and reads the serpent's self-enclosed desire as a kazav precisely because its pleasure immediately expires.,430Expanded source note: “Bread of falsehood”: the phrase is Mishlei 20:17, “Bread of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth will be filled with gravel.” Rashi reads it as the momentary sweetness of forbidden intimacy; Metzudas David and the straightforward sense include benefit acquired through deceit. Malbim broadens the image: gain obtained without rightful labor, and even false beliefs fed to the soul, may initially taste sweet but ultimately become gravel and spiritual death. R' Tzadok uses the verse at the level of inward motive. Pleasure detached from the lasting purpose of a mitzvah promises satisfaction yet cannot endure, and is therefore “bread of falsehood.” This does not classify every pleasure as false. The following paragraphs uncover a holy, life-giving root within desire; what must be removed is the concealing claim that private gratification is the act's final purpose.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד

whereas “the lip of truth shall be established forever” (Mishlei 12:19).431Expanded source note: Yaakov, truth, and enduring life: Taanis 5b records R' Yochanan's statement, 'Yaakov Avinu did not die.' When challenged by the Torah's account of embalming, mourning, and burial, he derives the teaching from Yirmiyah 30:10, which links Yaakov with his seed: just as his descendants are alive, he is alive. Rashi to Bereishis 49:33 notes that the Torah says Yaakov expired but does not use the word death. Ramban there explains that the souls of the righteous are bound in the bond of life and may retain a distinctive attachment to their purified spiritual garment; he does not deny the narrative of burial. The attribute behind this endurance is already assigned to Yaakov in Michah 7:20, 'You will give truth to Yaakov.' Mishlei 12:19 contrasts that permanence with falsehood: the lip of truth is established forever, whereas a lying tongue lasts only for a moment. R' Tzadok reads mortality spiritually as the end of what is false and self-enclosed. Taavah called 'bread of falsehood' promises a satisfaction that immediately ceases; emes joins a finite act to Hashem's enduring will and to future generations. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 147 makes Yaakov's freedom from the serpent's shame the paradigm for this rectification. Thus 'Yaakov did not die' is not merely a claim about biological continuance. It explains why an act wholly directed to building the covenantal seed participates in lasting truth, and why Se'if 8 can uncover an immortal, holy root beneath a desire that the serpent had clothed in transience and embarrassment.
וְעָווֹן זֶה שֶׁנֶּחְשַׁב לוֹ לְיִשַׁי לְפִי גְּדוּלָּתוֹ לְעָווֹן, נִתְוַוסַּף בּוֹ אוֹת הָאֱמֶת
And this avon, which was reckoned against Yishai solely according to his supreme stature as an iniquity, had added to it the letter of Truth [the vav];
כִּי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מִלְּבַד מִצְוַת עוֹנָה בְּעָלְמָא וּמִצְוַת ״לָעֶרֶב אַל תַּנַּח יָדֶךָ״ כְּשֶׁהִיא בַּת בָּנִים וּלְהוֹלִיד אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁקִּיֵּים פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה דְּיֵשׁ מִצְוָה לְכָל אָדָם

for the physical act, besides fulfilling the general mitzvah of conjugal duty (onah) and the precept “in the evening withhold not your hand” (Koheles 11:6) when she is capable of childbearing, to father children even after fulfilling procreation, which is a mitzvah incumbent upon every man (Yevamos 62b),432Expanded source note: Halachic background to Yishai's act: The Torah separately recognizes procreation and onah. 'Be fruitful and multiply' (Bereishis 1:28) obligates the man in p'ru u'rvu, while Shemos 21:10 establishes the husband's continuing conjugal obligation. Even after the minimum mitzvah of procreation has been fulfilled, R' Yehoshua teaches in Yevamos 62b from Koheles 11:6, 'In the morning sow your seed, and in the evening do not rest your hand,' that one should continue to build a family. Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 15:16, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 1:8, codify this continuing rabbinic duty. Onah is independently binding according to the couple's circumstances (Mishnah Kesubos 5:6; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 14:1; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 76), so marital union is not reduced to biological reproduction. Rambam, Hilchos De'os 3:2-3 and 5:4, adds the inward discipline: bodily acts should be directed toward knowing and serving Hashem, and marital life should combine sanctity, mutual willingness, and joy. R' Tzadok therefore identifies several objective layers of mitzvah in Yishai's deed - onah, continued family-building, and the actual bringing of a soul into the world - before the unique result is even considered. The birth of David, the future rectifier of Adam's failure and progenitor of Mashiach, magnifies the deed's truth but does not create its permissibility retroactively. This is why the trace of self-interest cannot turn the act into sin: halachically and teleologically it is mitzvah, while the se'if examines only the refinement of intent appropriate to Yishai's exceptional spiritual level.
בְּלֵידַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַמְתַקֵּן הַכֹּל עַד דִּיבוּקַּשׁ עָווֹן וְאֵינֶנּוּ וִיבוּלַּע הַמָּוֶת, כִּי יִתְגַּלֶּה הָאֱמֶת הַקַּיָּים לָעַד

in the birth of David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who rectifies everything until iniquity will be sought and be no more, and death will be swallowed up forever (Yeshayah 25:8), when the eternal Truth will be fully revealed,433Expanded source note: David as rectifier of Adam's mortality: Bamidbar Rabbah 14:12 teaches that Adam, who was destined to live one thousand years, gave seventy years of his life to David ben Yishai and therefore lived nine hundred and thirty. The kabbalistic tradition, cited by Recanati on the Torah, Bereishis 220, treats David's seventy years as life received from Adam for the work of completing the damaged human order. This provides the background to R' Tzadok's description of David as “the one who rectifies everything.” David's teshuvah and the Davidic future are bound to the reversal of Adam's legacy of sin and death, culminating in “death will be swallowed up forever” (Yeshayah 25:8). In the present se'if, the tikkun begins already in David's conception: the birth of the soul that will repair Adamic mortality reveals Yishai's act as a life-giving pe'ulas emes, while the serpent's minute husk of self-interest is what falls away.,434Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's larger framework: Tehillim 51:7, 'Behold, in iniquity was I formed,' is read here not as an accusation that Yishai committed an ordinary transgression, but as a disclosure of the primordial mixture that can remain even within a mitzvah. Shabbos 55b explicitly numbers Yishai among the four who died only be-etyo shel nachash, through the serpent's counsel and the mortality introduced through Adam, not through a sin of their own. Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 nevertheless applies the plene phrase be-avon even to the most pious, because embodied conception can contain a minute element of self-directed pleasure. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 147 supplies the closest parallel: the shame that entered after the serpent is evidence that human desire had ceased to be experienced as a transparent mitzvah, whereas Yaakov's rectification of that distortion belongs to the mystery that 'Yaakov did not die.' Pri Tzadik, Miketz 1, develops the same chain explicitly: Yishai's freedom from personal sin, the Midrash's be-avon malei, the serpent's implantation of self-enjoyment, and the work of uprooting that residue through Torah. This is a spiritual genealogy, not inherited halachic guilt. The act is judged as Yishai's mitzvah and David's birth as an immense good; only the nearly invisible inward admixture is called avon relative to Yishai's exceptional level. Se'if 8 therefore explains the 'root' named at the end of Se'if 7: David's teshuvah reaches beneath his visible deed to clarify the ancestral human drive itself, revealing that its ultimate source is holy life-giving desire rather than sin.
וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא פְּעוּלַּת אֱמֶת הֵפֶךְ הֶעָוֹן שֶׁהוּא שֶׁקֶר, לְהַגִּיד כִּי גַּם עָווֹן זֶה דָּבוּק בֶּאֱמֶת

it was certainly nothing other than an act of pure Truth, the very antithesis of iniquity which is falsehood, declaring that even this avon is bound to absolute Truth.435Expanded source note: Prophetic horizon and meforshim: Yirmiyah 50:20 speaks of the final restoration after the fall of Babylon: 'The iniquity of Israel will be sought and there will be none, and the sins of Yehudah will not be found, for I will forgive those whom I leave as a remnant.' Radak explains that sincere return and Divine forgiveness leave the accuser with no discoverable charge; the verse is not denial that sin once occurred but a promise of complete removal. Yeshayah 25:8, in a prophecy of Hashem's universal banquet and removal of disgrace, says that He will 'swallow up death forever' and wipe tears from every face. Pesachim 68a cites this verse as proof that the final giving of life is not followed by another death. The classical tradition contains different accounts of the stages of resurrection and the World to Come; R' Tzadok's point here is the shared symbolic axis: sin, falsehood, and death are temporary, whereas truth and the life rooted in Hashem endure. David is placed at that axis because his teshuvah repairs Adam's introduction of death and his royal seed leads toward Mashiach. The 'avon' surrounding Yishai's intention is therefore exposed as a covering, not the deed's essence. When the covering is removed, no independent sin remains to be found, and the birth of the one who will help rectify death is seen as pe'ulas emes, a deed of truth. This does not mean ordinary offenses disappear without teshuvah; it describes the completed clarification produced by teshuvah, in which the false admixture is erased and the holy act that it obscured stands revealed.
כִּי שֹׁרֶשׁ הַתַּאֲוָה וְהַחֵשֶׁק שֶׁל הַמַּשְׁפִּיעַ לַמּוּשְׁפָּע הוּא בְּעֶלְיוֹנֵי עֶלְיוֹנִים
For the supernal root of the desire and longing of the bestower [mashpia] toward the recipient [mushpa] originates in the highest transcendent realms,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהִמְשִׁיל בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לִכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּחָשׁוּק לַחֲשׁוּקָתוֹ מַמָּשׁ

just as Shir HaShirim allegorizes the love of the Blessed Name for the Congregation of Israel to that of a passionate lover for his beloved.436Expanded source note: Shir HaShirim as the holy root of desire: The rabbinic reading does not treat the Song's language of longing as accidental. R' Akiva declares in Yadayim 3:5 that all the Writings are holy and Shir HaShirim is the Holy of Holies. Rashi's introduction reads it as a sustained parable of a beloved wife who remembers her youthful closeness to her husband while in separation - Knesses Yisrael remembering and seeking Hashem. Shir HaShirim Rabbah consistently identifies the lovers with Hashem and Israel; for example, at 6:1 the nations question Israel about her Beloved, and Israel answers that their mutual cleaving cannot be severed. The Zohar deepens this imagery into the union of the Holy One and the Shechinah, the supernal source from which blessing and souls flow. R' Tzadok's terms mashpia and mushpa belong to that kabbalistic grammar: the giver's urge to bestow and the recipient's readiness to receive originate in a Divine pattern of relationship. He is not collapsing Divine love into physical appetite or declaring every desire holy as experienced. He distinguishes root from distortion. At its root, desire is the movement by which life and blessing pass from giver to receiver; the serpent's residue bends that movement inward toward isolated gratification and shame. The work of teshuvah is therefore not annihilation of the life-force but clarification of it. In Yishai's begetting of David, the future fruit reveals the source: the act participates in the highest yearning to give life, while its minute self-regarding husk can be removed. This prepares Se'if 9, where even the father's pleasure is shown to possess a side of truth because a son brings merit and continuity to his father.

items.h: The theme: The true, unblemished desire of Yaakov Avinu was directed purely toward raising offspring. Even in the mixture of bodily pleasure, a father's joy in bearing righteous progeny contains a dimension of genuine Truth (bara mezakeh aba). Through David HaMelech—the rectifier of the sin of Adam and the serpent's counsel—his father Yishai was retroactively vindicated, revealing that his pleasure was aligned with Truth, attached to the holy letter vav. Yet to the outer husk (kelipah) and relative to Yishai's transcendent holiness, this residue of self-gratification was accounted as deliberate iniquity (avon), whereas in David's mother it was reckoned merely an inadvertent sin (chet). David's entire apparent fall with Bas Sheva stemmed solely from this unrectified ancestral root in human conception—an act of taking what was destined "unripe" in privacy rather than in sanctity before all—which he later attributed to his ancestral origin.

p: וְעִיקַּר חֵשֶׁק הָאֱמֶת דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁאָמַר ״הָבָה״ וְגוֹמֵר, לְהַעֲמִיד תּוֹלָדוֹת נִתְכַּוֵּון וְלֹא הָיָה לוֹ שׁוּם מַחֲשָׁבָה וְכַוָּונָה אַחֶרֶת כְּלָל

And the essential yearning of Truth of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who said "Give [me my wife]" (Bereishis 29:21), was intended solely to raise up offspring, and he possessed no other thought or intention at all;437Expanded source note: Midrash, Rashi, Ramban, and R' Tzadok: Bereishis 29:21 records Yaakov's demand to Lavan, 'Give me my wife, for my days are fulfilled, that I may come to her.' Bereishis Rabbah 70:18 asks how even an undisciplined person could speak so openly. R' Aivu answers that Yaakov had been told that he would establish the twelve tribes; he was already eighty-four, and his words meant that he must begin producing those generations. Rashi incorporates both the chronological reading - the period associated with his mother's instruction and his service had reached its completion - and the Midrash's inward reading: 'that I may come to her' was said leholid toldos, to beget offspring. Ramban preserves the plain contractual setting. Yaakov was demanding the marriage for which he had served; 'I will come to her' means that he would marry her and continue to complete whatever service remained, not take her and abandon Lavan. The Midrash and peshat therefore address different questions: the latter explains the legal-temporal claim, while the former explains the exceptional candor of a tzaddik. Pri Tzadik, Bereishis 8, reads the Midrash as a restoration of Adam before the serpent: Yaakov did not experience the bodily self-enjoyment that produced shame after the sin, but knew the act only as bringing forth life. Pri Tzadik, Rosh Hashanah 7, Vayigash 11, and Beha'aloscha 6 repeat the same association among Yaakov's pure intention, 'they were not ashamed' (Bereishis 2:25), and 'Yaakov Avinu did not die' (Taanis 5b). This does not make immodest speech a general model. R' Tzadok treats Yaakov's wording as evidence possible only at his unique rung: because no false private claim was present, there was nothing for shame to conceal. The verse thus establishes the standard against which Yishai's nearly imperceptible admixture is measured.
וְעֵירְבּוּב תַּאֲוַת שֶׁקֶר דִּלְהַנָאָתוֹ, עִם עַצְמוֹ יֵשׁ בָּהּ צַד אֱמֶת, כִּי יֵשׁ בְּהוֹלָדַת בָּנִים הֲנָאָה לָאָב מִצַּד הָאֱמֶת דְּ״בָּרָא מְזַכֶּה אַבָּא״

and even the intermingling of the false desire for personal pleasure contains within itself an aspect of Truth, for in the begetting of children there is true satisfaction for the father from the side of Truth, as "a son brings merit to his father" (Sanhedrin 104a).438Expanded source note: 'A son brings merit to his father' in its Talmudic setting: Sanhedrin 104a is discussing the kings excluded from the World to Come. Amon is omitted in honor of his righteous son Yoshiyahu; when the Gemara asks why Menasheh is not likewise spared by the merit of his father Chizkiyahu, it answers: bara mezakeh abba, but abba lo mezakeh bara. A son's righteousness can count for the father, whereas a father's righteousness does not automatically rescue a corrupt son. The Gemara cites Devarim 32:39 to teach that Avraham does not simply save Yishmael and Yitzchak does not simply save Esav. Rashi's underlying logic is causal: the father has a share in the righteous child he raised. Maharsha sharpens it by observing that even some wicked fathers do not want their children to follow their path and may rebuke and train them toward goodness; the son's virtue therefore reveals a merit in the father that was not visible in the father's own conduct. Sotah 10b is not a second primary source for the phrase. Tosafos there cites Sanhedrin 104a while asking how David's prayer could raise Avshalom, a case that seems to run in the opposite direction, and offers qualifications concerning punishment already borne and the power of a father's prayer. Later halachic custom draws on the same principle to explain the special force of a child's Torah, mitzvos, and Kaddish for a parent. R' Tzadok uses the maxim more radically but still causally. David does not transfer an unrelated store of merit to Yishai. David is the fruit of Yishai's own life-giving act, and the fruit clarifies the root: the pleasure of producing a child capable of holiness, continuity, and rectification is itself a true paternal good. The klipah is the father's isolated self-enjoyment; bara mezakeh abba reveals that parent and child were never spiritually isolated in the first place.
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא הַמְתַקֵּן לְחֵטְא אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, זִכָּה לְאָבִיו בְּיִחוּד, שֶׁנִּתְבָּרֵר דְּגַם הֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ מִזֶּה הוּא הֲנָאַת אֱמֶת

And David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who is the rectifier of the sin of Adam HaRishon and the counsel of the serpent (etyo shel nachash), specifically brought merit to his father, clarifying that even his personal pleasure from this was a pleasure of Truth;
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינָהּ אוֹתָהּ הֲנָאַת הֶבֶל וְכוֹזֶבֶת שֶׁל דִּמְיוֹן הַיֵּצֶר הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ הַמְּכוּנָה בְּשֵׁם עָוֹן, רַק הַכֹּל נִטְפָּל לְאוֹת הַוָּא״ו שֶׁבּוֹ שֶׁהוּא אוֹת אֱמֶת

rather, it was not that futile and deceptive gratification born of the yetzer's imagination drawn from the serpent's counsel which is termed avon [iniquity], but was entirely subordinated to the letter vav within it, which is the letter of Truth.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם סוֹף סוֹף מִצַּד הַקְּלִיפָּה הַמַּקֶּפֶת וּמְכַסָּה לַפְּרִי וּמַעֲלִימָתוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לְעָוֹן, וּכְפִי גּוֹדֶל מַעֲלַת וּקְדוּשַׁת יִשַׁי נֶחְשַׁב זֶה לְעָוֹן מֵזִיד

Yet nevertheless, ultimately, from the perspective of the outer husk [kelipah] that surrounds, covers, and conceals the fruit, it was accounted as an avon, and according to the immense stature and sanctity of Yishai, this was reckoned as a deliberate iniquity.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּאִמּוֹ נֶחְשָׁב רַק לְחֵטְא, וְגַם דְּאֶצְלָהּ אֵין מַעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה בְּפֹעַל כָּל כָּךְ, דְּנָשִׁים אֵין מְצֻוּוֹת עַל פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה, רַק דְּהַנִּטְפָּל לְעוֹשֵׂי מִצְוָה כְּעוֹשֶׂה וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לָהּ לִהְיוֹת עֲדִיפָא מֵהָעוֹשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ

In contrast, with his mother it was reckoned only as an inadvertent sin [chet], and also because on her part there was not so much an actual mitzvah-action in practice, for women are not commanded in procreation (Yevamos 65b), but are merely considered like the performer under the principle that "one who assists those who perform a mitzvah is like one who performs it" (Menachos 93b), and she cannot possess higher status than the performer himself.439Expanded source note: Halachic and aggadic background: The Mishnah and Gemara in Yevamos 65b record the dispute between the Sages and R' Yochanan ben Beroka. The Sages exempt a woman from the individually defined command of p'ru u'rvu, deriving the obligation from the language of conquest in Bereishis 1:28 and from the command addressed in the singular to Yaakov in Bereishis 35:11. The halachah follows the Sages; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 15:2, and Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 1:13, rule that the man is commanded and the woman is not. Exemption is not a declaration that motherhood or her participation is spiritually neutral. The same sugya recognizes her independent interest in children, and the wider halachic tradition treats building and settling the world as an objective good in which both spouses participate. R' Tzadok explains her reward through Makkos 5b. There R' Akiva learns from the Torah's treatment of an additional witness who joins transgressors: if one attached to evildoers is punished with them, all the more does Hashem reward one attached to performers of a mitzvah as a performer. Thus nitpal le'osei mitzvah does not create the man's formal obligation in the woman; it describes her genuine share in the mitzvah-act and its reward. Nazir 23b supplies the comparison to aveirah lishmah. The sugya first states that an aveirah for Heaven is greater than a mitzvah not for its own sake, but after challenging this from the value of doing mitzvos even shelo lishmah, it refines the claim: Yael's aveirah lishmah is comparable to a mitzvah shelo lishmah. Rashi explains lishmah as for the sake of a mitzvah; Tosafos distinguish constructive shelo lishmah, which can mature into lishmah, from self-serving Torah used to attack others. R' Tzadok's kal vachomer is therefore conceptual, not permission to violate halachah. If even an objectively prohibited act performed for a uniquely saving heavenly purpose can possess spiritual value, then certainly a permitted marital act by the woman who enables her husband's mitzvah can become complete zechus when directed to Heaven. His terms avon and chatas measure degrees of inward alignment in this passage; they do not invent separate sacrificial liabilities or diminish the woman's essential role in bringing David into the world.

וְגַם תִּיקּוּנָהּ כְּתִיקּוּן הַחֵטְא שֶׁמִּתְהַפֵּךְ לִזְכוּת, כִּי כְּשֶׁכַּוָּונָתָהּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם אָז נֶחְשָׁב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לְמִצְוָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ גְּדוֹלָה, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן מַעֲשֶׂה דְּנִטְפָּל לְמִצְוָה כְּשֶׁהִיא לִשְׁמָהּ

And furthermore, her rectification is like the rectification of a sin which turns into a merit, for when her intention was for the sake of Heaven, the deed is considered a mitzvah; for behold, even a transgression for its own sake is great (Nazir 23b), all the more so an action that assists a mitzvah when performed for its own sake.

אֲבָל בְּכַוָּונָה לַהֲנָאָתָהּ אֵין גּוּף הַמַּעֲשֶׂה עַצְמָהּ מִצְוָה אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַנִּטְפָּל לָעוֹשֶׂה, וְעַל יְדֵי הַתִּיקּוּן דְּ״בָּרָא מְזַכֶּה לְשָׁרְשׁוֹ בָּאָבוֹת״ נַעֲשָׂה אֵצֶל אִמּוֹ לִזְכוּת גָּמוּר

But with an intent for personal pleasure, the bodily act itself is not a mitzvah except from the aspect of assisting the performer; and through the rectification wherein "a son brings merit to his ancestral root," it became for his mother a complete merit.

וְכָל חֵטְא דָּוִד הָיָה רַק מִצַּד זֶה, כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה, וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה אֶלָּא עַל חֵטְא, וּמֵהֵיכָן יָבוֹא לוֹ חֵטְא כֵּיוָן דִּכְבָר לִבּוֹ חָלָל

And David's entire "sin" stemmed solely from this side: since he was not personally suited for such an act except to teach the path of teshuvah (Avodah Zarah 4b), and repentance applies only over a sin, from where then could sin come upon him seeing that his heart was already hollow [of the yetzer hara] (Bava Basra 17a)?440Expanded source note: 'My heart is a void within me' in peshat, Chazal, Kabbalah, and R' Tzadok: Tehillim 109:22 belongs to David's prayer as a persecuted, impoverished man. Metzudas David reads chalal in its plain sense: his heart has become stricken and emptied by fear and grief; Malbim similarly connects it to the broken heart described earlier in the verse. Chazal deliberately reread the image as an account of inner mastery. Berachos 61b teaches that tzaddikim are judged by the yetzer tov and cites this verse; Rashi explains that David's yetzer hara was like something dead within him. Bava Basra 17a preserves an opinion that David too was among those over whom the yetzer hara did not rule, again deriving it from lev chalal. The Yerushalmi, Berachos 9:5, and the early kabbalistic Sefer HaBahir make the image more active: David could not make peace with the evil inclination, so he slew it in his heart; the Bahir attributes the victory to his uninterrupted attachment to Torah. R' Tzadok frequently cites this cluster. Divrei Sofrim section 28 says that David's heart was entirely clean of base appetite and that his trial with Bat-Sheva was therefore a test of a complete vessel, while Tzidkas HaTzadik section 248 insists that the power of cheshek itself remains the human being's greatness. 'Dead' does not mean that David ceased to possess will, passion, or freedom. It means that the yetzer no longer ruled as an autonomous inner claimant. That creates the se'if's problem: if David's own heart had already been emptied of such false appetite, the point of vulnerability had to lie deeper, in the inherited human root of his formation. His failure then served the purpose described earlier in the volume - to open and demonstrate the road of teshuvah from precisely that root.
וְעַל כֵּן הוּא רַק מִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ יְצִירָתוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו עַל יְדֵי כַּוָּונַת הֲנָאָה לְגַרְמֵיהּ, דַּעֲדַיִין לֹא תִּיקֵּן שׁוֹרֶשׁ זֶה מִקּוֹדֶם
Therefore it came only from the root of his formation from his parents through the intention of pleasure for oneself, since he had not yet rectified this root previously.
וְאַף שׁוֹרֶשׁ זֶה אֵינוֹ חֵטְא גָּמוּר, דְּגַם הוּא לֹא חָטָא בֶּאֱמֶת, וְכָל הָאוֹמֵר דָּוִד חָטָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא טוֹעֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שַׁבָּת נו עַמּוּד א)

And even this root was not an actual sin, for he too did not truly sin, and "whoever says David sinned is merely erring," as they said (Shabbos 56a);441Expanded source note: Textual clarification and the full Shabbos sugya: The subject of 'he too did not truly sin' here is David, not Yishai. The immediately following formula, 'whoever says that he sinned is merely mistaken,' is the statement of R' Shmuel bar Nachmani in the name of R' Yonasan in Shabbos 56a, not Shabbos 55b. The Gemara reads II Shmuel 12:9 with careful limits. David sought to do the evil described but did not commit the straightforward legal offenses attributed to him: Uriah was liable as one who rebelled against the king, though David should have judged him before the Sanhedrin, and David had valid marital capacity with Bat-Sheva because soldiers of the House of David wrote bills of divorce for their wives before battle. Rashi and Tosafos discuss whether those gittin operated immediately or conditionally and how Bat-Sheva's status was resolved. Malbim on II Shmuel 11:3 uses the same halachic framework, arguing that otherwise Bat-Sheva would have remained forbidden to David, their child would have had an invalid status, and David's later marriage and the choice of Shlomo could not stand. The sugya is not saying that David acted flawlessly. It preserves Nasan's rebuke, David's confession, and the punishments in II Shmuel 12, while relocating the wrong from formal adultery and unlawful execution to intention, procedure, scandal, and abuse of royal haste. Classical meforshim are not entirely uniform: Abarbanel reads the narrative's moral charges more literally, whereas Rashi, Tosafos, and Malbim develop the Talmudic defense. R' Tzadok consciously adopts the Gemara's strongest defense because his question is the origin of teshuvah in a heart already called chalal. If the visible deed were ordinary adultery, no ancestral theory would be required. By removing that legal description while retaining real fault, Shabbos 56a allows him to identify the remaining chet as the private, premature mode of taking what should have been received openly, responsibly, and in its Divinely appointed time.
וְגַם רְאוּיָה הָיְתָה לוֹ מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְרֵאשִׁית כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קז עַמּוּד א)

and she was also destined for him from the six days of Creation, as they said (Sanhedrin 107a).442Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's framework for this se'if: The argument is not that every experienced pleasure is holy, but that the power of desire has one created root whose truth or falsehood is determined by its direction. Michah 7:20 assigns emes to Yaakov, and the Midrash and Rashi on Bereishis 29:21 make Yaakov's startlingly direct words a disclosure of wholly purposeful desire: he sought the covenantal generations, not private gratification. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 248 supplies the general rule. The ikkar of a person is the cheshek in the heart; the same force is called yetzer tov when directed to good and yetzer hara when bent away from it. Machshavos Charutz 3:3 develops Yaakov's truth through Yosef: because Yosef's form resembled his father and Yaakov was immersed in Torah, which is called truth, even Yosef's dreams and imaginative pictures proved true rather than deceptive. Se'if 9 applies that grammar to Yishai and David. Sanhedrin 104a's bara mezakeh abba means that a righteous son can disclose and add merit to the father who generated and formed him. David's life therefore reveals that the paternal pleasure surrounding his conception was not empty self-enclosure; it secretly participated in the production of a soul who would rectify Adam and establish the Davidic line. The second half then applies the same distinction to David and Bat-Sheva. Shabbos 56a removes the simple legal picture of adultery, while Sanhedrin 107a says the match itself was destined but taken as an unripe fruit. Divrei Sofrim section 28 and Pri Tzadik, Emor 14, are close parallels: David's heart was fundamentally clear of base appetite, Bat-Sheva was the woman fit for him, and the failure lay in forcing a destined truth before its proper time and form. Teshuvah does not retroactively license haste or secrecy. It separates the enduring fruit from the klipah of self-appropriation, restoring the same cheshek to Hashem's timing, public responsibility, and kiddushin.,443Expanded source note: Bat-Sheva as the destined but unripe fruit: Sanhedrin 107a places the teaching inside the account of David's requested trial.
