David asked why the liturgy names the God of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov but not the God of David; Hashem answered that the Patriarchs had withstood trials, and warned David in advance that his own test would concern a married woman. After describing the episode, the school of R' Yishmael interprets Tehillim 38:18: Bat-Sheva daughter of Eliam was fit for David, but he ate her as a pagah, an unripe fruit. Rashi explains that he forced the hour and came to the destined relationship by means of transgression. The metaphor therefore holds destiny and responsibility together. A true future does not make every present path to it true; fruit taken before ripeness is the correct fruit damaged by wrong timing. R' Tzadok develops this repeatedly in Pri Tzadik, including Vayeishev 12, Pekudei 8, Kedoshim 14, Emor 14, and Eikev 19. Divrei Sofrim section 28 adds that the object of David's desire was not foreign to his holy root - Bat-Sheva and the Davidic-Messianic seed were genuinely his future - yet acting before the appointed disclosure made the act appear and function as private appetite. In this se'if R' Tzadok gives 'unripe' a precise social and halachic shape: David did not wait until he could take her befarhesya and through kiddushin. This is not merely a preference for publicity. Open marriage would have aligned personal desire with covenant, community, and recognized responsibility; secrecy isolated the pleasure from those truths. Teshuvah ripens the fruit by returning desire to its proper relationship and time. The adjoining citation to Shabbos 56a establishes that the root and ultimate match were not sinful; Sanhedrin 107a explains why taking them prematurely was nevertheless a genuine failure that required David's confession, suffering, and lifelong teaching of return.

וַאֲכִילַת פַּגָּה הוּא לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הִמְתִּין שֶׁיִּקָּחֶנָּה בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא וּבְקִדּוּשִׁין, רַק בְּצִנְעָא כְּמִתְכַּוֵּון רַק לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ לְבַד, וְלֹא כְּבָא לִיקַּח אִשָּׁה הָרְאוּיָה וְנִגְזַר לוֹ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם

And his "eating of unripe fruit" was only because he did not wait to take her publicly and with formal betrothal, but rather in secret like one intending only for personal pleasure, and not like one coming to wed a woman destined and decreed for him from Heaven.

וְזֶה שֶׁהִתְנַצֵּל שֶׁהוּא מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ בַּתּוֹלָדָה מֵאֲבוֹתָיו, וְגַם זֶה לֹא חֵטְא גָּמוּר, רַק דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים אֵינוֹ עֲשִׂיַּית רְצוֹן הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הָאֱמֶת שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בּוֹ

And this explains why he pleaded in defense that it stemmed from the root of his conception from his parents; and even this was not a complete sin, only that in any event it was not purely the fulfillment of the will of the Blessed Name alone, which is the ultimate Truth that the Blessed Name desires.

items.h: The theme: Man’s ultimate cleansing comes through the very brokenness of recognizing his bodily baseness. Although God desires inward truth in the innermost depths, He planted the evil inclination so that through humility and brokenness—symbolized by the hyssop (ezov)—Torah’s deepest mysteries are disclosed, and the penitent ascends to an incomparable joy that exceeds even the state of the wholly righteous.

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״הֵן אֱמֶת חָפַצְתָּ בַטֻּחוֹת״, הַיְינוּ גַּם בַּמַּעֲמַקִּים הַנֶּעֱלָמִים, דְּאַף שֶׁהַמַּעֲשֵׂה מִצְוָה צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת גַּם בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה וּבְמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב

And this is what he said afterward: “Behold, You desire truth in the inward parts” (Tehillim 51:8), meaning even in the hidden depths; for although the deed is a mitzvah, [truth] must reside in thought and in the depths of the heart as well;

אֲבָל תִּיקּוּנִי דְּ״בְסָתֻם חָכְמָה תוֹדִיעֵנִי״, דְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ בָּזֶה גַּם כֵּן חָכְמָה גְּדוֹלָה מַה שֶּׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע בָּעוֹלָם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״בָּרָאתָ יֵצֶר הָרָע״

but my rectification is that “in the hidden part You make me know wisdom,” for certainly there is also great wisdom in the fact that the Blessed Name created the evil inclination in the world, as they said, “You created the evil inclination” (Bava Basra 16a).
כִּידוּעַ דְּהַחָכְמָה, וְהִיא הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא חָכְמַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, לֹא נִתְּנָה לָאָדָם אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ יֵצֶר הָרָע, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּשַׁבָּת פט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א)

As is known, wisdom—which is the Torah, the wisdom of the Blessed Name—was given to man solely because the evil inclination resides within him, as they said (in Shabbos 89a);444Expanded source note: Why the Torah was given to beings with a yetzer hara: Kiddushin 30b states the foundational pairing, 'I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its seasoning'; Torah is not merely information about the struggle but the Divinely fashioned means of redirecting it. Shabbos 89a supplies R' Tzadok's more specific proof. When the angels claimed the Torah, Moshe answered from its commandments: they have no parents, commerce, jealousy, murder, adultery, theft, or evil inclination. The Torah's descent to humanity is therefore justified precisely by the low and conflicted conditions in which its wisdom must work. This does not shift moral responsibility to the Creator. Midrash Tanchuma, Bereishis 9, records Kayin's attempted defense, 'You created the evil inclination in me,' but the narrative preserves his accountability; creation of temptation explains the arena of choice, not the choice made within it. The contrast also clarifies 'in the hidden You teach me wisdom.' Rashi on Tehillim 51:8 understands that hidden wisdom as the wisdom to confess truthfully. Radak sees it as the insight by which David recognizes that his inward will was for Hashem even though desire overcame him. Malbim says moral wisdom is planted deep in the soul and must be drawn out from beneath the covering of matter. R' Tzadok combines all three: the yetzer creates the possibility of concealment and failure, while Torah and confession draw wisdom out of that concealment and reveal the act's true root. His claim that Hashem created the yetzer is therefore neither fatalism nor a plea of innocence. It explains why a failure can become the material of deeper Torah, provided the person accepts responsibility and allows the Torah to season, rather than merely suppress, the same power of desire.
וְהוֹלֶכֶת דַּוְוקָא לִמְקוֹם נָמוּךְ וּמִי שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ שְׁפֵלָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַעֲנִית ד סוֹף עַמּוּד א), וּדְחָכְמָה מְפוֹאָר דַּוְוקָא בִּכְלִי מְכוֹעָר
and it flows specifically to a low place and to one whose spirit is humble, as they said (in Taanis 7a), and that wisdom is glorified specifically within an unsightly vessel (Nedarim 50b);
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְהִתְקָרֵב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כַּאֲשֶׁר לִבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג וְנִשְׁבָּר בְּקִרְבּוֹ, דְּאָז מְגַלִּין לוֹ סִתְרֵי תוֹרָה כִּדִתְנַן (בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק אֵין דּוֹרְשִׁין)

for through this one can draw near to the Blessed Name when his heart is anxious and broken within him, at which time they reveal to him the secrets of the Torah, as we learned (Chagigah 13a).445Expanded source note: Humility, hidden Torah, and the hyssop of purification: Taanis 7a teaches in two linked images that Torah resembles water, which leaves a high place for a low one, and water, wine, and milk, which keep best in inexpensive vessels. The Gemara illustrates the second teaching when the emperor's daughter mocks R' Yehoshua ben Chananya as splendid wisdom in an unattractive vessel; he answers that royal wine spoils when stored in gold and silver. Rashi explains that Torah endures in him more because of the humility associated with the vessel. Maharal, Netiv HaTorah 2 and Netiv HaAnavah 8, makes the point metaphysical: humility is peshitus, freedom from self-imposed bulk and limitation, and is therefore the fitting receiver of Torah's non-material intellect. Chagigah 13a applies the same qualification specifically to sod: the chapter headings of the Merkavah are transmitted only to an av beis din and, according to the stricter version, only when his heart worries within him. Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim I:34, explains this as humility, submission, and intense fear of sin joined to wisdom; Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Shevat 2, likewise connects the worried heart with fitness to receive the concealed teachings. The hyssop image has concrete Torah background. Hyssop participates in the purification of a metzora (Vayikra 14:4-7) and in the ashes and sprinkling of the red heifer (Bamidbar 19:6, 18). Rashi and Radak on Tehillim 51:9 therefore hear David asking for purification like that of a metzora or one defiled by a corpse; Rashi on Vayikra 14:4 adds the moral symbolism that one raised like a cedar must lower himself like a worm and hyssop. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, cites that explanation directly: 'Cleanse me with hyssop' means that David's own lowliness becomes the instrument of purity, in accord with Sotah 5a, 'I am with the crushed one.' R' Tzadok's novelty is that the humiliation of discovering bodily weakness is not merely punishment. When it breaks self-certainty without breaking hope, it makes the heart a low place into which Torah and even its secrets can flow.

וְזֶהוּ ״תְּחַטְּאֵנִי בְאֵזוֹב״ — הַיְינוּ שִׁפְלוּת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד הַחֵטְא, שֶׁאַחַר כָּל הַיְגִיעָה בַּתּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה כְּשֶׁמַּגִּיעַ לִידֵי נִסָּיוֹן קַל בְּתַאֲוָה וַהֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית רוֹאֶה מַעֲשָׂיו מַעֲשֵׂה בְּהֵמָה

And this is: “Purge me with hyssop [ezov], and I shall be clean” (Tehillim 51:9)—namely, the humility drawn from the sin, where after all his toil in Torah and divine service, when he encounters a slight trial in bodily desire and pleasure, he sees his actions as the actions of a beast;
עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁפְלוּת הַזֶּה יוּכַל לִיטָּהֵר לְגַמְרֵי וּלְהַגִּיעַ לְמַעֲלָה יוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלָה
through this humility he can become completely purified and attain an even higher rung.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״תָּגֵלְנָה עֲצָמוֹת דִּכִּיתָ״, דְּמַה שֶּׁהוּא מִצַּד תּוֹלַדְתּוֹ מַה לָּאָדָם לַעֲשׂוֹת מִזֶּה כֵּיוָן שֶׁנּוֹלַד כָּךְ, וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הוּא שֶׁיְּצָרוֹ כֵּן וַהֲרֵי זֶה כְּאִלּוּ אַתָּה דִּכִּיתָ

And as he said afterward: “Let the bones You have crushed rejoice” (51:10); for regarding that which is due to his birth, what is a man to do since he was born thus, and the Blessed Name is the One Who formed him so, so that it is as though “You have crushed” them;
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּוְוקָא יָבוֹא לִידֵי גִּילָה, כִּי יִשְׁמַע שָׂשׂוֹן וְשִׂמְחָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה דַּוְוקָא מַה שֶּׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ מִקּוֹדֶם
but precisely through this he will arrive at exultation, hearing gladness and joy specifically on account of this, which he did not possess beforehand.
וְזֶהוּ הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין שֶׁגָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר כִּי יֵשׁ שָׁם שִׂמְחָה יְתֵירָה
And this is the place where penitents stand, which is greater, because there is found an extraordinary joy;

וְכַיָּדוּעַ הַמָּשָׁל לְמִי שֶׁהָיָה בֶּן יְחִידוֹ מֵרָחוֹק בַּשִּׁבְיָה אֵיזֶה זְמַן בֵּין אוֹיְבִים וּמְצֵרִים, כְּשֶׁשָּׁב לְבֵית אָבִיו יֵשׁ שִׂמְחָה יְתֵירָה כִּפְלֵי כִפְלַיִם לְאֵין עֵרֶךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה בִּהְיוֹתוֹ בְּבֵית אָבִיו תָּמִיד וְלֹא נִפְרַד מִמֶּנּוּ כְּלָל

and as is known from the parable of one whose only son was far away in captivity for some time among enemies and oppressors: when he returns to his father's house, there is an extraordinary joy, multiplied incomparably beyond what existed when he was in his father's house continuously, never separated at all.446Expanded source note: The joy unique to teshuvah: In the plain sense of Tehillim 51:10, David asks to hear through prophecy that he has been forgiven. Radak says the message would gladden a soul pained by sin and revive bones crushed by fear of God; Metzudas David connects the crushed bones to Nasan's harsh prophetic rebuke. Malbim keeps the purification imagery of the preceding verse: after the isolation and pain of a metzora, healing produces both outward rejoicing and inward joy. Berachos 34b records R' Abbahu's teaching that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place of baalei teshuvah, while R' Chiya bar Abba in R' Yochanan's name disputes it and reserves the highest hidden reward for those who never sinned. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, codifies the first view pastorally and ethically: a penitent must not imagine himself distant; he is beloved, and his reward is greater because he tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered a stronger inclination. Yoma 86b supplies the distinction central to this volume: teshuvah from fear reduces deliberate sins to inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love can transform them into merits. The captive-son parable explains the surplus of joy, not the desirability of captivity. Reunion after distance reveals and intensifies a bond that continuous residence never had to display. Accordingly, the Mishnah's warning in Yoma 8:9 that one may not plan to sin and repent remains fully in force. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, gives R' Tzadok's close parallel: 'whiter than snow' is not only removal of stain but the conversion of sins into merits, and beyond that the messianic clarification of 'very good.' In Se'if 10, 'the bones You crushed' are also the givens of birth that David did not choose. Their rejoicing means that teshuvah does not merely work around those givens; by redirecting the inherited power and producing a deeper humility and attachment, it turns the place of crushing itself into the source of a joy and closeness previously unavailable.
וְזֶהוּ אֲפִילּוּ אִם שָׁב רַק כְּמוֹת שֶׁהָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אִם שָׁב בְּמַעֲלוֹת יְתֵירוֹת שֶׁהִגִּיעוּ לוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַשִּׁבְיָה
And this holds true even if he returned merely as he was previously, and all the more so if he returned with superior virtues that accrued to him through the captivity.
וְזֶהוּ עַל יְדֵי הַכִּיבּוּס דְּ״מִשֶּׁלֶג אַלְבִּין״, שֶׁיָּשׁוּב יָפֶה הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר מִמַּה שֶּׁהָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם
And this is through the laundering of “I shall be whiter than snow” (51:9), that he shall return far more radiant than he was before.
וְכֵן בִּיקֵּשׁ בִּתְחִלַּת דְּבָרָיו ״הֶרֶב כַּבְּסֵנִי״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁיְּכֻבַּס כִּיבּוּס מְרוּבֶּה עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נָחֳוָור לְגַמְרֵי גַּם מֵחֵטְא שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת

And so he requested at the beginning of his words, “Wash me thoroughly [herev kabbeseini] from my iniquity” (51:4), that he be thoroughly laundered until he becomes completely white, even from the sin that was turned into inadvertence;
כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ בְּנַפְשׁוֹ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁרָאוּי לְהִתְלַבֵּן עַל יְדֵי הַכִּיבּוּס דִּתְשׁוּבָה יוֹתֵר מֵאוֹתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא נִתְלַכְלֵךְ
for he sensed within his soul the arousal of teshuvah from love, which is worthy of becoming whitened through the laundering of repentance even more than one who was never soiled at all.

וּבִרְאוֹתוֹ כִּי אַחַר כָּל תְּפִלָּתוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא רָצָה לְהוֹדִיעוֹ שֶׁנִּמְחַל, וְחָשַׁב אוּלַי חֵטְא זֶה דְּמִצַּד הַתּוֹלָדָה בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְתַקְּנוֹ לְגַמְרֵי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת עַד עֵת קֵץ שֶׁיְּבוּלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח

And seeing that after all his prayer the Blessed Name did not wish to inform him that he was pardoned, he thought that perhaps this blemish stemming from birth through the serpent's counsel cannot be rectified completely to become like merits until the End of Days, when death is swallowed up forever (Yeshayah 25:8);

וְעַל כֵּן חָזַר לְבַקֵּשׁ ״הַסְתֵּר פָּנֶיךָ״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהֶעָוֹן יִמָּחֶה לְגַמְרֵי, וְהַחֵטְא הַנִּשְׁאָר מִמֶּנּוּ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה שֶׁאֵין נִמְחֶה לְגַמְרֵי עַל כָּל פָּנִים יַסְתִּיר פָּנָיו

therefore he returned to plead, “Hide Your face from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities” (Tehillim 51:11), that the iniquity [avon] be utterly blotted out, and as for the sin [chet] remaining from it through the repentance from fear which is not totally erased, that He at least hide His face from it.447Expanded source note: R' Tzadok's map of Tehillim 51 in this se'if: Psalm 51 is David's confession after Nasan's rebuke, and verses 8-12 move from inward truth to purification, renewed joy, erasure of sin, and finally a newly created heart. The classical meforshim establish the range of the opening verse. Rashi reads 'You desire truth in the hidden parts' as David's truthful confession and identifies batuchos with the kidneys, the concealed seat of counsel. Radak says David's deeper will never sought rebellion; his regret proves that desire overpowered a will still directed toward Hashem. Metzudas David makes the verse strikingly close to this siman: Hashem demands truth even in the thoughts of the kidneys, and therefore the father's inward thought matters although the outward act was not sinful. Malbim explains that truth and moral wisdom lie deep within the soul but are covered by materiality, making failure possible. R' Tzadok joins these readings into a doctrine of root-rectification. Pri Tzadik, Balak 14, and Rosh Chodesh Av 3, identify batuchos with the kidneys whose counsel comes 'from afar,' from the hidden root; Torah can disclose true counsel at that depth. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, follows almost the entire sequence used here: hidden wisdom, purification through the lowliness of hyssop, whitening beyond snow, hiding and erasing sin, and a pure heart that makes the penitent like a new creature. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 39 adds that prayer and heavenly mercy can change even a compromised root, because 'create for me' denotes creation ex nihilo. Thus Se'if 10 is not excusing David through birth or the yetzer. It insists that teshuvah must reach beneath the legal act and conscious intention to inherited disposition itself. The same hidden region that carried the admixture also carries the wisdom by which it can be understood, humbled, and recreated.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא הִנִּיחַ אֶת שֶׁלּוֹ גַּם כֵּן וְהוֹסִיף לוֹמַר ״לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא״ וְגוֹמֵר, וּבְרִיאָה הוּא יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן

Nevertheless, he did not abandon his plea, adding: “Create in me a clean heart, O God; [and renew a steadfast spirit within me]” (51:12)—and “creation” implies ex nihilo [yesh me-ayin];448Expanded source note: From pardon to a newly created heart: 'He will swallow up death forever' is Yeshayahu 25:8, the prophetic promise that death and disgrace will finally disappear. Sukkah 52a links the end of death with the end of the yetzer by portraying Hashem's future slaughter of the evil inclination. David's fear in this se'if is therefore precise: perhaps the inherited trace of Adam and the serpent can be fully converted only when death's root is abolished. His next petitions form an ascending sequence. On 'Hide Your face from my sins and erase all my iniquities' (Tehillim 51:11), Radak explains that David asks that the sins no longer stand before Hashem for remembrance and punishment, and then asks that every iniquity be wiped away. Yet concealment and erasure are still less than positive renewal. Rashi and Metzudas David read 'Create for me a pure heart' (51:12) as protection against future failure; Radak adds Divine support so the yetzer no longer rules. Malbim distinguishes a heart whose material appetite is present by birth from a spirit distorted later by acquired false images: the former requires a new creation, while the latter can be renewed to its original straightness. Sukkah 52a's list of seven names for the yetzer makes David's wording explicit: God called it evil, Moshe uncircumcised, and David impure, inferred from his request for a pure heart. This is a spiritual analogy, not a new halachic status for permitted marital life. Pri Tzadik, Bo 4, applies the name to David's struggle with the admixture of desire; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17, says that a pure heart makes him like a new creature and turns the past into merits. Tzidkas HaTzadik section 39 states R' Tzadok's governing principle most sharply: prayer can overturn even the root, for beriah means existence from nonexistence. David therefore asks for more than acquittal. He asks Hashem to create within the very place of inherited self-directed pleasure a heart whose desire is transparent to Divine truth.
וּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה (נב סוֹף עַמּוּד א) מִזֶּה שֶׁגּוֹי קְרָאוֹ טָמֵא
and in Avodah Zarah (52a), [it is derived] from this that a gentile called it unclean.
וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ חֶטְאוֹ מֵאֲבוֹתָיו שֶׁכִּיוְּנוּ לַהֲנָאָתָן זֶה אֵינוֹ רַע הַפּוֹעֵל
And the ancestral root of his sin, that they intended for their own pleasure, is not an active evil;

דְּטַעַם הַטּוּמְאַת עֶרֶב, דִּבִּדְבַר מִצְוָה וּקְדוּשָׁה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ טוּמְאָה, רַק לְפִי שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּלֹא כַּוָּונָה לַהֲנָאָתוֹ אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים, מִזֶּה הֵיפֶךְ הַטָּהֳרָה

for the reason for evening-impurity [following marital relations, Vayikra 15:18] is that while in a matter of mitzvah and holiness impurity does not belong, since in this world it is impossible to act without an intention for personal pleasure even for the most pious of the pious, from this admixture arises the opposite of purity.

items.h: The theme: The distinction between the nations and Israel regarding the bodily origin of life. The wicked Bilaam could not conceive of holiness in procreation because he was entirely submerged in lust; but Israel’s essence is intrinsically holy, so any bodily impurity is merely temporary (tevilah and sunset purify it). While Scripture's plain sense says "in sin did my mother conceive me," Chazal read it as a term of purification (dikkuy). Because the complete rectification of this ancestral root was not yet revealed in his days, David pleaded for an ex nihilo creation of a clean heart, and offered the sacrifice of a broken spirit—the true offering that atones for the inadvertent residue of sin and leads upward to teshuvah from love.

p: וְאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע, שֶׁלֹּא הִשִּׂיג מְצִיאוּת טָהֳרָה וּקְדוּשָׁה בְּדָבָר זֶה, אָמַר ״מִי שֶׁהוּא טָהוֹר וְקָדוֹשׁ וּמְשָׁרְתָיו וְכוּלֵיהּ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (נִדָּה ל״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א), כִּי הוּא הָיָה מְשׁוּקָּע בְּזוּהֲמַת הַתַּאֲוָה

And that wicked one [Bilaam], who could not grasp the existence of purity and holiness in this matter, said, “Shall He who is pure and holy, whose ministers are pure and holy, [gaze at this?]”, as they said (Niddah 31a), because he was submerged in the filth of physical lust;449Expanded source note: Bilaam, holiness, and temporary ritual tum'ah: Niddah 31a:21 follows the teaching that Hashem 'sits and counts the quarterings of Israel,' awaiting the conception of a tzaddik. Bilaam objects, 'Would One who is pure and holy, and whose ministers are pure and holy, gaze upon this?' and the Gemara connects his blindness to 'the word of the man whose eye is shut' (Bamidbar 24:3). The adjacent passage says that Hashem assisted Leah's union with Yaakov that produced Yissachar (Bereishis 30:16). The setting is therefore not voyeurism but Divine partnership in bringing a holy life into being. Maharal, Netzach Yisrael 57:19, explains the conceptual dispute: Israel's seed proceeds from a hidden inward power, and what is inward is not ervah; Bilaam, whose own attachment was to zenus and exposed desire, had no access to that inward holiness and read the act only through his own corruption. This closely matches R' Tzadok's Dover Tzedek section 2, where Bilaam's da'as of the left stands opposite Moshe's life-giving da'as of the right. Halachically, the Torah itself prevents a false inference. Vayikra 15:16-18 states that an emission of seed, the garment on which it falls, and a man and woman after marital relations are impure until evening and require washing or immersion. Rashi on Vayikra 15:32 calls the baal keri's status tum'as erev, and Sefer Mitzvos Gadol, positive commandment 247, counts the impurity of semen and the resulting immersion as a Torah law. The category is ritual, not a declaration that a permitted or mitzvah-oriented union is morally sinful: the very same act can be lawful and holy while producing a short-lived tum'ah that limits access to sacred food or the Mikdash. Immersion begins purification, and nightfall completes it; this is the 'tovel u'ma'ariv shimsho' image used here. The lightness of the purification is precisely R' Tzadok's proof that the tum'ah is incidental rather than essential. Berachos 17a sharpens the metaphor: the 'leaven in the dough' is the yetzer that ferments and distorts an underlying will already directed to Hashem. R' Tzadok is thus not denying bodily desire or ritual impurity. He distinguishes their temporary admixture from the covenantal inwardness through which marriage, conception, and even the formation of a tzaddik can be sites of holiness. Bilaam's blindness is the inability to see that distinction.
אֲבָל אֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל עַם קָדוֹשׁ, אַף דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם מִטִּיפָּה שֶׁהַצַּדִּיק נוֹלָד יֵשׁ טוּמְאָה מִצַּד עֵירְבּוּב הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָּה, אֲבָל עַצְמוּתוֹ לֹא כֵן

but with Israel, a holy people, although in any event even from the seed through which a tzaddik is born there is ritual impurity on account of the mixture of the “leaven in the dough” [the serpent’s residue], its true essence is not so;
וְעַל כֵּן הַטּוּמְאָה רַק לְשָׁעָה, וְטוֹבֵל וּמַעֲרִיב שִׁמְשׁוֹ וְנִטְהָר, וּבִרְחִיצָה קַלָּה הוּא מִתְכַּבֵּס
therefore the impurity is only temporary: he immerses, awaits the sunset (he'erev shemesh), and is purified, and with a light washing it is cleansed.
וַחֲכָמִים דָּרְשׁוּ (בְּנִדָּה שָׁם עַמּוּד ב׳) ״בְּחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי אִמִּי״ — לִישָׁנָא דְּדִכּוּי וְטָהֳרָה
And the Sages expounded (in Niddah 31b) “in sin did my mother conceive me” (Tehillim 51:7) as an expression of cleansing and purity [dikkuy, related to mechatei];

אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁפְּשָׁטֵיהּ ״חֵטְא״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶהוּ רַק מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁלֹּא נִתְבָּרְרָה עֲדַיִין קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְגַמְרֵי, וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר בְּלָשׁוֹן דְּמִשְׁתַּמַּע לִתְרֵי אַפֵּי, וְהוּא חֵטְא וְדַם טָהֳרָה

even though its plain sense is “sin,” nevertheless that is only from the perspective of this world, wherein the holiness of Israel has not yet been fully clarified; wherefore it was stated in language bearing two meanings, referring both to sin and to blood of purity (dam tohar).450Expanded source note: The double reading of 'uv'chet yechematni imi' (Tehillim 51:7): Niddah 31b:3 records two views about the time of conception. R' Yitzchak in the name of Rav Ami associates conception with the onset of the menstrual period and cites 'be'avon cholalti'; R' Yochanan associates it with the time near immersion and cites 'uv'chet yechematni imi.' Rav Yitzchak explains that chet can be a term of dikuyi, cleansing, from 'vechitte et habayis' (Vayikra 14:52), rendered by the Targum as purification, and from 'techateini b'ezov v'et'har' - 'purge me with hyssop and I shall be pure' (Tehillim 51:9). Rashi on Niddah 31b explains the verse accordingly: the mother conceived after being cleansed from the blood of niddah. Yalkut Shimoni on Nach 765 preserves the same derash in its anthology of this psalm. The derash does not erase the ordinary meaning of chet. The classical meforshim emphasize that meaning from several angles. Rashi on Tehillim 51:7 reads David as acknowledging that human formation occurs through an arena in which many sins can arise, or through parents who are themselves fallible; 'yechematni' denotes heat. Ibn Ezra locates the point in the desire and yetzer planted in the human heart from birth. Radak stresses that sexual desire is natural and hence especially difficult to master, while explicitly refusing to make nature an exemption from responsibility; mastery is greater precisely because the drive is innate. Metzudas David connects David's particular failure with the same kind of desire present at conception. Malbim distinguishes avon, distortion of intellect caused by embodiment, from chet, failure through appetite, whose disposition accompanies conception. R' Tzadok deliberately preserves both sets of readings. In the manifest conditions of this world, where Israel's holiness has not been completely clarified, the verse truthfully says 'sin': bodily origin carries appetite and the se'or's admixture. At its root, however, the same word can mean purification because conception after immersion serves the creation of holy life. The philological two-sidedness becomes a theology of teshuvah: the surface defect is real, but it is not the final identity of the act or the person. Compare Siman 15 sections 94 and 103, where R' Tzadok returns to the leaven mixed into the formative drop and to the navel as the prenatal channel of vitality that requires healing at the root. The present derash is the seed of that later claim: repair must reach the inherited channel without confusing the channel's admixture with Israel's essential holiness.

וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁרָאָה בְּמַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ אָז כִּי לֹא נִתְבָּרֵר עֲדַיִין תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם לְגַמְרֵי, עַל כֵּן בִּיקֵּשׁ עַל בְּרִיאָה חֲדָשָׁה יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן: ״לֵב טָהוֹר״ לְגַמְרֵי, וּבָזֶה יְתוּקַּן הַכֹּל

Nevertheless, according to what he perceived in his thought then, that the complete rectification of the past was not yet clarified, he therefore pleaded for a new creation ex nihilo [yesh me-ayin]: a completely “clean heart” (Tehillim 51:12), whereby everything would be rectified.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהַשּׁוֹגֵג כַּפָּרָתוֹ בְּקָרְבָּן, עַל זֶה אָמַר שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ ״כִּי לֹא תַחְפֹּץ זֶבַח״ וְגוֹמֵר, ״זִבְחֵי אֱלֹהִים רוּחַ נִשְׁבָּרָה״ וְגוֹמֵר

And because the atonement for an inadvertent sin is through a sacrifice, he said there afterward: “For You desire not sacrifice... The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; [a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise]” (Tehillim 51:18–19);
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַזֶּבַח הַמְכַפֵּר לַשּׁוֹגֵג הַנַּעֲשֶׂה מִן הַמֵּזִיד עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, עַל יְדֵי הַלֵּב נִשְׁבָּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ לוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ

for this is the very sacrifice that atones for the inadvertent sin that was made out of the willful transgression through repentance, via the broken heart that he possesses afterward.451Expanded source note: The shogeg offering and the 'sacrifice' of a broken heart: Vayikra 4 establishes the chatas for specified inadvertent transgressions. Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, formulates the legal boundary precisely: one who inadvertently violates a negative command involving an act for whose intentional violation one is liable to kareis must bring a sin-offering. Not every mistake therefore carries a korban, and R' Tzadok is drawing an analogy from the Torah's paradigmatic shogeg, not issuing a new rule of sacrificial law. Yoma 86b supplies the transition: teshuvah from fear makes deliberate sins like inadvertent ones, whereas teshuvah from love makes them merits. Once rebellion has been removed, the deed's remaining imprint resembles a shogeg and still calls for kapparah. David's next words answer that need: 'You do not desire sacrifice ... the sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart You will not despise' (Tehillim 51:18-19). Radak explains that the sacrifice God desires is the broken spirit; a korban without a broken heart is rejected, while a broken heart is accepted even without a korban. Malbim distinguishes the inner ruach, which generates the soul's images, from the outer lev, seat of appetite and the power to govern it: both must be broken away from their old pattern, so that wisdom and fear replace corrupt images and desire is subdued. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, gives the practical structure beneath that brokenness: abandonment of the sin, removal from thought, resolve not to return, regret, and verbal confession. In Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, R' Tzadok gives the close parallel to this se'if: fear-based teshuvah cancels the willful status but leaves the ma'aseh and its defect in force, like an act performed unintentionally, and it therefore needs kapparah and refinement; love-based teshuvah receives Divine illumination that repairs the body of the act itself and turns it into merit. The 'broken spirit' is thus not self-loathing and does not replace an actual chatas when halachah obligates one. It is the inward offering of truthful regret and shame appropriate to the residue that fear-based return has not yet transformed. Precisely because the heart is broken before Hashem rather than merely frightened by punishment, Heaven can assist the penitent toward teshuvah from love. Compare Siman 15 section 103, where 'uv'chet yechematni imi' is tied to healing the prenatal root, and section 94, where the se'or leaves a trace even in the formative drop. Here R' Tzadok provides the mechanism of that root-healing: fear removes defiance, brokenness atones for the remaining shogeg-like imprint, and Divine love recreates the deed as merit.
דְּכָל זְמַן דְּלֹא נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, אִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, רוּחוֹ נִשְׁבָּרָה בְּקִרְבּוֹ לַאֲשֶׁר הִמְרָה פִּי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים

For as long as it has not been completely rectified to become like merits, if he returned in truth to the Blessed Name, his spirit is shattered within him over having rebelled against the word of the King of kings of kings;
וְהוּא נִכְלָם וּמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְהָרִים פָּנָיו לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּבָזֶה יְכוּפַּר לוֹ גַּם שִׁגְגָתוֹ
and he is humiliated and ashamed before himself, unable to lift his face before the Blessed Name, and through this his inadvertent transgression is likewise atoned.
וּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם יַעַזְרוּהוּ לְהַגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכֻיּוֹת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּרָכוֹת יב עַמּוּד ב) דְּהָעוֹבֵר עֲבֵירָה וּמִתְבַּיֵּישׁ מוֹחֲלִין מִשָּׁאוּל

And from Heaven they will assist him to reach teshuvah from love, that it may become like merits, as they said (Berachos 12b), that one who commits a transgression and is ashamed is forgiven [learned] from Shaul;
וּבְוַדַּאי שָׁאוּל שֶׁבּוֹשׁ אָז, כִּי הִרְגִּישׁ חֶטְאוֹ וְיָדַע שֶׁחָטָא, בְּוַדַּאי שָׁב וְנִתְחָרֵט כְּבָר עַל זֶה
and certainly Shaul, who was ashamed then because he recognized his transgression and knew that he had sinned, had certainly already repented and felt regret over it.
וּבְלָאו הָכִי נַמֵּי, כָּל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁעָבַר עֲבֵירָה וַדַּאי עָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (שָׁם יט עַמּוּד א), וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן מְשִׁיחַ ה׳ כְּשָׁאוּל

And even without this, any Torah scholar who commits a transgression has certainly performed teshuvah, as they said (Berachos 19a), and all the more so the anointed of Hashem like Shaul.452Expanded source note: Shaul's shame, repentance, and the limit of pardon: Berachos 12b:9-12 first cites Yechezkel 16:63 for the teaching that one who sins and is ashamed is forgiven, but rejects that proof because a community may be different. It then proves the rule from Shaul. When Shaul tells Shmuel that Hashem no longer answers him 'by prophets or by dreams' (I Shmuel 28:15), he omits the Urim VeTummim because recalling them would expose his destruction of Nov, the city of kohanim. That omission is the evidence of shame. The Gemara then reads Shmuel's 'tomorrow you and your sons will be with me' (28:19) as 'with me in my partition,' proof that Heaven pardoned him. Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 1:22, makes shame a high stage of teshuvah: contemplating Hashem's greatness, patience, and knowledge of one's hidden thoughts changes the radiance of the sinner's face and produces humiliation before the One against whom he rebelled. That is especially relevant here, because R' Tzadok explicitly includes yiras haromemus - awe of Divine exaltedness - within teshuvah from fear. Vayikra Rabbah 26:7 adds that Shmuel offered Shaul a choice: he could flee and survive, but if he accepted the attribute of justice he would be 'with me.' Shaul went to battle knowing that he and his sons would fall; the Midrash praises him for rejoicing in the justice that struck him. His shame was therefore not a passing feeling but acceptance of responsibility and judgment. Berachos 19a:6 adds the presumption used by R' Tzadok: if a Torah scholar transgressed at night, one should assume by day that he certainly repented. The Gemara limits this to matters affecting his own person; in monetary wrongs, repentance may not be presumed until restitution is made. That qualification guards the passage from becoming a license to substitute emotion for repair. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, likewise requires abandoning the act, regret, resolve, and confession. R' Tzadok's inference concerning Shaul is therefore strong but carefully limited: if an ordinary talmid chacham is presumed to return, all the more so Hashem's anointed king, whose shame and acceptance of judgment are explicit. Yet pardon is not the same as transformation into merit. Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, explains that fear-based return can leave the deed's imprint requiring kapparah, while love repairs the deed itself. Se'if 11 uses Shaul to show the full dignity and efficacy of shame - genuine forgiveness - while reserving the final conversion of the past into zechuyos for the Divine assistance that brings teshuvah from love.
אֲבָל לִהְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם כָּל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם הוּא רַק מִיִּרְאָה, וַאֲפִילּוּ אָדָם גָּדוֹל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִיִּרְאַת עֹונֶשׁ רַק מִיִּרְאַת רוֹמְמוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

But because every teshuvah stemming from man's initiative is always only from fear—and even for a great man, where it is not from fear of punishment but from awe of His Blessed exaltedness—453Expanded source note: The structure of Se'if 11: R' Tzadok links five sources into one progression. Niddah 31a interprets Bilaam's words, 'Who has counted the dust of Jacob, or numbered the quarterings of Israel' (Bamidbar 23:10), to mean that Hashem attends to Israel's marital unions, awaiting the drop from which a tzaddik will be formed. Bilaam's protest shows an outlook unable to distinguish bodily desire from the holy inward purpose that can work through it. Vayikra 15:16-18 then supplies the halachic model: an emission, and even permitted marital relations, produce a temporary ritual tum'ah that is removed through immersion and sunset. Niddah 31b reads 'uv'chet yechematni imi' (Tehillim 51:7) with a second sense, treating chet as cleansing, so the same word can point both to the admixture present in this world and to Israel's pure root. Tehillim 51:18-19 moves from animal sacrifice to the inner offering of a broken spirit, while Berachos 12b makes shame itself evidence of repentance and pardon. These are not separate prooftexts: temporary tum'ah, linguistic doubleness, brokenness, and shame all describe a stain that does not define the person's essence and can therefore be washed away. Berachos 17a names the obstructing admixture 'the leaven in the dough': Rashi explains it as the yetzer hara within the heart, while the prayer begins, 'It is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will.' That distinction between essential will and obstructing se'or is the background for R' Tzadok's statement that the admixture reaches even the drop from which a tzaddik is born but is not his atzmius. Dover Tzedek section 2 supplies the Bilaam parallel already implicit here: Bilaam's 'knowledge of the Most High' belongs to the da'as of the left, opposite Moshe's da'as of the right and its 'drug of life'; his corrupted knowledge projects its own filth onto the act and cannot perceive its holy root. Maharal, Netzach Yisrael 57:19, similarly explains that Israel's seed comes from an inward holy power, whereas Bilaam, attached to licentiousness, mistook inwardness for exposure and disgrace. The se'if's conclusion is developed almost word for word in Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1: teshuvah from fear removes willful rebellion but leaves the defect of the deed like a shogeg that still needs kapparah; teshuvah from love illuminates and repairs the deed itself, turning it into merit. Se'if 11 therefore maps the passage from Israel's unspoiled root, through a temporary admixture and fear-based return, to the heavenly gift of complete healing through love.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא רַק תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה דְּנַעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, וַעֲדַיִין צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה
it nevertheless remains only teshuvah from fear, through which [deliberate sins] are rendered like inadvertent ones, and he still requires atonement.

items.h: The theme: David HaMelech was the first to arouse the power of teshuvah from love that turns willful sins into merits, for Yehudah’s act preceded the Torah when teshuvah did not operate in full force, and in truth Tamar was no harlot but an act of levirate duty. Shaul likewise attained complete forgiveness through the deep shame that drained his blood—an atonement greater than sacrifices—yet his sin did not become merits without teshuvah from love, which was completed only when his sons accepted suffering on his behalf (bara mezakeh aba). Through complete teshuvah from love, the living can rectify even past departed generations, turning all former sins into merits and accomplishing universal restoration.

p: וְהָרִאשׁוֹן הַמְעוֹרֵר כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת הוּא דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא שֶׁ״הֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה״

And the first to awaken the power of teshuvah from love that [sins] become like merits is David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who is therefore described as having “raised up the yoke of repentance” (Moed Katan 16b, Avodah Zarah 5a);

וִיהוּדָה רֹאשׁ הַשֵּׁבֶט שֶׁהִתְחִיל בָּזֶה הָיָה קוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּאֵין הַחֵטְא נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא כָּל כָּךְ, דִּלִבְנֵי נֹחַ לֹא נֶאֶסְרָה קְדֵשָׁה, דְּהִיא אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּהִיא פְּנוּיָה

while Yehudah, the head of the tribe who initiated this, lived prior to the Giving of the Torah, when the transgression was not considered so severe a sin, for to the descendants of Noach a harlot [kedeshah] was not prohibited, since she may be classified as an unmarried woman,454Expanded source note: Yehudah and Tamar - law, confession, and the root of David: Bereishis 38:14-26 describes Tamar presenting herself as a kedeishah and Yehudah later confessing, 'She is more righteous than I.' The Noahide laws of forbidden relations in Sanhedrin 57b-58a prohibit adultery and specified relatives, but do not make consensual relations with an unmarried, unrelated woman the equivalent of adultery; thus the narrative term kedeishah should not automatically be read as the post-Sinai legal category. R' Tzadok also raises a deliberately hypothetical Israel-law defense: perhaps the transfer of the pledge before Hirah the Adullamite could be viewed as kiddushin before one witness. Kiddushin 65b records the dispute - Rav Kahana says such kiddushin need not be feared, while Rav Pappa says they must be. Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 42:2, rules that one witness does not effect kiddushin even when both parties admit it; the Rema preserves an opinion that is stringent when both admit. The bracketed argument here is therefore lomdus showing how little ordinary sexual wrongdoing need be assumed, not the normative ruling that one witness certainly creates marriage. Ramban on Bereishis 38:8 explains the deeper pre-Torah institution: the ancients knew a great benefit in yibbum, practiced it through the brother and then the nearest family redeemer, and called the wider form ge'ulah. The Torah later limited the legal mitzvah to a deceased childless brother's wife. Ramban on 38:24 stresses that a Noahide widow awaiting this custom was not thereby an eishes ish, and on 38:26 explains that if Shelah did not redeem Tamar, Yehudah was the next family redeemer. Hence 'raising the name of the dead' (Devarim 25:6; Rus 4:10) means preserving the dead man's place and continuity, not necessarily giving the child his personal name. Sotah 10b:11 praises Yehudah's public admission and records the heavenly confirmation, 'From Me these hidden things emerged'; Bava Metzia 59a derives from Tamar's discreet presentation of the pledges that one should accept the furnace rather than shame another publicly. Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 sets the entire episode within providence: while the family was occupied with Yosef's sale and mourning, Hashem was creating the light of Mashiach. R' Tzadok, Likkutei Ma'amarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:13, locates the power of hoda'ah and teshuvah in Yehudah, from whom David emerges; Pri Tzadik, Vayeishev 9:1, develops David and Mashiach as the completion of that power. Yet Yehudah acts before Torah and, on Ramban's account, within a genuine redemptive custom. That is why the se'if honors him as the tribal beginning while reserving the full post-Torah revelation of sins becoming merits for David.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵם נָהֲגוּ עַצְמָם כְּדִין יִשְׂרָאֵל
save that they conducted themselves according to the law of Israel.
[וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּדִינֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁקִּידְּשָׁהּ בִּפְנֵי רֵעֵהוּ הָעֲדוּלָּמִי, וּכְמַאן דְּאָמַר דְּחוֹשְׁשִׁין לְקִידּוּשִׁין בְּעֵד אֶחָד

[And even according to the laws of Israel, it is possible that he betrothed her before his Adullamite companion, in accordance with the authority who holds that we take into account betrothal witnessed by a single witness (Kiddushin 65b);
וְהִיא לֹא יָדְעָה דִּזְקוּקָה לְיִבּוּם, וְקוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נָהֲגוּ יִבּוּם בִּקְרוֹבִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ן], וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין שַׁיָּיכוּת לִתְשׁוּבָה כָּל כָּךְ

and she did not know that she was bound by levirate ties, while before the Giving of the Torah levirate marriage was practiced even among other relatives, as the Ramban wrote (Bereishis 38:8)]; nevertheless, repentance does not pertain here so strongly,
וְגַם אֵין כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה כָּל כָּךְ קוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה כֵּיוָן דְּאֵין נָהוּג בְּבֶן נֹחַ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי (לְעֵיל סִימָן א׳)
and the transformative power of teshuvah was likewise not so great prior to the Giving of the Torah, since repentance does not apply to a descendant of Noach as I wrote (above, Siman 1).
וְגַם דְּשָׁם עַל הָאֱמֶת לֹא הָיְתָה קְדֵשָׁה וְלֹא הָיָה חֵטְא כְּלָל, דְּאַדְּרַבָּא קִיֵּים הֲקָמַת שֵׁם הַמֵּתִים, וְעַל כֵּן הַמַּתְחִיל הָיָה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם

Furthermore, in truth she was no harlot and there was no sin at all, for on the contrary, he fulfilled the perpetuation of the name of the deceased; therefore the true initiator was David HaMelech, peace be upon him.

וְשָׁאוּל זָכָה גַּם כֵּן לִמְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה, דְּ״עִמִּי בִּמְחִיצָתִי״ דִּשְׁמוּאֵל, עַל כֵּן לֹא הָיָה עָלָיו עוֹד שׁוּם חֵטְא שֶׁנִּמְחַל עַל יְדֵי הַבּוּשָׁה דְּאָזֵיל סוּמְקָא וְנִשְׁפַּךְ דָּמוֹ

And Shaul likewise merited complete pardon, as Shmuel told him, “with me in my partition” (Berachos 12b), wherefore he bore no remaining sin, it having been forgiven through the shame wherein his redness departed and his blood was shed [as he blanched in shame];
דְּעָדִיף מִכֹּחַ הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת לְכַפֵּר עַל הַשּׁוֹגֵג הַנִּשְׁאָר

which is more potent than the power of sacrifices to atone for the remaining inadvertent sin.455Expanded source note: Shaul's shame and complete pardon: Berachos 12b:9-12 first states that one who sins and is ashamed is forgiven, then proves the rule from Shaul. When Shaul tells Shmuel that Hashem no longer answers him 'by prophets or by dreams' (I Shmuel 28:15), he omits the Urim VeTummim because mentioning them would expose his destruction of Nov, the priestly city. The omission is read as genuine shame. Shmuel's promise, 'Tomorrow you and your sons will be with me' (28:19), is then interpreted as 'with me in my partition,' proof that Heaven had pardoned him. Vayikra Rabbah 26:7 adds moral depth: Shmuel offered Shaul the possibility of fleeing, but Shaul accepted the attribute of justice and went to battle knowing what would happen to him and his sons. Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 1:22, describes shame before Hashem as a high stage of teshuvah, born from awareness of Divine greatness, patience, and knowledge of the hidden heart. Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah chapter 5, uses Shaul's omission and Shmuel's promise to show that shame is not merely embarrassment: it marks the sinner's withdrawal from identification with the sin. Bava Metzia 58b supplies R' Tzadok's physical image. The Gemara says that public humiliation resembles bloodshed because the red leaves the victim's face and pallor comes. The Gemara itself is warning against shaming another; R' Tzadok applies its physiology homiletically to the penitent's own shame before Heaven, as though his blood were offered. Tehillim 51:18-19 provides the sacrificial language: 'The offerings of God are a broken spirit; a broken and crushed heart You will not despise.' This comparison neither creates a new law of korban nor substitutes emotion for restitution, confession, and changed conduct (Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2). It explains inward kapparah for the shogeg-like residue left after deliberate rebellion is removed. Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, gives R' Tzadok's parallel formulation: fear-based teshuvah cancels the willful status but can leave the defect of the deed requiring kapparah; love-based teshuvah heals the deed itself and makes it merit. Shaul's shame is therefore fully effective as pardon, yet the se'if can still distinguish pardon from the later transformation of the past into zechuyos.
אֲבָל אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁנִּמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי, עֲדַיִין לֹא נֶחְשַׁב לִהְיוֹת עוֹד כִּזְכֻיּוֹת בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
Yet although it was completely pardoned, it was still not reckoned to become like merits without teshuvah from love;
וְעַל זֶה הוּצְרַךְ עוֹד לְעֹונֶשׁ בְּבָנָיו שֶׁאָז נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת

and for this he required a further punishment through his sons (II Shmuel 21), at which point it was completely rectified to become like merits.456Expanded source note: The seven descendants of Shaul and the declaration 'chosen of Hashem': II Shmuel 21:1-9 relates a three-year famine 'for Shaul and for the house of blood, because he put the Givonim to death.' The Givonim reject money and demand seven male descendants of Shaul; David delivers them, while sparing Mephiboshes son of Yonasan because of his oath. This episode immediately raises two Torah objections: 'Fathers shall not be put to death for children, nor children for fathers' (Devarim 24:16), and a hanged body may not remain overnight (21:23). Yevamos 78b-79a confronts both. R' Yochanan answers that it was preferable for a letter of Torah to be displaced in this exceptional case than for the Divine name to be profaned: the nations had to see that Israel's covenant with converts would be vindicated. The same sugya treats the bodies' extended exposure as a public lesson in the gravity of harming gerim. This is an extraordinary kiddush-Hashem setting, not a general license for courts to punish adult children for a father's crime. Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 12:24, cites the Givonim's pitiless demand for the seven as the reason David excluded them from joining the congregation, so Chazal preserve the moral complexity on both sides. Berachos 12b:13 then offers an alternative proof of Shaul's heavenly pardon. On the verse 'that we may hang them before Hashem in Giv'as Shaul, chosen of Hashem' (II Shmuel 21:6), a heavenly voice declared: 'chosen of Hashem.' Bamidbar Rabbah 8:4 expands the same reading: the human speakers said 'Giv'as Shaul,' and Heaven supplied 'chosen of Hashem.' The ordeal therefore did not fix Shaul eternally as rejected; once justice and public covenantal responsibility were completed, his chosenness was proclaimed anew. R' Tzadok joins this to the language of Bamidbar 16:7, 'the one whom Hashem chooses is the holy one': complete repair reveals that no portion of the person's history remains outside holiness. Yoma 86b supplies the conceptual bridge. Forgiveness removes liability, but only teshuvah from love converts willful sins into merits. Pri Tzadik, Vayigash 8:1, explains that the latter heals the body of the deed, not merely its willful classification. Thus R' Tzadok reads the suffering through Shaul's house and the later heavenly voice not as a contradiction to the pardon already proved in Berachos, but as the final passage from forgiven residue to a past wholly reintegrated as merit.
וְעַל כֵּן יָצָא אָז בַּת קוֹל: ״בְּחִיר ה׳״, וַ״אֲשֶׁר יִבְחַר ה׳ הוּא הַקָּדוֹשׁ״, שֶׁכָּל מַעֲשָׂיו בִּקְדוּשָׁה וְאֵין שׁוּם דָּבָר אֶצְלוֹ מִלְּבַר

Therefore a Heavenly Voice [bas kol] then issued forth, proclaiming: “the chosen of Hashem” (II Shmuel 21:6), and “he whom Hashem shall choose, he is the holy one” (Bamidbar 16:7), showing that all his deeds were in holiness and nothing in him lay outside [the realm of sanctity].
וּ״בָרָא מְזַכֶּה אַבָּא״, שֶׁיָּכוֹל לִזְכּוֹת גַּם לְאַחַר מִיתָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא תִּיקֵּן בְּחַיָּיו עַל יְדֵי בָּנָיו אַחֲרָיו

And “a son brings merit to the father” (Sanhedrin 104a), for [a father] can merit even after death that which he did not rectify during his lifetime through his children after him;457Expanded source note: David as the paradigm of teshuvah: Avodah Zarah 4b-5a first says that neither David nor Israel was naturally suited to the deed attributed to each: David's heart was already 'hollow within me' (Tehillim 109:22), and Israel had just declared at Sinai that it would obey. Their falls therefore became the Torah's answer to despair. If an individual sins, he is directed to David; if a community sins, it is directed to the generation of the Golden Calf. Both cases are needed, because an individual's sin is less public while a community possesses the greater power of collective prayer. The sugya then reads 'the saying of David son of Yishai ... the man raised on high' (II Shmuel 23:1) as David 'who raised the yoke of teshuvah.' The Zohar, Mishpatim 3:248, repeats this teaching and joins it to David's promise, 'I will teach transgressors Your ways, and sinners will return to You' (Tehillim 51:15): his story opens a path of return for ordinary sinners. Maharal, Tiferes Yisrael chapter 48, treats the individual and communal examples as a disclosure that teshuvah belongs to the providential order of Torah, not as permission to choose sin. The practical definition remains Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: abandonment of the act, regret, resolve for the future, and confession. Yoma 86b adds the level central here: return from fear makes willful sins like inadvertent ones, while return from love makes them merits. R' Tzadok develops David's distinctive role across his works. Resisei Layla 28 grounds return in the indestructible root of Israel: even after a person has sunk very low, the Divine promise 'I am with you ... and I will return you' preserves the point from which full teshuvah can grow. Tzidkas HaTzadik 254 reads David's kingship as inexhaustible longing rather than self-satisfied perfection; this is why his spiritual mode is teshuvah, always reaching beyond its present level. Pri Tzadik, Pinchas 15:2, joins the same Davidic power to Mashiach: the individual who returns awakens thoughts of return in all Israel. In this se'if, David is therefore 'first' not merely chronologically, but because after Matan Torah he reveals the full power of love-based teshuvah to transform an actual commanded past into a new source of merit.
לֹא בִּזְכוּתָם לְבַד, רַק עַל יְדֵי מַה שֶּׁהֵם מְקַבְּלִים עוֹנָשִׁים בִּשְׁבִילוֹ
not through their merits alone, but through their acceptance of sufferings on his behalf,
וּכְדֶרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״אֲבוֹתֵינוּ חָטְאוּ וְאֵינָם וַאֲנַחְנוּ עֲוֹנֹתֵיהֶם סָבָלְנוּ״
exactly as it is said: “Our fathers have sinned, and are not; and we have borne their iniquities” (Eichah 5:7);
וְקִיבְּלוּ עוֹנָשִׁים וּבָזֶה נִתְכַּפֵּר לָהֶם בְּגַן עֵדֶן
and they accepted punishments, and thereby atonement was achieved for [the fathers] in Gan Eden.
וְעַל כֵּן אוֹמֵר הַבֵּן ״הֲרֵינִי כַּפָּרַת מִשְׁכָּבוֹ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״א ב׳), וּפֵירַשׁ רַשִׁ״י דְּכָל עֹונֶשׁ הָרָאוּי לְאָבִיו יָבוֹא עָלָיו

And therefore a son recites, “Behold, I am an atonement for his resting place,” as they said (in Kiddushin 31b), which Rashi explains: that any punishment fitting to come upon his father should come upon him instead;
וְיוֹעִיל זֶה לְכַפֵּר נֶפֶשׁ אָבִיו שָׁם בִּמְקוֹם מְנוּחָתוֹ

and this avails to atone for his father’s soul there in the place of his eternal rest.458Expanded source note: 'A son brings merit to his father' - scope and limits: Sanhedrin 104a explains why Menasheh is omitted from one list of kings: the merit of his son Chizkiyahu benefits the father, whereas a father's merit does not similarly rescue a sinful son. Responsa Rashba V:49 explains the asymmetry in the world of souls. The child is an effect and continuation of the parent; when that continuation serves Hashem, the source acquires merit through what it produced. Sefer HaChinuch, mitzvah 598, uses precisely this principle to explain yibbum: the descendant established through the widow continues the deceased brother's place and benefits him in the world of souls. This also closes the circle with Yehudah and Tamar earlier in the se'if. Kiddushin 31b:11 states the halachic expression of honor after death: for twelve months, when repeating a parent's teaching, a child says, 'My father, my teacher - I am the atonement for his resting place.' Rashi explains it as accepting upon oneself any punishment due the parent. Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De'ah 240:9, codifies this formula within the first year and 'may his memory be a blessing' thereafter. Pri Tzadik, Pinchas 15:2, explicitly says that at times a person's repair comes through children and cites 'a son brings merit to his father.' Horayos 6a:7 gives a communal analogue. From the eglah arufah prayer, 'Atone for Your people Israel whom You redeemed' (Devarim 21:8), Rav Pappa derives that this atonement is fit to include even the generation redeemed from Egypt. Rashi there explains that a communal sin-offering does not die when members of the public die, because the dead can be included in the continuing community's kapparah. This does not mean that every private chatas can be offered after its owner's death. Nor is inherited punishment the ordinary criminal rule: Devarim 24:16 and Yechezkel 18 insist that each person is judged for his own sin, and Sanhedrin 27b limits punishment of descendants to those who continue their ancestors' deeds. The Shaul-Givonim episode is treated in Yevamos 79a as an exceptional kiddush-Hashem case. Eichah 5:7 - 'Our fathers sinned and are no more, and we have borne their iniquities' - describes descendants bearing the historical and spiritual consequences of an inherited breach, not a routine transfer of courtroom guilt. R' Tzadok's point is therefore organic and intergenerational: the parent's unfinished imprint can be repaired through the life, merit, or exceptional suffering of the continuation he brought into being. Resisei Layla 28 supplies the wider frame, describing Israel's generations as branches of one enduring root; later holiness can reach backward because the family and the people are not spiritually isolated units.
וְגַם בְּכַפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת וְעֶגְלָה עֲרוּפָה אָמְרוּ (בְּהוֹרָיוֹת ו׳ עַמּוּד א) דִּמְכַפְּרִין עַל דּוֹרוֹת שֶׁעָבְרוּ הַמֵּתִים
Furthermore, regarding the atonement of communal sacrifices and the decapitated heifer [eglah arufah], the Sages stated (in Horayos 6a) that they atone for departed past generations.
וְכֵן בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁנִּזְכֶּה לָשׁוּב כּוּלָּנוּ בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ בְּלֵב שָׁלֵם לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
And likewise, through teshuvah from love—which may we all merit to achieve speedily in our days with a whole heart before the Blessed Name—
נִזְכֶּה לְתַקֵּן כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת הַקּוֹדְמִים, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה חֲטָאֵי כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת וְיִהְיֶה תִּיקּוּן הַכֹּל
we will merit to rectify all preceding generations, so that the sins of all generations will become like merits, bringing about the complete rectification of all creation.

items.h: The theme: The universal pathway for every penitent returning to Hashem. Teshuvah necessarily begins from awe and fear (yirah), which represents the full scope of human initiative—anchored in the principle "I have set Hashem before me always" (the Rama's opening to Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim). Through constant brokenness and humility over the past, he first merits the pardon of inadvertent sins (mechilas hashogeg), becoming as one who never sinned. Thereafter, through perseverance (tahor yadayim yosif ometz), Heaven grants him supernal assistance to reach teshuvah from love (teshuvah me'ahavah), wherein all his former sins are transformed into merits.

p: וְכֵן הוּא סֵדֶר וְדֶרֶךְ כָּל הַבָּא לָשׁוּב אֶל ה׳: בַּהַתְחָלָה הוּא מִיִּרְאָה, שֶׁזֶּהוּ כָּל כֹּחַ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, רַק לְיִרְאָה

And such is the order and pathway of everyone who comes to return to Hashem: at the beginning it is from fear [and awe], for this constitutes the entire capacity of human initiative in the service of the Blessed Name, solely toward fear,

עַל יְדֵי ״שִׁוִּיתִי ה׳ לְנֶגְדִּי תָמִיד״ שֶׁהוּא כְּלָל גָּדוֹל בַּתּוֹרָה, שֶׁנִּזְדַּמֵּן בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ בְּפִי רַבֵּינוּ מֹשֶׁה אִיסֶרְלִישׂ זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה בַּהַגָּהָה דְּרֵישׁ ״אֹרַח חַיִּים״

through “I have set Hashem before me always” (Tehillim 16:8), which is a great principle in the Torah (as cited in the Rama, Orach Chaim 1:1), having been articulated through ruach hakodesh by Rabbeinu Moshe Isserles, of blessed memory, in his gloss at the opening of Orach Chaim,
שֶׁזֶּה הַתְחָלַת עֲבוֹדָה לָאָדָם הַבָּא לֵילֵךְ בְּדֶרֶךְ הַחַיִּים, לָדַעַת וּלְהַכִּיר שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ נִכְחוֹ תָּמִיד, וְצוֹפֶה וּמַבִּיט עַל כָּל דְּרָכָיו וּמַעֲלָלָיו

for this is the commencement of divine service for a person who comes to walk in the way of life: to know and recognize that the Blessed Name is before him always, watching and looking upon all his ways and deeds,
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יַגִּיעַ לְפַחַד וְיִרְאָה מִמֶּנּוּ יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְהַכְנָעָה וּבוֹשְׁתּוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ תָּמִיד
whereby through this he will arrive at dread and awe of Him, may He be blessed, and constant subjugation and shame before Him.
וְהַמִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא, הֲרֵי זֶה מַתְחִיל מֵחָדָשׁ לִיכָּנֵס לַעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
And one who awakens to repent after having sinned is beginning anew to enter the service of the Blessed Name;
וְ״רֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה״, שֶׁהוּא כָּל הַתּוֹרָה כּוּלָּהּ, הוּא ״יִרְאַת ה׳״, דְּהוּא תַּרְעָא לְאַעֲלָא גּוֹ מְהֵימְנוּתָא
and “the beginning of wisdom” (Tehillim 111:10), which encompasses the entirety of the Torah, is “the fear of Hashem,” which is the gate to enter into faith (Zohar I, 7b),
וְזֶה הַשַּׁעַר שֶׁכָּל בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גַּם כֵּן יָבוֹאוּ בוֹ בִּתְחִלַּת תְּשׁוּבָתָן
and this is the very gateway through which every penitent likewise must enter at the inception of his repentance.
וְאַחַר שֶׁשּׁוֹקֵד בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ וְחַטָּאתוֹ נֶגְדּוֹ תָּמִיד, לִהְיוֹת לִבּוֹ נִשְׁבָּר בְּקִרְבּוֹ
And after he is diligent in his repentance, his sin being ever before him (Tehillim 51:5) so that his heart remains broken within him,
עַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לִמְחִילַת הַשּׁוֹגֵג וְלִהְיוֹת כְּמִי שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא כְּלָל
through this he subsequently merits the forgiveness of the inadvertent sin, becoming as one who never sinned at all;
וַעֲדַיִין ״טְהָר יָדַיִם יֹסִיף אֹמֶץ״, שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה שֶׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם יְסַיְּיעוּהוּ לְהַגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה
and still “he that hath clean hands shall wax stronger and stronger” (Iyov 17:9), that he may merit assistance granted him from Heaven to attain teshuvah from love,
עַד שֶׁיָּשׁוּב הַכֹּל זְכֻיּוֹת, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת תִּיקּוּן הַתְּשׁוּבָה
until everything is converted into merits, which is the ultimate perfection of the rectification of repentance.

sections.en: Teshuvah through suffering and the acceptance of the penitent

items.h: תשובה על ידי יסורין וקבלת בעל התשובה.

The theme: Teshuvah through suffering (teshuvah al yedei yissurin) is the third mode identified in the Gemara (Yoma 86a). Rashi explains that one who repents through afflictions is called an “eved” [servant/slave], whereas one who repents from love or fear is called a “ben” [son]. R’ Tzadok analyzes this distinction, showing that while any sincere penitent is accepted and reaches the level of a baal teshuvah, an arousal originating purely from external affliction corresponds to the passive, receiving state of Nukva (ba’al l’ishah), rather than the proactive self-awakening of sons.

p: הַשְּׁלִישִׁי: עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, שֶׁלֹּא שָׁבוּ עַד שֶׁנִּתְיַיסְּרוּ

The third [mode]: through afflictions, where they did not repent until they were chastised [through suffering];459Expanded source note: Yoma 86a and Rashi - suffering as the occasion of return: Rav Yehudah's answer is 'here, from love or from fear; there, through sufferings.' Rashi defines the third case narrowly: 'one who did not return until he was afflicted with sufferings.' R' Tzadok elsewhere clarifies the boundary: one who has not yet been struck but repents because he fears that punishment may come is still returning from fear, albeit the lower fear of punishment. Actual suffering creates the third case because the pressure is already present. Chazal use the same image in Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:3:2: just as oil improves only through crushing, Israel is brought to repentance through crushing. Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 43 likewise closes its survey of the power of repentance by saying that Israel may return from distress, oppression, exile, and want. These passages describe an awakening; pain itself is not teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2, still requires abandonment of the sin, regret, resolution not to repeat it, and verbal confession. This also prevents confusion with the baraisa of the four divisions of atonement earlier on Yoma 86a. There, repentance has already occurred and sufferings are 'memarkin,' completing the cleansing of transgressions punishable by kareis or court death; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, and Rabbeinu Yonah, Shaarei Teshuvah 4:11, codify and develop that process. Here the sufferings precede the change of heart and provoke it. Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13:1, makes this very distinction and cites Achav and Menasheh: they returned only after the decree or affliction, yet their return was received. R' Tzadok's question is therefore not whether coercive pain is itself a mitzvah or kapparah, but whether the sincere choice made within that pressure remains permanently branded as a servant's response.

(כֵּן הוּא בְּרַשִׁ״י, וּלְאַפּוֹקֵי כְּשֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא בָּאוּ יִסּוּרִין רַק יָרֵא שֶׁלֹּא יָבוֹאוּ וְעַל יְדֵי כֵּן שָׁב, זֶה נִקְרָא מִיִּרְאָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁהִיא מַדְרֵגָה קְטַנָּה מִיִּרְאַת עֹונֶשׁ, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה בִּכְלַל מִיִּרְאָה)

(so it is in Rashi, excluding a case where afflictions have not yet arrived and he merely fears lest they come and repents on account of that, which is called [teshuvah] from fear — albeit a lower level of fear of punishment — yet nevertheless this too falls under the category of fear);
וְיַעֲיֵין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י הַחִילּוּק בֵּינֵיהֶם, דְּמֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה נִקְרָאִים ״בָּנִים״ וְעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין נִקְרָאִים ״עֲבָדִים״

and see Rashi there for the distinction between them: that through love and fear they are called “sons,” whereas through afflictions they are called “servants.”460Expanded source note: 'Sons' and 'servants' in the Yirmeyah verses: Yoma 86a juxtaposes 'Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness' (Yirmeyah 3:22) with 'Return, wayward sons ... for I am a Master to you' (3:14). Rashi on the Gemara reads the first address as the title granted to returners from love or fear, and ba'alti in the second as the language of mastery, hence servants. In the verse itself, Rashi on Yirmeyah explains ba'alti as 'I am your Lord, and it is not My honor to leave you in the enemy's hand.' Radak records both a marital reading - I shall take you again after divorce - and his father's alternative, 'I have wearied of you'; Malbim stresses renewed covenantal attachment even if only one from a city remains. On 3:22, Radak explains 'I will heal' as a metaphor: forgiveness with repentance heals the wound of the soul as medicine heals the body, while Rashi notes that the prophet teaches Israel the confession that follows, 'Behold, we have come to You.' Thus the sugya's son/servant contrast is a derashah built on the diction of the verses, not a denial of their broader prophetic promise. It also sets up R' Tzadok's challenge from Kiddushin 36a, where R' Meir holds that Israel is called children even when corrupt, and from Bava Basra 10a, where even R' Yehudah calls those presently doing God's will children. The kabbalistic tradition preserves the same tension. Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b explains 'Return, wayward sons': even while wayward, Israel normally remains rooted on the right side and is therefore still addressed as children; he cites R' Meir's rule, 'either way you are called sons.' R' Tzadok will therefore have to read 'servant' as the mode of the initial awakening under compulsion, not as the penitent's final and unchangeable identity. The following se'if accordingly turns from the titles themselves to the precise wording and textual logic of the Yoma passage.
וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן, כֵּיוָן דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַבֵּל תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ, וְהַגַּם שֶׁלֹּא שָׁב עַד אַחַר שֶׁבָּאוּ עָלָיו יִסּוּרִין, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִשֶּׁשָּׁב נִקְרָא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר

And this requires study: since the Holy One, blessed be He, accepts his repentance, even though he did not repent until after suffering came upon him, nonetheless, once he has returned he is termed a complete baal teshuvah;

דְּ״תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא״ כְּתִיב, וְדָרְשׁוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי (פֶּרֶק ב׳ דַּחֲגִיגָה הֲלָכָה א׳) ״עַד דִּכְדּוּכָהּ שֶׁל נֶפֶשׁ״, דַּאֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָה מְקַבְּלִין, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן עַל יְדֵי שְׁאָר יִסּוּרִין

for “You turn man to contrition [dakka]” (Tehillim 90:3) is written, which they expounded in the Yerushalmi (Chagigah 2:1) as “until the very crushing of the soul,” meaning that even at the threshold of death they accept [his return], and all the more so through other afflictions;
וּמִקְרָא מָלֵא (בְּפָרָשַׁת וָאֶתְחַנַּן) ״בַּצַּר לְךָ וּמְצָאוּךָ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְשַׁבְתָּ עַד ה׳״ וְגוֹמֵר
and there is an explicit verse (Devarim 4:30): “In your distress, when all these things have found you... you will return to Hashem your God”;

וּבְטַעֲנָה זוֹ בָּא מְנַשֶּׁה כְּשֶׁשָּׁב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין דְּמֶלֶךְ אַשּׁוּר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק י׳ דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין הֲלָכָה ב׳), וְנִתְקַבְּלָה תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בַּמַּתְנִיתִין דְּשָׁם

and with this very argument Menasheh approached when he repented through the tortures of the King of Assyria, as they said (in Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2), and his repentance was accepted according to Rabbi Yehudah in the Mishnah there;461Expanded source note: Menasheh as the extreme test of return under affliction: II Divrei HaYamim 33:10-17 supplies the biblical sequence that Melachim omits. Menasheh and his people ignore the prophets; the Assyrian commanders seize him, bind him in bronze, and take him to Bavel. 'When he was in distress' he entreats Hashem, humbles himself greatly, is heard, and is restored to Yerushalayim. He then removes the foreign gods, repairs the altar, offers peace and thanksgiving offerings, and commands Yehudah to serve Hashem. Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2 expands the ordeal: R' Levi says they placed him in a copper mule and heated it from below. After every idol failed him, Menasheh recalled Devarim 4:30-31, 'when you are in distress ... you shall return to Hashem your God.' The angels blocked the windows of heaven, arguing that an idolater who placed an image in the Heichal should not be received. Hashem answered, 'If I do not receive him, I lock the door before all penitents,' and dug a tunnel beneath the Throne of Glory to hear his prayer. Pesikta deRav Kahana 24:11 preserves the same homily and plays on va-ye'ater, 'He was entreated,' as though va-yachter, 'He tunneled'; Pirkei deRabbi Eliezer 43 places Menasheh among its classic proofs of the power of teshuvah. The Midrash does not romanticize his first prayer - he invokes Hashem only after testing every idol - but it also records the decisive outcome: 'Menasheh knew that Hashem, He is God' (II Divrei HaYamim 33:13), expressed in the Yerushalmi as 'there is judgment and there is a Judge.' Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13:1, uses this very case to prove that a return born in suffering is genuinely accepted. The tunnel symbolizes mercy opening a route beyond the accusing angels, not a bypass of repentance's inner requirements.

וְתַנָּא קַמָּא דְּפָלֵיג מִשּׁוּם דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּלֹא עָבַד תְּשׁוּבָה כִּמְבוֹאָר (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א), וְהַיְינוּ דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהִתְפַּלֵּל לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהִצִּילוֹ מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא שָׁב מֵחֲטָאָיו

and the First Tanna who disputes holds that he did not do genuine teshuvah, as explained (in Sanhedrin 103a), meaning that although he prayed to the Blessed Name and was saved, he nevertheless did not turn from his sins;462Expanded source note: The dispute over Menasheh - prayer, repentance, and the World to Come: Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2 lists Menasheh among the three kings with no share in the World to Come. R' Yehudah dissents from II Divrei HaYamim 33:13: 'He prayed to Him, He was entreated, heard his supplication, and returned him to Yerushalayim to his kingdom.' The Sages answer, 'To his kingdom He returned him, but not to life in the World to Come.' The Bavli, Sanhedrin 102b-103a, sharpens the dispute through Yirmeyah 15:4: R' Yehudah reads 'because of Menasheh' as an indictment of a generation that failed to repent although even Menasheh repented; the other opinion reads it as 'because Menasheh did not repent.' R' Yochanan then declares that one who says Menasheh has no share weakens the hands of penitents, and a baraisa calculates that he practiced repentance for thirty-three years after twenty-two years of sin; Rashi explains the arithmetic from the comparison with Achav's twenty-two-year reign. R' Tzadok follows the Bavli's formulation: a cry for rescue is not necessarily proof that the person abandoned his sins. That distinction accords with Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: teshuvah requires leaving the sin, regret, future resolve, and confession. Yet Rambam 2:1 also rules that even a person who returns only in old age or on the day of death is a baal teshuvah and is forgiven, though it is not the highest 'complete teshuvah' of confronting the same temptation with full strength and abstaining solely because of teshuvah. R' Tzadok's phrase 'complete baal teshuvah' in this se'if concerns the reality and acceptance of a sincere return, while his later analysis asks about its spiritual rank. See also Tzidkas HaTzadik 130, where R' Tzadok returns to the severe view of Menasheh and explains why denying the efficacy of such repentance would weaken all baalei teshuvah; and Siman 15, sections 95-96, for his fuller treatment of the tunnel beneath the Throne.

אֲבָל אִם שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת אֲפִילּוּ מִתּוֹךְ הַיִּסּוּרִין, הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) דְּגַם גְּאוּלָּה הַשְּׁלֵימָה הָעֲתִידָה יוּכְלוּ לִזְכּוֹת עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין מִמֶּלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן

but if one repents in truth, even from within afflictions, behold they said (in Sanhedrin 97b) that even the complete future Redemption can be merited through teshuvah provoked by suffering under a monarch as cruel as Haman;463Expanded source note: The three modes in this se'if are a taxonomy of what awakens the sinner to return: love, fear, or suffering. The immediate source is the final discussion on Yoma 86a, where Rav Yehudah reconciles Yirmeyah 3:22, 'Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness,' with 3:14, 'for I am a Master to you.' Rashi explains that one who returns from love or fear is called a son, whereas one who did not return until affliction struck is called a servant. This is distinct from the earlier baraisa on the same page, the four divisions of atonement: there the question is what completes kapparah after teshuvah, and suffering may cleanse severe sins even when it did not cause the return. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, codifies that atonement scheme; R' Tzadok is analyzing the later aggadic scheme of motives. The closest parallel in R' Tzadok's own writings is Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13:1. He asks why Israel could doubt whether repentance would be accepted when the Torah says so repeatedly, and answers that they knew repentance from fear and from love but did not yet know the third power, repentance awakened by suffering. The examples of Kayin, Achav, and Menasheh show that even this return is accepted. He connects it to Moshe's prayer, 'You return man until crushing' (Tehillim 90:3), and to Adam's astonishment after meeting Kayin: 'Such is the power of teshuvah, and I did not know' (Bereishis Rabbah 22:13; Pesikta deRav Kahana 24:11). Pri Tzadik, Chukas 3, supplies the upper end of the same ladder: teshuvah from love can disclose 'light that emerges from within darkness' and convert willful sins into merits. Siman 12 begins at the lower end - a person first broken open by pain - and asks whether a true return from there can ultimately attain the full dignity of sonship and of a complete baal teshuvah.,464Expanded source note: The 'king whose decrees are harsher than Haman's': Sanhedrin 97b-98a records the dispute of R' Eliezer and R' Yehoshua over whether redemption depends upon Israel first repenting. R' Yehoshua answers that if they do not repent, the Holy One sets over them a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, Israel repents, and He restores them to the good. Yerushalmi Taanis 1:1 gives the same teaching and joins it to Yirmeyah 30:7, 'it is a time of distress for Yaakov, and from it he shall be saved.' Megillah 14a supplies the historical model: the removal of Achashverosh's ring and its transfer to Haman accomplished more than forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses, because the decree returned Israel to the good. R' Tzadok repeatedly insists that this is not merely salvation of bodies. In Machshavos Charutz 6:1, the blow itself becomes the cure: Haman's decree brought Israel to complete teshuvah and to a renewed acceptance of Torah from love, so the source of danger became the source of rescue. Resisei Layla 58:3 says 'like Haman' precisely because the harshness is ultimately a provisional appearance whose purpose is to restore the heart to its Father in heaven. Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 adds the radical application used here: Mashiach can arrive in a generation wholly guilty, because God can bring the entire generation to repentance in a single moment and reveal the high root hidden beneath its failures. Siman 12, sections 9 and 11, will develop the same image as the Divine hand concealed within the apparently rejecting hand of Esav. The proof in the present se'if is exact: if return induced by suffering were intrinsically invalid or permanently second-class, it could not be the road to the complete future redemption. Once the response becomes true teshuvah rather than momentary panic, the coercive beginning does not cancel its redemptive power.
הֲרֵי דְּנִקְרָא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר הַגָּדוֹל מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר כָּל שֶׁשָּׁב בֶּאֱמֶת מֵחֲמַת הַיִּסּוּרִין
