so he is indeed called a complete baal teshuvah, who is greater than a complete tzaddik, provided he repents sincerely out of the suffering.465Expanded source note: 'Where baalei teshuvah stand': Berachos 34b records R' Abahu's teaching that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place occupied by baalei teshuvah, deriving it from Yeshayahu 57:19, 'peace, peace, to the far and to the near' - the one who had been far is named first. R' Yochanan disagrees and reads 'far' as one distant from sin from the outset; the Gemara therefore presents a real dispute about comparative rank. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, adopts R' Abahu's view and explains that the penitent has tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered a stronger inclination. This does not erase Rambam's distinction in 2:1 between the ideal case of 'complete teshuvah' - the same opportunity and full strength, with abstention solely because of repentance - and a later return in weakness, which is accepted but not the choicest form. R' Tzadok is pressing the aggadic claim at its deepest point: if a person genuinely abandons the sin after suffering awakens him, does the source of the awakening bar him from the baal-teshuvah advantage? Takanas HaShavin 3:1 explains R' Abahu metaphysically. The tzaddik remains within the measured order of Torah, prophecy, and wisdom, while the baal teshuvah broke the world's boundary and, in returning from the place to which he fell, discovers that God was present even there. Resisei Layla 54:9 similarly says that after sin, rescue, and atonement, the penitent can attain a light higher than the joy available through ordinary worldly service. Pri Tzadik, Shelach 14:3, preserves both sides of the Gemara by teaching that each can be true in a different respect. Thus 'greater than a complete tzaddik' here is not a blanket rule that pain automatically elevates. It is the possible rank of the person who uses pain to make a real inward return and then transforms the distance itself into greater closeness.

וְאִם כֵּן וַדַּאי דַּהֲרֵי הוּא מֵעַתָּה בִּכְלַל עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם דְּנִקְרָאִים ״בָּנִים״ וְלֹא ״עֲבָדִים״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י עַמּוּד א), וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְרַבִּי מֵאִיר (בְּקִדּוּשִׁין לו עַמּוּד א) דִּלְעוֹלָם נִקְרָאִים ״בָּנִים״

And if so, he certainly belongs henceforth to the category of those who fulfill the will of the Omnipresent, who are designated “sons” and not “servants,” as they said (Bava Basra 10a), and all the more so according to Rabbi Meir (Kiddushin 36a), who holds that under all circumstances they are called “sons”;466Expanded source note: Israel as sons even after sin: Bava Basra 10a contrasts two modes of relation to God. When Israel does the will of the Omnipresent it is called sons; when it does not, servants. Kiddushin 36a records the fuller dispute on 'You are sons to Hashem your God' (Devarim 14:1). R' Yehudah says the title sons depends upon behaving as sons; R' Meir says, 'either way you are called sons,' and brings verses that call Israel foolish sons, faithless sons, and corrupt sons. Rashi emphasizes the climax: even after the corruption of idolatry they can again be called 'sons of the living God' through repentance. Accordingly, R' Tzadok's argument works on both opinions. For R' Yehudah, the sincere penitent is now doing God's will and should be called a son; for R' Meir, the essential filial bond was never annulled. The Zoharic framework sharpens this second reading. Yahel Or on Zohar II 254b, drawing on Zohar III 36a-37a, explains that even when Israel's deeds are corrupt it remains rooted on the right side; the left may rule over it because of its deeds, but it does not become mixed with that side permanently. He therefore reads 'Return, wayward sons' literally: although wayward, they remain sons and are summoned to return, and he explicitly cites R' Meir in Kiddushin. The exceptional story of Acher marks the danger of believing oneself excluded, while Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 answers even that despair with 'until the crushing of the soul they receive.' R' Tzadok's wider theology is parallel: Takanas HaShavin 3:1 says the baal teshuvah can return from beyond the ordinary bounds of law because the Divine hand remains extended there, and Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 compares Israel to a rose among thorns whose root remains intact beneath the surrounding damage. The se'if's unresolved difficulty is therefore precise. 'Servant' cannot describe Israel's final essence after true teshuvah; it must name a stage, manner of awakening, or degree of revealed closeness, which the following sections will define.
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב עוֹד גִּירְסָא אַחֶרֶת וּפֵירוּשׁ אַחֵר דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע קוֹדֶם שֶׁתָּשׁוּבוּ
and as for what [Rashi] further wrote as an alternative textual reading and interpretation, that “I have become a master/husband to you [ba’alti]” (Yirmeyah 3:14) implies before you repent,

וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר כַּוָּונָתוֹ דְּעַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מְתַקְּנִים לְמַפְרֵעַ לַעֲקוֹר הַחֵטְא מֵעִיקָּרוֹ, כְּמוֹ חָכָם הָעוֹקֵר הַנֶּדֶר מֵעִיקָּרוֹ, דְּמִמֵּילָא אִגַּלַּאי מִילְּתָא הַשְׁתָּא דְּגַם לְמַפְרֵעַ הָיוּ מְרוּצִים

his meaning must be that through repentance one rectifies retroactively to uproot the sin from its inception, like a sage who uproots a vow from its root, whereby it is revealed now that they were accepted even retroactively.

וְאִם זֶה, לָא עֲדִיפָא דְּתִינַח תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה דְּהוּא כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, אֲבָל מִיִּרְאָה דְּכִשְׁגָגוֹת וְהַשּׁוֹגֵג עֲדַיִין צָרִיךְ סְלִיחָה, וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ אַכַּתִּי ״בָּעַלְתִּי בָכֶם״ גַּם מִקּוֹדֶם כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נֶעֱקַר עֲדַיִין לְגַמְרֵי

And if so, this is difficult: it works well for teshuvah from love, where [sins] become like merits, but for teshuvah from fear, which renders them like inadvertent errors where the inadvertent sin still requires pardon, “I was a master to you” would not yet apply to the period beforehand, since it has not yet been fully uprooted;
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין (צז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) מַיְיתֵי מִקְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ דִּבְלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל וְזֶה עִנְיָן אַחֵר, וְשָׁם פֵּירַשׁ רַשִׁ״י דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע בְּעַל כָּרְחֲכֶם וְכוּלֵיהּ

and in Sanhedrin (97b) they cite the verse of “I was a master to you” as referring to a state without any teshuvah at all, which is a different matter, and there Rashi explains that ba’alti denotes “against your will,” etc.,
וְשַׁפִּיר יְפוֹרַשׁ גַּם עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, דְּהוּא בְּעַל כָּרְחוֹ, וְלֹא מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה דְּהוּא מֵרְצוֹנוֹ שָׁב
and it can be well explained as referring to [teshuvah] through afflictions, which occurs against his will, unlike repentance from love and fear where he returns of his own free will;
וְעַל כֵּן פְּשָׁט ״בָּעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע וַדַּאי דִּמְפָרֵשׁ לֵיהּ אַעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and therefore the plain sense of ba’alti certainly implies that he interprets it as referring to repentance through suffering.

וְקָרוֹב יוֹתֵר דְּהוּא לְשׁוֹן בַּעַל לְאִשָּׁה וְלֹא אָדוֹן לְעֶבֶד, דִּכְשֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְעוֹרְרוֹ (עַל יְדֵי הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁמֵּבִיא עָלָיו) הוּא מִסִּטְרָא דְּנוּקְבָּא כְּאִשָּׁה הַמְקַבֶּלֶת מִבַּעְלָהּ

And it is closer [to the truth] that it is a term of a husband [ba'al] to a wife rather than a master to a slave: for when the Holy One, blessed be He, arouses him (through the afflictions He brings upon him), he is from the aspect of the feminine, like a wife who receives from her husband;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן ״בָּנִים״ הוּא דְּכוּרָא, זֶהוּ כְּשֶׁשָּׁבוּ מֵהִתְעוֹרְרוּת עַצְמָם מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
whereas “sons” corresponds to the masculine, representing a return that originates from their own awakening, out of love and fear;
וְגַם כְּפִי הַנּוּסְחָא אַחֲרָא דְּרַשִׁ״י קְרָא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ אֵלַי״ הַיְינוּ בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא דִּידְהוּ
and also according to Rashi’s alternate reading, the verse “Return to Me” refers to an awakening from below [it'aruta d'letata] on their part.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the Maharsha’s resolution of the Talmudic contradiction in Yoma 86a between “Return, wayward children” (Yirmeyah 3:22) and “for I am a master to you” (3:14). R’ Tzadok demonstrates the logical flaws in assuming the contradiction is between “repentance” and “no repentance,” proving that the questioner already knew both verses refer to forms of teshuvah, and that the difficulty lies in the discrepancy of scope: why one verse promises complete communal restoration while the other selects only “one from a city and two from a family.”

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שָׁם הִרְגִּישׁ בְּמַה שֶׁהִקְשֵׁיתִי מֵהַהוּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין
And then I saw that the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados there felt the difficulty I raised from that passage in Sanhedrin (97b),

וּפֵירֵשׁ כֵּן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר הַגִּירְסָא דְּהָרוּמְיָא, דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ מַשְׁמַע בִּתְשׁוּבָה דַּוְוקָא וּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל מִסַּנְהֶדְרִין, וּמְשַׁנֵּי דְּהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and explained that this must be the reading of the contradiction: that “Return” implies specifically with repentance, while “I was a master to you” implies without repentance as mentioned above from Sanhedrin, and the Gemara resolves that it refers to repentance through suffering — see there.467Expanded source note: The textual setting of Se'if 2 is the second of two adjacent derashos on Yoma 86a. First, R' Chama bar Chanina contrasts the beginning of Yirmeyah 3:22, 'Return, wayward sons,' with its conclusion, 'I will heal your waywardness.' Rashi explains that return from love uproots the sin from its beginning, whereas return from fear leaves the former blemish perceptible like the name of an invalid who has been healed. Rav Yehudah then contrasts that entire verse with Yirmeyah 3:14, 'for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family,' and the Gemara answers: here from love or fear, there through sufferings. Rashi's principal explanation reads the titles: returners from love or fear are called sons, while those who did not return until suffering struck are called servants. Rashi then records an alternate text: the contradiction is between 'Return to Me and I shall return to you' and 'I am already a Master to you' - the first describes Divine return after human repentance, the second Divine mastery before repentance. Maharsha rejects the need for that alternate text and preserves the standard editions; the next note gives his construction. Maharal, Netivos Olam, Netiv HaTeshuvah 2, offers an important conceptual parallel without relying on the Maharsha's three-clause mapping. 'Return ... I will heal' indicates an awakening that begins within the person; 'I am a Master to you' indicates an awakening initiated by God, who compels the person through suffering. Maharal thus distinguishes love, fear, and suffering as three grades of agency and associates them with Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov: love is inner attachment, fear is the person's own response to an external demand, and suffering is an arousal imposed from above. R' Tzadok accepts the reality of those three modes but tests whether the wording and chosen verses support either Rashi's labels or Maharsha's reconstruction. His wider teaching explains why the textual point matters. Resisei Layla 21 says that only after teshuvah from love will it be disclosed that Israel's sins too were within the Divine order established from Creation; Tzidkas HaTzadik 40 likewise defines the deepest repentance as the illumination in which deliberate sins become merits, while Tzidkas HaTzadik 52 and Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 13, show that suffering can begin a genuine national return. The se'if therefore does not reject repentance born from fear or pain. It asks how an externally forced beginning relates to the later inward return that heals and transforms. The halachic baseline remains Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2: abandonment of the sin, regret, resolution, and confession make the act teshuvah; the aggadic distinctions here concern its mode, depth, and revealed relationship to God, not whether pain automatically atones or whether a fearful penitent is excluded.,468Expanded source note: Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados to Yoma 86a - text, source, and R' Tzadok's critique: R' Shmuel Eliezer Edels (1555-1631) wrote Chiddushei Aggados to clarify the non-legal passages of the Bavli. Here he says that Rashi's alternate reading is forced and that 'all the text of the editions' should be maintained. He reads Yoma together with Sanhedrin 97b-98a. There R' Eliezer says that Israel is redeemed only if it repents; R' Yehoshua answers that if Israel does not repent, the Holy One will set over it a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman's, Israel will repent, and He will restore them to the good. In the following Scriptural exchange R' Yehoshua cites Yirmeyah 3:14, 'for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family,' as a promise of redemption not dependent upon an earlier voluntary return. Maharsha combines these passages and maps three phrases in Yoma onto three responses: 'Return, wayward sons' describes voluntary repentance from love; 'I will heal your waywardness' describes repentance from fear of punishment; and 'I am a Master to you' describes compelled repentance through sufferings, when God raises a Haman-like ruler and thereby restores Israel. This reading is theologically close to Maharal's distinction between human arousal and Divine compulsion, but R' Tzadok objects to its syntax. If the initial force of 'I am a Master' is that God acts before Israel repents, the Gemara should have answered explicitly that this too ends in teshuvah - the repentance produced by the harsh king and the sufferings. Its balanced formula, 'here ... and here ...,' implies that both verses were already understood to describe teshuvah and that the unresolved contrast lies in some other detail. His second objection is still more textual. Yirmeyah 3:14 itself begins, 'Return, wayward sons, says Hashem,' before continuing 'for I am a Master to you.' If the problem were simply son versus servant, or return versus no return, why did Rav Yehudah cite the later verse 3:22 - 'Return, wayward sons, I will heal your waywardness' - instead of allowing the apparent contradiction to stand within 3:14 itself? Classical peshat also cautions against turning ba'alti into a technical denial of repentance: Rashi on Yirmeyah understands it as Divine lordship and refusal to abandon Israel to the enemy; Radak records the covenantal-marital sense; Malbim emphasizes renewed attachment even when only a remnant returns. A later discussion in Marit HaAyin to Yoma insists that even repentance from fear restores the legal-spiritual title of son, and cites the Rashba's ruling that Israel remains children even in sin. Consistently, Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1-2 and 7:4, distinguishes the completeness and rank of repentance without saying that an awakening caused by fear or suffering is unreal once the sinner genuinely abandons the sin. R' Tzadok will therefore retain Maharsha's crucial Sanhedrin background but relocate the contradiction. In Se'if 3 he reads it in the endings of the verses: 3:22 promises healing to all who return from their own arousal, whereas 3:14 concludes that only 'one from a city' truly returns under an arousal from above and brings merit to the rest. This explains both the verses chosen by the Gemara and the phrase 'here ... here' without branding a sincere penitent permanently as a servant.
וּפֵירוּשׁ זֶה גַּם כֵּן אֵינוֹ מְחֻוָּור, דְּאִי לְסַלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ ״בָּעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה, לָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר ״כָּאן וְכוּלֵיהּ וְכָאן וְכוּלֵיהּ״

But this explanation too is not well clarified: for if it could enter your mind that ba’alti meant without repentance, the Gemara should not have formulated its answer as “here [it refers to...] and here [it refers to...]”;
לָא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמֵימַר הָכִי נַמֵּי עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה דְּמַעֲמִיד וְכוּלֵיהּ וְעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
rather, it should have said: “this too is through repentance, for He appoints a cruel king over them, etc., through afflictions”;

אֲבָל הַלָּשׁוֹן ״כָּאן וְכוּלֵיהּ״ מַשְׁמַע דְּיָדַע גַּם בְּסַלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ רָצָה לוֹמַר עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, רַק דְּהוּקְשָׁה לֵיהּ דִּבְאֵיזֶה דָּבָר לֹא דָּמֵי דְּעַל זֶה יִפּוֹל לְשׁוֹן הַשִּׁינּוּי, דְּכָאן בְּמִין זֶה דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה וְכָאן בְּזֶה

but the phrasing “here... and here...” implies that even in its initial assumption, the Gemara understood that ba’alti refers to repentance, and was troubled only by what difference exists between them that justifies the phrasing distinguishing one category of repentance from another.

וְאִי הַקּוּשְׁיָא דְּלָא דָּמֵי הוּא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ מַשְׁמַע אַתֶּם וּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ מַשְׁמַע אֲנִי וְעַל יָדִי, אִם הַקּוּשְׁיָא לָמָּה פְּעָמִים כָּךְ וּפְעָמִים כָּךְ, עַל זֶה לֹא תֵּירֵץ כְּלוּם בִּלְשׁוֹן ״כָּאן״

And if the difficulty of their divergence was that “Return” implies an initiative by you, while “I was a master” implies by Me, or why it is sometimes this way and sometimes that way, the Gemara resolved nothing of this by merely stating “here [from love or fear] and there [through suffering]”;
רַק הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר: הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַמְתִּין לָאָדָם, אִם שָׁב מֵעַצְמוֹ מוּטָב, וְאִם לָאו בְּעַלְתִּים כָּל כָּךְ
it should rather have stated: the Blessed Name waits for man; if he repents of his own accord, it is well, and if not, He coerces them thus;
וְאִם הַקּוּשְׁיָא אֵיךְ בַּמְּצִיאוּת לַהֲשִׁיבָם בְּעַל כָּרְחָם, זֶה וַדַּאי אֵינוֹ בְּגֶדֶר קוּשְׁיָא כְּלָל כְּלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא
and if the question was how in reality can people be made to repent against their will, this is certainly no question at all regarding Heaven.
וְגַם הַלָּשׁוֹן ״כָּאן וְכוּלֵיהּ״ אֵין נָכוֹן בָּזֶה, וְרֵישָׁא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר יָדַע גַּם הַמַּקְשֶׁה דְּהוּא מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
Furthermore, the phrasing “here... and here...” would not fit this, and the opening of “Return” the questioner already knew corresponds to love and fear;

וְתוּ יֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק בַּגִּירְסָא שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ מִקְּרָא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״, לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י וּמַהַרְשָׁ״א לָמָּה מַיְיתֵי הַאי קְרָא דְּאַחַר כָּךְ וְלֹא רֵישֵׁיהּ דִּקְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ עַצְמוֹ, דְּפָתַח גַּם כֵּן ״שׁוּבוּ בָנִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, דְּקָרֵי לְהוּ ״בָנִים״ וְאָמַר ״שׁוּבוּ״

and further, one must examine according to the text before us citing the verse “Return... I will heal your backslidings” (Yirmeyah 3:22): according to Rashi and Maharsha, why did it cite that later verse rather than the opening of the ba’alti verse itself (3:14), which likewise begins “Return, O backsliding children,” explicitly calling them “children” and bidding them to “return”?
וְאִי דְּבָעֵי לַאֲתוֹיֵי ״אֶרְפָּא״, דִּלְרַשִׁ״י הַיְינוּ מִיִּרְאָה, לוֹמַר דְּאַף מִיִּרְאָה נִקְרָאִים ״בָּנִים״, קָשֶׁה הָא גוּפֵיהּ מְנָא לֵיהּ

And if one suggests it wished to cite “I will heal,” which according to Rashi represents teshuvah from fear, to demonstrate that even through fear they are called “sons,” this itself is difficult: from where would he derive this?
דַּהֲלֹא יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לוֹמַר דְּמִיִּרְאָה לָא, אֵימָא אִין הָכִי נַמֵּי דִּבְסֵיפֵיהּ דְּ״אֶרְפָּא״ לֹא כְּתִיב ״בָּנִים״
For there is room to argue that through fear they are not [called sons], and one could say indeed that in the clause of “I will heal” the word “sons” is not written;

וּמִלְּשׁוֹן ״מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ אֵין לְדַיֵּיק דְּאַ״בָּנִים״ דְּרֵישֵׁיהּ קָאֵי, דִּבְהַאי קְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ נַמֵּי כְּתִיב ״בָּנִים״ בְּרֵישֵׁיהּ וְלֹא אָמַר דְּ״אֶתְכֶם״ אַ״בָּנִים״ דְּרֵישֵׁיהּ קָאֵי

and from the word “your backslidings” one cannot infer that it refers back to “sons” in the opening, because in that verse of ba’alti as well “sons” is written in its opening, yet the Gemara did not say that “I will take you” relates to the “sons” of the beginning;
וְהָתָם נִמְשָׁךְ טְפֵי לְרֵישֵׁיהּ מִמַּה שֶׁאָמַר ״כִּי אָנֹכִי״ וְגוֹמֵר, דְּמִלַּת ״כִּי״ מַשְׁמַע שֶׁקָּאֵי אַ״שׁוּבוּ״ דִּלְעֵיל
and there it is even more directly continuous with the opening because it says “for I [am a master to you],” where the word “for” connects directly to the preceding “Return.”

וּבֶאֱמֶת מֵהַאי טַעְמָא גַּם כֵּן דָּחֵיק לְפִי דִּבְרֵיהֶם שֶׁנִּצְטָרֵךְ לִהְיוֹת סַכִּינָא חָרִיפָא מְפַסְּקֵי קְרָאֵי, וּלְשׁוֹן ״כִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר מַשְׁמַע דְּפֵרוּשֵׁי מְפָרֵשׁ וְהַכֹּל עִנְיָן אֶחָד

And indeed, for this reason it is also forced according to their approach, requiring a “sharp knife to sever the verses,” whereas the word “for” indicates an ongoing explanation, the entire verse forming a single cohesive theme.

וְתוּ יֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק כְּפִי הַנּוּסְחָא בַּגְּמָרָא שֶׁלְּפָנֵינוּ מַסִּיק לְסֵיפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֶחָד מֵעִיר״ וְגוֹמֵר, דְּמַה דְּמַיְיתֵי לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב כּוּלּוֹ דְּ״וְלָקַחְתִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר הוּא לְלֹא צֹרֶךְ

And furthermore, one must examine why, according to the text in the Gemara before us, it cites the end of the verse of ba’alti, “one from a city and two from a family,” for citing the entire conclusion “and I will take you” seems unnecessary;
וּבְעֵין יַעֲקֹב הַגִּירְסָא ״וְגוֹמֵר״, וְגַם מִלַּת ״וְגוֹמֵר״ הוּא לְמוֹתָר אִם הָרוּמְיָא מִמִּלַּת ״בָעַלְתִּי״ לְבַד
while in Ein Yaakov the reading is simply “etc.”, yet even the word “etc.” is superfluous if the contradiction rested solely on the word ba’alti.

items.h: The theme: The true core of the Talmud’s question lies in the contrast of outcomes: the first verse promises universal communal return and healing for all Israel, whereas the second verse restricts the taking to “one from a city and two from a family.” R’ Tzadok explains that when teshuvah begins from below through love or fear, all who repent merit healing according to their level. But when repentance is triggered from Above through suffering, only rare individuals (“one from a city”) penetrate beyond the desire to escape pain and reach genuine teshuvah from love—who then merit to bring spiritual vindication to their entire city.

p: וְעַל כֵּן נִרְאֶה לְפָרֵשׁ דְּעִיקַּר הַקּוּשְׁיָא הוּא רַק מִסִּיּוּם לְשׁוֹן הַנִּזְכָּר, דְּהָתָם כְּתִיב ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְ״אֶרְפָּא״ לְכוּלָּם

Therefore it appears right to explain that the primary difficulty arises strictly from the concluding words mentioned: for there (Yirmeyah 3:22) it is written “Return” to all Israel and “I will heal” to all of them,
וְהָכָא כְּתִיב נַמֵּי ״שׁוּבוּ״ וּמְסַיֵּים דְּיִקַּח רַק ״אֶחָד מֵעִיר״ וְגוֹמֵר
whereas here (3:14) it is also written “Return,” yet it concludes that He will take only “one from a city and two from a family”;

וְגַם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין קיא רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א) ״אֶחָד מֵעִיר מְזַכֶּה כָּל הָעִיר״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, מְבוֹאָר מִכָּל מָקוֹם דְּרַק אֶחָד הוּא הַזּוֹכֶה וּמְזַכֶּה, וְאַמַּאי לֹא כוּלָּם, שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ כוּלָּם וְיִרְפָּא כוּלָּם וְיִזְכּוּ כָּל אֶחָד מֵהֶם

and even according to what is taught (Sanhedrin 111a) that “one from a city brings merit to the entire city,” it is still clear that only one is the individual who attains merit and bestows it, so why not all of them, seeing that the verse should have stated that all will return, all will be healed, and every one of them will merit personally?469Expanded source note: Sanhedrin 111a - source, meforshim, and the reach of one person's merit: This teaching appears in the closing aggadah of Perek Chelek, amid discussions of how many will be redeemed. On Yirmeyah 3:14, Reish Lakish first says devarim ki-kesavan, 'the words are literal': only one from a city and two from a family will be taken. R' Yochanan objects, 'It is not pleasing to their Master that you say this about them,' and expounds that one person's merit benefits the entire city and two benefit the entire family. The Gemara repeats the same exchange between Rav Kahana and Rav, making clear that the merciful reading is deliberate and not a casual paraphrase. Rashi explains the objection as: do not diminish Israel so drastically. Yalkut Shimoni on Nach 270:3 preserves this dispute as a midrash on the verse and thereby shows its independent place in the later aggadic source tradition. The peshat traditions need not deny the derash. R' Yosef Kara explains the simple sense as a future gathering of scattered survivors, collected one from this city and two from that family, who will later multiply in Zion. Malbim likewise reads 'one from a city' as the small remnant that God will nonetheless take and restore. Sanhedrin transforms that image of a remnant into collective merit: the few are not merely saved from the many; their merit becomes the means by which the many are saved. R' Tzadok adopts R' Yochanan's derash but gives it a precise role in the Yoma sugya. When suffering produces only a wish that suffering stop, the person has not yet made the pain into return for Hashem's sake. The 'one from a city' is the rare person in whom the arousal from Above becomes a genuine inward teshuvah, and he thereby brings merit to those whose response remains incomplete. A closely related baraisa in Yoma 86b states in R' Meir's name that because of one individual who repents, he and the whole world are forgiven, deriving this from Hoshea 14:5, 'I will heal their waywardness ... for My anger has turned from him' - 'from them' is not written, but 'from him.' Tzidkat HaTzadik 159 asks how one person's repentance can yield forgiveness for others and answers that the exceptional penitent awakens stirrings of teshuvah in their hearts as well; he also warns that not everyone can simply declare himself that singular individual. This supplies the inner mechanism for the present se'if: the one merits the city by beginning a real movement within it. The kabbalistic parallel is Zohar Chadash, Midrash HaNe'elam on Noach, near its conclusion: if even one congregation returns in teshuvah, the merit of that gathering can draw in the entire exile. The individual, congregation, city, and nation are therefore successive circles of one principle - an authentic point of return can become the channel of a collective redemption. The halachic boundary remains important. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:2-3, requires each sinner's own abandonment of the sin, regret, resolve, and confession; another person's merit does not perform those acts in his place. The aggadah describes collective favor, rescue, and awakening, not a legal substitution of one confession for another. This also prepares Se'if 4: even after the one has conferred merit, the prophetic call and daily bas kol continue to summon every other person to turn the externally granted opening into his own complete return.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר: כָּאן מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה, דִּבְהָכִי מִתּוֹקָם קְרָא דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר ״אֶרְפָּא״ וְגוֹמֵר דִּלְעֵיל
And to this the Gemara answers: here [where all are healed] it is from love and fear, whereby that former verse of “Return... and I will heal” is established;
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁשָּׁבוּ בְּעַצְמָם מֵאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּידְהוּ, כּוּלָּם זוֹכִים לִרְפוּאָה כָּל אֶחָד כְּפִי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
and since they repented of their own accord through an awakening from below, all of them merit healing, each according to his teshuvah.
וּקְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״, דְּמַשְׁמַע בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא הוּא שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ הַיְינוּ עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, בָּזֶה רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

But the verse of ba’alti, which implies that their return is driven by an awakening from Above through afflictions, in this case only “one from a city” repents in genuine truth to the Blessed Name,470Expanded source note: Yoma 86a and R' Tzadok's reading of the two verses: Rav Yehudah sets Yirmeyah 3:22, 'Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness,' against Yirmeyah 3:14, 'Return, wayward sons ... for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family.' The Gemara answers: here from love or fear, there through sufferings. Rashi and Maharsha, discussed in the preceding notes, locate the contrast in the titles 'sons' and 'servants,' or in voluntary versus compelled return. R' Tzadok instead asks why the Gemara cited the later verse 3:22 when verse 3:14 itself begins with the same summons, 'Return, wayward sons.' He therefore moves the contradiction to the endings. Verse 3:22 addresses all Israel and promises healing to all who return; verse 3:14 ends with only 'one from a city and two from a family.' The difference is not whether the latter people repent, but how the movement began. Love and fear are an it'aruta di-letata, an arousal initiated by the person, so each returner receives the healing corresponding to his own teshuvah. Suffering is an it'aruta di-le'eila, an arousal initiated from Above. Many seek only relief from pain; the rare 'one from a city' allows the suffering to awaken a return directed to Hashem Himself, and his merit then reaches the rest. This reading also preserves R' Tzadok's insistence in Se'if 1 that teshuvah born amid suffering can be complete once it becomes truthful and inward. The classical commentators help define the derash. Rashi on Yirmeyah 3:14 explains ba'alti as Divine lordship: Israel bears God's Name, and His honor does not permit Him to abandon them to their enemies. Radak records both the covenantal-marital sense - God will take Israel back after divorce - and the Targum's 'I desired you'; Malbim reads the verse as God's attachment to the children even where the earlier generation failed, promising to gather even a tiny remnant. These are peshat and covenantal readings, whereas R' Tzadok is explaining the Bavli's juxtaposition and the spiritual process implied by its answer. His terminology belongs to a larger pattern in his sefarim. Takanat HaShavin 5:4 contrasts the human demand, 'Return to Me,' with the hope that an arousal from Above will first draw Israel; there too, the enduring goal is that the upper awakening be followed by the person's own return. Tzidkat HaTzadik 159 explains that the repentance of a unique individual can benefit the whole world because it awakens thoughts of teshuvah in other hearts, not because his inner act mechanically replaces theirs. Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 14, similarly notices the movement in Hoshea from the singular 'Return, Israel' to the plural 'Take words with you and return,' treating individual return as capable of opening a communal movement. Thus the present se'if is not a theory of automatic atonement through pain. It is a theory of how a Divine interruption becomes human teshuvah, first in the exceptional individual and then, through him, in the community.
וְלֹא מִשּׁוּם לְהִנָּצֵל מֵהַיִּסּוּרִין עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְבַד, רַק שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַיִּסּוּרִין הוּא מִתְעוֹרֵר, וּמִשֶּׁנִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב הוּא שָׁב בֶּאֱמֶת וּמְזַכֶּה כָּל הָעִיר
and not merely to escape suffering thereby, but rather through the suffering he is awakened, and once awakened, he returns in authentic truth and brings merit to the entire city.
וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּלָא נִיחָא לְמָרַיְיהוּ לְמֵימַר עַל כָּל הַשָּׁבִים מִיִּסּוּרִים שֶׁאֵינָם בֶּאֱמֶת אֶלָּא אֶחָד בָּעִיר
And even if you say that their Master does not wish to assert of all who repent through suffering that only one in a city is sincere,
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהָכָא מַיְירֵי בִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה, וְלֹא מִבַּעְיָא לְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י דְּ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ הַיְינוּ מֵאַהֲבָה
one can answer that here it deals with complete teshuvah; and not only according to Rashi who explains that shovavim denotes teshuvah from love

(וְיֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק לְפִי דְּבָרָיו אַגִּירְסָא ב׳ דְּמַיְיתֵי דְּמוֹקֵי קְרָא דְּ״בָעַלְתִּי״ מֵאַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה, וְהָא כְּתִיב בֵּיהּ ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ דִּלְפִי דְּבָרָיו הַיְינוּ מֵאַהֲבָה, וְלָמָּה מַזְכִּיר גַּם מִיִּרְאָה, צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר לֵיהּ דְּקָאֵי גַּם אַמִּירְאָה)

(and one may observe according to his words on the second reading cited, which establishes the verse of ba’alti as referring to love and fear: behold, shovavim is written in it, which according to him signifies love, so why mention fear as well? Perforce he must hold it encompasses fear too);

אֶלָּא גַּם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי (בַּסִּימָן הַקּוֹדֵם) דְּ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ מַשְׁמַע מִיִּרְאָה וְכִשְׁגָגוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם קְרָא דְּ״לָקַחְתִּי״ דְּבַתְרֵיהּ הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁיִּזְכּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִזְכֻיּוֹת

but even according to what I wrote (in the preceding Siman 11) that shovavim indicates fear and inadvertence, nonetheless the subsequent phrase “and I will take you” refers to when they later merit that sins become merits.

וְכָךְ הַמִּדָּה דִּתְחִלַּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין דְּוַדַּאי אֵין תְּחִלָּתוֹ בָּא אֶלָּא בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת יִרְאָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ זוֹכֶה לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת מֵאַהֲבָה

And such is the principle: the beginning of teshuvah is from fear, and all the more so when repenting through suffering, where the start certainly comes only through an awakening of fear, and only afterward does he merit to return truly from love;

וְכִדִמְסַיֵּים הָתָם אַחַר כָּךְ ״אֶרְפָּא״, דְּהַיְינוּ כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי רְפוּאָה גְּמוּרָה שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, הָכִי נַמֵּי הָכָא דִּמְסַיֵּים ״וְלָקַחְתִּי״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה אַחַר כָּךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה

and just as it concludes there afterward “I will heal,” which means a complete cure where sins become merits, so too here where it concludes “and I will take you,” it means that he merits afterward teshuvah from love;
זֶהוּ רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר כְּשֶׁהַהַתְחָלָה בְּאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and this is attained by only “one from a city” when the inception was an awakening from Above through suffering.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמִּכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט בֶּאֱמֶת, דַּי שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כִּשְׁגָגוֹת כִּתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה שֶׁהֲרֵי תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ מִיִּרְאַת הַיִּסּוּרִין שֶׁבָּאוּ עָלָיו
And although he truly repents and regrets, which suffices to make them like inadvertent sins as in teshuvah from fear, since his repentance stemmed from fear of the suffering that befell him;

אוֹ גַּם אִם יִזְכֶּה לִמְחִילַת הַשּׁוֹגֵג, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְהִתְהַפֵּךְ עוֹד לִזְכֻיּוֹת — שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁלֵימוּת הַתִּיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁיִּהְיוּ רְאוּיִים לִגְאוּלָּה שְׁלֵימָה בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ

or even if he merits the pardon of the inadvertent sin, nevertheless to be transformed further into merits — which is the absolute perfection of teshuvah from love, rendering them worthy of complete Redemption speedily in our days —
לָאו כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה, אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי אֶחָד מֵעִיר הַזּוֹכֶה לְכָךְ וּמְזַכֶּה כָּל אֶחָיו עִמּוֹ שֶׁיִּזְכּוּ גַּם כֵּן לְתִיקּוּן הַגָּמוּר עַל יָדוֹ דַּוְוקָא
not every person merits this, except through “one from a city” who attains it and bestows merit upon all his brethren with him, so that they too attain full rectification specifically through him;

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כְּשֶׁשָּׁב בְּעַצְמוֹ מֵהִתְעוֹרְרוּתוֹ, אַף דִּתְחִלָּתוֹ מִיִּרְאָה, כָּל אָדָם יוּכַל לִזְכּוֹת אִם לֹא יִתְרַשֵּׁל בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ לְמֵאַהֲבָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּשֶׁתְּחִלָּתוֹ מֵאַהֲבָה

whereas when one returns on his own through his own awakening, even if his start was from fear, every individual can merit it if he does not grow lax in his repentance, advancing subsequently to love, and all the more so when his beginning was from love.

items.h: The theme: Even when teshuvah begins through suffering (where only "one from a city" reaches complete teshuvah from love), the prophetic call "Return, wayward sons" continues to resound, urging a return from love for all Israel. This divine voice (bas kol) goes forth every day. Even those initially awakened by affliction can subsequently elevate their return to teshuvah from love. Hashem guarantees that the prophetic call—implanted eternally in Scripture—will not return void; eventually, all Israel will return from love, for they are all "sons of the Lord your God."

p: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הַכָּתוּב צָוַוח ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, אַף דִּכְבָר ״בָּעַלְתִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְעוֹרַרְתִּי הַהַתְחָלָה עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, וְ״לָקַחְתִּי רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר״ הַמְזַכֶּה כּוּלָּם, שֶׁהוּא מִתּוֹךְ הַיִּסּוּרִין עַצְמָן הִתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת מֵאַהֲבָה

Nevertheless, the verse cries out “Return” (Yirmeyah 3:22), even though [it already stated] “I was a master to you” (3:14), and I aroused the beginning through suffering, “and I took only one from a city” who brings merit to all, he being the one who from within the suffering itself awakened to return truly from love;
עֲדַיִין גַּם הַשְּׁאָר הַנָּבִיא מְעוֹרְרָם בִּדְבַר ה׳ לָשׁוּב עוֹד מֵאַהֲבָה, דְּ״שׁוּבוּ בָנִים״ לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל קָאָמַר

still, the rest [of the people] too, the prophet arouses them with the word of Hashem to return further, out of love, for “Return, [wayward] children” is said to all Israel.471Teshuvah from love: Yoma 86b teaches that when one repents from love, intentional sins are transformed into merits; when one repents from fear, they are reduced to inadvertent sins. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6-7, describes the baal teshuvah as beloved and close to Hashem, and stresses that yesterday he was separated and today he is attached to the Shechinah. R’ Tzadok therefore says that even one initially moved only by suffering can afterward “return again from love.” The first movement may have been compelled by pain, but the daily Divine summons enables a second, freely chosen teshuvah that changes the quality of the entire past.,472Yirmeyahu 3:14 and 3:22 — the two prophetic calls underlying the entire discussion. Verse 14 says, “Return, wayward sons ... for I have been a Master to you; I will take you one from a city and two from a family,” while verse 22 says, “Return, wayward sons; I will heal your waywardness.” Yoma 86a places these verses in tension and distinguishes voluntary teshuvah from return awakened through suffering; Sanhedrin 111a interprets “one from a city” mercifully, that one person can bring merit to the whole city. Rashi explains ba’alti as Hashem’s lordship and covenantal claim over Israel; Radak records both the marital sense and the Targum’s sense, “I desired you”; Malbim emphasizes that Hashem gathers even a tiny remnant and restores it to Zion. R’ Tzadok’s point in this se’if is a further stage: even after the arousal from Above and the merit of the exceptional “one,” the command “Return, sons” continues to address every Jew. Collective merit opens the door, but it does not replace each person’s own inward return.

וְ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ לְרַשִׁ״י הַיְינוּ תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה; וְגַם לְדִידִי רָצָה לוֹמַר דִּכְבָר הֵם ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, וּמְעוֹרְרָם עוֹד לַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עֲדַיִין

And shovavim according to Rashi signifies teshuvah from love; and according to my own interpretation as well, it means that they are already shovavim [i.e., their sins rendered inadvertent] through the teshuvah born of suffering, and he arouses them further to continue and return still more.
רַק לָבוֹא מֵהַתְחָלַת הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין לְבַד לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה לֹא כָּל אָדָם זוֹכֶה
Except that to arrive from the initial awakening of suffering alone to teshuvah from love, not every person merits;
אֲבָל יוּכַל לְהִתְעוֹרֵר אַחַר כָּךְ בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת חֲדָשָׁה לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת, שֶׁלֹּא מֵהַיִּסּוּרִין לְבַד
but he is able to awaken afterward with a new awakening to return in truth, not from the suffering alone.
וְאַחַר דְּ״לָקַחְתִּי״ עַל יְדֵי אֶחָד מֵעִיר הַמְזַכֶּה כּוּלָּם, דְּלֵיכָּא עוֹד יִסּוּרִין (אוֹ אֲפִילּוּ לֹא נִסְתַּלְּקוּ עֲדַיִין), מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא מִתְעוֹרֵר עוֹד לָשׁוּב שֶׁלֹּא מֵחֲמָתָן

And after “I have taken” through the one from a city who brings merit to all, when there is no longer suffering (or even if it has not yet departed), he nevertheless awakens further to return, not on account of [the suffering].

וְדָבָר זֶה בְּיַד כָּל אֶחָד, לִזְכּוֹת גַּם אַחַר הָאַתְחַלְתָּא שֶׁעַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין; וְאַדְּרַבָּא נָקֵל עוֹד יוֹתֵר, מֵאַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר הִתְחִיל לָשׁוּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים אַף שֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין

And this matter is in the hand of each individual, to merit even after the beginning initiated by suffering; and on the contrary, it is even easier, since he has already begun to return in any event, even if it was through suffering.

וּבַת קוֹל יוֹצֵא בְּכָל יוֹם, כֵּן מוּבָא בַּסְּפָרִים [וְאוּלַי הוּא בְּאֵיזֶה מִדְרָשׁ, דְּבַגְּמָרָא חֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳ וּבִירוּשַׁלְמִי פֶּרֶק ב׳ דַּחֲגִיגָה וְרוּת רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק ״לִינִי הַלַּיְלָה״ וְקֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה עַל פָּסוּק ״טוֹב אַחֲרִית״ אֵין הַלָּשׁוֹן ״בְּכָל יוֹם״, רַק דְּאָז שָׁמַע אַחֵר הַבַּת קוֹל ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ]

And a Heavenly Voice [bas kol] goes forth every day, as brought in the sacred books [and perhaps it is in some Midrash, for in the Gemara Chagigah 15a, and in Yerushalmi Chagigah chapter 2, and in Ruth Rabbah on the verse “Tarry this night” (Ruth 3:13), and Koheles Rabbah on the verse “Better is the end” (Koheles 7:8), the phrase “every day” does not appear, only that Acher heard the bas kol “Return,” etc. then];473The daily bas kol: Avos 6:2 records that every day a heavenly voice goes forth from Chorev concerning the neglect of Torah. A parallel formulation, “Every day a bas kol goes forth and proclaims: Return, wayward sons,” is quoted in Sefer Chareidim and in Shelah, Aseres HaDibros, Yoma, Derech Chaim 137, in the name of the Zohar; it is also developed by Kedushas Levi, Ki Savo §7. Chagigah 15a, Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1, Rus Rabbah, and Koheles Rabbah preserve the particular bas kol heard by Acher: “Return, wayward sons — except for Acher.” The later mussar and chassidic tradition reads that episode together with the daily proclamation: the call is objectively renewed every day, though each person hears it only according to the openness of his heart. This is the source framework for R’ Tzadok’s phrase here.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהֵם הַהִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁנּוֹפְלִים בְּלֵב כָּל אָדָם, מִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִהְיוֹת לְבָבוֹ פָּנוּי לִשְׁמוֹעַ אוֹתוֹ קוֹל הַמְעוֹרְרוֹ

and it is known that these are the stirrings of teshuvah that fall into the heart of every person, whoever merits to have his heart clear to hear that voice arousing him.474“Stirrings of teshuvah that fall into every heart”: the Baal Shem Tov tradition explains the heavenly proclamations as the sudden thoughts of return that enter a person’s consciousness. Mekor Mayim Chayim, citing the Baal Shem Tov, asks who hears the daily bas kol and answers that the Creator’s awakening within the heart is itself the voice. Me’or Einayim, Vayera, writes that even a great sinner receives daily thoughts of teshuvah, which are a revelation of Hashem to him; Kedushas Levi says every Jew hears the call according to his level. Mesillas Yesharim 5 adds that thoughts born from reading or hearing rebuke can bring a person back without bodily suffering. R’ Tzadok joins these ideas: suffering may begin the awakening, but the inner thought of teshuvah is a continuing Divine invitation that the person must freely hear and answer.,475The “bas kol issuing every day, ‘Return, wayward sons!’” is cited by R’ Tzadok from the standard seforim. He notes that in the extant sources — Chagigah 15a, the Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1, Rus Rabbah (on “lodge the night,” Rus 3:13), and Koheles Rabbah (on “better is the end”) — the wording is not “every day” but rather the singular event in which Acher (Elisha ben Avuya) heard the bas kol. R’ Tzadok reads the daily “bas kol” as the perpetual stirrings of teshuvah that the prophetic word, fixed in Scripture, awakens in every generation’s hearts.
וְזֶה הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לֹא פָּסִיק לְעוֹלָם; גַּם עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַבַּת קוֹל יוֹצֵא גַּם כֵּן לְעוֹרְרוֹ לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם כֵּן
And this arousal never ceases; even through suffering, nevertheless the bas kol issues forth as well to awaken him to return in truth also.
וְרַק כְּשֶׁהוּא אֵין שׁוֹמֵעַ לְקוֹל הַבַּת קוֹל הַמְעוֹרְרוֹ, וְשָׁב רַק מֵחֲמַת הַיִּסּוּרִין, בָּזֶה הוּא רַק אֶחָד מֵעִיר שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִזְכּוֹת עַל יָדוֹ
And only when he does not listen to the voice of the bas kol arousing him, and returns solely on account of the suffering, in this case it is only “one from a city” through whom he must attain merit;

אֲבָל בְּיַד כָּל אָדָם הוּא גַּם אַחַר הַיִּסּוּרִין, דְּלֹא נִגְרַע כְּמוֹ בְּמַה שֶּׁהָיָה מִקּוֹדֶם, לְהִתְעוֹרֵר גַּם כֵּן עַל יְדֵי שְׁמִיעַת הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁהוּא דְּבַר הַנָּבִיא בִּדְבַר ה׳ הַקַּיָּים לְעוֹלָם

but it is in the hand of every person, even after the suffering—for he is not diminished compared to what he was before—to awaken as well by hearing the bas kol of “Return,” etc., which is the word of the prophet in the word of Hashem that endures forever.
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁנִּכְתְּבָה נְבוּאָתוֹ בְּסֵפֶר, דְּמִצְטָרֶכֶת לְדוֹרוֹת, הֲרֵי הַדִּיבּוּר קָבוּעַ וְקַיָּים וּפוֹעֵל לְדוֹרוֹת, בְּכָל דְּבַר ה׳

For since his prophecy was written in a book, being needed for [future] generations (Megillah 14a), the utterance is established, enduring, and effective for generations, regarding every word of Hashem,476Megillah 14a: after stating that forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses were recorded, the Gemara asks whether there were no others and answers that prophets actually arose in enormous numbers. Only “a prophecy needed for the generations was written; one not needed for the generations was not written.” In its plain sense, this explains the canon of Tanach: the recorded prophecies contain an enduring message for later generations. R’ Tzadok draws a stronger spiritual conclusion from the same rule. If the prophecy was written because it is needed for all generations, its speech is not merely historically relevant; it remains an active Divine utterance that continues to awaken the souls for whom it was preserved.
כְּעִנְיַן ״לְעוֹלָם ה׳ דְּבָרְךָ נִצָּב בַּשָּׁמָיִם״, וְנֶאֱמַר ״כֵּן יִהְיֶה דְבָרִי״ וְגוֹמֵר ״לֹא יָשׁוּב אֵלַי רֵיקָם כִּי אִם עָשָׂה אֶת״ וְגוֹמֵר ״שְׁלַחְתִּיו״

as in the concept of “Forever, O Hashem, Your word stands firm in the heavens” (Tehillim 119:89), and it says, “So shall My word be... it shall not return unto Me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it” (Yeshayah 55:11).477Tehillim 119:89, “Forever, Hashem, Your word stands firm in the heavens.” Radak, Ibn Ezra, Metzudas David, and Rambam in Moreh Nevuchim I:15 understand nitzav as permanence and unchanging endurance. Midrash Tehillim and Shemos Rabbah use the verse to teach that Hashem’s word and promise remain standing until fulfilled. The Baal Shem Tov, cited in Tanya, Shaar HaYichud VehaEmunah ch. 1, reads it ontologically: the letters of the Divine command that created the heavens remain within them continually, giving them existence at every moment. R’ Tzadok applies that chassidic principle to prophecy. The command “Return” remains “standing” in the world and continually gives life to new stirrings of teshuvah in Jewish hearts.

וְכָל דִּיבּוּרָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ מִפִּי נְבִיאָיו שֶׁנִּכְתְּבוּ בַּתַּנַ״ךְ הֵם פּוֹעֲלִים לְדוֹרוֹת עוֹלָם, בְּכָל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר, לְהוֹלִיד בִּלְבָבָם הִרְהוּרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וְהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לָשׁוּב

And all the utterances of the Blessed One from the mouths of His prophets that were recorded in Tanakh are operative for eternal generations, within all the souls of Israel, in every generation, to beget in their hearts stirrings of teshuvah and an awakening to return.478Yeshayah 55:10-11. The prophet compares Hashem’s word to rain and snow: they do not return upward before watering the earth, causing it to give birth and sprout, and producing seed and bread. So too, “My word ... shall not return to Me empty, but shall accomplish what I desired and succeed in that for which I sent it.” Rashi and Radak explain that the Divine promise will certainly be fulfilled; the agricultural comparison emphasizes that its effect may unfold through a process of hidden germination before becoming visible. This precisely supports R’ Tzadok’s language: the prophetic word planted in Tanach acts through the generations, “giving birth” to thoughts of teshuvah, even when its final fruit is not immediately apparent.
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מַבְטִיחַ דְּלֹא יָשׁוּב רֵיקָם, דְּסוֹף כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל לָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת

And the Blessed Name promises that it shall not return void, for ultimately all Israel will return in truth.479R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §10): “‘An individual who repents — he and the whole world are forgiven’; and Mashiach ben David will be the individual who repents in the full force of teshuvah, who will bring forgiveness to the whole world.” The se’if’s “one from a city” who repents wholly from love and brings merit to all — the power of the single penitent.,480“In the end all Israel will return in truth” is the formulation of Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:5: “All the prophets commanded concerning teshuvah ... and the Torah has already promised that Israel will ultimately perform teshuvah at the end of their exile, and immediately they will be redeemed.” His source is Devarim 30:1-3: “You shall return to Hashem your God ... and Hashem your God will return your captivity.” This is not merely a hopeful prediction but, in the Rambam’s halachic presentation, a promise embedded in Torah. R’ Tzadok reads Yeshayah’s “it shall not return empty” as the spiritual mechanism of that promise: the words of the prophets continue to work within Israel until the promised collective teshuvah becomes actual and true.
וְאַף שֶׁמִּתְקַיֵּים גַּם הַדִּיבּוּר ״כִּי אָנֹכִי בָּעַלְתִּי״ וְגוֹמֵר, שֶׁמְּעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין גַּם כֵּן
And although the utterance “for I was a master to you” is fulfilled as well, arousing through suffering too,

מִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם הַדִּיבּוּר ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ מֵאַהֲבָה כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל כּוּלָּם, שֶׁהֵם כּוּלָּם בָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, דִּכְתִיב ״בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם״, גַּם זֶה לֹא יָשׁוּב רֵיקָם

nevertheless, the utterance “Return,” etc., that all Israel in their entirety will return from love, for they are all children of His Name, may He be blessed, as it is written “You are children unto Hashem your God” (Devarim 14:1), this too shall not return void.

items.h: The theme: The Voice crying “Return” rings out most powerfully on Yom Kippur, especially when it falls on Shabbos, reaching every Jewish heart. This is when Elisha ben Avuyah (“Acher”) heard the Voice behind the Holy of Holies say “Return… except for Acher.” R’ Tzadok explains that this terrifying exclusion was not a final rejection. The very fact that Acher heard the Voice meant he was still being addressed; the exclusion was a severe divine provocation from the side of harsh judgment (Midas HaDin), meant to shatter his complacency and force him into a desperate, heartbroken cry for mercy. Had he understood this and pushed through the "closed door," Hashem's hand would have received him "in secret" (bamachteret), just as He did for the wicked King Menasheh.

p: וּכְפִי הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דַּחֲגִיגָה, וְכֵן הוּא בְּמִדְרַשׁ רוּת וְקֹהֶלֶת שָׁם, וְהוּבָא גַּם כֵּן בְּתוֹסָפוֹת חֲגִיגָה שָׁם, דְּאַחֵר שָׁמַע בַּת קוֹל זֶה מֵאֲחוֹרֵי בֵּית קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁחָל בְּשַׁבָּת

And according to the Yerushalmi in Chagigah (2:1), and so it is in Midrash Ruth and Koheles there, and cited as well in Tosafos to Chagigah (15a, s.v. shuvu), that Acher heard this bas kol from behind the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos;481Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 (9b): R’ Meir said to Acher, “You have all this wisdom, and you do not return [in teshuvah]?” He said, “I cannot.” “Why?” “Once I was passing before the Holy of Holies, riding on my horse on a Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos, and I heard a bas kol issuing from the Holy of Holies saying, ‘Return, O sons — except for Elisha ben Avuya, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.’” (So too Rus Rabbah and Koheles Rabbah, cited in Tosafos, Chagigah 15a.)
נִרְאֶה דְּעִיקַּר תּוֹקֶף הִתְעוֹרְרוּת זֶה הוּא בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, דְּאָז הוּא הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת לְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
it appears that the primary intensity of this awakening is on Yom Kippur, for then is the awakening for all the hearts of the Children of Israel,
דְּכִמְעַט אֵין אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲלֶה בִּלְבָבוֹ אָז אֵיזֶה הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בִּלְבָבוֹ
such that there is scarcely one of Israel in whose heart there does not arise then some stirring of teshuvah in his heart.
וְהוּא מֵאוֹתוֹ הַקּוֹל ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר הַמְפוֹצֵץ וְיוֹצֵא מִסּוֹף עוֹלָם וְעַד סוֹפוֹ, וְנִשְׁמָע לְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת מִבְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֲשֶׁר לֹא נִטְמְעוּ עֲדַיִין בֵּין הָעַמִּים לְגַמְרֵי

And this is from that very voice of “Return,” etc., which resounds and goes forth from one end of the world to the other, and is heard by all the hearts of the Children of Israel who have not yet assimilated completely among the nations.
דַּאֲפִילּוּ ״אַחֵר״ שֶׁנִּגְזַר עָלָיו ״חוּץ״ וְגוֹמֵר, מִכָּל מָקוֹם שָׁמַע הַבַּת קוֹל, וְלֹא לְחִנָּם שְׁמָעוֹ, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁגַּם הוּא הִתְעוֹרֵר
For even “Acher,” upon whom it was decreed “except [for Acher],” nevertheless heard the bas kol, and he did not hear it for naught; meaning that he too was awakened.
אֶלָּא שֶׁלִּבּוֹ הִתְעָהוּ לַחְשׁוֹב כִּי חָטָא כָּל כָּךְ עַד שֶׁאֵין הַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לוֹ עוֹד, וּמִן הַשָּׁמַיִם פּוֹתְחִין לַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא עַל יְדֵי הַשְּׁמִיעָה דְּ״חוּץ״

Only his heart led him astray to think that he had sinned so egregiously that teshuvah could no longer avail him, and from Heaven they “open the way for one who comes to defile himself” (Shabbos 104a) through the hearing of “except”.

מֵאַחַר דְּזֶה הַפְּתִיחָה, שֶׁמַּרְאִין לוֹ שֶׁאֵין מְעוֹרְרִים אוֹתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי כְּמוֹ לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, אֲבָל אַדְּרַבָּא מַרְאִין לוֹ פֶּתַח כְּאִלּוּ הוּא חוּץ מֵהֶם, וְהַיְינוּ מִצַּד הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר

For since this is the “opening”—in that they show him that they are not arousing him completely like all Israel, but on the contrary show him an opening as if he is excluded from them—and this stems from the bas kol of “Return,” etc.
וְכִידּוּעַ דְּגַם הוּא אִלּוּ נִתְחַזֵּק עִם כָּל זֶה וְשָׁב, הָיָה מוֹעִיל לוֹ, דְּאֵין לְךָ דָּבָר הָעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה

And it is known that had he too strengthened himself despite all this and repented, it would have availed him, for nothing stands in the way of teshuvah (Yerushalmi Peah 1:1).482R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §120): “So too the yetzer will be ‘the left repels and the right draws near’ — whereas with Elisha [ben Avuyah / Acher] the right also repelled; and although they said (Bereishis Rabbah 9) ‘very good — this is the yetzer hara,’ it is known that ‘all is according to what a person is’ — one whose measure is to subdue [the yetzer] and repel it entirely, and one whose measure is to transform it.” Exactly the se’if’s Acher, who heard the bas kol: for him even “the right repelled” — yet it was still in his power to rectify.
וְאַף בַּת קוֹל זֶה שֶׁשָּׁמַע, אַף שֶׁהָיָה לְטוֹרְדוֹ מִצַּד הַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אִלּוּ הָיָה בָּא לִיטַּהֵר הָיָה גַּם זֶה לְסִיּוּעַ לוֹ

And even this bas kol that he heard, though it served to drive him away from the aspect of “one who comes to defile himself,” nevertheless, had he come to purify himself, this too would have served to assist him.
דְּהָיָה לוֹ לְהִתְבּוֹנֵן: אִלּוּ לֹא חָפֵץ בּוֹ ה׳, לָמָּה הִשְׁמִיעֵהוּ בֶּאֱמֶת, וְאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חָפֵץ בְּמוֹת הַמֵּת
For he should have reflected: had Hashem not desired him, why did He let him hear it at all, seeing that the Blessed Name does not desire the death of the one who dies (Yechezkel 18:32).

וְלָמָּה זֶה יְגַלֶּה לוֹ שֶׁנִּדְחָה אִם לֹא כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לָשׁוּב עוֹד בְּחָזְקָה יוֹתֵר, לְהִתְמַרְמֵר לְפָנָיו יוֹתֵר, וּלְעוֹרֵר רַחֲמָיו רַבִּים עַל עַצְמוֹ וּלְהַרְבּוֹת בִּתְפִלָּה וְתַחֲנוּנִים

And why would He reveal to him that he was rejected, if not so that he should be aroused through this to return with even greater force, to embitter himself before Him even more, to awaken His abundant mercy upon himself, and to multiply prayer and supplications?
וְעִנְיָן מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ה׳ לְמֹשֶׁה בְּחֵטְא הָעֵגֶל לְהוֹדִיעַ מִנָּשָׁם וַחֲרוֹנוֹ עֲלֵיהֶם כְּדֵי שֶׁיִּתְפַּלֵּל בַּעֲדָם
Just as Hashem spoke to Moshe at the sin of the Golden Calf, informing [him] of their punishment and His wrath upon them, in order that he should pray on their behalf (Berachos 32a);

וְכֵן הוּא אֵצֶל ״אַחֵר״, לְעִנְיָן זֶה הוֹדִיעוּהוּ כְּדֵי לְעוֹרְרוֹ שֶׁיְּרַחֵם עַל עַצְמוֹ, אֵיךְ בֵּן חָבִיב כָּמוֹהוּ שֶׁזָּכָה כְּבָר לִיכָּנֵס בַּפַּרְדֵּס וּלְחַפֵּשׂ בְּגִנְזַיָּא דְּמַלְכָּא, נִטְרָד בְּפֶתַע פִּתְאוֹם, וּלְהָרִים קוֹל בְּכִי וְתַחֲנוּנִים לִפְנֵי אָבִיו שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם

and so it was with “Acher”: for this purpose they informed him, to arouse him to take pity on himself—how a beloved son like him, who had already merited to enter the Pardes (Chagigah 14b) and search in the treasuries of the King, is suddenly banished!—and to raise a voice of weeping and supplications before his Father in Heaven.

וּבְוַדַּאי רַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם מְרוּבִּים כְּרַחֵם אָב עַל בָּנִים, שֶׁאַף שֶׁזּוֹרְקוֹ לַחוּץ וְאוֹמֵר שֶׁלֹּא יַנִּיחוֹ עוֹד לִיכָּנֵס לְבֵיתוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עֵינָיו צוֹפִיּוֹת כָּל שָׁעָה שֶׁיָּשׁוּב, וִירַחֲמֵהוּ כִּי יֵיטִיב מַעֲשָׂיו

And certainly the mercy of Heaven is abundant, like a father’s mercy on his children, who even when he throws him outside and says he will never let him enter his house again, nevertheless his eyes watch every moment for his return, and he will have mercy on him when he improves his deeds.

וַאֲפִילּוּ אִם נִסְגְּרָה הַדֶּלֶת לְפָנָיו בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת מִפְּנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין, יָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פְּרוּסָה תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת לְקַבֵּל בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּפְסָחִים קי״ט עַמּוּד א׳)

And even if the door is closed before him in all the worlds because of the Attribute of Judgment, the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is spread out beneath the wings of the Chayos to receive penitents, as they said (in Pesachim 119a).483Pesachim 119a: “‘and the hands of a man beneath their wings’ (Yechezkel 1:8) — it is written yado [His hand, singular]: this is the hand of the Holy One, spread beneath the wings of the chayos, to receive penitents from the hand of the Attribute of Justice.” With Sanhedrin 103a, that the Holy One made for Menasheh “a kind of tunnel [machteres] in the firmament, to receive him in teshuvah,” bypassing the Attribute of Justice — the same “hand” that reaches out to draw in even the one whom strict justice would exclude.
וְהוּא הַמַּחְתֶּרֶת בָּרָקִיעַ שֶׁעָשָׂה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִמְנַשֶּׁה לְקַבְּלוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה מִפְּנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ג עַמּוּד א׳)
And this is the secret tunnel in the firmament that the Holy One, blessed be He, made for Menasheh to receive him in teshuvah despite the Attribute of Judgment, as they said (in Sanhedrin 103a);
כִּי הוּא הָיָה גַּם כֵּן דּוּגְמַת אַחֵר, דְּיָדַע כֹּחוֹ וּמָרַד, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי וּמִדְרָשׁוֹת שָׁם בְּטַעַם ״חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״, כִּי גַּם מְנַשֶּׁה הָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם גָּדוֹל

for he [Menasheh] was also akin to Acher, knowing His power yet rebelling (Sanhedrin 103a), just as they said in the Yerushalmi (Hagigah 2:1) and Midrashim there regarding the reason for “except for Acher,” for Menasheh too was a great Torah scholar.

items.h: The theme: The formidable greatness in Torah of the wicked Kings of Israel. Menasheh, Yarovam, and Achav were profound Torah scholars who distorted the pathways of Divine service (e.g., Yarovam interpreting the Golden Calf, Achav innovating the kissing of the idol). Despite their rebellion, their Torah possessed eternal reality. Menasheh was recognized as the greatest of the three; a halachah is established in his name, and Acher's Torah teachings are preserved in Pirkei Avos. Though judged in Gehinnom, their wisdom endures because the truth of Torah stems inherently from Hashem's wisdom, independent of human merit.

p: וּמִלְּבַד מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] עַל כָּל מְלָכִים הַפָּנִים ״שֶׁהָיוּ שׁוֹנִים בְּתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים״ רָצָה לוֹמַר בְּדַרְכֵי הָעֲבוֹדָה לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

And besides what is stated [in Sanhedrin 103b] regarding all those kings, that “they would study Toras Kohanim” [Vayikra], meaning the pathways of service to the Blessed Name;484Three kings — Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2 identifies them as Yerovam, Achav, and Menasheh, and states that they have no share in the World to Come. R’ Yehudah disagrees regarding Menasheh, citing II Divrei Hayamim 33:13, where his prayer is accepted and he is restored to Jerusalem; the Sages answer that he was restored to his kingdom, but not necessarily to life in the World to Come. R’ Tzadok’s point here does not erase that judgment. It sharpens the paradox: these rulers could possess extraordinary Torah attainment while directing their will in rebellion, so their knowledge increases both the enduring Torah that can be preserved and the gravity of their responsibility.,485Toras Kohanim — the traditional name of the Sifra, the tannaitic halachic Midrash on Sefer Vayikra. Its subjects include korbanos, kehunnah, tumah and taharah, and the laws of kedushah. Sanhedrin 103b records the many “faces” these kings expounded in Toras Kohanim, and Rashi explains that Menasheh renewed and expounded a new mode each year. R’ Tzadok reads “Toras Kohanim” inwardly as the Torah of avodah: Vayikra is the book of approaching Hashem through service and sanctification. Thus the astonishing feature is not merely their scholarship, but their penetration into the very paths of Divine service even during years in which their deeds opposed that knowledge.,486Sanhedrin 103b: “The Sages taught: Menasheh would learn fifty-five ‘faces’ [modes of exposition] in Toras Kohanim, corresponding to the years of his reign; Achav — eighty-five; Yerovam — one hundred and three.” Rashi: “he would learn fifty-five faces in Toras Kohanim — the book of Vayikra he would renew each and every year and expound it with pilpul.”
וּבַמִּשְׁנָה אָמְרוּ ״נֶגֶד שְׁנֵי מַלְכוּתוֹ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּכָל שָׁנָה הָיָה דּוֹרְשׁוֹ
and in the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 103b) they said “corresponding to the years of his reign,” see Rashi there that every year he would expound it;
הֲרֵי גַּם בִּשְׁנוֹת רִשְׁעוֹ לֹא זָז מִלִּדְרוֹשׁ רָזֵי תוֹרָה בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
behold, even during the years of his wickedness he did not cease from expounding the secrets of Torah in the service of the Blessed Name.
[וְיָרָבְעָם ק״ג נִרְאֶה לִי בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא עֵגֶל, כִּי הָיָה דּוֹרֵשׁ דְּרָשׁוֹת שֶׁל דּוֹפִי לִפְתּוֹר דַּרְכֵי עֲבוֹדָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּמַעֲשֵׂה הָעֵגֶל

[And Yarovam’s 103 [expoundings of Toras Kohanim] appears to me to be the gematria of egel (calf), for he would preach flawed exegeses to interpret the pathways of service to the Blessed Name through the making of the calf;

וְאַחְאָב פ״ה אוּלַי לְפִי שֶׁחִידֵּשׁ עֲבוֹדַת הַבַּעַל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, שֶׁעִיקַּר עֲבוֹדָתוֹ כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה קְצָת הָיָה בַּפֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְהִשְׁאַרְתִּי בְיִשְׂרָאֵל... כָּל הַפֶּה אֲשֶׁר לֹא נָשַׁק לוֹ״ (מְלָכִים א י״ט:י״ח)

and Achav’s 85, perhaps because he innovated the worship of Baal in Israel, the essence of whose worship, it appears somewhat, was with the mouth [peh, numerically 85], as it is said, “Yet I have left in Israel... every mouth that has not kissed him” (I Melachim 19:18).

וּכְרִיעַת הַבִּרְכַּיִם זֶהוּ הַשְׁתַּחֲוָאָה הַנְּהוּגָה בְּכָל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְאִיתַהּ גַּם בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בִּכְרִיעוֹת וְהִשְׁתַּחֲוָיוֹת בַּמִּקְדָּשׁ וּבִשְׁעַת תְּפִלָּה דְּכָרַע בְּ״מוֹדִים״ וְכַיּוֹצֵא (בְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא בִּבְרָכוֹת ל״א עַמּוּד א׳)

And the bowing of the knees is the prostration customary in all idol worship, and exists also in the service of the Blessed Name with bowing and prostration in the Temple and during prayer, as one bows at "Modim" and the like (as with Rabbi Akiva in Berachos 31a);
אֲבָל נְשִׁיקַת פֶּה נִרְאֶה דְּנִתְחַדֵּשׁ אָז עַל יְדֵי אַחְאָב בַּעֲבוֹדַת הַבַּעַל, וְאֵין כָּאן מָקוֹם לְהַאֲרִיךְ יוֹתֵר בָּזֶה]
but the kissing with the mouth, it appears, was innovated then by Achav in the worship of Baal; and this is not the place to elaborate further on this].
עוֹד מָצִינוּ [שָׁם ק״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] אַמְנַשֶּׁה בְּיִחוּד, אִתְחֲזֵי לֵיהּ בְּחֶלְמָא ״חַבְרָךְ קָרֵית״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְהוּא אָמַר אַכּוּלְהוּ שְׁלֹשָׁה מְלָכִים

We also find [there in Sanhedrin 102b] regarding Menasheh specifically, [that Rav Ashi] saw him in a dream [saying]: “You call me your colleague [chaver]?” etc., though [Rav Ashi] had spoken of all three kings;
וּמִכּוּלְהוּ לֹא בָּא אֵלָיו לְשָׁאֳלוֹ עַל זֶה אֶלָּא מְנַשֶּׁה, מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא הַגָּדוֹל שֶׁבָּהֶם וְשֶׁלּוֹ לְבַד הָיָה רָאוּי שֶׁיִּחֲרֶה לוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁקְּרָאוֹ ״חַבְרִין״

yet of them all, none came to question him on this except Menasheh, implying that he was the greatest of them, and for him alone was it fitting to be angered over being called "colleague".487Sanhedrin 102b: “Rav Ashi concluded [a lecture] on the three kings [who have no share in the World to Come], and said: Tomorrow we will begin with ‘our colleagues.’ Menasheh appeared to him in a dream and said: ‘Your colleague and your father’s colleague you call us?! From where do you begin to break bread for ha-motzi?’ He said: I do not know. [Menasheh] said: From where the crust hardens [in baking]. [Rav Ashi] said: Teach me, and tomorrow I will expound it in your name at the lecture.”
וְכֵן זָכָה שֶׁנִּקְבַּע הֲלָכָה בִּשְׁמוֹ בַּגְּמָרָא מֵהֵיכָן לְמִשְׁרֵא הַמּוֹצִיא, מַה שֶּׁגִּילָּה מֵחֲלוֹם וְנִדְרַשׁ מִשְּׁמוֹ, וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And he likewise merited that a halachah was established in his name in the Gemara—from where to cut the bread (Sanhedrin 102b)—which he revealed from the dream and was taught in his name, even though [according to the Mishna] he has no share in the World to Come.488The halachah of ha-motzi — Sanhedrin 102b relates that Menasheh asked Rav Ashi where one begins to break the loaf and answered: at the place that baked first, where the crust formed well. Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 167:1, rules that one breaks the bread at the place where it is well baked; the Rema discusses how this applies to the shape of ordinary loaves. The dream therefore preserves an operative halachic teaching in Menasheh’s name. For R’ Tzadok, this is evidence that a genuine point of Torah can remain fixed in the mesorah even when the person through whom it was revealed is himself under severe judgment.

[דְּשָׁם ק״ו עַמּוּד ב׳ גַּבֵּי דּוֹאֵג, גַּם אַחַר שֶׁאָמַר ״יִתָּצְךָ לָנֶצַח״ דְּלֹא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, הוּצְרַךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ ״וְיִסָּחֲךָ מֵאֹהֶל״ דְּלֹא לֵימְרוּ שְׁמַעְתְּתָא בִּשְׁמֵיהּ בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ

[For there, 106b, regarding Doeg: even after [David] said “He will break you down forever” (Tehillim 52:7), that he would have no share in the World to Come, he still needed to pray “and pluck you out of your tent” so that they would not recite teachings in his name in the Beis Midrash;

דְּאַף שֶׁאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֶפְשָׁר מִכָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁשְּׁמַעְתָּיו יִהְיוּ נֶאֱמָרִים מִשְּׁמֵיהּ אִלּוּ זָכוּ לְכָךְ, וְדוֹאֵג הָיָה זוֹכֶה לוּלֵי קִלְלַת דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם]

for even if one has no share in the World to Come, it is nevertheless possible that his teachings be stated in his name had they merited it, and Doeg would have merited it were it not for the curse of David HaMelech, peace be upon him].
וּכְאֱלִישָׁע אַחֵר, דְּשָׁנָה רַבִּי שְׁמוּעָה מִשְּׁמוֹ בְּאָבוֹת, אַף דְּהוּא עַצְמוֹ אָמַר עָלָיו [בַּחֲגִיגָה שָׁם עַמּוּד ב׳] ״לֹא נִין לוֹ וְלֹא נֶכֶד בְּעַמָּיו״ וְגוֹמֵר

And like Elisha Acher, in whose name Rebbi taught a tradition in Avos (4:20), even though [Rebbi] himself said of him [in Chagigah 15b] “He shall have neither son nor son's son among his people” (Iyov 18:19),489Acher’s teaching in Avos — Pirkei Avos 4:20 records explicitly in the name of Elisha ben Avuyah: one who learns as a child is compared to ink written on new paper, while one who begins learning in old age is like ink on erased paper. The meforshim explain that early learning is deeply engraved and retained, whereas later impressions are less readily fixed. This is the “teaching in Avos” to which R’ Tzadok refers: despite Acher’s fall, Chazal preserved his true Torah by name within the Mishnah’s chain of ethical teaching.,490“Neither son nor grandson” — Iyov 18:19 describes the obliteration of the wicked person’s continuity. Chagigah 15b applies the verse to Acher when his impoverished daughter came before Rebbe. Rebbe initially asked whether any of Acher’s seed still remained; she answered, “Remember his Torah and do not remember his deeds.” Fire then descended and touched Rebbe’s bench, demonstrating the enduring claim created by Torah even when its bearer acted disgracefully. This episode supplies the precise background for R’ Tzadok’s separation between Acher’s condemned conduct and the Torah teachings that continued in the beis midrash.
וַעֲדַיִין בְּיָמָיו הָיָה נִידּוֹן בְּגֵיהִנֹּם עַד שֶׁבָּא רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן וְהוֹצִיאוֹ מִשָּׁם כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם

and even in [Rebbi’s] days he was still being judged in Gehinnom until Rabbi Yochanan came and extracted him from there, as stated there.491Chagigah 15b: “When Acher died, they said [in Heaven]: let him not be judged [in Gehinnom], and let him not enter the World to Come. Let him not be judged — because he engaged in Torah; and let him not enter the World to Come — because he sinned. R’ Meir said: better that he be judged and [then] enter the World to Come; when I die I will raise smoke from his grave. When R’ Meir died, smoke rose from Acher’s grave [a sign he was being judged]. R’ Yochanan said: is it a mighty deed to burn one’s teacher? There was one [such disciple] among us, and can we not save him? If I take him by the hand, who will wrest him from me? [So he took hold of him and raised him up.] When R’ Yochanan died, the smoke ceased from Acher’s grave; the eulogizer said of him: ‘even the guard of the gate did not stand before you, our teacher.’”,492Cf. Siman 15 §90 and §95 (in this volume): Elisha ben Avuyah — “Acher,” the teacher from whom R’ Meir “learned a teaching” — recurs as the paradigm of one before whom “the gates of teshuvah were locked” (the bas kol “Return, wayward children — except for Acher,” Chagigah 15a), whom the Holy One nonetheless receives only “by way of a tunnel”; there too R’ Meir is “the one who illumines the eyes of the Sages” through the Torah he drew even from Acher.
וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהַשְּׁמוּעָה הָיָה שְׁגוּרָה בְּפִי הַחֲכָמִים בְּבֵית הַמִּדְרָשׁ עוֹד מִקּוֹדֶם בְּחַיֵּי רַבִּי מֵאִיר שֶׁנִּגְמַר דִּינוֹ לְמַעְלָה שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And it implies that the teaching was current in the mouths of the Sages in the Beis Midrash even earlier during the lifetime of Rabbi Meir, when his judgment had already been sealed on high that he would have no share in the World to Come;

וְכֵן רַבִּי מֵאִיר עַצְמוֹ דִּגְמַר שְׁמַעְתָּא מִפּוּמֵיהּ, לִימְּדָהּ לְתַלְמִידָיו; וְיֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים דִּבְכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״רַבִּי מֵאִיר״ ״אֲחֵרִים״, הוּא הַשְּׁמוּעוֹת דִּגְמַר מִפּוּמֵיהּ דְּ״אַחֵר״

and likewise Rabbi Meir himself, who learned the teaching from his mouth, taught it to his students; and some say that wherever “Rabbi Meir” is referred to as “Acherim [Others]” (Horayos 13b), it denotes the teachings he learned from the mouth of “Acher”.493R’ Meir’s selective reception — Chagigah 15b asks how R’ Meir could learn from Acher when Malachi 2:7 teaches that Torah should be sought from a teacher who resembles an angel of Hashem. The Gemara distinguishes an adult scholar, capable of discrimination, from a child. It describes R’ Meir as eating the date while discarding its peel and, in another image, eating the pomegranate’s interior while throwing away its rind. Rava adds that a talmid chacham is like a nut: even when the shell is soiled, the interior is not made repulsive. R’ Tzadok’s wording that R’ Meir absorbed the teaching and transmitted it means disciplined separation of authentic Torah from corrupted conduct, not an unrestricted license to follow a sinful teacher.
וְגַם בְּעוֹדוֹ נֶחְשָׁב לְמוֹרֵד, מִכָּל מָקוֹם יָדַע כֹּחוֹ שֶׁזֶּהוּ יְדִיעַת דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה אֲמִיתִּים וּשְׁמוּעוֹת הַנִּקְבָּעוֹת לְעָלְמֵי עַד

And even while he was still reckoned a rebel, he nevertheless recognized its power, that this is the knowledge of true words of Torah and teachings established for all eternity.494“He knew My power and rebelled against Me” — the full expression appears in Ruth Rabbah 6:4, Koheles Rabbah 7:8, and Yalkut Shimoni on Nach §974 in the account of the bas kol heard by Elisha ben Avuyah. It declares: “Return, wayward children … except for Acher, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” The phrase defines Acher’s rebellion as informed defiance rather than ignorance. In R’ Tzadok’s argument, that same genuine knowledge explains both sides of the paradox: his rebellion was more severe precisely because he knew, while the true Torah contained in that knowledge could still be separated from his choice and preserved.,495Torah that remains valid — Chagigah 15b states that just as mud on a nut does not render its interior repulsive, “a talmid chacham, although he has sinned, his Torah is not made repulsive.” The same sugya derives from Mishlei 22:17, “Hear the words of the wise, and set your heart to My knowledge” — not merely to their personal knowledge — that the listener must identify the Divine truth within the teaching. R’ Tzadok therefore distinguishes a timeless Torah insight from human cleverness: what becomes part of the enduring Torah of the beis midrash testifies that its inner source transcends the personal failure of the speaker.

דְּדָבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ מִצַּד חָכְמָה אֱנוֹשִׁיּוּת וְדֶרֶךְ חִידּוּד שֵׂכֶל לְבַד, דִּדְבַר חָכְמָה הַקַּיֶּימֶת לָעַד אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא הַנִּמְשֶׁכֶת מֵחָכְמָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, שֶׁהוּא וְדַעְתּוֹ וְחָכְמָתוֹ הַכֹּל אֶחָד

For this matter does not derive from human wisdom or merely by way of intellectual sharpness; for a word of wisdom that endures forever is none other than that which is drawn from His Blessed wisdom, for He, His knowledge, and His wisdom are all One (Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:10).496Divine knowledge and wisdom — Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 2:10, formulates that the Creator does not know through knowledge external to Himself: “He is the Knower, He is the known, and He is the knowledge itself — all is one.” R’ Tzadok extends this formulation here to chochmah: Torah wisdom that is eternally true is drawn from the Divine wisdom and is not merely an achievement of autonomous human intellect. This explains how an authentic teaching can possess permanent sanctity even when the individual who received it later rebelled; the enduring truth belongs at its root to Hashem’s wisdom, while the person remains accountable for the direction of his will and actions.,497R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Bereishis §2): “(Sanhedrin 103b) Menasheh would expound fifty-five ‘faces’ [modes] in Toras Kohanim, corresponding to the [years of] his two reigns — and Rashi [explains] he would renew [them] each year and expound from his own analysis; and they had a sense of the renewal of Torah every Shabbos and every month.” Exactly the se’if: these “great ones who rebelled” were, even so, immersed in the Torah, expounding its “faces.”

items.h: The theme: The deepest Torah insights (chiddushim) revealed to Moshe at Sinai stem from absolute cleaving to Supernal Wisdom (Da'as). When one who attains this level rebels ("knowing his Master yet rebelling"), strict Judgment (Midas HaDin) blocks the gates of teshuvah, hardening his heart as with Pharaoh. Even when he seeks to return, judgment agitates his mind away from repentance. Yet Hashem digs a "secret tunnel" (machteret) beneath the wings of the Chayos—manifesting through the bas kol "except for Acher"—appearing to reject him outwardly while secretly stirring the root of Adam Elyon, engraved in the Throne of Glory as the visage of Yaakov Avinu, whose seed remains bound to Hashem in the depths of the heart no matter how numerous their sins.

p: וְזֶהוּ הַדִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה שֶׁתַּלְמִיד וָתִיק עָתִיד לְחַדֵּשׁ שֶׁנִּגְלוּ לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִצַּד דְּבֵיקוּתוֹ בַּחָכְמָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה

And this is [the meaning of] the words of Torah that a veteran disciple is destined to innovate, which were revealed to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, from the aspect of his cleaving to the Supernal Wisdom,498Megillah 19b (and Yerushalmi Pe’ah 2:4): “Everything that a diligent disciple is destined to innovate was already given to Moshe at Sinai.” R’ Tzadok: such enduring Torah is reached only through da’as — cleaving to the supernal Wisdom — which is why even a “knowing rebel” like Acher, who had attained that knowledge, could transmit teachings that “stand forever,” for they flow from God’s own wisdom, “He and His knowledge being one” (cf. Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 2:10).,499Cf. Siman 15 §85 and §90 (in this volume), where the same motif of the “diligent disciple [talmid vatik]” recurs — Moshe shown R’ Akiva expounding “heaps of halachos” upon the crownlets, matters Moshe himself did not know (Menachos 29b), and the talmid vatik at Yavneh who “purifies the sheretz with a hundred and fifty reasons” — all as facets of the Torah “a diligent disciple is destined to innovate,” already given to Moshe at Sinai.
שֶׁעַל יָדוֹ זָכָה לְקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ לָהּ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיְדִיעָה וּבְדַעַת שֶׁהוּא הַהִתְחַבְּרוּת וְהַדְּבֵיקוּת בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

through which he merited the reception of the Torah into this world, and which cannot be attained except from the aspect of profound perception and Knowledge (Da'as), which is the bond and attachment to the Blessed Name.500Da’as as connection — the biblical root is “Adam knew Chavah” (Bereishis 4:1), where knowledge denotes intimate union. Pardes Rimmonim 23:4 explicitly explains that da’as is named from this verse because it means joining and unification, and R’ Tzadok himself states later in Takanas HaShavin 15:108 that yediyah is a language of “connection and deveikus.” Thus, in this se’if da’as is not information about Hashem but a bond through which the human mind becomes receptive to supernal Chochmah. That explains why the authentic chidush of a talmid vatik can already be included in Sinai: the disciple uncovers, through deveikus, a facet of the Divine wisdom already rooted in Torah.
וּמִי שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה זוֹ וְעִם כָּל זֶה מוֹרֵד, עָנְשׁוֹ מִצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין לִסְתּוֹם בְּפָנָיו דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה

And one who reached this exalted rung and nevertheless rebels, his punishment from the side of the Attribute of Judgment is to seal before him the portals of repentance,501“One who knows his Master and intends to rebel” — Sifra, Bechukosai, section 2:2, derives this definition from “If you will not listen to Me” and applies it as well to Nimrod and the people of Sedom: their added guilt was that they recognized their Master and deliberately opposed Him. Halachos Gedolos preserves the same teaching in its discussion of the stages of rejecting Torah. R’ Tzadok uses the phrase in its strongest sense: after da’as has become genuine attachment, rebellion is not ordinary weakness or ignorance but a conscious severing of a known bond, and therefore Middas HaDin can claim that the ordinary path of return should be closed.
