כְּעִנְיָן בְּפַרְעֹה, שֶׁאַחַר שֶׁבַּמַּכּוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת הֶרְאוּ לוֹ יְדִיעַת כֹּחַ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ כְּפִי כֹּחַ הַשָּׂגַת הָאוּמּוֹת וְעִם כָּל זֶה מָרַד, הָיָה בַּמִּשְׁפָּט לְהַכְבִּיד אֶת לִבּוֹ אַחַר כָּךְ, וְלֹא כִּשְׁאָר ״בָּא לִיטַּמֵּא״ דְּרַק פּוֹתְחִין

as was the case with Pharaoh: after they demonstrated to him in the initial plagues the perception of the Blessed Name's might according to the capacity of the nations, and he nevertheless rebelled, it was decreed by righteous judgment to harden his heart subsequently (Shemos 7:3), unlike an ordinary person who "comes to defile himself," for whom they merely open the path (Shabbos 104a).502Pharaoh’s hardened heart — Shemos 7:3 announces, “I shall harden Pharaoh’s heart”; after Pharaoh repeatedly hardens himself, the Torah first says explicitly, “Hashem hardened Pharaoh’s heart” at Shemos 9:12, and again at 10:1. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3, explains that a person may sin so greatly and so willingly that the punishment itself is the withholding of teshuvah, enabling full retribution; Pharaoh is his leading example. Ramban to Shemos 7:3 adds that the first refusals were Pharaoh’s own, while the later hardening both punished the earlier evil and prevented fear of the plagues from producing a merely coerced submission. R’ Tzadok reads this as the claim of Middas HaDin against one who has already been shown Divine power and nevertheless rebels.,503“One who comes to defile himself, they open for him; one who comes to purify himself, they assist him” — Yoma 38b, Menachos 29b, and Avodah Zarah 55a, expounding Mishlei 3:34. The academy of R’ Yishmael compares it to a merchant: the purchaser of foul-smelling kerosene is told to measure it himself, whereas those selling fragrant balsam help the purchaser so that all may share its scent. Rabbeinu Yonah to Avos 4:2 explains that “opening” means the sinner is left to the path he chose, while positive choice receives active Heavenly assistance. R’ Tzadok contrasts this normal rule with the exceptional judgment of a knowing rebel: Middas HaDin seeks not merely to leave the path open, but to disturb even his desire to return.
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין טוֹעֶנֶת גַּם בְּרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיָּדְעוּ וּמָרְדוּ לִהְיוֹת הַמִּשְׁפָּט כֵּן, דְּמָה נִשְׁתַּנּוּ אֵלּוּ מֵאֵלּוּ
And the Attribute of Judgment argues likewise concerning the wicked of Israel who knew and rebelled, demanding that the judgment be identical: wherein are these different from those?
וְאַף כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לָשׁוּב, לֹא דַּי שֶׁאֵין מְסַיְּיעִין, אֶלָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין טוֹרְדִין אֶת לְבָבוֹ לְהַסִּיחַ דַּעְתּוֹ מֵהַתְּשׁוּבָה
And even when he wishes to repent, not only is assistance withheld, but from the side of the Attribute of Judgment they confound his heart to divert his attention from teshuvah.

וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן קִיבּוּל הַתְּשׁוּבָה, כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקַבֵּל לְרָצוֹן, אָז מִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה, וּבְכָל עֵת מוֹסִיף וְהוֹלֵךְ, דְּכָל שֶׁבָּא לְהוֹסִיף לְטַהֵר הַסִּיּוּעַ מִן הַשָּׁמַיִם הוֹלֵךְ וּמִתְגַּבֵּר גַּם כֵּן

And this is the principle of the acceptance of teshuvah: for when the Blessed Name receives it favorably, then one mitzvah draws another mitzvah (Avos 4:2) and it continually increases, so that whenever one seeks to purify himself further, heavenly assistance likewise intensifies;504“A mitzvah draws another mitzvah” — Pirkei Avos 4:2. Rabbeinu Yonah explains that the reward of a mitzvah includes help and readiness to perform the next mitzvah, while the consequence of sin is increased entanglement in further sin. Rashi to Devarim 22:8 similarly explains the sequence from sending away the mother bird to building a home and making a parapet as “mitzvah draws mitzvah.” R’ Tzadok applies the principle specifically to accepted teshuvah: acceptance is not only the erasure of the past; it becomes visible in a growing current of siyata diShmaya that carries the penitent from one act of purification to the next.
וְאִם הִגִּיעַ לְכָךְ שֶׁמִּדַּת הַדִּין מְעַכֶּבֶת, אָז הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חוֹתֵר חֲתִירָה, הַיְינוּ כְּעִנְיַן הַכְּרוּז ״חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״

but if he reached a state where the Attribute of Judgment obstructs, then the Blessed Name digs a secret tunnel (machteret), which is exemplified by the proclamation “except for Acher.”505The hidden “tunnel” of teshuvah — II Divrei HaYamim 33:13 says of Menasheh, “He prayed to Him, and He was entreated [vaye’ater] by him.” Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2 relates that the ministering angels closed the windows of Heaven against Menasheh’s prayer, so the Holy One “dug him a tunnel beneath His Throne of Glory” and heard him; the Midrash reads vaye’ater as though vayeichater, “He dug.” The tunnel is a route concealed from the prosecutors and outside the ordinary order of judgment. R’ Tzadok now generalizes Menasheh’s episode: even when Middas HaDin blocks the revealed gates, Hashem can create a hidden passage that preserves the possibility of return.,506“Return, wayward children — except for Acher” — Chagigah 15a records the bas kol that Elisha ben Avuyah heard after his entry into the Pardes; the same sugya records R’ Meir repeatedly urging him to return. Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 and Ruth Rabbah 6:4 give the fuller formulation: “except for Elisha ben Avuyah, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” On the surface the proclamation excludes him. R’ Tzadok offers a deliberately deeper reading: the very fact that the exclusion was addressed to him and heard by him was a concealed summons, challenging him to push past the apparent rejection and prove that no Divine voice can finally abolish the possibility of teshuvah. This interpretation is R’ Tzadok’s theological development of the sugya, not its explicit wording.

דִּלִפְנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין מַרְאֶה שֶׁמַּדְחִין אוֹתוֹ וּמַכְבִּידִין אֶת לִבּוֹ בָּזֶה, וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא אַדְּרַבָּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת, אִם הִשְׂכִּיל לָדַעַת שֶׁזֶּהוּ הִתְעוֹרְרוּת דֶּרֶךְ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא יַנִּיחַ מִלִּדְפּוֹק עַל דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, לְהִתְקַבֵּל בִּידֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן שֶׁתַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת

For before the Attribute of Judgment He displays that he is being driven away and his heart hardened thereby, whereas in truth it is on the contrary a profound awakening—if he possessed the insight to realize that this is an awakening through the Torah, never to cease knocking upon the gates of repentance, to be received by the hands of Adam Elyon beneath the wings of the Chayos;507“Hands of a man beneath their wings” — Yechezkel 1:8 describes human hands beneath the wings of the chayos, while 1:26 describes above the throne “a likeness as the appearance of a man.” Kol Bo §66 cites the teaching that these are, as it were, the hands of the Holy One spread beneath the chayos to receive penitents from Middas HaDin. Zohar, Pekudei 786, interprets the hands as receptacles that receive prayers and ba’alei teshuvah and open entrances for them; Malbim to Yechezkel 1:8 connects their appearing to the transformation of the natural order through Israel’s teshuvah. R’ Tzadok joins this image to the hidden tunnel: the penitent rejected by the ordinary hierarchy is received from beneath the wings by the concealed “human” form of Divine mercy.,508R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §12): “The whole Oral Torah, and everything that a diligent disciple will one day innovate — for ‘there is nothing that is not hinted in the Torah’ — all is hinted in the ‘air between [the letters],’ in the tagin and crowns of the letters and the like; and this is the meaning of ‘flying in the air’ — the air between the script.” Exactly the se’if: the disciple’s future innovations were already given to Moshe at Sinai, hidden in the Torah’s very “air.”

הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, רַק מִצַּד הַהִתְבּוֹנְנוּת בְּמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, שֶׁמֵּהַמַּעֲמַקִּים שֶׁל כָּל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב הֵם דְּבוּקִים בְּשָׁרְשָׁם וּמְקוֹרָם, צוּרַת אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן שֶׁהוּא צוּרָתוֹ שֶׁל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַחֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד

meaning that the awakening does not occur in the revealed consciousness of his heart through the bas kol “Return,” etc., but from contemplating the innermost depths of the heart: that from the core depths, all the seed of Yaakov are bound to their source and root, the form of Adam Elyon, which is the visage of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, engraved upon the Throne of Glory (Chullin 91b).509Cf. Chullin 91b: the ministering angels “ascend and gaze at the form of Yaakov above” — his likeness [iqonin] engraved on the Throne of Glory; with Taanis 5b, “Yaakov Avinu did not die.” R’ Tzadok’s frame: all of Yaakov’s seed cleave to that supernal form, which is why the “hand beneath the wings” reaches even the rejected penitent.

דְּ״גָדוֹל כֹּחָן שֶׁל נְבִיאִים שֶׁמְּדַמִּין צוּרָה לְיוֹצְרָהּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, הַיְינוּ דְּכָל הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים אֵינוֹ מִצַּד עַצְמוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּלֵית מַחֲשָׁבָה תְּפִיסָא בֵּיהּ כְּלָל, רַק מִצַּד אֲצִילוּת וְהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת הַשָּׂגָה שֶׁרָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מוּשָּׂג לַנִּבְרָאִים, וְהִיא כְּפִי הַשָּׂגַת הַנִּבְרָאִים

For “great is the power of the prophets who liken the form to its Creator” (Bereishis Rabbah 27:1), meaning that the entirety of prophetic attainment is not of His Blessed Essence, in which no thought can grasp at all (Tikkunei Zohar 17a), but from the side of Emanation (Atzilus) and the downward unfolding of apprehension that the Blessed Name willed to be grasped by created beings according to their capacity;510“Great is the power of the prophets, who liken the form to its Creator” — Bereishis Rabbah 27:1, on prophetic descriptions such as Yechezkel 1:26, “upon the likeness of the throne was a likeness as the appearance of a man.” Maharal, Derech Chaim 3:14, stresses that this does not attribute a body to the Creator; it describes the prophetic comparison of the revealed Divine governance to the complete human form. Nefesh HaChaim II:5 develops the same Midrash in relation to the supernal pattern of the worlds, and R’ Tzadok, Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Tammuz §1, explains that Torah and prophecy speak in human terms about the middos Hashem emanated for governing creation. Here R’ Tzadok identifies Yaakov, the complete human form, as the created image through which this revealed order is apprehended.,511“No thought grasps Him at all” — the celebrated formulation of Tikkunei Zohar in Patach Eliyahu. Tanya, Likkutei Amarim ch. 4, explains the distinction: no created intellect can grasp the Holy One in His essence, yet through Torah and mitzvos the mind can cleave to His revealed will and wisdom. This is precisely the boundary R’ Tzadok draws here. The prophetic “likeness of Man,” the sefirotic attributes, and Yaakov’s form on the Throne describe the emanated mode Hashem willed creatures to apprehend; they are not a description of His unknowable Essence. The footnote therefore guards the passage against corporeal interpretation while preserving R’ Tzadok’s claim that revealed Divinity is ordered according to the perfected form of man.

וְהוּא הָאָדָם רֹאשׁ וְתַכְלִית הַנִּבְרָאִים, וְאֵין שָׁם הַשָּׂגָה אַחֶרֶת בַּאֲמִיתּוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ אֶלָּא מַה שֶּׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם לְמַטָּה, שֶׁזֶּה כָּל כַּוָּונַת בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָמוֹת כּוּלָּם, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה שָׁם אָדָם בַּעַל בְּחִירָה שֶׁיַּכִּיר וְיַשִּׂיג בִּבְחִירָתוֹ שֶׁיֵּשׁ שָׁם אֱלֹקִי בּוֹרֵא וּמַנְהִיג

and man is the pinnacle and purpose of all created beings, and there is no other perception of His Blessed reality except that which constitutes the perception of the perfected man below, for this is the entire intention of the creation of all worlds: that there exist a human being of free choice who will recognize and attain through his choice that there is a Divine Creator and Guide.
וְעַל כֵּן הַשָּׂגַת הָאֱלֹקוּת הַמַּשִּׂיג הוּא בְּדִמְיוֹן הַנְּבִיאִים כִּדְמוּת אָדָם, שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַהַשָּׂגָה הַמּוּשֶׂגֶת כְּפִי כֹּחַ וְדַעַת הָאָדָם

Therefore, the apprehension of Divinity that the prophet grasps is represented in the imagination of the prophets as the likeness of a man (Yechezkel 1:26), which represents the apprehension accessible according to the capacity and knowledge of man;

וְהוּא יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא הָאָדָם הַשָּׁלֵם שֶׁהָיָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּמִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה וְלֹא מֵת, דְּ״מַה זַּרְעוֹ בַּחַיִּים״ וְכוּלֵיהּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בְּתַעֲנִית ה עַמּוּד ב)

and this is Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who is the perfected man who existed in this world, whose bed was whole and who “did not die,” for “just as his seed is alive, [so is he alive],” as they said (in Taanis 5b);

הַיְינוּ דְּקוֹמַת הַכְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל, זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁבְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר, הֵן הֵם עַצְמוֹ קוֹמַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, רַק שֶׁמִּתְפָּרֶטֶת וּמִתְחַלֶּקֶת לִפְרָטֵי נְפָשׁוֹת הַרְבֵּה

meaning that the collective stature of Knesses Yisrael, the seed of Yaakov Avinu in every generation, is itself the very stature of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, except that it differentiates and divides into numerous individual souls.

וְכָל מִי שֶׁהוּא מִזֶּרַע יַעֲקֹב, אֲפִילּוּ הִגְדִּיל עֲוֹנוֹת עַד אֵין קֵץ, יְדֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן הַיְינוּ יַד יָמִין, מִדַּת הַחֶסֶד דְּ״יָדוֹ״ כְּתִיב כִּדְאִיתָא הָתָם (בִּפְסָחִים קיט עַמּוּד א)

And anyone of the seed of Yaakov, even if he magnified iniquities without limit, the hands of Adam Elyon—namely the right hand, the attribute of Chesed, for “His hand” (yado) is written as brought there (in Pesachim 119a) —

וְהוּא הַיָּמִין שֶׁהוּא יָד סְתָם לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הַחֵרוּם (בִּמְנָחוֹת לז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א), וּלְדִידֵיהּ הָנֵי קְרָאֵי דְּתַנָּא קַמָּא הָתָם (לו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב) יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דִּמְפָרֵשׁ בְּהוּ אַחַר כָּךְ יָמִין עַל כֵּן קָרֵי לִשְׂמֹאל סְתָם יָד, אֲבָל יָד סְתָמָא בִּדְלָא מְפָרֵשׁ אַחַר כָּךְ מִידִי הוּא יָמִין

and that is the right, which is an unqualified “hand” according to Rabbi Yishmael the Charum (Menachos 37a); and according to him, those verses cited by the First Tanna there (36b) are because they specify “right” subsequently, wherefore the left is termed an unspecified “hand,” but an unqualified hand where nothing is specified afterward is the right;
וְהִיא פְּרוּסָה בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת שֶׁבְּעוֹלַם הַכִּסֵּא דְּמִתַּמָּן אִתְגְּזַרוּ נִשְׁמָתִין
and it is stretched forth in a secret tunnel beneath the wings of the Chayos in the World of the Throne, from whence souls are hewn out,
שֶׁהִגִּיעַ הַפְּגָם גַּם לַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ דִּטְהוֹרָה הִיא, וְאֵין אָדָם זוֹכֶה לָהּ אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן כְּבָר הִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגַת קְדוּשָׁה וְטָהֳרָה
where the blemish reached even the soul (neshamah) within the brain, which is pure, and which a person does not merit unless he has already arrived at a rung of sanctity and purity.

items.h: The theme: The exceptional peril of high-level spiritual rebellion. Great souls like Acher and Menasheh who attained the level of neshamah (rooted in the World of Beriah and the first hei of the Tetragrammaton) can damage the very seat of divine wisdom within the mind, endangering their share in the World to Come. The wings of the Chayos screen off the light of Atzilus, where no evil can enter. When such a soul falls, divine judgment demands that he be rejected with the left hand; yet the right hand of Adam Elyon of Atzilus draws him near in secret (derech he'elam), hidden even from the conscious mind.

p: אֲבָל יֵשׁ פְּעָמִים אֲנָשִׁים גְּדוֹלִים כְּ״אַחֵר״ וּמְנַשֶּׁה שֶׁכְּבָר זָכוּ בְּמַדְרֵגָתָם לִנְשָׁמָה, וְאַחַר כָּךְ חוֹטְאִים, וְזֶה נִקְרָא ״יוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וּמוֹרֵד״, שֶׁיּוּכַל לִפְגּוֹם גַּם הַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ שֶׁשָּׁם הַחָכְמָה וְהַיְדִיעָה לְרִבּוֹנוֹ

But at times there are great men like Acher and Menasheh who already merited in their stature the level of neshamah, and afterward sin, which is termed “knowing his Master yet rebelling,” wherein he can blemish even the neshamah in the brain where resides wisdom and the perception of his Master;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ דְּאֵין לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
and through this he can reach the point of having no share in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 90a).
דְּנֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה, שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד ג׳ עוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה, הֵם נֶגֶד ג׳ אוֹתִיּוֹת אַחֲרוֹנוֹת דְּשֵׁם
For Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, which correspond to the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, parallel the final three letters of the Divine Name [Vav-Hei];
דְּהַנְּשָׁמָה הִיא נֶגֶד הֵ״א רִאשׁוֹנָה שֶׁהוּא סוֹד עָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי כַּנּוֹדָע, וְהִיא מֵהַבְּרִיאָה דְּרוּבּוֹ טוֹב וּמִיעוּטוֹ רַע, וְהֵם מְעַטִּים מִמַּדְרֵגָה זוֹ דְּרַע

for neshamah corresponds to the upper hei, which is the mystery of the World to Come, derived from Beriah which is mostly good and a minority evil, and they are few who fall into this minority of evil;
וְכַנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת הֵם הַחוֹצְצִים בְּעַד הַהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מֵהֶם, שֶׁהוּא הַשָּׂגַת הַנְּשָׁמָה לַנְּשָׁמָה דְּמֵאֲצִילוּת דְּשָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לְרַע כְּלָל

and the wings of the Chayos are the barriers screening off the attainment that is above them, which is the attainment of the inner soul of the soul (neshamah l'neshamah) from Atzilus, where evil has no existence at all.
וְזֶהוּ הַחֵלֶק אֱלֹקִי מַמָּשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּכָל אֶחָד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וּמִי שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ מוּבְטָח שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא עוֹד
And this is the veritable portion of God that exists within every single Jew (Iyov 31:2), and one who merits it is guaranteed that he will never sin again,
כִּי כְּבָר הִשְׁלִים כָּל אוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם הַכְּלוּלוֹת בּוֹ שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ חַיּוּתוֹ כְּטַעַם ״וְאַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם״, וּבִהְיוֹת הַשֵּׁם שָׁלֵם אֵין חִסָּרוֹן עוֹד כְּלָל

for he has already perfected all the letters of the Divine Name integrated within him from which his vitality derives, in the sense of “and You preserve them all” (Nechemyah 9:6), and when the Name is whole there is no deficiency at all.
וְגַם כַּאֲשֶׁר פָּגַם וְהַמִּשְׁפָּט לִהְיוֹת שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה וּמִדַּת הַדִּין מְקַטְרֵג
And even when he caused a blemish and the judgment requires that the left hand push away while the Attribute of Judgment prosecutes,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַיָּמִין דְּאָדָם דַּאֲצִילוּת מְקָרַבְתּוֹ, רַק לֹא דֶּרֶךְ הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת הָעוֹלָמוֹת דִּבְרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, וַעֲשִׂיָּה בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת

nevertheless the right hand of Adam of Atzilus draws him near; yet not through the downward descent of the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah in revelation,512R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMincha §57): “Is permitted; and a ‘rebel [poshea]’ is one who knows his Master and intends to rebel against Him. And this is ‘from the willful [zedim] hold [me] back’ — and thereby ‘I shall be clean of great transgression.’” Exactly the se’if: “one who knows his Master and rebels” — able to blemish even the neshama attained in his rung.
הַיְינוּ לְהָאִיר לוֹ בְּפֹעַל בְּמוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ וּמֵהֶם לִכְלֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה לְסַיְּיעָם בְּפֹעַל לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
meaning to illumine for him consciously in his brain and his heart and from them to the physical faculties to actively assist them in His Blessed service;

רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו מְעוֹרְרוֹ וּמְסַיְּיעוֹ דֶּרֶךְ הֶעְלֵם, שֶׁגַּם בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ וּמוֹחוֹ עַצְמָם הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם, וּכְעִנְיָן שֶׁאָמַרְנוּ מֵהָא דְּ״חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״

rather, the Blessed Name in His abundant mercy and kindness arouses him and assists him in a concealed manner, so that even within the conscious revelation of his own heart and mind it remains hidden, as we explained regarding “except for Acher.”

items.h: The theme: The secret of drawing near through rejection (ha-kiruv al yedei ha-dechiyah). According to the opinion in Menachos 37a that an unspecified "hand" refers to the left, the Divine outreach operates via the apparent rejection of the left hand, silencing the accusers who see him cast out. This is teshuvah through suffering (as with Menasheh), where God's hand extends through the aperture (dodi shalach yado min hachor). Just as Yaakov had to dress in Esav’s garments to receive the blessings from Yitzchak (the Attribute of Gevurah), so does Divine mercy cloak itself in the harsh garments of Esav—chastising Israel through cruel kings like Haman—in order to secretly extract and redeem the holy essence hidden deep within.

p: וְנִרְאֶה, דִּלְתַנָּא קַמָּא [דִּמְנָחוֹת שָׁם] דִּסְתָם יָד הוּא שְׂמֹאל, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּזֶה דְּהַהִתְקָרְבוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי הַדְּחִיָּיה

And it appears that according to the First Tanna [in Menachos 37a] who holds that an unspecified “hand” is the left, one may say that the drawing near is accomplished through the rejection itself:513An unspecified “hand” as the left — Menachos 37a records the first Tanna’s position that the right hand is called “his right hand [yad yemino]” but is not called simply yad without qualification; the sugya applies this to the placement of tefillin on the left arm. R’ Yosei HaChorem challenges the premise from Bereishis 48:17, while R’ Nasan derives the left arm by linking “you shall bind them” to right-handed writing, and Rav Ashi expounds yadkhah as yad kehah, the weaker hand. Rashi to Shemos 13:9 and Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 27:1, codify the practical halachah that tefillin are placed on the left arm. R’ Tzadok takes the Tanna’s linguistic rule beyond its halachic setting: yad without an openly stated “right” signifies the concealed left side of din.
דַּהֲרֵי כְּשֶׁאָמַר ״חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״ הֲרֵי בָּא לְדַחּוֹתוֹ, וְהוּא מִצַּד הַשְּׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה, וְזֶה עַצְמוֹ הוּא כְּדֵי לְקַבְּלוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנִּתְבָּאֵר

for when He said “except for Acher” He came to reject him, which is from the side of the left hand that pushes away, yet this itself was in order to receive him, as explained;514“The left repels and the right draws near” — Sotah 47a and Sanhedrin 107b warn that rejection must never be total: one hand may distance, but the stronger right hand must remain ready to receive. The Gemara contrasts this balance with Elisha’s rejection of Geichazi and Yehoshua ben Perachyah’s rejection of his disciple “with both hands.” The same page applies the formula to the yetzer, a child, and a wife. In R’ Tzadok’s reading, the Acher proclamation is itself a left-handed rejection whose hidden right hand remains present; the apparent exclusion is therefore not the cancellation of teshuvah but the concealed means by which the door is kept open.
וְזֶהוּ ״יָדוֹ״ כְּתִיב, דְּאֵין שָׁם הִתְגַּלּוּת יַד יָמִין שֶׁהוּא הַחֲסָדִים הַגְּלוּיִים דְּאָז הָיָה מָקוֹם לְמִדַּת הַדִּין לְקַטְרֵג

and this is why “His hand” is written, for there is no open manifestation of the right hand representing revealed kindnesses, which would give room for the Attribute of Judgment to prosecute;515The crimson garments of vengeance — Yeshayah 63:1-4 pictures the Divine Redeemer coming from Edom with reddened garments and explains, “I trod them in My anger ... for a day of vengeance was in My heart, and the year of My redemption had come.” Rashi explains that the prophecy concerns Hashem’s future vengeance upon Edom and that Scripture speaks in the imagery of a human warrior whose garments are stained in battle, “to convey to the ear what it can hear,” not to attribute corporeality to Hashem. Radak and Malbim likewise read the red garment as the visible form assumed by judgment against Edom. R’ Tzadok uses that image here to explain concealed mercy: the right hand of redemption can appear outwardly clothed in Edom’s crimson, destructive form while its inward purpose is the rescue and purification of Israel.
רַק אַדְּרַבָּא, הַקַּבָּלָה הוּא עַל יְדֵי יַד הַשְּׂמֹאל הַדּוֹחָה, דִּכְשֶׁרוֹאִין שֶׁנִּדְחָה נִסְתַּם פִּיּוֹת כָּל הַמְקַטְרְגִים, וּבָזֶה הוּא הַקֵּירוּב שֶׁבַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת

but on the contrary, the reception takes place through the rejecting left hand, for when they see that he is rejected, the mouths of all prosecutors are stopped, and herein lies the drawing near within the secret tunnel.

אוֹ אֶפְשָׁר דְּהַקֵּירוּב הוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין כְּעִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה בִּמְנַשֶּׁה, וְזֶהוּ בְּיַד שְׂמֹאל שֶׁנִּרְאֶה כְּפוֹגֵעַ בּוֹ מִדַּת הַדִּין לְהַעֲנִישׁוֹ, וּבֶאֱמֶת הוּא לְהֵיטִיב אַחֲרִיתוֹ וּלְעוֹרְרוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִתְשׁוּבָה

Or it is possible that the drawing near is accomplished through suffering, as was the case with Menasheh, which is through the left hand: where the Attribute of Judgment appears to strike him to punish him, whereas in truth it is to do good for him in his end and to awaken him through this to teshuvah;516Menasheh’s suffering as an awakening — II Divrei HaYamim 33:10-13 relates that after Menasheh ignored prophetic warning, the Assyrians seized him with hooks, bound him in bronze, and carried him to Bavel; “when he was in distress, he entreated Hashem ... humbled himself greatly ... and prayed,” and Hashem restored him to Jerusalem. Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 10:2 describes the captivity more sharply: his captors placed him in a heated copper vessel, and only when every idol failed did he remember the verses his father had taught him, especially Devarim 4:30-31, promising return “when you are in distress.” The later “tunnel beneath the Throne” was thus preceded by suffering that cracked the hardened exterior and awakened the memory of Torah. R’ Tzadok therefore calls the punishing left hand itself the first stage of Divine reception.

וְדָבָר זֶה נִקְרָא ״קַבָּלָה בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת״, כְּשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְעוֹרְרוֹ עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי הוּכְבַּד לִבּוֹ עַל יְדֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין הַסּוֹתֶמֶת לְפָנָיו דַּלְתֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה

and this is termed “reception in a secret tunnel,” when it is impossible to awaken him through the bas kol “Return,” etc., because his heart was hardened by the Attribute of Judgment that seals before him the portals of repentance.

״דּוֹדִי שָׁלַח יָדוֹ מִן הַחוֹר״ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ה:ד), שֶׁשָּׁם הַשְּׁרָצִים מְצוּיִים, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים רַבָּה] עַל פָּסוּק זֶה עַל בִּנְיַן בַּיִת שֵׁנִי עַל יְדֵי כּוֹרֶשׁ

“My beloved put forth his hand by the hole of the door” (Shir HaShirim 5:4), where creeping vermin are found, as they expounded in Shir HaShirim Rabbah (5:4) on this verse regarding the building of the Second Temple through Cyrus;517Shir HaShirim Rabbah (on 5:4): On “my beloved put his hand through the hole [min hachor], and my heart was moved for him” — expounded of the building of the Second Temple through Cyrus [Koresh], when the Divine “hand” reached in, as it were, to rouse the return from Bavel. The se’if’s image of the arousal that reaches even into the “hole” where the concealed “creeping things” are found.
וְשָׁם נִקְרָא ״דּוֹדִי״, דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הָיָה בְּאַהֲבָה וְחִבָּה וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין
and there He is called “my beloved,” for nevertheless it came about through love and affection and not through suffering;

וּכְשֶׁהוּא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין דְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״בְּמֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן״, זֶהוּ הַהִתְעוֹרְרוּת וּבַמַּחְתֶּרֶת עַל יְדֵי יַד שְׂמֹאל שֶׁנִּרְאֵית כְּדוֹחָה וְנִרְאֵית כְּמִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת בַּיָּדַיִם ״יְדֵי עֵשָׂו״

but when it occurs through the afflictions of the nations, as they said regarding “a king as harsh as Haman” (Sanhedrin 97b), this is the awakening within the secret tunnel through the left hand that appears to reject, appearing cloaked in the hands that are “the hands of Esav.”518A “king whose decrees are harsh as Haman” — Sanhedrin 97b records the dispute whether redemption depends upon voluntary teshuvah. R’ Yehoshua answers that if Israel does not return, the Holy One raises a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman’s, “and Israel repent, and He restores them to the good.” The pressure is not an alternative to teshuvah but the external instrument that exposes Israel’s buried will to return. R’ Tzadok develops this very source in Machshavos Charutz §6 together with Megillah 14a, where the removal of Achashverosh’s ring accomplished what forty-eight prophets had not: Haman’s threat awakened the nation. Here the hostile ruler is the garment of the hidden Divine hand.,519“The hands are the hands of Esav” — Bereishis 27:22 describes Yaakov’s voice emerging through hands made to appear like Esav’s. Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 contrasts the two powers: Yaakov rules through voice, prayer, and Torah, whereas Esav rules through the hands; Gittin 57b identifies “the hands of Esav” with the violent empire that destroyed the Temple and exiled Israel. R’ Tzadok reverses the image inwardly: when suffering comes through the hands of Edom, the external agent is indeed Esav, but the concealed purpose may be the hand of the “supernal Man” using that garment to awaken teshuvah. This does not excuse the oppressor; it identifies the redemptive intention hidden beneath the historical instrument.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ נִרְאִים יְדֵי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בְּשָׁעָה שֶׁבָּא לְקַבֵּל הַבְּרָכוֹת מִיִּצְחָק אָבִיו, שֶׁיָּדָיו הֵן הֵם יְדֵי אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן כִּי צוּרָתוֹ בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד

Just as the hands of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, appeared when he came to receive the blessings from his father Yitzchak: for his hands were the very hands of Adam Elyon, since his form is engraved upon the Throne of Glory;520R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §23): “In desire, they said (Sotah 47a) ‘the left repels and the right draws near’; and so in the Future this [particular] yetzer will not be slain, as the Zohar says (I, 137–138) that it is called ‘white [lavan],’ for the eye is ‘whitened’ [purified].” Exactly the se’if: the drawing-near comes precisely through the repelling — “the left repels and the right draws near.”,521Yaakov’s form engraved above — Bereishis Rabbah 68:12 interprets the angels “ascending and descending in him” (Bereishis 28:12) as ascending to see Yaakov’s image engraved above and descending to find him sleeping below. Ramban to Bereishis 33:20 cites the recurring teaching that Yaakov’s ikon is engraved upon the Throne of Glory and explains its sod as the dwelling of the Shechinah with Israel, especially in Eretz Yisrael. Rabbeinu Bachya develops the same identification of Yaakov with the supernal form. In the language of the preceding se’if, Yaakov is the perfected human form corresponding to the revealed order of the “supernal Man”; his earthly hands can therefore serve as the parable for the hidden Divine hands beneath the wings of the chayos.
וּכְשֶׁבָּא לִפְנֵי יִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא מִדַּת הַדִּין הוּצְרַךְ לָבוֹא בַּמַּחְתֶּרֶת

and when he came before his father Yitzchak who embodies the Attribute of Judgment (Gevurah), he was compelled to enter via a secret tunnel;522Yitzchak as Gevurah and din — the kabbalistic alignment of the Avos identifies Avraham with Chesed, Yitzchak with Gevurah or Pachad, and Yaakov with Tiferes, the harmonizing middah. Pardes Rimmonim 23:3 calls Gevurah “the middah of Yitzchak, the severe Attribute of Justice,” and Sha’arei Orah, Gate Eight, identifies Gevurah with Pachad Yitzchak and the heavenly power that executes judgment. This background explains the symbolic structure of the blessing episode for R’ Tzadok: Yaakov, the inward truth and synthesis of mercy with judgment, cannot receive the material blessing from the domain of unmixed din through an openly revealed right hand; he must approach through a garment recognizable to Yitzchak’s judicial gaze.

כִּי עֵשָׂו הָיָה לוֹ בִּגְדֵי הַחֲמוּדוֹת דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, שֶׁהָיָה לוֹבְשָׁן כְּשֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ אָבִיו, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהָיָה פּוֹשֵׁט טְלָפָיו וּמַרְאֶה הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ טָהוֹר וָטוֹב לִפְנֵי אָבִיו, וְהַפְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ טָמֵא אֵינוֹ נִגְלֶה בַּחוּץ

for Esav possessed the coveted garments of Adam HaRishon (Bereishis Rabbah 65:16), which he wore when attending his father, meaning that he stretched out his split hooves [like a swine] to show an outward garment pure and good before his father, while the inwardness that was entirely impure remained unrevealed externally.523Yaakov’s hidden approach — Bereishis 27:15-35 describes Rivkah clothing Yaakov in Esav’s garments and Yitzchak later saying, “Your brother came b’mirmah and took your blessing.” Targum Onkelos renders b’mirmah as b’chochmeta, “with wisdom,” emphasizing a divinely directed strategy rather than ordinary falsehood; Rashi similarly explains that the blessing came to the one who was truly fit to receive it under Rivkah’s prophetic direction. R’ Tzadok’s word machteres is his own conceptual bridge to the hidden “tunnel” of teshuvah: strict justice sees only Esav’s outer garment and therefore cannot prosecute, while the blessing is secretly transferred to Yaakov, its truthful inner recipient. The comparison explains the concealment; it is not a halachic identification of Yaakov with a burglar.
וְזֶה כָּל עִנְיַן עֵשָׂו: לְהַעֲרִים, לְהִתְעַטֵּף בִּלְבוּשׁ שֶׁל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וְצַדִּיק
And this is the entire character of Esav: to practice cunning, wrapping himself in the mantle of a Torah scholar and tzaddik;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק ״אִם בֵּין כּוֹכָבִים״ וְגוֹמֵר, דֶּעָתִיד לְהִתְעַטֵּף בְּטַלִּיתוֹ וְלֵישֵׁב אֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מוֹרִידוֹ

and as the Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse “Though you set your nest among the stars...” (Ovadyah 1:4), that in the future he is destined to wrap himself in his tallis and sit beside Yaakov, and the Holy One, blessed be He, will cast him down (Pesikta Rabbasi 12);
כִּי הוּא בְּיָדוֹ לְהַעֲלִים פְּנִימִיּוּתוֹ וּלְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ בִּלְבוּשׁ הַנִּרְאֶה טוֹב לֹא לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן הַגַּשְׁמִי בִּלְבַד, רַק גַּם בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת
for he has the capacity to conceal his interior and cloak himself in a garment appearing good, not only to the physical sight of the eye, but throughout all the spiritual worlds.

וְיִצְחָק אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה נְבִיא ה׳ וְטָעָה בּוֹ, וְרַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּעַצְמוֹ הוּא שֶׁיּוֹרִידוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״מִשָּׁם אוֹרִידְךָ נְאֻם ה׳״, שֶׁהוּא לְבַדּוֹ אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב וְיוֹדֵעַ פְּנִימִיּוּתוֹ

And Yitzchak Avinu, peace be upon him, was a prophet of Hashem and was mistaken in him; and only the Blessed Name Himself is the One Who will bring him down, as it is said, “From thence will I bring you down, says Hashem” (Ovadyah 1:4), for He alone is the One Who looks into the heart (I Shmuel 16:7) and knows his true interior.

items.h: The theme: The limitation of creaturely perception versus Hashem’s gaze upon the inward heart. Even great prophets like Shmuel and ministering angels judge according to the outward eye and external thoughts, whereas only Hashem knows the absolute inner truth of the heart. In the physical World of Action (Asiyah), ruled by strict Judgment (Midas HaDin, numerical equivalent of HaTeva, Nature), Esav dominates through outward deeds. To extract the physical blessings from Yitzchak (the realm of Judgment), Yaakov was required to cloak himself in Esav's garments—transforming that external garment of deception into the revelation of Israel’s inner truth, where even "the fragrance of his traitors" wafts the scent of Gan Eden.

p: אֲבָל הָאָדָם, אֲפִילּוּ נָבִיא גָּדוֹל כִּשְׁמוּאֵל, ״יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם״, וְכֵן מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת

But man, even a prophet as great as Shmuel, “looks on the outward appearance” (I Shmuel 16:7), and likewise the ministering angels;524Shmuel and Eliav — I Shmuel 16:6-7 relates that when Shmuel saw Eliav, his imposing appearance led him to say, “Surely Hashem’s anointed is before Him.” Hashem answered: “Do not look at his appearance or at the height of his stature ... for man sees with the eyes, but Hashem sees into the heart.” Rashi explains that Shmuel was initially drawn to the same outward signs of kingship that had distinguished Shaul; Radak notes that prophetic greatness does not mean that every uncommunicated human judgment is infallible; and Malbim contrasts visible qualities with the hidden dispositions required for kingship. R’ Tzadok uses this episode as the paradigm for the limit of every created knower: even the greatest prophet evaluates what has entered revelation, whereas Hashem alone knows the deepest point of the heart before it has become conscious thought or deed.

וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיּוֹדְעִים מַחֲשָׁבוֹת שֶׁבַּלֵּב לְפִי דַּעַת הַתּוֹסָפוֹת [שַׁבָּת י״ב עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״שֶׁאֵין״, גַּם בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה יֵשׁ פְּנִימִיּוּת שֶׁהוּא הָאֱמֶת שֶׁבְּעַצְמִיּוּתוֹ, וְחִיצוֹנִיּוּת מַה שֶּׁמַּרְאֶה אֶת עַצְמוֹ גַּם כֵּן לַחְשׁוֹב הַכֹּל לִפְנִים

and even though they know the thoughts of the heart according to the opinion of Tosafos [Shabbos 12b, s.v. she-ein], within thought itself there is also an inwardness, which is the truth of one's essence, and an externality, which is how one shows himself even [in his own mind] to think everything outwardly;525Tosafos, Shabbos 12b (s.v. she-ein): that the ministering angels do know the thoughts of the heart (unlike the view that they do not). R’ Tzadok qualifies: even so, there is an innermost stratum of thought that only Hashem knows — “Hashem sees to the heart” (I Shmuel 16:7) — the true self beneath even the thought with which a person deceives himself. (He references Mishnas Chachamim of the author of Menoras HaMaor, §92.)
וּפְנִימִיּוּת הַלֵּב אֵין מַכִּיר אֶלָּא הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ [וְעַיֵּין בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים לְהָרַב מֹשֶׁה חַגִּיז זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה סִימָן ל״ב]
and the inwardness of the heart none knows except the Blessed Name [see Mishnas Chachamim by Rabbi Moshe Chagiz, §32].

וּבְעוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה הַכֹּל לְפִי רוֹב הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וּלְפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת שֶׁבְּפֹעַל, דְּעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ לְעֵשָׂו כֹּחַ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל יְדֵי מִקְצָת מִצְוֹת קַלּוֹת שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה לִפְנִים וּלְהִתְיַיהֵר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י עַמּוּד ב׳]

And in the World of Action (Asiyah), everything is evaluated according to the majority of deeds and according to outward actualization; wherefore Esav possesses power in this world by virtue of a few minor mitzvos performed outwardly for ostentation, as they said [Bava Basra 10b];526Bava Basra 10b: the nations’ “kindness” and mitzvos are done for self-aggrandizement — “the kindness of the peoples is a sin” (Mishlei 14:34) — hence Esav’s foothold is only in the external, this-worldly realm, where “the abundance of the deed” and outward show count; whereas Israel’s worth is in the concealed inner will, which this world’s “hindrances” prevent from fully manifesting (Berachos 17a).
וְהַהֵיפֶךְ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּחִיצוֹנִיּוּתָם לֹא כֵן, דְּעַל כֵּן אֵין מוֹצִיא לְקַבֵּל רוֹב טוֹבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
and the opposite is true of Israel, whose externality is not thus, wherefore it does not produce the reception of the abundance of good in this world;

וְרַק הַפְּנִימִיּוּת כּוּלּוֹ אֱמֶת בִּלְתִּי לַה׳ לְבַדּוֹ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא: ״רְצוֹנֵנוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ״, לוּלֵי הַמְּעַכְּבִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְהִתְגַּלּוּת הַפְּנִימִיּוּת דְּרָצוֹן לִפְעוֹל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה

but their inwardness is entirely Truth, dedicated solely to Hashem alone, as is stated: “it is our will to perform Your will, etc.” (Berachos 17a), were it not for the hindrances in this world that obstruct the revelation of that inward will into actualized deeds.
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין הוּא הַמַּנְהִיג עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כִּידוּעַ דְּ״אֱלֹהִים״ בְּגִימַטְרִיָּא ״הַטֶּבַע״

And the Attribute of Judgment governs this world, as is known that Elokim is numerically equal to HaTeva [Nature, 86];527Elokim and nature — both א-להים and הטבע have the numerical value eighty-six. The Shelah, Torah Ohr to Terumah §27, uses this equivalence to describe the Divine Name Elokim as the concealed governance revealed through the stable order of nature. R’ Tzadok himself makes the same point in Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2:11: Elokim signifies mastery over all the forces of nature, and therefore equals ha-teva in gematria. The equation does not identify nature as an independent power; it means that what appears as impersonal law is itself Hashem’s hidden rule through the middah of din. This is precisely R’ Tzadok’s argument here: the world of outward action is administered through measurable consequence, while its inner Divine intention may remain concealed.

וְכֵן תְּחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין, רַק אַחַר כָּךְ שִׁיתֵּף מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים לְקִיּוּם הָעוֹלָם, וְהוּא מִדַּת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהוּא הַמְקַיֵּים הָעוֹלָם, דְּאִלְמָלֵא יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא הָיָה כָּל הַבְּרִיאָה

and likewise the beginning of Creation was conceived in the Attribute of Judgment, and only afterward did He associate the Attribute of Mercy for the world’s preservation (Rashi, Bereishis 1:1), which is the middah of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who sustains the world, for without Israel the entire Creation would not exist;528Justice joined with mercy in Creation — Bereishis Rabbah 12:15 explains the shift from “Elokim” in Bereishis 1:1 to “Hashem Elokim” in Bereishis 2:4: the world could not endure under strict din alone, so the Holy One joined the middah of mercy to it. Rashi to Bereishis 1:1 states this as: initially it arose in thought to create with din; seeing that the world would not endure, He gave precedence to mercy and joined it to din. Maharal clarifies that this is not a change of mind, God forbid, but two levels of the created order: din defines the truth and structure of existence, while mercy grants the possibility of endurance and repair. R’ Tzadok applies that cosmic pattern to teshuvah: the visible order judges the deed, but the merciful power sustaining the world preserves the hidden point from which return remains possible.,529Israel and Torah as the purpose of Creation — Bereishis Rabbah 1:4 and Rashi to Bereishis 1:1 expound “Bereishis” as “for the sake of Torah, which is called reishis, and for the sake of Israel, who are called reishis.” Shabbos 88a similarly interprets Yirmiyahu 33:25, “If not for My covenant day and night, I would not have established the laws of heaven and earth,” as teaching that the world’s continued existence depends upon Torah. R’ Tzadok links the two: Israel is not merely one nation within the created system but the bearer of the inward purpose for which that system exists. Therefore Yaakov, whose perfected offspring are Israel and whose middah harmonizes din and mercy, is described here as sustaining the world even when Israel’s outward conduct does not yet reveal its inner truth.
אֲבָל מִצַּד יִצְחָק הוּא הַכֹּל בְּמִדַּת הַדִּין
but from the aspect of Yitzchak, everything is governed by the Attribute of Judgment.
וּכְשֶׁ״דִּינָא יְתִב״, אָז כָּל צְבָא הַשָּׁמַיִם עוֹמְדִים מִימִינוֹ וּמִשְּׂמֹאלוֹ, מַיְימִינִים וּמַשְׂמְאִילִים, שֶׁהֵם הַבֵּית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה, וְהֵם אֵין יוֹדְעִים הַפְּנִימִיּוּת

And when “the judgment was set” (Daniel 7:10), all the host of heaven stand on His right and on His left, inclining toward acquittal and inclining toward guilt (Shabbos 56b), being the Heavenly Court, and they do not know the inwardness.530The Heavenly Court to the right and left — I Melachim 22:19 records Michayahu’s vision of Hashem seated upon His throne “and all the host of heaven standing by Him on His right and on His left.” Chazal ask how “right” and “left” can apply before Hashem and explain: those on the right advocate merit, while those on the left advocate liability. Rashi to Bereishis 1:26 cites this vision to explain Hashem’s consultation with the heavenly retinue, and Midrash Tanchuma, Mishpatim §6, develops it as the process by which a case is argued above. The angels judge from what is available within the created order of evidence and manifestation. R’ Tzadok’s point is that such a court cannot penetrate the innermost will known only to Hashem; mercy may therefore have to enter the judicial order in a concealed garment that even the prosecuting forces cannot challenge.

וְעַל כֵּן, כְּשֶׁבָּא יַעֲקֹב לְקַבֵּל בִּרְכַּת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִיִּצְחָק, הוּצְרַךְ לִלְבּוֹשׁ בִּגְדֵי עֵשָׂו, כִּי הוּא הָיָה אוֹהֵב עֵשָׂו מִצַּד הַלְּבוּשׁ הַנִּגְלֶה מִמֶּנּוּ לְפָנָיו בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

Therefore, when Yaakov came to receive the blessing of this world from Yitzchak, he was compelled to wear the garments of Esav, because [Yitzchak] loved Esav on account of the outward garment revealed before him in this world;531Yitzchak’s perception of Esav — Bereishis 25:27-28 says that Esav was “a man who knew hunting” and that Yitzchak loved him “because game was in his mouth.” Rashi, following Bereishis Rabbah 63:10, explains that Esav knew how to “hunt and deceive his father with his mouth,” asking ostentatious questions such as how to tithe salt and straw so that Yitzchak would think him exceptionally exacting in mitzvos. Midrash Aggadah adds that Yitzchak loved the image of piety that Esav presented, while Rivkah, who saw his conduct, recognized the deception. R’ Tzadok is not diminishing Yitzchak’s greatness; he is demonstrating the limitation built into judgment in this world: Yitzchak’s middah responds to the garment that has entered evidence, while the concealed truth of the person remains known in full only above.

וּכְשֶׁלָּבַשׁ יַעֲקֹב אוֹתוֹ לְבוּשׁ, וְהוּא כּוּלּוֹ אֱמֶת וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְרַמּוֹת וּלְהַרְאוֹת הַלְּבוּשׁ נֶגֶד הַפְּנִימִיּוּת, מִמֵּילָא אוֹתוֹ הַלְּבוּשׁ דְּעֵשָׂו נֶהְפַּךְ אֶצְלוֹ לְהַרְאוֹת הָאֱמֶת דְּעֵשָׂו שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ הַלְּבוּשׁ, וְהוּא הַלְּבוּשׁ שֶׁלּוֹ מֵאוֹתָם שֶׁבֵּירוּרוֹ שֶׁלֹּא כֵן בְּפֹעַל

and when Yaakov donned that garment, being entirely Truth and unable to deceive or present an outward garment contradictory to his inwardness, of itself that garment of Esav was transformed in him to reveal the inner truth of Esav contained within that garment, which is his garment from those whose outer actuality belies their inner reality.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחֵטְא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא בִּפְנִימִיּוּת, וְעַל כֵּן הֵרִיחַ בּוֹ יִצְחָק ״רֵיחַ בּוֹגְדָיו״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ל״ז עַמּוּד א׳]

And nevertheless, although the sin of Israel appears in the externality, wherefore Yitzchak smelled in him “the fragrance of his traitors [bogdav]” as they said [in Sanhedrin 37a],532“Although he sinned, he is Israel” — Sanhedrin 44a derives this principle from Yehoshua 7:11, “Israel has sinned,” said concerning Achan: even after sin, the essential name Israel remains. The Gemara illustrates it with a myrtle standing among thorns: it is still called a myrtle. Halachic authorities use the principle to explain why a Jewish transgressor remains obligated in mitzvos and retains basic Jewish status. R’ Tzadok repeatedly deepens it from legal identity into spiritual ontology; see Peri Tzadik, Pesach §8, and Takanas HaShavin §3: the root inherited from Yaakov cannot be uprooted, even when the revealed conduct is distorted. Thus the “garment of Esav” can cover a Jewish soul, but it cannot become its innermost identity.,533R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §14): “For man ‘looks to the eyes’ and to the revealed deed and the middos manifest through their expansion, but Hashem ‘looks to the heart,’ from which are ‘the issues of life,’ the source of the middos.” Exactly the se’if: man — even a prophet like Shmuel — and the angels too “see to the eyes”; only Hashem sees the hidden inner core.,534Sanhedrin 37a (and Bereishis Rabbah): On “and he smelled the scent of his garments [begadav]” (Bereishis 27:27) — “do not read begadav [his garments], but bogdav [his traitors]” — [teaching] that even Israel’s “traitors” are full of good deeds. R’ Tzadok reads it here as Yitzchak’s smelling “the scent of Gan Eden” through the shining of Yaakov’s inner core.
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי הֶאָרַת הַפְּנִימִיּוּת דְּיַעֲקֹב בְּבִיאָתוֹ אֵלָיו שֶׁנִּכְנַס עִמּוֹ רֵיחַ גַּן עֵדֶן, מִמֵּילָא הֵרִיחַ הַטּוֹב שֶׁבִּפְנִימִיּוּת בּוֹגְדָיו

yet through the illumination of the inwardness of Yaakov upon his arrival, when the scent of Gan Eden entered with him (Rashi, Bereishis 27:27), he consequently smelled the good hidden in the inwardness of his traitors;535The fragrance accompanying Yaakov — Bereishis 27:27 says that Yitzchak “smelled the fragrance of his garments” and blessed Yaakov. Rashi asks how goatskins, which normally have an unpleasant odor, could produce such fragrance and answers, following Bereishis Rabbah 65:22, that the scent of Gan Eden entered with Yaakov; “the field that Hashem blessed” is interpreted as a field of apples or the supernal garden. This source complements the Gemara’s derashah on begadav/bogdav cited in the existing note: the outward garment may be associated with betrayal, yet the inward fragrance reveals the holy root. R’ Tzadok reads the blessing scene as a disclosure of this paradox — Esav’s visible clothing is transformed by Yaakov’s inner truth until even the judge of externals perceives the scent of the hidden Edenic source.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר: ״הַיָּדַיִם״ וְכֹחוֹת הַפְּעוּלָּה — ״יְדֵי עֵשָׂו״, וְ״הַקּוֹל״ שֶׁהוּא הַפְּנִימִיּוּת — ״קוֹל יַעֲקֹב״
and therefore he said: the hands and faculties of action are “the hands of Esav,” but the voice, which is the inwardness, is “the voice of Yaakov” (Bereishis 27:22).

items.h: The theme: The secret strategy against strict Judgment: Mercy conceals itself within Judgment, reaching out beneath the wings of the Chayos. The right hand of Chesed clothes itself within the left hand of Gevurah, just as Adam Elyon cloaks Himself in the garments of Esav. This occurred in the days of Haman, where Hashem handed over the ring of dominion to a tyrant to arouse Israel from their spiritual slumber through suffering, bringing about a return that forty-eight prophets could not achieve. So too, in every generation and for every individual soul, the prophetic call to teshuvah resounds eternally, awakening the Jewish heart to its innate, unshakeable root of Truth.

p: וְזֶהוּ הָעֵצָה נֶגֶד מִדַּת הַדִּין, שֶׁמִּדַּת הָרַחֲמִים מַעֲלֶמֶת רַחֲמִים מִתַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת שֶׁאֵין נִרְגָּשׁ לְכָל הַמַּלְאָכִים וּבֵית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה בְּכָל הָעוֹלָמוֹת

And this is the counsel against the Attribute of Judgment: that the Attribute of Mercy conceals mercy beneath the wings of the Chayos, undetectable to all the angels and the Heavenly Court throughout all the spiritual worlds;536The concealed hands beneath the chayos — Yechezkel 1:8 describes “the hands of a man beneath their wings.” Chazal interpret this image as Hashem’s hands extended beneath the wings of the chayos to receive penitents “because of the Attribute of Justice”; see Kol Bo §66, which preserves the teaching and concludes, “His right hand is outstretched to receive those who return.” Zohar, Pekudei (Sulam §786), explains the “hands” as supernal receptacles that receive prayer and open entrances for those who seek return. Shem MiShmuel, Purim §5:12, applies the image specifically to hidden salvation: just as the penitent is received in a place inaccessible to accusation, Divine bounty can descend from a concealed source without the prosecuting forces sensing it. Rav Tzadok develops the same mechanism here. Mercy does not defeat din by denying truth; it clothes itself within the ordered world of din and works from beneath its wings, where the soul’s still-hidden capacity for teshuvah can be preserved and awakened.

וְזֶהוּ ״יָדוֹ״ כְּתִיב, שֶׁאֵין כָּאן אֶלָּא יָד אֶחָד, כִּי יַד יָמִין מִתְלַבֶּשֶׁת תּוֹךְ הַיַּד שְׂמֹאל (וּכִבְיָכוֹל אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן מִתְלַבֵּשׁ תּוֹךְ הַיַּד שְׂמֹאל), וְכִבְיָכוֹל אָדָם הָעֶלְיוֹן מִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּבִגְדֵי עֵשָׂו

and this is why “His hand” (yado, in the singular) is written, for there is only one revealed hand here, because the right hand is cloaked within the left hand (and as it were, Adam Elyon is cloaked within the left hand), cloaked, as it were, in the garments of Esav,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה עַל פָּסוּק ״חֲמוּץ בְּגָדִים״ שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לוֹבֵשׁ אָדוֹם כָּמוֹהוּ כְּשֶׁיָּבוֹא לִנְקוֹם מִמֶּנּוּ וּלְכַלּוֹתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי

in the manner the Sages of blessed memory expounded on the verse “with dyed garments” (Yeshayah 63:1), that the Holy One, blessed be He, dons red like him when He comes to take vengeance upon him and destroy him completely.537“Crimson garments” — Yeshayah 63:1-4 portrays the Divine warrior coming from Edom with blood-colored garments, proclaiming that the day of vengeance and the year of redemption have arrived. Rashi explains that the prophecy speaks in the imagery of human warfare “to convey to the ear what it can hear”: the Shechinah is depicted as clothed in garments stained by the defeat of Edom, while the subject is Hashem’s personal vengeance against Edom and its heavenly power. The anthropomorphic garment therefore does not describe His essence, God forbid, but the form in which His judgment becomes visible within history. Rav Tzadok reads the image inwardly: the red garment appears to belong to Esav and strict din, yet the One clothed within it is the “supernal Man,” whose purpose is Israel’s redemption. The very appearance of Edomite power can thus become the external clothing through which Edom is ultimately destroyed.

וְכֵן בְּכָל דּוֹר וָדוֹר, כְּשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהוֹשִׁיעַ לְיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּאֹפֶן אַחֵר, כְּבִימֵי הָמָן דְּהוּחְזְרוּ לְמוּטָב עַל יְדֵי זֶה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא הוֹעִיל לָהֶם מ״ח נְבִיאִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְגִלָּה י״ד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״גְּדוֹלָה הֲסָרַת טַבַּעַת וְכוּלֵיהּ״

And so it is in every generation when it is impossible to bring salvation to Israel in any other way, as in the days of Haman, where through this they were returned to good when forty-eight prophets could not avail them, as they said [Megillah 14a]: “Greater was the removal of the signet ring, etc.”;538Megillah 14a: “Forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses prophesied to Israel, and not one of them turned them back to the good; yet the removal of Achashverosh’s ring [and its transfer to Haman] turned them back to the good — hence, ‘greater was the removal of the ring than the forty-eight prophets.’” With Esther Rabbah, that “the King” (unspecified) in the Megillah alludes to the King of the world.
וּבְכָל מָקוֹם ״הַמֶּלֶךְ״ סְתָם בַּמְּגִלָּה בְּמַלְכּוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם הַכָּתוּב מְדַבֵּר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּמִדְרַשׁ אֶסְתֵּר]
and wherever “the King” is stated without qualification in the Megillah, Scripture speaks of the King of the Universe, as they expounded [in Midrash Esther Rabbah 3:10],

כִּי מַלְכּוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם כִּבְיָכוֹל הֵסִיר טַבַּעַת מֶמְשַׁלְתּוֹ לְשָׁעָה קַלָּה וּמְסָרָהּ לְהָמָן, כְּאִלּוּ הוּא הַמּוֹשֵׁל וְעוֹשֶׂה כִּרְצוֹנוֹ בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ וּבָאוּמָּה יִשְׂרְאֵלִית שֶׁהֵם כּוֹלְלִים כָּל הָעוֹלָמוֹת כּוּלָּם גַּם כֵּן

for the King of the Universe, as it were, removed the signet ring of His dominion for a brief moment and handed it to Haman, as though he were the master doing as he willed throughout the entire universe and over the Israelite nation, who also incorporate all the worlds.

וְזֶהוּ הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הַקְּדוּשָׁה בִּלְבוּשׁ שַׂק דְּהָמָן לִהְיוֹתָם יְשֵׁנִים מִן הַמִּצְוֹת, וְלֹא הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לְעוֹרְרָם אֶלָּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה שֶׁיִּשְׁלַח יָדוֹ מִן הַחוֹר בְּהִתְלַבְּשׁוֹ הַהֵיפֶךְ, שֶׁהַגְּזֵירָה ״לְהַשְׁמִיד וְלַהֲרֹג״ וְגוֹמֵר

And this is the cloaking of holiness in the sackcloth-garment of Haman, because they were asleep from the mitzvos and it was impossible to awaken them except in this manner: that He put forth His hand from the hole (Shir HaShirim 5:4) by cloaking Himself in the reverse appearance, through the decree “to destroy, to slay, and to exterminate” (Esther 3:13);539“Asleep from the mitzvos” — Esther 3:8 introduces Haman’s accusation, “There is one people.” Megillah 13b reads his word yeshno as yashnu: “they have fallen asleep from the mitzvos.” This does not necessarily mean that every mitzvah had ceased. Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Adar II §1, and Resisei Layla §20 explain that the accusation concerned the loss of inward vitality: mitzvos could be performed in a state resembling sleep, while the deepest Jewish will remained awake. This is the background to Rav Tzadok’s “sackcloth garment.” Esther 4:1 records Mordechai clothing himself in sackcloth when the decree became known; the external distress awakened the inner life that had become dormant. Haman saw sleep as proof that Israel’s covenantal core had disappeared. Rav Tzadok reverses that claim: sleep conceals life but does not extinguish it, and the blow from outside becomes the means by which the hidden point reawakens.,540The decree and its reversal — Esther 3:13 formulates Haman’s decree “to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate all the Jews.” The second royal letter deliberately repeats the same verbs, now granting the Jews power “to destroy, to kill, and to annihilate” the forces attacking them (Esther 8:11). The Megillah then states the governing principle: “v’nahafoch hu — the opposite occurred,” so that the Jews ruled over those who hated them (Esther 9:1). The reversal is deeper than a fortunate change of events. The language of destruction itself is transferred from Israel to Amalek, revealing that the threatening decree had become the instrument of its own undoing. This is Rav Tzadok’s meaning that holiness was clothed in Haman’s garment: within the visible decree lay a concealed Divine intention to awaken Israel, elevate its horn, and turn the power of “destroying” against Haman and the seed of Amalek.
וּבֶאֱמֶת הָיָה הַכַּוָּונָה לְהֵיפֶךְ: לְרוֹמֵם וּלְגַדֵּל קֶרֶן יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְלַהֲרוֹג וּלְאַבֵּד אֶת הָמָן וְזֶרַע עֲמָלֵק וְכָל אוֹיְבֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
yet in truth the intention was the exact opposite: to elevate and exalt the horn of Israel, and to slay and destroy Haman, the seed of Amalek, and all the enemies of Israel.

וְכֵן לֶעָתִיד, אִם יִצְטָרְכוּ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם לְמֶלֶךְ קָשֶׁה כְּהָמָן, יִהְיֶה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּקִרְבּוֹ, דְּ״לֵב מְלָכִים בְּיַד ה׳״, וְעַל יְדֵי אוֹתוֹ הִתְלַבְּשׁוּת בִּלְבוּשׁ עֵשָׂו יְאַבְּדוּ מִן הָעוֹלָם

And so in the future, if they should require, God forbid, a king as harsh as Haman, the Blessed Name will cloak Himself within him—for “the king’s heart is in the hand of Hashem” (Mishlei 21:1)—and through that very cloaking in the garment of Esav, He will eradicate him from the world;541A harsh king and the King’s heart — Sanhedrin 97b teaches that if Israel does not awaken to teshuvah, the Holy One may raise over them “a king whose decrees are as harsh as Haman’s,” through whom they return to the good. Mishlei 21:1 supplies the inner principle: “Like channels of water is the heart of a king in the hand of Hashem; He turns it wherever He desires.” The meforshim explain that a ruler may experience his plans as his own, while Providence directs their course toward an end he neither sees nor intends. Thus the teaching does not absolve a wicked ruler of responsibility; Haman chooses hatred and is punished for it. Yet his freely chosen wickedness is enclosed within a higher governance that redirects its consequences. Rav Tzadok calls this Hashem’s clothing within the harsh king: the external garment is Esav’s coercive power, but the hidden hand bends that power toward Israel’s teshuvah and the eventual destruction of the persecutor himself.
וְכֵן בְּכָל נֶפֶשׁ פְּרָטִי, דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״שֹׁמֵר אֱמֶת לְעוֹלָם״ (תְּהִלִּים קמ״ו:ו׳), הֵם זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ זֶרַע אֱמֶת, שֶׁלֹּא יִדַּח מֵהֶם נִדָּח

and likewise with every individual soul, for the Blessed Name “keeps truth forever” (Tehillim 146:6), they being the seed of Yaakov which is entirely seed of Truth (Yirmeyah 2:21), that no outcast shall be expelled from Him (II Shmuel 14:14);542“Hashem keeps truth forever” and the “seed of truth” — Tehillim 146:6 praises the Creator as “the One who keeps truth forever,” meaning that His covenantal faithfulness is not cancelled by delay or concealment. Yirmiyahu 2:21 calls Israel “entirely seed of truth,” even while rebuking the nation for having outwardly become like an alien vine. The contrast itself is Rav Tzadok’s point: deformation in conduct does not erase the original planting. Michah 7:20 associates truth specifically with Yaakov — “You will grant truth to Yaakov, kindness to Avraham” — and the meforshim explain that “truth” signifies the sure fulfillment of the covenant promised to his descendants. Rav Tzadok combines these verses ontologically. Israel is the seed of Yaakov, whose root is emes; therefore Hashem’s fidelity to truth includes continuously arranging means by which that root will again appear. Teshuvah is not the invention of a new identity but the reemergence of the true seed beneath its foreign growth.,543“No outcast shall be cast away” — II Shmuel 14:14 says that God “devises designs so that no banished one be banished from Him.” In its narrative setting, the wise woman of Tekoa argues for bringing Avshalom back from exile; later Jewish thought reads the verse as a general principle of Divine providence over every Jewish soul. Rav Tzadok makes this explicit in Resisei Layla §35: even those who are spiritually “lost” or “banished” will ultimately be awakened by the great shofar, because Hashem has promised that no outcast will remain cast away. Machshavot Charutz §9 and Peri Tzadik, Nasso §15, similarly describe an indestructible root of faith within Knesses Yisrael. This promise does not minimize sin or remove the need for punishment and teshuvah. It means that all the concealments, exiles, and corrective processes are ultimately ordered toward return rather than permanent severance.

וּמְעוֹרְרָם תָּמִיד לִתְשׁוּבָה עַל יְדֵי הַמ״ח נְבִיאִים שֶׁנִּקְבְּעָה נְבוּאָתָם לְדוֹרוֹת, בְּדִבְרֵי נְבוּאָתָם בְּאַזְהָרַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה מַרְעֶמֶת וּמַרְעֶשֶׁת בִּתְמִידוּת בַּלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

and He arouses them constantly to teshuvah through the forty-eight prophets whose prophecy was established for generations, their prophetic words resounding and shaking the hearts of the Children of Israel continuously with the call to repentance.544Prophecy fixed for the generations — Megillah 14a teaches that far more prophets arose in Israel than are recorded in Tanach; only “prophecy needed for the generations was written,” while prophecy needed only for its immediate hour was not. The same passage identifies the forty-eight prophets and seven prophetesses whose teachings entered the permanent canon. Their words are therefore not merely reports of past admonition. Their preservation testifies that their spiritual address remains necessary whenever the corresponding condition returns. Rav Tzadok explains in Tzidkas HaTzadik §72 that a miracle or prophetic event written for generations opened a lasting gate through which that Divine power can again be reached. Here he applies that principle to teshuvah: the prophetic cry continues to “thunder” in Jewish hearts because the words chosen for Scripture carry an enduring force designed for every later generation.,545R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §36): “That is, a multiplicity that is unified — and it is the Attribute of Mercy, which is ‘kindness within judgment,’ for such is the judgment: to have mercy on His children and do kindness with them; and this is [done] openly and publicly, for since such is the judgment there is no dread of accusation and no shame.” Exactly the se’if: the Attribute of Mercy hidden beneath the wings of the chayos — the “stratagem” by which mercy overcomes strict judgment.

וְכֵן כָּל מָקוֹם שֶׁחִידְּשׁוּ סוֹפְרִים אַחַר כָּךְ כָּל דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה הַמְקוּדָּשִׁים, וְאַף שֶׁאַחֲרֵיהֶם אוֹתָם שֶׁהָיוּ חֲכָמִים בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁכָּל דִּבְרֵיהֶם דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים

And likewise wherever the Scribes subsequently innovated all the sanctified words of the Sages of blessed memory, and even those after them who were true sages whose words are all the words of the Living God,546The authority of the soferim and rabbinic enactments — Devarim 17:11 commands Israel not to turn aside from the rulings of the authorized Torah court. Shabbos 23a asks how one may bless “Who commanded us” over the rabbinic mitzvah of Chanukah lights and answers: Rav Avya derives the command from “lo tasur,” while Rav Nechemiah cites “Ask your father and he will tell you; your elders and they will say to you” (Devarim 32:7). Rambam, Hilchos Mamrim 1:1-2, accordingly includes the received interpretations, enactments, decrees, and safeguards of the Great Court within the Torah’s obligation to heed the sages. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “what the soferim innovated” does not mean arbitrary invention detached from Sinai. It refers to Torah authority drawing forth the practical form needed by a later generation. Their sacred words can therefore serve as a further Divine awakening after the era of prophecy.,547“The words of the living God” — Eruvin 13b records the heavenly declaration concerning Beis Shammai and Beis Hillel: “These and those are the words of the living God,” even though practical halachah follows Beis Hillel. Gittin 6b similarly applies the phrase to differing interpretations that disclose complementary dimensions of one event. Rashi to Kesubos 57a explains that honest Torah reasoning is not falsehood merely because another sage reaches the opposite ruling: each view articulates the rationale that applies to the reality as that sage understands it, and changing circumstances may reveal the relevance of a different rationale. Rav Tzadok carefully limits his statement to those “who were sages in truth.” Their words possess life because they are genuine apprehensions within Torah, not personal rhetoric. Once articulated in holiness, they continue supplying later souls with the precise thought capable of awakening them from spiritual sleep.
דִּבְרֵיהֶם פּוֹעֲלִים בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת וּבְכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת לְעוֹרְרָם מִשְּׁנָתָם, וְאַשְׁרֵי הַמִּתְעוֹרֵר עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְבַד שֶׁאֵין צָרִיךְ יוֹתֵר
their words operate throughout all generations and in all hearts to awaken them from their slumber; and fortunate is he who awakens through this alone, needing nothing further.

items.h: The theme: The appointed season of teshuvah for all Israel during the Ten Days of Repentance (Aseres Yemei Teshuvah), when Hashem is found (behimatze'o). The awakening begins on Rosh Hashanah through the simple voice of the Shofar—the "voice of Yaakov"—which pierces sleep, awakens awe (teshuvah mi-yirah), and causes the Throne of Judgment (Korsei d'Dina) to be removed so Hashem sits upon the Throne of Mercy (Kisei Rachamim). The structure of the Ten Days rectifies the ten sefirotic rungs: the two days of Rosh Hashanah rectify the hidden cognitive head (Keser and Chochmah); the seven intermediate days rectify the seven building attributes of action (Chesed through Malchus); and Yom Kippur culminates in Binah of the heart through teshuvah from love (teshuvah ila'ah).

p: וּזְמַן תְּשׁוּבָה לַכֹּל הוּא בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁאָז נִקְרָא ״בְּהִמָּצְאוֹ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה י״ח עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁהוּא מָצוּי אֵצֶל כָּל יָחִיד

And the season of repentance for all is during the Ten Days of Repentance, when it is termed “while He may be found” (Yeshayah 55:6), as they said [Rosh Hashanah 18a] that He is accessible to every individual;548Rosh Hashanah 18a: On “seek Hashem while He may be found [b’himatzo]” (Yeshayah 55:6) — “these are the ten days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur,” when He is ‘found’ and near to every individual. The source for the se’if’s Ten Days of Teshuvah, when Hashem is “found.”
כִּי אָז הוּא בְּיִחוּד הַזְּמַן שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְעוֹרֵר כָּל יָחִיד מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל בְּחַדְרֵי לְבָבוֹ לָשׁוּב אֵלָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ
for then is uniquely the time when the Blessed Name arouses each individual of Israel in the chambers of his heart to return to Him, may He be blessed.

וְהַהַתְחָלָה עַל יְדֵי קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, דִּפְשׁוּטוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָרַמְבַּ״ם: ״עוּרוּ יְשֵׁנִים מִתַּרְדֶּמַתְכֶם״, וְ״הֲיִתָּקַע שׁוֹפָר בְּעִיר וְעָם לֹא יֶחֱרָדוּ״ הִיא תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה שֶׁהוּא כְּכָל הַתְחָלַת הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם

And the commencement is through the sound of the Shofar on Rosh Hashanah, whose plain meaning is as the Rambam wrote (Hilchos Teshuvah 3:4): “Awake, you sleepers, from your slumber”; and “Shall a horn be blown in a city, and the people not tremble?” (Amos 3:6) represents teshuvah from fear, which characterizes every beginning of teshuvah initiated by man;549The shofar as an awakening to teshuvah — Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 3:4, writes that although the command of shofar is a decree of Scripture, it contains an allusion: “Awake, sleepers, from your sleep; arise, slumberers, from your slumber; examine your deeds, return in teshuvah, and remember your Creator.” Amos 3:6 supplies the prophetic image: “Shall a shofar be sounded in a city and the people not tremble?” Pesikta de-Rav Kahana §24 applies this verse to the shofar of Rosh Hashanah and explains that Hashem does not desire the death of the wicked but sends the warning call so that they may awaken. Rav Tzadok therefore identifies this first movement as teshuvah from fear: the sound enters from without, shakes the person out of spiritual sleep, and begins the human response. Yet the Rambam’s language already points beyond fear alone — to self-examination, remembrance of the Creator, and the recovery of one’s true purpose.

וְזֶהוּ פְּעוּלָּתוֹ בַּלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְכֵן פּוֹעֵל לְמַעְלָה בְּקִיּוּם מִצְוָה זוֹ דְּהַשְׁמָעַת קוֹל שׁוֹפָר שֶׁהוּא ״הַקּוֹל קוֹל יַעֲקֹב״, קוֹל פָּשׁוּט הַמְעוֹרֵר עַל הַפְּנִימִיּוּת הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁכָּל רְצוֹנֵנוּ רַק לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ

and this is its operation in the hearts of the Children of Israel, and so it operates Above through the fulfillment of this mitzvah of sounding the Shofar: which is “the voice is the voice of Yaakov” (Bereishis 27:22), a simple, unadorned voice that awakens the concealed inwardness, testifying that our sole desire is to do His Blessed will.550“The voice, the voice of Yaakov” — Bereishis 27:22 contrasts Yaakov’s voice with Esav’s hands. Bereishis Rabbah 65:20 develops the contrast: Yaakov’s power is in his voice — Torah and prayer — and when that voice is heard in the synagogues and study halls, the hands of Esav do not rule. Rav Tzadok, Resisei Layla §52, similarly calls Torah and prayer “the sword of the mouth,” the spiritual weapon of Israel. In this se’if the shofar is identified with that same voice, but in its simplest and most inward form: not articulated words, but a plain cry preceding speech. The sound reaches the point of Yaakov that is prior to the complications of outward conduct. Thus the mitzvah does not merely announce judgment; it allows the essential Jewish voice to emerge, weakening the external “hands of Esav” and disclosing the soul’s bond with Hashem.,551The hidden will of Israel — Berachos 17a records R’ Alexandri’s prayer: “Master of the worlds, it is revealed and known before You that our will is to do Your will; and what prevents us? The leaven in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms.” Rashi explains the “leaven” as the evil inclination within the heart. The statement distinguishes the deepest ratzon from the forces that obstruct its appearance in action. Rav Tzadok repeatedly builds upon this teaching; see Resisei Layla §20, where even when Israel is “asleep from the mitzvos,” the heart remains awake and the true will remains attached to Hashem. The shofar’s simple voice reaches this pre-verbal ratzon. It does not excuse wrongdoing, because the external barriers must still be overcome through teshuvah; rather, it reveals the point from which genuine teshuvah becomes possible — the inward will that never consented to permanent separation.

וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה יַעֲלֶה זִכְרוֹנֵנוּ לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ לְטוֹבָה, כִּי יִסְתַּלֵּק כּוּרְסְיָא דְּדִינָא וְיֵשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא רַחֲמִים לְהִתְנַהֵג בַּחֲסִידוּת, וּמוֹחֵל עֲוֹנוֹת עַמּוֹ כִּי מַבִּיט עַל הַפְּנִימִיּוּת וְלֹא עַל חִיצוֹנִיּוּת הַמַּעֲשִׂים הַנִּגְלִים

And through this our remembrance ascends before Him for good, for the Throne of Judgment (Korsei d’Dina) is removed and He sits upon the Throne of Mercy (Kisei Rachamim) to conduct Himself with lovingkindness (Vayikra Rabbah 29:3), forgiving the iniquities of His people because He gazes at the inwardness and not at the externality of revealed actions.552Remembrance through the shofar — Rosh Hashanah 16a teaches: “Recite before Me kingship, remembrance, and shofar verses: kingship, so that you accept My kingship; remembrance, so that your remembrance rise before Me for good — and through what? Through the shofar.” The shofar is therefore not only a warning heard below; it is the means by which Israel’s remembrance ascends Above. Rambam, Commentary to Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 4:5, cites this teaching as the structure of the Rosh Hashanah service. Sefas Emes explains that the shofar’s voice is uniquely Israel’s own voice and brings the words of remembrance inward, “before” Hashem. Rav Tzadok reads this remembrance as the disclosure of the concealed inner identity. What is remembered is not a selective forgetting of deeds, but the covenantal root beneath them — the true Yaakov-point that can now awaken, repent, and redirect the revealed life.,553From the throne of judgment to the throne of mercy — Tehillim 47:6 says, “Elokim ascends with the teruah; Hashem with the sound of the shofar.” Yalkut Shimoni on Tehillim §754 explains: when the Holy One sits upon the throne of judgment, He is called Elokim; when Israel sounds the shofar, He rises from the throne of judgment and sits upon the throne of mercy, as indicated by the Divine Name of mercy in the second half of the verse. The change does not imply change in Hashem Himself, God forbid. It describes the mode through which His unchanging will is manifested toward the world. Rav Tzadok connects the transition to the shofar’s revelation of Israel’s inward truth: once the hidden desire to return is sounded, judgment itself can agree that the person is not exhausted by the visible record of failure and that mercy should guide the process of repair.,554The heart beneath the visible appearance — I Shmuel 16:7 teaches, “Man sees what is visible to the eyes, but Hashem sees into the heart.” In context, Shmuel was impressed by Eliav’s outward appearance, while Hashem disclosed that kingship depended upon the hidden heart. Rambam, Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 7:7, cites the verse to distinguish human judgment, which must proceed from available evidence, from Divine knowledge of inward truth. Rav Tzadok does not mean that revealed deeds are irrelevant; throughout his writings, teshuvah requires their repair. His point is that Rosh Hashanah judgment includes a dimension inaccessible to any created court: Hashem sees whether the sins express the soul’s final desire or are foreign garments covering a will that remains directed toward Him. The shofar gives voice to that hidden heart, allowing mercy to address the person according to the root from which return can grow.

וְשִׁבְעַת יָמִים שֶׁבֵּין רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה לְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הֵם יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן כָּל מַה שֶּׁפָּגַם בְּכָל הַשָּׁנָה [אוֹ הַשָּׁנִים שֶׁעָבְרוּ] כָּל יוֹם יוֹמוֹ, כִּידוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִיזַ״ל בְּסֵפֶר הַכַּוָּונוֹת

And the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur are days of repentance to rectify all that was blemished throughout the entire year [or past years], day by day, as is known from the Arizal in Sefer HaKavvanos;555Arizal, Sefer HaKavanos — the kabbalistic teachings of R’ Yitzchak Luria (as recorded by R’ Chaim Vital): the seven days between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur each correspond to a day of the week, each rectifying its own day of the year.

וְהַיְינוּ דְּשִׁבְעַת יָמִים אֵלּוּ שֶׁהֵם כּוֹלְלִים כָּל יְמֵי הַשָּׁבוּעַ, הֵם נֶגֶד שִׁבְעַת יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן הַכּוֹלְלִים שֶׁבַע מִדּוֹת הַיְּדוּעִים, שֶׁהוּא כְּלַל קוֹמַת אָדָם בְּכָל מִדּוֹתָיו וּפְעוּלוֹתָיו הַנִּגְלוֹת

meaning that these seven days, which encompass all the days of the week, correspond to the seven days of the supernal structure incorporating the seven lower attributes (middos), which constitute the full stature of man in all his revealed traits and actions.556The seven “days of building” — Kabbalistic literature calls the seven lower sefiros, from Chesed through Malchus, the seven middos or “days of building,” because through them the ordered, revealed world is built. The seven days of Creation are their temporal expression, and each governs a distinct pattern of conduct and relationship. This usage appears throughout later kabbalistic and chassidic works; for example, Likutei Halachos, Hilchos Nedarim 2:9, explicitly identifies “the seven days of building” with the seven middos and the revealed structure of the world. Rav Tzadok applies the correspondence practically: the seven weekdays between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur repair the revealed stature of the person — love, restraint, harmony, endurance, acknowledgment, bonding, and actual expression — while the holy days at the boundaries address the hidden roots from which those middos emerge.

דְּהַנִּסְתָּרוֹת הֵם ג׳ רִאשׁוֹנוֹת, שֶׁנֶּגְדָּם ב׳ יָמִים דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה, שֶׁהוּא קוֹמַת הָרֹאשׁ: חָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ, וְכֶתֶר שֶׁעַל גַּבֵּי הָרֹאשׁ הוּא הָעוֹמֶק רֵאשִׁית דְּמַחֲשָׁבָה הַנֶּעְלָם מֵהָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ, מְקוֹם לֵידַת הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן״, וְ״הַחָכְמָה מֵאַיִן תִּמָּצֵא״ כַּנּוֹדָע

For the hidden realms are the three upper sefirot (Chabad/Gartcha), paralleled by the two days of Rosh Hashanah, which represent the stature of the Head: Chochmah within the brain, and Keser above the head, which is the profound primal source of thought concealed from man himself, the birthplace of thought wherefore it is termed Yesh me-Ayin, as in “wisdom is found from Nothingness [me-ayin]” (Iyov 28:12);557“Wisdom is found from ayin” — Iyov 28:12 asks, “And wisdom, from where [me-ayin] is it found, and where is the place of understanding?” On the level of peshat, the verse emphasizes that the source of wisdom is hidden from ordinary human discovery. Kabbalistic interpretation reads ayin as the concealed level above articulated Chochmah, often associated with Keser: wisdom flashes into consciousness from a source that the thinker cannot yet grasp as a defined “something.” Chazal also read the verse ethically — Sotah 21b says Torah endures in one who makes himself “as nothing.” Rav Tzadok uses both resonances. Rosh Hashanah repairs the head and the primordial point of thought: Chochmah as the first knowable flash, and Keser as its unknowable birthplace. Teshuvah therefore begins not only by correcting particular ideas, but by returning the faculty of thought to the Divine ayin from which a new and truthful beginning can emerge.
וְהֵם קְדוּשָׁה אַחַת וְיוֹמָא אֲרִיכְתָּא, כִּי הָאַיִן אֵין תְּפִיסָה בּוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיֵּשׁ הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמֶּנּוּ
and they constitute one single sanctity and “one long day” (yoma arichta), because the transcendent Ayin cannot be grasped except through the Yesh [existence] that emanates from it.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא נֶגֶד הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ״ כַּנּוֹדָע

And Yom Kippur corresponds to the Binah within the heart, as in “his heart shall understand, and he shall return, and be healed” (Yeshayah 6:10);558Binah, the heart, and teshuvah — Yeshayah 6:10 joins the stages: “his heart understands, and he returns, and he is healed.” Megillah 17b cites this verse to explain why the blessing of teshuvah follows the blessing of understanding in the Amidah: understanding opens the path to return. Rosh Hashanah 17b further derives from the same verse that teshuvah tears up a person’s decree. In biblical and rabbinic usage, the heart is not merely the seat of emotion; it is the inward faculty that integrates knowledge into lived recognition.
