Rav Tzadok therefore associates Yom Kippur with Binah of the heart. The flash of awakening that began at Rosh Hashanah becomes comprehended, absorbed, and transformed into loving return. Healing is the final word of the verse because true Binah does not remain abstract: it reunites the divided person and restores the deeds and middos to their source.

וְהֵם תִּיקּוּן הַנֶּעְלָמוֹת: הַהַתְחָלָה בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה בִּתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, וְהַגְּמָר בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה, תְּשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה, תְּשׁוּבָה דְּאִתְחַזְיָא לְחַפָּאָה עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי

and these constitute the rectification of the hidden realms: the beginning on Rosh Hashanah through teshuvah from fear, and the completion on Yom Kippur through teshuvah from love—the Higher Teshuvah (teshuvah ila'ah), the repentance worthy to cover over all his deeds (Zohar III, 122a);559R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim §11): “As it says in the passage ‘seek Hashem while He may be found [b’himatzo], call upon Him [while He is near] — let the wicked forsake his way’ — the meaning being that this is the prayer one prays to Hashem, that He cause ‘the wicked to forsake his way,’ for the very power of teshuvah is in the hand of Hashem.” Exactly the se’if: the Ten Days, when Hashem is “found,” near to every individual, rousing each Jew in the chambers of his heart.,560Cf. Zohar (III, Acharei Mos 69b; and Vayikra 15a): “teshuvah tata’ah” — the lower heh, Malchus — versus “teshuvah ila’ah,” the upper heh, Binah. R’ Tzadok maps these onto Rosh Hashanah/Shabbos (teshuvah from fear, from man’s side) and Yom Kippur (teshuvah from love, “the teshuvah fit to atone for all his deeds”).
וְשִׁבְעַת יָמִים שֶׁבֵּינְתַיִם הוּא בְּתִיקּוּן הַנִּגְלוֹת בְּמִדּוֹת וּמַעֲשִׂים
and the seven intervening days effect the rectification of the revealed realms in character attributes (middos) and physical actions.

items.h: The theme: Shabbos Shuvah and Yom Kippur as the cosmic climax of teshuvah. Ordinary Shabbos corresponds to the lower hei (teshuvah tata'ah, from fear), whereas Yom Kippur (Shabbos Shabbason) corresponds to the upper hei (teshuvah ila'ah, from love). When Yom Kippur coincides with Shabbos, the spiritual arousal reaches peak intensity. It was precisely at that auspicious time, as Acher rode behind the Holy of Holies, that the Heavenly Voice (bas kol) reached even his deeply fallen heart. Because he mistook the apparent rejection of the left hand ("except for Acher") as final and did not discern the hidden right hand reaching to receive him, he failed to repent during life, requiring his disciples R' Meir and R' Yochanan to redeem him after death.

p: וְשַׁבָּת שֶׁבֵּינְתַיִם נִקְרָא ״שַׁבַּת תְּשׁוּבָה״ שֶׁבּוֹ מַפְטִירִין ״שׁוּבָה יִשְׂרָאֵל״, שֶׁהוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בַּלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יְדֵי קְרִיאַת דִּבְרֵי הַנְּבִיאִים הַמַּזְהִירִים עָלֶיהָ

And the intermediate Shabbos is called “Shabbos Teshuvah,” on which they read the Haftarah of “Return, O Israel” (Hoshea 14:2), which is the arousal of repentance in the hearts of the Children of Israel through reading the words of the prophets exhorting concerning it;561Shabbos Shuvah and its haftarah — Hoshea 14:2-3 begins, “Return, O Israel, unto Hashem your God, for you have stumbled through your iniquity; take words with you and return unto Hashem.” Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 13:19, records that on the Shabbos between Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur the haftarah is “Shuvah Yisrael.” Beis Yosef, Orach Chaim 428, treats this as the fixed practice and notes that the halachic sources themselves call the day Shabbos Shuvah. The reading is therefore not merely a name for the Shabbos. The prophet supplies the congregation with the very words of return — recognition of stumbling, confession, prayer, and trust in Divine healing. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the performative effect of sacred reading: the prophetic call heard publicly becomes an awakening within the Jewish heart.
כִּי לְעוֹלָם בְּשַׁבָּת הוּא זְמַן תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הַחְזָרַת הָעוֹלָמוֹת לִמְקוֹמָן כְּאָדָם הַמֵּשִׁיב נַפְשׁוֹ וּמַמְשִׁיךְ רוּחוֹ אֵלָיו כַּנּוֹדָע, וּבְשַׁבָּת זֶה בְּיוֹתֵר

for always on Shabbos is a time of teshuvah [lit., "return"], being the time of the worlds returning to their source, like a person restoring his soul and drawing his spirit back to himself as is known, and on this Shabbos all the more so.562Shabbos as return to the source — Beitzah 16a teaches that an additional soul is granted on the eve of Shabbos and departs after Shabbos, reading “Shavas va-yinafash” as the soul’s expanded life and subsequent withdrawal. Kabbalistic and chassidic literature describes Shabbos as “the ascent of the worlds”: their inward life rises from weekday dispersion and action toward its source. Rav Tzadok develops this directly in Resisei Layla §27 and §42, and in Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushas Shabbos 1:8, where the ascent enables the soul to unite with the source of its vitality. Takanas HaShavin 15:51 interprets “va-yinafash” as a person drawing breath and spirit inward and explicitly identifies this with the worlds’ return to their root. Thus Shabbos is intrinsically related to teshuvah: both are forms of hashavah, restoring what had spread outward to the place from which its true life comes.
וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הַנִּקְרָא ״שַׁבַּת שַׁבָּתוֹן״ כִּי הוּא הֵ״א רִאשׁוֹנָה דְּשֵׁם, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כָּל שַׁבָּת הוּא הֵ״א תַּחְתּוֹנָה

And Yom Kippur, which is called “Shabbos Shabbason” (Vayikra 16:31), corresponds to the upper hei of the Divine Name, whereas every ordinary Shabbos corresponds to the lower hei;563“Shabbos Shabbason” — Vayikra 16:31 calls Yom Kippur “a Shabbos of complete rest,” immediately after the promise, “On this day He shall atone for you, to purify you.” The designation is repeated in Vayikra 23:32 together with the command of affliction. The doubled expression marks a cessation deeper than ordinary weekday rest: work ceases, bodily self-assertion is subdued, and the person stands before Hashem for purification. Rav Tzadok reads this doubling in the language of the Divine Name. Ordinary Shabbos restores the revealed order to its source; Yom Kippur reaches the more concealed root of understanding and inward return. When both sanctities coincide, the two movements of return are intensified together.,564The two hehs and two levels of teshuvah — Zohar III 122a (Raaya Mehemna) interprets teshuvah as tashuv heh, “the heh shall return”: the lower heh corresponds to teshuvah tataah, and the upper heh to teshuvah ilaah. This formulation is explained at length in Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 4, which identifies the first heh of the Divine Name with Binah and the final heh with Malchus and revealed Divine speech. The lower return repairs the person’s revealed life and submission; the higher return restores inward understanding, love, and union at their source. Rav Tzadok applies this kabbalistic structure to sacred time: the ordinary Shabbos is associated with the final heh and the return of the revealed worlds, while Yom Kippur is associated with the first heh, the concealed mother-source from which a new spirit of purity descends.
וְהֵ״א הִיא הַפֶּתַח לְבַעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּמְנָחוֹת כ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳], וְזֶהוּ תְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה הַיְינוּ תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה שֶׁמִּצַּד הָאָדָם

and the letter hei is the opening for penitents, as stated [in Menachos 29b], representing the lower teshuvah (teshuvah tata'ah), which is repentance from fear initiated by man;565Menachos 29b: “‘For with Yah [be-Yah] Hashem formed worlds’ (Yeshayah 26:4) — this world [was created] with a heh and the World to Come with a yud. Why was this world created with a heh? Because it is like a portico [open below], that whoever wishes to leave may leave [the opening for sinners]. And why the little foot [of the heh, detached]? So that a penitent may be brought in. And why an opening at the top? To provide for penitents [mishum ba’alei teshuvah].” R’ Tzadok maps the lower heh to Shabbos / teshuvah from fear, and the upper heh to Yom Kippur / the higher teshuvah “from Hashem’s side.”

וְהֵ״א רִאשׁוֹנָה הִיא הַפֶּתַח לְבַעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בִּתְשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה דְּמִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, דְּ״אָשׁוּבָה אֲלֵיכֶם״, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה נִתְעוֹרֵר רוּחַ טָהֳרָה בַּלְּבָבוֹת דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּ״לִפְנֵי ה׳ תִּטְהָרוּ״ מִכֹּל חַטֹּאתֵיהֶם

and the upper hei is the opening for penitents in the higher teshuvah (teshuvah ila'ah) from the side of the Blessed Name, of “and I will return to you” (Malachi 3:7), through which a spirit of purity is awakened in the hearts of the Children of Israel, that “before Hashem you shall be clean” (Vayikra 16:30) from all their sins.566“Return to Me, and I will return to you” — Malachi 3:7 presents teshuvah as a reciprocal movement. Human beings first turn from estrangement toward Hashem; Hashem’s “return” then means a renewed revelation of closeness and assistance. Yechezkel 36:25-27 describes that Divine side of the process: “I will sprinkle pure water upon you,” give a new heart and a new spirit, and place My spirit within you so that you walk in My statutes. This is not a replacement for human choice, but the response that enables a partial awakening to become deep and enduring. Rav Tzadok calls the first movement teshuvah from man’s side and the second the higher teshuvah “from Hashem’s side”: after the lower opening, a spirit of purity is aroused within the hearts of Israel.,567“Before Hashem you shall be purified” — Vayikra 16:30 is expounded in Mishnah Yoma 8:9 and Yoma 85b. R’ Elazar ben Azaryah derives that Yom Kippur atones for sins between man and Hashem, whereas interpersonal wrongs require appeasing the injured person. R’ Akiva then declares: “Fortunate are you, Israel! Before Whom are you purified, and Who purifies you? Your Father in Heaven,” comparing Hashem to a mikveh that purifies the impure. The verse therefore has two complementary meanings. One must enter honestly “before Hashem,” including repairing obligations to others; yet the ultimate purifying power is Hashem Himself. Rav Tzadok hears in R’ Akiva’s formulation the higher teshuvah: Israel turns toward purification, and the Father in Heaven awakens and completes it from Above.

וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁחָל בְּשַׁבָּת, אָז הָאִתְעָרוּתָא בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, תּוֹקֶף וָעֹוז, עַל כֵּן אָז הִגִּיעַ הַבַּת קוֹל גַּם לְ״אַחֵר״, וּמִבֵּית קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים שֶׁשָּׁם הוּא מְקוֹם הַכַּפָּרָה וְהַסְּלִיחָה לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְנִיסַת כֹּהֵן גָּדוֹל לִפְנַי וְלִפְנִים

And when Yom Kippur falls on Shabbos, the spiritual arousal is with preeminent elevation, power, and might; therefore, at that time the Heavenly Voice reached even Acher, echoing from the Holy of Holies, which is the locus of atonement and forgiveness for all Israel upon the entry of the Kohen Gadol into the innermost Sanctuary;568Acher on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos — The precise source is Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 (9b). Elisha ben Avuyah told R’ Meir that he once rode past the House of the Holy of Holies on Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos and heard a bas kol emerge from the Holy of Holies: “Return, wayward children — except Elisha ben Avuyah, who knew My power and rebelled against Me.” The Bavli, Chagigah 15a, records the general statement “Return, wayward children, except Acher,” but does not include the Yerushalmi’s distinctive conjunction of Yom Kippur, Shabbos, and the Holy of Holies. Rav Tzadok deliberately highlights those details. At the strongest convergence of sacred time and sacred place, even the person who believed himself excluded heard the call of return. The tragedy was not that no call reached him, but that he interpreted the warning as an absolute closing of the gate rather than as the very pressure calling him to break through despair.,569R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech §14): “That teshuvah reaches the Throne of Glory, as it says, ‘Return, O Israel, unto Hashem your God’; and Rabbeinu Chananel explains [the greatness of teshuvah, that it reaches the Throne].” Exactly the se’if’s “Shabbos Teshuvah,” when we read “Return, O Israel” — the arousal of teshuvah through the prophets’ words, reaching to the Throne.,570The Kohen Gadol “within the innermost” — Vayikra 16:2 limits entry beyond the paroches, and Vayikra 16:12-17 prescribes the Kohen Gadol’s unique Yom Kippur service there with incense and blood. The chapter concludes that he atones for the innermost sanctuary, the Tent of Meeting, the altar, the kohanim, and “all the people of the congregation” (16:33-34). Mishnah Yoma 5:1 describes his entry into the Holy of Holies with the incense pan and the cloud of ketores. Chazal call this place lifnai ve-lifnim, “within the innermost,” because it lies beyond the ordinary modes of access and representation. Rav Tzadok connects the bat kol’s emergence from there with its content: the innermost sanctuary is the site where the hidden bond of all Israel is represented and where atonement reaches beneath the visible record of sin to the covenantal root.
וְהַסְּלִיחָה הַיְינוּ רַק עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה בֶּאֱמֶת בְּכָל הַלְּבָבוֹת, מֵעוּמְקָא דְּלִבָּא וּמֵאַהֲבָה גְּמוּרָה

and that forgiveness is accomplished solely through the awakening of teshuvah at that very hour in truth in all hearts, from the depth of the heart and out of complete love.571Atonement joined to inward teshuvah and love — Mishnah Yoma 8:8 teaches that death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah, while Yoma 85b discusses the scope of Yom Kippur’s independent power. Yoma 86b distinguishes teshuvah from fear, through which intentional sins become like errors, from teshuvah from love, through which intentional sins can become merits. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6-7, describes this higher return as restoring closeness: the person who had been distant becomes beloved, desired, near, and a friend. Rav Tzadok’s “depths of the heart” therefore means more than emotional intensity. It is the revelation that the soul’s deepest will belongs to Hashem, followed by a loving redirection of the very powers that had been misused. Yom Kippur’s pardon becomes fully manifest when the day’s Divine purification awakens that genuine inner return.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁבַּת קוֹל הַמְעוֹרֵר לִתְשׁוּבָה יוֹצֵא בְּכָל יוֹם, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת יְמֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּשַׁבָּת, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
And although the Heavenly Voice that awakens to teshuvah goes forth every day, all the more so during the Ten Days of Repentance, all the more so on Shabbos, and all the more so on Yom Kippur;
לֹא הִגִּיעַ עֲדַיִין שְׁעַת אִתְעָרוּתָא לְלֵב ״אַחֵר״ שֶׁנִּדְחָה כָּל כָּךְ עַד יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁחָל בְּשַׁבָּת
the hour of awakening did not reach the heart of Acher, who was so profoundly banished, until Yom Kippur that fell on Shabbos;
וְגַם זֶה כְּשֶׁרָכַב אֲחוֹרֵי בֵּית קָדְשֵׁי קָדָשִׁים, שֶׁהַמָּקוֹם גּוֹרֵם גַּם כֵּן לְהַכְנִיס קְצָת קְדוּשָׁה בַּלֵּב וְאֵיזֶה הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה
and this occurred specifically when he rode behind the Holy of Holies, for the sacred place likewise helped to introduce a measure of holiness into the heart and some stirring of teshuvah.

וְגַם זוֹ הָאִתְעָרוּתָא לוֹ דֶּרֶךְ שְׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וְלֹא פָּעַל בּוֹ כְּלוּם בִּשְׁעָתוֹ, וְאַדְּרַבָּא נִדְחָה יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי שְׁמִיעַת הַשְּׂמֹאל דּוֹחָה, וְלֹא הִרְגִּישׁ מֵהַיָּמִין מְקָרֶבֶת הַגְּנוּזָה וְנֶעֱלֶמֶת בָּזֶה

Yet even this awakening came to him via the left hand that pushes away as mentioned above, effecting nothing in him at that moment; on the contrary, he was pushed further away by hearing the rejecting left hand, failing to perceive the drawing right hand hidden and concealed within it;
וְלֹא זָכָה לְיִסּוּרִין שֶׁיְּבִיאוּהוּ לָשׁוּב בְּחַיָּיו, דְּגַם לָזֶה צָרִיךְ זְכִיָּה וּזְכוּת אָבוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה לִמְנַשֶּׁה
and he did not merit afflictions that would bring him to return during his lifetime, for even to receive that requires personal merit and ancestral merit (zechus avos), as was granted to Menasheh.
וְרַק בִּשְׁעַת דִּכְדּוּכָהּ שֶׁל נֶפֶשׁ עוֹרְרוֹ רַבִּי מֵאִיר לָשׁוּב מִפַּחַד יִסּוּרֵי הַמִּיתָה
And only at the hour of the crushing of his soul (dichduchah shel nefesh) did Rabbi Meir arouse him to return out of dread of the agony of death;

וּלְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיְתָה תְּשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה בְּכָל לְבָבוֹ, רַק מִפַּחַד הַמִּיתָה לְבַד, עַל כֵּן הוּצְרַךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לִשְׁנַיִם מִמִּשְׁפָּחָה לְזַכּוֹתוֹ וּלְהַבִיאוֹ לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בְּכֹחָם וּזְכוּתָם, וְהֵם רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן

and because it was not a complete repentance with all his heart, but born of fear of death alone, he therefore required afterward “two from a family” (Yirmeyah 3:14) to vindicate him and bring him into the World to Come through their power and merit, who were Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan.

items.h: The theme: The intercession of tzaddikim for fallen souls. While Abraham cannot unilaterally save Ishmael in the World of Truth where each receives his due reward, one who repented even out of fear of death at the threshold of life is received by Hashem as an inadvertent sinner (shogeg), whose atonement is completed through death. Yet strict Judgment prosecutes those who "knew their Master and rebelled." Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan overcame this barrier at the time of their departure (yoma d'hilula), when great supernal joy dispels all accusers, awakening vast compassion that allowed Acher’s repentance to be fully accepted.

p: וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּ״אֵין מִיָּדִי מַצִּיל״ כְּתִיב, וְלֹא אַבְרָהָם מַצִּיל יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנוֹ, כִּדְאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ד עַמּוּד א׳]
And although “there is none that can deliver out of My hand” (Devarim 32:39) is written, so that Abraham cannot deliver his son Ishmael, as stated [in Sanhedrin 104a];
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא אוֹהֲבוֹ וְרוֹצֶה לְהֵיטִיב לוֹ אֵין יָכוֹל בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּלֹא כְּהָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁכָּל אֶחָד נוֹטֵל חֶלְקוֹ הָרָאוּי לוֹ

and despite loving him and desiring to do good for him, he is unable to do so in the World to Come, for unlike this world, the World to Come is where each receives the portion fitting for him;572Sanhedrin 104a: “‘He has no son [nin] nor grandson among his people, and no remnant in his dwellings’ (Iyov 18:19) — ‘he has no nin’ — [meaning] a son; ‘nor grandson’ — a grandson. A father benefits a son, [but] a son does not benefit a father, as it is written, ‘and there is none that can deliver from My hand’ (Devarim 32:39) — Avraham cannot deliver Yishmael, Yitzchak cannot deliver Esav.” R’ Tzadok: in Olam Haba each receives strictly his own; Acher’s deliverers could act only because he himself had repented under the sufferings of death.
וְאִלּוּ לֹא שָׁב כְּלָל עַד שֶׁבַּמִּשְׁפָּט הָיָה אוֹבֵד כָּל חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ, וַדַּאי הֵם לֹא יָכְלוּ לַעֲשׂוֹת לוֹ כְּלוּם
and had [Acher] not repented at all, so that by strict judgment he would lose entirely his portion in the World to Come, they certainly could not have done anything for him;
רַק שֶׁשָּׁב מִתּוֹךְ יִסּוּרֵי מִיתָה, בָּזֶה אָמְרוּ ״אֶחָד מֵעִיר וּשְׁנַיִם מִמִּשְׁפָּחָה מַצִּילִין כּוּלָּם״

only because he repented from within the agony of death, in this context it was said that “one from a city and two from a family deliver them all” (Sanhedrin 111a).573“One from a city and two from a family” — Yirmiyahu 3:14 promises, “I will take you, one from a city and two from a family, and bring you to Tziyon.” Sanhedrin 111a records two readings. Reish Lakish initially takes the verse literally, while R’ Yochanan insists that “one from a city merits the entire city, and two from a family merit the entire family”; Rav gives the same response to Rav Kahana. Yoma 86a places this verse in the laws of teshuvah and distinguishes a return arising from love or fear from a return forced through suffering. Rav Tzadok combines the sugyos: Acher’s own deathbed return created the opening, while the merit of the two great sages could then carry and elevate one who had already begun to return. Their merit did not manufacture a share in Olam Haba for someone wholly detached from it; it activated the communal power Chazal locate in “one” and “two.”
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים לְעוֹלָם כָּל שֶׁשָּׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט, דְּאַף דְּנַעֲשָׂה רַק כִּשְׁגָגוֹת דְּצָרִיךְ עֲדַיִין כַּפָּרָה, דַּי לוֹ בְּדָבָר מוּעָט לְכַפָּרָה כְּקָרְבָּן

For the Blessed Name always accepts penitents whenever one returns and regrets; for although it is reduced merely to inadvertent sins which still require atonement, a minor vehicle of atonement suffices for him, like a sacrifice;574Hashem receives those who return — Tehillim 90:3 says, “You return man unto crushing, and say: Return, children of man.” Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1 applies this verse directly to Acher’s final illness. When he asked R’ Meir whether a penitent is accepted, R’ Meir answered that a person is received “until the crushing of the soul”; Acher then wept and died, and R’ Meir understood that his teacher had departed through teshuvah. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4-7, rules that a baal teshuvah must never imagine himself permanently distant: he is beloved and desired before the Creator, and teshuvah brings near those who had been far removed. Rav Tzadok therefore treats even repentance awakened by mortal suffering as genuine return, though the degree of its inwardness determines what further atonement is needed.

וְכֵן תַּעֲנִית דְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים שֶׁבָּא עַל זֶה לְכַפֵּר אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּשְׁגָגָה, דְּמִיעוּט חֶלְבּוֹ וְדָמוֹ נֶחְשָׁב כְּקָרְבָּן, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן הַמִּיתָה שֶׁשָּׁפַךְ דָּמוֹ לְגַמְרֵי דִּמְכַפֶּרֶת עַל זֶה

and so too the fast of Yom Kippur, which serves to atone after repentance has rendered it like an inadvertent deed, wherein the diminution of his fat and blood is reckoned as an offering, and all the more so death, which sheds his blood completely, atones for it.575Fasting as a korban — Berachos 17a records Rav Sheshes’s prayer after a fast. When the Beis HaMikdash stood, a sinner brought a korban whose fat and blood were offered and he was atoned; now, through fasting, “my fat and blood have diminished,” and Rav Sheshes asks that this diminution be regarded as though offered upon the mizbeiach. Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 2, cites this passage to explain that in the absence of an offering, a properly directed fast can serve as the gift brought after teshuvah to restore favor. Rav Tzadok applies the same imagery specifically to the Yom Kippur fast: the bodily diminution does not replace teshuvah, but functions as its sacrificial completion after the willful sin has already been reclassified through return.,576Death as the completion of atonement — Mishnah Yoma 8:8 teaches that death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah. Yoma 86a sets out the “divisions of atonement”: some sins are forgiven immediately through teshuvah, others require Yom Kippur, more severe sins require suffering, and desecration of the Divine Name is held in suspension until death completes the cleansing. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, codifies this structure and states that for chillul Hashem, teshuvah, Yom Kippur, and suffering suspend the judgment, while death brings the final atonement. Rav Tzadok’s comparison of death to the complete pouring out of blood is therefore not a claim that death automatically saves without repentance. It is the final meruk, the complete cleansing, once a real movement of teshuvah has already begun.

וְרַק שֶׁמִּדַּת הַדִּין מְקַטְרֶגֶת נֶגֶד הַיּוֹדֵעַ רִבּוֹנוֹ וּמוֹרֵד, דְּהָא דְּנֶחְשָׁב כִּשְׁגָגָה אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הוּא לְפִי שֶׁהַחֵטְא הָיָה רַק עַל יְדֵי רוּחַ שְׁטוּת שֶׁהִתְעָהוּ וְהֶעֱלִים מִמֶּנּוּ יְדִיעַת רִבּוֹנוֹ בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה וְעִידָּן דְּיִצְרָא הָרָע

Except that the Attribute of Judgment prosecutes against one who knows his Master and rebels; for the principle that it is reckoned inadvertent after repentance applies when the sin occurred solely through a spirit of folly (ruach shtus) that misled him and concealed from him the consciousness of his Master at that moment and season of the evil inclination;577The “spirit of folly” — Sotah 3a states: “A person commits a transgression only if a spirit of folly enters him,” deriving shetus from the Torah’s spelling of tisteh. The teaching does not remove responsibility; it explains how a person who truly knows Hashem can act against that knowledge. At the moment of sin, desire creates a temporary concealment in which the consequence and the person’s deeper allegiance are no longer fully present to consciousness. Berachos 17a expresses the same structure in the prayer, “Our will is to do Your will; what prevents us? The yeast in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms.” Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why ordinary teshuvah from fear can reduce a deliberate sin to the category of inadvertence: the return uncovers that the act was produced by a distorting spirit rather than by the soul’s deepest will. Acher, however, was described as one who “knew My power and rebelled,” so the Attribute of Justice could argue that his case required a deeper answer.
אֲבָל זֶה שֶׁיּוֹדֵעַ וּמוֹרֵד, יֵשׁ מָקוֹם לִטְעוֹן נֶגְדּוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יֵחָשֵׁב לְשׁוֹגֵג עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה כָּל שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁיֵּחָשְׁבוּ לִזְכֻיּוֹת

but for one who knows and rebels, there is room to argue against him that it should not be considered an inadvertent error through repentance, as long as he has not attained teshuvah from love wherein sins are reckoned as merits.578Cf. Siman 11 §1 and §3 (in this volume), which lay the foundation used here: teshuvah from fear uproots the prior evil intention so that willful sins (zedonos) become inadvertent ones (shegagos) — “a deed without intent” — because the sin came only through a “spirit of folly” that concealed the knowledge of one’s Master; whereas the “knowing rebel” needs teshuvah from love for the sins to be reckoned merits (“the iniquity of Israel shall be sought and there shall be none”).
וְעַל זֶה הוֹעִילוּ רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁעוֹרְרוּ מִדַּת הַדִּין בִּשְׁעַת פְּטִירָתָן

And on this score Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan availed, mitigating the Attribute of Judgment at the hour of their passing;579R’ Meir and R’ Yochanan on behalf of Acher — Chagigah 15b relates that after Acher died, the Heavenly Court said that he should neither be judged nor enter Olam Haba: his Torah shielded him from judgment, but his sins barred his entry. R’ Meir declared that it was better for him to be judged and afterward enter Olam Haba; when R’ Meir died, smoke rose from Acher’s grave. R’ Yochanan then objected: “There was one among us and we cannot save him? If I take him by the hand, who can remove him?” He said that when he died he would extinguish the smoke, and at his passing the smoke ceased. The Gemara describes the effect of their passing; Rav Tzadok explains its mechanism. Their intervention could operate because Acher’s own final tears constituted a beginning of teshuvah, allowing their merit to shift the case from absolute exclusion toward judgment, cleansing, and eventual restoration.

דְּיָדוּעַ דִּבְיוֹמֵי דְּהִילּוּלָא דְּצַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים כָּאֵלּוּ יֵשׁ שִׂמְחָה גְּדוֹלָה בְּעוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים, וּמֵרוֹב הַשִּׂמְחָה בְּטֵלִים כָּל הַמְקַטְרְגִים, וְאֵין שָׂטָן וְאֵין פֶּגַע רָע וְהָרַחֲמִים גּוֹבְרִים

for it is known that on the hillula-days of such consummate tzaddikim there is immense rejoicing in the supernal worlds, and from the abundance of that joy all accusers are nullified, there is no adversary and no evil occurrence, and mercy prevails;580The hilula of a tzaddik — In its ordinary Aramaic usage, hilula means a wedding celebration. Kabbalistic and chassidic sources use the term for the passing of a perfected tzaddik because the life’s avodah reaches its bond and culmination Above. The Idra Zuta, Zohar III 287b-296b, depicts the final day of R’ Shimon bar Yochai as an overwhelming revelation of Torah and attachment rather than merely a moment of loss. Rav Tzadok, Peri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer §1, explains that R’ Shimon’s day of passing is called his hilula because the Torah he revealed was then received and fixed in the hearts of Israel of his generation. Thus Rav Tzadok’s language here is not a general denial of mourning. It identifies the death of a wholly righteous person as a moment when the completed Torah and avodah of that soul become newly active in the upper and lower worlds.,581“There is no Satan and no evil mishap” — The phrase comes from I Melachim 5:18, where Shlomo describes the state of rest surrounding the building of the Beis HaMikdash. Shemos Rabbah 15:26 expands the verse: no evil touches the Divine throne, and the merits and prayers of the Avos make peace between Israel and their Father in Heaven. Zohar, Emor 25:126, similarly calls Shabbos the “day of the King’s hilula,” when distress, wrath, and pressure are forgotten from the world. Rav Tzadok applies this pattern to the hilula of a complete tzaddik. The abundance of revealed joy and union does not erase justice; it removes the dominance of prosecution, allowing the deeper Divine will of mercy and restoration to be heard. In that opening, souls whose ascent had been obstructed by accusation can be reconsidered and raised.
וְאָז יְכוֹלִים לְהַעֲלוֹת כַּמָּה נְשָׁמוֹת הַדְּחוּיוֹת מִפְּנֵי קִטְרוּג וּמִדַּת הַדִּין שֶׁגָּבְרָה עֲלֵיהֶם, וְעַל כֵּן יָכְלוּ לְזַכּוֹתוֹ
and at that moment they can elevate many souls that were rejected due to prosecution and the Attribute of Judgment that overpowered them; wherefore they were able to vindicate him;
וְלֹא שֶׁבְּכֹחָם הִצִּילוּהוּ, רַק שֶׁפָּעֲלוּ דְּנִתְקַבְּלוּ תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ בְּכֹחַ הָרַחֲמִים רַבִּים שֶׁנִּתְרַבּוּ בְּעוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים עַל יְדֵיהֶם

not that they delivered him by their independent power, but that they effected the acceptance of his repentance through the power of the abundant mercies multiplied in the supernal worlds through their agency.582R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §8): “And no one delivers him except Hashem Himself, who ‘sees to the heart’ — that he too, in the depths of his heart, is at root ‘circumcised’; and Pinchas, who is Eliyahu, the ‘angel of the covenant,’ was zealous for this — [over him] who ‘draws his foreskin’ and appears uncircumcised to human eyes.” Exactly the se’if: “there is none that can deliver” from the World to Come — none but Hashem, who alone sees the true inner root.

items.h: The theme: The halachic decree of tzaddikim over the Heavenly Court (tzaddik gozer ve-haKadosh Baruch Hu mekayem). Since Torah authority was granted to earthly courts below, their legal rulings establish the law throughout all supernal realms. Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan legally ruled that even a semblance of deathbed repentance (dimyon shel teshuvah) avails for an eminent scholar whose Torah cannot be extinguished by sin, establishing this principle permanently for all similar souls. Yet for any ordinary sinner who sincerely repents out of fear of death or affliction, the sin becomes an inadvertent error and death provides full atonement; but to transform the past into merits (zechuyos) and enter the supreme rung of baalei teshuvah, one requires the spiritual assistance of the righteous ("one from a city") or a renewed celestial awakening from Above to return out of love.

p: וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר שֶׁהָיָה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״וְתִגְזַר אֹמֶר וְיָקָם לָךְ״ (אִיּוֹב כ״ב:כ״ח), ״צַדִּיק גּוֹזֵר וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַיֵּים״

And one may also say that it occurred in the manner of “You shall also decree a thing, and it shall be established unto you” (Iyov 22:28): “a tzaddik decrees and the Holy One, blessed be He, fulfills” (Ta'anis 23a),
כִּי נַעֲשָׂה הוּא מַכְרִיעַ בְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַעְלָה, וַהֲלָכָה כְּמוֹתוֹ בִּגְזֵירוֹתָיו נֶגֶד גְּזֵירַת דִּינָא עִילָּאָה
for he becomes the decisive arbiter in the Heavenly Court, and the halachah accords with him in his decrees against the decree of the Supernal Judgment;
כִּי כָּל הַמִּשְׁפָּטִים בְּכָל עוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים הַכֹּל הוּא עַל פִּי הַתּוֹרָה, וְהַתּוֹרָה כְּבָר נִמְסְרָה לַתַּחְתּוֹנִים

for all judgments in all supernal worlds are determined entirely according to the Torah, and the Torah was already given over to the lower beings (Bava Metzia 59b);583“The Torah has already been handed to those below” — Devarim 30:12 declares, “It is not in Heaven.” Bava Metzia 59b applies this in the dispute over the oven of Achnai: even after a bas kol supported R’ Eliezer, R’ Yehoshua ruled, “It is not in Heaven,” and R’ Yirmiyah explained that once the Torah was given at Sinai, halachah is decided through the Torah’s own rules, including “after the majority shall you incline” (Shemos 23:2). The Holy One then said, “My children have triumphed over Me.” This is the foundational background for Rav Tzadok’s language. He is not granting a tzaddik an arbitrary power to overturn Torah; rather, because the Torah itself entrusted adjudication to the sages below, a valid Torah ruling becomes the operative truth even in the upper worlds. The calendar example and Rabbah bar Nachmani’s heavenly arbitration, cited in the following note, are applications of this same delegated authority.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לְעִנְיַן קְבִיעַת רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה: ״אֲנִי וְאַתֶּם נֵלֵךְ לְבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה, וְאִם עִיבְּרוּ בֵּית דִּין הַחֹדֶשׁ, הַדִּינִין שֶׁל מַעְלָה מִתְבַּטְּלִין מֵאוֹתוֹ יוֹם״

as they expounded regarding the sanctification of Rosh Hashanah: “I and you shall go to the earthly court; and if the court intercalates the month, the heavenly proceedings are suspended from that day” (Yerushalmi Rosh Hashanah 1:3);
וְכֵן בְּכָל סְפֵיקוֹת שֶׁבְּעִנְיְנֵי הַתּוֹרָה, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁמַּכְרִיעִים חֲכָמִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כֵּן הוּא הַהַכְרָעָה בְּכָל עוֹלָמוֹת עֶלְיוֹנִים
and so with all doubts in Torah matters: whatever the Sages determine in this world becomes the binding halachic determination across all supernal worlds,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק הַפּוֹעֲלִים, בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳] בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּקֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּמְתִיבְתָּא דִּרְקִיעָא לָקְחוּ רַבָּה בַּר נַחְמָנִי לְמַכְרִיעַ

as they related [in chapter HaPoalim, Bava Metzia 86a] that in a dispute between the Holy One, blessed be He, and the Heavenly Academy, they brought Rabbah bar Nachmani to be the decisive arbiter.584Bava Metzia 86a (Perek HaPoalim): in a dispute between the Holy One and the Heavenly Academy over a point of the laws of nega’im (baheres), “who shall decide? — Rabbah bar Nachmani, who said, ‘I am singular in [the laws of] nega’os, I am singular in [the laws of] ohalos.’” R’ Tzadok reads this, with the sugya on sanctifying the new moon (Rosh Hashanah 25a, “I and you, let us go to the court below”), as the principle that the earthly sages’ rulings determine the heavenly judgments — hence a tzaddik’s “decree” that Acher’s teshuvah be accepted is fulfilled as halachah.
וּגְזֵירַת הַצַּדִּיק הַמִּתְקַיֶּימֶת הַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא אוֹמֵר שֶׁכָּךְ רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת הַמִּשְׁפָּט, דְּזֶה נִקְרָא ״גְּזֵירָה״ שֶׁגּוֹזֵר בַּדִּין שֶׁכָּךְ רָאוּי לִהְיוֹת וְעַל כֵּן נִתְקַיֵּים

And the decree of a tzaddik that is fulfilled means that he rules that such ought to be the law, which is termed a “decree” (gezeirah), adjudicating legally that thus it is fitting to be, and therefore it is established;
וְכֵן הֵם גָּזְרוּ אַחַר כֵּן בַּמִּשְׁפָּט, וְהַכֹּל עַל יְדֵי הַהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ, אַף שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה תְּשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה רַק דִּמְיוֹן שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה

and so they decreed subsequently in judgment, all predicated upon the stirring of teshuvah he experienced prior to death, even though it was not a complete repentance but merely a semblance of repentance,
כִּלְשׁוֹנוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי מֵאִיר [בַּמִּדְרָשׁ וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי שָׁם]: ״דּוֹמֶה שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ תְּשׁוּבָה נִסְתַּלֵּק״, דְּמַשְׁמַע שֶׁאֵינָהּ תְּשׁוּבָה בְּרוּרָה רַק ״דּוֹמֶה״ וְכוּלֵיהּ

as indicated by the wording of Rabbi Meir [in the Midrash and Yerushalmi there]: “It appears that he departed amid repentance,” which implies not an absolute repentance, but only that it “appeared” so;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הֵם גָּזְרוּ וּפָסְקוּ שֶׁגַּם תְּשׁוּבָה זוֹ מוֹעִילָה לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם גָּדוֹל כְּמוֹתוֹ שֶׁאֵין עֲבֵירָה מְכַבָּה תּוֹרָתוֹ

yet nevertheless they decreed and ruled that even such a repentance avails for an eminent Torah scholar like him, whose Torah cannot be extinguished by sin (Sotah 21a).585“No sin extinguishes Torah” — Sotah 21a distinguishes between a mitzvah, whose protective light can be extinguished by sin, and Torah, whose enduring light is derived from “many waters cannot extinguish the love” (Shir HaShirim 8:7). The Gemara emphasizes that this does not mean Torah prevents a scholar from sinning or automatically erases judgment: Doeg and Achitofel possessed Torah and nevertheless fell. Chagigah 15b makes the distinction concrete in Acher’s case. The Heavenly Court initially said that he could neither be judged, because he had occupied himself with Torah, nor enter the World to Come, because he had sinned. His Torah remained real and protective, but his guilt also remained real. Rav Tzadok therefore uses the surviving Torah not as an exemption from teshuvah, but as the enduring holy core upon which R’ Meir and R’ Yochanan could rule that even Acher’s slight deathbed movement of return must be received.
וַאֲפִילּוּ תְּשׁוּבָה קַלָּה כָּזוֹ, וּלְיוֹדֵעַ וּמוֹרֵד כְּמוֹתוֹ, הוֹעִילָה עַל יְדֵי גְּזֵירַת רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
And even so slight a repentance, and for one who knew and rebelled like him, availed through the decree of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yochanan;

וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי שֶׁהוּא דֶּרֶךְ גְּזֵירָה וּפְסַק שֶׁלָּהֶם, לֹא לוֹ לְבַד הוֹעִילָה, רַק לְמִי שֶׁכָּל כַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן, אַחַר שֶׁכְּבָר נִפְסְקָה הֲלָכָה עַל פַּעַם שֶׁתִּתְקַבֵּל תְּשׁוּבָה כָּזוֹ לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁכַּיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ

and as I wrote that this operated by way of their judicial ruling and decree, it availed not for him alone, but for anyone akin to him as well, once the halachah was established that such repentance is accepted for a scholar of his kind.

וְכָל זֶה הוּצְרְכוּ לְגַבֵּי דִּידֵיהּ וּבְדִמְיוֹן שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד; אֲבָל הַשָּׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט בֶּאֱמֶת עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מִפַּחַד הַיִּסּוּרִין אוֹ אֲפִילּוּ מִפַּחַד הַמִּיתָה, דְּכָל זֶה בִּכְלַל תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה דְּמוֹעִילָה לִהְיוֹת כִּשְׁגָגוֹת עַל כָּל פָּנִים, וְשׁוּב יִסּוּרִין זוֹ מִיתָה שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ מְכַפְּרִין לְגַמְרֵי

And all this intercession was required specifically for him, given only a mere semblance of repentance; but for one who repents and regrets in truth through suffering, even if it is out of fear of suffering or even dread of death, all of this is included in teshuvah from fear, which avails to render sins like inadvertent errors in any case, whereupon the agony of death subsequently completes full atonement;586Teshuvah from fear and from love — Yoma 86b records two teachings of Reish Lakish: through teshuvah, deliberate sins become like inadvertent transgressions, and through teshuvah they can even become merits. The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction: when one returns from fear, the deliberate sins are reckoned as shegagos; when one returns from love, they are transformed into merits. Rav Tzadok applies this distinction with precision. Fear awakened by suffering or impending death can be genuine teshuvah and can remove the status of defiant intentionality; the suffering, Yom Kippur, or death that follows can then complete the required atonement. Yet that first stage does not itself confer the creative elevation in which the former fall becomes a source of greater attachment. That requires the second, deeper return from love.

אֶלָּא דִּלִזְכּוֹת עַל יְדֵי זֶה לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, וּלְהִתְקָרֵב לְגַמְרֵי לִמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין הַגָּדוֹל מִמְּקוֹם הַצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים, בָּזֶה צָרִיךְ סִיּוּעַ הָ״אֶחָד מֵעִיר וּשְׁנַיִם מִמִּשְׁפָּחָה״ מִבַּחַיִּים, לְהַכְנִיס שֵׁנִית הַתְּשׁוּבָה בְּעוּמְקָא דְּלִבָּא מֵאַהֲבָה

however, to merit through this that sins be converted into merits, and to draw near completely to the place where penitents stand, which is greater than the station of the wholly righteous, in this one requires the assistance of the “one from a city and two from a family” from the living, to implant teshuvah a second time into the depth of the heart out of love;587“The place where baalei teshuvah stand” — Berachos 34b records a dispute. R’ Abbahu teaches that “in the place where penitents stand, even the wholly righteous do not stand,” deriving it from “peace, peace, to the far and to the near” (Yeshayah 57:19), with the formerly distant penitent named first. R’ Yochanan interprets the verse differently and places the wholly righteous first. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:4, adopts the exalted description of the baal teshuvah: he is beloved as though he had never sinned, and his reward is especially great because he tasted sin, separated from it, and conquered his inclination. Rav Tzadok’s wording here follows this higher conception. Forgiveness through fear restores the sinner and cleanses the offense; reaching the distinctive “place” above the wholly righteous requires teshuvah from love, which converts the very distance and struggle into a new depth of closeness.
אוֹ שֶׁמִּן הַשָּׁמַיִם יְעוֹרְרוּהוּ שֵׁנִית עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל דְּ״שׁוּבוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ הַמַּשְׁמִיעַ בְּחַדְרֵי הַלֵּב לָשׁוּב מֵאַהֲבָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

or that from Heaven they awaken him anew via the Heavenly Voice of “Return,” etc., which resounds within the chambers of the heart to return out of love, exactly as I have written.588R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §22): “‘A tzaddik decrees and the Holy One fulfills’ (Taanis 23a) — [as in] ‘you shall decree a thing and it will be established for you’; and he too [the tzaddik] ‘fulfills’ [what he has decreed].” Exactly the se’if: “you shall decree a thing and it will be fulfilled” — the tzaddik decrees and the Holy One carries it out.

items.h: ארבעה חילוקי כפרה.

The theme: Analysis of the first of the four categories of atonement (arba'ah chilukei kapparah, Yoma 86a): one who transgresses a positive commandment (aseh) and repents is forgiven immediately ("does not move from there before he is pardoned"), derived from "Return, backsliding children." Rashi and the Maharsha interpret "shovavim" and "meshuvatam" as cessation and inaction—failing to toil in positive mitzvos. This includes negative commandments lacking action (lav she-ein bo ma'aseh), as well as evil and foreign thoughts of the heart, particularly idolatrous thoughts (hirhurei avodah zarah). While an olah [burnt offering] is brought for sinful thoughts (Vayikra Rabbah 7), it functions merely as a royal gift (doran) after repentance has already effected essential forgiveness.

p: אַרְבָּעָה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה הֵן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳]: אִם עָבַר עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה וְשָׁב, אֵינוֹ זָז מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁמּוֹחֲלִין לוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״שׁוּבוּ בָנִים שׁוֹבָבִים״

Four categories of atonement exist, as they said [in Yoma 86a]: if one transgressed a positive commandment and repented, he does not move from there before they pardon him, as it is said, “Return, O backsliding children” (Yirmeyah 3:14);589Yoma 86a: “R’ Masya ben Cheresh asked R’ Elazar ben Azaryah in Rome: have you heard [of] the four categories of atonement that R’ Yishmael would expound? He said: they are three, and teshuvah [accompanies] each one. (1) One who transgressed a positive commandment and repented — he does not stir from there until they forgive him, as it says (Yirmeyah 3), ‘Return, wayward sons.’ (2) One who transgressed a negative commandment and repented — teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones, as it says (Vayikra 16), ‘for on this day He shall atone for you [from all your sins].’ (3) One who transgressed [prohibitions bearing] kareis or court-death and repented — teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend, and sufferings scour, as it says (Tehillim 89), ‘I will punish their transgression with a rod and their iniquity with plagues.’ (4) But one who has desecration of the Name in his hand — there is no power in teshuvah to suspend, nor in Yom Kippur to atone, nor in sufferings to scour; rather, all of them suspend, and death scours, as it says (Yeshayah 22), ‘and it was revealed in My ears [by] Hashem of Hosts: this iniquity shall not be atoned for you until you die.’”
וּמִשּׁוּם דִּמְסַיֵּים ״כִּי [אָנֹכִי בָעַלְתִּי בָכֶם]״ וְגוֹמֵר ״וְלָקַחְתִּי [אֶתְכֶם]״ וְגוֹמֵר
and because it concludes “for [I am a master to you]” and “and I will take [you]”;
וּמִלְּשׁוֹן רַשִׁ״י שָׁם מַשְׁמַע דְּכִיוֵּון לִקְרָא דְּבַתְרֵיהּ דִּמְסַיֵּים ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״ מַשְׁמַע מִיָּד, וְעַיֵּין מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב רַשִׁ״י

while from the language of Rashi there, it implies that he directed to the subsequent verse (3:22) which concludes “I will heal your backslidings,” implying immediately; and see what Rashi wrote.590Yoma 86a, and Rashi: on “one who transgressed a positive commandment and repented — he does not stir from there until they forgive him, as it says, ‘Return, wayward sons,’” Rashi comments: “‘Return, sons’ — and immediately I will heal [you]; you have learned that there is a sin which is atoned by teshuvah alone.” (Note: there are two verses in Yirmeyah 3 beginning “Return, wayward sons” — v. 14: “Return, wayward sons, says Hashem, for I am a Master to you, and I will take you one from a city and two from a family and bring you to Zion”; and v. 22: “Return, wayward sons, I will heal your waywardness; behold, we have come to You, for You are Hashem our God.”)
וְנִרְאֶה דִּמְפָרֵשׁ ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ לְשׁוֹן שְׁבִיתָה וּבִיטּוּל, שֶׁמִּתְבַּטֵּל מִמַּעֲשֵׂה הַמִּצְוֹת
And it appears that he interprets shovavim as an expression of cessation (shevisah) and neglect (bittul), that one desisted from the performance of the mitzvos;

וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת שֶׁכָּתַב שֶׁרָאָה לְפָרֵשׁ עַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה, דְּ״מְשׁוּבָתָם״ [וְעַיֵּין שָׁם שֶׁמֵּבִיא קְרָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא מְשׁוּבוֹתֵיכֶם״] לְשׁוֹן מְנוּחָה שֶׁאֵין מִתְעַמֵּל לְקַיֵּים מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and then I saw in the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados that he wrote that he saw fit to interpret in this manner, that meshuvatam [and see there that he cites the verse “I will heal your backslidings”] is a term of resting, wherein one does not exert himself to fulfill a positive commandment, see there.591Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados (Yoma 86a): “‘Return, wayward sons’ — I have seen an interpretation of this: that Scripture likened the sickness of the soul to the sickness of the body. For there is a sickness of the body [that comes to] one who desires to eat but, because he does not exert himself in any labor, brings upon himself bodily sickness — as it says, ‘the desire of the sluggard slays him, for his hands refuse to labor’ (Mishlei 21:25), and ‘by the sweat of your brow you shall eat bread’ (Bereishis 3:19). So too regarding the sickness of the soul: ‘I will heal mi-shuvasam’ — meaning, from their rest [menuchasam], that they already had, having not toiled to fulfill a positive commandment, whereby the soul’s sickness reaches them; and upon his returning from his ‘rest’ to perform a positive commandment, he is healed immediately — and this is what they said, ‘and he repents, he does not stir,’ etc., that he is healed [at once].”
וּלְפִי זֶה הַיְינוּ דַּוְוקָא בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, וְיֵשׁ לִכְלוֹל בָּזֶה לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן עֲבֵירָה בְּשֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה

And according to this, it refers specifically to the omission of a positive commandment, and one may include within this a negative commandment that lacks physical action (lav she-ein bo ma'aseh), which is likewise a transgression of passive inaction (shev ve-al ta'aseh);592A “negative commandment that has no action” — Makkos 2b states the general rule: “Every negative commandment that has no action, one is not lashed for it.” Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2, codifies the rule and lists the exceptional cases of a false oath, temurah, and cursing another with the Divine Name. Sefer HaChinuch §241 explains that the classification turns on whether the prohibition can be violated without an act; even if an incidental physical act accompanies a particular violation, the prohibition remains a lav she-ein bo maaseh when its essential transgression is inward or passive. Rav Tzadok is not reclassifying such a lav as a positive commandment for ordinary halachah. He is proposing, within R’ Yishmael’s categories of atonement, that its passive “sit and do not act” quality may place it alongside omission of an aseh; in the following se’if he tests this proposal against the Gemara’s unqualified category of “one who transgressed a negative commandment.”

וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר כָּל הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה וּמַחֲשָׁבוֹת רָעוֹת וְזָרוֹת, עַל זֶה נוֹפֵל בְּיִחוּד לְשׁוֹן ״שׁוֹבָבִים״, כְּמוֹ [בִּישַׁעְיָה נ״ז:י״ז] ״שׁוֹבָב בְּדֶרֶךְ לִבּוֹ״, וְהוּא הַתָּר אַחַר כָּל הָעוֹלֶה בְּלִבּוֹ מֵהִרְהוּרֵי הַיֵּצֶר רָע, וְכֵן גֹּבַהּ לֵב וְלֵב רַגָּז

and needless to say, all sinful thoughts and evil, foreign deliberations: upon this specifically applies the expression shovavim, as in “backsliding in the way of his heart” (Yeshayah 57:17), which refers to one who wanders after whatever arises in his heart from the incitements of the evil inclination, and likewise arrogance of heart and an agitated heart;593Sinful thoughts — Yoma 29a teaches, “Hirhurei aveirah are more difficult than the transgression,” using the aroma of meat as its mnemonic. Rav Tzadok returns to this teaching in Takanas HaShavin 15:12. There he distinguishes two measures of severity: for practical Torah law, an actual deed remains more severe according to its stated prohibition and punishment; yet before Hashem, Who examines the heart, an entrenched thought may stain the intellectual soul more deeply and obstruct closeness to the Shechinah. He cites Rabbeinu Bachya, Kad HaKemach (entry “Purity of the Heart”), for this inward reading. That later passage clarifies the present se’if: placing thoughts within the category atoned by teshuvah alone does not make them spiritually trivial. It means that because their transgression is located in the heart rather than in an external act, their direct repair is the heart’s own return.,594Cf. Isaiah 57:17 (Sefaria’s link-graph connects this verse to Takanat HaShavin 13:1): “For the iniquity of his covetousness I was angry and I smote him, hiding [My face] and was wroth; yet he went on, wayward in the way of his heart [וַיֵּלֶךְ שׁוֹבָב בְּדֶרֶךְ לִבּוֹ].” R’ Tzadok reads “shovav” here as the license one grants to whatever arises in the heart — the paradigm of a sin committed “by sitting still,” atoned by teshuvah alone.,595“Following whatever arises in his heart” — Bamidbar 15:39 commands, “You shall not stray after your hearts and after your eyes.” Sifrei Shelach §115 and Berachos 12b interpret “after your hearts” as heretical thought, “after your eyes” as thoughts of immorality, and “after which you stray” as idolatry. Ramban ad loc. explains that the verse warns against allowing contemplation to develop into skepticism or idolatrous belief; the tzitzis are to redirect sight into remembrance of Hashem’s commandments. Rav Tzadok’s wording is exact: the wrong is not merely that an unwanted thought first appears, but that one grants it permission, follows it, and lets it become the “way of his heart.” This is why Yeshayah’s “wayward in the way of his heart” becomes his model for inward shovavus.,596“Haughtiness of heart” and “a raging heart” — Mishlei 16:5 says, “Every proud heart is an abomination to Hashem.” Sotah 4b derives that arrogance resembles idolatry and denial of the Divine root, also citing “your heart will be lifted and you will forget Hashem” (Devarim 8:14). “A raging heart” echoes Devarim 28:65; Rashi explains lev ragaz as a trembling or fearful heart, while Nedarim 22a places the verse in its discussion of anger and emotional turmoil. Rambam, Hilchos De’os 1:1, treats anger, settledness, pride, humility, desire, and related qualities as dispositions of the soul; in 2:2-3 he prescribes deliberate retraining and especially radical distance from arrogance and anger. Rav Tzadok therefore includes these examples among inward transgressions: even where no discrete outward act can be isolated, teshuvah must restore the heart’s dispositions and not merely correct visible behavior.

וַאֲפִילּוּ הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּנֶעֱנָשִׁים עָלֶיהָ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״ט עַמּוּד ב׳], וְיֵשׁ עַל זֶה אַזְהָרַת לָאו דְּ״לֹא יִהְיֶה לְךָ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַמְבַּ״ם [רֵישׁ הִלְכוֹת יְסוֹדֵי הַתּוֹרָה], הוּא לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה

and even thoughts of idolatry, for which one is punished as they said [in Kiddushin 39b], and regarding which there is the negative admonition “You shall have no other gods” as the Rambam stated [beginning of Hilchos Yesodei HaTorah 1:6], it is a negative commandment without physical action.597R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Rosh HaShanah §15): “They reckoned (Yoma 86a) four categories of atonement, and [regarding] the severe ones — teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend and sufferings scour; and for idolatry, as in the generation of Enosh, there is a chillul Hashem that only death scours; only that one who delights in the Shabbos for the sake of Heaven is ‘better than a thousand fasts.’” Exactly the se’if’s framework — R’ Yishmael’s four levels of atonement, from a positive commandment up to chillul Hashem.,598Kiddushin 39b (verbatim): “But perhaps he was contemplating idolatry, and it is written: ‘so as to seize the House of Israel by their heart’ (Yechezkel 14:5)” — i.e., though “a bad thought the Holy One does not join to a deed,” an idolatrous thought He does join, so one is held culpable for it. Rambam, Yesodei HaTorah 1:6: the prohibition “you shall have no other gods before Me” (Shemos 20:3) forbids even entertaining idolatry in thought — a “negative commandment that has no action” (there being no physical deed).
וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה [פָּרָשָׁה ז׳] אִיתָא דְּאֵין עוֹלָה בָּאָה אֶלָּא עַל הִרְהוּר הַלֵּב, וְכֵן הוּא בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [פֶּרֶק ח׳ דְּיוֹמָא רֵישׁ הֲלָכָה ז׳] וּפֶרֶק א׳ דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת [הֲלָכָה ו׳]

And in Vayikra Rabbah [parashah 7:3] it is stated that an olah [burnt offering] comes only for sinful contemplation of the heart, and so it is in the Yerushalmi [Yoma 8:7] and chapter 1 of Shevuos [1:6];

וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהַיְינוּ הִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּיֵשׁ עֹונֶשׁ וְצָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה, וְכֵן קְרָא דְּאִיּוֹב דְּמַיְיתֵי שָׁם ״וּבֵרְכוּ אֱלֹהִים בִּלְבָבָם״ מַשְׁמַע דְּהַיְינוּ הִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

and it implies that this refers to thoughts of idolatry, for which there is punishment and which requires atonement, and so too the verse from Iyov cited there, “and cursed God in their hearts” (Iyov 1:5), implies thoughts of idolatry.599Vayikra Rabbah 7:3 and its parallel Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7 (= Shevuos 1:6), verbatim: “the olah atones only for a musing of the heart. What is the reason? ‘[As for] that which rises upon your spirit’ (Yechezkel 20:32). And so Job says, ‘and he rose early in the morning and offered burnt-offerings according to the number of them all,’ etc. (Iyov 1:5) — [this shows] that the olah atones for a musing of the heart” (attributed there to R’ Shimon bar Yochai). The proof-verse Iyov 1:5 (verbatim): “for Job said, perhaps my children have sinned and blasphemed God in their hearts [וּבֵרְכוּ אֱלֹהִים בִּלְבָבָם]” — read as a musing of idolatry, which requires atonement. Zevachim 7b: an olah that comes for [the nullification of] a positive commandment is “a mere gift [doron],” offered when one comes “to greet the face of the King” — since teshuvah has already atoned; R’ Tzadok extends this to the olah for a sinful musing.

וְאַף דִּבִתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד נִתְכַּפֵּר, הָעוֹלָה לְדוֹרוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּזְבָחִים ז׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] לְעִנְיַן כַּפָּרָה אַעֲשֵׂה דְּמֵהַאי טַעְמָא הוּא דּוֹרוֹן בְּעָלְמָא, וְהָכִי נַמֵּי לְהַוַּיִּקְרָא רַבָּה וְהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּכַפָּרָה אַהִרְהוּר

And although through repentance alone atonement is achieved, the olah is brought as a tribute-gift (doran), just as they said [in Zevachim 7b] regarding atonement for a positive commandment, that for this reason it is merely a gift; and so too according to Vayikra Rabbah and the Yerushalmi regarding atonement for sinful thought.
וְנִרְאֶה דְּלָא פְּלִיגֵי אַהַגְּמָרָא שָׁם, דְּגַם הִרְהוּר בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה, דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה הוּא בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

And it appears that they do not dispute the Gemara there, for thought is also subsumed under positive commandments, since a negative commandment lacking action is categorized under positive commandments as I wrote;
וְהַגְּמָרָא נָקַט הַמָּצוּי טְפֵי וְהַמִּדְרָשׁ נָקַט הֶחָמוּר טְפֵי
and the Gemara cited the more common case [omission of a positive command], while the Midrash cited the more severe case [sinful thought of idolatry];
וְאַף דְּנִתְכַּפֵּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד, צָרִיךְ לְהָבִיא אַחַר כָּךְ עוֹלָה לְדוֹרוֹן כְּשֶׁיָּבוֹא לְהַקְבִּיל פְּנֵי הַמֶּלֶךְ, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּזְבָחִים שָׁם]
and although he was atoned through teshuvah alone, he must subsequently bring an olah as a tribute-gift when coming to greet the presence of the King, as they said [in Zevachim 7b].

items.h: The theme: Halachic classification of negative commandments lacking stripes (lav she-ein bo malkus). Does the leniency of immediate pardon apply to all violations lacking bodily punishment, or strictly to passive inaction (shev ve-al ta'aseh)? R' Tzadok analyzes whether a negative commandment breached through active commission (kum ve-aseh)—or a positive command breached actively—can be forgiven immediately through teshuvah alone. He demonstrates that while the severity of punishment dictates the severity of atonement (such as kares for neglecting circumcision or the Pesach offering), an unqualified negative command requires Yom Kippur, which raises the question of whether an olah for idolatrous thoughts is genuinely a non-obligatory tribute or an independent, fifth category of atonement where repentance suspends and the olah atones.

p: וּשְׁאָר לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי, כָּל שֶׁעֲבֵירָתָן בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה מַשְׁמַע דְּאֵינָן בִּכְלָל

And regarding other negative commandments for which they do not administer lashes, according to what I wrote, wherever their transgression is performed through an active deed (kum ve-aseh), it implies that they are not included [in the leniency of immediate forgiveness];600Negative commandments for which lashes are not administered — Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2, gathers several distinct classes: a lav without an action; a lav that serves as the warning for a court-death offense; a lav assigned to monetary repayment; a lav repaired by a positive commandment [lav ha-nitak la-aseh]; and a general or composite prohibition [lav she-bichlalos]. The absence of lashes does not turn these into permissions or erase their status as Torah prohibitions. Rav Tzadok’s question is narrower: since Rashi links the gradation of atonement to the Torah’s gradation of punishment, should every non-lashed lav receive the lighter atonement of an aseh, or does R’ Yishmael’s unqualified phrase “one who transgressed a negative commandment” retain them in the second category?

וַאֲפִילּוּ עֲשֵׂה אִם עוֹבֵר עָלֶיהָ בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה, וּכְגוֹן לָאו הַבָּא מִכְּלַל עֲשֵׂה דְּהוּא נֶחְשָׁב עֲשֵׂה וַעֲבֵירָתוֹ בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּאֵינוֹ בִּכְלָל

and even a positive commandment, if one transgresses it through an active deed—such as a negative prohibition derived implicitly from a positive commandment (lav ha-ba miklal aseh), which is legally classified as a positive command yet breached through active commission—one may say according to what I wrote that it is not included;601A “negative derived from a positive” [lav ha-ba mi-klal aseh] is an act forbidden only by inference from the Torah’s positive formulation. The established rule is “lav ha-ba mi-klal aseh — aseh”: it is classified as a positive commandment rather than as a punishable lav. Rashi to Devarim 23:21 applies the rule to interest taken from a Jew, inferred from the permission to take interest from a gentile. Rambam, Hilchos Maachalos Asuros 2:1-3, applies it to species excluded from “these are the animals that you may eat,” and Hilchos Issurei Biah 1:8 applies it to relationships excluded by a positive formulation. Rav Tzadok points out the tension created by such cases: their formal category is aseh, yet the violation itself occurs through an active deed, not through passive failure to perform a mitzvah.
וּסְתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מַשְׁמַע דְּכָל עֲשֵׂה קָאָמַר
yet the unqualified language of the Gemara implies that it refers to any positive commandment.

וּכְפִי דִּבְרֵי רַשִׁ״י שָׁם דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וּפָקַדְתִּי״ דְּמִסְּבָרָא אוֹקֵי הַקַּל לַקַּלָּה, עַיֵּין שָׁם, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר לֹא כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר מַהַרְשָׁ״א שָׁם בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת דְּמוֹקְמִינַן אַעֲשֵׂה הַקַּלָּה שֶׁאֵינוֹ בְּמַעֲשֶׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And according to Rashi’s comment there (s.v. ufakadti), that through logical deduction we assign the lighter atonement to the lighter transgression, see there, one may say: it is not as the Maharsha said there in Chiddushei Aggados, that we establish it upon the lighter positive commandment that lacks action, see there;
רַק קוּלָּא דַּעֲשֵׂה הוּא לְפִי שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ מַלְקוּת, דְּמַה דְּאַשְׁכְּחַן דְּהַתּוֹרָה הֵקֵלָּה בְּעָנְשׁוֹ זֶה חָשְׁבִינַן לְקוּלָּא לְעִנְיַן כַּפָּרָתוֹ גַּם כֵּן

rather, the leniency of a positive commandment is because it carries no lashes; for wherever we find that the Torah was lenient regarding its punishment, we reckon that as a leniency regarding its atonement as well;602Rashi, Yoma 86a (s.v. u-fakadti): “‘I will punish their transgression with a rod’ — you have learned that there is a sin that requires sufferings; and by logic we set the light [sin] to the light [scouring] and the severe to the severe.” Maharsha (s.v. avar): “‘One transgressed [a positive commandment], etc., as it says: Return, wayward sons, I will heal their waywardness’ — implying that by teshuvah alone they forgive him; and since we find four categories of atonement in these verses, and per Rashi that by logic we establish this verse on the lightest — namely a positive commandment — for it is logical to reckon the punishment of a transgressor of a mere positive commandment (‘sits and does nothing’) lighter than a transgressor of a negative commandment (‘who transgresses by an act’); and for this reason a positive commandment overrides a negative commandment, since the positive is fulfilled by an act.” (R’ Tzadok reads Rashi’s “light” as bearing no lashes, not the Maharsha’s “not by an act.”)
וּכְמוֹ דְּמַחְמִירִינַן בְּכַפָּרָה בְּחֹמֶר הָעֹונֶשׁ בְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין
just as we are stringent regarding atonement corresponding to the severity of punishment in offenses liable to spiritual excision (kares) and court-imposed executions (misos beis din).
וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם פֶּסַח וּמִילָה שֶׁהֵם מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה וְעוֹבֵר עֲלֵיהֶם בְּשֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה, כֵּיוָן דְּחַיָּיב כָּרֵת עֲלֵיהֶם הֵם בִּכְלַל חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת לְחֹמֶר הַכַּפָּרָה

And certainly, the Paschal lamb (Pesach) and Circumcision (Milah), which are positive commandments transgressed through passive inaction, since they carry liability to kares, are included within offenses of kares regarding the severity of their atonement;603Pesach and milah are the exceptional positive commandments whose deliberate neglect bears kareis. Mishnah Kerisos 1:1 concludes its list of thirty-six kareis-liabilities: “the Paschal offering and circumcision are positive commandments.” Thus they remain mitzvos aseh in formal classification, but their punishment places them among the severe offenses for the fourfold atonement system. Their omission does not generate a chatas when inadvertent: Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, limits the fixed sin-offering to an inadvertent violation of an active negative commandment bearing kareis. This supports Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the category of the commandment and the severity assigned by its punishment.
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא כָּל שֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה קַל, רַק הַקּוּלָּא תָּלוּי בַּמַּה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ עֹונֶשׁ
wherefore not every passive inaction is lenient, but leniency depends rather upon the absence of punishment;
וּלְפִי זֶה הָיָה נִרְאֶה דְּגַם כָּל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין יִהְיֶה לְעִנְיָן זֶה בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה
and according to this, it would seem that all negative commandments for which one is not flogged should likewise be included in this category of positive commandments.
אַךְ סְתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא שֶׁאָמְרוּ אַחַר כָּךְ ״עָבַר עַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ וְלֹא אָמְרוּ דַּוְוקָא לָאוִין שֶׁלּוֹקִין, מַשְׁמַע דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר כָּל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה

However, the unqualified language of the Gemara stating subsequently, “if one transgressed a negative commandment, etc.,” without specifying prohibitions carrying lashes, implies that it means any negative commandment;
וְאַף דִּגְבֵי עֲשֵׂה נָקַט סְתָם וְעִם כָּל זֶה עֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ כָּרֵת אֵינוֹ בִּכְלָל וְכִמְבוֹאָר בִּלְשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק א׳ מִתְּשׁוּבָה הֲלָכָה ד׳]
and even though regarding positive commands it spoke generally, yet a positive command carrying kares is excluded as explained by the Rambam [Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4],
בָּזֶה סָמַךְ עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ בַּחֲמוּרוֹת ״חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת״, דְּכוֹלֵל כָּל חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת, בֵּין מִמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה בֵּין מִמִּצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה

in this he relied upon what was stated subsequently regarding severe offenses, “those liable to kares,” which includes all who incur excision, whether from a positive or negative commandment;604Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4: “If he transgressed kareis-bearing or court-death-bearing prohibitions and repented — teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend, and the sufferings that come upon him complete the atonement. But if he has desecration of the Name, even though he repented and Yom Kippur came and he is [still] in his teshuvah and sufferings befell him — he is not fully atoned until he dies.” The Rambam counts kareis from either a positive or negative commandment in the “severe” category — which is why the Gemara’s earlier unqualified “positive commandment” need not itself exclude the kareis-bearing aseh.
וְנָקַט מִקּוֹדֶם מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה וּמִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה סְתָם, וּרְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר חוּץ מֵחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין שֶׁזָּכַר אַחַר כָּךְ
and it cited initially positive and negative commandments without qualification, meaning: except for those liable to kares and execution by the court, which it specified afterward;
אֲבָל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין דְּאֵין נִזְכָּר, מַשְׁמַע דְּהֵם בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה
but non-punishable negative commandments, which were not separately mentioned, implies they remain included in negative commandments.

וּלְפִי זֶה נִרְאֶה דְּגַם לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וְאַף שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, וְכֵן הִרְהוּר דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּהוּא בְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

And according to this, it appears that even a negative commandment without action is included in negative commandments despite lacking action, and likewise thoughts of idolatry, which fall under a negative commandment without action as I wrote.

וְאִם כֵּן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בִּזְבָחִים שָׁם] ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״, הַיְינוּ רַק לְמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דִּמְכַפֶּרֶת אַעֲשֵׂה, אֲבָל לְהַוַּיִּקְרָא רַבָּה אַהִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לָאו דּוֹרוֹן, דִּצְרִיכָה לִגְמוֹר הַכַּפָּרָה קוֹדֶם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

And if so, one must say that what they said [in Zevachim 7b], that an olah is a tribute-gift, applies only to what they stated there that it atones for positive commands; but according to Vayikra Rabbah regarding thoughts of idolatry, it is not a mere gift, but is necessary to complete atonement prior to Yom Kippur.

וְאִם כֵּן אִיכָּא ה׳ חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, וְחַטָּאת דְּלָאו דּוֹרוֹן הַהִיא אַשּׁוֹגֵג דְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּבָאָה לְשׁוֹגֵג בִּמְקוֹם הַיִּסּוּרִין הַצְּרִיכִין לְמֵזִיד, אֲבָל עוֹלָה אַהִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה זֶה חִילּוּק כַּפָּרָה מְחוּדָּשׁ, דְּבָזֶה תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת

And if so, there would be five categories of atonement! And a sin offering (chatas), which is not a gift, is brought for an inadvertent sin of kares, replacing the afflictions required for intentional sin; whereas an olah for thoughts of idolatry would constitute an innovative category of atonement, wherein repentance suspends and the olah atones.605Rav Tzadok’s “five categories” are an analytical synthesis, not a separate fivefold baraisa. The standard fourfold structure is R’ Yishmael’s in Yoma 86a. Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1, explains the chatas as the required offering for an inadvertent active lav bearing kareis; it therefore supplies, for the inadvertent sinner, the cleansing that sufferings complete for a willful offender after teshuvah and Yom Kippur. By contrast, Vayikra Rabbah 7:3 and Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7 associate the olah with a musing of the heart, while Zevachim 7b calls an olah brought for an ordinary neglected aseh a “gift” after teshuvah has already atoned. Rav Tzadok concludes that if idolatrous thought remains within the negative-commandment category, its olah cannot be only a gift: teshuvah suspends and the olah completes the atonement. That sacrificial subcategory is the additional, fifth division proposed here.

items.h: The theme: Analysis of the Mishnah in Yoma 85b. The Mishnah lists chatas and asham as atoning offerings, omitting the olah—supporting Rava’s view (Zevachim 7b) that the olah is a tribute rather than an atoning sacrifice. Furthermore, the Mishnah states that repentance atones for positive commandments and negative commandments. The Gemara clarifies that "negative commandments" here refers strictly to a negative commandment tied to a positive command (lav ha-nitak la-aseh), because fulfilling the positive command rectifies the violation, equating it with an aseh. However, in Yoma 86a, "You shall not take [the Name in vain] and anything similar" refers to prohibitions carrying lashes. R' Tzadok reconciles these sources, demonstrating that "nitak la-aseh" in the Gemara serves as a paradigm for all negative commandments lacking lashes.

p: וּבַמִּשְׁנָה [יוֹמָא פ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳] חָשֵׁיב חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם דִּמְכַפֵּר וְלֹא עוֹלָה, וְזֶה רְאָיָה לִדְרָבָא [בִּזְבָחִים שָׁם] דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן וְלֹא לְכַפָּרָה
And in the Mishnah [Yoma 85b], it enumerates chatas and asham as atoning, but not olah, which provides proof for Rava [in Zevachim 7b] that an olah is a gift and not for essential atonement;
וּמִיהוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה שָׁם אִיתָא דִּתְשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַמִּצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה וּמִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא מוֹקֵי אַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה

however, in the Mishnah there it is taught that repentance atones for positive commandments and negative commandments, and see there in the Gemara (Yoma 86a) that it establishes it upon a negative commandment tied to a positive command (lav ha-nitak la-aseh).606Mishnah, Yoma 85b: “The chatas and the definite asham atone; death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah. Teshuvah atones for light transgressions — for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment; and for the severe ones it suspends until Yom Kippur comes and atones.” Gemara there: “Now, [if] it atones for a negative commandment, need [it be said that it atones] for a positive commandment?! Rav Yehudah said, this is what it means: for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment linked to a positive [nitak la-aseh]. (And the Gemara then asks:) And for a full negative commandment, no? — [But] contrast this [with a baraisa]: ‘these are the light ones — a positive commandment and a negative commandment’ (Yoma 86a), except for lo tisa and all that resembles it.” Rashi: “‘except for lo tisa’ — it entered the [questioner’s] mind [in the difficulty] because it is written [of it] ‘He will not hold guiltless’ (Shemos 20:7). ‘And all that resembles it’ — a full negative commandment.” Cf. Shevuos 21a, that lo tisa (a false oath) bears lashes administered by the earthly court, notwithstanding “He will not hold guiltless.”
וְלִכְאוֹרָה מַשְׁמַע דַּוְוקָא הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, דְּאַף דְּעָבַר אַלָּאו אִי מְקַיֵּים הָעֲשֵׂה תִּיקֵּן עֲבֵירַת הַלָּאו וְעַל כֵּן לֹא חֲמִיר מֵעֲשֵׂה

And superficially, it implies specifically a prohibition tied to a positive command, for although he transgressed a negative command, if he fulfills the positive command he rectifies the violation, wherefore it is no more severe than an aseh;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן שְׁאָר לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין כְּגוֹן לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת, וְאֶפְשָׁר גַּם לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה לֹא, מִדְּנָקַט רַק הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה

whereas other negative commandments that lack lashes, such as a generalized negative command (lav she-biklalos), and perhaps also a prohibition without action, would not be included, since it cited only a prohibition tied to a positive command.

אַךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁאִיתָא [שָׁם פ״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] ״לֹא תִשָּׂא וְכָל דְּדָמֵי לֵיהּ״, מַשְׁמַע דַּוְוקָא לָאו שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מַלְקוּת דּוּמְיָא דְּ״לֹא תִשָּׂא״ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ מַלְקוּת, כִּמְבוֹאָר [בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת כ״א עַמּוּד א׳] דְּבֵית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַטָּה מַלְקִין

Yet from what is taught [there, Yoma 86a], “You shall not take [the Name of the Lord in vain] and anything similar to it,” it implies specifically a negative command carrying lashes, akin to “You shall not take” which incurs lashes, as explained [in Shevuos 21a] that the earthly court administers lashes for it;
וְרַשִׁ״י שָׁם דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְכָל״ כָּתַב ״לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר״, וְהוּא לִישָׁנָא דְּבָרַיְיתָא שֶׁמַּיְיתֵי הַגְּמָרָא שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ
and Rashi there (s.v. ve-khol) wrote “a complete negative commandment,” which is the phrasing of the Baraisa cited by the Gemara subsequently;

וְאַף דְּכָתַב לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה סְתָם מַשְׁמַע רַק לְאַפּוֹקֵי הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִדְּנָקַט ״לֹא תִשָּׂא״ וּלְאַשְׁמוֹעִינַן דְּדָמֵי לֵיהּ מַשְׁמַע לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דְּמַלְקוּת, דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי הֲוָה לֵיהּ לְמִינְקַט לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה אַחֶרֶת שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַלְקוּת

and although writing an unqualified "negative commandment" would seem merely to exclude a prohibition tied to a positive command, nevertheless, since it cited “You shall not take” to teach that which is similar to it, it implies a negative command carrying lashes, for otherwise it should have cited another negative command that carries no lashes;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה״ חֲדָא נָקַט, וְהוּא הַדִּין שְׁאָר לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין

and one must say that what the Gemara stated, “tied to a positive command,” was merely one example, and the same law applies to other negative commandments that do not incur lashes.607R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek §1): “One cannot bring a ‘gift [doron]’ from mitzvos and good deeds until he first removes the evil; and ‘abstaining from transgressions’ is the middah of night, for one who walks in darkness must first see [that he not stumble] into pits and be harmed, and [only] afterward does he see the fitting way.” Exactly the se’if: the olah is a “gift,” not [strictly] a means of atonement — a gift presupposes the evil has already been removed.

items.h: The theme: Reconciling the Mishnah in Yoma 85b with the Baraisa of Rabbi Yishmael (Yoma 86a). The Mishnah does not follow the fourfold categorization of Rabbi Yishmael, for its conclusion groups all severe sins (chamurot) under a single rule—repentance suspends and Yom Kippur atones—without distinguishing offenses of kares and court executions. Furthermore, Rabbi Yishmael differentiates aseh from lo ta'aseh, indicating that his category of aseh includes positive commandments alone (and not lav ha-nitak la-aseh). Tosafos in Shevuos 12b resolves this by explaining that the Mishnah's term "atones" (mechafrot) does not mean total absolution, but rather that repentance "suspends" (toline), showing that the Mishnah did not intend to detail Rabbi Yishmael's complete classification.

p: וּמִיהוּ מַתְנִיתִין שָׁם לָא אָתְיָאן כְּחִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, שֶׁהֲרֵי תָּנֵי סֵיפָא ״חֲמוּרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר״ וְלֹא תָּנֵי חֲלוּקָּה אַחֶרֶת

However, the Mishnah there does not align with the categories of atonement of Rabbi Yishmael, for the conclusion teaches: “severe transgressions, repentance suspends and Yom Kippur atones,” and it does not teach another category;608Mishnah, Yoma 85b: “The chatas and the definite asham atone; death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah. Teshuvah atones for light transgressions, for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment; and for the severe ones it suspends until Yom Kippur comes and atones.”
וּמַשְׁמַע דְּכָיֵיל הַכֹּל בַּחֲמוּרוֹת גַּם כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין, וּכְבָרַיְיתָא דְּבַגְּמָרָא [שָׁם פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳]
and it implies that it encompasses everything within "severe transgressions," including kares and court-imposed executions, like the Baraisa in the Gemara [there, 86a];
וּבְלָאו הָכִי, מִדְּתָנֵי בְּמַתְנִיתִין ״מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה וּמִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה״, וְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל פַּלְגִינְהוּ בִּתְרַתֵּי
and even without this: since the Mishnah taught together “positive commandments and negative commandments,” whereas Rabbi Yishmael divided them into two separate categories,
מַשְׁמַע דְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הַיְינוּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה לְבַד
it implies that the positive commandment of Rabbi Yishmael is a positive commandment alone;
דְּאִי גַּם הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, הֲוָה לֵיהּ לוֹמַר מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה וּמִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה כִּבְמַתְנִיתִין, וְלִיתְנֵי בְּאִידָךְ חֲלוּקָּה מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר כִּבְבָרַיְיתָא דִּלְעֵיל

for if it included also a prohibition tied to a positive command, he should have said “positive commandments and negative commandments” as in our Mishnah, and taught in the other category “a complete negative commandment” as in the Baraisa above.609The [second] baraisa, Yoma 86a: “Come and hear: since it says at Chorev [regarding] teshuvah, ‘and He will hold guiltless’ [i.e. ‘clears’]— could it be that even lo tisa [a false oath] is among them [atoned by teshuvah alone]? The verse teaches: ‘He will not hold guiltless.’ Could it be that even the other liable-to-negatives are so [i.e. teshuvah alone does not atone them]? The verse teaches: ‘His Name’ — it is [only for] His Name that He does not clear, but He does clear [i.e. teshuvah alone atones] the other liable-to-negatives. (It thus emerges that teshuvah alone atones every negative, even one not nitak la-aseh.) It is a dispute among tannaim, for it was taught: ‘For what does teshuvah atone? For a positive commandment and a negative commandment linked to a positive; and for what does teshuvah [merely] suspend, with Yom Kippur atoning? For kareis, court-death, and a full negative commandment.’” R’ Tzadok refers to this second baraisa, since per the Gemara’s conclusion the first is like our Mishnah.
וְעַל כֵּן דְּהוּא כָּיֵיל כָּל מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וַעֲשֵׂה רָצָה לוֹמַר מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה לְבַד
Therefore, he subsumed all negative commandments under the category of negative commandments, and "positive" means a positive commandment alone;
