וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע בְּתוֹסָפוֹת [שְׁבוּעוֹת י״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״לֹא זָז״ שֶׁהִקְשׁוּ אַהָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל מֵהַךְ מַתְנִיתִין, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and so it implies in Tosafos [Shevuos 12b, s.v. lo zaz], who raised a difficulty against Rabbi Yishmael from this Mishnah, see there;610Tosafos, Shevuos 12b (s.v. lo zo): “‘he does not stir from there until they forgive him’ — and although we learned in the Mishnah in the last chapter of Yoma (85b) that teshuvah atones ‘for a positive commandment and a negative commandment,’ and it also says in Chagigah (5a) that whoever does a thing and regrets it, they forgive him immediately, even as [with] other transgressions — [that] is not complete forgiveness, but rather they lighten the judgment for him; whereas for a positive commandment they forgive completely.”
וּמְבוֹאָר דִּפְשִׁיטָא דְּהַךְ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה הַיְינוּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה לְבַד וְלֹא לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה
and it is clear that it was obvious to them that this "positive commandment" means a positive command alone, and not a prohibition tied to a positive command.
וְהֵם תֵּירְצוּ דְּלָא פְּלִיג אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, עַיֵּין שָׁם כַּוָּונָתָם דְּ״מְכַפְּרִין״ דְּמַתְנִיתִין לָאו כַּפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה אֶלָּא כְּ״תוֹלִין״ דְּבָרַיְיתָא

And they resolved that the Mishnah does not dispute Rabbi Yishmael, see there that their intention is that “atone” in the Mishnah does not mean complete atonement, but rather like “suspends” in the Baraisa;
וְעַל כֵּן לָא קַשְׁיָא גַּם כֵּן מֵחֲמוּרוֹת אִי רָצָה לוֹמַר גַּם חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין
and therefore it is also not difficult from severe offenses, if one wishes to say it includes those liable to kares and executions by the court;
דְּהָא רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר דִּתְשׁוּבָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים תּוֹלִין וְצָרִיךְ תַּרְוַויְיהוּ לִתְלוֹת, וְלִתְלִיָּיה דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל קָרֵי מַתְנִיתִין ״מְכַפְּרִין״
for behold, Rabbi Yishmael says that repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, requiring both of them to suspend, and to that suspension of Rabbi Yishmael the Mishnah applied the term “atone”;

וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּכָיֵיל בְּהֶדְיָא גַּם כֵּן מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר, וּבָזֶה יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי גַּם כֵּן, מַתְנִיתִין לָא נָחֵית לְזֶה דְּכַפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

and even though it explicitly encompasses also a complete negative commandment, wherein Yom Kippur atones completely as well, the Mishnah did not concern itself with detailing that complete atonement of Rabbi Yishmael.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the apparent contradiction between the Mishnah in Yoma 85b and the Baraisa of Rabbi Yishmael (Yoma 86a) concerning negative commandments. If “atones” (mechafrot) in the Mishnah merely means “suspends” (toline), why does the Mishnah group full negative commandments with severe sins? R’ Tzadok explores whether the Tannaim dispute the entire scheme—allowing repentance alone to fully atone even for complete negative commandments—and examines the views of Tosafos in Shevuos 12b and Chagigah 5a, alongside the Turei Even regarding prohibitions lacking lashes (lav she-ein bo malkus) and withholding a worker’s wage (ovesh sechar sachir).

p: אַךְ הָא קָשֶׁה: אִי ״תּוֹלִין״ דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל הַיְינוּ ״מְכַפְּרִין״ דְּמַתְנִיתִין, אִם כֵּן קָשֶׁה מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר, אַמַּאי תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה עַד יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים כְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין

But this is difficult: if “suspends” of Rabbi Yishmael is equivalent to “atones” in the Mishnah, then regarding a full negative commandment, why does repentance suspend until Yom Kippur just like offenses liable to kares and court executions?
וַהֲרֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל אוֹמֵר עַל זֶה ״תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה״ כִּבְלָאו תַּעֲשֶׂה הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה דִּכְהֲדָדֵי נִינְהוּ, וּלְהַךְ ״תּוֹלָה״ קָרֵי מַתְנִיתִין ״מְכַפְּרִין״

For behold, Rabbi Yishmael says regarding this that repentance suspends, just as with a negative commandment tied to a positive command (lav ha-nitak la-aseh), for they are identical, and to that suspension the Mishnah applies the term “atones”;

וְאִם כֵּן גַּם בְּלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר כֵּן, דַּהֲרֵי גְּמָרָא מְפָרֵשׁ מִיִּתּוּרָא דְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּמִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה דַּוְוקָא קָאָמַר מַתְנִיתִין, וּכְאִידָךְ בָּרַיְיתָא דְּבַגְּמָרָא שָׁם, וּפְלִיגֵי אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

and if so, it should be the same for a full negative commandment, for the Gemara explains from the redundancy of “positive commandment” that the Mishnah specifically meant a negative commandment tied to a positive command, matching the other Baraisa in the Gemara there which disputes Rabbi Yishmael.611Mishnah, Yoma 85b: “The chatas and the definite asham atone; death and Yom Kippur atone together with teshuvah. Teshuvah atones for light transgressions — for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment; and for the severe ones it suspends until Yom Kippur comes and atones.” Gemara there: “Now, [if] it atones for a negative commandment, need [it be said that it atones] for a positive commandment?! Rav Yehudah said, this is what it means: for a positive commandment and for a negative commandment linked to a positive [nitak la-aseh]. (And the Gemara then asks:) And for a full negative commandment, no? — [But] contrast this [with a baraisa]: ‘these are the light ones — a positive commandment and a negative commandment’ (Yoma 86a), except for lo tisa and all that resembles it.” Rashi: “‘except for lo tisa’ — it entered the [questioner’s] mind [in the difficulty] because it is written [of it] ‘He will not hold guiltless’ (Shemos 20:7). ‘And all that resembles it’ — a full negative commandment.” Cf. Shevuos 21a, that lo tisa (a false oath) bears lashes administered by the earthly court, notwithstanding “He will not hold guiltless.”
וְאִם כֵּן מַאי מַקְשׁוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת מִמַּתְנִיתִין אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְנִדְחֲקוּ לְתָרֵץ, כֵּיוָן דְּעַל כָּרְחֲךָ פְּלִיגֵי, אִם כֵּן נֵימָא דִּפְלִיגֵי בְּכוּלְּהוּ

And if so, why did Tosafos raise a difficulty from the Mishnah against Rabbi Yishmael and press themselves to resolve it; since perforce they dispute, let us say that they dispute across all the categories!

וְאִין הָכִי נַמֵּי דִּמְכַפְּרִין לְגַמְרֵי, וּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ לְתַנָּא דְּמַתְנִיתִין דְּנִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה דָּמֵי לַעֲשֵׂה לְכַפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי, וְחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין דָּמֵי לְמִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גְּמוּרָה דְּסַגִּי בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

And indeed they would hold that [repentance and Yom Kippur] atone completely: the Tanna of the Mishnah holding that a prohibition tied to a positive command is like an aseh to atone completely, while offenses of kares and court executions are like a full negative commandment, for which Yom Kippur suffices

[וּמִזֶּה לֹא הִקְשׁוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת מִשּׁוּם דִּבְמַתְנִיתִין לֹא מְפָרֵשׁ בְּהֶדְיָא חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין, אַךְ בַּבָּרַיְיתָא מְפָרֵשׁ, וּבִשְׁבוּעוֹת שָׁם נַמֵּי מְפָרְשִׁינַן חֲמוּרוֹת כֵּן, עַיֵּין שָׁם]

[and Tosafos did not question from this because in the Mishnah offenses of kares and court executions are not explicitly detailed, though the Baraisa details them, and in Shevuos there we likewise interpret “severe sins” this way, see there];
וְאוּלַי לֹא בָּעוּ לְאַפּוֹשֵׁי פְּלוּגְתָּא בְּמַה דְּאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּלָא פְּלִיגֵי
and perhaps they did not wish to multiply disputes where it is possible to maintain that they do not dispute,
וְרַק בְּמִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר דִּבְלָאו הָכִי תַּנָּאֵי נִינְהוּ בְּיוֹמָא שָׁם, דִּלְחַד תַּנָּא תְּשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת גַּם אַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר
but only regarding a full negative commandment, where in any case Tannaim dispute in Yoma there, since according to one Tanna repentance atones even for a full negative commandment.
וּכְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת דְּהַךְ ״מְכַפְּרִין״ הַיְינוּ ״תּוֹלִין״, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהַיְינוּ כִּדְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, דְּכָל מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה תּוֹלִין בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד
And according to what I wrote regarding Tosafos, that “atones” means “suspends,” one may say that it aligns with Rabbi Yishmael, that all negative commandments are suspended by repentance alone;
וְדִבְרֵיהֶם בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת הוּא כְּתֵירוּץ בַּתְרָא [בְּחֲגִיגָה ה׳ עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״הָא״

and their words in Shevuos accord with the second resolution [in Chagigah 5a, s.v. ha],612Chagigah 5a: “R’ Chanina bar Pappa said: whoever does a thing and then regrets it — they forgive him immediately, as it says (Malachi 3), ‘and they did not fear Me’ — [implying] had they feared Me, they would be forgiven immediately.” Tosafos (there): “It is written regarding one who withholds a hired worker’s wages, which is a negative commandment; and it disagrees with R’ Yishmael in the last chapter of Yoma (86a), who said [for a negative] teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones — and [yet] there is another baraisa that says teshuvah atones for a positive commandment and a negative commandment [linked to a positive]. Moreover, one may distinguish among types of teshuvah: there is [one who] repents and they forgive him immediately, and [one who] repents and they forgive him but not completely, and there is still a punishment, and that punishment they suspend. And that which we say in Shevuos (12b) [that] one who transgresses a positive commandment and regrets it does not stir from there until they forgive him — that is complete forgiveness; and if he repents with all his heart, through sufferings his iniquities are atoned.”
וּלְתֵירוּץ קַמָּא שָׁם בָּרַיְיתָא דְּעַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר תְּשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת פְּלִיגֵי אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל
whereas according to the first resolution there, the Baraisa holding that repentance atones for a full negative commandment disputes Rabbi Yishmael.
וּמַה שֶּׁהֵבִיאוּ שָׁם מִבָּרַיְיתָא וְלֹא מִמַּתְנִיתִין דְּיוֹמָא שָׁם, הַיְינוּ מִשּׁוּם דְּמַתְנִיתִין מוֹקְמִינַן בְּנִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, אֲבָל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר מוֹדֵי לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

And why they cited from the Baraisa there rather than from the Mishnah in Yoma is because we establish the Mishnah upon a prohibition tied to a positive command, whereas on a full negative commandment it agrees with Rabbi Yishmael;
וְהָתָם בְּעוֹשֶׁק שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר קָיְימֵי, וְהֵם לְשִׁיטָתָם [בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא ס״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״לַעֲבוֹר״ דְּלוֹקִין אַכּוֹבֵשׁ שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and there [in Chagigah 5a] they deal with withholding a worker's wage, and they follow their consistent view [in Bava Metzia 61a, s.v. la'avor] that lashes are incurred for withholding a worker's wage, see there.613Tosafos, Bava Metzia 61a, s.v. la’avor alav bishnei lavin — withholding wages and lashes: The Gemara asks why the Torah repeats the prohibition of robbery and applies “lo tigzol,” where ordinary robbery is already known, to withholding a hired worker’s wages. Tosafos distinguish the two applications: ordinary robbery is a lav ha-nitak la-aseh, because restitution remains due, and therefore does not receive lashes; when the verse is applied to withholding wages, Tosafos state that lashes can apply. This is the local premise Rav Tzadok imports into Tosafos, Chagigah 5a. He therefore treats the case there as a full, lash-bearing negative commandment rather than as a non-lashed prohibition grouped with an aseh. Consequently, Tosafos’ citation must reach the broader Yoma baraisa that allows teshuvah to atone even beyond the category of nitak la-aseh.

[וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בְּטוּרֵי אֶבֶן חֲגִיגָה שָׁם כָּתַב לְתָרֵץ קוּשְׁיַת הַתּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם, דְּכָל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּיוֹמָא בְּלָאו הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, וְכוֹבֵשׁ שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר אֵין לוֹקֶה דְּנִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה וְגַם הוּא לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

[And then I saw in Turei Even on Chagigah there that he resolved Tosafos’ difficulty by positing that all negative commandments lacking lashes are included under aseh, as stated in Yoma regarding a prohibition tied to an aseh, and one who withholds a worker's wage does not receive lashes because it is tied to an aseh and is also a prohibition without action, see there;614Turei Even on Chagigah 5a — alternative classification and Rav Tzadok’s objection: Turei Even, the Talmudic commentary of R’ Aryeh Leib Ginzburg (author of Sha’agas Aryeh), resolves Tosafos’ difficulty by grouping prohibitions that do not receive lashes with the lighter, aseh-like category for the hierarchy of atonement. In his analysis, withholding a hired worker’s wages is both linked to the continuing duty of payment and a lav she-ein bo maaseh; it therefore receives no lashes and can fit the Mishnah’s immediate-atonement category without creating a broad dispute with R’ Yishmael. Rav Tzadok does not merely reject that taxonomy in the abstract. He argues that it cannot explain Tosafos themselves, because Tosafos, Bava Metzia 61a, explicitly say that when “lo tigzol” is applied to withholding wages, lashes can apply. Tosafos in Chagigah are therefore discussing a full negative commandment. This forces Rav Tzadok to identify their source as the broader Yoma baraisa, and illustrates his method of reading each Rishon according to that Rishon’s own local halachic position.
וּבֶאֱמֶת תּוֹסָפוֹת לְשִׁיטָתָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וְהִנֵּה פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן דְּכָל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין בִּכְלָל]
and in truth Tosafos follows its own system as I wrote, and behold it was obvious to him as well that all prohibitions lacking lashes are included].
וְעַל כֵּן מַיְיתֵי הַבָּרַיְיתָא דְּגַם בְּלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר דְּמַלְקוּת דּוּגְמַת ״לֹא תִשָּׂא״ תְּשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת
Therefore it cited the Baraisa teaching that even for a full negative commandment carrying lashes akin to “You shall not take,” repentance atones;

וּלְפִי זֶה שָׁם תְּלָתָא תַּנָּאֵי בָּזֶה: דִּלְמַתְנִיתִין יַחַד בָּרַיְיתָא בְּנִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה וְכַדּוֹמֶה דְּלֵיכָּא מַלְקוּת תְּשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת, וּלְאִידָךְ בָּרַיְיתָא אֲפִילּוּ לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר נַמֵּי חוּץ מִ״לֹא תִשָּׂא״, וּלְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דַּוְוקָא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה לְבַד

and according to this there are three Tannaitic views on this: according to the Mishnah together with one Baraisa, for a prohibition tied to an aseh and the like where there are no lashes, repentance atones; according to the other Baraisa, even for a full negative command as well, except for “You shall not take”; and according to Rabbi Yishmael, solely for a positive commandment alone.

items.h: The theme: Analysis of the commentary Tosafos Yom HaKippurim citing Retzuf Ahavah on the dispute between the Mishnah and Rabbi Yishmael. The Retzuf Ahavah struggled with Tosafos in Shevuos, assuming that a prohibition tied to a positive command is identical to an aseh according to Rabbi Yishmael, and wondered why withholding a worker's wage was treated as a full negative command. R’ Tzadok demonstrates that the commentator overlooked Tosafos in Bava Metzia 61a and Chagigah 5a (which hold that withholding wages incurs lashes), and clarifies why the Rishonim specifically cited the Baraisa over the anonymous Mishnah.

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בְּסֵפֶר תּוֹסָפוֹת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים [יוֹמָא פ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] הֵבִיא מִסֵּפֶר רְצוּף אַהֲבָה [סִימָן ש״י] הִקְשָׁה אַתּוֹסָפוֹת שְׁבוּעוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר: הָא בְּיוֹמָא מוֹקְמִינַן לַהּ בְּלָאו הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה וְהַיְינוּ עֲשֵׂה, וּפְשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ דְּהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן עֲשֵׂה בִּדְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

And then I saw in the book Tosafos Yom HaKippurim [Yoma 85b], who cited from Retzuf Ahavah (§310) questioning the aforementioned Tosafos in Shevuos: behold, in Yoma we establish the Mishnah upon a prohibition tied to a positive command, which is categorized as an aseh, and it was obvious to him that this is likewise an aseh in Rabbi Yishmael's scheme;615Tosafos Yom HaKippurim and Ratzuf Ahavah §310 — background and the opening difficulty: Tosafos Yom HaKippurim, R’ Moshe ibn Chaviv’s commentary on Yoma, cites Sefer Ratzuf Ahavah §310. Ratzuf Ahavah asks: Yoma 85b establishes the Mishnah’s negative commandment as a lav ha-nitak la-aseh, which is not lashed because it has a positive rectification; why, then, do Tosafos in Shevuos understand R’ Yishmael’s ‘positive commandment’ as an aseh alone? He answers in Rav Tzadok’s direction: R’ Yishmael’s wording is literal, and the absence of lashes does not by itself transfer a lav into the aseh atonement class. The issue is the tannaitic classification of the prohibition, not only its technical malkus rule.
וְהוּא יִשֵּׁב דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹסָפוֹת כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּבָרַיְיתָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דַּוְוקָא קָאָמַר
and he resolved the words of Tosafos just as I wrote, that the Baraisa of Rabbi Yishmael means strictly a positive commandment.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ הֵבִיא תּוֹסָפוֹת דַּחֲגִיגָה הַנִּזְכָּר וְיַעֲיֵין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ עַל זֶה, וְהֵבִיא מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר שָׁם כֵּן גַּם בְּסֵפֶר שָׁם דְּעוֹשֶׁק שְׂכַר שָׂכִיר לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר, וְתָמַהּ עַל זֶה דְּהוּא נִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And see there afterward that he cited the aforementioned Tosafos in Chagigah, examining it at length, bringing what Rabbi Elazar wrote there and in his book that withholding a worker's wage is a full negative command, wondering at this since it is tied to an aseh, see there;616Cf. Chagigah 5a; Tosafos there; and Bava Metzia 61a — why withholding wages is decisive: Chagigah 5a reads Malachi 3:5 as placing severe sins together with withholding a worker’s wage, and R’ Chanina bar Pappa then says that regret brings immediate forgiveness. Tosafos ask against R’ Yishmael, who requires Yom Kippur for a negative commandment, and answer either from another baraisa or by distinguishing incomplete forgiveness from complete forgiveness. Tosafos, Bava Metzia 61a, are decisive for Rav Tzadok: when ‘lo tigzol’ is applied to withholding wages, they state that lashes can apply. Their Chagigah case is therefore a full lav, not merely a non-lashed nitak la-aseh; Rav Tzadok reads Tosafos consistently across tractates.
וְאִשְׁתְּמִיטְתֵיהּ תּוֹסָפוֹת דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא הַנִּזְכָּר דִּמְפוֹרָשׁ דְּלוֹקִין, וְגַם מִדִּבְרֵיהֶם בַּחֲגִיגָה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל מוּכָח כֵּן
and he overlooked the aforementioned Tosafos in Bava Metzia (61a) where it is explicit that they administer lashes, as is also proven from their words in Chagigah mentioned above.
וְהוּא כָּתַב דְּמַאי שְׁנָא מִבָּרַיְיתָא אַחֵר, רָצָה לוֹמַר בָּרַיְיתָא דִּתְשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַעֲשֵׂה וְלֹא תַעֲשֶׂה הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And he wrote asking why this Baraisa is different from another Baraisa, meaning the Baraisa holding that repentance atones for an aseh and a prohibition tied to an aseh, see there;
וְתָמוּהַּ, אִם כֵּן לָמָּה לָהֶם לְבָרַיְיתָא, הֲוֵי לָהֶם לְהָבִיא מֵהַמִּשְׁנָה, וּסְתַם מִשְׁנָה נַמֵּי פְּלִיגָא אַדְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּנִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה

and it is astonishing: if so, why did they need to cite a Baraisa? They should have cited the Mishnah, for an anonymous Mishnah likewise disputes Rabbi Yishmael regarding a prohibition tied to an aseh!
וְעַל כֵּן כַּוָּונָתָם לְאִידָךְ בָּרַיְיתָא, וּמִשּׁוּם דְּהַהִיא לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

Therefore, their intent was directed to the other Baraisa, specifically because that one deals with a full negative commandment, exactly as I wrote.617Cf. Yoma 86a — the ‘other baraisa’ and why the Mishnah is insufficient: Yoma 86a presents two tannaitic formulations: one limits immediate atonement to an aseh and a lav ha-nitak la-aseh, while another derives that Hashem absolves those liable for the other prohibitions, apart from the exceptional false oath. If Tosafos meant only the Mishnah’s nitak la-aseh case, the Mishnah itself already sufficed. Their phrase ‘another baraisa’ therefore points to the broader source that includes a full negative commandment.

items.h: The theme: Critique of the Asarah Ma'amaros (by the Rama MiFano). The Rama MiFano asserts that all negative commandments lacking lashes atone through repentance alone—including generalized prohibitions, prohibitions derived from positive commands, prohibitions without action, prohibitions tied to positive commands, and prohibitions remediable by restitution (nitan l'tashlumin). He suggests that while an olah atones for these, repentance atones independently without a sacrifice. R' Tzadok critiques this formulation, demonstrating that if an olah functions as a mere gift (doran) because repentance alone suffices, the mechanism of atonement for non-punishable prohibitions remains unresolved, leaving what seemed obvious to the Rama MiFano as a matter requiring deep examination.

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [מַאֲמַר חֲקוֹר דִּין, חֵלֶק א׳ רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק י״ח] דְּכָל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין כְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה בָּזֶה, לְהִתְכַּפֵּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד

And then I saw in Asarah Ma'amaros [Ma'amar Chakor Din, Part I, start of ch. 18] that all negative commandments lacking lashes are equated to positive commandments in this regard, to be atoned through repentance alone;
וְהֵן: לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת, וְהַבָּא מִכְּלַל עֲשֵׂה, וְשֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, וְהַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, וְהַנִּיתָּן לְתַשְׁלוּמִין וְקִיֵּים הָעֲשֵׂה וְשִׁילֵּם

and they are: a generalized negative command, a prohibition derived from a positive command, a prohibition lacking action, a prohibition tied to a positive command, and a prohibition given to financial restitution, provided he fulfilled the positive command and paid;
אֲבָל הַנִּיתָּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין מִפְּנֵי חוּמְרוֹ אֵין לוֹקִין וְאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל זֶה

but a prohibition serving as an admonition for death by court execution, which does not incur lashes due to its greater severity, is excluded from this.618Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chakor Din I:18; Sifra and Rashi; Rambam and Makkos — the proposed class of non-lashed lavim: Rema mi-Fano states that teshuvah alone atones immediately for a positive commandment and for lavim not punished by lashes—such as a lav she-bichlalus, one inferred from an aseh, one without action, one nitak la-aseh whose corrective aseh was fulfilled, and one given to payment—and says that although an olah also atones, here he discusses atonement arising from the person’s own regret. Yad Yehudah links this to Sifra and Rashi on Vayikra 1:4, where an olah reconciles for an aseh and a lav ha-nitak la-aseh. Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2, lists the same categories for the laws of lashes; however, Makkos 15b and Rambam 16:4 show they are not one uniform status, since a nitak la-aseh can become lash-bearing when its aseh is not fulfilled. Rav Tzadok therefore questions deriving one lighter rule of kapparah merely from the absence of lashes.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם כָּתַב: וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁעוֹלָה גַּם כֵּן כַּפָּרָתָן, הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן בְּכַפָּרָה דְּמִמֵּילָא
And see there that he wrote: although an olah likewise atones for them, with what are we dealing here? With an atonement that occurs automatically through repentance;
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּמְפָרֵשׁ [אוֹת ג׳] הֵבִיא דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים מוּבָא בְּרַשִׁ״י בַּחוּמָשׁ עַיֵּין שָׁם
and see there in the commentary [note 3] citing Toras Kohanim as quoted by Rashi on the Chumash (Vayikra 1:4), see there;
וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן בְּרַשִׁ״י בַּגְּמָרָא דִּזְבָחִים [ה׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מַאן״, וְשָׁם כָּתַב רַק הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, וְהוּא כָּתַב עַל כָּל לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין

and so it is in Rashi in the Gemara in Zevachim [5b, s.v. man], where he mentioned only a prohibition tied to a positive command, whereas the Rama MiFano applied it to all negative commandments lacking lashes.

אֲבָל תָּמוּהַּ מַה דְּמַשְׁמַע מִדְּבָרָיו דְּעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת כְּכַפָּרָה דִּתְשׁוּבָה, אֶלָּא דְּהָכָא מַיְירֵי בְּכַפָּרָה שֶׁמֵּהָאָדָם עַצְמוֹ וְאֵין צָרִיךְ דָּבָר אַחֵר, עַיֵּין שָׁם בַּמְפָרֵשׁ [אוֹת ד׳]

But it is astonishing that his words imply that an olah atones just like the atonement of repentance, except that here we deal with an atonement originating from the person himself needing no external vehicle, see there in the commentary [note 4];

וְנִרְאֶה דְּאִשְׁתְּמִיטְתֵיהּ גְּמָרָא [דִּזְבָחִים ז׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״ מִשּׁוּם דִּבְלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״ וּבִתְשׁוּבָה סַגִּי, וְאִם כֵּן אֵינוֹ כַּפָּרָתָן כְּלָל

and it appears that he overlooked the Gemara [Zevachim 7b] mentioned above that an olah is a tribute-gift, because without repentance “the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination” (Mishlei 21:27) and with repentance it suffices alone, and if so the offering is not their essential atonement at all!

וְלִכְאוֹרָה מִשָּׁם רְאָיָה לִדְבָרָיו דְּגַם לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין תְּשׁוּבָה סַגִּי, לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּגַם עֲלַיְיהוּ עוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת, וְאַמַּאי קָאָמַר ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״ אִי בְּהוּ לָא סַגִּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד

And superficially there is proof from there for his words, that for prohibitions lacking lashes repentance alone suffices, according to what I wrote that an olah atones for them as well; for why would the Gemara state that an olah is a tribute-gift if regarding them repentance alone did not suffice?
וְגַם לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי מִלְּשׁוֹן רַשִׁ״י בְּהַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה מִיהַת מוּכָח כֵּן וְנֶגֶד מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
And also according to what I wrote from Rashi’s language on a prohibition tied to an aseh, this is proven, contradicting what I wrote above.

וְאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּאִין הָכִי נַמֵּי רָבָא קָאָמַר רַק דְּאִיכָּא עוֹלָה דְּדוֹרוֹן בְּכַפָּרָה דַּעֲשֵׂה, וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּקְרָא כְּתִיב ״לְכַפֵּר״ לָאו דַּוְוקָא דְּהָא אַעֲשֵׂה לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ, וְאִין הָכִי נַמֵּי דְּאַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

And one may suggest that indeed Rava meant only that there exists an olah of tribute in the atonement of an aseh, and although Scripture writes “to make atonement” (Vayikra 1:4) it is not precise since for an aseh alone you cannot find an independent atonement; yet indeed for a prohibition tied to an aseh you can find it according to Rabbi Yishmael,
וְלֹא נָחֵית לְבָאֵר זֶה, דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים רוֹב עוֹלָה הַבָּא עַל עֲשֵׂה הוּא דּוֹרוֹן
and he did not descend to elaborate this, because in any event the majority of burnt offerings brought for an aseh are gifts.

וְהוּא כָּתַב שָׁם מַסְקָנָא דְּמִילְּתָא כְּאִלּוּ הוֹכִיחַ זֶה מִקּוֹדֶם, וְאֵין שָׁם הוֹכָחָה, רַק [בְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק ט״ז] כָּתַב כֵּן גַּם כֵּן בִּפְשִׁיטוּת מִדַּעְתּוֹ, בְּלָאו הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה וְקִיֵּים עֲשֵׂה דְּמִתְכַּפֵּר מִיָּד

And [the Rama MiFano] wrote there his conclusion as if he had proven this beforehand, yet there is no proof there; only [at the beginning of ch. 16] he wrote likewise simply from his own reasoning, that for a prohibition tied to an aseh where he fulfilled the aseh, he is atoned immediately.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם כָּתַב: ״וְאִם לָאו וְכוּלֵיהּ מִתְכַּפֵּר קְצָת וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And see there that he wrote: “and if not, he is atoned somewhat, etc.”, see there;619Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din, part 1, ch. 16: “Four categories of atonement R’ Yishmael would expound, and R’ Elazar ben Azaryah explained: they are three, and teshuvah [accompanies] all of them — for upon the nullification of a positive commandment [teshuvah] alone atones immediately. And there are those who teach in it ‘he does not stir from there until they forgive him,’ and so it is taught in the first chapter of Shevuos. And the intent is to distinguish between the nullification of a bare positive commandment and the light ones among the negatives — for even though their law is like a positive commandment and one is not lashed for them, they still require further [atonement]: for one who transgresses a negative nitak la-aseh, if through teshuvah he fulfilled the positive linked to it, he is atoned completely at once; and if not, he has in hand two transgressions, and through teshuvah he is atoned somewhat and his punishment is lightened, but he has no complete forgiveness until Yom Kippur comes.” Mefaresh (letter ו): “For he did not fulfill the positive, [so] he has in hand a transgression of the negative and a transgression of the positive; and through teshuvah one of them is atoned — namely the nullification of the positive in it — and therefore his punishment is lightened. And this is [the meaning of] the Mishnah, according to Rav Yehudah, [that] for a negative nitak la-aseh teshuvah atones — meaning it atones the portion of the positive in it; but in any case, from the side of the negative in it, he still has forty [lashes] on his shoulder and is subject to lashes until Yom Kippur comes, since it is like a full negative, of which R’ Yishmael said teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones.”
וּמַשְׁמַע קְצָת דִּמְפָרֵשׁ כֵּן הַגְּמָרָא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הַמְפָרֵשׁ [שָׁם אוֹת ו׳] דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר בְּלֹא קִיֵּים הָעֲשֵׂה, וּמְכַפֵּר אַעֲשֵׂה אֲבָל אַלָּאו לוֹקֶה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and it implies somewhat that he explains the Gemara thus, as the commentator wrote [note 6], that it refers to where he did not fulfill the positive command, so it atones for the aseh while for the negative command he incurs lashes, see there.
וְתָמוּהַּ בְּעֵינַי: אַעֲשֵׂה פְּשִׁיטָא, וּמַאי שְׁנָא מִשְּׁאָר עֲשֵׂה? וְגַם מַתְנִיתִין קָאָמַר ״מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה״, מְבוֹאָר דְּאַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה מְכַפֵּר, לֹא אַעֲשֵׂה

And this is astonishing in my eyes: regarding the aseh it is obvious, for wherein is it different from any other positive command? And furthermore, the Mishnah explicitly states “negative commandments,” showing clearly that it atones for the negative command, not merely for the positive!

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ מִתּוֹסָפוֹת שְׁבוּעוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר מְפָרֵשׁ דִּבְרֵיהֶם גַּם כֵּן בְּלֹא קִיֵּים הָעֲשֵׂה דְּלוֹקֶה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נוֹחַ לְהִתְכַּפֵּר מִשְּׁאָר חַיָּיבֵי מַלְקוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And see there afterward that from the aforementioned Tosafos in Shevuos he interprets their words likewise as referring to where he did not fulfill the aseh and incurs lashes, yet it is easier to achieve atonement than for other offenses carrying lashes, see there;
וְהוּא תָּמוּהַּ גַּם כֵּן בְּעֵינַי: דְּמַאי שְׁנָא מִשְּׁאָר לָאוִין הַלּוֹקִין כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא קִיֵּים הָעֲשֵׂה, וּכְמַאן דְּאָמַר ״לֹא קִיֵּים לוֹקֶה״

and this too is astonishing in my eyes: wherein does it differ from other negative commandments carrying lashes, once he failed to fulfill the positive command, in accordance with the authority who holds that failing to fulfill incurs lashes?
וְגַם לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מַה מַּקְשֶׁה מִמַּתְנִיתִין אַבָּרַיְיתָא, וּמַתְנִיתִין לְפִי דְּבָרָיו בְּלֹא קִיֵּים וְלֹא מְכַפֵּר אַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה רַק אַעֲשֵׂה

And I also do not understand how he questions from the Mishnah against the Baraisa, when the Mishnah according to his explanation deals with non-fulfillment and does not atone for the negative command at all, but only for the positive!
וְנִרְאֶה דְּהָדַר בֵּיהּ מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַב תְּחִלָּה, וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת מְפָרֵשׁ דְּגַם אַלֹּא תַעֲשֶׂה מְכַפֵּר אַף דְּלֹא קִיֵּים
And it appears that he retracted from what he wrote initially, and Tosafos explains that it atones even for the negative command despite non-fulfillment;
אֲבָל תֵּימַהּ: מְנָא לֵיהּ לְהַקְשׁוֹת וּלְהִדָּחֵק וּלְפָרֵשׁ מַתְנִיתִין בִּדְלָא קִיֵּים, וְלֹא בִּדְקִיְּימוֹ לַעֲשֵׂה דְּבָזֶה מִתְכַּפֵּר גַּם לְרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל

but it is wondrous: from where did he derive to question, force himself, and interpret the Mishnah as dealing with non-fulfillment, rather than where he fulfilled the positive command, wherein it atones according to Rabbi Yishmael as well?

וְאוּלַי מִשּׁוּם דְּאִם גַּם לָזֶה קָרֵי ״מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה״ וְאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, אִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּבָרַיְיתָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל גַּם כֵּן אֵין זֶה בִּכְלָל, וַעֲדַיִין קָשֶׁה אַהֲדָדֵי, וְעַל כֵּן מְפָרֵשׁ זֶה בְּלֹא קִיֵּים

And perhaps it is because if one terms this a “negative commandment” and excludes it from positive commandments, perforce the positive commandment of Rabbi Yishmael’s Baraisa likewise excludes it, so the contradiction remains, and therefore he explains it as dealing with non-fulfillment;
אֲבָל לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מִי דְּחָקוֹ לְפָרֵשׁ כֵּן, וּבְעֵינַי הוּא זָר וְתָמוּהַּ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וּפְשָׁטֵיהּ דְּתוֹסָפוֹת שְׁבוּעוֹת דְּלֹא כְּוָותֵיהּ
but I do not know what compelled him to interpret thus, and in my eyes it is foreign and astonishing as I wrote, and the plain reading of Tosafos in Shevuos does not accord with him.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם [פֶּרֶק י״ז] מֵהַתּוֹסָפוֹת דַּחֲגִיגָה וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב: ״וְלֵיכָּא לְמֵימַר אֶלָּא דְּפָלֵיג אֲפִילּוּ דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְכוּלֵיהּ״
And see there [ch. 17] from Tosafos in Chagigah, and what he wrote: “and one cannot say other than that it disputes even Rabbi Yishmael, etc.”;

לֹא יָדַעְתִּי מִי דְּחָקוֹ לָזֶה, וַהֲלֹא תַּנָּאֵי הוּא וְתוֹסָפוֹת הֵבִיאוּ בָּרַיְיתָא דְּאִידָךְ תַּנָּא וְכַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וְאוּלַי בָּא לְהַעֲמִידוֹ כִּסְתַם מִשְׁנָה וְאֵינוֹ מוּכְרָח, וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי מַאי ״וְלֵיכָּא לְמֵימַר״ דְּקָאָמַר

I do not know what compelled him to this: is it not a dispute of Tannaim, where Tosafos cited the Baraisa of the other Tanna as mentioned above? Perhaps he sought to establish it like an anonymous Mishnah, but it is not compelling, and I do not know what he meant by stating “one cannot say”.620Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din, part 1, ch. 17: “In Chagigah, first chapter, R’ Chanina bar Pappa said: whoever does a thing and regrets it, they forgive him immediately — and we do not read ‘for all his iniquities,’ as is proven from Tosafos there and in the first chapter of Shevuos. Except that they said in Chagigah that R’ Chanina bar Pappa disagrees with R’ Yishmael, and there is nothing to say except that he disagrees with Rav Yehudah’s interpretation of the Mishnah at the end of Yoma; for we are astonished at it, ‘now [that] teshuvah atones for a negative, need [it be said] for a positive?!’ — and Rav Yehudah explained it [as] a negative nitak la-aseh, while R’ Chanina bar Pappa said [the Mishnah] teaches ‘not [only] this but even this,’ and would establish the stam Mishnah as not in accordance with R’ Yishmael.”
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב הוּא לְתָרֵץ דְּלָא פְּלִיגֵי מִשּׁוּם דְּנִיתָּן לְתַשְׁלוּמִין וְאֵין לוֹקֶה, וְהוּא עַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ דִּבְלָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקֶה מוֹדֶה

And what he wrote to resolve that they do not dispute because it is given to financial restitution and does not incur lashes, this follows his own path that for prohibitions lacking lashes [Rabbi Yishmael] agrees;
וּמֵהַתּוֹסָפוֹת דְּלֹא תֵּירְצוּ כֵּן יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין רְאָיָה, דְּהֵם לְשִׁיטָתָם דְּלוֹקֶה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and from Tosafos, who did not resolve it thus, one may say there is no counter-proof, for they follow their own view that lashes are administered, as mentioned above.
וְהִנֵּה הָא דִּמוֹחֲלִין עַל כָּרְחֲךָ בְּשֶׁשִּׁילֵּם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הַמְפָרֵשׁ [אוֹת ט״ו]
And behold, that they pardon him applies perforce only when he paid restitution, as the commentator wrote [note 15];
אַךְ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: מִי לָא עָסְקִינַן בְּעוֹשֶׁק שְׂכִיר גֵּר דְּמַיְירֵי בֵּיהּ נַמֵּי קְרָא שָׁם וּמֵת הַגֵּר, דְּהַשְׁתָּא לֵיכָּא תַּשְׁלוּמִין וְלוֹקֶה

yet one may say: could we not be dealing with withholding the wages of a convert-worker, with whom the verse there also deals, where the convert died without heirs, so that now restitution is inapplicable and he incurs lashes?
וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים אֵין לוֹ רְאָיָה לְהָרַמַ״ע בָּזֶה, וּלְכָן מַה דִּפְשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ, לְדִידִי מִיבַּעְיָא טוּבָא

In any event, the Rama MiFano has no definitive proof in this matter; wherefore that which was simple and obvious to him, to me remains deeply questioning and unresolved.621Cf. Zevachim 7b; Mishlei 21:27; Bava Metzia 61a with Tosafos; Gittin 39a — Rav Tzadok’s two tests: Rava calls the olah a doron: without teshuvah, ‘the offering of the wicked is an abomination,’ and after teshuvah the essential atonement is already complete, so the korban cannot be the operative kapparah. Rav Tzadok’s final worker case applies the same scrutiny to payment. Bava Metzia makes withholding wages an additional violation of lo tigzol, and Tosafos state that this lav can carry lashes. Gittin records that a convert who dies without heirs leaves ownerless property. If the unpaid worker was such a convert and died, restitution can no longer be made while the lav remains; payment therefore cannot by itself establish Rema mi-Fano’s lighter atonement category.

items.h: The theme: R’ Tzadok found in the Mishnas Chachamim (§2, letter ו), in the name of the author’s father, who “sensed.” Inferred from the fact that an olah is a “gift” and [yet] atones for a nitak la-aseh — that a nitak la-aseh too suffices with teshuvah [alone]. The author rejected this: one may say [Rava] speaks of a plain olah, which is for those liable for a positive commandment, common every day in every person.

p: וּמָצָאתִי בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים [סִימָן ב אוֹת ו] בְּשֵׁם אָבִיו, הִרְגִּישׁ מֵהָא דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״ וּמְכַפֵּר אַהַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, דְּגַם נִיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה דַּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה

And I found in the book Mishnas Chachamim [section 2, letter vav] in the name of his father, who noted the difficulty from the fact that an olah is a gift and atones for [a negative commandment] tied to a positive one, that for [a negative commandment] tied to a positive one, repentance alone should also suffice;622Sefer Mishnas Chachamim §2, letter ו — background and argument: This work on the 613 mitzvos was composed by R. Yosef Hochgelernter, son of R. Yaakov Yitzchak, and is arranged with the analytical divisions Yavin Shemuah and Tzafnas Paneach. R’ Tzadok quotes a teaching recorded in the father’s name: if Zevachim 7b calls the olah a doron, yet an olah also addresses a lav ha-nitak la-aseh, teshuvah must already have completed its essential kapparah. The author limits “doron” to the ordinary olah for neglect of an aseh; R’ Tzadok then tests that distinction through the coercion passages in Rosh Hashanah and Arachin.
וְהוּא דָּחָה זֶה, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר בִּסְתָם עוֹלָה קָאָמַר דְּהוּא עַל חַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה, הַמָּצוּי בְּכָל יוֹם בְּכָל אָדָם
and he deflected this, saying that one can say it was speaking of an ordinary olah, which is for those liable for [transgressing] a positive commandment, which is common every day for every person;

אֲבָל הֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִכָּל מָקוֹם מֵהָא דְּחַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה מְמַשְׁכְּנִין, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת [רֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ו עַמּוּד א] סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״יַקְרִיב״ הַטַּעַם דְּמִתְכַּפֵּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה, וְקָפָסֵיק וְתָנֵי כָּל חַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה אַף אַהַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

but he brought a proof regardless from the fact that those liable for positive commandments are exacted collateral, and in Tosafos [Rosh Hashanah 6a] at the end of the entry beginning "yakriv" the reason [given] is that one is atoned through repentance, and it categorically teaches "all who are liable for a positive commandment," even for [a negative commandment] tied to a positive one, see there.623Rosh Hashanah 6a: “‘he shall bring it’ (Vayikra 1:3) — teaches that they compel him [to bring his offering]”; the discussion concerns a voluntary olah. Tosafos (s.v. yakriv): “for every positive commandment too they compel [performance], as it says in the chapter Naarah she-Nispatesah (Kesubos 40b). And if you ask: [regarding] that which we learned in the chapter ha-Omer Mishkali (Arachin 21a), ‘those liable for chataos and ashamos are not distrained, [but] those liable for olos and shelamim are distrained [in order to compel them to bring].’ And if you ask: and for olos, why does he need distraint more than for chataos and ashamos, seeing that in the first chapter of Zevachim (6a) it says that olos too atone for those liable for a positive commandment? One may answer: since we say elsewhere (Yoma 86a) that if he did teshuvah he does not stir from there until they forgive him, he is [already] atoned by teshuvah — and it is not like chataos and ashamos.”
וְאֵינוֹ מוּכְרָח, דְּהָא עוֹלָה לָאו חוֹבָה הִיא, וְרַשִׁ״י [עֲרָכִין כ״א עַמּוּד א] כָּתַב דְּמֵהַאי טַעְמָא מְמַשְׁכְּנִין

And this is not a compelling proof, for an olah is not an obligation, and Rashi [Arakhin 21a] wrote that it is for this reason that collateral is exacted;624Vayikra 1:3; Arachin 21a; Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Maaseh HaKorbanos 14:1, 17: An ordinary olah may begin as a neder or nedavah; once undertaken, beis din may distrain and compel the owner until he says “I desire.” Rashi contrasts this with chataos and ashamos, for which no distraint is needed because their owners require them for kapparah. This sharpens R’ Tzadok’s distinction: the sin itself does not create a compulsory olah-debt; the obligation arises only after the person vows or designates it. Thus coercion cannot prove that teshuvah alone fully atones for every lav ha-nitak la-aseh.
וּנְהִי דְּתוֹסָפוֹת לָא נְהִירָא לְהוּ זֶה, דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם אִי מְכַפֵּר לֹא פָּשַׁע
and even though this was not clear to Tosafos, since in any case if it atones he has not been negligent;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם זֶה אֱמֶת דְּאֵינוֹ חוֹבָה, דְּהָא לֹא כְּתִיב קְרָא לְחִיּוּבָא עַל הָעוֹבֵר לְהָבִיא אֶלָּא דְּאִי מֵבִיא מִתְכַּפֵּר
nevertheless it is true that it is not an obligation, for no verse is written obligating the transgressor to bring it, rather only that if he brings it he is atoned.
וּלְפִי זֶה גַּם אִי לָאו הַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה צָרִיךְ לְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים לְכַפֵּר, יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מִיהַת גּוֹמֵר כַּפָּרָתוֹ, וְאַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מִיהַת אֵין צָרִיךְ מִיָּד

And according to this, even if a negative commandment tied to a positive one requires Yom Kippur to atone, Yom Kippur at any rate completes his atonement, and after Yom Kippur at any rate he does not need [to bring it] immediately.
וְלֹא דָּמֵי לְחַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת, דְּאִמַּעוּט [בִּכְרֵיתוֹת כ״ה עַמּוּד ב] ״חֲטָאִים דְּבַר קָרְבָּן״, דְּזֶהוּ בְּקָרְבַּן חוֹבָה דְּחַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת

And it is not comparable to those liable for sin-offerings and guilt-offerings, which were excluded [in Kerisos 25b] as "sins subject to a sacrifice," for that is regarding an obligatory sacrifice of sin-offerings and guilt-offerings;625Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Kerisus 25b: The fourfold atonement framework distinguishes a regular lav, for which teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones, from sins requiring further cleansing. Obligatory chataos and definite ashamos remain due even after Yom Kippur because they are “sins subject to a korban.” R’ Tzadok contrasts that continuing sacrificial debt with a voluntary olah: once the relevant completion of kapparah has occurred, the olah is not still owed as a compulsory korban, so one may suspect that the sinner will delay and rely upon Yom Kippur instead of bringing it.

אֲבָל עוֹלָה דְּאֵינוֹ חוֹבָה לֹא מִקְּרֵי ״חֵטְא בַּר קָרְבָּן״ לְהַצְרִיכוֹ לְכַפָּרָתוֹ אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, וְשַׁפִּיר חָיְישִׁינַן דְּפָשַׁע וּמַמְתִּין עַד אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְיִתְכַּפֵּר

but an olah, which is not an obligation, is not termed a "sin subject to a sacrifice" to require it for his atonement after Yom Kippur, and we rightly suspect that he is negligent and waits until after Yom Kippur and will be atoned.

וְתוֹסָפוֹת דְּנָקְטֵי ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ הַיְינוּ בִּסְתָם עוֹלָה דַּעֲשֵׂה, וְאִין הָכִי נַמֵּי דְּאַהַנִּיתָּק לַעֲשֵׂה חָיְישִׁינַן דְּיַמְתִּין עַל יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, וְלָכֵן עֲדַיִין דָּבָר זֶה צָרִיךְ יִשּׁוּב וְהֶכְרֵעַ

And Tosafos, who cited "does not move," etc., meant regarding an ordinary olah for a positive commandment, but indeed for [a negative commandment] tied to a positive one we suspect he might wait for Yom Kippur, and therefore this matter still requires resolution and decision.626R’ Tzadok — parallel (Et HaOchel §10): “‘And one who brings a gift [doron]’ — [is] like one who brings first-fruits; and their eating is like a korban, for they themselves are like the altar, as the Sages said at the end of Chagigah that ‘their whole body is fire,’ as it says, ‘is not My word like fire?’” The se’if’s olah-as-gift, which atones for a nitak la-aseh: the doron offered to draw near, on the model of first-fruits and the korban.

sections.en: Complete teshuvah and immediate forgiveness for positive commandments

items.h: תשובה גמורה ומחילה מיידית על ביטול מצוות עשה.

The theme: The wording “he does not stir from there [until they forgive him]” — which the Tosafos Yom. HaKippurim scrutinized (citing the Mahari“t: why”he does not stir," and how does one derive. Immediacy from “Return, wayward sons” when “I will heal their waywardness” reads as future?).

p: וְלָשׁוֹן ״אֵינוֹ זָז מִשָּׁם״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁדִּקְדֵּק בּוֹ בְּ״תוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים״ בְּשֵׁם מַהֲרִי״ט עַיֵּין שָׁם

And the expression "he does not move from there," etc., which was analyzed carefully in Tosefos Yom HaKippurim in the name of the Maharit, see there;627Sefer Tosafos Yom HaKippurim by R’ Moshe ibn Chaviv (first published 5447 / 1687), and this is its language: “‘Transgressed a positive commandment and repented — he does not stir from there,’ etc. The Mahari”t in his derashos (p. 232) asked: what is this “he does not stir” that it says — and until how much would it enter your mind that [atonement] would be suspended? And moreover, how does he derive from “Return, wayward sons” that “he does not stir from there” — behold, “I will heal their waywardness” implies the future? And he answered [there], see there. And it is difficult to me: whence did the Rav z“l [Mahari"t] to explain that what is written here,”transgressed a positive commandment," deals with a rebel who returned to his corruption? And therefore it appears to me to explain like the approach of Rashi and the Rambam, and along the way I will resolve the difficulty of Tosafos. And R’ Shimon and R’ Yehoshua ben Korchah say: either way (even if they repented in private) we accept them — that is, even though he repented in concealment and not in public, as it says, “Return, wayward sons,” even though he is still wayward, for he repented in secret and not openly; and so the Rambam ruled at the end of ch. 3 of [Hilchos] Teshuvah. And according to this it says: ‘transgressed a positive commandment and repented’ — even though the teshuvah is in concealment, we do not say let us wait until he repents in public; rather he does not stir from there until they forgive [him], as it says, “Return, wayward sons,” even though he is still wayward, for he did not repent in public — and this is “I will heal your waywardness” [future], meaning that the Holy One will help him to repent in concealment such that he will return also in public."

יֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְפִי דַּעַת רַמְבַּ״ם וְכָל הַמְפָרְשִׁים בְּהָא דְּ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה״ וְכוּלֵיהּ ״שֶׁבָּאת״ וְכוּלֵיהּ ״בְּאוֹתָהּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ דִּתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵהַמּוּבְחָר צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת דַּוְוקָא שֶׁבָּאת וְכוּלֵיהּ

one can say, according to the opinion of the Rambam and all the commentators regarding [the Talmudic statement], "What is the case of a penitent?", etc., "that it comes to him," etc., "with the same," etc., according to its plain meaning that a complete and choice repentance requires specifically that it comes [to his hand again], etc.628Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1: “What is complete teshuvah? One to whose hand came a matter in which he had transgressed, and it is possible for him to do it [again], yet he separated and did not do it because of teshuvah — not out of fear and not from failure of strength. How so? One who had relations with a woman in sin, and after time secluded himself with her, he still in his love for her and in his bodily vigor, and in the [same] province in which he transgressed, yet he separated and did not transgress — this is a complete baal teshuvah. This is what Shlomo said, ‘and remember your Creator in the days of your youth’ (Koheles 12:1). And if he repented only in his old age, at a time when it is impossible for him to do what he used to do — although it is not choice teshuvah, it avails him, and he is a baal teshuvah.” And the language in the Gemara, Yoma 86b, which Rabbeinu mentions below: “What is a baal teshuvah? Rav Yehudah said: for example, one to whose hand came a matter of transgression a first time and a second time, and he separated from it — with that [same] woman, at that [same] time, in that [same] place.”

נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ רַק בְּעוֹבֵר עַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״שֶׁבָּאת דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל״, דְּלֹא כָּל שַׁעְתָּא מִתְרַחֵשׁ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה לְפָנָיו וּבְאוֹתוֹ הַגָּווֶן וְהָעִנְיָן שֶׁעָבַר

It appears that this is only when transgressing a negative commandment, as it says "that the matter of transgression comes to his hand and he is saved," since not at every moment does the matter of transgression happen before him and in the same manner and context that he [previously] transgressed.
וְגַם צָרִיךְ לִהְיוֹת אוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ דַּוְוקָא שֶׁכְּבָר טָעַם טַעַם אִיסּוּר הַהוּא וְהַיֵּצֶר מְסִיתוֹ וּמִתְגַּבֵּר נֶגְדּוֹ בָּזֶה יוֹתֵר, וְלֹא תַּאֲוַת כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שָׁווֹת

And it also needs to be specifically that very same transgression, since he has already tasted the taste of that prohibition and the evil inclination incites him and overcomes him more in this [regard], and the desire for all transgressions is not equal.

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּעוֹבֵר עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, דְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה הוּא בָּא מִצַּד עַצְלוּת וּקְרִירוּת שֶׁאֵינוֹ רוֹצֶה לְהַטְרִיחַ גּוּפוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת הַמִּצְוָה וְכָל הַמִּצְוֹת שָׁווֹת בָּזֶה

Whereas when transgressing a positive commandment, the nullification of a positive commandment comes from laziness and coldness, where one does not want to trouble his body to perform the mitzvah, and all commandments are equal in this regard.
וְאֵין לְךָ רֶגַע שֶׁאֵין מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מוּכֶנֶת לִפְנֵי הָאָדָם לְקַיְּימָהּ כְּגוֹן לִימּוּד תּוֹרָה וֶאֱמוּנַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּ״אָנֹכִי ה׳״ וְגוֹמֵר, וְאַהֲבָתוֹ וְיִרְאָתוֹ וְכַדּוֹמֶה

And there is no moment when a positive commandment is not ready before a person to fulfill it, such as Torah study and faith in the Blessed Name from "I am Hashem," etc., and loving Him and fearing Him, and the like.629Constant positive commandments. Rambam, Sefer HaMitzvos, aseh 1, 3, and 4, counts faith from “Anochi,” love from Devarim 6:5, and fear from Devarim 10:20; Hilchos Talmud Torah 1:8 requires every Jew to establish Torah study by day and night from Yehoshua 1:8. Biur Halachah 1:1, quoting Sefer HaChinuch, describes six mitzvos whose obligation is constant and says that every moment one contemplates them he fulfills an aseh. This supplies the halachic background to Rav Tzadok’s word “prepared”: unlike the recurrence of a particular forbidden temptation, faith, love, fear, and Torah study are immediately available modes of present obedience.
וְגַם הַתְּשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ, שֶׁהוּא שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁבִּיטֵּל, הִיא עַצְמָהּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
And the repentance itself, where he returns and regrets the positive commandment that he nullified, is itself a positive commandment.
וַהֲרֵי לְפָנָיו מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁהוּא מְקַיְּימָהּ עַתָּה, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ דַּוְוקָא אוֹתָהּ מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה עַצְמָהּ

So behold, before him is the positive commandment of repentance which he is fulfilling now, and there is no need for that specific positive commandment itself to come to his hand.630Teshuvah as a positive commandment. Ramban to Devarim 30:11 reads “this commandment” as the return described in 30:1-2, possible “at all times and in all places,” through mouth and heart. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, formally counts verbal confession as the positive commandment when one repents. Rav Tzadok himself, Takanat HaShavin 9:1, distinguishes the inward turning—which can make a person righteous through sincere resolve—from vidui, “a positive commandment in its own right.” Here, “the positive commandment of teshuvah” means that the present act of return is itself obedience; the penitent therefore need not wait for the identical neglected aseh to recur. The wording accords directly with Ramban while retaining Rav Tzadok’s earlier distinction concerning vidui.
וְגַם לְגִירְסָא דִּילַן ״שֶׁבָּאת פַּעַם אַחַת וּשְׁתַּיִם״, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּבְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה אֵין צָרִיךְ לָזֶה וְאֵין צָרִיךְ בֵּירוּר עַל יְדֵי בִּיאָה לְיָדוֹ כְּלָל

And also according to our text "that it came once and twice," one can say that for a positive commandment there is no need for this, and there is no need for clarification through it coming to his hand at all;
דְּרַק בִּדְבַר עֲבֵירָה דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה אַאוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה בְּיִחוּד שֶׁל יִתְקְפֶנּוּ יִצְרוֹ שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה
for only regarding a matter of transgression, where the repentance is for that specific transgression uniquely because his inclination overpowers him, is this applicable.
אֲבָל בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּבְכָל קִיּוּם מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה סַגִּי, אֵין צָרִיךְ בָּזֶה בֵּירוּר כְּלָל שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ
But regarding a positive commandment, according to what I wrote, since any fulfillment of a positive commandment suffices, there is no need in this for any clarification of it coming to his hand.

דְּאֵין לְךָ אָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַיֵּים כַּמָּה מִצְוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם, וַאֲפִילּוּ הָרֵיקָנִין שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כְּרִימּוֹן, וַאֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹף חֲגִיגָה]

For there is no person in Israel who does not fulfill several commandments every day, and even the empty ones in Israel are as full of commandments as a pomegranate, and even the transgressors of Israel, as they said [at the end of Chagigah].631Cf. Chagigah 27a (Sefaria’s link-graph connects this to Takanat HaShavin 14:1), verbatim: “Reish Lakish said: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel — [derived] a fortiori from the golden altar: just as the golden altar, which has upon it only the thickness of a gold dinar, [yet] for many years the fire has no power over it — the sinners of Israel, who are ‘full of mitzvos like a pomegranate,’ as it is written, ‘like a slice of pomegranate is your temple [rakatekh]’ (Shir HaShirim 4:3) — read not ‘rakatekh’ but ‘reikanin shebakh’ [the empty ones among you] — all the more so.” R’ Tzadok invokes this to show that every Jew always has fulfilled positive commandments to his credit, so the “recurrence test” is unnecessary for atoning a nullified aseh.

items.h: The theme: That one should not nullify any further mitzvah is likewise impossible — as they said (Zevachim 7a) that an olah brought “on condition that I owe nothing” is invalid, since there is no Jew who does not owe a positive commandment. Indeed, even “on condition that he already offered an olah that day” fails. For from that offering until now he inevitably nullified some positive commandment (the constant mitzvos, like Torah study — the moment one lets his mind go idle he nullifies a positive commandment).

p: וְלָעִנְיָן שֶׁלֹּא יְבַטֵּל עוֹד שׁוּם מִצְוָה, זֶה גַּם כֵּן אִי אֶפְשָׁר
And regarding not nullifying any commandment again, this too is impossible.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּזְבָחִים ז עַמּוּד א] ״עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֵין מְחוּיָּב כְּלוּם – פְּסוּלָה, שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה״

And as they said [Zevachim 7a], "On the condition that he is not obligated in anything—it is invalid, for there is no person in Israel who is not obligated in a positive commandment."632Cf. Zevachim 7a (Sefaria’s link-graph, anchored to Takanat HaShavin 14:2), verbatim: “And Rava said: a chatas that one slaughtered for one who owes nothing is invalid, for there is no person in Israel who does not owe a positive commandment [שֶׁאֵין לְךָ אָדָם בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּיב עֲשֵׂה].” R’ Tzadok applies the principle to an olah conditioned on owing nothing: since every Jew perpetually owes some positive commandment (e.g., a momentary lapse in Torah study), such a condition can never be satisfied.
וּמַשְׁמַע אֲפִילּוּ עַל מְנָת שֶׁהִקְרִיב כְּבָר עוֹלָה בְּאוֹתוֹ יוֹם, גַּם כֵּן אֵין לְךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה מִשְּׁעַת הַקְרָבַת עוֹלָה עַד עַתָּה

And it implies that even on the condition that he already brought an olah on that same day, there is also no [person], etc., who is not obligated in a positive commandment from the time of offering the olah until now.

דְּאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִינָּצֵל בְּכָל שָׁעָה מִבִּיטּוּל עֲשֵׂה כְּמִצְוַת תַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה וְכַדּוֹמֶה מִמִּצְוֹת הַתְּמִידוּת, שֶׁכְּשֶׁמְּפַנֶּה רֶגַע אַחַת לִבּוֹ לַבַּטָּלָה, מְבַטֵּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה וְאֵין לְךָ אָדָם נִיצּוֹל מִזֶּה

For it is impossible to be saved at every moment from nullifying a positive commandment such as the commandment of Torah study and similar continuous commandments, because when one turns his heart to idleness for a single moment, he nullifies a positive commandment, and there is no person saved from this.
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ה עַמּוּד א] ״פִּשְׁפֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא – יִתְלֶה בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה״

Therefore they said [Berachos 5a], "If he examined and did not find [a sin]—he should attribute it to the neglect of Torah study."633Cf. Berakhos 5a (Sefaria’s link-graph, anchored to Takanat HaShavin 14:2), verbatim: “Rava — and some say Rav Chisda — said: if a person sees that sufferings befall him, let him examine his deeds, as it says, ‘let us search our ways and examine [them], and return to Hashem’ (Eichah 3:40). [If] he searched and did not find [a sin to account for them], let him attribute it to nullification of Torah [study], as it says, ‘happy is the man whom You afflict, Hashem, and teach him from Your Torah’ (Tehillim 94:12).” R’ Tzadok’s point: because bittul Torah is unavoidable for nearly everyone, the penitent always has a residual “positive commandment” owing — hence the daily Hashiveinu.
דְּדָבָר זֶה מָצוּי אֵצֶל כָּל אָדָם, אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁפִּשְׁפֵּשׁ וְלֹא מָצָא לוֹ שׁוּם חֵטְא, וּמִסְּתָמָא שׁוֹקֵד עַל הַתּוֹרָה כָּל הַיּוֹם
For this matter is common with every person, even a completely righteous person who examined and found no sin, and presumably studies Torah diligently all day long.

וְעִם כָּל זֶה יוּכַל לִתְלוֹת בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה אֵיזֶה רְגָעִים, אִם לֹא יְחִידִים הַשְּׂרִידִים כְּרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וַחֲבֵרָיו תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים הָאֲמִיתִּים, שֶׁכָּל שִׂיחָתָם וְהִרְהוּר לִבָּם גַּם בְּמִילֵי דְּעָלְמָא הַכֹּל דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה

Yet despite this he could attribute it to the neglect of Torah study for some moments, except for unique individuals, the remnants, such as Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and his colleagues, the true Torah scholars, whose every conversation and thought of their heart, even in worldly matters, is entirely words of Torah.634The “conversation” of true Torah scholars. Sukkah 21b derives from Tehillim 1:3, “and his leaf does not wither,” that even the conversation of talmidei chachamim requires study. The teaching follows R’ Shimon’s report that two halachos were learned from Rabban Gamliel’s seemingly incidental conversation. Rashi to Tehillim 1:3 explains that even what appears secondary or waste-like in a sage serves a purpose; Maharal, Tiferes Yisrael ch. 59, calls such speech the “leaf” that clothes and expresses the inner fruit of wisdom. Rav Tzadok limits the stronger claim—that worldly speech and thought are themselves Torah—to rare, fully integrated scholars such as R’ Shimon bar Yochai and his circle. It is therefore an exceptional spiritual level, not a general dispensation for ordinary idle conversation.
וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה דְּעַל כֵּן תִּיקְּנוּ בַּתְּפִלָּה בִּרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״ שָׁלֹשׁ פְּעָמִים בְּכָל יוֹם, וַאֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר
And apparently, this is why they instituted in the prayer the blessing of "Hashiveinu" three times every day, even for a completely righteous person;
דְּאֵין לְךָ שֶׁאֵין מְחוּיָּב עֲשֵׂה בְּבִיטּוּל תּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה, דְּעַל זֶה מְבַקְּשִׁים ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ לְתוֹרָתֶךָ וְקָרְבֵנוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ

for there is no one who is not liable for [the neglect of] a positive commandment in the neglect of Torah and service, for regarding this we request "Return us to Your Torah and draw us near," etc.635Hashiveinu in the three daily prayers. Berakhos 26b records that Shacharis, Minchah, and Maariv were instituted by the Avos and aligned by the Sages with the daily offerings. Megillah 17b states that the Men of the Great Assembly fixed the Amidah in its order and placed teshuvah after understanding. The blessing itself asks: “Return us, our Father, to Your Torah; bring us near, our King, to Your service; and restore us in complete teshuvah before You.” Rav Tzadok reads these three clauses as a recurring accounting for Torah, avodah, and teshuvah itself. Because the Amidah returns morning, afternoon, and evening, each prayer addresses new spiritual deficits that arose since the previous one.
וְ״הַחֲזִירֵנוּ״ וְכוּלֵיהּ הוּא עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת תְּשׁוּבָה עַצְמָהּ
And "And bring us back," etc., is regarding the nullification of the commandment of repentance itself.

וְאַף דִּכְבָר שָׁב שַׁחֲרִית וְנִתְכַּפֵּר מִיָּד, וּלְתַנָּא קַמָּא דְּבָרַיְיתָא [יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב] אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְכַּפֵּר וְנִמְחַל אֵין לוֹ לְהַזְכִּירָם עוֹד אֶלָּא אִם כֵּן שׁוֹנֶה בָּהֶם, וְאֵין צָרִיךְ לָשׁוּב וְלַחֲזוֹר וְלָשׁוּב עַל חֵטְא אֶחָד

And although he already repented in the morning and was atoned immediately, and according to the first Tanna of the Baraisa [Yoma 86b] after he is atoned and forgiven he should not mention them again unless he repeats them, and there is no need to repent and return and repent over a single sin;636Repeating confession after forgiveness. Yoma 86b records a dispute. The tanna kamma says that sins confessed on one Yom Kippur should not be confessed again unless they were repeated; R’ Eliezer ben Yaakov says repeated confession is praiseworthy, citing Tehillim 51:5, “my sin is always before me.” Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:8, rules that one may confess them again even while remaining steadfast in teshuvah. Rav Tzadok deliberately argues here even according to the tanna kamma: the three daily requests are not needless repetition of one already-forgiven act, because fresh omissions accumulate between Shacharis, Minchah, and Maariv. His proof therefore does not depend on rejecting the Rambam’s ruling.

בָּזֶה חוֹזְרִים וּמְבַקְּשִׁים לָשׁוּב בְּכָל פַּעַם עַל מַה שֶּׁהוֹסִיף לַחֲטוֹא מִשַּׁחֲרִית לְצָהֳרַיִם וּמִצָּהֳרַיִם לְעַרְבִית, דְּאֵין לְךָ אָדָם שֶׁנִּיצּוֹל בְּכָל שָׁעָה וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי:

[nevertheless] in this we return and request to repent every time for what he additionally sinned from morning to noon, and from noon to evening, for there is no person who is saved at every moment, as I wrote.

items.h: The theme: The daily liturgy's juxtaposition of Hashiveinu and Salach Lanu. For a positive commandment, pardon is granted immediately upon repentance without requiring the test of facing the identical temptation (she-ba'as l'yado). The opening of the gates of forgiveness in Hashiveinu allows the petitioner in Salach Lanu to plead for severe offenses (chamurot), where Hashem, in His abundant mercy (HaMarbeh li'slo'ach), is appeased through supplication to pardon even without Yom Kippur and suffering.

p: וְהִסְמִיכוּ לָזֶה בִּרְכַּת ״סְלַח לָנוּ״, דְּמִיָּד אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה בָּאָה הַסְּלִיחָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְגִלָּה י״ז עַמּוּד ב׳]
And they juxtaposed to this [in the Shemoneh Esreh] the blessing of "Forgive us" (Salach Lanu), for immediately following repentance comes forgiveness, as they said [in Megillah 17b];
וְהַיְינוּ עַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּמוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד, שֶׁעַל זֶה מִתְוַודֶּה וּמְבַקֵּשׁ בְּבִרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״, וְעַל זֶה הַסְּלִיחָה בָּאָה מִמֵּילָא כַּדִּין תֵּיכֶף לַתְּשׁוּבָה

and this refers to a positive commandment for which they pardon immediately, concerning which one confesses and petitions in the blessing of "Return us" (Hashiveinu), and on this forgiveness comes automatically by law immediately following repentance.637Cf. Megillah 17b (Sefaria’s link-graph, anchored to Takanat HaShavin 14:3): in the fixed order of the Shemoneh Esreh, the berachah of pardon (Selach Lanu) was placed immediately after the berachah of teshuvah (Hashiveinu) — “and why did they see [fit] to say pardon after teshuvah? As it is written (Yeshayah 55:7), ‘let the wicked forsake his way, and the man of iniquity his thoughts, and let him return to Hashem and He will have mercy on him, and to our God, for He abundantly pardons.’” R’ Tzadok reads the sequence as teshuvah for the nullified positive commandment, followed at once by pardon.
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁנִּפְתְּחוּ שַׁעֲרֵי סְלִיחָה וּמְחִילָה, מוֹסִיף לְבַקֵּשׁ עַל סְלִיחַת חֵטְא וָפֶשַׁע שֶׁהֵם הַחֲמוּרוֹת
And once the gates of forgiveness and pardon have been opened, he continues to petition for the forgiveness of "sin and transgression" (chet va-fesha), which are the severe offenses;

וּלְכָךְ מְסַיֵּים ״הַמַּרְבֶּה לִסְלוֹחַ״, דְּהַסְּלִיחוֹת בְּרִיבּוּי: גַּם מִלְּבַד מַה שֶּׁהַדִּין נוֹתֵן לִסְלוֹחַ, הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בְּרוֹב רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו מִתְפַּיֵּיס בְּתַחֲנוּנִים לִמְחוֹל גַּם עַל הַחֲמוּרוֹת בְּלֹא יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְיִסּוּרִין, וְלֹא דֶּרֶךְ וִיתּוּר רַק עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַתְּפִלָּה

and therefore he concludes "[Blessed are You, Hashem, the gracious One Who] abundantly forgives," for the pardons are in abundance: even beyond what strict law dictates to forgive, the Blessed Name in His abundant mercies and kindnesses is appeased through supplications to pardon even for the severe offenses without Yom Kippur and suffering—not by way of arbitrary waiver, but through repentance and prayer;

וּכִצְלוֹתֵיהּ דְּרָבָא וְרַב הַמְנוּנָא זוּטֵי [בִּבְרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: ״וּמַה שֶּׁחָטָאתִי מָרֵק בְּרַחֲמֶיךָ וְלֹא עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין״, וְהַיְינוּ גַּם בְּאוֹתָם הַצְּרִיכִין יִסּוּרִין לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה

and like the prayer of Rava and Rav Hamnuna Zuti [in Berachos 17a]: "and what I have sinned, scour in Your mercies and not through suffering," which refers even to those offenses that ordinarily require suffering to scour and complete atonement.638Cf. Berakhos 17a (Sefaria’s link-graph, anchored to Takanat HaShavin 14:3), verbatim: “Rava, after his prayer, would say thus: ‘My God, before I was formed I was unworthy, and now that I have been formed it is as if I had not been formed; I am dust in my life, all the more so in my death; behold I am before You like a vessel full of shame and disgrace. May it be Your will, Hashem my God, that I sin no more, and what I have sinned before You scour in Your abundant mercy — but not through sufferings and evil illnesses.’ And this is the confession of Rav Hamnuna Zuti on Yom Kippur.” R’ Tzadok cites this to show that even severe sins can be scoured “in Your mercy” — through teshuvah and prayer — rather than through suffering. Bava Kamma 50a warns that one who says the Holy One is “vateran” forfeits his life, citing Devarim 32:4: “all His ways are justice.” Rav Tzadok therefore stresses that this merciful scouring is not an arbitrary waiver; teshuvah and tefillah are the divinely established means through which mercy operates within justice.
וְזֶהוּ בִּרְכַּת ״סְלַח״ שֶׁהִסְמִיכוּ לְ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״, דְּזֶה צָרִיךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ בְּכָל יוֹם הַסְּלִיחָה לְהִנָּצֵל מִיִּסּוּרִין
And this is the blessing of "Forgive us" which they juxtaposed to "Return us," for this one must request every day: forgiveness in order to be saved from suffering;
וּבִרְכַּת ״הֲשִׁיבֵנוּ״ עַצְמָהּ הִיא עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה תּוֹרָה וַעֲבוֹדָה וּתְשׁוּבָה הַמְפוֹרָשׁ בָּהּ, דְּדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּצֵל בְּכָל יוֹם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

while the blessing of "Return us" itself is for the neglect of the positive commandments of Torah, service, and teshuvah made explicit in it, since from this failure it is impossible to be spared every day, as I wrote.
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר מוּכְרָח מִזֶּה דִּלִמְחִילָה אַמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה אֵין צָרִיךְ לִתְנַאי שֶׁתָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ

And if so, it is well proven from this that for the pardon of a positive commandment through repentance, there is no need for the prerequisite that [the same temptation] come to his hand [and he resist];

וְיֵשׁ לְהַכְרִיחַ נַמֵּי כֵּן מֵהָא דִּזְבָחִים [שָׁם ז׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״, דְּ״הֵיכִי דָּמֵי, אִי דְּלֵיכָּא תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאִי דְּאִיכָּא תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וּמָה רְאָיָה, דִּלְמָא שֶׁשָּׁב וְלֹא בָּא לְיָדוֹ וְנִיצּוֹל

and one can likewise prove this from that passage in Zevachim [7b] that "an olah is a tribute-gift," where it asks: "What are the circumstances? If there is no repentance, etc., and if there is repentance, etc."; for what proof is there? Perhaps it refers to one who repented, but it did not yet come to his hand again and he was saved from it?639Zevachim 7b: “And Rava said: an olah is a gift. How so? If there is no teshuvah — [then] ‘the offering of the wicked is an abomination’ (Mishlei 21:27). And if there is teshuvah — (why do I need the olah?) But it was taught: ‘[one who] transgressed a positive commandment and repented does not stir from there until they forgive him’! Rather, learn from this that it [the olah] is a gift.” Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1–2, distinguishes teshuvah gemurah—facing the same sin with the same ability and refraining—from a lower level of teshuvah that nevertheless avails and makes one a baal teshuvah; even deathbed teshuvah brings forgiveness. Rav Tzadok therefore treats the later test as perfection of teshuvah, not a prerequisite for its present effect; his special application to a missed positive commandment is his own analysis.

וּמְבוֹאָר בָּרַמְבַּ״ם דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֹא נִיצּוֹל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת וְלֹא לְגַמְרֵי, וּבְוַדַּאי דְּיָצָא מִכְּלַל ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״ כֵּיוָן דְּהַשְׁתָּא מִיהַת שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט, וְעַל זֶה בָּאָה הָעוֹלָה לִהְיוֹת נִמְחָל מְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה

And it is explained in the Rambam (Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1) that even if he was not tested and saved, repentance nevertheless avails, though not completely; and certainly he has departed from the category of "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" since now, at any rate, he repents and regrets, and for this the olah comes to effect complete pardon.
וְעַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דִּבְעֲשֵׂה מוֹדֵי דְּלָא שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה, וְהַיְינוּ דְּמַיְיתֵי בָּרַיְיתָא דְּ״לֹא זָז מִשָּׁם וְכוּלֵיהּ״

Therefore one must say that regarding an aseh he agrees that this [requirement of facing the test] does not apply, and that is why the Gemara cites the Baraisa that "he does not move from there [before he is pardoned], etc.";
וּלְשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז״ בָּא לִרְמֹז דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ שֶׁיָּבוֹא לְיָדוֹ וִיקַיֵּים, רַק מִיָּד נִמְחָל
and the expression "does not move" comes to intimate that there is no need for it to come to his hand and he fulfill it, but rather he is immediately pardoned;
וַאֲפִילּוּ יוֹסִיף לַעֲבוֹר אַחַר כָּךְ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עַל הַקּוֹדֵם נִמְחַל לְגַמְרֵי, וּבְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה הוּא תְּשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה כָּל שֶׁמִּתְחָרֵט בִּשְׁעָתוֹ לְגַמְרֵי

and even if he should transgress again afterward, nevertheless for the past he is completely pardoned, and for a positive commandment it is considered complete teshuvah so long as he regrets sincerely at that moment.640R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §21): “This is the teshuvah and the atonement, as it says, ‘and his heart understands and returns, and it is healed for him [ve-rafa lo].’” Exactly the se’if: Selach Lanu is placed adjacent [to Hashiveinu], for immediately after teshuvah comes pardon (Megillah 17b) — “he understands and returns, and it is healed.”

items.h: The theme: The spiritual purpose of the olah as a tribute-gift (doran). Since repentance alone grants immediate pardon for a positive commandment, the subsequent offering is an act of pious devotion (derech eretz) that demonstrates renewed zeal, paralleled today by the daily statutory prayers. This tribute elevates the quality of the pardon: in teshuvah from fear, it transforms sins from inadvertent errors into merits (zechuyos); in teshuvah from love, where the sin is already erased as though it never existed, the tribute completes the ascent into absolute merits.

p: וּמִיהוּ כָּל זֶה לְשִׁיטַת הָרִאשׁוֹנִים, אֲבָל לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל [אוֹת ט׳] דְּגַם בַּחֲמוּרוֹת כֵּן, קָשֶׁה הַלָּשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז מִשָּׁם״ דְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה

However, all this follows the approach of the Rishonim; but according to what I wrote above [section 9] that even for severe transgressions this is so [that one is termed a tzaddik immediately upon repentance], the expression "he does not move from there" regarding a positive commandment is difficult.
וְאוּלַי הָא גּוּפֵיהּ קָא מַשְׁמַע לָן בָּזֶה, דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה
And perhaps this itself is what it comes to teach us: that he does not need an olah to scour and complete the atonement;

וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּבָאָה עַל חַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה, וְעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ מַה אֵיזֶה צוֹרֶךְ לְתִיקּוּן הָעֲשֵׂה דְּבִיטֵּל, וְקָא מַשְׁמַע לָן דְּאֵינָהּ רַק דּוֹרוֹן, שֶׁמִּדַּת דֶּרֶךְ אֶרֶץ לַחוֹטֵא אַף שֶׁנִּמְחַל לְהָבִיא עוֹד דּוֹרוֹן לְהִתְרַצּוֹת

and even though [the olah] comes for those liable for omitting a positive commandment, so that there is some need to rectify the positive commandment he neglected, it comes to teach us that it is merely a tribute-gift (doran), for it is proper etiquette (derech eretz) for a sinner, even after he has been pardoned, to bring a gift to appease [the King];

וְהַתְּפִלּוֹת שֶׁבִּמְקוֹם תְּמִידִין תִּיקְּנוּם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת כ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳], הֵם בִּמְקוֹם הָעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן לִמְחַיְּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה בַּזְּמַן הַזֶּה, וְהָעֲבוֹדָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב בִּתְפִלָּה הוּא בִּמְקוֹם עֲבוֹדַת הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת בְּבֵית הַמִּקְדָּשׁ בְּפֹעַל

and the prayers, which were instituted in place of the daily offerings (temidin) as they said [in Berachos 26b], stand in place of the olah of tribute for those liable for positive commandments in this era, and the service of the heart in prayer takes the place of the sacrificial service in the Beis HaMikdash in practice.641Berakhos 26b; Taanis 2a; Rambam, Hilchos Tefillah 1:1: Berakhos teaches that the fixed prayers correspond to the daily offerings; even the view that the Avos instituted prayer agrees that the Sages aligned it with the korbanos. Taanis derives ‘service with all your heart’ (Devarim 11:13) as prayer. Rambam codifies daily prayer as a positive command, while its number, formula, and fixed times are rabbinic. Rav Tzadok joins these layers: the Amidah replaces the tamid and olah service, while avodah shebalev expresses the servant’s renewed desire after forgiveness.

וְכָךְ רָאוּי לְעֶבֶד שֶׁחָטָא בְּהִתְעַצְּלוּת עֲבוֹדָתוֹ: אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט וַאֲדוֹנוֹ מָחַל לוֹ, יֵשׁ לוֹ לְהוֹסִיף מִשֶּׁלּוֹ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת עֲבוֹדָה לְרַבּוֹ מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִצְטַוָּוה, לְהַרְאוֹת חִשְׁקוֹ וּרְצוֹנוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדַת רַבּוֹ, וְשֶׁהוּא מוּכָן וְזָרִיז מֵעַתָּה לַעֲבוֹדָתוֹ

And so it is fitting for a servant who sinned through laziness in his service: after he regretted and his master pardoned him, he should add on his own initiative devotion in serving his master beyond what was commanded, to demonstrate his longing and desire for his master's service, and that he is now prepared and zealous for his service;

אֲבָל אֵין זֶה מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְהַצְרִיכוֹ זֶה לְתוֹעֶלֶת הַמְּחִילָה שְׁלֵימָה, דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מוֹחֵל מִיָּד, וְאֵינוֹ זָז אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַחֲרָטָה מִמְּקוֹמוֹ לְהוֹסִיף לְהִשְׁתַּדֵּל בְּאֵיזֶה עֲבוֹדָה לְצֹרֶךְ הַמְּחִילָה, אֶלָּא מוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד תֵּיכֶף שֶׁנִּתְחָרֵט וְשָׁב בְּלִי זִיזָה לְעִנְיָן אַחֵר וּפְעוּלָּה אַחֶרֶת

but this is not from the side of the Blessed Name to require this of him for the efficacy of full pardon, for the Blessed Name pardons immediately, and [the sinner] does not need to move from his place after teshuvah and regret to exert himself in further service for the need of pardon; rather, they pardon immediately, the moment he regrets and repents, without moving to any other matter or action;
וְדַיֵּיק זֶה מִקְּרָא דְּ״אֶרְפָּא״ מִיָּד
and he derived this from the verse “I will heal,” immediately.
וּמֵהָכָא הוּא דִּדָיְיקִינַן מִבִּזְבָחִים שָׁם דְּ״עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן״, וְלָא תֵּימָא תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְעוֹלָה מְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה וְלָא קָרֵינַן בֵּיהּ ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״

And from here is what we infer in Zevachim (7b) that an olah is a tribute-gift, and do not say that repentance suspends and the olah scours the atonement without it being termed "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination";642Zevachim 7b; Yoma 86a: Rava proves that an olah is a gift: without teshuvah it is ‘the offering of the wicked’; with teshuvah, the baraisa says that one who violated a positive commandment ‘does not stir’ before being forgiven. Yoma states this as immediate forgiveness and links teshuvah to ‘I will heal your backsliding’ (Yirmiyahu 3:22; cf. Hoshea 14:5). Rav Tzadok therefore reads the healing as taking effect with the return itself; the olah cannot complete the pardon, but follows it as a gift.

דְּגַם בַּחֲמוּרוֹת דְּצָרִיךְ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים אוֹ גַּם יִסּוּרִין אוֹ גַּם מִיתָה לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד לֹא מִבַּעְיָא דְּיָצָא מִכְּלַל שֵׁם רָשָׁע, אֶלָּא אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיק גָּמוּר נַמֵּי מִיקְרֵי כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל [אוֹת ט׳] מִן הַמְפוֹרָשׁ [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] ״עַל מְנָת שֶׁאֲנִי צַדִּיק אֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר – שֶׁמָּא הִרְהֵר תְּשׁוּבָה״, וְרָשָׁע גָּמוּר מַשְׁמַע גַּם בְּכָל עֲבֵירוֹת הַחֲמוּרוֹת

for even in severe offenses where one requires Yom Kippur, or also suffering, or also death to scour the atonement, nevertheless through repentance alone, not only has he departed from the designation of wicked, but he is even called a complete tzaddik, as I wrote above [section 9] from what is explicit [in Kiddushin 49b]: “on condition that I am a righteous man, even if he is completely wicked—perhaps he contemplated repentance in his heart,” and “completely wicked” implies even regarding all the severe transgressions;643Cf. Kiddushin 49b (Sefaria’s link-graph, anchored to Takanat HaShavin 14:4), verbatim: “‘[Be betrothed to me] on condition that I am righteous’ — even [if he was] a completely wicked man she is betrothed, [for] perhaps he entertained thoughts of teshuvah in his mind. ‘[On condition that] I am wicked’ — even [if he was] a completely righteous man she is betrothed, [for] perhaps he entertained a matter of idolatry in his mind.” R’ Tzadok infers that a single thought of teshuvah, even from “a completely wicked man,” instantly reclassifies him as righteous.
וּמִיָּד שֶׁשָּׁב הֲרֵי הוּא נִקְרָא צַדִּיק אַף שֶׁמְּחוּסַּר כַּפָּרָה עֲדַיִין, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן דְּלָא קָרֵינַן בֵּיהּ ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״
and immediately upon repenting he is called righteous even though he still lacks full atonement, and all the more so we do not apply to him “the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination”;

עַל כֵּן מַיְיתֵי שָׁם לְשׁוֹן הַךְ בָּרַיְיתָא דְּ״לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵיהּ״, דִּמְבוֹאָר דִּתְשׁוּבָה מְכַפֶּרֶת לְגַמְרֵי מִיָּד בְּלֹא הוֹסָפַת עוֹד דָּבָר, וְכֵיוָן דִּבְלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר, עַל כֵּן כָּל עוֹלָה רַק לְדוֹרוֹן

therefore it cites there the text of this Baraisa of “he does not move, etc.,” from which it is clear that repentance atones completely and immediately without the addition of any further element; and since without repentance it is impossible [to bring a sacrifice], perforce any olah is solely a tribute-gift.

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה דְּעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַעֲשֵׂה, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״עוֹלָה וְכוּלֵיהּ אֵינָהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ כַּפָּרָה מַמָּשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ יְעוּיַּן שָׁם, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״עוֹלָה״, צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּגַם לְהַךְ דּוֹרוֹן קָרֵי ״כַּפָּרָה״
