And what was written there prior to this, that an olah atones for a positive commandment—see Rashi there (s.v. olah, etc., "it is not, etc., actual atonement, etc.", see there) and Tosafos (s.v. olah)—one must say that to this tribute-gift too it applies the term “atonement”;644Zevachim 7b, Rashi and Tosafos; Yoma 86b: Rashi compares the olah to a gift brought when greeting the king after appeasement; it does not produce the initial pardon. Tosafos notes that it is nevertheless called an atonement for a positive commandment. Yoma distinguishes teshuvah from fear, which makes willful sins like errors, from teshuvah from love, which makes them merits. Rav Tzadok’s further staging is his own proposal: the gift-olah may deepen love and elevate the repaired past—either upgrading fear-based return toward merit, or turning a sin already erased through love into a positive source of closeness. Thus ‘kapparah’ here means added rectification, not delayed forgiveness.
אַף שֶׁכְּבָר נִתְכַּפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי, מִכָּל מָקוֹם בַּהֲבָאַת דּוֹרוֹן הוּא מוֹסִיף אַהֲבָה, וּמִמֵּילָא גַּם הַכַּפָּרָה בְּתִיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם הִיא בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת

for even though he was already completely atoned, nevertheless through bringing the tribute he increases love, and consequently the atonement in rectifying the past is achieved with greater elevation;
וְאֶפְשָׁר דִּבִתְשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה דִּזְדוֹנוֹת כִּשְׁגָגוֹת, עַל יְדֵי הָעוֹלָה שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ מִתְאַהֵב לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
and it is possible that in teshuvah from fear where intentional sins become like inadvertent ones, through the subsequent olah he becomes beloved to the Blessed Name and they become like merits;

וְאֶפְשָׁר גַּם בִּתְשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה לֹא מִיָּד נַעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת, רַק דִּבְהָא עֲדִיפָא מִתְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאָה, דְּמִיָּד שֶׁשָּׁב נִמְחָה הֶעָוֹן לְגַמְרֵי וְאֵינוֹ כִּשְׁגָגָה גַּם כֵּן, רַק הוּא כְּמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא כְּלָל

and it is also possible that even in teshuvah from love they do not immediately become like merits, but in this it is superior to teshuvah from fear: that as soon as he repents the iniquity is utterly erased and is not even like an inadvertent sin, but he is as though he never sinned at all;645R’ Tzadok — parallel (Poked Akarim §4): “Even if he only contemplated teshuvah in his heart, he is at once a ‘complete tzaddik’ — from the side of Hashem [who searches the heart].” Exactly the se’if’s principle, applied even to the severe sins: teshuvah alone already makes one a “tzaddik,” so that “he does not stir from there” marks not a delay but the immediacy of the return.
וְעַל יְדֵי דּוֹרוֹן הָעוֹלָה בְּחַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה [וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים וְיִסּוּרִין בְּחַיָּיבֵי לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין] הוּא שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה כִּזְכֻיּוֹת
and through the tribute of the olah in positive commandments [and Yom Kippur and suffering in negative commandments and capital offenses], it is transformed into merits;

וְשַׁפִּיר אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכְּבָר כִּיפֵּר לְגַמְרֵי בִּמְחִילָה גְּמוּרָה וְהוּא רַק דּוֹרוֹן, כֵּיוָן דְּעַל יְדֵי הַדּוֹרוֹן נִתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם יוֹתֵר, קָרֵי לֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן ״כַּפָּרָה״ עַל הַקּוֹדֵם

and rightly so: although he was already completely atoned with full forgiveness and it is merely a tribute, since through the tribute the past is rectified further, it is likewise termed “atonement” for the past.

items.h: The theme: The Yerushalmi’s ruling on conditional atonement (ha-omer ein olah mechaperes). In Yerushalmi Yoma 1:7, one who declares that his olah should not atone does not receive atonement, implying that the Yerushalmi views the olah as an actual atoning agent rather than a mere gift. R' Tzadok rejects the interpretation of the Pnei Moshe and Korban HaEdah regarding Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel's statement ("a mortal cannot tell the King: 'You are no King'"). Instead, following the Yafeh Mareh, he demonstrates that Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel refers to Yom Kippur, which atones against one's will because Hashem's sovereign kingship is absolute; whereas a sacrificial offering depends upon human action and intent, allowing man to stipulate whether his deed shall take effect.

p: אַךְ לְשׁוֹן הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [פֶּרֶק א׳ דְּיוֹמָא רֵישׁ הֲלָכָה ז׳] ״הָאוֹמֵר אֵין עוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת וְכוּלֵיהּ אֵין מְכַפֶּרֶת לוֹ״ עַד כָּאן, עַיֵּין שָׁם

However, the wording of the Yerushalmi [Yoma 1:7]: “One who says: let the olah not atone, etc., it does not atone for him,” thus far, see there;646Yerushalmi Yoma 8:7 (42a): “One who says, ‘an olah does not atone [at all],’ [or says,] ‘an olah does not atone for me’ — it does atone (for he alone erred and supposed that it does not atone, and his error does not change the truth). [But if he said,] ‘I do not want it to atone for me’ — it does not atone for him against his will.”

מַשְׁמַע דְּבָאָה לְכַפָּרָה מַמָּשׁ, דְּאִי רַק לְדוֹרוֹן, וְהַכַּפָּרָה הַמְּתוֹסֶפֶת עַל יָדוֹ הוּא מִמֵּילָא עַל יְדֵי הַדּוֹרוֹן שֶׁהֵבִיא, אִם כֵּן אֵין הֲבָאָתָהּ לְכַפָּרָה וְשַׁפִּיר קָאָמַר ״אֵינָהּ מְכַפֶּרֶת״

implies that it comes for actual atonement; for if it were only a tribute, and the additional atonement achieved through it occurs automatically through the tribute he brought, then its presentation is not for atonement and he has stated accurately that “it does not atone”;

וְכֵן אֲפִילּוּ אָמַר ״אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁתְּכַפֵּר״, הֲרֵי מִכָּל מָקוֹם הֵבִיא הַדּוֹרוֹן, וְלָמָּה לֹא יֵצֵא הוֹסָפַת הַכַּפָּרָה הַבָּאָה עַל יְדֵי הֲבָאַת דּוֹרוֹן אֲפִילּוּ בְּלֹא רְצוֹנוֹ לְכַפָּרָה, כֵּיוָן דְּבֶאֱמֶת אֵינוֹ כַּפָּרָה רַק דּוֹרוֹן

and likewise, even if he said "it cannot atone," behold in any event he brought the tribute, so why would the added atonement that comes through presenting a tribute not take effect even without his desire for atonement, since in truth it is not an atonement but a tribute?
וּבִכְרֵיתוֹת [ז׳ עַמּוּד א׳] אִיתָא אַחַטָּאת פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּאַבַּיֵּי וְרָבָא עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְעוֹלָה לֹא נִזְכַּר

And in Kerisos [7a] the dispute of Abaye and Rava is taught regarding a sin-offering (chatas), see there, and an olah is not mentioned;647Kerisus 7a: “One who says, ‘let my chatas not atone for me’ — Abaye says: it does not atone; Rava says: it atones.” (Here the dispute is stated regarding a chatas; the olah is not mentioned — which R’ Tzadok takes as consistent with the Bavli’s view that the olah is only a gift.)
וְנִרְאֶה דְּתַלְמוּדִין לְטַעְמֵיהּ דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן, וְהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי פָּלֵיג עַל זֶה, וְעַיֵּין בְּכוֹרוֹת [כ״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] וּבְרַשִׁ״י יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and it appears that our Talmud [the Bavli] follows its reasoning that an olah is a tribute, whereas the Yerushalmi disputes this; and see Bechoros [26b] and Rashi, see there.648Bechoros 26b: “Or perhaps, since an olah too atones for a positive commandment, he does not delay it.” Rashi: “that an olah atones for a positive commandment, as we say in Yoma (36a), that the olah atones the sin of [neglecting] shichechah and pe’ah.” (The Bavli assumes the olah atones for a positive commandment — supporting R’ Tzadok’s reading that the Bavli holds the olah to be a “gift”/atonement for a nullified aseh.)

וְעַיֵּין בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַפְּנֵי מֹשֶׁה [פֶּרֶק א׳ דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת הֲלָכָה ו׳] דִּמְפָרֵשׁ הָא דְּאָמַר רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ: ״לֹא כּוּלָּהּ מִן הַדֵּין בַּר נָשׁ מֵימַר לְמַלְכָּא לֵית אַתְּ מֶלֶךְ״, בָּא לַחֲלוֹק אַדִּלְעֵיל וְלוֹמַר דְּאִיפְּכָא מִסְתַּבְּרָא, וּדְבְקָרְבָּן מְכַפֵּר בְּעַל כָּרְחָךְ דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הִקְרִיב, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And see in the commentary of Pnei Moshe [Shevuos 1:6] who explains that which Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel stated there afterward: “It is not within the power of a man to say to the King: ‘You are no King’,” that he came to dispute the preceding statement and to say that the reverse is logical, that a sacrifice atones against his will since he offered it in any event, see there;649Yerushalmi Shevuos 1:6; Pnei Moshe, Korban HaEdah; Yefeh Mar’eh on Yerushalmi Yoma 8, siman 3, s.v. mechaper; Peri Tzadik, Purim §1: The Yerushalmi contrasts a korban, whose atonement can depend on the owner’s will, with Yom Kippur, whose atonement expresses the King’s rule. Pnei Moshe reads R’ Chanina b. R’ Hillel as reversing the preceding logic; Korban HaEdah distinguishes a voluntary korban from Yom Kippur fixed by Hashem. Rav Tzadok rejects those constructions and reads R’ Chanina as directly explaining Yom Kippur: a person cannot cancel the King’s sovereignty, whereas he may condition an atonement effected through his own korban. He reports that Yefeh Mar’eh explains the passage the same way. A close parallel appears in Peri Tzadik: ‘the essence of the day atones’ even when observance is forcibly prevented, provided the Jew still knows that it is Yom Kippur. Thus the atonement here proceeds from Hashem’s revealed kingship, not from a human ritual act.
וְרָצָה לוֹמַר: זֶהוּ פְּשִׁיטַת תַּלְמוּדִין הַנִּזְכָּר דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן, וְדַוְוקָא בְּעוֹלָה קָאָמַר
and he meant to say: this is the premise of our Talmud mentioned above that an olah is a tribute, and he stated it specifically regarding an olah.
אַךְ בֶּאֱמֶת פֵּירוּשׁוֹ דָּחוּק וְרָחוֹק מְאוֹד בְּעֵינַי בְּמַשְׁמַע לְשׁוֹן הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי, וְגַם פֵּירוּשׁ הַקָּרְבַּן הָעֵדָה שָׁם בָּזֶה דָּחוּק
But in truth, his explanation is very forced and far-fetched in my eyes according to the meaning of the Yerushalmi's language, and the explanation of the Korban HaEdah there on this is also forced.
וּלְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט בְּהֵיפֶךְ מִדִּבְרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם, דְּרַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל אַדִּלְעֵיל קָאֵי, לְפָרֵשׁ טַעְמָא דְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר בְּעַל כָּרְחָךְ

And in my opinion, the plain meaning is the exact opposite of both their words: that Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel refers to the earlier statement, to explain the reason why Yom Kippur atones against one's will [even if one denies its atonement]:

דְּכַפָּרָתוֹ מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר פְּנֵי מַלְכוּתוֹ, וְלֹא וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁאֵין לוֹמַר ״אֵינְךָ מֶלֶךְ״, דִּבְעַל כָּרְחָךְ הוּא מוֹלֵךְ עָלָיו וְעַל כֵּן בְּעַל כָּרְחָךְ הוּא מְכַפֵּר

for its atonement is from the side of the Blessed Name and the revelation of the light of the presence of His Sovereignty, and one cannot say "You are not King," for against your will He reigns over him, and therefore against your will He atones;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן קָרְבָּן דְּבָא לְכַפֵּר עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֶׂה דִּידֵיהּ, בְּדִידֵיהּ תַּלְיָא שֶׁלֹּא יִתְכַּפֵּר עַל יְדֵי זֶה, דִּבְיַד הָאָדָם לְהַתְנוֹת עַל מַעֲשָׂיו בִּפְעוּלוֹתָיו כִּרְצוֹנוֹ

whereas a sacrifice, which comes to atone through his own action, depends upon him that he should not be atoned through it, for it is in the power of a person to place conditions upon his actions and deeds as he wills;
וְאַדְּרַבָּא, דִּבְרֵי רַבִּי חֲנַנְיָה בַּר הִלֵּל מְסַיְּיעִים וּמַסְכִּימִים עִם הַקּוֹדֵם
and on the contrary, the words of Rabbi Chananyah bar Hillel support and agree with the preceding ruling!
וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי בְּ״יְפֵה מַרְאֶה״ שָׁם [בְּיוֹמָא סִימָן ג׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מְכַפֵּר״ פֵּירֵשׁ כֵּן, וְלֹא יָדַעְתִּי לָמָּה נָאדוּ הֵם מִפֵּירוּשׁ זֶה הַפָּשׁוּט וּבָרוּר:

And then I found in Yafeh Mareh there [Yoma, section 3, s.v. mechaper] that he explained thus, and I do not know why they strayed from this simple and clear interpretation.650R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Vayishlach §4): “(Bava Kamma 119a) Yaakov, with that ‘gift [doron],’ saved himself from the ‘bloodshed’ of Esav — ‘and there is no judgment without judgment.’” The se’if’s olah: a “gift [doron]” that nonetheless atones — as Yaakov’s gift to Esav both appeased and shielded him."

items.h: The theme: According to the Talmud Yerushalmi, an olah [burnt offering] functions as an actual instrument of atonement (le-khapparah mamash) rather than a mere gift, scouring and completing atonement prior to Yom Kippur in a manner analogous to Yom Kippur's effect on negative commandments. For an ordinary positive commandment (aseh), repentance alone grants immediate pardon ("does not move from there before he is pardoned"), so no sacrifice is required. However, for sinful contemplation of idolatry (hirhur avodah zarah)—which carries the status of a negative commandment lacking physical action (lav she-ein bo ma'aseh)—repentance suspends and the olah scours the atonement. The Tannaitic list of four categories of atonement omits sacrificial offerings entirely, just as it omits chatas and asham, focusing strictly on the calendar and existential vehicles of atonement (repentance, Yom Kippur, suffering, and death).

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים מוּכְרָח מֵהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּעוֹלָה לְכַפָּרָה
And in any event, it is proven from the Yerushalmi [Yoma 1:7] that an olah is brought for actual atonement;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּמְמָרֶקֶת הַכַּפָּרָה, דּוּגְמַת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים בְּחַיָּיבֵי לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה
and one must say that it holds that it scours and completes the atonement, analogous to the function of Yom Kippur for those liable for negative commandments.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְדִידֵיהּ, הַלָּשׁוֹן ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ בַּבָּרַיְיתָא דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בְּחַיָּיבֵי עֲשֵׂה, דְּמַיְיתֵי לַהּ גַּם שָׁם (עַיֵּין שָׁם), הוּא לְטַעְמֵיהּ שָׁם וְשָׁם

And one can say according to [the Yerushalmi], the phrase "he does not move from there, etc." in the Baraisa of Rabbi Yishmael regarding those liable for an aseh [Yoma 86a], which it also cites there (see there), is consistent with its own reasoning in both places:
דְּעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת אַהִרְהוּר וְלֹא אַעֲשֵׂה

that an olah atones for sinful contemplation (hirhur) and not for [omission of] a positive commandment;651Yerushalmi Yoma 8:6–7 (42a; parallel Yerushalmi Shevuos 1:6) derives from Yechezkel 20:32 and Iyov 1:5 that an olah atones for hirhur halev, and then restates R’ Yishmael’s categories: for an aseh, teshuvah brings immediate forgiveness; for a lav, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for kareis or court-death, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend and suffering scours; for chillul Hashem, death completes the cleansing. Kiddushin 40a teaches that an evil thought is ordinarily not joined to an act, but idolatrous thought is exceptional, based on “that I may seize the House of Israel in their heart” (Yechezkel 14:5). Rambam, Hilchos Avodah Zarah 2:3, codifies the prohibition against following thoughts that uproot Torah principles and states that it carries no lashes because it involves no act. These sources underlie Rav Tzadok’s classification of hirhur avodah zarah as a lav she-ein bo maaseh. His further conclusion—that in the Yerushalmi teshuvah suspends and the olah scours this inward sin before Yom Kippur—is his analytical reading, not an explicit fifth baraisa.
וְהִרְהוּר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה, וּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ
and contemplation of idolatry is a negative commandment lacking physical action, which it holds is not included in the positive commandment category of "he does not move, etc."
וְהַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּפָלֵיג אַתַּלְמוּדִין גַּם בָּזֶה דְּלֹא בָּא אַעֲשֵׂה, מִשּׁוּם דְּאַעֲשֵׂה ״לֹא זָז״ וְכוּלֵיהּ וְלֹא צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה

And this is the reason that it disputes our Talmud [Bavli] in this as well, holding that it does not come for a positive commandment, because for a positive commandment "he does not move from there [before being pardoned]" and does not require an olah at all;
אֲבָל הִרְהוּר (עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה) דְּהוּא כְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה צָרִיךְ לְעוֹלָה, וּמְמָרַקְתּוֹ קוֹדֶם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
whereas contemplation (of idolatry), which is classified as a negative commandment lacking action, requires an olah, and it scours his atonement prior to Yom Kippur;
וּשְׁאָר לָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל כָּל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה דְּצָרִיךְ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
while other negative commandments lacking action are subsumed under ordinary negative commandments, requiring Yom Kippur.
וְהָא דְּלֹא חָשֵׁיב חֲמִשָּׁה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, דְּהִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְעוֹלָה מְמָרֶקֶת
And that it does not enumerate five categories of atonement, where for sinful contemplation repentance suspends and the olah scours:
מִלְּבַד דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלָא מַיְירֵי מֵעֲבֵירָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
besides the fact that one may answer that the Baraisa does not deal with transgressions confined to the heart;
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלָא מַיְירֵי מִכַּפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת
one can also say that it does not deal with the atonement of sacrifices at all,
כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלָא חָשֵׁיב חַיָּיבֵי חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת
just as it does not enumerate those liable for sin-offerings (chata'os) and guilt-offerings (ashamos),
דְּנַמֵּי אֵינָן בְּלֹא תְּשׁוּבָה דְּ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״, דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְהֵן מְמָרְקִין הַכַּפָּרָה בְּלֹא יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

which likewise cannot atone without repentance, since "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination" (Mishlei 21:27), where repentance suspends and they scour the atonement without requiring Yom Kippur,
כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה מִלְּשׁוֹן הַמִּשְׁנָה דְּיוֹמָא [שָׁם פ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״חַטָּאת וְאָשָׁם וַדַּאי מְכַפְּרִין, מִיתָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפְּרִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״
as appears from the wording of the Mishnah in Yoma [85b]: "A sin-offering and an unconditional guilt-offering atone; death and Yom Kippur atone, etc.";

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּגְּמָרָא דִּמְכַפְּרֵי כַּפָּרָה גְּמוּרָה, וְגַם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים אֵין מְכַפֵּר בְּלֹא הֵם, דְּגַם אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים צָרִיךְ לַהֲבִיאָן לְמָרֵק כַּפָּרָתָן עַל יָדָם דַּוְוקָא

and see there in the Gemara (Yoma 86a) that they effect complete atonement, and Yom Kippur does not atone without them, for even after Yom Kippur one must bring them to scour atonement specifically through them;652Yoma 85a–b distinguishes the complete atonement of a chatas and definite asham from the incomplete protection of an asham talui: even after Yom Kippur, one who owes a chatas or definite asham must still bring it. Zevachim 7b, citing “the offering of the wicked is an abomination” (Mishlei 21:27), establishes that a korban cannot atone without prior teshuvah; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1, likewise rules that a sin- or guilt-offering atones only after teshuvah and verbal confession. Rav Tzadok therefore explains that R’ Yishmael’s general categories omit sacrificial mechanisms—not because korbanos are ineffective, but because that baraisa classifies the broad paths of atonement. Chatas, asham, and according to this Yerushalmi an olah for sinful thought, are separate korban-based completions.
וַאֲפִילּוּ הָכִי לָא חֲשָׁבִינְהוּ בַּהֲדֵי חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּלָא מַיְירֵי הָתָם מִכַּפָּרַת קָרְבָּנוֹת
and even so, it did not enumerate them among the four categories of atonement; perforce, it did not deal there with the atonement of sacrifices,
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא נָקַט גַּם כַּפָּרָה דְּעוֹלָה
and therefore it likewise did not include the atonement of an olah.
וּמַתְנִיתִין דְּנָקַט ״חַטָּאוֹת וַאֲשָׁמוֹת מְכַפְּרִין״ וְלֹא גַּם עוֹלָה, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּהָנֵי אֵין בָּאִין אֶלָּא לְכַפָּרָה וּפְסִיקָא לֵיהּ
And the Mishnah, which cited "sin-offerings and guilt-offerings atone" and not an olah as well, one can say is because these are brought solely for atonement and the matter is definitive;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן עוֹלָה דְּבָאָה נְדָבָה גַּם כֵּן, וְלֹא פְּסִיקָא לֵיהּ לוֹמַר דִּמְכַפֶּרֶת, כֵּן נִרְאֶה בָּזֶה בְּשִׁיטַת הַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי
whereas an olah is brought as a voluntary freewill gift (nedavah) too, so it is not definitive to state that it atones; thus it appears regarding the methodology of the Yerushalmi.

[וּלְפִי זֶה מוּכָח מֵהַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי דְּלָאו שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה בִּכְלַל לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וּבַהֲדָא דְּאֵין מוּכְרָח דְּתַלְמוּדִין פָּלֵיג עֲלֵיהּ, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין לְאַפּוֹשֵׁי פְּלוּגְתָּא מִמַּה דְּלָא אַשְׁכְּחַן]:

[And according to this, it is proven from the Yerushalmi that a negative commandment lacking physical action is included in the category of negative commandments; and in this matter, where it is not compelled that our Talmud disputes it, one should maintain that we do not multiply disputes beyond what is explicitly found].

sections.en: The sin of wasteful emission of seed and its rectification through teshuvah

items.h: עוון הוצאת זרע לבטלה ותיקונו על ידי תשובה.

The theme: The legal classification of the sin of wasteful emission (hotza'as zera l'vattalah). Because the Torah contains no explicit negative prohibition against it, it is classified by Tosafos (Sanhedrin 59b) as an offshoot of the positive commandment of procreation (peru u'revu). Although transgressed through active commission (kum ve'aseh), it falls under the category of positive commandments that atone through repentance alone without requiring Yom Kippur. Midrashic associations with murder and idolatry (Niddah 13a) or the derashah on "you shall not commit adultery" (lo tin'af) are homiletic supports (asmachta), not formal biblical negative prohibitions carrying corporal lashes.

p: וְהִנֵּה עֲוֹן דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הָיָה נִרְאֶה לִי לִפְשׁוֹט דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, שֶׁהֲרֵי לֹא מָצִינוּ עָלָיו שׁוּם אַזְהָרָה בַּתּוֹרָה בְּהֶדְיָא

And behold, regarding the iniquity of wasteful emission of seed, it seemed clear to me to resolve that it is likewise included in the category of positive commandments, for we find no explicit prohibition against it anywhere in the Torah;
וְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת [סַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְהָא״ כָּתְבוּ דְּמִי שֶׁמְּצֻוֶּוה עַל פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ מְצֻוֶּוה שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁחִית זֶרַע, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and Tosafos [Sanhedrin 59b, s.v. ve-ha] wrote that whoever is commanded concerning procreation is commanded not to destroy seed, see there;653Tosafos, Sanhedrin 59b (s.v. veha periyah u-reviyah): “But procreation — it is astonishing: from where do we [derive] that it was not stated to the Noahides? And if [it is inferred] because it is not counted among the seven [Noahide] commandments — [that proves nothing, for] it says above (58b) that a ‘rise-up-and-do’ [positive commandment] is not counted. And one may say that it is a ‘sit-and-do-not’ [i.e. also has a negative aspect] as well — for one who is commanded regarding procreation is commanded not to destroy seed.”
מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דִּפְרוּ וּרְבוּ, וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי נֶעֶנְשׁוּ עָלֶיהָ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל דְּגַם בְּנֵי נֹחַ הָיוּ מְצֻוִּין אָז עַל זֶה

which implies that it is subsumed under the positive commandment of procreation, and for this reason they were punished for it in the generation of the Flood, because the descendants of Noach were also commanded concerning this at that time.654Bereishis 1:28, 6:12, and 9:7; Sanhedrin 59b; Bereishis Rabbah 28:8. The command of procreation begins with Adam and is restated to Noach; Sanhedrin treats it as a pre-Sinai command, while Tosafos identifies destruction of seed as its negative aspect. The Torah and Midrash describe the Flood generation as corrupting the generative order of “all flesh.” R’ Tzadok therefore connects their punishment to violation of the then-binding command of procreation.
וְאִם כֵּן הִיא בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, דְּאַף שֶׁעוֹבֵר בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה נִתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל [אוֹת י״ג] דְּסַגִּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד

And if so, it falls within the category of a positive commandment, where although one transgresses through active commission, it was explained above [Siman 13] that repentance alone suffices for it;655Yoma 86a; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 13. R’ Yishmael teaches that one who violates a positive commandment and repents is forgiven immediately. R’ Tzadok’s earlier analysis is that the atonement category follows the source of the obligation: if the prohibition is included within “be fruitful and multiply,” it remains an aseh-category offense even though the violation is committed actively. This is the proposition for which he next cites Mishnas Chachamim.
וְשָׁם כָּתַבְתִּי כֵּן מִדְּנַפְשַׁאי מִסְּתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא, וְעַתָּה רָאִיתִי כֵּן גַּם בְּסֵפֶר מִשְׁנַת חֲכָמִים [סִימָן ב׳ אוֹת ו׳], עַיֵּין שָׁם
and there I wrote this independently from the plain, unqualified language of the Gemara, and now I have found it stated likewise in the book Mishnas Chachamim [section 2, note 6], see there.

וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּבְנִדָּה [י״ג עַמּוּד ב׳] יָלְפִינַן לֵיהּ מִקְּרָא דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ — ״לֹא יְהֵא וְכוּלֵיהּ״, הָיָה נִרְאֶה לִי לִפְשׁוֹט דְּאֵין זֶה דְּרָשָׁא גְּמוּרָה וּלְהַיוֹת הַלָּאו אָתֵי לְהָכִי וּלְהַיוֹת בִּכְלַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, דְּגוּף הַלָּאו בְּנִיאוּף גָּמוּר

And although in Niddah [13b] we derive it from the verse “You shall not commit adultery” (Shemos 20:13) — [read as] “there shall not be, etc.” — it seemed clear to me to resolve that this is not an absolute scriptural exegesis meaning that the negative command comes specifically for this and classifies it under formal negative commandments, for the literal body of the negative prohibition refers to actual adultery;656Mishnas Chachamim §2, letter ו. Mishnas Chachamim, by R’ Moshe Chagiz, is cited here as independent support for R’ Tzadok’s rule that an offense classified under a positive commandment remains in the immediate-teshuvah category even when the violation is committed through an affirmative act. The citation confirms the methodological point developed in Siman 13; it is not a separate source for the Niddah derashah discussed below.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֵפֶר הַמִּצְוֹת לָרַמְבַּ״ם [מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה שמ״ז] דְּנִכְפְּלָה בָּזֶה אַזְהָרָה, וְהֵבִיא כֵּן מֵהַמְּכִילְתָּא ״לֹא תִנְאָף לָמָּה נֶאֱמַר וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and as they said in the Rambam's Sefer HaMitzvos [negative commandment 347], that the prohibition was repeated regarding this, citing from the Mekhilta: “'You shall not commit adultery' — why was this stated, etc.?”, see there;
וְכֵן הוּא בְּסֵפֶר הַחִנּוּךְ [מִצְוָה ל״ה], וְלֹא כָּתְבוּ שָׁם מֵאִיסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה כְּלָל, וְעַל כֵּן דְּהִיא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא

and so it is in Sefer HaChinuch [mitzvah 35], and they made no mention there of the prohibition of wasteful emission of seed at all; perforce, it is merely an asmachta [a rabbinic homiletic support].657Niddah 13b: “R’ Elazar said: what is [the meaning of] that which is written (Yeshayah 1:15), ‘your hands are full of blood’? — these are those who commit adultery with the hand (‘one who emits seed in vain’). The academy of R’ Yishmael taught: ‘you shall not commit adultery’ — let there not be in you adultery, whether by hand or by foot.” Sefer HaMitzvos (Rambam, negative 347) brings from the Mechilta that the Torah doubled the prohibition of adultery — one [statement] for punishment and one for warning — and does not learn from this doubling any prohibition of wasteful emission of seed, implying it is an asmachta.
וְהָרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק כ״א מֵהִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה הֲלָכָה י״ח] כָּתַב שֶׁאִיסּוּר גָּדוֹל הוּא, וְלֹא כָּתַב שׁוּם מִקְרָא מִן הַתּוֹרָה עַל זֶה
And the Rambam [Hilchos Issurei Biah 21:18] wrote that it is a grave prohibition, yet cited no biblical verse from the Torah for it;
וְאַף שֶׁכָּתַב שָׁם דְּהוּא כְּאִלּוּ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים, וְהוּא מֵהַגְּמָרָא [שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳], וְשָׁם אִיתָא גַּם כֵּן כְּאִלּוּ עוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה
and although he wrote there that he is as one who sheds blood, which is derived from the Gemara [Niddah 13a], where it is also taught that he is as one who serves idols;
וּבָזֶה בְּוַדַּאי אֵין רוֹצֶה לוֹמַר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּמוֹ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה מַמָּשׁ, וְהוּא הַדִּין נַמֵּי לְעִנְיַן שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים
and in this he certainly does not mean that it is literal idolatry, and the same principle applies to bloodshed;
לֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא ״כְּאִלּוּ״, וְלֹא שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בִּכְלַל אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים
he stated only "as if," and not that it is subsumed under the formal prohibition of bloodshed;
דַּהֲרֵי אֲפִילּוּ עַל עוּבָּרִין וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁלֹּא הוֹצִיא רֹאשׁוֹ אֵין חַיָּיבִין עָלָיו בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
for behold, even for fetuses that have not emerged headfirst, an Israelite is not executed for murder;

וַאֲפִילּוּ בְּנֵי נֹחַ דְּחַיָּיבִין עַל הָעוּבָּרִין, דַּוְוקָא עוּבָּרִין אִתְרַבּוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] מֵ״הָאָדָם בַּדָּם״, אֲבָל הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל אַזְהָרַת שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים

and even for descendants of Noach who are held liable for fetuses, fetuses specifically were included [in Sanhedrin 57b] from the phrase "man in man" (Bereishis 9:6), but wasteful emission is not included in the prohibition of bloodshed,
וְכִדְמוּכָח מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּאַזְהָרָתוֹ רַק מִשּׁוּם מִצְוַת פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ

as proven from the words of Tosafos cited above, that its prohibition is rooted solely in the positive commandment of procreation.658Niddah 13a; Bereishis 38:10; Rambam, Issurei Biah 21:18; Sanhedrin 57b. Niddah derives liability to death from Onan—“it was evil in the eyes of Hashem… and He put him to death”—and compares the sin to bloodshed and idolatry. The Rambam codifies it as a “great prohibition” and repeats the bloodshed comparison, but does not place it under the homicide prohibition. Sanhedrin derives a Noahide’s liability for killing a fetus from “the blood of man within man”; R’ Tzadok distinguishes a fetus from seed that has not entered fetal existence. The comparisons therefore express extraordinary severity, while Tosafos’ operative source remains the duty of procreation.
וְגַם בַּסְּמַ״ג [לָאוִין קכ״ו] כָּתַב בִּלְשׁוֹן רַמְבַּ״ם הַנַּ״ל כְּדַרְכּוֹ
And in the Semag [Negative Mitzvos 126] he likewise wrote in the language of the aforementioned Rambam according to his style;
וְשָׁם [רֵישׁ הֲלָכָה צ״ז] הֵבִיא מִדְּרָשַׁת חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה ״תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר לֹא תִנְאָף וְאֵין נִיאוּף אֶלָּא בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ״
and there [in note 97] he cited the derashah of the Sages: "Scripture teaches: 'You shall not commit adultery,' and adultery applies only to a married woman";

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם [סוֹף סִימָן ק״ג] מֵבִיא עוֹד דְּרָשָׁא דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת [מ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳] ״אַזְהָרָה לְעוֹקֵב וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וְהַהוּא דְּנִדָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל לֹא מַיְיתֵי כְּלָל, נִרְאֶה וַדַּאי דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא

and see there [end of section 103] where he brings another derashah from Shevuos [47b] as a warning against fraud, yet that teaching from Niddah mentioned above he does not cite at all; it appears certain that he holds it to be merely an asmachta.659Semag, Lavin 126 (following the Rambam); and end of §103: “and we further expound in Shevuos (47b): from ‘you shall not commit adultery [lo tinaf]’ — ‘do not cause adultery [lo tagrim ni’uf]’ — a warning to the ‘okeiv’ who abets the adulterer (the Aruch explains: who goes about ‘on his heels [akeivav]’ to bring women to another for adultery).” The Semag does not cite the Niddah derashah at all.

items.h: The theme: The position of the Sefer Mitzvos Katan (Semak, §292), which lists the prohibition not to destroy seed as a distinct biblical negative command under the verse "lo tin'af". R' Tzadok investigates the textual variant in the Semak ("lo teheneh l'af", do not bring pleasure to wrath) versus the Talmudic reading ("lo tehei becha ni'uf", there shall be no adultery within you). He suggests that the Semak may not have intended to define it as a classical negative commandment carrying stripes, but rather categorized it as an independent biblical prohibition of passive restraint (shev ve'al ta'aseh) modeled after the structure of negative commands.

p: אַךְ בַּסְּמַ״ק [רֵישׁ סִימָן רצ״ב] בְּלָאוִין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא שֶׁבְּאֵבֶר הַמִּילָה כָּתַב: שֶׁלֹּא לְהַשְׁחִית זֶרַע, כִּדְכְתִיב ״לֹא תְהַנֶּה לָאַף״

However, in the Semak [start of §292], under the biblical negative commandments pertaining to the organ of circumcision, he wrote: "not to destroy seed, as it is written: lo teheneh l'af [do not give pleasure to wrath]";
[נִרְאֶה דְּהָיָה בְּגִירְסָתוֹ כֵּן בַּגְּמָרָא, וּלְפָנֵינוּ הַגִּירְסָא ״לֹא תְהֵא בְּךָ נִיאוּף״

[it appears that such was his textual reading in the Gemara, whereas before us the reading in Niddah 13b is "there shall be no adultery within you";660Sefer Mitzvot Katan §292; Niddah 13b; Bereishis 38:10. R’ Yitzchak of Corbeil places this prohibition in the seventh division of the Semak, among mitzvos connected with milah. He cites “lo tinaf,” the derashah concerning adultery by hand or foot, the warning to one who assists an adulterer, and Onan’s death. The entry establishes that the Semak regards destruction of seed as a Torah prohibition of exceptional severity; Rav Tzadok’s question is narrower—whether the Semak intended an independent, formally enumerated full lav, or used “lo tinaf” as scriptural support within his practical compendium.

וּבְפֵירוּשׁ רַשִׁ״י שֶׁסְּבִיב הָרִי״ף פֶּרֶק ח׳ שְׁרָצִים פֵּירֵשׁ מִדְּלָא כְּתִיב ״לֹא תִנְאַף אִשָּׁה״, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְכֵן הוּא בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת בְּנִדָּה שָׁם, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and in Rashi surrounding the Rif (Shabbos, ch. 8) he explained that this is derived from the fact that it is not written "you shall not commit adultery with a woman," see there, and so it is in the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados in Niddah there, see there;
וּבָרִי״ף שָׁם מְסַיֵּים ״וּקְרֵי בֵּיהּ לֹא תַנְאִיף״

and in the Rif there he concludes: "and read into it: lo tan'if [do not cause adultery]";661Niddah 13b; Rif, Shabbos, ch. 8; Shevuos 47b. Niddah records the school of R’ Yishmael: “lo tinaf”—there shall not be adultery among you, by hand or foot. The Rif preserves the wording “lo tehei bekha niuf” and reads the verse homiletically, while Shevuos vocalizes it “lo tanif,” a warning against enabling another’s adultery. Rav Tzadok therefore resists using the same ordinary reading for two different derashos. His proposed reflexive vocalization—“do not perform an act of adultery upon yourself”—is a conjectural reconciliation of the textual traditions, not the printed wording of the Bavli.
וְלֹא הֵבַנְתִּי זֶה, דְּזֶהוּ דְּרָשָׁא אַעוֹקֵב וְכוּלֵיהּ וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת שָׁם, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and I did not understand this, for that is the derashah applied to an extortioner as they said in Shevuos 47b, see there;

וְאוּלַי טָעוּת סוֹפֵר תּוֹסָפוֹת הָיָה, וְכַוָּונָתוֹ עַל שִׁינּוּי הַנִּיקּוּד לִקְרוֹתוֹ הַנּוּ״ן קְמוּצָה וְהָאָלֶ״ף בְּצֵירֵי, דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר לֹא תִּתְפַּעֵל, וְהַיְינוּ לֹא יִהְיֶה בְּךָ בְּעַצְמְךָ וּבִלְבַדְּךָ מַעֲשֵׂה הַנִּיאוּף]

and perhaps it was a scribal error, and his intent was regarding an alteration of the vocalization, reading the nun with a kamatz and the alef with a tzeireh, meaning a reflexive form: that the act of adultery shall not occur within yourself alone];
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם הֵבִיא גַּם דְּרָשָׁא דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת
and see there that he also cited the derashah of Shevuos.
וְאֶפְשָׁר קְצָת דְּלָא לְאַשְׁווֹיֵי פְּלוּגְתָּא, וּבִפְרָט נֶגֶד הַסְּמַ״ג שֶׁכְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה מֵהַקְדָּמָתוֹ נִגְרָר אַחֲרָיו תָּדִיר, דְּגַם כָּאן אֵין כַּוָּונָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה לָאו גָּמוּר

And it is somewhat possible to suggest, in order not to establish a dispute, especially against the Semag whom he consistently follows according to his introduction, that here too his intent was not that this constitutes an absolute formal negative command;662Semak, Introduction and §292; Semag, Negative Commandment 126. The Semak’s introduction explicitly directs readers to the Sefer HaMitzvos of R’ Moshe of Coucy—the Semag—and presents the Semak as a seven-day practical handbook of obligations relevant in exile, not merely a fresh count of the 613. Its framework also includes rabbinic obligations. The Semag treats destruction of seed as a grave prohibition and cites Niddah, but does not count the “lo tinaf” derashah as a separate full negative commandment. Rav Tzadok therefore suggests that the Semak may list the subject separately for practical study while remaining aligned with the Semag’s formal classification.

כִּי הוּא לֹא בָּא לִמְנוֹת הַתַּרְיַ״ג מִצְוֹת וּשְׁסָ״ה לָאוִין שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, וּמָנָה גַּם מִצְוֹת דְּרַבָּנָן כִּמְגִלָּה וַחֲנוּכָּה וּנְטִילַת יָדַיִם וְכַדּוֹמֶה, וְכֵן לָאוִין דְּרַבָּנָן כְּכָל שְׁנִיּוֹת דִּרְבָּנָן, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּסוֹף הַסִּימָנִים שֶׁבְּרֵישׁ הַסֵּפֶר, אֶלָּא שֶׁזֶּה מָנָה בֵּין לָאוִין דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא

for he did not come to enumerate strictly the 613 mitzvos and 365 prohibitions of the Torah, having counted rabbinic mitzvos such as Megillah, Chanukah, and washing hands, as well as rabbinic prohibitions such as secondary incestuous relations (sheniyos), see the list of sections at the beginning of the book, though he did list this among biblical negative commands;
אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹמַר אֵין כַּוָּונָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּזֶה אַזְהָרַת לָאו גָּמוּר, רַק הוֹאִיל וְהוּא אִיסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וְאִיסּוּרוֹ שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹת כְּכָל אִיסּוּרֵי לָאוִין
but one may say his intention was not that this represents a formal negative prohibition, but since it is a biblical prohibition whose injunction is passive restraint like all negative commands,
עַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ הָיָה מַזְכִּירוֹ בְּסִימָן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ לִמְנוֹת אִיסּוּר בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵינוֹ נִכְלָל בִּשְׁאָר אִיסּוּרֵי עֲרָיוֹת וְחַיָּיבֵי לָאוִין

according to his organizational method he mentioned it in a distinct section to enumerate a distinct prohibition, seeing that it is not subsumed within other forbidden unions and ordinary negative commandments;

וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁחֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה סְמָכוּהוּ אַאַזְהָרַת לָאו דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״, מַיְיתֵי עַל זֶה הַאי קְרָא, וְאַף שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רַק אַסְמַכְתָּא, דְּלֹא נָחֵית הָכָא לְעִנְיַן אַזְהָרַת לָאו גָּמוּר דַּוְוקָא מִמִּקְרָא זֶה

and since the Sages anchored it upon the prohibition of "you shall not commit adultery," he cited this verse, even though it is merely an asmachta, for he did not intend here to imply a formal negative command specifically from this verse;
אַךְ פַּשְׁטוּת דְּבָרָיו לֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן
yet the plain sense of his words does not seem to imply this.

items.h: The theme: Even if viewed as a negative command under "lo tin'af", it does not carry lashes (lav she-ein bo malkus) because it constitutes a generalized prohibition (lav she-biklalos), which embraces multiple distinct offenses under a single verse. According to the Rama MiFano in Asarah Ma'amaros, all negative commandments lacking lashes atone like positive commandments through repentance alone. While prohibitions that serve as warnings for court-imposed death penalties (nitan l'azharas misas beis din) do not atone through repentance alone, this exclusion applies only to the capital offense itself; an auxiliary non-capital act included within the general verse lacks lashes due to its generalized nature, not due to capital severity, and therefore retains the leniency of atoning through repentance alone.

p: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נִרְאֶה, גַּם לְפִי דְּבָרָיו אֵינוֹ מֵהַלָּאוִין הַלּוֹקִין, מֵאַחַר שֶׁכָּתַב דִּבִכְלַל זֶה גַּם כֵּן אַזְהָרָה לְעוֹקֵב וְכוּלֵיהּ, אִם כֵּן הָוֵי לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת

And nevertheless it appears that even according to his words, it is not among the negative commandments that incur lashes, since he wrote that within this is also included a warning to an extortioner, etc.; if so, it constitutes a generalized prohibition (lav she-biklalos);
וְאִם כֵּן הָא אִיכָּא הָרַמַ״ע בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל [אוֹת י״ג] שֶׁכָּתַב דְּגַם לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה בָּזֶה

and if so, there is the opinion of the Rama MiFano in Asarah Ma'amaros cited above [Siman 13], who wrote that a generalized prohibition is likewise classified like an aseh in this regard [atoning through repentance alone].663Shevuos 47b; Aruch, s.v. עקב; Semag, Lavin §103. Shimon ben Tarfon asks, “From where is the warning to the okeiv after an adulterer?” and derives it from “lo tinaf,” read “lo tanif” — do not cause or facilitate adultery. The Aruch, cited by the Semag, explains the okeiv as one who goes about “on his heels” to procure a woman for another man’s adultery. Since the Semak includes both the adulterous act and the assisting conduct beneath the same Scriptural expression, Rav Tzadok treats the warning as a composite prohibition rather than as a dedicated lav for wasteful emission.664Rambam, Sefer HaMitzvos, Shoresh 9; Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2; Rema mi-Fano, Chakor Din I:18. A lav she-bichlalus is one Torah negative that embraces several distinct prohibited acts or meanings. Rambam explains that when two or more prohibitions issue from one undifferentiated lav, the verse is counted as one commandment and does not generate ordinary lashes for each branch; he codifies that a lav she-bichlalus does not carry lashes. Rema mi-Fano consequently includes it among the lighter non-lashed prohibitions whose atonement follows the category of an aseh. This is the formal bridge Rav Tzadok uses here.

וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּכָאן הָוֵי גַּם כֵּן לָאו שֶׁנִּיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, דְּהָאַזְהָרָה קָאֵי בְּנִיאוּף דְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ גָּמוּר וּלְהַזְהִיר הָאִשָּׁה דְּלָא נָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִ״לֹא תִתֵּן שְׁכָבְתְּךָ״

And although one might argue that here it is also a negative command serving as a warning for a court-imposed death penalty, since the warning applies to actual adultery with a married woman and to warn the woman, which is not derived from "you shall not lie carnally" (Vayikra 18:20),
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּסְּמַ״ג שָׁם וּבְסֵפֶר הַמִּצְוֹת שָׁם, עַיֵּין שָׁם

as stated in the Semag and Sefer HaMitzvos there, see there;665Vayikra 18:20; Sefer HaMitzvos, Negative Commandment 347; Semag, Lavin §103. “To your fellow’s wife you shall not give your emission” is phrased to the male adulterer and therefore does not by itself warn the married woman. Rambam cites the Mechilta that “lo tinaf” was repeated to warn both parties—“the man and the woman”—while the first verse warns the man alone. The Semag likewise places “lo tinaf” alongside the adultery warning and also records its separate derashah concerning the okeiv. This is why Rav Tzadok can view the same broad expression as containing both a capital adultery warning and a distinct noncapital branch.

וּבְכְהַאי גַּוְונָא דְּיֵשׁ בִּכְלָלוֹ אַזְהָרָה לְאִיסּוּר דְּמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין חָשְׁבִינַן לֵיהּ גַּם כֵּן ״נִיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין״ שֶׁלֹּא לִלְקוֹת אַף בְּהָאִיסּוּר הַנִּכְלָל בּוֹ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין

and in such a case where it contains within its scope a warning for a capital crime, we consider it likewise as "given for the warning of a court execution" so as not to administer lashes even for the subsidiary prohibition included within it that carries no death penalty,

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּעֵירוּבִין י״ז עַמּוּד ב׳], וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּתוֹסָפוֹת סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״לָאו״, וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת [סַנְהֶדְרִין ס״ג עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מִשּׁוּם״, [פ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״הִכָּהוּ״

as they stated [in Eruvin 17b], and see Tosafos there (s.v. lav), and Tosafos [Sanhedrin 63a, s.v. mishum, and 85a, s.v. hikahu];666Eruvin 17b; Tosafos ad loc.; Tosafos, Sanhedrin 63a and 85a. Eruvin supplies the model for a verse whose scope may contain both a capital and a noncapital branch. R’ Yonasan objects to lashes for crossing the Shabbos boundary because “al yetzei ish mimkomo” could also function as the warning for carrying from one domain to another, a capital Shabbos offense; the Gemara invokes the rule that a lav given as the warning for court-imposed death does not carry lashes. Rav Ashi ultimately distinguishes the wording “yetzei” from “yotzi,” but Rav Tzadok cites Tosafos for the broader analytical issue: when one Scriptural warning encompasses a death-bearing act and another act with no death penalty, the lighter branch may also lack lashes because the shared lav was not formulated as an ordinary warning for lashes.
וּבְלָאו שֶׁנִּיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין נִתְבָּאֵר שָׁם מֵהָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת דְּאֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל זֶה

and regarding a negative command given as a warning for a court execution, it was explained from the Asarah Ma'amaros that it is excluded from this leniency;667Rema mi-Fano, Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chakor Din I:18. The passage lists lighter lavim treated like an aseh for immediate atonement — including a lav she-bichlalus, a lav inferred from a positive formulation, and an actionless lav — but does not place a lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din in that lenient group. Rav Tzadok reads the omission as reflecting the usual severity of a warning attached to a capital offense. His present chiddush limits that exclusion to the genuinely capital act itself, rather than a separate, lighter branch that merely shares the same broad verse.
נִרְאֶה לִי דְּלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁאוֹתוֹ אִיסּוּר עַצְמוֹ נִיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, אֶלָּא שֶׁהִתְרוּ בוֹ לְמַלְקוּת וְלֹא לְמִיתָה
it seems to me that he said this only when that specific transgression itself was given as a warning for a death penalty, where they warned him for lashes instead of death,
דִּבְכְהַאי גַּוְונָא הוּא עִיקַּר הָא דְּנִיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין [בְּמַכּוֹת י״ג עַמּוּד ב׳] וּבָרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק י״ח מֵהִלְכוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין הֲלָכָה ב׳], עַיֵּין שָׁם

for in such a case lies the primary principle of a prohibition given for the warning of a court death penalty [Makkos 13b] and in the Rambam [Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2], see there.668Makkos 13b; Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2. Rava explains the dispute concerning a lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din where the offender was warned for lashes rather than execution: R’ Akiva holds that even then the capital-warning lav does not produce lashes. Rambam rules accordingly that every lav serving as the warning for a court-death offense — such as “lo tinaf” or the Shabbos labor prohibition — is not punishable by lashes. This is Rav Tzadok’s “primary” form: the very act now before us is itself the capital offense. He contrasts it with the derivative form, where the particular branch has no death liability at all.669Editor’s clarification — two applications of lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din. The first is the direct case of Makkos 13b: the act itself carries court-imposed death, but the offender was warned for lashes; R’ Akiva still exempts him because the lav serves the capital offense. Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 18:2, codifies that a capital-warning lav—such as “lo tinaf” or the Shabbos labor prohibition—does not carry lashes. The second, discussed by Tosafos in Eruvin and Sanhedrin, is derivative: one broad verse includes both a capital act and a lighter branch, and the lighter branch may also lack lashes because the shared lav was not formulated as an ordinary lashes-warning. Rav Tzadok argues that Rema mi-Fano’s exclusion from immediate atonement applies to the first, intrinsically severe form, not necessarily to the lighter derivative branch.

אֲבָל כְּהַאי דַּאֲמַרַן שֶׁאוֹתוֹ עִנְיָן אֵין בּוֹ מִיתָה כְּלָל, רַק הוֹאִיל בְּחֵלֶק הַלָּאו שֶׁלְּאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין אֵין בּוֹ מַלְקוּת גַּם בְּאִידָךְ שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ מַלְקוּת כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא נִיתַּן הַלָּאו לְאַזְהָרַת מַלְקוּת

But in a case such as ours where that specific matter carries no death penalty at all, and only because the portion of the verse warning against the capital crime carries no lashes, lashes likewise do not apply to the subsidiary clause included within it since the verse was not formulated for lashes;
דָּבָר זֶה מַה שֶּׁאֵין לוֹקִין עָלָיו אֵינוֹ מִפְּנֵי חֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה עָנְשׁוֹ חָמוּר, דַּהֲרֵי בְּהַהִיא לֵיכָּא עֹונֶשׁ מִיתָה הֶחָמוּר כְּלָל
this exemption from lashes is not due to any intrinsic severity in the act or because its punishment is more severe, for in this specific act there is no severe death penalty whatsoever;
בִּכְהַאי גַּוְונָא יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא אָמַר הָ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ לְהַעֲדִיפוֹ מִשְּׁאָר לָאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין כְּלָל
in such a case, one may say that the Asarah Ma'amaros did not intend to set it apart from other negative commandments that lack lashes at all,
דְּלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין לְהַחְמִיר בְּעָנְשָׁם כִּמְבוֹאָר בִּדְבָרָיו שָׁם, עַיֵּין שָׁם
for he spoke only where lashes are omitted due to greater severity of punishment, as explained in his words there, see there.
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר הַךְ פְּטוּר דְּמִשּׁוּם נִיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, אֲפִילּוּ אִי נִפְטַר רַק מִשּׁוּם זֶה, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּלְהָ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ הוּא בִּכְלַל עֲשֵׂה בָּזֶה

And if so, this exemption on the grounds of being given for the warning of a court execution, even if exempt solely because of this, according to the Asarah Ma'amaros is categorized under positive commandments in this regard [attoning through repentance alone];

וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן דְּהוּא לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת גַּם כֵּן דְּפָטוּר בְּלָאו הָכִי, וְלֹא יִגָּרַע כֹּחוֹ מִשּׁוּם דְּיֵשׁ בִּכְלָלוֹ גַּם אַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, כֵּיוָן דְּלֹא קָאֵי הַמִּיתַת בֵּית דִּין אַפְּרָט זֶה:

and all the more so since it is also a generalized prohibition which is exempt from lashes regardless, and its standing should not be diminished simply because its general scope includes a capital warning, since the death penalty does not apply to this specific detail.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ד׳–ז׳

The theme: The definition of "adultery by hand or foot" (mena'ef b'yad o b'regel). The derashah from "you shall not commit adultery" (lo tin'af) refers strictly to unnatural manual or pedal friction mimicking the act of coitus with a woman. In contrast, emission induced through contemplation (hirhur) and erection without such physical mimicry violates only the positive command of procreation (peru u'revu). This distinction explains why the Sages in Yevamos 76b permitted a medical arousal test (using colored garments) to verify marital fitness: since the emission is prompted by passive sight and thought rather than the pseudo-adulterous friction of the negative command, it was permitted for the overriding purpose of procreation.

p: וּבִתְשׁוּבָה כָּתַבְתִּי עוֹד, דְּאֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּדִיּוּק לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא שָׁם: ״לֹא תְהֵא בְּךָ נִיאוּף, בֵּין בְּיָד בֵּין בְּרֶגֶל״
And in a responsum I wrote further that it is possible to say that the precise phrasing of the Gemara there (Niddah 13b): "There shall be no adultery within you, whether by hand or by foot,"

דְּדַוְוקָא מְנָאֵף בְּיָד אוֹ רֶגֶל שֶׁמַּכְנִיס הָאֵבֶר תּוֹךְ יָדוֹ אוֹ בֵּין רַגְלָיו עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַכְנָסָתוֹ בְּאִשָּׁה, שֶׁדּוֹמֶה לְנִיאוּף דְּאִשָּׁה, הוּא דְּאִתְרַבִּי אִיסּוּר מִ״לֹא תִנְאָף״, שֶׁזֶּהוּ דֶּרֶךְ נִיאוּף

means that specifically one who "commits adultery" with hand or foot—inserting the organ into his hand or between his feet in the manner of entry into a woman, which resembles adultery with a woman—is what was included in the prohibition derived from "You shall not commit adultery," for this constitutes a manner of adultery;
אֲבָל הַמְהַרְהֵר וּמִתְקַשֶּׁה וּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל הַזֶּה, וְאִיסּוּרוֹ רַק מִשּׁוּם מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה
but one who contemplates, experiences an erection, and emits seed wastefully is not included in this category, and his prohibition derives solely from the positive commandment of procreation.
וּרְאָיָה מֵהָא [דִּיבָמוֹת ע״ו עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״מַנְחֵיהּ לֵיהּ אַבֵּי פוֹקְרֵי וּמַקְרֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ, מַעַבְרֵיהּ קַמֵּיהּ בִּגְדֵי צִבְעוֹנִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And a proof is from that passage [in Yevamos 76b]: "They place him upon a dunghill and he experiences a seminal emission... they parade before him colored garments, etc.," see there;
וּבְבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל [סִימָן כ״ה סְעִיף קָטָן ב׳] וּבִבְכוֹר שׁוֹר [בְּנִדָּה שָׁם] מַיְיתֵי לַהּ לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם דְּהוּתַּר הַאי אִיסּוּר לְצֹרֶךְ כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and in the Beis Shmuel [Even HaEzer 25:2] and Bechor Shor [Niddah 13b] they cite it to derive from there that this prohibition was permitted for a necessity of such a nature, see there;670Beis Shmuel, Even HaEzer 25:2; Bechor Shor on Niddah 13a. Beis Shmuel considers a diagnostic case in which a woman’s blood may have come from her husband and tentatively permits emission to determine its source. He cites the examination in Yevamos 76a, but says the proof can be rejected and leaves the matter tzarich iyun. Bechor Shor states more directly that Yevamos intentionally induces emission to determine whether the man is fit to enter the congregation. These Acharonim establish a need-based precedent but do not explain why the usual Torah prohibition yields. Rav Tzadok supplies the classification: the test is not derekh niuf and is performed to restore the possibility of procreation itself.671Yevamos 76a: [regarding one whose membrum was punctured, to determine his fitness to marry into the congregation] “Rava son of Rabbah sent to Rav Yosef: let our master teach us, how do we act [to test whether emission opens the puncture]? He said to him: we bring warm barley bread and place it abei pukri [near the orifice] and he emits — and we observe him. Abaye said: is everyone Yaakov our father, of whom it is written (Bereishis 49:3) ‘my strength and the first of my vigor,’ [meaning] that he never saw an emission in his days?! Rather, Abaye said: we pass before him colored garments [‘of a woman, and he muses upon a woman and emits’]. Rava said: is everyone Barzilai the Gileadi [steeped in licentiousness]?! Rather, it is clearest as we said originally.”
אֲבָל לֹא בֵּאֲרוּ הַטַּעַם בֶּאֱמֶת לָמָּה הוּתַּר אִיסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, וּלְהַסְּמַ״ק בְּלָאו, מִשּׁוּם צֹרֶךְ הַבְּדִיקָה דְּשָׁם
yet they did not truly explain the reason why a biblical prohibition—and according to the Semak, a negative commandment—was permitted merely on account of the need for the medical examination there.

וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי נִיחָא, דְּשָׁם דְּמַקְרֵי עַל יְדֵי הַחִימּוּם אוֹ הַהִרְהוּר וְלֹא כְּדֶרֶךְ הַמְנָאֲפִים, אֵין אִיסּוּרוֹ מִשּׁוּם לָאו דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ גַּם לַסְּמַ״ק, רַק נִלְמַד מִמִּצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה

But according to what I wrote it is well resolved: for there, since the emission occurs through bodily warmth or contemplation and not in the manner of adulterous friction, its prohibition is not under the negative commandment of "You shall not commit adultery" even according to the Semak, but is derived solely from the mitzvah of procreation;
וְאִם כֵּן שָׁם דְּהַבְּדִיקָה הוּא לְצֹרֶךְ מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה לְהַכְשִׁירוֹ בַּקָּהָל, מִשּׁוּם הָכִי הוּתַּר
and if so, there, where the examination is for the very sake of the mitzvah of procreation to declare him fit to marry into the congregation, for that reason it was permitted.
וּלְפִי זֶה גַּם לַסְּמַ״ק לֹא כָּל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּלָאו, וּבְלָאו הָכִי הוּא יְחִידָאָה נֶגֶד רַמְבַּ״ם וּסְמַ״ג וְסֵפֶר הַחִנּוּךְ

And according to this, even according to the Semak not every instance of emitting seed wastefully violates a negative command; and regardless, he is a solitary authority (da'as yachid) against the Rambam, the Semag, and Sefer HaChinuch.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the responsum of the Pnei Yehoshua regarding whether wasteful emission carries the penalty of rabbinic disciplinary lashes (makas mardus). The Pnei Yehoshua argued that because the Rambam lists only excommunication (nidui) and not makas mardus, the derashah on "lo tin'af" must be a mere asmachta, asserting that makas mardus applies only to rabbinic enactments and not to biblical prohibitions lacking lashes. R' Tzadok refutes this assertion, proving from a half-measure of forbidden food (chatzi shi'ur) and the negative command of bal yera'eh that makas mardus indeed applies to biblical infractions without action. The absence of lashes in the Rambam does not prove the verse is an asmachta, because generalized negative prohibitions (lav she-biklalos) are biblically exempt from Torah lashes.

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת פְּנֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ [חֵלֶק ב׳ הַנִּדְפָּס מֵחָדָשׁ סִימָן מ״ד] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְהַשְּׁאֵלָה הַשְּׁנִיָּה״, כָּתַב גַּם כֵּן דְּהַךְ דְּרָשָׁא דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ בִּלְתִּי סָפֵק דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא

And then I saw in the responsa of Pnei Yehoshua [Part II, §44, s.v. ve-hashe'elah hasheniyah] that he likewise wrote that this derashah from "You shall not commit adultery" is undoubtedly a mere asmachta;
וְהֵבִיא רְאָיָה מֵרַמְבַּ״ם הַנַּ״ל שֶׁלֹּא כָּתַב דְּלוֹקִין עַל זֶה, וַאֲפִילּוּ מַכּוֹת מַרְדּוּת לֹא כָּתַב אֶלָּא בְּנִדּוּי וְכוּלֵיהּ

and he brought proof from the aforementioned Rambam who did not write that lashes are administered for it, and did not even write disciplinary lashes (makas mardus), but only excommunication (nidui), etc.;672Responsa Pnei Yehoshua, II, §44 (s.v. veha-she’eilah ha-sheniyah). The responsum addresses a patient whose physicians believed that emitting seed could cure him. Pnei Yehoshua permits it when the medical benefit is certain, explaining that the comparisons to bloodshed and forbidden relations express severity rather than the formal law of yehareg ve’al ya’avor. He further calls the derashah from “lo tinaf” an asmachta, arguing from Rambam’s omission of both Torah lashes and makkos mardus. Rav Tzadok accepts neither proof: the absence of Torah lashes can follow from lav she-bichlalus or lav ha-nitan l’azharas misas beis din, and Rambam’s silence about makkos mardus is not itself dispositive.
דְּדָבָר זֶה שֶׁאֵינוֹ תַּקָּנַת חֲכָמִים זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה רַק נִלְמַד מִקְּרָאֵי וְאֵין בּוֹ לָאו, אֵין לוֹקֶה מַכּוֹת מַרְדּוּת, וּכְמוֹ לְשׁוֹן הָרָע וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

for a matter that is not a positive rabbinic enactment, but is merely derived from Scripture and contains no negative command, does not receive makas mardus, like evil speech (lashon hara) and similar matters, see there at length.
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מִדְּאֵין לוֹקִין אֵין רְאָיָה, דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּהוּא לָאו שֶׁבִּכְלָלוֹת אוֹ נִיתַּן לְאַזְהָרַת מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

And what he wrote based on the absence of biblical lashes is no proof, for one can say it is because it is a generalized negative command (lav she-biklalos) or given as a warning for a court-imposed death penalty, as mentioned above.
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּגַם מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת אֵין לוֹקֶה בְּאִיסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא אֶלָּא בְּאִיסּוּרִין דְּרַבָּנָן — לֵיתָא
And what he wrote—that one does not receive disciplinary lashes for a biblical prohibition of this kind, but only for rabbinic prohibitions—is incorrect;
דְּגַם בְּאִיסּוּר חֲצִי שִׁיעוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וְאֵין בּוֹ לָאו, מְבוֹאָר בָּרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק א׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת חָמֵץ וּמַצָּה הֲלָכָה ז׳] דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת, עַיֵּין שָׁם

for even regarding the biblical prohibition of a half-measure (chatzi shi'ur), which contains no specific negative command, it is explicit in the Rambam [Hilchos Chametz U’Matzah 1:7] that he receives makas mardus, see there;673Rambam, Hilchos Chametz uMatzah 1:3, 1:7; Hilchos Deos 7:2–3. Rambam rules that deliberate consumption of less than a kezayis of chametz—although prohibited by Torah law without the ordinary measure for Torah punishment—receives makkos mardus. He likewise gives makkos mardus for retaining chametz without an act, even though the Torah lashes do not apply. In Hilchos Deos he places lashon hara within “lo telech rachil” and stresses its exceptional gravity. These rulings support Rav Tzadok’s central response: makkos mardus is not limited to newly enacted rabbinic prohibitions, and the absence of an explicit penalty in a particular chapter does not prove that no disciplinary punishment exists.
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מִלְּשׁוֹן הָרָע, שָׁם יֵשׁ לָאו דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל ״לֹא תֵלֵךְ רָכִיל״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב [פֶּרֶק ז׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת הֲלָכָה ב׳], אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה

and what he cited from evil speech: there exists an explicit negative commandment, which is included in "You shall not go up and down as a talebearer" (Vayikra 19:16) as the Rambam wrote [Hilchos De'os 7:2], only that it lacks physical action;
וּמְבוֹאָר שָׁם [בְּפֶרֶק א׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת חָמֵץ וּמַצָּה הֲלָכָה ג׳] בְּלָאו דְּ״בַּל יֵרָאֶה״ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת
and it is explained there [Hilchos Chametz U’Matzah 1:3] regarding the negative command of bal yera'eh [owning leaven] which lacks physical action that one receives makas mardus!

וְהָא דְּלֹא כָּתַב בְּהִלְכוֹת דֵּעוֹת דְּלוֹקֶה מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת גַּבֵּי לְשׁוֹן הָרָע וּרְכִילוּת, אוּלַי מִשּׁוּם דִּפְרִיצֵי בְּהוּ כּוּלֵי עָלְמָא וְלֹא מַשְׁמַע כָּל כָּךְ לֶאֱינָשֵׁי, וְגַם אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְיַסֵּר הַכֹּל

And the fact that he did not write in Hilchos De'os that one receives makas mardus for evil speech and talebearing, is perhaps because everyone is prone to breach them and people do not realize its gravity, and it is also impossible to flog everyone;
אוֹ דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ לְחֹמֶר הָאִיסּוּר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב [שָׁם הֲלָכָה ג׳] לֹא נִיתְּנָה לְכַפָּרָה בְּמַכַּת מַרְדּוּת
or he held that due to the extreme gravity of the prohibition, as he wrote [there, Halachah 3], it is not granted atonement through makas mardus.

אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא בָּא לְכַפָּרָה כְּמַלְקוּת דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא, דְּכֵיוָן שֶׁלָּקָה הֲרֵי הוּא כְּאָחִיךָ, רַק לִרְדּוֹת הָעוֹבְרִים שֶׁלֹּא יִפְרְצוּ, וְאִם כֵּן כָּל שֶׁכֵּן אִי חֲמִיר טְפֵי אוֹ פְּרִיצֵי טְפֵי דְּרָאוּי לְיַסֵּר וְלִרְדּוֹת

However, makas mardus does not come for spiritual atonement like biblical lashes—where once flogged he is restored as "your brother"—but merely to discipline transgressors so they do not breach fences, and if so, all the more so if it is more severe or more widely breached, it would be appropriate to chastise and discipline.674Makkos 23a; Devarim 25:3; Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 24:4. The Mishnah expounds “veniklah achicha le’einecha”: once the offender has received the Torah-prescribed lashes, he is again “your brother,” expressing judicial atonement and restored standing. Makkos mardus has a different function. Rambam describes the court’s extraordinary authority to strike or otherwise discipline when needed to strengthen Torah observance and prevent breach. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes fixed Torah lashes, which complete a formal kapparah, from discretionary chastisement intended to subdue ongoing transgression and protect the communal fence.

אֲבָל בְּלָאו הָכִי אֵין דַּרְכּוֹ שֶׁל רַמְבַּ״ם לִכְתּוֹב בְּכָל אִיסּוּרִין כּוּלָּם דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא אוֹ דְּרַבָּנָן עֹונֶשׁ מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת, וְיֵשׁ הַרְבֵּה דְּכָוָותֵיהּ אַף דְּוַדַּאי יֵשׁ בְּהוּ עֹונֶשׁ מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת לֹא פֵּירֵשׁ בְּחִיבּוּרוֹ, וְכָתַבְתִּי מִזֶּה כְּבָר בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר

But regardless, it is not the style of the Rambam to record the penalty of makas mardus across every single biblical or rabbinic prohibition, and there are many comparable cases where although makas mardus certainly applies, he did not specify it in his code, and I have already written of this elsewhere.

items.h: The theme: Resolving the Rambam's view through his Commentary on the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 7:4). The Rambam records excommunication (nidui) for self-induced erection and emission because nidui is a more severe sanction than makas mardus, and courts do not administer both simultaneously. Crucially, the Rambam himself cites the textual variant "lo teheneh l'af" (do not derive pleasure in the nose) as a biblical derashah from "lo tin'af", but applies it to inhaling perfumes placed upon illicit nakedness (ervah). This explains the ruling in Hilchos Issurei Biah 21:3 and reveals that the Maggid Mishneh sought its source from distant passages in Shabbos 62b only because he lacked access to the Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah. This derashah represents a genuine biblical prohibition without biblical lashes, like chatzi shi'ur.

p: וּבַהַאי דַּאֲתֵינַן יֵשׁ לוֹמַר, כֵּיוָן דְּכָתַב נִדּוּי דַּעֲדִיפָא מִמַּכַּת מַרְדּוּת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּפְסָחִים נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳], וּבָזֶה יֵשׁ חִיּוּב נִדּוּי אֲפִילּוּ בִּמְקַשֶּׁה עַצְמוֹ לְבַד, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לִכְתּוֹב עוֹד מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת דְּתַרְתֵּי לָא עָבְדִינַן

And in this matter that we have addressed, one can say: since the Rambam recorded excommunication (nidui), which is more severe than disciplinary lashes as they said [in Pesachim 52a], and in this matter there is a liability to nidui even for deliberately causing an erection alone, all the more so for emitting seed wastefully, it was inappropriate to write makas mardus as well, for we do not administer two punishments;
וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁכָּתַב מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת אֵין מְנַדִּין, וְהָכָא דִּמְנַדִּין וְעָבְדֵי בֵּיהּ הֶחָמוּר לֹא כָּתַב מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת

and where he writes makas mardus they do not excommunicate, whereas here where they excommunicate and apply the more severe penalty, he did not record makas mardus;675Pesachim 52a — nidui compared with makkos mardus. Rav Yosef punished Rav Nasan bar Asya for violating the second festival day. In one version he chose excommunication and explained that it was more severe than lashes; the alternate version chose lashes for a Torah scholar because excommunication was too severe for him. Rav Tzadok uses this comparison to suggest why Rambam records nidui here without also listing makkos mardus: the more severe sanction may replace the lesser one. The Gemara itself compares their severity; the broader rule that both are not administered together is Rav Tzadok’s inference.
אֲבָל מִדְּלֹא מַיְיתֵי כְּלָל בָּזֶה קְרָא דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״, מַשְׁמַע וַדַּאי דְּלָא סְבִירָא לֵיהּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בָּזֶה לָאו גָּמוּר
but from the fact that he does not cite the verse "You shall not commit adultery" at all in this context, it certainly implies that he does not hold that there is an absolute negative command here.

וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת לָרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק ז׳ דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין] מִשְׁנַת ״הַבָּא עַל הַזָּכוּר״, כָּתַב: ״וּמִי שֶׁבָּא דֶּרֶךְ אֵבָרִים וְכוּלֵיהּ [זֶה כָּתַב גַּם בְּחִיבּוּרוֹ בְּפֶרֶק כ״א מֵהִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה]

And then I found in the Commentary on the Mishnah by the Rambam [Sanhedrin, ch. 7, on the Mishnah "He who lies with a male"], he wrote: "And one who engages in unnatural contact through limbs, etc. [this he wrote also in his Code, Hilchos Issurei Biah 21:1],

אוֹ מְשַׁמֵּשׁ בְּאֵבֶר מֵאֵבָרָיו לְכַוָּונַת הֲנָאָה בְּאֵיזֶה אֵבֶר שֶׁנָּגַע מֵאֶבְרֵי גּוּפוֹ כְּאוֹתָן הַמִּתְעַנְּגִים בְּיָד וָרֶגֶל, וְזֶה הַמַּעֲשֶׂה מֵהַזְּנוּת קוֹרִין אוֹתוֹ חֲכָמִים מְנָאֲפִים בְּיָד וּבְרֶגֶל, וְכֵן וְכוּלֵיהּ, כָּל זֶה אָסוּר וּמַכִּין לָעוֹבֵר מַלְקוּת

or uses one of his limbs with the intention of gratification against whichever limb of the body he touches, like those who indulge with hand and foot, and this act of immorality the Sages call 'committing adultery by hand and by foot,' etc., all of this is forbidden and they strike the transgressor with lashes,
וְכָל אֵלּוּ נִכְלָלִין בִּב׳ לָאוִין וְכוּלֵיהּ: ״לֹא תִקְרְבוּ לְגַלּוֹת עֶרְוָה״ וְכוּלֵיהּ, ״לְבִלְתִּי עֲשׂוֹת מֵחֻקּוֹת״ וְגוֹמֵר
and all of these are included under two negative commandments: 'None of you shall approach to uncover nakedness' (Vayikra 18:6), and 'that you commit not any one of these abominable customs' (18:30);

וְכֵן אָסוּר לְהָרִיחַ בִּבְשָׂמִים שֶׁעַל הָעֶרְוָה וְכוּלֵיהּ, אֲבָל אֵינוֹ חַיָּיב עַל זֶה מַלְקוּת, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָמַר: ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ — ״לֹא תְהַנֶּה לָאַף״, לְפִי שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין מִדְּרָשָׁא, עַד כָּאן

and likewise it is forbidden to smell perfumes upon forbidden nakedness, etc., but one is not liable to lashes for this, even though it said: 'You shall not commit adultery [lo tin'af]' — 'do not derive pleasure in the nose [lo teheneh l'af],' because they do not administer biblical lashes based on an exegesis (derasha)," thus far.676Rambam, Peirush HaMishnayos, Sanhedrin 7:4; Issurei Biah 21:2; Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai 20:13 — limb-contact and the nose-derashah: Rambam places limb-based gratification under Vayikra 18:6 and 18:30, but separately derives the ban on smelling an ervah’s perfume from “lo tinaf—lo tehaneh la’af,” stating that Torah lashes do not follow from a derashah. Issurei Biah nevertheless assigns makkos mardus to intentional smelling or gazing. Shabbos, cited by the Maggid Mishneh, describes women using perfume to arouse men. Rav Tzadok distinguishes that case from Rambam’s exact nose-derashah and treats the latter as a Torah prohibition without Torah lashes. In Se’if 8 Rav Tzadok draws a further conclusion from Rambam’s wording: “hand and foot” can describe limb-based contact with an ervah rather than wasteful emission. Mekhilta de-Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai preserves separate “lo tinaf” interpretations concerning pleasure through the nose and sin through hand, foot, eye, and heart. That Midrash supports separating the derashos, but it does not state Rav Tzadok’s precise physical interpretation.
וְהִנֵּה גַּם הוּא גּוֹרֵס הָא דְּ״לֹא תְהַנֶּה לָאַף״ שֶׁבַּסְּמַ״ק הַנַּ״ל, אֲבָל הוּא מְפָרֵשׁ אַרֵיחַ מִבְּשָׂמִים שֶׁמֵּרִיחַ וְנֶהֱנֶה בְּאַפּוֹ

Behold, the Rambam too had the textual reading of "do not derive pleasure in the nose" found in the aforementioned Semak, but he explains it as referring to the scent of perfumes, where one smells and derives pleasure in his nose!
וּמִכָּאן לָקַח אִיסּוּר זֶה שֶׁכָּתַב [בְּפֶרֶק כ״א מֵהִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה הֲלָכָה ג׳], וּדְמַכִּין עַל זֶה מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת כֵּיוָן דְּנִלְמַד מִקְּרָא
And from here he took this prohibition that he recorded [in Hilchos Issurei Biah 21:3], and that they administer makas mardus for it since it is derived from Scripture.
וְהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד שָׁם צִיֵּין לְשַׁבָּת [ס״ב עַמּוּד ב׳], וְשָׁם נִזְכַּר עֹונֶשׁ הַנָּשִׁים הַמַּתִּיזוֹת בִּבְשָׂמִים לְהַכְנִיס יֵצֶר הָרָע בַּבַּחוּרִים, וַהֲוָה לֵיהּ לוֹמַר זֶה
And the Maggid Mishneh there cited Shabbos [62b], where mention is made of the punishment of women who sprayed perfumes to inject the evil inclination into young men, and he should have stated this;
אֲבָל מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב הוּא עַל הָאֲנָשִׁים הַמְּרִיחִים לֹא לָקַח מֵהַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, רַק מֵהַהִיא דְּ״לֹא תְהַנֶּה לָאַף״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב בְּעַצְמוֹ בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת הַנַּ״ל

but what the Rambam wrote concerning men who smell the perfumes he took not from that passage, but from that derashah of "do not derive pleasure in the nose," as he wrote himself in his Commentary on the Mishnah.

וְהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד לֹא רָאָה פֵּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת, וְגַם לֹא הָיָה לְפָנָיו הַנּוּסְחָא בַּגְּמָרָא כֵּן רַק כִּלְפָנֵינוּ וְלֹא בְּאֵיזֶה בָּרַיְיתָא אַחֶרֶת, וְעַל כֵּן הוּצְרַךְ לְבַקֵּשׁ מִמֶּרְחָק
And the Maggid Mishneh did not see the Commentary on the Mishnah, nor did he have that variant reading in the Gemara (having only our text), wherefore he was compelled to search from afar.
וּמִלְּשׁוֹן פֵּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת מַשְׁמַע דִּדְרָשָׁא גְּמוּרָה דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא הוּא, דְּלֹא כָּתַב דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא, רַק דְּמִדְּרָשָׁא לָא מַלְקִינַן

And from the language of the Commentary on the Mishnah it implies that this is a full biblical derashah, for he did not write that it is an asmachta, but only that they do not administer Torah lashes based on a derashah;677Yoma 74a; Sanhedrin 54a — a Torah prohibition without Torah lashes. R’ Yochanan rules that chatzi shiur is prohibited by Torah law because it can combine into the full measure, deriving inclusion from “all fat,” although the prescribed Torah punishment requires the full measure. Sanhedrin discusses the rule “ein onshin min hadin”: even a valid legal inference does not automatically create a corporal penalty without an explicit penal source. Rav Tzadok applies the same structure here. “Lo tehaneh la’af” may establish a Torah-level prohibition, while the plain warning of “lo tinaf” remains directed to actual adultery; therefore no Torah lashes follow from this secondary derashah.
וְהַיְינוּ עַל דֶּרֶךְ חֲצִי שִׁיעוּר, דְּאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאָסוּר מִן הַתּוֹרָה לְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מֵרִיבּוּיָא דְּ״כָל״, אֵין לוֹקִין
meaning in the manner of a half-measure (chatzi shi'ur), which although forbidden biblically according to Rabbi Yochanan from the inclusionary word "any" (kol), does not incur lashes;
וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ דְּאֵין עוֹנְשִׁין מִן הַדִּין, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁקַּל וָחֹמֶר הוּא אַחַת מִי״ג מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן דְּרָשָׁא כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִי״ג מִדּוֹת

and akin to the principle that they do not punish based on logical deduction (ein onshin min hadin), even though an a fortiori argument (kal va-chomer) is one of the thirteen hermeneutical principles by which the Torah is expounded, and all the more so an exegesis of this kind which is not among the thirteen principles.
וְטוּבָא יֵשׁ כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ מִדְּרָשָׁא דִּקְרָא וְהוּא אִיסּוּר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וְאֵין לוֹקִין
And there are numerous cases of this kind that are derived from a scriptural derashah, constituting a biblical prohibition yet incurring no biblical lashes;
וְאַף שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ מִגּוּף לְשׁוֹן הָאַזְהָרָה, אֵין עִיקַּר אַזְהָרַת הַלָּאו אֶלָּא עַל נִיאוּף מַמָּשׁ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ
and even though they expounded it from the very wording of the prohibition, the primary scriptural warning of the negative command addresses literal adultery according to its plain sense.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the textual origins of "lo teheneh l'af" and its kabbalistic versus halachic interpretations. Neither the Rambam nor the Semak identified the exact rabbinic source of "lo teheneh l'af." Commentators on the Semak cited Niddah 13b regarding wasteful emission, which forces an allegorical interpretation based on the Zohar (Bereishis 57a): that one must not give pleasure or vitality to the destroying angel of wrath named Af. R' Tzadok demonstrates that the Rambam's literal reading (pleasure of scent to the physical nose, af) is far superior, concluding that the textual reading in Niddah likely contained an alternative clause (davar acher), or that the phrase originated from an independent, non-extant Baraisa that was preserved in ancient manuscripts of the Semak.

p: וְהִנֵּה רַמְבַּ״ם וְסַמַ״ק עַצְמָם לֹא הֶרְאוּ מְקוֹם הַמַּאֲמָר ״לֹא תְהַנֶּה לָאַף״
And behold, the Rambam and Semak themselves did not indicate the source of the dictum "do not derive pleasure in the nose";
וְרַק בַּסְּמַ״ק שָׁם צִיֵּין הַמְצַיֵּין מַרְאֵה מָקוֹם לְנִדָּה, לְפִי שֶׁשָּׁם מַיְיתוּ מִמִּקְרָא זֶה לְאִיסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
and only in the Semak there did the cross-referencing glossator mark a reference to Niddah (13b), because there they cite this verse for the prohibition of wasteful emission of seed.
וְצָרִיךְ לִדְחוֹק וּלְפָרֵשׁ לְפִי דְּבָרָיו, דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר: שֶׁלֹּא יִגְרוֹם הֲנָאָה לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמַּשְׁחִית הַנִּקְרָא ״אַף״

And according to his words, one would be forced to interpret with difficulty that it means: that he should not cause gratification to the destroying angel named Af [Wrath],678Niddah 13b; Sefer Mitzvot Katan §292 — the divergent readings: The standard Bavli text reads “lo tinaf — lo tehei [bekha] ni’uf/no’ef, bein ba-yad bein ba-regel,” and contains no phrase “lo tehaneh la-af.” The Semak, however, prints “lo tinaf, lo tehaneh la-af” and the later source-reference points to Niddah. Rav Tzadok is therefore addressing a textual problem, not merely explaining the printed Gemara. His report that a parchment Semak dated 5109 (1349) agrees with the printed wording shows that the Semak reading is old, but it does not prove that Niddah itself contained that reading.
כִּידוּעַ בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [פָּרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית נ״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבַּעֲוֹן זֶה יָהֵיב חֵילָא וְתוּקְפָּא לְרוּחַ מְסָאֲבָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם
as is known in the Holy Zohar [Bereishis 57a] that through this sin one gives strength and dominion to the spirit of impurity, see there;
וְהוּא דָּחוּק, וְיוֹתֵר נִרְאֶה כְּפֵירוּשׁ רַמְבַּ״ם הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

yet this is forced, and it appears far more plausible according to the explanation of the Rambam mentioned above [referring to the physical nose];679Zohar, Bereishis 57b — giving power to the spirit of impurity: (with the Sulam translation): “‘for the wickedness of man was great’ (Bereishis 6:5) — they committed all the transgressions, yet their punishment was not sealed until they spilled blood in vain upon the earth. And who are they? They are those who corrupt their way (their seed) upon the earth. And this is what is written, ‘only evil all the day’ (ibid.); it is written here ‘only evil,’ and it is written there (Bereishis 38:7) ‘and Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil in the eyes of Hashem.’ R’ Yosi said: is not ‘evil’ [the same as] ‘wicked’? He said to him: no — ‘wicked’ [applies] even [to] one who raised his hand against his fellow though he did nothing to him, as it says, ‘and he said to the wicked one, why do you strike your fellow’ — ‘struck’ is not said, but ‘strike.’ But ‘evil’ is called only one who corrupts his way and defiles himself and defiles the earth, and gives power and might to the spirit of impurity called ‘evil,’ as it says ‘only evil all the day’; and he does not enter the palace of Hashem and does not see the face of the Shechinah, since through this sin the Shechinah departs from the world. Come and see: when a person is defiled (through this sin), he is not remembered by the Holy One for good, and at all times he is remembered for evil, from that spirit of impurity called ‘evil.’” Rav Tzadok cites this passage only to supply the spiritual idea behind a possible reading of “Af”; the Zohar itself does not interpret the Semak’s wording. Compare Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim §12, where Rav Tzadok likewise discusses pegam ha-bris in Zoharic terms while stressing that teshuvah cleanses the defect and reveals Israel’s underlying holiness.
אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ הוּא בַּבָּרַיְיתָא דְּנִדָּה שָׁם, וּדְמַסַּיֵּים עַל זֶה: ״בְּיָד וּבְרֶגֶל״, אִם אֵין לוֹמַר כֵּן
except that this is not the text in the Baraisa of Niddah there, and it concludes upon it: "by hand and by foot," unless one says thus:
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דִּלְפִי דַּעַת הָרַמְבַּ״ם הָיָה הַגִּירְסָא: ״דָּבָר אַחֵר: אֵלּוּ הַמְנָאֲפִים בְּיָד וּבְרֶגֶל״, וְזֶהוּ דְּרָשׁ אַחֵר

And one must say that according to the opinion of the Rambam the textual reading was: "Another explanation (davar acher): these are those who commit adultery by hand and by foot," this being a distinct exegesis

[680Pesikta Rabbati 24 — an independent “lo tehaneh ha-af” tradition: On “lo tinaf,” the Midrash reads “lo tehaneh ha-af mimek.” This supplies a source outside the printed Niddah for the phrase and supports Rav Tzadok’s suggestion that the Semak may have drawn it from another baraisa or midrash. The Pesikta does not contain Rav Tzadok’s proposed words “davar acher,” so separating the two derashos in that exact form remains Rav Tzadok’s textual reconstruction.ואולי גם בסמ"ק יש חיסור לשון וצריך לומר תחלה כלשון הגמרא ואחר כך דבר אחר לא תהנה לאף
[and perhaps in the Semak too there is a textual omission, and it should read initially like the language of the Gemara and afterward: "Another explanation: do not derive pleasure in the nose";
וְאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁדָּבָר זֶה לוּקַּח מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר וּמֵאֵיזֶה בָּרַיְיתָא אַחֶרֶת וְאֵינוֹ בַּבָּרַיְיתָא דְּנִדָּה כְּלָל
and it is possible that this phrase was taken from elsewhere and from some other Baraisa, and is not in the Baraisa of Niddah at all;
אֲבָל רָאִיתִי בַּסְּמַ״ק כְּתַב יָד יָשָׁן עַל קְלָף מִשְּׁנַת ק״ט גַּם כֵּן הַגִּירְסָא כִּבִדְפוּס]:
but I saw in an ancient parchment manuscript of the Semak from the year 5109 [1349 CE] that the reading is likewise identical to the printed edition].

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ח׳–י״א

The theme: Analyzing the Rambam’s interpretation of “adulterers by hand and by foot” (menafim b’yad u’v’regel). In his Commentary on the Mishnah, the Rambam interprets this not as wasteful emission, but as unnatural, licentious manual or pedal stimulation with a married woman. The Talmudic phrase “by foot” cannot literally describe self-stimulation, which would require the term “thighs” (yerechayim).
