Because adultery biblically pertains to a married woman (eshes ish), the Rambam establishes this act under the biblical negative injunction “do not draw near to uncover nakedness” (lo sikrevu), punishable by lashes, while viewing the homiletic link to “lo tin’af” as a stringency without practical halachic bearing.

p: וְהִנֵּה מִפֵּירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָיוֹת הַנַּזְכָּר לְעֵיל מְבוֹאָר פֵּירוּשׁ אַחֵר עַל הָא דִּ״בְיָד וָרֶגֶל״ גַּם כֵּן
And behold, from the aforementioned Commentary on the Mishnah a different interpretation is clarified regarding that [dictum] of "by hand and by foot" as well:
דְּאֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר אַהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּיָד וָרֶגֶל, רַק עַל הַמַּכְנִיס וּמְמָעֵךְ בְּאֶצְבְּעוֹת יָדָיו אוֹ רַגְלָיו בְּאִשָּׁה כְּדֶרֶךְ נִיאוּף

that it did not intend to refer to the wasteful emission of seed by hand and by foot, but rather to one who inserts and rubs with the fingers of his hands or his feet in a woman in the manner of adultery.
וְאַף דִּבְנִדָּה שָׁם מִקַּמֵּי הָכִי אִיתָא לְשׁוֹן ״הַמְנָאֲפִים בַּיָּד״ עַל פָּסוּק ״יְדֵיכֶם דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ״, דְּקָאֵי אַעֲוֹן זֶה דְּשַׁיָּיךְ ״דָּמִים מָלֵאוּ״

And although in Niddah [13b] prior to this there is found the expression "those who commit adultery by hand" upon the verse "your hands are full of blood" (Yeshayah 1:15), which refers to this iniquity where "full of blood" applies;
וְכֵן הוּא בָּרַמְבַּ״ם [בְּהִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה שָׁם] לָשׁוֹן זֶה אַעֲוֹן זֶה
and so it is in the Rambam [Hilchos Issurei Biah 21:18], this expression regarding this iniquity:
שָׁם נָקַט רַק ״יָד״, וְכֵן בַּקְּרָא כְּתִיב רַק ״יְדֵיכֶם״, אֲבָל בְּרֶגֶל מַמָּשׁ לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ

there it cited only "hand," and likewise in the verse it is written only "your hands," whereas with an actual foot you cannot find it [for self-emission];681Niddah 13b; Yeshayah 1:15; Rambam, Issurei Biah 21:18 — two adjacent formulations: The Gemara first explains “your hands are full of blood” as referring to “those who commit adultery with the hand,” and immediately afterward records the academy of R’ Yishmael’s exposition of “lo tinaf” as adultery “with hand or foot.” Rambam applies the first formulation specifically to wasteful emission and likewise speaks only of the hand. Rav Tzadok argues that this does not determine the second teaching: if it begins a separate unit, Rambam’s Peirush HaMishnayos can read “hand and foot” as sexual contact with a forbidden woman. The separation of the two clauses is Rav Tzadok’s analysis; the printed Gemara itself places them consecutively.
וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים לָאו אוֹרְחֵיהּ לְשַׁפְשֵׁף בָּאֵבֶר לְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, וְלֹא הֲוָה לֵיהּ לוֹמַר ״רֶגֶל״ אֶלָּא ״יְרֵכַיִם״
and in any event it is not the usual way to rub against the organ for wasteful emission, and it should not have said "foot" but rather "thighs" (yerechayim).
וְאַף דִּמְצִינוּ בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי בִּקְרָאֵי דְּקָרְאוּ גַּם לַיְּרֵכַיִם ״רַגְלַיִם״, כְּבָר אָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת ק״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] בְּכוּלְּהוּ דְּהוּא לְלִישָׁנָא מְעַלְּיָא

And although we find in several places in Scripture that they termed even the thighs "feet," they already stated [in Yevamos 103a] regarding all of them that this is an expression of euphemism (lishana me'alya);
וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ כְּלָל הָכָא גַּבֵּי הַמְנָאֲפִים בְּעַצְמָם, דְּשַׁפִּיר הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר בָּזֶה ״יְרֵכַיִם״

and it does not apply here at all regarding the adulterers themselves, where it could well have said in this context "thighs."682Yevamos 103a — “feet” as a euphemism for the thighs or private area: While defining the anatomical boundary of regel for chalitzah, the Gemara tests verses that seem to use “feet” for the upper leg or private area. It first explains Devarim 28:57 by the birthing position, and then calls the expressions in II Shemuel 19:25, I Shemuel 24:4, Shoftim 3:24, and Shoftim 5:27 “lishana ma’alya,” refined euphemistic speech. Rav Tzadok’s point is that this convention does not naturally explain a technical description of the offenders themselves: there the baraisa could have stated “thighs” directly if that were its intended physical mechanism.
גַּם מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״רֶגֶל״ לְשׁוֹן יָחִיד, וּבְחַד יָרֵךְ לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ לְהַקִּיף הָאֵבֶר כְּבְיָד, וְהָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר לְשׁוֹן רַבִּים
Also, what they said "foot" in the singular: for with one thigh you cannot find the ability to enclose the organ as with a hand, so it should have used the plural;
וְגַם מֵהָא דְּדָרְשִׁינַן עַל ״לֹא תִנְאָף״, וַחֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה אָמְרוּ דְּאֵין נִיאוּף אֶלָּא בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ
and also from the fact that we expound it upon "You shall not commit adultery," and the Sages of blessed memory stated that adultery applies only to a married woman,
רָצָה לוֹמַר דְּאִין הָכִי נַמֵּי גַּם הָכָא בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ קָאֵי, אֶלָּא שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְנָאֵף מַמָּשׁ בְּאֵבְרוֹ רַק בְּיָד וָרֶגֶל

it means that indeed here too it refers to a married woman, except that he does not commit actual adultery with his organ, but rather with hand and foot;683Rashi on Shemos 20:13 and Devarim 5:17 — ni’uf denotes adultery with a married woman: Rashi states that the Torah’s term ni’uf refers specifically to relations with an eshes ish, citing the formulations of Vayikra 20:10 and Yechezkel 16:32. Rav Tzadok applies that lexical rule to the derashah in Niddah: “with hand and foot” would still concern an eshes ish, although the prohibited act is performed through other limbs rather than intercourse. Neither Rashi nor the cited verses spell out that extension; it is Rav Tzadok’s inference from the continued use of the word ni’uf.
וְאַיְידֵי דְּמַיְיתֵי לְעֵיל ״מְנָאֵף בַּיָּד״ דְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, מַיְיתֵי גַּם כֵּן מִין אַחֵר מִמְּנָאֲפִים בְּיָד וָרֶגֶל, וְלֹא קָאֵי אַקּוֹדֵם
and since it cited above "committing adultery by hand" regarding wasteful emission, it likewise cited another category of adulterers by hand and foot, and it does not connect to the preceding case.

וְאַף דִּבְרִי״ף [פֶּרֶק ח׳ שְׁרָצִים] הַגִּירְסָא ״כִּדְתָנֵי דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל וְכוּלֵיהּ״ וּמַיְיתֵי לַהּ אַדִּלְעֵיל, וְכֵן הָא דִּמְסַיֵּים עֲלַהּ ״קְרֵי בֵּיהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ מַשְׁמַע כֵּן כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל

And although in the Rif [Shabbos, ch. 8] the reading is "as was taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael, etc." and he connects it to the preceding, and likewise the fact that it concludes upon it "read into it, etc." implies thus as I wrote above;
וְגַם בְּהָרַב הַמַּגִּיד [בְּהִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה] הֶעְתִּיק הַלָּשׁוֹן ״דִּתְנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and also the Maggid Mishneh [Hilchos Issurei Biah] transcribed the text as "taught in the school of Rabbi Yishmael," see there;684Rif, Shabbos, ch. Shemoneh Sheratzim; Maggid Mishneh, Issurei Biah 21:18; Niddah 13b — the opening connective: The Rif’s wording “ke-detanna d’vei R’ Yishmael” explicitly joins the hand-and-foot derashah to the preceding statement about “adulterers with the hand,” and the Maggid Mishneh preserves a similarly connective wording. The standard printed Bavli begins simply “tanna d’vei R’ Yishmael,” which can be read as a new teaching. Rav Tzadok therefore proposes that Rambam’s text lacked the opening connective and that he treated the passage independently. This is a reconstruction of Rambam’s textual basis, not an explicit manuscript report in the Rif or Maggid Mishneh.
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר לִפְנֵי רַמְבַּ״ם הָיָה הַגִּירְסָא ״תָּנָא דְּבֵי רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל״ בְּלֹא דָּלֶ״ת כִּלְפָנֵינוּ, וּמְפָרֵשׁ לַהּ עִנְיָן בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ
one can say that before the Rambam the reading was "The school of Rabbi Yishmael taught" without the letter dalet [meaning "for"], just as in our text, and he explains it as an independent matter;
וְלֹא זָכַר עַל זֶה הַדְּרָשׁ מִ״לֹא תִנְאָף״, כִּי דַּאֲדְרָשָׁא לָא מַלְקִינַן
and he made no mention regarding this of the derashah from "You shall not commit adultery," because based on an exegesis (derasha) they do not administer lashes;
וְהוּא מַיְיתֵי עַל זֶה לָאו גָּמוּר דְּ״לֹא תִקְרְבוּ״ לְמַלְקוּת גַּם כֵּן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and he brings for this the complete negative commandment "Do not approach" (Vayikra 18:6) for lashes as well, as mentioned above.
וְהָא דִּדְרָשׁוּהוּ גַּם כֵּן מִ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ הוּא לְהַחְמִיר עָלָיו, לוֹמַר שֶׁקְּרָא אַחְשְׁבֵיהּ לְהַאי כִּמְנָאֵף מַמָּשׁ
And that they expounded it also from "You shall not commit adultery" was to be stringent upon him, to indicate that Scripture considered this one as a literal adulterer;
וּבְחִיבּוּרוֹ לֹא כָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם זֶה, דְּאִיסּוּרוֹ וְחִיּוּב מַלְקוּת הוּא לָמַד מִכְּלַל חִבּוּק וְנִישּׁוּק וּמִקַּל וָחֹמֶר דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים דְּהָוֵי קְרֵיבָה, וְלֹא צָרִיךְ לְפָרֵשׁ

and in his Code the Rambam did not write this, because its prohibition and liability to lashes he derived from the general category of embracing and kissing and by an a fortiori argument that in any event it constitutes illicit proximity (kerivah), and he had no need to elaborate;
וְהַחֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ שֶׁדְּרָשׁוּהוּ מִקְּרָא דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ אֵין בּוֹ נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לְדִינָא
and the stringency within it, that they expounded it from the verse "You shall not commit adultery," has no practical halachic difference.

items.h: The theme: According to the Rambam, there is no scriptural derashah linking wasteful emission to "lo tin'af". In his Commentary on the Mishnah, the Rambam attributes the severe warnings against erection and emission to rabbinic elaboration (chachamim bi'arahu), explicitly noting that courts do not administer lashes for such acts. R' Tzadok clarifies that the phrase "they do not obligate lashes" excludes even rabbinic disciplinary lashes (makas mardus), for in that same context the Rambam uses the unqualified word "lashes" to refer to rabbinic floggings for illicit seclusion (yichud).

p: וּלְפִי זֶה לָרַמְבַּ״ם לֵיכָּא שׁוּם דְּרָשׁ מִקְּרָא דְּ״לֹא תִנְאָף״ אַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
And according to this, according to the Rambam there is no scriptural derashah from the verse "You shall not commit adultery" regarding one who emits seed wastefully.
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָה אַחַר כָּךְ כָּתַב: ״וּכְבָר הִזְהִירוּ חֲכָמִים הַרְבֵּה עַל הַהִרְהוּר וְכוּלֵיהּ
And see there in the Commentary on the Mishnah afterward, he wrote: "And the Sages have already warned extensively against sinful contemplation, etc.,

וְהֶאֱרִיכוּ לָשׁוֹן לְאַיֵּים וּלְהַפְחִיד כָּל הַמַּקְשֶׁה עַצְמוֹ לָדַעַת וְהַמּוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, וּבֵאֲרוּ שֶׁכָּל זֶה אָסוּר, אֲבָל אֵינָם מְחַיְּיבִין מַלְקוּת בְּשׁוּם דָּבָר בְּכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ״, עַד כָּאן

and extended their words to threaten and intimidate anyone who deliberately causes himself an erection and emits semen wastefully, and explained that all of this is forbidden; but they do not obligate lashes for anything comparable to it," thus far.685Rambam, Peirush HaMishnayos, Sanhedrin 7:4 — warnings without lashes: Rambam summarizes Niddah’s warnings against hirhur, deliberate arousal, and wasteful emission, then states that they are forbidden but carry no lashes. Since he cites verses and assigns lashes elsewhere in this exposition, Rav Tzadok infers that Rambam does not derive wasteful emission from “lo tinaf.” This classification is Rav Tzadok’s inference.
הִנֵּה יִיחֵס אִיסּוּר זֶה לַחֲכָמִים שֶׁבֵּאֲרוּהוּ, וְלֹא מַיְיתֵי עָלֶיהָ שׁוּם דְּרָשׁ מִקְּרָא כִּדְמַיְיתֵי לִפְנֵי זֶה אַמֵּרִיחַ כַּנַּ״ל
Behold, he attributed this prohibition to the Sages who explained it, and did not cite for it any scriptural derashah as he cited prior to this regarding smelling perfumes, as mentioned above.
[וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב ״דְּאֵינָם מְחַיְּיבִין מַלְקוּת״ נִרְאֶה דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר גַּם מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת וּמַלְקוּת דְּרַבָּנָן
[And what he wrote, that "they do not obligate lashes," it appears means even makas mardus and rabbinic lashes;
דְּשָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה כָּתַב: כְּשֶׁיִּתְיַיחֵד עִם הָעֶרְוָה אוֹ עִם פְּנוּיָה מַלְקִין לִשְׁנֵיהֶם, וְהוּא מֵהַגְּמָרָא [קִדּוּשִׁין פ״א עַמּוּד א׳], וְרָצָה לוֹמַר מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת דְּרַבָּנָן

for there prior to this he wrote: when one is secluded with a forbidden relation (ervah) or with an unmarried woman (penuyah), they administer lashes to both, which is from the Gemara [Kiddushin 81a], and he meant rabbinic makas mardus,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַשִׁ״י, דְּמַלְקוּת דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא לֵיכָּא אֲפִילּוּ בְּיִחוּד דְּעֶרְוָה, דְּמַיְיתֵי [שָׁם פ׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] רֶמֶז מֵהַתּוֹרָה מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין בּוֹ אַזְהָרַת לָאו

as Rashi stated, that biblical lashes do not exist even for seclusion with an ervah, for although they cite a scriptural allusion [Kiddushin 80b], it nonetheless contains no formal negative prohibition;686Kiddushin 81a and Rashi — yichud receives makkos mardus: Rav states “malkin al ha-yichud”; Rav Ashi ordinarily limits this to a penuyah to avoid suspicion concerning a married woman’s children. Rashi glosses “malkin” as “mardus,” and Rambam likewise excludes an eshes ish. Thus unqualified “lashes” can mean rabbinic disciplinary lashes.687Kiddushin 80b — a Torah remez, not an explicit lav: R’ Yochanan derives a Torah remez from a son’s permitted seclusion with his mother, implying prohibition with other arayos. The verse’s plain subject is idolatrous enticement. Rav Tzadok therefore sees an allusion without an explicit lav, so ordinary Torah lashes do not follow; that conclusion is his inference.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן יִחוּד דִּפְנוּיָה דְּהוּא מִגְּזֵירַת בֵּית דִּינוֹ שֶׁל דָּוִד כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כ״א רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳]
and all the more so seclusion with a penuyah, which is an enactment from the court of King David, as found [in Sanhedrin 21b];
וַהֲרֵי דְּקָרֵי גַּם לְמַכַּת מַרְדּוּת שָׁם בִּסְתָם ״מַלְקוּת״
and behold, he termed even makas mardus there with the unqualified word "lashes";
וְאִם כֵּן כָּאן שֶׁמִּיעֵט מִמַּלְקוּת, הַיְינוּ גַּם מִמַּכַּת מַרְדּוּת הַקּוֹדֵם
and if so, here where he excluded from lashes, it means even from the aforementioned makas mardus;
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר לְשׁוֹן ״אֵינָם מְחַיְּיבִים״, דְּהַיְינוּ שֶׁהַחֲכָמִים לֹא חִיְּיבוּ עַל זֶה מַלְקוּת, וְזֶהוּ מַכַּת מַרְדּוּת שֶׁמֵּחִיּוּב חֲכָמִים]:

and therefore he used the phrase "they do not obligate," meaning that the Sages did not obligate lashes for this, which refers to makas mardus that stems from rabbinic obligation].688Sanhedrin 21b and Avodah Zarah 36b — David’s yichud decree: After Amnon and Tamar, Rav Yehudah reports David’s decree. Avodah Zarah distinguishes Torah-level yichud with an eshes ish, David’s extension to a penuyah, and the later extension to a non-Jewish woman; Yad Ramah discusses the wording. Thus penuyah-yichud is rabbinic and its lashes are makkos mardus.

items.h: The theme: The consensus of the Rishonim and the Zohar (Vayeshev 188a) applies "by hand or foot" to wasteful emission. Being derived by exegesis rather than an explicit negative command, it atones through repentance alone according to the Asarah Ma'amaros, or at least in conjunction with Yom Kippur. While the Shulchan Aruch (Even HaEzer 23) notes that this sin is "more severe than all transgressions in the Torah" based on the Zohar (which compares it to murder, destroying one's own children), halachic reality proves it cannot be literally worse than murder: murder carries court execution and requires martyrdom (yehareg v'al ya'avor), whereas this sin carries no lashes and is set aside to save a mother's life (Ohalos 7:6).

p: וּמִיהוּ כָּל הָרִאשׁוֹנִים מְפָרְשֵׁי לַהּ אַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
Nevertheless, all the Rishonim explain it as referring to one who emits seed wastefully;

וְגַם בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב קפ״ח עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וַיֵּרַע״ אִיתָא: ״וְאַפֵּיק זַרְעָא לְמַגָּנָא בִּידָא אוֹ בְּרַגְלָא״, הִזְכִּיר גַּם כֵּן לְשׁוֹן ״בְּרֶגֶל״ אַהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
and in the Holy Zohar [Vayeshev 188a, s.v. vayera] it is stated: "and emitted seed in vain by hand or by foot," mentioning likewise the expression "by foot" regarding wasteful emission.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם, כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא רַק מִדְּרָשָׁא, אֶפְשָׁר דִּלְכוּלֵי עָלְמָא לֹא חֲמִיר מַעֲשֶׂה לְעִנְיַן תְּשׁוּבָה

And nevertheless, since it is derived solely from an exegesis (derasha), it is possible that according to all authorities its deed is not more severe than a positive commandment regarding repentance;689Niddah 13b; Zohar, Vayeshev 188a — “hand or foot” and spiritual defilement: Niddah places the teaching “lo tinaf — by hand or by foot” beside the phrase “adulterers with the hand.” The Rishonim discussed in the preceding se’ifim read it as wasteful emission. The Zohar states explicitly that one brings out seed in vain “by hand or by foot” and describes the resulting obstruction from the divine palace and the face of the Ancient of Days. Rav Tzadok accepts this identification here, while distinguishing the Zohar’s description of spiritual defilement from the formal halachic category and atonement process.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לְהָ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ דְּלֹא גָּרַע מִלָּאוִין שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין

and all the more so according to Asarah Ma'amaros, for it is no worse than negative commandments that do not incur lashes.690Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din I:18; Yoma 86a — atonement follows legal classification: Rema mi-Fano groups several Torah prohibitions that do not receive ordinary lashes with the lighter atonement class, analogous in this respect to a positive commandment. Yoma 86a supplies the underlying hierarchy of teshuvah and atonement. Rav Tzadok therefore argues that even if the “lo tinaf” derashah is Torah-based, its lack of an explicit, independently punishable lav may prevent it from receiving the full severity of an ordinary negative commandment. The precise placement of this offense is Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not an explicit ruling of Yoma or Asarah Maamaros.

וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּלֹא כְּהָ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״, וּדְגַם זֶה דְּלֵיכָּא לָאו מְפוֹרָשׁ — כֵּיוָן דְּאִיסּוּרוֹ מִן הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁלֹּא לַעֲשׂוֹת, וְעוֹבֵר בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה וְלֹא בְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה כִּבְשֵׁב וְאַל תַּעֲשֶׂה, לָא דָּמֵי לְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה

And even if you say that the halachah does not follow the Asarah Ma'amaros, and that even where there is no explicit negative command, since its biblical prohibition is a command of restraint yet breached through active commission (kum ve-aseh) rather than passive omission (shev ve-al ta'aseh), it does not resemble a positive commandment:
עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּצֵירוּף יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מִיהַת מְכַפֵּר כְּמוֹ שֶׁיִּתְבָּאֵר בַּחֲלוּקָּה הַב׳
in any event, in combination with Yom Kippur it certainly atones, as will be explained in the second category of atonement.
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁמְּבוֹאָר [בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סוֹף סִימָן כ״ג] דַּעֲוֹן זֶה חָמוּר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה
And although it is stated [in Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 23:1] that this iniquity is more severe than all transgressions in the Torah,
עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל דְּלָאו דַּוְוקָא, וְאִיסּוּר כָּרֵת [דְּנִדָּה] חָמוּר מִינֵּיהּ

see the Beis Shmuel there that this is not literal, for an offense of spiritual excision (kares) such as intercourse with a niddah is more severe than it;691Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 23:1; Beis Shmuel — “more severe than all sins” is not a literal halachic ranking: Shulchan Aruch calls the offense “more severe than all transgressions in the Torah,” following the Beis Yosef’s citation of the Zohar. Beis Shmuel, citing the practical comparison recorded by Chelkas Mechokek from Sefer Chassidim, explains that the phrase cannot mean that it overrides every formally graver prohibition; a kareis-level sexual prohibition is certainly more severe in halachic consequence. Rav Tzadok reads the formulation as exceptional severity among offenses of a comparable legal class, without minimizing the Zohar’s warning.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף דְּהֵבִיא זֶה מֵהַזֹּוהַר, וְהוּא [בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שָׁם] דְּ״בְכָל חוֹבִין דְּאִסְתָּאַב בַּר נָשׁ בְּהַאי עָלְמָא, דָּא אִיהוּ חוֹבָא דְּאִסְתָּאִיב בֵּיהּ יַתִּיר בְּהַאי עָלְמָא וּבְעָלְמָא דְּאָתֵי״, עַד כָּאן

and see the Beis Yosef there who cited this from the Zohar [Vayeshev 188a]: "of all the sins whereby a man defiles himself in this world, this is the sin through which he is defiled most in this world and in the World to Come," thus far.

וְאַף דִּסְתִימוּת לְשׁוֹן הַזֹּוהַר וְשֻׁלְחָן עָרוּךְ הַנַּ״ל ״חָמִיר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת מַמָּשׁ״, אֶפְשָׁר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁכַּיּוֹצֵא בוֹ קָאָמְרֵי שֶׁאֵין עֲלֵיהֶם אֲפִילּוּ אִיסּוּר לָאו מְפוֹרָשׁ, וְלֹא מֵהַחֲמוּרוֹת מֵהֶם

And although the plain wording of the Zohar and the Shulchan Aruch implies literally more severe than all transgressions, it is possible they meant more severe than all comparable transgressions that lack an explicit scriptural prohibition, and not more severe than those inherently weightier.

וּמִיהוּ בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [פָּרָשַׁת וַיְחִי רי״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] אִיתָא: ״וּלְהַאי טָרְדִין בְּהַהוּא עָלְמָא יַתִּיר מִכּוּלְּהוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְכוּלְּהוּ סָלְקִין וְהַאי לָא סָלֵיק, וְאִם תֹּאמַר שְׁאָר חַיָּיבִין דְּקָטְלֵי בַּר נָשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ, אִינּוּן קָטְלֵי בַּר נָשׁ אָחֳרָא וְהַאי קָטִיל בְּנוֹי וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

However, in the Holy Zohar [Vayechi 219b] it is taught: "And this one they banish in that world more than all of them... and all ascend whereas this one does not ascend; and if you say what of other sinners who kill a man, they kill another man while this one kills his own children, etc.," see there;692Zohar, Vayechi 219b — “all ascend, but this one does not ascend”: The Zohar calls one who destroys his seed “evil,” compares the act to killing his own children, and describes a unique obstruction to seeing the Shechinah and ascending from judgment. Rav Tzadok does not dismiss this language. He argues that it describes a particularly deep spiritual blemish and impediment to ascent, not a formal equation with intentional murder for court punishment, yehareg ve’al ya’avor, or the standard categories of teshuvah. That distinction between mystical consequence and halachic classification is Rav Tzadok’s own resolution.
וְהִנֵּה מַשְׁמַע דְּעָנְשׁוֹ חָמוּר מֵרוֹצֵחַ גָּמוּר שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים
and behold, this implies that his punishment is more severe than a literal murderer who sheds blood!
אֲבָל הוּא דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא נִיתַּן לֵיאָמֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אִיסּוּר זֶה חָמוּר מִשְּׁפִיכַת דָּמִים מַמָּשׁ שֶׁחַיָּיבִין עָלָיו מִיתָה, וּבְהַהִיא אֲפִילּוּ מַלְקוּת לֵיכָּא
But this is something that cannot be said: that this prohibition should be more severe than literal bloodshed for which one is executed by court, whereas in this sin there are not even lashes;
וְרוֹצֵחַ ״יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבוֹר״, וּבְהַהִיא פְּשִׁיטָא דְּלָא אָמְרִינַן ״יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבוֹר״, וּמוּתָּר לְצֹרֶךְ רְפוּאַת גּוּפוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת פְּנֵי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ שָׁם

and regarding a murderer the law is "be killed and do not transgress" (Sanhedrin 74a), whereas in this sin it is obvious that we do not say "be killed and do not transgress," and it is permitted for medical healing as they stated in the responsa of Pnei Yehoshua there;
וְהֵבִיא רְאָיָה מִמִּשְׁנָה [סוֹף פֶּרֶק ז׳ דְּאָהֳלוֹת] שֶׁמְּחַתְּכִין הַוָּלָד בְּמֵעֶיהָ שֶׁחַיֶּיהָ קוֹדְמִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and he brought proof from the Mishnah [Ohalos 7:6] that they dismember a fetus within its mother's womb to save her, because her life takes precedence, see there.693Responsa Pnei Yehoshua II §44; Ohalos 7:6; Sanhedrin 74a — medical need and the limits of the murder analogy: Pnei Yehoshua permits the act when physicians determine that it is certainly needed for treatment, reasoning that the comparisons to bloodshed and forbidden relations express gravity rather than the formal rule of yehareg ve’al ya’avor. He supports this by an a fortiori argument from Ohalos: before birth, a fetus endangering its mother may be dismembered because her life takes precedence; once the head emerges, one life may not be displaced for another. The Mishnah does not directly classify semen as a fetus. Rav Tzadok uses the responsum to show that the Zoharic murder comparison cannot create the legal status of murder established in Sanhedrin 74a.

items.h: The theme: The Zoharic severity of this sin pertains specifically to metaphysical estrangement from the Divine Presence ("does not gaze upon the countenance of the Shechinah"). The Zohar does not describe worse physical torments in Gehinnom than for other transgressions, but rather an absolute spiritual barrier preventing entry into supernal chambers (palterin). This explains the phrase "and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem" (vayerah b'einei Hashem): the offense is uniquely severe specifically in the "eyes of Hashem," signifying an inward blemish that repels intimacy with the Creator.

p: אֲבָל שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה בֵּאֲרוּ בְּעָנְשׁוֹ דְּ״לָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא״
But there prior to this they explained regarding his punishment that "he does not behold the countenance of the Shechinah";
וְכֵן [בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיֵּשֶׁב שָׁם] דְּ״לָא עָאל וְלָא חָמֵי סְבַר אַפֵּי עַתִּיק יוֹמִין״
and likewise [in Parashas Vayeshev there] that "he does not enter and does not gaze upon the pleasant countenance of the Ancient of Days";
וְכֵן [בְּפָרָשַׁת בְּרֵאשִׁית שָׁם] דְּ״לָא עָאל בִּפְלַטְרִין וְלָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא״
and likewise [in Parashas Bereishis 57a] that "he does not enter the royal palace (palterin) and does not behold the countenance of the Shechinah";
וְכֵן [בְּפָרָשַׁת אֱמֹר צ׳ עַמּוּד א׳] רֵישׁ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְלָא״
and likewise [in Parashas Emor 90a, start of s.v. v'la].
הִנֵּה עִם כָּל תּוֹקֶף הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבַּעֲוֹן זֶה, לֹא אָמְדוּ בָּזֶה עָנְשֵׁי גֵּיהִנָּם חֲמוּרִים בְּיוֹתֵר מִבִּשְׁאָר עֲבֵירוֹת

Behold, with all the intensity of the impurity in this iniquity, they did not assess for it harsher punishments of Gehinnom than for other sins;694Zohar, Vayechi 219b; Vayeshev 188a; Bereishis 57a; Emor 90a — barred from the presence of the Shechinah: These passages apply Tehillim 5:5, “evil shall not dwell with You,” to the Torah’s description of Er and Onan as “evil in the eyes of Hashem” (Bereishis 38:7, 10). They call the offender ra and bar him from the heavenly palace and from beholding the Shechinah or Atik Yomin; Vayechi adds that other guilty souls ascend while this one does not. A parallel in Zohar Mishpatim uses the same language. Rav Tzadok infers that the distinctive emphasis is exclusion from divine proximity and higher ascent, not an explicitly greater Gehinnom punishment.
רַק כָּל חֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ בְּהֶעְדֵּר הַמַּעֲלָה דִּרְאִיַּית פְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה, וּמְנִיעַת הַכְּנִיסָה לְמַדְרֵיגוֹת עֶלְיוֹנוֹת
but rather its entire severity consists in the deprivation of the supreme attainment of beholding the Divine Presence, and the withholding of entry into the highest rungs.
וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן ״הַאי לָא סָלֵיק״ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין עוֹלֶה לְמַעֲלָה עֶלְיוֹנָה
And likewise, the expression "this one does not ascend" mentioned above means that he does not ascend to the supernal height;
וְכִדִמְסַיֵּים שָׁם גַּם כֵּן דְּ״לֵית לָן חַיָּיבַיָּא דְּלָא חָמֵי אַפֵּי שְׁכִינְתָּא בַּר מֵהַאי״
and as it concludes there as well: "we have no sinner who does not behold the face of the Shechinah except for this one."
וּבְפָרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל [רי״ד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּ״לֵית חוֹבָא דְּקַשְׁיָא קַמֵּיהּ קֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא כְּהַאי וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַל חוֹבָא דָּא כְּתִיב: ׳וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳׳ וְגוֹמֵר״

And in Parashas Vayakhel [214b]: "there is no sin as severe before the Holy One, blessed be He, as this, etc.; regarding this sin it is written: 'And it was evil in the eyes of Hashem' (Bereishis 38:10)."695Zohar, Vayakhel 214b; Bereishis 38:7, 10 — “evil in the eyes of Hashem” specifically: The Zohar calls this sin uniquely difficult “before the Holy One” and cites the Torah’s description of Er and Onan as “evil in the eyes of Hashem.” Rav Tzadok reads the wording precisely: its exceptional severity concerns the divine “eyes,” the Shechinah and closeness to Hashem, rather than the formal halachic ranking of punishments. That distinction is Rav Tzadok’s own analysis.
הִנֵּה בְּכָאן פֵּירֵשׁ שֶׁקּוֹשִׁי חֵטְא זֶה מִכָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת הוּא קַמֵּיהּ קֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא דַּוְוקָא, דְּמַיְיתֵי עַל זֶה קְרָא דְּ״בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״, דְּלֹא נִמְצָא כֵּן בְּחֵטְא אַחֵר

Behold, here he explained that the singular severity of this sin above all other transgressions is specifically before the Holy One, blessed be He, for he cites concerning this the verse "in the eyes of Hashem," which is not found formulated thus with any other sin;
וְכֵן בְּעֵר נֶאֱמַר ״רַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״ (שָׁם:ז׳), וּבְכָל הָנֵי דּוּכְתֵּי בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ מַיְיתֵי גַּם כֵּן מִקְרָא הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and likewise regarding Er it is said "was wicked in the eyes of Hashem" (Bereishis 38:7), and in all these passages in the Holy Zohar it cites this verse as well;
וְכְלַפֵּי עֵינֵי ה׳ דַּיְיקָא עָוֹן זֶה חָמוּר וְרַע יוֹתֵר מֵהַכֹּל:
and specifically toward the eyes of Hashem is this iniquity judged more severe and evil than everything.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים י״ב–ט״ו

The theme: Resolving the apparent paradox of this sin's severity. Relative to human jurisprudence, the world of angels, and actual physical damage, sins carrying Torah lashes, court executions, or spiritual excision (kares) are far weightier. The Zohar’s assessment that this sin is worse than all transgressions refers strictly to "in the eyes of Hashem"—the spiritual contamination (tum'ah) that repels the Shechinah and stains the intellectual soul (nefesh hasichlis) within the heart. This parallels the Talmudic dictum that "sinful thoughts are worse than the sin itself" (hirhurei aveirah kashim me-aveirah, Yoma 29a), which addresses internal psychic defilement rather than earthly liability.

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר לְפִי זֶה שַׁפִּיר, דְּדַוְוקָא הוּא נֶגֶד כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת כּוּלָּם בְּעִנְיַן הַטּוּמְאָה הַמְרַחֶקֶת מִפְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה וּכְלַפֵּי שְׁמַיָּא דַּוְוקָא

And one can well say according to this: it is specifically weighed against all transgressions in the category of the spiritual defilement that estranges from the presence of the Shechinah, and specifically relative to Heaven;
אֲבָל מִצַּד הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וַאֲפִילּוּ מִצַּד עוֹלַם הַמַּלְאָכִים, וַדַּאי כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁהֶחְמִירָה תּוֹרָה בְּאַזְהָרָתָם וּבְעָנְשָׁם הֵם חֲמוּרִים יוֹתֵר

whereas from the perspective of man in this world, and even from the perspective of the world of angels, certainly all the transgressions regarding which the Torah was stringent in their prohibition and punishment are far more severe;
וְדָחֵי הָא מִקַּמֵּי הָא כְּדִבְרֵי הַסֵּפֶר חֲסִידִים שֶׁמֵּבִיא בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל שָׁם
and this sets aside that, in accordance with the words of Sefer Chassidim cited in the Beis Shmuel there [Even HaEzer 23];

אוֹ לְעִנְיַן ״יֵהָרֵג וְאַל יַעֲבוֹר״ וּלְהִתְרַפֹּאות לִדְחוֹתָהּ מִפְּנֵי פִּיקּוּחַ נֶפֶשׁ, דִּכְשֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אוֹתָם מִצַּד הַדִּין שֶׁנִּדְחָה מִפְּנֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר הֶחָמוּר, שׁוּב גַּם בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ אֵינוֹ רַע

or regarding the principle of "be killed and do not transgress," and undergoing medical healing to set it aside in the face of saving life (pikuach nefesh), for when one performs them according to the halachic ruling that it is overridden before a weightier consideration, it is no longer evil in the eyes of Hashem either.696Shulchan Arukh, Even HaEzer 23:1; Beit Shmuel ad loc.; Sefer Chassidim — mystical severity versus operative halachah: Shulchan Arukh repeats the Zoharic description that this offense is “more severe than all transgressions.” Beit Shmuel, quoting Sefer Chassidim, shows that the phrase is not a literal ranking for practical law: where a person faces a graver forbidden relationship, the lesser wrong does not displace the Torah’s formal hierarchy, and danger to life likewise governs according to ordinary halachic rules. Rav Tzadok uses this distinction to say that an act permitted or required by a higher rule is not “evil in the eyes of Hashem”; the exceptional severity concerns spiritual distance from the Shechinah, not a new rule of yehareg ve’al ya’avor or pikuach nefesh.

וְגוּף חֹמֶר הָאִיסּוּרִים לְעִנְיַן דִּיחוּי וְכַיּוֹצֵא בְּכָל דָּבָר דְּנַפְקָא מִינַּהּ לְדִינָא וּלְגַבֵּי הָאָדָם, הוּא כְּפִי חוּמְרֵי הָאַזְהָרוֹת וְהָעֳנָשִׁים הַמְפוֹרָשִׁים בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁאָנוּ רוֹאִים שֶׁהֶחְמִירָה בְּאֵיזֶה דָּבָר

And the essential severity of prohibitions regarding precedence and any practical halachic ramification concerning man is determined strictly by the severity of the warnings and punishments made explicit in the Torah, wherever we see that it treated an issue stringently;
וְגַם לְעִנְיַן עָנְשֵׁי שָׁמַיִם בְּגֵיהִנָּם וַדַּאי הֵם חֲמוּרִים יוֹתֵר, וְאִם כֵּן הוּא עֹונֶשׁ שָׁמַיִם
and likewise regarding heavenly punishments in Gehinnom, [the explicit biblical crimes] are certainly more severe, since that is an explicit heavenly punishment;
אֲבָל חֹמֶר עָוֹן זֶה הוּא רַק בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ לְבַדּוֹ וּלְעִנְיַן הַהִתְקָרְבוּת לְפָנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ
but the singular gravity of this iniquity exists solely "in the eyes of Hashem" and regarding spiritual proximity before Him, may He be blessed.
וַהֲרֵי זֶה עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּיוֹמָא כ״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה קָשִׁים מֵעֲבֵירָה״

And behold, this follows the manner of that which is taught [in Yoma 29a]: "sinful thoughts are worse than the sin itself";697Yoma 29a and Rashi — “thoughts of transgression are harder than transgression”: The Gemara states that sinful thoughts are “harder” than the act and compares them to the appetite-provoking aroma of meat. Rashi explains “harder” physically: desire weakens the body more than the completed act. Rav Tzadok follows the broader reading found among other Rishonim and in Kad HaKemach—that thought can produce a deeper stain in the intellectual soul—while expressly maintaining that the deed remains more severe for punishment and practical halachah.
וְאַף דְּרַשִׁ״י שָׁם פֵּירֵשׁ ״קָשִׁים לַגּוּף״, כָּל הָרִאשׁוֹנִים לֹא פֵּירְשׁוּ כֵּן
and although Rashi there explained "harder on the physical body," all the Rishonim did not explain it thus;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ גַּם כֵּן בְּסֵפֶר כַּד הַקֶּמַח לְרַבֵּינוּ בַּחְיֵי [אוֹת טָהֳרַת הַלֵּב] לְפָרֵשׁ כִּפְשָׁטֵיהּ לְעִנְיַן קוֹשִׁי הַחֵטְא וְטוּמְאַת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, וּלְפִי שֶׁהַהִרְהוּר בַּלֵּב וּמְטַמֵּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַשִּׂכְלִית הַשּׁוֹכֶנֶת שָׁם, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

and as was likewise stated in Kad HaKemach of Rabbeinu Bachya [under Tohoras HaLev] explaining it according to its plain sense regarding the gravity of the sin and the defilement of the soul, since contemplation resides in the heart and defiles the intellectual soul that dwells there, see there at length.698Kad HaKemach, Taharas HaLev — thought defiles the intellectual soul: Rabbeinu Bachya distinguishes bodily traits, corrected through deeds, from intellectual traits, which govern thought. Because the soul’s root and human thought are closely joined, corrupt thought directly contaminates the soul dwelling in the heart; this is his explanation of Yoma’s statement that sinful thoughts are “harder.” Rav Tzadok adopts that soul-centered explanation only for the hidden, inward dimension before Hashem, not to reduce the greater legal severity of an actual transgression. Chovos HaLevavos similarly distinguishes inward duties known fully to the Creator from outward conduct judged by humanly revealed standards.
וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁמַּעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ בְּפֹעַל חֲמוּרָה הַרְבֵּה יוֹתֵר לְכָל דָּבָר מֵהַהִרְהוּר
And certainly the actual deed of transgression in practice is far more severe in every respect than the mere contemplation;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁטּוּמְאָתָהּ בַּנֶּפֶשׁ קָשָׁה יוֹתֵר, זֶהוּ רַק לִפְנֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הַבּוֹחֵן לְבָבוֹת שֶׁיִּרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב לְבַד
and even though its spiritual defilement within the soul is harsher, this is solely before the Blessed Name Who examines hearts, Who looks into the heart alone;
וְהוּא מִצַּד הַנִּסְתָּרוֹת אֲשֶׁר אֵין גָּלוּי אֶלָּא ״לַה׳ אֱלֹהֵינוּ, וְלָנוּ וּלְבָנֵינוּ הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹת אֶת כָּל דִּבְרֵי הַתּוֹרָה״
and this belongs to the hidden realms which are revealed only "unto Hashem our God, but the revealed things belong to us and to our children to do all the words of this law" (Devarim 29:28),
וְאֵין לָנוּ אֶלָּא כְּפִי מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה מַה שֶּׁהֶחְמִירָה בְּאַזְהָרוֹתֶיהָ:

and we have only that which aligns with the judgment of the Torah according to the stringencies of its explicit prohibitions.699I Samuel 16:7; Devarim 29:28 — Hashem sees the heart, while Torah law governs revealed action: Hashem tells Shmuel that a person sees what is visible, whereas Hashem “sees the heart.” Devarim assigns “the hidden things” to Hashem and “the revealed things” to us and our children “to perform all the words of this Torah.” Rav Tzadok joins the verses to separate two measures: Hashem alone assesses the concealed impurity of thought and inner distance, while human obligation and practical ranking follow the Torah’s revealed warnings and punishments. This synthesis is Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not an explicit legal rule stated by either verse.

items.h: The theme: The core evil of wasteful emission stems from the sinful contemplation (hirhur) that generates it. In Niddah 13b, the verse "and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem" (vayerah b'einei Hashem, spoken of Er and Onan) is applied to one who brings himself to lustful thoughts. Because Hashem does not combine an evil thought with action (machashavah ra'ah ein HaKadosh Baruch Hu mitztaref l'ma'aseh), punishment is incurred only when the obsessive thought culminates in physical emission. Because its core severity lies in the defilement of internal thought, it is healed through the internal repentance of the heart (u'levavo yavin v'shav v'rafa lo).

p: וְעָוֹן זֶה גַּם כֵּן נִמְשָׁךְ מֵהַהִרְהוּר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁחִבְּרָם רַמְבַּ״ם בְּפֵירוּשׁ הַמִּשְׁנָה שָׁם יַחַד
And this iniquity likewise is drawn from sinful contemplation, just as the Rambam linked them together in the Commentary on the Mishnah there;

וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בְּנִדָּה שָׁם]: ״כָּל הַמֵּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לִידֵי הִרְהוּר אֵין מַכְנִיסִין אוֹתוֹ בִּמְחִיצָתוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, כְּתִיב הָכָא: ׳וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳׳ וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and so they stated [in Niddah 13b]: "Whoever brings himself to lustful contemplation is not brought into the partition of the Holy One, blessed be He, for it is written here: 'And it was evil in the eyes of Hashem,' etc.," see there.
וְהִנֵּה קְרָא דְּ״וַיֵּרַע״ אַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה קָאֵי, שֶׁהָיָה דָּשׁ בִּפְנִים וְזוֹרֶה בַּחוּץ, וּמַיְיתֵי זֶה אַהִרְהוּר

Behold, the verse "and it was evil" refers to one who emits seed wastefully, for [Onan] threshed within and scattered without, yet the Talmud applies this to contemplation;700Rambam, Peirush HaMishnayos, Sanhedrin 7:4; Niddah 13a-b — thought, arousal, and the completed act: The Rambam groups the Sages’ warnings against sinful thought, deliberate arousal, and wasteful emission, while noting that these prohibitions do not carry lashes. Niddah first invokes Er and Onan and then states that one who brings himself to sinful thought is not admitted into the Holy One’s “compartment,” linking “it was evil in the eyes of Hashem” with “evil shall not dwell with You” (Tehillim 5:5). Rav Tzadok reads this sequence as showing that the act is the realized outcome of sustained thought, while the distinctive spiritual stain begins in the heart.
מְבוֹאָר מִזֶּה דְּעִיקַּר חֹמֶר עָוֹן זֶה, וּמַה דְּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳, הוּא מִפְּנֵי הַהִרְהוּר
it is clear from this that the essential gravity of this iniquity, and that which is "evil in the eyes of Hashem," is on account of the contemplation.

וּלְפִי שֶׁמַּחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה אֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְצָרֵף לְמַעֲשֶׂה, אֵין נֶעֱנָשׁ עָלֶיהָ אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיָּצָא לִפְעוֹל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה בְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה שֶׁהָא נִמְשָׁךְ וּבָא מֵהַהִרְהוּר

And since the Holy One, blessed be He, does not combine an evil thought with action (Kiddushin 40a), one is not punished for it until it issues into concrete action through the wasteful emission of seed, which was drawn and produced by that contemplation.701Kiddushin 40a — a bad thought is not joined to an act unless it “bears fruit”: The Gemara says that Hashem does not ordinarily combine a bad thought with a deed, but qualifies this: a thought that produces fruit is joined to the deed, whereas one that produces no fruit is not. Rav Tzadok applies that distinction here. Passing thought alone is not treated as the completed transgression; when the thought is deliberately prolonged until it issues in action, the deed embodies the thought and exposes its full severity.
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״מֵבִיא לְהִרְהוּר״, הַכַּוָּונָה בְּהִרְהוּר הַיּוֹצֵא לִפְעוֹל בְּמַעֲשֶׂה כְּמַעֲשֵׂה עֵר וְאוֹנָן דְּמַיְיתֵי
And also what they said, "whoever brings himself to contemplation," refers to contemplation that issues into actual deed like the acts of Er and Onan which it cites;
וּסְתָם מְהַרְהֵר הַמֵּבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְכָךְ, שֶׁהוּא הַמַּעֲמִיק בְּהִרְהוּרוֹ וְאֵינוֹ פּוֹסֵק, סוֹפוֹ לָבוֹא לְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה
and an ordinary contemplator who brings himself to this—deepening his contemplation without ceasing—will ultimately come to wasteful emission.
וּמִדְּנָקְטֵיהּ עַל שֵׁם הַהִרְהוּר, מַשְׁמָעוֹ דְּזֶהוּ עִיקַּר הַחֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ, וּמִשּׁוּם דְּהִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה קָשִׁים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
And since the Talmud formulated it in terms of contemplation, it implies that this is its essential severity, because "sinful thoughts are worse [than the sin]" as mentioned above;
וּמִטַּעַם זֶה בְּלָאו הָכִי לָא קַשְׁיָא מֵהַסֵּפֶר חֲסִידִים שֶׁמֵּבִיא בְּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל שָׁם
and for this reason it is also not difficult from Sefer Chassidim cited in the Beis Shmuel there:

דִּלְעִנְיַן בִּיאַת עֲרָיוֹת אוֹ נִדָּה מִתּוֹךְ אוֹתוֹ הַהִרְהוּר עַצְמוֹ פְּשִׁיטָא דְּחָמוּר טְפֵי, דַּהֲרֵי מִצַּד הַהִרְהוּר אֵין חִילּוּק, וְהָכָא אִיכָּא עוֹד חֹמֶר מַעֲשֵׂה הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ

for regarding illicit intercourse with forbidden relations or a niddah arising from that very same contemplation, it is obvious that it is more severe, for on the side of contemplation there is no difference, and here there is additionally the severity of the act of transgression itself!
וְלֹא אָמְרוּ דְּחָמִיר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת אֶלָּא בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵינָם בִּפְגַם הַבְּרִית, אוֹ שֶׁאֵין בָּאִים מִתּוֹךְ תֹּרֶף הַעֲמָקַת הַהִרְהוּר כְּעָוֹן זֶה רַק מִתּוֹךְ פְּגִיעַת הָעֶרְוָה לְפָנָיו

And they said that it is graver than all sins only regarding those that do not involve the blemish of the Covenant (pegam ha-bris), or that do not arise from the depth of profound contemplation like this sin, but merely from suddenly encountering an illicit situation before him.
וְהָא דְּאֵין מַכְנִיסִין לִמְחִיצָתוֹ, הַיְינוּ לְפַרְגּוֹדָא דִּבְזֹוהַר הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
And that which was stated, "they do not bring him into His partition," refers to the supernal curtain (pargoda) in the Zohar mentioned above.
וּמִתְבָּאֵר כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּכָל הַחֹמֶר הוּא מִצַּד הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה הַקָּשִׁים
And it is clarified as I wrote: that the entire severity derives from the harshness of sinful thoughts;
וְעַל הִרְהוּרֵי עֲבֵירָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב וַדַּאי דְּסַגִּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב לְבַד כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי [בְּאוֹת י״ג]
and for sinful thoughts of the heart, internal repentance of the heart alone certainly suffices, as I wrote [in Siman 13];
וְכָל הַחֹמֶר שֶׁבּוֹ הוּא רַק קוֹדֶם שֶׁשָּׁב, אֲבָל אַחַר דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב״ הֲרֵי נִטְהַר הַלֵּב וְ״רָפָא לוֹ״:
and all the severity within it applies only prior to repentance, but once "his heart understands and he repents," the heart is purified and "he is healed" (Yeshayah 6:10).

items.h: The theme: The prophetic term "shovavim" (backsliding sons) specifically designates one who strays after the lusts of his heart (shovav b'derech libo). In Yeshayah 57, the phrase "the righteous man perishes" (ha-tzaddik avad) is stated twice in the context of this specific sin, where the sinner forfeits the spiritual title of Tzaddik, which represents guardianship of the Covenant (shomer ha-bris). It is precisely to this state that the promise applies: "Return, backsliding children; I will heal your backslidings" (shuvu vanim shovavim, erpa meshuvoseichem).

p: וְעִיקַּר לְשׁוֹן ״שׁוֹבָבִים״ דִּבִקְרָא הַנִּדְרָשׁ עַל הַמְּחִילָה מִיָּד, מוֹרֶה עַל הַהוֹלֵךְ שׁוֹבָב בְּדֶרֶךְ לִבּוֹ
And the essential scriptural term shovavim [backsliding/wayward], which is expounded as receiving immediate pardon, points to one who walks backsliding in the way of his heart (Yeshayah 57:17);
וּמִקְרָא דְּ״וַיֵּלֶךְ שׁוֹבָב וְכוּלֵיהּ״ [בִּישַׁעְיָה נ״ז] נֶאֱמַר ב׳ פְּעָמִים ״הַצַּדִּיק אָבָד״
and near the verse "and he went on backsliding, etc." [in Yeshayah 57], it states twice "the righteous man perishes" (57:1);
שֶׁהִיא כּוּלָּהּ מְדַבֶּרֶת בְּעָוֹן זֶה בְּיִחוּד, שֶׁהַחוֹטֵא בּוֹ הוּא אוֹבֵד מַדְרֵיגַת וּמִדַּת ״צַדִּיק״ הָרוֹמֵז לְשׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע
which entirely speaks of this specific iniquity, wherein the one who stumbles in it loses the spiritual level and attribute of "Tzaddik," which alludes to the guardian of the Covenant as is known;
וְכֵן מִקְרָא דְּ״הַנֵּחָמִים בָּאֵלִים וְגוֹמֵר״ הָאָמוּר שָׁם [בְּנִדָּה שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳] עַל זֶה
and so too the verse "you that inflame yourselves among the terebinths" (Yeshayah 57:5), which is applied there [in Niddah 13a] to this sin;
וְהַחוֹטֵא בָּזֶה נִקְרָא ״שׁוֹבָב״, וְעָלָיו נֶאֱמַר: ״שׁוּבוּ וְגוֹמֵר אֶרְפָּא וְגוֹמֵר״:

and one who stumbles in this is termed shovav, and concerning him it was proclaimed: "Return, O backsliding children, and I will heal your backslidings" (Yirmeyah 3:22).702Yeshayah 57:1, 5, 17-19; Yirmiyahu 3:22; Niddah 13a; Zohar, Mishpatim 232 — waywardness, the tzaddik, and healing: Yeshayah 57 moves from “the tzaddik is lost” and the verse expounded in Niddah concerning wasted seed to “he went wayward in the path of his heart,” followed by “I have seen his ways and I will heal him” and peace for the distant and near. Yirmiyahu likewise says, “Return, wayward children; I will heal your waywardness.” The Zohar reads Yeshayah’s promise as healing prepared when deliberate sinners return. Rav Tzadok connects this scriptural cluster with the kabbalistic association of tzaddik, yesod, and bris: the sinner loses that level, but heartfelt teshuvah purifies the heart and restores healing.

items.h: The theme: Reconciling the Zohar’s statement that "there is no repentance for this sin" (Vayechi 219b). Early authorities (kadmonim) cried out against taking this literally, since nothing stands in the way of repentance (ein lecha davar she-omeid bifnei ha-teshuvah). The Zohar itself in Parashas Noach (62a) and Vayakhel (214b) clarifies that this applies only when one does not perform "higher, complete teshuvah" (tiyuvta da-chazya le-chafaya al kol ovdoi). Halachically, repentance in the heart transforms even an absolute rasha into a tzaddik in an instant (Kiddushin 49b); the Talmud in Niddah 13a calls one who improperly holds his organ "wicked for a single hour" (rasha sha'ah achas), proving that through immediate subsequent regret and repentance, the status of wickedness is promptly removed.

p: אַךְ בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [וַיְחִי שָׁם] תְּנַן, אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוּדָה: ״לֵית לָן חוֹבָא בְּעָלְמָא דְּלָא אִית לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה בַּר מֵהַאי״
However, in the Holy Zohar [Vayechi 219b] we learned, Rabbi Yehudah said: "We have no sin in the world for which there is no repentance except for this one";
הִנֵּה מַגְרִיעַ כֹּחַ חֵטְא זֶה דְּלָא מְהַנֵּי לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל
behold, this minimizes the power of this sin as if repentance does not avail for it at all!
וּכְבָר צָוְוחוּ עַל זֶה קַמָּאֵי, שֶׁהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה
And the early masters already cried out over this, for behold nothing stands in the way of repentance;

וּבְפָרָשַׁת נֹחַ [ס״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״כָּל חֲטוֹאֵי דְּבַר נָשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ תַּלְיָין בִּתְשׁוּבָה, וְחֶטְאָה דְּאוֹשֵׁיד זַרְעָא וְכוּלֵיהּ נִכְתָּם עֲוֹנֵךְ וְכוּלֵיהּ, בַּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה סַגִּי״, עַד כָּאן

and in Parashas Noach [62a]: "All sins of man depend upon repentance, but the sin of spilling seed... 'your iniquity is marked before Me' (Yirmeyah 2:22), except through abundant repentance," thus far;703Zohar, Vayechi 219b; Zohar, Noach 62a; Reishit Chokhmah, Sha’ar HaKedushah 17 — “no teshuvah” means no ordinary teshuvah: The Zohar’s severe formulation is: “לית לן חובא בעלמא דלא אית ליה תשובה, בר מהאי” — “there is no sin in the world without teshuvah except this one.” Yet a manuscript reading of Zohar Noach preserved by Reishit Chokhmah adds: “בר בחילא דתיובתא תקיפא” — “except through the power of forceful teshuvah.” Background: the passages describe an unusually deep blemish in bris/yesod and the consequent loss of closeness to the Shechinah; they do not overturn the Torah’s general principle that repentance remains possible. Reishit Chokhmah resolves the texts by explaining that ordinary regret is insufficient: the repair must include profound teshuvah, Torah/chokhmah, and humility, corresponding to the depth of the damage. He also cites R. Yehudah Chalguah’s Tzafnat Pa’aneach, which explains that “he has no teshuvah” means that the required return is so difficult that the sinner is not readily assisted and may tire before completing it; persistent return can nevertheless open the door. Rav Tzadok adopts this resolution: there is no license for despair, but the teshuvah and tikkun must be proportionate to the blemish.704Zohar, Vayakhel 214b; Reishit Chokhmah, Sha’ar HaKedushah 17 — complete teshuvah repairs the whole spiritual structure: After describing the severity of damage to the covenant, the Zohar qualifies its warning: “והני מילי כד לא עבד תיובתא שלימתא, תיובתא דאיהי אתחזיא לחפייא על כל עובדוי” — “these words apply when he did not perform complete teshuvah, a teshuvah fit to cover all his deeds.” The background to “all his deeds” is the kabbalistic identification of bris with yesod, called kol because it gathers and transmits the preceding middos. Reishit Chokhmah therefore explains that a blemish there is not treated as an isolated failure: it affects the person’s entire spiritual stature and requires a whole-person repair through teshuvah, Torah, corrected conduct, and renewed holiness. His explanation supplies the mefaresh for the Zohar’s broad language: complete teshuvah does not merely cancel punishment; it rebuilds the channels damaged by the sin. Rav Tzadok extends this principle to a deficiency reaching the root of the soul and its bond with the body. The greater the original disruption, the more comprehensive the return must be—but the Zohar’s qualification itself establishes that complete teshuvah can reach and repair it.
וְהָנֵי ג׳ מִלּוֹת ״בַּר וְכוּלֵיהּ״ מוּקָפִים כִּי בִּסְפָרִים יְשָׁנִים אֵינוֹ, וְנוֹסַף מִתּוֹךְ אֵיזֶה נוּסְחָא אַחֲרָא כְּתַב יָד
and these three words "except through, etc." are bracketed because in older editions they do not appear, having been added from some alternative manuscript reading;
כִּי בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה [שַׁעַר הַקְּדוּשָׁה פֶּרֶק י״ז] כָּתַב דִּבְמִקְצָת נוּסְחָאוֹת בְּסִפְרֵי כְּתַב יָד כָּתוּב: ״בַּר בְּחֵילָא דִּתְיוּבְתָּא תַּקִּיפָא״
for in Reishis Chochmah [Sha'ar HaKedushah, ch. 17] he wrote that in several manuscript versions it is written: "except through the power of forceful repentance";
וְזֶה נִרְאֶה כְּסוֹתֵר הַלָּשׁוֹן דְּפָרָשַׁת וַיְחִי הַנַּ״ל שֶׁסָּתַם בְּעַד הַתְּשׁוּבָה לְגַמְרֵי
and this appears to contradict the phrasing of Parashas Vayechi mentioned above which sealed the door against repentance entirely.

אֲבָל גַּם [בְּפָרָשַׁת וַיַּקְהֵל שָׁם] אַחַר שֶׁהֶאֱרִיךְ בְּגוּף פְּגַם הַפּוֹגֵם בַּבְּרִית אָמַר: ״וְהָנֵי מִילֵּי כַּד לָא עֲבַד תְּיוּבְתָּא שְׁלֵימָתָא, תְּיוּבְתָּא דְּחַזְיָא לְחַפָּיָא עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי״, עַד כָּאן

But also in Parashas Vayakhel [214b], after elaborating on the blemish of the one who damages the Covenant, it states: "And these words apply only when he did not perform a complete repentance, a repentance worthy of covering over all his deeds," thus far.

אַךְ עֲדַיִין צָרִיךְ טַעַם עַל שֶׁהֶחְמִיר בִּתְשׁוּבַת עָוֹן זֶה כָּל כָּךְ, שֶׁכְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי הוּא קַל אֲפִילּוּ מִלָּאוִין הַלּוֹקִין לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן מֵחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין לְעִנְיַן הַתְּשׁוּבָה

Yet one still requires an explanation as to why it was so stringent regarding the repentance of this iniquity, which according to what I wrote is lighter even than negative commandments carrying lashes according to all views, and all the more so compared to those liable for excision and court execution regarding repentance!

וּכְבָר נִזְכַּר לְעֵיל מֵהָא [דְּקִדּוּשִׁין מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּאֵין לְךָ רָשָׁע בְּשׁוּם עֲבֵירָה שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב צַדִּיק גָּמוּר עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר תְּשׁוּבָה בַּלֵּב בִּלְבַד בְּרֶגַע אֶחָת

And it was already mentioned above from that passage [Kiddushin 49b] that there is no wicked person in any sin who is not reckoned a complete tzaddik through a mere thought of repentance in the heart in a single moment,
דְּשָׁם סְתָמָא אָמַר: ״אֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע גָּמוּר״, מַשְׁמַע בְּכָל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם וְאֵין אֶחָד יוֹצֵא מֵהַכְּלָל
for there it stated categorically "even a completely wicked person," implying regarding all sins in the world without a single exception;
וְגַם [בְּנִדָּה שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳] קָרֵי לֵיהּ ״רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם״
and also [in Niddah 13a] it calls him "wicked for a single hour before the Omnipresent,"

וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהַכַּוָּונָה מִשּׁוּם דְּהָתָם לֹא בָּא לְהֵזִיד לְהַרְשִׁיעַ וְלַעֲבוֹר כְּלָל, רַק מִתּוֹךְ שֶׁיֶּאֱחֹז בָּאַמָּה חָיְישִׁינַן שֶׁיִּתְחַמֵּם וְיָבוֹא לְהִרְהוּר וּלְהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה

and it implies that the meaning is because there he did not come intentionally to do wickedness and transgress at all, but only that through holding the organ we suspect he may become heated and arrive at contemplation and wasteful emission;705Kiddushin 49b; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 8:5; Marit HaAyin; Niddah 13a — immediate spiritual status and the longer process of kapparah: Kiddushin rules: “על מנת שאני צדיק — אפילו רשע גמור מקודשת, שמא הרהר תשובה בדעתו” — if a man betroths a woman “on condition that I am righteous,” even a complete sinner creates a doubtful kiddushin, because perhaps he contemplated teshuvah. The Rambam codifies this explicitly as kiddushin misafek, showing that an inward turn can have immediate halachic significance even before its outward history is known. Niddah similarly speaks of a person making himself “רשע שעה אחת לפני המקום” — “wicked for one moment before the Omnipresent,” emphasizing that spiritual status can change from one moment to the next. Marit HaAyin asks how a complete sinner can already be called righteous when serious sins may still require Yom Kippur or suffering for full atonement. He answers that teshuvah begins the kapparah and changes the person’s status immediately, while the completion of kapparah may follow later. This distinction is central to Rav Tzadok: sincere teshuvah can make a person a tzaddik at once and therefore removes every basis for despair, even though full cleansing and repair may still demand the deeper process described in the preceding sources.

וּבְוַדַּאי אִם יֶאֱרַע לוֹ כָּךְ, חֶזְקָתוֹ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לִבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג עַל זֶה, וְיִהְיֶה שָׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט בַּלֵּב עַל כָּל פָּנִים, וּבְהָכִי סַגִּי שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה נִקְרָא רָשָׁע עוֹד בִּכְלָל

and certainly if such befell him, his presumption is that afterward his heart will be anxious over this, and he will repent and regret in his heart at any rate, and this suffices that he should no longer be called wicked at all;
אֶלָּא דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּשְׁעָתוֹ מִיהַת הָוֵי רָשָׁע, וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּלֹא יִהְיֶה רָשָׁע גַּם שָׁעָה אֶחָת:
rather, in any case during that moment he was wicked, and therefore it warned that one should not become wicked even for a single hour.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ט״ז–י״ט

The theme: Analyzing the dictum of Akavya ben Mahalalel in Eduyos 5:6: "Better for me to be called a fool all my days than to become wicked before the Omnipresent for a single hour" (mutav li l'hikarei shoteh kol yamai v'lo e'aseh rasha sha'ah achas lifnei HaMakom). The Sages offered to appoint him Av Beis Din if he retracted four halachic traditions. R' Tzadok questions the phrasing "wicked for a single hour": if he retracted falsely, he would remain a sinner misguiding the public his entire life; if he merely compromised for political appointment, how could the Sages expect a giant of his stature to act corruptly for power? Why would he fear being called a "fool" for refusing to rule against the truth, and why did he add "lest they say he retracted for the sake of power"?

p: וְאִיבְרָא מָצִינוּ לָשׁוֹן זֶה [בְּפֶרֶק ה׳ דְּעֵדֻיּוֹת מִשְׁנָה ו׳] גַּבֵּי עֲקַבְיָא, וְשָׁם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי
And indeed we find this expression [in Eduyos 5:6] regarding Akavya [ben Mahalalel], and there what I wrote [regarding physical desire and subsequent regret] does not apply;

אֲבָל גַּם לְעִנְיַן מַעֲשֵׂה הָרֶשַׁע לִכְאוֹרָה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שָׁם ״שָׁעָה אַחַת״, דְּאִם יַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ מִדַּעְתּוֹ בְּשֶׁקֶר לְהוֹרוֹת בְּהֵיפֶךְ, עַל כֵּן יִהְיֶה כָּל יָמָיו כֵּן מוֹרֶה בְּהֵיפֶךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁהוּא הָאֱמֶת כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ

but regarding the act of wickedness itself, superficially "a single hour" is likewise inapplicable there: for if he were to retract his legal opinion falsely to instruct contrary to his conviction, he would continually rule all his days contrary to what is true in his mind!706Mishnah Eduyot 5:6–7; Mishnah Chagigah 2:2; Tosafos Yom Tov; Ben Yehoyada — Akavya’s refusal and “a rasha for one moment”: The Mishnah states: “Akavya, recant the four matters that you used to say, and we will make you Av Beis Din over Israel.” He answered: “Better that I be called a fool all my days than that I become a rasha before the Omnipresent for one moment, so that they should not say: for the sake of office he recanted.” Av Beis Din was the senior judicial office alongside the Nasi; Chagigah 2:2 describes the first of each zug as Nasi and the second as Av Beis Din. The next Mishnah supplies essential background: at death Akavya told his son to abandon his four rulings, because Akavya had received them from a majority, whereas his son had heard the minority view only from him and the opposing view from the majority. His refusal was therefore fidelity to his own received mesorah, not rejection of majority rule for others. Tosafos Yom Tov reads two reasons: he would not recant falsely before God; moreover, even if he genuinely changed his view, he would decline the office lest people attribute the change to ambition. Ben Yehoyada offers another reading: the Sages sought practical submission to their majority tradition, and the appointment would ultimately remove suspicion that Akavya had lied earlier; “one moment” refers to the interim before all four rulings and the appointment were completed. Rav Tzadok distinguishes these explanations from the Mishnah’s wording and develops his own analysis in this and the following se’ifim.
וְהָיָה קְצָת אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּאִם הָיָה מַטְעֶה אוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה חוֹזֵר בֶּאֱמֶת, וַדַּאי דְּלֹא הָיָה חוֹזֵר אֶלָּא לְשָׁעָה
And it was somewhat possible to suggest: that had he misled them without truly retracting, he certainly would have retracted only temporarily for a brief moment,
וְאַחַר שֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אָב בֵּית דִּין הָיָה חוֹזֵר לְדַעְתּוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹנָה, וּמִשֶּׁעָלָה שׁוּב לֹא הָיוּ מוֹרִידִין אוֹתוֹ בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה שֶׁנֶּחְלַק עִם הַחֲכָמִים בְּאֵיזֶה דִּינִים
and after being appointed Av Beis Din he would return to his original position, and once elevated they would not depose him merely because he disputes the Sages in a few legal rulings;
וְרַק לְכַתְּחִלָּה לֹא רָצוּ לְמַנּוֹתוֹ עַד שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר, אֲבָל אֵין בָּזֶה כְּדֵי לְהוֹרִידוֹ אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְמַנָּה כְּלָל, וּ״מַעֲלִין בַּקֹּדֶשׁ וְלֹא מוֹרִידִין״
for only ab initio did they decline to appoint him until he retracted, but that provides no grounds to remove him once appointed, as "we elevate in holiness and do not demote" (Berachos 28a);
וְשַׁפִּיר הָוֵי פְּעוּלַּת הָרֶשַׁע רַק שָׁעָה אַחַת, וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר לְשׁוֹן ״רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת״

and rightly so the act of deceitful wickedness would last only a single hour, wherefore he used the phrasing "wicked for a single hour."707Megillah 9b; Menachos 99a–b — “we ascend in holiness and do not descend”: The phrase is a general rule governing an object or person already elevated to a higher sacred function. Menachos applies it when the lechem hapanim is transferred from a silver table to a gold one: “מעלין בקודש ולא מורידין.” Megillah gives the closer personal example. When a substitute Kohen Gadol served because the regular Kohen Gadol was disqualified temporarily, Rabbi Yosi says the substitute later serves neither as Kohen Gadol nor as an ordinary Kohen; he may not remain Kohen Gadol because of possible hostility, and he may not return to ordinary service “משום מעלין בקודש ולא מורידין.” Rav Tzadok uses this principle analogically in his provisional explanation: once Akavya had been appointed Av Beis Din, a later return to his original rulings would not automatically erase the elevation merely because he disagreed with the Sages on several halachos. The Gemara itself discusses priestly status, not Akavya or judicial appointment; the extension to Av Beis Din is Rav Tzadok’s proposed application, introduced here only to explain how the imagined deception could have lasted “one moment.” He immediately rejects that scenario on moral and textual grounds.
אֲבָל אֵין זֶה מְחֻוָּור כְּלָל, דַּהֲרֵי הֵם בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ לַחֲזוֹר בֶּאֱמֶת וְלֹא לְהַטְעוֹתָם, וְ״שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עַוְלָה וְלֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב״
But this is entirely unsatisfactory: for behold, they asked him to retract sincerely and not to deceive them, and "the remnant of Israel shall not do iniquity nor speak lies" (Tzefanyah 3:13),
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אָדָם גָּדוֹל כַּעֲקַבְיָא בֶּן מַהֲלַלְאֵל חָלִילָה שֶׁיַּטְעֶה אוֹתָם

and all the more so a titan like Akavya ben Mahalalel, God forbid that he would deceive them!708Zephaniah 3:13; Mishnah and Bartenura, Eduyot 5:6 — truthfulness and Akavya’s stature: The complete verse reads: “שארית ישראל לא יעשו עולה ולא ידברו כזב ולא ימצא בפיהם לשון תרמית” — “the remnant of Israel shall do no wrong, speak no falsehood, and no deceitful tongue shall be found in their mouths.” In context, the prophet describes the purified remnant that will live without injustice or deception. Rav Tzadok cites the middle clause to rule out his own tentative hypothesis that Akavya might have feigned agreement merely long enough to receive office. The Mishnah itself makes that suggestion especially implausible. Rabbi Yehudah declares that the Temple courtyard never closed upon anyone in Israel equal to Akavya “in wisdom and fear of sin”; Bartenura explains the praise as exceptional humility and yiras chet. Tosafos Yom Tov likewise argues that such stature makes deliberate degradation of Shemaya and Avtalyon inconceivable. These comments do not directly answer Rav Tzadok’s grammatical question about “one moment,” but they supply the ethical background for his rejection: the proposed stratagem would require deliberate falsehood toward the Sages, whereas the entire portrait of Akavya is one of uncompromising truthfulness and reverence.
וְאִם הֶחְשִׁיב זֶה לְמַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע לַחֲזוֹר מִקַּבָּלָתוֹ וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ, לֹא הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר ״שָׁעָה אַחַת״
And if he considered it an act of wickedness to recant his tradition and teach contrary to the law according to his understanding, he should not have said "a single hour";
וּמֵהֵיכָן תֵּיתֵי לוֹ לוֹמַר לְעִנְיַן שֶׁלֹּא יַטְעֶה אוֹתָם דָּבָר שֶׁלֹּא בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ וְלֹא יַעֲלֶה עַל לֵב שֶׁיַּעֲשֶׂה זֶה שֶׁיִּצְטָרֵךְ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא יַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן

and whence would it occur to him to address deceit—something they never asked him to do, and which would never enter anyone's mind that he would contemplate doing—that he would need to state he will not do so?
וּבְלָאו הָכִי יֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״חֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵיהּ וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אָב בֵּית דִּין״, וְאֵיךְ סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בִּשְׁבִיל שְׂרָרָה
And regardless, one must examine what they said to him: "Retract... and we will make you Av Beis Din": how could it enter your mind that he would recant for the sake of political power?!

וְאִם כַּוָּונָתָם הָיָה שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בֶּאֱמֶת לְבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַמְּרוּבִּים, לֹא הָיָה לָהֶם לוֹמַר הָא דְּ״נַעֲשֶׂךָ אָב בֵּית דִּין״ אִם בַּדִּין הוּא שֶׁיְּבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ וְיַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ

And if their intent was that he retract sincerely to subordinate his opinion to the majority, they should not have mentioned "we will make you Av Beis Din" if the law itself dictates that he yield his opinion and retract!

גַּם זוּלַת זֶה הָיָה לָהֶם לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן מִקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר, וְאִם אֵינוֹ בַּדִּין שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר — וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ אַחַר כָּךְ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ז׳] ״אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי מִפִּי הַמְּרוּבִּים וְכוּלֵיהּ״ — גַּם בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּהוּ אָב בֵּית דִּין לֹא סָלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין

Moreover, they should have simply asked him to retract on legal grounds beforehand; and if the law did not require him to retract—as he explained afterward [Mishnah 7]: "I heard from the mouth of the majority, etc."—even to be made Av Beis Din how could it enter anyone's mind that he would illegitimately compromise?
וּמַשְׁמָעוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן דְּאָמְרוּ לוֹ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּהוּ אָב בֵּית דִּין, וְזֶה צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר
Yet the plain phrasing implies that they told him to retract in order that they appoint him Av Beis Din, which requires explanation!
וְגַם מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״מוּטָב לִי לְהִקָּרֵא שׁוֹטֶה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר, דְּמֵהֵיכָן תֵּיתֵי יִקְרָאוּהוּ שׁוֹטֶה עַל שֶׁלֹּא רָצָה לַחֲזוֹר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין בִּשְׁבִיל הַשְּׂרָרָה
And also his statement: "Better for me to be called a fool, etc." requires explanation: why would anyone call him a "fool" for refusing to rule unlawfully for the sake of power?

וְאִם הֵם נֶחְלְקוּ עִמּוֹ בְּזֶה גּוּפֵיהּ, שֶׁהָיוּ סְבוּרִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְבַטֵּל דַּעְתּוֹ לְדַעַת הָרַבִּים וְהוּא סָבוּר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ לְבַטֵּל, לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לְקָרוֹתוֹ שׁוֹטֶה בִּשְׁבִיל זֶה אִם הוּא לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ אֵינוֹ רַשַּׁאי לַחֲזוֹר

And if they disputed with him regarding this fundamental issue—they holding that he must yield to the majority while he held he must not—it is unfitting to label him a "fool" for adhering to what he believes the halachah strictly prohibits him from conceding!

גַּם צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר מַה שֶּׁאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים בִּשְׁבִיל שְׂרָרָה חָזַר בּוֹ״, וּמַה עִנְיַן ״שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים״ אִם בְּלָאו הָכִי אֵין רַשַּׁאי לַחֲזוֹר בּוֹ כְּלָל

Furthermore, what he added afterward: "lest they say he retracted for the sake of power" requires explanation: what relevance has public perception ("lest they say") if in any case he is legally forbidden to retract?
וּבְתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב שָׁם נִדְחַק דְּ״חֲדָא וְעוֹד״ קָאָמַר, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And the Tosafos Yom Tov there was forced to explain that he offered two distinct reasons ("one reason and furthermore another"), see there;
אֲבָל פְּשַׁט הַלָּשׁוֹן ״שֶׁלֹּא וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וְלֹא אָמַר ״וְשֶׁלֹּא״, מַשְׁמַע דַּחֲדָא מִלְּתָא הוּא וְסִיּוּם דְּבָרָיו הָרִאשׁוֹנִים:

but the plain language "lest, etc."—omitting the connective letter vav ("and lest")—implies that it is a single continuous thought, serving as the conclusion of his opening words.709Tosafos Yom Tov on Eduyot 5:6 — “one reason, and moreover another”: Commenting on “so that they should not say,” Tosafos Yom Tov writes: “חדא ועוד קאמר” — the Mishnah gives one reason and then an additional reason. His explanation is that Akavya first says he will not recant merely for office and become a rasha before the One Who examines hearts. He then adds that even if he were to recant sincerely, he would still not accept appointment as Av Beis Din, because observers might say that he changed his ruling for authority. This reading separates the clauses: the first concerns objective wrongdoing before God; the second concerns maris ayin and suspicion in the eyes of people. Rav Tzadok explicitly finds this forced. The Mishnah says “שלא יהיו אומרים,” not “ושלא יהיו אומרים”; grammatically, he argues, the final clause sounds like the explanation or completion of “become a rasha for one moment,” not a second independent consideration. That linguistic observation creates the central problem of Se’if 15: if the wicked act is abandoning what Akavya believes to be true, why is it only momentary, and why is public suspicion the defining explanation? The subsequent se’ifim continue Rav Tzadok’s resolution.

items.h: The theme: Akavya’s halachic stance on transmitting personal traditions. On his deathbed, Akavya instructed his son: "Retract... it is better to set aside the words of an individual and uphold the words of the majority." When his son asked why he himself had never retracted, Akavya answered: "I received my tradition from the mouth of the majority, and they received from the mouth of the majority; I stood by my tradition, and they stood by theirs; but you have heard from an individual [me] and from the majority—it is better to set aside the individual." This reveals that Akavya never taught outside students, tutoring only his son in private seclusion, since all official academies studied directly under the Sanhedrin.

p: וְעַל כֵּן נִרְאֶה, דְּבֶאֱמֶת הֲרֵי אָמְרוּ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ז׳] דִּבִשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ אָמַר לִבְנוֹ: ״חֲזוֹר בְּךָ וְכוּלֵיהּ, מוּטָב לִדְחוֹת דִּבְרֵי הַיָּחִיד וְכוּלֵיהּ״

Therefore it appears: for in truth, behold they stated [Eduyos 5:7] that at the hour of his death he said to his son: "Retract... it is better to set aside the words of an individual and uphold the words of the majority";
וּמִמַּה שֶּׁאָמַר ״וְלָמָּה לֹא חָזַרְתָּ? אָמַר לוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ״, מְבוֹאָר דְּלֹא אָז הוּא שֶׁנִּתְחַדֵּשׁ לוֹ דָּבָר זֶה

and from his son's query, "Why then did you not retract?", and his response, it is clear that this was not a novel realization conceived only then:710Mishnah Eduyos 5:7, Bartenura, and Tosafos Yom Tov - Akavya's received tradition: The Mishnah continues: “בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ... אֲנִי שָׁמַעְתִּי מִפִּי הַמְרֻבִּים... אֲבָל אַתָּה שָׁמַעְתָּ מִפִּי הַיָּחִיד וּמִפִּי הַמְרֻבִּין; מוּטָב לְהַנִּיחַ דִּבְרֵי הַיָּחִיד וְלֶאֱחֹז בְּדִבְרֵי הַמְרֻבִּין.” At death Akavya instructed his son to leave Akavya's ruling for the majority's. Akavya had not formed a private opinion; he preserved a ruling received from a group. Tosafos Yom Tov, citing Raavad, explains either that the earlier authorities were divided, or that each side regarded its transmitters as the majority. Bartenura notes that Akavya says “better,” not simply “obligatory,” because his own mesorah also came from many; his son, however, heard Akavya as an individual against the public tradition. Rav Tzadok thus distinguishes between a teacher's fidelity to what he personally received and a listener's duty to follow the operative majority. In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae to Rif, Shabbos 22:2, he states the same rule: “כְּלָלָא דְּיָחִיד וְרַבִּים... קְרָא כְּתִיב אַחֲרֵי רַבִּים לְהַטּוֹת.”
רַק כָּךְ הָיָה דַּעְתּוֹ מֵעוֹלָם, דְּהוּא אֵין יָכוֹל לְבַטֵּל דְּבָרָיו שֶׁשָּׁמַע מֵהַמְּרוּבִּים, אֲבָל הַשּׁוֹמֵעַ מִמֶּנּוּ יֵשׁ לוֹ לִדְחוֹת דְּבָרָיו

rather, such was his lifelong legal position: that he himself could not nullify traditions he personally received from the majority of his teachers, but anyone hearing from him as a lone master must set aside his words before the collective majority.
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר לוֹ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ, לְפִי שֶׁכָּל יְמֵי חַיָּיו הָיָה בְּנוֹ אֶצְלוֹ וּבְבֵיתוֹ וְלֹא הָיָה מוֹרֶה לְעַצְמוֹ, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא הוּצְרַךְ לוֹמַר לוֹ זֶה אֶלָּא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ

And that he told him this only at the hour of death was because all his days his son resided with him in his home and never issued practical legal rulings independently, wherefore he had no reason to instruct him thus until his passing;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ תַּלְמִידִים אֲחֵרִים כְּלָל אֶלָּא בְּנוֹ לְבַד
and one must say that he had no other disciples at all, but his son alone:
דְּאִם לֹא כֵן, הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר זֶה עוֹד בְּחַיָּיו לְהַתַּלְמִידִים כְּשֶׁפֵּירְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ, אוֹ בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָתוֹ גַּם לְתַלְמִידָיו
for otherwise, he should have instructed this during his lifetime to disciples when they departed from him, or at his death to his disciples as well.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ, דְּאָז כָּל הַתַּלְמִידִים הָיוּ לוֹמְדִים לִפְנֵי הַסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְהָאָב בֵּית דִּין שֶׁהָיָה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
And perforce, at that time all aspiring scholars studied before the Sanhedrin and the presiding Av Beis Din of Israel,
וְהוּא, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְמַנָּה אָב בֵּית דִּין, הָיָה יוֹשֵׁב בָּדָד בְּבֵיתוֹ וְלֹא לָמַד אֶלָּא עִם בְּנוֹ לְבַד:
while he, not having been appointed Av Beis Din, sat in solitude in his home, studying solely with his son.

items.h: The theme: The Sages did not ask Akavya to abandon his private tradition, but rather to instruct public students to follow the majority. Since an Av Beis Din shapes national practice, the Sages feared students would follow his minority ruling. Akavya personally agreed that students must follow the majority, but refused to implement this change simultaneously with his appointment, citing the biblical imperative "you shall be clean before Hashem and before Israel" (ve-hiyisem nekFinancialyim me-Hashem u-mi-Yisrael): the public would misinterpret his shift as selling his integrity for high office, making him appear wicked before Heaven.

p: וּלְפִי זֶה יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״חֲזוֹר וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אָב בֵּית דִּין״ אֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁהוּא יַחֲזוֹר לְעַצְמוֹ
And according to this, one can explain: that which they said, "Retract and we will make you Av Beis Din," did not mean that he should recant his private conviction;
רַק לְפִי שֶׁהָיָה שׁוֹנֶה לִבְנוֹ כֵּן, וּכְשֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אָב בֵּית דִּין יִשְׁנֶה גַּם לַתַּלְמִידִים כֵּן
but rather, because he taught his son thus, and upon being appointed Av Beis Din he would teach public students thus;

וְאַף שֶׁהַתַּלְמִידִים יִשְׁמְעוּ דִּבְרֵי הַמְּרוּבִּים, אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּגָּרְרוּ אַחַר דַּעְתּוֹ בִּהְיוֹת אָב בֵּית דִּין וּמוּפְלָא שֶׁבַּסַּנְהֶדְרִין וְגָדוֹל שֶׁבְּכָל חֲכָמִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם מִשְׁנָה ו׳]

and even though the students would hear the words of the majority, they might be drawn after his ruling by virtue of his office as Av Beis Din, the preeminent scholar of the Sanhedrin, and the greatest of all the Sages, as they stated [Mishnah 6];
וְיִרְבּוּ אַחַר כָּךְ הַנִּגְרָרִים אַחֲרָיו עַד שֶׁיִּתְבַּטְּלוּ דִּבְרֵיהֶם

and subsequently those drawn after him would multiply until the majority ruling was undermined.711Mishnah Chagigah 2:2; Eduyos 5:6; Sanhedrin 88b - the Av Beis Din shapes public Torah: Mishnah Chagigah identifies the zugos: “הָרִאשׁוֹנִים הָיוּ נְשִׂיאִים, וּשְׁנִיִּים לָהֶם אַב בֵּית דִּין”; Bartenura explains that their recurring disputes were between each generation's Nasi and Av Beis Din. Eduyos praises Akavya: “שֶׁאֵין עֲזָרָה נִנְעֶלֶת... בְּחָכְמָה וּבְיִרְאַת חֵטְא כַּעֲקַבְיָא.” Sanhedrin describes unresolved questions rising through the courts and being decided by vote - “רַבּוּ הַמְטַמְּאִים טִמְּאוּ; רַבּוּ הַמְטַהֲרִין טִהֲרוּ” - and a qualified judge being promoted toward the Great Sanhedrin. This is the institutional background for Rav Tzadok's inference: appointing Akavya would place an exceptionally authoritative teacher at the center of national transmission, not merely grant him honor. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the Sages' request as directed to what he would teach the students, lest reverence for him eventually displace the operative majority. That application is Rav Tzadok's interpretation, not an explicit statement of the Mishnah.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ ״חֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵיהּ״ — הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִלְמוֹד לַתַּלְמִידִים כְּדַעְתּוֹ, וְיֹאמַר לָהֶם שֶׁיִּסְמְכוּ אַהַמְּרוּבִּים
And regarding this they said "Retract": meaning that he should not teach disciples according to his personal view, but instruct them to rely upon the majority;
וְזֶהוּ כַּדִּין, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר גַּם הוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ לִבְנוֹ
and this was entirely in accordance with the law, exactly as he himself told his own son!
וְלֹא בִּקְשׁוּ שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בְּעַצְמוֹ וְיֹאמַר מַה שֶּׁהוּא שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין כְּפִי שְׁעָתוֹ וּשְׁמוּעָתוֹ, רַק שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר בְּעִנְיַן לִימּוּדוֹ לַתַּלְמִידִים
And they never asked that he abandon his personal conviction and speak falsely contrary to his received tradition, but only that he adapt his pedagogical instruction to public disciples;
וּבָזֶה הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם לְמַנּוֹתוֹ אָב בֵּית דִּין, דְּאֵין עוֹד חֲשַׁשׁ תַּקָּלָה לַתַּלְמִידִים
and this was sufficient for them to appoint him Av Beis Din, for there would be no apprehension of stumbling for the students,
מֵאַחַר שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁהוּא בְּעַצְמוֹ לֹא יַחֲזוֹר מִשְּׁמוּעָתוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֹאמַר לַתַּלְמִידִים שֶׁיַּנִּיחוּ דַּעְתּוֹ וְיִתְפְּסוּ דַּעַת הָרַבִּים
since although he personally would not abandon his tradition, he would instruct students to set aside his opinion and grasp the ruling of the majority.
וְאִם כֵּן הֵם בִּקְשׁוּ מִמֶּנּוּ דָּבָר שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת בַּדִּין כְּפִי דַּעַת עַצְמוֹ גַּם כֵּן, וְגַם הוּא מֵעַצְמוֹ הָיָה עוֹשֶׂה כֵּן כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
If so, they asked of him something that he was legally bound to do according to his own perspective, and which he would have done of his own accord as mentioned above;
רַק לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בִּקְשׁוּ זֶה מִמֶּנּוּ וּכְדֵי לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ אָב בֵּית דִּין, נִמְנַע מֵהַטַּעַם שֶׁסִּיֵּים: ״שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים וְכוּלֵיהּ״
except that because they requested it of him as a prerequisite to make him Av Beis Din, he demurred for the reason he concluded: "lest they say [he retracted for power]."
וְזֶה הָיָה עִיקַּר טַעְמוֹ: דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁעַד עַתָּה לֹא לִימֵּד לַתַּלְמִידִים רַק לִבְנוֹ בִּלְבַד כְּשִׁיטָתוֹ, וְלֹא יָדְעוּ שֶׁדַּעְתּוֹ בֶּאֱמֶת שֶׁאֲחֵרִים יִגָּרְרוּ אַחַר הַמְּרוּבִּים

And this was his primary reason: since until now he had taught no disciples other than his son according to his private ruling, and the public did not know that he held that others must follow the majority,
אִם עַתָּה עַל פִּי בַּקָּשָׁתָם יַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן כְּשֶׁיִּתְמַנֶּה אָב בֵּית דִּין, יֹאמְרוּ שֶׁבִּשְׁבִיל הַשְּׂרָרָה חָזַר שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין
if he were now to concede upon their request upon being appointed Av Beis Din, the world would say that he compromised unlawfully for the sake of political power!

וַהֲרֵי מָצִינוּ חֲכָמִים אָסְרוּ כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד, וּבְשַׁבָּת [כ״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] אִיתָא: ״מְנָא תֵּימְרָא דְּחָיְישִׁינַן לַחֲשָׁד וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וְהַיְינוּ מִקְּרָאֵי דְּמַיְיתֵי דְּגַם הַתּוֹרָה חָשְׁשָׁה לַחֲשָׁד גַּבֵּי פֵּאָה

And behold, we find that the Sages prohibited numerous permissible acts on account of suspicion (chashad), and in Shabbos [23a] it is taught: "From where do we know that we are concerned for suspicion?", citing verses showing that the Torah itself guarded against suspicion regarding the corner of the field (pe'ah);
וּבְפֶרֶק ג׳ דִּשְׁקָלִים [מִשְׁנָה ב׳] יָלְפִינַן מִקְּרָא דְּ״וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר ל״ב:כ״ב), עַיֵּין שָׁם
and in Shekalim [3:2] we derive this from the verse: "and you shall be guiltless before Hashem and before Israel" (Bamidbar 32:22), see there;
וּמֵאַחַר דְּגַם מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ מְקַיֵּים דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים נִקְרָא ״רָשָׁע״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנִדָּה י״ב עַמּוּד א׳], כָּל שֶׁכֵּן בָּזֶה דְּנִלְמַד מִקְּרָא
