and since whoever disregards rabbinic enactments is branded "wicked" as they said [in Niddah 12a], all the more so in this matter which is anchored in Torah verses:
הָעוֹבֵר וּמֵבִיא עַצְמוֹ לַחֲשָׁד, הֲרֵי זֶה רָשָׁע לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם גַּם כֵּן, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵין שָׁם בֶּאֱמֶת שׁוּם מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע כְּלָל
one who transgresses and brings himself into suspicion is accounted wicked before the Omnipresent as well, even though in objective truth there is no evil action at all!
וְאִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר מַה שֶּׁאָמַר ״שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיוּ אוֹמְרִים וְכוּלֵיהּ״ הוּא נִמְשָׁךְ לְטַעַם אֶל הַקּוֹדֵם, דּמִפְּנֵי כֵן יִהְיֶה נֶחְשָׁב רָשָׁע לַמָּקוֹם גַּם כֵּן:

If so, his concluding phrase "lest they say, etc." follows as the direct reason for his opening statement: that by arousing public suspicion, he would be reckoned wicked before the Omnipresent as well.712Shabbos 23a; Shekalim 3:2; Niddah 12a - avoiding reasonable suspicion: Shabbos asks, “מְנָא תֵּימְרָא דְּחָיְשִׁינַן לַחֲשָׁד?” and answers that the Torah required pe'ah at the field's end, among other reasons, “מִפְּנֵי הַחֲשָׁד.” Shekalim requires the treasurer to enter without anything that could conceal coins, because “אָדָם צָרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַמָּקוֹם,” citing “וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּים מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל.” Bartenura explains that observers might otherwise say he hid Temple funds in a folded garment, tefillin, or amulet. Niddah adds Rava's premise that one who disregards the Sages' requirements is termed a rasha. Rav Tzadok combines these sources: even an honest act may violate the duty to remain clean before Israel when it knowingly creates credible suspicion. In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Novellae to Rif, Berachos 1:5, he similarly writes, “לִיזָּהֵר וְלִבְרֹחַ מִפְּנֵי חֲשָׁד.” Akavya's “that they not say” is therefore not concern for reputation alone; preventable suspicion itself becomes a temporary spiritual fault.

items.h: The theme: Why Akavya termed this suspicion "wicked for a single hour." Public suspicion would have been temporary: had he compromised solely for power, he would have reverted to his personal rulings once securely established in office; seeing him consistently teach the majority position would ultimately prove to the public that his compliance was authentic. Yet Akavya refused to tolerate even temporary suspicion. This clarifies the Talmudic expression "wicked for a single hour" (rasha sha'ah achas): it describes a situation where future events will retroactively reveal that no sin was committed, yet during that initial hour of suspicion the person stands compromised before Heaven.

p: אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת הַךְ חֲשָׁדָא אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא לְשָׁעָה וּבַתְּחִלָּה, אֲבָל אַחַר כָּךְ כְּשֶׁיִּרְאוּ שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק וְעוֹמֵד כֵּן בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ לְגַבֵּי הַתַּלְמִידִים, וַדַּאי דְּלֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ עוֹד

But in truth, this suspicion would have lasted only temporarily at the outset; for afterward, when they saw that he firmly maintained his pedagogical retraction before the students, they certainly would suspect him no longer;
שֶׁאִם הָיָה רַק מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה, אַחַר שֶׁנִּתְמַנָּה הֲוָה לֵיהּ לַחֲזוֹר לְדַעְתּוֹ הָרִאשׁוֹנָה דְּשׁוּב לֹא יַעֲבִירוּהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
for had he conceded purely for the sake of power, once appointed he should have reverted to his original view, seeing that they would not depose him, as I wrote above.
וְזֶה וַדַּאי לֹא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק אַחַר כָּךְ בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ כְּדֵי שֶׁלֹּא יֹאמְרוּ שֶׁחָזַר מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה
And they certainly would not suspect him of perpetuating his retraction merely to prevent people from gossiping that he retracted for power:

דְּהַחֲשָׁד וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם עַל חֲזָרָתוֹ מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר לְעוֹלָם וְיוֹרֶה שֶׁלֹּא כַּדִּין מִפְּנֵי שְׂרָרָה, דְּהָוֵי חֲשָׁד אַמַּעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע לְהַכְשִׁיל רַבִּים בְּהוֹרָאָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ כַּדִּין לְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ

for suspicion and slander regarding retracting for power apply only if he were to permanently teach unlawful rulings for prestige, which represents suspicion of an ongoing wicked act of leading the public into error contrary to his own legal conviction;
אֲבָל אִם אַחַר כָּךְ חָזַר לְהוֹרָאָתוֹ, הֲרֵי אַדְּרַבָּא, עַל יְדֵי הִתְמַנּוּתוֹ לְאָב בֵּית דִּין מַחֲזִיק הוֹרָאָתוֹ וְיִמְנַע רַבִּים מִמִּכְשׁוֹל כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ

whereas if he subsequently returned to his original instruction, on the contrary, through his appointment as Av Beis Din he would establish his true ruling and prevent the multitude from stumbling according to his view!
אַף שֶׁהִטְעָה אֶת הַחֲכָמִים בְּמַה שֶּׁאָמַר לָהֶם שֶׁחָזַר בּוֹ, וְנָהַג עִמָּהֶם מִנְהַג רַמָּאוּת וְעָבַר עַל ״מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק״ וְעַל ״שְׁאֵרִית יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב״

Even though he would have deceived the Sages in claiming to retract, practicing deceit and violating "keep far from a false matter" (Shemos 23:7) and "the remnant of Israel shall not speak lies,"713Shemos 23:7; Tzefaniah 3:13; Shevuos 30b-31a - truth remains the governing rule: The Torah says, “מִדְּבַר שֶׁקֶר תִּרְחָק,” and the Navi describes Israel's perfected remnant: “לֹא יַעֲשׂוּ עַוְלָה וְלֹא יְדַבְּרוּ כָזָב וְלֹא יִמָּצֵא בְּפִיהֶם לְשׁוֹן תַּרְמִית.” Shevuos derives numerous judicial safeguards from the unusual command to distance oneself from falsehood, not merely to avoid an explicit lie. Sforno explains that a judge must avoid wording that a dishonest litigant could exploit; Malbim reads Tzefaniah as excluding wrong in deed, falsehood in speech, and calculated deception in thought. Rav Tzadok is therefore not dismissing these prohibitions. He is testing whether the cited cases are narrow deviations that serve an already-established halachic truth. A parallel in Kometz HaMinchah II:1 observes that sometimes false intermediate steps can become “דֶּרֶךְ לְהַגִּיעַ עַל יָדוֹ לָאֱמֶת,” yet Peri Tzadik, Vayetzei 1:1, stresses Yaakov's fear of even a “שֶׁמֶץ פְּגַם הַשֶּׁקֶר.” Together they illuminate Rav Tzadok's balance: purpose matters, but good intent is not a general license to deceive.
מָצִינוּ כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא שֶׁהָיוּ מַטְעִים לַחֲכָמִים כְּדֵי לְהַעֲמִיד הַדִּין עַל אֲמִיתּוֹ
we find comparable instances where masters misled colleagues to establish the halachah upon its true foundation,
עַל דֶּרֶךְ הַאי דִּיבָמוֹת [קט״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] ״אֲמַר לֵיהּ סָפְדִי וְכוּלֵיהּ, וּלְפוּם שִׁקְרָא אִינְהוּ כְּרַבָּנָן סְבִירָא לֵיהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

along the lines of that passage in Yevamos [116b]: "He said to him: lament... and through this ruse they conformed to the Sages, etc.," see there;714Yevamos 116b; Meiri - satisfying a disputed condition without fabricating the underlying case: Rabbi Yehudah required a woman who reported her husband's death to appear in mourning; the Chachamim did not. When a woman came before his court, advisers told her, “סִפְדִי בַּעְלִיךְ, קִרְעִי מָאנִיךְ, סִתְרִי מַזְיֵיךְ.” The Gemara asks, “אַלְּפוּהָ שִׁיקְרָא?” and answers, “אִינְהוּ כְּרַבָּנַן סְבִירָא לְהוּ... כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִישְׁרְיָהּ.” The Meiri formulates the limit: when a recognized beis din permits the matter without that condition, one may guide the litigant to appear before the stricter beis din in a manner that satisfies its condition, and this is not treated as מיחזי כשיקרא. No evidence of the husband's death was invented; the advisers held that she was already halachically permitted and arranged the presentation so Rabbi Yehudah would also permit her. Rav Tzadok cites this as the milder model: an external appearance is adjusted to secure what the advisers understand to be the true ruling. It does not establish permission to falsify facts on which the דין itself depends.
וְאַף לוֹמַר שֶׁקֶר כְּהַאי דְּשַׁבָּת [קט״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] ״אֲמַר לֵיהּ אֲתָא אִיגַּרְתָּא מִמַּעַרְבָא וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י

and even to utter an untruth, as in Shabbos [115a]: "He said to him: a letter arrived from the West, etc.," see Rashi there;715Shabbos 115a; Rashi - an invented report used to stop a real violation: The Gemara permits preparing vegetables on Yom Kippur only “מִן הַמִּנְחָה וּלְמַעְלָה מִפְּנֵי עָגְמַת נֶפֶשׁ.” When Rabbah saw his household beginning too early, “אָמַר לְהוּ: אֲתַאי אִיגַּרְתָּא מִמַּעְרָבָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן דְּאָסַר.” Rashi explains his purpose in four words: “כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיקַבְּלוּ מִינֵּיהּ” - so they would accept the correction from him. Unlike the Yevamos case, this was an outright invented report, but it was used to stop conduct that was genuinely premature under the very rule being discussed. Rav Tzadok therefore treats it as the stronger precedent for a pedagogic falsehood directed toward immediate compliance with the דין. The source still does not say that any mitzvah-purpose permits lying; its force is narrower: Rabbah did not distort the halachah, gain personally, or create false evidence. He used a claimed authority to make his household heed the correct restriction.
וּבְעֵירוּבִין [נ״א עַמּוּד א׳] ״לָא תְּנָא לֵיהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי אֶלָּא כִּי הֵיכֵי דְּלִיקַבְּלַהּ מִינֵּיהּ״
and in Eruvin [51a]: "He did not teach it according to Rabbi Yose, but framed it so that he would accept it from him";
וְכֵן הַאי דְּקִדּוּשִׁין [נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳] ״אַפְּכוּהָ וְשַׁדְּרוּהָ וְכוּלֵיהּ״, פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י, וְכַדּוֹמֶה

and so that passage in Kiddushin [52b]: "they inverted it and sent it, etc.," as Rashi explained there, and similar instances.716Eruvin 51a; Kiddushin 44b with Rashi - altered attribution to secure an honest ruling: In Eruvin, Rabbah told Rav Yosef to rely on his identification of their Shabbos residence and attributed the rule to Rabbi Yosi. The Gemara clarifies: “לָא תְּנָא לֵיהּ כְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי, אֶלָּא כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִיקַבֵּל לַהּ מִינֵּיהּ, מִשּׁוּם דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי נִימּוּקוֹ עִמּוֹ.” In Kiddushin, after Shmuel and Karna disputed a minor's betrothal, the scholars “אַפְכוּהָ שַׁדְּרוּהָ לְקַמֵּיהּ דְּרַב.” Rashi explains that they reversed the names because Rav loved Shmuel; by placing Karna's ruling in Shmuel's name they could test whether Rav would concede to the substance rather than react to the speaker. These cases concern attribution, not manufactured legal facts. Rav Tzadok uses them to show that Chazal sometimes separated a teaching from its stated source so the listener would evaluate or accept the correct דין. He then states his own limit: this technique does not resolve an individual-versus-majority dispute; it only removes the specific suspicion of a wicked act when the actor sincerely seeks to preserve what he regards as the lawful tradition.

וְהַגַּם דְּזֶה לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ בְּיָחִיד נֶגֶד רַבִּים, מִכָּל מָקוֹם אֵין בָּזֶה חֲשָׁד שֶׁל מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע וּלְזוּת שְׂפָתַיִם אִם הוּא עוֹמֵד עַל דַּעְתּוֹ וְרוֹצֶה לְהַחֲזִיק שְׁמוּעָתוֹ מִפִּי רַבִּים גַּם נֶגֶד הַמְּרוּבִּים עַל יְדֵי הַטְעָאָה

And although this principle does not apply for an individual against a majority, nevertheless there is no suspicion of ongoing wickedness and slander if he stands by his tradition from many teachers even against his contemporaries through a tactical ruse;
וְכֵיוָן דְּיֵשׁ שָׁם דְּבַר שֶׁל זְכוּת בְּמַעֲשֶׂה זוֹ שֶׁהוּא עוֹשֶׂה כַּדִּין וְעוֹד מִתְכַּוֵּין לְמִצְוָה, לָא שַׁיָּיךְ חֲשָׁדָא
and since there is an aspect of merit in this act—acting lawfully in his eyes and intending a mitzvah—suspicion does not apply.
וְאִם כֵּן אִלּוּ לֹא הָיָה חוֹזֵר בֶּאֱמֶת, וַדַּאי שֶׁהָיָה אַחַר כָּךְ חוֹזֵר לְדַעְתּוֹ
And if so, had he not retracted sincerely, he certainly would have reverted to his original ruling afterward;
וְאִם כֵּן כְּשֶׁיִּרְאוּ שֶׁעוֹמֵד בַּחֲזָרָתוֹ, וַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא יַחְשְׁדוּהוּ עוֹד שֶׁעָשָׂה מִפְּנֵי הַשְּׂרָרָה, וְיֵדְעוּ שֶׁהַחֲזָרָה בֶּאֱמֶת:
wherefore when they saw him permanently maintain his pedagogical retraction, they certainly would no longer suspect him of having acted for power, and would recognize that his retraction was genuine.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים כ׳–כ״ב

The theme: The dispute between the Sages and Akavya ben Mahalalel regarding temporary suspicion (chashad l'sha'ah). The Sages held that one need not avoid a suspicion that will soon be resolved and proven false; hence they urged him to accept the post of Av Beis Din. Akavya, however, held that during the very hour people suspect him of compromising for power, he is considered wicked before Heaven because he is not "guiltless before Israel." In contrast to this mere appearance of evil, one who improper touches his organ (Niddah 13a) commits a concrete offense in that moment, becoming genuinely "wicked for a single hour" until he repents.

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּזֶה טַעַם הַחֲכָמִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״חֲזוֹר וְנַעֲשֶׂךָ אָב בֵּית דִּין״ וְלֹא חָשׁוּ לַחֲשָׁדָא
And one can say that this was the reasoning of the Sages who said to him, "Retract and we will make you Av Beis Din," and were not concerned for suspicion:
דְּלֹא מָצִינוּ חֲשָׁשַׁת חֲשָׁדָא בְּכָל מָקוֹם, וְכֵן הָא דְּיָלְפִינַן מִקְּרָאֵי הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, אֶלָּא לְעִנְיַן חֲשָׁד גָּמוּר שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֵר בְּדַעְתָּם כֵּן
for we do not find concern for suspicion everywhere, nor in that which we derive from the verses cited above, except regarding an enduring suspicion that would remain fixed in people's minds;
אֲבָל חֲשָׁד לְשָׁעָה וְאַחַר כָּךְ יִתְבָּרֵר לָהֶם הָאֱמֶת וְיָסוּר הַחֲשָׁד, לֹא מָצִינוּ לָחוּשׁ לָזֶה
but regarding a temporary suspicion where afterward the truth will be clarified to them and the suspicion will dissipate, we find no precedent to be concerned for this.
וַעֲקַבְיָא חָיֵישׁ שֶׁלֹּא לֵיעָשׂוֹת שָׁעָה אַחַת וְכוּלֵיהּ, דִּיֵּיק שַׁפִּיר לוֹמַר ״שָׁעָה אַחַת״
And Akavya was scrupulous not to become [wicked for] a single hour, etc., speaking with exactitude when he said "a single hour":
דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם בְּאוֹתוֹ שָׁעָה שֶׁיַּחְשְׁדוּהוּ וְיַחֲזִיקוּהוּ הַבְּרִיּוֹת לְרָשָׁע, נַעֲשָׂה רָשָׁע גַּם לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה מִיהַת
for nevertheless, during that hour when people suspect him and hold him to be wicked, he becomes wicked before the Omnipresent during that hour at least;
דַּהֲרֵי אָז אֵינוֹ נָקִי מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל, וְעָבַר בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה עַל מַה שֶּׁאָמְרָה תּוֹרָה ״וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּים [מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל]״ וְגוֹמֵר

for behold, at that time he is not clean before Israel, having violated in that hour what the Torah stated: "and you shall be guiltless before Hashem and before Israel" (Bamidbar 32:22).717Bamidbar 32:22; Mishnah Shekalim 3:2; Shabbos 23a with Bartenura and Rashi - the scope of suspicion: Moshe told Gad and Reuven that after fulfilling their public obligation they would be “וִהְיִיתֶם נְקִיִּם מֵה׳ וּמִיִּשְׂרָאֵל.” Shekalim applies this to the Temple treasurer: “אָדָם צָרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַבְּרִיּוֹת כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לָצֵאת יְדֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” He entered without anything that could appear to conceal coins; Bartenura explains the suspicion that later wealth came from the chamber. Shabbos likewise requires a Chanukah light at each of two differently facing entrances when townspeople might see one entrance and infer that the mitzvah was neglected; Rashi identifies that concrete inference. These cases create an appearance liable to remain. Rav Tzadok's limitation - that Chazal did not generally legislate for a momentary suspicion certain to be disproved - is his own inference, not an explicit rule in the sources. Akavya nevertheless accepted the stricter personal standard: during that interval he was not yet “clean before Israel.” Rav Tzadok similarly writes in Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Berachos 1:5, “לִיזָּהֵר וְלִבְרֹחַ מִפְּנֵי חֲשָׁד.”
וּמִיהוּ לֹא דָּמֵי הַךְ לְהַהִיא דְּנִדָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
However, this case is not comparable to that passage in Niddah [13a] mentioned above:
דְּשָׁם הָוֵי מַעֲשֵׂה חֵטְא וְרֶשַׁע גָּמוּר בִּשְׁעָתוֹ אֶלָּא שֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ יָשִׁיב
for there it is an actual act of sin and complete wickedness in that moment, only that he will subsequently repent.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּלָא דָּמֵי לְהָא דְּ״אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ [בְּמִשְׁנָה יוֹמָא פ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]
And although it is not comparable to that dictum, "If one says: 'I will sin and repent,' they do not grant him the opportunity [to repent]" [Yoma 85b]:
דְּהָכָא אֵין בָּא לַחֲטוֹא, רַק דְּמִתּוֹךְ שֶׁאוֹחֵז בַּאֲמָתוֹ חָיְישִׁינַן דְּיָבוֹא לְחִימּוּם עַל יְדֵי הִרְהוּר וּגְרִיַּית יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁיִּתְקְפֶנּוּ, וְאֵין חוֹטֵא עַל סְמַךְ שֶׁיָּשׁוּב

for here he does not set out to sin, but merely because he holds his organ we suspect he may come to heated passion through lustful contemplation and incitement of the yetzer hara which will overpower him, and he does not sin relying on the assumption that he will repent;718Niddah 13a; Maharal, Netiv HaPerishus 3 - an actual aveirah for “one moment”: Rabbi Eliezer taught: “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא לַעַז עַל בָּנָיו... וְאַל יַעֲשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” The conflict is between avoiding public suspicion and avoiding contact that may produce prohibited arousal. The Gemara asks, “וְכָל כָּךְ לָמָּה?” and answers that the concern is an actual emission for no purpose, citing Onan: “וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה.” Maharal explains the comparison to a flood: wasting the human power of generation undoes the divinely ordered gathering from which future life proceeds, parallel to the Flood's undoing of the gathered waters. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes the cases. Akavya's deed may be innocent while observers temporarily misunderstand it; in Niddah the feared act itself is sinful at that moment. Later regret can repair the person, but it does not make that moment a non-act. He borrows Rabbi Eliezer's phrase “one moment” while separating objective wrongdoing from temporary public suspicion.
רַק אֲנַן אָמְרִינַן בְּעַצְמֵנוּ כֵּן דְּוַדַּאי הוּא שֶׁיָּשִׁיב אַחַר כָּךְ וְיִתְחָרֵט מֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא בָּא לַעֲבוֹר בִּזְדוֹנוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
rather, we ourselves say that he will certainly repent afterward and regret it, since he did not intend to transgress willfully, as mentioned above;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם בִּשְׁעָתוֹ מִיהַת עוֹבֵר עַל דָּבָר שֶׁאֵין הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא הָאָדָם גַּם לְשָׁעָה אַף שֶׁיָּשׁוּב
nevertheless, during that moment at least he transgresses against that which the Blessed Name does not desire a person to transgress even for a moment, even though he will repent;
[וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּעַל כֵּן אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לָשׁוּב, אֶלָּא דִּבְיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳ אָתוּ עֲלַהּ מִטַּעַם אַחֵר וְדַוְוקָא בְּב׳ פְּעָמִים, עַיֵּין שָׁם]:

[and perhaps for this reason they do not grant him the opportunity to repent, though in Yoma 86a they derived it from a different reason, and specifically when repeated twice, see there].719Mishnah Yoma 8:9; Yoma 87a with Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 4:1 - relying on future repentance: The Mishnah states: “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב, אֶחֱטָא וְאָשׁוּב, אֵין מַסְפִּיקִין בְּיָדוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה.” Yoma explains the repetition: “כֵּיוָן שֶׁעָבַר אָדָם עֲבֵירָה וְשָׁנָה בָּהּ... נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ כְּהֶיתֵּר.” Rashi says that after repetition the sin feels permitted, obstructing repentance. Rambam lists “הָאוֹמֵר אֶחְטָא וְאָשׁוּב” among the severe acts that impede teshuvah because the future remedy is built into the present decision to sin. Rav Tzadok distinguishes Niddah: the person does not intend to transgress on condition that he later repent; Chazal fear that contact may awaken the yetzer, and Rav Tzadok predicts later regret after an unplanned lapse. His bracket asks whether even this may impede teshuvah, while noting that Yoma formally emphasizes repetition. In Takanat HaShavin 10:8 he explains that one who plans to sin in order to become a baal teshuvah cannot reach full regret, because the sin never appeared truly evil. Resisei Layla 38 likewise distinguishes mistakenly treating an aveirah as a mitzvah from knowingly relying on later repentance.

items.h: The theme: God's ultimate desire for uprightness versus the heightened rung of the penitent. Even according to Rabbi Abbahu that "in the place where penitents stand, the wholly righteous cannot stand" (Berachos 34b), Hashem takes no pleasure in the deeds of the wicked (eino chafetz b'ma'aseihen shel resha'im). Hashem created man upright (yashar) so that he should never sin, and does not wish man to be wicked even for a single hour. Yet Akavya applied this so stringently that he considered even temporary public suspicion a state of being "wicked for a single hour," willingly accepting the label of a "foolish pietist" (chassid shoteh) by forfeiting the holy post of Av Beis Din to avoid even fleeting suspicion.

p: וְאַף לְמַאן דְּאָמַר [בְּרָכוֹת ל״ד עַמּוּד ב׳] ״בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״ דְּעָדִיף מִצַּדִּיק גָּמוּר
And even according to the authority who holds [in Berachos 34b] that "in the place where penitents stand, [the wholly righteous cannot stand]," that he is greater than a wholly righteous person,

מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא בְּאֵלֶּה חָפֵץ ה׳, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה ב׳]: ״אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה מֵהֶן חָפֵץ וְכוּלֵיהּ, כֵּיוָן דִּכְתִיב וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאֵינוֹ חָפֵץ בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים״

nevertheless Hashem does not desire these [sins], as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 2:5]: "One might not know in which of them He delights... until it is written... He does not delight in the deeds of the wicked";
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּיְפֵה תֹּאַר בְּשֵׁם יֵשׁ אוֹמְרִים דְּהַךְ אַגָּדָה סְבִירָא לַהּ דְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר עָדִיף מִבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and see the Yefeh To'ar there in the name of some commentators who explain that this Midrashic aggadah holds that a wholly righteous person is greater than a penitent, see there;720Berakhot 34b; Bereishis Rabbah 2:5; Yefeh To’ar; Maharal, Netiv HaTeshuvah 4; Peri Tzadik, Shelach 6 - higher teshuvah does not make sin desirable: Berakhot records R’ Abahu’s teaching: “מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין, צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים אֵינָם עוֹמְדִין”; R’ Yochanan instead ranks the complete tzaddik higher. Bereishis Rabbah has R’ Abahu ask, “אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה מֵהֶם חָפֵץ,” and conclude: “בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים חָפֵץ, וְאֵינוֹ חָפֵץ בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים.” Yefeh To’ar cites an explanation that the uncertainty concerns repentant sinners versus complete tzaddikim, with the conclusion favoring the latter. Rav Tzadok argues oppositely: because the same R’ Abahu ranks baalei teshuvah higher, one might mistakenly infer that Hashem desires the fall which produces their later ascent. “עָשָׂה הָאֱלֹקִים אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר” rejects that inference. Maharal explains that R’ Abahu values the baal teshuvah’s greater overcoming after attachment to sin, while R’ Yochanan values never having that attachment. Peri Tzadik states the boundary explicitly: one might think “שֶׁיְּקַלְקְלוּ מִקּוֹדֶם וְאַחַר כָּךְ יַעֲשׂוּ תְשׁוּבָה,” but “לְכַתְּחִלָּה בְּוַדַּאי חָלִילָה לַחְשׁוֹב כֵּן.” Teshuvah can transform a past fall; Hashem’s original desire remains uprightness.
וְתֵימַהּ, דְּהִיא בְּעַצְמוֹ הַפְּלוּגְתָּא [מִפֶּרֶק אֵין עוֹמְדִין]
and it is astonishing, for that is the very dispute in the chapter Ein Omedin [Berachos 34b];

וַהֲרֵי שָׁם רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ הוּא דְּאָמַר זֶה דְּ״בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף, וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ עַל הַהַגָּדָה שֶׁבִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and behold, there it is Rabbi Abbahu who stated that "in the place where penitents stand, etc." that a penitent is greater, and he himself authored the aggadah in Bereishis Rabbah cited above, see there!
וַאֲבָל לְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט לְהֵיפֶךְ: דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ לְטַעְמֵיהּ דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף
But in my opinion the plain explanation is the reverse: Rabbi Abbahu is entirely consistent with his view that a penitent is greater,
וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי אָמַר ״דְּאֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ בְּאֵיזֶה חָפֵץ״: דִּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר צַדִּיק גָּמוּר עָדִיף פְּשִׁיטָא דְּחָפֵץ יוֹתֵר בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים

and for this reason he framed it, "I do not know in which He delights": for according to the one who holds a wholly righteous person is greater, it is obvious that He delights more in the deeds of the righteous;

אֲבָל לְדִידֵיהּ דְּבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עָדִיף, הָיָה אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רוֹצֶה יוֹתֵר בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים כְּדֵי שֶׁיָּשׁוּב אַחַר כָּךְ וְיַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּדוֹלָה יוֹתֵר
but according to him that a penitent is greater, it might have been possible to say that the Blessed Name prefers the deeds of the wicked so that he will subsequently repent and attain a higher rung;
וְהוּצְרַךְ לִלְמוֹד מִקְּרָא דְּאֵין חָפֵץ וְכוּלֵיהּ, כִּי ״הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כט) שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא כְּלָל, וְאֵין רוֹצֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה רָשָׁע אֲפִילּוּ שָׁעָה אַחַת

therefore he had to derive from Scripture that He does not delight in this, for "God made man upright" (Koheles 7:29) so that he should never sin, and He does not want him to be wicked even for a single hour.

אֲבָל הָכָא, דְּאֵין כָּאן מַעֲשֵׂה רֶשַׁע בֶּאֱמֶת כְּלָל רַק שֶׁהַבְּרִיּוֹת חוֹשְׁדִין אוֹתוֹ לְשָׁעָה, כֵּיוָן דְּאַחַר כָּךְ יִסְתַּלֵּק הַחֲשָׁד יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין חָשׁוּב רָשָׁע לַמָּקוֹם כְּלָל אֲפִילּוּ בִּשְׁעָתוֹ

But here, where in truth there is no act of wickedness at all, but merely that people suspect him temporarily, since afterward the suspicion will dissipate, one could argue that he is not considered wicked before the Omnipresent at all, even in that hour;
אֶלָּא שֶׁעֲקַבְיָא הֶחְמִיר עַל עַצְמוֹ לְהַחְשִׁיב גַּם זֶה לְרִשְׁעוּת שָׁעָה אַחַת, דִּבְאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה שֶׁהַבְּרִיּוֹת מַחְשִׁיבִין אוֹתוֹ לְרָשָׁע הוּא כְּרָשָׁע לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם

except that Akavya was stringent with himself to consider even this a state of wickedness for a single hour, for in that hour when people consider him wicked he is as one wicked before the Omnipresent.
וּבָזֶה יָדַע שֶׁאֲחֵרִים יַלְעִיגוּ עָלָיו וְיֹאמְרוּ שֶׁהוּא חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה בָּזֶה, לְהַנִּיחַ הִתְמַנּוּת אָב בֵּית דִּין בְּסַנְהֶדְרֵי גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל

And in this he knew that others would mock him and say that he is a "foolish pietist" (chassid shoteh) in this matter, for relinquishing the appointment of Av Beis Din in the Great Sanhedrin of all Israel,
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּזֶה וַדַּאי מַעֲלָה וְהִתְעַלּוּת גָּדוֹל לַנֶּפֶשׁ גַּם כֵּן כֵּיוָן שֶׁהוּא מַעֲלָה בַּקֹּדֶשׁ
which certainly contains great spiritual elevation and ascension for the soul as well, being an elevation in holiness;
דְּעַל כֵּן גְּדוֹלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מָצִינוּ שֶׁהָיוּ מִתְאַוִּים לַנְּשִׂיאוּת, וְקָרֵי לַהּ [בְּרָכוֹת כ״ח רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] ״כַּסָּא דְּמוֹקְרָא״
wherefore we find that giants of Israel yearned for the presidency of the Sanhedrin, which is termed [in Berachos 28a] "a seat of honor";
וּבְוַדַּאי לֹא חָמְדוּ לְכָבוֹד בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, רַק לְהַמַּעֲלָה דִּקְדוּשָׁה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לְנַפְשֵׁי יִשְׂרָאֵל
and certainly they did not covet honor in this world, but rather the spiritual sanctity it bestows upon the souls of Israel;
וְהַחֲכָמִים שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ ״חֲזוֹר וְכוּלֵיהּ״ הָיוּ סְבוּרִים דְּאֵין כְּדַאי לִהְיוֹת זֶה בִּשְׁבִיל חוּמְרַת חֲשָׁשַׁת הַחֲשָׁד דִּלְשָׁעָה
and the Sages who said to him "Retract, etc." held that it is inappropriate to forfeit this on account of the stringency of a fleeting suspicion.

וְעַל זֶה אָמַר ״מוּטָב לְהִקָּרֵא שׁוֹטֶה וְכוּלֵיהּ״, דִּבִשְׁבִיל זֶה שַׁפִּיר שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹמַר דְּיַחְשִׁיבוּהוּ לְשׁוֹטֶה, דְּמָצִינוּ חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה [בְּסוֹטָה כ״א עַמּוּד ב׳] כְּשֶׁדּוֹחֶה דָּבָר גָּדוֹל בִּשְׁבִיל אִיסּוּר קַל, עַיֵּין שָׁם, כֵּן נִרְאֶה בָּזֶה

And regarding this he said, "Better for me to be called a fool, etc.," for on account of this it is very fitting to say that they would consider him a fool, as we find the concept of a foolish pietist [in Sotah 21b] who forfeits a great mitzvah on account of a minor prohibition, see there; so it appears in this matter.721Berakhot 28a with Rashi; Sotah 21b - nesius, public responsibility, and chasid shoteh: When R’ Elazar ben Azarya was offered the nesius after Rabban Gamliel’s removal, his wife warned that he too might be removed. He answered: “לִשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ אִינִישׁ יוֹמָא חֲדָא בְּכָסָא דְמוֹקְרָא, וּלְמָחָר לִיתְּבַר” - use a precious goblet for one day even if it breaks tomorrow. Rashi explains that it is an expensive glass cup whose owner should use it for the opportunity and distinction it affords. When Rabban Gamliel was restored, the Sages preserved a share of leadership for R’ Elazar because “מַעֲלִין בַּקֹּדֶשׁ וְאֵין מוֹרִידִין.” This supplies the background for Rav Tzadok’s inference that nesius may represent genuine elevation through serving and teaching Klal Yisrael, not merely worldly honor. Sotah defines “חָסִיד שׁוֹטֶה” through one who refuses to look at a drowning woman in order to rescue her. His error is allowing a secondary concern to displace an immediate, greater obligation. Rav Tzadok applies the category analogically: the Sages could view refusal of the Av Beis Din position because of a temporary suspicion as sacrificing a major public Torah responsibility for an unusually remote stringency. Akavya’s “better to be called a fool” means that he knowingly accepted that criticism rather than relax his personal standard. The spiritual reading of nesius and its application to Akavya are Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not explicit statements of either Gemara.

וּמִתְבָּאֵר שַׁפִּיר גַּם מִשָּׁם, דְּמַשְׁמָעוּת לָשׁוֹן זֶה דְּ״שָׁעָה אַחַת״ הַיְינוּ כְּשֶׁאַחַר כָּךְ יִתְגַּלֶּה דְּגַם עַתָּה לֵיכָּא רִשְׁעוּת, וְזֶהוּ בְּהַהוּא דְּנִדָּה רַק עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם:

And it is well clarified from there as well, that the meaning of this phrase "a single hour" refers to a situation where afterward it is revealed that even previously there was no true wickedness; and in that passage in Niddah this occurs solely through repentance that rectifies the past.722Niddah 13a with Rashi and Maharal - actual momentary sin versus a suspicion later disproved: The Sages objected that one who does not hold himself while urinating may appear physically impaired, causing aspersions on his children. R’ Eliezer answered: “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא לַעַז עַל בָּנָיו... וְאַל יַעֲשֶׂה עַצְמוֹ רָשָׁע שָׁעָה אַחַת לִפְנֵי הַמָּקוֹם.” The Gemara asks, “וְכָל כָּךְ לָמָּה?” and identifies the concern as an actual forbidden emission, citing Onan: “וַיֵּרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳ אֲשֶׁר עָשָׂה.” Rashi explains that contact produces warmth and may cause the emission. Maharal explains the comparison to bringing a flood upon the world: wasting man’s generative power reverses the divinely ordered preservation of future life, paralleling the Flood’s undoing of creation’s order. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes this case from Akavya’s. In Niddah, the feared deed itself is wrong at that moment; later teshuvah repairs the past but does not reveal that no aveirah occurred. Akavya would not actually corrupt a ruling: observers would temporarily suspect that he had recanted for office, while his later conduct could reveal that their suspicion had never described his deed. Rav Tzadok extends the phrase “one moment” from objective wickedness later repaired to a momentary public judgment later disproved. That extension is his analysis, not an explicit equation made by Niddah.

items.h: The theme: Critique of early and later kabbalistic explanations for why the Zohar states that repentance does not avail for wasteful emission. The Reishis Chochmah explains that lower teshuvah (teshuvah tata'ah, mere abstention from evil) is insufficient, requiring higher teshuvah (teshuvah ila'ah) with heartfelt crying, while others suggest it requires mortifications (sigufim) to rectify all limbs, or a spiritual level above the domain of teshuvah (Ilimah of the Ramak). The Shelah suggests that teshuvah is difficult because one who falls into this sin repeats it many times. R' Tzadok rejects all these solutions: according to the Talmudic four categories of atonement (arba'ah chilukei kapparah), this sin requires no mortifications and is no weightier than an ordinary negative commandment. Moreover, the Zohar addresses the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, which applies even to one who stumbled only a single time and immediately felt true regret.

p: וְעַיֵּין בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה שָׁם כָּתַב דְּלָא מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה, דְּהַיְינוּ סוּר מֵרָע לְבַד, אֶלָּא צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה [בִּצְעָקָה שֶׁמִּלִּבּוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם]

And see in Reishis Chochmah [Sha'ar HaKedushah, ch. 17] who wrote that lower repentance (teshuvah tata'ah)—which is mere turning away from evil alone—does not avail, but rather one requires higher repentance (teshuvah ila'ah) [with a cry from his heart, see there];
וּבְשֵׁם הָרַב יְהוּדָה חַלְגְּוָאָה בְּסֵפֶר צָפְנַת פַּעְנֵחַ כָּתַב דִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה מִפְּנֵי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ סִגּוּפִים הַרְבֵּה שֶׁיִּלְאֶה לַעֲשׂוֹתָם
and in the name of Rabbi Yehudah Chalgava in the book Tzofnas Pane'ach he wrote that its repentance is difficult because it requires numerous afflictions (sigufim) that one will weary of performing;
וְעוֹד תֵּירֵץ דְּצָרִיךְ עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן כָּל הָאֵבָרִים
and he further resolved that one must rectify all bodily limbs through repentance;
וּבְשֵׁם הָרַמַ״ק בְּסֵפֶר אֵילִימָה כָּתַב דְּצָרִיךְ דָּבָר שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה מִמְּקוֹם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

and in the name of the Ramak in Sefer Ilimah he wrote that it requires an illumination from above the realm of Teshuvah [i.e., Keser], see there at length.723Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaKedushah 17:20-24; R. Yehudah Chalgua, Tzafnas Paneach; Ramak, Elimah; Tzidkat HaTzadik 132 - lower and upper teshuvah: Reishis Chochmah writes: “אֵין הַדָּבָר תָּלוּי בִּתְשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה... דְּהַיְינוּ בְּסוּר מֵרַע,” and concludes that the return must rise “עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ לִתְשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה,” through a heartfelt cry that reaches above ordinary judgment. He cites Tzafnas Paneach: “תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה עַד מְאֹד... צָרִיךְ סִיגּוּפִים הַרְבֵּה.” His second explanation is structural: the blemish is “כְּאִלּוּ פָּגַם כָּל הַשִּׁיעוּר קוֹמָה,” requiring “תְּשׁוּבָה תַּקִּיפָא כְּאִלּוּ פָּגַם כָּל אֵיבָרָיו.” The Ramak’s Elimah places the damage in Chochmah, above the usual locus of teshuvah in Binah, and therefore speaks of repair “above the place of teshuvah.” These are kabbalistic descriptions of the depth of repair, not a denial that teshuvah exists. Rav Tzadok uses the same vocabulary in Tzidkat HaTzadik 132: upper teshuvah awakens “מִי הַחָכְמָה שֶׁהוּא הַשֹּׁרֶשׁ לַשֹּׁרֶשׁ,” where the Jewish soul remains pure. Here he questions whether that mystical depth can create a separate halachic system of atonement.
וְכָל זֶה אֵינוֹ מַסְפִּיק לְיַישֵּׁב גּוּף הַדָּבָר שֶׁהֶחְמִירוּ בִּתְשׁוּבַת עָוֹן זֶה כָּל כָּךְ, וְהוּא נֶגֶד ד׳ חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה שֶׁהָיָה רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל דּוֹרֵשׁ

And all of this is insufficient to resolve the fundamental problem of why they were so stringent regarding repentance for this iniquity, for this contradicts the four categories of atonement that Rabbi Yishmael expounded;
דִּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְפִי דַּעְתִּי אֵין צָרִיךְ לְכַפָּרַת עָוֹן זֶה סִגּוּפִים וְיִסּוּרִים מְמָרְקִים כְּלָל
for according to what I have written, in my opinion the atonement for this iniquity does not require mortifications and scouring afflictions at all,
וְאֵין בּוֹ חֹמֶר לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר מִשְּׁאָר מִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה לְעִנְיַן כַּפָּרָה

and it possesses at most no greater severity than any ordinary negative commandment regarding atonement.724Yoma 86a; Tosefta Yoma 4:9; Shaarei Teshuvah 4:6; Takanat HaShavin 13:1 - the four categories govern basic atonement: R. Elazar ben Azaryah answers: “שְׁלֹשָׁה הֵן, וּתְשׁוּבָה עִם כָּל אֶחָד וְאֶחָד.” For a negative commandment, “תְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים מְכַפֵּר”; for kareis or a court-imposed death penalty, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend punishment and suffering completes the cleansing; chillul Hashem requires death for the final cleansing. The Tosefta gives the same graded framework. Rabbeinu Yonah adds an important distinction: even after repentance has atoned for a neglected positive commandment, an olah may still “תּוֹסִיף עַל כַּפָּרָתוֹ וְיוֹסִיף לְהִתְרַצּוֹת” - increase acceptance and reconciliation. Thus forgiveness, completed kapparah, and fuller spiritual restoration are related but not identical. Rav Tzadok makes this distinction earlier in Takanat HaShavin 13:1, describing the later offering as “דורון בעלמא” after forgiveness. His argument here is that R. Yishmael’s scheme was stated comprehensively for Torah transgressions. Unless this sin falls into kareis, death, or chillul Hashem, extraordinary mortifications cannot become a new condition for basic kapparah. “Upper” or “complete” teshuvah may describe full rectification of the spiritual damage, but it cannot silently become a fifth category replacing the explicit order of Chazal.
וּבַשְּׁלָ״ה [שַׁעַר הָאוֹתִיּוֹת, אוֹת קְדוּשָׁה] הֵבִיא תֵּירוּץ הָרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה דְּצָרִיךְ בָּזֶה לְתַקֵּן כָּל אֵבָרָיו
And in the Shelah [Sha'ar HaOtiyos, letter Kedushah] he cited the resolution of the Reishis Chochmah that one must rectify all of his limbs;
וְהוּא כָּתַב לְתָרֵץ, לְפִי שֶׁהָרָגִיל בְּחֵטְא זֶה הוּא חָטָא בּוֹ כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים, וְעַל כֵּן תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ קָשָׁה לַעֲשׂוֹת הַסִּגּוּפִים עַל כָּל פַּעַם, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

and [the Shelah] himself wrote to explain that because one who is accustomed to this sin commits it multiple times, his repentance is difficult because he must perform mortifications for each individual occurrence, see there at length;725Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyot, Kedushah; Reishis Chochmah 17:22, 24; Rokeach; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 3:1; Zohar, Vayakhel 214b; Peri Tzadik, Ki Savo 12 - repetition and intrinsic repair: The Shlah explains that this concealed sin is easily repeated, so the penitential regimen would have to correspond to every occurrence; the sinner’s years can therefore be consumed by teshuvah while “בְּרֹב לֹא תַּשְׁלִים.” Reishis Chochmah similarly requires persistence year after year, remembering “כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים הִכְעִיס אֶת בּוֹרְאוֹ.” The background is the Rokeach’s teshuvas ha-mishkal and related disciplines, which prescribe practices proportionate to the act; they are not R. Yishmael’s four categories of kapparah. Rambam supplies a general limit: “אָסְרוּ חֲכָמִים שֶׁיְּהֵא אָדָם מְסַגֵּף עַצְמוֹ בְּתַעֲנִית.” This does not reject every targeted correction, but it shows that self-mortification is not automatically the essence of teshuvah. Rav Tzadok’s textual objection is that the Zohar speaks about the sin itself: “וְהָנֵי מִילֵי כַּד לָא עָבַד תְּיוּבְתָא שְׁלֵימָתָא... לְחַפְּיָא עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי,” without distinguishing one occurrence from many. Reishis Chochmah likewise explains an intrinsic blemish to the whole spiritual stature. In Peri Tzadik, Ki Savo 12, Rav Tzadok quotes this Zohar and adds: “עַל יְדֵי תּוֹרָה יֵשׁ תַּקָּנָה לִפְגָם זֶה,” together with prayer and crying. Repetition may increase the burden, but it cannot explain the Zohar’s unique characterization of the sin itself.
וּכְבָר קְדָמוֹ גַּם בָּזֶה הָרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ בְּדִבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְצָרִיךְ לְהַתְמִיד״, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and the Reishis Chochmah himself already preceded him in this afterward (s.v. v'tzarich lehasmid), see there.
וְזֶה וַדַּאי אֵין מַסְפִּיק: אֲפִילּוּ נוֹדֶה לְגוּף צֹרֶךְ הַסִּגּוּפִים לְקַבָּלַת תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ
And this is certainly insufficient: even if we were to concede the fundamental necessity of mortifications for the acceptance of his repentance,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם דִּבְרֵי הַזֹּוהַר מְבוֹאָר דִּמְדַבְּרִים מִגּוּף חֵטְא זֶה בְּעַצְמוּתוֹ, וְלֹא מִצַּד רִיבּוּי הַפְּעָמִים
nevertheless, the words of the Zohar clearly speak of the intrinsic essence of this sin in itself, and not on account of the multiplication of offenses,
שֶׁזֶּה אֶפְשָׁר גַּם בַּחֲטָאִים אֲחֵרִים שֶׁהוּרְגַּל כַּמָּה פְּעָמִים
for habitual repetition is equally possible with other transgressions that one repeats many times!
וְכֵן בְּחֵטְא זֶה שֶׁשָּׁב וְנִיחָם מִיָּד אַחַר פַּעַם הָרִאשׁוֹן וְלֹא חָטָא יוֹתֵר
Furthermore, what of this sin where one repented and felt deep remorse immediately after the first instance and never sinned again?
וּבַזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ לֹא חִילְּקוּ בֵּין פַּעַם אֶחָד לְהַרְבֵּה, וְאֵין נִרְאֶה כְּלָל דְּאָתֵי מִכֹּחַ רִיבּוּי הַחֲטָאִים:
Yet in the Holy Zohar they drew no distinction between a single occurrence and many, so it does not appear at all that this severe stringency derives merely from the numerical repetition of sins.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים כ״ג–כ״ו

The theme: Critique of proofs from the Generation of the Flood. The Reishis Chochmah and the Shelah cite Noach’s warnings to the Generation of the Flood to prove that teshuvah avails for this sin, understanding the Zohar’s denial of repentance as an assertion that the sinner remains completely unatoned, as if he never repented. R’ Tzadok rejects this deduction: for Bnei Noach, teshuvah merely rescinds impending physical destruction (as in Nineveh), whereas for Israel, teshuvah effects metaphysical erasure of the past, rendering the soul as if it had never sinned. Thus, the Generation of the Flood offers no proof against the Zohar’s statement.

p: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרֵאשִׁית חָכְמָה וְכֵן בַּשְּׁלָ״ה שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ רְאָיָה דִּמְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁנֹּחַ הִתְרָה בָּהֶם שֶׁיָּשׁוּבוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּמִּדְרָשׁ וּבְרַשִׁ״י בַּחֻמָּשׁ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And see there in Reishis Chochmah and likewise in the Shelah, who brought a proof that repentance avails from the Generation of the Flood, since Noach warned them to repent, as they said in the Midrash and in Rashi on the Chumash (Bereishis 6:14), see there;
וְנִרְאֶה דְּהֵבִינוּ דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּוהַר דְּלָא מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא לְגַמְרֵי כְּאִלּוּ לֹא שָׁב כְּלָל וּכְאִלּוּ עֲדַיִין עוֹמֵד בְּרִשְׁעוֹ

and it appears they understood that what the Zohar said—that repentance does not avail—means that it is completely as if he did not repent at all and as if he still persists in his wickedness;726Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaKedushah 17:25; Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Hilchos Bi’ah 1:35; Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 5:6; Rashi, Bereishis 6:14 — Noach’s warning proves that return could avert the Flood: Reishis Chochmah writes: “וּרְאָיָה שֶׁגַּם... יֵשׁ לָהֶם תְּשׁוּבָה, שֶׁהֲרֵי דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל... נִתְעַכֵּב נֹחַ בַּעֲשִׂיַּת הַתֵּבָה כְּדֵי לְהַכְרִיז לָהֶם שֶׁיַּחְזְרוּ וְיַעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה.” The Midrash itself says, “מֵאָה וְעֶשְׂרִים שָׁנָה הָיָה מַתְרֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, שֶׁמָּא יַעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה,” and describes Noach repeatedly explaining the Ark until they refused to return. Rashi states the purpose even more briefly: “אוּלַי יָשׁוּבוּ.” The Shlah uses this as a challenge to an absolute reading of the Zohar: “וְעַל כָּל זֹאת רָצָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁיַּעֲשׂוּ תְּשׁוּבָה וְיִמְחֹל לָהֶם.” Background: the long construction made the approaching judgment visible and gave the generation time to abandon its corrupt conduct. Rav Tzadok accepts that this disproves the claim that repentance would leave them presently wicked and doomed regardless. He limits the proof, however: an offered escape from punishment does not yet establish that the former spiritual blemish could be erased as though it had never occurred.

וְזֶה וַדַּאי דָּבָר תָּמוּהַּ וְזָר מְאוֹד, וַאֲפִילּוּ תֵּימָא דְּלֹא תִּיקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ כְּלָל, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֹּל שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁבִין וְלֹא הָיוּ חוֹטְאִים עוֹד, וַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ נֶעֱנָשִׁים בְּעֹונֶשׁ הַמַּבּוּל לִכְלָיוֹן הָעוֹלָם כּוּלָּם בִּשְׁבִילוֹ יֹאבְדוּ גַּם לְגַמְרֵי

and this is certainly astonishing and very strange, for even if you say that he did not rectify the past through his repentance at all, nevertheless, had they repented and ceased sinning, they certainly would not have been punished with the destruction of the Flood, causing the entire world to perish completely on their account!
וּבִבְנֵי נֹחַ בְּלָאו הָכִי לֹא מָצִינוּ שֶׁנִּתְּנָה לָהֶם תְּשׁוּבָה לְכַפָּרַת הַקּוֹדֵם כְּלָל, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי [לְעֵיל אוֹת א׳] מִזֶּה בְּשֵׁם הַמִּדְרָשׁ וְהָרִאשׁוֹנִים

Moreover, regarding descendants of Noach, in any event we do not find that repentance was granted to them for retroactive atonement of the past at all, as I wrote [above, Siman 1] concerning this in the name of the Midrash and the Rishonim;727Midrash Tanchuma, Ha’azinu 4:1; Takanas HaShavin 1:1 — Noahide teshuvah and the difference between future healing and retroactive atonement: Tanchuma distinguishes Israel’s covenantal gift of atonement: “עוֹשֶׂה תְּשׁוּבָה, נוֹשֵׂא לוֹ פָּנִים. יָכוֹל לַכֹּל? תַּלְמוּד לוֹמַר: אֵלֶיךָ, וְלֹא לְאֻמָּה אַחֶרֶת.” Rav Tzadok cites this passage together with the Ramah miPano and R. Yitzchak Abarbanel in his opening siman. There he supplies the distinction governing the present se’if: “וְרַק רְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא זֶה יֵשׁ גַּם בְּגוֹיִם,” whereas “תִּיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם” means that the prior sin itself is removed—“יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ.” In other words, a Noahide can cease the evil and thereby no longer be subject to a decree whose basis is continuing wickedness; this is real return from the present course. The special Torah chiddush of kapparah for Israel goes further: it can transform the relationship to the past, ultimately leaving the person “כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם.” Rav Tzadok therefore reads the earlier authorities precisely, not as denying all moral change to the nations, but as denying the uniquely Jewish power of teshuvah to uproot and repair the former act itself.
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַתְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעֶלֶת לָהֶם לְבַטֵּל הָעֹונֶשׁ הַנִּגְזָר כִּדְאַשְׁכְּחַן בְּאַנְשֵׁי נִינְוֵה
but nevertheless, repentance avails for them to annul an impending decreed punishment, as we find with the people of Nineveh;
וְהַזֹּוהַר מְדַבֵּר בִּתְשׁוּבָה שֶׁהִיא מוֹעִילָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל עֲוֹן הַקּוֹדֵם וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה כְּאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם, וְעַל זֶה אֵין רְאָיָה מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל:

whereas the Zohar speaks of the repentance that avails for Israel to atone for past iniquity and render him as though he had never sinned in his life, and regarding this there is no proof from the Generation of the Flood.728Yonah 3:8–10; Taanis 16a; Zohar, Vayechi 219b and Vayakhel 214b; Reishis Chochmah 17:20–25 — Nineveh proves cancellation of the decree, not complete erasure: Nineveh was commanded, “וְיָשֻׁבוּ אִישׁ מִדַּרְכּוֹ הָרָעָה,” and Scripture concludes: “וַיַּרְא הָאֱלֹהִים אֶת מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם כִּי שָׁבוּ מִדַּרְכָּם הָרָעָה... וְלֹא עָשָׂה.” Taanis emphasizes that God did not see merely their sackcloth or fasting, but their changed deeds. This establishes Rav Tzadok’s “רְפוּאָה לְהַבָּא”: the conduct ceased and the threatened punishment was withdrawn. The Zohar’s severe wording—“לֵית לָן חוֹבָא בְּעָלְמָא דְּלָא אִית לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה, בַּר מֵהַאי”—addresses the deeper repair of the prior blemish. Its qualification in Vayakhel is decisive: “וְהָנֵי מִילֵי כַּד לָא עָבַד תְּיוּבְתָא שְׁלֵימָתָא... לְחַפָּאָה עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי.” Reishis Chochmah explains that ordinary teshuvah tata’ah—merely turning from the act—is insufficient for such a comprehensive blemish; teshuvah ila’ah, crying, Torah, and whole-person repair are required. Thus the Flood and Nineveh demonstrate that no sinner should despair or remain in wickedness, but they do not by themselves prove the Zohar’s higher category: complete repair of the earlier damage.

items.h: The theme: The four categories of Rabbi Yishmael apply to every sin. Under the Tannaitic framework, every transgression in the Torah finds atonement, at least in conjunction with Yom Kippur. The Shelah quotes the Rokeach as asserting that whoever incurs a death penalty requires bodily afflictions equivalent to death, and that one who emits seed wastefully is liable to death. R’ Tzadok refutes this application: the Rokeach stated "afflictions as harsh as death" exclusively regarding capital offenses executed by an earthly court (misos beis din), whereas for spiritual excision (kares) he required only scouring afflictions without equating them to death, and certainly not for an offense that does not even carry kares.

p: אַךְ מֵאַרְבָּעָה חִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה דְּרַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל, שֶׁכָּלַל בָּהֶם כָּל הָעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה, וַדַּאי מְבוֹאָר דִּמְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה לְכַפָּרַת הַקּוֹדֵם גַּם כֵּן עַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּצֵירוּף יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים

But from the four categories of atonement of Rabbi Yishmael (Yoma 86a), which encompass all the transgressions in the Torah, it is certainly clear that repentance avails to atone for the past as well, at least in conjunction with Yom Kippur;
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּשְּׁלָ״ה דִּבְרוֹקֵחַ כָּתַב דִּבַעֲבֵירָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֹונֶשׁ מִיתָה צָרִיךְ סִגּוּפִים הַשָּׁוִים לְמִיתָה, וְהַמּוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה, עַד כָּאן

and see in the Shelah there, who cited that the Rokeach wrote that for a transgression carrying the punishment of death one requires mortifications equivalent to death, and one who emits seed wastefully is liable to death, thus far;729Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Shaarei Teshuvah 4:6; Resisei Layla 41; Machshavot Charutz 15:5 — teshuvah remains operative in every category of atonement: Rabbi Yishmael’s formulation is: “שלשה הן, ותשובה עם כל אחד ואחד” — “there are three additional divisions, and teshuvah accompanies each one.” The baraisa then distinguishes: for a positive commandment, forgiveness is immediate; for a negative commandment, teshuvah suspends and Yom Kippur atones; for kareis or a court death penalty, teshuvah and Yom Kippur suspend and suffering completes the cleansing; and for chillul Hashem, death completes it. The Rambam codifies the same order, while Rabbeinu Yonah emphasizes that the later stages do not replace teshuvah but complete kapparah and renewed acceptance. Background: Rav Tzadok is answering the claim that this sin lies wholly outside teshuvah. Because Rabbi Yishmael’s scheme was stated as a comprehensive classification of Torah transgressions, even its gravest category begins with teshuvah; the additional agents determine when the earlier stain is fully cleansed. In Resisei Layla 41 Rav Tzadok describes Israel’s distinctive power as “לתקן הקודם עד דזדונות נעשים כזכיות” — to repair the past until deliberate sins become merits. In Machshavot Charutz 15:5 he adds that for this particular blemish complete repair requires teshuvah joined to Torah. Thus his present inference is limited but decisive: the Zohar cannot mean that sincere return has no effect; the remaining question is what completes the prior repair.
וְתָמוּהַּ, דִּבְרוֹקֵחַ כָּתוּב זֶה עַל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין, עַיֵּין שָׁם [בְּהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה סִימָן י״א] בְּבָא עַל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ
and it is astonishing, for in the Rokeach [Hilchos Teshuvah, §11] this was written regarding those liable to court executions, see there regarding one who cohabits with a married woman;
אֲבָל בְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת [שָׁם סִימָן ז׳ וְסִימָן י״ד], אַף דְּהִצְרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן לְסִגּוּפִים וְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא כָּתַב שָׁם ״קָשֶׁה כְּמִיתָה״ כְּלָל, עַיֵּין שָׁם

whereas regarding those liable to excision (kares) [there, §7 and §14], although he likewise required mortifications and scouring afflictions, he did not write there "as harsh as death" at all, see there;
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּהַהִיא דְּגַם כָּרֵת לֵיכָּא:

and all the more so regarding this sin where not even excision applies!730Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Hilchos Bi’ah 1:49; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7, 11, 14 — “suffering like death” is stated for a formal court-death transgression: The Shlah writes: “אם יש עונש מיתה, צריך לעשות לו סיגופים השוים למיתה; והמוציא זרע לבטלה חייב מיתה” — when a sin carries death, the penitent requires mortifications corresponding to death, and one who emits seed in vain is called liable to death. He is combining the Rokeach’s four modes of teshuvah with Niddah 13a’s description of Onan. Rav Tzadok tests that combination against the Rokeach’s actual wording. In §11, concerning adultery, the Rokeach says: “שהוא כמיתה, יסבול צער קשה כמיתה” — because it is like death, he should endure suffering as harsh as death. But in §§7 and 14, concerning intercourse with a niddah and other kareis-level cases, the Rokeach prescribes fasting, lashes, cold, confession, and restraint without using the phrase “like death.” Background: the Rokeach calibrates teshuvas ha-kasuv to the Torah’s stated punishment. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes a fixed halachic category of misas beis din from the Gemara’s “חייב מיתה” concerning Onan, which may express heavenly punishment or exceptional severity rather than place the act in the same formal class. He does not minimize the aveirah; he questions whether the Rokeach himself supports the Shlah’s exact measure. The following se’ifim continue that legal analysis, while Machshavot Charutz 15:5 supplies the broader conclusion that teshuvah together with Torah can repair the earlier blemish.

items.h: The theme: Analysis of "liability to death" for wasteful emission and its derivation from Onan. In Niddah 13a, Chazal derive that one who emits seed wastefully is liable to death from Onan. R' Tzadok engages in an extensive halachic excursus analyzing whether this applied to Bnei Noach through the mitzvah of procreation, or through the verse "and he shall cleave unto his wife" (v'davak b'ishto, Sanhedrin 58a), from which sodomy and bestiality are derived. He demonstrates that while heavenly retribution took Onan's life, wasteful emission is not enumerated among biblical capital crimes or among fixed deaths at the hands of Heaven (misah bidei Shamayim). Unlike statutory divine death penalties, Talmudic warnings that an act incurs death (e.g., teaching halachah before one's master, sleeping before Ma'ariv, neglecting hand-washing) do not equate an offense to kares, nor do they require scouring mortifications for repentance.

p: וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה הוּא מֵהַגְּמָרָא דְּנִדָּה [שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳] וְלָמְדוּ מִקְּרָא דְּאוֹנָן, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And what he wrote, that he is liable to death, is from the Gemara in Niddah [13a], where they derived it from the verse concerning Onan, see there.
[וְיֵשׁ לְעַיֵּין קְצָת: מַה רְאָיָה מַיְיתֵי מִקּוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה, דְּהָיוּ בִּכְלַל בְּנֵי נֹחַ דְּאַזְהָרָתָן הִיא מִיתָתָן וְהָיוּ חַיָּיבִין מִיתָה בִּידֵי אָדָם עַל זֶה גַּם כֵּן

[And one must examine somewhat: what proof can be brought from the era prior to the Giving of the Torah, when they were categorized as Bnei Noach, regarding whom their prohibition is their death penalty (Sanhedrin 57a), and they were liable to capital execution by man for this as well;731Niddah 13a; Bereishis 38:9–10; Rashi — Onan and the Gemara’s phrase “liable to death”: The Gemara states: “כל המוציא שכבת זרע לבטלה חייב מיתה, שנאמר: וירע בעיני ה׳ אשר עשה וימת גם אותו” — “Anyone who emits seed in vain is liable to death, as it is stated: ‘What he did was evil in Hashem’s eyes, and He put him to death also.’” The verse concerns Onan, who “שחת ארצה לבלתי נתן זרע לאחיו” — destroyed [his seed] upon the ground so as not to provide offspring for his brother. Rashi explains: “דש מבפנים וזורה מבחוץ,” intercourse was begun normally but completed externally. Background: the Gemara cites a narrative of punishment by Heaven; the verse does not formulate a permanent beis-din penalty or list this act among the Torah’s fixed chayavei misah. That distinction drives Rav Tzadok’s question. Since Onan lived before Matan Torah, when the patriarchal family still stood within the legal framework of Bnei Noach, how can his death by Heaven establish the exact post-Sinai classification for a Jew? Earlier in this siman (15:1–4), Rav Tzadok likewise notes that the Rambam calls the act an “איסור גדול” and cites the Gemara’s comparisons, but does not identify a distinct Torah death-penalty. Se’if 23 therefore accepts the Gemara’s severity while investigating what kind of “death liability” the proof from Onan actually establishes.
דַּהֲרֵי קוֹדֶם מַתַּן תּוֹרָה נִצְטַוּוּ אַפְּרוּ וּרְבוּ דְּזֶה בִּכְלָלוֹ
for behold, prior to the Giving of the Torah they were commanded concerning procreation, within which this is subsumed;
וְהָא דְּלֹא חָשֵׁיב לֵיהּ בְּז׳ מִצְוֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ, וּמִשּׁוּם דְּלֹא נִשְׁנָה בְּסִינַי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין [נ״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳]
and that it was not enumerated among the Seven Mitzvos of Bnei Noach is because it was not repeated at Sinai, as they said in Sanhedrin [59a];
הַיְינוּ מִסִּינַי וְאֵילָךְ דְּנִיטְּלָה מֵהֶם, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר רַשִׁ״י [שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״לֹא״
meaning from Sinai onward it was removed from them, as Rashi said [there, 59a, s.v. lo];

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּטַ״ז אֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר [סִימָן א׳ סְעִיף קָטָן ב׳] וּבְטוּרֵי אֶבֶן [בְּרֵישׁ מִלּוּאִים לַחֲגִיגָה] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״לֹא לְתֹהוּ״ וּבְמִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ [פֶּרֶק י׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת מְלָכִים], יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ, וְעַל כֵּן נֶעֶנְשׁוּ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל

and as stated in the Taz [Even HaEzer 1:2], in the Turei Even [Chagigah, Milu'im, s.v. lo l'sohu], and in the Mishneh LaMelech [Hilchos Melachim 10:7], see there at length, and for this reason they were punished in the Generation of the Flood.732Sanhedrin 59a–b; Rashi; Tosafos; Mishneh LaMelech, Melachim 10:7; Ramban and Rashba on Niddah 13a — procreation before and after Sinai: The governing rule is: “כל מצוה שנאמרה לבני נח ונשנית בסיני — לזה ולזה נאמרה; לבני נח ולא נשנית בסיני — לישראל נאמרה ולא לבני נח.” Rashi explains that before Sinai the Noahides were commanded, but when Israel “יצאו לקדושה” they remained bound while an unrepeated command was removed from the nations from Sinai onward. The Mishneh LaMelech therefore writes that it is “פשיטא” that all Bnei Noach were obligated in peru u’revu until Sinai. Tosafos adds the direct connection used here: “מי שמצווה על פריה ורביה מצווה שלא להשחית זרע” — one commanded to reproduce is commanded not to destroy seed. The opposing Rishonim separate the prohibitions. As quoted by the Mishneh LaMelech, the Ramban and Rashba argue that women, although not commanded in peru u’revu, are still forbidden to destroy seed, and “הכל לקו על זה במבול” — everyone was punished for this at the Flood. Rav Tzadok is mapping these positions, not merely citing authorities in agreement: Tosafos supplies a derivative of peru u’revu; Ramban and Rashba show an independent prohibition but leave its Noahide source difficult. His own earlier discussion in 15:1–4 already frames this dispute, and the present se’if proposes a textual source that may resolve both the prohibition and its omission as a separate eighth Noahide commandment.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּמִשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ שָׁם לִפְנֵי זֶה הֵבִיא מֵרַמְבַּ״ן וְרַשְׁבָּ״א [נִדָּה שָׁם] דְּגַם מִי שֶׁאֵין מְצֻוֶּוה אַפְּרוּ וּרְבוּ אָסוּר בְּהַשְׁחָתַת זֶרַע, דְּהַכֹּל לָקוּ בַּמַּבּוּל

And see there in the Mishneh LaMelech prior to this, where he cited from the Ramban and Rashba [Niddah 13a] that even one who is not commanded in procreation is forbidden to destroy seed, for all were stricken in the Flood;

וּדְזֶה דְּלֹא כְּתוֹסָפוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ, אֶלָּא דְּלֹא יָדַע הֵיכָן רְמִיזָא אִיסּוּר זֶה לְבֶן נֹחַ, וְגַם אַמַּאי לֹא מְנָאוֹ בִּכְלַל ז׳ מִצְוֹת בְּנֵי נֹחַ, וְהִנִּיחַ בְּקוּשְׁיָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and this diverges from Tosafos in Sanhedrin (59b) who held it is subsumed under procreation; yet [the Mishneh LaMelech] did not know where this prohibition is alluded to for a Ben Noach, nor why it was not enumerated among the Seven Mitzvos, leaving it in difficulty, see there.

וְנִרְאֶה דִּלְפִי דַּעְתִּי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר, דִּכְמוֹ דְּדָרְשִׁינַן [סַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ח עַמּוּד א׳] ״וְדָבַק״ — וְלֹא בְּזָכָר, ״בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ״ — וְלֹא בְּאֵשֶׁת חֲבֵירוֹ, ״וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד״ — יָצְאוּ בְּהֵמָה וְחַיָּה וְכוּלֵיהּ

And it appears in my opinion that one may say: just as we expound [in Sanhedrin 58a] "and he shall cleave" (Bereishis 2:24)—and not to a male; "unto his wife"—and not to the wife of his fellow; "and they shall be one flesh"—excluding domestic and wild beasts;733Sanhedrin 58a; Rambam, Hilchos Melachim 9:5; Bereishis Rabbah 18:5 — Rav Tzadok’s proposed derivation from “cleave to his wife”: The Gemara expounds Bereishis 2:24: “ודבק — ולא בזכר; באשתו — ולא באשת חבירו; והיו לבשר אחד — מי שנעשים בשר אחד, יצאו בהמה וחיה שאין נעשים בשר אחד.” The Rambam codifies these phrases as the source for the Noahide arayos of another man’s wife, a male, and an animal. Bereishis Rabbah gives the same grouping and adds the principle that a prohibition written for Bnei Noach is enforced with death. None of these sources explicitly mentions emitting seed in vain. Rav Tzadok therefore marks his next step as his own chidush: “לפי דעתי יש לומר.” When seed is deliberately scattered outside, there is no enduring “דיבוק,” the act is not completed “באשתו” in the Torah’s procreative sense, and no “בשר אחד” can result. He proposes that the act may thus be included in the same verse-generated Noahide arayos complex, just as male intercourse and bestiality are not counted as independent Noahide commandments but are subsumed under arayos. This explains both where the warning could be hinted and why it does not appear as an eighth item. The note must remain carefully limited: Sanhedrin supplies the textual categories; the extension to this act is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive construction, offered to answer the Mishneh LaMelech’s unresolved question.
הָכִי נַמֵּי יֵשׁ לִלְמוֹד מִזֶּה אִיסּוּר דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, דְּלֵיכָּא דִּיבּוּק וְלֹא בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ וְלֹא נַעֲשָׂה בָּזֶה ״לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד״ כְּשֶׁזּוֹרֶה בַּחוּץ
so too one may derive from this the prohibition of wasteful emission, for there is no cleaving, nor is it within his wife, nor does it become "one flesh" when he scatters outside!
וּכְמוֹ דְּזָכוּר וּבְהֵמָה לֹא נִמְנוּ בִּפְנֵי עַצְמוֹ בִּבְנֵי נֹחַ וְהֵם בִּכְלַל גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, וְאַף שֶׁאֵינָם מִכְּלַל הָעֲרָיוֹת כֵּיוָן דְּמִקְּרָא אֶחָד נִלְמַד אִיסּוּרָם

And just as homosexuality and bestiality were not enumerated independently for Bnei Noach, being subsumed under illicit relations (gilui arayos) although they are not classic familial relations, because their prohibition is derived from a single verse;
הָכִי נַמֵּי מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּנִלְמַד גַּם כֵּן מֵאוֹתוֹ מִקְרָא וְדָמְיָא נַמֵּי לְהוּ, כְּלָלוּהוּ בְּגִילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת
so too with wasteful emission, which is derived from that very same verse and resembles them, they subsumed it under gilui arayos.
וְגַם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דְּהַמִּשְׁנֶה לַמֶּלֶךְ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל כָּתַב רַק הֵיכִי רְמִיזָא לִבְנֵי נֹחַ, נִרְאֶה דִּלְיִשְׂרָאֵל סְבִירָא לֵיהּ כְּסַמַ״ק הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּנִלְמַד מִ״לֹא תִנְאָף״

And one can also say that the Mishneh LaMelech mentioned above asked only where it is alluded to for Bnei Noach, because for Israel he assumed according to the Semak that it is derived from "You shall not commit adultery";
וּכְבָר נִתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא, וְאִם כֵּן וַדַּאי גַּם לְיִשְׂרָאֵל צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּאֵין אִיסּוּרוֹ אֶלָּא מִ״וְדָבַק״ וְגוֹמֵר הַנֶּאֱמַר לִבְנֵי נֹחַ דְּגַם יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּכְלָל

but it was already explained that this is an asmachta, and if so, for Israel as well one must say that its prohibition stems solely from "and he shall cleave, etc." stated to Bnei Noach, in which Israel is included,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [קִדּוּשִׁין כ״א סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״אֵשֶׁת״, דִּבְאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּגוֹי אִיכָּא עֲשֵׂה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל מִ״וְדָבַק״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

in the manner Tosafos wrote [Kiddushin 21b, s.v. eshes] that regarding the wife of a gentile there is a positive command for an Israelite derived from "and he shall cleave," see there;734Tosafos, Kiddushin 21b; Niddah 13b; Bereishis Rabbah 18:5; Resisei Layla 41 — Israel’s inclusion and the difference between earthly and heavenly punishment: Tosafos writes regarding a captive gentile married woman: “מכל מקום איכא עשה, דכתיב ודבק באשתו — ולא באשת חבירו” — even for a Jew there remains a positive command derived from the verse addressed to Bnei Noach. Rav Tzadok uses that model to argue that Israel can remain included in “ודבק…באשתו…לבשר אחד,” even when the Noahide obligation itself changed after Sinai. Niddah 13b then calls those who sin “דרך איברים” — by non-intercourse use of the limbs — “בני מבול,” people deserving the Flood. Rav Tzadok reads this as more than a historical label: it identifies the intrinsic heavenly consequence associated with the corruption that produced the Flood. He therefore distinguishes two planes. Human law may punish a Noahide more readily because “אזהרתן זו היא מיתתן” and social order requires stricter external enforcement; this does not prove that the identical beis-din penalty applies to Israel. Heavenly punishment, however, reflects the spiritual damage itself, and Rav Tzadok argues that Israel’s greater sanctity can make that damage greater, not smaller. This accords with his broader formulation in Resisei Layla 41 that Israel’s root remains bound to Hashem even through sin, enabling deeper repair but also giving Jewish action greater spiritual consequence. Thus the proof from Onan can establish grave heavenly liability without placing the act in the formal category of kareis or court-imposed death.

וְכֵיוָן דְּלֹא נִשְׁנָה אִיסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בְּסִינַי לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, מִמֵּילָא שָׁאַמְרִינַן דְּגַם לְדִידְהוּ מִסִּינַי וְאֵילָךְ נִיטַּל מִבְּנֵי נֹחַ וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי לֹא חֲשָׁבוּהוּ בְּז׳ מִצְוֹת וּכְמוֹ לְהַתּוֹסָפוֹת

and since the prohibition of wasteful emission was not explicitly repeated at Sinai for Israel, we say that from Sinai onward it was removed from Bnei Noach as well, and for this reason they did not count it among the Seven Mitzvos, as in Tosafos.

וְלֹא דָּמֵי לְמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ מֵאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּגוֹי, דְּשָׁם אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נִשְׁנָה בְּסִינַי לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וּלְגַבֵּי הַגּוֹי הוּא אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּגוֹי כְּמוֹ גַּבֵּי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל
And it is not comparable to the wife of a gentile, for there adultery with an Israelite woman was repeated at Sinai;

מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בָּזֶה לֹא מְהַנֵּי מַה דְּנִשְׁנָה גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת בְּסִינַי, וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּמֵחַד קְרָא נָפְקָא לֵיהּ בִּבְנֵי נֹחַ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן דְּאִיסּוּר זֶה לֹא נִשְׁנָה בְּסִינַי עַל כֵּן נִיטַּל מֵהֶם
whereas here it does not avail that general gilui arayos was repeated at Sinai, for since this specific prohibition was not repeated at Sinai, it was removed from them.

וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים בְּנֵי נֹחַ הָיוּ אָז מוּזְהָרִים מִזֶּה וְנֶהֱרָגִין עָלָיו כְּמוֹ עַל גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, אַף דְּהוּא רַק בַּעֲשֵׂה וְלָאו הַבָּא מִכְּלַל עֲשֵׂה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ה׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] רֵישׁ דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מוּכָן״

In any event, Bnei Noach were then warned concerning this and executed for it just as for gilui arayos, even though it is only a positive command and a negative command derived from a positive, as Tosafos stated [Avodah Zarah 5b, s.v. mukan];
וְאִם כֵּן מַאי רְאָיָה מִזֶּה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
and if so, what proof is there from this for an Israelite?
וְאוּלַי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִזֶּה רְאָיָה לְהַסּוֹבְרִים דְּמֵהָאָבוֹת וְאֵילָךְ יָצְאוּ מִכְּלַל בְּנֵי נֹחַ, עַיֵּין בְּפָרָשַׁת דְּרָכִים [דְּרוּשׁ א׳]
And perhaps one might say this proves the view that from the Patriarchs onward they departed from the status of Bnei Noach, see Parashas Derachim [Derush 1].

אַךְ בְּנִדָּה [שָׁם עַמּוּד ב׳] אִיתָא: ״דֶּרֶךְ אֵבָרִים בְּנֵי מַבּוּל נִינְהוּ״, וּמַשְׁמַע דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר עֹונֶשׁ מַבּוּל מַמָּשׁ אִלּוּ הָיוּ כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ נִכְשָׁלִים בּוֹ וְאַלְמָלֵא הַשְּׁבוּעָה שֶׁלֹּא יָבִיא מַבּוּל, וַהֲרֵי לָמְדוּ גַּם מֵעֹונֶשׁ דּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל לְיִשְׂרָאֵל

But in Niddah [13b] it is taught: "Those who engage in unnatural contact through limbs are like those belonging to the Generation of the Flood," implying literal punishment of the Flood had the entire world stumbled in it were it not for the oath never to bring a Flood (Yeshayah 54:9), so behold they derived a lesson from the Flood for Israel as well!
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר, דְּאַף עַל גַּב דִּלְעִנְיַן עֹונֶשׁ בִּידֵי אָדָם הֶחְמִירָה תּוֹרָה בִּבְנֵי נֹחַ, לְעִנְיַן עֹונֶשׁ בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם אֵין חִילּוּק
And one must say: although regarding human execution the Torah was more stringent with Bnei Noach, regarding punishment by the hands of Heaven there is no difference:
דְּדִינֵי אָדָם שֶׁהֵם לְתִיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם שֶׁיִּתְיָירְאוּ מֵעֹונֶשׁ בֵּית דִּין בָּזֶה צְרִיכִים לִגְזוֹר בִּבְנֵי נֹחַ טְפֵי דִּפְרִיצֵי טְפֵי
for human jurisprudence exists for social order so they fear court punishment, wherefore they must decree more stringently upon Bnei Noach who are more lawless;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן דִּינֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁהוּא נִמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד פְּגַם הָעֲבֵירָה עַצְמָהּ, אַדְּרַבָּא יִשְׂרָאֵל לְמַעֲלָתָם פּוֹגְמִים בְּחֶטְאָם טְפֵי מֵאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם]
whereas heavenly judgments derive from the spiritual blemish of the transgression itself, in which Israel, owing to their spiritual elevation, blemish in their sin far more than the nations].
וְהַיְינוּ לְעִנְיַן עֹונֶשׁ שָׁמַיִם, וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה לַשָּׁמַיִם קָאָמַר, וְלֹא דָּמֵי וַדַּאי לְחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת גַּם כֵּן
And this applies to heavenly punishment, meaning liability to death from Heaven, and it is certainly not comparable to those liable for excision (kares) either.

וְאַף דִּבְעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת [מַאֲמַר חֲקוֹר דִּין חֵלֶק א׳ פֶּרֶק י״ח] כָּתַב בִּפְשִׁיטוּת דְּגַם חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם בִּכְלַל חַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת לְהַצְרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין לְכַפָּרָתוֹ

And although in Asarah Ma'amaros [Chakor Din 1:18] he wrote simply that those liable to death at the hands of Heaven are included among those liable for kares to require scouring afflictions for atonement;
הֲרֵי פֵּירֵשׁ שָׁם: כְּגוֹן זָר שֶׁשִּׁימֵּשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְכוֹבֵשׁ נְבוּאָתוֹ וַחֲבֵירָיו וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם
behold, he specified there: such as a non-Kohen who served in the Temple, one who suppresses his prophecy, and their companions, see there;
וְהֵם אוֹתָם הַשְּׁנוּיִים בַּמִּשְׁנָה [סַנְהֶדְרִין פ״ט עַמּוּד א׳] וּבַבָּרַיְיתָא [שָׁם פ״ג עַמּוּד א׳], עַיֵּין שָׁם
and these are the statutory cases taught in the Mishnah [Sanhedrin 89a] and Baraisa [83a], see there;
וְהַיְינוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁלָּמְדוּ מִקְּרָא שֶׁזֶּהוּ עָנְשׁוֹ הַקָּבוּעַ לְדוֹרוֹת

which refers to those derived from verses as a fixed statutory penalty for generations.735Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chakor Din I:18; Sanhedrin 83a and 89a; Rambam, Hilchos Sanhedrin 19:2; Ramban — a fixed Torah category of misah bidei Shamayim: Rav Tzadok reports the Asarah Maamaros as treating the formally defined chayavei misah bidei Shamayim like chayavei kareis for the need of teshuvah together with purifying suffering. The source-category is juridically identifiable. Sanhedrin 83a introduces an enumerated baraisa, “ואלו הן שבמיתה” — “These are the ones [liable] to death,” and derives its cases from verses, including a non-kohen who performs the service and a tamei kohen who serves. The Mishnah at 89a likewise states: “הכובש את נבואתו… מיתתו בידי שמים, שנאמר אנכי אדרש מעמו” — one who suppresses his prophecy, disregards a prophet’s words, or violates his own prophecy dies by Heaven, based on “I will require it from him.” The Rambam codifies this defined class in Hilchos Sanhedrin. Ramban supplies a close conceptual parallel on Shemos 22:21: although the Torah threatens death for oppressing a widow or orphan, Chazal did not count it among the baraisa’s chayavei misah bidei Shamayim, because it is not the same fixed legal category as verses such as “ומתו בו כי יחללוהו.” In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Rav Tzadok similarly analyzes chayavei misah bidei Shamayim as a recognized halachic class alongside kareis. His conclusion here is therefore limited but exact: the Asarah Maamaros refers to punishments permanently assigned by Torah to an offense, not every sin for which death once occurred or for which Chazal use the phrase “liable to death.”

וְזֶה לֹא נִמְנָה שָׁם וְלֹא בָּרַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק י״ט מֵהִלְכוֹת סַנְהֶדְרִין הֲלָכָה ב׳], דְּלֹא מָצִינוּ שֶׁקְּבָעַתּוּ תּוֹרָה בְּעֹונֶשׁ זֶה, רַק מַה שֶּׁמָּצִינוּ שֶׁאֵיזֶה אָדָם נֶעֱנַשׁ מִיתָה עַל עָוֹן זֶה, אֲבָל לֹא נִתְבָּאֵר שֶׁיִּהְיֶה זֶה לְעֹונֶשׁ קָבוּעַ עַל חֵטְא זֶה

But this sin was not enumerated there, nor in the Rambam [Hilchos Sanhedrin 19:2], for we do not find that the Torah established it as a statutory penalty, but merely that specific individuals [Er and Onan] were punished with death for this iniquity, with no indication that this constitutes a fixed penalty for this sin;
וְגַם עַל בִּיטּוּל פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה נֶעֱנַשׁ חִזְקִיָּה מִיתָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת י׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳], וְלֹא נִמְנָה בֵּין חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם
and for neglecting procreation Chizkiyahu was likewise punished with death as they said [Berachos 10a], yet it is not counted among statutory deaths at the hands of Heaven;

וְכַיּוֹצֵא בוֹ בְּעֵירוּבִין [ס״ג עַמּוּד א׳] בְּמוֹרֶה הֲלָכָה בִּפְנֵי רַבּוֹ וְכַדּוֹמֶה, כָּל אֵלּוּ לֹא נִמְנוּ בִּכְלַל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁחִיְּיבָתַם תּוֹרָה מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם, וְלֹא לְאֵלּוּ כִּוֵּון הָעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת לְהַשְׁווֹתָם לְחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת

and likewise in Eruvin [63a] regarding one who issues a halachic ruling in the presence of his master, and similar cases, none of which are categorized among statutory capital offenses where the Torah commanded death by Heaven, and it was not to these that Asarah Ma'amaros intended to equate to kares.736Berachos 10a and 4b; Eruvin 63a and 21b; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 5:2 — several uses of “liable to death” outside the formal list: Berachos 10a relates that Yeshayahu told Chizkiyahu, “כי מת אתה ולא תחיה,” explaining, “משום דלא עסקת בפריה ורביה” — he would die because he had not engaged in procreation. When Chizkiyahu defended himself by citing his vision of unworthy children, Yeshayahu answered: “בהדי כבשי דרחמנא למה לך? מאי דמפקדת איבעי לך למעבד” — do not enter Hashem’s hidden calculations; perform what you were commanded. Yet failure to fulfill peru u’revu is not enumerated in Sanhedrin’s fixed misah bidei Shamayim list. Eruvin 63a similarly says: “בפניו — אסור וחייב מיתה,” and records the tradition, “כל המורה הלכה בפני רבו חייב מיתה”; the Rambam codifies that warning in Hilchos Talmud Torah. Rav Tzadok then adduces an even broader use. Berachos 4b declares, “כל העובר על דברי חכמים חייב מיתה,” but the Gemara itself asks why this language appears specifically there and answers that it stresses the danger of being overcome by sleep or establishes that Maariv is obligatory. Eruvin 21b applies the same phrase to rabbinic safeguards and illustrates it through Rabbi Akiva’s refusal to eat without netilas yadayim in prison. These sources demonstrate genuine severity and possible heavenly punishment, but not one uniform atonement classification. Rav Tzadok’s distinction is that an incident, warning, or forceful rabbinic formulation does not by itself become the Torah-defined category that the Asarah Maamaros equates with kareis.

וַהֲרֵי מָצִינוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת ד׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּגַם כָּל הָעוֹבֵר עַל דִּבְרֵי חֲכָמִים חַיָּיב מִיתָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם לְעִנְיַן הַיָּשֵׁן קוֹדֶם תְּפִלַּת עַרְבִית, וְכֵן בְּעֵירוּבִין [כ״א עַמּוּד ב׳] לְעִנְיַן נְטִילַת יָדַיִם, וְאַף דְּקָרוּ לְהוּ שָׁם ״חֲמוּרוֹת״ מֵהַאי טַעְמָא, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And behold, we find [in Berachos 4b] that whoever violates rabbinic enactments is liable to death (regarding one who sleeps before Ma'ariv), and in Eruvin [21b] regarding washing hands, and although they termed them "severe" for this reason;
מִכָּל מָקוֹם וַדַּאי אֵין לְדַמּוֹתָם לְחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת לְעִנְיַן חֹמֶר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וּלְהַצְרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין, וְלֹא חֲמִירֵי מִבִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא כְּלָל
nevertheless one certainly cannot equate them to kares regarding the severity of repentance to require scouring afflictions, for they are no graver than neglecting a biblical positive command;

וְלֹא אָמַר אֶלָּא בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁחִיְּיבָתַן תּוֹרָה לְעֹונֶשׁ הַחֵטְא, וְלֹא בְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה שֶׁאָמְרוּ רַבָּנָן, וַאֲפִילּוּ שֶׁנִּמְצָא שֶׁנֶּעֶנְשׁוּ כֵּן כָּל שֶׁלֹּא קָבְעָה תּוֹרָה הָעֹונֶשׁ לְהַחֵטְא כִּבְכָל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁמָּנוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה:

and [the Rama MiFano] spoke solely of offenses where the Torah formally prescribed excision or death by Heaven as the statutory punishment for that sin, and not of offenses where the Rabbis used homiletic expressions of liability to death, nor even where individuals were divinely executed, so long as the Torah did not fix it as the statutory penalty for that crime.

items.h: The theme: The fasts prescribed by the Rokeach for wasteful emission are not scouring afflictions (yissurin memarkin). In Hilchos Teshuvah (§20), the Rokeach prescribes a forty-day fast for wasteful emission, omitting the severe mortifications he requires elsewhere for kares (such as cohabiting with a niddah). For rabbinic and non-capital negative commands, the Rokeach likewise prescribes fasts (e.g., twenty fasts for illicit embraces). Fasts for non-capital sins serve as "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal) to counterbalance bodily pleasure, or as a proactive tribute-gift, rather than an essential requirement for atonement, because teshuvah suspends judgment until Yom Kippur arrives, and should death occur beforehand, death itself scours the sin.

p: וְתֵדַע עוֹד, דִּבְרוֹקֵחַ [שָׁם סִימָן כ׳] סִדֵּר תְּשׁוּבָה לְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה תַּעֲנִית מ׳ יוֹם, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְלֹא כָּתַב עוֹד צֵירוּף סִגּוּפִים שֶׁכָּתַב [בְּסִימָן ז׳ וְי״ד] בְּבוֹעֵל נִדָּה וְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת

And you should further know: for in the Rokeach [there, §20] he arranged the regimen of teshuvah for wasteful emission as a forty-day fast, see there, and did not add the combination of severe mortifications that he prescribed [§7 and §14] for one who cohabits with a niddah and those liable for kares;

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב תַּעֲנִיּוֹת — כֵּן מַצְרְכוּ [שָׁם סִימָן י״ג] כ׳ תַּעֲנִית בְּהַ״ב עַל קוּרְבָה דְּגִילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם, שֶׁהוּא רַק בְּלָאו גַּם לְרַמְבַּ״ם הַמַּחְמִיר, וְעַיֵּין בְּשַׁ״ךְ יוֹרֶה דֵּעָה [סִימָן קנ״ז סְעִיף קָטָן י׳]

and as for writing fasts, he likewise required [there, §13] twenty fasts (on Mondays and Thursdays) for illicit physical contact (kerivah d'arayos), which is merely a negative commandment even according to the strict view of the Rambam, see the Shach [Yoreh De'ah 157:10];737Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7, 14, and 20 - forty fasts, but different accompanying disciplines: The Rokeach writes in §20: “מי שהשחית זרע בחשק תאותו יתענה מ׳ יום, וישמור נפשו ולא יראה פני אשה... ומכל ייחוד” - one who destroyed seed through desire fasts forty days and must guard against sights, perfume, and seclusion that could rekindle the sin. For intercourse with a niddah, however, §7 says: “הרי נתחייב כרת על בעילתו... ילקה ויתענה לא פחות מארבעים יום,” together with lying on the ground, black clothing, repeated confession, and tears. Section 14 adds: “יתענה ארבעים יום רצופין, וילקה בכל יום, ולא יאכל בשר ולא ישתה יין... ולא ירחץ,” and prescribes exposure to cold water. Thus the numerical fast may coincide, but the kareis cases receive a fuller regimen explicitly keyed to the Torah penalty. Rav Tzadok's inference is internal to the Rokeach: §20's forty days and protective fences do not equal the teshuvas ha-kasuv of §§7 and 14. He does not minimize the aveirah; he identifies the Rokeach's graduated prescriptions.
