In Machshavot Charutz 15:5 Rav Tzadok supplies the broader repair for this blemish: “אין לזה תיקון רק על ידי התורה” - after teshuvah, Torah is essential to repairing what preceded, so fasting is not presented as the entire process.738Rokeach §13; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Bi'ah 21:1; Ramban, Hasagos to Lo Sa'aseh 353; Shach, Yoreh De'ah 157:10 - affectionate contact: Rokeach §13 rules: “המנשק נשים ומחבקן וממשמשן בלא שכיבה יתענה שני וחמישי ושני... וירחיק מפתח ביתה שלא יבוא לידי עבירה” - one who kisses, embraces, or fondles women without intercourse fasts Monday-Thursday-Monday and erects a protective boundary. Rambam defines the Torah prohibition narrowly: “שחיבק ונישק דרך תאוה ונהנה בקירוב בשר הרי זה לוקה מן התורה,” deriving it from “לא תקרבו לגלות ערוה.” Ramban disputes that independent biblical lav, arguing that non-intercourse proximity is generally a rabbinic fence or an asmachta, though it remains prohibited. The Shach surveys the dispute, favors Rambam for intercourse-oriented affection, and stresses that even Rambam speaks only “דרך תאוה וחיבת ביאה”; he also records that Torah lashes for such proximity apply only regarding arayos punishable by kareis. Rav Tzadok therefore deliberately grants the stricter premise: even if the contact is a Torah lav, it is not itself kareis. That sharpens his question. Since the Rokeach's opening atonement scheme says that a lav requires teshuvah and Yom Kippur rather than scouring suffering, why prescribe BaHaB? Rav Tzadok tests whether the fast is teshuvas ha-mishkal for pleasure, an attempt to accelerate cleansing, or a distinct devotional gift - the distinction developed in the next se'if.
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ [שָׁם סִימָן א׳] כָּתַב הַחִלּוּקֵי כַּפָּרָה, דִּבְמִצְוֹת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה אֵין צָרִיךְ לְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and [the Rokeach] himself [there, §1] recorded the categories of atonement, stating that for a negative commandment one does not require scouring afflictions, see there.
וְעַיֵּין [שָׁם בְּסִימָן ו׳] כָּתַב דְּצָרִיךְ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל כְּפִי הַהֲנָאָה
And see [there, §6] where he wrote that one requires fasts for "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal) corresponding to the forbidden pleasure;
אֲבָל שָׁם כְּפִי הַנִּרְאֶה קָאֵי אַפְּנוּיָה נִדָּה דְּפָתַח בֵּיהּ [שָׁם בְּסִימָן ג׳] שֶׁהוּא מֵחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת דְּצָרִיךְ לְיִסּוּרִין
but there, it appears, he referred to an unmarried woman who is a niddah, with which he opened [§3], which is an offense of kares that requires afflictions.
וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּקָאֵי כְּשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְמָרֵק הַכַּפָּרָה קַמֵּי יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים דְּצָרִיךְ לִמְחוֹצֵי לָאוִין, וּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּהָכִי נַמֵּי לִמְחַיְּיבֵי לָאוִין בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה

And it is possible that he refers to one who wishes to scour and complete atonement prior to Yom Kippur, which applies to violators of negative commands, holding that the same applies to those who breach prohibitions through active commission;
אַךְ מִלְּבַד דִּסְתִימוּת דְּבָרָיו לֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן, אֵינוֹ נִרְאֶה גַּם כֵּן צֹרֶךְ לָזֶה
but besides the fact that his unqualified words do not imply this, there is also no halachic necessity for it:
כֵּיוָן דְּהַתְּשׁוּבָה תּוֹלָה לְהָגֵן בַּעֲדוֹ עַד שֶׁיַּגִּיעַ יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים
since repentance suspends judgment to shield him until Yom Kippur arrives;
וְאִם יָמוּת מִקּוֹדֶם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, הֲרֵי הַמִּיתָה מְמָרֶקֶת, מַה צֹּרֶךְ לְסִגּוּפֵי הַתַּעֲנִית לְמָרֵק:

and should he die prior to Yom Kippur, behold death scours the sin, so what need is there for the mortifications of fasting to scour it?739Yoma 86a; Shevuos 8b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4 - suspension, atonement, and Rav Tzadok's question: R. Yishmael's divisions state: “עבר על לא תעשה ועשה תשובה - תשובה תולה ויום הכיפורים מכפר”; for kareis and court-death offenses, “תשובה ויום הכיפורים תולין ויסורין ממרקין”; and for chillul Hashem, all three suspend while “מיתה ממרקת.” Rambam codifies the same hierarchy: an ordinary lav is completed by Yom Kippur, whereas kareis and court-death cases require suffering, and chillul Hashem is completed only by death. Shevuos 8b clarifies the function of suspension. When R. Zeira suggests that suspension means one who dies is free of the sin, Rava answers: “אם מת - מיתה ממרקת,” and concludes that suspension is “להגן עליו מן היסורין” - protection from suffering until the completing atonement arrives. Rav Tzadok applies that logic to the Rokeach. If fasts for a lav are merely punitive scouring intended to finish Yom Kippur's work early, teshuvah already protects the penitent in the interim, and death would cleanse if it came first. There is therefore no evident need for voluntary mortification as meruk. Rav Tzadok is not denying the value of fasting; he rejects this explanation of its function. Se'if 26 instead develops a non-punitive purpose: the fast as a doron replacing an olah.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים כ״ז–ל׳

The theme: The true role of fasting in repentance as a surrogate offering (doran). In Moed Katan 25a, Rav Huna fasted forty days merely because his tefillin strap inadvertently flipped over—an act devoid of physical pleasure where "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal) does not apply. In Berachos 17a, a fast is explicitly defined as replacing a sacrificial offering, where the diminution of fat and blood parallels the altar. Since an olah [burnt offering] was brought as a gift (doran) even after full pardon for omitting a positive commandment, voluntary fasts nowadays replace the olah to appease and draw near to Hashem, both after repentance and when offering heartfelt prayer.

p: וּבֶאֱמֶת מָצִינוּ בַּגְּמָרָא בְּכַמָּה דּוּכְתֵּי שֶׁהִתְעַנּוּ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת הַרְבֵּה עַל דְּבָרִים קַלִּים
And in truth we find in the Gemara in several places that they fasted numerous fasts over minor matters,
כְּהַאי דְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן [כ״ה עַמּוּד א׳] בְּרַב הוּנָא דְּאִתְהֲפֵיךְ רְצוּעָה דִּתְפִלִּין לֵיהּ וִיתֵיב אַרְבָּעִים תַּעֲנִיּוֹת
like that incident in Moed Katan [25a] regarding Rav Huna, whose tefillin strap became inverted and he sat forty fasts;

וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה בְּמֵזִיד חַס וְשָׁלוֹם, וְכִדְמַשְׁמַע גַּם כֵּן מִלְּשׁוֹן ״אִתְהֲפִיכָא״ דְּמַשְׁמַע מִמֵּילָא וּמֵעַצְמוֹ בְּלֹא דַּעְתּוֹ, אֶלָּא שֶׁהָיָה קְצָת פְּשִׁיעוּת עַל שֶׁלֹּא הִשְׁגִּיחַ שֶׁלֹּא יִתְהַפֵּךְ

and certainly it was not done intentionally, God forbid, as is also implied by the term ishpicha [it became inverted], which implies on its own without his knowledge, save that there was a slight negligence in not being vigilant that it should not invert;740Moed Katan 25a; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 33:3 - Rav Huna's forty fasts for a reversed tefillin strap: The Gemara records Rav Huna's exceptional care: “דְּיוֹמָא חַד אִתְהֲפִיכָא לֵיהּ רְצוּעָה דִתְפִילִּין וִיתֵיב עֲלַהּ אַרְבְּעִין תַּעֲנִיָּתָא” - one day a tefillin strap turned over and he observed forty fasts. The underlying halachah is significant: Shulchan Aruch codifies the halachah leMoshe miSinai that the straps must be “שְׁחוֹרוֹת מִבַּחוּץ,” with their black side outward. Yet the Gemara says that the strap “turned over”; it does not describe a deliberate violation. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the episode as an inadvertent occurrence enabled, at most, by slight insufficient care. Neither the Gemara nor Shulchan Aruch presents forty fasts as the ordinary halachic remedy. The incident's force here is conceptual: Rav Huna responded intensely to a lapse that involved no forbidden pleasure and therefore could not be explained as measure-for-measure deprivation. The fast may express renewed reverence and personal self-offering after a defect in kavod ha-mitzvah. Mishnah Berurah 33:19 stresses the practical duty to inspect and restore the straps' blackness; Rav Huna's forty fasts remain an exceptional personal avodah, not a universal schedule.
וְשָׁם אֵינוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁל הֲנָאָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל שֶׁל הַהֲנָאָה מֵהָאִיסּוּר
and there it was not a matter of physical pleasure that would require "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal) to counterbalance forbidden pleasure.

אֲבָל עִיקַּר הַתַּעֲנִית הוּא בִּמְקוֹם קָרְבָּן, כִּמְבוֹאָר [בִּבְרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: ״אָדָם חוֹטֵא וּמַקְרִיב קָרְבָּן וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְעַכְשָׁו יָשַׁבְתִּי בְּתַעֲנִית וְכוּלֵיהּ, חֶלְבִּי וְדָמִי שֶׁנִּתְמַעֵט כְּאִלּוּ הִקְרַבְתִּיו וְכוּלֵיהּ״

Rather, the primary function of fasting is in place of a sacrificial offering, as explained [in Berachos 17a]: "When the Temple stood, a person sinned and offered a sacrifice... and now I have sat in fasting... may my fat and blood that were diminished be considered as if I offered them, etc.";741Berakhot 17a; Vayikra 1:4 with Rashi and Ramban; Zevachim 6a; Shlah - fasting as korban and the olah as doron: Rav Sheshet prayed after a fast: “אָדָם חוֹטֵא וּמַקְרִיב קָרְבָּן... וְעַכְשָׁיו יָשַׁבְתִּי בְּתַעֲנִית וְנִתְמַעֵט חֶלְבִּי וְדָמִי... כְּאִלּוּ הִקְרַבְתִּיו לְפָנֶיךָ עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ.” This is a prayer of symbolic self-offering, not a claim that fasting literally recreates sacrificial law. On “וְנִרְצָה לוֹ,” Rashi says the olah appeases for an aseh and a lav repaired by an aseh. Ramban sharpens the point: after the sinner has returned, he may no longer bear the basic guilt yet remain not fully acceptable before the King; “וּבַמֶּה יִתְרַצּוּ אֶל אֲדוֹנֵיהֶם? בַּדּוֹרוֹן הַזֶּה.” Zevachim likewise reasons that an olah can cover several positive-commandment failures: “כֵּיוָן דְּאִיכָּא כַּמָּה עֲשֵׂה גַּבֵּיהּ מְכַפְּרָא.” Rav Tzadok distinguishes that minimum formal efficacy from voluntary abundance: one olah can suffice, while one capable of more may increase gifts. The Shlah, Aseres HaDibros, Yoma, Ner Mitzvah 2:9, makes the sequence explicit: first firm remorse and abandonment of sin, and only afterward “יַקְרִיב קָרְבַּן תַּעֲנִיּוֹת.” This supports Rav Tzadok's claim that the fast follows teshuvah and Yom Kippur as doron, rather than functioning as punitive scouring.
וַהֲרֵי גַּם עוֹבֵר אַמִּצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּמוֹחֲלִין עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיָּד, גַּם כֵּן מֵבִיא עוֹלָה לְדוֹרוֹן
and behold, one who transgresses a positive commandment, for which they pardon immediately upon repentance, likewise brings an olah as a tribute-gift (doran);
וְעַתָּה שֶׁאֵין לוֹ קָרְבָּנוֹת, הַתַּעֲנִית הוּא בִּמְקוֹם דּוֹרוֹן הַקָּרְבָּן
and now that he has no sacrifices, fasting stands in place of the sacrificial tribute!
וְאִם עַל כַּפָּרַת מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מְבִיאִין דּוֹרוֹן, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן עַל מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה גַּם אַחַר יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים צָרִיךְ דּוֹרוֹן גַּם כֵּן לְרַצּוֹת, וְעַל זֶה הֵם הַתַּעֲנִיּוֹת

And if for the atonement of a positive commandment one brings a gift, all the more so for a negative commandment, even after Yom Kippur, one requires a gift to appease, and toward this end serve the fasts:
אֲפִילּוּ עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה קַלָּה צָרִיךְ תַּעֲנִית יוֹם אֶחָד עַל כָּל פָּנִים לְדוֹרוֹן בִּמְקוֹם עוֹלָה
even for the omission of a minor positive commandment one requires at least one day's fast as a tribute-gift in place of an olah.

וְאַף עַל גַּב דִּבְחַד עוֹלָה סַגִּי לְכַפֵּר עַל כַּמָּה מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה דְּגַבֵּיהּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּזְבָחִים ו׳ עַמּוּד א׳], זֶהוּ לְעִנְיַן חִיּוּב הַדּוֹרוֹן דְּנִלְמַד מִקְּרָא, וּכְשֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְהָבִיא יוֹתֵר סַגִּי לֵיהּ בְּהָכִי

And although one olah suffices to atone for several positive commandments incumbent upon him as they said [in Zevachim 6a], this applies to the statutory requirement of tribute derived from Scripture, where if he cannot bring more this suffices;
אֲבָל וַדַּאי מִי שֶׁהַיְּכוֹלֶת בְּיָדוֹ הָיָה מַרְבֶּה לְהָבִיא קָרְבְּנוֹת נְדָבָה לְדוֹרוֹן כְּפִי יְכָלְתּוֹ, אִישׁ כְּבִרְכָתוֹ
but certainly whoever possessed the means would generously multiply voluntary offerings as a gift according to his ability, each man according to his blessing;

וְזֶהוּ גַּם עַל בִּיטּוּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אַעֲבֵירַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה וּבְקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה דִּצְרִיכֵי לְהַרְבּוֹת בְּדוֹרוֹן אַחֲרֵי רִיצּוּי הַפְּרַקְלִיט דִּתְשׁוּבָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים, וְאֵינָם בְּתוֹרַת סִגּוּפִים וּלְמֵירוּק כְּלָל

and this applies likewise to the omission of a positive commandment, and all the more so to the violation of a negative commandment through active commission, where they must multiply tribute after the appeasement of the advocates of repentance and Yom Kippur, and they are not in the category of mortifications and scouring at all.

וְעַל זֶה הֵם הַתַּעֲנִיּוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ מִתְעַנִּין: כְּשֶׁהָיוּ צְרִיכִין לְהִתְפַּלֵּל עַל אֵיזֶה עִנְיָן הָיוּ עוֹשִׂין בְּקָרְבְּנוֹת הָעוֹלָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר [שְׁמוּאֵל א ז:ט] ״וַיַּעֲלֵהוּ עוֹלָה וְגוֹמֵר וַיִּזְעַק וְגוֹמֵר, וַיְהִי שְׁמוּאֵל מַעֲלֶה הָעוֹלָה וְגוֹמֵר״

And to this purpose correspond the fasts that they would fast: when they needed to pray over some matter they would accompany it with burnt offerings, as it is said [I Shmuel 7:9]: "and offered it for a whole burnt-offering... and Samuel cried... and as Samuel was offering up the burnt-offering, etc.";
וְכֵן [שָׁם י״ג:י״ב] בְּשָׁאוּל ״הַגִּישׁוּ אֵלַי הָעֹלָה וְגוֹמֵר״, וְאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ ״וּפְנֵי ה׳ לֹא חִלִּיתִי וָאֶתְאַפַּק וָאַעֲלֶה הָעֹלָה״
and likewise [ibid. 13:9, 12] regarding Shaul: "Bring hither the burnt-offering to me... and I had not made entreaty unto Hashem; I forced myself therefore, and offered the burnt-offering";
הִנֵּה שֶׁהָיוּ מַקְרִיבִים עוֹלוֹת לְצֹרֶךְ הַתְּפִלָּה עַל מַה שֶּׁהָיוּ צְרִיכִים, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַקָּרְבָּנוֹת הָיוּ מִתְקָרְבִים לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְכֵן עַתָּה עַל יְדֵי הַתַּעֲנִית

behold, they would offer burnt offerings for the purpose of prayer concerning whatever they needed, for through the offerings they drew near to the Blessed Name, and so it is now through fasting;742I Samuel 7:9-10 and 13:9-13 with Rashi - an olah joined to petition, but never a substitute for obedience: At Mitzpah, “וַיַּעֲלֵהוּ עוֹלָה... וַיִּזְעַק שְׁמוּאֵל אֶל ה' בְּעַד יִשְׂרָאֵל וַיַּעֲנֵהוּ ה'”; while Shmuel was offering, Hashem routed the Philistines. Shaul later explained his own offering: “וּפְנֵי ה' לֹא חִלִּיתִי, וָאֶתְאַפַּק וָאַעֲלֶה הָעֹלָה.” Rashi reads “וָאֶתְאַפַּק” as forcing his heart against its desire to wait for Shmuel. Rav Tzadok notices that in both narratives the olah is bound to seeking divine favor: it accompanies crying out or “entreating the face of Hashem,” illustrating korban as an act of kirvah placed alongside petition. The contrast also limits the analogy. Shmuel's offering joins national return to Hashem and obedient prayer; Shaul's offering, brought against the prophetic instruction, is immediately rebuked: “נִסְכָּלְתָּ, לֹא שָׁמַרְתָּ אֶת מִצְוַת ה'.” A gift cannot replace submission to the King. Thus when Rav Tzadok compares a fast to an olah, he means an added doron after the underlying teshuvah and obligations are in place, not an independent mechanism that overrides them or guarantees acceptance.
וּמָצִינוּ גַּם כֵּן [תַּעֲנִית י״א סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] דְּאַף בְּלִי שׁוּם צֹרֶךְ כְּלָל, לֹא לִתְפִלָּה וְלֹא לִתְשׁוּבָה, הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית נִקְרָא ״קָדוֹשׁ״ בִּדְמָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ

and we also find [in Ta'anis 11a] that even without any functional necessity at all—neither for prayer nor for repentance—one who sits in fasting is termed "holy" if he has the physical endurance to afflict himself,
וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיוּ מַקְרִיבִין עוֹלוֹת נְדָבָה לִהְיוֹת לְרֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ לְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לְבַד:

which is exactly analogous to offering voluntary burnt offerings solely to provide a sweet savour unto the Blessed Name alone.743Taanis 11a-b; Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos De'os 3:1; Dover Tzedek - when voluntary fasting can be called holy: The sugya preserves both sides. Shmuel says, “כָּל הַיּוֹשֵׁב בְּתַעֲנִית נִקְרָא חוֹטֵא,” learning from the nazir who afflicted himself by abstaining from wine. Rabbi Elazar answers that he is “נִקְרָא קָדוֹשׁ,” and the Gemara limits this praise: “הָא דְּמָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ, הָא דְּלָא מָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ” - it depends whether the person can bear the deprivation. Rashi explains the holiness through the cleansing accomplished by the fast, but the continuation warns that a talmid chacham may not fast when it diminishes “מְלֶאכֶת שָׁמַיִם.” Rambam accordingly rejects habitual asceticism and calls continual self-denial a bad path. Rav Tzadok invokes only the qualified view: where the fast is genuinely controlled avodah and does not damage one's duties, it can resemble a voluntary olah offered solely as reiach nichoach. In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvos 2:10, he explains “דְּמָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ” as mastery of the body - “שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מוֹשֵׁל עַל הַגּוּף” - rather than bodily impairment. The source therefore allows devotional nedavah while denying a blanket endorsement of self-mortification.

items.h: The theme: Analysis of the Ba'al HaTanya in Iggeres HaTeshuvah. R' Tzadok rejoices to find his thesis—that fasts serve as a sacrificial tribute (doran) rather than scouring afflictions—explained in the Tanya. However, he respectfully questions the Tanya’s assertion that wasteful emission carries statutory liability to death from Heaven (chayav misah bidei Shamayim) equating it to kares and requiring scouring mortifications. The Rama MiFano in Asarah Ma'amaros enumerates only statutory cases of death from Heaven (Sanhedrin 83a), and the Rokeach himself prescribes fasts—not afflictions—for this sin.

p: וְשׁוּב מָצָאתִי מְבוֹאָר כִּדְבָרַי בְּעִנְיַן הַתַּעֲנִית לִתְשׁוּבָה בְּסֵפֶר הַתַּנְיָא לְהָרַב מֶחֱבָר מֵהַרְ״שׁ זַלְמָן זִכְרוֹנוֹ לִבְרָכָה [בְּאִגֶּרֶת הַתְּשׁוּבָה פֶּרֶק ב׳], יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ וְאַהְנְיַין מְאוֹד

And then I found explained in accordance with my words regarding the role of fasting in repentance in the book Tanya by the author, our Master Rav Shneur Zalman, of blessed memory [in Iggeres HaTeshuvah, ch. 2], see there at length, and it pleased me greatly;

אֲבָל שָׁם [סוֹף פֶּרֶק א׳] רָאִיתִי שֶׁכָּתַב בִּפְשִׁיטוּת דְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּעֵר וְאוֹנָן, דִּינוֹ כְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת לְעִנְיָן זֶה לְהַצְרִיךְ סִגּוּפִים לְהִנָּצֵל מֵעֹונֶשׁ יִסּוּרִין שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה הַמְּמָרְקִין, עַיֵּין שָׁם

but there [at the end of ch. 1] I saw that he wrote simply that one who emits seed wastefully, who is liable to death at the hands of Heaven as stated regarding Er and Onan, is legally equated to those liable for excision (kares) in this regard, to require mortifications in order to be spared the heavenly scouring afflictions, see there.744Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah, chs. 1-2 - teshuvah is not fasting; fasting can serve two later functions: The Baal HaTanya first states, “וְלֹא כְּדַעַת הֶהָמוֹן, שֶׁהַתְּשׁוּבָה הִיא הַתַּעֲנִית.” Torah teshuvah is abandonment of sin, sincere return, and confession; even where suffering completes atonement, Hashem brings the suffering after an accepted return. He then distinguishes a second goal: after the sin and its punishment have been forgiven, the penitent may still seek restored favor before the King. The olah was therefore “דּוֹרוֹן לְאַחַר שֶׁעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה וְנִמְחַל לוֹ הָעוֹנֶשׁ,” and without the Mikdash, “הַתַּעֲנִית הוּא בִּמְקוֹם קָרְבָּן.” This is the point Rav Tzadok says accords with his analysis in the preceding se'if: the many fasts of Chazal over comparatively light lapses cannot all be punitive scouring; they can be voluntary korban-like acts that renew ratzon and kirvah. The distinction is essential. A fast may be undertaken to avert or lighten suffering, or as a post-forgiveness doron, but it is not the definition of teshuvah and cannot replace cessation of the sin. The Tanya's later examples from the Arizal, including fasts for rabbinic violations, reinforce Rav Tzadok's claim that the mere existence or number of fasts does not by itself establish the formal severity-classification of the underlying aveirah.
הִנֵּה פְּשִׁיטָא לֵיהּ נֶגֶד מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וְאִם קַבָּלָה נְקַבֵּל וְאִם לַדִּין יֵשׁ תְּשׁוּבָה
Behold, this was obvious to him contrary to what I have written; and "if it is a received tradition we shall accept it, but if it is an inference of legal logic, there is an answer" (Yevamos 76b):

דִּלְדַעְתִּי הָיָה נִרְאֶה פָּשׁוּט כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, וְדִבְרֵי הָרַמַ״ע בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ הַנַּ״ל מְסַיְּיעִין לִי, דְּלֹא חָשֵׁיב אֶלָּא חַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם שֶׁמָּנוּ חֲכָמִים בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין, וְכֵן דִּבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ כַּנַּ״ל

for in my opinion the plain truth seemed as I wrote, and the words of the Rama MiFano in Asarah Ma'amaros cited above support me, for he enumerated strictly the statutory liabilities to death by Heaven listed by the Sages in Sanhedrin (83a), and so too the words of the Rokeach as mentioned above;
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ מַיְיתֵי שָׁם מֵרוֹקֵחַ שֶׁכָּתַב סִגּוּפִים לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת, וְלֹא הֵעִיר דְּלֹא כָּתַב כֵּן לְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה

and [the Ba'al HaTanya] himself cites there from the Rokeach who prescribed mortifications for those liable for kares, yet did not notice that the Rokeach did not prescribe such mortifications for wasteful emission!

וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּהַתַּעֲנִיּוֹת הֵם הַסִּגּוּפִים, וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב ״דִּינוֹ כְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת״ אֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר לְהַשְׁווֹתָם לְגַמְרֵי, רַק לְעִנְיַן דִּצְרִיכִין יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין, אֲבָל סַגִּי בָּזֶה בְּיִסּוּרִין קַלִּים טְפֵי

And one must say that the fasts are themselves the mortifications, and what he wrote—that his law is like those liable for kares—did not mean to equate them entirely, but only regarding the need for scouring afflictions, wherein lighter afflictions suffice for this;
אֲבָל כְּבָר נִתְבָּאֵר עֶשְׂרִים תַּעֲנִיּוֹת גַּם לְאִיסּוּר לָאו לְבַד, אֶלָּא דְּכָאן הִרְבָּה בְּמִסְפַּר הַצּוֹמוֹת

but it was already explained that twenty fasts are required even for a mere negative commandment, except that here the number of fasts was increased.745Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah 1; Sanhedrin 83a; Rokeach; Ohr Zarua LaTzadik - the disputed comparison to kareis: The Tanya writes of wasteful emission, “שֶׁחַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם... וְדִינוֹ כְּחַיָּיבֵי כְרֵיתוֹת לְעִנְיָן זֶה,” explaining that the fasts and mortifications described by the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim can help avoid Heavenly suffering and hasten cleansing. Rav Tzadok does not minimize the sin or reject penitential discipline; he challenges the legal inference. Sanhedrin's formal list concerns offenses for which the Torah fixed misah bidei Shamayim as a standing punishment, whereas the death of Er and Onan does not by itself prove inclusion in that enumerated class. His earlier textual comparison is also important: the Rokeach prescribes forty fasts here, but reserves an added complex of lashes and other mortifications for kareis cases, while prescribing fasts even for ordinary lavin. Thus a schedule of fasts cannot prove full equivalence to kareis. Rav Tzadok offers a narrow reconciliation: “דִּינוֹ כְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת” may mean only that some cleansing suffering is appropriate, though lighter than that required for actual kareis. This measured reading matches his halachic method in Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Mitzvos 3:5, where he treats the named category of misah bidei Shamayim as carrying defined legal consequences rather than as a loose description for every sin concerning which death-language appears.

וְהוּא כָּתַב דְּסִפְרֵי הַמּוּסָר וּבְרֹאשָׁם הָרוֹקֵחַ וְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים כָּתְבוּ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת וְסִגּוּפִים לְעוֹבֵר עַל כְּרִיתוֹת וּמִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין, וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי הוּצְרַךְ לוֹמַר דְּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה גַּם כֵּן כְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת, דְּלֹא כָּתַב בִּשְׁמָם תַּעֲנִיּוֹת לַעֲבֵירוֹת אֲחֵרוֹת:

And [the Tanya] wrote that the ethical works, foremost among them the Rokeach and Sefer Chassidim, prescribed fasts and mortifications for those violating kares and court executions, wherefore he was compelled to state that wasteful emission is likewise like kares, assuming they never prescribed fasts for other transgressions.

items.h: The theme: The Rishonim explicitly prescribed fasts for ordinary negative commands and interpersonal sins. The Ba'al HaTanya attributes fasts for non-capital transgressions exclusively to the Ari, while limiting the early Rishonim to kares and death from Heaven. R' Tzadok shows that the Rokeach repeatedly established fast regimens for non-capital offenses lacking excision or death from Heaven: illicit physical affection, stealing, and interpersonal grievances after financial restitution. In the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, forty fasts and lashes are prescribed for relations with an unmarried woman who immersed—an offense carrying no death penalty whatsoever—proving that the Rishonim instituted fasts broadly across all categories of sin.

p: וְאַחַר כָּךְ [בְּפֶרֶק ב׳] שֶׁכָּתַב תַּעֲנִיּוֹת לְדוֹרוֹן, כָּתַב: ״וְעַל יְסוֹד זֶה לִימֵּד הָאֲרִ״י מִסְפַּר צוֹמוֹת לְכַמָּה עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם כָּרֵת וְלֹא מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם וְכוּלֵיהּ״, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

And afterward [in ch. 2], where [the Tanya] wrote of fasts as a tribute-gift (doran), he wrote: "And upon this foundation the Ari taught the specific number of fasts for numerous transgressions that contain neither kares nor death by Heaven, etc.," see there;
הִנֵּה יִיחֵס דָּבָר זֶה לְהָאֲרִיזַ״ל, אֲבָל לְהָרִאשׁוֹנִים יִיחֵס רַק תַּעֲנִיּוֹת לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וּמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּחַיָּיבֵי מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם

behold, he attributed this concept to the Arizal, whereas to the Rishonim he attributed fasts only for those liable for kares and wasteful emission as liable to death by Heaven;746Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah 2 - the Arizal systematized exact fast-counts even for lighter sins: After defining the fast as a post-forgiveness doron, the Baal HaTanya writes: “וְעַל יְסוֹד זֶה, לִימֵּד הָאֲרִיזַ״ל לְתַלְמִידָיו... מִסְפַּר הַצּוֹמוֹת לְכַמָּה עֲוֹנוֹת וַחֲטָאִים, אַף שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶן כָּרֵת וְלֹא מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם.” He gives anger, with 151 fasts; stam yeinam, a rabbinic prohibition, with seventy-three; and neglect of prayer, a rabbinic positive commandment, with sixty-one. Rav Tzadok is not questioning the Arizal's authority. His question concerns the historical and halachic inference: the Tanya presents the Arizal as extending numbered fast-regimens to lighter offenses after discussing the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim mainly in connection with kareis, capital sins, and wasteful emission. Rav Tzadok therefore checks whether the Rishonim themselves already prescribed fasting beyond those severe classes. The Tanya's own explanation supports the importance of that inquiry: fasting can reveal “רָצוֹן הָעֶלְיוֹן” like a korban and need not measure the statutory punishment of the sin. As Se'ifim 26-27 established, the same discipline may serve restored favor, deterrence, remorse, or cleansing; its number alone cannot classify the aveirah.
וְחִידּוּשׁ דְּלֹא רָאָה בְּדִבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב, שֶׁסִּידֵּר תַּעֲנִית עַל חִבּוּק וְנִישּׁוּק נָשִׁים וּמִשְׁמוּשָׁן דְּלֵיכָּא כָּרֵת וְלֹא מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם
and it is wondrous that he did not notice what the Rokeach wrote, who arranged fasts for embracing, kissing, and caressing women, where there is neither kares nor death by Heaven!
וְכֵן כָּתַב שָׁם [סִימָן י״ד] עַל חִבּוּק וְנִישּׁוּק אִשְׁתּוֹ נִדָּה, [וּבְסִימָן ט״ו] עַל גּוֹנֵב וְגוֹזֵל אַחַר שֶׁהֶחֱזִירוֹ
And so he wrote there [§14] for embracing and kissing his wife who is a niddah; [and in §15] for stealing and robbing after he returned the stolen property;
[וּבְסִימָן ט״ז] כָּתַב עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת הָיָה לוֹ לְהִתְעַנּוֹת וְלִלְקוֹת, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן עַל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין וְעַל חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְכוּלֵיהּ

[and in §16] he wrote: "for all transgressions one should fast and receive lashes, all the more so for those liable to court execution and kares, etc.";747Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§13-16 - penitential disciplines extend beyond kareis and follow concrete repair: The Rokeach's cases are broader than a list limited to kareis or misah bidei Shamayim. For embracing and kissing forbidden women he prescribes a Monday-Thursday-Monday fast; for embracing and kissing one's niddah wife, fasting and confession; and for theft or robbery after the money has been returned, “יִלְקֶה וְיִתְעַנֶּה וְיֵאָנַח וְיִתְחָרֵט וְיִתְוַדֶּה.” His general formulation is decisive: “עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת הָיָה לוֹ לְהִתְעַנּוֹת וְלִלְקוֹת, כָּל שֶׁכֵּן עַל חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין וְעַל חַיָּיבֵי כָרֵת.” The “all the more so” distinguishes the severe categories from the wider practice rather than restricting fasting to them. In sins against another person, the order is also essential: appeasement and restitution precede the personal fast or symbolic lashes. These disciplines supplement, but never replace, returning what was taken and obtaining forgiveness. As discussed above in Se'if 25, Rambam and Ramban dispute whether lustful embracing and kissing constitute a separately punishable Torah lav; neither treats the contact itself as the completed relation carrying kareis. Rav Tzadok consequently uses the Rokeach as direct evidence that the presence of fasts—even lashes—does not by itself prove a formal Heavenly-death classification.
הִנֵּה כָּתַב לְהֶדְיָא תַּעֲנִית גַּם מַלְקוּת עַל כָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאֵינָן חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת
behold, he explicitly recorded fasting and lashes for all transgressions that do not incur kares!

וְכֵן כָּתַב שָׁם עַל הַרְבֵּה עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבֵּין אָדָם לַחֲבֵירוֹ שֶׁאֵין בָּהֶם כָּרֵת וּמִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם לְהִתְעַנּוֹת וְלִלְקוֹת אַחַר הַפִּיּוּס לַחֲבֵירוֹ וַחֲזָרַת מָמוֹן, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ
And so he wrote there regarding many interpersonal sins lacking kares and death by Heaven, requiring fasting and lashes after placating one's fellow and restoring the money, see there at length.

גַּם בְּ״דַּרְכֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה״ שֶׁבְּסוֹף תְּשׁוּבוֹת מַהֲרַ״ם מֵרוֹטֶנְבֶּרְג דְּפוּס פְּרָאג, הַמְקוּבָּל מִיְּסוֹד הָרוֹקֵחַ, אִיתָא כָּל הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְעוֹד הוֹסִיף וּבְתַעֲנִיּוֹת מְרוּבִּים, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

Also in Darkhei HaTeshuvah at the end of the responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg (Prague edition), received from the foundation of the Rokeach, all the above is found, with even more numerous fasts added, see there;748Maharam of Rothenburg, Darkei HaTeshuvah; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 1:4 with Raavad and Kessef Mishneh - forty fasts without misah bidei Shamayim: The penitential appendix printed with the Prague responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, received from the tradition of the Rokeach, prescribes: for relations with “פְּנוּיָה שֶׁטָּבְלָה לְנִידָּתָהּ,” one set of lashes and forty fasts. Since she immersed, the act is not the niddah offense that carries kareis; yet the schedule equals the forty days assigned there to wasteful emission. The remaining prohibition of relations outside marriage requires qualification. Rambam writes, “כָּל הַבּוֹעֵל אִשָּׁה לְשֵׁם זְנוּת בְּלֹא קִדּוּשִׁין לוֹקֶה מִן הַתּוֹרָה,” under לא תהיה קדשה. Raavad limits kedeshah to a woman made available to everyone, and Kessef Mishneh observes that Rambam elsewhere likewise implies lashes only when “הִיא מוּכֶנֶת לְכָךְ.” Rav Tzadok's phrase “לְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר... אִיסּוּר לָאו שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין” reads the isolated case within that narrower application: unquestionably forbidden, but not a fixed misah bidei Shamayim offense. His proof is therefore methodological. Equal numbers of fasts can express teshuvas hamishkal, a protective fence, or an inherited penitential regimen; they do not establish equal punishments or equal halachic categories.
וְשָׁם כָּתַב גַּם כֵּן עַל פְּנוּיָה שֶׁטָּבְלָה לְנִדָּתָהּ: מַלְקִין פַּעַם אַחַת וּמ׳ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת
and there he wrote likewise regarding relations with an unmarried woman who immersed for her niddah status: they administer lashes once and forty fasts
[וְאִם הִיא נִדָּה הֶחְמִיר טְפֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּשִׁינּוּי מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ בְּרוֹקֵחַ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל עַל זֶה]
[and if she is a niddah he was more stringent, see the variation from the Rokeach on this];

הִנֵּה קָצַב מִסְפַּר הַתַּעֲנִיּוֹת גַּם עַל זֶה כִּבְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, וְאַף דְּאֵין בּוֹ מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם לְדִבְרֵי הַכֹּל, וּלְכָל הַיּוֹתֵר הוּא רַק אִיסּוּר לָאו שֶׁאֵין לוֹקִין, עַיֵּין רַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק א׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת אִישׁוּת הֲלָכָה ד׳]:

behold, he fixed the number of fasts for this identically to wasteful emission, even though it carries no death by Heaven according to all opinions, being at most a negative prohibition lacking lashes, see Rambam [Hilchos Ishus 1:4]!

items.h: The theme: Fasting in the early pietistic tradition as therapeutic subjugation (hachna'as ha-yetzer). In the Rokeach and Sefer Chassidim, fasts and bodily disfigurement (such as letting hair and nails grow wildly, Sanhedrin 25a) were not statutory atonement formulas, but pastoral strategies to break the power of lust and demonstrate genuine brokenness of heart (lev do'eg). Rav Huna fasted forty days not as an objective tariff, but because grief over his slight negligence made it impossible to eat. Because internal subjugation varies per individual, fixed fasting quotas are not absolute halachic requirements, but subjective remedies tailored to each person's spiritual struggle.

p: וֶאֱמֶת בְּרוֹקֵחַ לֹא נִזְכָּר מֵעִנְיַן תַּעֲנִית לְדוֹרוֹן
And in truth, in the Rokeach there is no explicit mention of fasting serving as a tribute-gift (doran);
וְהָנֵי דְּהוּשְׁחֲרוּ שִׁנָּיו מִפְּנֵי תַּעֲנִיּוֹתָיו שֶׁמֵּבִיא בַּעַל הַתַּנְיָא [שָׁם בְּפֶרֶק ב׳] נִזְכָּר גַּם בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים [סִימָן תרי״ז]
and those sages whose teeth turned black from fasting, cited by the author of the Tanya [ch. 2], are likewise mentioned in Sefer Chassidim [§617];
וְשָׁם כָּתַב: ״וְאִלּוּ הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חָפֵץ בַּתַּעֲנִיּוֹת הָיָה מְצַוֶּוה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, אֶלָּא שֶׁיַּכְנִיעַ לִבּוֹ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ׳וְהָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה שֶׁיִּרְאוּ מִלְּפָנָיו׳״

and there he wrote: "And had the Holy One, blessed be He, desired fasts, He would have commanded them to Israel; rather, He desires that one humble his heart, as it is said: 'and God has so made it, that men should fear before Him' (Koheles 3:14)";
וְכֵן כָּתַב שָׁם [בְּרֵישׁ הַסִּימָן] ״יְסַגֵּף עַצְמוֹ לְהַכְנִיעַ יִצְרוֹ״
and so he wrote there [at the start of the section]: "he should afflict himself to humble his yetzer,"
מַשְׁמַע שֶׁזֶּהוּ רַק עֵצָה שֶׁיָּשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת בְּהַכְנָעַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי וְשֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב לְכִסְלָה עוֹד
which implies that this is merely therapeutic counsel that he return in truth through the total subjugation of the inclination, never returning to folly.
וּמָצִינוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין כ״ה עַמּוּד א׳] בְּמוֹצִיא טְרֵיפָה מִתַּחַת יָדוֹ דְּרַבֵּי מַזְיֵיהּ וְטוּפְרֵיהּ, וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י ״לְנַוֵּול עַצְמוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה״
And we find [in Sanhedrin 25a] regarding a butcher who sold non-kosher meat that he let his hair and fingernails grow, which Rashi explains: "to disfigure himself to perform teshuvah";

וְהַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן לְהַכְנִיעַ יִצְרוֹ עַל יְדֵי זֶה, וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [קִדּוּשִׁין מ׳ עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״וְיַעֲשֶׂה״ בְּשֵׁם רַבֵּינוּ חֲנַנְאֵל אַהָא דְּיִצְרוֹ מִתְגַּבֵּר יֵלֵךְ וְכוּלֵיהּ וְיִלְבַּשׁ שְׁחוֹרִים וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and this likewise was to humble his yetzer through this, along the lines of what Tosafos wrote [Kiddushin 40a, s.v. v'ya'aseh] in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel on the dictum "if one sees that his yetzer overpowers him, let him go to a place where he is not known and don black, etc.," see there.749Sefer Chasidim §617; Sanhedrin 25a with Rashi - self-denial must express genuine inner submission: Sefer Chasidim does not present fasting as an independent object desired by Heaven. It first limits the practice: “אֵין הַיָּחִיד מְסַגֵּף עַצְמוֹ בְּתַעֲנִית שֶׁמָּא יִצְטָרֵךְ לַבְּרִיּוֹת,” yet when the inclination is overpowering, “יְסַגֵּף עַצְמוֹ לְהַכְנִיעַ יִצְרוֹ.” It further warns that a fast which produces anger or diminishes a teacher's, scribe's, or worker's duty is counterproductive, and concludes: “אִלּוּ הָיָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא חָפֵץ בְּתַעֲנִיּוֹת... אֶלָּא שֶׁיִּכָּנַע לִבּוֹ.” The blackened teeth of Rabbi Yehoshua and Rabbi Elazar ben Azariah are cited in that context. The Tanya uses these episodes to illustrate fasting as a post-forgiveness doron; Rav Tzadok observes that Sefer Chasidim itself emphasizes submission and prevention. Sanhedrin sharpens the point. A butcher caught selling treifah let his hair and nails grow; Rashi explains, “לְנַוֵּל עַצְמוֹ לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה.” Rava nevertheless feared that this could be staged, so reliable rehabilitation required an unobserved costly choice: returning a valuable lost object or discarding a valuable treifah of his own. External mortification is therefore meaningful only when it accompanies a changed will and conduct, not as a mechanically sufficient tariff.750Kiddushin 40a; Tosafos in the name of Rabbeinu Chananel; Berachos 56a - breaking the yetzer and spontaneous remorse: Rabbi Ilai teaches that one whose inclination overpowers him should travel where he is unknown, dress and wrap himself in black, and then “יַעֲשֶׂה מַה שֶּׁלִּבּוֹ חָפֵץ.” Tosafos immediately records Rabbeinu Chananel's limiting explanation: “חַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁהֻתַּר לוֹ לַעֲבֹר עֲבֵירָה”; rather, the hardship of travel, unfamiliar lodging, and black clothing “מְשַׁבְּרִים יֵצֶר הָרָע וּמוֹנְעִים אָדָם מִן הָעֲבֵירָה.” The abasement is a preventive strategy directed at the particular strength of the yetzer, not permission to sin and not a standardized punishment after the fact. Rav Tzadok then offers a second reading of exceptional fasts: they may emerge naturally from authentic regret. In Berachos, Bar Hedya interprets the dream-verse to Rava: “פָּסֵיד עִסְקָךְ וְלָא אַהֲנִי לָךְ לְמֵיכַל מֵעוּצְבָּא דְּלִבָּךְ” - grief itself can make eating impossible. Rav Huna's forty fasts may therefore describe the intensity of his broken heart rather than a prescribed count. This does not negate Se'if 26's doron model; it shows that the narrative alone cannot establish a rule equal for every penitent. In Dover Tzedek, Kuntres Ner HaMitzvot 2:10, Rav Tzadok similarly reads “דְּמָצֵי לְצַעוֹרֵי נַפְשֵׁיהּ” as mastery that does not damage avodas Hashem; mortification is judged by the spiritual change it produces and the person's actual capacity.
וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּהַהוּא דְּרַבֵּי וְכוּלֵיהּ הוּא סִימָן עַל שֶׁשָּׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט בֶּאֱמֶת, דְּמִתּוֹךְ חֲרָטָתוֹ הוּא מִצְטַעֵר וְלִבּוֹ דּוֹאֵג עַל יְדֵי שֶׁעָבַר לַמְרוֹת מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים

And it is possible that letting his hair grow was an outward sign of authentic grief and regret: that from the depth of remorse he is distressed, his heart anxious over having rebelled against the King of kings of kings,
מִתּוֹךְ יְגוֹנוֹ וְצַעֲרוֹ לֹא יוּכַל לְהִתְנָאוֹת בְּקִישּׁוּטֵי גּוּפוֹ כְּדֶרֶךְ הַשְּׁרוּיִים בְּצַעַר
and out of deep sorrow he cannot adorn his body, as is the manner of those in profound mourning;

וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ זֶה יֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם כֵּן בְּתַעֲנִיּוֹת דְּרַב הוּנָא דְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, שֶׁמִּתּוֹךְ צַעֲרוֹ עַל מַה שֶּׁבָּא לְיָדוֹ כָּךְ לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַכְנִיס אוֹכֶל לְפִיו מִגּוֹדֶל מְרִירוּת לִבּוֹ

and in this manner one may likewise explain the fasts of Rav Huna in Moed Katan mentioned above: out of sorrow over what occurred at his hand, he simply could not bring food into his mouth from the immense bitterness of his heart;
וְעַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת נ״ו עַמּוּד א׳]: ״וְלָא אַהֲנֵי לָךְ לְמֵיכַל מֵעוּצְבָּא דְּלִבָּךְ״
and along the lines of what they said [in Berachos 56a]: "and food was of no pleasure to you because of the grief of your heart."
וְכָל עִנְיָנִים אֵלּוּ לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לְצַוּוֹת וּלְהַזְהִיר לְבַעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עַל זֶה, וְלִקְבּוֹעַ מִסְפַּר תַּעֲנִיּוֹת מְיוּחָד לְכָל עֲבֵירָה שָׁוֶוה לְכָל אֶחָד

And regarding all such subjective manifestations of sorrow, it is inappropriate to command them as formal ordinances upon a penitent, nor to fix an identical quota of fasts for each transgression applicable equally to everyone;
וְדָבָר זֶה תָּלוּי הַכֹּל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא אָדָם בְּהִשְׁתַּקְּעוּתוֹ בָּעֲבֵירָה וְהִתְגַּבְּרוּת הַיֵּצֶר נֶגְדּוֹ:
for this matter depends entirely on the nature of the individual: the extent of his immersion in the sin, and the intensity of the yetzer's dominion over him.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ל״א–ל״ג

The theme: The foundation of the Rokeach's fasting regimens is "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal), instituted to counterbalance the bodily pleasure enjoyed in sin, rather than statutory scouring afflictions (yissurin memarkin). Since the Rokeach separately lists scriptural repentance (teshuvah ha-kasuv) for offenses of excision (kares) and court executions (misos beis din), it follows that teshuvah ha-mishkal applies across all transgressions as a sacrificial tribute-gift (doran). For positive commandments, one offers additional positive service to offset past laziness; for negative prohibitions violated for pleasure, one offers bodily distress to counterbalance that pleasure.

p: וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה, יְסוֹד דִּבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ בְּמִסְפַּר הַצּוֹמוֹת הוּא מִצַּד ״תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל״ שֶׁהִצְרִיךְ שָׁם [בְּסִימָן ו׳ וְי׳] נֶגֶד הַהֲנָאָה בַּעֲבֵירָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם וְנִזְכַּר לְעֵיל

And apparently, the foundation of the words of the Rokeach regarding the number of fasts is based on "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal), which he required there [§6 and §10] to counterbalance the pleasure enjoyed in the sin, see there and as mentioned above;
וְאַף דְּשָׁם קָאֵי אַחַר כָּךְ מֵחַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין, מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַשְׁמַע דְּלֹא כָּתַב זֶה בִּמְקוֹם הַיִּסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין

and even though there he deals subsequently with those liable to court executions, nevertheless it implies that he did not write this in place of scouring afflictions;751Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§6-11; Yoma 86a - four forms of teshuvah and two distinct kinds of suffering: The Rokeach organizes the penitent's avodah into four categories. Teshuvas ha-ba'ah is passing the same test when Providence returns it; teshuvas ha-geder creates fences that prevent a relapse; teshuvas ha-mishkal measures pain against the pleasure or ease of the sin; and teshuvas ha-kasuv corresponds to the punishment written by the Torah. Rav Tzadok's reading depends on keeping the last two separate. The earlier fast-counts are introduced as mishkal, whereas the later sections prescribe hakasuv for kareis and misas beis din. They therefore cannot simply be the “יסורין ממרקין” of Rabbi Yishmael's baraisa in Yoma, which assigns suffering specifically to the formal categories of kareis and court death. This distinction also explains why mishkal can appear for lighter prohibitions: it addresses the sinner's attachment and benefit, not the statutory punishment. In Tzidkas HaTzadik 73, Rav Tzadok describes a deeper teshuvas hamishkal that Heaven arranges by returning an equivalent test; the fixed practices of the Rokeach are humanly available approximations, not a declaration that every offense has the same halachic severity.

שֶׁהֲרֵי כָּתַב אַחַר כָּךְ ״תְּשׁוּבַת הַכָּתוּב״ לִסְבּוֹל יִסּוּרִין בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין נֶגֶד עֹונֶשׁ הַכָּתוּב בָּהֶם, וּמַשְׁמַע דְּזֶהוּ הַשִּׁיעוּר לְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין

for behold, he wrote afterward regarding "scriptural repentance" (teshuvah ha-kasuv) to endure afflictions for those liable to kares and court executions corresponding to the punishment written concerning them, implying that this is the statutory measure for scouring afflictions.
וְאִם כֵּן נִרְאֶה, דְּיִסּוּרִין שֶׁבְּמִשְׁקַל הַהֲנָאָה שֶׁכָּתַב מִקּוֹדֶם אֵינוֹ לְיִסּוּרִין הַמְּמָרְקִין שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין
And if so, it appears that the afflictions balancing pleasure which he wrote previously are not the scouring afflictions required for kares and court executions;
וְאִם כֵּן מַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא גַּם בְּכָל עֲבֵירוֹת, וְלֹא כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
and if so, it implies that it applies across all transgressions, and not as I wrote above.
וְאֶפְשָׁר דְּנָפְקָא לֵיהּ זֶה מֵעוֹלָה דְּדוֹרוֹן לְמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
And it is possible that he derived this from the olah [burnt offering] of tribute brought for omitting a positive commandment,

דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּלְפִי שֶׁבִּיטֵּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה מִצַּד הִתְעַצְּלוּתוֹ בַּעֲבוֹדַת ה׳, צָרִיךְ כְּשֶׁשָּׁב לַעֲשׂוֹת תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל לְהוֹסִיף מַעֲשֵׂה עֲבוֹדָה לְדָבָר שֶׁלֹּא נִתְחַיֵּיב בָּהּ בַּהֲבָאַת קָרְבָּן נֶגֶד הִתְעַצְּלוּתוֹ

holding that because he neglected a positive commandment due to laziness in the service of Hashem, when he repents he must perform "commensurate repentance" by adding active service in an uncommanded matter through bringing an offering to counterbalance his laziness;
וְאַף שֶׁנִּמְחַל עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה מִיָּד, מִכָּל מָקוֹם צָרִיךְ לְרִיצּוּי דּוֹרוֹן לַעֲשׂוֹת דָּבָר הַשָּׁקוּל נֶגֶד הָעֲבֵירָה
and although he was pardoned through repentance immediately, he nonetheless requires the appeasement of a tribute-gift by doing something commensurate to the sin;
וְעַל כֵּן בַּעֲבֵירַת מִצְוַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה בְּקוּם וַעֲשֵׂה לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ, רִיצּוּי הַדּוֹרוֹן הוּא בְּמִשְׁקַל הַצַּעַר נֶגֶד הֲנָאַת עֲבֵירָה
therefore, in transgressing a negative commandment through active commission for self-gratification, the appeasing tribute consists of a weight of distress balancing the pleasure of the sin.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם [סִימָן ו׳] כָּתַב לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל דַּהֲנָאָה בִּנְשִׁיקָה וּמִשְׁמוּשׁ וְהַעֲרָאָה [הַיְינוּ נוֹסָף עַל גְּמַר בִּיאָה]: יִתְעַנֶּה מ׳ יוֹם וְלֹא יֹאכַל בָּשָׂר וְכוּלֵיהּ וְיִצְטַעֵר בִּשְׁכִיבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ

And see there [§6], where he wrote regarding teshuvah ha-mishkal for the pleasure of kissing, touching, and initial penetration [in addition to full intercourse]: he shall fast forty days, refrain from meat, and afflict himself in sleep, etc.;

[752Rokeach §§6 and 10; Zevachim 7b; Ramban on Vayikra 1:4 - weighing pain against pleasure as a post-forgiveness doron: The Rokeach states the principle explicitly: “יְשַׁקֵּל צַעֲרוֹ כְּנֶגֶד הֲנָאָתוֹ שֶׁנֶּהֱנָה.” His examples combine fasting with abstention from meat and wine, diminished comfort in sleep, and removal of the habits that nourished the desire. The forty days are therefore only one element in a broader reversal of the pleasure. Rav Tzadok proposes the conceptual source from the olah. Zevachim teaches that an olah can obtain favor for several neglected positive commandments; Ramban explains “וְנִרְצָה לוֹ” as a gift after pardon, restoring the servant's welcome before the King. Rav Tzadok's inference is that mishkal performs a comparable ritzui: after teshuvah has removed the rebellion, the penitent adds voluntary avodah opposite the mode of failure. For a missed mitzvas aseh, he adds service; for an active prohibition pursued for enjoyment, he accepts measured deprivation. This is an interpretation of the Rokeach, not an explicit Talmudic equation. A parallel in Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 4:2, describes teshuvas hamishkal as making the “כּוֹבֶד עֹנֶג הָעֲבֵירָה” negligible beside the “כּוֹבֶד מְרִירוּת הַתְּשׁוּבָה.”וּבְסִימָן ז׳] לִתְשׁוּבַת הַכָּתוּב וְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת כָּתַב: יִשְׁכַּב בְּקוֹשִׁי וְכוּלֵיהּ וְיִתְעַנֶּה מ׳ יוֹם וְכוּלֵיהּ
[and in §7] for scriptural repentance for kares, he wrote: he shall sleep with discomfort and fast forty days, etc.;
[וְזֶהוּ הַשִּׁיעוּר דְּיִסּוּרִין שֶׁל חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת, וּלְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין מַשְׁמַע דְּצָרִיךְ טְפֵי וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב שָׁם רֵישׁ סִימָן י״א
[and this is the measure of afflictions for kares, whereas for court executions it implies one requires more, as he wrote at the beginning of §11;

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב שָׁם [בְּסוֹף הַסִּימָן] דִּכְשֶׁלֹּא אֲסָרַתָּהּ עַל בַּעְלָהּ דַּי כִּבְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת תַּעֲנִית מ׳ יוֹם וְיִשְׁכַּב [כֵּן צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר, וְטָעוּת סוֹפֵר מַה שֶּׁכָּתוּב ״וְיֵשֵׁב״] עַל הָאָרֶץ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and what he wrote at the end of that section—that when she did not become forbidden to her husband, it suffices with forty fasts and sleeping upon the ground as with kares, see there;753Rokeach §§7, 11 and 14 - teshuvas ha-kasuv follows the Torah's punishment category, not the pleasure alone: For a kareis offense the Rokeach writes, “יִשְׁכַּב בְּקוֹשִׁי... וְיִתְעַנֶּה לֹא פָחוֹת מֵאַרְבָּעִים יוֹם,” together with lashes, confession and withdrawal from frivolity. For adultery he prescribes “יִסּוּרִין קָשִׁין כְּמִיתָה,” such as ice, snow or insects, because teshuvas ha-kasuv mirrors the written death-penalty. Yet the same number forty also appears in other sections, with different accompanying practices. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the regimen cumulatively: the number by itself does not identify the punishment class; continuity, intensity, lifelong conduct and the consequences of the act supply the distinction. He also corrects the text at the end of §11 from “וְיֵשֵׁב” to “וְיִשְׁכַּב” on the ground. When the act did not prohibit the woman to her husband, the Rokeach compares the fasting and lying regimen to kareis; when it did, the continuing confession and mortification are more extensive. Rav Tzadok's point is exegetical and halachic: the Rokeach's internal headings and gradations must govern the interpretation, rather than treating every occurrence of forty fasts as interchangeable.
נִרְאֶה דְּזֶהוּ לְעִנְיַן יְמֵי הַתַּעֲנִית שֶׁכָּתַב מִקּוֹדֶם לְהִתְעַנּוֹת בְּכָל יוֹם וְכוּלֵיהּ וּבְכָל מִינֵי סִגּוּף וְצַעַר מֵאַחַר שֶׁאֲסָרַתָּהּ וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם
it appears this refers to the duration of fasting mentioned earlier, to fast daily with all manners of affliction once she became forbidden, see there,
וְכַוָּונָתוֹ עַל סִגּוּף דְּתַעֲנִית וּשְׁכִיבָה עַל גַּבֵּי קַרְקַע, וּמַצְרִיךְ בְּכָל יוֹם הַיְינוּ כָּל יְמֵי חַיָּיו
referring to the affliction of fasting and sleeping on the ground, requiring it "every day," meaning all the days of his life;
וְכֵן הוּא גַּם כֵּן בְּהֶדְיָא בְּסוֹף תְּשׁוּבוֹת מַהֲרַ״ם שָׁם: לְהִתְוַודּוֹת כָּל יָמָיו וְלָשׂוּם שַׂק וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְעַל זֶה כָּתַב כָּאן דַּוְוקָא כְּשֶׁאֲסָרַתָּהּ

and so it is explicitly at the end of the responsa of Maharam there: to confess all his days and wear sackcloth, see there, and regarding this he wrote here that it applies specifically when she became forbidden;754Responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, penitential order - continuing confession and sackcloth address an enduring breach: Rav Tzadok cites the penitential order printed at the end of the Prague responsa of Maharam, which draws heavily on the Rokeach. Its language requires the offender “לְהִתְוַדּוֹת כָּל יָמָיו וְלָשׂוּם שַׂק,” alongside the specified fasts and bodily restrictions. Rav Tzadok reads “בְּכָל יוֹם” in the Rokeach accordingly: not that every day of life is a fast, but that confession, humility and the renunciation of former indulgence become an ongoing posture. This is especially intelligible where the sin produced a lasting human consequence, such as forbidding a married woman to her husband; a short numerical regimen cannot by itself match the continuing damage. The printed penitential orders are thus layered: a limited fast-count, repeated vidui, and sometimes lifelong signs of submission. Rav Tzadok does not present these as an alternative definition of Torah teshuvah, which remains abandonment of the sin and sincere return. He uses them to explain the Rishonim's additional avodah of mishkal, hakasuv and ritzui after the core teshuvah. This reading also prevents the dramatic ascetic language from being flattened into a single universal schedule detached from the person's act and its consequences.
אֲבָל מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב בִּתְחִלַּת דְּבָרָיו לֵישֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח וְלִפְנֵי נְמָלִים, שֶׁהוּא לְיִסּוּרִין הַקָּשִׁין כְּמִיתָה, זֶה הוּא גַּם בְּשֶׁלֹּא אֲסָרַתָּהּ
but what he wrote at the beginning of his words—to sit in ice and before ants, which constitutes afflictions as harsh as death—applies even when she did not become forbidden.
וְעַיֵּין בְּפִסְקֵי מַהֲרָאִ״י [סִימָן נ״ה] מֵבִיא מִפִּסְקֵי רַבֵּינוּ מֹשֶׁה מִירְזְבוּרְק: בְּחִילּוּל שַׁבָּת בִּמְלָאכָה דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא סַגִּי בְּתַעֲנִית מ׳ יוֹם
And see in Piskei Maharai [§55] citing from the rulings of Rabbeinu Moshe of Merseburg: for desecrating Shabbos with a biblical labor, forty fasts suffice,
וְאַף דְּהוּא חַיָּיב מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין וּבִסְקִילָה הַחֲמוּרָה, וְכִדְאִיתָא שָׁם בְּנִדָּתוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב שֶׁהָיְתָה נִרְדֶּפֶת וּקְצָת אֲנוּסָה
even though it incurs court execution by severe stoning, as found there regarding a niddah who was pursued and coerced;
וְכֵן כָּתַב [שָׁם סִימָן ס׳] דִּבְנִרְדָּף הֵקֵלּוּ
and so he wrote [§60] that they were lenient regarding one who was coerced;

אֶלָּא דְּשָׁם מַשְׁמַע דְּכָתַב זֶה עַל מַה שֶּׁאֵין צָרִיךְ הַתַּעֲנִיּוֹת רְצוּפִים, דִּבְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת צָרִיךְ גַּם כֵּן רְצוּפִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רוֹקֵחַ שָׁם [בְּסוֹף סִימָן י״א], עַיֵּין שָׁם

except that there it implies that he wrote this to waive the requirement of consecutive fasts, for regarding kares consecutive fasts are required as the Rokeach wrote [§11], see there.755Piskei Mahari §§55, 60; Magen Avraham 334:33; Mishnah Berurah 334:77-81; Sefer Chasidim §181 - forty days can be deterrence or mishkal, not a severity chart: Piskei Mahari records forty fasts even for a Torah Shabbos labor carrying sekilah, and also for crossing techumin. The Magen Avraham preserves the striking extension: “אֲפִלּוּ בִּתְחוּמִין דְּרַבָּנַן,” while the Mishnah Berurah explains that the practice may apply to either a biblical or rabbinic violation and varies with coercion, loss and the sinner's attitude. This alone disproves any automatic equation between forty days and one fixed punishment. Rav Tzadok notes Mahari's stated educational concern, “דְּלָא יְזַלְזְלוּ” - that Shabbos not be treated lightly - and distinguishes consecutive fasts used for the graver category from a nonconsecutive corrective schedule. Sefer Chasidim makes the mishkal element even clearer. When a man carried his money on Shabbos, the sage ordered him to distribute that money or its value to embarrassed poor people and offered no substitute when he refused. The correction directly removes the benefit for which he violated Shabbos. Rav Tzadok therefore concludes that such rulings may function as deterrence, restitution of the enjoyed gain, or voluntary ritzui; their shared number does not establish equal intrinsic severity or the same requirement for kapparah.

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם וְשָׁם מַצְרִיךְ תַּעֲנִית מ׳ יוֹם גַּם בִּתְחוּמִין דְּהִיא דְּרַבָּנָן, וְגַם לְמַאן דְּאָמַר דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא אֵין בּוֹ כָּרֵת וּמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וּמַיְיתֵי לֵיהּ מָגֵן אַבְרָהָם [סִימָן של״ד סְעִיף קָטָן ל״ג]
And see there that he requires forty fasts even for traversing Shabbos boundaries (techumin), which is rabbinic (or lacking kares and execution even if biblical), cited by the Magen Avraham;

וְזֶה וַדַּאי אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשְׁווֹתָם, וְנִרְאֶה דְּעִיקַּר טַעְמוֹ בָּזֶה כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב [שָׁם סִימָן נ״ה] דְּלֹא יְזַלְזְלוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וְאֵינוֹ מֵעִיקַּר הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְהַצֹּרֶךְ לְכַפָּרָה
and this certainly cannot be equated, the primary reason being "lest people treat it lightly," and not out of the core requirement for atonement.
וּבְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים [סִימָן קפ״א] כָּתַב: אֶחָד חִלֵּל שַׁבָּת וְנָשָׂא כַּסְפּוֹ, וְאָמַר לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה לְחַלֵּק הַכֶּסֶף אוֹ שָׁוְיוֹ לַעֲנִיִּים, וְלֹא נָתַן לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה אַחֶרֶת, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And in Sefer Chassidim [§181] he wrote: a man desecrated Shabbos by carrying his money, and he instructed him to distribute the money or its value to the poor, giving him no other repentance, see there;
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּלֹא הוֹצִיא לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים רַק טִלְטוּל מוּקְצֶה דְּרַבָּנָן
and one must say that he did not carry into the public domain, but merely handled rabbinic muktzeh;

וְלֹא צָרִיךְ תַּעֲנִית רַק לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל, דְּזֶה צָרִיךְ בְּכָל אִיסּוּרִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי, לְפִי שֶׁעָשָׂה לַהֲנָאָתוֹ שֶׁלֹּא יִגְנְבוּ כַּסְפּוֹ, עַל כֵּן אָמַר לְחַלֵּק וּלְסַלֵּק הֲנָאָתוֹ מֵהָאִיסּוּר וְהָעֲבֵירָה עַל יְדֵי זֶה]:
and he needed no fast, but only teshuvah ha-mishkal to eliminate the financial benefit derived from the prohibition, by distributing the money to the poor.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the twin requirements in the Rokeach (§11) regarding cohabitation with a niddah: forty fasts, lashes, and sitting in ice for the duration of roasting and swallowing an egg. Both are necessary: one fulfills scriptural repentance (teshuvah ha-kasuv), while the other fulfills commensurate repentance (teshuvah ha-mishkal). The roasting of an egg corresponds to Rabbi Akiva’s definition of the time required for cohabitation (Sotah 4a), requiring physical distress equal to the duration of forbidden pleasure. For wasteful emission, the Rokeach lists forty fasts solely to balance the pleasure of emission, omitting other mortifications because manual and oral fondling are absent.

p: וּבְסִימָן [י״א] בְּנִדָּה כָּתַב הָרוֹקֵחַ: יִתְעַנֶּה מ׳ וְיִלְקֶה וְלֹא יֹאכַל בָּשָׂר וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאַחַר כָּךְ כָּתַב: לֵישֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח כְּשִׁיעוּר צְלִיַּית בֵּיצָה וְגוֹמְעָהּ לְפָחוֹת מִגּ׳ יוֹם וְכוּלֵיהּ, בֵּין אֵינוֹ מִתְעַנֶּה, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And in §11 regarding a niddah, the Rokeach wrote: he shall fast forty days, receive lashes, and not eat meat, etc., and afterward wrote: to sit in ice for the duration of roasting an egg and swallowing it for at least three days, even when not fasting, see there;
וְנִרְאֶה דְּתַרְוַויְיהוּ צְרִיכֵי: אֶחָד לִתְשׁוּבַת הַכָּתוּב, וְהַב׳ לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל

and it appears that both are required: one for scriptural repentance, and the second for commensurate repentance.756Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7 and 14; Orchos Tzadikim, Shaar HaTeshuvah - two regimens for two functions: The Rokeach's niddah order first states: “יִתְעַנֶּה אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם רְצוּפִים וְיִלְקֶה בְּכָל יוֹם,” together with abstention from meat, wine, hot food and washing. It then adds a different practice: sitting in cold water or ice for the time specified, “בֵּין מִתְעַנֶּה בֵּין אֵינוֹ מִתְעַנֶּה.” Rav Tzadok reads the duplication as intentional. The forty-day discipline, lashes and continuing restrictions belong to teshuvas ha-kasuv - a regimen reflecting the Torah's kareis category. The measured cold exposure belongs to teshuvas hamishkal - pain set opposite the particular bodily pleasure of the act. This also explains why §11 prescribes an hour of severe cold for adultery, whereas §14 uses the much shorter halachic measure of the act itself: the first resembles punishment “כְּמִיתָה,” while the second weighs duration against duration. Orchos Tzadikim preserves substantially the same forty-day niddah order, showing that it circulated as a structured penitential tradition rather than a single undifferentiated fast. Rav Tzadok's larger point is that multiple practices may accompany one sin for different purposes; one cannot infer from the number forty alone whether a practice is basic kapparah, written-punishment correspondence, or post-forgiveness ritzui.

וְכֵן נִרְאֶה מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַב הַשִּׁיעוּר דִּצְלִיַּית וְכוּלֵיהּ וְלֹא כָּתַב ״שָׁעָה אַחַת״ [כִּבְסִימָן י״א], מְבוֹאָר דְּטַעְמוֹ בָּזֶה שֶׁזֶּה שִׁיעוּר טוּמְאָה לְרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא [בְּסוֹטָה ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳] דְּקַיְימָא לָן כְּוָותֵיהּ

And so it appears from his specifying the duration of roasting an egg rather than "one hour": for this is the duration of cohabitation according to Rabbi Akiva [Sotah 4a], in accordance with whom the halachah is established,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר [סִימָן קע״ח סְעִיף ד׳], וְצָרִיךְ לִסְבּוֹל הַצַּעַר כְּשִׁיעוּר זְמַן הַהֲנָאָה, וְזֶהוּ לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל

as stated in Even HaEzer [178:4], requiring one to endure distress equal to the duration of the pleasure, which fulfills teshuvah ha-mishkal.757Sotah 4a; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 178:4; Tzidkas HaTzadik 73 - the measure of roasting and swallowing an egg: The Gemara defines the minimum seclusion capable of tumah as the time for intercourse and ha'ara'ah. Among its practical measures, one baraisa gives R. Akiva “כְּדֵי לִצְלוֹת בֵּיצָה,” and the Gemara resolves the variant traditions: “אֵימָא כְּדֵי לִצְלוֹת בֵּיצָה וּלְגוֹמְעָהּ.” Shulchan Aruch accordingly rules that stirah requires “כְּדֵי לִצְלוֹת בֵּיצָה וּלְגָמְעָהּ.” The Rokeach's use of this exact formula for sitting in ice is therefore not merely a picturesque time estimate. Rav Tzadok infers that it deliberately mirrors the halachically defined duration of the pleasure and act, making it a classic teshuvas hamishkal. This derivation is Rav Tzadok's interpretive reconstruction; neither Sotah nor Even HaEzer discusses penitential ice. The contrast with the Rokeach's “one hour” in the adultery section is decisive for him: a fixed hour expresses harsh suffering analogous to death, while the egg-measure expresses proportionality to the act. In Tzidkas HaTzadik 73, Rav Tzadok describes the deepest hamishkal as Providence returning the same circumstance and the penitent overcoming it. Here the Rokeach's measured bodily practice functions as a humanly available analogue when the original test cannot or should not be recreated.
וּבִתְשׁוּבוֹת מַהֲרַ״ם שָׁם כָּתַב לְהִתְעַנּוֹת שָׁנָה רִאשׁוֹנָה שֵׁנִי וַחֲמִישִׁי וְלִלְבּוֹשׁ שַׂק וְג׳ מַלְקִיּוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And in the responsa of Maharam there, he wrote to fast Mondays and Thursdays during the first year, wear sackcloth, and receive lashes three times, see there;758Responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, penitential order; Rokeach §14 - substituting an extended fast schedule for omitted mortifications: The penitential order printed with Maharam distinguishes an unimmersed woman, where the act carries niddah-kareis, from one who immersed. For the former it prescribes three floggings, Monday-and-Thursday fasting through the first year, increased supplication and sackcloth; for the latter, one flogging and forty fasts. Rav Tzadok compares this with the Rokeach, who combines forty consecutive fasts and lashes with food restrictions, and then separately requires the measured ice practice. Maharam does not mention that ice regimen. Rav Tzadok therefore suggests that the longer BaHaB schedule, together with sackcloth and repeated lashes, may compensate for the omitted mortifications and effectively supply more than one forty-day layer. This is an inference from the two texts, not an explicit equation stated by Maharam. It also explains why one should not compare the printed numbers in isolation: the total penitential package includes continuity, permitted non-fast days, clothing, confession, lashes, diet and other bodily restraints. Earlier in this siman Rav Tzadok separated core teshuvah from additional ritzui; here he further separates the components within that ritzui. Two authorities may pursue the same purposes through different combinations of fasting and mortification, so a divergent schedule need not mean a dispute about whether teshuvah or Yom Kippur has already achieved basic forgiveness.
וְלֹא כָּתַב הַאי דְּקֶרַח, וְעַל כֵּן הוֹסִיף בַּתַּעֲנִיּוֹת שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לְפִי זֶה ב׳ פְּעָמִים מ׳ יוֹם
and he did not record sitting in ice, wherefore he increased the fasts to twice forty days;
וּבְשֵׁנִי וַחֲמִישִׁי דְּשָׁנָה רִאשׁוֹנָה, שֶׁהוּא מִסְּתָמָא חוּץ מִיָּמִים שֶׁאֵין מִתְעַנִּין בְּמוֹעֲדוֹת וְרֹאשׁ חֹדֶשׁ וַחֲנוּכָּה וּפוּרִים, הוּא קְצָת יוֹתֵר
and Mondays and Thursdays of the first year (excluding festive days) amounts to slightly more;
וְאֶפְשָׁר הוּא נֶגֶד שְׁאָר סִגּוּפִים הַנִּזְכָּר בְּרוֹקֵחַ בִּתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל וְהַכָּתוּב בְּעִנְיַן הַשְּׁכִיבָה וַאֲכִילַת בָּשָׂר שֶׁלֹּא נֶאֱמַר כָּאן
and perhaps this balances the other mortifications mentioned in the Rokeach regarding sleeping and refraining from meat.
וּבְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה שֶׁכָּתַב רוֹקֵחַ מ׳ יוֹם, הוּא לְמִשְׁקַל הַהֲנָאָה לְבַד
And regarding wasteful emission, where the Rokeach prescribed forty days, it is solely to balance the pleasure;
וּלְפִי שֶׁאֵין שָׁם הֲנָאַת מִשְׁמוּשׁ וְנִישּׁוּק וְהַעֲרָאָה, עַל כֵּן לֹא כָּתַב בָּזֶה שְׁאָר סִגּוּפִין הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and because manual and oral fondling are absent, he did not record those other mortifications here.
וּבְבִיאַת פְּנוּיָה לְפִי זֶה הָיָה צָרִיךְ לְכָל חִיּוּב תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל שֶׁבְּרוֹקֵחַ [סִימָן ג׳] הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
And for relations with an unmarried woman, one should logically require all the elements of teshuvah ha-mishkal in Rokeach [§3];
אֶלָּא שֶׁבִּתְשׁוּבוֹת מַהֲרַ״ם הֵקֵל גַּם בָּזֶה בְּתַעֲנִית מ׳ יוֹם לְבַד
but in the responsa of Maharam he was lenient with forty fasts alone,
וְאֶפְשָׁר סְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּפְנוּיָה שֶׁאֵין מוּפְקֶרֶת רַק אִיסּוּר דְּרַבָּנָן וְקַל
holding that an unpromiscuous unmarried woman violates only a rabbinic prohibition and is lighter.
וְגַם בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים [סִימָן קע״ז] וּמוּבָא בְּחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק וּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל [רֵישׁ סִימָן כ״ג] מַשְׁמַע דְּאִיסּוּר הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חָמוּר מֵאִיסּוּר פְּנוּיָה שֶׁאֵין נִדָּה
And in Sefer Chassidim [§177], cited in Chelkas Mechokeik and Beis Shmuel [Even HaEzer 23], it implies that wasteful emission is graver than relations with a non-niddah unmarried woman;
וְרַק נִדָּה אוֹ עֲרָיוֹת חֲמִירֵי מִינַּהּ וְנִדְחֶה מִפְּנֵיהֶם, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and only niddah or incestuous relations are graver, taking precedence over it, see there;759Sefer Chasidim §176; Chelkas Mechokek and Beis Shmuel, Even HaEzer 23:1; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 1:4 - relative severity is context-dependent: Sefer Chasidim rules that when a man fears imminent failure with a married woman, niddah or another ervah, “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זַרְעוֹ וְאַל יֶחֱטָא בְּאִשָּׁה,” followed by ice in winter or forty summer fasts. Chelkas Mechokek and Beis Shmuel cite this ruling to qualify the Shulchan Aruch's phrase that wasting seed is “חָמוּר מִכָּל עֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁבַּתּוֹרָה”: it cannot be an absolute halachic ranking, because it is set aside to prevent arayos or niddah. Rav Tzadok draws a more precise hierarchy from the case. Wasting seed may be treated more severely than relations with a non-niddah unmarried woman, yet it remains lighter than niddah and forbidden relations. The Rambam complicates the comparison by ruling: “כָּל הַבּוֹעֵל אִשָּׁה לְשֵׁם זְנוּת בְּלֹא קִדּוּשִׁין לוֹקֶה מִן הַתּוֹרָה,” under lo tihyeh kedeishah; the Raavad and other Rishonim limit that Torah category to a woman made available promiscuously. Rav Tzadok therefore frames Maharam's leniency as possibly following the narrower view, where an unmarried woman who is not hefker carries only a lighter prohibition. The conclusion is methodological: penitential severity, rhetorical severity and formal malkus are distinct measures and must not be collapsed into one scale.
וּלְרַמְבַּ״ם דְּלוֹקִין אַפְּנוּיָה, נִרְאֶה דְּחָמִיר מֵהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּלֵיכָּא מַלְקוּת:
while according to the Rambam who holds that lashes are incurred for an unmarried woman, it is graver than wasteful emission which carries no lashes.

items.h: The theme: The equivalence between sitting in ice and forty fasts in Sefer Chassidim and Maharam of Rothenburg. In Sefer Chassidim, sitting in ice in winter balances forty fasts in summer as alternate expressions of teshuvah ha-mishkal. The text in Maharam stating "he shall fast forty days and sit in ice" is a scribal error and must be read "or sit in ice" (o yeishev), as one suffices. The forty-day quota does not derive from "murdering a potential child," since forty fasts are also assigned to relations with an unmarried woman where no potential life is destroyed; rather, forty days corresponds to the forty days of fetal formation (yetziras ha-valad), balancing the intense heat of the entire body experienced during emission.

p: וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים כָּתַב: לְכַפָּרַת הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה בַּקֶּרַח בַּחֹרֶף אוֹ מ׳ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת דְּקַיִץ, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And see in Sefer Chassidim where he wrote: for the atonement of wasteful emission, [sit] in ice in winter or [fast] forty fasts in summer, see there;
וְהַיְינוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל דְּאוֹתָהּ הֲנָאָה דְּסַגִּי בַּחֲדָא מִינַּיְיהוּ כַּנַּ״ל

which aligns with teshuvah ha-mishkal, where one of these options suffices to balance the pleasure, as mentioned above;760Sefer Chasidim §§167, 176; Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 - ice or forty fasts as alternative teshuvas hamishkal: Sefer Chasidim rules in the emergency case: “מוּטָב שֶׁיּוֹצִיא שִׁכְבַת זַרְעוֹ וְאַל יֶחֱטָא בְּאִשָּׁה,” but adds, “צָרִיךְ כַּפָּרָה: יֵשֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח בִּימֵי הַחֹרֶף אוֹ יִתְעַנֶּה אַרְבָּעִים יוֹם בִּימֵי חַמָּה.” The word “אוֹ” is central to Rav Tzadok's reading: cold and fasting are alternative forms of one repair, not two cumulative stages of indispensable kapparah. In §167 Sefer Chasidim explains the bodily logic - if the body was heated through sin, it should be cooled - yet concludes that a teacher may not direct the penitent to kill himself, invoking “דִּרְשׁוּנִי וִחְיוּ.” This places a limit around the entire practice. Rav Tzadok therefore classifies it as teshuvas hamishkal, a measured reversal of the pleasure and heat absorbed through the act. In Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 he develops the principle: sinful pleasure becomes like forbidden substance absorbed into the soul, and proportional suffering can “expel” that absorbed enjoyment; Torah and renewed mitzvah-life can also cleanse it. Thus Sefer Chasidim's regimen expresses additional ritzui and purification after sincere teshuvah. Its severity does not by itself prove a formal category of kareis or misah bidei Shamayim.
וְכֵן כָּתַב [שָׁם סִימָן קס״ז] לְעִנְיָן זֶה בַּקֶּרַח לְבַד, וּמִשּׁוּם דִּבְרוֹתְחִין קִלְקְלוּ, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם, וְהַיְינוּ כְּנֶגֶד הֲנָאַת הָעֲבֵירָה
and so he wrote [§167] requiring ice alone, because "in boiling heat they corrupted" (Sanhedrin 108b), see there, counterbalancing the heat of the sinful pleasure.
[וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרֵישׁ הַסִּימָן כָּתַב: לְחַיָּיב כָּרֵת שֶׁבְּמַלְקוּת נִפְטַר צָרִיךְ לִתְשׁוּבָה דָּבָר הַשָּׁקוּל לְמַלְקוּת אוֹ לְכָרֵת
[And see at the beginning of that section where he wrote: for an offense of kares that is exempt through lashes, one requires a repentance commensurate to lashes or kares;

וּבַחֹרֶף יֵשֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח כְּמַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁדִּבֵּר עִמָּהּ מֵהָעֲבֵירָה עַד גְּמָרָהּ, וְיַעֲשֶׂה כֵּן תָּדִיר כָּל זְמַן שֶׁיֵּשׁ קֶרַח, וּבִימוֹת הַחַמָּה בִּנְמָלִים, וּבִזְמַן שֶׁאֵין קוֹר וָחֹם יִתְעַנֶּה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and in winter he shall sit in ice for the duration of his speaking with her from the inception of the sin until its completion, doing so continually as long as there is ice, in summer among ants, and in temperate seasons he shall fast, see there;
וְזֶהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר הָרוֹקֵחַ גַּבֵּי חַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין: יִסּוּרִין כְּמִיתָה וְלֹא בְּג׳ יָמִים לְבַד
which matches what the Rokeach stated regarding court executions: afflictions as harsh as death, and not for three days alone;
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם אַחַר כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ כְּשֶׁאֲסָרַתָּהּ אַבַּעְלָהּ לְהַחְמִיר יוֹתֵר
and see what he wrote regarding a married woman when she became forbidden to her husband to be even more stringent;
וְכֵן בְּרֵישׁ הַסִּימָן דְּפָתַח בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ, מַשְׁמַע דְּגַם בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ כֵּן כְּשֶׁלֹּא אֲסָרַתָּהּ, וְאֵין מְחַלֵּק בֵּין חַיָּיבֵי מִיתוֹת בֵּית דִּין לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת

and so at the start of the section opening with a married woman, it implies that it is so even when she did not become forbidden, drawing no distinction between court executions and kares;761Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §§7, 11, 14; Orchos Tzadikim 26:103; Menoras HaMaor, Hilchos Teshuvah 18; Kesubos 33b - two different measures of suffering: The Rokeach tradition contains two distinct formulations. For adultery, Orchos Tzadikim preserves: since the act carries court-imposed death, “יִסְבֹּל צַעַר הַקָּשֶׁה כַּמָּוֶת,” including an hour in snow or ice throughout the winter and comparable summer suffering. By contrast, Menoras HaMaor states for kareis-level arayos: “יֵשֵׁב בַּקֶּרַח כְּשִׁעוּר צְלִיַּת בֵּיצָה וְגוֹמְעָהּ,” with fasting between three and forty days. The first imitates the gravity of the written punishment; the second measures pain against the duration and pleasure of the act. Rav Tzadok uses this contrast to explain why the ice prescribed for wasted seed may suffice once: its function is hamishkal, not a substitute for death. He nevertheless flags a difficulty in the Rokeach's language comparing such suffering to lashes. Kesubos distinguishes “הַכָּאָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהּ קִצְבָּה” from unlimited coercive flogging; fixed Torah lashes are lighter than death, while unlimited beating can be harsher. Therefore one cannot create a single hierarchy from the words “lashes,” “kareis,” and “like death.” The total context - duration, repetition, purpose and accompanying restrictions - determines whether a regimen corresponds to punishment, breaks desire, or supplies post-forgiveness ritzui.
וְאַף שֶׁמְּדַמֶּה זֶה לְיִסּוּרֵי מַלְקוּת, וּמַלְקוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם קִצְבָּה קַל מִמִּיתָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּכְתוּבּוֹת ל״ג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳, וְצָרִיךְ עִיּוּן]
and although he compares this to lashes, lashes have a defined limit and are lighter than death as stated in Kesubos 33b, and this requires study];
וּמַשְׁמַע דְּסַגִּי בְּפַעַם אַחַת
and it implies that a single instance of sitting in ice suffices;
וְלֹא דָּמֵי לִבְיאַת חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת, דְּאִיכָּא הֲנָאָה טְפֵי בְּבִיאַת אִשָּׁה מִבְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and it is not comparable to cohabitation with those liable to kares, where there is far greater pleasure in coitus with a woman than in wasteful emission, as mentioned above.

וּבִתְשׁוּבוֹת מַהֲרַ״ם שָׁם כָּתַב: דְּיִתְעַנֶּה מ׳ יוֹם כְּנֶגֶד יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד, וְיֵשֵׁב בַּמַּיִם בַּחֹרֶף כְּנֶגֶד צְלִיַּית בֵּיצָה, וְכָל אוֹתָם מ׳ יוֹם לֹא יֹאכַל בָּשָׂר וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And in the responsa of Maharam there, he wrote: he shall fast forty days corresponding to the formation of the fetus, sit in cold water in winter for the duration of roasting an egg, and throughout those forty days refrain from meat, see there;762Responsa of Maharam of Rothenburg, penitential order; Rashi on Bereishis 7:4; Sefer Chasidim §176; Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 - why forty days correspond to formation: The penitential order printed with Maharam says that one who wasted seed should fast forty days “כְּנֶגֶד יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד,” sit in winter water for the egg-roasting measure, avoid meat, wine and hot food, and confess with a firm resolution not to return. Rav Tzadok proposes that its “וְיָשַׁב” should read “אוֹ יָשַׁב,” because Sefer Chasidim explicitly offers ice or forty summer fasts as alternatives. The forty-day symbolism has an established source: Rashi explains the Flood's forty days as “כְּנֶגֶד יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד,” because that generation corrupted human formation. Rav Tzadok nonetheless rejects the idea that Maharam is treating wasted seed literally as fetal bloodshed. The same penitential collection assigns forty fasts to relations with an immersed unmarried woman, where no destroyed fetus is involved. He therefore reads the number as a measure of bodily pleasure: the whole body is heated toward procreation, and forty days of restraint answer the forty-day process of formation; the winter water directly counters the immediate heat. This fits Tzidkas HaTzadik 262, where teshuvas hamishkal removes the pleasure absorbed by the soul. The number forty is thus a symbolic measure of ritzui, not proof of misah bidei Shamayim or a fifth category of basic kapparah.
וְנִרְאֶה דְּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב ״וְיֵשֵׁב״ טָעוּת סוֹפֵר, וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר ״אוֹ יֵשֵׁב״, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים דִּבְחַד מִינַּיְיהוּ סַגִּי
and it appears that what he wrote, "and sit," is a scribal error, and must read "or sit" (o yeishev), as stated in Sefer Chassidim that one of them suffices.
וְטַעְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב לְשִׁיעוּר מ׳ יוֹם אֵין רְצוֹנוֹ לוֹמַר מִפְּנֵי שֶׁהוּא כְּשׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים דְּוָלָד עַל כֵּן צָרִיךְ לְתַקֵּן מ׳ יוֹם נֶגֶד יְצִירָתוֹ
And his reason for the forty-day measure does not mean that because he is like a murderer of a potential child he must rectify forty days corresponding to its formation;
שֶׁהֲרֵי גַּם בְּבִיאַת פְּנוּיָה כָּתַב שִׁיעוּר מ׳ יוֹם וְשָׁם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ שְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים דְּוָלָד
for behold, regarding an unmarried woman he likewise prescribed forty days, where no destruction of potential life applies!
רַק כַּוָּונָתוֹ לָתֵת טַעַם לְמִשְׁקַל הַהֲנָאָה זוֹ בְּכָךְ, לְפִי שֶׁהַגּוּף נִתְחַמֵּם לְהוֹצָאַת וָלָד שֶׁהוּא חִימּוּם כָּל הַגּוּף כּוּלּוֹ לִיצִירַת וָלָד
Rather, his intention was to provide a rationale for this measure of pleasure: since the body is heated for the emission of seed with a total warmth that has the capacity to form a child,
עַל כֵּן שִׁיעֲרוּ הָעִינּוּי לְדוֹרוֹן נֶגֶד הַהֲנָאָה בְּשִׁיעוּר יְמֵי יְצִירַת הַוָּלָד:
they consequently calibrated the affliction of the tribute-gift to counterbalance that pleasure according to the forty days of fetal formation.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ל״ד–ל״ט

The theme: The fasts of the Rokeach versus the fasts of the Arizal. The Rokeach bases his fasts on "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal), which derives from the sacrificial tribute-gift (doran) of the olah. The Ari does not calibrate the tribute strictly according to physical pleasure, prescribing eighty-four fasts for wasteful emission to effect rectification in higher metaphysical worlds. As the Rama MiFano wrote in Pelach HaRimmon, the Kabbalah of the early masters compared to the Ari is like the literal sense (peshat) compared to the esoteric mystery (sod); each master formulated the requirements of appeasement (ritzui) according to his level of mystical perception.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים נִרְאֶה טַעַם סִגּוּפֵי עָוֹן זֶה לְרוֹקֵחַ וְסִיעָתוֹ מִשּׁוּם ״תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל״
And in any event, it appears that the rationale for the mortifications of this iniquity according to the Rokeach and his school is on account of "commensurate repentance" (teshuvah ha-mishkal);
וְטַעַם ״תְּשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל״ עַצְמוֹ, שֶׁלֹּא הֶרְאָה לוֹ רוֹקֵחַ מָקוֹר
and the rationale of teshuvah ha-mishkal itself, for which the Rokeach did not indicate a Talmudic source

[כִּלְ״תְּשׁוּבַת הַבָּאָה״ שֶׁמֵּבִיא מִגְּמָרָא [דְּיוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳], וּ״תְשׁוּבַת הַגָּדֵר״ הֲגַם דְּהוּא לֹא מַיְיתֵי מִגְּמָרָא, הוּא מְבוֹאָר בְּפֶרֶק ״זֶה בּוֹרֵר״ (סַנְהֶדְרִין כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳) בִּמְשַׂחֲקֵי בְּקוּבְיָא דַּאֲפִילּוּ בְּחִנָּם לָא עָבְדֵי, וּמַלְוֶה בְּרִבִּית אֲפִילּוּ לְגוֹי לֹא מַלְוֶה, וּמַפְרִיחֵי יוֹנִים אֲפִילּוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר לָא עָבְדֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם

[unlike "responsive repentance" (teshuvah ha-ba'ah when facing identical temptation) which he cites from the Gemara [Yoma 86b]; and "protective repentance" (teshuvah ha-geder), which although he does not cite a Gemara, is clarified in chapter Zeh Borer (Sanhedrin 25b) regarding dice players who must refrain from playing even for free, usurers who must not lend on interest even to a gentile, and pigeon-flyers who must not fly them even in the desert, see there;763Yoma 86b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:1; Tzidkas HaTzadik 73 — teshuvas haba’ah tests the transformed choice: Yoma defines the complete returnee: “הֵיכִי דָמֵי בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה? ... שֶׁבָּאת לְיָדוֹ דְּבַר עֲבֵירָה פַּעַם רִאשׁוֹנָה וּשְׁנִיָּה וְנִיצַּל הֵימֶנָּה,” specifically “בְּאוֹתָהּ אִשָּׁה, בְּאוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק, בְּאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם.” Rambam codifies the principle: “זֶה שֶׁבָּא לְיָדוֹ דָּבָר שֶׁעָבַר בּוֹ ... וּפֵרַשׁ וְלֹא עָשָׂה מִפְּנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה,” while desire and strength remain. This is not a punishment imposed on the body, but evidence that the inner decision has changed under equivalent conditions.
