Rav Tzadok therefore says the Rokeach can point to an explicit Gemara for teshuvas haba’ah, whereas the proportional suffering of teshuvas hamishkal lacks such a direct Talmudic formulation. In Tzidkas HaTzadik 73 he adds an important safeguard: a person may not deliberately recreate a forbidden test; rather, Hashem sometimes arranges “אוֹתוֹ פֶּרֶק וְאוֹתוֹ מָקוֹם,” and the successful refusal reveals that the return has become genuine. Thus teshuvas haba’ah verifies freedom from the former hold of the sin; it is not the source for a fixed number of fasts.764Sanhedrin 25b; Zevachim 7b; Takanas HaShavin 15:31; Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 — from teshuvas hageder to the olah-doron root of hamishkal: Sanhedrin describes rehabilitation by dismantling the framework of the offense: dice-players cease “אֲפִילּוּ בְּחִנָּם,” lenders on interest refrain “אֲפִילּוּ לְגוֹי,” and pigeon-racers desist “אֲפִילּוּ בַּמִּדְבָּר.” This is teshuvas hageder: the person builds a boundary stronger than the minimum prohibition and demonstrates that the former occupation no longer governs him. Rav Tzadok then seeks a conceptual source for the Rokeach’s separate teshuvas hamishkal. Zevachim states: “עוֹלָה — דּוֹרוֹן הִיא.” Rava reasons that without teshuvah the offering is “זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה,” while after teshuvah the sinner has already been forgiven; the olah therefore enters afterward as a gift of renewed favor. Rav Tzadok proposes that the Rokeach understood proportional counter-suffering in the same post-forgiveness category: pleasure was used to rebel, so an opposite exertion becomes a fitting doron and restores willing service. In Se’if 31 he applies this even to lesser prohibitions, and in Tzidkas HaTzadik 262 explains that forbidden pleasure becomes absorbed in the soul and may be expelled through measured pain, Torah, and renewed mitzvah-life. The source is therefore the logic of ritzui, not a new indispensable condition of basic mechilah.
וּ״תְשׁוּבַת הַכָּתוּב״ הוּא מִדְּבָרִים שֶׁצָּרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין לְחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וְחַיָּיבֵי מִיתַת בֵּית דִּין, אֲבָל לִ״תְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל״ לֹא נִמְצָא שׁוֹרֶשׁ בַּגְּמָרָא]

and "scriptural repentance" (teshuvah ha-kasuv), which derives from the principle that scouring afflictions are required for kares and court executions; but for teshuvah ha-mishkal no explicit root is found in the Gemara]
הוּא מֵהָא דְּעוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן
is derived from the principle that an olah is a tribute-gift (doran).
וְהָאֲרִ״י אֵין מְפָרֵשׁ הַדּוֹרוֹן כְּמִשְׁקַל הֲנָאָה, וְעַל כֵּן קָבַע תַּעֲנִיּוֹת הַרְבֵּה גַּם לַעֲבֵירוֹת שֶׁאֵין כָּל כָּךְ הֲנָאָה
And the Ari does not explain the tribute-gift as counterbalancing pleasure, and therefore he fixed numerous fasts even for transgressions that contain little pleasure;
וְכֵן לְמוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה הוֹסִיף עַד פ״ד תַּעֲנִיּוֹת, כִּי אֵין הַדּוֹרוֹן כְּפִי מִשְׁקַל הַהֲנָאָה דַּוְוקָא, וּבְוַדַּאי דְּאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים

and likewise for wasteful emission he increased up to eighty-four fasts, because the tribute is not calibrated specifically to the weight of pleasure, and certainly "these and those are the words of the Living God" (Eruvin 13b).
וּבַשְּׁלָ״ה שָׁם רָמַז גַּם כֵּן לְדִבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ״י בְּתִיקּוּן עָוֹן זֶה
And in the Shelah there he likewise alluded to the words of the Rokeach and the Ari regarding the rectification of this iniquity

[וְתֵימַהּ שֶׁכָּתַב זֶה אַחַר מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּצָרִיךְ יִסּוּרִין כְּמִיתָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וַהֲרֵי שְׁנֵיהֶם הָרוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ״י לֹא כָּתְבוּ בָּזֶה אֶלָּא מִסְפַּר תַּעֲנִיּוֹת וְלֹא יִסּוּרִין כְּמִיתָה כְּלָל]

[and it is wondrous that he wrote this after writing that one requires afflictions as harsh as death as mentioned above, when behold, both the Rokeach and the Ari wrote regarding this strictly a count of fasts, and not afflictions as harsh as death at all!],
וּדְאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וּכְשֶׁרוֹצֶה לְתַקֵּן הַפְּגָם בְּיוֹתֵר וּבְעוֹלָם יוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹן צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה בְּיוֹתֵר, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and that both are the words of the Living God, and when one seeks to rectify the blemish more extensively and in a higher world, one requires a greater repentance, see there;765Shlah, Shaar HaOtiyos, Kedushah; Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaTeshuvah 7; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah 3; Rema MiPano, introduction to Pelach HaRimon — different depths of one true repair: The Shlah, drawing on Reishis Chochmah, accepts both the Rokeach’s regimen and the Arizal’s tikkunim as “אֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹקִים חַיִּים,” adding that one who seeks to repair the blemish “בְּעוֹלָם יוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹן” requires a deeper teshuvah. Tanya records the Arizal’s figure explicitly: “פ״ד תַּעֲנִיּוֹת,” and presents the dispute whether repeated acts require repeated series like separate chata’os or can be addressed like one olah covering several positive-commandment failures. Its accepted practical compromise is three series, yet it sharply limits fasting when health or Torah study will suffer and permits redemption through tzedakah. The number is therefore a kabbalistic form of ritzui and tikkun, not a simple measurement of physical pleasure. Rav Tzadok uses this to explain why the Arizal can require more than the Rokeach without contradicting him: the doron reaches additional spiritual worlds. He cites Rema MiPano’s introduction to Pelach HaRimon, which treats the Ramak and earlier kabbalists in relation to the Arizal as progressively deeper levels rather than mutually exclusive systems. At the same time, Rav Tzadok questions the Shlah’s phrase “יסורין כמיתה”: the actual Rokeach and Arizal schedules cited here prescribe fasts, not literal death-like suffering. Greater tikkun must not be confused with a formal Torah punishment category.
וְהַיְינוּ כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי: צָרִיךְ דּוֹרוֹן יוֹתֵר לִהְיוֹת רָצוּי גַּם בָּעוֹלָמוֹת הָעֶלְיוֹנִים בְּיוֹתֵר וְגָבֹהַּ מֵעַל גָּבֹהַּ
meaning, as I wrote: one requires a greater tribute-gift to be accepted and beloved in the highest spiritual realms, high above high;
וְכָל אֶחָד יִיסֵּר לְפִי מַדְרֵיגַת הַשָּׂגָתוֹ
and each master formulated his guidance according to the level of his perception.

וְכִידוּעַ מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב הָרַמַ״ע בְּהַקְדָּמַת סֵפֶר ״פֶּלַח הָרִמּוֹן״, דְּקַבָּלַת הָרַב מֹשֶׁה קוֹרְדּוֹבֵירִי וְהָרִאשׁוֹנִים נֶגֶד קַבָּלַת הָאֲרִ״י כְּמַדְרֵגַת הַפְּשָׁט נֶגֶד הַסּוֹד, עַיֵּין שָׁם:

And as is known from what the Rama MiFano wrote in the introduction to Pelach HaRimmon, that the Kabbalah of Rabbi Moshe Cordovero and the Rishonim compared to the Kabbalah of the Ari is like the level of peshat [literal sense] compared to sod [esoteric secret], see there.

items.h: The theme: The four levels of Pardes parallel the four worlds of ABYA and the four letters of the Tetragrammaton. The higher mystical rectifications revealed through the Arizal address spiritual elevations inaccessible in earlier generations. The sacrificial tribute (doran) does not withhold basic forgiveness (kapparah), but rather enables the penitent to attain the ultimate level of intimacy accessible to a wholly righteous tzaddik ("the King has brought me into His chambers").

p: וְיָדוּעַ ד׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת פַּרְדֵּ״ס שֶׁיֵּשׁ בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַתּוֹרָה, הֵם נֶגֶד ד׳ עוֹלָמוֹת אֲבִי״עַ וְנֶגֶד ד׳ אוֹתִיּוֹת הַשֵּׁם

And it is known that the four levels of Pardes (Peshat, Remez, Derush, Sod) in the attainment of the Torah correspond to the four worlds of ABYA (Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah) and to the four letters of the Divine Name;

וְכָל אֶחָד הִשִּׂיג כְּפִי מַדְרֵיגַת הַשָּׂגָתוֹ, וְעַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ דִּבֵּר בְּעִנְיַן הָרִיצּוּי לְהַגִּיעַ לְאוֹתָן מַדְרֵיגוֹת הַשָּׂגָה שֶׁנִּתְגַּלּוּ עַל יְדֵי הָאֲרִיזַ״ל שֶׁלֹּא נוֹדְעוּ עֲדַיִין מִקּוֹדֶם וְלֹא הָיוּ יְכוֹלִים לְהַגִּיעַ לְכָךְ

and each master perceived according to the level of his attainment, speaking according to his pathway regarding the appeasement required to reach those levels of perception revealed through the Arizal, which were not yet known previously and which they could not reach;766Or HaChaim, Shemos 32:6; Shaarei Kedushah I 2:8; Shaar Maamarei Razal, Shabbos 8; Etz Chaim 42:17; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:44; Resisei Layla 35; Tzidkas HaTzadik 134 — PaRDeS, ABiYA, and ascent from one level of attainment to another: PaRDeS is the familiar acronym for peshat, remez, derash, and sod—the plain, allusive, homiletical, and esoteric dimensions of Torah. Or HaChaim makes the correspondence used here explicit: “הַפְּשָׁט אוֹרוֹ מֵאִיר בְּעוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה, רֶמֶז בְּעוֹלַם הַיְּצִירָה, דְּרָשׁ בְּעוֹלַם הַבְּרִיאָה, סוֹד בְּעוֹלַם הָאֲצִילוּת”—peshat illumines Asiyah, remez Yetzirah, derash Beriah, and sod Atzilus. Shaarei Kedushah presents the four modes of Torah-study as vehicles for the soul’s ascent, while Shaar Maamarei Razal and Etz Chaim relate the worlds to the four letters of Havayah: yud to Atzilus, the first heh to Beriah, vav to Yetzirah, and the final heh to Asiyah. These worlds are graded modes of Divine disclosure, from revealed unity to increasingly differentiated and concretized reception; a teaching may therefore be true on one level without exhausting a higher one. Rav Tzadok develops this in Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:44. Hashem did not establish unrelated systems; “אוֹתוֹ הַסֵּדֶר שֶׁבָּאֲצִילוּת הוּא עַצְמוֹ בִּבְרִיאָה... בִּיצִירָה... בַּעֲשִׂיָּה”—the same order repeats from Atzilus through Asiyah, though it descends into different forms of being. He also maps the worlds within the person: the hidden root of unified attachment corresponds to Atzilus; apprehension in which knower and known remain distinct to Beriah; the heart and ruach to Yetzirah; and recognition embodied in action to Asiyah. Resisei Layla 35 adds that Atzilus is what Hashem makes apprehensible of His otherwise unlimited light, and “כְּפִי מִדַּת הַשָּׂגָתָם הוּא... מִדַּת הַהַשָּׂגָה הַנֶּאֱצֶלֶת”—the revealed apprehension corresponds to the recipients’ attainment. Rav Tzadok therefore does not treat earlier authorities as mistaken: each spoke truth from the chamber and capacity then accessible. Tzidkas HaTzadik 134 supplies the direct teshuvah parallel. There is no fixed end to a person’s levels, and “כְּפִי מַעֲלַת הָאָדָם וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ כָּךְ הִיא תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ.” A sin may have been genuinely repaired “בְּכָל דַּרְגִין וְעוֹלָמוֹת” on the lower level, leaving no trace there; yet upon ascent it becomes newly visible according to the higher standard and calls for deeper teshuvah. This is the bridge in this se’if: the earlier tikkun sufficed for the level then revealed, while the Arizal’s disclosures opened a higher chamber and therefore a fuller ritzui. The correspondences come from the cited sources; their application here is Rav Tzadok’s analysis.
וְעַל כֵּן הָיָה דַּי לָהֶם מִתִּיקּוּן שֶׁנִּתְגַּלָּה אָז כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהָיָה הַצֹּרֶךְ אָז לַמַּדְרֵיגָה שֶׁהָיוּ יְכוֹלִים לְהַגִּיעַ
wherefore the rectification revealed in their time was sufficient for them, according to the need of that era for the spiritual level they were able to attain.

וְרִיצּוּי הַדּוֹרוֹן הוּא כְּדֵי שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְתַכְלִית הַמַּדְרֵיגָה שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר לְהַגִּיעַ, עַל יְדֵי הָרִיצּוּי הַגָּמוּר שֶׁ״הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו״ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים א:ד)

And the appeasement of the tribute-gift is designed to enable one to reach the ultimate spiritual peak accessible to a consummate tzaddik, through that total appeasement whereof it is said: "The King has brought me into His chambers" (Shir HaShirim 1:4);767Shir HaShirim 1:4; Yalkut Shimoni 982; Tanna DeBei Eliyahu Rabbah 6 — “The King brought me into His chambers”: Shir HaShirim says, “הֱבִיאַנִי הַמֶּלֶךְ חֲדָרָיו.” Yalkut Shimoni applies the verse to R’ Akiva, who entered Pardes and emerged in peace, and also interprets the chambers as the hidden treasuries of heaven, Gan Eden, and “חַדְרֵי תוֹרָה.” Tanna DeBei Eliyahu compares it to a king taking his beloved by the hand into innermost rooms and teaches that each talmid chacham has inner chambers in Torah. These readings illuminate Rav Tzadok’s use of the verse. It is not a source for a formal requirement to perform a particular fast or mortification. It is the image of complete ritzui after forgiveness: the penitent is not merely released from liability but restored to intimate access and higher Torah-attainment. The Midrashic link to R’ Akiva’s entry into Pardes also echoes the PaRDeS framework at the beginning of this se’if.
וְכָל תִּיקּוּנֵי תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁל הַקַּדְמוֹנִים כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי אֵינָם לְעִיכּוּב הַכַּפָּרָה לְגַמְרֵי, רַק לְהַגִּיעַ גַּם כֵּן לָרִיצּוּי הַגָּמוּר
and all the regimens of teshuvah of the early masters, as I wrote, do not withhold essential atonement, but serve solely to attain this complete appeasement;
וְאַף בְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת וּמִיתַת בֵּית דִּין אֵין הַסִּגּוּפִים שֶׁקָּצְבוּ לְיִסּוּרִים הַמְּמָרְקִים לְבַד
and even for those liable to kares and court executions, the mortifications they designated are not strictly scouring afflictions,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּדִבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ שֶׁקָּצַב מִלְּבַד זֶה לִתְשׁוּבַת הַמִּשְׁקָל, שֶׁהוּא בִּמְקוֹם הַדּוֹרוֹן עַל פִּי דַּרְכּוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל:

as I wrote regarding the words of the Rokeach, who designated in addition to them teshuvah ha-mishkal, which takes the place of the tribute-gift according to his methodology as mentioned above.768Yoma 86a; Zevachim 7b; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah — kapparah, yissurin memarkin, and the separate doron: Yoma distinguishes the stages of atonement by category: for kareis and court-death offenses, “תְּשׁוּבָה וְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים תּוֹלִין, וְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין” — repentance and Yom Kippur suspend, while suffering completes the cleansing. Zevachim, by contrast, calls the olah “דּוֹרוֹן הִיא”: without teshuvah the offering is rejected as a sacrifice of the wicked, while after teshuvah the person has already been forgiven; the offering restores favor. The Rokeach’s teshuvas hamishkal prescribes measured fasts or suffering corresponding to the transgression. Rav Tzadok’s chiddush is to separate these functions. He does not deny Yoma’s required cleansing where it applies; he argues that not every mortification listed by the early pietists is that indispensable stage. Some are an additional doron — a discipline of appeasement and repair that elevates the penitent beyond mechilah toward complete ritzui. This distinction is Rav Tzadok’s analysis, not an explicit statement of Yoma, Zevachim, or the Rokeach.

items.h: The theme: Critique of the Ba'al HaTanya's deduction from Sefer Chassidim. The Ba'al HaTanya derived that wasteful emission requires scouring mortifications like kares from the fasts listed in the Rokeach and Sefer Chassidim. R' Tzadok shows that mortifications for non-capital sins serve strictly as a tribute-gift (doran). Furthermore, regarding a positive commandment carrying kares, the Tosafos Yom HaKippurim (Yoma 85b) suggested that even an aseh carrying kares atones immediately through repentance alone.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים נִרְאֶה דְּבַעַל הַתַּנְיָא לָמַד זֶה מִדִּבְרֵי הָרוֹקֵחַ וְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים שֶׁסִּידְּרוּ תַּעֲנִיּוֹת וְסִגּוּפִים לִתְשׁוּבָה עַל זֶה
And in any event, it appears that the author of the Tanya derived this from the words of the Rokeach and Sefer Chassidim who arranged fasts and mortifications for repentance over this;
וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי אֵינוֹ רְאָיָה כְּלָל מִיהָא
but according to what I wrote, there is no proof whatsoever from this!
וְאַף דִּבְסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים שָׁם הֵבִיא בָּזֶה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״דִּכְאִלּוּ מֵבִיא מַבּוּל וּכְאִלּוּ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים״

And although in Sefer Chassidim there he cited regarding this that "it is as though he brings a flood and sheds blood,"769Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 1; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah §20; Sefer Chasidim §167 — Severe penitential regimens do not by themselves determine the formal atonement category: The Baal HaTanya writes that the classic mussar works, foremost the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim, prescribe numerous fasts and mortifications for sins carrying kareis or beis-din death, and likewise for wasteful emission of seed, which he classifies as death by Heaven from the deaths of Er and Onan; for the purpose of avoiding heavenly suffering he therefore treats it like kareis. The Rokeach prescribes forty fast-days together with practical safeguards against renewed arousal, while Sefer Chasidim prescribes cold-water mortification. Rav Tzadok is not denying that these Rishonim regarded the offense with extraordinary severity. His precise argument is methodological: the quantity and harshness of a teshuvah regimen may be intended to restore favor and refine the person in proportion to the damage, and therefore cannot alone prove that the offense belongs legally to the kareis-or-death class whose essential kapparah requires yissurin. The classification as death by Heaven is explicit in the Tanya; the inference that it was derived from the Rokeach and Sefer Chasidim is Rav Tzadok’s own reconstruction.
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּלְעִנְיַן הַסִּגּוּף לְדוֹרוֹן תָּלוּי גַּם כֵּן כְּפִי חֹמֶר הָעָוֹן, וְאַף עַל פִּי דְּאֵין בּוֹ כָּרֵת

one can say that regarding mortification for a tribute-gift, it depends likewise upon the severity of the iniquity, even though it carries no kares;770Niddah 13a; Yeshayah 57:5; Bereishis 6:12; Sefer Chasidim §167 — “As though he brings a Flood” and “as though he sheds blood”: Niddah describes conduct likely to cause wasteful emission as though it brings a Flood upon the world, linking it to “all flesh had corrupted its way,” and R’ Yitzchak and R’ Ami compare the emission itself to bloodshed through the derashah that reads shochatei, “those who slaughter children,” as sochetei, “those who squeeze out.” Rashi explains that the Flood generation corrupted through heated passion and was punished measure for measure with heated waters. Sefer Chasidim turns these images into penitential practice, prescribing immersion or sitting in icy water to cool the bodily heat that produced the sin. These statements explain why a doron-oriented tikkun may be unusually demanding. Rav Tzadok nevertheless distinguishes an aggadic comparison expressing destructive spiritual potential from a formal Torah category of homicide, kareis, or statutory death; that distinction continues his analysis from the opening se’ifim of this siman.
וְגַם בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה, אַף שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה אָמְרָה דֶּרֶךְ כְּלָל ״הָעוֹלָה מְכַפֶּרֶת לְדוֹרוֹן עַל כָּל מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה״
and regarding a positive commandment as well, although the Torah stated as a general rule that an olah atones as a tribute for any positive commandment,
עַתָּה שֶׁאֵין לָנוּ קָרְבָּנוֹת מִסְּבָרָא וַדַּאי יֵשׁ חִילּוּק בֵּין עֲשֵׂה חֲמוּרָה לַקַּלָּה בְּעִנְיַן סִגּוּפִים שֶׁעוֹשִׂים לְרִיצּוּי דּוֹרוֹן

now that we have no sacrifices, by logical reasoning there is certainly a distinction between a severe aseh and a light aseh regarding the fasts performed for the appeasement of tribute;771Zevachim 7b; Rashi, s.v. olah doron hi; Yoma 86a; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 2 — The olah restores favor after the sinner has already been pardoned: Rava reasons that an olah cannot effect the first pardon for neglect of a positive commandment: without teshuvah, “the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination,” while after teshuvah the offender “does not move from his place until he is forgiven.” The olah is therefore a doron. Rashi compares it to one who offended a king, secured appeasement through an advocate, and then brings a gift when admitted again before the king. Iggeres HaTeshuvah applies this distinction to voluntary fasting after genuine teshuvah: the fast is not the essence of forgiveness, but a means of becoming as beloved and welcome as before the sin. Rav Tzadok adopts the same structure here. Basic mechilah follows the halachic category of the offense; the additional regimen may vary with its severity because it seeks fuller ritzui and renewed closeness. A parallel appears in Tzidkas HaTzadik §134: a person may have completely repaired a sin on his present level, yet when he ascends, a deeper form of teshuvah becomes appropriate. That later refinement does not retroactively mean that the earlier forgiveness was incomplete.
אֲבָל אֵין בָּזֶה עִנְיָן לְיִסּוּרִין מְמָרְקִין דְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת שֶׁהֵם מְעַכְּבִין הַכַּפָּרָה
but this has nothing to do with the scouring afflictions of kares that withhold essential atonement!
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי דְּהוּא רַק מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה: אוֹ מִ״וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ״, אוֹ בִּכְלַל ״פְּרוּ וּרְבוּ״
And all the more so according to what I wrote: that it is merely a positive commandment, either derived from "and he shall cleave unto his wife" or subsumed under "be fruitful and multiply."

הִנֵּה גַּם בְּמִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה דְּחַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת דְּנִתְבָּאֵר [לְעֵיל אוֹת י״ג] בִּפְשִׁיטוּת מִלְּשׁוֹן הָרַמְבַּ״ם דְּהוּא בִּכְלַל חַיָּיבֵי כָּרֵת, וְכֵן הוּא גַּם כֵּן בַּעֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת שָׁם בִּפְשִׁיטוּת

Behold, even regarding a positive commandment carrying kares [such as circumcision or the Paschal lamb]—which was explained above [Siman 13] as plainly categorized under kares according to the Rambam and Asarah Ma'amaros—

רָאִיתִי עַתָּה בְּ״תוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים״ [בְּיוֹמָא פ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁכָּתַב בְּיִשּׁוּב דִּבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם [פֶּרֶק א׳ מֵהִלְכוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה הֲלָכָה ב׳] מִקּוּשְׁיַת הַכֶּסֶף מִשְׁנֶה שָׁם מֵהָא דִּשְׁבוּעוֹת [י״ב סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]
I have now seen in Tosafos Yom HaKippurim [Yoma 85b], who wrote in resolving the words of the Rambam [Hilchos Teshuvah 1:2] from the difficulty raised by the Kesef Mishneh from Shevuos [12b]:
דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם ״הַאי עֲשֵׂה הֵיכִי דָּמֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ״ קָאֵי אַעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת דְּמֵחֲמוּרוֹת, עַיֵּין שָׁם

that what they said there, "What are the circumstances of this positive command, etc.?", refers to a positive commandment carrying kares which belongs to the severe category, see there;772Tosafos Yom HaKippurim on Yoma 85b; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:2 and 1:4; Kesef Mishneh; Shevuos 12b — An aseh whose neglect carries kareis: The Rambam distinguishes the general categories of atonement and states that one who violates a positive commandment and repents is forgiven immediately. The Kesef Mishneh discusses how this formulation relates to the sugya in Shevuos, which asks what type of positive commandment remains for the Yom Kippur scapegoat to atone after teshuvah has already atoned. Tosafos Yom HaKippurim explains the sugya’s “this aseh—what are its circumstances?” as referring to an unusually severe positive commandment whose neglect itself carries kareis, such as the obligations of Korban Pesach or circumcision. On his reading, the rule “he does not move from there until he is forgiven” still follows the mitzvah’s positive-command form, even where kareis marks the gravity of its neglect. Rav Tzadok invokes this as direct support for the governing distinction of Siman 15: severity may enlarge the need for ritzui, safeguards, and later purification without automatically transferring the offense into the atonement schedule of a full negative prohibition or a kareis transgression. This is the view he draws from Tosafos Yom HaKippurim; it should not be presented as an uncontested reading of every Rishon or Acharon.
וּמְבוֹאָר דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּגַם מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד נִמְחָל, כִּדְמַיְיתֵי בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם (עַל זֶה) הָא דְּ״לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם:

and it is clear that he holds that even a positive commandment carrying kares is pardoned through repentance alone, as the Gemara cites there (concerning this) that "he does not move from there [before being pardoned], etc.," see there.

items.h: The theme: Refutation of Tosafos Yom HaKippurim. In Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4, the Rambam explicitly states that immediate pardon applies strictly to a positive commandment lacking excision (she-ein bo kares). The author of Tosafos Yom HaKippurim suggested that the verse "Return, backsliding children" applies to idolatry—interpreted as the positive commandment of rebuke (tochechah) or where one knew only the positive command. R' Tzadok refutes this: the failure to rebuke does not incur excision, and whoever unintentionally violates an offense of kares requires a sin-offering (chatas) alongside repentance, proving that repentance alone cannot grant immediate pardon for an aseh carrying kares.

p: וְאִיבְרָא שֶׁהוּא כָּתַב זֶה אַלִּיבָּא דְּרַמְבַּ״ם, וּכְבָר תָּמְהוּ עָלָיו שֶׁלֹּא רָאָה דִּבְרֵי רַמְבַּ״ם עַצְמוֹ [שָׁם הֲלָכָה ד׳] שֶׁכָּתַב: דַּוְוקָא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ כָּרֵת ״לֹא זָז וְכוּלֵיהּ״

And indeed, he wrote this according to the Rambam, and commentators already wondered at him for failing to notice the words of the Rambam himself [Halachah 4], who explicitly wrote: strictly for a positive commandment lacking kares does "he not move from there, etc.";
גַּם מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב שָׁם דִּקְרָא ״שׁוּבוּ בָנִים וְגוֹמֵר״ דְּיָלְפִינַן מִינֵּיהּ דַּעֲשֵׂה נִמְחָל מִיָּד קָאֵי בַּעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת, דִּבַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה מַיְירֵי כִּדְמוֹכְחֵי קְרָאֵי

likewise, what he wrote there—that the verse "Return, O backsliding children" from which we derive that an aseh is pardoned immediately refers to an aseh carrying kares, because it deals with idolatry as proven by the verses

[773Yoma 86a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 1:4; Minchas Chinuch, mitzvah 364:14 — the Rambam limits immediate pardon to an aseh without kareis: Rabbi Yishmael’s formulation in the Gemara says generally that one who violated an aseh and repented is forgiven immediately. The Rambam adds the decisive qualification “she-ein bah kareis,” excluding such positive commandments as milah and the Korban Pesach, whose neglect carries kareis. The Minchas Chinuch likewise places an aseh carrying kareis within the more severe atonement category. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the Rambam’s wording as substantive, not incidental: the objective punishment attached to the neglected command determines its seder ha-kapparah. Compare the preceding se’ifim, where immediate mechilah is distinguished from the further stages of kapparah, ritzui, and doron.דְּכָל הַפָּרָשָׁה שֶׁבְּיִרְמְיָה ג׳ קָאֵי אַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שֶׁעָבְדוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם]
[for the entire chapter in Yirmeyah 3 addresses the idolatry they served, see there],
וּמַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ עֲשֵׂה בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּתוֹכָחָה שֶׁלֹּא הוֹכִיחוּ, אוֹ הֵיכִי דְּלֹא יָדְעוּ לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּלָאו אֶלָּא בַּעֲשֵׂה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

finding an aseh in idolatry either in the command of rebuke (tochechah) where they failed to admonish, or where they recognized idolatry through a positive command rather than a negative command, see there at length:774Yirmiyahu 3:6–22; Tosafos Yom HaKippurim to Yoma 85b–86a, s.v. Amar Rabbi Yehudah — the idolatry setting of “Return, wayward children”: The prophecy repeatedly describes worship “upon every high mountain,” “under every leafy tree,” and adultery “with stone and with wood”; the call “Shuvu banim shovavim, erpa meshuvoseichem” therefore arises in an explicit avodah-zarah context. Tosafos Yom HaKippurim asks how this verse can prove that an ordinary aseh is forgiven immediately and suggests either that the aseh was the failure to rebuke the idolaters, or that the sinner knew only a positive formulation of the prohibition. Rav Tzadok challenges both answers: the failure to rebuke has no kareis of its own, while ignorance of the lav does not remove the objective kareis and korban-chatas status of the act.
תָּמוּהַּ מְאוֹד, דְּאַעֲשֵׂה דְּתוֹכָחָה לֵיכָּא כָּרֵת, וְרַק הָעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה בְּכָרֵת וְלֹא מִי שֶׁאֵין מוֹכִיחַ
is exceedingly astonishing, for regarding the aseh of rebuke there is no excision, and only the one who actually worships idols incurs kares, not the one who omits rebuke!

וְאַף דְּנֶעֱנַשׁ מִטַּעַם עַרְבוּת כְּשֶׁלֹּא מִיחָה, הֲרֵי מְפוֹרָשׁ [בִּשְׁבוּעוֹת ל״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּגַם רְשָׁעִים דְּעָלְמָא שֶׁהָיָה בְּיָדָם לִמְחוֹת וְלֹא מִיחוּ אֵין נֶעֱנָשִׁים אֶלָּא בַּדִּין הַקַּל, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And although one is punished on grounds of communal responsibility (arevut) when failing to protest, it is explicit [in Shevuos 39b] that even wicked people who had the power to protest and did not are punished only under the lighter penalty, see there;775Shevuos 39b; Shabbos 54b–55a; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 6:7 — arvus, protest, and derivative punishment: Shevuos distinguishes the principal sinner from others who could have protested: in ordinary transgressions, the sinner receives his own judgment, wicked members of his family a severe derivative judgment, and other wicked people who failed to protest only the lighter judgment. Shabbos and the Rambam nevertheless teach that one able to rebuke who remains silent is “seized” for the other’s sin and may be punished severely. Rav Tzadok’s point is categorical: arvus can create real liability, but it does not make the non-protester the direct idolater or assign the non-protester the idolater’s kareis. This distinction also prepares the continuation in Se’if 37, where he returns to the deaths decreed for failure to protest in Shabbos 55a.

וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּיָדַע רַק בַּעֲשֵׂה, מִלְּבַד דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר כֵּיוָן דְּכָרֵת דִּידֵיהּ עַל הַלָּאו נֶאֱמַר וְלֹא עַל הָעֲשֵׂה, וְהוּא יָדַע מֵהַכָּרֵת אַף עַל גַּב דְּלֹא יָדַע מֵהַלָּאו, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּרֵת דִּידֵיהּ חָמוּר

and what he wrote that he knew only the aseh: besides the fact that his kares applies to the negative command and not to the positive, and if he knew of kares even while ignorant of the prohibition his kares is severe;
בְּלָאו הָכִי נַמֵּי הֲרֵי גַּם שׁוֹגֵג דְּחַיָּיבֵי כְּרִיתוֹת חַיָּיב חַטָּאת
regardless, an inadvertent violator of kares is obligated to bring a sin-offering (chatas)!
וְהַיְינוּ עִם הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי ״זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֵבָה״
And that is in conjunction with repentance, for otherwise "the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination";
וְרַק עוֹלָה דּוֹרוֹן, אֲבָל חַטָּאת לָאו דּוֹרוֹן, דְּאֵין לוֹ כַּפָּרָה בִּתְשׁוּבָה לְבַד, וַאֲפִילּוּ עִם יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים עַד שֶׁיָּבִיא חַטָּאת

and only an olah is a tribute-gift, whereas a chatas is not a gift, for he has no atonement through repentance alone, nor even with Yom Kippur, until he brings the chatas!776Vayikra 4:27–35; Mishnah Yoma 8:8; Rambam, Hilchos Shegagos 1:1 and Hilchos Teshuvah 1:1; Zevachim 7b — a chatas completes kapparah and is not merely a doron: An inadvertent violation of a lav whose intentional violation carries kareis obligates a chatas. The Rambam rules that the offering itself cannot atone without teshuvah and verbal confession; conversely, teshuvah and Yom Kippur do not cancel the outstanding korban obligation. This differs from an olah, which Zevachim describes as a gift brought after the basic pardon. Rav Tzadok uses that formal distinction as a test of the proposed reading: if the deed objectively belongs to the kareis/chatas class, knowing the kareis while being unaware of the lav cannot transform it into a light aseh that is forgiven immediately. This continues his distinction in Se’ifim 34–35 between essential kapparah and the additional doron of complete ritzui.
וְאִם כֵּן אֵיךְ אָמְרוּ עַל זֶה דְּמוֹחֲלִין מִיָּד, וּמִי עָדִיף יָדַע בְּהַכָּרֵת וַעֲשֵׂה וְשָׁגַג בְּלָאו מֵאִלּוּ שָׁגַג בַּכֹּל, דְּלֹא נִתְכַּפֵּר עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד:

And if so, how could they state regarding this that he is pardoned immediately? Is one who was conscious of kares and the aseh yet unaware of the negative command superior to one who erred regarding everything, who is not atoned through repentance alone?!

items.h: The theme: Failure to protest incurs heavenly death, yet atones through repentance alone. In Shabbos 55a, the righteous of Jerusalem were punished with death from Heaven because they failed to protest public sins ("begin at My sanctuary", Yechezkel 9:6). This positive commandment carries liability to death by Heaven, directly akin to the derivation of wasteful emission from Onan. We see that an omission of an aseh resulting in death by Heaven is pardoned through repentance alone. Furthermore, Onan's death occurred specifically because his act destroyed the mitzvah of procreation, whereas wasteful emission where procreation is not subverted does not carry statutory death.

p: וּמִיהוּ גּוּף דְּבָרָיו אֱמֶת דִּקְרָא בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה קָאֵי
However, the substance of his words is true, that the verse in Yirmeyah addresses idolatry;

וְעַיֵּין שָׁם [יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד א׳] סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״עָבַר עַל עֲשֵׂה״ הוּקְשָׁה לֵיהּ אֵיךְ מַיְיתֵי לַהּ הַאי קְרָא אַעֲשֵׂה וְשָׁם קָאֵי אַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, וְתֵירֵץ דְּקָאֵי אַאוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא הוֹכִיחוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and see there [Yoma 86a, end of s.v. avar al aseh] where it was difficult to him how the Gemara cites this verse for an aseh when it refers to idolatry, and he resolved that it refers to those who failed to rebuke, see there;777Tosafos Yom HaKippurim on Yoma 85b–86a, s.v. avar al aseh; Yirmiyahu 3:6–22 — the author’s first answer and Rav Tzadok’s reading of his retraction: The source verse for immediate forgiveness of an aseh, “Return, wayward children; I will heal your waywardness,” appears in a prophecy whose surrounding verses explicitly describe idolatry on the high places and under the leafy trees. Tosafos Yom HaKippurim therefore asks how a verse spoken in an avodah-zarah setting can prove the rule for an ordinary positive commandment. His first answer identifies the relevant aseh as the bystanders’ failure to rebuke the idolaters; his second treats the worshippers as people who knew the Divine command only through its positive formulation. As explained in the expanded notes to Se’if 36, Rav Tzadok rejects the second answer because ignorance of the lav does not remove the deed’s objective kareis and chatas classification. Here he observes that the later discussion returns to the first answer—failure to rebuke—and takes that as the author’s operative resolution. The conclusion that this constitutes a retraction is Rav Tzadok’s reading of the sequence; it is not an explicit statement by Tosafos Yom HaKippurim.
הִנֵּה הָדַר בֵּיהּ בְּעַצְמוֹ מִתֵּירוּץ ב׳ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וְתָפַס תֵּירוּץ א׳
behold, he himself retracted from the second resolution mentioned above and adopted the first resolution.
וְהַגַּם דְּמִזֶּה אֵין רְאָיָה לַעֲשֵׂה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ כָּרֵת וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לִדְאָתֵינַן עֲלַהּ נִרְאֶה שַׁפִּיר לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם
And although from this there is no proof for an aseh carrying kares, nevertheless for our subject matter it is very fitting to derive a lesson from there:
דְּהָרֵי מְבוֹאָר [בְּשַׁבָּת נ״ה עַמּוּד א׳] דְּנִגְזַר ״מִמִּקְדָּשִׁי תָּחֵלּוּ״ עַל שֶׁלֹּא מִיחוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם, הֲרֵי דְּנִתְחַיְּיבוּ מִיתָה לַשָּׁמַיִם עַל זֶה

for it is explained [in Shabbos 55a] that it was decreed: "begin at My sanctuary" (Yechezkel 9:6) against those who did not protest, see there, showing that they incurred death by Heaven for this!778Shabbos 54b–55a; Yechezkel 9:4–6; Rashi; Petach Einayim; Rambam, Hilchos De’os 6:7 — “From My sanctified ones shall you begin” and punishment for failing to protest: The Gemara describes righteous people in Yerushalayim who groaned over the public abominations and had fulfilled the Torah “from alef to tav,” yet did not protest. Middas HaDin argued that, although Hashem knew the sinners would not listen, the righteous themselves could not know that with certainty; the protective mark was therefore reversed, and “u-mi-mikdashi tacheilu” is read as “begin with My sanctified ones.” Rashi and the surrounding sugya frame their fault as the neglected obligation to protest, while the Rambam rules generally that one who can rebuke and remains silent is “seized” for the sinner’s wrongdoing. Petach Einayim records the difficulty especially relevant here: failure to fulfill the positive commandment of rebuke is not ordinarily listed as an offense carrying death, yet these righteous people died because of it. Rav Tzadok uses the episode as an actual instance of death decreed from Heaven for neglect of an aseh and argues that teshuvah alone can nevertheless address the aseh-category. His formulation should not be mistaken for a codified rule that every failure to rebuke carries a statutory misah bidei Shamayim; the Gemara recounts an exceptional communal judgment, and Rav Tzadok draws an analogy from the severity of its consequence.
וַהֲרֵי זֶה חַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם דּוּגְמַת מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דְּיָלְפִינַן מֵאוֹנָן
And behold, this represents liability to death at the hands of Heaven, directly analogous to wasteful emission derived from Onan;
וַחֲזֵינַן דְּגַם עֲשֵׂה דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה בִּידֵי שָׁמַיִם כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא, מַה שֶּׁרָאִינוּ מִי שֶׁנִּתְחַיְּיבוּ מִיתָה עַל זֶה, מְהַנֵּי לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה לְבַד
and we see that even for an aseh where we find individuals who incurred death by Heaven for it, repentance alone avails!
וְגַם בְּעִיקָּר דִּפְשִׁיטָא לְהוּ דְּכָל מוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה חַיָּיב מִיתָה אַף דְּבַגְּמָרָא אִיתָא סְתָם, צָרִיךְ יִשּׁוּב

Furthermore, regarding the basic premise taken for granted by commentators that anyone who emits seed wastefully is liable to death, even though in the Gemara it is stated categorically, this requires careful resolution:
כֵּיוָן דְּמֵאוֹנָן יָלְפִינַן לַהּ, וְשָׁם מְבוֹאָר בַּכָּתוּב דְּהָיָה שֶׁלֹּא לְהָקִים זֶרַע וּלְבַטֵּל מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה

since we derive it from Onan, and there it is explicit in Scripture that his motive was not to raise up seed and to nullify procreation,779Bereishis 38:8–10; Niddah 13a; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Bi’ah 21:18; Shulchan Aruch, Even HaEzer 23:1 — Onan as the source of the Gemara’s unqualified death-language: Rabbi Yochanan states without qualification that one who emits seed in vain is liable to death and proves it from Onan. The narrative, however, gives a particular motive: Onan repeatedly spilled the seed “lest he give seed to his brother,” directly frustrating Yehudah’s command to establish offspring for the deceased Er. The Rambam and Shulchan Aruch codify a broad prohibition against wasteful emission and stress its exceptional gravity, but they do not derive in these passages a separate formal death-penalty category for every circumstance. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes two questions: the prohibition and severity are general, while the literal death-liability inferred from Onan may depend on the additional element of deliberately defeating procreation. This proposed limitation is Rav Tzadok’s chiddush; Niddah itself applies Rabbi Yochanan’s statement in general language and does not articulate the qualification.

יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דַּוְוקָא בְּבִיטּוּל מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה, דִּמְצִינוּ עֹונֶשׁ זֶה גַּם בְּחִזְקִיָּה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וְגַם עֵר שֶׁמֵּת עַל חֵטְא זֶה אָמְרוּ [יְבָמוֹת ל״ד עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁרָצָה שֶׁלֹּא תִּתְעַבֵּר, עַיֵּין שָׁם, וּבִיטְּלוּ מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה

one can say it applies specifically to the subversion of procreation, which punishment we find likewise with Chizkiyahu as mentioned above; and Er too who died for this sin, they stated [Yevamos 34b] acted so that she would not become pregnant, see there, thus nullifying procreation;780Berachos 10a; Yevamos 34b; Bereishis 38:7–10; Machshavos Charutz 15:4 — Chizkiyahu, Er, and the common element of frustrating procreation: Yeshayah told Chizkiyahu that he would die because he had not married and engaged in peru u-revu; Chizkiyahu’s prophetic knowledge that unworthy children would emerge did not permit him to neglect the command. Yevamos explains that Onan prevented conception because the offspring would be attributed to his brother, while Er acted so that Tamar would not become pregnant and lose her beauty; “He slew him also” links their deaths to the same conduct. Rav Tzadok identifies the common denominator as the intentional diversion of the generative act away from establishing seed. This fits his broader presentation in Machshavos Charutz 15:4: peru u-revu is the first mitzvah given before Adam’s sin, Adam’s post-sin separation is associated there with the “sin of Er,” and the birth of Sheis represents return and repair—“the end is embedded in the beginning.” That parallel supplies conceptual background for his emphasis here on procreation as the root-purpose of the faculty. It does not independently prove his narrower halachic claim that literal death-liability applies only when peru u-revu is actually frustrated.
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁאֵין בָּטֵל מִפְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה, בָּזֶה אֵין לִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם דְּחַיָּיב מִיתָה כְּלָל
but where procreation is not being subverted, one cannot derive from there that he is liable to death at all.
וְאַף עַל גַּב דְּהַגְּמָרָא מַיְיתֵי לַהּ אַאוֹחֵז וּמַשְׁתִּין
And although the Gemara (Niddah 13a) applies this to one who improperly holds his organ while urinating,

מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן דְּעִיקַּר הָעָוֹן בִּכְלָלוֹ מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה, מַיְיתֵי לְעִנְיַן חֹמֶר הָעָוֹן, אַף דְּבָזֶה אִיכָּא חִיּוּב מִיתָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הָעָוֹן חָמוּר שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ גַּם חִיּוּב מִיתָה:

nevertheless, since the root of this iniquity is linked to procreation, it cited it to demonstrate the ultimate severity of the iniquity, showing that in its most extreme manifestation it incurs liability to death.781Niddah 13a; Rashi; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Bi’ah 21:18–19 — why the Gemara cites the death-statement regarding one who holds himself while urinating: The immediate sugya is not a husband refusing conception. It forbids a man from holding the organ while urinating because stimulation may lead to wasteful emission, and Rabbi Yochanan’s death-language from Onan is introduced to explain the extreme caution. Rashi reads the passage as demonstrating how grave the danger is, and the Rambam similarly places strict safeguards around conduct that can lead to emission. Rav Tzadok acknowledges that this context appears broader than actual nullification of peru u-revu. His answer is that Chazal may cite the most severe consequence found within the general class in order to establish the gravity of every instance, even when the particular case does not itself carry literal death-liability. Thus he is not reducing the prohibition; he is separating an aggadic statement of class-wide severity from the narrower formal question governing the order of kapparah in this siman. This distinction is his interpretive proposal and is not expressly stated by the Gemara or the Rambam.

items.h: The theme: The true meaning of the Zohar's statement that "repentance does not avail" for wasteful emission. It does not deny fundamental forgiveness, which would contradict the foundational principle of teshuvah and the Talmudic precedent of David and Bas Sheva. Rather, it refers to the supernal appeasement of the tribute-gift (doran): restoring the soul to the pristine heights of a lifelong guardian of the Covenant (shomer ha-bris) who never blemished his vitality. While teshuvah from love generally converts sins into merits (zechuyos), for this specific iniquity, the unique celestial elevation attained by Rashbi and his disciples remains closed to one who actively stained the Covenant, accessible exclusively to the wholly righteous.

p: וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים, כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהֵבִינוּ כּוּלָּם דְּדִבְרֵי הַזֹּוהַר דְּ״אֵין לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה״ הַיְינוּ לְגוּף מְחִילַת הֶעָוֹן וְהַכַּפָּרָה, וַדַּאי הוּא דָּבָר תָּמוּהַּ וְזָר, וְכָל מַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ בָּזֶה הֵם דְּבָרִים דְּחוּקִים וּרְחוֹקִים

And in any event, according to what commentators understood—that the Zohar's statement that "there is no repentance for him" applies to the essential pardon and atonement of the iniquity—it is certainly astonishing and strange, and everything written on this is forced and far-fetched;
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן כְּפִי פַּשְׁטוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן דְּאֵין לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה כְּלָל, דְּזֶה וַדַּאי דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר

and all the more so according to the literal wording that he has no repentance at all, which is certainly an impossibility!782Zohar I, Vayechi 219b; Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaKedushah 17:69, 85; Shaarei Kedushah II 8:8; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah ch. 4 — “there is no teshuvah” and the classic resolutions: The Zohar records R’ Yehudah’s severe formulation that every sin has teshuvah except this one, and that other sinners ultimately behold the Shechinah whereas this sinner does not. The statement was never understood uniformly as an absolute denial of return. Shaarei Kedushah records a textual tradition adding that repair is possible through an exceptionally powerful and constant teshuvah. Reishis Chochmah first asks the same basic question raised here—Menasheh and even the gravest sinners were accepted—and explains that ordinary teshuvah tata’ah is insufficient, while a more difficult teshuvah ila’ah, joined with Torah, humility, sustained crying, and complete repair, can reach above the damaged level. The Tanya cites that explanation explicitly: the Zohar cannot mean that the universal principle “nothing stands before teshuvah” has an exception; rather, lower teshuvah does not suffice and higher teshuvah is required. Rav Tzadok accepts the inviolability of essential teshuvah but proposes a different narrowing. In this se’if, “no teshuvah” does not refer to basic mechilah and kapparah at all. It refers to the final restoration of ritzui—to stand again in the innermost chambers as though the covenant had never been blemished, and even to transform the past into a positive source of ascent. This is Rav Tzadok’s own synthesis of the Zohar with the universal power of teshuvah; it should be distinguished from the Reishis Chochmah–Tanya explanation of teshuvah tata’ah and teshuvah ila’ah.
דַּהֲרֵי אִיסּוּר אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ וַדַּאי חָמוּר מִינֵּיהּ, וְכִמְבוֹאָר גַּם כֵּן בְּסֵפֶר חֲסִידִים הַמּוּבָא בְּחֶלְקַת מְחוֹקֵק וּבֵית שְׁמוּאֵל וְנִזְכַּר לְעֵיל

For behold, the prohibition of a married woman is certainly more severe than it, as explained likewise in Sefer Chassidim cited in the Chelkas Mechokeik and Beis Shmuel and mentioned above;783Sefer Chasidim §176; Chelkas Mechokek, Even HaEzer 23:1; Beis Shmuel 23:1 — the comparison with a married woman or a niddah: Sefer Chasidim rules that when a person fears an imminent fall into relations with a married woman or with a niddah, it is better to avoid that graver transgression even through the lesser wrongdoing discussed here, followed by a demanding penitential regimen. Chelkas Mechokek quotes the ruling verbatim. Beis Shmuel uses it to qualify the Shulchan Aruch’s statement that this sin is “more severe than all transgressions”: that phrase cannot be a literal halachic ranking above adultery or niddah, because Sefer Chasidim itself prefers it when those are the only alternatives. The passage does not make the lesser act permissible in an ordinary situation and does not diminish its gravity; it establishes the hierarchy when two wrongs directly conflict. Rav Tzadok employs the comparison as a kal vachomer about teshuvah: if the objectively graver category of eshes ish is not excluded from repentance, the Zohar’s phrase cannot mean that the essential forgiveness of this lesser category is metaphysically impossible. His conclusion depends on separating the Zohar’s language of extraordinary spiritual damage from the formal halachic ranking of prohibitions.

וּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּדָוִד בְּבַת שֶׁבַע שֶׁהָיָה בְּאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ אָמְרוּ [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה ד׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה רָאוּי לְכָךְ אֶלָּא לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁאִם חָטָא יָחִיד וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and regarding the incident of David with Bas Sheva, which involved a married woman, they stated [in Avodah Zarah 4b] that he was not fit for that deed save to teach the power of teshuvah, that if an individual sinned they say to him: go to the individual [David], see there;
הֲרֵי דְּגַם לְאֵשֶׁת אִישׁ הֶחָמוּר מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן לָזֶה

showing that even for the severe sin of a married woman repentance avails, and all the more so for this sin!784Avodah Zarah 4b; Shabbos 56a; Sanhedrin 107a; II Shmuel 11–12 — David and Batsheva as the paradigm of teshuvah for an individual: R’ Yochanan teaches in the name of Rashbi that David was not naturally suited to the episode with Batsheva—“my heart is hollow within me”—but the fall was allowed so that an individual sinner would have a public model of return: “If an individual sinned, they say to him, go to the individual,” namely David. The broader Chazal picture is deliberately complex. Shabbos states that “whoever says David sinned is mistaken” and explains that soldiers in David’s army wrote bills of divorce to their wives; the same sugya nevertheless speaks of what David sought to do and identifies a remaining fault in the matter of Uriyah. Sanhedrin describes David’s confession, suffering, and request that his forgiveness become known. Rav Tzadok is not resolving every legal detail of Batsheva’s marital status. He invokes the episode in the form in which Scripture and the teshuvah-sugya present it: the paradigmatic, publicly perceived sexual failure from which David returned and through which the road of teshuvah was taught to every individual. Thus, even where Chazal qualify the technical category of eshes ish, the episode remains a stronger proof against reading the Zohar as barring essential forgiveness. Rav Tzadok’s point is the revealed power of teshuvah in the gravest apparent case, not a new ruling on David’s halachic liability.
אֲבָל כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל בַּתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁסִּידְּרוּ רוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ״י, דְּאֵינָם לְעַכֵּב הַכַּפָּרָה רַק לְדוֹרוֹן, וְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

But according to what I wrote above regarding the regimens of repentance arranged by the Rokeach and the Ari—that they do not withhold essential atonement but serve as a tribute-gift (doran), each according to his mystical rung as mentioned above:

נִרְאֶה לִי פָּשׁוּט דְּגַם הַזֹּוהַר כַּוָּונָתוֹ לְעִנְיַן הָרִיצּוּי דְּדוֹרוֹן, שֶׁיִּתְרַצֶּה לְגַמְרֵי לַעֲלוֹת וְלֵירָאוֹת פְּנֵי ה׳ בְּמַדְרֵיגוֹת עֶלְיוֹנוֹת כְּצַדִּיק גָּמוּר שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית שֶׁלֹּא חָטָא מֵעוֹלָם

it seems plain to me that the Zohar's intent likewise addresses the appeasement of the tribute-gift: to be completely received in favor so as to ascend and behold the face of Hashem in the highest rungs like a consummate tzaddik, a guardian of the Covenant who never sinned in his life.785Zevachim 7b; Tanya, Iggeres HaTeshuvah chs. 1 and 4; Rokeach, Hilchos Teshuvah — kapparah, cleansing, and the later “gift” of ritzui: Zevachim distinguishes the advocate who first secures reconciliation from the gift presented afterward: an olah is a doron only after the advocate has appeased the king. Iggeres HaTeshuvah uses this distinction to explain the fasts and mortifications recorded by the Rokeach and other sifrei mussar. The essence of teshuvah is abandonment of sin, regret, confession, and a true return to Hashem; the additional practices belong to gmar hakapparah, cleansing, and restored favor after the basic return. Rav Tzadok has developed the same structure throughout the preceding se’ifim, but with a sharper relational vocabulary. Mechilah removes the barrier created by guilt; the doron produces complete ritzui, renewed closeness, and permission to enter the King’s inner chambers. Therefore, when he says that the Rokeach’s and Arizal’s programs are “not to prevent kapparah, only for a gift,” he is not dismissing them as optional decoration. They address a real second stage, but that stage is not a prerequisite for the sinner to be accepted as a baal teshuvah. His reading of the Zohar in this se’if is built on that distinction: “no teshuvah” cannot negate the first stage; it limits the highest form of the second—full restoration to the intimacy and spiritual access of one whose covenant was never damaged.
וּבְכָל הָעֲבֵירוֹת הוּא כֵּן, דִּבִתְשׁוּבָה גְּמוּרָה מֵאַהֲבָה זְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ כִּזְכֻיּוֹת וַעֲלֵיהֶם חָיֹה יִחְיֶה
And across all other transgressions this is so: through complete repentance from love, intentional sins are transformed into merits (zechuyos) and upon them he shall live (Yechezkel 18:21);

וְהַיְינוּ אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה הָרְאוּיָה וְהַבָּאַת הַדּוֹרוֹן, אַחַר כָּךְ חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת מְקוֹרָב וּבֶן בַּיִת כְּבַתְּחִלָּה בְּעֹוז יוֹתֵר, מֵאַחַר שֶׁגַּם הָעֲבֵירוֹת עוֹלִים לְחֶשְׁבּוֹן מִצְוֹת

meaning that after proper repentance and the presentation of the tribute-gift, he returns to be intimate and an inhabitant of the Palace as at the beginning with even greater strength, since the sins themselves ascend into the tally of mitzvos.786Yoma 86b; Yechezkel 33:19; Sefer HaIkkarim IV:25; Kli Yakar on Bereishis 25:1 — teshuvah from love and willful sins becoming merits: Reish Lakish gives two descriptions of the transformed past: through one form of teshuvah, deliberate sins become like inadvertent errors; through teshuvah from love, they become actual merits, based on “when the wicked turns from his wickedness and does justice and righteousness, by them he shall live.” The Gemara resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing teshuvah from fear from teshuvah from love. Sefer HaIkkarim asks why repentance should do more than erase guilt and explains that the sinner’s powerful love, effort, and reversal can itself generate new merit. Kli Yakar offers the image of the foul-smelling chelbenah becoming part of the fragrant ketores: the formerly negative element is integrated into Divine service. Rav Tzadok reads “by them he shall live” strongly—the very transgressions become a source of life because the distance, longing, and return produce a closeness unavailable in the same form beforehand. His phrase “a member of the household” expresses the completed ritzui that follows the fitting teshuvah and doron. He then identifies the Zohar’s limitation precisely here: not that the sinner remains unforgiven, but that this particular blemish cannot be converted into the same affirmative spiritual capital or restore the exact unblemished access of the complete covenant-guardian.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ בַּזֹּוהַר דִּבַעֲבֵירָה זוֹ לָא מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבָה לִהְיוֹת כִּזְכֻיּוֹת וּכְמִקֶּדֶם לְגַמְרֵי אֲפִילּוּ אַחַר כָּל הַדּוֹרוֹנוֹת
And regarding this the Zohar stated that in this iniquity repentance does not avail to transform sins into merits and restore him completely as before, even after all tribute-gifts!
וְהָרוֹקֵחַ וְהָאֲרִ״י דִּבְּרוּ כְּפִי מַדְרֵגָתָם, מְהַנֵּי תְּשׁוּבַת כָּל אֶחָד לְאוֹתָהּ מַדְרֵיגָה שֶׁהִשִּׂיג שֶׁיּוֹעִיל

And the Rokeach and the Ari spoke according to their rungs, each master’s repentance availing for that specific mystical plane which he attained as efficacious;787Tzidkas HaTzadik §134; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:44; see the expanded PaRDeS–ABiYA note to Se’if 34 — “each according to his level” in Rav Tzadok’s own system: Rav Tzadok explains in Tzidkas HaTzadik that there is no fixed ceiling to a person’s ascent and therefore no single final measure of teshuvah. A sin may be genuinely repaired relative to a lower level; when the person rises, the same past reappears as a deficiency measured against the newly attained light, requiring a deeper return. Dover Tzedek supplies the metaphysical background: Hashem did not create unrelated systems; the same ordered structure descends through Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, becoming progressively more revealed and embodied. Human mind, heart, soul-powers, and action mirror those worlds. Se’if 34 applied that principle to the four modes of Torah, PaRDeS, and to the tikkunim revealed in different generations. Accordingly, Rav Tzadok’s statement that the Rokeach and the Arizal spoke “according to their level” does not mean that one was mistaken or that their prescribed teshuvah was ineffective. Each tikkun was fully meaningful within the spiritual chamber opened to that sage and generation. Rashbi’s disclosure describes a still higher threshold. At that level, an earlier repair can remain valid for mechilah and for the ritzui then attainable, yet still be insufficient to recreate the completely unblemished standing demanded by the higher chamber.
וּמַעֲלַת רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי בְּהַשָּׂגָתוֹ וּמַה שֶּׁגִּילָּה לְחַבְרַיָּא שֶׁלּוֹ גְּבוֹהָה מִכּוּלָּם
while the stature of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai in his attainment and what he revealed to his holy fellowship is higher than all of them,
כִּידוּעַ מִזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ מַה שֶּׁאָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ, וְכֵן עַל כָּל בְּנֵי דּוֹרוֹ שֶׁאָמַר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה כְּדָרָא דָּא וְשֶׁלֹּא יִתְגַּלֶּה עוֹד כֵּן עַד בִּיאַת מָשִׁיחַ

as is known from the Holy Zohar what he stated concerning himself, and likewise concerning all the members of his generation: that there will never be another generation like this, nor will such secrets be revealed again until the coming of the Messiah;788Zohar III, Pinchas 241b; Tikkunei Zohar 42a; Sukkah 45b — Rashbi’s generation and secrets reserved until Mashiach: In the Zohar’s account, R’ Abba declares that even had the Torah been given only in the form “here is Bar Yochai—My Torah and My secrets,” that would have sufficed for the world. He laments Rashbi’s eventual departure and says that until King Mashiach arrives there will not be another generation like the one in which R’ Shimon dwells. Tikkunei Zohar similarly records a disclosure described as something not destined to be revealed again until the days of Mashiach. These passages provide the background for Rav Tzadok’s claim that Rashbi and his circle spoke from a level of attainment above the ordinary tikkunim available in earlier or later generations. Sukkah’s description of Rashbi and his son as the rare bnei aliyah who can enter to receive the Shechinah without permission clarifies Rav Tzadok’s “member of the household” metaphor. The sources do not themselves formulate Rav Tzadok’s precise distinction between forgiveness and restoration of rank. That is his synthesis: the Zohar’s severe phrase measures the possibility of returning to Rashbi’s exceptional, quasi-Messianic degree of direct access, not the possibility of repentance, forgiveness, or a holy life at the level genuinely available to the penitent.
וּכְפִי הַשָּׂגַת מַדְרֵיגָתָם אָמְרוּ שֶׁבְּחֵטְא זֶה אֵין תְּשׁוּבָה מוֹעִיל שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵגָה גְּבוֹהָה כָּזוֹ
and according to the height of their spiritual attainment, they stated that for this sin repentance cannot avail to reach so exalted a station,
שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְהַגִּיעַ לָזֶה אֶלָּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם מֵעוֹלָם כְּלָל:
which none can attain save a consummate tzaddik, a guardian of the Covenant who never blemished his holiness in any way.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים מ׳–מ״ג

The theme: The unique metaphysical stature of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai, his son Rabbi Elazar, King Chizkiyahu, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi. In their generations, the rainbow never appeared, for their consummate purity of the Covenant (sheleimus kedushas ha-bris) shielded the world from the decree of the Flood. Chizkiyahu was worthy of being Mashiach—attaining eternal life (chayei olam)—which is accessible only to those entirely free from the instigation of the Primordial Serpent (ityo shel nachash). Like Yaakov Avinu who never experienced a nocturnal emission and "did not die," and Eliyahu the Angel of the Covenant who lives forever, Rashbi and his son were the supreme "men of ascent" (bnei aliyah) who enter the Divine Presence without an intermediary escort.

p: וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וַחֲבֵירָיו הָיוּ יְחִידִים בְּדָבָר זֶה, שֶׁעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ל״ה]: ״לְדֹרֹת״ חָסֵר, פְּרָט לְדוֹרוֹ שֶׁל חִזְקִיָּה וְשֶׁל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי

And Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai and his companions were unique in this matter, wherefore they said [in Bereishis Rabbah 35:2]: "'for generations' [l'doros, Bereishis 9:12] is written defectively [lacking the letters vav], excluding the generation of Chizkiyahu and that of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai,
שֶׁלֹּא הָיוּ צְרִיכִין לְאוֹת קֶשֶׁת נֶגֶד עֹונֶשׁ מַבּוּל הַבָּא עַל פְּגַם הַבְּרִית
who did not require the sign of the rainbow against the punishment of the Flood which comes for the blemish of the Covenant.
וְעַל חִזְקִיָּה אָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין צ״ד עַמּוּד א׳] דְּבִקֵּשׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַעֲשׂוֹתוֹ מָשִׁיחַ

And regarding Chizkiyahu they stated [in Sanhedrin 94a] that the Holy One, blessed be He, sought to make him Mashiach,789Bereishis Rabbah 35:2; Ramban on Bereishis 9:12–16; Etz Yosef ad loc.; see also Kesubos 77b — the deficient spelling of “l’doros” and generations that required no rainbow: The Torah calls the rainbow the sign of the covenant that the world will never again be destroyed by a Flood. Bereishis Rabbah reads the deficient spelling of l’doros as excluding two generations that did not require this sign. One opinion names the generations of Chizkiyahu and the Anshei Knesses HaGedolah; R’ Chizkiyah substitutes the generation of Rashbi for the latter. Etz Yosef notes that the continuation concerning Rashbi and R’ Yehoshua ben Levi supports the tradition that no rainbow appeared in Rashbi’s generation. The rainbow is therefore not itself the punishment; it is the protective covenantal sign displayed when the generation otherwise requires protection from a Flood. Rav Tzadok adds a further thematic identification: because the Flood is associated with the corruption of “all flesh,” the absence of the sign reflects a generation whose tzaddikim supplied an exceptional communal protection rooted in kedushas habris. That final causal formulation is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis; the Midrash itself states the absence of the rainbow and the merit of those generations, but does not explicitly define their merit as perfection of the covenant.

וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, דְּעַל מָשִׁיחַ נֶאֱמַר: ״חַיִּים שָׁאַל מִמְּךָ נָתַתָּה לּוֹ וְגוֹמֵר״ (תְּהִלִּים כ״א:ה׳), כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוּכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳]: ״אֵינוֹ מְבַקֵּשׁ אֶלָּא חַיִּים וְגוֹמֵר״

meaning that he would merit eternal life, for regarding Mashiach it is said: 'He asked life of You, You gave it to him, even length of days forever and ever' (Tehillim 21:5), as they said [in Sukkah 52a]: 'he asks for nothing but life, etc.';790Sanhedrin 94a; Yeshayahu 9:6; Rashi ad loc.; Ben Yehoyada on Sanhedrin 94a — Chizkiyahu as a potential Mashiach: Chazal expound the closed mem in l’marbeh hamisrah: the Holy One sought to make Chizkiyahu the Mashiach and Sancheriv the final Gog and Magog. Middas HaDin objected that David had sung many songs, whereas Chizkiyahu had not sung after his miracles; the opportunity therefore remained unrealized. Rashi cites this derashah in his commentary to Yeshayahu. Ben Yehoyada explains that the statement may mean that Chizkiyahu was to receive qualities, victories, and revelations resembling those of the final Mashiach, even if the complete final redemption was not yet actualized. Rav Tzadok uses the very possibility as evidence of Chizkiyahu’s extraordinary wholeness. His next step—that this messianic suitability reflects perfected kedushas habris and a capacity for eternal life—is an interpretive link developed here, not the explicit reason supplied by Sanhedrin, which focuses on Chizkiyahu’s failure to sing.791Sukkah 52a; Tehillim 21:5 — Mashiach ben David asks only for life: The Gemara contrasts Mashiach ben Yosef, who is slain, with Mashiach ben David. When Hashem invites Mashiach ben David to request anything, he asks only for life. Hashem answers that David had already prophesied this request and its fulfillment: “Life he asked of You; You gave it to him, length of days for ever and ever.” The immediate context is the survival of Mashiach ben David after he sees the death of Mashiach ben Yosef. Rav Tzadok reads the verse’s continuation, “for ever and ever,” in its strongest eschatological sense: the completed Mashiach-state includes victory over ordinary mortality. He then connects that life to complete removal of the bodily root of the serpent. The Gemara supplies the promise of life; the specific dependence on shleimus kedushas habris is Rav Tzadok’s explanatory framework.
וְדָבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שְׁלֵימוּת קְדוּשַׁת הַבְּרִית
and this matter is impossible except through the consummate perfection of the holiness of the Covenant,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל [רֵישׁ סִימָן ו׳] בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁמֵּתוּ בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, דְּזֶהוּ עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֲדַיִין שׁוֹרֶשׁ תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית בַּלֵּב בְּעִנְיָן זֶה

and as I wrote above [start of Siman 6] regarding those who died solely through the instigation of the Primordial Serpent (ityo shel nachash), for that counsel of the Serpent is that there still remains a root of bodily lust in the heart regarding this matter;792Bava Basra 17a; Shabbos 55b; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 6 — those who died only through the serpent and Rav Tzadok’s “root of bodily desire”: Bava Basra lists four exceptionally righteous people—Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav—who died only because of the primordial serpent’s counsel or contamination, not because of personal sin. The same tradition appears in Shabbos. In that sugya, “the serpent’s counsel” explains why death remained in the world even for a person whose own deeds did not warrant it. Earlier in Siman 6, Rav Tzadok gives the phrase a more inward application: the universal mortality introduced by Adam’s sin corresponds to a still-unrectified root of bodily desire, especially in the sphere of the covenant. A person can therefore be free of actual transgression and still remain subject to death because the root inherited from the serpent has not been totally transformed. This psychological-kabbalistic identification is Rav Tzadok’s own development of the Gemara. It allows him here to distinguish the four who were personally sinless yet mortal from Yaakov, Eliyahu, Rashbi, and the other figures whom he associates with a more complete uprooting of that root.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּהָיָה נָקִי מִזֶּה וְלֹא רָאָה קֶרִי מֵעוֹלָם, דִּרְאוּבֵן ״רֵאשִׁית אוֹנוֹ״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית מ״ט:ג׳), לֹא מֵת

whereas Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who was pure from this and never experienced a seminal emission in his life, Reuven being 'the first of his strength' (Bereishis 49:3), did not die (Ta'anis 5b);
וְכֵן אֵלִיָּהוּ מַלְאַךְ הַבְּרִית חַי לְעוֹלָם

and likewise Eliyahu, the Angel of the Covenant, lives forever.793Bereishis 49:3 with Rashi and Bereishis Rabbah 98:4; Taanis 5b; II Melachim 2:11; Malachi 3:1; Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer ch. 29 — Yaakov and Eliyahu: On “Reuven…reishis oni,” Rashi, following Bereishis Rabbah, explains that Reuven came from Yaakov’s first seminal drop and that Yaakov had never experienced a seminal emission beforehand. Taanis teaches, “Yaakov Avinu did not die,” deriving it from the comparison between Yaakov and his living descendants; the Gemara acknowledges the embalming and burial but defines his continuing life on a deeper plane. Eliyahu ascended in a whirlwind rather than undergoing an ordinary death and is identified in the prophetic and midrashic tradition with the “angel of the covenant,” who attends the covenant of circumcision and will herald redemption. Rav Tzadok combines these distinct traditions into a single causal pattern: purity of the covenant corresponds to an enduring form of life. None of the cited texts explicitly states the full equation “never seeing keri caused Yaakov not to die,” nor do they prove that Eliyahu’s ascent occurred because he was the angel of the covenant. That synthesis belongs to Rav Tzadok and continues his argument from Siman 6 that death persists while the serpent’s bodily root persists.
וְרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי דְּגַם כֵּן לֹא נִרְאֶה הַקֶּשֶׁת בְּיָמָיו כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּכְתוּבּוֹת ע״ז עַמּוּד ב׳], נִכְנַס חַי לְגַן עֵדֶן
And Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, in whose days the rainbow was likewise never seen as they said [in Kesubos 77b], entered alive into Gan Eden;

וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי שָׁם שְׁאָלוֹ עַל זֶה, דְּלוּלֵי זֶה לֹא הָיָה יָכוֹל לִיכָּנֵס לִמְקוֹמוֹ וּמְחִיצָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי וּלְהַשִּׂיג מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ, וְגַם לֹא הָיָה אֵלִיָּהוּ הַמַּכְרִיז לְפָנָיו ״פַּנּוּ מָקוֹם״

and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai questioned him there concerning this, for were it not so, he would not have been able to enter into the station and partition of Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai to attain his rung, nor would Eliyahu have proclaimed before him: 'Make way!';794Kesubos 77b; Bereishis Rabbah 35:2; Pischei Einayim and Haflaah on Kesubos 77b — R’ Yehoshua ben Levi, Gan Eden, and the rainbow test: R’ Yehoshua ben Levi uniquely attached himself to sufferers from ra’atan while learning Torah, trusting Torah’s protection. At his death the Angel of Death was commanded to fulfill his wishes; R’ Yehoshua saw his place in Gan Eden, leaped inside, and remained there because he had never sought release from an oath. Eliyahu proclaimed before him, “Make way for the son of Levi.” He then met Rashbi, who asked whether a rainbow had appeared in his days. Although no rainbow had actually appeared, R’ Yehoshua answered yes because he did not wish to claim merit for himself. Bereishis Rabbah preserves a related version in which Eliyahu brings R’ Yehoshua to Rashbi and the rainbow determines whether he is worthy to behold Rashbi. Pischei Einayim discusses the relationship between the versions and the possibility that a rainbow might be seen in a distant region while the tzaddik’s own place remained protected; Haflaah analyzes why the test was necessary. Rav Tzadok reads the episode as a test of spiritual compatibility: entry into Rashbi’s section required the same order of world-protecting purity. The Gemara itself presents righteousness, humility, Torah, and the absent rainbow; the particular identification with kedushas habris is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.

וְרַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי נִסְתַּלֵּק בְּמִלַּת ״חַיִּים עַד הָעוֹלָם״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹף הָאִידְרָא זוּטָא דְּהַאֲזִינוּ], וּדְשָׁמְעוּ קוֹל ״אֹרֶךְ יָמִים וְגוֹמֵר וְחַיִּים שָׁאַל וְגוֹמֵר״

and Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai departed this world with the word 'life forevermore' (chayim ad ha-olam), as they related [at the end of the Idra Zuta, Ha'azinu, Zohar III, 296b], and a heavenly voice was heard declaring: 'Length of days... he asked life of You...';795Zohar, Idra Zuta 42:195 and 43; Tehillim 133:3; Mishlei 3:2; Tehillim 21:5 — Rashbi’s final word, the surrounding fire, and the voices of life: Immediately before the account of Rashbi’s passing, the Idra explains the flow of blessing into the Kodesh HaKodashim through the verse “for there Hashem commanded the blessing—life for evermore.” R’ Abba then records that the holy lamp did not finish saying the word chayim before his speech ceased. The room was filled with overpowering light and fire; after the fire departed, Rashbi was seen lying on his right side with a smiling face. R’ Abba heard one voice reciting “length of days and years of life” and another “life he asked of You.” The Zohar nevertheless also says that Rashbi “departed from the world” and describes his burial. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the scene mystically rather than as a denial of the visible passing: Rashbi’s departure was sealed inside the word chayim and manifested a share in the enduring life promised to Mashiach and attributed to Yaakov. The exact sequence also clarifies Rav Tzadok’s phrase “with the word life for evermore”: the preceding discourse contained the full verse, while Rashbi’s audible speech ceased at chayim.
וְהַיְינוּ דְּזָכָה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה בּוֹ מָשִׁיחַ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל, וּכְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּלֹא מֵת רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
meaning that he attained the eternal life that Mashiach will merit as mentioned above, and like Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who did not die except to outward appearances in this world;
וְכֵן רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בְּנוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא פ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּנְפַק קָלָא מֵעִילִּיתֵיהּ
and so too Rabbi Elazar his son, as they related [in Bava Metzia 84b] that a voice went forth from his upper attic;
וְכֵן נִתְבָּאֵר לְעֵיל [סוֹף סִימָן ו׳] בְּרַבִּי וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי שָׁם מִגְּמָרָא דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא שָׁם

and so it was explained above [end of Siman 6] regarding Rebbe, that Rabbi Elazar ben Rabbi Shimon was greater than he, as I wrote there from the Gemara in Bava Metzia there.796Bava Metzia 84b; Takanas HaShavin, end of Siman 6 — R’ Elazar b’Rashbi’s preserved body and the voice from his attic: Before his death R’ Elazar b’Rashbi instructed his wife not to surrender him immediately for burial. His body remained in the attic for many years without decay; when a hair was pulled, blood appeared, and litigants would stand at the doorway and hear a voice from the attic declaring who was liable and who was innocent. The Gemara later describes his burial and the honor shown to him. The “voice” in Rav Tzadok’s wording is thus not merely an undefined heavenly echo: it belongs to the narrative of a body that continued to function as a locus of judgment after death. Earlier, at the end of Siman 6, Rav Tzadok compares this preservation with the traditions about Rebbi’s continuing return to his home, while arguing that R’ Elazar’s level was still greater. He treats incorruptibility and continued spiritual activity as signs that the flesh itself had been refined by kedushas habris. The Gemara reports the wonders; the placement of R’ Elazar within Rav Tzadok’s graded theory of eternal life is Rav Tzadok’s own reading.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי [סוּכָּה מ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה מוּעָטִים, וְאִם שְׁנַיִם הֵן אֲנִי וּבְנִי הֵן״
And therefore Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai stated [Sukkah 45b]: "I have seen the men of ascent (bnei aliyah), and they are few... and if they are two, they are myself and my son";
וּמַסִּיק שָׁם דְּהֵם דְּעָיְילֵי בְּלָא בַּר לְקַבֵּל פְּנֵי שְׁכִינָה, וּמִשּׁוּם הָכִי נִקְרָאִים ״בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה״ שֶׁהֵם כִּבְנֵי בַּיִת לִיכָּנֵס כִּרְצוֹנָם:

and the Gemara concludes there that they are those who enter without permission to receive the Divine Countenance, and for this reason they are called "men of ascent," for they are like members of the royal household, entering at will.797Sukkah 45b; Rashi ad loc.; see the Rashbi note to Se’if 38 — “bnei aliyah” and entering without permission: Rashbi says that he has seen the bnei aliyah and they are few; if there are only two, they are Rashbi and his son. The Gemara distinguishes between those who enter to behold the Divine Presence with permission and the still rarer figures who enter without permission. Rashi explains bnei aliyah as those whose spiritual ascent brings them before the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok turns the legal image of entry “without permission” into the relational image used throughout these se’ifim: they are bnei bayis, members of the King’s household, whose complete ritzui allows them to enter at will. This is the highest degree of the “King brought me into His chambers” discussed in Se’if 34. The Gemara establishes Rashbi and R’ Elazar’s exceptional access; Rav Tzadok connects that access to an entirely unblemished covenant and therefore to the life-state described in this se’if. The expanded Rashbi note in Se’if 38 supplies the broader Zoharic background for his claim that Rashbi’s generation stood at a uniquely elevated, quasi-Messianic level.

items.h: The theme: Adam HaRishon's inability to eradicate the root of the Serpent's instigation. Before the sin, Adam dwelt in Gan Eden and could partake of the Tree of Life to live forever; after the sin, he was banished lest he put forth his hand, for repentance could not annul the physical decree of mortality. During the 130 years of fasting and separation from his wife (Eruvin 18b), Adam was termed a "great pietist" (chassid gadol) who guarded against every waking lustful thought (hinnazeh mi-kol shemetz hirhur). Nevertheless, because his bodily heart had not yet been purified from the physical inclination, involuntary nocturnal emissions (keri l'onso) occurred, inadvertently generating spirits, demons, and lilin (ruchin v'shedin v'lilin).

p: וְדָבָר זֶה זוֹכֶה רַק מִי שֶׁלֹּא טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא מֵעוֹלָם, כְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא שֶׁהָיָה מִשְׁכָּנוֹ בְּגַן עֵדֶן
And this supreme state is merited only by one who never tasted the taste of sin in his life, like Adam HaRishon prior to the sin, whose dwelling was in Gan Eden,
וְשָׁם הָיָה יָכוֹל לֶאֱכוֹל שֶׁהָיָה מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וָחַי לְעוֹלָם
and there he was able to eat of the Tree of Life and live forever;

וְאַחַר הַחֵטְא גּוֹרַשׁ מִשָּׁם: ״פֶּן יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וְגוֹמֵר״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג:כב), דְּעַל זֶה לֹא הוֹעִיל לוֹ תְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁיּוּכַל לְתַקֵּן הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ וּלְבַטֵּל גְּזֵירַת הַמִּיתָה, עַיֵּין [לְעֵיל סִימָן ג׳]

but after the sin he was banished from there: "lest he put forth his hand, etc." (Bereishis 3:22), for regarding this repentance did not avail him to rectify the root of the Serpent's instigation and abolish the decree of death, see [above, Siman 3].798Bereishis 2:8–9; 3:22–24; Ramban on Bereishis 3:22 — Gan Eden, the Tree of Life, and immortality: The Torah first places Adam in Gan Eden, with the Tree of Life in the garden. After the sin, Hashem declares that Adam might take from that tree, eat, and “live forever,” and therefore banishes him and guards the path to it. Ramban explains that the Tree of Life was created to confer enduring life; eating from it after the sin would have annulled, or at least suspended, the newly imposed decree of death. Before the sin Adam did not need to eat from it, because he lived in obedient harmony with the Divine command. Rav Tzadok reads this narrative as more than a physical restriction: Gan Eden and access to the Tree of Life represent the state of a person who has never internalized sin. Once the taste of sin entered human experience, ordinary teshuvah could restore obedience and forgiveness, but not automatically recreate the untouched pre-sin condition. The verses and Ramban establish the connection between the tree and life; the formulation that only one who never tasted sin fully possesses this level is Rav Tzadok’s spiritual application.799Bava Basra 17a; Shabbos 55b; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 3; Machshavot Charutz 20:13 — teshuvah and the remaining root of the serpent: Chazal identify exceptionally righteous people who died only through “the counsel of the serpent,” meaning that mortality introduced by Adam’s sin remained even where no personal transgression required death. Rav Tzadok uses that tradition to distinguish forgiveness of an act from total repair of the human condition. In Machshavot Charutz he writes that Adam was a “great chasid” and began teshuvah during his 130 years of fasting, yet did not attain the complete teshuvah later revealed through David and ultimately Mashiach, who restores access to the Tree of Life. Thus “teshuvah did not avail him” here does not mean that Adam’s repentance was rejected. It means that his repentance did not yet uproot the deepest bodily residue of the serpent or reverse the universal decree of death. This is the same distinction developed earlier in Takanas HaShavin: kapparah and genuine spiritual repair may be present while a still deeper root awaits transformation.

וְגַם בְּאוֹתָן ק״ל שָׁנָה שֶׁיָּשַׁב בְּתַעֲנִית לָשׁוּב מֵחֶטְאוֹ, הוֹלִיד רוּחִין, שֵׁדִין וְלִילִין מִשִּׁכְבַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסֵיהּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּעֵירוּבִין י״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]
