And even during those 130 years that he sat in fasting to repent from his sin, he generated spirits, demons, and lilin from inadvertent seminal emissions that he experienced involuntarily, as they said [in Eruvin 18b],
וְקָרוּ לֵיהּ שָׁם ״חָסִיד גָּדוֹל״

and they designated him there "a great pietist";800Eruvin 18b:10–12; Bereishis 5:3 — Adam’s 130 years, “a great chasid,” and involuntary emissions: R’ Yirmeyah ben Elazar teaches that during the 130 years in which Adam was under ban he produced “spirits, demons, and liliths,” deriving this from the verse that only at age 130 did Adam father a son “in his likeness and image.” The Gemara challenges this from R’ Meir’s teaching that Adam was a great chasid: after seeing that death had been decreed through him, he fasted, separated from his wife, and wore fig garments for 130 years. The Gemara resolves the contradiction: the destructive beings came from semen “that he saw involuntarily.” The full passage is essential to Rav Tzadok’s argument. Adam’s ascetic teshuvah was real and earned the designation “great chasid,” yet involuntary bodily emission still occurred. Rav Tzadok therefore understands the event as evidence of a residue beneath conscious thought and choice. The Gemara explicitly calls the emission involuntary; the conclusion that it reveals an unpurified root of bodily desire is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation.
אֶלָּא דַּאֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִטְהַר הַלֵּב מִתַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית שֶׁלֹּא לְהוֹצִיא בָּשָׂר, דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה בָּא לִידֵי טוּמְאָה בַּלַּיְלָה לְאוֹנְסוֹ
yet even the most pious of the pious whose heart has not yet been thoroughly purified from bodily lust to eliminate fleshly passion, through this comes to nocturnal impurity involuntarily;
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא לְאוֹנְסוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוֹלִיד בָּזֶה רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין וְהוֹסִיף כֹּחַ בְּסִטְרָא דִּמְסָאֲבוּ רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן

and although it was entirely involuntary, he nevertheless generated through this spirits, demons, and lilin, augmenting power to the realm of defilement, God protect us!801Machshavot Charutz 15:10 and 20:13; cf. Takanas HaShavin, Siman 6 — Adam’s 130 years in Rav Tzadok’s broader system: Rav Tzadok repeatedly treats the Eruvin narrative as a foundational defect in the covenant. Machshavot Charutz 15:10 links Adam’s production of spirits, demons, and liliths during those 130 years to the serpent’s corruption of human generative power, and presents Avraham and Sarah’s eventual fertility as part of its repair. Machshavot Charutz 20:13 goes further: ordinary death serves to rectify the defect begun by Adam “through the counsel of the serpent” in those years; Adam began teshuvah, but its completion appears through David and Mashiach, with renewed access to the Tree of Life. Se’if 40 adds the sharp implication that even an involuntary event can have objective spiritual consequences and can strengthen forces of impurity, despite the absence of conscious sin. Rav Tzadok is not assigning ordinary halachic guilt for an accident. He is distinguishing culpability from spiritual causation: an act may be involuntary and still disclose—and give expression to—a bodily root not yet wholly transformed.
וּבְוַדַּאי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהִרְהֵר בַּיּוֹם וְעָבַר עַל ״וְנִשְׁמַרְתָּ מִכֹּל דָּבָר רָע״ — שֶׁלֹּא יְהַרְהֵר וְכוּלֵיהּ

And it was certainly not through contemplating by day and violating "and you shall keep yourself from every evil thing" (Devarim 23:10)—that one must not engage in lustful thoughts by day (Avodah Zarah 20b);
אַף שֶׁעֲדַיִין לֹא נִתְּנָה תּוֹרָה לְהַזְהִיר עַל זֶה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לָא הֲווֹ קָרֵי לֵיהּ ״חָסִיד גָּדוֹל״, וְגַם זֶה לֹא הָיָה קֶרִי לְאוֹנְסוֹ כֵּיוָן דְּהוּא בְּהִרְהוּרוֹ הֵבִיא עַצְמוֹ לְכָךְ

for although the Torah had not yet been given to warn of this, nevertheless they would not have termed him "a great pietist," nor would this be classified as an involuntary emission since through his own contemplation he would have brought it upon himself;
וְעַל כֵּן וַדַּאי נִזְהַר בְּתַכְלִית מִכָּל שֶׁמֶץ הִרְהוּר:

wherefore he was certainly scrupulous to the ultimate degree against every trace of contemplation.802R’ Tzadok — parallel (Likkutei Maamarim §10): “This was the dwelling of Adam before the sin; and afterward he was expelled — ‘lest [he stretch out his hand and take also of the Tree of Life].’” Exactly the se’if: this level [of purity in the act] is attained only by one who never tasted sin — like Adam before the sin, dwelling in Gan Eden.803Devarim 23:10–11; Kesubos 46a; Avodah Zarah 20a; Shaarei Teshuvah 3:40 — daytime thought and genuine oness: From “you shall guard yourself from every evil thing,” R’ Pinchas ben Yair derives that a person must not entertain thoughts by day that bring him to impurity at night. Avodah Zarah applies the same verse to guarding one’s sight, and Shaarei Teshuvah emphasizes that the prohibition includes thought even where the person does not intend to act upon it. This establishes the distinction used by Rav Tzadok: an emission caused by a person’s deliberate thoughts is not complete oness, because he brought himself to the result. Since Eruvin both calls Adam’s emission involuntary and calls him a great chasid, Rav Tzadok concludes that Adam must have guarded himself from every conscious trace of such thought. His final step is deeper than the halachic derashah: even where conscious causation is absent, spontaneous bodily pleasure may reveal the still-present root of the serpent. That metaphysical claim prepares Se’if 41, which analyzes complete external compulsion and the continuing need for purification.

items.h: The theme: Even an involuntary nocturnal emission (keri l'onso) contains an element of levity (kalus rosh), defilement, and bodily pleasure. Even when caused by the exhaustion of travel (as with the pious man in Shabbos 127a, identified with Rabbi Yehudah ben Beseira in Berachos 22a), the Sages required immersion in a mikveh or washing with nine kavvin of water before studying Torah, because Torah must be acquired in dread, awe, trembling, and sweat (eimah, yirah, reses, v'zei'ah). As long as man is not entirely freed from the instigation of the Serpent, the subconscious physical pleasure experienced during sleep produces forces of impurity. The antidote is Torah study—the divine spice (tavlin) given at Sinai to liberate man from the yetzer hara.

p: אֲבָל גַּם בְּאוֹנֶס גָּמוּר מִטֹּרַח הַדֶּרֶךְ כְּהַאי דְּחָסִיד אֶחָד [בְּשַׁבָּת קכ״ז עַמּוּד ב׳], גַּם כֵּן יֵשׁ בּוֹ טוּמְאָה וְצָרִיךְ טְבִילָה וְגַם לְדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳]

But even in a case of absolute duress from the fatigue of travel, like that incident of a certain pious man [in Shabbos 127b], there is likewise impurity within it and it requires immersion, even for speaking words of Torah as they stated [in Berachos 22a];804Shabbos 127b; Temurah 15b; Rashi ad loc.; Berachos 22a–b — the “certain chasid,” involuntary emission, and Torah study: Shabbos relates that a certain chasid redeemed a Jewish girl from captivity, kept her beneath his feet at the inn to protect her, and the next morning “descended, immersed, and taught his students.” The story does not explicitly identify the cause of his immersion. Rav Tzadok reads it as an involuntary emission caused by the exertion of the journey, rather than marital relations. Rashi identifies the anonymous “certain chasid” used in such narratives as either R’ Yehuda ben Bava or R’ Yehuda bar Ilai, in accord with the general rule stated in Temurah; Rav Tzadok argues that this case is the same R’ Yehuda discussed in Berachos. Berachos grounds the ancient restriction on Torah study in the juxtaposition of teaching Torah to the revelation at Sinai: just as Sinai was received with awe, fear, trembling, and perspiration, Torah must be approached in the same spirit. The sugya also distinguishes ordinary and involuntary emissions and discusses forty se’ah versus nine kav. Thus the immersion and the Sinai standard are explicit; the identification of the incident, its physical cause, and its use as proof of a wholly involuntary occurrence are Rav Tzadok’s careful reconstruction.
וְשָׁם אִיתָא בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּרָאָה קֶרִי, מַשְׁמַע בְּשֵׁינָה וּלְאוֹנְסוֹ, לֹא בְּתַשְׁמִישׁ הַמִּטָּה
and there it is taught regarding the incident of Rabbi Yehudah [ben Beseira] that he experienced a seminal emission, which implies during sleep and involuntarily, not through marital relations;
וְהוּא נִקְרָא גַּם כֵּן ״חָסִיד אֶחָד״ בִּסְתָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּתְמוּרָה ט״ו סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳], וּמַיְיתֵי לַהּ רַשִׁ״י שַׁבָּת שָׁם
and he is likewise referred to simply as "a certain pious man" as they stated [in Temurah 15b], cited by Rashi in Shabbos there;
וְהַקָּרוֹב דְּהַיְינוּ עוּבְדָא דְּשַׁבָּת, שֶׁלֹּא לִתְלוֹת רְאִיַּית קֶרִי לְאוֹנְסוֹ בְּאוֹתוֹ גּוּף קָדוֹשׁ ב׳ פְּעָמִים אוֹ בְּב׳ חֲסִידִים

and it is probable that this is the identical incident recorded in Shabbos, so as not to attribute involuntary emissions to that holy body twice or to two separate pious sages.805Temurah 15b; Rashi on Shabbos 127b — identifying the anonymous chasid: Temurah states that whenever the Gemara says “an incident involving a certain chasid,” the subject is either R’ Yehuda ben Bava or R’ Yehuda bar Ilai. Rashi repeats this rule directly on the Shabbos narrative. Rav Tzadok prefers R’ Yehuda bar Ilai because Berachos records an incident involving “R’ Yehuda” who experienced an emission and immersed before Torah study. He then proposes that both passages describe one event, rather than attributing the same rare involuntary occurrence twice to one sacred body or separately to two chasidim. The sources support the two possible identities; the choice of R’ Yehuda bar Ilai and the unification of the narratives are Rav Tzadok’s inference.
וְטַעַם טְבִילָה לְדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה מְבוֹאָר בִּבְרָכוֹת שָׁם: לְפִי שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִלְמוֹד בְּאֵימָה, בְּיִרְאָה, בְּרֶתֶת וּבְזֵיעָה
And the reason for immersion prior to Torah study is explained in Berachos there: because one must study with dread, with awe, with trembling, and with sweat;
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״מִכָּאן״, שֶׁבַּעַל קֶרִי אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִתּוֹךְ קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ וְזַחוּת הַדַּעַת
and see Rashi there (s.v. mikan): that one who experiences an emission does so only out of levity (kalus rosh) and haughtiness of spirit (zachus ha-da'as).
וְאִם כֵּן, דְּגַם לְאוֹנְסוֹ צָרִיךְ עַל כָּרְחֲךָ [לוֹמַר] דְּגַם זֶה מִקַּלּוּת רֹאשׁ
And if so, that even for an involuntary emission immersion is required, perforce you must say that this too stems from a subtle levity;
וְאַף דְּחָלִילָה לִקְדוֹשֵׁי עֶלְיוֹן שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לָהֶם שׁוּם רֶגַע קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם בְּהָקִיץ וְלֹא זַחוּת דַּעַת
and although God forbid that holy supernal masters should possess even a moment of levity or haughtiness while awake,
מִכָּל מָקוֹם, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא נִיצּוֹלוּ מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ לְגַמְרֵי לִהְיוֹת ״לֵב בָּשָׂר״ כַּלֶּעָתִיד וּכְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם

nevertheless, so long as they have not been completely delivered from the instigation of the Serpent so as to possess a "heart of flesh" (Yechezkel 36:26) as in the Future and like Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,

גַּם בַּמַּה דַּחֲזָא לְאוֹנְסֵיהּ בְּשֵׁינָה לֹא נִיצּוֹל מֵהַרְגָּשַׁת הֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית בִּשְׁעָתוֹ בִּשְׁנָתוֹ, וְגַם זֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ וְזַחוּת דַּעַת וְגוֹרֵם תּוֹלֶדֶת כֹּחוֹת טוּמְאָה רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן

even in that which he experiences involuntarily during sleep, he is not spared from the sensation of physical pleasure in that moment of sleep, and this too is accounted as a subtle levity and haughtiness, causing the generation of forces of impurity, God protect us!806Yechezkel 36:26; Bereishis 49:3 with Rashi; Yevamos 76a — a heart of flesh and Yaakov’s exceptional bodily purity: Yechezkel describes the future transformation as the removal of the heart of stone and the gift of a heart of flesh. Rav Tzadok reads this not as increased sensuality, but as a living heart wholly responsive to holiness after the serpent’s corruption has been removed. Rashi explains Yaakov’s description of Reuven as “the first of my vigor” to mean that Yaakov had never previously experienced an emission; Yevamos invokes that purity as an exceptional standard, asking rhetorically whether everyone is like Yaakov Avinu. These sources establish Yaakov’s extraordinary bodily sanctity and the future replacement of the stony heart. Rav Tzadok’s further point is that a holy person may be entirely free of conscious levity while an involuntary sensation during sleep still reveals a bodily layer not yet transformed to Yaakov’s level or to the future state. He is describing spiritual residue, not assigning deliberate halachic guilt for an accident.

וְעַל זֶה תִּיקְּנוּ חֲכָמִים הַטְּבִילָה אוֹ רְחִיצָה בְּט׳ קַבִּין, שֶׁבְּכָךְ הוּא נִטְהָר מֵאוֹתוֹ רוּחַ הַטּוּמְאָה וְזַחוּת דַּעַת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִזֶּה, וְיוּכַל לִידָּבֵק בִּמְאוֹר וּקְדֻשַּׁת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁהוּא עֵץ חַיִּים

And for this reason the Sages instituted immersion [in a mikveh] or washing with nine kavvin of water, through which one is cleansed of that spirit of impurity and haughtiness drawn from it, enabling him to cleave to the luminary and sanctity of the Torah which is the Tree of Life;
כִּי עַל יָדָהּ דְּבוּקִים בְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, הִיא הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּקְרֵאת כֵּן [בְּשַׁבָּת י׳ עַמּוּד א׳, ל״ג עַמּוּד ב׳], וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם נָטַע בְּתוֹכֵנוּ״

for through it we cleave to eternal life, being the Torah which is termed thus [in Shabbos 10a, 33b], as is recited: 'and planted eternal life within us';807Berachos 22a–b; Rambam, Hilchos Krias Shema 4:8; Shabbos 10a and 33b — nine kav, the later status of Ezra’s enactment, and Torah as eternal life: Berachos records Ezra’s immersion enactment and the later provision of nine kav for a healthy person who experienced an involuntary emission. The same sugya presents purification as preparation for Torah’s Sinai-like awe. The Rambam rules, however, that the enactment did not spread throughout Israel and ultimately lapsed; Jews therefore study Torah and recite Shema in this state because words of Torah do not contract ritual impurity. Immersion or nine kav remained a voluntary practice of added purity, not the binding prerequisite it once was. Shabbos calls Torah “eternal life” in contrast to ordinary temporal needs, both in the discussion of prolonged prayer and in Rashbi’s response to worldly labor after leaving the cave. Rav Tzadok uses the older purification structure and this language of eternal life to explain how water removes the lingering spirit of frivolity and allows renewed attachment to Torah as the spiritual Tree of Life. His passage explains the inner meaning of the practice; it should not be read as reversing the later halachic ruling.
וְעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה יוּכַל לְתַקֵּן גַּם כֵּן הַכֹּל, דְּעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: ״בָּרָאתִי יֵצֶר הָרָע, בָּרָאתִי לוֹ תּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין״

and through the Torah one can likewise rectify everything, concerning which they stated [Bava Basra 16a]: 'I created the evil inclination, and I created the Torah as its antidote-spice';808Bava Basra 16a; Kiddushin 30b — the evil inclination, death, and Torah as the divinely created antidote: Bava Basra identifies the Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death as three manifestations of one force, and connects the evil inclination to the Flood verse “only evil all day.” The exact declaration “I created the evil inclination, and I created Torah as its antidote” appears in Kiddushin, where Hashem promises that those engaged in Torah are not surrendered into the inclination’s hand; the same sugya instructs a person confronted by it to draw it into the beis midrash, where Torah melts stone and shatters iron. Rav Tzadok’s citation of Bava Basra brings the creation-level unity of temptation and death, while Kiddushin supplies the explicit “Torah as antidote” formulation. Read together, they support his claim that Torah does not merely distract from desire: it is the remedy created for the very root from which desire and mortality emerge.
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא קְרָאוֹ ״רַע״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוּכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳] מִקְּרָא דְּ״רַע מִנְּעֻרָיו״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ח:כא), שֶׁהוּא בַּחֵטְא דְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל
and the Holy One, blessed be He, called it 'evil' as they stated [in Sukkah 52a] from the verse 'is evil from his youth' (Bereishis 8:21), which was stated regarding the Generation of the Flood,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁבַּבְּרִיאָה שֶׁבְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, שֶׁהִיא מִצַּד הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁבָּרָא עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע וְהַבְּחִירָה לָאָדָם לֶאֱכוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ

which stems from the root of the yetzer hara in Creation via the Serpent's instigation, originating from the Blessed Name Who created the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil and endowed man with free choice to eat from it,
שֶׁמִּזֶּה נִכְנַס הַרְגָּשַׁת תַּאֲווֹת הַגּוּפָנִיּוֹת לַלֵּב וְלֹא כִּמְקוֹדֶם דְּ״לֹא יִתְבֹּשָׁשׁוּ״ (שָׁם ב:כה)

from which the feeling of physical bodily desires entered the heart, unlike their initial state wherein 'they were not ashamed' (Bereishis 2:25);809Bereishis 2:25; 3:7; 6:5; 8:21; Sukkah 52a — shame, the Flood, and the name “evil from youth”: Before the sin, Adam and Chavah were unclothed and “were not ashamed”; immediately after eating from the Tree of Knowledge their eyes opened, they recognized their nakedness, and covered themselves. Before the Flood the Torah says that every formation of the human heart was “only evil all day,” and after the Flood Hashem says that the inclination of the human heart is evil from youth. Sukkah cites the latter verse as the name Hashem Himself gives the evil inclination: “evil.” Rav Tzadok joins these stages into one history. The Tree of Knowledge introduced self-conscious bodily desire; its root later expanded into the corruption of the Flood generation; and the post-Flood verse identifies that inclination as embedded from youth. The verses and Gemara establish the sequence and terminology. The unification of shame, bodily desire, the Flood, and the serpent’s counsel is Rav Tzadok’s theological synthesis.
וּבְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה נַעֲשׂוּ חֵרוּת מִיֵּצֶר הָרָע, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה תַּבְלִין יוּכְלוּ לְתַקֵּן זֶה
and at the Giving of the Torah they became free from the yetzer hara (Eruvin 54a), for through the Torah as a spice they are able to rectify this,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם [בְּסוֹף הִלְכוֹת אִיסּוּרֵי בִּיאָה פֶּרֶק כ״ב הֲלָכָה כ״א] דְּאֵין הַתַּאֲווֹת אֶלָּא בְּלֵב פָּנוּי מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה:

as the Rambam wrote [Hilchos Issurei Biah 22:21] that lustful thoughts dwell only in a heart devoid of words of Torah.810Shabbos 146a; Avos 6:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Eikev 8; Takanas HaShavin §4; Rambam, Hilchos Issurei Biah 22:21 — Sinai, freedom, and filling the heart with Torah: Shabbos teaches that at Sinai the serpent’s pollution ceased from Israel. Avos reads “engraved [charus] upon the tablets” as freedom, declaring that the only truly free person is one occupied with Torah. Midrash Tanchuma applies the same wordplay to freedom from the Angel of Death, with related traditions adding freedom from exile or suffering. Rav Tzadok consistently combines these teachings and describes the first Tablets as freedom from the evil inclination, foreign domination, and death—the restoration, for a moment, of the state later promised for the future. After the Golden Calf that complete condition was lost, but Torah remained the antidote through which its repair can be regained. The Rambam concludes Hilchos Issurei Biah with the practical expression of this principle: a person should turn his mind to Torah and broaden it with wisdom, because forbidden thoughts become dominant only in a heart empty of wisdom. Rav Tzadok therefore moves from Sinai’s collective purification to the individual discipline of filling the heart with Torah.

items.h: The theme: The generation of Rabbi Yehudah bar Ilai ("a woman that fears Hashem, she shall be praised") versus the generations of Moshe, Yehoshua, and Chizkiyahu ("grace is deceitful and beauty is vain", Sanhedrin 20a). While early leaders possessed innate soul-purity (chein v'yofi) that kept them untainted by bodily lust from birth, Rabbi Yehudah attained angelic purity strictly through personal human toil (yir'as Hashem), studying Torah amid abject poverty. When he bathed before Shabbos and robed in white linen fringed with techeiles, he radiated the supernal countenance (or panim) of Adam HaRishon prior to the sin, uniting love and awe (d'chilu u'rechimu) and binding his soul to the Eternal Life of the Torah.

p: וְעַל דּוֹרוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן רַבִּי אִלְעָאִי אָמְרוּ [סַנְהֶדְרִין כ׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״׳אִשָּׁה יִרְאַת ה׳ הִיא תִתְהַלָּל׳ (מִשְׁלֵי ל״א:ל׳) — וַעֲדִיפֵי מִדּוֹרוֹ דְּמֹשֶׁה וִיהוֹשֻׁעַ וּדְחִזְקִיָּה״

And concerning the generation of Rabbi Yehudah ben Rabbi Ilai they stated [in Sanhedrin 20a]: "'A woman that fears Hashem, she shall be praised' (Mishlei 31:30)—and they are greater than the generations of Moshe, Yehoshua, and Chizkiyahu,"
שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ ״חֵן וְיוֹפִי״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהֵם הָיוּ נְפָשׁוֹת נְקִיּוֹת מִתּוֹלָדָה
who represented 'grace and beauty,' meaning that they were souls born pure from their inception:

כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִיָּד שֶׁנּוֹלַד: ״וַתֵּרֶא אוֹתוֹ כִּי טוֹב הוּא״ (שְׁמוֹת ב:ב), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁנּוֹלַד מָהוּל, וְהַיְינוּ צַדִּיק כִּי טוֹב, הֵיפֶךְ ״הָרַע בְּעֵינֵי ה׳״

as is said of Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, immediately at birth: 'she saw him that he was good' (Shemos 2:2), and the Sages of blessed memory expounded that he was born circumcised (Sotah 12a), which is the tzaddik called 'good' (Yeshayah 3:10), the antithesis of that which is 'evil in the eyes of Hashem';811Sanhedrin 20a; Rashi ad loc. — “grace,” “beauty,” and Torah learned under hardship: The Gemara gives several readings of “Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain; a woman who fears Hashem, she shall be praised.” In the reading used here, “grace” denotes the generation of Moshe and Yehoshua, “beauty” the generation of Chizkiyahu, and “a woman who fears Hashem” the generation of R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai. It then records that six of his students shared one cloak and nevertheless engaged in Torah. Rashi explains the earlier generations as extraordinarily devoted to Torah and Chizkiyahu’s generation as still greater, while the final reading praises Torah sustained amid poverty and oppression. The Gemara explicitly establishes the comparative hierarchy through difficult circumstances. Rav Tzadok deepens that contrast: “grace and beauty” signify holiness naturally rooted in the soul, whereas the praise of yiras Hashem belongs to sanctity acquired through personal struggle.812Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Pri Tzadik, Tazria 8:1; Machshavot Charutz 15:12 - inherited spiritual root and Torah joined to yirah: Pri Tzadik reads “Grace is deceitful and beauty is vain; a woman who fears Hashem, she shall be praised” as a statement about Torah itself: even serious Torah activity pursued only as spiritual “grace” or “beauty,” without yiras Shamayim, remains false and vaporous; yirah is the enduring inner substance. Machshavot Charutz teaches the complementary truth that every Jew is created from the good root of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov, and that an indelible imprint of that original light remains even after later failure. Together these passages illuminate the distinction drawn here. A naturally pure root is genuine and powerful, but the final praise belongs to Torah and holiness made one’s own through yirah and avodah.
וְכֵן יְהוֹשֻׁעַ מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף

and so too Yehoshua, who stemmed from the seed of Yosef [the exemplar of guarding the Covenant];813Shemos 2:2; Sotah 12a; Bamidbar 13:8; Bereishis 39:7–12; Sotah 36b; Yeshayah 3:10 — Moshe’s innate “goodness” and Yehoshua’s descent from Yosef: Sotah offers several explanations of “she saw that he was good”: Moshe was named Tov or Toviyah, was fit for prophecy, was born circumcised, or filled the house with light. Rav Tzadok selects the interpretation of circumcision and joins it to “say of the righteous that he is good,” treating “good” as the opposite of the “evil in the eyes of Hashem” associated with blemish of the covenant. Bamidbar identifies Yehoshua as Hoshea son of Nun from Ephraim, and thus a descendant of Yosef. Yosef’s resistance to Potiphar’s wife, elaborated in Sotah, made him the paradigmatic guardian of the covenant. The genealogy is explicit; Rav Tzadok’s conclusion that Yehoshua inherited a soul naturally clean of bodily desire is a spiritual reading of that lineage.814Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Takanat HaShavin 4:1; Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 20:1 - Moshe’s Sinai-level and the first versus second tablets: Earlier in Takanat HaShavin, Rav Tzadok describes Moshe’s level at Matan Torah as complete freedom from subjugation, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death. Pri Tzadik develops a crucial two-stage model. At the first tablets, “Anochi” was implanted directly in Israel’s heart and “You shall have no other gods” uprooted the alien power of the yetzer; the freedom was bestowed from Above. After the sin, the second tablets began with “Carve for yourself”: the person must first carve and refine the stony heart, and only then can the same Torah become engraved within it and produce freedom from the yetzer. This is a close parallel to Se’if 42’s movement from the native “grace and beauty” associated with Moshe’s generation to the acquired yirah and Torah-labor exemplified by R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai.
וְחִזְקִיָּה אָמַר עַל עַצְמוֹ: ״זְכָר [נָא] אֲשֶׁר הִתְהַלַּכְתִּי [לְפָנֶיךָ בֶּאֱמֶת וּבְלֵבָב שָׁלֵם] וְהַטּוֹב בְּעֵינֶיךָ [עָשִׂיתִי]״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ל״ח:ג׳), שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ ״הָרַע בְּעֵינָיו״

and Chizkiyahu said of himself: 'Remember now how I have walked before You in truth and with a whole heart, and have done that which is good in Your sight' (Yeshayah 38:3), which is the opposite of 'evil in His sight';
וְהָיָה בָּטוּחַ בְּעַצְמוֹ שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה עָלָיו שׁוּם טַעֲנָה מִשֶּׁמֶץ חֵטְא בָּעוֹלָם
and he was confident that there was no complaint against him of any trace of sin in the world,
דְּגַם מַה שֶּׁבִּיטֵּל פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה הָיָה בִּתְמִימוּת וּלְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם כְּפִי דַּעְתּוֹ, דַּחֲזָא בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ

for even his abstention from procreation was done with integrity and for the sake of Heaven according to his understanding, because he foresaw through Divine Inspiration that unworthy children would descend from him (Berachos 10a).
וְהַגַּם דִּקְרָא צָוַוח: ״אֵין אָדָם צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב [וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא]״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כ), צָרִיךְ לוֹמַר דְּדָיֵיק ״בָּאָרֶץ״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁהוּא שָׁקוּעַ בְּאַרְצִיּוּת גַּם כֵּן

And although Scripture proclaims: 'For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that does good, and sins not' (Koheles 7:20), one must say that it states with precision 'upon earth' (ba-aretz), meaning one who is immersed in earthliness as well,815Melachim II 20:1–3; Berachos 10a; Koheles 7:20 — Chizkiyahu’s prayer, prophetic calculation, and the limits of his claim: When Chizkiyahu became mortally ill, he prayed: “Remember how I walked before You in truth and with a whole heart, and did what was good in Your eyes.” Berachos explains that Yeshayah attributed the decree to Chizkiyahu’s failure to engage in procreation. Chizkiyahu answered that he had seen through ruach ha-kodesh that unworthy children would issue from him; Yeshayah replied that he must perform the command and leave the hidden outcomes to Hashem. The Gemara therefore does not validate his practical decision. Rav Tzadok’s narrower point is about motive: the calculation was sincere and for Heaven according to Chizkiyahu’s understanding, not an expression of lust or self-interest. He then rereads Koheles’ “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and never sins” by emphasizing “on earth,” a derash that distinguishes souls immersed in ordinary earthliness from exceptional figures whose root lay beyond it.816Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Machshavot Charutz 15:4 - procreation, Adam’s separation, the sin of Er, and complete repair: Rav Tzadok identifies peru u-revu as the Torah’s first mitzvah, commanded to Adam before the sin, and the direct opposite of the conduct of Er, who did not desire the continued existence of seed. After the sin, Adam separated from his wife and thereby encountered the “sin of Er” even through an involuntary occurrence; after teshuvah he returned to union and fathered Sheis, from whom the world was established. Rav Tzadok calls this “the end embedded in the beginning”: complete repair returns the final, damaged point to the first Divine purpose. This provides important context for Chizkiyahu. His calculation was sincere and prophetic in motive, yet abstention from peru u-revu still touched the primal command through which human generative power is directed toward life and continuity.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אוֹתָם שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לָהֶם שׁוּם שַׁיָּיכוּת לְעִנְיְנֵי אַרְצִיּוּת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּלָל
whereas those holy individuals possessed no connection to the mundane affairs of this world at all.
אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן רַבִּי אִלְעָאִי זָכָה עַל יְדֵי יִרְאַת ה׳, שֶׁהוּא מַה שֶּׁה׳ שׁוֹאֵל מֵעִמָּךְ, שֶׁהוּא רַק בְּהִשְׁתַּדְּלוּת אָדָם וְלֹא מִצַּד שָׁרְשׁוֹ

But Rabbi Yehudah ben Rabbi Ilai attained his level through fear of Hashem (yir'as Hashem), which is that which 'Hashem asks of you' (Devarim 10:12), depending purely on human exertion and not on hereditary soul-root;817Devarim 10:12; Berachos 33b — yiras Shamayim as the sphere of human effort: “What does Hashem your God ask of you except to fear Hashem” is the source for the principle that everything is in the hands of Heaven except fear of Heaven. Berachos stresses both sides: yirah is the one realm entrusted to human choice, yet it is also Hashem’s unique treasure and no small achievement. Rav Tzadok applies that principle to R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai. Unlike the “grace and beauty” of souls whose purity was native to their root, his greatness was won through effort, poverty, Torah, and fear of Heaven. The distinction between inherited spiritual disposition and acquired holiness is Rav Tzadok’s interpretation; the Gemara supplies the foundation that yirah depends upon the person’s own avodah.818Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Yisrael Kedoshim 6:5; Resisei Layla 54:12 - human effort preparing the vessel for a higher gift: Yisrael Kedoshim distinguishes what lies within human reach from the higher illumination that cannot be seized directly. A person first sanctifies the body through mitzvos, the heart through avodah and yirah, and the mind through Divine wisdom; only after completing that avodah can the encompassing light of the soul’s supernal root be drawn upon him as a gift from Heaven. Resisei Layla similarly teaches that the temporary freedom from the yetzer experienced at Sinai and on Yom Kippur is “according to what the person is,” and that repeated human effort opens the point of a needle until Hashem opens it like the entrance of the Sanctuary. Thus Se’if 42 does not deny the soul-root. It teaches that the higher root becomes revealed and enduring through the person’s own yirah and exertion.

דְּזֶה נִקְרָא ״חֵן וְיוֹפִי״: מִי שֶׁבְּשׁוֹרֶשׁ נָקִי מִתַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת, וְזֶה לֹא יֶאֱרַע לוֹ שׁוּם מִקְרֶה גַּם לְאוֹנְסוֹ מֵאֵיזֶה חִימּוּם וְטֹרַח דֶּרֶךְ וְכַדּוֹמֶה שֶׁיֶּאֱרַע לִבְנֵי אָדָם

for that is termed 'grace and beauty': one whose root is innately pure from bodily lusts, so that no nocturnal accident occurs to him even involuntarily through bodily warmth, travel exhaustion, and the like, as commonly occurs to human beings,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת ע״ו עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״אַטּוּ כּוּלֵי עָלְמָא יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ, אַטּוּ כּוּלֵי עָלְמָא בַּרְזִלַּי וְכוּלֵיהּ״

as they stated [in Yevamos 76b]: 'Is everyone then Yaakov Avinu... is everyone Barzillai HaGiladi?';819Yevamos 76a; Bereishis 49:3 with Rashi — Yaakov, Barzilai, and deliberately induced arousal: To test whether a puncture invalidated a man for marriage into the congregation, Rav Yosef proposed warm barley bread near the organ. Abaye objected, “Is everyone Yaakov Avinu,” and suggested passing colored women’s garments before him; Rava countered, “Is everyone Barzilai,” and returned to the original test. Rashi explains Yaakov’s “first of my vigor” as his first seminal drop, because he had never previously experienced an emission. The sugya invokes Yaakov as an exceptional standard of bodily purity, but its test is deliberately induced while the subject is awake. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes it from a guarded person asleep: heat joined to intentional stimulation can operate even where an entirely involuntary occurrence would not. That final distinction is his inference from the sequence of the sugya.820Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Pri Tzadik, Emor 14:1 - Rav Tzadok’s direct parallel to the “certain chasid” and R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai: This is Rav Tzadok’s most direct parallel to the present discussion. He cites the incident in Shabbos 127b and Rashi’s identification of an anonymous “certain chasid” as either R’ Yehuda ben Bava or R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai. He then cites the very hierarchy used in Se’if 42 - Moshe and Yehoshua as “grace,” Chizkiyahu as “beauty,” and R’ Yehuda’s generation as “a woman who fears Hashem.” Yet the Gemara still records that an involuntary occurrence befell that chasid. Rav Tzadok says the passage was written to strengthen broken hearts: an unwanted bodily event does not by itself prove moral consent, loss of yirah, or severance from kedushah. The person’s inward fear of Hashem and lifelong avodah remain the decisive measure.

וְהַגַּם דְּשָׁם מְבוֹאָר דְּגַם מִי שֶׁכְּיַעֲקֹב יִפְעוֹל הַחִימּוּם אַבֵּי פוֹקְרֵי, שָׁם הוּא בְּהָקִיץ לִרְצוֹנוֹ וְלֹא לְאוֹנְסוֹ, וְעוֹשִׂין כְּדֵי לְהוֹלִיד בְּלִבּוֹ הִרְהוּר כְּהַאי דְּבִגְדֵי צִבְעוֹנִין שָׁם

and although it is explained there that even for one like Yaakov bodily warmth on a dunghill would take effect, there it was done while awake, deliberately, and with stimuli designed to arouse contemplation like colored garments,
וּבְצֵירוּף הַהִרְהוּר יִפְעוֹל הַחִימּוּם, וְלֹא לְמִי שֶׁנִּזְהָר מֵהִרְהוּר וּבְשֵׁינָה
and in conjunction with contemplation bodily warmth takes effect, but not for one who guards against contemplation during sleep.

אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה בֶּן רַבִּי אִלְעָאִי זָכָה אַחַר כָּךְ לָזֶה בְּכֹחַ הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה, עַד שֶׁאָמְרוּ עָלָיו [בְּשַׁבָּת כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁהָיָה דּוֹמֶה לְמַלְאַךְ ה׳ צְבָאוֹת, וּמַלְאָךְ הוּא נָקִי מִתַּאֲווֹת

Yet Rabbi Yehudah ben Rabbi Ilai attained this subsequently through the power of his intense toil in the Torah, until they said of him [in Shabbos 25b] that he resembled an angel of the Lord of Hosts, and an angel is completely free from lusts;821Shabbos 25b — R’ Yehuda b’R Ilai appearing like an angel on Erev Shabbos: Rav describes R’ Yehuda’s Erev Shabbos practice: they brought him a basin of hot water, he washed his face, hands, and feet, wrapped himself in fringed sheets, and sat resembling an angel of Hashem of Hosts. The passage explicitly connects washing, the fringed garment, and his angelic appearance. It does not itself say that he thereby became wholly free of bodily desire. Rav Tzadok reads the angelic image as the visible culmination of his Torah effort: the acquired yirah of R’ Yehuda had refined the body until, in the illumination of Shabbos, it displayed a purity usually associated with beings beyond physical desire.
וְזֶה הָיָה בִּלְבִישַׁת סְדִינִין הַמְצוּיָּיצִין, דְּצִיצִית בְּחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת רוֹמֵז לְיִרְאָה כִּידוּעַ
and this occurred when he donned his fringed linen cloak, for the tzitzis with the thread of techeiles alludes to fear (yirah) as is known;
וְאַחַר הָרְחִיצָה לִכְבוֹד שַׁבָּת שֶׁהִתְחִיל לְהִתְנוֹצֵץ הֶאָרָה מִקְּדֻשַּׁת שַׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא בְּבִיטּוּל הַיֵּצֶר

and after washing in honor of Shabbos, when the radiance of the holiness of Shabbos began to scintillate—which is a foretaste of the World to Come in the nullification of the yetzer—822Menachos 43b; Berachos 57b — tzitzis, techeiles, and Shabbos as a semblance of the World to Come: Menachos teaches that tzitzis is equivalent to all the mitzvos, that seeing leads to remembering and doing, and that one diligent in the mitzvah merits receiving the Shechinah; its proof joins “you shall see it” to “Hashem your God you shall fear, and Him you shall serve.” Berachos calls Shabbos a semblance of the World to Come. These sources support Rav Tzadok’s joining of the fringed garment, yirah, Shabbos, and revelation of the Divine Presence. His more specific symbolism—white linen as love and techeiles as fear—and his description of the Shabbos illumination as a temporary nullification of the inclination are kabbalistic interpretations, not statements made explicitly in these two sugyos.823Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 20:1; Divrei Soferim 33:3 - Torah engraved in the heart as freedom from the yetzer and death: Pri Tzadik explains that when Torah is engraved on the heart it becomes “freedom upon the tablets” - freedom from the evil inclination - and that even after the first tablets were broken, one who personally carves the stony heart can recover that same inner freedom. Divrei Soferim states even more broadly that Torah produces freedom from both the yetzer and the Angel of Death, and connects the completed heart to “in the light of the King’s face is life,” before which the forces rooted in death have no standing. These passages supply Rav Tzadok’s larger conceptual setting for R’ Yehuda’s angelic appearance on Erev Shabbos: Torah and yirah had not merely restrained desire from outside; they had refined the bodily vessel until the light of life could become visible in his face.
זָכָה לְהָאוֹר פָּנִים שֶׁל אָדָם בְּשַׁבָּת שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה י״א]: ״דְּבֵרְכוֹ וְקִדְּשׁוֹ״
he merited the radiant countenance of man on Shabbos whereof they expounded [in Bereishis Rabbah 11:2] on 'and He blessed it and sanctified it' (Bereishis 2:3);

וְהַיְינוּ בְּאוֹר פָּנִים שֶׁהָיָה לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: לְמוֹצָאֵי שַׁבָּת נִיטַּל זִיווֹ וְנִטְרַד מִגַּן עֵדֶן, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״מְשַׁנֶּה פָנָיו וַתְּשַׁלְּחֵהוּ״ (אִיּוֹב י״ד:כ׳)

meaning the radiant countenance that Adam HaRishon possessed prior to the sin, as they said there: at the conclusion of Shabbos his radiance was removed and he was banished from Gan Eden, as it is said: 'You change his countenance, and send him away' (Iyov 14:20);
וְלֶעָתִיד שֶׁיְּתוּקַּן זֶה יַחֲזוֹר זִיווֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם פָּרָשָׁה י״ב]

and in the Future when this is rectified his radiance will return, as they stated [ibid. 12:6];824Bereishis Rabbah 11:2 and 12:6; Iyov 14:20; Shoftim 5:31 — Adam’s Shabbos radiance and its future restoration: Bereishis Rabbah teaches that although Adam sinned before Shabbos, his honor remained with him through the holy day; only after Shabbos was his radiance taken and he was driven from Gan Eden, as expressed by “You change his face and send him away.” The later passage lists radiance among six qualities taken from Adam and says that they will not return to their perfection until the coming of the descendant of Peretz. For the restored radiance it cites, “Those who love Him are like the sun going forth in its strength.” Rav Tzadok uses these Midrashim to explain R’ Yehuda’s shining Shabbos face as a present glimpse of Adam’s pre-sin splendor and of the future rectification.
וְזֶהוּ הַמְּאוֹר פָּנִים לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ [סוֹטָה פֶּרֶק י״ג] שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לְכָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם כְּפִי תּוֹרָתוֹ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and this is the luminous countenance of the World to Come mentioned in Tanna D'vei Eliyahu [Sotah, ch. 13] which will shine for every Torah scholar according to his Torah, see there.825Tanna d’Vei Eliyahu Zuta, chapter 12 — the future light of the face according to one’s Torah: The Midrash compares the evil inclination to an iron wall that servants must climb in order to approach the King. Those who overcome it are crowned with a radiance likened to “those who love Him are like the sun in its strength.” It then asks whether one who learned much and one who learned little will possess the same facial light in the World to Come, and answers that each person’s radiance corresponds to his Torah. Rav Tzadok brings this future measure into the present: R’ Yehuda’s face already shone in this world because his Torah, learned through privation and fear, had begun to reveal the light normally reserved for the perfected world.

וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה זָכָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְ״חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר [פָּנָיו]״ (קֹהֶלֶת ח:א), כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים מ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] עַל יְדֵי שְׁקִידָתוֹ בַּתּוֹרָה מִתּוֹךְ הַדֹּחַק יוֹתֵר מִכָּל הַדּוֹרוֹת כַּנַּ״ל

And Rabbi Yehudah merited in this world that 'a man’s wisdom makes his face to shine' (Koheles 8:1), as they stated [in Nedarim 49b], through his diligence in Torah amid poverty and oppression more than all other generations;826Nedarim 49b; Koheles 8:1 — “a person’s wisdom makes his face shine” in R’ Yehuda: R’ Tarfon observed that R’ Yehuda’s face was radiant. R’ Yehuda first attributed it to beets; when a matron suspected wine, he swore that he tasted wine only for Kiddush, Havdalah, and the four cups, which caused him prolonged pain. When a heretic compared his appearance to prosperous sinners, he answered that those occupations were forbidden and described the many privies required by his physical condition. The Gemara’s answer is the verse, “a person’s wisdom makes his face shine.” The setting excludes wealth, indulgence, and bodily ease. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the visible radiance as the fruit of Torah diligence amid hardship, completing Sanhedrin’s praise of R’ Yehuda’s generation.
וְהָאוֹר פָּנִים שֶׁאָדָם זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה לִשְׁמָהּ, זֶהוּ זִיווֹ דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לְאוֹר פְּנֵי מֶלֶךְ חַיִּים

and the radiant countenance that a person merits through Torah studied purely for its own sake (Torah lishmah) is the very radiance of Adam HaRishon prior to the sin, meriting the light of the King's Countenance of Life;
וְזֶהוּ כְּשֶׁנִּתְעַטֵּף בִּסְדִינִין הַמְצוּיָּיצִין, שֶׁהוּא חִיבּוּר אַהֲבָה וְיִרְאָה
and this was realized when he robed in fringed linen cloaks, which represents the union of Love and Awe:
כִּי סָדִין לָבָן שֶׁל פִּשְׁתָּן רוֹמֵז לְמִדַּת הָאַהֲבָה, וְחוּט שֶׁל תְּכֵלֶת לְיִרְאָה
for the white sheet of linen alludes to the attribute of Love (Chesed), and the thread of blue techeiles alludes to Awe (Gevurah);
וְאוֹרַיְיתָא בִּדְחִילוּ וּרְחִימוּ פָּרְחָא לְעֵילָּא
and the Torah studied in awe and love ascends on high (Tikkunei Zohar, Tikkun 10),
וְנַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ סַם חַיִּים לִידָּבֵק עַל יְדֵי זֶה בְּחֵי הָעוֹלָמִים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ, דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא וְקֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא חַד:

becoming for him an elixir of life (sam chayim) to cleave through it to the Life of the Worlds, blessed be His Name, for the Torah and the Holy One, blessed be He, are One.827Taanis 7a; Tikkunei Zohar, tikkun 10; Zohar, Acharei Mos 73a; Tanya, chapter 39 — Torah lishmah, love and fear, and the elixir of life: Taanis states explicitly that one who engages in Torah for its own sake finds his Torah becoming an elixir of life, citing “it is a Tree of Life to those who grasp it,” while Torah pursued improperly can become the opposite. The Tikkunei Zohar teaches that service lacking fear and love does not fly upward; Tanya explains that revealed or awakened love and fear give Torah and mitzvos the power to ascend and be incorporated in Divine unity. The Zohar’s formulation that Torah and the Holy One are one underlies Rav Tzadok’s final movement: Torah studied with both love and fear becomes not merely information but living attachment to the Life of all worlds. His identification of the white garment with love and the techeiles thread with fear supplies the symbolic form of that union.828Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Yisrael Kedoshim 6:5; Takanat HaShavin 15:43 - Torah lishmah, bodily sanctification, and “your world in your lifetime”: Yisrael Kedoshim teaches that Torah gives eternal life and that mitzvos performed according to Torah extend its holiness into every limb, until the body itself becomes saturated with the life-giving dew of Torah. The immediate continuation of this work, Se’if 43, then carries Se’if 42’s facial radiance into the blessing “May you see your world in your lifetime, and may your face shine,” identifying it with the rare level of the bnei aliyah who encounter the Shechinah in this world. The ending of Se’if 42 is therefore a bridge, not an isolated image: Torah lishmah joined to love and fear sanctifies the body, reveals Adam’s lost radiance, and opens a present foretaste of the perfected life normally reserved for the World to Come.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים מ״ד–מ״ז

The theme: The blessing "may you see your world in your lifetime" (olamkha tireh b'chayecha, Berachos 17a) refers to the luminous countenance of Adam HaRishon before the sin and entering the presence of the Ancient of Days (Atik Yomin) as a ben aliyah. Rabbi Yehudah’s dictum that "there is no repentance for this sin" applies to reaching this supreme rung, attained only by the rarest giants who never actively damaged the Covenant (shelo pagam ha-bris b'fo'al). Adam HaRishon drew his foreskin (meshukh b'orlaso) through the Serpent's instigation; even his 130 years of ascetic repentance could not grant reentry into Gan Eden to eat of the Tree of Life and live forever, because once that defilement penetrates the physical frame, its only purification is bodily decomposition in the dust.

p: וְזֶהוּ מַדְרֵיגוֹת ״עוֹלָמְךָ תִּרְאֶה בְּחַיֶּיךָ״ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת י״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]
And this is the level of "may you see your world in your lifetime" that they stated [in Berachos 17a];
וּמְסַיֵּים שָׁם: ״וּפָנֶיךָ יַזְהִירוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ — הַיְינוּ אוֹר הַפָּנִים
and it concludes there: "and your face shall shine, etc."—which is the luminous countenance (or ha-panim);
״וּפְעָמֶיךָ יָרוּצוּ לִשְׁמוֹעַ דִּבְרֵי עַתִּיק יוֹמִין״ — הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מִבְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה
"and your feet shall run to hear the words of the Ancient of Days"—meaning that he will be among the men of ascent (bnei aliyah).

וְהַךְ מֵימְרָא [דְּפָרָשַׁת וַיְחִי] דְּ״לֵית לֵיהּ תְּשׁוּבָה״ הוּא מִדִּבְרֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה, דְּדָבָר זֶה זָכוּ לָהּ רַק יְחִידֵי הַדּוֹרוֹת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, דְּעַל כֵּן אָמַר רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי דְּהֵן מוּעָטִים

And that teaching [in Zohar, Parashas Vayechi 219b] that "he has no repentance" is from the words of Rabbi Yehudah, for this attainment was merited only by the unique individuals of the generations in this world, wherefore Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai stated that they are few.829Zohar, Vayechi 219b (Sulam translation): “For we have learned: whoever brings out his seed in vain is called ‘evil’ and does not see the face of the Shechinah, as it says, ‘for You are not a God who desires wickedness; evil shall not dwell with You,’ and it is written ‘and Er, Yehudah’s firstborn, was evil.’ Here too [Yeshayah 3:11], ‘woe to the wicked, evil’ — woe to that wicked one who is evil, who made himself evil; for ‘the recompense of his hands shall be done to him’ — the meaning being, whoever [uses] his hands to bring out and destroy his seed in vain — him they punish in the world of truth more than [for] all [the transgressions]. Come and see: ‘evil shall not dwell with You’ — and all of them ascend [from Gehinnom] but this one does not ascend. And if you say, the other wicked who killed people — come and see: they all ascend and he does not ascend; what is the reason? They killed other people, but this one killed his own children and spilled much blood. Come and see: of the other wicked of the world it is not written ‘and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem,’ and here it is written ‘and it was evil in the eyes of Hashem what he did.’ R’ Yehudah taught: there is no transgression in the world for which there is not teshuvah, except for this; and there are no wicked who do not see the face of the Shechinah except for this, as it is written ‘evil shall not dwell with You’ at all. R’ Yitzchak said: happy are the righteous in this world and in the World to Come; of them it is written, ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever’ (Yeshayah 60:21).”830Berachos 17a; Rashi and Maharsha ad loc. - “May you see your world in your lifetime” and the radiance of the face: Rashi explains the opening blessing on the practical level: may all the needs of “your world” be found during your lifetime. Maharsha reads the formula as a deliberately ordered blessing that begins in this world and continues through the World to Come, the generations of redemption, and resurrection; he links “may your face shine” to “a person’s wisdom illuminates his face” (Koheles 8:1). Rav Tzadok reads the same words at their highest spiritual register. “Your world” is not a generic reward but the particular chamber and portion of Divine life suited to this soul, tasted while still embodied. The facial light is the outward sign that inward Torah and attachment have begun to disclose that future portion in the present. This is an interpretive deepening of the Gemara, not a replacement of Rashi’s plain meaning.831Kisvei Rav Tzadok - Yisrael Kedoshim 6:5; Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 20:1; Divrei Soferim 33:3 - a present foretaste of eternal life: Yisrael Kedoshim teaches that after a person sanctifies body, heart, and mind through mitzvos, avodah, yirah, and Torah, an encompassing light from the hidden root of the soul can rest upon him; this is the same supernal root disclosed by the crowns of Sinai and by freedom from the yetzer and death. Pri Tzadik explains that Torah engraved on the heart becomes the Tree of Life and gives a genuine form of freedom even after the first tablets were broken. Divrei Soferim joins this to “in the light of the King’s face is life.” These passages clarify the present se’if: “seeing one’s world” means that the life normally concealed in one’s future portion becomes perceptible now, and “the light of the face” is its embodied trace.
וּבַגְּמָרָא דְּסוּכָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל אִיתָא: ״אִם שְׁנַיִם וְכוּלֵיהּ״ וְלֹא אָמַר פָּחוֹת
And in the Gemara in Sukkah (45b) mentioned above it is taught: "if they are two, etc.," and he did not say fewer;

וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [פָּרָשָׁה ל״ה] אִיתָא: ״וְאִם חַד הוּא אֲנָא הוּא״, וְשָׁם לֵיתָא הַלָּשׁוֹן ״רָאִיתִי״, וְאָמַר כְּפִי הַמְּצִיאוּת דְּעַל כָּל פָּנִים אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִהְיוֹת פָּחוֹת מֵאֶחָד שֶׁעָלָיו הָעוֹלָם עוֹמֵד, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם״ (מִשְׁלֵי י:כה)

while in Bereishis Rabbah [35:2] it is taught: "and if he is one, I am he," and there the wording "I have seen" is absent, and he stated it according to metaphysical reality, for in any event it is impossible for there to be fewer than one upon whom the world stands, as it is said: "the righteous man is an everlasting foundation" (Mishlei 10:25).832Sukkah 45b: “And Chizkiyah said, R’ Yirmeyah said in the name of Rashbi: I have seen the members of the [supernal] ascent, and they are few — if they are a thousand, I and my son are among them; if they are a hundred, I and my son are among them; if they are two, they are I and my son. But are they so few? Did not Rava say: there are eighteen thousand [tzaddikim] who stand before the Holy One, as it is said ‘around, eighteen thousand’? It is no difficulty: this [refers to those] who gaze through the clear glass [aspaklaria ha-me’irah], and that [refers to those] who do not gaze through the clear glass. And those who gaze through the clear glass — are they so few? Did not Abaye say: the world has no fewer than thirty-six tzaddikim who receive the face of the Shechinah every day, as it is said ‘praiseworthy are all who wait [chochei] for Him’ — [the numerical value of] ‘lo’ [ל"ו] in gematria is thirty-six? It is no difficulty: this [refers to those] who enter with permission, and that [refers to those] who enter without permission.” [Those who enter [Hashem’s presence] without asking permission are few.]833Sukkah 45b; Bereishis Rabbah 35:2 - the several counts of the bnei aliyah: The Bavli records Rashbi’s graded formulation: if the highest group numbers one thousand, one hundred, or only two, he and his son are included. It then distinguishes eighteen thousand who stand before Hashem, thirty-six who greet the Shechinah daily, those who see through an illuminating glass, and the exceedingly few who enter without requesting permission. Bereishis Rabbah gives a different ladder - thirty, twenty, ten, five, two, and finally one - and concludes, “if there is one, I am he.” Rav Tzadok treats the difference in wording precisely. The Midrash speaks of the minimum necessary for the world’s endurance; the Bavli’s “I have seen” speaks from Rashbi’s actual spiritual vision, in which he knew at least himself and his son as members of that innermost class.834Bava Basra 75a; Yevamos 49b; Maharsha on Sukkah 45b - distinct chambers and degrees of seeing the Shechinah: Chazal say that in the future every righteous person has a canopy appropriate to him and that one may be “scorched” by another’s canopy, teaching that spiritual reward and perception are individually measured. Yevamos distinguishes Moshe’s clear lens from the other prophets’ non-clear lens. Maharsha applies the hierarchy in Sukkah to differing degrees of apprehension: the larger numbers truly receive the Shechinah, but not with the same clarity or unrestricted access. Rav Tzadok’s language of an “olam” or royal chamber should therefore not be flattened into a single experience. Every tzaddik may possess genuine light and a genuine chamber, while the title bnei aliyah in its strictest sense belongs to those whose entry is immediate and whose perception is exceptionally clear.
וּבַגְּמָרָא אָמַר ״רָאִיתִי״, דִּכְבָר נִסְתַּכֵּל וְרָאָה בְּאַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא הַמְּאִירָה שֶׁלּוֹ בִּבְנֵי עֲלִיָּה
And in the Gemara he said "I have seen," because he had already gazed and perceived through his luminous mirror (aspaklaria ha-me'irah) into the men of ascent;
וְאַף שֶׁלֹּא הִסְתַּכֵּל לִרְאוֹת כַּמָּה הֵם, דַּהֲרֵי אָמַר ״אִם וְכוּלֵיהּ״, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עַל בְּנוֹ שֶׁהָיָה עִמּוֹ בְּצַוְותָּא תָּמִיד כְּבָר רָאָה וְיָדַע שֶׁהוּא מִבְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה

and although he had not gazed to determine how many they were, for behold he said "if, etc.," nevertheless regarding his son who was constantly in his company, he had already seen and known that he was among the men of ascent;
וְעַל כֵּן סִיֵּים בִּבְ׳ דִּכְבָר יָדַע שֶׁבְּאוֹתוֹ הַדּוֹר יֵשׁ ב׳ וַדַּאי מִבְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה
and therefore he concluded with two, for he already knew that in that generation there were certainly two among the men of ascent.
וּלְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ הַגְּדוֹלָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ אֶלָּא מִי שֶׁהוּא צַדִּיק יְסוֹד עוֹלָם שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם הַבְּרִית בְּפֹעַל מִיהַת מִיָּמָיו בְּאֵיזֶה חֵטְא

And to this exalted rung none can attain except one who is a righteous foundation of the world who never in his days blemished the Covenant in actual deed through any sin.835Mishlei 10:25; Sanhedrin 93b; Kisvei Rav Tzadok - “the righteous person is the foundation of the world” and covenantal yesod: The verse contrasts the wicked person swept away by the storm with “the tzaddik, an everlasting foundation.” Chazal repeatedly understand the righteous as sustaining the world, while the language of yesod also carries the covenantal meaning developed throughout this work: the power of life, continuity, and faithful transmission. Rav Tzadok does not claim that every ordinary failure removes a person from the category of tzaddik. Here he defines the exceptional threshold for the innermost bnei aliyah: the foundation itself must never have been actively severed. This explains why the discussion moves immediately from Rashbi’s world-sustaining rank to Adam’s blemish of the covenant. The issue is not whether Adam repented or was forgiven, but whether the original foundation remained entirely unbroken.
וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, שֶׁאָמְרוּ [סַנְהֶדְרִין ל״ח עַמּוּד ב׳] מִקְּרָא דְּ״עָבְרוּ בְרִית״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ו:ז) שֶׁהָיָה מָשׁוּךְ בְּעָרְלָתוֹ
And Adam HaRishon, concerning whom they expounded [in Sanhedrin 38b] from the verse "they like Adam have transgressed the covenant" (Hoshea 6:7) that he extended his foreskin,
דְּעַל יְדֵי עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ בְּחֵטְא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לִידִיעַת רַע וְהַרְגָּשַׁת תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית פָּגַם הַבְּרִית, גּוֹרַשׁ מִגַּן עֵדֶן

for through the Serpent's instigation in the sin of the Tree of Knowledge, whereby he arrived at the consciousness of evil and the sensation of bodily lust, he blemished the Covenant, and was banished from Gan Eden;836Sanhedrin 38b; Hoshea 6:7; Zohar, Bereishis 43:434; Pri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1 - Adam “drew his foreskin” as a covenantal rupture: The Gemara derives from “they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant” that Adam was described as one who drew or extended the foreskin. The Zohar explains the phrase spiritually: he separated the holy covenant from its proper place, abandoned it, and attached himself to the side of orlah through the serpent’s persuasion. Pri Tzadik identifies the same act as the first blemish of the covenant, joined to the first deviation toward denial and concealment from Hashem. Rav Tzadok is therefore not asserting a merely anatomical event. He reads Chazal’s phrase as the inner meaning of the Tree-of-Knowledge sin: bodily desire became self-conscious and autonomous, and the life-force that should have remained transparently bound to Divine purpose became mixed with the serpent’s will.837Cf. Sanhedrin 38b — the source R’ Tzadok cites regarding Adam: among the teachings that Adam “was a heretic” / “drew back his foreskin [moshech b’orlaso]” the Gemara adduces the verse of Hoshea 6:7, “and they, like Adam, transgressed the covenant” — read as a blemish of the covenant (bris milah), which R’ Tzadok links to the sensation of bodily desire that entered through the sin of the Tree of Knowledge.838Eruvin 18b; Rashi ad loc.; Machshavot Charutz 15:4 - Adam’s 130 years of fasting, separation, and involuntary emission: R’ Meir calls Adam “a great chasid”: when he saw that death had been decreed through him, he fasted, separated from Chavah, and wore fig-leaf restraints for 130 years. The Gemara nevertheless states that destructive beings issued from seed emitted involuntarily. The passage is essential to Rav Tzadok’s argument. Adam’s teshuvah was authentic, prolonged, and severe, and the remaining occurrence is explicitly described as oness rather than chosen indulgence. Machshavot Charutz adds that after this period Adam returned to Chavah and fathered Sheis, repairing the world’s foundation through holy continuity. Even so, the involuntary residue showed that the serpent’s bodily admixture had not yet been restored to the untouched state preceding the sin.
וְהוּשְׂמוּ הַכְּרוּבִים וְלַהַט וְגוֹמֵר ״לִשְׁמֹר אֶת דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג:כד)
and the Cherubim and the flaming sword were placed "to keep the way of the Tree of Life" (Bereishis 3:24),
דְּגַם אַחַר כָּל הַתְּשׁוּבָה וְתַעֲנִיּוֹת ק״ל שָׁנָה וּבִפְרִישָׁה מֵאִשָּׁה וְהַתַּאֲווֹת, לֹא יָכוֹל לְתַקֵּן שֶׁיּוּכַל לָשׁוּב לְגַן עֵדֶן וְלֶאֱכוֹל מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים לִזְכּוֹת לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם

for even after all the repentance, the 130 years of fasts, and the abstention from his wife and desires, he could not rectify enough to return to Gan Eden and eat from the Tree of Life to merit eternal life;839Bereishis 3:22-24; Rashi, Ramban, and Sforno; Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 20:1 - the guarded road to the Tree of Life: The Torah explicitly joins eating from the Tree of Life with living forever and places the keruvim and revolving flame to guard its road after Adam’s expulsion. The classical meforshim explain that immortality while evil remains mixed into the person would perpetuate the damaged condition; removal from Eden therefore protects the order of repair, not merely a physical location. Pri Tzadik identifies the first tablets and Torah in its pure engraving with the Tree of Life, freedom from the yetzer, and freedom from death. After the sin, the heart must first be carved and purified. Rav Tzadok’s conclusion here follows that structure: profound teshuvah can restore holiness and life, but literal return to the original Edenic body requires the final removal of the mixture introduced by the serpent.
כִּי זוּהֲמָא זוֹ מִשֶּׁנִּקְלְטָה בַּגּוּף אֵין לָהּ תַּקָּנָה אֶלָּא קְבוּרָה וְשֶׁיָּשׁוּב אֶל הֶעָפָר כְּשֶׁהָיָה:

because this defilement (zuhama), once absorbed into the physical body, has no remedy except burial, that he return to the dust as he was.840Shabbos 146a; Bereishis Rabbah 12:6; Kesubos 77b; Resisei Layla 54:12 - burial, the serpent’s contamination, and rare bodily entry into Gan Eden: Chazal describe the serpent as introducing a zuhama into humanity and list life, radiance, stature, and other gifts among the qualities lost through Adam and destined for restoration with redemption. Rav Tzadok interprets burial and return to dust as part of that purification: the present composite body is dissolved before its perfected reconstruction. This is a mystical account of spiritual embodiment, not a medical claim. Kesubos presents R’ Yehoshua ben Levi’s bodily entrance into Gan Eden as a singular exception achieved through extraordinary Torah and self-sacrifice, and even there Rashbi tests his rank by asking whether a rainbow appeared in his days. Resisei Layla emphasizes that permanent removal of the yetzer belongs to the future completion; present revelations are exceptional anticipations of that final state.

items.h: The theme: The cessation of defilement at Mount Sinai and the spiritual lineage of Yaakov versus Esav and Yishmael. At Sinai, Israel’s defilement ceased (paskah zuhamasan, Shabbos 146a), an achievement perfected in Yaakov Avinu whose bed was flawless and who never tasted death. In contrast, Esav and Yishmael inherit the root of the Serpent’s defilement—the Cherubim and the flaming sword that guard the Tree of the Torah. These represent the two gates of the heart: murder (the flaming sword, Esav) and adultery/wasteful emission (the perverted Cherubim, Yishmael). While Yishmael personally repented through Avraham’s prayer, his descendants remain inherently uncircumcised in flesh and spirit.

p: וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁעָמְדוּ עַל הַר סִינַי פָּסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שַׁבָּת קמ״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳], וּלְחַד מַאן דְּאָמַר שָׁם פָּסַק מִימוֹת יַעֲקֹב
And the Children of Israel who stood at Mount Sinai, their defilement ceased, as they stated [in Shabbos 146a], and according to one authority there it ceased from the days of Yaakov;
וְאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, כִּי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם פָּסְקָה מִמֶּנּוּ הַזּוּהֲמָא לְגַמְרֵי דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא מֵת

and these and those are the words of the Living God, for from Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, the defilement ceased entirely, wherefore he did not die;841Shabbos 146a: “When the serpent came upon Chavah he injected into her a pollution [zuhama]; Israel, who stood at Mount Sinai — their pollution ceased.” The source for the se’if’s cessation of the serpent’s filth at Sinai.842Cf. Shabbos 146a — the source R’ Tzadok cites: “when the serpent came upon Chavah, he cast pollution [zuhama] into her; [when] Israel stood at Mount Sinai, their pollution ceased; the gentiles, who did not stand at Mount Sinai, their pollution did not cease.” The dispute R’ Tzadok references (that it ceased “from the days of Yaakov”) reflects the view that the Patriarch’s descendants were already prepared for this cleansing, realized in actuality at Sinai.843Shabbos 146a; Taanis 5b; Pri Tzadik, Pidyon Haben 1:1 — Yaakov’s purification and Sinai’s national actualization: Shabbos records two formulations. One teaches that the serpent’s pollution ceased from Israel at Sinai; R’ Abba bar Kahana says that it had already ceased after three generations, when Yaakov fathered twelve tribes “in whom there was no blemish.” Taanis adds, “Yaakov Avinu did not die,” deriving his continuing life from the life of his seed. Pri Tzadik explicitly reconciles the views in the manner used here: Yaakov himself attained the condition of Adam before the corruption, and his complete family established the holy preparedness of Jewish offspring; at Sinai that potential became an actual national state, extending through the whole people. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “these and these are the words of the living God” therefore distinguishes personal root, inherited readiness, and collective realization rather than treating the two traditions as contradictory.

וְעַל כֵּן בְּזַרְעוֹ לֹא הָיָה שׁוּם דֹּפִי, הַיְינוּ שֶׁכּוּלָּם מוּכָנִים וּמְעוּתָּדִים גַּם כֵּן לְהַגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת פְּסִיקַת הַזּוּהֲמָא, וְזָכוּ לָהּ בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת כֵּן בְּפֹעַל בְּכָל הָאוּמָּה

and therefore in his seed there was no blemish, meaning that all of them were primed and destined likewise to attain the cessation of defilement, meriting it at the Giving of the Torah to be realized in practice throughout the entire nation.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק הוֹלִידוּ עֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִיפָּסֵק מֵהֶם כְּלָל

This was not so with Avraham and Yitzchak, who fathered Esav and Yishmael, the root of defilement that can never cease from them at all;844Sifrei Devarim 343:6; Kometz HaMinchah 2:14 and 2:79 — the Torah offered to the nations and Rav Tzadok’s Esav–Yishmael pairing: Sifrei depicts Hashem offering the Torah to the nations. Esav refuses “You shall not murder,” citing the sword as his inherited way; Ammon and Moav refuse “You shall not commit adultery”; Yishmael refuses “You shall not steal,” citing his ancestral brigandage. Rav Tzadok follows an additional Zoharic tradition preserved in Kometz HaMinchah: Seir is confronted with murder and Paran with adultery, so Esav and Yishmael embody the two distorted “arms” of the false world—aggressive force and self-serving desire. Kometz HaMinchah explains that these are corruptions of true gevurah and chesed. The present se’if therefore should not be read as quoting the Sifrei’s allocation verbatim; it develops the Zoharic mapping used consistently in Rav Tzadok’s own writings.
דְּעַל כֵּן כְּשֶׁהֶחֱזִיר עֲלֵיהֶם הַתּוֹרָה לֹא רָצוּ לְקַבֵּל וְאָמְרוּ: ״מַה כְּתִיב בָּהּ? לֹא תִרְצַח, לֹא תִנְאָף״
wherefore when He offered the Torah to them (Avodah Zarah 2b), they refused to accept it, asking: "What is written in it? 'You shall not murder,' 'You shall not commit adultery'";
שֶׁהֵם ב׳ שָׁרְשֵׁי כֹּחוֹת הַיֵּצֶר הַיּוֹשֵׁב עַל ב׳ מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב, וְהֵם שָׁרְשָׁם בְּב׳ כֹּחוֹת הָרָע הַלָּלוּ

which are the two root powers of the inclination dwelling at the two entrances of the heart, their essence rooted in these two evil forces.845Berachos 61a; Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim 14:1 — the yetzer between the two openings of the heart: Rav says that the evil inclination resembles a fly and sits “between the two openings of the heart.” The Gemara supplies the image but does not identify those two openings with particular sins. Rav Tzadok interprets the divided heart through the paired roots of jealousy/aggression and desire: murder is the false form of gevurah, while adultery and uncontrolled gratification are the false form of chesed. Peri Tzadik adds that the yetzer can even appear on the right, presenting itself as if it were counseling good. The English wording “two chambers” reflects the heart’s two-sided structure, but the cited Bavli’s exact expression is “two openings.”
וְהֵם ״הַכְּרֻבִים וְלַהַט הַחֶרֶב״ הַשּׁוֹמְרִים דֶּרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים, הִיא הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁלֹּא יִגַּע בָּהֶם מִי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ זוּהֲמַת נָחָשׁ הַקַּדְמוֹנִי

And they are "the Cherubim and the flame of the sword" that guard the way of the Tree of Life—which is the Torah—preventing anyone possessing the root defilement of the Primordial Serpent from touching them:
שֶׁהוּא נִדְבָּק אָז בַּכְּרוּבִים שֶׁהֵם כִּמְעָר אִישׁ וְלִוְיוֹת

for such a person is bound to the perverted Cherubim which resemble the embrace of a man and his consort (Yoma 54a);846Bereishis 3:24; Mishlei 3:18; Sukkah 5b; Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 20:1 — the keruvim, the revolving flame, and Torah as the Tree of Life: After Adam’s expulsion, the Torah places the keruvim and the flaming, revolving sword to guard the road to the Tree of Life. Mishlei calls Torah “a Tree of Life to those who grasp it,” and Pri Tzadik identifies Torah engraved upon the heart with that life-giving state. Sukkah explains the name keruv as ke-ravya, “like a child,” because in Babylonia a child was called ravya; this is the basis of Rav Tzadok’s association with youthful impulse and “sin of youth.” Rav Tzadok then interiorizes the Edenic guardians: unrefined desire and murderous anger stand at the entrance to Torah’s eternal life. The verse itself describes the guarding beings; the identification of their negative counterpart with these two inner powers is Rav Tzadok’s symbolic synthesis.

וּבִקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא יִחוּד קֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וּשְׁכִינְתֵּיהּ וּדְבֵיקוּת כְּנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל בַּאֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְאַתֶּם הַדְּבֵקִים [בַּה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם] חַיִּים [כֻּלְּכֶם הַיּוֹם]״ (דְּבָרִים ד:ד), דְּזוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם

whereas in holiness, this represents the supernal union of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and the cleaving of the Congregation of Israel to their Father in Heaven, as it is said: "But you that did cleave unto the Lord your God are alive every one of you this day" (Devarim 4:4), meriting thereby eternal life.
וְ״זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה עָשָׂה הָאֱלֹהִים״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:יד), שֶׁנִּדְבָּק בְּסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא עַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה וְנִיאוּף, וְהֵם ב׳ קְלִיפּוֹת הַטְּמֵאוֹת

And "God has made even the one over against the other" (Koheles 7:14), for one cleaves to the Other Side (Sitra Achra) through wasteful emission and adultery, which are the two totally impure husks;847Devarim 4:4; Koheles 7:14; Nefesh HaChaim I:6 — holy attachment and its opposing counterfeit: “You who cleave to Hashem your God are all alive today” makes deveikus the source of life. “This corresponding to that God made” teaches that the created order contains opposing structures. Rav Tzadok applies that symmetry to covenantal attachment: holiness joins Knesses Yisrael to Hashem and His Shechinah, while misuse of the same life-force produces attachment to the opposing side. Nefesh HaChaim similarly explains that human deeds attach a person and the worlds either to holiness or, God forbid, to impurity. The full language of Divine unification is kabbalistic; the verses establish life through attachment and the structural principle of opposition, while Rav Tzadok supplies their specific covenantal application.848Niddah 13a — wasted seed, bloodshed, and the severity of misdirected life-force: The Gemara says that deliberate emission of seed in vain is punishable by death at the hand of Heaven, compares it to shedding blood, and in another formulation to idolatry. Its bloodshed comparison rests on the destruction of potential descendants. Rav Tzadok uses this severe rabbinic equation to join the two apparent opposites discussed here: unbounded desire and murderous destruction both detach life-force from its intended holy continuity. The Gemara does not name “two impure kelipos”; that terminology is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic organization of the rabbinic moral parallels.

וּמִילּוּי תַּאֲווֹת בְּהֶיתֵּר שֶׁקּוֹרֵא לוֹ רַמְבַּ״ן [רֵישׁ פָּרָשַׁת קְדוֹשִׁים] ״נָבָל בִּרְשׁוּת הַתּוֹרָה״ וְשֶׁעַל זֶה נִצְטַוּוּ ״קְדֹשִׁים תִּהְיוּ״ (וַיִּקְרָא י״ט:ב׳) הוּא מִקְּלִיפַּת נוֹגַהּ כִּידוּעַ

while indulging physical desires in permitted matters—termed by the Ramban [Vayikra 19:2] "a scoundrel with the Torah's permission," regarding which they were commanded "You shall be holy"—stems from the husk of Kelipas Nogah as is known.849Ramban on Vayikra 19:2 — “a scoundrel with the Torah’s permission” and sanctifying what is permitted: Ramban explains that “You shall be holy” requires more than avoiding explicitly forbidden relations and foods. A person can remain technically within permitted conduct yet become consumed by marital indulgence, meat, wine, or vulgar speech—a naval birshus haTorah. The Torah therefore commands restraint, cleanliness, and measured use even of what is allowed. Rav Tzadok accepts that ethical category and adds the kabbalistic classification of kelipas nogah: permitted desire is mixed and capable of elevation, unlike intrinsically forbidden impurity, but when pursued for itself it still blocks complete holiness. “Kelipas nogah” is Rav Tzadok’s explanatory framework, not Ramban’s own term.
וּכְרוּבִים, דְּהַיְינוּ כְּרַבְיָא, בְּיֵצֶר לֵב הָרַע מִנְּעוּרָיו וְחַטַּאת נְעוּרִים
And the Cherubim—having the faces of youths (k'ravya, Chagigah 13b)—allude to the evil inclination of the heart from youth and the sins of youth;
וּמִי שֶׁנָּקִי מִזֶּה הוּא נִדְבָּק בְּלַהַט הַחֶרֶב שֶׁהוּא הָרְצִיחָה וּשְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים וְקִנְאָה וָכַעַס
and one who is clean of lust may yet become ensnared in the flaming sword, which is murder, bloodshed, jealousy, and anger.
וְעֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל שָׁרְשָׁם בְּאֵלֶּה, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה לֹא יָכְלוּ לְהַגִּיעַ לְדֶרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים וּלְקַבֵּל הַתּוֹרָה, כִּי כָּל הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים וַאֲפִילּוּ מוּלֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

And Esav and Yishmael have their root in these evil traits, wherefore they could not attain the way of the Tree of Life nor receive the Torah, for all the gentiles are uncircumcised, even those among the nations who practice circumcision (Nedarim 31b);850Nedarim 31b — “circumcised” and “uncircumcised” as covenantal identities: The Mishnah rules that a vow concerning “the uncircumcised” follows covenantal identity rather than anatomy: an uncircumcised Jew is not included in that designation, while a physically circumcised member of the nations is. It proves that Scripture commonly calls the nations “uncircumcised.” Rav Tzadok employs this halachic language spiritually. Physical circumcision alone does not establish the inner state he is discussing; the decisive question is whether the person and lineage are rooted in the covenant’s holiness. The Mishnah states a rule of vow terminology and Israel’s covenantal name; Rav Tzadok extends it to his account of the serpent’s root and access to Torah’s Tree of Life.

וְרַק יִשְׁמָעֵאל עַצְמוֹ שֶׁנִּימּוֹל עַל יְדֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּבִרְצוֹת ה׳, זֶה שֶׁעָשָׂה תְּשׁוּבָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה, וְהוֹעִילָה לוֹ תְּפִלַּת אַבְרָהָם: ״לוּ יִשְׁמָעֵאל יִחְיֶה [לְפָנֶיךָ]״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ז:י״ח) — עָלָיו לְבַד

and only Yishmael personally who was circumcised by Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, with Divine favor, repented as the Sages stated (Bava Batra 16b), Avraham's prayer "Oh that Yishmael might live before You!" (Bereishis 17:18) availing for him alone;851Bereishis 17:18–20; Bava Basra 16b; Rashi on Bereishis 25:9 — Avraham’s prayer and Yishmael’s personal teshuvah: Avraham prayed, “Would that Yishmael live before You,” and Hashem answered that He had heard concerning Yishmael and would bless him, while reserving the covenant’s continuation for Yitzchak. Bava Basra teaches that Yishmael repented during Avraham’s lifetime, inferred from his allowing Yitzchak to precede him at Avraham’s burial; Rashi cites the same proof. Rav Tzadok therefore carefully singles out Yishmael himself from the collective root attributed here to his descendants. His circumcision, Avraham’s prayer, and his eventual submission to Yitzchak made personal teshuvah possible without transferring the covenantal election from Yitzchak.
אֲבָל כָּל זַרְעוֹ, אַף שֶׁנִּמּוֹלִים, הֵם עֲרֵלִים בֶּאֱמֶת כִּי שָׁרְשָׁם בָּרָע שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָעָרְלָה, כִּי כוּלָּם בְּשַׂר עָרְלָה דִּ״בְשַׂר חֲמוֹרִים בְּשָׂרָם״ (יְחֶזְקֵאל כ״ג:כ׳)

but all his descendants, even when circumcised, are truly uncircumcised because their root is in evil which is the root of the foreskin, being all flesh of foreskin, whose "flesh is as the flesh of donkeys" (Yechezkel 23:20);
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק ״שְׁבוּ לָכֶם פֹּה עִם הַחֲמוֹר״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית כ״ב:ה׳) דְּהוּא גַּם עַל יִשְׁמָעֵאל שֶׁהָיָה מִב׳ נְעָרָיו שֶׁעִמּוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה:

and as they expounded on the verse "Abide ye here with the donkey" (Bereishis 22:5), which applies likewise to Yishmael who was one of the two youths accompanying him, as the Sages of blessed memory stated (Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer, ch. 31).852R’ Tzadok — parallel (Yisrael Kedoshim §9): “For at Sinai the serpent’s pollution [zuhama] ceased from them; and according to one view, [it had already ceased] from the days of Yaakov.” Exactly the se’if: Israel who stood at Sinai — their pollution ceased.853Yechezkel 23:20; Bereishis 22:3–5 with Rashi; Yevamos 62a — “flesh of donkeys” and the two attendants at the Akeidah: Yechezkel uses the graphic phrase “whose flesh is the flesh of donkeys” in a prophetic denunciation of Yerushalayim’s lust for Egypt; Rav Tzadok borrows its imagery for uncontrolled bodily desire. At the Akeidah, Avraham told his attendants, “Remain here with the donkey.” Yevamos interprets the phrase in its legal discussion of a Canaanite slave as “a people comparable to a donkey,” meaning absence of ordinary lineage in that halachic context. Rashi, following Midrash, identifies Avraham’s two attendants as Yishmael and Eliezer. Rav Tzadok joins these separate texts homiletically. They are rabbinic and prophetic metaphors about covenant, lineage, and subjection to physicality—not a biological characterization of any contemporary ethnicity.

items.h: The theme: The distinction between the uncircumcised status of gentiles and the holy seed of Israel. Adam HaRishon was created circumcised; through free choice he allowed the yetzer’s defilement into his heart, extending his foreskin (meshukh b'orlaso) and becoming fully uncircumcised. This established the root for gentiles to be born uncircumcised. Conversely, Israel descends from Yaakov, who retained the pristine state of Adam before the sin, wherefore even an uncircumcised Israelite is legally designated "circumcised." Cain avoided bodily lust but clung to the flaming sword of murder; his imperfect repentance left a residue of defilement (keina d'msavuta). The Cherubim precede the flaming sword at the entrance to Gan Eden because evil originates in bodily desire before escalating into violence.

p: וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן נוֹלַד מָהוּל, דְּ״הָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כט)
And Adam HaRishon was born circumcised, for "God made man upright" (Koheles 7:29);
אֶלָּא שֶׁנִּיתַּן בּוֹ כֹּחַ הַבְּחִירָה לְהִתְפַּתּוֹת עַד שֶׁיַּכְנִיס זוּהֲמַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע לְלִבּוֹ וְיוּכַל לְהַמְשִׁיךְ עָרְלָתוֹ וְלִהְיוֹת עָרֵל
but he was endowed with the capacity of free choice to be seduced until he admitted the defilement of the yetzer hara into his heart, enabling him to draw his foreskin and become uncircumcised;
וְלֹא כְּמָהוּל הַמָּשׁוּךְ דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ לַחֲזוֹר וּלְמוּלוֹ אֶלָּא מִדְּרַבָּנָן מִשּׁוּם מַרְאִית הָעַיִן לְבַד
