and not like a circumcised man whose foreskin was artificially drawn, who does not biblically require recircumcision save rabbinically for appearances alone (Yevamos 72b);854Midrash Tanchuma, Noach 5; Koheles 7:29; Pri Tzadik, Tzav 7:1 and Shemos 4:1 — Adam created circumcised and upright: Midrash Tanchuma counts Adam among those created or born circumcised, while Koheles states that “God made man upright.” Pri Tzadik joins these teachings directly: Adam’s native condition was circumcised and holy; only through his free choice in eating from the Tree of Knowledge did a covering of foreskin become drawn over that holiness. In Shemos, Rav Tzadok adds that because this occurred within the six days of Creation, the defect entered the natural pattern of human birth, so Adam’s descendants were thereafter born uncircumcised. This is the closest internal parallel to the opening of the se’if. The Midrash establishes Adam’s original wholeness, and the verse establishes upright creation; the explanation that the foreskin signifies the serpent’s pollution and was transmitted as a birth-root is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
אֲבָל הוּא נַעֲשָׂה אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא עָרֵל גָּמוּר בְּהַמְשָׁכָה זוֹ
rather, after he sinned he became completely uncircumcised through this extension;
וּמִזֶּה נַעֲשָׂה שׁוֹרֶשׁ לְלֵידַת הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים שֶׁכּוּלָּם צֶאֱצָאֵי אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן

and from this was forged the root for the birth of gentiles as uncircumcised, all being descendants of Adam HaRishon.855Yevamos 72a; Nimukei Yosef on Yevamos 24a; Sefer HaChinuch 282 — the ordinary halachic status of a mashuch: Rav Huna teaches that a person who was circumcised and later appears uncircumcised because the skin was drawn forward remains circumcised by Torah law; the Sages treated him as uncircumcised because he looks like an arel. The Rishonim explain that the requirement to circumcise him again is rabbinic. Rav Tzadok deliberately contrasts that ordinary case with Adam. Adam had never fulfilled a commanded act of circumcision and then merely lost its appearance; rather, according to Rav Tzadok, he transformed his primordial, created wholeness into a genuine root of orlah through the sin itself. This distinction is conceptual and homiletic. It should not be read as a new practical halachic category beyond the laws stated in Yevamos and the poskim.856Sanhedrin 38b; Pri Tzadik, Tzav 7:1 — “Adam drew his foreskin” as a covenantal rupture: Sanhedrin includes the opinion that Adam HaRishon was moshuch be’orlaso, deriving it from “like Adam, they transgressed the covenant.” Commentators differ over the literal mechanics and meaning of that statement. Pri Tzadik reads it in the same spiritual sense as this se’if: Adam was created circumcised, but by choosing the Tree of Knowledge he drew over himself an orlah that concealed holiness; consequently, later human birth carried the defect. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “complete uncircumcised one” therefore describes the depth of the primordial covenantal rupture, not merely an anatomical observation. It explains why the ordinary rabbinic rule of a mashuch cannot exhaust the Aggadah’s meaning.
וְזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל צֶאֱצָאֵי יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שָׁרְשָׁם מִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁקּוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
Whereas the seed of Israel, descendants of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, have their root in the primal stature of Adam HaRishon prior to the sin, which Yaakov Avinu merited;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה בְּלֹא פְּסוֹלֶת, שֶׁגַּם עַרְלֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָאִים מוּלִים

and through this his bed was perfect without dross, so that even uncircumcised Israelites are legally termed "circumcised" (Nedarim 31b);857Nedarim 31b; Shabbos 146a; Taanis 5b; Pri Tzadik, Pidyon Haben 1:1 — Yaakov’s complete root and Israel’s covenantal name: Nedarim rules that “circumcised” and “uncircumcised” function as covenantal identities: even an uncircumcised Jew is included among the circumcised, while a physically circumcised gentile is included among the uncircumcised. Shabbos records that the serpent’s pollution ceased at Sinai, and another opinion places its cessation in Yaakov’s complete family; Taanis states that Yaakov did not die. Pri Tzadik reconciles these sources by distinguishing Yaakov’s personal return to the condition of Adam before the sin, the holy preparedness of his complete offspring, and the national actualization at Sinai. Se’if 45 applies that same structure: Israel’s covenantal identity is rooted in Yaakov’s restored Adamic root, even when an individual still lacks the physical mitzvah of milah.
וְהַגּוֹיִם בְּהֵיפֶךְ, שֶׁהֵם מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הָעָרְלָה וְהַזּוּהֲמָא שֶׁנִּקְלַט וְנִשְׁרַשׁ בּוֹ אַחַר הַחֵטְא
and gentiles are the reverse, stemming from the root of the foreskin and defilement absorbed and entrenched within him after the sin.
וְעַל כֵּן נִמְנַע מִמֶּנּוּ הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה לְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי לְבַטֵּל גְּזֵירַת הַמִּיתָה

Therefore complete repentance was withheld from him to rectify entirely so as to abolish the decree of death;858Bereishis 3:22–24; Bava Basra 17a; Shabbos 55b; Machshavos Charutz 20:13 — accepted teshuvah without annulment of death: After the sin, Adam is expelled lest he eat from the Tree of Life and live forever. Chazal identify exceptionally righteous people who died only through the serpent’s counsel, showing that Adam’s death-decree remained embedded in humanity even where no personal sin required death. Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains that Adam’s teshuvah was real but did not yet restore the untouched pre-sin condition or uproot the deepest bodily residue. Machshavos Charutz describes the completion of that repair as unfolding through David and ultimately Mashiach. Thus the se’if does not mean that Adam was denied forgiveness. “Complete teshuvah was withheld” means that his repentance did not cancel mortality or return the entire human root to its original immortality.
וְגַם אַחַר תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ הוֹצִיא זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה לְאוֹנְסוֹ וְהוֹלִיד רוּחִין, שֵׁדִין וְלִילִין
and even after his repentance he emitted seed wastefully through nocturnal accidents, fathering spirits, demons, and lilin;
וְזֶה מִצַּד שֶׁלֹּא נִטְהַר עֲדַיִין מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא דִּידִיעַת רַע וְהֶרְגֵּשׁ תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and this occurred because he had not yet been purified from the root defilement of knowing evil and physical bodily lust, as mentioned above;
וְזֶהוּ שְׁמִירַת הַכְּרוּבִים לְדֶרֶךְ עֵץ הַחַיִּים

and this is the guarding of the Cherubim over the way to the Tree of Life.859Eruvin 18b; Machshavos Charutz 15:10 and 20:13; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 15, Se’if 40 — Adam’s 130 years and involuntary emission: Eruvin teaches that during Adam’s 130 years of fasting, separation, and penitential discipline, destructive beings came from semen he emitted involuntarily. The same passage calls him a “great chasid,” making clear that the event was not presented as deliberate misconduct. Rav Tzadok uses this to distinguish culpability from spiritual condition: an involuntary event can reveal that the bodily root of desire has not yet been fully transformed, even where there is no conscious sinful thought. Machshavos Charutz links those years to the serpent’s corruption of generative power and to the long historical repair of the covenant. The present se’if continues the argument of Se’if 40. It does not classify an involuntary bodily event as a chosen sin; it treats it as evidence, within Rav Tzadok’s metaphysical framework, of an unfinished primordial purification.860Bereishis 3:24; Mishlei 3:18; Sukkah 5b — the keruvim and the guarded way to the Tree of Life: The Torah places the keruvim and the flaming, revolving sword at the entrance to Eden “to guard the way to the Tree of Life.” Mishlei identifies Torah as “a Tree of Life to those who grasp it.” Sukkah explains keruv as ke-ravya, “like a child,” supplying the linguistic basis for Rav Tzadok’s association with youthful impulse. Rav Tzadok reads the Edenic guardians inwardly: the residue of bodily desire blocks direct access to Torah’s immortal life, while the flaming sword represents the later development of destructive anger and bloodshed. The verses describe the guardians and the Tree; the mapping of desire and murder onto their order is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis, continued from Se’if 44.
וְקַיִן הָיָה נָקִי מִזֶּה, אֲבָל נִדְבַּק בְּלַהַט הַחֶרֶב וּרְצִיחָה
And Cain was pure from lust, but became bound to the flaming sword and murder;
וְגַם אַחַר תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ לֹא נִטְהַר מִזֶּה לְגַמְרֵי וְנִשְׁאַר ״קֵינָא דִּמְסָאֲבוּתָא״ כַּנּוֹדָע, כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא לֹא יָכוֹל לְסַלֵּק

and even after his repentance he was not purified from this completely, remaining a "nest of defilement" (keina d'msavuta) as is known, because he could not banish the root of defilement;861Bereishis Rabbah 22:13; Vayikra Rabbah 10:5 — Cain’s teshuvah and its partial effect: Bereishis Rabbah relates that Cain emerged from judgment rejoicing and told Adam, “I performed teshuvah and reached a compromise.” Vayikra Rabbah explains that according to one view teshuvah accomplished half: Cain had been sentenced to be both na and nad, but after repentance only part of the decree remained. These sources establish both the reality and the limitation of his teshuvah. Rav Tzadok therefore does not deny that Cain repented. His point is that the deep root expressed in murder was not wholly purified, just as Adam’s repentance did not annul death. The Midrash’s “compromise” provides the precise background for the se’if’s distinction between accepted repentance and complete uprooting of a primordial defect.862Tomer Devorah 4:2; Zoharic tradition of “kina d’masavusa”; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 8 and 13 — Cain as a “nest of impurity” and the power of teshuvah: Tomer Devorah quotes the kabbalistic description of Cain as kina d’masavusa, a “nest of impurity,” rooted in the serpent’s side, yet insists that he was not beyond repair: “If you improve, you will be elevated.” The expression denotes a concentration of impure powers, not the absence of free choice. Rav Tzadok’s Shabbos Shuvah teachings analyze Cain’s “I repented and compromised” as a revelation of how far teshuvah can reach, even when the repentance is incomplete or accompanied by suffering. Se’if 45 holds both truths together: Cain’s teshuvah was received, but the root of anger and murder was not yet wholly transformed. This is why Rav Tzadok can cite Cain as a penitent while still describing a residue of kina d’masavusa.

וְגַם זֶה מִכְּלַל שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״רַע״ בַּעֲוֹן דְּהוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן כְּאִלּוּ שׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים, וּמִזֶּה נִמְשַׁךְ אַחַר כָּךְ בְּקַיִן לְשׁוֹפֵךְ דָּמִים

and this too belongs to the root of the yetzer hara called "evil" in the iniquity of wasteful emission—which is likewise compared to shedding blood—and from this it extended subsequently in Cain into literal bloodshed;863Niddah 13a — deliberate waste of seed compared with bloodshed, and the limits of the comparison: Niddah speaks in severe terms about deliberate emission of seed in vain and records the comparison “as though he sheds blood,” because potential life is destroyed. Rav Tzadok uses that equation structurally: the root of misdirected generative desire can unfold into the opposite pole of actual bloodshed, as seen later in Cain. The Gemara’s statement concerns deliberate conduct. Adam’s emission in Eruvin is explicitly described as involuntary, so the two passages must not be collapsed into a single judgment of culpability. Rav Tzadok is tracing a common spiritual root between distorted desire and destruction; he is not assigning the legal or moral status of intentional bloodshed to an involuntary event.
וְעַל כֵּן הַכְּרוּבִים קוֹדְמִים וְאַחַר כָּךְ לַהַט הַחֶרֶב, כִּי הַתְחָלַת הָרָע הוּא בְּהַרְגָּשַׁת הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ חֵטְא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת בִּידִיעַת הָרָע:

wherefore the Cherubim precede and only afterward appears the flaming sword, for the inception of evil lies in lustful sensation, which is the root of the sin of the Tree of Knowledge in the consciousness of evil.864R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §1): “This depends on the power of choice within him, in which the evil inclination does not leave him [at rest] — for ‘God made man upright,’ [yet placed in him the power of choice].” Exactly the se’if: Adam was born circumcised and “upright,” only that the power of choice was placed in him.865Bereishis 3:6 and 4:8; Kometz HaMinchah 2:14 and 2:79 — desire before murder and the two corrupted powers: The Torah first describes the Tree as desirable to the eyes and then, in the next generation, records Cain’s murder of Hevel. Rav Tzadok sees an ordered development: self-directed desire is the first entry of evil into conscious human experience; jealousy and murderous anger are its hardened external consequence. In Kometz HaMinchah he repeatedly pairs adultery or uncontrolled desire with murder as the two primary corruptions associated with Yishmael and Esav, distorted forms of chesed and gevurah. The order of keruvim before the flaming sword therefore mirrors the order of the Torah’s narrative. This is a theological and psychological reading of the sequence, not a claim that every experience of desire mechanically produces violence.

items.h: The theme: The esoteric meaning of "And now, lest he put forth his hand and take also of the Tree of Life" (Bereishis 3:22). In Bereishis Rabbah 21:6, "and now" (v'atah) indicates that Hashem opened an entrance to repentance. R' Tzadok asks: if Adam repented, why was he forbidden from the Tree of Life? The Torah's redundant phrasing—"put forth his hand" (yishlach yado) and "also" (gam)—indicates that repentance arouses a longing to grasp the esoteric depths of the Torah (penimiyus ha-Torah). However, if one enters the mystical secrets while bodily lust still stains the heart, the Torah turns into a deadly poison (sama d'mosa), as occurred to Acher who "cut the shoots" (kitzetz ba-netios) and the followers of Shabbetai Zvi. Only when man attains the unblemished Divine Image (tzelem Elokim)—realized in Yaakov Avinu whose likeness is engraved upon the Throne of Glory—can he fuse directly with the Tree of Life.

p: וְנֶאֱמַר: ״וְעַתָּה פֶּן [יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וְלָקַח גַּם מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְאָכַל וָחַי לְעֹלָם]״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ג:כב)
And it is said: "And now, lest he put forth his hand, and take also of the tree of life, and eat, and live for ever" (Bereishis 3:22);
וְאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ״א] שֶׁפָּתַח לוֹ לִתְשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאֵין ״פֶּן״ אֶלָּא לָאו, אָמַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יִשְׁלַח וְכוּלֵיהּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 21:6] that He opened for him an entrance to repentance, etc., and "lest" (pen) means "no"—the Holy One, blessed be He, said: shall he put forth, etc., see there.
וְהַדָּבָר זָר לִהְיוֹת מְפַסְּקָא קְרָאֵי, וְלוֹמַר דְּמִלַּת ״פֶּן״ שֶׁבָּאֶמְצַע הוּא תְּשׁוּבַת אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן עַל זֶה, דָּבָר שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַכְנִיסוֹ בְּמַשְׁמַע הַכָּתוּב

And it is strange to divide the verse, suggesting that the word "lest" in the middle constitutes Adam HaRishon's response refusing repentance, which cannot be reconciled with the plain text;866Bereishis Rabbah 21:6: “‘And now, lest he send forth his hand [and take also from the Tree of Life]’ — R’ Abba bar Kahana said: [this] teaches that the Holy One opened for him a door of teshuvah. ‘And now [ve-atah]’ — there is no ‘ve-atah’ except an expression of teshuvah, as it is stated (Devarim 10:12): ‘and now, Israel, what does Hashem ask of you, but to fear.’ And he [Adam] says: ‘pen [lest],’ and there is no ‘pen’ except a negative — the Holy One said: ‘let him send forth his hand and eat also from the Tree of Life’ — I wonder! — ‘and if he eats he lives forever.’ Therefore, ‘and Hashem God sent him out from the Garden of Eden.’ Once He sent him out, He began to lament over him and say, ‘behold, the man was like one of us.’” And see [the editor’s note] on p. 15 there, where he also explains this midrash.
וְגַם הוּא נֶגֶד הַבָּרַיְיתָא דְּעֵירוּבִין הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל שֶׁעָשָׂה בֶּאֱמֶת תְּשׁוּבָה ק״ל שָׁנָה, וְכֵן הוּא גַּם בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כ״ב], וְעַיֵּין לְעֵיל [סִימָן ג׳]

and it also contradicts the Baraisa in Eruvin (18b) mentioned above that he truly repented 130 years, and so it is in Bereishis Rabbah, see [above, Siman 3];867Eruvin 18b; Bereishis Rabbah 22:13; Takanas HaShavin §3; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 8, 13, and 17 — Adam’s actual teshuvah and the meaning of incomplete restoration: Eruvin calls Adam a “great chasid” and records that, after recognizing that death entered the world through him, he fasted, separated from Chavah, and wore fig-leaf belts for 130 years. Bereishis Rabbah likewise depicts him learning the power of teshuvah from Kayin and then reciting “Mizmor shir le-yom haShabbos.” Rav Tzadok analyzes these traditions repeatedly: Adam certainly repented, but the repentance did not yet restore the entire human root to its untouched pre-sin condition or erase mortality and the bodily residue described in the surrounding se’ifim. Thus the apparent contradiction is only verbal. The Midrash’s “opening to teshuvah” and Eruvin’s 130 years establish genuine repentance; Rav Tzadok’s phraseology here concerns the difference between accepted teshuvah and total primordial repair.
אֲבָל וַדַּאי אֵין מִקְרָא יוֹצֵא מִפְּשׁוּטוֹ שֶׁהַכֹּל דִּבְרֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
rather, a verse never departs from its plain meaning (Shabbos 63a), the entire statement being the words of the Blessed Name.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהַדָּבָר קָשֶׁה: מֵאַחַר דְּפָתַח לִתְשׁוּבָה, אֵיךְ אָמַר ״פֶּן יִשְׁלַח וְגוֹמֵר״, וְאִם יָשׁוּב לָמָּה לֹא יִשְׁלַח וְגוֹמֵר, וּתְשׁוּבָה מְבַטֶּלֶת הַגְּזֵירָה

But the matter remains difficult: once He opened the door to repentance, why did He say "lest he put forth his hand, etc."? If he repents, why should he not put forth his hand, since repentance annuls the decree?!868Shabbos 63a; Ramban on Bereishis 3:22 — preserving peshat while uncovering the concealed meaning: Shabbos states the interpretive rule that “a verse never departs from its plain meaning.” Ramban, commenting directly on “and now, lest he send forth his hand,” emphasizes that the Garden, the trees, and the threatened acquisition of eternal life possess a real revealed meaning, while also insisting that the episode has a lofty concealed dimension and that “the overt and the concealed are both true.” Rav Tzadok adopts precisely this two-level method. He rejects a reading that breaks the verse into unrelated speakers and first preserves the straightforward divine statement; only afterward does he explain why Chazal placed the opening to teshuvah beside the guarding of the Tree of Life. His reading is therefore an added inner layer, not a replacement of the verse’s grammar or historical sense.869Vayikra Rabbah 10:5; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 8:6 — teshuvah can annul a decree: Vayikra Rabbah records differing formulations of the power of teshuvah and prayer. One view learns from Kayin that repentance removed half of the decree of being “na va-nad”; another teaches that teshuvah can annul the entire decree, and the Midrash later declares explicitly that its power can cancel both a decree and an oath, as illustrated by Yechonyah. Shir HaShirim Rabbah repeats this principle. Rav Tzadok’s question—if Adam truly returned, why should the decree still bar him from the Tree of Life?—is therefore grounded in an established teaching of Chazal, not merely in abstract logic. His answer distinguishes ordinary cancellation of punishment from the deeper question of whether the inner bodily root has become fit for immortal Torah-life.

אֲבָל דִּקְדּוּק לְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב שָׁם: ״פֶּן יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ וְלָקַח גַּם מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְגוֹמֵר״, דְּמִלַּת ״יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ״ וּמִלַּת ״גַּם״ יִתּוּר לָשׁוֹן, וַהֲוָה לֵיהּ לוֹמַר ״פֶּן יִקַּח מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים״

However, by scrutinizing the wording of Scripture: "lest he put forth his hand and take also from the Tree of Life," the words "put forth his hand" and "also" are redundant, for it should simply have said "lest he take from the Tree of Life"!
מְבוֹאָר דְּהַכַּוָּונָה בַּמַּה שֶּׁהִסְמִיךְ זֶה לְ״וְעַתָּה״, שֶׁהוּא הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תְּשׁוּבָה

It is clear that the intent of juxtaposing this to "and now" (v'atah)—which represents the arousal of repentance—is this:870Bereishis 3:22–24; Ramban ad loc. — why the Tree of Life was guarded after Adam gained choice: Ramban explains that the Tree of Life was created to grant everlasting life to those who ate from it. Had Adam eaten after the sin, the decree of death would have been nullified entirely or its appointed time would have been displaced. Before the sin Adam did only what he was commanded and did not require the tree; afterward, once moral choice had entered him, the tree had to be guarded. Rav Tzadok reads the Torah’s expanded wording—“send forth his hand” and “also”—as indicating more than accidental eating: an awakened penitent might actively reach toward the highest source of life before his inner condition had been fully repaired. Ramban supplies the literal and metaphysical stakes; Rav Tzadok explains the sequence as a warning against grasping an eternal attainment prematurely.
דְּלוּלֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה וַדַּאי יוֹסִיף לְהִשְׁתַּקֵּעַ בָּרָע וְלֹא יִקְרַב לְעֵץ הַחַיִּים כְּלָל
without repentance, he would certainly sink deeper into evil and would never draw near to the Tree of Life at all;
רַק כְּשֶׁיִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב, אָז אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּקְרַב לְעֵץ הַחַיִּים, וְהוּא הַשָּׂגַת פְּנִימִיּוּת הַתּוֹרָה

only when he awakens to repent is it possible that he will draw near to the Tree of Life, which is the attainment of the inner mysteries of the Torah (penimiyus ha-Torah).871Mishlei 3:18; Tanna DeVei Eliyahu Rabbah 1; Pri Tzadik, Ha’azinu 2 and 13; Machshavos Charutz 15:8 — the Tree of Life as Torah: Mishlei calls wisdom “a Tree of Life to those who grasp it,” and Tanna DeVei Eliyahu identifies the Tree of Life with Torah. Pri Tzadik repeatedly uses this identification for both Written and Oral Torah. Machshavos Charutz places Torah at the center of the Garden as the life-source from which all its trees draw nourishment; it further explains that after Adam’s sin even the human reception of Torah became entangled with the categories of the Tree of Knowledge—pure and impure, permitted and forbidden, valid and invalid. Rav Tzadok’s “inner dimension of Torah” therefore means the Torah as it is apprehended at its unmingled life-root, before the learner’s unresolved desire colors the knowledge. The primary sources identify Torah with life; the distinction between outer clarification and inner, Edenic apprehension is Rav Tzadok’s developed framework.872Takanas HaShavin 6:77; Kometz HaMinchah 2:77; Divrei Soferim 36:3 — Torah-life, the serpent, and the right manner of grasping it: Elsewhere in Takanas HaShavin, Rav Tzadok states that the guarded Tree of Life is Torah and that Israel’s souls, having accepted Torah at Sinai, are attached to eternal life even though its full revelation is hidden in this world. Kometz HaMinchah identifies Yaakov with the Tree of Life and explains that Torah joins Israel to the Holy One; the same Torah is an elixir of life to those who “turn right” in it, but can become the serpent and an elixir of death when approached from the distorted side. Divrei Soferim describes Yaakov as attached to the living God and as one who “did not die” because he partook of the Tree of Life, Torah. These passages form the immediate internal background for Se’if 46’s movement from Adam’s guarded access to Yaakov’s perfected access.
וְיָדוּעַ דְּמִי שֶׁאֵין לְבָבוֹ מְנוּקֶּה מִתַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת, אִם יִרְצֶה לִיכָּנֵס לִפְנִימִיּוּת הַחָכְמָה וְהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁאֵין שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹ, נַעֲשֵׂית לוֹ סַמָּא דְּמוֹתָא

And it is known that one whose heart is not purified from physical desires, if he seeks to enter into the inner wisdom and mystical perception that does not belong to him, it becomes for him a deadly poison (sama d'mosa);
כְּ״אַחֵר״ שֶׁקִּיצֵּץ בַּנְּטִיעוֹת, וְאָמְרוּ [בַּחֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד ב׳] לְפִי שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה נָקִי אַגַּב אִימֵּיהּ, שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ אֵיזֶה רַע בַּשּׁוֹרֶשׁ שֶׁלֹּא נִתְנַקָּה מִמֶּנּוּ מִקּוֹדֶם

as with Acher who "cut the shoots" (Chagigah 14b), regarding whom they said [Chagigah 15b] that he was not pure on account of his mother, possessing an innate evil at his root from which he had not cleansed himself beforehand;873Cf. Chagigah 14b–15b — the source R’ Tzadok invokes: the account of “the four who entered the pardes,” of whom “Acher” (Elisha ben Avuya) “cut down the plantings”; the Gemara/aggadah attributes his fall in part to a defect present from before his birth (his mother having passed by houses of idolatry, or eaten of their offerings, while pregnant) — supporting R’ Tzadok’s thesis that one not wholly cleansed at the root is harmed rather than helped by entering the esoteric.874Yoma 72b; Chagigah 14b–15b; Peri Tzadik, Parshas Zachor 9; Likkutei Maamarim, On Sefer Yehoshua 4 — when exalted Torah becomes an elixir of death: Yoma warns that Torah without inner integrity and fear of Heaven can become a “potion of death”; it condemns a scholar whose inside does not match his outside and describes pure Torah as Torah learned with a heart protected from sinful distraction. Chagigah’s Acher “cut down the plantings” after entering Pardes. Rav Tzadok interprets cutting the plantings as separating a revealed spiritual power from the divine unity that gives it life—taking “malchus” or created reality as independent of its upper source. Peri Tzadik similarly describes mistaken entry into Pardes as a failure of faithfulness, while the Yehoshua essays connect Acher’s fall with externalized wisdom and duality. The preserved note supplies the biographical Aggadah; this companion note explains Rav Tzadok’s broader diagnosis: the danger is not hidden Torah itself, but receiving it through an uncleansed and separating consciousness.
וְכֵן כַּת שַׁבְּתַי צְבִי שֶׁם רְשָׁעִים יִרְקַב, נִרְאֶה דְּנַעֲשׂוּ נוֹאֲפִים עַל שֶׁעָסְקוּ בַּנִּסְתָּרוֹת בְּעוֹד לְבָבָם מָלֵא תַּאֲווֹת

and so the sect of Shabbetai Zvi, may the name of the wicked rot, who became licentious adulterers because they engaged in esoteric mysteries while their hearts were filled with lusts.875Machshavos Charutz 1:6 — Rav Tzadok’s polemical use of the Sabbatean collapse: Machshavos Charutz names Shabtai Tzvi together with another notorious claimant as examples of people whose intense asceticism and imagined holiness strengthened fantasy rather than truth, allowing the serpent’s temptation to cast them “from a high roof into a deep pit.” This is the closest internal parallel to the sharp historical reference in our se’if. Rav Tzadok is using the Sabbatean disaster as a spiritual caution: self-declared elevation, esoteric knowledge, and extreme practices cannot substitute for purification of character and submission to Torah. His statement that the sect became morally corrupt is a polemical-theological diagnosis within his writings; it should not be mistaken for a complete neutral history of the movement or a claim that study of Kabbalah itself produces corruption.

וְכֵן אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן: אִלּוּ הָיָה מְתַקֵּן לְגַמְרֵי חֵטְא דְּעֵץ הַדַּעַת לִהְיוֹת כְּקוֹדֶם שֶׁחָטָא, נֶעְדָּר מִמֶּנּוּ יְדִיעַת הָרָע כָּל עִיקָּר, אָז וַדַּאי הָיָה רָאוּי לֶאֱכוֹל מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים

And likewise Adam HaRishon: had he rectified the sin of the Tree of Knowledge completely so as to be as he was prior to the sin—totally devoid of the consciousness of evil—then he would certainly have been worthy to eat of the Tree of Life;
וּלְכָךְ נִבְרָא לְצֹרֶךְ הָאָדָם, דְּכָל הַבְּרִיאָה הָיָה בִּשְׁבִילוֹ, וְאוֹרַיְיתָא וְקֻדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא וְיִשְׂרָאֵל כּוּלָּא חַד

and for this the Tree of Life was created for the sake of man, for the entire Creation was made for him, and the Torah, the Holy One, blessed be He, and Israel are entirely One (Zohar III, 73a);876Bereishis Rabbah 1:4; Sanhedrin 37a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8; Resisei Layla 41:1 — creation for humanity, Torah, and Israel: Bereishis Rabbah reads “Bereishis” as creation for Torah and for Israel, both called “first.” Sanhedrin teaches that humanity began with one person so that each individual may recognize the immeasurable significance of a single life and of the world entrusted to him. Rav Tzadok brings these strands together: Israel represents the completed root-form of Adam for whose recognition of God the created order was intended, and Torah contains every root-letter of the souls of Israel. Yisrael Kedoshim therefore says that if even one essential soul-root had been absent at Sinai, Torah itself would have been lacking; Resisei Layla describes Yaakov and Israel as the purpose for which the world is ultimately named. Se’if 46’s “for his sake” is not license for human domination, but a statement that creation reaches its purpose when the human image becomes transparent to divine life through Torah.
וְיִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָאָדָם שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ נִבְרָא הָעוֹלָם, וְהוּא אֶחָד וּמִתְאַחֵד מַמָּשׁ עִם עֵץ הַחַיִּים הוּא הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהוּא הַנִּשְׁמַת חַיִּים שֶׁנָּפַח בְּאַפָּיו

and Israel is the root of Man for whose sake the universe was created, uniting in literal oneness with the Tree of Life, which is the Torah, the breath of life (nishmas chayim) breathed into his nostrils;877Bereishis 2:7; Zoharic principle cited in Yisrael Kedoshim 8:1 and 10:8 and Resisei Layla 41:1 — “the Holy One, Torah, and Israel are one”: The Torah says that God breathed into Adam’s nostrils a “breath of life.” Rav Tzadok repeatedly invokes the teaching that the Holy One, Torah, and Israel are one, and explains its three aspects: Torah is the holiness attained through human effort; Israel is the inherited holy root of the congregation descending from the Avos; and the Holy One is the transcendent holiness that sanctifies them from above. Resisei Layla links this unity to the verse of divine breathing—“one who blows, blows from within”—so the human soul’s deepest life is not an independent substance severed from its Source. Se’if 46 consequently aligns the breath of life, the Tree of Life, and the living God as distinct expressions of one life-root, while still preserving the Creator–creature distinction in lived existence.
וְהַכֹּל שׁוֹרֶשׁ אֶחָד שֶׁל חַיִּים: זֶה נִקְרָא ״נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים״, וְזֶה ״עֵץ חַיִּים״, וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא ״אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים״

and all constitute a single root of life: this is termed the "breath of life" (nishmas chayim), that is the "Tree of Life" (eitz chayim), and the Holy One, blessed be He, is the "Living God" (Elokim chayim);
אֲבָל זֶהוּ כְּשֶׁהוּא בִּשְׁלֵימוּת הַצֶּלֶם אֱלֹהִים שֶׁבִּתְחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה
but this applies only when he stands in the perfection of the Divine Image (tzelem Elokim) of primal Creation,
וְזֶהוּ יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁצוּרָתוֹ חֲקוּקָה בְּכִסֵּא הַכָּבוֹד:

which is Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, whose visage is engraved upon the Throne of Glory (Chullin 91b).878Yirmiyahu 10:10; Devarim 5:23; Kometz HaMinchah 2:77; Divrei Soferim 36:3 — one root of “living God,” living soul, and living Torah: Tanakh calls Hashem “the living God” and describes the voice heard at Sinai as the voice of the living God. Torah is called life and a Tree of Life, while Adam receives a living soul from divine breath. Rav Tzadok does not equate these expressions indiscriminately; he traces their relationship of source and reception. Kometz HaMinchah describes Torah as the staff that joins the Holy One and Israel, and Divrei Soferim identifies Yaakov’s enduring life with attachment to Torah and to Elokim Chayim. The “one root” in this se’if therefore means that divine life is the source, Torah is its revealed life-pattern, and the perfected human soul receives and embodies that pattern. Adam’s incomplete image cannot safely seize the life-pattern; Yaakov’s complete image can be described as engraved at its heavenly root.879Chullin 91b; Rashi on Bereishis 28:12; Peri Tzadik, Nasso 15 and Vayigash 13; Resisei Layla 10, 28, 41, and 45; Takanas HaShavin 12:7 — Yaakov’s image engraved on the Throne: Chazal describe the angels ascending to view Yaakov’s image above and descending to compare it with the person sleeping below; Rashi explains that his likeness was engraved upon the Throne of Glory. Rav Tzadok expands this into a central anthropology. Yaakov is the restored “form of Adam,” the line of truth and Torah, whose complete household includes the soul-roots of Israel. Resisei Layla says that his engraved form includes all Jewish souls and joins the lower seven qualities with the upper three in a unified human form; Takanas HaShavin 12 explains that every generation of Israel is a further articulation of Yaakov’s single spiritual stature. Pri Tzadik identifies Yaakov’s beauty with Adam’s original beauty. The closing sentence of Se’if 46 thus answers its opening problem: the Tree of Life is fitting not for spiritual ambition alone, but for the fully integrated divine image exemplified by Yaakov.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים מ״ח–נ׳

The theme: The esoteric meaning of "lest he put forth his hand and take also of the Tree of Life" (Bereishis 3:22). If one reaches for the inner secrets of Torah (penimiyus ha-Torah) while the defilement of knowing evil still resides in the heart, he does not cleave to the Tree of Life; rather, he stretches forth his hand from a distance, severing the holy vitality and drawing it into the external realm—an act termed "cutting the shoots" (kitzetz ba-netiot). Eradicating this innate defilement is beyond human capacity, requiring Hashem to recreate the heart ex nihilo ("Create for me a pure heart, O God", Tehillim 51:12), transforming the "heart of stone" into a "heart of flesh."

p: אֲבָל הַחֲשָׁשׁ ״פֶּן וְגוֹמֵר גַּם מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה בּוֹ עֲדַיִין זוּהֲמַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת דִּידִיעַת רַע שֶׁלֹּא נִתְקַן לְגַמְרֵי, וְיִקַּח מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים גַּם כֵּן מְצוֹרָף לַאֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת הַקּוֹדֵם

But the apprehension "lest... [take] also of the Tree of Life" means that there would still linger within him the defilement of the Tree of Knowledge in the consciousness of evil that had not been thoroughly rectified, and he would take from the Tree of Life as well, combined with his prior eating from the Tree of Knowledge;
וְזֶהוּ לְשׁוֹן ״יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ״, שֶׁלֹּא יִתְקָרֵב אֶל עֵץ הַחַיִּים עַצְמוֹ לְהִתְדַּבֵּק וּלְהִתְאַחֵד עִמּוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה רָאוּי לְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא

and this is the meaning of the expression "he put forth his hand": that he would not draw near to the Tree of Life itself to cleave and unite with it, as had been fitting for Adam HaRishon prior to the sin;880Bereishis 3:22; Ramban ad loc.; Takanas HaShavin 15:46; Machshavos Charutz 15:8 — taking “also” from the Tree of Life while the Tree of Knowledge remains mixed within: The verse fears that Adam might “send forth his hand and take also from the Tree of Life, and eat, and live forever.” Ramban explains that after human choice had been corrupted, access to the Tree was barred so that the decree of death would not be nullified. Rav Tzadok’s preceding se’if reads “and now” as an awakening of teshuvah; the present se’if then makes a further derash on “also”: the danger is not life-giving Torah itself, but joining it to an unrepaired knowledge of evil. Machshavos Charutz explains that after Adam’s sin even the Torah’s Tree-of-Life light is encountered through the mixed categories of the Tree of Knowledge. The verse and Ramban establish the guarded Tree; the specific conjunction of the two trees is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis.

דְּאַחַר כָּךְ, אַף שֶׁיִּתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁלֹּא יֻפְלַט מִקִּרְבּוֹ יְדִיעַת הָרָע וְלִהְיוֹת כְּמוֹ קוֹדֶם, הֲרֵי הוּא עוֹמֵד מְרוּחָק מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וְלֹא יָכוֹל לִיקַּח מִפִּרְיוֹ אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי שְׁלִיחוּת וְהוֹשָׁטַת הַיָּד

for afterward, even if he arouses himself to repent, as long as the consciousness of evil is not thoroughly purged from within him to be as he was before, he stands distant from the Tree of Life and cannot take of its fruit except through stretching forth and extending the hand;
וְזֶהוּ לְשׁוֹן ״יִשְׁלַח יָדוֹ״, שֶׁהוּא כְּלוֹקֵחַ דָּבָר הַמְרוּחָק מִמֶּנּוּ וְאֵין לוֹ חִיבּוּר וְשַׁיָּיכוּת עִמּוֹ, רַק שֶׁיָּכוֹל לְהוֹשִׁיט יָד וְלִיקַּח

and this is the expression "he put forth his hand": like one who grasps an object far removed from him with which he has no intrinsic bond or affinity, merely possessing the capacity to reach out a hand and seize it;
וְאֵין הוּא מִתְקָרֵב אֶל הָעֵץ הַחַיִּים, אֶלָּא לוֹקֵחַ מֵעֵץ הַחַיִּים וּמַפְרִידוֹ מִמֶּנּוּ וּמְקָרְבוֹ אֵלָיו

and he does not draw near to the Tree of Life, but rather seizes from the Tree of Life, detaching it from its source and drawing it down to himself;881Devarim 30:14; Resisei Layla 10:1; Kometz HaMinchah 2:77 — Torah internalized as life versus Torah grasped externally: The Torah is described as “very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it,” not as an object held at a distance. Resisei Layla identifies genuine deveikus with cleaving to Torah, truth, and the spiritual form of Yaakov; Kometz HaMinchah describes Torah as the Tree of Life and the staff that joins Israel to Hashem, while the same staff can become a serpent when approached from the wrong side. Rav Tzadok’s image of merely stretching out a hand therefore distinguishes external acquisition from inner identification. This is his conceptual reading of the verse, not a claim that the physical gesture itself is inherently defective.
וְזֶה נִקְרָא ״קִיצוּץ בַּנְּטִיעוֹת״, וּמַכְנִיס דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה לַחִיצוֹנִים רַחֲמָנָא לִיצְלַן, כְּעִנְיַן ״וְלָרָשָׁע [אָמַר אֱלֹהִים] מַה לְּךָ לְסַפֵּר [חֻקָּי] וְגוֹמֵר״ (תְּהִלִּים נ:טז)

and this is termed "cutting the shoots" (kitzetz ba-netiot), introducing words of Torah into the domain of the external forces, God protect us, along the lines of "But unto the wicked God said: What have you to do to declare My statutes, etc." (Tehillim 50:16).882Chagigah 14b–15a; Tikkunei Zohar, tikkunim 69–70; Resisei Layla 27:1; Likkutei Maamarim, On Sefer Yehoshua 4; Machshavos Charutz 15:17 — “cutting down the plantings”: Chagigah relates that four entered Pardes and that Acher “cut down the plantings.” The Tikkunei Zohar explains this image as separating Malchus from the higher sefiros, treating the manifested kingdom as detached from its living source. Rav Tzadok repeatedly applies that structure to religious error: one takes the lower expression of Divine wisdom as an independent power and thereby produces dualism, idolatry, or distorted action. Here, drawing Torah toward an unrepaired self instead of drawing the self into Torah is called the same “cutting”: the branch is appropriated while its unity with the root is denied.883Tehillim 50:16–17; Yoma 72b; Taanis 7a; Peri Tzadik, Shemos 4; Tzidkas HaTzadik 39 — recounting Torah while casting its words behind: The Psalm rebukes the wicked: “What have you to recount My statutes … while you hate discipline and cast My words behind you?” Yoma teaches that a scholar whose inside does not match his outside is not a true Torah scholar, and that Torah can become a potion of death; Taanis similarly distinguishes Torah pursued for its own sake from Torah misused. Rav Tzadok does not teach that a sinner should abandon ordinary Torah study—his writings repeatedly present Torah and teshuvah as the path of repair. His warning is narrower and more severe: esoteric Torah must not be appropriated as spiritual power while the heart actively resists the discipline that makes it a Tree of Life.
וּבִכְנִיסָה לַפַּרְדֵּ״ס, שֶׁהוּא לִהְיוֹת מִבְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה, לִהְיוֹת צוֹפֶה בְּנִסְתְּרוֹת חַדְרֵי מֶלֶךְ מַלְכֵי הַמְּלָכִים
And regarding entry into Pardes—which means to be among the men of ascent (bnei aliyah), gazing into the hidden chambers of the King of kings of kings:
אֲפִילּוּ מִי שֶׁאֵינוֹ רָשָׁע, רַק שֶׁאֵינוֹ נָקִי לְגַמְרֵי מִשָּׁרְשׁוֹ, אֵין זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹ, וְאֵין לוֹ לִדְרוֹשׁ וְלַחְקוֹר בַּמֻּפְלָא מִמֶּנּוּ

even one who is not wicked, but merely unpurified from his innate root of defilement, this domain does not belong to him, and he must not search or delve into that which is too wondrous for him (Chagigah 13a);884Chagigah 14b; Sukkah 45b; Ramban on Bereishis 3:22; Takanas HaShavin 15:43; Peri Tzadik, Parshas Zachor 9 — Pardes, the King’s chambers, and the few bnei aliyah: Chagigah’s entry into Pardes is the classic image of ascent into hidden wisdom. Sukkah says that the bnei aliyah are few, distinguishes those who see through a clear glass and those who do not, and further distinguishes those who may enter only with permission from those who may enter without it. Ramban describes earthly Gan Eden as corresponding to supernal chambers. Rav Tzadok already developed the rarity of the bnei aliyah in Se’if 43 and elsewhere identifies entry into Pardes with approaching the King’s hidden chambers. The common point is not exclusivity for its own sake, but the need for a vessel proportionate to the revelation.885Chagigah 13a; Ben Sira 3:21–22 as cited there; Rambam, Moreh Nevuchim I:32; Ramban, Introduction to the Torah; Peri Tzadik, Parshas Zachor 9 — limits of investigation: Chagigah sets a boundary on speculation and cites Ben Sira: “Do not investigate what is wondrous beyond you, and do not search what is concealed from you; contemplate what you have been permitted.” Rambam explains that forcing the intellect beyond its capacity can damage rather than perfect it; Ramban invokes the same teaching as a rule of humility before the Torah’s secrets. Rav Tzadok applies the principle personally: the problem is not the existence of hidden wisdom, but entering a level for which one’s character and root have not yet become a fitting vessel.
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: ״יָהֵב חָכְמְתָא לְחַכִּימִין״ (דָּנִיֵּאל ב:כא) — וְלֹא לְטִפְּשִׁין, שֶׁהָיוּ מוֹצִיאִין אוֹתָהּ בִּמְקוֹמוֹת הַמְטוּנָּפִים

and concerning this it is stated: "He gives wisdom unto the wise" (Daniel 2:21)—and not to fools (Berachos 55a), who would bring it into soiled places.886Daniel 2:21; Berachos 55a; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:1; Tzidkas HaTzadik 39 — “He gives wisdom to the wise”: Daniel praises Hashem Who “gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those who know understanding.” Berachos derives that Hashem grants wisdom to one who already possesses wisdom, and pairs the verse with “in the heart of every wise-hearted person I have placed wisdom.” The first wisdom is the prepared heart—the humility, moral discipline, and desire for truth that make further revelation receivable. Yisrael Kedoshim distinguishes holiness attained through human effort from the higher holiness bestowed from above; Tzidkas HaTzadik adds that prayer is needed even to repair the root. Rav Tzadok’s contrast with fools therefore concerns the absence of a vessel, not mere intellectual ability.
וְעִנְיַן הַחֲשָׁשׁ זֶה דְּ״פֶן וְגוֹמֵר״ — שֶׁלֹּא יוּסַר שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַזּוּהֲמָא מִלֵּב לְגַמְרֵי
And the essence of this apprehension "lest, etc." is that the root of defilement would not be thoroughly removed from the heart;
כִּי דָּבָר זֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר רַק עַל יְדֵי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר לֶעָתִיד: ״וַהֲסִרֹתִי אֶת לֵב הָאֶבֶן [מִבְּשַׂרְכֶם] וְנָתַתִּי לָכֶם לֵב בָּשָׂר״ (יְחֶזְקֵאל ל״ו:כו)

for this achievement is impossible except through the Blessed Name alone, as is stated concerning the Future: "and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you a heart of flesh" (Yechezkel 36:26);
וְאָמְרוּ: ״לֵב לְהוֹצִיא בָּשָׂר״, שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ לֵב הָאֶבֶן הַמְשׁוּקָּע בְּגַשְׁמִיּוּת

and they expounded: "a heart that repels fleshly lust" (lev l'hotzi basar, Shabbat 110b), which is the antithesis of the stony heart sunk in corporeal materialism.887Shabbos 146a; Shabbos 55b with Rashi; Machshavos Charutz 18:5; Takanas HaShavin 6:77 and 15:44–46 — the root of the serpent’s pollution: Shabbos 146a teaches that the serpent cast pollution into Chavah and that Israel’s pollution ceased at Sinai. Shabbos 55b nevertheless speaks of exceptionally righteous people who died only through “the counsel of the serpent,” and Rashi explains that expression as the primordial decree introduced through the serpent’s advice rather than through a personal sin. Rav Tzadok distinguishes levels: Sinai removed the pollution from Israel collectively, but later sin could again uncover its structure within the individual; ordinary teshuvah repairs guilt, while the complete uprooting of the primordial knowledge of evil requires a transformation of the created heart itself.888Yechezkel 36:25–27; Radak ad loc.; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:4; Machshavos Charutz 18:5 — the divine removal of the heart of stone: The prophecy proceeds from cleansing waters to a new heart and spirit: Hashem removes the heart of stone, gives a heart of flesh, places His spirit within Israel, and causes them to walk in His statutes. Radak explains the new heart as receptive and willing to accept Hashem’s word with love; the stone heart is wicked and hard, whereas the flesh heart is soft and prepared for good. Rav Tzadok emphasizes the verbs of Divine action. Human fasting and discipline can subdue desire, but the final removal of the inward compulsion fixed into nature after Adam’s sin is Hashem’s future act.889Zohar, Toldos 56; Peri Tzadik, Vayigash 11 and Vayeitzei 4; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:4; Takanas HaShavin 6:75 — “a heart to bring forth flesh”: The Zohar asks the meaning of “a heart of flesh” and answers: a heart for bringing forth flesh, and not for another purpose. In context, the future inclination will remain only for the holy need of procreation and will be awakened by Hashem rather than burning constantly for self-gratification. Rav Tzadok cites this teaching throughout his writings to show that the life-force of desire is not annihilated; it is whitened and redirected until it serves life without self-serving pollution. The “heart of flesh” is therefore the opposite of the “heart of stone” sunk in physicality, not the absence of embodied human life.
וְכֵן אָמַר דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: ״לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא לִי [אֱלֹהִים]״ (תְּהִלִּים נ״א:י״ב), וּבְרִיאָה הוּא יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן
And so David HaMelech, peace be upon him, prayed: "Create for me a pure heart, O God" (Tehillim 51:12), and creation (beriah) signifies something from nothing (yesh me-ayin):
שֶׁאַף שֶׁכְּבָר הֲרָגוֹ לַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בְּתַעֲנִית כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְלִבִּי חָלַל [בְּקִרְבִּי]״ (שָׁם ק״ט:כ״ב)
for although he had already slain his yetzer hara through fasting as he said, "and my heart is slain within me" (ibid. 109:22; Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5);

אַחַר שֶׁרָאָה בְּאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה שֶׁאֵינוֹ כֵן, דְּהוּא לֹא יָדַע מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ דְּלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי אֶלָּא וְכוּלֵיהּ וְשֶׁבֶּאֱמֶת רְאוּיָה לוֹ, שֶׁהֲרֵי הַנָּבִיא אָמַר לוֹ שֶׁחָטָא וְנֶעֱנַשׁ עַל זֶה

after he witnessed in that incident [of Bas Sheva] that it was not so—for he did not know the rabbinic dictum that he was not fit for that deed save to teach repentance and that in truth she was destined for him, since the prophet Nathan declared to him that he sinned and he was punished for it;890Tehillim 51:12; Tzidkas HaTzadik 39; Peri Tzadik, Va’eschanan 2–3, Vayeishev 9, and Sukkos 34 — “Create for me a pure heart” as a new creation: David asks, “Create for me a pure heart, O God, and renew a steadfast spirit within me.” Rav Tzadok repeatedly makes the same lexical point found here: beri’ah denotes creation from nothing, so David did not ask merely for restraint or improvement but for a heart whose purity could be renewed at the root. Peri Tzadik, Va’eschanan explains that after all David’s effort appeared to have failed, his cry reached the Divine power to create a new vessel; Vayeishev joins this to the promised “new heart” of Israel. This is one of the clearest internal parallels to the present se’if.891Tehillim 109:22; Bava Basra 17a; Machshavos Charutz 18:5; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:53; Tzidkas HaTzadik 68 — David’s “hollow heart” and conquest of the yetzer: Bava Basra records one view that David belongs among those over whom the evil inclination did not rule, citing “my heart is hollow within me”; the opposing view reads the verse as a description of his suffering. Rav Tzadok consistently follows the traditional interpretation that David made the yetzer “dead” through fasting and intense struggle. Machshavos Charutz distinguishes that humanly achieved killing from the future Divine slaughter of the yetzer, which removes its created root so that it cannot return. The incident therefore exposed to David that even an extraordinary personal conquest was not yet identical with the final transformation promised by the prophets.
וְחָשַׁב שֶׁיֵּשׁ בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ רָע מִזּוּהֲמַת עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהִנָּקוֹת מִזֶּה כְּלָל

and he thought that there remained within him an evil root from the defilement of the Serpent's instigation from which it is impossible to be cleansed by natural means at all;892Avodah Zarah 4b–5a; Sanhedrin 107a; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 17; Divrei Soferim 28 — David was “not fit for that incident”: Avodah Zarah says that David was not naturally fit for that incident, just as Israel was not naturally fit for the Golden Calf; both events became an opening that teaches the power of teshuvah to individuals and to the community. Sanhedrin also records David’s request to be tested and the failure that followed. Rav Tzadok combines these strands carefully: David’s inner spiritual level was beyond the ordinary rule of the yetzer, yet the event remained a real sin that demanded confession, punishment, and return. Its providential role as a paradigm of teshuvah does not erase human accountability.893II Shmuel 12:7–14; Radak and Abarbanel ad loc.; Peri Tzadik, Bo 4 — Nathan’s rebuke, forgiveness, and continuing consequences: Nathan tells David, “You are the man,” details the wrongdoing, and announces its consequences. David responds, “I have sinned to Hashem”; Nathan then says that Hashem has removed his sin and he will not die, while temporal consequences remain. The meforshim distinguish forgiveness of the sinner’s ultimate standing from the earthly effects and punishments that still unfold. Rav Tzadok therefore refuses to use the aggadah that David was “not fit” for the incident to cancel the plain prophetic judgment. The prophet named the act a sin, David confessed it, and the ensuing suffering remained part of its rectification.894Shabbos 55b; Bava Basra 17a; Rashi ad loc.; Machshavos Charutz 18:5; Takanas HaShavin 6:77 — “the counsel of the serpent”: The Gemara says that four exceptionally righteous people died only through “the counsel of the serpent.” Rashi explicitly explains עטיו as עצתו: the serpent’s advice to Chavah brought the decree of death upon Adam’s descendants even where no personal sin deserved it. Rav Tzadok uses the phrase inwardly for the inherited structure implanted by the primordial sin—the possibility that knowledge of evil still exists in the heart’s root. David feared that his failure revealed such a root within him; therefore he asked not only for pardon, but for a newly created pure heart.
וְעַל כֵּן בִּקֵּשׁ עַל בְּרִיאָה חֲדָשָׁה יֵשׁ מֵאַיִן לֵב טָהוֹר, וַהֲסָרַת לֵב הַטָּמֵא וְהָאֶבֶן שֶׁמִּכְּבָר בּוֹ:
therefore he pled for a brand new creation ex nihilo of a pure heart, and the total removal of the impure, stony heart that had previously dwelt within him.

items.h: The theme: The innate truth of Yaakov Avinu versus the temporary lapse of Israel at the Golden Calf. Yaakov was formed from primal Truth—the antithesis of physical lusts which are fleeting falsehood ("bread of deceit", Mishlei 23:3). At Sinai, when Israel's souls departed at the first utterance, their stony hearts were removed and replaced with hearts of flesh, making them immortal like the angels. Though the Golden Calf caused them to forfeit actual immortality ("indeed you shall die like Adam", Tehillim 82:7), the prefix "like" (k'adam) denotes resemblance rather than literal identity. Unlike Adam who became truly uncircumcised, Israel's blemish is superficial; in their inner depths, Hashem remains the rock of their heart (tzur levavam), and their core will is to perform His will.

p: וְיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם נוֹצַר בְּתוֹלָדָה כֵּן מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הָאֱמֶת, שֶׁהוּא הֵיפֶךְ כָּל תַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״לֶחֶם שֶׁקֶר״ וְכָזָב, דָּבָר הַפּוֹסֵק

And Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, was formed from birth in this state from the root of Truth, which is the antithesis of all bodily desires termed "bread of deceit" (Mishlei 23:3) and falsehood, a transient thing that ceases;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן ״שְׂפַת אֱמֶת תִּכּוֹן לָעַד״ (מִשְׁלֵי י״ב:י״ט), שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּחַיֵּי עוֹלָם הַקַּיָּים לָעַד, וְתוֹרָה דִּכְתִיב בָּהּ אֱמֶת
unlike "the lip of truth shall be established forever" (ibid. 12:19), which is the root of eternal life enduring forever, and the Torah whereof Truth is written (Mishlei 23:23);
שֶׁזָּכָה לָזֶה עַל יְדֵי יְגִיעַת אֲבוֹתָיו אַבְרָהָם וְיִצְחָק בַּהֲסָרַת הַזּוּהֲמָא, וּלְהָבִיא נֶפֶשׁ נְקִיָּה כָּזוֹ לָעוֹלָם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִקְרָא הוּא לְבַדּוֹ לָהֶם ״זֶרַע״

which he attained through the toil of his fathers Avraham and Yitzchak in removing defilement, bringing such a pure soul into the world that he alone should be designated unto them as holy "seed";895Mishlei 20:17; Rashi ad loc.; Mishlei 12:19; Maharal, Netivos Olam, Nesiv HaEmes 1; Likkutei Maamarim, On Sefer Yehoshua 13 — “bread of falsehood” and the transience of desire: Mishlei calls “bread of falsehood” initially sweet, but says that afterward the mouth is filled with gravel; Rashi identifies this “bread” specifically with adultery. Mishlei then contrasts “the lip of truth,” which endures forever, with falsehood, which lasts only for a moment. Maharal explains that truth possesses stability from within, whereas falsehood eventually collapses because it lacks a real foundation. Rav Tzadok’s Likkutei Maamarim on Sefer Yehoshua makes the present association explicit: illicit desire is called “bread of falsehood” because its pleasure is temporary, while Hashem, whose seal is truth, is the opposite of such momentary gratification. These sources supply the textual and conceptual background for Se’if 48’s contrast between bodily desire and enduring life.896Michah 7:20; Malachi 2:6; Taanis 5b; Resisei Layla 10:1; Peri Tzadik, Nasso 15:1; Takanas HaShavin 6:4 — Yaakov, Torah, truth, and enduring life: Scripture associates truth with Yaakov — “You will give truth to Yaakov” — and calls Torah “the Torah of truth.” Taanis teaches that “Yaakov Avinu did not die,” explaining that as his descendants remain alive, so does he. Rav Tzadok repeatedly unites these ideas: Resisei Layla identifies attachment to Yaakov’s form with attachment to Torah and truth; Peri Tzadik presents Yaakov’s measure of truth as something that endures forever; and Takanas HaShavin links his image engraved upon the Throne to humility and the perfected human form. Se’if 48 therefore develops an established Rav Tzadok pattern: Yaakov, truth, Torah, and life are different expressions of one enduring root.897Bereishis 21:12; Nedarim 31a; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:1; Resisei Layla 41:1 — “in Yitzchak,” but not all of Yitzchak: Hashem tells Avraham, “Through Yitzchak shall offspring be called yours.” Nedarim excludes Yishmael through the word “Yitzchak,” and then excludes Esav through the derashah “in Yitzchak” — but not all of Yitzchak — leaving Yaakov as the covenantal seed. That is the Talmudic source for Yaakov alone being called the fathers’ seed. Rav Tzadok adds a spiritual history: Resisei Layla describes the avodah of Avraham and Yitzchak as producing Yaakov’s perfectly straight line, while Yisrael Kedoshim distinguishes holiness acquired through human effort from the inherited holiness transmitted through the fathers. The legal derashah identifies Yaakov; the account of the fathers’ labor removing pollution is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis.
וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִבְנָה אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, שֶׁזָּכוּ כוּלָּם לָזֶה בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה
and from him was constructed the Israelite nation, who all attained this at the Giving of the Torah:

עַל יְדֵי שֶׁבְּדִבּוּר רִאשׁוֹן יָצְאָה נִשְׁמָתָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, שַׁבָּת פ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳] וְהוּסַר לֵב הָאֶבֶן מֵהֶם, וְעַל יְדֵי טַל שֶׁל תְּחִיָּה שֶׁהוּחְזַר הוּחְזַר לֵב בָּשָׂר

through the fact that at the first Divine utterance their souls departed as they said [in Shabbat 88b], the heart of stone being removed from them, and through the dew of resurrection wherewith they were restored, a heart of flesh was returned to them.898Shabbos 88b; Shir HaShirim 5:6; Tehillim 68:10; Takanas HaShavin 4:1 — death and revival at each Divine utterance: R’ Yehoshua ben Levi teaches that with every utterance from Hashem at Sinai, Israel’s souls departed, as indicated by “my soul went out when He spoke.” Hashem then brought down the dew with which He will revive the dead and restored them, deriving this from “You poured down abundant rain, O God; when Your inheritance was weary, You sustained it.” This is the direct Aggadic source for the death-and-revival described here. Earlier in Takanas HaShavin, Rav Tzadok presents Matan Torah as temporary release from the evil inclination, death, and subjugation; Se’if 48 reads the repeated revival as a transformation of the human vessel into a foretaste of resurrection.899Yechezkel 36:26–27; Radak ad loc.; Zohar, Toldos 56; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:4; Takanas HaShavin 15:47 — the heart of stone and the heart of flesh: Yechezkel promises that Hashem will remove the heart of stone, give Israel a new heart and spirit, and place His own spirit within them so that they will keep His statutes. Radak explains the heart of flesh as a soft, receptive heart prepared to accept the good, in contrast to a wicked heart hardened like stone. The Zohar interprets “heart of flesh” as a heart whose generative impulse exists only to bring forth flesh in holiness, rather than for self-serving desire. Rav Tzadok’s preceding se’if stresses that the final uprooting of the stone heart is a Divine act. Se’if 48’s claim that this occurred at Sinai is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis of the Sinai revival with Yechezkel’s future promise; Shabbos 88b itself does not use the heart-of-stone language.
וְעַל כֵּן הָיוּ רְאוּיִם אָז לִהְיוֹת חֵרוּת מִמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת כִּי נִסְתַּלְּקָה הַזּוּהֲמָא לְגַמְרֵי, וְכַלֶּעָתִיד אַחַר תְּחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים

And therefore they were worthy at that moment to be free from the Angel of Death, for the defilement was completely eliminated, as it will be in the Future following the Resurrection of the Dead;900Shabbos 146a; Shemos Rabbah 41:7; Vayikra Rabbah 18:3; Avodah Zarah 5a; Peri Tzadik, Shavuos 20:1; Divrei Soferim 33:3 — Sinai, the end of pollution, and freedom from death: Shabbos teaches that the serpent’s pollution ceased from Israel when they stood at Sinai. The Midrash reads “engraved [charus] upon the tablets” as “freedom [cheirus]” from the Angel of Death, exile, or suffering. Avodah Zarah preserves a dispute: one Tanna limits Sinai’s freedom to national subjugation, while R’ Yosei says the Torah was accepted so that the Angel of Death would no longer rule over Israel. Rav Tzadok consistently develops the latter Midrashic strand. Peri Tzadik connects Torah engraved in the heart with freedom from the yetzer, and Divrei Soferim joins Torah to freedom from both the yetzer and death. Thus Se’if 48 follows a specific authoritative view rather than presenting an uncontested conclusion of every source.
אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי [אֱלֹהִים אַתֶּם וּבְנֵי עֶלְיוֹן כֻּלְּכֶם] אָכֵן כְּאָדָם תְּמוּתוּן״ (תְּהִלִּים פ״ב:ו׳–ז׳)
except that sin caused it, as it is said: "I said: You are godlike beings, and all of you sons of the Most High; nevertheless you shall die like Adam" (Tehillim 82:6–7);
״וֵאלֹהִים וּבְנֵי עֶלְיוֹן״ הַיְינוּ בַּהֲסָרַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי כְּמַלְאָכִים
"godlike beings and sons of the Most High" meaning with the total removal of the yetzer like angels;
״וּכְאָדָם״ הַיְינוּ שֶׁחָטְאוּ דּוּגְמַת אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁפָּגְמוּ בַּבְּרִית גַּם כֵּן

and "like Adam" meaning that they sinned after the pattern of Adam HaRishon, blemishing the Covenant as well;901Tehillim 82:6–7; Avodah Zarah 5a; Takanas HaShavin 4:1; Peri Tzadik, Shavuos 20:1 — “I said: You are godlike … yet like Adam you shall die”: Avodah Zarah applies these verses to Israel at Sinai and after the Golden Calf. “You are godlike, and all of you children of the Most High” means that they had reached an angel-like state beyond the rule of death; it does not ascribe divinity to human beings. When they “ruined their deeds,” mortality returned: “Yet like Adam you shall die.” Rav Tzadok describes the same reversal as the loss of the freedom granted with the first tablets — freedom from the yetzer and death — after which the second tablets required the human work of carving the stony heart.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיָּקֻמוּ לְצַחֵק״ (שְׁמוֹת ל״ב:ו׳) — זֶה גִּילּוּי עֲרָיוֹת
as they expounded on the verse "and rose up to play" (Shemos 32:6)—this denotes illicit sexual relations (gilui arayos, Bereishis Rabbah 53:11);
דְּכָל שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה דְּעֵגֶל הָיָה רַק בִּשְׁבִיל תַּאֲוָה זוֹ
for the entire root of the idolatry of the Golden Calf was solely for the sake of this lust,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ס״ג עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״לֹא עָבְדוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה אֶלָּא לְהַתִּיר עֲרָיוֹת בְּפַרְהֶסְיָא״

as they stated [in Sanhedrin 63b]: "Israel served idolatry only to permit illicit sexual relations in public."902Shemos 32:6; Rashi ad loc.; Bereishis 39:17; II Shmuel 2:14; Shemos Rabbah 41:7 — “they rose to make merry”: Rashi explains that the word letzachek in the Golden Calf narrative includes sexual immorality and bloodshed, alongside the idolatry explicit in the surrounding verses. He supports these meanings from the same verb in the episode of Yosef and Potiphar’s wife and from the deadly “play” between the warriors of Avner and Yoav; the Midrash also associates the episode with the killing of Chur. Rav Tzadok emphasizes arayos as the inward desire motivating the idolatrous permission structure, but that emphasis does not erase the other dimensions contained in the Biblical and Midrashic account.903Kisvei Rav Tzadok — Takanas HaShavin 6:4 and 15:44–45; Peri Tzadik, Chanukah 2:1; Likkutei Maamarim, On Sefer Yehoshua 13 — bodily desire as a root of idolatrous estrangement: Across his writings Rav Tzadok maps the corrupted forms of desire, aggression, and honor to the opposing roots represented by Yishmael, Esav, and the distortion of Yaakov’s truth. Se’ifim 44–45 traced how desire can develop into aggression and idolatrous separation; Peri Tzadik identifies the husks of desire and honor as forces opposing Torah; and Likkutei Maamarim calls illicit desire a momentary falsehood opposed to Hashem’s seal of truth. This internal framework explains why Rav Tzadok treats the Golden Calf not merely as an abstract theological error, but as a religious mechanism created to authorize bodily desire. The preserved Sanhedrin note that follows supplies the direct Talmudic statement.904Cf. Sanhedrin 63b — the source R’ Tzadok cites: “R’ Yehuda said in the name of Rav: Israel knew that idolatry has no substance; they worshipped idolatry only in order to permit themselves arayos in public” — grounding his reading that the root of the Golden Calf was the very bodily desire under discussion.
אֲבָל אָמַר ״כְּאָדָם״ בְּכָ״ף הַדִּמְיוֹן, דְּמוֹרֶה בְּכָל מָקוֹם ״לֹא מַמָּשׁ״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּאֵיכָה רַבָּתִי א:א] עַל פָּסוּק ״הָיְתָה כְּאַלְמָנָה״

Yet it says "like Adam" (k'adam) with the comparative letter kaf, which denotes in all places "not literally," as they stated [in Eichah Rabbah 1:1] on the verse "she is become as a widow";905Taanis 20a; Sanhedrin 104a; Rashi on Eichah 1:1 — the kaf of comparison: On the words “she became like a widow,” Chazal stress: like a widow, but not an actual widow — rather, like a woman whose husband has traveled overseas and intends to return. The kaf marks resemblance without complete identity. Rav Tzadok transfers that grammatical principle to “like Adam”: Israel’s sin resembled Adam’s covenantal failure and restored mortality, but did not reproduce every aspect of his rupture. The Talmudic source discusses Jerusalem’s bond with Hashem; its application to Adam and the covenant is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive move.
וְהַיְינוּ כִּי אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן חָזַר לִהְיוֹת עָרֵל מַמָּשׁ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
meaning that Adam HaRishon reverted to being literally uncircumcised as mentioned above;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם עֲרֵלִים נִקְרָאִים מוּלִים, וְהָעָרְלָה הוּא רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן כְּמוֹ בְּמָשׁוּךְ

whereas Israel, even when physically uncircumcised, are halachically termed "circumcised," and the foreskin is merely an outward appearance, as with one whose foreskin is drawn;906Sanhedrin 38b; Hoshea 6:7; Zohar, Bereishis 43:434; Peri Tzadik, Mishpatim 4:1; Resisei Layla 58:3 — Adam “drew his foreskin”: Sanhedrin reads “they, like Adam, transgressed a covenant” as teaching that Adam was mashuch be’orlaso. The Zohar interprets this spiritually: he separated the holy covenant from its place, cleaved to the foreskin, and followed the serpent’s counsel. Rav Tzadok repeatedly links the Tree-of-Knowledge sin with the first blemish of bodily covenant and with the later mixture of self-directed desire in Adam’s descendants. Accordingly, the phrase here that Adam “actually became uncircumcised” follows an Aggadic and kabbalistic description of covenantal rupture; it should not be read as a medical or historical claim detached from that interpretive tradition.907Nedarim 31b; Yevamos 72a; Machshavos Charutz 15:11; Peri Tzadik, Shemos 1:1 — Israel’s covenantal identity and the mashuch: Nedarim rules that a vow concerning “the circumcised” includes even an uncircumcised Jew, while a circumcised non-Jew remains within the category called “uncircumcised”; the terms express covenantal identity, not anatomy alone. Yevamos further teaches that one whose foreskin was drawn forward remains circumcised by Torah law, although the Sages required correction because he appears uncircumcised. Rav Tzadok uses both principles to distinguish the visible covering from Israel’s essential root: even when the covenant is obscured in conduct and appearance, its inherited identity is not converted into the root of the nations.
וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּ״אָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם״ (שְׁמוּאֵל א ט״ז:ז׳) נִרְאֶה עָרְלָה וּפְגַם בַּבְּרִית וְנִגְזַר מִיתָה
and in this world where "man looks on the outward appearance" (I Shmuel 16:7), there appears a foreskin and a blemish in the Covenant, wherefore death was decreed;
אֲבָל עַל הָאֱמֶת ״ה׳ יִרְאֶה לַלֵּבָב״, דְּהוּא יִתְבָּרַךְ צוּר לְבָבָם וְחֶלְקָם

but in ultimate Truth "Hashem looks on the heart," for He, may He be blessed, is the rock of their heart and their portion (Tehillim 73:26);908I Shmuel 16:7; Tehillim 73:26; Takanas HaShavin 12:7; Resisei Layla 28:1 and 50:2 — appearance, the heart, and Israel’s hidden root: Hashem tells Shmuel that a human being sees what appears to the eyes, while Hashem sees the heart. The Psalmist calls Hashem “the Rock of my heart and my portion forever.” Rav Tzadok explains elsewhere that every Jewish soul remains rooted in the supernal form of Yaakov: the upper end of the cord is bound to the Throne, while even the lowest and most distant souls remain attached at the other end. Se’if 48 applies that doctrine to covenantal failure. Visible sin is real, incurs judgment, and can produce death; nevertheless, it does not by itself define the deepest identity that Hashem sees within the heart.
וְכָל הַפְּגָמִים אֵינוֹ מִמַּעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, רַק מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר הַיּוֹשֵׁב עַל מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב
and all blemishes do not stem from the inner depths of the heart, but solely from the yetzer that sits upon the entrances of the heart;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: ״גָּלוּי וְיָדוּעַ שֶׁרְצוֹנֵנוּ [לַעֲשׂוֹת רְצוֹנְךָ] וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְרַק הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה גּוֹרֵם הַכֹּל״ (בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳):

and as they said: "It is revealed and known before You that our will is to perform Your will, and what prevents us? The yeast in the dough [the yetzer hara]" (Berachos 17a).909R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §30): “The Name Havayah is the middah of ‘truth to Yaakov,’ which is literally the opposite of imagination [dimyon].” Exactly the se’if: Yaakov was formed from the root of truth — the very opposite of the serpent [the power of illusion].910Berachos 17a; Rashi ad loc.; Rambam, Hilchos Gerushin 2:20; Peri Tzadik, Sukkos 47:1; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:1 — the inner will and the “leaven in the dough”: R’ Alexandri’s prayer declares that Israel’s will is to do Hashem’s will, while the “leaven in the dough” and the subjugation of kingdoms obstruct it. Rashi identifies the leaven as the evil inclination in the heart. Rambam similarly explains that a Jew’s underlying will is to belong to Israel, perform the mitzvos, and avoid sin, although the yetzer can overpower him. Rav Tzadok joins this inherited inner holiness to the obligation of avodah. This teaching does not erase responsibility or consequences; it distinguishes the deepest ratzon from the force obstructing its expression.

items.h: The theme: Yom Kippur, the scapegoat to Azazel, and the rectification of the Covenant. On Yom Kippur, the awakening of Understanding in the heart (Binah she-ba-lev) reveals that all Israel are inherently righteous ("and your people are all righteous", Yeshayah 60:21), meaning guardians of the Covenant. The scapegoat to Azazel atones for the deeds of Uzza and Azael (Yoma 67b), the fallen angels who became the root of absolute evil and the husk (Kelipah) of Balaam. Through wasteful emission, the Queen of Sheba sought the esoteric knowledge of Balaam's husk (Da'as d'Kelipah); hence Balaam’s judgment in Gehinnom is through boiling semen (Gittin 57a). While the seventy nations derive from pure evil, Israel incorporates a mixture of good and evil that is completely sifted and redeemed on Yom Kippur.

p: וְזֶהוּ עִנְיַן יוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים דְּ״בַיּוֹם הַזֶּה יְכַפֵּר [עֲלֵיכֶם לְטַהֵר אֶתְכֶם]״ (וַיִּקְרָא ט״ז:ל׳)
And this is the concept of Yom Kippur, that "on this day shall atonement be made for you, to cleanse you" (Vayikra 16:30):
שֶׁאָז הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב שֶׁהוּא הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ אֲכִילָה וְלֹא שְׁתִיָּה
for then is the awakening of Understanding within the heart (Binah she-ba-lev), which is the World to Come wherein there is neither eating nor drinking (Berachos 17a);
שֶׁאָז יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ
when "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none" (Yirmeyah 50:20);
וְאָז כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ס:כא), כִּדִתְנַן [רֵישׁ פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק, סַנְהֶדְרִין צ׳ עַמּוּד א׳]

and then all Israel possess a portion in the World to Come, as it is said: "Your people also shall be all righteous" (Yeshayah 60:21), as we learned [Sanhedrin 90a];911Vayikra 16:30; Mishnah Yoma 8:9 — Yom Kippur atonement and purification: The Torah promises that on this day atonement will be made to cleanse Israel “before Hashem.” The Mishnah derives that Yom Kippur atones for sins between a person and Hashem, but not for injuries to another person until the offended party is appeased; it also states that one who plans to sin because Yom Kippur will atone is not granted that atonement. Rav Tzadok’s language of the inward heart explains the spiritual depth of the day’s purification. It does not remove the halachic requirements of teshuvah, confession, restitution, and reconciliation.912Berachos 17a; Dover Tzedek 3:15; Pri Tzadik, Yom Kippur 5:1 — the World to Come, fasting, and the heart: Berachos describes the World to Come as having no eating, drinking, commerce, jealousy, hatred, or rivalry; the righteous instead delight in the radiance of the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok repeatedly treats Yom Kippur’s abstention from bodily needs as a present-world resemblance to that state and links the day to the hidden root of the soul. His identification of the World to Come with Binah and its awakening in the heart is a kabbalistic synthesis. The Gemara itself supplies the nonphysical description, but does not state the sefirah-language used here.913Yirmiyahu 50:20; Radak ad loc.; Yisrael Kedoshim 7:13 — sins sought but not found: Yirmiyahu foretells a future in which Israel’s iniquity will be sought and not found, because Hashem will forgive the surviving remnant. Radak emphasizes that the verse concerns the future perfected redemption, not the ordinary moral condition of every period. Rav Tzadok applies that future truth to Yom Kippur as a temporary disclosure of the soul’s deepest holy root. The prophetic verse therefore describes forgiveness and transformation; Rav Tzadok’s inward-heart reading explains how that future state can be anticipated on the sacred day.
וְ״צַדִּיק״ הַיְינוּ שׁוֹמֵר הַבְּרִית
and "tzaddik" denotes one who guards the Covenant.
וְלֹא הוֹצִיאוּ שָׁם עוֹבְרֵי עֲבֵירָה בִּפְגַם הַבְּרִית מֵחֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
And the Mishnah did not exclude there those who transgressed in blemishing the Covenant from their portion in the World to Come,
דְּבֶאֱמֶת מִצַּד עֹומֶק הַלֵּב שֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אָז הֵם כּוּלָּם כֵּן

for in absolute truth, from the perspective of the depth of the heart that will be revealed then, they are all truly righteous guardians of the Covenant.914Sanhedrin 90a; Yeshayahu 60:21 — “all Israel have a portion” and “your people are all righteous”: The opening Mishnah of Perek Chelek states that all Israel have a portion in the World to Come and cites “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever.” The Mishnah immediately lists severe exceptions, showing that the statement establishes Israel’s covenantal baseline rather than erasing accountability. Rav Tzadok reads “all righteous” at the deepest root of the Jewish soul, from which eventual return remains possible. This is an interpretation of the collective promise alongside, not instead of, the Mishnah’s explicit moral boundaries.915Nedarim 31b; Machshavos Charutz 15:11; Pri Tzadik, Shemos 1:1 — Israel’s enduring covenantal identity: Nedarim rules that even an uncircumcised Jew is included when a vow refers to “the circumcised,” while a circumcised non-Jew is not included; the terms follow covenantal identity, not anatomy alone. Rav Tzadok develops this into a spiritual principle: Israel inherits a holy foundation from the Avos, and even visible failure does not convert that root into the opposing identity. Calling every Israelite a guardian of the covenant “at the root” is Rav Tzadok’s theological extension of the Mishnah; it does not mean that an actual covenantal transgression is permitted or without consequence.
וְכֵן בְּיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת זֶה, ״וְנָשָׂא הַשָּׂעִיר [אֹתוֹ] עֲוֹנֹתָם [אֶל אֶרֶץ גְּזֵרָה]״ (וַיִּקְרָא ט״ז:כ״ב) לַעֲזָאזֵל
And likewise on Yom Kippur this revelation occurs, through "and the goat shall bear upon him all their iniquities unto a land not inhabited" (Vayikra 16:22) to Azazel;
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא ס״ז עַמּוּד ב׳] לְכַפֵּר עַל מַעֲשֵׂה עֻזָּא וַעֲזָאֵל
and they stated [in Yoma 67b]: to atone for the deeds of Uzza and Azael,

הֵם גַּם כֵּן אֱלֹהִים שֶׁחָטְאוּ וְהֶחֱטִיאוּ בְּדוֹר הַמַּבּוּל, עַל יְדֵי שֶׁקִּטְרְגוּ בִּבְרִיאַת אָדָם וְהֶרְאָה לָהֶם הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּ״אַל תָּדִין חֲבֵירְךָ עַד שֶׁתַּגִּיעַ לִמְקוֹמוֹ״ (אָבוֹת ב:ד)

who were angelic beings (elohim) that sinned and caused sin in the Generation of the Flood, because they prosecuted against the creation of man, and the Blessed Name showed them: "Judge not your fellow until you come into his place" (Avos 2:4);916Vayikra 16:8–10, 21–22; Yoma 67b; Ramban on Vayikra 16:8 — Azazel and the removal of sin: The Torah places both goats before Hashem, assigns them by lot, and sends one to the wilderness bearing Israel’s confessed iniquities. Yoma records the school of R’ Yishmael’s interpretation that Azazel atones for the deed of Uza and Azael. Ramban stresses that the goat is not an independent offering to another power; the entire service fulfills Hashem’s command, and both goats remain “before Hashem.” Rav Tzadok adopts the Aggadic-kabbalistic layer to describe the return of externalized sin to its corrupt root, while the Torah’s plain service remains an act of Divine worship alone.917Avos 2:4; Rabbeinu Yonah ad loc. — “Do not judge your fellow until you reach his place”: The Mishnah warns a person not to presume how he would withstand another’s circumstances. Its purpose is humility, compassion, and caution in judgment; it does not declare wrongdoing innocent. Rav Tzadok applies the maxim dramatically to Uza and Azael: the angels who accused humanity discovered, upon entering embodied existence, the force of temptation they had judged from afar. This application explains why their fall becomes a lesson in moral humility while preserving responsibility for the fall itself.
כִּי הֵם כְּשֶׁבָּאוּ לָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַגּוּפָנִי נַעֲשָׂה מֵהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע וְכֶתֶר דִּקְלִיפָּה וְסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא
for when they descended into this physical world, there emerged from them the root of evil, the Crown of the Kelipah (Keser d'Kelipah) and the Other Side;
וִינִיקַת בִּלְעָם מֵהֶם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּזֹוהַר בָּלָק] וְהוּא הַדַּעַת דִּקְלִיפָּה כִּידוּעַ
and the sustenance of Balaam drew from them as they stated [in Zohar, Balak 208a], he being the Knowledge of the Kelipah (Da'as d'Kelipah) as is known.
וּמַלְכַּת שְׁבָא שֶׁהִיא הַמַּלְכוּת דִּקְלִיפָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּתַרְגּוּם אִיּוֹב א:טו] עַל ״שְׁבָא״ — לִילִית וְגוֹמֵר
And the Queen of Sheba, who is the Sovereignty of the Kelipah (Malchus d'Kelipah) as stated [in Targum Iyov 1:15] on "Sheba"—identifying her with Lilith, etc.;

בִּקְּשָׁה לַעֲמוֹד עַל הַשָּׂגַת הַדַּעַת דִּקְלִיפָּה דְּבִלְעָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּוהַר [שָׁם קצ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳], וְאָמַר לַהּ עַל יְדֵי הוֹצָאַת זֶרַע לְבַטָּלָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם — הוּא הַיְסוֹד דִּקְלִיפָּה

sought to understand the perception of the Da'as d'Kelipah of Balaam as they related in the Zohar [ibid. 194b], and he told her it is attained through wasteful emission of seed, see there, which is the Foundation of the Kelipah (Yesod d'Kelipah);918Sifrei Devarim 357; Bamidbar 24:4, 16; Kisvei Rav Tzadok — Moshe and Bilaam, pure and corrupted da’as: Sifrei derives from “no prophet arose in Israel like Moshe” that a prophetic counterpart arose among the nations—Bilaam—then contrasts their modes of revelation. Bilaam is called one who “knows the knowledge of the Most High” and sees while fallen, whereas Moshe stands with Hashem. Rav Tzadok treats this parallel as equality of extraordinary cognitive reach but opposition of moral vessel: Moshe’s da’as is surrendered to holiness, while Bilaam’s knowledge is appropriated by desire and impurity.
