The Midrash compares prophetic capacities; the characterization of pure versus corrupted da’as is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.919For elaboration — in Yoma 67b: “The school of R’ Yishmael taught: Azazel — [so called] because it atones for the deed of Uza and Azael.” Rashi: “Angels of destruction who descended to earth in the days of Naamah, the sister of Tuval-Cain; and of them it is said, ‘and the sons of the gods saw the daughters of man’” — i.e., Yom Kippur atones for arayos. And the Zohar, Balak 194a asks: what was the “vision of Shakkai” that Bilaam saw? And it answers: the vision of Uza and Azael, who are “fallen and open of eyes.” And Uza and Azael sinned and caused the generation of the Flood to sin through arayos — as they said in Rosh Hashanah 12a that they sinned with boiling semen, and therefore the waters of the Flood were boiling, measure for measure. And in Iyov 1:15, among Iyov’s afflictions it says: “and Sheba fell [upon them] and took them, and the lads they smote by the edge of the sword”; and in the Targum: “and Lilith, queen of Zemargad, fell suddenly.” And likewise in the Zohar there, 194b: the queen of Sheba asked Shlomo the King how great was the power of Bilaam, and how it is possible to seize the serpents that he used for his sorceries; and he answered her that through Bilaam’s emitting boiling semen, out of longing and desire for the sake of those serpents, he would seize them and rule over them.
וְכֵן הוּא דִּינוֹ דְּבִלְעָם בְּשִׁכְבַת זֶרַע רוֹתַחַת כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק הַנִּיזָּקִין, גִּיטִּין נ״ז עַמּוּד א׳]
and likewise Balaam’s judgment in Gehinnom is with boiling semen, as they stated [in Gittin 57a];
דְּמִשָּׁם מִינִיקַת הַקְּלִיפָּה שֶׁלּוֹ מִדּוֹר הַמַּבּוּל דִּבְרוֹתְחִין קִלְקְלוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה י״ב עַמּוּד א׳]

for from there stems the sustenance of his husk, from the Generation of the Flood who corrupted in boiling heat as they stated [in Rosh Hashanah 12a].920Gittin 57a; Rosh Hashanah 12a — measure for measure in Bilaam and the Flood: Gittin’s Aggadah says that Bilaam is punished in boiling semen, reflecting his role in drawing Israel into sexual corruption. Rosh Hashanah teaches that the generation of the Flood “sinned with boiling heat and was judged with boiling heat,” interpreting the Flood waters as scalding through a verbal analogy. Rav Tzadok connects the two teachings as manifestations of one root: desire experienced as consuming heat becomes its own measure-for-measure judgment. These are Aggadic descriptions of moral consequence, not physical or medical claims about the afterlife.
וְהֶרְאָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא כִּי מֵהֶם נֶגְדָּה כָּל קוֹמַת הַקְּלִיפָּה שֶׁמִּשָּׁם הַמְשָׁכַת כָּל ע׳ אוּמּוֹת שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ רַע גָּמוּר

And the Holy One, blessed be He, demonstrated that from them was erected the entire stature of the Kelipah, whence is drawn the vitality of all seventy nations, which is absolute evil;921Devarim 32:8; Rashi ad loc.; Shemos 1:5 — seventy nations and seventy souls: The Torah says that Hashem established the boundaries of the peoples “according to the number of the children of Israel.” Rashi explains that the seventy nations correspond to the seventy souls of Yaakov’s household who descended to Egypt. Rav Tzadok uses this correspondence dynamically: the national powers have parallel possibilities within Israel, so their temptations can appear in Jewish life without becoming Israel’s essential root. The Biblical and Rashi sources establish the numerical correspondence; the mapping of every national power into opposed inner potentials is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive framework.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בִּבְנֵי אָדָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ עֵירוּב טוֹב וָרָע, אַף דְּיֵשׁ רַע גָּמוּר יֵשׁ גַּם כֵּן טוֹב גָּמוּר דְּזֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה, וְעַל יְדֵי שְׁלִיטַת הָאָדָם בְּאָדָם מְעוֹרָבִים יַחַד

unlike human beings who possess a mixture of good and evil: for even where there is absolute evil there is also absolute good, being one opposite the other, and through "man ruling over man" (Koheles 8:9) they are intermingled together;922Koheles 7:14; Chagigah 15a — “this corresponding to that” and paired possibilities: Koheles teaches that God made one thing corresponding to another. Chagigah records two explanations: R’ Meir describes corresponding features within creation, while R’ Akiva interprets the verse as righteous and wicked, Gan Eden and Gehinnom, with each person possessing potential portions in both. Rav Tzadok applies this paired structure inwardly to the mixed world of good and evil. The verse does not teach that good and evil are equal authorities; rather, human freedom encounters opposed possibilities under the sovereignty of the one Creator.923Koheles 8:9; Resisei Layla 52:5; Takanas HaShavin 6:70 — “man rules over man to his harm”: Koheles observes a time when one person rules another to his own detriment. Following the Arizal, Rav Tzadok repeatedly reads the verse as the temporary rule of the “lawless man” over holy humanity, which ultimately harms the oppressor: domination enables holiness to reclaim sparks and resources trapped within the opposing power. Takanas HaShavin earlier applies this principle to exile, where Israel gathers its displaced spiritual abundance from among the nations. The verse’s plain sense concerns harmful human rule; the language of extracting holy sparks is the kabbalistic interpretation used here.
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בַּחֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳]: ״זָכָה — נוֹטֵל חֶלְקוֹ וְחֵלֶק חֲבֵירוֹ בְּגַן עֵדֶן, וְהַלָּה נוֹטֵל חֵלֶק שְׁנֵיהֶם בְּגֵיהִנָּם״, כִּי נִפְרָד הַטּוֹב מִן הָרָע

and regarding this they stated [in Chagigah 15a]: "If he merits, he takes his portion and the portion of his fellow in Gan Eden; and that one takes both their portions in Gehinnom," for the good is cleanly severed from the evil;
וְזֶהוּ ע׳ נֶפֶשׁ דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל נֶגֶד ע׳ אוּמּוֹת:

and this corresponds to the seventy souls of the Children of Israel (Bereishis 46:27) arrayed against the seventy nations of the world.924R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek §2): “This is the matter of Yom Kippur — ‘for on this day He shall atone for you, to purify you.’” Exactly the se’if: Yom Kippur, “on this day He atones,” the day of the awakening of the [supernal] purity.925Chagigah 15a; Yeshayahu 61:7; Yirmiyahu 17:18 — the doubled portions of the righteous and wicked: R’ Akiva’s teaching in Chagigah assigns every person a potential portion in both Gan Eden and Gehinnom. One who becomes righteous receives his own portion and the unused portion of another in Gan Eden; one who becomes wicked receives both portions in Gehinnom. Rav Mesharshiya supports the double portions from verses in Yeshayahu and Yirmiyahu. Rav Tzadok reads this not as arbitrary transfer but as the final sorting of what was intermingled: realized good joins holiness, while rejected evil bears the consequences of both lost possibilities.926Machshavot Charutz 19:8; Resisei Layla 52:5; Takanas HaShavin 6:70 — separation, self-destruction of evil, and gathered sparks: Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains that an impure power survives only because some spark of good gives it vitality. When that good is extracted and restored to holiness, the remaining evil has no independent permanence and collapses. Machshavot Charutz describes a holy spark emerging precisely from deep entanglement; Resisei Layla shows hostile rule becoming the instrument of its own defeat; and Takanas HaShavin describes Israel gathering displaced spiritual abundance through exile. The present conclusion gathers these themes: the enduring good is incorporated into holy souls, while evil stripped of borrowed vitality disintegrates.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים נ״א–נ״ד

The theme: Yom Kippur effects the absolute severance of evil from Israel. When the scapegoat is dispatched to the wilderness, all iniquities are returned to their demonic source—the external "yeast in the dough"—leaving Israel pure as ministering angels, with the Satan silenced. This reveals the inward depth of the heart (tzur levavam), demonstrating that sins were only an external facade of this world. Repentance that reaches Binah in the heart (u'levavo yavin v'shav) accesses the hidden light of the World to Come (alma d'iskasya). This explains why the station of the penitent exceeds that of the wholly righteous: while the tzaddik corresponds to Yesod (the sixth day of Creation, upholding the world of action), the penitent ascends to Shabbos—the seventh day, a foretaste of the World to Come—where even the yetzer hara is retroactively transformed into "very good" (tov me'od).

p: וּבְיוֹם הַכִּפּוּרִים הוּא הַהַפְרָדָה, דְּאַחַר כָּךְ ״וְיַעֲקֹב נָסַע סֻכֹּתָה״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ל״ג:י״ז), וְנָקַט בַּיָּין בְּיָדוֹ לוֹמַר דְּהוּא נָצַח [וַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ל׳]

And on Yom Kippur the complete severance occurs, after which "and Jacob journeyed to Succoth" (Bereishis 33:17), holding the spear (bayin, the lulav) in his hand to proclaim that he has triumphed [Vayikra Rabbah 30:2];
וְשׁוֹלְחִין הָעֲווֹנוֹת לִמְקוֹם שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע, כִּי הַכֹּל מִשָּׁם, מֵהַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה
and they dispatch the iniquities to the locus of the root of evil, for everything originated from there, from the yeast in the dough;
וְיִשְׂרָאֵל נִשְׁאֲרוּ נְקִיִּים לְגַמְרֵי כְּמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת
and Israel remain entirely pure like the ministering angels;
וְעַל כֵּן אָז אֵין רְשׁוּת לַשָּׂטָן לְקַטְרֵג כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳]

and therefore at that time the Satan has no permission to prosecute, as they said [in Yoma 20a];927Vayikra Rabbah 30:2: “R’ Avin said: a parable — [comparable] to two who entered before the judge, and we do not know which of them won; but the one who goes out [holding] his branch [ai] in his hand [i.e., who leaves brandishing his palm-branch], we know that he is the victor. So too Israel and the nations of the world come and accuse before the Holy One on Rosh Hashanah, and we do not know who won; but by [the fact] that Israel go out from before the Holy One with their lulavim and their esrogim in their hands, we know that Israel are the victors. Therefore Moshe warns Israel and says to them: ‘and you shall take for yourselves on the first day.’”928Bereishis 33:17; Vayikra Rabbah 30:2; Pri Tzadik, Motzaei Yom Kippur 11:1 — from Yom Kippur’s judgment to Sukkos victory: Bereishis records that Yaakov journeyed to Sukkos. Vayikra Rabbah compares Israel emerging with lulav and esrog to a litigant leaving court with the sign of victory in hand. Rav Tzadok brings the two texts together: after Yom Kippur separates confessed sin from Israel’s inward root, Sukkos displays the resulting victory and restored holiness. The Torah’s journey and the Midrash’s courtroom parable are distinct sources; their placement in a single spiritual sequence is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis.929Berachos 17a; Resisei Layla 25:1 — the “leaven in the dough” and Israel’s inward will: R’ Alexandri’s prayer says that Israel’s true will is to perform Hashem’s will, while “the leaven in the dough” and subjugation to foreign kingdoms obstruct it. The Gemara identifies an inner impediment; it does not deny choice or responsibility. Rav Tzadok uses the prayer to distinguish the holy desire at the root of the heart from the alien admixture that produces actual sin. Resisei Layla similarly explains that Israel’s failures arise within a divinely ordered condition of deficiency and repair, while the enduring point of dependence upon Hashem remains their defining spiritual root.930Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 46; Ramban on Vayikra 16:8 — Israel like the ministering angels on Yom Kippur: Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer depicts Sammael himself acknowledging that Israel resemble the ministering angels on Yom Kippur: they abstain from food and drink, stand in prayer, make peace, and emerge clean of sin. Ramban cites this teaching while stressing that the Azazel service is wholly commanded worship of Hashem, not an offering to an independent power. Rav Tzadok reads the angelic comparison as disclosure of Israel’s purified inward root. It presupposes the day’s teshuvah and avodah and does not cancel the Mishnah’s requirements of confession, reconciliation, and genuine return.
כִּי אָז נִתְגַּלָּה מַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, דְּ״צוּר לְבָבָם וְחֶלְקָם אֱלֹהִים לְעוֹלָם״ (תְּהִלִּים ע״ג:כ״ו), וְשֶׁכָּל הַחֲטָאִים רַק לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

for then the depths of the heart are revealed: that "God is the rock of their heart and their portion forever" (Tehillim 73:26), and that all sins were merely an outward appearance in this world;931Cf. Yoma 20a — the source R’ Tzadok invokes: “On Yom Kippur the Satan has no permission to accuse — [the numerical value of] ‘ha-satan’ [השטן] is three hundred and sixty-four,” the number of days (of the solar year) on which he may accuse, excluding Yom Kippur — which R’ Tzadok reads as the day the concealed depth of the Jewish heart is laid bare, leaving no foothold for accusation.932Tehillim 73:26; Resisei Layla 25:1 — “the Rock of my heart and my portion forever”: The Psalmist contrasts failing flesh and heart with God as the enduring “Rock of my heart and my portion forever.” Rav Tzadok reads the verse as naming a Divine attachment deeper than unstable bodily and emotional states. Resisei Layla explains that visible Jewish failure belongs to a created process of deficiency and completion, while Israel’s ultimate dependence upon Hashem is not displaced. The verse itself voices trust amid frailty; the claim that sins are only “to the sight of the eye” describes Rav Tzadok’s inward-root perspective, not a denial that acts in this world are real and morally consequential.933Yirmiyahu 2:21; Michah 7:20; Machshavot Charutz 7:1; Yisrael Kedoshim 5:7 — Yaakov’s “seed of truth”: Yirmiyahu calls Israel a planted “seed of truth” precisely while rebuking its corruption, and Michah identifies truth with Yaakov. Rav Tzadok develops the tension: Yaakov’s descendants possess a point of truth that “is established forever,” even when it is concealed by the falsehood of this world. Machshavot Charutz says that every Jew retains this enduring point, while Yisrael Kedoshim describes truth as hidden in earthly coverings until it finally grows and becomes manifest. Holy origin therefore grounds the possibility and necessity of teshuvah; it does not reclassify wrongdoing as harmless.
אֲבָל נֶגֶד הִתְגַּלּוּת הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב אֵין שָׂטָן וְאֵין פֶּגַע רָע
but before the revelation of Understanding within the heart (Binah she-ba-lev), there is no adversary and no evil occurrence;
דְּזֶה הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הַמּוּשְׁרָשׁ בְּכָל זַרְעוֹ, שֶׁהֵם זֶרַע אֱמֶת שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ לַה׳ וְאֵין פְּסֹולֶת וְרַע כְּלָל

for this is the root of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, implanted within all his seed, who are a seed of Truth entirely devoted to Hashem, possessing no dross or evil whatsoever.934Berachos 17a; Machshavot Charutz 7:1; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7:11 — the inward root beyond accusation: Berachos places “a bad mishap” and the evil inclination among the forces from which one asks rescue, showing that evil is experienced as a genuine threat in ordinary life. Rav Tzadok nevertheless distinguishes this field of struggle from the deepest covenantal point: Machshavot Charutz describes a truth in every member of Yaakov’s seed that cannot be extinguished, and Peri Tzadik says that the same root remains attached to Hashem even when its revelation is obscured. “No Satan and no evil affliction” therefore concerns the revealed root on Yom Kippur, not permanent immunity from temptation, judgment, or consequences.
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתְּשׁוּבָה דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ו:י), שֶׁמֵּאִיר מַעֲמַקֵּי הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב
And this is likewise the root of repentance whereof it is said "his heart shall understand, and he shall return" (Yeshayah 6:10), which radiates from the depths of Understanding within the heart;
וְהוּא הַשָּׂגַת אוֹר עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא הָעָלְמָא דְּאִתְכַּסְיָא בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְנִתְגַּלָּה עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁמְּשִׁיב כָּל הַדְּבָרִים לְשָׁרְשָׁם

and this is the attainment of the light of the World to Come, which is the concealed realm (alma d'iskasya) within this world, unveiled through repentance which restores all things to their root;935Yeshayahu 6:10; Megillah 17b; Takanas HaShavin 1:1 and 8:1 — understanding, return, and healing: Yeshayahu joins the heart’s understanding with return and healing: “its heart understands, and it returns, and it is healed.” Megillah uses this verse to explain why the blessing of teshuvah follows the blessing of understanding in the Amidah. Rav Tzadok makes the sequence metaphysical: binah within the heart is the beginning of teshuvah, first as an inward turning and afterward as full repair. Takanas HaShavin opens with this principle and later distinguishes the initial healing produced by the heart’s return from the more complete rectification of the past. The sefirah-language is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic exposition of the prophetic and liturgical sources.936Berachos 17a; Pri Tzadik, Shavuot 22:1, Rosh Chodesh Shvat 1:1, and Devarim 10:1 — Binah, the World to Come, and the concealed world: Berachos describes the World to Come as beyond eating and drinking, with the righteous enjoying the radiance of the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok repeatedly identifies Binah with teshuvah and with the “World to Come”: Pri Tzadik calls Binah the upper mother and Eden from which the healing power of return flows; elsewhere he calls it the heart’s inward understanding and the “upper Shabbos” preceding the seven days of creation. The Bavli supplies the nonphysical image of the World to Come. Its identification with Binah and the concealed world, and the claim that teshuvah briefly reveals that light within this world, belong to Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic synthesis.
וְזֶהוּ הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִים שֶׁאֵין צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים יְכוֹלִים לַעֲמוֹד
and this is the station where penitents stand, where even the wholly righteous cannot stand (Berachos 34b);
כִּי צַדִּיק גָּמוּר הוּא הַיְסוֹד עוֹלָם, דְּעַל כֵּן נִבְרָא אָדָם בְּיוֹם ו׳ שֶׁהוּא הִתְגַּלּוּת מִדַּת הַיְסוֹד

for the wholly righteous person embodies Yesod Olam, wherefore man was created on the sixth day, which is the manifestation of the attribute of Yesod;937Berachos 34b — the disputed rank of baalei teshuvah and complete tzaddikim: R’ Abahu teaches that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place occupied by baalei teshuvah, deriving precedence from “peace, peace, to the far and to the near.” R’ Yochanan disagrees and applies the prophets’ promises to penitents while reserving the unseen reward for those righteous from the outset. Rav Tzadok follows R’ Abahu in this se’if because teshuvah reveals a level of return to the hidden source beyond the ordinary structure of a perfected life. The next se’if explicitly returns to R’ Yochanan’s view and seeks to preserve both teachings as “the words of the living God.”938Mishlei 10:25; Bereishis 1:26–31; Tzidkat HaTzadik 190; Peri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6:4 — the tzaddik as the world’s foundation: Mishlei calls the righteous person “an everlasting foundation,” and Bereishis places Adam’s creation on the sixth day, at the completion of the work of creation. Rav Tzadok reads these facts through the sefirotic order: the sixth attribute is Yesod, the channel that gathers and sustains the preceding powers, and the complete tzaddik embodies that stable foundation. Tzidkat HaTzadik associates Yaakov and Yosef with truth, life, and the heart’s covenantal foundation; Peri Tzadik describes Yaakov’s complete offspring as wholly rooted in holiness. The equation of the sixth day with the sefirah of Yesod is kabbalistic, not the plain sense of Bereishis or Mishlei.
כִּי הוּא הַיְסוֹד שֶׁעָלָיו עוֹמֵד כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ וְכָל הַבְּרִיאָה שֶׁבְּו׳ יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן
for he is the foundation upon which the entire universe and the whole creation of the six days of the cosmic structure stand;
וְאַחַר שֶׁחָטָא וְשָׁב נִיתַּן לוֹ יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, שֶׁהוּא גַּם כֵּן מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּאָז הוּא קִיבּוּל הַתְּשׁוּבָה

and after he sinned and repented, the day of Shabbos was given to him, which is likewise a foretaste of the World to Come, for then is the reception of repentance;939Berachos 57b; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 5:1 and 21:3 — Shabbos as a foretaste of the World to Come and the source of return: Berachos calls Shabbos a microcosm and one-sixtieth of the World to Come. Pri Tzadik explains that the first Shabbos protected Adam after his sin and revealed the possibility of teshuvah; every Shabbos therefore awakens return, and Shabbos Shuvah transmits that power with special intensity into the days leading to Yom Kippur. He also calls Yom Kippur a humanly realized “Shabbos Shabbason” that repairs the six days of action. The Gemara establishes Shabbos as a taste of the World to Come; its role as the spiritual reception and diffusion of teshuvah is Rav Tzadok’s developed interpretation.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן ״מִזְמוֹר שִׁיר לְיוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת״ (תְּהִלִּים צ״ב:א׳) כְּשֶׁנּוֹדַע לוֹ כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה כ״ב]
and therefore Adam HaRishon proclaimed "A Psalm, a Song for the Sabbath day" (Tehillim 92:1) when the power of repentance became known to him, as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 22:13];

דְּכָל כֹּחָהּ הוּא מִצַּד יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת, דְּ״רָאָה כָּל אֲשֶׁר [עָשָׂה וְהִנֵּה] טוֹב מְאֹד״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית א:לא), דְּגַם הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע שֶׁהוּא רַע הוּא חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת ״טוֹב מְאֹד״ אַחַר הַתְּשׁוּבָה

for its entire power stems from the aspect of the Sabbath day, when "He saw every thing that He had made, and, behold, it was very good" (Bereishis 1:31), so that even the yetzer hara, which was evil, is transformed into "very good" following repentance (Bereishis Rabbah 9:7);940Bereishis Rabbah 22:13 and 9:7; Pri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 5:1; Resisei Layla 42:1 — Adam’s song and the yetzer restored to “very good”: Bereishis Rabbah relates that Adam learned the power of teshuvah from Cain and immediately recited “A psalm, a song for the day of Shabbos.” A separate Midrash calls the evil inclination “very good” because without directed ambition people would not build, marry, have children, or conduct commerce. Rav Tzadok joins the teachings: teshuvah does not declare the sinful act good; it returns the underlying drive to the constructive purpose for which it was created. Pri Tzadik connects this discovery to the first Shabbos, while Resisei Layla explains that Shabbos reveals how even the force presently experienced as evil belongs ultimately within the Creator’s “very good” design.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה ״שָׁבַת וַיִּנָּפַשׁ״ (שְׁמוֹת ל״א:י״ז), שֶׁיָּדוּעַ שֶׁהוּא כְּאָדָם הַמִּתְנַפֵּשׁ וּמוֹשֵׁךְ נְשִׁימָתוֹ וְרוּחַ שֶׁבְּאַפָּיו אֵלָיו

and through this "He ceased from work and was refreshed" (Shemos 31:17), which is known to be like a person who catches his breath, drawing his breath and the spirit of his nostrils back into himself;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עֲלִיַּית הָעוֹלָמוֹת בְּשַׁבָּת, דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן הֲשָׁבָה לַמָּקוֹר, אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד שְׁכִינָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ בַּתַּחְתּוֹנִים, וּ״מְלֹא כָל הָאָרֶץ כְּבוֹדוֹ״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ו:ג):

which constitutes the elevation of the worlds on Shabbos, being likewise a restoration unto the Source, though from the aspect of His Divine Presence dwelling below, where "the whole earth is full of His glory" (Yeshayah 6:3).941Shemos 31:17; Beitzah 16a; Machshavot Charutz 10:1; Resisei Layla 54:2 — “He rested and was refreshed”: The Torah says that on the seventh day Hashem “ceased and was refreshed.” Beitzah reads va-yinafash as an allusion to the additional Shabbos soul and the sorrow when it departs. Rav Tzadok develops the word’s ordinary image of catching one’s breath: after activity reaches completion, the worker draws his powers inward and rests in their source. Machshavot Charutz describes Shabbos as the final power that completes a work by gathering spirit and soul back to the doer, and Resisei Layla compares its cool repose to the World to Come. The cosmic ascent described here is the kabbalistic analogue of that inward gathering.942Yeshayahu 6:3; Midrash Tanchuma, Nasso 16; Peri Tzadik, Nasso 5:1–2 and Acharei Mot 8:1 — ascent without abandoning the lower world: Yeshayahu proclaims that “the whole earth is full of His glory.” Midrash Tanchuma teaches that Hashem desired a dwelling in the lower worlds and that the Avos and Moshe progressively restored the Shechinah after sin had driven it upward. Rav Tzadok therefore qualifies the language of Shabbos ascent: the created powers return to their source, yet the purpose remains Divine indwelling below. Pri Tzadik links Shabbos, va-yinafash, teshuvah, and the Shechinah’s residence in the heart. The verse and Midrash establish pervasive glory and the lower dwelling; the terminology of ascending worlds describes their kabbalistic harmonization, not Divine absence from earth.

items.h: The theme: The lower unity versus the higher unity in repentance. The lower unity (yichuda tata'ah) corresponds to "Blessed be the name of His glorious Kingdom forever" and lower repentance (teshuvah tata'ah, mere cessation from sin), which Adam attained. The prophets, gazing through an unpolished mirror (aspaklaria she-einah me'irah), prophesied exclusively concerning this rung of the penitent, whereas the concealed reward of the World to Come ("eye has not seen", Yeshayah 64:3) is reserved for the wholly righteous. David HaMelech established higher repentance (teshuvah ila'ah), which penetrates the heart's depths and grasps Binah, enabling one to "see his world in his lifetime" and transcend death. At this transcendent rung, sins are retroactively understood as part of the hidden Divine design (kavshei d'Rachmana), where Hashem sovereignly orchestrated the historical descent of souls to bring forth the light of Mashiach.

p: וְזֶהוּ יִחוּדָא תַּתָּאָה דְּ״בָּרוּךְ שֵׁם כְּבוֹד מַלְכוּתוֹ לְעוֹלָם וָעֶד״, וְהוּא תְּשׁוּבָה תַּתָּאָה שֶׁזָּכָה לָהּ גַּם אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן עַל יְדֵי הַסּוּר מֵרָע לְבַד

And this is the lower unity (yichuda tata'ah) of "Blessed be the name of His glorious Kingdom forever and ever," which embodies lower repentance (teshuvah tata'ah), merited even by Adam HaRishon through mere turning away from evil alone;
וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ [בְּרָכוֹת ל״ד עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״כָּל הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא נִתְנַבְּאוּ אֶלָּא לְבַעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, אֲבָל צַדִּיק גָּמוּר וְכוּלֵיהּ״

and concerning this they stated [in Berachos 34b]: "All the prophets prophesied only concerning penitents, but regarding a wholly righteous person: 'Eye has not seen, O God, beside You' (Yeshayah 64:3)";943Pesachim 56a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:13 — “Baruch Shem” and the lower unity: Pesachim relates that when Yaakov feared a defect among his children, they declared that Hashem was One in their hearts just as in his; Yaakov answered, “Blessed is the Name of the glory of His kingship forever and ever.” Rav Tzadok calls this yichuda tata’ah, the lower unity: Divine kingship is recognized from within an apparently separate and concealed world. Yisrael Kedoshim contrasts it with the fully revealed unity represented by Shema. Thus “lower Yehudah” is not a lesser allegiance to Hashem, but the confession of unity precisely within earthly concealment, where return, choice, and kingship are experienced.944Tzidkat HaTzadik 132; Takanas HaShavin 11:7, 15:22; Pri Tzadik, Sh’lach 7:2 — lower and upper teshuvah: Rav Tzadok distinguishes teshuvah tata’ah from teshuvah ila’ah. The lower return begins with human awakening, fear, regret, and turning from evil; it repairs conduct and removes the immediate hold of sin. The upper return reaches Binah, the source above the corrupted root, where the deepest source of Israel is wholly good and even the past can be transformed. Takanas HaShavin elsewhere explicitly identifies “turning from evil alone” with the lower level and describes the upper level as Hashem’s answering return and added sanctification. The distinction is one of depth and completion, not a suggestion that practical abandonment of sin can be bypassed.
וּפְלִיגָא אַדְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ דְּ״מָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״
which disputes the view of Rabbi Abbahu that "in the place where penitents stand, [the wholly righteous cannot stand]";
וְאֵלּוּ וָאֵלּוּ דִּבְרֵי אֱלֹהִים חַיִּים, וְהַשָּׂגַת הַנְּבִיאִים בְּאַסְפַּקְלַרְיָא שֶׁאֵינָהּ מְאִירָה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִרְאוֹת אוֹר הַגָּנוּז לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא

and these and those are the words of the Living God, for through the prophetic perception of an unpolished mirror (aspaklaria she-einah me'irah) it is impossible to behold the light concealed for the righteous in the Future;945Berachos 34b; Eruvin 13b — two rankings of the penitent and the complete tzaddik: R’ Yochanan reserves “no eye has seen” for one righteous from the outset and applies prophetic consolation to penitents. R’ Abahu reverses the priority, teaching that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place of baalei teshuvah. Rav Tzadok invokes the general principle of Eruvin, “these and those are the words of the living God,” to treat the dispute as describing two valid dimensions: stable purity has an unseen perfection of its own, while return from distance can reach a source unavailable through an unbroken path. The Gemara presents competing rankings; Rav Tzadok’s reconciliation is an interpretive synthesis.946Yevamos 49b; Ramban on Bereishis 17:1 — the non-illuminating glass and the limits of prophetic sight: Yevamos distinguishes Moshe, who perceived through an illuminating glass, from the other prophets, who perceived through a glass that does not illuminate. Ramban explains that prophetic vision remains an authentic encounter while being received through differing degrees of mediation. Rav Tzadok uses that distinction to explain why prophecy can disclose the days of Mashiach yet not the fully hidden light of the World to Come. “No eye has seen” marks not a defect in prophecy, but a level that is not an object of ordinary visionary perception. The identification of that hidden light with the reward of the complete tzaddik belongs to his reading of Berachos.
וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לְטַעְמֵיהּ שָׁם דְּ״כָל הַנְּבִיאִים וְכוּלֵיהּ לִימוֹת הַמָּשִׁיחַ, אֲבָל לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and Rabbi Yochanan follows his reasoning there that "all the prophets prophesied only for the Days of the Messiah, but as for the World to Come, 'eye has not seen, etc.'";
דִּלְנָבִיא לְפָנִים יִקָּרֵא ״הָרֹאֶה״ (שְׁמוּאֵל א ט:ט), דְּהַשָּׂגָתוֹ עַל יְדֵי עַיִן רוֹאָה
for a prophet was formerly called "the seer" (I Shmuel 9:9), his perception operating through the seeing eye;
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמַר לִשְׁמוּאֵל רַבָּן שֶׁל נְבִיאִים: ״אַל תַּבֵּט [אֶל מַרְאֵהוּ] וְגוֹמֵר, כִּי לֹא אֲשֶׁר יִרְאֶה הָאָדָם, כִּי הָאָדָם יִרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וְגוֹמֵר״ (שְׁמוּאֵל א ט״ז:ז׳)

wherefore He said to Shmuel, the master of prophets: "Look not on his countenance... for man looks on the outward appearance, but Hashem looks on the heart" (I Shmuel 16:7).947I Shmuel 9:9 and 16:7 — the seer, the eyes, and the heart: Scripture notes that a prophet was formerly called a ro’eh, a seer. When Shmuel evaluates Yishai’s sons, Hashem warns him not to look at appearance or stature: a person sees what is visible to the eyes, but Hashem sees the heart. Rav Tzadok makes the episode programmatic. Even the master prophet can perceive only the revealed form unless Hashem discloses the inward heart, while David’s chosenness lies precisely in that concealed interior. The verses establish the contrast between external sight and Divine knowledge of the heart; Rav Tzadok applies it to the contrast between prophetic sight and the heart-depth of upper teshuvah.
כִּי דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הַגֶּבֶר שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה
For David HaMelech, peace be upon him, was the man who raised up the yoke of higher repentance (teshuvah ila'ah, Moed Katan 16b),
שֶׁהוּא מַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין״, וְזוֹכֶה לְהַשָּׂגַת הַבִּינָה לִבָּא שֶׁהוּא עָלְמָא עִילָּאָה דְּעַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה

which issues from the depths of the heart where "his heart understands," meriting the attainment of Understanding of the heart, which is the supernal realm whereof "eye has not seen";948Moed Katan 16b; Avodah Zarah 5a; Pri Tzadik, Shavuos 19:1 and Va’eschanan 3:1 — David established the yoke of upper teshuvah: Chazal expound “the man raised on high” as David, who established the yoke of teshuvah and became the model for an individual who returns. Pri Tzadik identifies David’s root with the upper hei, Binah, and the verse “then you will understand fear of Hashem”: his return reaches the depths of the heart and opens a path beyond the ordinary standing of the complete tzaddik. Rav Tzadok does not erase David’s confession, rebuke, or consequences. His claim is that David’s accepted return revealed a previously hidden power by which even profound failure can become the beginning of renewed attachment and life.
דְּאֵין בּוֹ הַשָּׂגָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֶלָּא לְמִי שֶׁזּוֹכֶה לִרְאוֹת עוֹלָמוֹ בְּחַיָּיו
which cannot be attained in this world except by one who merits to see his world in his lifetime;
הַיְינוּ שֶׁכְּבָר תִּיקֵּן הַכֹּל, גַּם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, וְזוֹכֶה לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם כִּי אֵין מִיתָה בְּלֹא חֵטְא

meaning that he has already rectified everything, even the root of the Serpent's instigation, meriting eternal life, for there is no death without sin (Shabbos 55a).949Berachos 17a; Pri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer 4:1 and 6:2; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:20 — “May you see your world in your lifetime”: The Sages blessed one another, “May you see your world in your lifetime.” Rav Tzadok explains that the World to Come is the revelation of the primordial light hidden in Torah and knowledge of Hashem; an exceptional person may taste or “see” that light while still alive. Pri Tzadik associates the blessing with inward Torah illumination, while Yisrael Kedoshim stresses that during earthly life it remains a sight and foretaste rather than complete possession. In this se’if, David’s upper teshuvah makes such sight possible because the heart has already begun to return to the future world’s source of life.
וְאַף דְּאִיתּוֹתַב הַךְ מַאן דְּאָמַר [בְּשַׁבָּת נ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳]
And although that authority was refuted [in Shabbos 55b],
הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין צָרִיךְ חֵטְא גָּמוּר בְּפֹעַל, וְרַק כָּל שֶׁלֹּא בִּיטֵּל זוּהֲמַת הַיֵּצֶר לְגַמְרֵי זֶהוּ עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ דְּמֵתוּ בָּהּ אוֹתָן דְּחָשֵׁיב שָׁם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל

that refutation means that actual sin in practice is not required, and merely failing to eliminate the defilement of the yetzer entirely constitutes the Serpent's instigation, by which those four individuals enumerated there died, as I wrote above;950Shabbos 55b; Bava Basra 17a; Machshavos Charutz 11:6 — death, sin, and the serpent’s counsel: Shabbos records the assertion “there is no death without sin” and then refutes it from four exceptionally righteous people who died only through the serpent’s counsel: Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav. Bava Basra preserves the same list. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes a chosen, concrete transgression from the inherited root introduced through Adam: even where no personal act warrants death, mortality can remain because the primordial mixture has not yet been wholly removed. Machshavos Charutz assigns Mashiach the final repair of that root. This is a metaphysical account of mortality, not a charge that those four secretly committed ordinary sins.
וּלְגַבַּיְיהוּ גַּם זֶה נֶחְשָׁב חֵטְא, דִּסְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד
and relative to their stature, even this subtle trace is considered a sin, for "round about Him it storms exceedingly" (Tehillim 50:3);
וְהַכָּתוּב קְרָאוֹ ״בְּעָווֹן״ מָלֵא גַּבֵּי יִשַׁי, דִּלְגַבֵּי דִּידֵיהּ נֶחְשַׁב זֶה לְעָווֹן מַה שֶּׁכִּיוֵּון לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ
and Scripture wrote "in iniquity" (b'avon, Tehillim 51:7) with a full vav regarding Yishai, for relative to him his intention for personal pleasure was accounted an iniquity;
וּלְגַבֵּי אִמּוֹ, דְּמִסְּתָמָא הָיְתָה גַּם כֵּן צַדֶּקֶת גְּדוֹלָה שֶׁזָּכְתָה לְבֵן כָּזֶה, נֶחְשַׁב לְחֵטְא
and relative to David's mother, who was presumably a great righteous woman to merit such a son, it was reckoned merely an inadvertent sin (chet);
וְלוֹ שֶׁהָיָה גָּדוֹל יוֹתֵר נֶחְשַׁב לְעָווֹן וְנוֹסַף הַוָּי״ו

while to Yishai who was greater, it was accounted an iniquity (avon), with the letter vav added.951Tehillim 50:3 and 51:7; Yevamos 121b; Pri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Tammuz 3:2 — the exacting measure applied to Yishai and David’s mother: Chazal interpret “around Him it storms greatly” to mean that Hashem is exacting with those nearest to Him even to a hair’s breadth. Tehillim describes David’s conception with the terms avon and chet, while Chazal count Yishai among those who died only through the serpent’s counsel. Rav Tzadok reads the words by a relative spiritual scale: for people free of ordinary transgression, the faint residue of self-directed pleasure can be called a defect because of their exceptional closeness. Pri Tzadik makes the same connection to Yishai. This is neither a legal condemnation of marital intimacy nor an accusation against David’s mother; it is Rav Tzadok’s language of elevated spiritual exactness.952Pri Tzadik, Shavuos 19:1; Machshavos Charutz 7:15; Takanas HaShavin 5:8 — the added hei and increased holiness: Rav Tzadok attributes to the Ari the symbolic rule that an added letter of the Divine Name signals an added measure of holiness and attachment. His own writings repeatedly associate the lower hei with revealed kingship and lower teshuvah, and the upper hei with Binah and the higher return exemplified by David. Here the added hei marks a more refined spiritual status and therefore a more exacting use of the word avon. This is a kabbalistic letter-symbolism invoked by Rav Tzadok, not the grammatical or historical plain meaning of the name or verse, and it should be kept distinct from the Gemara’s legal categories of sin.
וְיָדוּעַ מֵהָאֲרִ״י שֶׁבְּכָל מָקוֹם שֶׁנּוֹסַף אוֹת מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת שֵׁם הֲוָיָ״ה מוֹרֶה תּוֹסֶפֶת קְדוּשָׁה וְדִיבּוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, וְשֶׁמֵּאִתּוֹ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים

And it is known from the Ari that wherever a letter of the Tetragrammaton is added, it indicates an augmentation of holiness and cleaving unto the Blessed Name, signifying that deep divine decrees (kevuoshim) issued from Him;

כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּסוֹף מַכּוֹת, כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳] בִּיהוּדָה וְתָמָר [וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה, פָּרָשָׁה פ״ה]: דְּרָצָה לֵילֵךְ, וְרָמַז הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַמַּלְאָךְ הַמְמוּנֶּה עַל הַתַּאֲוָה וְכוּלֵיהּ

in the manner taught [at the end of Makkos 23b and in Bereishis Rabbah 85:8] regarding Yehudah and Tamar: that he wished to pass by, but the Holy One, blessed be He, signaled to the angel appointed over lust, etc.;
וְהָיָה דּוֹמֶה שֶׁעָשָׂה עֲבֵירָה וּבָעַל קְדֵשָׁה
and it appeared outwardly as if he committed a sin and cohabited with a harlot;
וְעַל כֵּן תְּחִלָּה רָצָה לֵילֵךְ כִּי יִצְרוֹ הָיָה מָסוּר בְּיָדוֹ, וְלֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה אִלּוּ הָיָה עֲבֵירָה

wherefore initially he wished to pass by, for his yetzer was surrendered into his hand, and he would never have engaged in that deed had it been an actual sin;953Cf. Makkos 23b — the source R’ Tzadok invokes regarding Yehuda and Tamar: among the three things the earthly court did with which the Heavenly court concurred, a bas kol went forth and said, “mimeni yatz’u kevushim [from Me these hidden things went out]” — confirming that Yehuda’s union with Tamar, from which Mashiach descends, was providentially arranged from Above and not a mere transgression.954Bereishis Rabbah 85:8 — Yehudah, Tamar, and the angel appointed over desire: The Midrash says that Yehudah initially sought to pass Tamar, but Hashem sent the angel appointed over desire, asking from where kings and great leaders would arise; it then reads “he turned to her” as occurring against his initial will. The same passage begins with a warning that a person must guard himself carefully from sexual stumbling. Rav Tzadok draws on the providential layer to explain the concealed origin of Davidic kingship. The Aggadah is not permission to follow desire or to treat ordinary prohibited conduct as secretly commanded. It describes this singular ancestral event while preserving the Torah’s moral seriousness and Yehudah’s later public acknowledgment.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא הָיָה עָסוּק לִבְרוֹא אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ
rather, the Holy One, blessed be He, was occupied with creating the light of Mashiach,
שֶׁהוּא מִתְגַּלֶּה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה עַל יְדֵי הַהֶסְתֵּר וְהֶעְלֵם הַקּוֹדֵם בְּכָל יְמֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַדּוֹמֶה לְלַיְלָה שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ חֹשֶׁךְ
which is revealed in this world through the preceding concealment throughout all the days of this world, which resembles a night of utter darkness;
וְיֵעָדֵר אוֹר מֵרוֹב הִשְׁתַּקְּעוּת שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְשִׁעְבּוּד מַלְכוּת

where light is absent from the depth of immersion caused by the yeast in the dough and the subjugation of the kingdoms;955Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 — Hashem was creating the light of King Mashiach: Bereishis Rabbah portrays every participant as occupied with a different visible concern after Yosef’s sale, while Hashem was occupied with “creating the light of the King Mashiach” through Yehudah’s developing family. The Midrash deliberately holds rebuke, suffering, human action, and hidden redemption together. Rav Tzadok takes this as a paradigm: the messianic light enters history under concealment and can initially appear opposite to its ultimate purpose. The source does not say that every wrongful act is automatically redemptive. It teaches that Divine providence can prepare redemption within a morally complex history whose participants remain responsible for their choices.
וּבְקַדְרוּת דְּצַפְרָא גּוֹבֵר הַחֹשֶׁךְ יוֹתֵר, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּעִקְּבָתָא דִּמְשִׁיחָא
and in the twilight before dawn darkness intensifies, as the Sages stated regarding the Footsteps of the Messiah (ikvesa d'Meshicha);
וּמִשָּׁם דַּיְיקָא ״יְקַבֶּצְךָ [ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ] וּמִשָּׁם יִקָּחֶךָ״ (דְּבָרִים ל:ד)
and precisely from there "will the Lord your God gather you, and from there will He fetch you" (Devarim 30:4);
כִּי אוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מַעְלָה הוּא אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר גַּם בְּתוֹךְ הַחֹשֶׁךְ
for the supernal Light is a light that shines even within the darkness,
וּמְבָרֵר דִּ״לְכָל בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הָיָה אוֹר בְּמוֹשְׁבֹתָם״ (שְׁמוֹת י:כג) גַּם בִּימֵי הַחֹשֶׁךְ
clarifying that "all the children of Israel had light in their dwellings" (Shemos 10:23) even in the days of darkness;
דְּ״כִּי אֵשֵׁב בַּחֹשֶׁךְ ה׳ אוֹר לִי״ (מִיכָה ז:ח), וְ״גַּם כִּי אֵלֵךְ [בְּגֵיא צַלְמָוֶת לֹא אִירָא רָע כִּי] אַתָּה עִמָּדִי״ (תְּהִלִּים כ״ג:ד׳)

for "though I sit in darkness, Hashem shall be a light unto me" (Michah 7:8), and "yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Tehillim 23:4);956Sotah 49b; Devarim 30:4; Shemos 10:23; Michah 7:8; Tehillim 23:4 — light within the darkness before redemption: Sotah describes the footsteps of Mashiach as an age of intensified brazenness, confusion, and absent truth. Yet the Torah promises that even from the furthest exile Hashem will gather and take Israel. The Exodus already supplied the image: darkness covered Egypt while Israel had light in its dwellings. Michah and Tehillim add that when one sits in darkness Hashem becomes one’s light, and even in the valley of death’s shadow “You are with me.” Rav Tzadok reads these sources together: the darkness can intensify near dawn, but the higher light is present within concealment and becomes the means of gathering rather than proof of abandonment.
דְּכָל הַחֲטָאִים יִהְיוּ כַּשָּׁנִים הַלָּלוּ שֶׁסְּדוּרוֹת וּבָאוֹת מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית
so that all sins will retroactively be recognized like those cosmic years that have been ordered and advancing since the six days of Creation (Shabbos 89b);
הַיְינוּ דְּהַכֹּל מְסוּדָּר מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁרָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן, וּמִמֶּנּוּ יָצְאוּ כְּבוּשִׁים

meaning that everything was sovereignly ordered by the Blessed Name Who willed it to be so, and from Him issued these hidden decrees.957Shabbos 89b; Machshavos Charutz 4:3 and 11:3; Pri Tzadik, Chanukah 6:1 — sins arranged from the six days of Creation: Shabbos expounds “if your sins are like years” as sins arranged and coming from the six days of Creation, yet becoming white as snow. Rav Tzadok reads this as a future disclosure that even the darkness through which Israel passed was encompassed within the Creator’s primordial plan of darkness followed by light. Machshavos Charutz and Pri Tzadik connect that disclosure with Davidic teshuvah, through which intentional sins can ultimately be transformed into merits. This is an eschatological clarification after genuine teshuvah. It does not permit a person now to call a chosen violation God’s will, ignore halachah, or evade present responsibility and repair.
אֶלָּא שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא עוֹלַם הַבְּחִירָה, דָּבָר זֶה ״כִּבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא״ שֶׁהוּא טָמִיר וְנֶעְלָם אֵיךְ הַכֹּל מִידִיעַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

Except that in this world, which is the world of free choice, this matter belongs to the "secrets of the Merciful One" (kavshei d'Rachmana), hidden and concealed as to how all harmonizes with the omniscience of the Blessed Name;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ קוּשְׁיַת הַיְּדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה שֶׁכָּתַב רַמְבַּ״ם שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג יְדִיעָתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
which is the classical dilemma of Foreknowledge versus Free Choice formulated by the Rambam (Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5), that it is impossible for the human mind to grasp His knowledge;
וּדְבָרָיו חַיִּים וְקַיָּימִים, שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לַעֲמוֹד עַל זֶה אֵיךְ יִכּוֹנוּ יַחְדָּו:

and his words are living and enduring: that in this world it is impossible to comprehend how they coexist together.958Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5; Pri Tzadik, Beha’aloscha 12:2; Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 3:7 — Divine knowledge and human choice: Rambam asks how Hashem’s complete foreknowledge can coexist with a person’s ability to choose otherwise. He answers that Divine knowledge is not external to Hashem as human knowledge is, and therefore its manner is beyond human comprehension. Nevertheless, he insists without qualification that human deeds are in the person’s hands, Hashem does not compel the act, and judgment by deeds is a foundation of prophecy. Rav Tzadok accepts both sides. Pri Tzadik cites Rambam and “My thoughts are not your thoughts,” while Dover Tzedek says the unity can be grasped only at a level inaccessible to ordinary intellect. Thus hidden providential order never cancels practical free choice in this world.

items.h: The theme: Divine foreknowledge versus human responsibility in Chizkiyahu, David, and the daughters of Lot. When Chizkiyahu foresaw through the Holy Spirit that wicked sons (Menasheh) would issue from him, the prophet Yeshayah rebuked him: "What have you to do with the secrets of the Merciful One?" (Berachos 10a). Although free choice governs this world, Mashiach will illuminate how every descent was preordained since Creation. David is described as a "lost treasure" found in Sodom ("I have found David My servant... in Sodom", Tehillim 89:21; Bereishis Rabbah 41:4), for the seed of Mashiach was extracted from the absolute nadir of bodily lust—Lot and his daughters. While the daughters of Lot were immersed in lust, their intention was elevated to preserve human existence ("and bring forth seed from our father", Bereishis 19:32), which Chazal identify with the royal seed of Mashiach.

p: וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת י׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] בְּחִזְקִיָּה, דַּחֲזָא בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ דִּיהוֹן לֵיהּ בְּנִין דְּלָא מַעֲלוּ: ״בַּהֲדֵי כִּבְשֵׁי [דְּרַחֲמָנָא לָמָּה לָךְ] וְכוּלֵיהּ״

And therefore they stated [in Berachos 10a] regarding Chizkiyahu, who foresaw through the Holy Spirit that he would father unworthy children: "What have you to do with the secrets of the Merciful One? [Do that which you are commanded]";
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁרוֹאֶה בְּרוּחַ הַקֹּדֶשׁ מִקּוֹדֶם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן, אִם כֵּן הַדָּבָר מְסוּדָּר כֵּן מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ וְאֵינוֹ בִּבְחִירָה
for since he foresaw through Divine Inspiration that it would be so, the matter was already ordained by the Blessed Name and seemingly outside free choice!
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁגַּם זֶה אֱמֶת דְּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַבְּחִירָה בְּיַד אָדָם, וְעַל כֵּן הָרְשָׁעִים נִידּוֹנִים עַל חֶטְאָם

And although it is equally true that in this world free choice is given to man, wherefore the wicked are judged for their sin;959Berakhot 10a — Chizkiyahu’s vision and the obligation to act: Chizkiyahu withheld from marriage because he saw through ruach ha-kodesh that unworthy children would emerge from him. Yeshayahu answered: “Why involve yourself with the hidden matters of the Merciful One? What you were commanded, you must do.” The Gemara’s practical teaching is unequivocal: foreknowledge of an outcome does not release a person from mitzvah or responsibility. Rav Tzadok then explores the deeper metaphysical question raised by the very truth of that vision; he does not use hidden knowledge to weaken halachic obligation.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַה שֶּׁהוּא מַשִּׂיג מִצַּד הַיְּדִיעָה, אִם הַיְּדִיעָה אֱמֶת אֵיךְ נֶחְשָׁב לְחֵטְא, אַף שֶׁפְּשַׁט הַדָּבָר נֶעְלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה ״בַּהֲדֵי כִּבְשֵׁי וְכוּלֵיהּ״

nevertheless, from the perspective of Foreknowledge, if that knowledge is absolute truth, how is it accounted a sin? Even though the inner resolution is concealed in this world as "the secrets of the Merciful One."960Nefesh HaChaim, Gate I 22 — commanded action rather than speculation: Rav Chaim of Volozhin cites Yeshayahu’s answer to Chizkiyahu as a rule of avodah: “What you were commanded, you must do; what is pleasing before the Holy One, let Him do.” A person is charged with the revealed will of Torah, not with calculating the hidden Divine plan. Rav Tzadok’s discussion belongs to the plane of ultimate clarification by Mashiach; until then, it cannot function as permission to disregard command, accountability, or ordinary moral judgment.
וּמָשִׁיחַ שֶׁיֵּצֵא מֵחֲלָצָיו, הוּא יְגַלֶּה וְיָאִיר אוֹר הַשָּׂגָה זוֹ וְכִבְשֵׁי דְּרַחֲמָנָא הַלָּלוּ אֵיךְ הַכֹּל מְסוּדָּר מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית

And Mashiach, who will issue from his loins, will reveal and illuminate the light of this perception and these divine mysteries, demonstrating how everything was orchestrated from the six days of Creation;961Sanhedrin 94a; Dover Tzedek §4 — Chizkiyahu and the unrealized possibility of Mashiach: Chazal teach that Hashem sought to make Chizkiyahu Mashiach. Rav Tzadok repeatedly associates Chizkiyahu’s trust and ruach ha-kodesh with a messianic mode of perception, while also explaining why that light was not fully revealed through him. Se’if 52 continues that line: Chizkiyahu perceived a hidden arrangement, but the complete illumination of how providence and choice unite is assigned to the descendant who will bring the messianic rectification to completion.
כִּי הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ בָּרָא יֵצֶר הָרָע וּבָרָא רְשָׁעִים, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּל יְמֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַבְּחִירָה בִּידֵי אָדָם, וְדָבָר זֶה סָתוּם וְנֶעְלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

for the Blessed Name created the yetzer hara and created the wicked (Bava Batra 16a), yet throughout the duration of this world free choice remains in human hands, a paradox sealed and concealed in this world.962Shabbos 89b; Machshavos Charutz 4:3 and 11:3; Pri Tzadik, Beha’aloscha 12:2 — “ordered from the six days of Creation”: Shabbos expounds “though your sins be like years” as sins that have been ordered and coming since the six days of Creation. Rav Tzadok frequently reads this as the future disclosure that the darkness preceding light was included in the primordial order, while insisting that within the present world choice and judgment remain binding. In Pri Tzadik he explicitly invokes the Rambam: human thought cannot understand how foreknowledge does not cancel choice. The future whitening of sins describes their rectification after teshuvah, not advance authorization to sin.963Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:1–5 — Divine knowledge and human freedom: The Rambam establishes free choice as a foundation of Torah and judgment, then asks how it can coexist with Hashem’s infallible knowledge. His answer is that Hashem and His knowledge are one, unlike human knower and knowledge; therefore the manner of Divine knowing is beyond human comprehension. Nevertheless, human deeds remain genuinely in human hands. This supplies the classical framework for Rav Tzadok’s statement that both truths stand: choice governs avodah in this world, while the reconciliation with Divine knowledge remains among the hidden matters.

וְעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר: ״מָצָאתִי דָּוִד עַבְדִּי״ (תְּהִלִּים פ״ט:כ״א), כִּי הֲקָמַת עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה דְּדָוִד, שֶׁזָּכָה לִהְיוֹת חַי וְקַיָּים עַל יְדֵי תִּיקּוּן כָּל הַחֲשֵׁיכוּת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And therefore it is stated: "I have found David My servant" (Tehillim 89:21): for the raising of the yoke of repentance by David, who merited to be "alive and enduring" through rectifying all the darkness of this world,
אוֹר זֶה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא אָבוּד מִכָּל אָדָם וְאֵינוֹ מִתְגַּלֶּה אֶלָּא דֶּרֶךְ מְצִיאָה

this light in this world was lost to all men, being discovered only through the unexpected manner of a "find";964Psalms 89:21; Bereishis Rabbah 41:4–5 — “I found David My servant” in Sodom: The verse says, “I have found David My servant.” The Midrash asks, “Where did I find him? In Sodom,” connecting David’s line to Lot and the daughters who were “found.” The language of finding signifies a holy root concealed where ordinary expectation would not seek it. Rav Tzadok develops this into a principle of Mashiach: the final light emerges from profound concealment and then reveals how holiness survived and was refined through the darkness.
וְאָמְרוּ: ״הֵיכָן מְצָאתִיו? בִּסְדוֹם, דִּכְתִיב: ׳[שְׁתֵּי] בְנֹתֶיךָ הַנִּמְצָאֹת׳ (בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ט:ט״ו)״
and they expounded: "Where did I find him? In Sodom, as it is written: 'your two daughters that are found' (Bereishis 19:15; Bereishis Rabbah 41:4)";
וְאֵין לְךָ בְּנֵי אָדָם גְּרוּעִים בְּשִׁיקּוּעַ בְּכָל מִינֵי תַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּאַנְשֵׁי סְדוֹם, וְלוֹט בִּשְׁבִיל כֵּן נִתְחַבֵּר עִמָּהֶם

and you have no people as degraded in immersion in all manners of physical lusts of this world as the people of Sodom, with whom Lot associated for that very reason;965Pri Tzadik, Sukkos 23:2 — the hidden Torah of Mashiach located in Sodom: Rav Tzadok’s close parallel states that the soul of David and Mashiach was present in Sodom and associates it with the future Torah of Mashiach, an illumination unlike the ordinary attainments of this world. He contrasts Sodom’s destruction with the concealed spark found there. This supports the se’if’s claim that the messianic light appears by metziah: not because Sodom’s conduct becomes holy, but because a hidden spark is extracted from a place dominated by corruption.966Genesis 13:13; 18:20; Ezekiel 16:49–50 — the corruption of Sodom: Scripture describes the people of Sodom as exceedingly wicked and sinful and identifies arrogance, abundance, ease, neglect of the poor, and abomination among their sins. Rav Tzadok’s phrase “sunk in every bodily desire” is a theological characterization of that corrupt civilization. It does not turn later descendants into embodiments of Sodom, nor does the holy spark found there excuse the society’s cruelty and sin; the contrast between the setting and the concealed messianic root is precisely his point.
וְאֵין לְךָ מְגוּנֶּה מֵהַבִּיאָה עַל בְּנוֹתָיו שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַשִּׁיקּוּעַ בַּתַּאֲווֹת
and you have nothing as abhorrent as cohabitation with his daughters, which represents the ultimate nadir of immersion in lust!
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: ״מִי שֶׁלָּהוּט אַחַר בּוּלְמוּס שֶׁל עֲרָיוֹת, סוֹף מַאֲכִילִין אוֹתוֹ מִבְּשָׂרוֹ״

As they stated: "Whoever is consumed with a ravenous hunger (bulmus) for illicit relations, in the end they feed him from his own flesh" (Bereishis Rabbah 51:10);967Bereishis Rabbah 51:11 — “the bulmus of forbidden relations”: The Midrash applies a severe measure-for-measure formulation to Lot: one who is consumed by the bulmus of forbidden relations is ultimately fed from his own flesh. The rhetoric depicts desire that has become ravenous and self-destructive. Rav Tzadok cites it to describe the depth of the surrounding corruption from which the line of Moav had to be purified, not to erase the distinction between Lot’s conduct, his daughters’ intentions, and the later halachic status of their descendants.
וּלְשׁוֹן ״בּוּלְמוּס״ הַיְינוּ תּוֹקֶף תַּאֲוָה הַנּוֹגֵעַ עַד חַיּוּתוֹ מַמָּשׁ, כְּעִנְיַן ״אֲחָזוֹ בּוּלְמוּס״ דְּיוֹמָא [פ״ג עַמּוּד א׳]
and the term bulmus denotes a violent craving that borders upon his very life, like the life-threatening seizure of hunger in Yoma [83a];
אֶלָּא שֶׁהֵן כִּיוְּנוּ לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנָזִיר כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳], וְעַל כֵּן נְקֵבוֹתֵיהֶם מוּתָּרוֹת

except that they intended for the sake of Heaven as they stated [in Nazir 23b], wherefore their female descendants (Moabite and Ammonite women) were permitted to marry into Israel;968Yoma 83a–b — bulmus as life-threatening hunger: In halachic usage, bulmus is a dangerous state of overpowering hunger for which one feeds the patient immediately, even on Yom Kippur, until his sight returns. Rav Tzadok borrows that term metaphorically for desire touching the perceived life-force itself. The comparison explains intensity; it does not create a halachic equivalence between illness and sin. His language tracks how a drive can feel indispensable to life and therefore require a long process of clarification.969Nazir 23a–b; Horayos 10b — Lot’s daughters and aveirah lishmah: Chazal cite the daughters of Lot in discussing an act outwardly transgressive yet intended for the sake of Heaven, because they believed the world had been destroyed and sought its continuation. The same sugya distinguishes their initiative and rewards the elder for preceding to what she understood as a mitzvah. Rav Tzadok preserves the paradox: genuine holy intention was present, while the act and its surrounding desire still required purification across generations. Aveirah lishmah is an exceptional Aggadic category, not a general license to violate halachah.970Cf. Nazir 23a–b — the source R’ Tzadok cites regarding Lot’s daughters: “‘a transgression [performed] for its own sake [aveirah lishmah] is greater than a mitzvah [performed] not for its own sake’ — for the elder daughter, who [openly] called her son ‘Moav [me-av, from father],’ the Torah rewarded her descendant Rus to enter Israel four generations before the younger’s.” The Gemara establishes their intent was for the sake of Heaven — to perpetuate the world they believed destroyed — which R’ Tzadok makes the crux of Mashiach’s descent through them.
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא קַמָּא ל״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״בְּכִירָה שֶׁקִּדְּמָה לִדְבַר מִצְוָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and so they stated [in Bava Kamma 38b]: "The elder daughter who preceded for the purpose of a mitzvah, etc.";

וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ אָמְרוּ: ״בְּכִירָה שֶׁפָּתְחָה בִּזְנוּת פִּרְסְמָהּ הַכָּתוּב״, וְכֵן בְּרַשִׁ״י [פָּרָשַׁת וַיֵּרָא, בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ט:ל״ז] וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה [סוֹף פָּרָשָׁה נ״א] פְּלִיגֵי אָמוֹרָאֵי בָּזֶה

whereas in the Midrash they stated: "The elder who initiated with promiscuity, Scripture publicized her," and so in Rashi [Bereishis 19:37] and Bereishis Rabbah the Amoraim dispute this;971Bava Kamma 38b — reward and the differing names of Moav and Ammon: The Gemara says the elder daughter, who preceded in the matter she regarded as a mitzvah, merited an earlier allowance for her female descendants: Ruth entered the congregation generations before Naamah. At the same time, the Torah treats the public naming “Moav,” from father, more critically than the younger daughter’s more veiled “Ben-Ammi.” Chazal therefore hold together merit for intention and initiative with criticism of immodesty; Rav Tzadok likewise refuses to flatten the episode into either pure holiness or pure lust.972Rashi on Genesis 19:33 and 19:37; Bereishis Rabbah 51:12–13 — publicizing the elder daughter and the dispute over motive: Rashi notes that Scripture openly marks the elder daughter’s initiative and the name Moav, while treating the younger more discreetly. Bereishis Rabbah records opposing evaluations: one Amora emphasizes that the conception of Moav began for the sake of Heaven, while another emphasizes promiscuous motive. Rav Tzadok says both are true because mixed intention can contain a real concern for the world’s survival together with inherited appetite. His synthesis is interpretive; the Midrash itself preserves the tension.
וּבְוַדַּאי כָּל דִּבְרֵיהֶם אֱמֶת, דִּלְהַיוֹתָן בְּנוֹת לוֹט מִסְּתָמָא הָיוּ מְשׁוּקָּעוֹת בַּתַּאֲווֹת גַּם כֵּן
and certainly all their words are true: for being the daughters of Lot, they were presumably immersed in lust as well;
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם כָּאן מְפָרֵשׁ בַּכָּתוּב כַּוָּונָתָם לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם גַּם כֵּן, שֶׁאָמְרוּ: ״וּנְחַיֶּה מֵאָבִינוּ זָרַע״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ט:ל״ב), שֶׁכִּיוְּנוּ לְקִיּוּם עוֹלָם

yet Scripture explicitly reveals that their intention was likewise for the sake of Heaven, saying "that we may preserve seed of our father" (Bereishis 19:32), aiming for the preservation of the world;
וּבִבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה שָׁם אָמְרוּ: ״׳זֶרַע׳ הַבָּא מִמָּקוֹם אַחֵר — זֶה מָשִׁיחַ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם:

and in Bereishis Rabbah there they stated: "'Seed' that comes from another place—this is the King Messiah," see there.973Bereishis Rabbah 51:10; Genesis 19:32 — “seed from another place,” the King Mashiach: On “let us preserve seed from our father,” the Midrash reads not merely a son but “seed that comes from another place—this is the King Mashiach.” The daughters believed that no other human future remained and sought to rebuild the world. Rav Tzadok explains that their longing attached, in hidden form, to the one through whom the whole world will be repaired. The messianic result does not retroactively sanctify every element of the deed; it reveals the holy point that endured through later refinement.974Bereishis Rabbah 51:10: “R’ Tanchuma in the name of R’ Shmuel: ‘and let us keep alive seed from our father [zera]’ — ‘let us keep alive a son from our father’ is not written here, but rather ‘let us keep alive seed from our father’ — [meaning] that seed which comes from another place. Which is it? This is the King Mashiach.” And there, [51:]13: “Rav Huna said: from the beginning of Moav’s conception it was not for the sake of promiscuity but for the sake of Heaven. R’ Simon said: from the beginning of Moav’s conception it was not for the sake of Heaven but for the sake of promiscuity.”

items.h: The theme: The transmission of the soul of Mashiach through historical acts combining physical desire with transcendent divine intention. The entire unfolding of Mashiach’s lineage evolved through acts that appeared outwardly driven by bodily lust, yet concealed an ultimate purpose for the sake of Heaven: the daughters of Lot, Yehudah and Tamar, and Yishai with his wife. When Yehudah was aroused by Tamar, Hashem signaled the angel of lust to bring forth the royal seed; when Yishai sought his maidservant to purify his line (as explained by the Rama MiFano), his wife entered secretly, and Hashem infused Yishai with passion for his own pleasure so that David would be conceived in this paradoxical mystery ("behold, in iniquity I was brought forth", Tehillim 51:7). Mashiach will ultimately clarify that all physical desires of Israel were sovereignly orchestrated from the six days of Creation to birth holiness out of darkness.

p: וְנִרְאֶה לִי, לְפִי שֶׁהוּא קִיּוּם כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ לֹא נִבְרָא אֶלָּא בִּשְׁבִילוֹ, שֶׁיָּבוֹא וִיתַקֵּן הַכֹּל כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בִּתְחִלַּת הַבְּרִיאָה

And it appears to me, because he constitutes the sustenance of the entire universe—the whole world having been created solely for his sake (Sanhedrin 98b)—that he should come and rectify everything as it existed at the inception of Creation;
וְכַוָּונָתָם לְקִיּוּם כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ עַל יָדוֹ אַחַר שֶׁנֶּחְרַב, שֶׁהָיוּ סְבוּרִים שֶׁכָּל הַהַשְׁאָרָה מֵהֶם, הֲרֵי בָּאוּ לְתַקֵּן כָּל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ אַחַר הַקִּלְקוּל

and their intention was directed toward the preservation of the entire universe through him following the destruction of Sodom, believing that all human survival depended upon them, coming to rectify the entire universe following its ruin;
וְתִיקּוּן הָעוֹלָם הוּא עַל יְדֵי מָשִׁיחַ
and the ultimate rectification of the world is achieved through Mashiach;
וּבִשְׁבִיל חֶשְׁקָם זֶה שֶׁהָיָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם זָכוּ לְכָךְ בֶּאֱמֶת, לִהְיוֹת אוֹתוֹ זֶרַע מֵהֶם אַחַר זִיכּוּךְ הַרְבֵּה דּוֹרוֹת מִפְּסֹולֶת הַכַּוָּונָה דִּזְנוּת שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם גַּם כֵּן

and on account of this longing which was for the sake of Heaven, they truly merited that this royal seed should descend from them, following the refinement through many generations of the dross of lustful intent that was also present within them.975R’ Tzadok — parallel (Dover Tzedek §4): “This was revealed to Chizkiyahu, whom the Holy One wished to make Mashiach (Sanhedrin 94a) — for he too was at this level, that he said, ‘I sleep on my bed and You [do battle for us].’” Exactly the se’if: Chizkiyahu saw by ruach ha-kodesh [the level of the Mashiach’s soul].
וְכָל הִשְׁתַּלְשְׁלוּת נֶפֶשׁ דְּמָשִׁיחַ בָּעוֹלָם הָיָה עַל יְדֵי עִנְיָנִים כָּאֵלּוּ, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מַחֲשֶׁבֶת תַּאֲוָה וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם
And the entire descent of the soul of Mashiach into the world transpired through such paradoxes: that there should be an external thought of bodily lust, yet inwardly directed for the sake of Heaven;
וְזֶה יְבָרֵר מָשִׁיחַ בְּכָל תַּאֲווֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּהַכֹּל מְסוּדָּר מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ
and this Mashiach will clarify regarding all the lusts of Israel: that everything was sovereignly ordered from the six days of Creation by the Blessed Name!
וְזֶהוּ בְּרִיאַת אוֹרוֹ בְּמַעֲשֶׂה דִּיהוּדָה שֶׁהָיָה עַל יְדֵי הִתְעוֹרְרוּת תַּאֲוָה גּוּפָנִית וְלֹא בְּכַוָּונָה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם, דַּהֲרֵי רָמַז לַמַּלְאָךְ דְּתַאֲוָה

And this is the creation of his light in the incident of Yehudah, which occurred through the stirring of bodily lust and not through conscious intent for the sake of Heaven, for behold, Hashem signaled the angel of lust;976Bereishis Rabbah 85:1; Yevamos 77a — the messianic line emerging through concealment: Bereishis Rabbah portrays the tribes, Yosef, Reuven, and Yaakov as occupied with loss and repentance while the Holy One was already ‘creating the light of the King Mashiach’ through Yehudah’s descent. Yevamos later has David say that he thought he had only now arrived, but discovered that his existence was already ‘written in the scroll,’ linking him to the daughters of Lot. Rav Tzadok gathers these sources into a single pattern: the genealogy of Mashiach is repeatedly hidden inside situations whose immediate appearance does not disclose their final redemptive purpose.977Nazir 23a–b; Horayos 10b — mixed desire and intention for the sake of Heaven: Chazal discuss the daughters of Lot under the exceptional heading of an act whose external form is transgressive while its intention seeks the world’s survival. They simultaneously preserve criticism of immodest elements and reward the elder daughter’s initiative. Rav Tzadok extends the motif to the descent of the messianic soul, where a real holy intention can coexist with unresolved bodily desire. This is an Aggadic analysis of mixed motive and later purification, not a general halachic license for ‘aveirah lishmah.’978Shabbos 89b; Takanas HaShavin 10:2; Resisei Layla 21:1 — ‘ordered from the six days of Creation’: Shabbos interprets sins ‘like years’ as matters ordered and coming since the six days of Creation. Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains that only after teshuvah can it be revealed that darkness was included in the route to a greater light and that intentional sins can be transformed into merits. Takanas HaShavin 10 stresses that the sinner still bears judgment and requires atonement; Resisei Layla explicitly places the clarification after teshuvah from love. Se’if 53 therefore speaks about Mashiach’s retrospective disclosure, while ordinary avodah remains governed by choice, command, and accountability.979Genesis 38:14–26; Bereishis Rabbah 85:1 — the creation of Mashiach’s light through Yehudah and Tamar: The Torah records Yehudah’s encounter, Tamar’s safeguarding of the identifying objects, and Yehudah’s public admission, ‘She is more righteous than I.’ Bereishis Rabbah sets the episode within the Holy One’s hidden work of creating the light of Mashiach. The biblical narrative supplies the deed and the confession; the Midrash identifies its redemptive future; Rav Tzadok interprets the bodily awakening itself as part of the concealment through which that future entered history.980Bereishis Rabbah 85:8 — the angel appointed over desire: The Midrash says Yehudah sought to pass by, but the Holy One summoned the angel responsible for desire, asking from where kings and great leaders would otherwise arise; ‘he turned to her’ is read as against his will. This is the direct source for Rav Tzadok’s language. The Midrash does not erase Yehudah’s later responsibility to recognize and confess; rather, it places an otherwise hidden Divine purpose behind the encounter.
אֲבָל גַּם הִתְעוֹרְרוּת הַתַּאֲוָה לֹא הָיָה מִצִּדּוֹ, רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ דְּעוֹרֵר בּוֹ כֹּחַ תַּאֲוָה הַגּוּפָנִיּוֹת בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
yet even that stirring of lust did not originate from him, but from the Blessed Name Who awakened within him the force of bodily desire at that hour,
וּלְבָרֵר בָּזֶה שֶׁכָּל תַּאֲווֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת דְּזֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל הַכֹּל מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא רָצָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה כֵּן

to clarify through this that all physical desires of the seed of Israel are ultimately from the Blessed Name, Who willed that it should be so.981Likkutei Maamarim, Compositions on the Festivals 16:38 — Divine dispatch versus an ordinary temptation: Rav Tzadok elsewhere carefully distinguishes the Yehudah narrative from cases in which a tempting angel merely attacks a person. In Yehudah’s case, he says, the Holy One specifically summoned the angel because the deed belonged to the concealed Divine purpose; in ordinary temptation the individual can and must resist. This companion passage prevents the present se’if from being read as a universal claim that every impulse is coercive or that human responsibility disappears.982Takanas HaShavin 6:73 — Davidic desire directed toward an enduring Divine purpose: In an earlier internal parallel, Rav Tzadok describes the root of David’s desire as directed toward the partner destined from the six days of Creation and toward the enduring building of the Davidic kingdom, not toward a passing pleasure. He then develops the traditions concerning Yishai and the maidservant. Se’if 53 advances the same thesis: the holy root is not the bodily appetite as such, but the Divine purpose that will ultimately be separated from its temporary mixture with self-directed pleasure.

וְכֵן בְּיִשַׁי, אָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ מֵאִשְׁתּוֹ וְרָצָה לָבוֹא עַל שִׁפְחָתוֹ, וּפֵירֵשׁ הָרַמַ״ע בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [מַאֲמַר חֲקוֹר דִּין חֵלֶק ב׳ פֶּרֶק י״א] לְטַהֵר זַרְעוֹ

And so with Yishai, the Sages of blessed memory stated that he separated from his wife and sought to come unto his maidservant, which the Rama MiFano explained in Asarah Ma'amaros [Chakor Din 2:11] as an effort to purify his seed from doubts regarding Moabitess descent;
וּמִסְּתָמָא לֹא הָיָה דָּוִד ״בֶּן תְּמוּרָה״ חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

and presumably David was not a "child of substitute intimacy" (ben temurah, Nedarim 20b), God forbid;983Shabbos 55b; Bava Basra 17a — Yishai died only through the serpent’s decree: Both sugyos count Yishai among four people who died ‘through the counsel of the serpent,’ meaning that no personal transgression made them liable to death. Rav Tzadok therefore refuses to attribute an ordinary grave sexual sin to Yishai. His reading of the later conception tradition seeks a form consistent with Yishai’s exceptional righteousness, while treating even a minute trace of self-oriented pleasure as ‘iniquity’ relative to so elevated a person.984Midbar Kedemos, letter Yod §20; Chomas Anach on II Samuel 23:1 — the later received tradition about Yishai’s household: The Chida records a tradition that Yishai, troubled by the status of his Moabite ancestry, arranged to be with a maidservant so that his future seed would be unquestionably permitted; the maidservant informed Yishai’s wife, who entered in her place and preserved the secret. The Chida presents this as material found in an older manuscript tradition, not as an explicit account in Tanakh or the Bavli. Rav Tzadok adopts this later Aggadic tradition and offers his own harmonizing reconstruction of its details.985Rema MiFano, Asarah Maamaros, Chikur Din III:10, cited by Pardes Yosef on Bereishis 29:31 — ‘to purify his seed’: Later commentators cite the Rema MiFano as explaining that Yishai’s contemplated union with the maidservant was intended to remove a perceived genealogical doubt from his descendants. The background is not a denial of the accepted law, but anxiety over whether the exclusion of Ammon and Moav applied to women. Rav Tzadok uses this motive to show that the plan began from religious scruple, even though the final conception had to emerge through a different hidden arrangement.986Nedarim 20b; Rashi, Ran, and Tur, Even HaEzer 25 — the category of ‘ben temurah’: Nedarim lists ‘children of substitution’ among unions blemished by disordered intention. Rashi and the Ran explain this as intending one wife while being with another; the Tur also records the broader formulation of directing one’s mind toward another woman. Rav Tzadok explicitly rejects applying this category to David. Pardes Yosef, citing the Rema MiFano, explains that Yishai had given identifying signs that were transmitted to his wife, removing culpable mistaken identity. The se’if’s conclusion rests on that harmonization, not on minimizing Chazal’s warning about marital intention.
וּכְדְבָאתָה אִשְׁתּוֹ בַּמִּקְוֶוה בִּשְׁעַת הַרְגֵּל דָּבָר, מִסְּתָמָא הִגִּידָה לוֹ הָאֱמֶת
and when his wife entered the chamber following her immersion at the appointed time, she presumably told him the truth,
כִּי הִיא צַדֶּקֶת וְכַוָּונָתָהּ לַשָּׁמַיִם לְהָקִים הַזֶּרַע שֶׁנִּתְכַּוְּונוּ לוֹ בְּנוֹת לוֹט כַּנַּ״ל, וּבְוַדַּאי דְּלֹא רָצְתָה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה דַּעְתּוֹ לְאַחֶרֶת

for she was a righteous woman whose intention was for the sake of Heaven to establish the royal seed intended by the daughters of Lot as mentioned above, and she certainly did not wish his thoughts to be directed toward another;987Midbar Kedemos, letter Yod §20 — the mother’s secrecy and righteousness; Rav Tzadok’s added inference: The Chida’s version says Yishai’s wife preserved the maidservant’s secret even when her pregnancy was misunderstood. Rav Tzadok adds that, at the decisive moment, she presumably disclosed the truth to Yishai so that his mind would not remain directed toward another. That disclosure is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive inference, designed to reconcile the tradition with the laws of ‘ben temurah’; it should not be presented as a verbatim statement of the earlier source.988Nedarim 20b; Tur, Orach Chaim 240 and Even HaEzer 25 — the mind must be present with one’s spouse: Chazal’s warning against ‘drinking from one cup while setting one’s eyes on another’ treats inward marital presence as morally significant, even when the physical union is otherwise permitted. Rav Tzadok’s insistence that Yishai’s wife would not allow his mind to remain on the maidservant protects precisely this principle. The discussion should be read with dignity: it concerns fidelity of intention between spouses, not sensational reconstruction of private conduct.
וְלִהְיוֹת הוּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר, וְחָשַׁב אָז אוּלַי הַהֲלָכָה דְּגַם עַמּוֹנִית אֲסוּרָה וְלֹא רָצָה לְהוֹלִיד עוֹד מִיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית כְּדִבְרֵי הָרַמַ״ע, וַדַּאי שֶׁהָיָה רוֹצֶה לִפְרוֹשׁ מִמֶּנָּה

and since he was a consummate tzaddik who suspected that perhaps the halachah forbids even an Ammonite or Moabite woman and refused to father any further children with an Israelite woman as the Rama MiFano explained, he certainly would have sought to separate from her;989Yevamos 76b–77a — ‘an Ammonite, but not an Ammonite woman; a Moabite, but not a Moabite woman’: The Mishnah permits female Ammonite and Moabite converts immediately. The Gemara recounts the fierce challenge to David’s legitimacy and Amasa’s testimony from the court of Shmuel that the Torah bars the males, not the females. The uncertainty attributed to Yishai in the later tradition is therefore a historical fear before or around the public establishment of that received halachah, not a continuing normative doubt. Ruth’s and David’s entry into Israel is fully valid in halachah.
וּבְוַדַּאי גַּם אָז רָמַז הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לַמַּלְאָךְ דְּתַאֲוָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא פֵּירֵשׁ
and certainly then, too, the Holy One, blessed be He, signaled to the angel of lust so that he did not separate!
וְזֶהוּ ״בְּעָווֹן״ מָלֵא, דְּעַל יְדֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא בָּא לוֹ הַתַּאֲוָה לַהֲנָאַת עַצְמוֹ אָז, דְּכָךְ רָצָה הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ כַּוָּונָה לַהֲנָאָתוֹ

And this is the esoteric meaning of "in iniquity" (b'avon) written with a full vav: through the Holy One, blessed be He, desire for personal pleasure was instilled in him at that moment, for thus the Blessed Name willed that he should possess intent for his own enjoyment;
וּבֶאֱמֶת גַּם זֶה מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ, לְהוֹצִיא נֶפֶשׁ יְקָרָה כָּזוֹ מִכַּוָּונָה כָּזוֹ דַּוְוקָא, וּלְבָרֵר כַּנַּ״ל:

and in absolute truth this too was orchestrated by the Blessed Name: to extract so precious a soul specifically out of such bodily intention, and to clarify the cosmic mysteries as mentioned above.990Yevamos 77a; Pri Tzadik, Sukkos 23:2 — a precious messianic soul extracted from concealment: Yevamos links David both to Ruth the Moabite and Naamah the Ammonite and calls his ancient emergence a wonder already written in the scroll. Pri Tzadik says the soul of David and Mashiach was ‘found’ in Sodom and associates it with the future Torah of Mashiach. Rav Tzadok’s phrase ‘a precious soul from such a base vessel’ describes extraction and purification: the precious soul is not evidence that the surrounding appetite or apparent degradation was itself holy, but that holiness could survive concealment and be separated from it through generations of Torah and teshuvah.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים נ״ה–נ״ט

The theme: David HaMelech's teshuvah for the incident with Bas Sheva. Just as Yishai was pure of bodily lust and was infused with desire by Hashem to bring forth the soul of David, so too David had already slain his yetzer hara through fasting and was made to stumble solely by Divine design to instruct the world in repentance (Avodah Zarah 4b).
