Through his higher repentance (teshuvah ila'ah)—sacrificing his very life through ecstatic love until his soul expired and was restored with a "pure heart" (lev tahor) as at Mount Sinai—David rectified the instigation of the Serpent (ityo shel nachash) and became "alive and enduring" (chai v'kayam) like Yaakov Avinu and Eliyahu.

p: וְעַל כֵּן הִזְכִּיר זֶה דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּתְשׁוּבָתוֹ אַמַּעֲשֶׂה דְּבַת שֶׁבַע
And therefore David HaMelech, peace be upon him, mentioned this in his repentance over the incident with Bas Sheva:
דְּגַם הוּא לֹא הָיָה רָאוּי לְאוֹתָהּ מַעֲשֶׂה, רַק מֵהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ הָיָה לוֹ זֶה שֶׁיִּכָּשֵׁל לְהוֹרוֹת תְּשׁוּבָה
that he too was not fit for that deed, and only from the Blessed Name was it orchestrated that he should stumble, in order to instruct the world in repentance (Avodah Zarah 4b);
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּ״הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי״ גַּם כֵּן מַמָּשׁ דּוּגְמַת זֶה, דְּלֹא הָיָה יִשַׁי רָאוּי לְכָךְ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

and therefore he said "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity" (Tehillim 51:7) likewise as a literal replica of this, for Yishai was not fit for such lust as mentioned above,991Avodah Zarah 4b–5a — David was not naturally suited to that incident, but became the paradigm of individual teshuvah: The Gemara places David beside Israel at the Golden Calf: neither stood at a spiritual level naturally suited to the failure, yet their fall opened a path of return—David for the individual and Israel for the community. This does not mean the act became permitted or unreal. The same sugya calls it a sin for which teshuvah was required, and Sanhedrin 107a records confession, suffering, and atonement. Rav Tzadok reads the providential role as explaining why the test entered David’s life, while preserving moral responsibility within the revealed world of choice.
דְּהָיָה מְנוּקֶּה בֶּאֱמֶת גַּם מֵהַרְגֵּשׁ הֲנָאָה כְּלָל, רַק בְּאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה רָצָה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְהַכְנִיס בּוֹ תַּאֲוָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

being truly pure even from any sensation of pleasure at all, save that at that hour the Holy One, blessed be He, willed to inject lust into him as mentioned above.992Tehillim 51:7; Rashi and Radak ad loc.; Vayikra Rabbah 14:5 — ‘Behold, in iniquity I was formed’: Rashi explains that human formation occurs through bodily union, a sphere in which many failures can arise; Radak similarly treats the verse as David’s recognition that sexual appetite belongs to embodied human nature and therefore demands exceptional mastery. Radak also cites the derash that the word avon is written full: even the most pious person cannot be entirely without some trace of self-oriented pleasure. Rav Tzadok’s specific link to Yishai’s concealed conception tradition is an additional interpretive layer; it is not the plain meaning asserted by Rashi or Radak.
וְזֶהוּ הִתְנַצְּלוּת גַּם כֵּן עַל חֶטְאוֹ דְּדָוִד, דְּהוּא גַּם כֵּן כֵּן, דִּכְבָר הֲרָגוֹ לַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בְּתַעֲנִית וְלֹא הָיָה בּוֹ הַרְגֵּשׁ הֲנָאָה
And this is likewise the justification regarding David's sin: that his condition was identical, having already slain his yetzer hara through fasting (Bava Batra 17a), possessing no lustful sensation;
רַק הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ רָצָה לְנַסּוֹתוֹ וְהִכְנִיס בְּלִבּוֹ תַּאֲוָה, וּכְדֵי לְתַקֵּן אַחַר כָּךְ בִּתְשׁוּבָה וּלְהוֹרוֹת לְכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ

but the Blessed Name willed to test him and introduced passion into his heart, in order that he rectify it afterward through repentance and instruct the entire world.993Bava Basra 17a; Avodah Zarah 4b; Sanhedrin 107a — ‘my heart is hollow within me’ and the yetzer subdued through fasting: Bava Basra records an opinion that the evil inclination had no sway over David, citing ‘my heart is hollow within me’; Avodah Zarah uses the same verse to explain why he was not naturally fit for the incident. Sanhedrin adds that David’s body had been weakened by severe fasting and suffering. Rav Tzadok combines these strands into the image of David having ‘killed’ the yetzer through fasting. The Gemara itself preserves another reading of the verse—as describing David’s anguish—so Rav Tzadok is choosing and synthesizing one traditional line, not erasing the dispute.994Sanhedrin 107a — David asked to be tested and failed: The Gemara warns that a person should never bring himself into a trial: David asked to be tested like the Patriarchs, was told that the test would involve forbidden desire, and failed. This source supplies the immediate background for Rav Tzadok’s phrase that Hashem ‘wished to test him.’ Its practical lesson is caution, humility, and avoidance of temptation. The hidden providential purpose described by Rav Tzadok can be recognized only retrospectively through teshuvah; it cannot be used beforehand to seek danger or suspend the Torah’s boundaries.995II Shmuel 12:7–14; Sanhedrin 107a — prophetic rebuke, confession, and consequences remain fully real: Nasan HaNavi tells David, ‘You are the man,’ names the wrongdoing, and announces consequences. David answers, ‘I have sinned to Hashem’; forgiveness removes the death penalty, but suffering and historical consequences remain. Sanhedrin likewise depicts David accepting afflictions and undergoing a period of isolation. Rav Tzadok’s ‘defense’ therefore does not mean exoneration. It identifies a deeper providential function in the fall and the repair, while the revealed prophetic judgment continues to govern accountability.
וְזָכָה לִהְיוֹת ״דָּוִד מֶלֶךְ יִשְׂרָאֵל חַי וְקַיָּים״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כ״ה עַמּוּד א׳]
And he merited to be "David, king of Israel, lives and endures," as they stated [in Rosh Hashanah 25a],
שֶׁלָּזֶה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לִזְכּוֹת אֶלָּא צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וְאֵלִיָּהוּ וְכַדּוֹמֶה
which none can merit except a consummate tzaddik like Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, Eliyahu, and the like,
אוֹ בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה גָּמוּר כְּדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁתִּיקֵּן גַּם הָעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ

or a consummate penitent like David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who rectified even the instigation of the Serpent;996Rosh Hashanah 25a; Ramban on Bereishis 38:29; Rabbeinu Bachya on Bereishis 38:30 — ‘David, king of Israel, lives and endures’: Rosh Hashanah records this phrase as the sign sent when the new moon was sanctified. Ramban and Rabbeinu Bachya connect the Davidic dynasty, descending from Peretz, with the moon: it diminishes, disappears, and is renewed. The saying therefore expresses the enduring covenant of Davidic kingship through apparent eclipse. Rav Tzadok gives the phrase an inward dimension as well: David’s complete teshuvah renews life after spiritual collapse, making the waxing moon a model of a life-force restored rather than extinguished.997Taanis 5b; II Melachim 2:11 — Yaakov and Eliyahu as models of life beyond ordinary death: Taanis teaches that Yaakov Avinu did not die, grounding his continued life in the enduring life of his descendants; II Melachim describes Eliyahu ascending in a storm with a fiery chariot rather than undergoing ordinary burial. Rav Tzadok places them beside David as examples of a life rooted beyond the usual hold of death. His distinction is conceptual: Yaakov and Eliyahu exemplify the complete tzaddik, whereas David reaches enduring life through the fully repaired path of the baal teshuvah.998Shabbos 55b; Bava Basra 17a; Takanas HaShavin 15:48; Machshavos Charutz 18:5 — repairing ‘the counsel of the serpent’: The Gemara speaks of exceptionally righteous people who died only through ‘the counsel of the serpent,’ meaning the primordial decree of mortality rather than a personal sin. Earlier in this siman Rav Tzadok distinguished ordinary conquest of desire from the future Divine removal of its created root; Machshavos Charutz similarly separates human suppression from the final uprooting of the serpent’s pollution. Se’if 54 claims that David’s complete teshuvah touched this deeper root: not merely forgiveness of one deed, but renewal at the level where mortality and disordered desire first entered human nature.
אַף שֶׁהָיָה עָלָיו טַעֲנָה מִפְּגַם הַבְּרִית, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר ״וְהָרַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ עָשִׂיתִי״ (תְּהִלִּים נ״א:ו׳), דְּזֶה נִקְרָא ״רַע בְּעֵינָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ״

even though there was a claim against him regarding a blemish of the Covenant, as he said: "and done that which is evil in Your sight" (Tehillim 51:6), for this sin is specifically termed "evil in His sight, blessed be He";
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״לֵב טָהוֹר בְּרָא וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and therefore he prayed "Create for me a pure heart, etc."
כִּי מִי שֶׁפָּגַם בְּחֵטְא בְּפֹעַל, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לְתַקֵּן שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתַּאֲוָה לְגַמְרֵי שֶׁיֶּאֱחֹז בְּעֵץ הַחַיִּים לְתַקֵּן גַּם עֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
For one who blemished the Covenant through actual sin in deed cannot rectify the root of lust completely so as to grasp the Tree of Life and rectify the Serpent's instigation,
אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה דַּחֲזְיָא לְחַפָּיָא עַל כָּל עוֹבָדוֹי

except through the repentance worthy of covering over all his deeds (Zohar III, 214b);999Tehillim 51:6; Bereishis 38:10; Takanas HaShavin 11:10 — ‘what is evil in Your eyes I have done’: David confesses, ‘I have done what is evil in Your eyes.’ The Torah uses a closely related expression of Onan’s destruction of seed: ‘What he did was evil in the eyes of Hashem.’ Rav Tzadok reads the verbal echo as associating David’s confession with the covenantal sphere and with the inner root of desire. This is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive linkage; the Psalm itself does not explicitly identify the phrase with that particular transgression. His purpose is to explain why David asks not only for pardon but for purification of the heart’s source.1000Tehillim 51:12; Tzidkas HaTzadik 39 and 130; Peri Tzadik, Va’eschanan 2 and Sukkos 34 — ‘Create for me a pure heart’ as a new creation: Rav Tzadok repeatedly emphasizes that beri’ah denotes creation from nothing. David therefore does not ask only that an existing heart be restrained or polished; he asks Hashem to create a new inward vessel where the prior root appeared beyond repair. Tzidkas HaTzadik teaches that prayer can transform even a person’s root, and Peri Tzadik describes David’s cry as reaching Divine mercy for an entirely new heart. The verse thus becomes the central proof that teshuvah can renew the person at a level deeper than habit or ordinary self-discipline.1001Reishis Chochmah, Shaar HaKedushah 17:24; Takanas HaShavin 15:22 — teshuvah ‘fit to cover all his deeds’: Reishis Chochmah uses this formulation for a complete teshuvah that repairs the whole person when the covenantal faculty has been blemished, because that faculty is described as integrating the full spiritual structure. Earlier in Takanas HaShavin, Rav Tzadok cites this stringent tradition while arguing that no sin is outside the power of return. The rhetoric is intentionally grave, but its conclusion is not despair: the required repair must involve the entire personality—thought, desire, conduct, Torah, prayer, and renewed attachment to Hashem.
הַיְינוּ כְּעֵין תְּשׁוּבַת רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר בֶּן דּוֹרְדְיָא [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה י״ז עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁיָּצְתָה נַפְשׁוֹ מִתּוֹךְ מְרִירוּת לִבּוֹ
meaning like the repentance of Rabbi Elazar ben Dordaya [in Avodah Zarah 17a] whose soul departed amid the bitterness of his heart;
וְכֵן מִי שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לָזֶה עַל יְדֵי תּוֹקֶף הָאַהֲבָה כְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

and likewise one who attains this through the sheer intensity of love, like Israel at the Giving of the Torah as mentioned above;1002Avodah Zarah 17a — Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya and teshuvah from the depth of the heart: After a life of extreme sexual wrongdoing, Elazar ben Durdaya concluded, ‘The matter depends only upon me,’ wept until his soul departed, and was proclaimed destined for the World to Come; the Heavenly voice even called him ‘Rabbi.’ Rav Tzadok invokes this as the extreme image of teshuvah that overturns the whole self. It is not a normative instruction that repentance must cause physical death. The Gemara presents an exceptional case in which total inner rupture accompanied return; ordinary halachic teshuvah remains confession, abandonment of sin, regret, and a firm future commitment.1003Shabbos 88b; Takanas HaShavin 15:48; Peri Tzadik, Vayeishev 9 — souls departing and the dew of resurrection at Sinai: Shabbos teaches that with every Divine utterance Israel’s souls departed—‘my soul went out when He spoke’—and Hashem revived them with the dew destined to resurrect the dead. Earlier in this siman Rav Tzadok used that event to describe the removal of the heart of stone and the reception of a new heart. Peri Tzadik likewise links a newly created heart with Israel’s single heart at Sinai. Se’if 54 compares David’s love-driven self-transcendence to this pattern: the old life expires in attachment, and life is returned from a purer source.
וְכֵן דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגַת אַהֲבָה זוֹ עַד כְּלוֹת הַנֶּפֶשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר: ״כָּלְתָה נַפְשִׁי [לִתְשׁוּעָתְךָ] וְגוֹמֵר״ (תְּהִלִּים קי״ט:פ״א)
and so David HaMelech, peace be upon him, attained this degree of love unto the expiration of the soul, as he said: "My soul pines for Your salvation, etc." (Tehillim 119:81);
וְנֶאֱמַר: ״אֵלֶיךָ ה׳ נַפְשִׁי אֶשָּׂא״ (שָׁם כ״ה:א׳), דִּמְסַר גַּרְמֵיהּ לְמִיתָה מַמָּשׁ עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת הַנֶּפֶשׁ בִּמְקוֹרָהּ בְּחֵי הַחַיִּים יִתְבָּרַךְ שְׁמוֹ

and it is said: "Unto You, O Hashem, do I lift up my soul" (ibid. 25:1), surrendering himself to literal death through the cleaving of the soul to its Source in the Life of all life, blessed be His Name;1004Tehillim 84:3; Dover Tzedek, Eruvin 1:4; Kometz HaMinchah 2:50 — ‘my soul yearns and even pines’ as kelos hanefesh: The Psalm describes longing for Hashem’s courtyards until ‘my heart and my flesh sing to the living God.’ Dover Tzedek explains that contemplation of Hashem’s holiness produces an overwhelming yearning to reach the hidden Divine light; Kometz HaMinchah identifies the same ‘consumption of the soul’ with love. Rav Tzadok therefore reads David’s phrase literally as the summit of ahavah, where desire is no longer turned toward bodily possession but is gathered entirely toward the Source of life.1005Tehillim 25:1; Resisei Layla 37; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:2 — ‘To You, Hashem, I lift my soul’ as mesirus nefesh and renewed life: Resisei Layla reads the verse as surrendering all personal powers to Hashem; Dover Tzedek describes complete ‘with all your soul’ as an actual self-offering through love, yet adds that the radiance of the King’s face is itself life and therefore immediately returns a new life-force. This is the closest internal parallel to the end of the se’if. David’s soul rises toward its source, but the Source of life restores it—as at Sinai—now capable of receiving the newly created pure heart and overcoming the serpent’s pollution at its root.
רַק שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ חוֹזֵר לְהַחֲיוֹתוֹ כִּבְמַתַּן תּוֹרָה וְיוּכַל לְהַחְזִיר לוֹ לֵב טָהוֹר
only that the Blessed Name restores him to life as at the Giving of the Torah, returning to him a pure heart;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לְסִילּוּק הַזּוּהֲמָא דְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ לְגַמְרֵי:

and through this he merits the complete elimination of the defilement of the Serpent's instigation.1006R’ Tzadok — parallel (Tzidkas HaTzadik §108): “David came upon Bas Sheva — which was a rectification of the blemish of the covenant [tikkun al kilkul ha-bris].” Exactly the se’if: David mentioned this in his teshuvah regarding the deed of Bas Sheva — the rectification of the very root of the bris.

items.h: The theme: The intellectual vision of Rashbi versus prophetic perception. Rashbi beheld the "men of ascent" through the eye of Wisdom (Chochmah), which surpasses prophecy (Bava Batra 12a), grasping realities that physical eyes cannot see. The prophets only perceived the lower level of the penitent and could not gaze upon the transcendent reward of the wholly righteous ("eye has not seen"). Rabbi Yochanan, being a lifelong tzaddik from the seed of Yosef who never blemished the Covenant, taught that "eye has not seen" belongs strictly to the wholly righteous; but Rabbi Abbahu perceived that higher teshuvah ascends even higher. When Rabbi Abbahu wept on his deathbed that he had "toiled in vain" (yagati l'rik, Tehillim 73:13, rik alluding to keri), he feared a blemish in the Covenant, yet Hashem showed him thirteen rivers of balsam oil, proving his beauty mirrored Yaakov Avinu and Adam HaRishon before the sin.

p: וְהֵם בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה הַמּוּעָטִים שֶׁרָאָה רַבִּי שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן יוֹחַאי
And these are the few men of ascent (bnei aliyah) that Rabbi Shimon ben Yochai beheld (Sukkah 45b);
וּרְאִיָּתוֹ וְהַשָּׂגָתוֹ הָיָה בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַחָכְמָה דְּעָדִיף מִנְּבוּאָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י״ב עַמּוּד א׳]

and his vision and perception were rooted in the attainment of Wisdom, which is superior to prophecy as they said [in Bava Batra 12a];1007Sukkah 45b; Rashi ad loc.; Ramban, Sha’ar HaGemul §52 — the few “members of the ascent”: Rashbi says that he saw the members of the ascent and that they are few. The Gemara distinguishes them from the larger circles of righteous people: the highest group sees through an illuminating partition and enters before the Shechinah without requesting permission. Rashi identifies them as the class that receives the Divine Presence. Ramban explains this language of “seeing” as an elevation of intellectual apprehension. Rav Tzadok therefore uses bnei aliyah as a precise description of an exceptionally rare spiritual rank, not merely as a general title for good people.1008Bava Basra 12a; Takanas HaShavin 3:2; Resisei Layla 52:7 — wisdom is greater than prophecy: The Gemara teaches that although prophecy was removed from the prophets after the Churban, it was not removed from the Sages, and concludes that a chacham is greater than a prophet. Rav Tzadok explains the distinction: prophetic apprehension is comparable to vision, which presents a bounded image, whereas wisdom can reason toward a concealed root that no created eye directly sees. The Talmud supplies the hierarchy; the contrast between “seeing of the eye” and “seeing of the intellect,” and its application to the hidden order of teshuvah and the World to Come, is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive synthesis.
כִּי אֵינוֹ נִקְרָא רְאִיַּית הָעַיִן כִּדְנְבִיאִים, רַק רְאִיַּית הַשֵּׂכֶל
for this is not called sensory sight like that of the prophets, but the perception of the intellect;
וּבַשֵּׂכֶל אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג מִי שֶׁרָאוּי לְכָךְ גַּם מַה שֶּׁעַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּלָל

and through the intellect one who is worthy can grasp even that which eye has never seen in this world at all.1009Yeshayahu 64:3; Berachos 34b; Peri Tzadik, Shelach 14:3 — “no eye has seen”: R’ Yochanan applies “no eye has seen, God, besides You” both to the World to Come and to the reward of complete tzaddikim, beyond what the prophets described. R’ Abahu disagrees and teaches that baalei teshuvah stand where complete tzaddikim cannot stand. Peri Tzadik explains that both statements express true aspects of different spiritual orders. Se’if 55 builds upon this dispute: prophetic sight reaches the revealed scale of reward, while the deepest transformation of teshuvah belongs to a concealed order that can be approached through wisdom but is not pictured in ordinary prophetic vision.

וְעַל כֵּן הוּא רָאָה מַדְרֵיגַת בְּנֵי עֲלִיָּה, אֲבָל הַנְּבִיאִים לֹא רָאוּ בִּנְבוּאָתָם מַדְרֵיגַת הַצַּדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים, הַיְינוּ כְּאֵלִיָּהוּ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוּם שֶׁמֶץ חֵטְא אֲפִילּוּ מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ

Therefore he perceived the station of the men of ascent, whereas the prophets in their prophetic visions did not see the ultimate station of the wholly righteous—namely, like Eliyahu who possesses no trace of sin, even from the Serpent's instigation,
דְּגַם כֵּן נִקְרָא עָווֹן לְגַבֵּי צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל

which is likewise reckoned an iniquity relative to a consummate tzaddik, as mentioned above.1010Bava Basra 17a; II Melachim 2:11; Takanas HaShavin 15:54–55 — Eliyahu and the “counsel of the serpent”: Bava Basra lists exceptionally righteous people who died only because mortality entered the world through the primordial serpent, rather than through personal sin. Scripture describes Eliyahu’s departure in a whirlwind rather than an ordinary death. Rav Tzadok joins these traditions and treats Eliyahu as the paradigm of a tzaddik whose refinement reaches even the inherited residue of Adam’s fall. That final formulation is his spiritual reading; the cited sources themselves do not state that Eliyahu “rectified the counsel of the serpent” in these exact terms.
וְכֹל שֶׁלֹּא הִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ עָלָיו נֶאֱמַר: ״[כִּי אָדָם אֵין צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא]״ (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כ)
And whoever has not attained to this rung, concerning him it is said: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that does good, and sins not" (Koheles 7:20);
הַיְינוּ מִי שֶׁהוּא עֲדַיִין שָׁקוּעַ בְּאַרְצִיּוּת וְהֶרְגֵּשׁ הֲנָאוֹת גּוּפָנִיּוֹת, אַף שֶׁהוּא צַדִּיק בְּפֹעַל וְעוֹשֶׂה טוֹב, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יֶחֱטָא בְּאֵיזֶה דָּבָר מַה

meaning one who is still immersed in earthliness and the sensation of physical pleasures: even though he is righteous in deed and performs good, it is impossible that he will not stumble in some slight matter,
אֶלָּא שֶׁשָּׁב וּמִתְחָרֵט מִיָּד וְהוּא בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה, וּמִמַּדְרֵגָתָם דִּבְּרוּ נְבִיאִים בְּהַשָּׂגָתָם מִמַּרְאוֹת הַנְּבוּאָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

only that he repents and regrets immediately, being a ba'al teshuvah, and concerning their level spoke the prophets in their prophetic visions in this world.1011Koheles 7:20; Metzudas David ad loc.; Tzidkas HaTzadik §164 — “there is no righteous person on earth who does good and does not sin”: The verse teaches universal human fallibility, and Metzudas David explains that even a righteous person cannot be assumed never to stumble. Rav Tzadok gives special weight to the words “on earth”: one who remains embodied within earthly sensation can be righteous in deed and nevertheless encounter some failure, followed by immediate remorse and return. His distinction between the completely purified tzaddik and the righteous person who repeatedly becomes a baal teshuvah is an interpretive development of the verse, not a denial of the verse’s plain warning about human limitation.
וְרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁהָיָה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר שֶׁלֹּא פָּגַם בַּבְּרִית מֵעוֹלָם, כִּי הָיָה מִזַּרְעָא דְּיוֹסֵף כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת כ׳ עַמּוּד א׳]
And Rabbi Yochanan, who was a consummate tzaddik who never blemished the Covenant, being from the seed of Yosef as they said [in Berachos 20a],

וְלֹא יָדַע מִמַּדְרֵיגַת בַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה עִילָּאָה דַּחֲזְיָא לְחַפָּיָא וְכוּלֵיהּ שֶׁיּוּכַל לְתַקֵּן גַּם פְּגַם הַבְּרִית לְגַמְרֵי אַחַר הַחֵטְא עַד שֶׁיִּזְכֶּה לְמַדְרֵיגַת צַדִּיק גָּמוּר וּבְנֵי עֲלִיָּה

did not fathom the transcendent rung of higher teshuvah worthy of covering all sins, which can rectify even the blemish of the Covenant completely after the sin until one merits the stature of a consummate tzaddik and the men of ascent;1012Berachos 20a; Bereishis 49:22; Peri Tzadik, Kedoshim 12:1 — R’ Yochanan, Yosef, and guarded holiness: R’ Yochanan says that he descends from Yosef, over whose seed the evil eye has no dominion. The Gemara also explains that Yosef’s eye refused to feed upon what was not his, and therefore the evil eye cannot rule over him. Peri Tzadik interprets R’ Yochanan’s beauty and his conduct at the gates of immersion as expressions of complete shemiras habris, following Yosef’s pattern. Rav Tzadok’s description of R’ Yochanan as a complete tzaddik in this area rests upon that Aggadic and Chassidic reading; it is not a general halachic judgment about personal perfection.1013Reishis Chochmah, Sha’ar HaKedushah 17:24 — “teshuvah fit to cover all his deeds”: Reishis Chochmah uses the Zoharic expression teshuvah shehi chazya lechafya al kol ovdoi for a return strong enough to repair a covenantal blemish that affects the person’s whole spiritual form. Rav Tzadok adopts this language for an “upper teshuvah” that reaches the root from which conduct emerges, rather than correcting only the isolated act. This teaching intensifies the demand of teshuvah; it does not excuse the transgression, erase responsibility, or permit a person to rely beforehand upon a future mystical repair.
כִּי כָּל אֶחָד מַשִּׂיג רַק כְּפִי מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ, וְעַל כֵּן הִשִּׂיג הוּא הַמַּדְרֵיגָה דְּ״עַיִן לֹא רָאָתָה״ רַק לְצַדִּיק גָּמוּר

for each master perceives strictly according to his own spiritual level, and therefore he assigned the rung of "eye has not seen" solely to the wholly righteous.1014Berachos 34b; Takanas HaShavin 3:2; Tzidkas HaTzadik §164; Peri Tzadik, Pesach Sheni 2:2 — R’ Yochanan and R’ Abahu: The Gemara records a genuine dispute: R’ Yochanan places complete tzaddikim beyond the prophetic description given to baalei teshuvah, while R’ Abahu places baalei teshuvah beyond complete tzaddikim. Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains that both are “the words of the living God.” The orderly ascent of the complete tzaddik and the leap of the baal teshuvah reveal different dimensions of perfection. Thus the statement that R’ Yochanan “did not know” the upper baal teshuvah means that this level lay outside the spiritual standpoint expressed by his teaching, not that he lacked knowledge in the ordinary sense.

אֲבָל רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ, אָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [פֶּרֶק ג׳ דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה הֲלָכָה ה׳] דְּהֶרְאוּ לוֹ לִפְנֵי פְּטִירָתוֹ י״ג נַהֲרֵי אֲפַרְסְמוֹן, וְאָמַר: ״אֲנִי אָמַרְתִּי לְרִיק יָגַעְתִּי״ (יְשַׁעְיָה מ״ט:ד׳)

But regarding Rabbi Abbahu, they related in the Yerushalmi [Avodah Zarah 3:1] that before his passing they showed him thirteen rivers of pure balsam oil, whereupon he exclaimed: "Then I said: I have labored in vain (l'rik yagati)!" (Yeshayah 49:4);1015Yeshayahu 49:4; Yalkut Shimoni, Nach §468; Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 3:1 — R’ Abahu and the thirteen rivers: At R’ Abahu’s passing he was shown thirteen rivers of pure balsam. When he asked for whom they were prepared and was told that they were his, he exclaimed, “All these for Abahu? And I said: I labored in vain.” The Midrash explains that Hashem shows the righteous their future reward near death, so that their souls become satisfied and sleep. The source portrays astonishment and humility. Rav Tzadok adds a more searching interpretation: the words la-rik reveal that R’ Abahu had feared that some root of his labor remained unrectified.
וְיָדוּעַ [בַּכַּוָּונוֹת] עַל ״לֹא נִיגַע לָרִי״ק״ שֶׁהוּא אוֹתִיּוֹת קֶרִ״י, דִּכְזֶה הוּא חַס וְשָׁלוֹם יְגִיעַת בָּשָׂר לָרִיק
and it is known [from the Kavvanos of the Ari] on the prayer "that we may not labor in vain (la-rik)" that rik has the letters of keri, for such is, God forbid, the toil of the flesh in vain;
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ עַל זֶה: ״וְלֹא נֵלֵד לַבֶּהָלָה״ — הַיְינוּ רוּחִין וְשֵׁדִין וְלִילִין
and likewise they expounded on "nor bring forth for terror" (Yeshayah 65:23): this refers to spirits, demons, and lilin;
וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁנָּתַן לָנוּ תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת וְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם נָטַע וְגוֹמֵר נִזְכֶּה לָזֶה לְעָבְדוֹ בְּלֵבָב שָׁלֵם

and because He gave us the Torah of truth and planted eternal life within us, we merit through this to serve Him with a whole heart,1016Yeshayahu 65:23; Radak ad loc.; Midrash Tanchuma, Kedoshim 14 — “they shall not labor in vain”: In its plain sense, the verse promises that Israel’s labor and children will no longer be lost to calamity. Radak contrasts this future blessing with the curse in which enemies consume a person’s work. Tanchuma connects the verse with the future removal of the evil inclination, when parents will bear children in joy rather than terror. Rav Tzadok’s reversal of the letters ריק into קרי is a kabbalistic remez concerning wasted generative power; it should be clearly distinguished from the verse’s peshat and treated with the reverence appropriate to sensitive bodily matters.
הַיְינוּ בְּב׳ הַלְּבָבוֹת גַּם בְּיֵצֶר הָרָע לְאַכְפַּיָּא, שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה בּוֹ שׁוּם שׁוֹרֶשׁ מִזּוּהֲמַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע, ״לְמַעַן לֹא [נִיגַע לָרִיק] וְגוֹמֵר״
meaning with both inclinations, subjugating the yetzer hara so that no trace of the yetzer's defilement remains, "that we may not labor in vain, etc.";
דְּעַל יְדֵי זֶה יְבוֹעַר רוּחַ הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁבְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ, וּמְחַלֵּל לִבּוֹ לְגַמְרֵי וְלֹא נִיגַע וְכוּלֵיהּ

for through this the spirit of impurity at its root is purged, thoroughly slaying the heart so that we do not labor in vain;1017Mishnah Berachos 9:5; the blessing after Torah reading; Takanas HaShavin 15:48, 50, and 54 — serving with both inclinations: The Mishnah interprets “with all your heart” as service with both the good inclination and the evil inclination. The blessing over Torah calls it “the Torah of truth” and says that Hashem “planted eternal life within us.” Rav Tzadok joins these formulations: Torah does not merely suppress bodily force from the outside; at its highest level it redirects the second heart until it too serves Hashem, thereby revealing the planted root of life. Earlier se’ifim connected this transformation with the removal of the heart of stone, Shabbos, and David’s prayer for a newly created pure heart.
וְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ שֶׁחָשַׁב עַל עַצְמוֹ דְּיָגַע לָרִיק, עַל כֵּן חָשַׁד עַצְמוֹ מִפְּגַם הַבְּרִית שֶׁלֹּא תִּיקְּנוֹ [וְעַיֵּין בִּתְשׁוּבַת חַוַּת יָאִיר סִימָן קנ״ב] לְגַמְרֵי

and Rabbi Abbahu, who thought of himself that he had labored in vain, suspected himself of an involuntary blemish of the Covenant that he had not fully rectified [see Responsa Chavvos Yair, §152];1018Kisvei Rav Tzadok — Takanas HaShavin 15:48 and 15:54–56; Peri Tzadik, Vaeschanan 3:1; Tzidkas HaTzadik §§108, 130 — rectifying the root: Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains “create for me a pure heart” as a new creation from nothing, capable of repairing a defect that ordinary gradual effort cannot reach. Se’if 48 associates this with removing the serpent’s pollution; Se’if 54 applies it to David’s complete teshuvah; and Se’if 56 will describe R’ Abahu’s reward as revealed while still concealed within this world. This internal chain clarifies why R’ Abahu’s self-suspicion is not despair. It is the humility that precedes recognition that Hashem can recreate and purify even the deepest root.1019Chavos Yair §152 explains puzzling expressions of Chazal that appear as though [the sages] disparaged their colleagues; and among his words he addresses the words of R’ Abahu, who seemingly disparaged R’ Zeira (Sanhedrin 29b), explaining that their conducts differed — R’ Abahu would derive benefit from this world, and R’ Zeira would mortify himself — and [R’ Abahu] spoke in accordance with his own approach. And likewise in Kesuvos 62a they said that R’ Abahu and R’ Yochanan were “of those brought forth from the West [mimafkeni d’ma’arva],” and therefore were obligated in a [regular conjugal] onah.
וּבֶאֱמֶת אָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא פ״ד עַמּוּד א׳] דְּשׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ מֵעֵין דְּיַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
yet in truth they stated [in Bava Metzia 84a] that the beauty of Rabbi Abbahu was a reflection of the beauty of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him,
שֶׁזָּכָה עַל יְדֵי הַתּוֹרָה לִמְאוֹר פָּנִים דְּ״חָכְמַת אָדָם תָּאִיר פָּנָיו״ (קֹהֶלֶת ח:א), כִּדְקָרֵי עָלָיו רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [פֶּרֶק עַרְבֵי פְסָחִים סוֹף הֲלָכָה א׳]

having merited through the Torah the radiant countenance of "a man's wisdom makes his face to shine" (Koheles 8:1), as Rabbi Yochanan proclaimed over him in the Yerushalmi [Pesachim 10:1];1020Koheles 8:1; Bava Metzia 84a; Peri Tzadik, Chayei Sarah 8:1 — wisdom, beauty, and the light of the face: Koheles says that a person’s wisdom illuminates his face. Bava Metzia describes a chain of reflected beauty: Rav Kahana’s beauty resembled R’ Abahu’s, R’ Abahu’s resembled Yaakov’s, and Yaakov’s resembled Adam’s. Rav Tzadok reads this not as an aesthetic ranking but as the outward radiance of an inward human form restored toward its original wholeness. Peri Tzadik similarly links clarified life, the Davidic quality of enduring existence, and the perfected root of the fathers. The preserved note that follows supplies the Gemara’s fuller wording and immediate context.1021Cf. Bava Metzia 84a — the source R’ Tzadok draws upon: “whoever wishes to see something of the beauty of R’ Yochanan, let him bring a silver goblet as it emerges from the smith’s crucible, fill it with the red seeds of a pomegranate, encircle its rim with a garland of red roses, and set it between sun and shade — that radiance is a semblance of R’ Yochanan’s beauty”; and there too, “the beauty of Rav Kahana is a semblance of R’ Abahu’s beauty, [and] the beauty of R’ Abahu is a semblance of the beauty of Yaakov Avinu.”
וְדְיַעֲקֹב מֵעֵין אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן, הַיְינוּ קוֹדֶם הַחֵטְא
and the beauty of Yaakov was a reflection of Adam HaRishon prior to the sin;
וְאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן הָיָה רָאוּי לִחְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, אֲבָל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם דְּלֹא מֵת הָיָה בְּהֶעְלֵם מִצַּד הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּקָבְרוּ קָבְרַיָּא

and Adam HaRishon was fit to live forever in overt manifestation in this world, whereas Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, who did not die, possessed this immortality in concealment from the perspective of this world, wherein the embalmers embalmed him and the undertakers buried him (Ta'anis 5b);1022Taanis 5b; Yirmiyahu 30:10; Bereishis 49:33–50:13 — Yaakov did not die, yet was buried: R’ Yitzchak derives “Yaakov Avinu did not die” by comparing Yaakov with his descendants: just as his seed remains alive, so does he. Rav Nachman immediately objects that Yaakov was eulogized, embalmed, and buried, and the Gemara leaves the Scriptural derashah standing beside those visible events. Rav Tzadok makes that tension central. Adam before the sin was fit for manifest unending life; Yaakov possesses enduring life at the root, but in this world it remains concealed beneath the ordinary appearance of death and burial.
וְזֶה נִקְרָא ״מֵעֵין״, כְּמוֹ שַׁבָּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהַהַרְגֵּשׁ בּוֹ בְּתַכְלִית הַהֶעְלֵם
and this is called "a reflection" (me'ein), like Shabbos which is a foretaste of the World to Come, where the spiritual perception within it is profoundly concealed;

וּדְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ מֵעֵין יַעֲקֹב, דְּאֵצֶל יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִכָּל מָקוֹם נִתְגַּלָּה שֶׁיֵּשׁ הֶעְלֵם, דְּמִדְּרַשׁ הַמִּקְרָא מִיהַת נוֹדַע דִּבְאֶמֶת לֹא מֵת, וְאֶצְלוֹ הָיָה גַּם הַהֶעְלֵם בְּהֶעְלֵם:

and Rabbi Abbahu's beauty was a reflection of Yaakov: for with Yaakov Avinu it was revealed through the verses of Scripture that he did not die, whereas with Rabbi Abbahu even that concealment was itself hidden.1023Berachos 57b; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos 2:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:56 — Shabbos as a “semblance” of the World to Come: Berachos calls Shabbos one-sixtieth of the World to Come. The comparison means a genuine but partial taste, not identity with the future state. Peri Tzadik explains that the World to Come remains hidden from a person immersed in this world, while Shabbos allows its holiness to be received as a Divine gift within time. Rav Tzadok applies the same structure to R’ Abahu: his likeness to Yaakov is real, but even the hidden life that becomes discernible in Yaakov remains hidden again in R’ Abahu. Se’if 56 develops this double concealment through the vision of reward before death.

items.h: The theme: The thirteen rivers of balsam oil and the thirteen attributes of mercy (yud-gimmel middos shel rachamim). The thirteen rivers shown to Rabbi Abbahu represent the reward of the World to Come experienced in this world, fulfilling "I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with Your likeness" (Tehillim 17:15). In the World to Come there is no eating or drinking, only the delight of the Shechinah's radiance; experiencing this in life renders physical death merely like peaceful sleep. The thirteen rivers correspond to the thirteen attributes of mercy and the thirteen corrections of the supernal beard (yud-gimmel tikunei dikna). Rabbi Yochanan, drawing from strict judgment (Gevurot), lacked a beard and held that only the wholly righteous receive this reward. Rabbi Abbahu, through a lifetime of brokenness and bitter anxiety, aroused the abundant mercies of the supernal beard, proving that the station of the ba'al teshuvah surpasses that of the tzaddik.

p: וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [דַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה שָׁם] אָמְרוּ אַהָא דְּרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ דְּי״ג נַהֲרֵי, הַגִּירְסָא: דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַרְאֶה לָהֶם מַתַּן שְׂכָרָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְהֵן שְׂבֵעִים וִישֵׁנִים

And in the Yerushalmi [Avodah Zarah 3:1] regarding the thirteen rivers of Rabbi Abbahu, the textual reading is: that the Holy One, blessed be He, shows them the reward of their labor in this world, and they are sated and fall asleep;
דְּרְאִיַּית י״ג נַהֲרֵי הוּא רְאִיַּית עוֹלָמוֹ בְּחַיָּיו בְּעוֹדוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הַשָּׂכָר דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא

for the vision of the thirteen rivers represents beholding one's world in his lifetime while still in this world, which is the reward of the World to Come;1024Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 3:1; Yalkut Shimoni, Nach §468 — reward shown before death: The tradition concerning R’ Abahu says that near his passing Hashem showed him thirteen rivers of pure balsam. Yalkut Shimoni explains the broader pattern: Hashem shows the righteous their future reward while they are still in this world; their souls become satisfied, and they sleep. The source itself emphasizes consolation at the moment of departure. Rav Tzadok develops this into a doctrine of hidden life: the vision is not merely information about reward, but a present taste of the World to Come that transforms death into sleep.
וְהוּא עִנְיַן הַשְּׂבִיעָה כְּעִנְיַן ״אֶשְׂבְּעָה בְהָקִיץ תְּמוּנָתֶךָ״ (תְּהִלִּים י״ז:ט״ו)
and this is the spiritual satiation of "I shall be satisfied, when I awake, with Your likeness" (Tehillim 17:15);
דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵין בּוֹ אֲכִילָה וְכוּלֵיהּ, רַק נֶהֱנִין מִזִּיו הַשְּׁכִינָה (בְּרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳)
for in the World to Come there is no eating or drinking, but the righteous sit with their crowns on their heads and enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah (Berachos 17a);
וְ״אֶשְׂבְּעָה בְהָקִיץ״ הוּא הַשָּׂגַת שְׂבִיעָה זוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

and "I shall be satisfied, when I awake" denotes attaining this very satiation within this world;1025Berachos 17a; Peri Tzadik, Lag BaOmer 4:1, 6:2, and 8:1; Kedushas Shabbos 1:8 — “see your world in your lifetime”: The Sages blessed one another, “May you see your world in your lifetime.” Rav Tzadok repeatedly explains this as receiving in this world a disclosure of the hidden light and knowledge reserved for the World to Come. Peri Tzadik connects it with becoming a “son of the World to Come” while alive, and Kedushas Shabbos identifies Shabbos as a recurring taste of this state. Se’if 56 applies the same pattern to R’ Abahu’s vision: future reward enters present awareness without ceasing to belong to a concealed world.1026Tehillim 17:15; Rashi and Radak ad loc. — “I shall be satisfied, upon awakening, with Your image”: David contrasts the satisfaction of the wicked from worldly plenty with his own hope to behold Hashem in righteousness and be satisfied when he awakens. Rashi relates the awakening to the resurrection, while Radak explains it as awakening from the sleep of death to apprehend Divine glory. Rav Tzadok reads the verse dynamically: a tzaddik may attain a measure of that future satisfaction before death, so that the later awakening has already begun within life.1027Berachos 17a; Shemos 24:11; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 8:2 — delighting in the radiance of the Shechinah: The Gemara says that the World to Come contains no eating, drinking, procreation, commerce, jealousy, hatred, or competition; rather, the righteous enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah. Rambam explains that these expressions describe incorporeal intellectual delight and closeness to Hashem, not bodily consumption. Rav Tzadok uses the language of satisfaction carefully: the thirteen rivers are a spiritual apprehension represented through an image of abundance, not a claim that the future reward is physical balsam.
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הַמִּיתָה אַחַר כָּךְ רַק כִּשְׁינָה בְּעָלְמָא, וְהוּא גַּם כֵּן דְּלֹא מֵת, אֶלָּא שֶׁגַּם הָא דְּלֹא מֵת הוּא בְּהֶעְלֵם

and through this, death thereafter is merely like falling asleep, which is likewise a state of not dying, except that his immortality remains concealed.1028Daniel 12:2; Berachos 57b; Taanis 5b; Takanas HaShavin 15:54–56 — death as sleep and concealed life: Daniel calls the dead “those who sleep in the dust,” and Berachos calls sleep one-sixtieth of death. Taanis nevertheless teaches that Yaakov Avinu did not die, even while acknowledging the visible facts of eulogy, embalming, and burial. Rav Tzadok combines these strands: for one who has already touched the life of the World to Come, death is analogous to sleep, while the enduring life remains concealed from ordinary earthly perception. This is theological interpretation, not a denial of physical death or mourning.
וּמִסְפַּר י״ג נַהֲרֵי שֶׁנִּמְצָא גַּם בְּתַלְמוּדִין [תַּעֲנִית כ״ה עַמּוּד א׳] בִּשְׂכַר עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וַדַּאי הוּא נֶגֶד י״ג מִדּוֹת שֶׁל רַחֲמִים
And the tally of thirteen rivers, found likewise in our Talmud [Ta'anis 25a] regarding the reward of the World to Come, certainly corresponds to the thirteen attributes of mercy;
שֶׁזּוֹכִים לָהֶם עַל יְדֵי עֵסֶק הַתּוֹרָה בְּי״ג מִדּוֹת שֶׁהַתּוֹרָה נִדְרֶשֶׁת דְּהֵם זֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה כִּידוּעַ
which one merits through engrossment in the Torah through the thirteen hermeneutical principles by which the Torah is expounded, which parallel one another as is known;
וְיָדוּעַ דְּהַי״ג מִדּוֹת הֵם י״ג תִּיקּוּנֵי דְּדִיקְנָא

and it is known that the thirteen attributes of mercy are the thirteen corrections of the supernal beard (yud-gimmel tikunei dikna).1029Taanis 25a (and Yerushalmi Avodah Zarah 3:1): The reward stored for the tzaddikim — “thirteen rivers of balsam [afarsemon]” that they will delight in in the Future — R’ Tzadok’s image for the thirteen “rivers” of divine goodness.1030Taanis 25a — R’ Elazar ben Pedas and the thirteen rivers: The Bavli’s account concerns R’ Elazar ben Pedas, who accepted continued poverty rather than ask that creation be restarted for the possibility of improved fortune. Hashem promised him thirteen rivers of pure balsam in the World to Come. The parallel number supports Rav Tzadok’s comparison, but the personalities and immediate settings must remain distinct: R’ Abahu’s vision appears in the Yerushalmi-Midrashic tradition, whereas Taanis records a promise to R’ Elazar ben Pedas.1031Shemos 34:6–7; Rosh Hashanah 17b; Rabbeinu Tam, Tosafos ad loc. — the thirteen attributes of mercy: The Torah reveals Hashem’s attributes of compassion after the sin of the Golden Calf. Rosh Hashanah teaches that Hashem showed Moshe the order of prayer and covenanted that these attributes would not return empty. The precise enumeration is discussed among the Rishonim, but the unit is classically known as the Thirteen Attributes of Mercy. Rav Tzadok interprets the thirteen rivers as a corresponding flow of mercy received by the baal teshuvah; that numerical correspondence is his kabbalistic synthesis, not the plain statement of the Gemara in Taanis.1032Baraisa of R’ Yishmael; Sifra, Introduction; Takanas HaShavin 3:2 and 15:55–56 — thirteen hermeneutical principles: The Baraisa of R’ Yishmael enumerates thirteen principles through which Torah law is expounded. They belong to the disciplined transmission of Torah shebe’al peh, not to unrestricted symbolic interpretation. Rav Tzadok links them to the thirteen attributes of mercy: through faithful Torah study, human understanding becomes a vessel for Divine compassion. This association continues his broader teaching that wisdom can disclose a hidden order that prophetic sight does not directly picture.1033Zohar III, Nasso, Idra Rabbah 131b–134b; Sha’ar HaKavanos, Derushei Dikna — the thirteen tikkunei dikna: Kabbalistic literature represents the supernal channels of compassion as thirteen arrangements of the beard. The beard is therefore a symbol of mature, overflowing mercy rather than a biological measure of holiness. Rav Tzadok draws upon this symbolic vocabulary when he connects thirteen rivers, thirteen attributes, thirteen Torah principles, and hadras panim. The connection belongs to the kabbalistic interpretive layer and should not be confused with the Gemara’s literal explanation of R’ Yochanan’s appearance.
וּבְבָבָא מְצִיעָא [שָׁם עַמּוּד א׳] דְּשׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן לֹא חָשֵׁיב דְּלֹא הָיָה לוֹ הַדְרַת פָּנִים זָקָן
And in Bava Metzia [84a], where the beauty of Rabbi Yochanan is excluded from the listing because he lacked the facial glory of a beard;
הַיְינוּ דְּהַבַּעַל תְּשׁוּבָה צָרִיךְ לְעוֹרֵר מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים רַבִּים לְרַחֵם עָלָיו וּלְקַבְּלוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה הֲגַם שֶׁחָטָא
this means: a penitent must awaken abundant mercy from the supernal beard to show compassion upon him and accept him in repentance despite his sin;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן צַדִּיק גָּמוּר אֵין לְמִדַּת הַדִּין לְקַטְרֵג עָלָיו, וְהוּא מִתְנַהֵג הַכֹּל עַל פִּי מִדַּת הַדִּין, דְּעַל כֵּן סְבִיבָיו נִשְׂעֲרָה מְאֹד

whereas with a consummate tzaddik, the Attribute of Judgment has no cause to prosecute him, and all his conduct is aligned with strict justice, wherefore "round about Him it storms exceedingly";1034Bava Metzia 84a — R’ Yochanan’s beauty and the absence of hadras panim: The Gemara praises R’ Yochanan’s extraordinary beauty, yet excludes him from the chain linking Rav Kahana, R’ Abahu, Yaakov, and Adam because he lacked hadras panim, explained there as a beard. Rav Tzadok turns this physical distinction into a spiritual symbol: R’ Yochanan represents the complete tzaddik governed by clarity and judgment, while R’ Abahu’s greater facial splendor signifies mercy awakened through teshuvah. The symbolic contrast is Rav Tzadok’s reading; the Bavli itself does not assign these spiritual types to the two Sages.1035Tehillim 50:3 and 89:8; Yevamos 121b — “around Him it storms mightily”: Yevamos derives from these verses that Hashem is exacting with those closest to Him even to a hairsbreadth. The teaching warns that spiritual greatness increases accountability; it does not authorize harshness toward others or imply that every tragedy reveals a specific sin. Rav Tzadok uses it to characterize the standpoint of the complete tzaddik, against whom the attribute of judgment has no accusation except the most exacting measure.
וְעַל כֵּן רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן שֶׁהָיָה צַדִּיק גָּמוּר כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל וִינִיקָתוֹ מֵהַגְּבוּרוֹת
wherefore Rabbi Yochanan who was a consummate tzaddik as mentioned above, his spiritual nourishment deriving from Gevurot—
דְּעַל כֵּן עָנֵישׁ וְקָטֵיל בְּעוּבְדָא דְּרַב כָּהֲנָא [בְּבָבָא קַמָּא קי״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] וּדְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ [בָּבָא מְצִיעָא פ״ד סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]
wherefore he punished and slew with his gaze in the incident of Rav Kahana (Bava Kamma 117a) and Reish Lakish (Bava Metzia 84a)—
לֹא הָיָה לוֹ זָקָן, דְּהוּא חוֹתָמָיו שֶׁל בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה
lacked a beard, which is the supernal seal of the penitent,
שֶׁזּוֹכִים בִּתְשׁוּבָתָם לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם עַל יְדֵי דְּבֵיקוּת הָאַהֲבָה בִּכְלוֹת הַנֶּפֶשׁ

who merit through their repentance eternal life through the passionate cleaving of love unto the expiration of the soul;1036Bava Kamma 117a: The narrative of Rav Kahana — who slew the informer and fled to Eretz Yisrael, to R’ Yochanan; R’ Tzadok cites it among the accounts of the Sages’ guarded holiness.1037Bava Metzia 84a: The narrative of Reish Lakish — the bandit who became R’ Yochanan’s disciple and brother-in-law — and his death after R’ Yochanan’s “bandit” remark. R’ Tzadok reads the whole account, as in Siman 10, as being to Reish Lakish’s praise.1038Bava Kamma 117a; Bava Metzia 84a; Takanas HaShavin 10 and 15:56 — Rav Kahana and Reish Lakish: The preserved notes identify the two narratives. In Bava Kamma, R’ Yochanan’s reaction to Rav Kahana leads to grave consequences before Rav Kahana is restored; in Bava Metzia, the dispute with Reish Lakish leads to illness, death, and R’ Yochanan’s overwhelming grief. Rav Tzadok reads these episodes through R’ Yochanan’s root in gevurah, while elsewhere emphasizing the greatness of Rav Kahana and the praise of Reish Lakish’s teshuvah. The narratives should therefore be studied as morally complex Aggadah, not reduced to approval of punishment or anger.
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי זֶה, כַּמַּיִם הַפָּנִים, מְעוֹרֵר אַהֲבַת הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ אֵלָיו מִמִּידַּת רַחֲמָיו וַחֲסָדָיו
through which, "as in water face answers to face" (Mishlei 27:19), he arouses the love of the Blessed Name toward him from the attribute of His mercies and kindnesses;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה זוֹכֶה לְהַדְרַת פָּנִים יוֹתֵר, וְהוּא ״הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ שֶׁהִשִּׂיג רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ עַל פִּי מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לָהּ לִפְנֵי פְּטִירָתוֹ
and through this he merits a greater facial glory, which is "the place where penitents stand" attained by Rabbi Abbahu according to his rung before his passing,
עַל יְדֵי הַמְּרִירוּת שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ כָּל יְמֵי חַיָּיו עַל יְדֵי מַחֲשַׁבְתּוֹ דִּ״לְרִיק יָגַעְתִּי״

on account of the bitterness he experienced all the days of his life through his humble thought that "I have labored in vain";1039Mishlei 27:19; Rashi and Rabbeinu Yonah ad loc.; Resisei Layla 37:1 — “as water reflects the face”: Just as water returns the face presented to it, one heart awakens a corresponding response in another. Rashi explains the verse as reciprocal human feeling; Rabbeinu Yonah applies it to the heart’s response. Rav Tzadok extends the principle upward: self-surrendering love and teshuvah awaken a disclosure of Divine love and mercy. This is not a mechanical guarantee that emotion compels Heaven, but a description of covenantal reciprocity when the person genuinely turns toward Hashem.
וּמִי שֶׁלֹּא טָעַם טַעַם חֵטְא אֵינוֹ יוֹדֵעַ מְרִירוּת שֶׁל הַבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה, וְאֵין יָכוֹל לְהַשִּׂיג גּוֹדֶל הַמַּדְרֵיגָה שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהַגִּיעַ עַל יְדֵי זֶה:

and one who has never tasted the taste of sin does not know the bitterness of the penitent, and cannot comprehend the supreme height that can be reached through it.1040Berachos 34b; Avodah Zarah 17a; Takanas HaShavin 15:54–56; Tzidkas HaTzadik §164; Peri Tzadik, Pesach Sheni 2:2 — the bitterness and height of teshuvah: R’ Abahu teaches that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place of baalei teshuvah, while R’ Yochanan gives priority to the tzaddik who was distant from sin from the beginning. R’ Elazar ben Durdaya shows how radical remorse can reach the point of the soul’s departure. Rav Tzadok maintains that both Talmudic positions are true in different orders: steady purity has one perfection, and a return from distance can awaken otherwise inaccessible mercy. Se’if 56 concludes that one who never tasted sin cannot experientially know this bitterness; it does not praise sin or recommend seeking failure, but explains the unique transformation available after responsibility, remorse, and complete return.

items.h: The theme: The beauty of the righteous in Gan Eden compared to a cup of gold. In the Baraisa of Maseches Gan Eden, the least radiant countenance in Gan Eden resembles the beauty of Yosef and Rabbi Yochanan, likened to pomegranate seeds in a goblet of gold facing the sun. A Torah scholar initially appears to an unlearned person (am ha'aretz) like a flagon of gold; once he engages in familiar conversation, he appears like silver (Sanhedrin 52b). Korach claimed that "all the congregation are holy," arguing that the unlearned, whose mitzvos are as full as pomegranate seeds (partuta d'rumana, Berachos 57a), equal scholars. Yet the scholar tastes the inner juice of the pomegranate (asis rimoni, Shir HaShirim 8:2), extracting the divine essence while discarding the external shell, as Rabbi Meir did with Acher (Chagigah 15b).

p: וּבַבָּרַיְיתָא [דְּמַסֶּכֶת גַּן עֵדֶן] בְּמַעֲלַת הַצַּדִּיקִים בְּגַן עֵדֶן אִיתָא: ״וְהַכֵּיעוּר שֶׁבָּהֶם דּוֹמִין פָּנָיו לְיוֹסֵף הַצַּדִּיק וּלְדִמְיוֹן רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, וּכְפִרְטֵי רִמּוֹנִים בְּכוֹס שֶׁל זָהָב מוּקָּף נֶגֶד הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ״, עַד כָּאן

And in the Baraisa [of Maseches Gan Eden] on the stature of the righteous in Gan Eden it is taught: "And the least radiant among them has a countenance resembling Yosef the Righteous and the likeness of Rabbi Yochanan, like seeds of pomegranate in a cup of gold set against the sun," thus far;
וְדוֹמֶה בָּזֶה לְמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא שָׁם]: ״הַאי מַאן דְּבָעֵי לְמֶחֱזֵי שׁוּפְרֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן, נַיְיתֵי כָּסָא דְּכַסְפָּא וְכוּלֵיהּ״

and this is similar to what they stated [in Bava Metzia 84a]: "One who wishes to see the beauty of Rabbi Yochanan should bring a cup of silver, etc.";1041Maseches Gan Eden; Bava Metzia 84a — the later Gan Eden baraisa and R’ Yochanan’s radiance: The passage is cited here from Maseches Gan Eden, a later midrashic description of the righteous in Gan Eden rather than a tractate of the Bavli. Its gold cup, pomegranate seeds, and sunlight imagery closely reworks the Bavli’s description of R’ Yochanan’s beauty. Rav Tzadok reads the physical imagery symbolically: even the lowest visible rank of the righteous reflects the perfected human beauty associated with Yosef and R’ Yochanan. The baraisa supplies the image; the hierarchy of spiritual types developed from it is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.

כָּאן אָמְרוּ ״שֶׁל זָהָב״, כִּי אָמְרוּ [סַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ב רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״תַּלְמִיד חָכָם דּוֹמֶה לִפְנֵי עַם הָאָרֶץ בַּתְּחִלָּה לְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל זָהָב, סִפֵּר עִמּוֹ דּוֹמֶה לְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל כֶּסֶף וְכוּלֵיהּ״

here it specifies "of gold," for they stated [in Sanhedrin 52b]: "A Torah scholar appears before an unlearned person at first like a flagon of gold; once he converses with him, he appears like a flagon of silver, etc.";
עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דְּקָאֵי אַעֲדַת קֹרַח הַנִּזְכָּר מִקּוֹדֶם, וּמַשְׁמַע דְּחָשֵׁיב לְקוֹרַח עַם הָאָרֶץ

see Rashi there who explains that this applies to the company of Korach, which implies that he considered Korach an am ha'aretz;1042Sanhedrin 52b; Rashi ad loc. — gold, silver, and earthenware in the am ha’aretz’s perception: The Gemara says that a Torah scholar first appears to an am ha’aretz like a golden vessel, after ordinary conversation like silver, and after receiving benefit from him like earthenware. The passage describes the observer’s declining reverence through familiarity and dependency; it does not say that the scholar’s intrinsic Torah stature changes. Rashi connects the surrounding discussion with Korach’s assembly. Rav Tzadok therefore contrasts gold and silver as modes of perceived honor while probing how Korach’s great learning could coexist with opposition to Moshe.1043Cf. Bava Metzia 84a — the source R’ Tzadok draws upon: “whoever wishes to see something of the beauty of R’ Yochanan, let him bring a silver goblet as it emerges from the smith’s crucible, fill it with the red seeds of a pomegranate, encircle its rim with a garland of red roses, and set it between sun and shade — that radiance is a semblance of R’ Yochanan’s beauty”; and there too, “the beauty of Rav Kahana is a semblance of R’ Abahu’s beauty, [and] the beauty of R’ Abahu is a semblance of the beauty of Yaakov Avinu.”

וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ אָמְרוּ דְּחָכָם גָּדוֹל הָיָה וּמִטּוֹעֲנֵי הָאָרוֹן, וְאָמְרוּ: ״קוֹרַח שֶׁפִּקֵּחַ הָיָה, מָה רָאָה לִשְׁטוּת זֶה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר רַבָּה י״ח:ג׳), וּמַשְׁמַע דְּהוּא הָיָה הַתַּלְמִיד חָכָם הַגָּדוֹל בְּכוּלָּם

yet in the Midrash they said that he was a great sage and among the bearers of the Ark, asking: "Korach, who was clever, what saw he to this folly?" (Bamidbar Rabbah 18:3), implying that he was the greatest scholar of them all!1044Bamidbar Rabbah 18:3; Midrash Tanchuma, Korach 2; Rashi on Bamidbar 16:7; Peri Tzadik, Korach 8:2 — Korach’s greatness and folly: The Midrash calls Korach a great sage and one of the bearers of the Ark. Rashi asks, “Korach, who was clever, what did he see that led him to this folly?” and answers that his vision of distinguished descendants misled him. Rav Tzadok emphasizes that Torah knowledge does not protect a person who uses it to contest the Torah’s living transmission. Peri Tzadik similarly explains that Korach opposed Moshe through confidence in his own Torah attainment. The sources preserve both truths: Korach possessed real greatness, and that greatness became implicated in his rebellion.
אֲבָל הַכַּוָּונָה, דְּיָדוּעַ דְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹת כָּל הַתַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל בְּכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת
But the inner meaning is: it is known that Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, is the root of the souls of all the Torah scholars of Israel throughout all generations,
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַב הָאֲרִיזַ״ל עַל לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא ״מֹשֶׁה שַׁפִּיר קָאָמְרַתְּ״ דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר תַּלְמִיד חָכָם

as the Arizal wrote on the Talmudic idiom "Moshe, you have spoken well!" (Shabbos 101b), which addresses every eminent Torah scholar;1045Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Galus Mitzrayim 6:1; writings of the Arizal — Moshe as the root of Torah knowledge: Rav Tzadok cites the Arizal’s explanation of the Talmudic expression “Moshe, you have spoken well”: Moshe is the root of the da’as found in the Torah scholars of every generation, because his soul embraces the general revelation of Torah. This is a doctrine of spiritual rootedness, not an equation of every scholar with Moshe Rabbeinu. Se’if 57 uses it to explain the severity of Korach’s dispute: denying Moshe’s unique elevation attacked the source through which the differentiated levels of Torah are transmitted.
וְהֵם בָּאוּ לַחֲלוֹק עַל שְׁמוֹ בְּטַעֲנַת: ״כָּל הָעֵדָה כֻּלָּם קְדֹשִׁים... וּמַדּוּעַ תִּתְנַשְּׂאוּ״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר ט״ז:ג׳)
and [Korach and his assembly] came to dispute his authority with the argument: "all the congregation are holy... wherefore then lift ye up yourselves?" (Bamidbar 16:3);
הַיְינוּ דְּאֵין הִתְנַשְּׂאוּת לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם עַל עַם הָאָרֶץ, דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״ וְיָרְשׁוּ אֶרֶץ וְעוֹלָם הַבָּא

meaning that a Torah scholar has no superiority over an am ha'aretz, for "Your people are all righteous" and inherit the earth and the World to Come;1046Bamidbar 16:3; Ramban and Sforno ad loc.; Bamidbar Rabbah 18 — “the entire congregation is holy”: Korach’s claim began from a true premise: Israel had received holiness and the Divine Presence dwelled among them. Ramban and Sforno explain, however, that he used that shared holiness to challenge the appointments and distinctions commanded through Moshe. The error was not affirming Jewish holiness, but treating essential holiness as proof that no ordered roles or degrees of Torah authority could exist. Rav Tzadok preserves the premise while rejecting the conclusion: every Jew is holy, yet Torah scholars can embody a higher revealed attainment.1047Yeshayahu 60:21; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1; Peri Tzadik, Shoftim 11:1 — universal Jewish rootedness and differentiated attainment: “Your people are all righteous; they shall inherit the land forever” is the verse used by the Mishnah for Israel’s share in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok elsewhere notes that even Jews empty of Torah possess mitzvos and covenantal distinction. This essential share does not mean that all spiritual accomplishments are equal, nor does it remove judgment or responsibility. Se’if 57 distinguishes the unseverable root shared by Israel from the additional inward light attained through Torah.
כִּי גַּם רֵיקָנִים שֶׁבְּיִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כְּרִמּוֹן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת נ״ז עַמּוּד א׳], זֶה אַעַם הָאָרֶץ שֶׁהוּא רֵיקָן מִדִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה

for even the empty ones of Israel are as full of mitzvos as a pomegranate as they said [in Berachos 57a], which refers to an am ha'aretz who is empty of Torah knowledge.1048Kesubos 62a; Bava Metzia 84a; Chagigah 14a — distinguishing the Aggadic biographies of R’ Yochanan and R’ Abahu: Kesubos records two related feats: when a bathhouse collapsed, R’ Abahu saved the two servants supporting him; when stairs collapsed beneath R’ Yochanan, he lifted Rav Ami and Rav Asi. Bava Metzia describes R’ Yochanan’s exceptional beauty. The title “esteemed before Caesar” in Chagigah is applied to R’ Abahu. The bracketed biographical gloss in the present text appears to combine these traditions. This distinction does not alter Rav Tzadok’s argument, which depends chiefly on the Bavli’s image of R’ Yochanan’s beauty.
וּמִילּוּי הַמִּצְוֹת הוּא דּוּגְמַת מִילּוּי הָרִמּוֹן מִפַּרְצִידֵי וּפַרְטוּתָא דְּרוּמָּנָא

And the fulfillment of mitzvos is modeled after the filling of the pomegranate with seeds (partuta d'rumana);1049Eruvin 19a; Berachos 57a; Resisei Layla 52:8; Peri Tzadik, Shoftim 11:1 — “even the empty among you are full of mitzvos”: Chazal compare even the reikanin of Israel to a pomegranate filled with seeds. Berachos interprets dream imagery of pomegranates in relation to mitzvos and Torah. Rav Tzadok repeatedly uses this teaching to describe Jews who lack developed Torah knowledge yet retain a treasury of concrete mitzvah acts. “Empty” is therefore relative to Torah attainment, not a declaration that the person has no spiritual worth; neither does the praise erase failures that require teshuvah.
אֲבָל בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: ״יְצַפֶּה לַתּוֹרָה, דִּכְתִיב: ׳מֵעֲסִיס רִמֹּנִי׳ (שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים ח:ב)״ — הוּא הַנִּמְצָץ מֵהָרִמּוֹן

but regarding a Torah scholar they said there: "let him anticipate Torah, as it is written: 'of the juice of my pomegranate' (Shir HaShirim 8:2)"—which is the sweet essence sucked from the pomegranate;
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּחֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד ב׳] עַל ״אַחֵר״ שֶׁהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם וּבַעַל עֲבֵירוֹת בְּפֹעַל, דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר רִמּוֹן מָצָא, תּוֹכוֹ אָכַל
and therefore they stated [in Chagigah 15b] regarding Acher who was a Torah scholar yet a sinner in practice, that Rabbi Meir found a pomegranate: he ate the inside,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁמָּצַץ הָעָסִיס, וּקְלִיפָּתוֹ זָרַק, שֶׁכָּל גּוּף הַפַּרְצִידֵי הַנִּשְׁאָר אַחַר הַמְּצִיצָה הָיָה קְלִיפָּה

meaning he sucked the juice, and discarded its rind, for the entire physical substance of the seeds remaining after the juice is extracted was discarded as a husk;1050Shir HaShirim 8:2; Berachos 57a; Takanas HaShavin 15:57; Resisei Layla 52:8 — seeds and the juice of the pomegranate: Shir HaShirim speaks of “the juice of my pomegranate.” Rav Tzadok distinguishes the pomegranate’s many edible seeds, symbolizing discrete mitzvah deeds, from the juice drawn inward from them, symbolizing Torah apprehended and absorbed in the heart. This is an interpretive metaphor, not a halachic ranking that permits neglect of action. Torah’s inward understanding and mitzvos performed through the limbs remain mutually necessary; the comparison explains why the scholar’s revealed form differs from that of the mitzvah-observant am ha’aretz.1051Cf. Chagigah 15b — the source R’ Tzadok cites regarding “Acher”: when the sages questioned how R’ Meir could learn Torah from Elisha ben Avuya after he went astray, they answered with the parable, “R’ Meir found a pomegranate; he ate its inside and discarded its peel [rimon matza, tocho achal, klipaso zarak]” — extracting the Torah while casting off the corruption.
וְעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ בַּעֲלֵי מִצְוֹת אֵין בָּהֶם עָסִיס, אֲבָל הַפַּרְצִידֵי טוֹבִים לְמַאֲכָל
while the unlearned masters of mitzvos possess no juice, yet their physical seeds are wholesome for food.
וְתוֹרָה הוּא הַפְּנִימִיּוּת וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
And the Torah is the inwardness and root of the souls of Israel, which originate from the letters of the Torah,
וְעִיקָּרוֹ בְּהַשָּׂגַת הַחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ וּבִינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וְאֵין בָּהּ שַׁיָּיכוּת בְּאֶבְרֵי הַגּוּף רַק מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁמּוֹצִיא בַּפֶּה:

its essence residing in the perception of Wisdom in the brain and Understanding in the heart, having no connection to the physical limbs except through what one utters with the mouth.1052Chagigah 15b; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 4:1 — R’ Meir learning from Acher was exceptional: The preserved note gives the Gemara’s pomegranate parable: R’ Meir took the nourishing inside of Acher’s Torah and discarded the corrupt peel. Rambam rules ordinarily that Torah should be learned from a teacher whose conduct is proper, and the Gemara treats R’ Meir’s capacity as exceptional. Rav Tzadok uses the image to distinguish inward Torah from corrupted behavior; it must not be read as minimizing Acher’s transgression or as general permission to seek Torah from spiritually destructive sources.

items.h: The theme: Speech as the culmination of action, and the holiness of Israel's physical body. Speech (Malchus, mouth) is the boundary of action, for moving the lips is legally reckoned a deed (akimas sefasav havei ma'aseh). On Shabbos, the scholar's delight transcends physical speech, basking in internal intellectual ecstasy. For the unlearned, Shabbos sanctifies the physical body through festive eating, like partaking of the Manna. Even a sinner in Israel is compared to a burned Sefer Torah upon his death (Shabbos 105a; Rosh, Moed Katan 59), because even the empty are full of mitzvos as a pomegranate. The joyful rejoicing over the destruction of the wicked applies strictly to idolaters and heretics who sin defiantly to provoke Heaven (l'hakh'is), whereas the innate spark of Judaism in the seed of Yaakov remains indelibly bound to the Living God.

p: וְזֶהוּ סוֹף כָּל מַדְרֵיגוֹת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, כִּידוּעַ דְּמַלְכוּת פֶּה
And this is the culmination of all levels of action, as is known that Malchus is the Mouth (Patach Eliyahu);
כִּי הַדִּבּוּר אֵינוֹ מַעֲשֶׂה גָּמוּר בְּפֹעַל בְּגוּף הַדִּבּוּר, רַק עֲקִימַת שְׂפָתַיִם נֶחְשָׁב מַעֲשֶׂה
for speech is not a complete physical act in the substance of speech itself, only that the movement of the lips is legally reckoned an action (Sanhedrin 65b);
וּבַתּוֹרָה הוּא רַק הַהוֹצָאָה מִכֹּחַ לַפּוֹעַל וּבְהִתְגַּלּוּת מַה שֶּׁאֶפְשָׁר לְגַלּוֹת

and in the Torah speech serves merely to bring potential into actuality and reveal what can be expressed;1053Yeshayahu 58:13; Shabbos 118a; Rambam, Hilchos Shabbos 30:7–10; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos — bodily delight as sanctified avodah: The Navi calls Shabbos “a delight,” and Chazal praise honoring it through food and bodily rest. Rambam codifies both kavod and oneg while directing them toward the sanctity of the day. Rav Tzadok explains that mitzvos are performed through the limbs, so Shabbos reveals that the Jewish body itself can become a vessel of holiness. This is not unrestricted indulgence: bodily pleasure becomes mitzvah when ordered toward Shabbos, gratitude, and attachment to Hashem.
אֲבָל עִיקַּר הַהַשָּׂגָה הוּא בַּלֵּב בְּחָכְמָה וּבִינָה שֶׁהֵם לְמַעְלָה מִזּ׳ יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן שֶׁהֵם יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה
but the essential perception resides in the heart in Wisdom and Understanding, which transcend the seven days of the cosmic structure (the days of action).
וְשַׁבָּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהוּא הַשְּׁבִיתָה מִמַּעֲשֶׂה, אַף מֵהַדִּבּוּר בַּתּוֹרָה בְּפֹעַל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת קי״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳]

And Shabbos is a foretaste of the World to Come, being the cessation from labor, even from vocalized speech in Torah in practice as they said [in Shabbos 119b],1054Devarim 8:3; Mechilta deRabbi Yishmael, Beshalach, Vayassa 2; Yoma 75b; Peri Tzadik on Shabbos and the manna — manna and Torah entering the heart: The manna taught that human life proceeds from the word of Hashem, and the Mechilta associates the generation sustained by manna with the fullest reception of Torah. Chazal also describe the manna as suited to each person without ordinary bodily burden. Rav Tzadok treats Shabbos eating as a recurring likeness of manna: physical nourishment, when sanctified, quiets material obstruction and helps Torah penetrate the heart. The comparison is spiritual and functional, not a claim that ordinary Shabbos food acquires the miraculous substance of manna.1055Mishlei 6:23 and 20:27; Zoharic language of nehora zuta; Resisei Layla 52:8 — the mitzvah-lamp and the soul-lamp: Mishlei calls a mitzvah a lamp and Torah light, and calls the human soul “the lamp of Hashem.” Rav Tzadok combines the verses with the kabbalistic expression nehora zuta, a “small light” present in every Jewish soul. Even where the broad illumination of Torah has not been attained, a mitzvah can uncover this inner spark within the body. “Small” describes concealment and limited revelation, not insignificance; the spark remains a demand for further Torah, mitzvos, and teshuvah.
רַק בְּהַשָּׂגַת הָעוֹנֶג לְתַלְמִיד חָכָם בְּהַשָּׂגַת דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם עֹונֶג לְמַעְלָה מִזֶּה
consisting rather in the intellectual delight of the Torah scholar in grasping words of Torah, than which there is no greater pleasure;
וְהַדִּבּוּר בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה עִם חֲבֵירוֹ מַעֲלִים וּמְכַסֶּה הַהַשָּׂגָה בַּלֵּב כִּידוּעַ

and vocalized speech in Torah with one's fellow conceals and veils internal perception in the heart as is known.1056Sanhedrin 44a; Shabbos 105b; Taanis 5b; Takanas HaShavin 12:7 and 15:57 — “although he sinned, he remains Israel”: Sanhedrin teaches that Achan remained “Israel” despite grave sin. Shabbos compares the departure of a Jewish soul to a Torah scroll being burned, and Taanis roots Yaakov’s enduring life in the continuing life of his descendants. Rav Tzadok joins these sources into the claim that the soul-root of the seed of Yaakov cannot be severed. This essential identity is not immunity from consequences: the same sources demand judgment, mourning, and repair. It explains why teshuvah remains possible and why sin does not become the deepest definition of the Jew.
וּלְעַמֵּי הָאָרֶץ בַּעֲלֵי מִצְוֹת שֶׁהוּא בִּיגִיעַת בָּשָׂר וְאֶבְרֵי הַגּוּף, שֶׁכָּל הַמִּצְוֹת בִּפְעוּלַּת הָאֵבָרִים
And for the unlearned whose service consists in the performance of mitzvos through the toil of the flesh and the bodily limbs, all mitzvos operating through physical organs;
עַל זֶה הוּא מִצְוַת שַׁבָּת בְּעוֹנֶג הַגּוּף, שֶׁגַּם בָּזֶה יֵשׁ קְדוּשָׁה גְּדוֹלָה בְּשַׁבָּת כִּי הַגּוּף קָדוֹשׁ דִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל גַּם כֵּן דָּבוּק בַּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ

toward this end the mitzvah of Shabbos directs bodily delight, for in this too there is supreme holiness on Shabbos, since the holy body of the Children of Israel is likewise cleaved unto the Blessed Name;1057Peri Tzadik, Vayetzei 8:1; Zoharic teaching on Israel and Torah — Torah’s letters as the root of Jewish souls: Rav Tzadok writes that the words of Torah are the root of the souls of Israel and describes the traditional correspondence between the souls of Israel and the letters and component parts of Torah. This is a kabbalistic account of spiritual rootedness: each soul has a distinct share in the one Torah, while the Torah as a whole embraces the collective soul of Israel. It is not a claim that personal identity can be reduced to a simple count of visible letters. Se’if 58 therefore continues the preceding se’if: mitzvos sanctify the limbs, while Torah reveals the inward form from which the soul itself receives life.1058Tikkunei Zohar, Petichas Eliyahu; Berachos 61a — “chochmah is the brain” and “binah is the heart”: Petichas Eliyahu maps chochmah to the brain and binah to the heart: chochmah is the inward point of thought, while binah is the heart’s power to understand and develop it. Berachos likewise describes the heart as understanding and discerning. Rav Tzadok is using this established symbolic anatomy, not proposing a medical theory. His point is that the principal acquisition of Torah occurs in inward consciousness — insight, comprehension, and integration — before it is expressed through the bodily organs.1059Devarim 30:14; Eruvin 54a; Rambam, Hilchos Talmud Torah 3:12 — Torah “in your mouth and in your heart”: The Torah itself joins mouth and heart: “the matter is very near to you, in your mouth and in your heart, to do it.” Chazal strongly encourage audible study, teaching that one who opens his mouth in Torah retains and clarifies his learning. Rav Tzadok does not diminish verbal learning. Rather, he distinguishes the mouth as Torah’s point of bodily emergence from the inward wisdom and understanding that give the words their living content. Speech is the bridge by which hidden attainment becomes teachable and shareable.
וְכָל אֲכִילַת שַׁבָּת כַּאֲכִילַת הַמָּן שֶׁפּוֹעֵל לְהַכְנִיס דִּבְרֵי תּוֹרָה בַּלֵּב
and all eating on Shabbos is like eating the Manna, operating to instill words of Torah into the heart;
גַּם מִי שֶׁלֹּא זָכָה לְאוֹר תּוֹרָה, זוֹכֶה עַל יְדֵי הַנֵּר דְּמִצְוָה גַּם כֵּן לְהָאִיר לוֹ בַּגּוּף הֶחָשׁוּךְ

even one who has not merited the light of Torah merits through the "candle of mitzvah" (Mishlei 6:23) that light shines for him within the dark body,1060Tikkunei Zohar, Petichas Eliyahu; Peri Tzadik, Vaera 7:1 — “malchus is the mouth; it is called the Oral Torah”: Petichas Eliyahu identifies malchus with the mouth and with Torah Shebe’al Peh. Rav Tzadok repeatedly uses this formula to describe the final disclosure of an inward Divine idea in articulated language and practical halachah. “Malchus is the mouth” is therefore a kabbalistic structure: what begins as hidden wisdom descends until it can be spoken, received, and enacted. The source supplies the symbolic identification; Se’if 58 applies it to the gradation from inward Torah knowledge to outward speech.1061Sanhedrin 65a; Kerisos 4a; Bava Metzia 90b — movement of the lips as an act: Several Talmudic discussions treat the physical movement of the lips as a form of action, although the precise halachic result varies by context. Rav Tzadok adopts the underlying distinction: speech is not a full bodily deed like an act performed by the limbs, yet it possesses a minimal physical act through articulation. Calling it the “end” of the levels of action means that speech stands at the boundary between inward thought and outward deed; it does not establish that every spoken word has the same legal status as a complete physical act.
בְּ״נֵר ה׳ נִשְׁמַת אָדָם״ (שָׁם כ:כז) שֶׁהוּא נְהוֹרָא זוּטָא דְּיֵשׁ לְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, דְּכוּלָּם קְדוֹשִׁים וּדְבוּקִים בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים

through "the spirit of man is the lamp of Hashem" (ibid. 20:27), which is the small light (nehora zuta) possessed by every single Jew, for all are holy and cleaved unto the Living God;1062Devarim 6:6; Mishlei 2:10; Takanas HaShavin 15:59 — revelation in speech and acquisition in the heart: “These words shall be upon your heart,” and “wisdom shall enter your heart,” locate Torah’s lasting acquisition within the person. Speech brings an insight from potential into communicable actuality, but the spoken formulation can reveal only what language is capable of carrying. Rav Tzadok develops the complementary side in the following se’if: conversation can also cover the fullness of an inward apprehension because words necessarily delimit it. Se’if 58 is not opposing speech and understanding; it orders them, with inward comprehension as the source and speech as its finite revelation.1063Tikkunei Zohar, Petichas Eliyahu; Sefer Yetzirah, ch. 4 — chochmah and binah above the “seven days of building”: Kabbalistic terminology calls the seven lower middos — from chesed through malchus — the “seven days of building,” because they structure the manifested order reflected in the seven days of creation. Chochmah and binah belong to the upper intellectual powers that precede and direct those manifest attributes. Rav Tzadok’s phrase is therefore a hierarchy of concealment and revelation, not a chronological statement that wisdom and understanding exist outside Torah practice. Their inward light must ultimately descend through the middos into speech and action.
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ: ״אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא, יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא״ (סַנְהֶדְרִין מ״ד עַמּוּד א׳)
wherefore they stated: "Even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite" (Sanhedrin 44a),
דְּשׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת הַיַּהֲדוּת שֶׁבּוֹ שֶׁמִּצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתָן שֶׁל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְנַתֵּק

for the root holiness of Judaism within him, deriving from the soul-root of the seed of Yaakov, can never be severed.1064Berachos 57b; Zohar, Bereishis 78; Resisei Layla 1:1 — Shabbos as a semblance of the World to Come: Berachos lists Shabbos among the experiences that provide a taste of the World to Come, and the Zohar similarly calls Shabbos its likeness. Rav Tzadok explains that this resemblance lies in release from the strain and fragmentation of weekday activity. The World to Come is not earned by passive inactivity; it is the revealed fruit of the Torah and mitzvos cultivated in this world. Shabbos allows a person to taste that completed state by resting from creative labor and receiving holiness as a present reality.1065Shabbos 119b: “The world endures only for the sake of the breath of schoolchildren [hevel tinokos shel beis raban]” — the breath “in which there is no sin”; and one does not interrupt the children even to build the Temple.1066Yerushalmi Shabbos 15:3; Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 290:2; Takanas HaShavin 15:58–59 — Torah study on Shabbos and contemplative “cessation”: The Yerushalmi states that Shabbos and festivals were given for engagement in Torah and also teaches, “as the Holy One ceased from utterance, so you should cease from utterance,” referring to weekday-oriented speech. Halachah accordingly assigns substantial Shabbos time to Torah study. Rav Tzadok’s phrase about ceasing even from Torah speech describes an exceptionally inward level in which the scholar rests in apprehended Torah delight without needing to externalize every insight. It is not a practical instruction to stop learning or teaching Torah on Shabbos.1067Tehillim 119:97, 103; Avos 6:4; Peri Tzadik, Kedushas Shabbos — the pleasure of inward Torah attainment: The Psalmist describes Torah as the object of constant love and meditation and says that its words are sweeter than honey. Chazal portray the life of Torah as the deepest happiness available even amid material simplicity. Rav Tzadok identifies the scholar’s Shabbos delight with the moment when Torah is no longer merely information spoken aloud but an inwardly tasted reality. This pleasure does not replace disciplined study; it is its ripened fruit, when chochmah and binah become settled in the heart and the person experiences attachment to Hashem through the Torah itself.
וּבְשַׁבָּת [ק״ה עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּאָדָם מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁמֵּת אֲפִילּוּ דְּלָאו אָדָם כָּשֵׁר, דּוֹמֶה לְסֵפֶר תּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּשְׂרַף
And in Shabbos [105b] it is taught that when an ordinary Israelite dies, even one who was not an upright man (adam kasher), he is compared to a Torah scroll that was consumed by fire;
וּפֵירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י, דְּאֵין לְךָ רֵיק מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת
and Rashi explains: for there is no empty Jew who does not possess Torah and mitzvos;
וּמַשְׁמַע דַּאֲפִילּוּ רָשָׁע וּבַעַל עֲבֵירוֹת נַמֵּי, שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כְּרִמּוֹן
which implies that even a wicked person and habitual transgressor is included, for even the sinners of Israel are as full of mitzvos as a pomegranate;
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע לְשׁוֹן ״דְּלָאו אָדָם כָּשֵׁר״ עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאִיתָא [שָׁם קמ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״אֵין ׳לֹא טוֹב׳ אֶלָּא רַע״

and so implies the phrase "not an upright man," along the lines of that which is taught [ibid. 149b]: "'not good' means evil";1068Cf.
