Shabbos 105b — the source R’ Tzadok builds upon: “whoever is present at the departure of the soul is obligated to tear [his garment] — to what is this comparable? To a Torah scroll that is burned” (over which one must tear, per Moed Katan 26a) — Rashi adding that “there is no empty one among Israel who has no Torah and mitzvos.”1069Eruvin 19a; Shir HaShirim 6:7 — even the “empty ones” are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate: Reish Lakish teaches that even the sinners of Israel retain a fullness of mitzvos, and the same passage describes them as ultimately accepting the justice of Divine judgment. The image does not deny sin, punishment, or the need for teshuvah. It identifies real good deeds that remain part of the person and are not retroactively erased by later corruption. Rav Tzadok uses that enduring content to explain why even a deeply fallen Jewish soul can still be compared to a Torah scroll.
וְכֵן הוּא בָּרֹא״שׁ [פֶּרֶק אֵלּוּ מְגַלְּחִין סִימָן נ״ט] בְּשֵׁם מַהֲרַ״ם מֵרוֹטֶנְבֶּרְג
and so it is in the Rosh [Moed Katan, ch. 3, §59] in the name of Maharam of Rothenburg
[וּבִדְפוּס יָשָׁן שֶׁכָּל סִימָנֵי הַמַּסֶּכְתָּא נִסְמְנוּ יַחַד הוּא בְּסִימָן ק״ו] מִלְּשׁוֹן רַשִׁ״י הַנַּ״ל

[and in older editions where all sections of the tractate are numbered consecutively it is §106] derived from the language of Rashi above;1070Shabbos 149b; Mishlei 17:26; Tehillim 5:5 — “there is no ‘not good’ except evil”: The Gemara uses this formulation in discussing one who causes another person to be punished: even a righteous person who becomes the instrument of punishment is described there with the language of “not good,” because evil does not dwell within the Divine partition. Rav Tzadok borrows the phrase to sharpen the wording “not a fit person.” This is a linguistic and moral association; it does not mean that every occurrence of “not good” creates the same halachic category.
וּדְמַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר ״בַּאֲבֹד רְשָׁעִים רִנָּה״ (מִשְׁלֵי י״א:י׳), זֶהוּ בְּעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה אוֹ עוֹשִׂים לְהַכְעִיס וּמִינִין
and that which is stated "when the wicked perish, there is joy" (Mishlei 11:10) applies exclusively to an idolater, heretics, or those who transgress defiantly to provoke Heaven (l'hakh'is);
וְנִדְחַק בַּהֲרוּגֵי בֵּית דִּין דְּאֵין מִתְאַבְּלִין דְּ״בַּאֲבוֹד וְגוֹמֵר״, דְּהוּא כִּלְהַכְעִיס מַה שֶּׁמָּסְרוּ עַצְמָן לְמִיתָה כְּשֶׁהִתְרוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם:

and he was hard-pressed to explain why they do not mourn for those executed by a court on the grounds of "when the wicked perish," explaining that it is considered like defiant provocation because they surrendered themselves to death when warned, see there.1071Rosh, Moed Katan, ch. Eilu Megalchin §59: “And that which we say, ‘at the time the soul departs one is obligated to tear’ — Rabbeinu Meir wrote that he heard in the name of R’ Yonah, of blessed memory, that this applies to a person who is not wicked; but for a wicked and suspect person one is not obligated to tear — rather, on the contrary, one should rejoice, as it is written ‘at the destruction of the wicked, joyous song.’ And [Rabbeinu Meir] wrote that this did not appear correct to him, for we say in Perek HaOreg (105b): to what is this comparable? To a Torah scroll that was burned, over which one is obligated to tear — and Rashi explained there: and the soul of a Jew too resembles it, for there is no empty one among them who has no Torah and mitzvos. Rather, it appears to me that one is obligated to tear over everyone at the time the soul departs — except for an apostate to idolatry, for whoever acknowledges it denies the whole Torah, or one who transgresses one of all the mitzvos stated in the Torah ‘to provoke,’ who is like an idolater, for we hold in the last chapter of Horayos (11a) that an apostate who eats neveilos ‘to provoke’ is a transgressor. And this is what is taught in Mesechta Semachos (ch. 2:10): one who separates from the ways of the community — one does not occupy oneself with him in any matter; their brothers and relatives don brightly-colored garments and wrap themselves in white and eat and drink and rejoice that the enemy of the Omnipresent has perished, as it is stated: ‘do I not hate those who hate You, Hashem?’ — and this verse is adduced in Perek Kol Kisvei HaKodesh (115a) regarding heretics. And it concludes that there is no difference whether he died in his wickedness or was killed in his wickedness — since he was killed by beis din, for whom killing is by law, he has no atonement at the time of burial until he sees the pain of the grave.”1072Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:6; Semachos 2:10; Rosh, Moed Katan 3:59 — formal mourning, inward grief, and those executed by beis din: The Mishnah states that the relatives of one executed by the court do not observe formal mourning, although they do grieve inwardly, because mourning begins only after the judicial atonement has been completed. Semachos and the Rosh discuss separate exclusions for those who sever themselves from the community or act defiantly against the Torah. Rav Tzadok is questioning how far those exclusions explain the Torah-scroll comparison; he is not collapsing the practical halachic distinctions between aveilus, aninus, grief, and the status of different transgressors.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ס׳–ס״ד

The theme: Analyzing the execution of criminals and the status of sinners as a burned Torah scroll. One who commits a capital crime in the face of formal judicial admonition (hasra'ah) does not act out of pure defiance to spite Heaven (l'hakh'is), but is blinded by fleeting lust or vengeance. Furthermore, since all executed criminals confess before death (Sanhedrin 43b), their teshuvah removes any designation of apostasy. The Ramban in Toras HaAdam (cited in Beis Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 340) questioned the Talmudic ruling that one rends garments over any deceased Jew as over a burned Torah scroll (Shabbos 105b): why rend when a scroll requires rending only when burned by force (bi-zro'a, Moed Katan 26a)?

p: וְאֵין בּוֹ טַעַם לְהַחְשִׁיבוֹ ״לְהַכְעִיס״ בִּשְׁבִיל קַבָּלַת הַהַתְרָאָה, אֶלָּא שֶׁהַתַּאֲוָה דִּלְהַנָּאַת שָׁעָה עִוְּורָה עֵינָיו שֶׁלֹּא לָחוּשׁ לְמַה שֶּׁיִּהְיֶה

And there is no valid reason to classify him as acting "to spite" Heaven merely because he accepted the judicial admonition (hasra'ah), but rather the craving for momentary pleasure blinded his eyes from being concerned about what will follow;
וְכַדֶּרֶךְ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״עָרֵב לָאִישׁ לֶחֶם שָׁקֶר, וְאַחַר יִמָּלֵא פִיהוּ חָצָץ״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ:יז), וּמַתְעֶה נַפְשׁוֹ שֶׁיּוּכַל לִבְרוֹחַ וּלְהִמָּלֵט

and in the manner stated: "Bread of falsehood is sweet to a man, but afterward his mouth shall be filled with gravel" (Mishlei 20:17), deluding himself into thinking that he will be able to flee and escape;1073Mishlei 20:17 — “bread of falsehood is sweet to a person, but afterward his mouth is filled with gravel”: The verse contrasts the immediate sweetness of dishonest gain with its bitter end. Rav Tzadok applies that psychology to a sinner who accepts a warning yet proceeds: desire narrows attention to the moment and suppresses the future consequence. This explains the act without excusing it. The offender remains responsible precisely because the warning made the consequence known, even though appetite overwhelmed that knowledge in practice.
וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן בְּרוֹצֵחַ הָעוֹשֶׂה לְמַלֹּאות תַּאֲוַת נִקְמָתוֹ בְּאוֹיְבוֹ, דְּהוּא אֵינוֹ חוֹשֵׁשׁ אֲפִילּוּ יְמִיתוּהוּ גַּם כֵּן
and all the more so regarding a murderer who acts to fulfill his lust for vengeance against his enemy, who is unconcerned even if they put him to death as well,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּיבָמוֹת קי״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״׳תָּמוֹת נַפְשִׁי עִם פְּלִשְׁתִּים׳ (שׁוֹפְטִים ט״ז:ל׳) קָאָמְרָה״

after the manner they said [in Yevamos 118b]: "She says: 'Let my soul die with the Philistines!' (Shoftim 16:30)";1074Yevamos 118a; Shoftim 16:30 — “let my soul die with the Philistines”: The Gemara uses Shimshon’s words as a description of a person willing to suffer loss so long as another is harmed as well. Rav Tzadok applies the pattern to vengeance: a murderer may disregard his own punishment in order to injure his enemy. The comparison analyzes a destructive motive; it does not claim that every murderer acts from the identical psychological state.
וְגַם הוּא כָּתַב רַק ״כְּמוֹ לְהַכְעִיס״, אֲבָל אֵין בָּזֶה טַעַם, כֵּיוָן דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא עוֹשֶׂה רַק לְמַלֵּא תַּאֲוָתוֹ וְלֹא לְהַכְעִיס יוֹצְרוֹ
and [the Rosh] also wrote merely that it is "like spite," yet there is no logical ground for this, since in any event he acts solely to satisfy his personal desire and not to spite his Creator.
וְתוּ נִרְאֶה, דְּהַדִּין תָּמוּהַּ מִסַּנְהֶדְרִין [מ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּכָל הַמּוּמָתִין מִתְוַודִּין
And furthermore it appears that this ruling is astonishing from Sanhedrin [43b], that all who are executed confess;
וְכֵיוָן שֶׁהִתְוַודָּה וְשָׁב, אַף שֶׁהוּא בִּשְׁעַת מִיתָה, וַדַּאי דְּאֵין לְהַחְשִׁיבוֹ עוֹד כִּמוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס

and since he confessed and repented, even though it was at the moment of death, certainly one must no longer reckon him as an apostate out of spite!1075Cf. Sanhedrin 43b — the source R’ Tzadok invokes: “when he was about ten cubits from the place of stoning, they say to him, ‘confess,’ for such is the way of all who are put to death that they confess — for whoever confesses has a share in the World to Come” — which R’ Tzadok reads as evidence that even the executed transgressor is a penitent, not one who acts “to provoke.”1076Sanhedrin 44a; Rashi ad loc. — “Israel, even though he sinned, is still Israel”: The statement is made regarding Achan, whose transgression brought guilt upon the community. Rashi explains that the covenantal name Israel remains even while the sinner is held responsible. Rav Tzadok’s argument here follows the same twofold structure: identity is not erased, and guilt is not minimized. Se’ifim 57–58 prepared this conclusion by identifying mitzvos with the sanctification of the limbs and Torah with the inward root of the soul.
וּבֶאֱמֶת לְשׁוֹן רַשִׁ״י הַנַּ״ל שֶׁ״אֵין לְךָ רֵיק וְכוּלֵיהּ״, מַשְׁמַע דְּעַל כָּל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַיּוֹתֵר גְּרוּעִים נַמֵּי קָאָמַר
And in truth the language of Rashi above, that "there is no empty Jew, etc.," implies that he speaks regarding all the most degraded transgressors of Israel as well;
וּכְמוֹ דְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל לֹא נֶעֱקַר גַּם מִמּוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס וְעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, דְּגַם בּוֹ מִכָּל מָקוֹם יֵשׁ גַּם תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת

and just as the name of Israel is never uprooted even from an apostate out of spite and an idolater, for within him too there are nevertheless both Torah and mitzvos.1077Resisei Layla 52:8; Pri Tzadik, Shoftim 11:1 — Rav Tzadok on the mitzvos hidden within every Jew: Resisei Layla invokes the pomegranate teaching even regarding the sinners of Israel, while Pri Tzadik explains that every Jew is distinguished through some combination of Torah, prayer, or deeds of kindness, and that gemilus chasadim remains accessible even to one lacking learning or fluent prayer. These passages do not equate all lives morally. They explain the indestructible residue of holy action from which return can begin.
וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין [ל״ט עַמּוּד ב׳] אִיתָא הָא דְּ״בַּאֲבֹד רְשָׁעִים״ אַאַחְאָב
And in Sanhedrin [39b] that verse "when the wicked perish [there is song]" is applied to Ahab;
וְשָׁם [ק״ג עַמּוּד א׳] אָמְרוּ שֶׁהָיָה שׁוֹנֶה פ״ה פָּנִים בְּתוֹרַת כֹּהֲנִים, אִם כֵּן הָיָה מָלֵא תּוֹרָה
and there [103a] they stated that he was expounding eighty-five facets in the Priestly Code (Toras Kohanim), so that if so, he was filled with Torah;
וְכֵן בְּמִצְוֹת אָמְרוּ [שָׁם ק״ב עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּהֶהֱנָה תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים מִנְּכָסָיו וְהָיָה וַותְרָן בְּמָמוֹנוֹ
and likewise regarding mitzvos they stated [there, 102b] that he benefited Torah scholars from his property and was generous with his money;
וּצְדָקָה נִקְרָא בְּדִבְרֵי חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת בְּשֵׁם סְתָם ״מִצְוָה״, כִּי זֶהוּ הַמִּצְוָה שֶׁעוֹשִׂין בְּכָל עֵת

and charity is termed in the words of our Sages of blessed memory in several places by the unqualified name of "mitzvah," for that is the mitzvah performed at all times.1078Sanhedrin 39b; Megillah 10b — rejoicing at the removal of wickedness and Divine sorrow over destruction: Sanhedrin applies “at the destruction of the wicked there is song” to the death of Achav, but immediately asks whether the Holy One rejoices in the downfall of the wicked. The broader Aggadic answer distinguishes the benefit and song experienced when evil is removed from the Divine attitude toward the destruction of His creatures. Rav Tzadok’s discussion similarly permits moral judgment of wickedness while still treating the loss of a Jewish soul as a profound loss.1079Sanhedrin 102b — Achav’s honor for Torah and generosity to Torah scholars: The Gemara says that Achav received twenty-two years of kingship because he honored the Torah, which is written with twenty-two letters, and that his generosity and support of Torah scholars offset half of his accumulated guilt in the heavenly accounting. The same sugya describes the extraordinary severity of his idolatry. Rav Tzadok cites this precisely to show that authentic Torah honor and mitzvah-merit can coexist with grave corruption without either side being denied.1080Sanhedrin 103b — Achav’s eighty-five interpretations in Toras Kohanim: The Baraisa reports that Achav could teach Toras Kohanim in eighty-five ways. Torah knowledge therefore did not immunize him against idolatry or guarantee a share in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok does not present learning as a substitute for obedience. He uses the report to establish that the Torah acquired by a Jewish soul remains a real spiritual possession even when the person’s chosen conduct contradicts it.
אֲבָל בְּלָאו הָכִי כְּבָר עָמַד הָרַמְבַּ״ן בְּ״תוֹרַת הָאָדָם״ וּמוּבָא בְּבֵית יוֹסֵף [יוֹרֶה דֵּעָה סִימָן ש״מ] מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ לְחִיּוּב קְרִיעָה דְּדוֹמֶה לְסֵפֶר תּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּשְׂרַף
But without this, the Ramban in Toras HaAdam (cited in Beis Yosef, Yoreh De'ah 340) already noted regarding the obligation to rend garments upon one who is compared to a burned Torah scroll:
הָא בְּסֵפֶר תּוֹרָה לֹא אָמְרוּ אֶלָּא ״בִּזְרוֹעַ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּמוֹעֵד קָטָן כ״ו סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]
behold, regarding a Torah scroll they required rending only when burned by violent force (bi-zro'a), as they stated [in Moed Katan 26a]!
וְנִדְחַק דְּמָשָׁל בְּעָלְמָא אָמְרוּ, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And he was forced to answer that they spoke merely by way of metaphor, see there.1081Beis Yosef, Yoreh Deah §340: “And that which he [the Tur] wrote, ‘and Rashi explained that he could still have studied, etc.’ — thus the Ramban wrote in his name in the Sefer Toras HaAdam, and wrote upon it that the matter is difficult, to say that one tears over the future; and moreover, if by law even for a Torah scroll one does not tear except [when it is burned] ‘by force,’ as in the incident that occurred. But to me it appears that the soul in the body is like the [Divine] Names in the parchments, and it is [meant] only as a parable, to say that it is a great loss and a great dread, and a person is obligated to tear over it as though a Torah scroll were burned before him. Alternatively, one may say: just as one tears over it, so does one tear over those who fulfill its mitzvos — for when it [the scroll] is burned, the mitzvos of its writing are lost, and at the death of the doer, the mitzvos of action are lost; therefore one tears over every person of Israel, and even over a woman — end of his language. And in the Rashi commentary that we possess it is not written as the Ramban wrote in his name; for in Perek R’ Eliezer he wrote [regarding] a Torah scroll that was burned, that the one who sees is obligated to tear, [and that] the soul of a Jew that is taken resembles it, for there is no empty one among Israel who has no Torah and mitzvos; and in Perek Eilu Megalchin [25a] he wrote [regarding] a Torah scroll, that the Torah is called a ‘lamp,’ as it is written ‘for a mitzvah is a lamp and Torah is light,’ and the soul is called a ‘lamp,’ as it is written ‘the lamp of God is the soul of man’ — end of his language.”1082Mishlei 6:23; Mishlei 20:27; Rashi to Moed Katan 25a; Ramban, Toras HaAdam — Torah and the soul as lamps: The Torah is called light and the mitzvah a lamp, while the human soul is called “the lamp of Hashem.” Rashi and the authorities cited by the Beis Yosef use these parallel images to illuminate the comparison between a departing soul and a burned Torah scroll. Ramban adds that the soul within the body resembles the sacred Names written upon parchment. The analogy therefore concerns both the deeds and Torah embodied during life and the sacred soul that made such embodiment possible.
וַעֲדַיִין צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר: דְּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מַה דִּימָּה לְסֵפֶר תּוֹרָה וְלִלְמוֹד מִשָּׁם לִקְרוֹעַ
And it still requires explanation: why did the Talmud compare a deceased Jew to a Torah scroll at all in order to derive the obligation of rending garments from there?

וְגַם הָאַחֲרוֹנִים עָמְדוּ בָּזֶה, עַיֵּין בְּסֵפֶר תִּפְאֶרֶת לְמֹשֶׁה [סוֹף סִימָן ש״מ], וּבִשְׁבוּת יַעֲקֹב [חֵלֶק א׳ סִימָן פ״ה], וּתְשׁוּבַת חֲכַם צְבִי [סִימָן י״ז], וְלֹא הֶעֱלוּ בָּזֶה דָּבָר בָּרוּר רַק כְּדִבְרֵי הָרַמְבַּ״ן הַנַּ״ל:

And the Acharonim likewise addressed this, see Tiferes L'Moshe [end of §340], Shevus Ya'akov [Part I, §85], and the Responsa of Chacham Tzvi [§17], and they did not conclude in this matter anything clear beyond the aforementioned words of the Ramban.1083Chacham Tzvi §17 raises a difficulty with the comparison between the burning of a Torah scroll “by force” and the passing of a person of Israel, and explains that the burning of a Torah scroll “by force” means that one is unable to save it — and likewise, at the passing of a person of Israel, which one is unable to prevent, it is called “by force.”1084Takanat HaShavin 15:57–59 and 15:93–95 — Rav Tzadok’s synthesis and its limits: The preceding se’ifim distinguish mitzvos expressed through the body from Torah rooted in the inward soul; the present se’if applies both dimensions even to a sinner. Later in this siman, Rav Tzadok returns to Achan and to the principle that the name Israel is not severed, describing the holy root as sometimes imprisoned beneath thought, speech, and action but never annihilated. This is Rav Tzadok’s theological synthesis. It does not erase punishment, restitution, repentance, or the practical rulings of the laws of mourning.

items.h: The theme: Natural death as an act of force (bi-zro'a). Natural death is considered an act of violent coercion (bi-zro'a) executed by the prosecuting Satan, who is the evil inclination and the Angel of Death (Bava Batra 16a). Since an earthly court would not sentence this individual to death, his passing is reckoned an act of violence, obligating those present to rend their garments as over a Torah scroll burned by force. Conversely, those executed by a court on biblical grounds or heretics and defiant apostates whom society is commanded to execute (Avodah Zarah 26b) are not considered killed by unlawful force, and concerning them Scripture states, "when the wicked perish, there is song."

p: וּלְדַעְתִּי נִרְאֶה, דְּכָל מִיתַת אָדָם נֶחְשָׁב ״בִּזְרוֹעַ״ עַל יְדֵי קִטְרוּג הַמְקַטְרְגִים וּמַשְׂטִינִים
And in my opinion it appears that every death of a person is accounted an act of violent force (bi-zro'a) via the prosecution of the accusers and adversaries;
וְהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ ״לֹא יַחְפֹּץ בְּמוֹת הַמֵּת״ (יְחֶזְקֵאל י״ח:ל״ב), רַק מִצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין הַמְקַטְרֶגֶת עַל יְדֵי הַשָּׂטָן הָעוֹלֶה וּמְקַטְרֵג

for the Blessed Name "has no pleasure in the death of him that dies" (Yechezkel 18:32), and it occurs only from the perspective of the Attribute of Judgment prosecuting through the Satan who ascends and prosecutes;
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ הַמַּלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת, שֶׁבְּכֹחַ קִטְרוּגוֹ זֶה יוֹרֵד וְנוֹטֵל נְשָׁמָה

and he is himself the Angel of Death, who by the force of this accusation descends and takes the soul;1085Yechezkel 18:23, 18:32, and 33:11 — Divine desire, judgment, and repentance: The verses explicitly state that Hashem does not desire the death of the wicked or of the dying person, but that he turn from his way and live. Their plain meaning is a summons to teshuvah and life, not a denial that judgment may require punishment. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 7:6, accordingly describes teshuvah as bringing the penitent close to the Divine Presence. Rav Tzadok’s formulation distinguishes this revealed will for life from the prosecuting operation of middas ha-din; that distinction is his theological synthesis, while responsibility, judgment, and the obligation to repent remain fully intact.
וְהוּא עַצְמוֹ הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע וְהַמֵּסִית לְהַעֲבִירָהּ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳], וְהַכֹּל מִמֶּנּוּ

and he is himself the yetzer hara who incites to transgression as they stated [in Bava Batra 16a], and everything originates from him.1086Bava Basra 16a — Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death: The Gemara first teaches that the accuser descends and misleads, ascends and prosecutes, receives permission, and then takes the soul; Reish Lakish then states that Satan, the evil inclination, and the Angel of Death are one. The sugya describes three functions of one accusing force, not three independent powers. Rav Tzadok uses this Aggadah to explain the sequence of enticement, accusation, permission, and death. In his broader writings, Pri Tzadik, Shavuos 20:1, and Divrei Sofrim 33:3 connect Torah engraved in the heart with freedom from both the yetzer and the Angel of Death; that is Rav Tzadok’s later spiritual synthesis, not the Gemara’s plain legal meaning.
וְהַיְינוּ ״בִּזְרוֹעַ״, כָּל שֶׁאֵין מְחוּיָּב מִיתָה בְּבֵית דִּין וּבֵית דִּין שֶׁל מַטָּה הָיוּ פּוֹטְרִין אוֹתוֹ
And this is categorized as "by violent force" (bi-zro'a): whenever he is not liable to execution by a court and an earthly court would exempt him;
אַף דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נָתַן רְשׁוּת לַשָּׂטָן לְהַשְׂטִין וְלִהְיוֹת רְשָׁעִים תִּרְדֹּף רָעָה, וְהַכֹּל בְּמִשְׁפָּט וּבְדִין שֶׁל מַעְלָה

even though the Holy One, blessed be He, gave permission to the Satan to accuse so that evil pursues the wicked, and all is conducted with justice and divine judgment on high,1087Sanhedrin 46b; Mishnah Sanhedrin 6:6; Moed Katan 27a — mourning and those executed by beis din: The Mishnah rules that relatives of persons executed by beis din do not observe ordinary mourning, although they grieve inwardly, because aninus is a matter of the heart; the Gemara also discusses when formal mourning begins, at the closing of the grave. Rambam, Hilchos Avel 1:9, codifies that those executed by beis din are not mourned in the regular manner. Rav Tzadok draws a conceptual contrast between a death carried out through the Torah court’s sentence and an ordinary death that, from the standpoint of the earthly court, was not judicially imposed.1088Mishlei 11:10; Avodah Zarah 26b — severe rhetoric and its halachic-historical limits: “At the destruction of the wicked there is song” is a wisdom-text statement about the removal of entrenched evil, while Avodah Zarah records the ancient category of heretics whom one would lower and not raise. The existing note preserves Rav Tzadok’s citation. For practical halachah, later authorities sharply restrict application: Chazon Ish, Yoreh De’ah 2:16, explains that coercive measures presuppose an era of manifest providence and effective rebuke, whereas in an age of concealment they can deepen alienation and are replaced by efforts of love and return. Rav Tzadok’s discussion is therefore historical and theological, not a license for private violence or contemporary targeting.1089Rosh, Moed Katan 3:59, citing Maharam of Rothenburg; II Samuel 19:1 — appetite, defiance, and Avshalom: Maharam explains that the obligation to tear at the departure of a Jewish soul extends even to a sinner who acts from appetite or neglects a mitzvah because of difficulty, provided he is not a denier or one who sins specifically to provoke. He adduces David’s mourning for Avshalom, despite Avshalom’s grave transgressions and rebellion, because his motive was the desire to rule rather than ideological defiance. Rav Tzadok adopts that distinction to explain why moral failure does not automatically erase the person’s remaining Torah and mitzvos; the distinction does not excuse the misconduct or remove accountability.
מִכָּל מָקוֹם לְגַבֵּי דִּידַן, מֵאַחַר דִּכְפִי מִשְׁפְּטֵי הַתּוֹרָה הַמְּסוּרִים לָנוּ אֵין עָלָיו מִשְׁפַּט הַמָּוֶת, נֶחְשָׁב כִּבִזְרוֹעַ, וְעַל כֵּן דִּמּוּהוּ לְנִשְׂרַף בִּזְרוֹעַ

nevertheless relative to us, since according to the laws of the Torah committed into our hands he bears no sentence of death, it is accounted as if taken by violent force, and therefore they compared him to a Torah scroll burned by violence.
אֲבָל הֲרוּגֵי בֵּית דִּין דִּבְדִין קָטְלִינַן לְהוּ
However, those executed by a court, whom we execute lawfully according to the decree of the court;
וְאַף דְּשָׁב וּמִתְוַודֶּה אֵין בֵּית דִּין שֶׁלְּמַטָּה מוֹחֲלִין לוֹ, וְאָנוּ מְמִיתִין אוֹתוֹ בְּיָדֵינוּ עַל פִּי מִצְוַת הַתּוֹרָה, לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לְדַמּוֹתוֹ לִבִזְרוֹעַ

and even though he repented and confessed, the earthly court does not pardon him, and we execute him with our own hands pursuant to the commandment of the Torah, it is inappropriate to compare him to one destroyed by violent force.
וְהָכִי נַמֵּי מוּמָר לְהַכְעִיס וְעוֹבֵד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, שֶׁהֵם בִּכְלַל הַמִּינִין דְּמוֹרִידִין כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳]
And so too an apostate out of spite and an idolater, who fall into the category of heretics whom one casts down as they said [in Avodah Zarah 26b]:
כֵּיוָן דִּבְדִין לְהוֹרִידָן וּלְהֲמִיתָם בְּיָדַיִם, גַּם כְּשֶׁמֵּתוּ מֵעַצְמָן לֹא הָוֵי בִּזְרוֹעַ, דְּהָא דִּינָא הָכִי וְכוּלֵי עָלְמָא מְצֻוִּין לְבַעֲרוֹ

since it is lawful to cast them down and execute them directly, even when they die on their own it is not considered an act of violent force, for such was the law and everyone is commanded to eradicate them;1090Avodah Zarah 26b: [Heretics, informers, and the like] “are lowered [into a pit] and not raised up [moridin v’lo ma’alin]” — one may bring about their death and need not save them. R’ Tzadok invokes this as the din for one utterly sunk in the sin.
וּבִכְהַאי גַּוְונָא הוּא שֶׁאָמְרוּ דִּ״בְאַבְדָן רִנָּה״
and in such a case it was stated that "when they perish, there is song" (Mishlei 11:10);
וְאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם גַּם כֵּן תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת וְהֵם כְּסֵפֶר תּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּשְׂרַף, אֵינוֹ כְּנִשְׂרַף בִּזְרוֹעַ, כֵּן נִרְאֶה בְּעֵינַי בְּטַעַם זֶה:
and although they too possess Torah and mitzvos and resemble a burned Torah scroll, it is not like one burned by unlawful force; thus it appears in my eyes regarding this reason.

items.h: The theme: The fire of Gehinnom has no dominion over Torah scholars and Jewish sinners (Chagigah 27a). Rabbi Abbahu derived from the Golden Altar that the fire of Gehinnom has no power over Torah scholars whose entire bodies are fire; Reish Lakish derived from the Golden Altar that it has no power over the sinners of Israel who are full of mitzvos as a pomegranate. Tosafos (Chagigah 27a) reconciles this by stating that Reish Lakish excludes habitual bodily sinners (posh'ei Yisrael b'gufan). Yet Three Kings (such as Yerovam) were eminent scholars, and smoke ascended from Acher's grave to judge him (Chagigah 15b), proving that the fire of Gehinnom indeed affects scholars.

p: וּלְעוֹלָם גַּם כּוּלְּהוּ מְלֵאִים תּוֹרָה וּמִצְוֹת, כָּל שֶׁהֵם מִזֶּרַע יַעֲקֹב שֶׁמִּטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה דְּלֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח
And inherently they are all filled with Torah and mitzvos, so long as they stem from the seed of Yaakov whose bed is complete and from whom no outcast shall be expelled;
וּבְסוֹף חֲגִיגָה [כ״ז עַמּוּד א׳] אָמַר רַבִּי אֲבָהוּ אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים אֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֶטֶת בָּהֶן לְפִי שֶׁכָּל גּוּפָן אֵשׁ

and at the end of Chagigah [27a] Rabbi Abbahu said in the name of Rabbi Elazar: Torah scholars—the fire of Gehinnom has no dominion over them, because their entire body is fire (Yirmeyah 23:29);1091II Samuel 14:14; Sanhedrin 44a — “the banished one is not banished” and enduring Jewish identity: The verse states that God devises means so that a banished person not remain banished from Him. In its narrative context, the wise woman of Tekoa pleads for Avshalom’s return; Chazal and later Jewish thought read the phrase more broadly as expressing the possibility of ultimate return. Sanhedrin 44a states, regarding Achan, “Israel—even though he has sinned, he remains Israel.” Neither source denies judgment or the need for teshuvah. Rav Tzadok’s claim that the seed of Yaakov remains inwardly connected to Torah and mitzvos is his covenantal synthesis: sin can conceal and damage that bond, but does not convert moral failure into a new biological or ethnic essence.

וְאַחַר כָּךְ אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: אֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֶטֶת בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, קַל וָחֹמֶר מִמִּזְבַּח הַזָּהָב דְּעָלָיו כְּעוֹבִי דִּינָר זָהָב וְכוּלֵיהּ, פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דִּמְלֵאִים מִצְוֹת כְּרִמּוֹן וְכוּלֵיהּ

and afterward Reish Lakish stated: the fire of Gehinnom has no dominion over the sinners of Israel, by an a fortiori argument from the Golden Altar upon which was gold the thickness of a gold dinar, etc., how much more so the sinners of Israel who are as full of mitzvos as a pomegranate, etc.;1092Chagigah 27a; Eruvin 19a; Resisei Layla 52:8; Pri Tzadik, Shoftim 11:1 — fire, the golden altar, and the pomegranate: Chagigah presents two separate kal va-chomer teachings: Torah scholars are compared to fire because “My word is like fire,” while the sinners of Israel are compared to the gold plating of the altar because even the “empty” among Israel are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate. These are Aggadic images of the enduring effect of Torah and mitzvah, not a scientific description of fire or an exemption from accountability. Eruvin 19a supplies the broader context of Avraham raising his descendants from Gehinnom, subject to the sugya’s stated exceptions. Rav Tzadok develops the pomegranate image in Resisei Layla and Pri Tzadik: concrete mitzvos remain stored within a Jew and can become the point from which return begins; this is his interpretive synthesis rather than the plain meaning of the kal va-chomer.1093Chagigah 27a: “R’ Abahu said in the name of R’ Elazar: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over Torah scholars — [by] a kal va-chomer from the salamander: if a salamander, which is an offspring of fire, [such that] one who smears its blood [on himself], the fire has no power over him — Torah scholars, whose whole body is fire, as it is written ‘is not My word like fire, says Hashem,’ all the more so. Reish Lakish said: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel — [by] a kal va-chomer from the golden altar: if the golden altar, upon which there is only [gold] the thickness of a golden dinar, [and yet] for many years the fire had no power over it — the sinners of Israel, who are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate, as it is written ‘like a slice of pomegranate is your temple [rakasech]’ — read not ‘rakasech’ but ‘the empty ones [reikanin] among you’ — all the more so.” Tosafos: “‘The fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel, etc.’ — it appears to me that [this is] not [regarding] ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ for we say in Rosh Hashanah (17a) [that regarding] ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed; rather, it speaks of some [partial] sinners, and because Avraham raises them all [from Gehinnom] except one who has relations with a gentile-woman, whose foreskin is drawn over him, as it says at the start of Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a). And that which we say at the end of HaZahav (Bava Metzia 58b), ‘all descend and ascend except three’ — that is not speaking of Gehinnom, but of another place to be judged; and even the one judged, after twelve months they ascend, and are judged no more than a full year.”
וְאָמְרוּ בָּזֶה לְשׁוֹן ״אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ״, וְלֹא ״רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר״ כְּמִי שֶׁבָּא לַחֲלוֹק, מַשְׁמַע דְּמָר אָמַר חֲדָא וּמָר אָמַר חֲדָא וְלָא פְּלִיגֵי

and they phrased this as "Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said," and not "Reish Lakish says" as one who comes to dispute, implying that one master stated one teaching and the other master stated another teaching, and they do not dispute;
וְזֶה תֵּימַהּ לִכְאוֹרָה: דְּאִם גַּם בְּכָל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל אֵין שׁוֹלֵט, מַה צֹּרֶךְ לְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר לוֹמַר רַק בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם וּמִפְּנֵי שֶׁגּוּפָן אֵשׁ

and this is astonishing superficially: for if the fire has no dominion even over all the sinners of Israel, what need was there for Rabbi Elazar to state it specifically regarding a Torah scholar because his body is fire?
וְתוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם כָּתְבוּ, דְּלָאו אַפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן קָאָמַר, דַּעֲלֵיהֶם אָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה י״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: ״גֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה וְהֵם אֵינָן כָּלִין״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And Tosafos there wrote that Reish Lakish did not speak of the sinners of Israel who sin with their bodies (posh'ei Yisrael b'gufan), regarding whom they said [in Rosh Hashanah 17a]: "Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed," see there;
וּלְפִי דִּבְרֵיהֶם יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּבְתַלְמִיד חָכָם אֲפִילּוּ הֵם פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן גַּם כֵּן אֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט

and according to their words, one can say that for a Torah scholar, even if he belongs to the sinners of Israel with their bodies, the fire of Gehinnom likewise has no dominion;1094Rosh Hashanah 17a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 3:5–6 — categories of judgment and the meaning of “sinners with their bodies”: Rosh Hashanah distinguishes several categories: ordinary intermediate people, “sinners of Israel with their bodies,” heretics and related deniers, and those who cause the public to sin. The severe phrase that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not consumed belongs to specified categories in that Aggadic account; it is not a blanket characterization of every sinner. Rambam codifies the relevant distinctions while emphasizing that repentance before death changes a person’s standing. Rav Tzadok is testing how Tosafos’ limitation in Chagigah fits the wider sugya; he is not asserting that Torah scholarship nullifies punishment irrespective of deliberate rebellion.1095Chagigah 27a: “R’ Abahu said in the name of R’ Elazar: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over Torah scholars — [by] a kal va-chomer from the salamander: if a salamander, which is an offspring of fire, [such that] one who smears its blood [on himself], the fire has no power over him — Torah scholars, whose whole body is fire, as it is written ‘is not My word like fire, says Hashem,’ all the more so. Reish Lakish said: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel — [by] a kal va-chomer from the golden altar: if the golden altar, upon which there is only [gold] the thickness of a golden dinar, [and yet] for many years the fire had no power over it — the sinners of Israel, who are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate, as it is written ‘like a slice of pomegranate is your temple [rakasech]’ — read not ‘rakasech’ but ‘the empty ones [reikanin] among you’ — all the more so.” Tosafos: “‘The fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel, etc.’ — it appears to me that [this is] not [regarding] ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ for we say in Rosh Hashanah (17a) [that regarding] ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed; rather, it speaks of some [partial] sinners, and because Avraham raises them all [from Gehinnom] except one who has relations with a gentile-woman, whose foreskin is drawn over him, as it says at the start of Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a). And that which we say at the end of HaZahav (Bava Metzia 58b), ‘all descend and ascend except three’ — that is not speaking of Gehinnom, but of another place to be judged; and even the one judged, after twelve months they ascend, and are judged no more than a full year.”
אֲבָל [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם] אִיתָא הָא דְּ״גֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה״ עַל מַחֲטִיאֵי הָרַבִּים כְּיָרָבְעָם וַחֲבֵירָיו
but [in Rosh Hashanah there] that statement of "Gehinnom is consumed" is stated regarding those who cause the multitude to sin, like Jeroboam and his companions;

וּבְסַנְהֶדְרִין [ק״ג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] אַהָא דְּג׳ מְלָכִים שֶׁהֵן יָרָבְעָם וַחֲבֵירָיו, אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר: ״נִפְתַּח בְּחַבְרִין״, פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י: שֶׁהָיוּ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים כְּמוֹתֵינוּ, וְאַחַר כָּךְ בְּרַבְרְבָתָא

and in Sanhedrin [103b] on the Three Kings who are Jeroboam and his companions, Rabbi Elazar said: "Let us open with our colleague"—Rashi explaining: who was a Torah scholar like us—and afterward with the kings;
הֲרֵי דְּגַם עַל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם אָמְרוּ כֵּן

showing that they stated this regarding a Torah scholar as well!1096Sanhedrin 102b–103b with Rashi — Rav Ashi’s “colleagues” and the three kings: The Mishnah lists Yaravam, Achav, and Menashe among the kings who have no share in the World to Come. When Rav Ashi announced that the next lesson would begin with “our colleagues,” Rashi explains that these kings were learned scholars like the sages themselves. The continuation, in which Menashe appears to Rav Ashi and demonstrates superior halachic knowledge, rebukes scholarly condescension while leaving the kings’ grave sins fully condemned. Rav Tzadok uses Rashi’s wording to show that great Torah knowledge and catastrophic wrongdoing can coexist; Torah merit therefore cannot be reduced to a claim that the scholar never enters judgment.
וּמִיהוּ אֶפְשָׁר לוֹמַר, דְּמֵהָא דְּ״הֵם אֵינָן כָּלִין״ אֵין קוּשְׁיָא
However, one can say that from the statement "they are not consumed" there is no difficulty:
דְּהָא דְּ״אֵין שׁוֹלֵט״, וְלֹא אָמְרוּ ״דְּאֵין נִכְנָסִים כְּלָל״, מְבוֹאָר דְּנִכְנָסִים רַק שֶׁהָאוּר אֵין שׁוֹלֵט
for that phrase "has no dominion," rather than stating "they do not enter at all," makes it clear that they enter, only that the fire does not dominate them;
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ [בִּמְנָחוֹת ק׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁגַּם לְמֶלֶךְ שֶׁהוּא תַּלְמִיד חָכָם הוּכַן
and so they stated [in Menachos 100a] that Topheth was prepared even for a king who is a Torah scholar;
וְאִם כֵּן עַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּאֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר שֶׁאֵין שׁוֹלֵט כְּלָל שֶׁאֵין מַרְגִּישׁ כְּוִיַּית הָאֵשׁ, דְּאִם כֵּן לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ נִכְנָסִין וְלָמָּה הוּכַן לוֹ
and if so, perforce it does not mean that the fire has no effect at all such that he feels no burning, for if so, for what purpose do they enter and why was it prepared for him?
וְגַם אָמְרוּ [חֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד ב׳] בְּ״אַחֵר״, דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר הֶעֱלָה עָשָׁן מִקִּבְרוֹ לְדַיָּינֵיהּ, הֲרֵי דְּשָׁלַט בּוֹ הָאֵשׁ אַף שֶׁהָיָה תַּלְמִיד חָכָם

And they also related [in Chagigah 15b] regarding Acher, that Rabbi Meir caused smoke to ascend from his grave to judge him, showing that the fire held dominion over him even though he was a Torah scholar;
וּמֵעִיקָּרָא שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״דְּלָא לְדַיָּינֵיהּ״ בִּשְׁבִיל הַתּוֹרָה, הַיְינוּ שֶׁלֹּא לְהַכְנִיסוֹ כְּלָל בְּגֵיהִנָּם
and initially when the heavenly court ruled not to judge him on account of his Torah, that meant not to bring him into Gehinnom at all,
דְּמֵאַחַר שֶׁדָּנוּהוּ שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לוֹ עוֹלָם הַבָּא, נָתְנוּ לוֹ שְׂכַר תּוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַפֵּחַ שֶׁלֹּא יִדּוֹן וְיִצְטַעֵר כְּלָל בְּצַעַר גֵּיהִנָּם

for since they judged that he would have no share in the World to Come, they gave him the reward of his Torah—which the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold—that he should not be judged or suffer in the agony of Gehinnom;
וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר אָמַר לְדוּנּוֹ וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה לוֹ עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְעַל כָּל פָּנִים חֲזֵינַן דְּשָׁלַט אַף שֶׁכָּל גּוּפוֹ אֵשׁ:
while Rabbi Meir prayed that he be judged so that he might ultimately enter the World to Come; yet in any event we see that the fire dominated him even though his entire body was fire!

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the Maharsha's view on Acher. The Maharsha (Chagigah 15b) resolved the question of why fire dominated Acher by explaining that he was worse than an ordinary scholar because "he knew his Master and intended to rebel." R' Tzadok refutes this distinction: the Talmudic statement that the fire of Gehinnom has no power over a scholar is unqualified (stam), based on the verse "Is not My word like fire?" (Yirmeyah 23:29), which counterbalances all sins. Acher was filled with Torah—Rabbi Meir ate the fruit of his mouth and discarded his shell. Although Acher initially spoke of "two powers" (shtei rashuyos), his subsequent failure to repent was not spiteful (l'hakh'is), but despair caused by the Heavenly Voice declaring "Return, backsliding children, except for Acher," causing him to pursue worldly pleasures out of appetite (l'tei'avon).

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א שָׁם הִרְגִּישׁ בָּהָא, וְנִדְחַק דְּ״אַחֵר״ גָּרַע, דְּיָדַע וְנִתְכַּוֵּין לִמְרוֹד, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And then I saw in the Maharsha there that he was sensitive to this difficulty, and was forced to answer that Acher was worse because he knew his Master and intended to rebel, see there;1097Chagigah 15b: it is related that in heaven they did not wish to judge “Acher” — for to bring him into Gan Eden was impossible, since he had sinned; and to punish [him] in Gehinnom [was also impossible, since he had engaged in Torah].
וְלָשׁוֹן שֶׁאָמְרוּ כָּאן בִּסְתָם ״דְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם אֵין שׁוֹלֵט״, מַשְׁמַע בְּכָל עִנְיָן שֶׁיֶּחֱטָא
yet the phrasing stated here categorically that the fire has no dominion over a Torah scholar implies in whatever manner he may sin;
וְגַם לְפִי הַטַּעַם מִשּׁוּם ״הֲלוֹא כֹה דְבָרִי כָּאֵשׁ״ (יִרְמְיָה כ״ג:כ״ט), מַשְׁמַע גַּם כֵּן נֶגֶד כָּל חֲטָאִים כֵּיוָן דְּאֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט
and likewise according to the rationale based on "Is not My word like fire?" (Yirmeyah 23:29), it implies against all sins, since the fire of Gehinnom cannot dominate.
וַהֲלֹא גַּם ״אַחֵר״ הָיָה מָלֵא תּוֹרָה, דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר גְּמַר מִפּוּמֵיהּ וְתוֹכוֹ אָכַל
And was not Acher likewise filled with Torah, seeing that Rabbi Meir learned from his mouth and ate his inner fruit (Chagigah 15b)?
וְגַם בַּגְּמָרָא [שָׁם ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳] אִיתָא, דְּרַק מִשּׁוּם הַכְּרוּז דְּ״חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״ אָמַר: דְּלִיתְהֲנֵי מֵהַאי עָלְמָא
And in the Gemara [ibid. 15a] it is explicitly stated that solely because of the proclamation "except for Acher" did he say: "Let me at least enjoy this world";
וְעַל כֵּן מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ דְּנִתְכַּוֵּין לִמְרוֹד, דְּהַיְינוּ לְהַכְעִיס, שֶׁהוּא בִּכְלַל מִינִין [דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם] דְּגֵיהִנָּם כָּלָה — זֶה הָיָה בַּתְּחִלָּה שֶׁאָמַר ״ב׳ רְשֻׁיּוֹת״

therefore what they said—that he intended to rebel, meaning to spite Heaven, which falls under the category of heretics (Rosh Hashanah 17a) where Gehinnom is consumed—that was only at the beginning when he uttered the heresy of "two independent powers";
וְאַחַר כָּךְ מַה שֶּׁלֹּא שָׁב הָיָה רַק עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁלֹּא יוֹעִיל כִּדְאִיתָא שָׁם, וּלְתֵיאָבוֹן עָבֵיד וְלֹא הָיָה לְהַכְעִיס:

but subsequently, his failure to repent was solely due to the Heavenly Voice whereby he assumed that repentance would not avail, as stated there, so that he transgressed out of appetite (l'tei'avon) and not out of spite (l'hakh'is).1098Chagigah 15a–b; Yerushalmi Chagigah 2:1; Maharsha; Tzidkas HaTzadik 39; Resisei Layla 27:1 — Acher, the bas kol, and obstructed return: The Bavli records that Elisha ben Avuyah heard the heavenly proclamation “Return, wayward children—except Acher,” concluded that repentance would not be accepted, and pursued this-worldly pleasure; it also records R’ Meir’s effort that he be judged and ultimately brought to the World to Come. The Yerushalmi preserves additional encounters in which R’ Meir continues to call him back. Maharsha distinguishes Acher’s initial knowing rebellion from his later despair-driven conduct. Rav Tzadok repeatedly treats Acher as the paradigm of Torah severed from its living root: Tzidkas HaTzadik warns against Torah possessed externally while the heart resists its discipline, and Resisei Layla analyzes “cutting the plantings” as separation from unity. This explains Rav Tzadok’s distinction between initial defiance and later appetite; it does not make the sins involuntary or remove responsibility.

items.h: The theme: The definition of the fire's "dominion" (ein sholetet). "Dominion" means total destruction and annihilation (l'khaloto). The fire of Gehinnom inflicts intense pain upon a Torah scholar to purge his sins, but it cannot consume his soul into ashes. In Rosh Hashanah 17a, the sinners of Israel who sin with their bodies (posh'ei Yisrael b'gufan) are burned after twelve months, their bodies consumed and their ashes scattered under the feet of the righteous; hence the fire does hold destroying dominion over them. Why then was Rabbi Elazar’s teaching regarding scholars necessary? The Talmud defines a bodily sinner as "a skull that does not put on tefillin," but Tosafos notes that a scholar engrossed in Torah is exempt from tefillin, making it impossible for a true scholar to ever be categorized as a bodily sinner.

p: אֲבָל לְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט דִּלְשׁוֹן ״אֵין שׁוֹלֵט״ הַיְינוּ לְכַלּוֹתוֹ, שֶׁזֶּהוּ שְׁלִיטַת הָאוּר הַשּׂוֹרֵף וּמְכַלֶּה הַכֹּל
But in my opinion the plain meaning of "has no dominion" is to consume him entirely, for that is the absolute dominion of fire that burns and reduces everything to ash;
וּלְתַלְמִיד חָכָם אֵין מְכַלֶּה, אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם מַכְאִיב לוֹ וּמְקַבֵּל הַדִּין מִיִּסּוּרֵי הַכְּוִיּוֹת דְּאוּר
whereas regarding a Torah scholar it does not consume him, though it certainly pains him and he receives judgment through the agony of burns;
וְאִם כֵּן הֲרֵי גַּם [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה] אַיָּרָבְעָם שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּ״הֵם אֵינָן כָּלִין״, אַף דְּהוּא לְרָעָתָם, דְּמַשְׁמַע דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר דְּאִשָּׁם לֹא תִכְבֶּה לְעוֹלָם

and if so, behold even in Rosh Hashanah regarding Jeroboam where they said "they are not consumed," although this is to their detriment—implying that their fire will never be quenched (Yeshayah 66:24);1099Chagigah 27a — “the fire of Gehinnom has no power over Torah scholars”: The Gemara derives this Aggadic teaching by a kal va-chomer from the salamander: if one who anoints himself with the product of fire is protected from fire, all the more so Torah scholars, whose entire bodies are fire through the words of Torah. The sugya does not state that a scholar can never experience judgment or pain. Rav Tzadok therefore reads “has no power” narrowly as inability to consume and annihilate, while allowing corrective suffering. This is his interpretive resolution of the sugya’s wording, not an explicit distinction stated by the Gemara itself.
גַּם אַחַר שֶׁגֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה לִשְׁאָרֵי רִשְׁעֵי עוֹלָם, בָּהֶם אֵשׁ הַגֵּיהִנָּם נֶאֱחָז בְּגוּפָן וְאֵין כָּבָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם כֵּיוָן דְּהֵם אֵין כָּלִין הֲרֵי אֵין הָאוֹר שׁוֹלֵט לְכַלּוֹתָם

so that even after Gehinnom ceases for other wicked of the world, in them the fire of Gehinnom clings to their body and is not quenched, nevertheless since they are not consumed, the fire does not dominate them to obliterate them.
וְקוּשְׁיַת הַתּוֹסָפוֹת מִפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן, וּבָזֶה הַקּוּשְׁיָא שַׁפִּיר
And regarding the difficulty of Tosafos from the sinners of Israel with their bodies: on this point the question is well founded;
דִּבְאֶמֶת בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם הָא דְּ״גֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״ עַל הַמִּינִין וַחֲבֵירֵיהֶם אָמְרוּ
for in truth in Rosh Hashanah there, that statement that "Gehinnom is consumed, etc." was stated regarding heretics and their companions;
אֲבָל הָא דְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן, בְּרֵישָׁא שָׁם אָמְרוּ דִּלְאַחַר י״ב חֹדֶשׁ גּוּפָן כָּלָה וְנִשְׁמָתָן נִשְׂרֶפֶת וְרוּחַ מְפַזַּרְתָּן תַּחַת רַגְלֵי צַדִּיקִים

but regarding the sinners of Israel with their bodies, in the opening clause there they stated that after twelve months their body is consumed, their soul is burned, and a wind scatters them beneath the feet of the righteous;1100Rosh Hashanah 17a — separate classes of punishment must not be conflated: The sugya first describes ordinary intermediate people, then “sinners of Israel with their bodies,” whose punishment is stated as twelve months followed by consumption of body and burning of soul, and separately lists minim, informers, deniers, and those who caused the public to sin, concerning whom it says that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not consumed. Rav Tzadok’s correction depends on keeping these clauses distinct. The severe descriptions are Aggadic accounts of posthumous judgment; they do not function as medical claims, and they do not remove the efficacy of sincere repentance before death.
וּבָזֶה הַקּוּשְׁיָא שַׁפִּיר דַּהֲרֵי שׁוֹלֵט שֶׁנִּשְׂרָף וְנַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר
and in this the question is well placed, for behold the fire dominates them so that they are burned and turned to ash!
וּמַה שֶּׁסִּיְּימוּ ״מִגֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה״ עַל כֵּן טָעוּת סוֹפֵר הוּא, דַּהֲרֵי לֹא אָמְרוּ שָׁם זֶה אַפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן כְּלָל

And that Tosafos concluded citing "from Gehinnom is consumed," perforce that is a scribal error, for they did not state that phrase regarding the sinners of Israel with their bodies at all.1101Tosafos, Chagigah 27a, s.v. talmidei chachamim — the citation problem: Tosafos asks how the statement that fire has no power over Torah scholars accords with the punishment of “sinners of Israel with their bodies.” Rav Tzadok observes that a concluding reference to “Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed” belongs in Rosh Hashanah to a different and more severe group, not to the immediately cited category. He therefore proposes a scribal error. This is a textual-critical judgment by Rav Tzadok based on the structure of Rosh Hashanah 17a; it should not be presented as an established manuscript reading unless corroborated independently.
וּלְפִי זֶה עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ לוֹמַר הָא דְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם אִיצְטְרִיךְ לְפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן
And according to this, one could still suggest that the teaching regarding a Torah scholar was necessary for a scholar who is a sinner of Israel with his body;
אַךְ בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם אָמְרוּ: ״פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן מַאי נִיהוּ? קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין״
yet in Rosh Hashanah there they asked: "Who are the sinners of Israel with their bodies? A skull that does not put on tefillin";
וּבְתוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם כָּתְבוּ דְּהָעוֹסֵק בַּתּוֹרָה פָּטוּר מִתְּפִלִּין, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and in Tosafos there they wrote that one who is actively engrossed in Torah is exempt from tefillin, see there;
אִם כֵּן לָא מַשְׁכַּחַתְּ לַהּ כְּלָל תַּלְמִיד חָכָם פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן, כֵּיוָן דִּגְבֵיהּ לֵיכָּא חֵטְא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין:
if so, you cannot find at all a Torah scholar who is categorized among the sinners of Israel with their bodies, since for him the sin of not wearing tefillin does not exist!

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ס״ה–ס״ח [1102: Rosh Hashanah 17a, Tosafos s.v. karkafta; Mechilta — tefillin, Torah study, and contempt for a mitzvah: Rav identifies “sinners of Israel with their bodies” with a skull that does not don tefillin. Tosafos cites the Mechilta that one occupied in Torah is exempt from tefillin, then records Rabbeinu Tam’s narrower explanation: the severe category concerns one for whom the mitzvah itself is contemptible, whereas fear of failing the requirement of a clean body does not place a person in that class. Rav Tzadok initially uses the Torah-study exemption to question whether the category can apply to a Torah scholar at all. The discussion distinguishes legal exemption, weakness or apprehension, and deliberate degradation of a mitzvah; it does not equate every lapse in tefillin with ideological rebellion.] [1103: Rosh Hashanah 17a: “‘The sinners of Israel with their bodies’ (who descend to Gehinnom and are judged there twelve months, and after twelve months their body is consumed and their soul is burned and a wind scatters them beneath the soles of the feet of the righteous) — what are they? Rav said: the skull [karkafta] that does not don tefillin.” Tosafos: “‘The skull that does not don tefillin’ — if he engages in Torah, he is like one who dons tefillin, for it says in the Mechilta: one who engages in Torah is exempt from tefillin. And Rabbeinu Tam explains that here [it is] when the mitzvah is despised upon him, that the straps of tefillin on his head are contemptible to him; but if he fears to don [them] because we require a clean body, like Elisha ‘the man of wings’ [baal kenafayim] — this certainly does not have upon him the law of ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies.’ And all these [teachings] of our sugya are [regarding] when he did not repent; but [if] he repented, we say in Yoma (86a) that teshuvah suspends and death scours.”]

The theme: The definition of "sinners of Israel with their bodies" (posh'ei Yisrael b'gufan). In Rosh Hashanah 17a, the Talmud defines this as "a skull that does not put on tefillin." The Rama MiFano in Asarah Ma'amaros suggested that tefillin is merely an example, applying equally to anyone who despises any biblical commandment. R' Tzadok rejects this: "with their bodies" denotes a mitzvah performed directly upon the physical body itself, unlike tzitzis which is on the garment, or circumcision where refraining is driven by dread of physical pain rather than disdain. Tefillin involves neither monetary loss nor pain; thus, deliberately avoiding it reveals contempt for a bodily mitzvah. For gentiles, "sinning with their bodies" means sexual transgression (aveirah), because their essential root is embedded in evil, whereas for a Jew, lust stems merely from the external "yeast in the dough."

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר גַּם עַל זֶה, לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַב בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [מַאֲמַר מְקוֹר דִּין חֵלֶק ה׳ פֶּרֶק ג׳], דְּ״קַרְקַפְתָּא דְּלָא מַנַּח תְּפִלִּין״ פֵּירוּשׁ בְּעָלְמָא וְלָאו דַּוְוקָא, רַק הוּא הַדִּין אִם מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת בְּזוּיָה עָלָיו, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

And one can also suggest regarding this, according to what was written in Asarah Ma'amaros [Mekor Din 5:3], that "a skull that does not put on tefillin" is merely an illustrative example and not literal, the same law applying if any other mitzvah is held in contempt by him, see there at length;
אַךְ לְדַעְתִּי לֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן, דְּמַאי שְׁנָא דְּנָקַט ״תְּפִלִּין״ מִכָּל מִצְוֹת

but in my opinion it does not imply thus, for why did it specify tefillin out of all commandments?1104Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chakor Din V:3 — whether tefillin is an example or the defining case: R. Menachem Azariah of Fano interprets Rav’s phrase ‘a skull that does not don tefillin’ as the paradigm of a person who treats a mitzvah with contempt, extending the category to contempt for another commandment. Rav Tzadok records that approach and then argues from the Gemara’s specific wording that tefillin is not merely an interchangeable example. The broader rule belongs to the Asarah Maamaros; Rav Tzadok’s narrower reading is his own textual inference from b’gufan and from Rav’s selection of tefillin.
וְנִרְאֶה מִשּׁוּם דִּלְשׁוֹן ״בְּגוּפָן״ הַיְינוּ בְּמִצְוָה שֶׁבַּגּוּף, וְאֵין מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת בְּגוּפוֹ מַמָּשׁ, דְּצִיצִית הוּא בְּבִגְדוֹ

And it appears that it is because the phrase "with their bodies" denotes a commandment performed directly upon the body, and there is no other mitzvah performed upon the physical body itself, for tzitzis is worn upon one's garment;
אַף דְּאִיכָּא מִילָה, אִם לֹא מָהֲלוּהוּ בְּקַטְנוּתוֹ אָבִיו וּבֵית דִּין וְעַתָּה אֵין רוֹצֶה לָמוּל אֶת עַצְמוֹ
and although there is circumcision, where his father and the court did not circumcise him in his youth and now he refuses to circumcise himself;
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר כֵּיוָן דְּזוֹ צַעֲרָא דְּגוּפָא, מַה שֶּׁאֵין רוֹצֶה הוּא לְפִי שֶׁאֵין רוֹצֶה לַחְבּוֹל בְּעַצְמוֹ, וְלֹא מִשּׁוּם שֶׁמִּצְוֹת בְּזוּיוֹת
one can say that since this involves bodily pain, his refusal is because he does not wish to inflict injury upon himself, and not because the commandments are despised;
עַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ רַק ״תְּפִלִּין״, דִּכְשֶׁיֶּשְׁנָם לְפָנָיו וְאֵין מַנִּיחַ הוּא מִשּׁוּם דִּבְזוּיוֹת, כֵּיוָן דְּאֵין בָּזֶה לוֹ הֶפְסֵד מָמוֹן וְלֹא צַעַר בַּגּוּף וְלֹא טִרְחָא כָּל כָּךְ

therefore they stated specifically "tefillin," for when they are present before him and he refuses to don them, it is purely because they are held in contempt, since it entails neither monetary loss, nor physical pain, nor significant exertion.1105Milah, bodily pain, and moral classification — Kiddushin 29a; Rambam, Hilchos Milah 1:2: After a father and beis din fail to circumcise a child, the obligation ultimately rests upon the adult himself. Rav Tzadok nevertheless distinguishes refusal rooted in fear of bodily injury from contempt for the mitzvah. He is not excusing the continuing obligation or removing accountability; he is classifying motive for purposes of the Aggadic category under discussion. This anticipates his broader method throughout Takanas HaShavin: involuntary pressure, appetite, weakness, and defiant disparagement are morally and spiritually distinct even when the external omission may look similar.1106Tefillin as an embodied covenantal sign — Devarim 6:8; Menachos 36b; Shabbos 49a: The Torah commands that the words be bound ‘as a sign upon your hand’ and placed ‘between your eyes,’ making tefillin a mitzvah worn directly on the body. Chazal require a clean body for tefillin and discuss their sanctity and constant awareness. These sources explain why failure may arise from practical or halachic concern rather than contempt. Rav Tzadok’s argument therefore focuses on a person for whom tefillin are available and who refuses them without financial loss, bodily pain, or substantial burden; only then does he infer degradation of the mitzvah.
וּמִמַּה שֶּׁאָמַר ״בְּגוּפָן״ מַשְׁמַע דְּדַוְוקָא הוּא, שֶׁמִּצְוָה שֶׁבַּגּוּף בְּזוּיָה עָלָיו וְלֹא מִצְוָה אַחֶרֶת, וּדְלֹא כְּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״
And from the phrasing "with their bodies," it implies that it is precise: that a mitzvah performed on the body is held in contempt by him and not any other mitzvah, unlike Asarah Ma'amaros;
וְכֵן בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁאָמְרוּ ״בַּעֲבֵירָה״, וְלֹא אָמְרוּ בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה וּשְׁפִיכַת דָּמִים, הַיְינוּ גַּם כֵּן מִשּׁוּם דְּבָעֵינַן עֲבֵירָה שֶׁבַּגּוּף דַּוְוקָא

and likewise regarding the nations of the world where they defined their bodily sin as sexual transgression (aveirah), and did not say idolatry and bloodshed, this is likewise because a sin performed specifically with the body is required.1107Rosh Hashanah 17a — ‘sinners of Israel with their bodies’: The Bavli identifies this class as ‘a skull that did not don tefillin,’ while the corresponding class among the nations is described as sin through sexual transgression. The sugya itself does not explain why these two cases are parallel. Rav Tzadok’s se’if supplies an interpretive structure: for Israel, contempt for a mitzvah resting directly upon the body reveals rebellion at the bodily covenantal level; for the nations, bodily appetite itself defines the category. This is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis of the two clauses, not the Gemara’s explicit explanation.

וּמַה שֶּׁלֹּא אָמְרוּ גַּם זֶה בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל, נִדְחַק בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם בְּרֵישׁ הַפֶּרֶק וּבְסוֹפוֹ], דְּמִשּׁוּם דְּלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ זֶה שֶׁיֵּעָשֶׂה עַל יְדֵי דְּזִלְזוּלָהּ בְּעֵינָיו בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אֶלָּא בַּגּוֹיִם, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And as for why they did not define this likewise for Israel, the Asarah Ma'amaros was hard-pressed to explain [ibid.], suggesting that committing sexual sin out of disdain for the prohibition does not occur in Israel but only among gentiles, see there;
וְאֵין בּוֹ טַעַם, וּלְדַעְתִּי פָּשׁוּט דַּעֲבֵירָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהּ תַּאֲוָה סְתָמָא לְתֵיאָבוֹן, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמִילָה
yet there is no substance to this, and in my opinion it is simple: a sin involving physical lust is presumed to be driven by appetite (l'tei'avon), just as I wrote regarding circumcision;
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא לָא הָוֵי ״פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן״ אִם לֹא דֶּרֶךְ זִלְזוּל וּבִזּוּי
and in an Israelite such a case is not categorized as "sinners of Israel with their bodies" unless performed by way of defiance and contempt;
דְּמַה שֶּׁעוֹשֶׂה מִצַּד תַּאֲוָה הוּא מִצַּד יֵצֶר הַבּוֹעֵר וְאֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְעֶצֶם גּוּפוֹ

for what he does out of lust stems from the burning inclination and has no intrinsic attachment to the essence of his body;1108Rav Tzadok on appetite, bodily desire, and the essential self — Resisei Layla 5; Takanas HaShavin, Siman 15, Se’ifim 59–63: In Resisei Layla 5 Rav Tzadok describes the darkness of this world as the pull of bodily desire and associates Gehinnom’s corrective judgment with immersion in appetite. Here, however, he distinguishes an Israelite’s act under the ‘burning inclination’ from the essence of the person’s body: desire can overpower choice without becoming the deepest covenantal identity. Contemptuous rejection is graver because it expresses identification with the rebellion. This does not permit wrongdoing or erase responsibility; it explains why Rav Tzadok differentiates chosen disparagement from an act committed under appetite, while still requiring repentance and rectification.

אֲבָל בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם גַּם לְתֵיאָבוֹן הוּא בִּכְלַל פּוֹשְׁעִים בְּגוּפָן, דְּשָׁרְשָׁן בָּרָע וְלֹא מִצַּד הַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה רַק מִצַּד הָעִיסָה עַצְמָהּ, וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ זֶה רַק בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם:

whereas among the nations of the world, even sinning out of appetite is included among bodily sinners, for their very root is in evil, not stemming merely from the "yeast in the dough" but from the substance of the dough itself, wherefore they stated this solely regarding the nations of the world.

items.h: The theme: Reconciling the protection of mitzvos with the judgment of bodily sinners. In Asarah Ma'amaros, disdaining even a single divine statute categorizes one as a bodily sinner. If Reish Lakish teaches that the fire of Gehinnom has no dominion over Jewish sinners because they are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate, does this protection apply to bodily sinners whose transgressions outweigh their merits (rubo avonos)? In Sotah 21a, "sin extinguishes a mitzvah" (aveirah mekhabah mitzvah) means that sin weakens the protective shield against future incitement of the yetzer hara, but it does not extinguish the mitzvah's power to shield from divine retribution (haganah mi-pur'anus). In Eruvin 19a, sinners pass through Gehinnom weeping (ovrei b'emek ha-baka), which R' Tzadok explains as suffering the pain of fire without being consumed, after which Avraham Avinu draws them out.

p: וּבַ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם] מְבוֹאָר גַּם לְפִי דְּבָרָיו דַּאֲפִילּוּ מְזַלְזֵל רַק בְּחֹק אֶחָד דֶּרֶךְ בִּזּוּי כֵּן
And in Asarah Ma'amaros [ibid.] it is explained even according to his words that even if one treats a single statute with contempt by way of disdain, it is so;
וְכֵן לְשׁוֹן הַגְּמָרָא מַשְׁמַע אֲפִילּוּ מְזַלְזֵל רַק בִּתְפִלִּין לְבַד
and so the language of the Gemara implies: even if he disdains tefillin alone;
וְאַף שֶׁקָּאֵי בְּרוּבּוֹ עֲווֹנוֹת כִּדְאִיתָא בַּגְּמָרָא שָׁם, הַיְינוּ בַּעֲבֵירַת לֹא תַעֲשֶׂה, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מְקַיֵּים כָּל מִצְוֹת עֲשֵׂה
and even though the Talmud deals with one whose sins are the majority (rubo avonos), this refers to the violation of negative commandments, while he nevertheless fulfills all positive commandments.
וְאִם כֵּן עֲדַיִין קָשֶׁה, דִּלְפוּם טַעְמָא דִּיהֵיב רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ לְפִי שֶׁמְּלֵאִים מִצְוֹת, גַּם פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן נַמֵּי

And if so, it remains difficult: according to the rationale provided by Reish Lakish that they are full of mitzvos, this should protect the sinners of Israel with their bodies as well!1109Rosh Hashanah 17a — majority sins and Rav Tzadok’s test case: The baraita distinguishes several judgment categories. It states that ‘sinners of Israel with their bodies’ are judged for twelve months when their deeds are predominantly sinful, while a person whose merits and sins are evenly balanced but who also bears this bodily offense passes through a refining fire. Rav identifies the offense as a ‘skull that did not don tefillin.’ The Gemara does not state that a person’s majority of sins must consist specifically of negative-commandment violations while every positive commandment is fulfilled. Rav Tzadok constructs that possibility as a logical test of Reish Lakish’s rationale: a person can accumulate many violations and nevertheless remain ‘full of mitzvos.’ His conclusion is therefore an inference about how the two sugyos fit together, not the explicit wording of Rosh Hashanah.

וְאַף שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוֹטָה כ״א עַמּוּד א׳] ״עֲבֵירָה מְכַבָּה מִצְוָה״, שָׁם אָמְרוּ סְתָם עֲבֵירָה וּמַשְׁמַע אֲפִילּוּ יְחִידִית וְאֵיזֶה שֶׁיִּהְיֶה, וְלֹא בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן דַּוְוקָא וּבַהֲדֵי רוֹב עֲווֹנוֹת דַּוְוקָא, וְלֹא בִּשְׁקוּלִים וּמֶחֱצָה עַל מֶחֱצָה

And although they stated [in Sotah 21a] that "a sin extinguishes a mitzvah," there they stated an unqualified sin, implying even a single transgression of any kind, and not specifically a bodily sinner, nor specifically one with a majority of sins, nor one whose deeds are balanced half and half.
אֲבָל שָׁם לֹא מַיְירֵי מֵהֲגָנָה מִפּוּרְעָנוּת, אֶלָּא מֵהַצָּלַת הַחֵטְא וּמִיֵּצֶר הָרָע
But there it does not deal with protection from physical retribution (haganah mi-pur'anus), but rather with rescue from sin and the yetzer hara;
כִּמְבוֹאָר שָׁם בַּסּוּגְיָא, דְּבֵין לְרַב יוֹסֵף בֵּין לְרָבָא בְּהָכִי הוּא דְּמַפְלִיג בֵּין תּוֹרָה לְמִצְוָה, לְמָר בְּעִידָּנָא דְּלָא עָסֵיק וּלְמָר בְּעִידָּנָא דְּעָסֵיק

as explained in the passage there, that both according to Rav Yosef and according to Rava it is regarding this that they distinguish between Torah and mitzvah (whether while actively engaged or when not actively engaged);1110Sotah 21a — protection from calamity and rescue from sin: On ‘for a mitzvah is a lamp and Torah is light’ (Mishlei 6:23), the Bavli distinguishes maginna, shielding from punishment or misfortune, from matzla, rescuing a person from the evil inclination. Rav Yosef holds that a mitzvah protects and rescues while one performs it, but afterward only protects; Torah protects and rescues even afterward. Rava concludes that Torah protects and rescues while one studies it and afterward only protects, whereas a mitzvah protects but does not rescue in either period. Thus, for both views, mitzvah-performance retains a protective merit against calamity; their dispute concerns its preventive force against subsequent sin and the time at which that force operates. Rav Tzadok accordingly does not read ‘a transgression extinguishes a mitzvah’ as erasing the deed, its accountability, or its reward.

וְעַל זֶה אָמְרוּ הַטַּעַם דַּ״עֲבֵירָה מְכַבָּה״, דְּהַהַצָּלָה עַל יְדֵי דְּמִצְוָה גּוֹרֶרֶת מִצְוָה, אֲבָל עֲבֵירָה גּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה וְהוּא מְכַבֶּה כֹּחַ הַמִּצְוָה שֶׁכְּנֶגְדָּהּ וְנִשְׁאָר שָׁקוּל לִבְחִירָתוֹ

and on this they stated the rationale that "sin extinguishes": for protection occurs because a mitzvah draws another mitzvah, whereas a sin draws another sin, extinguishing the spiritual momentum of the corresponding mitzvah so that he remains balanced in his free choice;
וּלְרָבָא דְּקָאֵי בְּעִידָּנָא דְּעָסֵיק, קָאֵי אַעֲבֵירָה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת

and according to Rava, who addresses the time when one is actively engaged, it refers to a preceding sin.1111Pirkei Avos 4:2 — ‘a mitzvah draws a mitzvah’ and continued free choice: Ben Azzai teaches that one mitzvah leads to another and one transgression leads to another. Rabbeinu Yonah explains that repetition habituates the soul: a mitzvah draws a person nearer to divine service, whereas sin makes the spirit more accessible to the inclination. Bartenura adds that Heaven places another mitzvah before one who has chosen well. Tosafos Yom Tov stresses the moral asymmetry: one who comes to purify is assisted, but one who comes to defile is merely given an opening and is not assisted in wrongdoing. Rav Tzadok’s formulation here — that the contrary momentum of a transgression can neutralize the mitzvah’s preventive force and leave the person ‘balanced’ for choice — is his synthesis of these teachings. Pri Tzadik, Beshalach 14:1, likewise treats the chain of acts as a process that can expose error and awaken repentance, not as the removal of responsibility.
אֲבָל לְעִנְיַן הֲגָנָה מִפּוּרְעָנוּת, מְבוֹאָר שָׁם דִּלְתַרְוַויְיהוּ אֵין חִילּוּק בָּזֶה בֵּין מִצְוָה לְתוֹרָה, עַיֵּין שָׁם
However, regarding protection from retribution, it is explained there that according to both authorities there is no distinction between a mitzvah and Torah study, see there;
וְגַם סְתִימוּת הַלָּשׁוֹן ״פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל״ מַשְׁמַע דִּבְכָל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל קָאָמַר, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל

and likewise the unqualified language "the sinners of Israel" implies that he speaks of all sinners of Israel, as I wrote above;1112Pri Tzadik, Kuntres Amalah shel Torah 6:4 — the enduring mitzvah-content of Israel: Rav Tzadok there joins the teaching that even the ‘empty’ of Israel are full of mitzvos like a pomegranate with Sotah’s rule that a transgression can extinguish a mitzvah but cannot extinguish Torah. He explains that even a sinner retains a root and hold in Torah because it is ‘an inheritance of the congregation of Yaakov,’ and that joining a sacred communal act can awaken the buried point of Jewish holiness. This internal parallel clarifies the present argument: an aveirah may darken the active light by which a particular mitzvah draws another mitzvah, yet it does not retroactively make the person devoid of all mitzvah-deeds or sever the covenantal root. Rav Tzadok’s claim preserves judgment and the need for teshuvah; it does not imply that prior merits authorize later misconduct or cancel halachic accountability.
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע גַּם כֵּן [בְּעֵירוּבִין י״ט עַמּוּד א׳] דְּפָרִיךְ אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ מִקְּרָא דְּ״עֹבְרֵי בְּעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא״ (תְּהִלִּים פ״ד:ז׳)
and so it implies in Eruvin [19a], which challenges Reish Lakish from the verse "Passing through the valley of weeping" (Tehillim 84:7);
וְאִם אִיתָא דְּיֵשׁ פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן דְּשׁוֹלֵט בָּהֶם, לוֹקְמֵיהּ לִקְרָא בְּהָכִי

for if it were true that there are bodily sinners of Israel over whom fire holds dominion, let the Gemara resolve the verse with them!1113Eruvin 19a: “Reish Lakish said: the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel — [by] a kal va-chomer from the golden altar [as quoted above]. [The Gemara asks:] but that which is written, ‘those who pass through the valley of weeping [emek ha-bacha]’ [implying they pass through Gehinnom]? — [The Gemara answers:] those [are] the ones liable at that moment in Gehinnom, and Avraham Avinu comes and raises them and receives them — except a Jew who came upon the daughter of a gentile [bas oved kochavim], whose foreskin is drawn, and [Avraham] does not recognize him” — [i.e.,] does not recognize him as a Jew, and therefore does not save him.
וְהָא לָא קַשְׁיָא לְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל, דְּרַק אֵין שׁוֹלֵט לְכַלּוֹתָן
And this is not difficult according to what I wrote above: that the fire merely lacks dominion to annihilate them;
אִם כֵּן שַׁפִּיר עוֹבְרִים וּבוֹכִים מִפְּנֵי הַיִּסּוּרִין
if so, they rightly pass through and weep on account of the painful chastisements;
דְּיֵשׁ לוֹמַר הַיְינוּ דִּמְשַׁנֵּי: הַהוּא דִּמְחַיְּיבֵי הַהוּא שַׁעְתָּא, וְאָתֵי אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם וּמַסֵּיק:

for one can say this is why the Gemara answers: that refers to those who are condemned to punishment for that initial hour, after which Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, comes and draws them up.1114Eruvin 19a — weeping, judgment, and Avraham’s raising of the sinners of Israel: The Gemara first describes transgressors who pass through the ‘valley of weeping,’ shed tears, and acknowledge the justice of judgment. It then states that the fire of Gehinnom ‘has no power’ over the sinners of Israel because even their empty ones are full of mitzvos, and resolves the apparent contradiction by saying that those presently liable enter, but Avraham Avinu comes and raises them. The Bavli itself places suffering, acknowledgment, and rescue in one Aggadic sequence. Rav Tzadok’s more precise reconciliation — that the fire can afflict and refine but cannot consume or annihilate their covenantal being — is his interpretive synthesis of that sequence. The imagery is Aggadic and theological, not a medical or scientific description; it affirms both moral accountability and ultimate non-annihilation, and it offers no permission for wrongdoing.

items.h: The theme: Analyzing the three who descend to Gehinnom and never ascend (Bava Metzia 58b). Tosafos in Chagigah 27a, Bava Metzia 58b, and Rosh Hashanah 17a implies that the fire lacks dominion only because Avraham Avinu extracts them immediately, which does not apply to those judged for twelve months. R' Tzadok refutes this: since even temporary entry involves intense weeping and pain, "no dominion" must mean the fire cannot consume them into oblivion, rendering the duration (one hour versus twelve months) immaterial. The three who descend and do not ascend (including one who cohabits with a married woman) descend for illicit sexual relations (isqei chinam, Eruvin 19a). Avraham extracts them through the sign of circumcision (bris milah), unless one cohabited with an Aramean woman (bo'el aramis), drawing down a foreskin that prevents Avraham from recognizing him.

p: וּמֵהַתּוֹסָפוֹת [חֲגִיגָה שָׁם] מַשְׁמַע, דְּרַק מִשּׁוּם דְּאַבְרָהָם מַסֵּיק מִיָּד אֵין שׁוֹלֵט, מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּנִידּוֹנִין י״ב חֹדֶשׁ, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם
And from Tosafos [Chagigah 27a] it implies that solely because Avraham extracts them immediately does the fire lack dominion, which is not so for those judged twelve months, see there;
וְכֵן מַשְׁמַע בְּתוֹסָפוֹת [בָּבָא מְצִיעָא נ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״חוּץ״, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם
and so it implies in Tosafos [Bava Metzia 58b, s.v. chutz], see there
[וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתְבוּ מֵחֲגִיגָה קַל וָחֹמֶר מִסַּלְמַנְדְּרָא צָרִיךְ עִיּוּן, דְּהַהוּא בְּתַלְמִיד חָכָם וְהָתָם בְּכָל יוֹרְדִין דְּעָלְמָא קָאֵי]

[and what they cited from the a fortiori argument of the salamander in Chagigah requires study, for that applies to a Torah scholar whereas here it addresses ordinary sinners who descend];1115Bava Metzia 58b: “R’ Chanina said: all descend to Gehinnom except three. ‘All’?! Can it enter your mind [that all descend]? Rather, say: all who descend to Gehinnom ascend, except three who descend and do not ascend. And these are they: one who comes upon a married woman, one who whitens his fellow’s face in public, and one who calls his fellow by a derogatory name.” Tosafos: “Thus is its explanation: all who descend ascend immediately, and the fire of Gehinnom has no power over them, as we say in Perek Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a) [by] a kal va-chomer from the golden altar, and in the last chapter of Chagigah (27a) [where] he made a kal va-chomer from the salamander — except three who do not ascend immediately; but some of them are judged forever, such as [the heretics], and some ascend after twelve months, such as [the sinners of Israel]. And yet it is difficult that [R’ Chanina] did not count ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ such as the skull that does not don tefillin, of whom we say in Rosh Hashanah that they descend and are judged there twelve months, and afterward their body and soul are burned.”
וְכֵן [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה י״ז עַמּוּד א׳] סוֹף דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״כִּי״, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and so in Rosh Hashanah [17a, end of s.v. ki], see there.1116Bava Metzia 58b: “R’ Chanina said: all descend to Gehinnom except three. ‘All’?! Can it enter your mind [that all descend]? Rather, say: all who descend to Gehinnom ascend, except three who descend and do not ascend. And these are they: one who comes upon a married woman, one who whitens his fellow’s face in public, and one who calls his fellow by a derogatory name.” Tosafos: “Thus is its explanation: all who descend ascend immediately, and the fire of Gehinnom has no power over them, as we say in Perek Osin Pasin (Eruvin 19a) [by] a kal va-chomer from the golden altar, and in the last chapter of Chagigah (27a) [where] he made a kal va-chomer from the salamander — except three who do not ascend immediately; but some of them are judged forever, such as [the heretics], and some ascend after twelve months, such as [the sinners of Israel]. And yet it is difficult that [R’ Chanina] did not count ‘the sinners of Israel with their bodies,’ such as the skull that does not don tefillin, of whom we say in Rosh Hashanah that they descend and are judged there twelve months, and afterward their body and soul are burned.”
וְהוּא תָּמוּהַּ בְּעֵינַי: כֵּיוָן דְּהַהוּא שַׁעְתָּא עַל כָּל פָּנִים שׁוֹלֵט לִכְוָותָם וּמִתְיַיסְּרִין, מִדְּבוֹכִין וּמוֹרִידִין דְּמָעוֹת וּמַצְדִּיקִין הַדִּין

And this is astonishing in my eyes: since during that initial hour the fire in any event holds dominion to burn them and they suffer, as evidenced by the fact that they weep, shed tears, and justify the divine decree;
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּרָצָה לוֹמַר דְּאֵין שׁוֹלֵט לְכַלּוֹתָם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל
and perforce it means that the fire lacks dominion to consume them into annihilation, as I wrote above;
אִם כֵּן מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ בֵּין שָׁעָה אַחַת וְעוֹלֶה מִיָּד אוֹ אַחַר י״ב חֹדֶשׁ, כֵּיוָן דְּסוֹף סוֹף אֵין שׁוֹלֵט לְכַלּוֹת
if so, what practical difference is there between suffering one hour and ascending immediately versus suffering twelve months, since ultimately the fire does not dominate to annihilate them?
וּשְׁלִיטָה לִשְׁעָתוֹ אִיכָּא דְּנִיתְיַיסְּרוּ, מַאי נַפְקָא מִינַּהּ אִם הוּא זְמַן מוּעָט אוֹ זְמַן רָב
And as for temporary dominion to afflict them with burns, what difference does it make whether it lasts a short duration or a long duration?

וְגַם לְפִי דִּבְרֵי תּוֹסָפוֹת דְּבָבָא מְצִיעָא נִצְטָרֵךְ לוֹמַר, דְּגַם הָנֵי ג׳ דְּהָתָם אֵינוֹ בִּכְלַל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם אֵין שׁוֹלֵט, וַחֲדָא מִינַּיְיהוּ אֵשֶׁת אִישׁ

Moreover, according to Tosafos in Bava Metzia we would be forced to say that those three sinners mentioned there are excluded from the sinners of Israel over whom fire lacks dominion, one of whom is one who cohabits with a married woman;
וְלֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן בְּעֵירוּבִין שָׁם, דְּאָמַר אַחַר כָּךְ: ״גֵּיהִנָּם, שֶׁהַכֹּל יוֹרְדִין עַל עִסְקֵי חִנָּם״, פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י: עֲרָיוֹת
yet it does not imply thus in Eruvin [19a], which states subsequently: "Gehinnom, into which all descend on account of unprovoked matters," which Rashi explains: illicit sexual relations (arayos);
וּמַשְׁמַע לְפִי שֶׁזֶּהוּ עֲבֵירָה הַשְּׁכִיחָה יוֹתֵר וּמִיעוּטוֹ הַמָּצוּי כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בָּבָא בַּתְרָא [קס״ה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]

and this implies that because this is the most rampant transgression and a prevalent minority (Bava Batra 165a);1117Bava Basra 165a — prevalence language, not a universal characterization: The Gemara states: ‘Most [people] in robbery, a minority in sexual matters, and all in lashon hara,’ then immediately narrows the final clause to avak lashon hara. Rav Tzadok cites only the ‘minority in arayos’ clause to explain why Eruvin can use sexual wrongdoing as a common paradigm for descent to Gehinnom.
