However, according to this that they outlast and wear away Sheol, it implies that Sheol is completely consumed and no further fire remains; if so, they would be released from judgment, and that phrase "they are not consumed" would turn out to be to their advantage!
וְכֵן רָאִיתִי שֶׁפֵּירֵשׁ בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ שָׁם [חֵלֶק ה׳ סוֹף פֶּרֶק ד׳] עַל מַה שֶּׁאִיתָא בְּסוֹטָה [ט׳ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״חִצַּי כָּלִין וְהֵן אֵין כָּלִין״, עַיֵּין שָׁם
And so I saw explained in Asarah Ma'amaros [Part V, end of ch. 4] on what is stated in Sotah [9a]: "My arrows are consumed, but they are not consumed," see there;
וְשָׁם [פֶּרֶק ה׳] דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״אֵין לוֹ כְּבִיָּה לְעוֹלָם״ הַיְינוּ כָּל יְמֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

and there [ch. 5], that what they stated—"it has no quenching forever"—means throughout all the days of this world, see there at length;1164Sotah 9a; Malachi 3:6; Devarim 32:23 - 'My arrows are consumed, but they are not': In its original context, the teaching explains Israel's covenantal endurance. Other nations are not struck and then struck again because the first blow leaves no recovery, whereas 'you, children of Yaakov, are not consumed' despite repeated punishment; therefore, 'My arrows are consumed, but they are not consumed.' Rav Tzadok reports that the Asarah Maamaros applies this pattern to the ending of punishment. His difficulty is deliberate: the original maxim is an advantage of Israel, so survival by offenders who are worse than 'sinners of Israel with their bodies' appears paradoxically superior unless continued existence can itself be a form of loss.
וּלְפִי זֶה גַּם לָהֶם יֵשׁ קִיּוּם אַחַר כָּךְ לְטוֹב בְּלֹא יִסּוּרִין, וְקָשֶׁה מַאי שְׁנָא
and according to this, they too would subsequently possess existence for the good without afflictions, and it is difficult: wherein are they distinct?

אַךְ אֶפְשָׁר דְּיִהְיוּ עֲדִיפֵי מִפּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּגוּפָן שֶׁנִּכְלִים וְנַעֲשִׂין אֵפֶר, וְהֵם גְּרוּעֵי טוּבָא מִינַּיְיהוּ וְכִמְבוֹאָר גַּם כֵּן מֵהַגְּמָרָא שָׁם וּמִסְּבָרָא, וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם פֶּרֶק ג׳ וּפֶרֶק ד׳]

Yet is it possible that they should be superior to the bodily sinners of Israel who are consumed and made into ashes, when they are vastly more corrupt than them, as is clarified from the Gemara there and from logical reasoning, and see in Asarah Ma'amaros [ibid., ch. 3 and 4]?
וְאוּלַי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: כֵּיוָן דְּהָנֵי אֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, קִיּוּמָם אָז גַּם בְּלֹא יִסּוּרֵי גֵּיהִנָּם הוּא לְרַע לָהֶם
And perhaps one can say: since these heretics have no portion in the World to Come, their enduring existence then, even without the active torments of Gehinnom, is itself an evil unto them;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת קנ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״הַלָּלוּ אוֹכְלִין וְהַלָּלוּ רְעֵבִין וְכוּלֵיהּ, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר וְכוּלֵיהּ: ׳[הִנֵּה עֲבָדַי יָרֹנּוּ מִטּוּב לֵב] וְאַתֶּם תִּצְעֲקוּ מִכְּאֵב לֵב [וּמִשֵּׁבֶר רוּחַ תְּיֵלִילוּ]׳ (יְשַׁעְיָה ס״ה:י״ד)״:

and as they expounded [in Shabbos 152b]: "These eat and these are hungry, etc., as it is said: 'Behold, My servants shall sing for joy of heart, but you shall cry for sorrow of heart, and shall wail for vexation of spirit' (Yeshayah 65:14)."1165Shabbos 153a: The parable of the king who invited his servants to a feast — “the wise adorned themselves [and sat ready], and these [who came ready] eat and drink, and these [who did not] stand and watch”; the reward of those prepared for the World to Come.1166Shabbos 153a; Yeshayahu 65:13-14 - punishment through exclusion from the feast: The parable does not describe annihilation or the flames of Gehinnom. Both the prepared and unprepared servants remain present, but the prepared eat, drink, and rejoice while the unprepared hunger, thirst, feel shame, and cry from pain of heart. Rav Tzadok uses this model to distinguish bare existence from participation in the good of the World to Come. On his proposal, existence after Gehinnom has ended may still be profoundly adverse when a person beholds the feast but has no share in it. The Gemara itself does not identify the Rosh Hashanah classes with this parable; that connection is Rav Tzadok's suggested resolution.

items.h: The theme: The ultimate triumph of good in the World to Come according to Asarah Ma'amaros and the Dorshei Reshumos. The Rama MiFano establishes that eternity exists exclusively within the attribute of goodness (ein lecha davar nitzchi ela b'middas ha-tov); hence, when Gehinnom wears away, all evil is obliterated and only goodness remains. The Talmudic description of hunger in Shabbos 152b represents a lower rung, whereas in the higher World to Come there is no eating or drinking (Berachos 17a). This aligns with the ancient allegorical exegetes (Dorshei Reshumos, Sanhedrin 104b) who held that all the Three Kings and Four Commoners will ultimately enter the World to Come, for in the final cosmic rectification evil will have no reality, and not a single soul of Israel will be cast away (lo yidach mimenu nidach).

p: אַךְ מִמַּה שֶּׁכָּתַב בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם סוֹף פֶּרֶק ד׳] דְּאֵין לְךָ דָּבָר נִצְחִי אֶלָּא בְּמִדַּת הַטּוֹב
However, from what was written in Asarah Ma'amaros [ibid., end of ch. 4], that there is nothing eternal except within the attribute of goodness;
וְכֵן כָּתַב [בְּפֶרֶק ה׳] דִּבְהַנְהָגַת עוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵין רַע כָּל עִיקָּר
and so he wrote [in ch. 5], that in the divine governance of the World to Come there is no evil whatsoever;
מַשְׁמַע דִּכְשֶׁיִּכְלֶה גֵּיהִנָּם יִכְלֶה כָּל רַע וְיִהְיֶה רַק טוֹב
it implies that when Gehinnom ceases, all evil will be eradicated and only good will exist;
וּמַשְׁמַע לְפִי זֶה גַּם אוֹתָם רְשָׁעִים שֶׁאֵין כָּלִים יִהְיֶה לָהֶם אָז טוֹב

and it implies according to this that even those wicked who are not consumed will then experience good;1167Asarah Maamaros, part 5, ch. 1: “And this is the reason [for] ‘Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed,’ which we explain according to what the Sages explained in the verse ‘I will spend My arrows upon them [chitzai achaleh bam]’ — just as there the arrows are consumed [spent], which is the ultimate of sufferings, so here Gehinnom is consumed, which is the ultimate of the punishment; for the arrows and the Gehinnom do not cease all the days of their being, from being wrathful against them and rebuking them — however, ultimately they are not consumed. And Gehinnom itself is called thus, that it is ‘a valley of illicitness [gei shel chinam],’ and its explanation is a deep pit into which they descend on account of illicit matters. And the souls that were purified — they raise them [to] the emissaries of Gan Eden and say ‘here they are, take them’; and regarding only the examined souls that need no purification do they cry to them ‘here, take them and go,’ as is clarified in the Zohar. And in truth, there is nothing eternal except in the attribute of good.” There, ch. 5: “Thus we have learned that the fire of Gehinnom has no eternal extinguishing — but with a cessation [of wrath].”
וְכֵן כָּתַב שָׁם [בְּסוֹף פֶּרֶק ה׳] שֶׁרְשָׁעִים עוֹד אֵינָם, רַק יֶשְׁנָם בִּמְצִיאוּת שָׁקֵט וְשַׁאֲנָן, עַיֵּין שָׁם

and so he wrote there [end of ch. 5], that the wicked are no more, existing solely in a peaceful and tranquil reality, see there.1168Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chikur Din V:5 — “the wicked are no more” without annihilation: R. Menachem Azariah da Fano argues that the fire of Gehinnom lacks extinguishing only within the present order of the world; when that order ends, evil itself has no further standing. He reads “sins will cease” rather than “sinners,” and explains “the wicked are no more” to mean that their degraded mode of wickedness disappears, while they remain “in a quiet and tranquil existence.” The tranquility is therefore not a reward for wickedness, but the consequence of evil no longer existing as an active reality. Rav Tzadok adopts this universal-rectification framework and asks which level of the World to Come can contain it.
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר: אַף דְּרַשִׁ״י בְּשַׁבָּת שָׁם פֵּירֵשׁ זֶה לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְכֵן בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה אָמְרוּ: ״מִשִּׁלּוּמַת רְשָׁעִים בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא״

And one must say: although Rashi in Shabbos there explained this sorrow as occurring in the World to Come, and so in Bereishis Rabbah [33:1] they expounded: "from the retribution of the wicked in the World to Come";
יָדוּעַ דְּכַמָּה מַדְרֵיגוֹת בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא יֵשׁ

it is known that there are multiple distinct levels within the World to Come;1169“Several levels in the World to Come” — Rambam, Ramban, and Be’er Sheva: Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 8:2, uses “World to Come” for the incorporeal life of the soul, where there is no eating or drinking. Ramban, Sha’ar HaGemul 69–70, reserves the ultimate World to Come for the enduring state after resurrection, with body and soul reunited. Be’er Sheva on Sanhedrin 90a explicitly gathers several rabbinic uses of the term, including the world of souls, resurrection, and the messianic era. Rav Tzadok’s statement should therefore be read as a distinction among stages or meanings of Olam Haba, not as a rejection of either Talmudic passage.
וְשָׁם [בְּשַׁבָּת] מַשְׁמַע שֶׁיֵּשׁ אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה, וּבִבְרָכוֹת [י״ז עַמּוּד א׳] אִיתָא דְּאֵין בּוֹ אֲכִילָה וּשְׁתִיָּה וְכוּלֵיהּ

and there [in Shabbos] it implies that there is eating and drinking, whereas in Berachos [17a] it is taught that there is no eating and drinking in it, etc.1170Shabbos 153a and Berachos 17a — feast imagery and non-physical delight: Shabbos presents a mashal of servants summoned to the king’s feast; Rabbi Meir’s teaching says that both groups sit, but the prepared eat and drink while the unprepared hunger and thirst, citing Yeshayahu 65:13–14. Berachos states that in the World to Come there is no eating or drinking, and that the righteous instead enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah. Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 8:2, and Radak on Yeshayahu 65:13 treat bodily eating language as a metaphor for spiritual apprehension and delight. The sources can therefore be reconciled either as different stages, as Rav Tzadok proposes, or as parable versus literal description; the Shabbos passage itself is introduced as a parable.
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ד סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּכוּלָּם בָּאִין לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
And one can explain that what the allegorical exegetes (Dorshei Reshumos) stated [in Sanhedrin 104b]—that all of them [Doeg, Achitophel, Korach, and Balaam] enter the World to Come;
שֶׁהֵם הִשִּׂיגוּ אוֹתָהּ מַדְרֵיגָה דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁאֵין מְצִיאוּת לָרָע עוֹד כְּלָל
was because they grasped that ultimate transcendental level of the World to Come where evil has no existence whatsoever;
וְאָז גַּם כָּל רִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַיּוֹתֵר גְּרוּעִים ״לֹא יִדַּח מִמֶּנּוּ נִדָּח״ (שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ד:י״ד), דְּהֵם אֵין כָּלִים וּבָאִים לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

and at that time, even all the most degraded sinners of Israel, "no outcast shall be expelled from Him" (II Shmuel 14:14), for they are not utterly destroyed and will enter the World to Come.1171Sanhedrin 104b; Pri Tzadik, Pesach 8 and Bamidbar 5 — the dorshei reshumos: The Gemara’s derashah concerns the three kings and four commoners named by the Mishnah as having no share in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok elsewhere explains “dorshei reshumos” as tzaddikim who discern the residual imprint of Israel’s holy root even in souls submerged in the lowest condition; in Pri Tzadik, Pesach 8, he adds that their insight reaches beyond ordinary human reason. Se’if 72 thus invokes a recurring doctrine in Rav Tzadok’s writings: visible corruption can obscure, but not erase, the deepest Jewish root. This Aggadic counter-reading does not cancel the Mishnah’s warning on the level to which that warning applies.1172II Shmuel 14:14; Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chikur Din V:1 — “no banished one remains banished”: In its biblical setting, the woman of Tekoa urges David to devise a way to restore Avshalom, saying that God “devises plans so that one banished from Him not remain banished.” Later kabbalistic and Chasidic works develop the phrase into a principle of ultimate return. The Asarah Maamaros itself invokes it when suggesting that even the sixth and harshest class may eventually be examined and rectified through hidden divine wisdom; Rav Tzadok in Pri Tzadik, Pesach 8, similarly says that the future correction of the wicked son lies beyond human comprehension. Rav Tzadok’s use here is therefore part of his broader theology of the indestructible root of Israel, not a literal conclusion drawn from Avshalom’s immediate history.1173Cf. Sanhedrin 104b — the source R’ Tzadok cites: the dorshei reshumos (interpreters of allusions) taught that “all of them [even the wicked kings and commoners enumerated as having no share in the World to Come] come into the World to Come, as it says (Tehillim 60): ‘Gilead is Mine and Menasheh is Mine, etc.’” — which R’ Tzadok reads as their having attained the ultimate level of the World to Come in which evil no longer exists.

items.h: The theme: Reconciling the Ra'avad's ruling in Eduyos on the twelve-month judgment of heretics. In Eduyos (end of ch. 2), the Ra'avad comments on the verse "and it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another... shall all flesh come to worship before Me" (Yeshayah 66:23), stating that even heretics who denied fundamental tenets (kofrim ba-ikkar) are judged in Gehinnom for only twelve months. Commentators wondered at this from the Baraisa of Rosh Hashanah. R' Tzadok resolves this: on the Great Day of Judgment following the Resurrection, heretics who were not previously purified will undergo an intense, final twelve-month purgation, after which Gehinnom and all evil will be eradicated, enabling even them to be included within "all flesh" who bow before Hashem.

p: וְיֵשׁ לְיַישֵּׁב בָּזֶה דִּבְרֵי הָרַאֲבַ״ד בְּפֵירוּשׁוֹ לְעֵדֻיּוֹת [סוֹף פֶּרֶק ב׳] אַהָא דְּמִשְׁפַּט רְשָׁעִים בְּגֵיהִנָּם מִקְּרָא דְּ״וְהָיָה מִדֵּי חֹדֶשׁ בְּחָדְשׁוֹ וְגוֹמֵר״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ס״ו:כ״ג)

And through this one can resolve the words of the Ra'avad in his commentary to Eduyos [end of ch. 2] regarding the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom derived from the verse "and it shall come to pass, that from one new moon to another, etc." (Yeshayah 66:23):
כָּתַב: ״וּבְמִשְׁפַּט רְשָׁעִים מַיְירֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ, אוֹתָם שֶׁכָּפְרוּ בָּעִיקָּר וְכוּלֵיהּ דִּינָם י״ב חֹדֶשׁ״
he wrote: "And it deals with the judgment of the wicked, etc., those who denied the fundamental principle, etc., their judgment is twelve months";
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת תָּמַהּ עַל זֶה מִבָּרַיְיתָא דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה
and see the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados there who was astonished at this from the Baraisa of Rosh Hashanah (which states they are judged for generations);
וּבְתוֹסְפוֹת יוֹם טוֹב שָׁם כָּתַב לְהַגִּיהַּ, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם

and in the Tosafos Yom Tov there he wrote to emend the text, see there.1174Eduyos 2:10: “The judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months, as it says (Yeshayah 66): ‘and it shall be from month to month [midei chodesh b’chodsho]’; R’ Yochanan ben Nuri says: from Pesach until Shavuos, as it says (ibid.): ‘from Shabbos to Shabbos [midei Shabbos b’Shabbato].’” Raavad: “the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months, as it is written ‘and it shall be from month to month, all flesh shall come to bow before Me’ — since it says ‘in his month’ it implies in that same month, i.e., from Nisan to Nisan or from Tishrei to Tishrei; and it says ‘all flesh shall come to bow before the Omnipresent,’ and it deals with the judgment of the wicked, as it is written ‘and they shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men, etc.’ — and they are those who denied the essential and have chillul Hashem in their hand; but [other wicked], their judgment is twelve months.” Maharsha: “and there is astonishment in the matter, for this verse does not deal with the judgment of twelve months but forever, as it is written ‘for their worm shall not die and their fire shall not be extinguished’; and so it is explicitly explained in the first chapter of Rosh Hashanah: ‘but the righteous [do not descend].’”1175Tosafos Yom Tov on Eduyos 2:10 — emending the Raavad or defending his reading: The Raavad links Yeshayahu 66:23–24 to those who deny the essential principles, yet concludes that ‘other wicked’ are judged for twelve months. Tosafos Yom Tov inserts or clarifies the words ‘other wicked’ and says that this reading is required by Seder Olam and Rosh Hashanah 17a: the exceptional classes are distinct from the ordinary twelve-month group. Rav Tzadok takes a different route. Rather than solve the difficulty only by emendation, he preserves the Raavad’s association of the verse with the exceptional group and relocates their twelve-month sentence to a final judgment after resurrection. The se’if is therefore a proposed defense of the Raavad’s conceptual reading, not a repetition of the Tosafos Yom Tov’s correction.
וּלְפִי מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי יֵשׁ לוֹמַר, דְּמִמַּה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״גֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה״, עַל כָּרְחֲךָ הַךְ ״לֹא תִכְבֶּה״ לָאו לְעוֹלָם הוּא
And according to what I wrote, one can say: from the fact that they stated "Gehinnom ceases," perforce that phrase "shall not be quenched" is not absolute eternity;
וּמְפָרֵשׁ דְּקָאֵי לְיוֹם הַדִּין הַגָּדוֹל, וְאָז כָּל רְשָׁעִים כְּבָר קִבְּלוּ דִּינָם וְאֵשׁ שֶׁלָּהֶם נִכְבָּה

and he explains that it refers to the Great Day of Judgment, when all other wicked have already received their judgment and their fire is quenched;1176Rosh Hashanah 17a; Pesachim 54a — ‘their fire shall not be quenched’: Rosh Hashanah applies Yeshayahu 66:24 to the exceptional classes, saying that they are judged ‘for generations of generations,’ and then states that Gehinnom is consumed while they are not. Pesachim cites the same unquenched-fire language when teaching that the fire of Gehinnom, created on the second day, has no extinguishing forever. Rav Tzadok’s explanation is a harmonization: the phrase need not mean that each offender’s active sentence is literally endless; it can mean that the fire is not extinguished before the remaining judgment is completed. Neither Gemara explicitly states that the exceptional group receives only twelve months after resurrection; that is the novel reconciliation proposed here.
וְאֵלּוּ עֲדַיִין לֹא קִבְּלוּ כָּל עָנְשָׁם, וְאֵשׁ שֶׁלָּהֶם עֲדַיִין לֹא תִכְבֶּה עַד שֶׁקִּבְּלוּ מִשְׁפָּטָם
whereas these heretics have not yet completed their full punishment, and their fire is not quenched until they receive their judgment;
וְאָז הֵם יְבַלּוּן הַשְּׁאוֹל, כִּי בִּגְמַר דִּינָם יִבְלֶה וְיִכְלֶה שֶׁהוּא מְעוּכָּב רַק בִּשְׁבִילָם

and then they will wear away Sheol, for upon the completion of their judgment Sheol will wear away and cease, its existence having been extended solely for their sake.1177Tehillim 49:15 and Rashi — who ‘consumes’ Sheol?: The phrase ‘ve-tzuram levalos Sheol’ is difficult, and modern translations also note its uncertainty. Rashi, following the Bavli, reads the form of the wicked as outlasting or wearing away Sheol: Gehinnom ends while they do not. Rav Tzadok develops that reading causally — Sheol remains operative only for their sake, and when their sentence is complete they, as it were, bring Sheol itself to its end. This interpretation is deliberately provisional. In the following se’if he cites a Seder Olam wording that can be read as God consuming their form and their form being destined for consumption in Sheol, and he acknowledges that this may overturn the present explanation.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר כָּאן מִסֵּיפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא: [וְאַף דִּקְרָא דְּ״וְהָיָה״ קָדִים, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הוּא נִשְׁנָה גַּם לְאַחֲרָיו לוֹמַר דְּקָאֵי גַּם עַל זֶה] ״וְהָיָה מִדֵּי וְגוֹמֵר״

And regarding this he expounded from the conclusion of the verse [and although the verse "And it shall come to pass" precedes, it is repeated afterward to indicate that it applies to this as well]: "And it shall come to pass from one new moon to another, etc.";
דְּמִשְׁפָּטָם אָז הוּא רַק י״ב חֹדֶשׁ מֵאוֹתוֹ יוֹם הַדִּין שֶׁאַחַר תְּחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים

that their judgment at that time lasts only twelve months from that Day of Judgment following the Resurrection of the Dead;1178The Great Day of Judgment after resurrection — Ran, Ramban, and Asarah Maamaros: Ran on Rosh Hashanah 3b identifies the baraisa of the three groups with the judgment after resurrection, ‘the great and awesome day of Hashem.’ Ramban, Sha’ar HaGemul 64, likewise places the universal Day of Judgment and resurrection at the close of the messianic era, before the enduring World to Come. The Asarah Maamaros, Maamar Chikur Din V:1, as explained by Yad Yehuda, further allows for souls not rectified in the judgment following death to return to Gehinnom for the judgment of resurrection. These sources provide the eschatological structure for Rav Tzadok’s phrase ‘from that Day of Judgment’; his additional claim that the final term is exactly twelve months remains his own reconciliation of the Raavad with the baraisa.
וְאַחַר כָּךְ יִכְלֶה גֵּיהִנָּם וְכָל הָרָע מִן הָעוֹלָם, וְיִתּוּקְנוּ גַּם הֵם שֶׁיָּבוֹאוּ בִּכְלַל ״כָּל בָּשָׂר לְהִשְׁתַּחֲוֺת לְפָנַי״, וּכְדוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל:

and afterward Gehinnom and all evil will be eradicated from the world, and they too will be rectified so that they enter within the scope of "all flesh to worship before Me," in accordance with the Dorshei Reshumos mentioned above.1179Yeshayahu 66:23–24; Sanhedrin 104b — ‘all flesh’ after the final judgment: Yeshayahu first depicts ‘all flesh’ coming from month to month and Shabbos to Shabbos to bow before Hashem, and then depicts those worshippers going out to view the rebels whose fire is not quenched. On the plain level, ‘all flesh’ contrasts with the rebels. Mishnah Eduyos derives the twelve-month measure from the calendar language of the first verse. Rav Tzadok reads the sequence dynamically: once the rebels’ final judgment is completed and evil itself ends, they too can enter the category of ‘all flesh.’ This depends on the dorshei reshumos’ teaching that even the kings and commoners listed as excluded ultimately come to the World to Come, and on Rav Tzadok’s broader doctrine of universal rectification; it is not the straightforward contextual meaning of the verses.

items.h: The theme: The textual variant in Seder Olam Rabbah (end of ch. 3). In Seder Olam Rabbah, the Baraisa reads: "not only that, but Sheol wears away and their form wears away (tzurasam l'valos li-She'ol)." This phrasing implies that their spiritual form is ultimately worn away as an intensification of their punishment, and that the external fire of Gehinnom was simply incapable of annihilating them earlier. However, R' Tzadok notes that in the Tosefta of Sanhedrin the text matches the Talmud Bavli, invoking the halachic rule: "set aside one source in the presence of two" (semi chada mikamei tartei).

p: וּמִיהוּ רָאִיתִי בְּסֵדֶר עוֹלָם רַבָּא [סוֹף פֶּרֶק ג׳] דְּשָׁם אִיתָא הַךְ בָּרַיְיתָא
However, I saw in Seder Olam Rabbah [end of ch. 3] where this Baraisa is taught;

וְשָׁם אִיתָא: ״וְלֹא עוֹד אֶלָּא שֶׁשְּׁאוֹל בָּלָה [הוּא כִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב: ׳לְבַלּוֹת׳] וְהֵן וְכוּלֵיהּ, ׳מִזְּבֻל לוֹ׳ (תְּהִלִּים מ״ט:ט״ו) — מִזְּבוּלוֹ מְבַלֶּה צוּרָתָם, וְצוּרָתָם לְבַלּוֹת לִשְׁאוֹל״, עַד כָּאן

and there it is taught: "Not only that, but Sheol wears away [matching the scriptural term 'to wear away'] and they, etc., 'from its dwelling' (Tehillim 49:15)—from His dwelling He wears away their form, and their form wears away to Sheol," thus far;
מְבוֹאָר דְּסוֹף צוּרָתָם לְהִתְבַּלּוֹת גַּם כֵּן

it is clear that their form is ultimately worn away as well;1180Seder Olam Rabba, ch. 3: “the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months, as it says (Yeshayah 66): ‘and it shall be from month to month, etc.’; R’ Yochanan ben Nuri said: from Pesach until Shavuos, as it says: ‘and from Shabbos to Shabbos.’ After twelve months the sinners of Israel, who transgressed the Torah and the mitzvos, their soul is consumed and their body is consumed and Gehinnom [makes them] ash, and Gehinnom casts them out and the wind scatters them beneath the soles of the feet of the righteous, as it says (Malachi 3): ‘and you shall trample the wicked, etc.’ But one who denied the resurrection of the dead, and those who say there is no Torah from Heaven, and those who scoff at the words of the Sages — Gehinnom is locked before them and they are judged within it forever and ever, as it says (Yeshayah 66): ‘and they shall go out and look, etc.’; and not only that, but that Sheol is consumed and they are not consumed, as it says (Tehillim 49): ‘and their form is for Sheol to consume, from His abode [mi-zvul lo]’ — from His abode He consumes their form, and their form is [given] to consume Sheol.”1181Seder Olam Rabbah 3 — the longer recension and the baraisa’s two categories: Seder Olam first assigns twelve months to ordinary sinners of Israel who transgressed Torah and mitzvos; it then introduces a separate group with ‘but’ — sectarians, informers, deniers of resurrection or Torah from Heaven, scoffers at the Sages, and others — for whom Gehinnom is locked and whose judgment is described as enduring. Its text then adds the clauses ‘from His abode He wears out their form, and their form wears out Sheol.’ The existing footnote preserves the full wording. Rav Tzadok’s question here is therefore not whether the exceptional group is included in the ordinary twelve-month sentence, but whether the added Seder Olam gloss teaches that their form itself ultimately reaches an end after Sheol can no longer consume it.
וְגַם לְשׁוֹן ״וְלֹא עוֹד וְכוּלֵיהּ״ מַשְׁמַע דְּבָא לְהוֹסִיף בָּזֶה בְּפוּרְעָנוּתָם, וְלֹא כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי

and the phrase "not only that, etc." implies that it comes to add an intensification to their punishment, and not as I wrote;1182Tehillim 49:15 — competing parses of ‘ve-tzuram levalot Sheol’: The verse is syntactically difficult, and the Masoretic text itself preserves a ketiv/qere at ‘ve-tziram/ve-tzuram.’ The Bavli and Tosefta quote it for the concise proposition ‘Sheol ends, but they do not end’; Rashi likewise explains that the form of the wicked outlasts Gehinnom. Seder Olam’s expanded gloss pulls in the opposite direction as well: ‘from His abode He wears out their form,’ so that their form can eventually be consumed by God even though it first outlasts and, as it were, wears out Sheol. Rav Tzadok treats this as an Aggadic textual interpretation, not as the uncontested peshat of the verse.1183‘And not only’ — an intensification that reopens Se’if 73: The connective ve-lo od ella normally adds a further and more severe consequence. Rav Tzadok therefore reads the longer Seder Olam wording as increasing the punishment: not only does Gehinnom fail to finish them, but their form is ultimately consumed from the divine abode. That reverses the proposal of the preceding se’if, where the ending of Gehinnom was presented as the stage after which final restoration could occur. His phrase ‘and not as I wrote’ is an explicit provisional retraction; the next se’if continues the investigation through Maharsha rather than treating the issue as closed.
וּלְפִי זֶה מַשְׁמַע, הָא דְּאֵין נִבְלִים מִקּוֹדֶם עַל יְדֵי גֵּיהִנָּם הוּא לְפִי שֶׁאֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם יְכוֹלָה לִשְׁלוֹט לְבַלּוֹתָם
and according to this it implies that their not wearing away earlier through Gehinnom was because the fire of Gehinnom could not dominate to wear them away.
אֲבָל אֵינִי יוֹדֵעַ אִם זוֹ הַגִּירְסָא מְדוּקְדֶּקֶת
But I do not know if this reading is precise;
דִּבְתוֹסֶפְתָּא דְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם הַגִּירְסָא כַּבַּגְּמָרָא
for in the Tosefta of Sanhedrin there the reading matches our Gemara;
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר: סְמִי חֲדָא מִקַּמֵּי תַּרְתֵּי:

and one can say: set aside one solitary textual reading before two authoritative sources.1184Chagigah 27a — when the fire of Gehinnom ‘has no dominion’: Reish Lakish teaches that the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel because even the ‘empty’ among them are full of mitzvos. That teaching can illuminate Rav Tzadok’s inference that Gehinnom may punish without being able to consume. It should not, however, be transferred mechanically to every person in Rosh Hashanah’s exceptional list, which includes heretics, informers, deniers, and those who caused the public to sin. Rav Tzadok therefore says only ‘according to this it implies’: the inability of Gehinnom to annihilate them is deduced from the disputed Seder Olam reading, not stated directly by Chagigah, and it does not remove judgment or suffering.1185‘Sami chada mi-kamei tartei’ — weighing one recension against two: The phrase ‘remove one before two’ is used in Talmudic and later commentary when one report or textual formulation conflicts with two concordant ones; Tosafos on Beitzah 38a is a classic example. Here the Tosefta and the Bavli both preserve the shorter statement ‘Sheol ends and they do not end,’ without Seder Olam’s added clause that God consumes their form. Rav Tzadok therefore considers setting aside the single longer reading before the two matching witnesses. Yet he deliberately writes ‘I do not know whether this reading is precise’: he does not erase Seder Olam’s wording dogmatically, but records the textual tension and leaves the conclusion open for further analysis.

items.h: The theme: The Maharsha’s interpretation of "they are not consumed" and the textual variants regarding the ashes of sinners. The Maharsha (Rosh Hashanah 17a) explains that heretics are not consumed so that they remain an eternal disgrace ("and they shall be ashamed", Yeshayah 66:5). The phrase "they are judged for generations" applies strictly to the duration of this world where generations exist, whereas in the World to Come there is no procreation and no generations. The Maharsha notes that "becoming ashes" refers to the physical body rather than the soul. Support for this appears in the Tosefta ("their soul is consumed and their body is burned") and Seder Olam Rabbah; yet in the Talmud Bavli, the burning of the soul implies that the soul's separate existence ceases completely.

p: וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א בְּחִדּוּשֵׁי אַגָּדוֹת [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם] כָּתַב: דְּ״הֵם אֵין כָּלִין״ לֹא לִמְעַלְיוּתָא כְּהַאי דְּסוֹטָה, רַק לִגְרִיעוּתָא, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ לְחֶרְפּוֹת עוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְנִרְאֶה בְשִׂמְחַתְכֶם וְהֵם יֵבֹשׁוּ״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ס״ו:ה׳), עַיֵּין שָׁם

And then I saw in the Maharsha in Chiddushei Aggados [Rosh Hashanah 17a] who wrote: that "they are not consumed" is not to their advantage as in Sotah, but to their degradation, that they should be an everlasting reproach, as it is said: "that your joy may be seen, and they shall be ashamed" (Yeshayah 66:5), see there;
וְזֶהוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל מֵהַגְּמָרָא דְּשַׁבָּת, וְלֹא כְּהָ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״

and this aligns with what I wrote above from the Gemara in Shabbos, and not like Asarah Ma'amaros.1186Maharsha, Rosh Hashanah 17a: “‘Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed, etc.’ In the first chapter of Sotah we say, regarding the calamity of Israel, that ‘half are consumed and they [the arrows] are not consumed, etc.’ — and that is to [their] benefit, as Rashi [explains] in the Chumash; and this curse, according to the calamity, is a blessing — ‘half are consumed and they are not consumed.’ But here, in the judgment of these complete wicked in Gehinnom, it does not appear that it too speaks to [their] benefit, that ‘Gehinnom is consumed and they, etc.’ And one may say that it means thus: that they too are not consumed like the group of the sinners of Israel, etc. — that being consumed in their body is to [their] detriment — [and] here, regarding the heretics, etc., that they are not consumed, [it is] for eternal disgrace, and as it is written ‘and it shall be seen in your joy, and they shall be ashamed.’ However, that which it said to them, [that] they are judged ‘for generations of generations,’ requires explanation: since Gehinnom is consumed, how does it say they are judged for generations of generations? — and analyze it well.”1187Shabbos 153a; Yeshayahu 65:13–14 and 66:5 — survival can itself be deprivation: Rabbi Meir’s teaching in Shabbos does not describe the unprepared servants as annihilated. Both groups remain at the royal feast, but the righteous eat, drink, and rejoice while the others hunger, thirst, and experience shame. This supplies the model Rav Tzadok invokes against the Asarah Maamaros: continued existence may intensify exclusion rather than constitute a benefit. Maharsha’s prooftext, ‘it shall be seen in your joy, and they shall be ashamed,’ similarly defines the punishment through contrast with the joy of the righteous. These are Aggadic images of participation in, or deprivation from, divine delight; they are not a literal claim about physical nutrition in the World to Come.1188Berachos 17a — ‘no procreation’ and the limit of ‘generations of generations’: Rav teaches that the World to Come has no eating, drinking, procreation, commerce, jealousy, hatred, or rivalry; the righteous instead enjoy the radiance of the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok infers from the absence of procreation that the phrase ‘for generations of generations’ can describe the entire remaining span of this world, while biological generations still succeed one another, without extending beyond the transition to the World to Come. Neither Berachos nor Rosh Hashanah states that reconciliation explicitly. The existing Yad Yehuda note records a different reading, counting four ‘generations’ and allowing repeated cycles of judgment and rectification.
וּמַה שֶּׁהוּקְשָׁה לֵיהּ שָׁם הָא דְּ״נִידּוֹנִין לְדוֹרֵי דוֹרוֹת״ וְהִנִּיחַ בְּקוּשְׁיָא, לֹא קָשֶׁה כְּלָל
And what was difficult to him there—that they are judged "for generations of generations," which he left unresolved—is not difficult at all:
דְּהַהִיא כָּל יְמֵי עוֹלָם הַזֶּה קָאֵי שֶׁיֵּשׁ שָׁם דּוֹרוֹת
for that applies throughout all the days of this world wherein generations exist;
וְגֵיהִנָּם כָּלָה לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דִּבְעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין לוֹ כְּבִיָּה
and Gehinnom ceases in the World to Come, whereas in this world its fire has no quenching;
וְאָז אֵין פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳] וְאֵין עוֹד דּוֹרוֹת
and then there is no procreation as they stated [in Berachos 17a], so that there are no further generations;
וְעַיֵּין בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם פֶּרֶק א׳] עַל לְשׁוֹן ״דּוֹרֵי דוֹרוֹת״, וּבְפֵירוּשׁ ״יַד יְהוּדָה״ [אוֹת כ״ה]
and see in Asarah Ma'amaros [ibid., ch. 1] on the phrase "generations of generations," and in the commentary Yad Yehudah [note 25].
וְעַיֵּין עוֹד שָׁם בַּמַּהַרְשָׁ״א לִפְנֵי זֶה, דְּהָא דְּ״יִהְיֶה אֵפֶר״ לֹא אַנְּשָׁמָה קָאֵי אֶלָּא הַגּוּף, דְּאֵין כָּלָה לְגַמְרֵי רַק נַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And see further in the Maharsha prior to this: that the statement "they become ashes" does not refer to the soul but to the body, which is not completely annihilated but turned to ash, see there;1189Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din, part 5, ch. 1, Yad Yehuda commentary, os 25: “and this is the expression ‘generations [doros]’ that comes in the Gemara — for the minimum of ‘dorei [generations]’ is two, ‘doros [generations of]’ [another] two, and that is four; and since after four generations they ascend from Gehinnom for rectification, they return to Gehinnom for the judgment of the resurrection, if they are not rectified in the judgment of death.” Maharsha, Rosh Hashanah 17a: “‘their soul is burned, etc.’ — although the soul is a spiritual thing, we find regarding it the expression ‘burning’; but what [is intended by it is the removal of its light and radiance].”1190Rosh Hashanah 17a; Maharsha — soul, body, burning, and ash: The Bavli distinguishes the subjects and verbs: the body is consumed, the soul is burned, and the wind disperses them beneath the feet of the righteous. Maharsha explains that ‘burning’ applied to a non-material soul means the removal of its light and radiance, not material combustion; the image of ash therefore belongs most naturally to the bodily remainder. Rav Tzadok finds support for a transformed residue rather than simple nonexistence, yet he remains cautious because the Bavli’s wording does not itself say that the body merely becomes ash. The entire discussion is metaphysical and exegetical, not an anatomical or scientific account.
וּלְפִי דַּעְתּוֹ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר כְּדִבְרֵי ״יַד יְהוּדָה״ הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דְּאֵין נִשְׂרָף לְגַמְרֵי
and according to his opinion one can say like the words of Yad Yehudah mentioned above that the soul is not burned completely.
וְסַעַד לְדִבְרֵי מַהַרְשָׁ״א מָצָאתִי בַּתּוֹסֶפְתָּא שָׁם הַגִּירְסָא: ״נַפְשָׁן כָּלָה וְגוּפָן נִשְׂרַף וְגֵיהִנָּם פּוֹלְטָתַן וְנַעֲשִׂין אֵפֶר וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם

And support for the Maharsha's words I found in the Tosefta there, where the reading is: "their soul is consumed and their body is burned and Gehinnom expels them and they become ashes, etc.," see there;
וּמִלָּשׁוֹן זֶה מְבוֹאָר דְּאַגּוּף קָאֵי

and from this phrasing it is clear that becoming ashes refers to the body;1191Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:1; Seder Olam Rabbah 3; Rosh Hashanah 17a — three textual forms: The Tosefta reads: ‘their soul is consumed, their body is burned, Gehinnom casts them out, they become ash, and the wind scatters them.’ Seder Olam reads: ‘their soul is consumed, their body is consumed, they become ash, Gehinnom casts them out, and the wind disperses them.’ The Bavli reverses the first pair: ‘their body is consumed and their soul is burned,’ then mentions the wind. These changes in verb and sequence are precisely why Rav Tzadok weighs each recension separately. The Tosefta’s placement makes ‘they become ash’ follow the bodily burning most naturally, but the variants do not by themselves settle whether ‘consumed’ means total disappearance, loss of former form, or transformation into a remnant capable of later rectification.
וּבְסֵדֶר עוֹלָם רַבָּה [שָׁם] הַגִּירְסָא: ״נַפְשָׁן כָּלָה וְגוּפָן כָּלָה וְהֵן נַעֲשִׂין אֵפֶר וְגֵיהִנָּם פּוֹלְטָתַן וְכוּלֵיהּ״
and in Seder Olam Rabbah [ibid.] the reading is: "their soul is consumed and their body is consumed and they become ashes and Gehinnom expels them, etc.";
וְאָמַר בְּתַרְוַויְיהוּ לְשׁוֹן ״כָּלָה״, וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מִדְּאִיחַר לְגוּף מַשְׁמַע דְּאַגּוּף קָאֵי
and it applied to both the term "consumed," yet since it placed the body later, it implies that becoming ashes refers to the body;
אֲבָל לְפִי הַגִּירְסָא בְּתַלְמוּדִין לֹא מַשְׁמַע כֵּן
but according to the reading in our Talmud [Bavli] it does not imply thus,
וְגַם לַגִּירְסָא דְּשָׁם, לְשׁוֹן ״כָּלָה״ אַנֶּפֶשׁ אִי אֵינוֹ אֵפֶר מַשְׁמַע דְּנִכְלָה לְגַמְרֵי:
and even according to the reading there, the term "consumed" applied to the soul, if it does not mean ash, implies that it is completely annihilated.

items.h: The theme: The ultimate resurrection of the ashes of sinners through the intercession of the righteous. In Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah (ch. 3), the righteous advocate on behalf of sinners who performed mitzvos. Hashem commands: "Heal them"; the righteous stand upon the dust of the wicked, plead for mercy, and Hashem raises them up from beneath their feet ("and you shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet", Malachi 3:21). The use of the word "dust" (afar) indicates that the decomposed body will be resurrected. The Rama MiFano (Asarah Ma'amaros, Chakor Din 3:7) independently intuited this profound truth: the ashes of Jewish sinners can be kneaded (bar gibul), destined to be reconstituted into life through the compassionate tears of the righteous passing through the Valley of Weeping.

p: וְעַיֵּין בְּתַנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ [רַבָּה פֶּרֶק ג׳] אִיתָא, דְּצַדִּיקִים יְלַמְּדוּ זְכוּת אַהָרְשָׁעִים שֶׁעָסְקוּ בְּמִצְוֹת

And see in Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah [ch. 3] where it is taught that the righteous will plead merit for the wicked who engaged in mitzvos;1192Tosafos Yom Tov on Eduyos 2:10, citing Raavad — the proposed emendation and its scope: On the Mishnah’s twelve-month judgment, Tosafos Yom Tov cites Raavad and proposes that Yeshayahu’s final vision concerns those who denied a foundational principle and also bear chillul Hashem, whereas other wicked are judged for twelve months. He says that this emendation is supported by Seder Olam and the opening chapter of Rosh Hashanah. The proposal clarifies which category receives which duration; it does not decide the separate question occupying Rav Tzadok here — whether the terms ‘consumed,’ ‘burned,’ and ‘ash’ describe absolute annihilation or a changed state from which restoration can still occur. Rav Tzadok therefore records the emendation as evidence without treating it as the final resolution.
וְיֹאמַר לָהֶן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: ״רַפְּאוּ אוֹתָן״, וְהוֹלְכִין וְעוֹמְדִין עַל עַפְרָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים וּמְבַקְּשִׁין עֲלֵיהֶם רַחֲמִים
and the Holy One, blessed be He, will say to them: "Heal them"; and they go and stand upon the dust of the wicked and plead for mercy upon them,
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַעֲמִידָן מֵעֲפַר רַגְלֵיהֶם, שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְעַסּוֹתֶם רְשָׁעִים וְכוּלֵיהּ״, עַיֵּין שָׁם
and the Holy One, blessed be He, raises them up from the dust of their feet, as it is said: "and you shall tread down the wicked, etc." (Malachi 3:21), see there;
וּמִדְּקָרֵי ״עָפָר״ וְלֹא ״אֵפֶר״ כִּלְשׁוֹן הַכָּתוּב דְּמַיְיתֵי, מַשְׁמַע גַּם כֵּן דְּקָאֵי אַגּוּף הַנִּרְקָב וְנַעֲשָׂה עָפָר שֶׁיָּקוּם בִּתְחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים

and from his calling it "dust" (afar) rather than "ashes" (efer) like the verse cited, it implies that this refers to the decomposed physical body that turned to dust, which will rise at the Resurrection of the Dead;1193Tanna d’vei Eliyahu Rabba, ch. 3: “In the future the Holy One will sit in His study-hall and the righteous of the world will sit before Him, and they will discuss and debate in Scripture, in Mishnah, in halachos and aggados, and declare of the impure ‘impure’ and of the pure ‘pure’ — of the impure in its place and of the pure in its place. And afterward they bring the wicked and judge them before them, and some are judged thirty days, and some are judged sixty days, and some are judged three months, and some are judged six months; the rule of the matter — our Rabbis taught in the Mishnah: the judgment of the wicked in Gehinnom is twelve months. And afterward the righteous stand before the Holy One and say before Him: Master of the world, when we were in that world, these people would rise early and stay late to the synagogue and would recite Shema and perform the other mitzvos. And the Holy One says to them: if they did so, heal them. Immediately the righteous go and stand over the dust of the wicked and beseech mercy upon them, and the Holy One raises them from the dust of their feet, as it says (Malachi 2): ‘and you shall trample the wicked, for they shall be ash beneath the soles of your feet.’”1194Tanna d’vei Eliyahu Rabbah 3 — restoration is linked to retained mitzvah merit and righteous advocacy: The chapter first describes graded periods of judgment, culminating in the Mishnah’s maximum of twelve months. Only afterward do the righteous plead that these particular people rose early and stayed late in the synagogue, recited Shema, and performed other mitzvos. The Holy One responds, ‘If they did so, heal them,’ and the righteous then pray over their dust. The passage therefore does not state an undifferentiated restoration of every wicked person. Its stated basis is surviving mitzvah-credit, together with the intercession of the righteous, and it leaves intact the separate severe categories described in Rosh Hashanah, the Tosefta, and Seder Olam.1195Malachi 3:19–21 and Tanna d’vei Eliyahu Rabbah 3 — from efer to afar: The verse says that the wicked will be efer, ash, beneath the soles of the righteous. Tanna d’vei Eliyahu retells the scene as the righteous standing over the wicked’s afar, dust, and God raising them me-afar ragleihem, from the dust at their feet. Rav Tzadok treats this deliberate change of noun as an exegetical clue: ordinary bodily decay produces dust capable of resurrection, whereas ash suggests the result of burning. The inference belongs to the midrashic wording, not to the plain wording of Malachi. The surrounding verses themselves juxtapose destructive fire with the ‘sun of righteousness’ that bears healing.1196Daniel 12:2; Ezekiel 37:1–14 — awakening from dust and the rebuilding of the body: Daniel describes sleepers in the earth’s dust who awaken, some to eternal life and some to everlasting reproach. Ezekiel’s vision depicts dry bones reassembled with sinews, flesh, skin, and spirit, followed by the promise that God will open graves and raise His people. These passages provide the scriptural background for Rav Tzadok’s conclusion that afar may denote the bodily substrate from which resurrection occurs. They do not themselves identify the ‘ash’ of Rosh Hashanah with normal grave-dust; that identification depends on the altered wording of Tanna d’vei Eliyahu and the broader argument of this se’if.
אֶלָּא דְּשָׁם מַשְׁמַע דְּצַדִּיקִים הוֹלְכִים לִמְקוֹמָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים לִשְׁאוֹל לַעֲמוֹד עַל עַפְרָם
except that there it implies that the righteous go to the place of the wicked in Sheol to stand upon their dust;
וּבַגְּמָרָא וְתוֹסֶפְתָּא וְסֵדֶר עוֹלָם רַבָּה אָמְרוּ, דְּרוּחַ מֵבִיא הָאֵפֶר לִמְקוֹם הַצַּדִּיקִים לְגַן עֵדֶן

whereas in the Gemara, Tosefta, and Seder Olam Rabbah they stated that a wind brings the ashes to the place of the righteous in Gan Eden.1197Rosh Hashanah 17a; Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:1; Seder Olam Rabbah 3 — beneath the righteous, but not expressly ‘Gan Eden’: The Bavli says that after twelve months a wind disperses the punished beneath the soles of the righteous. The Tosefta adds that Gehinnom casts them out, they become ash, and the wind scatters them; Seder Olam similarly says that Gehinnom expels them and the wind disperses them beneath the righteous. None of these recensions explicitly names Gan Eden. Rav Tzadok’s description of the ash being brought to the righteous ‘in Gan Eden’ interprets the destination from their location. Tanna d’vei Eliyahu presents the complementary spatial image: instead of the remnant being carried to the righteous, the righteous go and stand over the wicked’s dust.
וּמִדְּבָרָיו לָמַדְנוּ, דְּאַף הֵם אֵין נִשְׁאָרִים וְנִכְלִים, רַק עַל יְדֵי זֶה שֶׁנִּתְפַּזְּרִים תַּחַת הַצַּדִּיקִים חוֹזְרִים לָקוּם וְלִחְיוֹת
And from his words we learned that even these bodily sinners do not remain annihilated, but through being scattered beneath the feet of the righteous they return to rise and live;
וְאִם כֵּן לָא קַשְׁיָא מַה שֶּׁכָּתַבְתִּי, דְּשַׁפִּיר עֲדִיפֵי מִמִּינִים אֲפִילּוּ אִי גַּם הֵם אֵין כָּלִים אַחַר שֶׁגֵּיהִנָּם כָּלָה
and if so, what I wrote is not difficult, for they are indeed superior to the heretics, even if the heretics are likewise not consumed after Gehinnom ceases.

וְשׁוּב רָאִיתִי בַּ״עֲשָׂרָה מַאֲמָרוֹת״ [שָׁם רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ז׳] כָּתַב מִדְּנַפְשֵׁיהּ: דְּאֵפֶר זֶה בַּר גִּיבּוּל הוּא, וַעֲתִידִים לִחְיוֹת עַל יְדֵי דִּמְעוֹת הַצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁיַּעַבְרוּ בְּעֵמֶק הַבָּכָא

And then I saw in Asarah Ma'amaros [Part III, start of ch. 7] who wrote from his own reasoning: that this ash can be kneaded with moisture (bar gibul), and they are destined to be revived through the tears of the righteous passing through the Valley of Weeping
[לֹא יָדַעְתִּי לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ לְמַאי דְּאָזֵיל הוּא לְגִירְסַת תַּלְמוּדִין דְּרוּחַ מַפְרִיחַ הָאֵפֶר לְגַן עֵדֶן כַּנַּ״ל] לְהַחֲיוֹתָן, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

[I do not know why this is necessary according to our Talmudic text where the wind scatters the ashes into Gan Eden, as mentioned above] to revive them, see there at length;1198Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din, part 5, ch. 7: “‘And you shall trample the wicked, for they shall be ash beneath the soles of your feet’ — behold, this is a wondrous promise, that kindness and truth will return to the other group that was counted fifth. And behold, this ash they will not tread with shoes, for its end is to become holy ground, and it is fit for kneading [bar gibbul] at the gates of tears that were not locked. This is only [because] it is a positive commandment for the righteous, that they pass through the valley of weeping — this is Gehinnom — to revive these lost ones, as Yechezkel did, who revived the dead, and it is written ‘and He led me around them round about’; the righteous too, who fear His blessed name, whom Malachi mentioned at the end of his prophecy, will pass through the valley of weeping. And it suffices for the general intent in this book to explain it according to its plain sense, that they weep there in prayer and supplications, and from the abundance of their tears and the tears of the sinners in their souls — who will be roused to weep with them — they will make that valley like a spring, like the waters that trickle, which Yechezkel mentioned, which are destined to go out from beneath the threshold of the Sanctuary, as we learned in Shekalim and Middos; and it is the purification of Gehinnom of which we spoke. And with this arousal, ‘a rain of goodwill God will shake down,’ and He will sprinkle upon them pure waters from the supernal waters that are suspended by [His] utterance, [known] to those who know their secret, and from there [are] the storehouses of the dew of the resurrection of the dead. And then, even upon these lost ones, the Teacher will bestow blessings, and they will go from strength to strength, until, after a long time, they reach [the point of] being counted with the righteous — that is the chosen host that fears the God of gods in Zion.”1199Psalms 84:7–8; Eruvin 19a; Ezekiel 37; Asarah Maamaros, Chakor Din V:7 — the Valley of Weeping and revival through the righteous: Eruvin identifies those ‘passing through the Valley of Weeping’ with persons then liable in Gehinnom, whom Avraham raises and receives. The Asarah Maamaros expands that image: the righteous pass through Gehinnom, their tears turn the valley into a spring, the ash is ‘fit for kneading,’ and the waters or dew of resurrection restore the lost. Its model also invokes Ezekiel, who was led around the dry bones before they lived. Rav Tzadok accepts the central idea of revival through the righteous because Tanna d’vei Eliyahu states it explicitly, while questioning why the righteous must travel there according to the Asarah Maamaros’ own reading that the wind has already carried the ash to the righteous. His final praise marks independent convergence upon the same teaching, not proof that the Asarah Maamaros had cited that midrash.
וְלֹא מַיְיתֵי דִּבְרֵי הַתַּנָּא דְּבֵי אֵלִיָּהוּ רַבָּה הַנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל דִּמְפוֹרָשׁ כֵּן, וְזָכָה לְכַוֵּון הָאֱמֶת מֵעַצְמוֹ:
and he did not cite the words of Tanna D'vei Eliyahu Rabbah mentioned above where this is explicit, having merited to perceive the truth on his own!

items.h: The theme: The fire of Gehinnom holds no dominion over the essential soul-root of Israel. The fire of Gehinnom exists to eradicate absolute evil, consuming the root and branch of the nations like thorns burned in fire (Yeshayah 33:12). But regarding Israel, it is written: "Let sins cease (yitamu chata'im), not sinners (chot'im)" (Berachos 10a). The soul-root of every Jew remains cleaved unto the Living God ("for the portion of Hashem is His people", Devarim 32:9). When Hoshea was told to exchange Israel, Hashem answered: "They are My children, the children of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov" (Pesachim 87a). A Jew's sins originate merely from the thorns that surround the rose (as'a v'shoshana)—the yetzer crouching at the doorway of the heart (Bereishis 4:7). Although the yetzer enters as a traveler and eventually takes over like a homeowner, the deep root of the Jewish heart remains pure.

p: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מַה דְּ״אֵין אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׁוֹלֵט״ צָרִיךְ בֵּיאוּר, דְּאַף דְּחוֹזְרִין לָקוּם הוּא עַל יְדֵי תְּפִלַּת הַצַּדִּיקִים, אֲבָל אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם שׂוֹרַפְתָּן לְגַמְרֵי

And nevertheless, that the fire of Gehinnom "has no dominion" requires explanation: for even though they rise again, that is through the prayer of the righteous, whereas the fire of Gehinnom burns them completely!
וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר: דִּבְלָאו הָכִי קָשֶׁה מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּעֵירוּבִין שָׁם] לְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דִּקְרָא ״וְאִשָּׁם לֹא תִכְבֶּה״ בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

And one can say: regardless, it is difficult what they answered [in Eruvin 19a] to defend Reish Lakish, that the verse "their fire shall not be quenched" speaks of the sinners of the nations of the world;
וַהֲרֵי בַּבָּרַיְיתָא [דְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה שָׁם] מְפוֹרָשׁ דְּהוּא בְּמִינִין וְכוּלֵיהּ, וּכְגוֹן יָרָבְעָם מֵרִשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל הַחוֹטְאִים בְּאוֹתָן דְּבָרִים, וְלֹא בְּאוּמּוֹת

when behold, in the Baraisa [Rosh Hashanah 17a] it is explicit that this verse applies to heretics, such as Jeroboam among the wicked of Israel who sinned in these matters, and not to gentiles!1200Rosh Hashanah 17a: “The sinners of Israel with their bodies and the sinners of the nations of the world with their bodies descend to Gehinnom and are judged there twelve months; after twelve months their body is consumed and their soul is burned and a wind scatters them beneath the soles of the feet of the righteous, as it says: ‘and you shall trample the wicked, for they shall be ashes beneath the soles of your feet.’ But the heretics and the informers and the epikorsim, who denied the Torah, and who denied the resurrection of the dead, and who separated from the ways of the community, and who cast their terror in the land of the living, and who sinned and caused the public to sin — like Yaravam ben Nevat and his fellows — descend to Gehinnom and are judged there for generations of generations, as it says: ‘and they shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who transgressed against Me, etc.’; Gehinnom is consumed and they are not consumed, as it says: ‘and their form is for Sheol to consume.’”
תּוּ יֵשׁ לְדַקְדֵּק מַה שֶּׁמּוּבָא [בְּעֵירוּבִין] שֶׁהִקְשָׁה ״דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ״, מַה עִנְיָן לְהַעֲמִיד בְּקוּשְׁיָאתָם מִדְּרָשַׁת רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ דְּ״פָּשְׁעֵי וְאָזְלֵי״
Furthermore, one must scrutinize the Talmudic question in Eruvin challenging "Reish Lakish against Reish Lakish": why frame the difficulty from Reish Lakish's exposition that they continuously sin,
וְאֵין הַקּוּשְׁיָא מִזֶּה רַק מִגּוּפֵיהּ דִּקְרָא מֵ״אִשָּׁם לֹא תִכְבֶּה״, וַהֲוָה לֵיהּ לוֹמַר רַק ״קָשֶׁה אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ״
when the question derives not from that teaching, but from the verse itself, "their fire shall not be quenched," so the Gemara should simply have said: "This is difficult against Reish Lakish"?

[1201Eruvin 19a: “R’ Yehoshua ben Levi said: what is [the meaning of] that which is written (Tehillim 84): ‘those who pass through the valley of weeping make it a spring; the early rain also covers it with blessings [moreh]’? ‘Those who pass [ovrei]’ — these are people who transgress the will of the Holy One; ‘the valley [emek]’ — that they deepen Gehinnom for them; ‘the weeping [ha-bacha]’ — that they weep and shed tears like a spring of the deep; ‘the early rain also covers it with blessings’ — that they justify upon themselves the judgment and say before Him: Master of the world, You judged well, You acquitted well, You condemned well, and You established Gehinnom well for the wicked and Gan Eden for the righteous. Is that so? But R’ Shimon ben Lakish said: the wicked, even at the entrance of Gehinnom, do not repent, as it says: ‘and they shall go out and look upon the corpses of the men who transgressed against Me, etc.’ — ‘who transgressed’ is not said, but rather ‘the transgressors [ha-poshim],’ [implying] that they transgress and go on forever. It is no difficulty: this (justifying the judgment) [refers to] the sinners of Israel; that (continuing to transgress) [refers to] the sinners of the idolaters. So too it is reasonable — for if not, there is a difficulty [of] Reish Lakish upon Reish Lakish” (Rashi: “for if so — since Reish Lakish establishes this verse, ‘their fire shall not be extinguished,’ regarding the sinners of Israel, [it is] a difficulty of his upon his own”). The continuation of the Gemara is cited in note 57.וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״שֶׁאִם כֵּן״: וְהָא דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מוֹקֵי וְכוּלֵיהּ, וְאֵינוֹ מוּבָן, דְּהָא בְּדִבְרֵי רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אֵין רְאָיָה בְּאֵיזֶה פּוֹשְׁעִים קָאֵי אִם הוּא בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דַּוְוקָא]

[and see Rashi there (s.v. she'im kein): that Reish Lakish established his teaching upon the sinners of Israel, which is difficult to understand, for in the words of Reish Lakish there is no proof regarding which sinners he spoke, whether specifically Jewish sinners];
וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לְהַקְשׁוֹת ״דְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אַדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ״ רַק אִם הַקּוּשְׁיָא מִדְּרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
and it is unfitting to formulate a contradiction between two statements of Reish Lakish unless the difficulty is derived from Reish Lakish's own words!
וְנִרְאֶה דְּפֵירוּשׁ ״אֵין שׁוֹלֵט בָּהֶם״ הַיְינוּ בְּעַצְמִיּוּתוֹ וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹ אֵין לוֹ שׁוּם שְׁלִיטָה כְּלָל, וַאֲפִילּוּ לְהַכְאִיב לוֹ

Rather, it appears that the explanation of "the fire has no dominion over them" means that over the essential core and soul-root of a Jew the fire has no dominion whatsoever, not even to afflict him with pain;1202Chagigah 27a - 'the fire of Gehinnom has no power over the sinners of Israel': Reish Lakish derives this teaching from the golden altar: although its gold coating was only the thickness of a dinar and fire burned upon it for many years, the fire did not master it; all the more so the 'empty ones' of Israel, who are nevertheless filled with mitzvos like a pomegranate. Read literally and in isolation, the statement sounds like complete immunity. Rosh Hashanah 17a, however, still assigns bodily sinners of Israel a period of judgment. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes between punishment that burns away acquired evil and dominion over the person's essential root: the fire may affect what surrounds or conceals the root, but it cannot possess or extinguish the covenantal core. That reconciliation is Rav Tzadok's synthesis; Chagigah itself does not spell out this distinction.
וְעִיקַּר אוּר שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם הוּא לְכַלּוֹת וּלְבַעֵר הָרָע מִן הָעוֹלָם
for the primary purpose of the fire of Gehinnom is to consume and eradicate evil from the world;

וְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם ״קוֹצִים כְּסוּחִים״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ל״ג:י״ב) מִשָּׁרְשָׁם וּבָאֵשׁ יִצַּתּוּ, ״לִהַט אֹתָם הַיּוֹם הַבָּא... אֲשֶׁר לֹא יַעֲזֹב לָהֶם שֹׁרֶשׁ וְעָנָף״ (מַלְאָכִי ג:יט), שֶׁיִּכְלוּ וִיבוֹעֲרוּ לְגַמְרֵי

and the nations of the world are "as thorns cut down" (Yeshayah 33:12) from their very root, ignited in fire: "the day that comes shall burn them up... that it shall leave them neither root nor branch" (Malachi 3:19), being entirely consumed and eradicated.1203Isaiah 33:12 and Malachi 3:19-21 - cut thorns, consuming fire, and 'root and branch': Isaiah describes peoples becoming like burnings of lime and like cut thorns kindled in fire. Malachi depicts the coming day burning the arrogant and evildoers like stubble, leaving neither root nor branch, while the righteous tread the wicked as ash. Rav Tzadok combines these prophetic images into a contrast between evil that is uprooted at its source and the sins of Israel that can be burned away while a good root remains. The verses themselves speak in broad prophetic language; their assignment to the precise metaphysical categories developed here is Rav Tzadok's interpretive construction.
אֲבָל בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, ״יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים״ כְּתִיב, וְלֹא ״חוֹטְאִים״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת י׳ רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]
But regarding the sinners of Israel, "Let sins cease" is written (Tehillim 104:35), and not "sinners," as they expounded [in Berachos 10a];
כִּי שׁוֹרֶשׁ כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל דְּבוּקִים בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים, שֶׁ״חֵלֶק ה׳ עַמּוֹ״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ב:ט׳)

for the root of all the souls of Israel is cleaved unto the Living God, for "the portion of Hashem is His people" (Devarim 32:9);1204Berakhot 10a; Maharsha, Chiddushei Aggados - 'sins' rather than 'sinners': When Rabbi Meir prayed that violent neighbors should die, Beruriah directed him to the wording 'let chata'im cease,' not 'let chot'im cease,' and to the continuation, 'and the wicked will be no more.' He therefore prayed for them to repent, and they did. Maharsha explains that chata'im can be read as the sins themselves, so that the persons remain alive while their wrongdoing ends. Rav Tzadok extends that derashah into an account of identity: once the sins are removed, the hidden good root is revealed and the person is no longer a rasha. The Gemara's explicit teaching concerns prayer and teshuvah; the language of an indestructible spiritual root is Rav Tzadok's further theological application.

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין ל״ו עַמּוּד א׳] דַּאֲפִילּוּ לֵית בְּהוּ הֵימָנוּתָא וּפָלְחֵי לַעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה, דְּיֵאָמֵר לָהֶם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א), וּלְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן כְּאִלּוּ אֵינָם עַמּוֹ

and as they stated [in Kiddushin 36a] that even when they lack faith and worship idols, where it is said of them "you are not My people" (Hoshea 1:9), appearing outwardly as if they are not His people;
שֶׁהֵם חֵלֶק ה׳, מַאֲמִינִים בְּנֵי מַאֲמִינִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת צ״ז רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]
in truth they remain the portion of Hashem, believers the descendants of believers, as they stated [in Shabbos 97a];
וְזֶרַע יַעֲקֹב מִטָּתוֹ שְׁלֵימָה, שֶׁאֵין בְּלִבָּם אֶלָּא אֶחָד כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּפְסָחִים נ״ו עַמּוּד א׳]

and the seed of Yaakov whose bed is complete have in their hearts nothing other than the One, as they stated [in Pesachim 56a].1205Cf. Kiddushin 36a — the source R’ Tzadok cites: the dispute whether “you are children [banim atem] to Hashem your God” applies unconditionally — R’ Meir holding “whether you conduct yourselves as children or not, you are called children” — which R’ Tzadok reads together with Hoshea (that even when Israel are called “not My people,” the root of their souls, “believers, sons of believers,” is never severed).1206Shabbat 97a; Pesachim 56a and 87a-b - believers, one heart, and children who cannot be exchanged: The Holy One rebukes Moshe for suspecting Israel and calls them 'believers, children of believers.' Yaakov's sons declare, 'Just as there is only One in your heart, so there is only One in our hearts.' In the Hoshea passage, after the prophet suggests replacing Israel with another nation, God teaches him through his own family that Israel remain 'My children, the children of My tested ones, the children of Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov,' and requires him to seek mercy for them. Rav Tzadok joins these distinct sugyos to the preceding Kiddushin teaching as cumulative evidence that visible estrangement and even idolatry do not sever the deepest covenantal bond. Each passage has its own immediate context; the unified doctrine of a permanently attached soul-root is his synthesis.
דְּהוֹשֵׁעַ קְרָאָם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ בִּשְׁבִיל שֶׁאָמְרוּ לוֹ: ״הַחֲלִיפֵם בְּאוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת״, כְּמוֹ שֶׁמּוּבָא [שָׁם פ״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]
For Hoshea designated them "not My people" because when told to prophesy he said: "Exchange them for another nation," as related [in Pesachim 87a];
שֶׁהָיָה סָבוּר שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לְנַתֵּק שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַיַּהֲדוּת עַל יְדֵי רִיבּוּי הַחֲטָאִים חַס וְשָׁלוֹם
because he presumed that it was possible to sever the name of Israel and the root of Judaism through the multitude of sins, God forbid;
עַד שֶׁאָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא: ״בָּנַי הֵם, בְּנֵי בְּחוּנַי וְכוּלֵיהּ״, וְשֶׁיְּבַקֵּשׁ רַחֲמִים לְבַטֵּל הַגְּזֵירוֹת שֶׁבִּשְׁבִילוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם עַמּוּד ב׳]

until the Holy One, blessed be He, said to him: "They are My children, the descendants of My beloved ones, Avraham, Yitzchak, and Yaakov," commanding him to plead for mercy to annul the decrees brought about through him, as they related [ibid. 87b];
כִּי כַּאֲשֶׁר הַצַּדִּיק שֶׁבַּדּוֹר לְמַטָּה מַסְכִּים לְמִדַּת הַדִּין הַמְקַטְרֶגֶת, נִסְתַּתְּמוּ טַעֲנַת מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים וְנִגְמַר הַדִּין, וּמִצַּד מִדַּת הַדִּין הָיָה כֵּן

for when the leading tzaddik of the generation below consents to the prosecuting Attribute of Judgment, the pleas of the Attribute of Mercy are sealed and judgment is decreed, and from the perspective of strict justice it was indeed so;
אֲבָל בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת מִדַּת הָרַחֲמִים הִשִּׂיג דִּ״בִמְקוֹם אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר [לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם בְּנֵי אֵל חָי]״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א)

but through the awakening of the Attribute of Mercy he perceived that "in the place where it was said unto them: 'You are not My people,' it shall be said unto them: 'You are the sons of the living God'" (Hoshea 2:1);
דְּכַאֲשֶׁר יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים, וּרְשָׁעִים עוֹד אֵינָם, וְנִשְׁאָר הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַטּוֹב
that when sins cease, the wicked are no more, and the holy root remains.
כִּי כָּל חֲטָאֵיהֶם הֵם רַק מִצַּד הַהוֹצֵי וְחוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים לְאָסָא וְשׁוֹשַׁנָּה
For all their sins stem merely from the brambles and thorns that encircle the myrtle and the rose (Vayikra Rabbah 23:3);
וְיֵצֶר הָרָע יוֹשֵׁב עַל ב׳ מִפְתְּחֵי הַלֵּב בַּפְּתִיחָה וּבַהַתְחָלָה, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״לַפֶּתַח חַטָּאת רֹבֵץ״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ד:ז)
and the yetzer hara perches at the two entrances of the heart at the threshold and inception of action, as it is said: "sin couches at the door" (Bereishis 4:7);
וְהַצַּדִּיקִים שֶׁלִּבָּם בִּרְשׁוּתָן אֵין מַנִּיחִין אוֹתוֹ לִיכָּנֵס
and the righteous whose heart is under their sovereignty (Bereishis Rabbah 34:10) do not permit it to enter;
וְהָרְשָׁעִים הֵן בִּרְשׁוּת לִבָּם, שֶׁכֵּיוָן שֶׁנִּכְנַס, אַף שֶׁתְּחִלָּתוֹ הֵלֶךְ וְאוֹרֵחַ, בַּסּוֹף נַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת
whereas the wicked are under the sovereignty of their heart, so that once it enters, though initially it behaves like a wayfarer and guest, in the end it becomes the master of the house (Sukkah 52b),
שֶׁמְּמַלֵּא כָּל חַדְרֵי הַלֵּב עַד שֶׁשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַטּוֹב נֶעְלָם לְגַמְרֵי, וְנַעֲשָׂה הוּא בַּעַל הַבַּיִת וּכְאִלּוּ שָׁרְשׁוֹ רָע:
filling all the chambers of the heart until the holy root of goodness is completely concealed, and the yetzer dominates the house as if the person's root were entirely evil.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים פ׳–פ״ג

The theme: The distinction between those who forfeit their share in the World to Come and the intrinsic sanctity of the Jewish soul. All Israel possesses a portion in the World to Come because "Your people are all righteous" (Yeshayah 60:21). Those enumerated in the Mishnah as lacking a portion are not excluded as exceptions from the general rule of Israel; rather, their profound sins caused the "lamp of Hashem, the soul of man" (ner Hashem nishmas adam) to become obscured, as sin progressively extinguishes the lamp of mitzvah until one reaches total idolatry and uproots his manifest Jewishness. Yet in the Future, Mashiach ben David will eradicate the root of evil and death stemming from the Serpent, revealing that all sins derived merely from the surrounding defilement and not from the soul's essential root, restoring the primordial light of Creation to all.

p: וְהֵן הֵם אוֹתָם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

And they are those who have no portion in the World to Come;1207Sukkah 52b - the yetzer as traveler, guest, and master of the house: Rava reads Nasan's parable to David as a progression: at first the yetzer hara is called a helekh, a passing traveler; afterward an ore'ach, a guest; and finally an ish, the established man of the house. Rav Tzadok uses this progression to explain how repeated consent allows an initially external impulse to fill the chambers of the heart until the good root is completely hidden and the evil appears to be the person's very essence. The Gemara supplies the psychological progression; the conclusion that this produces the appearance of an evil root and the category of 'no share in the World to Come' is Rav Tzadok's application here.
וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים וְגוֹמֵר״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ס:כא)
whereas all Israel have a portion in the World to Come, for "Your people also shall be all righteous, etc." (Yeshayah 60:21);
וְעַל כֵּן אוֹתָם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא הֵם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ וְאֵינָם בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
and therefore those who have no portion in the World to Come are categorized as "not My people" (Hoshea 1:9) and are not included in the general rule of Israel;
דְּעַל כֵּן לֹא אָמְרוּ ״חוּץ מֵאֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם וְכוּלֵיהּ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁמּוּבָא בְּכָל מָקוֹם דְּחָשְׁבִינַן כְּלָל וּמוֹצִיא אֵיזֶה מֵהַכְּלָל

which is why the Mishnah did not state "except for these who do not have, etc.," as is found in every other place where the Tannaim state a general rule and exclude specific exceptions from the rule;1208Sanhedrin 90a, Mishnah: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says (Yeshayah 60): ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory.’ And these are the ones who have no share in the World to Come: one who says there is no resurrection of the dead from the Torah, and [one who says] there is no Torah from Heaven, and an epikoros. R’ Akiva says: also one who reads the external books, and one who whispers over a wound and says ‘all the illness that I placed in Egypt I will not place upon you, for I am Hashem your healer.’ Abba Shaul says: also one who pronounces the [Divine] Name by its letters.”1209Sanhedrin 90a - 'All Israel' and 'these have no share': The Mishnah first states the universal rule, 'All Israel have a share in the World to Come,' and then introduces the listed cases with ve'elu she'ein lahem, 'and these are the ones who have no share.' Rav Tzadok makes a precise inference from the fact that it does not say chutz me'elu, 'except these': the second clause is not a simple external exception cut away from Israel's essential covenant, but describes persons in whom sin has concealed the aspect by which they are counted as His people and inheritance. When that concealment is removed, the universal opening can again be revealed. This grammatical-ontological distinction is Rav Tzadok's interpretation; the Mishnah itself states the rule and the exclusion without explaining their reconciliation.
אֲבָל אֵלּוּ אֵינָם מוּצָאִים מֵהַכְּלָל, דְּמִי שֶׁהוּא מִכְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהֵם עַמּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ וְנַחֲלָתוֹ, אִי אֶפְשָׁר שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

rather, these individuals are not excluded exceptions from the rule, for whoever belongs to the collective of Israel—who are His people, blessed be He, and His inheritance—it is impossible that he should lack a portion in the World to Come.
אֲבָל אֵלּוּ חֲטָאֵיהֶם גָּרְמוּ, דְּ״נֵר ה׳ נִשְׁמַת אָדָם״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ:כז), שֶׁהוּא הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּ״צוּר לְבָבִי וְגוֹמֵר״ (תְּהִלִּים ע״ג:כ״ו), שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לִבָּן שֶׁל יִשְׂרָאֵל

However, regarding these individuals, their sins caused that "the spirit of man is the lamp of Hashem" (Mishlei 20:27)—which is the inner root of "God is the rock of my heart, etc." (Tehillim 73:26), the Holy One, blessed be He, being the heart of Israel (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2)—
נֶאֱפַל וְנֶחְשַׁךְ עַל יְדֵי עֲבֵירָה שֶׁמְּכַבָּה נֵר מִצְוָה הַמְּאִירָה לְהַצִּיל מִן הַחֵטְא

became darkened and obscured through sin, which extinguishes the lamp of mitzvah that shines to save a person from sin;1210Proverbs 20:27; Psalms 73:26; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2:1; Sotah 21a - the soul-lamp, Israel's heart, and the mitzvah-lamp: Proverbs calls the human soul 'the lamp of Hashem,' while the psalmist calls God 'the Rock of my heart and my portion forever.' Shir HaShirim Rabbah explicitly asks where the Holy One is called 'the heart of Israel' and answers from that verse. Sotah distinguishes the temporary protection of a mitzvah, compared to a lamp, from the enduring light of Torah, and adds that a transgression can extinguish a mitzvah but cannot extinguish Torah. Rav Tzadok combines these sources into layered imagery: sin can darken the operative mitzvah-lamp and hide the inward divine root, but it does not prove that the root itself has ceased to exist.
כִּי עֲבֵירָה הַגּוֹרֶרֶת עֲבֵירָה כְּדַרְכּוֹ שֶׁל יֵצֶר הָרָע: הַיּוֹם אוֹמֵר עֲשֵׂה כָּךְ, וּמָחָר וְכוּלֵיהּ
for sin draws another sin in the manner of the yetzer hara: today it tells him, "Do this," and tomorrow it tells him, "Do that" (Shabbos 105b),
וְעַד שֶׁאוֹמֵר לוֹ ״לֵךְ עֲבוֹד עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה״ שֶׁהוּא עֲקִירַת הַיַּהֲדוּת לְגַמְרֵי
until it eventually says to him, "Go and serve idols," which is the total uprooting of Judaism;
דִּ״יהוּדִי״ נִקְרָא עַל שֵׁם הַכְּפִירָה בַּעֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְגִלָּה י״ג רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]
for a "Jew" (Yehudi) is defined specifically by the repudiation of idolatry, as they stated [in Megillah 13a];
כִּי לָמוּד הוּא אוֹתוֹ הַשֵּׁבֶט לְבַעֵר עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה צ״ט]

for that tribe [Yehudah] was habituated to eradicate idolatry, as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 99:8];1211Shabbat 105b; Megillah 13a; Bereishit Rabbah 94:3 - the yetzer's progression and the name Yehudi: Shabbat describes the craft of the evil inclination: today it tells a person to do one thing, tomorrow another, until it tells him to worship idolatry; the Gemara identifies the 'foreign god' within the body with the yetzer hara. Megillah teaches that anyone who repudiates idolatry is called a Yehudi, explaining why Mordechai from Binyamin bears that title. The standard citation for this teaching is Megillah 13a, notwithstanding the parenthetical 17a in the present text. Bereishit Rabbah relates that idolatrous images were engraved on Pharaoh's wagons, Yehudah burned them, and 'that tribe was accustomed to burn idolatry.' Rav Tzadok uses this cluster to make resistance to idolatry the defining root of Yehudah and, through the name Yehudi, of Jewish identity.
וְעַל כֵּן מָשִׁיחַ בֶּן דָּוִד מִזַּרְעוֹ, שֶׁהוּא יְבַעֵר כָּל שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע מִן הָעוֹלָם
and therefore Mashiach ben David descends from his seed, for he will eradicate the entire root of evil from the world,
עַד שֶׁיְּבֻלַּע גַּם הַמָּוֶת הַבָּא מִזּוּהֲמַת נָחָשׁ, שֶׁהוּא הַתְחָלַת שׁוֹרֶשׁ זוּהֲמַת הָרָע בָּאָדָם, שֶׁלֹּא יִרְבַּץ עוֹד גַּם אֵצֶל הַפֶּתַח

until death itself—which originated from the defilement of the Serpent, the initial root of evil within man—is swallowed up forever (Yeshayah 25:8), so that sin shall no longer couch at the door.1212Shabbat 146a; Isaiah 25:8; Genesis 4:7 - serpent-contamination, death, and sin at the entrance: The Aggadah in Shabbat says that the serpent introduced contamination into Chavah and that Israel's contamination ceased at Sinai. Isaiah promises that God will 'swallow death forever,' while the warning to Kayin depicts sin as crouching at the entrance, desiring to master the person. Rav Tzadok joins these images into a single account of evil as an attached pollution whose first human root is the serpent and whose final expression is death. His further claim that Mashiach ben David will eradicate that entire root, so that it no longer crouches even at the entrance, is a theological synthesis of these passages rather than the explicit statement of any one of them.
וְאָז יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ, כִּי כָּל הַחֲטָאִים כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ
And then "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none" (Yirmeyah 50:20), for all sins will be made as white as snow (Yeshayah 1:18),
כַּאֲשֶׁר יִתְגַּלֶּה שֶׁהַכֹּל הָיָה רַק בְּסִיבַּת הַיֵּצֶר וְהַזּוּהֲמָא הַסּוֹבֶבֶת וְלֹא מֵעֶצֶם שָׁרְשָׁם
when it is revealed that everything occurred solely due to the external incitement of the yetzer and the surrounding defilement, and not from the essence of their soul-root;
וּכְשֶׁיְּבוֹעַר זֶה, יַחֲזוֹר לְהָאִיר נֵרוֹ כִּבְרִאשׁוֹנָה
and when this defilement is eradicated, his lamp will shine once again as at the beginning;
וְהוּא הָאוֹר שֶׁל שֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית הַגָּנוּז לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא, שֶׁיִּהְיוּ כוּלָּם צַדִּיקִים, דְּאָז יִתְגַּלּוּ עִנְיָנָם הַכֹּל שֶׁהוּא כֵּן:

and this is the primordial Light of the six days of Creation concealed for the righteous in the Future, when they will all be righteous, for at that time the true reality of all their matters will be revealed to be so.1213R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §9): “‘your people are all righteous’ — the guardians of the covenant, for they are all called by [His name].” Exactly the se’if: “all Israel have a share in the World to Come, for ‘your people are all righteous.’”1214Jeremiah 50:20; Isaiah 1:18; Chagigah 12a - vanished iniquity, whitening, and the concealed primordial light: Jeremiah foretells a time when Israel's iniquity will be sought and will not be found, because God will pardon the remnant; Isaiah says that sins red as scarlet can become white as snow. Chagigah teaches that the light created on the first day allowed vision from one end of the world to the other, was concealed from corrupt generations, and was stored for the righteous in the future. Rav Tzadok links these teachings: when the surrounding corruption is removed, the original lamp shines again and the hidden first light reveals the truth of 'your people are all righteous.' Chagigah itself does not identify the primordial light with each person's restored soul-lamp; that identification is Rav Tzadok's application here.

items.h: The theme: The perspective of the Dorshei Reshumos on the remnant spark (reshimu) and the prophecy of Balaam. In this world, the full light of Mashiach remains hidden; yet the ancient allegorical masters (Dorshei Reshumos) perceived the indelible holy imprint (reshimu) that endures within even the most degraded sinners, just as a decaying body in the grave retains the bone of luz from which it will rise at the Resurrection. Balaam recognized this distinction ("Who has counted the dust of Jacob, or numbered the fourth part of Israel?", Bamidbar 23:10), realizing that in every reproductive drop of an Israelite there is an element called "tzaddik." In Israel, a mitzvah performed for selfish benefit still renders a person completely righteous (Rosh Hashanah 4a), whereas among gentiles, lack of pure intent taints the deed (Bava Batra 10b).

p: וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהַשִּׂיג זֶה, שֶׁעֲדַיִין אֵין הִתְגַּלּוּת מֵאוֹרוֹ שֶׁל מָשִׁיחַ
And in this world it is impossible to perceive this, for as yet there is no open manifestation of the light of Mashiach;
רַק דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת אָמְרוּ שֶׁכּוּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
only the Dorshei Reshumos stated that all of them possess a portion in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 104b),
שֶׁהֵם הִשִּׂיגוּ רְשִׁימוּ הַנִּשְׁאָר מֵאוֹר הַנִּיתָּק מֵהֶם עַל יְדֵי תֹּקֶף הַחֲטָאִים הַבָּאִים עַל יְדֵי יֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁנִּתְגַּבֵּר עֲלֵיהֶם

for they perceived the holy impression (reshimu) that remains from the divine light that was severed from them through the intensity of the sins brought about by the yetzer hara that overpowered them;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁמִּגּוּף הָאָדָם, הֲגַם שֶׁיָּשׁוּב אֶל הָאָרֶץ כְּשֶׁהָיָה וְנַעֲשָׂה תַּרְוַוד רָקָב וְעַפְרָא בְּעָלְמָא, הוּא חוֹזֵר וְקָם בִּתְחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים אוֹתוֹ גּוּף עַצְמוֹ
