and just as with the physical body of a person: even though it returns to the earth as it was and turns into a ladleful of dust and earth, that very same body rises again at the Resurrection of the Dead;1215Sanhedrin 90a, Mishnah: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says (Yeshayah 60): ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory.’ And these are the ones who have no share in the World to Come: one who says there is no resurrection of the dead from the Torah, and [one who says] there is no Torah from Heaven, and an epikoros. R’ Akiva says: also one who reads the external books, and one who whispers over a wound and says ‘all the illness that I placed in Egypt I will not place upon you, for I am Hashem your healer.’ Abba Shaul says: also one who pronounces the [Divine] Name by its letters.”1216Sanhedrin 104b; Bamidbar Rabbah 14:1 - the dorshei reshumos and the explicit exclusion of Bilaam: The Bavli passage in which the dorshei reshumos derive from Tehillim 60 that the listed kings and commoners ultimately enter the World to Come appears on Sanhedrin 104b, not 94b as printed in the bracketed citation here. The Bavli's exposition names Achav, Menasheh, Yaravam, Achitofel, Geichazi, and Doeg, but does not include Bilaam. Bamidbar Rabbah makes the limitation explicit: 'All of them have a share in the World to Come except Bilaam.' Rav Tzadok reads this omission as substantive: the Jewish sinners retain a surviving reshimu of their original good root, whereas Bilaam's evil is described as rooted in his very source rather than as a foreign layer that can be removed.1217Mishnah Oholos 2:2; Sanhedrin 91b - complete decay and resurrection of the same embodied person: The halachic term melo tarvad rakav, a ladleful of human decay, describes the residue of a corpse after the flesh has decomposed. Sanhedrin teaches that at judgment God returns the soul to the body and judges them together, and it derives from 'I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal' that just as wounding and healing occur in one person, death and revival occur in one person. The same sugya says that the resurrected arise with their former bodily defects and are then healed. These teachings support Rav Tzadok's analogy: physical dissolution does not mean replacement by a different person; the original embodied identity is reconstituted. His comparison of that continuity to a spiritual reshimu is a further mystical application.
וְעַל זֶה אָמַר אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע: ״מִי מָנָה עֲפַר יַעֲקֹב וּמִסְפָּר אֶת רֹבַע [יִשְׂרָאֵל]״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ״ג:י׳)
and concerning this that wicked one [Balaam] said: "Who has counted the dust of Jacob, or numbered the fourth part of Israel?" (Bamidbar 23:10),
כִּי הוּא הִשִּׂיג מַעֲלַת פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
for he grasped the inner elevation of the sinners of Israel and of those who lack a portion in the World to Come,
דְּיֵשׁ לָהֶם קְצָת שַׁיָּיכוּת עִם מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ שֶׁגַּם הוּא נִמְנָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה עִם אוֹתָם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
who possess a certain affinity with his own level, since he too is enumerated in the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a) among those who have no portion in the World to Come.
אֲבָל דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת לֹא דָּרְשׁוּ עָלָיו, כִּי הוּא לֹא נִכְלַל עִמָּהֶם
But the Dorshei Reshumos did not apply their homily to him, for he was not included with them;
וּבְבַמִּדְבַּר רַבָּה [רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה י״ד] מְפוֹרָשׁ ״חוּץ מִבִּלְעָם״
and in Bamidbar Rabbah [14:1] it is explicit: "except for Balaam";
כִּי הוּא שָׁרְשׁוֹ רַע וְלֹא שֶׁנִּיתַּק מִמֶּנּוּ, וְלֹא נִמְצָא בּוֹ רְשִׁימוּ כְּלָל
for his very root is evil, and not that the light was merely severed from him, possessing no holy reshimu whatsoever.
וְהוּא הִכִּיר מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּהּ: ״דְּמֵרֹאשׁ צֻרִים אֶרְאֶנּוּ״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ״ג:ט׳), מֵהַתְחָלַת הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ דְּ״צוּר לְבָבִי וְחֶלְקָם ה׳״

And he recognized the supreme quality of Israel therein: "For from the top of the rocks I see him" (Bamidbar 23:9), looking from the inception of the root of "the rock of my heart and their portion is Hashem,"
שֶׁאַף שֶׁהִגְדִּילוּ עֲווֹנוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב לֹא נִיתַּק לְגַמְרֵי
that even when they multiplied iniquities, the good root was never completely severed;
וְעַל כֵּן: ״מָה אֶקֹּב לֹא קַבֹּה אֵל״ (שָׁם:ח׳), וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: אַף בִּזְמַן שֶׁהָיָה רְאוּיִם לִקְלָלָה
and therefore: "How shall I curse, whom God has not cursed?" (ibid. 23:8), which the Sages expounded: even at a time when they were deserving of a curse (Sanhedrin 105b);
״כִּי לֹא הִבִּיט אָוֶן וְגוֹמֵר״ (בַּמִּדְבָּר כ״ג:כ״א), דְּזֶהוּ אֲפִילּוּ שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם עָמָל וְאָוֶן
"He has not beheld iniquity in Jacob, neither has He seen perverseness in Israel" (ibid. 23:21), meaning even when iniquity and trouble are present within them.
וְהָא כְּשֶׁיּוֹרְדִים דְּיוֹרְדִים עַד לֶעָפָר שֶׁהוּא הַיְרִידָה לַמַּדְרֵיגָה הַיּוֹתֵר תַּחְתּוֹנָה

And when they descend into sin, they descend unto the dust, which is the lowest possible level;1218Bamidbar 23:8-10, 21; Berachos 7a - Bilaam's oracle and Rav Tzadok's inward reading: The Torah places together Bilaam's declarations 'How can I curse whom God has not cursed?', 'from the top of the rocks I see him,' 'who has counted the dust of Yaakov,' and 'He has not beheld iniquity in Yaakov.' Berachos explains the first statement historically: God did not express the moment of anger during Bilaam's mission, so his intended curse had no opening. Rav Tzadok reads the same oracle on an additional inward plane. The 'rocks' signify Israel's primordial root, the 'dust' the lowest possible descent, and 'He has not beheld iniquity' does not deny actual sin; it means that sin does not wholly sever the good root. This ontological reading is Rav Tzadok's synthesis of the verses, not the plain explanation of the Bavli.
וְגַם זֶה ״מִי מָנָה... וְסָפַר רִבְעִיָּיתֵיהֶם״, וְאָמְרוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה: טִיפָּה לְהַצְדִּיק מִצַּד ״וְעַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״

and regarding this too: "Who has counted... or numbered their cohabitations (riv'eihem)?", which the Sages expounded: that Hashem scrutinizes the seminal drop to declare it righteous (Niddah 31a), because "Your people are all righteous";
וּבְכָל רֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ טִיפָּה הַנִּקְרָא ״צַדִּיק״, דְּעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִסְמֵית עֵינוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע וְכוּלֵיהּ
and in every cohabitation of an Israelite there is a drop termed "tzaddik," over which revelation the eye of that wicked one was blinded (Niddah 31a).
כִּי זֶהוּ הַהֶבְדֵּל שֶׁבֵּין יִשְׂרָאֵל לָעַמִּים שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה ד׳ עַמּוּד א׳]

For this is the fundamental difference between Israel and the nations of the world that they stated [in Rosh Hashanah 4a]:1219Cf. Niddah 31a — the source R’ Tzadok cites: “the man whose eye is open [shesum]” (Bamidbar 24:3) — one of his eyes was blinded — and the aggadah connects it to his having gazed upon the tents of Israel (“who has counted the dust of Yaakov, and the number of a quarter of Israel”), which R’ Tzadok reads as Bilaam’s perception of the “drop that is called righteous” in every Jew.
דְּעוֹשֶׂה מִצְוָה לְקַבֵּל פְּרָס וּלְהַנָּאַת עַצְמוֹ בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נִקְרָא ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״
one who performs a mitzvah in order to receive a reward and for his own benefit, in an Israelite he is called "a complete tzaddik";
וּבְאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם חָשֵׁיב לֵיהּ הֶחְמִיץ עַל יְדֵי זֶה

whereas among the nations of the world he is considered to have spoiled the deed through this;1220Rosh Hashanah 4a; Bava Basra 10b - a mitzvah performed for personal benefit in Israel and among the nations: Rosh Hashanah rules that a Jew who gives charity so that his children should live or so that he should merit the World to Come is called a complete tzaddik. The Gemara distinguishes Cyrus: a conditional good deed by a Jew remains meritorious because failure of the condition does not cause him to regret serving God, whereas the gentile case may reveal that the act depended entirely on the benefit. Bava Basra develops the other side of the distinction through several readings of 'the kindness of the nations is sin': their charity may be performed to prolong dominion, to obtain glory, or to taunt Israel. Rav Tzadok therefore treats self-interest in Israel as a secondary admixture surrounding a mitzvah-deed, but in the cited gentile cases as an intention that can define the deed itself.
וְכֵן [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּנֶחְשָׁב חֵטְא לָהֶם כְּשֶׁאֵין עוֹשִׂין אֶלָּא לְהִתְגַּדֵּר וְכַדּוֹמֶה, שֶׁאֶצְלָם מַחֲשָׁבָה זוֹ הִיא הָעִיקָּר
and so [in Bava Batra 10b], that it is reckoned a sin for them when they act solely for self-aggrandizement and the like, because with them this selfish thought is the primary essence;

דְּמִטַּעַם זֶה בְּהוּ מַחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה מִצְטָרֵף לְמַעֲשֶׂה וְלֹא טוֹבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [פֶּרֶק א׳ דְּפֵאָה הֲלָכָה ד׳] וְתוֹסָפוֹת [קִדּוּשִׁין ל״ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳], וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל לְהֵיפֶךְ:

for which reason with them an evil thought is combined with deed while a good thought is not, as stated in the Yerushalmi [Peah 1:4] and Tosafos [Kiddushin 39b], whereas with Israel the opposite is true.1221Kiddushin 39b-40a; Yerushalmi Peah 1:1:51 - how thought is joined to deed: The Bavli states that ordinarily God does not join an evil thought to an act, while a thought of idolatry is exceptional because Scripture says that God takes hold of the house of Israel 'in their heart.' It further distinguishes a bad thought that produces fruit from one that never comes to action. The Yerushalmi gives the broader contrast cited by Rav Tzadok: for Israel, a good thought is joined to deed and a bad thought is not; among the nations the pattern is reversed, with a bad thought joined and a good thought not joined. Rav Tzadok uses this Aggadic rule to express the same root distinction as the preceding sources. It is not a general license to ignore intention in practical halachah, where motive can matter in many specific laws.

items.h: The theme: The theological trap of Balaam’s counsel at Shittim. Procreation is a positive commandment; even though the instigation of the Serpent introduces selfish bodily pleasure into intimacy ("in iniquity was I brought forth", Tehillim 51:7), with an Israelite we evaluate the deed itself as a holy mitzvah. Balaam, termed the "flatterer" (machlik lashon), sought to seduce Israel by telling them that sins could never strip them of their sanctity. His trap was to incite them to cohabit with Midianite and Moabite women (bi'as aramis), where the child follows the gentile mother and no holy seed is produced, uprooting the child from Israel and extending a spiritual foreskin over the father. Balaam misled the nations to prostitute their daughters and seduced Zimri into believing that through a "transgression for the sake of Heaven" (aveirah lishmah) they could bring holy seed into the world.

p: וּפְרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה הוּא מִצְוַת עֲשֵׂה
And procreation is a positive commandment;
אֲבָל מִצַּד זוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ אֲפִילּוּ חָסִיד שֶׁבַּחֲסִידִים מִתְכַּוֵּין לְהַנָּאַת עַצְמוֹ
yet on account of the defilement of the Serpent, even the most pious of the pious has some intent for his own pleasure;
וּמִצַּד הַמְשָׁכַת הַזּוּהֲמָא לְכָל הַדּוֹרוֹת דְּ״[הֵן] בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי [אִמִּי]״ (תְּהִלִּים נ״א:ז׳)

and through the transmission of this defilement to all generations, "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Tehillim 51:7);1222Bereishis 1:28; Tehillim 51:7; Yevamos 103b - the mitzvah of procreation and the serpent's contamination: The Torah's first command to humanity is 'be fruitful and multiply.' Yevamos teaches, in the Aggadic account of the serpent and Chavah, that the serpent implanted contamination into humanity; Israel's contamination ceased at Sinai, whereas the nations who did not stand at Sinai retained it. The verse 'in iniquity I was formed, and in sin my mother conceived me' describes the frailty accompanying human generation. Rav Tzadok does not treat marital procreation as sinful: the deed remains a positive commandment. His synthesis distinguishes the purified covenantal root revealed at Sinai from the residual bodily impulse toward self-gratification. That admixture can accompany even a mitzvah without redefining the essential deed or the Jewish root.
אֲבָל בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל אָזְלִינַן בָּתַר הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁהוּא מִצְוָה, וְנֶחְשָׁב בָּזֶה ״צַדִּיק גָּמוּר״, וּמִזֶּה נִמְשָׁךְ דְּ״עַמֵּךְ כֻּלָּם צַדִּיקִים״
but with an Israelite we follow the physical deed which is a mitzvah, wherein he is reckoned a complete tzaddik, and from this flows the truth that "Your people are all righteous";
וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים שֶׁנִּמְשְׁכוּ מִצַּד הַזּוּהֲמָא הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִצַּד כַּוָּונַת הֲנָאָה לְגַרְמֵיהּ, אֵינָן נוֹגְעִים לְהַעֶצֶם וְהַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ
and all sins that were drawn from the defilement stemming from self-gratification do not touch the essential core and soul-root.
וְעַל דָּבָר זֶה נִקְרָא אוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע ״מַחֲלִיק לָשׁוֹן״, שֶׁהֱסִיתָם בָּזֶה לְמַעֲשֵׂה דְּשִׁטִּים
And concerning this matter that wicked one was termed "a flatterer of tongue" (Sanhedrin 106a), who incited them through this philosophy to the incident of Shittim;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּדְבָרִים רַבָּה [רֵישׁ פָּרָשָׁה ב׳] שֶׁזֶּה הָיָה כָּל כַּוָּונָתוֹ, לְגַלּוֹת לְיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאֲפִילּוּ יַגְדִּילוּ חֲטָאִים לֹא יֹאבְדוּ מַעֲלָתָם

and as they stated in Devarim Rabbah that this was his entire scheme: to reveal to Israel that even if they multiply sins, they will never lose their spiritual distinction;1223Rosh Hashanah 4a; Sanhedrin 90a; Devarim Rabbah 1:2 - the deed, the enduring root, and Bilaam's smooth tongue: Rosh Hashanah calls a Jew who gives charity so that his children should live or so that he should merit the World to Come a 'complete tzaddik'; the self-interested condition does not erase the mitzvah-act. The Mishnah in Sanhedrin introduces the share of all Israel in the World to Come with 'your people are all righteous.' Devarim Rabbah identifies the 'smooth-tongued' man of Mishlei with Bilaam: his flattering prophecies made Israel haughty, and they fell at Shittim. The Midrash states the sequence of flattery, pride, and fall. Rav Tzadok supplies the inner mechanism: Bilaam weaponized the true teaching that Israel's root survives sin, turning assurance of an enduring root into a pretext for recklessness. This does not remove judgment for the deed.
וְזֶה הָיָה הָעֵצָה רָעָה שֶׁלּוֹ, לַהֲסִיתָם עַל יְדֵי זֶה לַחֲטוֹא בְּבִיאַת אֲרַמִּית דִּוְלָדָהּ כְּמוֹתָהּ
and this was his malicious counsel: to entice them through this realization to sin through cohabiting with an Aramean woman, where her offspring possesses her gentile status (Kiddushin 68b);
וּמִטִּיפָּה זוֹ לֹא יֵצֵא זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל וְצַדִּיק כְּלָל, וְאֵין מְקַיֵּים בָּזֶה מִצְוַת פְּרִיָּה וּרְבִיָּה דְּלֹא נִקְרָא זַרְעוֹ
and from this drop no seed of Israel or righteous child will issue at all, failing to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation since the child is not legally attributed to him;
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן טַעַם דְּמִימְשְׁכָא עָרְלָתוֹ, אֲבָל גַּם זֶה אֶצְלוֹ הוּא רַק דְּלָא מַבְשְׁקַר, וְלֹא שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עָרֵל בֶּאֱמֶת חַס וְשָׁלוֹם

and this is likewise the reason that his foreskin is drawn down, though for the Israelite himself this is merely an outward concealment so that Avraham does not recognize him, and not that he becomes an actual uncircumcised gentile, God forbid;
אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם זַרְעוֹ נֶעֱקַר לְגַמְרֵי מִקְּדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל

yet nevertheless his physical seed is totally uprooted from the holiness of Israel.1224Sanhedrin 106a; Kiddushin 68b; Sanhedrin 44a - Bilaam's counsel, maternal lineage, and a drawn foreskin: Sanhedrin attributes the Shittim strategy to Bilaam, who advised exploiting Israel's vulnerability to sexual sin. Kiddushin derives that the child of a non-Jewish woman is not called the Jewish father's son but her son; the offspring follows the mother's status. Rav Tzadok therefore explains the counsel as an attempt to produce descendants outside Jewish lineage, not merely to induce a private transgression. Sanhedrin also describes Achan as one who drew his foreskin, yet the same sugya teaches: 'Even though he sinned, he is Israel.' Rav Tzadok joins these points carefully: the sinner's own covenantal identity is not literally converted into non-Jewish identity, even when the covenant is outwardly obscured, but offspring from this prohibited union is not absorbed into the father's Jewish lineage.
וְהוּא הִתְעָם בְּחַלְקוּת לְשׁוֹנוֹ, שֶׁהוּא חָשַׁב דִּלְעוֹלָם לֹא יֵעָקֵר טִיפָּה הַנִּמְשֶׁכֶת מִקְּדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל מִקְּדֻשָּׁתָהּ
And he deceived them with his smooth tongue, for he claimed that a drop issuing from the holiness of an Israelite could never be severed from its sanctity,
דְּתָלוּי בְּרוֹבַע יִשְׂרָאֵל דְּהָעִיקָּר הוּא מִשְׁפַּחַת אָב, וּדְיִקָּלֵט קְדוּשָׁה עַל יְדֵי זֶה גַּם בַּזֶּרַע שֶׁיּוֹלִידוּ בְּנוֹת הַגּוֹיִם מֵהֶם
arguing that it depends upon the seed of Israel where lineage follows the paternal house, and that holiness would be absorbed through this even into the offspring born of gentile women;
וּבָזֶה הֵסִית גַּם אוֹתָם לְהַפְקִיר בְּנוֹתָם, מַה שֶּׁכְּבָר גָּדְרוּ כָּל הָאוּמּוֹת, כְּדֵי לִקְלוֹט עַל יְדֵי זֶה בְּזַרְעָם קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהוּא כְּמוֹ ״עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ״

and through this he incited the Midianites to prostitute their daughters—breaching the moral fences established by the nations—in order to absorb the sanctity of Israel into their seed, presenting it as "a transgression for the sake of Heaven";

וְכֵן זִמְרִי שֶׁטָּעַן ״בַּת יִתְרוֹ מִי הִתִּיר לְךָ״ (סַנְהֶדְרִין פ״ב עַמּוּד א׳), חָשַׁב שֶׁגַּם הַנּוֹלָדִים מֵאֵלּוּ יֵחָשְׁבוּ עַל זֶרַע יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהוּא בָּא לְהַכְנִיס גַּם מֵהֶם תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי שְׁכִינָה

and so Zimri who challenged Moshe: "Who permitted the daughter of Yisro to you?" (Sanhedrin 82a), thought that the children born of these unions would be reckoned as the seed of Israel, seeking to bring them under the wings of the Shechinah.
וַ״עֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ״ הִיא כְּ״מִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּנָזִיר כ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳]
And "a transgression for the sake of Heaven" is like "a mitzvah not for the sake of Heaven" as they stated [in Nazir 23b];
וּבְיִשְׂרָאֵל אָזְלִינַן בָּתַר הַמַּחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה, וּבָאוּמּוֹת אַחַר מַעֲשֶׂה הָרָע
and with an Israelite we evaluate according to the good internal thought, while with the nations according to the evil outward deed;
הֵיפֶךְ בְּמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ

the opposite of a mitzvah performed for ulterior motives.1225Sanhedrin 82a; Nazir 23b - Zimri's argument and the limits of aveirah lishmah: Sanhedrin records Zimri's challenge to Moshe: 'The daughter of Yisro - who permitted her to you?' The sugya presents this as the defiant argument accompanying Zimri's public act, not as a validated halachic defense; the act remains within the law concerning relations with a non-Jewish woman. Nazir teaches that an aveirah performed for the sake of Heaven can be greater than a mitzvah performed not for its own sake, using Yael as the paradigm, and immediately balances this with the rule that one should engage in Torah and mitzvos even not for their own sake because this can lead to service for its own sake. Rav Tzadok analyzes Zimri's claimed good intention within that conceptual comparison, but the good intention does not authorize the prohibited act or cancel its punishment.
וְהָאוּמּוֹת הֵם מְקַבְּלִים שְׂכַר מִצְוֹת קַלּוֹת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And the nations of the world receive the reward for their minor mitzvos in this world;
וְגַם מַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה שֶׁאֵינָהּ כְּלוּם, מִכָּל מָקוֹם עַל אוֹתָהּ עֲבֵירָה אֵין נֶעֱנָשִׁים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה רַק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
and likewise a good thought which produces nothing tangible, nevertheless for that transgression they are not punished in this world but in the World to Come;
וְאֵין הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מְקַפֵּחַ שְׂכַר מַחֲשָׁבָה טוֹבָה שֶׁלָּהֶם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה מִיהַת, כִּבְמִצְוָה שֶׁלֹּא לִשְׁמָהּ מֵהַמַּחֲשָׁבָה רָעָה בִּשְׁבִיל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה

and the Holy One, blessed be He, does not withhold the reward of their good intention in this world at least, like a mitzvah not for its own sake where the evil intent is rewarded on account of the deed;
וְאֵצֶל יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא בְּהֵיפֶךְ, דַּעֲבֵירָה לִשְׁמָהּ כְּהַאי, עַל הַמַּעֲשֶׂה יֵשׁ עֹונֶשׁ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
whereas with Israel it is the reverse: for such a transgression for the sake of Heaven, there is punishment for the physical act in this world.
וְהוּא וְהֵם שֶׁמְּבַקְּשִׁים רַק טוֹבַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה יְעָצָם עֵצָה זוֹ
And Balaam and the nations, who seek solely the material benefit of this world, formulated this counsel;
וְזֶהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע דְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם, שֶׁהֵם מְבַקְּשִׁים רַק טוֹבוֹת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְחַיֵּי שָׁעָה וְלֹא חַיֵּי עוֹלָם
and this is the root of evil of the nations of the world: that they seek solely the pleasures of this world and temporal life (chayei sha'ah), and not eternal life (chayei olam);
וְאוֹתוֹ רָשָׁע הָיָה מַשִּׂיג מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְשֶׁיֵּשׁ חַיֵּי עוֹלָם, וְעִם כָּל זֶה לֹא בִּקֵּשׁ הוּא לִידָּבֵק בָּהֶם וּלְהַשִּׂיג חַיֵּי עוֹלָם
and that wicked one perceived the supreme stature of Israel and that eternal life exists, yet despite this he never sought to cleave unto them and attain eternal life;

כִּי הֵם כָּל קִיּוּמָם רַק בְּחַיֵּי שָׁעָה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת לְחַיֵּי עוֹלָם כְּשֶׁיְּבוֹעַר הָרָע, כִּי אֵין לָהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב כְּלָל שֶׁיִּהְיֶה נִשְׁאָר אַחַר בִּיעוּר הָרָע:

for their entire existence is confined to the temporal life of this world, possessing no connection to eternal life when evil is eradicated, because they possess no innate root of goodness that could endure following the eradication of evil.1226Avodah Zarah 3a; Pesachim 118a; Bamidbar 23:10 - limited reward and the refusal of eternal attachment: Avodah Zarah teaches both that the nations can receive reward for commandments they observe and that the full time of receiving reward belongs to the future; their reward is not simply denied. Pesachim states the broader principle that the Holy One does not withhold the reward of any creature. Rav Tzadok applies this with precision: a limited good intention attached to an evil deed may receive a limited benefit in this world, while the deed remains punishable and does not create an eternal root. Bilaam himself said, 'May my soul die the death of the upright, and may my end be like his,' showing awareness of Israel's enduring destiny. Rav Tzadok's criticism is that he desired their end without choosing their life of attachment; admiration for eternal life did not become covenantal cleaving.1227R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Ki Seitzei §6): “For they [the nations] are the root of the serpent’s pollution, from whom it did not cease; for conversion [does not fully uproot it].” Exactly the se’if: “be fruitful and multiply” is a positive commandment, but from the side of the serpent’s pollution [it is bound up with the sin’s root].

items.h: The theme: The seven individuals who have no portion in the World to Come. The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a) enumerates seven individuals lacking a portion in the World to Come: six from Israel (Three Kings and Three Commoners) and the seventh, Balaam, from the nations of the world. These seven incorporate all souls who forfeit their portion based on deeds. The six days of Creation correspond to the six rungs of action in this world ("today to perform them", Eruvin 22a); from these six rungs of earned reward, Jewish sinners are excluded because their deeds in this world merit no reward. However, the seventh rung in the World to Come corresponds to the holy Sabbath—a pure, unearned gift (matnas chinam) granted exclusively to Israel ("Was not Esau Jacob's brother? yet I loved Jacob", Malachi 1:2). From this seventh transcendental rung of unearned divine grace, not a single soul of Israel is cast away—only Balaam, who belongs to the nations of the world.

p: וּבַמִּשְׁנָה מָנוּ שִׁבְעָה דְּאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא: שִׁשָּׁה מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל וְהַשְּׁבִיעִי בִּלְעָם מֵאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם
And in the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a) they enumerated seven individuals who have no portion in the World to Come: six from Israel and the seventh, Balaam, from the nations of the world;
וּמִסְּתָמָא שִׁבְעָה אֵלּוּ כּוֹלְלִים כָּל הַנְּפָשׁוֹת שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, דְּוַדַּאי הָיוּ יוֹתֵר מִשִּׁבְעָה אֵלּוּ

and presumably these seven encompass all the souls that lack a portion in the World to Come, for there were certainly more than these seven;1228Sanhedrin 90a, Mishnah: “All Israel have a share in the World to Come, as it says (Yeshayah 60): ‘and your people are all righteous, they shall inherit the land forever, the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, in which to glory.’ And these are the ones who have no share in the World to Come: one who says there is no resurrection of the dead from the Torah, and [one who says] there is no Torah from Heaven, and an epikoros. R’ Akiva says: also one who reads the external books, and one who whispers over a wound and says ‘all the illness that I placed in Egypt I will not place upon you, for I am Hashem your healer.’ Abba Shaul says: also one who pronounces the [Divine] Name by its letters.”
רַק שֶׁכָּל דָּבָר חָלוּק לְו׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת כִּידוּעַ, וְכָל אַחַת כּוֹלֵל מַדְרֵגָה מְיוּחֶדֶת

but every matter is divided into six levels as is known, each one incorporating a specific rung:1229Sanhedrin 90a - from seven named figures to seven archetypal levels: The Mishnah lists three kings and four commoners among those who have no share in the World to Come. Six are Israelites - Yeravam, Achav, Menashe, Doeg, Achitofel, and Geichazi - while Bilaam is the sole figure from the nations. The Mishnah presents named individuals and does not state that these seven exhaust every excluded soul or that each represents a separate cosmic level. Rav Tzadok therefore makes an interpretive move: he reads the number seven typologically, with each person embodying a distinct mode within a complete sevenfold structure. This explains why a short list can stand for a much broader spiritual classification.
וּכְמוֹ שִׁבְעַת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית: שֵׁשֶׁת יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, וְיוֹם הַשְּׁבִיעִי שַׁבָּת מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְכֵן שֵׁשֶׁת אַלְפֵי שָׁנִים דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
matching the seven days of Creation: six days of action, and the seventh day Shabbos which is a foretaste of the World to Come, and likewise the six thousand years of this world;
כָּךְ יֵשׁ גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁהוּא זְמַן הַקִּיבּוּל שָׂכָר עַל הַמַּעֲשִׂים

so too is it in the World to Come, which is the time of receiving the reward for deeds:1230Berachos 57b; Avodah Zarah 9a, 3a - Shabbos, six millennia, and deed versus reward: Berachos calls Shabbos both a semblance of the World to Come and one-sixtieth of it. Tanna d'vei Eliyahu in Avodah Zarah describes the world as a six-thousand-year process, while Avodah Zarah also expounds 'today to do them' as limiting mitzvah-performance to this world and places the receiving of reward afterward; the same sugya says that one who labored on the eve of Shabbos will eat on Shabbos. Rav Tzadok combines these teachings into one architecture: six levels correspond to the arena of action, and the seventh corresponds to repose and reception. The cited sugyos provide the analogies; they do not themselves enumerate seven compartments within the World to Come.
דִּימֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה דְּ״הַיּוֹם לַעֲשׂוֹתָם״ (עֵרוּבִין כ״ב עַמּוּד א׳) הֵם שֵׁשׁ מַדְרֵיגוֹת
for the days of action of this world, of "today to perform them" (Eruvin 22a), constitute six rungs;
וּמֵאֵלּוּ הַמַּדְרֵיגוֹת נִדְחוּ אוֹתָם שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁמִּצַּד מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין לָהֶם שׁוּם קִיבּוּל שָׂכָר, וְהוּא גַּם בְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל

and from these six rungs of earned reward are excluded those who have no portion in the World to Come, who on account of their deeds in this world have no claim to reward, which applies even to the sinners of Israel.
וּמַדְרֵיגָה הַשְּׁבִיעִית דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד יוֹם הַשַּׁבָּת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁאֵינוֹ יוֹם הַמַּעֲשֶׂה, רַק מַתָּנָה טוֹבָה שֶׁנָּתַן הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל

But the seventh rung of the World to Come, which corresponds to the Sabbath day of this world that is not a day of physical labor, is a precious gift that the Holy One, blessed be He, gave to Israel (Shabbos 10b);1231Shabbos 10b; Sanhedrin 58b; Yeshayahu 61:5 - the seventh level as gift rather than labor: Shabbos records the Holy One's message to Moshe: 'I have a good gift in My treasure house, and Shabbos is its name, and I seek to give it to Israel.' Sanhedrin derives from 'day and night shall not cease' that a gentile who establishes a day of complete cessation is liable, expressing the distinct covenantal status of Israel's Shabbos. Yeshayahu's future vision says that strangers will tend Israel's flocks and serve as plowmen and vinedressers. Rav Tzadok joins these separate sources conceptually: the nations' contribution is expressed through constructive activity in the settled world, whereas Israel's seventh level is a covenantal gift of rest. The Gemara and the verse do not themselves formulate this complete contrast.
דְּגוֹי שֶׁשָּׁבַת חַיָּיב מִיתָה (סַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳), דְּמֵהֶם אֵין לְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא נִיחָא אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה שֶׁעוֹסְקִים בְּיִשּׁוּב הָעוֹלָם
for a gentile who rests on Shabbos is liable to death (Sanhedrin 58b), because from them the Holy One, blessed be He, derives satisfaction solely through physical labor in civilizing the world,
דִּלְכָךְ נוֹצְרוּ לִהְיוֹת אִכָּרִים וְכוֹרְמִים לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
for which they were created, to be plowers and vinedressers for Israel (Yeshayah 61:5);
וְעַל כֵּן רַק חֲסִידֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, אוֹתָם שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם שְׂכַר מַעֲשִׂים שֶׁפָּעֲלוּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְשֵׁם שָׁמַיִם וְלֹא לְגַרְמַיְיהוּ

and therefore only the pious of the nations of the world have a portion in the World to Come (Tosefta Sanhedrin 13:2), namely those who possess the reward of actual deeds performed in this world for the sake of Heaven and not for selfish benefit.1232Tosefta Sanhedrin 13; Rambam, Hilchos Melachim 8:11; Bava Basra 10b - chassidei umos and motive: The Tosefta infers from 'all the nations that forget God' that there are righteous people among the nations who do have a share in the World to Come. Rambam defines one of the pious among the nations as a person who accepts and carefully fulfills the seven Noahide commandments because the Holy One commanded them in the Torah and informed Moshe that the descendants of Noach had previously been commanded. Bava Basra criticizes acts of gentile charity motivated only by self-exaltation, political survival, or taunting, and distinguishes them from the conditional charity of an Israelite. Rav Tzadok's phrase 'for the sake of Heaven and not for themselves' synthesizes these sources around covenantal motive; it should not be read as denying every form of reward for any gentile deed with mixed motives, since Avodah Zarah 3a explicitly recognizes reward for a non-commanded performer.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל נֶאֱמַר: ״הֲלוֹא אָח [עֵשָׂו לְיַעֲקֹב נְאֻם ה׳] וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב״ (מַלְאָכִי א:ב)
Unlike Israel, regarding whom it is said: "Was not Esau Jacob's brother? says Hashem; yet I loved Jacob" (Malachi 1:2);
אַף שֶׁהֵם אַחִים דּוֹמִים זֶה לָזֶה בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם, זֶה אָהוּב בְּלֹא טַעַם, כְּעִנְיַן ״וְחַנֹּתִי אֶת אֲשֶׁר אָחֹן״ (שְׁמוֹת ל״ג:י״ט)

even though they are brothers resembling one another in their external deeds, this one is beloved unconditionally without formal reason, as in "and I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious" (Shemos 33:19);
אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן וּכְדַאי, מֵאוֹצָר שֶׁל מַתְּנַת חִנָּם שֶׁאֵינוֹ לְפִי הַמַּעֲשִׂים רַק מִצַּד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ, דְּהוּא רַק לְיִשְׂרָאֵל לְבַד

even though he is neither worthy nor deserving, drawn from the celestial treasury of unearned gifts (matnas chinam, Berachos 7a) which is not determined by deeds but by soul-root, belonging to Israel alone;
וּמִצַּד מַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא אֵין שׁוּם נֶפֶשׁ מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל נִדְחָה, אֶלָּא בִּלְעָם שֶׁהוּא מֵאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם:

and from the perspective of this seventh transcendental rung of the World to Come, not a single soul of Israel is ever cast away, but only Balaam, who belongs to the nations of the world.1233Malachi 1:2-3; Berachos 7a; Shemos Rabbah 45:6; Bamidbar Rabbah 14:1 - root-love, free grace, and Bilaam's exception: Malachi places Yaakov and Esav side by side as brothers and nevertheless declares God's love for Yaakov. Berachos interprets 'I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious' as grace even for one who is not worthy, and Shemos Rabbah describes a great treasury from which God grants freely to one who lacks earned merit. Bamidbar Rabbah records the dorshei reshumos' teaching that the listed sinners ultimately have a share except for Bilaam. Rav Tzadok unites these texts: beyond the levels measured by deeds lies a seventh, gratuitous share rooted in Israel's identity as Yaakov's seed; Bilaam remains outside that root. The exact seven-level metaphysics is Rav Tzadok's synthesis, not an explicit statement of any one source.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים פ״ד–פ״ח

The theme: The knot of the Tefillin (kesher shel tefillin) shown to Moshe Rabbeinu and the mystery of the unearned celestial treasury (otzar shel matnas chinam). In Berachos 7a, Hashem revealed to Moshe the knot of the Tefillin from behind (Shemos 33:23). In Hashem's Tefillin it is written: "Who is like Your people Israel, a unique nation upon earth?" (I Divrei HaYamim 17:21). The knot of the Tefillin—shaped like the letter dalet—symbolizes the indelible attachment (hiskashrus) between Israel and their Father in Heaven even when they are impoverished in mitzvos (dalus me-ha-mitzvos) and face away from Him (bechinas achorayim). The letter shin embossed upon the head-tefillin (with its three-headed and four-headed sides) represents the Seven Shepherds, the Patriarchs, and the perfection of the Covenant (kedushas ha-bris). Opposite these stand the seven levels of Gehinnom and the seven individuals lacking a share in the World to Come, where Balaam represents total, irredeemable evil devoid of eternal life, a state that never exists in any soul of Israel.

p: וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק עַל כָּל פָּנִים, שֶׁאוֹצָר זֶה שֶׁלֹּא נִתְגַּלָּה גַּם לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֶלָּא הָרְשִׁימוּ מִמֶּנּוּ

And all Israel possess a portion in any event, for this celestial treasury [of unearned gifts] was not revealed even to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, in this world, save for its impression (reshimu);
רָצָה לוֹמַר מַה שֶּׁגִּילָּה לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְצִיאוּת לְאוֹצָר זֶה
meaning that which the Holy One, blessed be He, revealed to him: that there exists such a treasury;
וְהוּא הַקֶּשֶׁר שֶׁל תְּפִלִּין שֶׁהֶרְאָה לוֹ בְּמַרְאֵה אֲחוֹרַיִם

and this is the knot of the Tefillin which He showed him in the vision of the back (Berachos 7a, on Shemos 33:23);1234Shemos Rabbah 45:6; Menachos 35b - the hidden treasury and the “back” of the tefillin: Shemos Rabbah relates that God showed Moshe the storehouses of reward and then a great treasury from which He grants freely to one who has no earned reward, on “I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious.” Menachos expounds “you shall see My back” as the knot of the Divine tefillin. Neither source uses the term reshimu or says that Moshe perceived only an impression. Rav Tzadok joins the two aggados: Moshe is shown that a treasury of gratuitous grace exists, while its inward content remains beyond revelation in this world; the visible “back” and knot become the trace of that concealed bond.
דִּתְפִלִּין דְּמָארֵי עָלְמָא כְּתִיב בְּהוּ: ״[וּ]מִי כְּעַמְּךָ יִשְׂרָאֵל גּוֹי אֶחָד [בָּאָרֶץ]״ (דִּבְרֵי הַיָּמִים א י״ז:כ״א)

for in the Tefillin of the Master of the Universe it is written: "And who is like Your people Israel, a nation one in the earth?" (I Divrei HaYamim 17:21; Berachos 6a);1235Berachos 6a - what is written in the tefillin of the Master of the world: The Gemara answers with “Who is like Your people Israel, one nation in the land,” then explains mutual singularity: Israel declares Hashem One, and Hashem makes Israel a unique nation. Rav Tzadok uses this not merely as praise written inside the tefillin, but as the content of the permanent attachment symbolized by their knot. The Gemara states the reciprocal praise; the extension to Israel’s bond even in an “achorayim” condition is his interpretation.
וְהַקֶּשֶׁר הוּא הַהִתְקַשְּׁרוּת שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם עִם אֲבִיהֶם שֶׁבַּשָּׁמַיִם גַּם בִּהְיוֹתָם בִּבְחִינַת אֲחוֹרַיִם
and the knot represents the bond of attachment that they possess with their Father in Heaven even when they are in the state of "back" (achorayim);
שֶׁהוּא בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵין עוֹשִׂין רְצוֹנוֹ שֶׁל מָקוֹם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ל״ט עַמּוּד א׳] שֶׁאֵינָם אָז פָּנִים בְּפָנִים
which is at a time when they do not perform the will of the Omnipresent, as they stated [in Bava Batra 39a] that they are not then face to face;
וְהוּא קֶשֶׁר שֶׁל דָּלֶ״ת הַמּוֹרֶה עַל דַּלּוּתָם מֵהַמִּצְוֹת

and it is a knot shaped like the letter dalet, pointing to their poverty (dalus) in mitzvos.1236Cf. Bava Basra 99a — the source R’ Tzadok cites: the dispute about the keruvim — “how did they stand? When Israel do the will of the Omnipresent [they face] one another; and when Israel do not do the will of the Omnipresent, their faces are turned [away], one from the other” — which R’ Tzadok reads as the “back [achorayim]” aspect, the enduring bond (the tefillin-knot) that remains even when Israel are estranged.
וּבִפְנִים בַּבַּיִת הוּא הַשִּׁי״ן מֵהַשֵּׁם הַמּוֹרֶה עַל קְדֻשַּׁת הַבְּרִית כַּנּוֹדָע, שֶׁהוּא קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל

And inward upon the capsule of the head-tefillin is the embossed letter shin from the Divine Name Sha-dai, which alludes to the holiness of the Covenant as is known, which is the essential sanctity of Israel;
שֶׁאֵין הָעָרְלָה נִקְרֵאת אֶלָּא לְשֵׁם אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

for the foreskin is designated solely upon the name of the nations of the world (Nedarim 31b);1237Menachos 35a-b; Mishnah Nedarim 3:11 - dalet, shin, and covenantal identity: Menachos treats both the shin embossed on the head-tefillin and the knot shaped as a dalet as halachos transmitted to Moshe at Sinai; it also connects “you shall see My back” to the knot. The Mishnah rules that even an uncircumcised Israelite is included in “the circumcised,” whereas even a circumcised gentile remains included in “the uncircumcised,” because the name orlah is applied to the nations. Rav Tzadok reads these fixed forms inwardly: the outward dalet signifies Israel’s poverty of deeds, while the shin of the bayis points to an indelible holiness of the covenant. Those symbolic meanings are not stated in the halachic sources themselves.
וְהֵם ב׳ שִׁינִי״ן שֶׁל ג׳ רָאשִׁים וְד׳ רָאשִׁים נֶגֶד ז׳ רוֹעִים
and these are two letters shin—one of three heads and one of four heads—corresponding to the Seven Shepherds (Sukkah 52b);
שֶׁהֵם כּוֹלְלִים כָּל קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל וּדְבֵיקוּתָם בְּז׳ מִדּוֹת הָעֶלְיוֹנוֹת דֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים כַּנּוֹדָע
who encompass the entirety of the holiness of Israel and their cleaving unto the seven supernal divine attributes (middos) of the Living God as is known.
אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הוּא הַתְחָלַת בִּנְיַן אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית
Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, is the inception of the construction of the Israelite nation;
וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁהוּא מְשִׁיחַ אֱלֹהֵי יַעֲקֹב, הוּא סוֹף שְׁלֵימוּתָם בְּבִיעוּר הָרָע וְגִילּוּי דְּבֵיקוּתָם לְגַמְרֵי

and David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who is the anointed of the God of Yaakov (II Shmuel 23:1), is the ultimate culmination of their perfection in the eradication of evil and the total revelation of their cleaving;
וְשִׁי״ן דְּג׳ רָאשִׁים הוּא נֶגֶד ג׳ אָבוֹת כִּידוּעַ
and the shin of three heads corresponds to the Three Patriarchs as is known.
וְזֶה לְעֻמַּת זֶה הֵם גַּם כֵּן ז׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת בָּרָע
And "God has made even the one over against the other" (Koheles 7:14), there being likewise seven rungs in the realm of evil:
כְּמוֹ ז׳ שֵׁמוֹת לְיֵצֶר הָרָע שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסוּכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד א׳], וְז׳ שֵׁמוֹת לְגֵיהִנָּם [בְּעֵירוּבִין י״ט עַמּוּד א׳], וְז׳ מְדוֹרֵי גֵּיהִנָּם הַנִּזְכָּר בַּזֹּוהַר וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ

matching the seven names of the yetzer hara stated [in Sukkah 52a], the seven names of Gehinnom [in Eruvin 19a], and the seven compartments of Gehinnom mentioned in the Zohar and Midrash;1238Sukkah 52a; Eruvin 19a; Zohar, Pekudei 53:838 - a sevenfold structure of evil and punishment: Sukkah enumerates seven names of the evil inclination: evil, uncircumcised, impure, enemy, stumbling block, stone, and hidden one. Eruvin enumerates seven names of Gehinnom: Sheol, Avaddon, Be’er Shachas, Bor Shaon, Tit HaYaven, Tzalmaves, and Eretz HaTachtis. The Zohar explicitly aligns seven chambers of Gehinnom with the seven names of the evil inclination. These sources establish the sevenfold parallel that Rav Tzadok invokes; his use of it to classify the seven excluded figures as corresponding spiritual levels is the next interpretive step.
וְכֵן ז׳ אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
and likewise these seven individuals who have no portion in the World to Come:
ג׳ מְלָכִים נֶגֶד ג׳ אָבוֹת
the Three Kings (Yerovam, Achav, Menasheh) opposite the Three Patriarchs;
וּבִלְעָם נֶגֶד דָּוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בִּקְדֻשָּׁה
and Balaam opposite David HaMelech, peace be upon him, in holiness;
שֶׁהוּא שְׁלֵימוּת הָרָע לְגַמְרֵי בְּלִי שׁוּם טוֹב מֵחַיֵּי עוֹלָם, וְזֶה לֹא נִמְצָא בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל:

Balaam embodying the absolute culmination of evil without any element of good belonging to eternal life, which state is never found in any soul of Israel.1239Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 32:42; Sukkah 52b; Sanhedrin 90a; II Shmuel 23:1 - three, four, and the holy counterpart to Bilaam: Halachah requires a three-headed shin on one side of the head-tefillin and a four-headed shin on the other. Sukkah identifies seven shepherds with David in the center, while Sanhedrin’s Mishnah lists three kings and four commoners among those with no share, Bilaam being the sole figure from the nations. David is called “the anointed of the God of Yaakov.” Rav Tzadok overlays these separate sevens: the three-headed shin with the Patriarchal root, the complete seven with Israel’s shepherds, the three wicked kings as opposites to the Patriarchs, and Bilaam as the negative counterpart to David. The individual correspondences are Rav Tzadok’s typology, not an explicit identification in the cited texts.

items.h: The theme: The root of the soul in Israel versus outward manifestation in deeds. The Dorshei Reshumos grasped the seventh transcendental rung where all Israel possess a portion in the World to Come. In this world, the expansion of the yetzer may totally obscure the good root within the heart, causing a person to lose the earned portion of deeds. Yet by virtue of the essential soul-root (mitzad ha-shoresh), he remains an Israelite. Hence halachah rules that an apostate's marriage remains valid (kiddushav kiddushin), based on the dictum "even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite" (Sanhedrin 44a). R' Tzadok refutes the view of the Rashdam (Even HaEzer 10) who argued that this Talmudic principle was a minority view or a mere homily (asmachta).

p: וּמִמַּדְרֵיגָה זוֹ הִשִּׂיגוּ דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת הָרְשִׁימוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּכוּלָּם יֵשׁ לָהֶם
And from this seventh transcendent rung the Dorshei Reshumos grasped the indelible impression (reshimu) when they stated that all of them possess a portion in the World to Come;
וְהַכֹּל אֱמֶת, דְּמִצַּד מַדְרֵיגוֹת הָרִאשׁוֹנוֹת אֵין לָהֶם
and all is absolute truth: from the perspective of the initial six rungs of earned reward they have none,
וּבְמַדְרֵיגַת הַזַּיִ״ן חָשֵׁיב הַתַּנָּא גַּם כֵּן רַק בִּלְעָם
whereas in the seventh rung the Tanna likewise excludes only Balaam;
כִּי יַעֲקֹב נָטַל לְחֶלְקוֹ הָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְעַל כֵּן כָּל זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
for Yaakov acquired the World to Come as his portion, wherefore all the seed of Yaakov have a share in the World to Come;
וְאַף דְּיֵשׁ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, גַּם הֵם מִצַּד שֶׁהֵם מִזֶּרַע יַעֲקֹב וּמִכְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא

and even those of whom it was stated that they lack a portion, they too, from the aspect that they stem from the seed of Yaakov and belong to Israel, ultimately possess a portion in the World to Come.1240Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:1-2; Sanhedrin 104b - “all Israel” and the dorshei reshumos: The Mishnah first states, “All Israel have a share in the World to Come,” and then enumerates both doctrinal offenders and seven named figures who “have no share.” It does not formulate the latter as a grammatical exception with the word chutz. Later, the Gemara records that the dorshei reshumos said that all of the enumerated figures ultimately enter the World to Come and interpreted verses as referring to each of them. Rav Tzadok reconciles the two formulations by distinguishing the share revealed and earned through conduct in this world from a deeper share rooted in Israelite identity. That two-level resolution is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis; the Mishnah and Gemara themselves preserve the apparent tension.1241Yalkut Shimoni on Torah 111:2; Midrash Tanchuma, Terumah 9:3 - Yaakov’s portion in the World to Come: The midrashic tradition portrays Yaakov and Esav as dividing the two worlds: Esav takes this world and Yaakov takes the World to Come. Tanchuma adds that Yaakov ultimately receives two portions - sustenance in this world and inheritance in the World to Come - while Esav possesses only his temporal portion. Rav Tzadok treats this not merely as Yaakov’s personal reward but as an inherited root belonging to all “the seed of Yaakov.” The extension from the patriarch’s portion to an indestructible share within every Israelite is his interpretive development of the midrash.
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא אָמְרוּ לְשׁוֹן ״חוּץ״ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
And therefore the Mishnah did not use the exclusionary phrase "except," as mentioned above;
וְרוֹמֵז גַּם לָזֶה, דְּאַף אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם, הֵם גַּם כֵּן מִכְּלַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם מִצַּד שֶׁהֵם גַּם כֵּן מִיִּשְׂרָאֵל
alluding likewise to this: that even these who seemingly have none are essentially included within "all Israel who have," from the aspect that they are inherently part of Israel;
וּמַה שֶּׁאֵין לָהֶם הוּא מִצַּד הִתְגַּבְּרוּת הָרָע בַּחֲלַל הַלֵּב עַד שֶׁנֶּעְלַם וְנִתְכַּסָּה שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַטּוֹב שֶׁבּוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְגַמְרֵי
and that which they lack a portion is on account of the dominance of evil in the hollow of the heart until the good root within them in this world is entirely concealed and veiled;
וְעַל כֵּן מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כְּבָר יָצָא מִכְּלַל שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל וְזֶרַע יַעֲקֹב
wherefore, from the perspective of overt manifestation in this world, he has departed from the collective name of Israel and the seed of Yaakov,
כִּי אוֹתוֹ חֵלֶק רָע הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט וּמְמַלֵּא כָּל מַעֲמַקֵּי לִבּוֹ אֵין לוֹ שַׁיָּיכוּת לְשׁוֹרֶשׁ יַעֲקֹב וְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל כְּלָל
for that evil element which spreads and fills all the depths of his heart has no affinity with the root of Yaakov and the name of Israel whatsoever;
וְעַל כֵּן בְּחֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁמִּצַּד הַמַּעֲשִׂים דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה אֵין לָהֶם, אֲבָל מִכָּל מָקוֹם מִצַּד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ יֵשׁ לָהֶם
wherefore, in the reward of the World to Come that is earned through the deeds of this world they have none, yet from the perspective of their essential root they certainly have.
וּמִצַּד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַזֶּה קַיְימָא לָן: דְּמוּמָר, אֲפִילּוּ נִטְמַע בֵּין הָעַמִּים, קִידּוּשָׁיו קִידּוּשִׁין וְשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלָיו

And by virtue of this inner root, the halachah is established: an apostate, even if assimilated among the nations, his marriage is legally binding (kiddushav kiddushin), and the name of Israel remains upon him (Yevamos 47b);1242Yevamos 47b; Rambam, Hilchos Ishus 4:15; Tur, Even HaEzer 44:1 - the apostate’s betrothal: Yevamos rules that after a convert has immersed and emerged, he is “like an Israelite in every respect”; even if he later reverts and betroths a Jewish woman, he is called an apostate Israelite and his kiddushin are valid. Rambam states the broader rule that an Israelite apostate who willingly worships idolatry nevertheless effects complete kiddushin and requires a get. The Tur likewise rules that an apostate’s kiddushin are valid, while recording and rejecting a dissenting view concerning public Shabbos desecration and idolatry. Rav Tzadok reads the operative halachah as a legal expression of the enduring Jewish root beneath the person’s revealed conduct.
וְיֵשׁ גְּאוֹנִים סוֹבְרִים דְּאֵין קִידּוּשָׁיו קִידּוּשִׁין, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּטוּר וּבֵית יוֹסֵף [בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן מ״ד]
and there are Geonim who hold that his marriage is not binding, as cited in the Tur and Beis Yosef [Even HaEzer 44];
וְהָרַשְׁדָּ״ם [בְּאֶבֶן הָעֵזֶר סִימָן י׳] הֶאֱרִיךְ לְבָאֵר דְּאֵינוֹ דֵּעָה דְּחוּיָה
and the Rashdam [Even HaEzer, §10] elaborated to explain that this Geonic view is not a rejected opinion,
דְּטַעְמָם: דְּהָא דְּ״אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא״ מֵעָכָן יָלְפִינַן, וְאֵין לָנוּ אֶלָּא דְּכָוָותֵיהּ
arguing that their rationale is that the dictum "even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite" was derived from Achan (Yehoshua 7:11), and we have only a case comparable to him;
וְאַף שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין מ״ד רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳] דְּעָבַר עַל ה׳ חוּמְשֵׁי תוֹרָה, לָאו דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל הוּא, יְעוּיַּן שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ

and even though they stated [in Sanhedrin 44a] that Achan transgressed all five books of the Torah, that is not unanimous, see there at length.1243Tur, Even HaEzer 44:1; Responsa Maharashdam, Even HaEzer 10 - the recorded Geonic dissent: The Tur cites an opinion that a public Shabbos desecrator or idolater is treated like a complete gentile for kiddushin, then says that this does not appear correct. Maharashdam argues that the opinion cannot simply be dismissed. He limits “although he sinned, he remains Israel” to a sinner comparable to Achan, suggests that the statement that Achan violated all five books may be a single-author derivation or an asmachta, and explores whether the Yevamos rule refers only to partial reversion or creates no more than a stringent or doubtful kiddushin. Rav Tzadok directly contests those textual moves in the remainder of the se’if.1244Sanhedrin 44a: “‘Israel sinned’ (Yehoshua 7:11) — R’ Abba bar Zavda said: even though he sinned, he is [still] Israel [af al pi she-chata Yisrael hu]. R’ Abba said: this is what people say — a myrtle that stands among thorns, its name is myrtle and they call it myrtle.”
וּבֶאֱמֶת לֹא נִמְצָא מַאן דְּפָלֵיג עַל זֶה
But in truth, no authority is found who disputes this exposition;
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב מִלְּשׁוֹן רַשִׁ״י שָׁם דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״פְּשִׁיטָא״, עַיֵּין שָׁם: אֲפִילּוּ יִהְיֶה זֶה דִּקְדּוּק קָשֶׁה אַרַשִׁ״י גּוּפֵיהּ, אָנָה מָצָא מַאן דְּפָלֵיג

and as for what the Rashdam deduced from the language of Rashi there (s.v. peshita): even were this a difficult textual precision on Rashi himself, where did he find any Tanna or Amora who disputes it?
אֲבָל בֶּאֱמֶת פָּשׁוּט דְּרַשִׁ״י נָקַט רַבִּי אִילְעָא גּוּפֵיהּ
Rather, the plain explanation is that Rashi specified that it is the statement of Rabbi Il'a himself,
מִשּׁוּם דְּאִי לָאו הָכִי, מִכֹּחַ הַקּוּשְׁיָא ״פְּשִׁיטָא״ הָיִינוּ אוֹמְרִים דְּהַאי מַאן דְּאָמַר פָּלֵיג וְלֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לְהַקְשׁוֹת כָּל כָּךְ בִּפְשִׁיטוּת ״פְּשִׁיטָא״

because otherwise, under the force of the Talmud's challenge ("this is obvious!"), we would have assumed that another authority disputes it, so the Gemara could not have asked so simply "it is obvious!";
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר דְּהוּא רַבִּי אִילְעָא גּוּפֵיהּ וְלֵיכָּא דְּפָלֵיג
wherefore Rashi clarified that it is Rabbi Il'a himself who formulated both statements and there is no disputant whatsoever;
וּמֵהֵיכָן תֵּיתֵי לַאֲפּוֹשֵׁי פְּלוּגְתָּא וּלְהַמְצִיא דְּלָא דִּבְרֵי הַכֹּל הוּא
and whence would one invent a dispute and fabricate that this is not universally accepted?
וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב דְּהוּא אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא, הוּא זָר בְּעֵינַי לְאוֹמְרוֹ כָּאן
And what the Rashdam wrote—that the verse regarding Achan is a mere asmachta [homiletic support]—is astonishing in my eyes to assert here;
דְּדָבָר זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ בְּעִנְיַן דִּין דְּיֵשׁ שֶׁהוּא דְּרַבָּנָן וְאַסְמְכוּהּ אַקְּרָא
for an asmachta applies strictly to a legal rule that is rabbinic in origin and anchored homiletically upon a verse;
אֲבָל יַלְפּוּתָא אַסִּפּוּר עִנְיָן שֶׁהָיָה, מַה שַּׁיָּיךְ אַסְמַכְתָּא בְּעָלְמָא בָּזֶה:

but regarding a textual derivation based on an actual historical biblical event, what relevance has a mere asmachta to this?1245Sanhedrin 44a and Rashi - the force of “peshita” and the claim of asmachta: The Gemara first attributes to R’ Ilai in the name of R’ Yehuda bar Masparta the teaching that Achan violated all five books of the Torah, and immediately attributes to the same authority the teaching that Achan concealed his circumcision. It then asks “peshita,” because the latter appears included in the former. Maharashdam infers from Rashi’s reference to R’ Ilai himself that other Sages may dispute the five-book teaching. Rav Tzadok argues the opposite: Rashi names R’ Ilai precisely because the question depends on the two statements sharing one authority; otherwise there would be no plain “peshita.” He further objects that calling this an asmachta is unnatural, since the argument is an aggadic inference from the scriptural account of an event rather than a rabbinic law merely supported by a verse.

items.h: The theme: The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah on whether Israel is called "children of God" when they sin. The Rashba (Responsa, Part I, §124 and §212) rules in accordance with Rabbi Meir (Kiddushin 36a) that whether obedient or disobedient, Israel is always termed "children of the Living God" (banei El chai). In contrast, Rabbi Yehudah holds that when they do not act as children, they are not termed children. When Israel left Egypt, Hashem proclaimed: "Israel is My firstborn son; send forth My son that he may serve Me" (Shemos 4:22–23). Death for a gentile leads to eternal perdition; but for an Israelite, death is "very good" (tov me'od, Bereishis Rabbah 9:5), for it purges the outer defilement and refines the holy soul. The Mishnah deliberately concealed the ultimate universal portion of all Israel in the World to Come, lest the frivolous use it as an excuse for moral laxity, just as Balaam did.

p: אֲבָל יֵשׁ לוֹמַר דִּתַלְיָא בִּפְלוּגְתָּא דְּתַנָּאֵי רַבִּי יְהוּדָה וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר [בְּקִדּוּשִׁין שָׁם]
But one can say that this matter depends upon the Tannaitic dispute between Rabbi Yehudah and Rabbi Meir [in Kiddushin 36a]:
[וְשׁוּב זָכִיתִי וּמָצָאתִי בִּתְשׁוּבוֹת הָרַשְׁבָּ״א [חֵלֶק א׳ סִימָן קכ״ד וְסִימָן רי״ב] שֶׁהֵבִיא גַּם כֵּן לְעִנְיָן זֶה הַךְ פְּלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה
[and then I merited to find in the Responsa of the Rashba [Part I, §124 and §212] who likewise cited for this issue this dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah,
וּדְקַיְימָא לָן כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מִשּׁוּם דְּדָיֵיק קְרָאֵי, עַיֵּין שָׁם וְאַהְנְיַין]
and that the halachah follows Rabbi Meir because his textual proofs are more precise, see there, and it brought me great joy];
דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר הוּא דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ דִּלְעוֹלָם נִקְרָאִים ״בְּנֵי אֵל חָי״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א)

for Rabbi Meir holds that in all circumstances they are termed "children of the Living God" (Hoshea 2:1);1246Responsa Rashba I:194 and I:242 - why the halachah follows R' Meir here: Although the usual rule in a dispute between R' Meir and R' Yehuda favors R' Yehuda, the Rashba rules here like R' Meir because R' Meir carefully proves his position from a chain of verses. In the responsa, this conclusion supports the continuing Israelite status of an apostate and its halachic consequences. Rav Tzadok says that he found these responsa after developing the issue as a tannaitic dispute. His further explanation - that an indestructible root of holiness remains beneath the person's revealed state - is a metaphysical development beyond the Rashba's legal ruling.1247Kiddushin 36a: “It was taught: ‘you are children to Hashem your God’ — at the time you conduct yourselves in the manner of children, you are called children; [if] you do not conduct yourselves in the manner of children, you are not called children — the words of R’ Yehuda. R’ Meir says: either way you are called children, as it says (Yirmeyah 4): ‘they are foolish children,’ and it says (Devarim 32): ‘children in whom there is no faithfulness,’ and it says (Yeshayah 1): ‘seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly,’ and it says (Hoshea 2): ‘and it shall be, in the place where it is said to them, you are not My people, it shall be said to them, children of the living God.’ What is [the point of each] ‘and it says’? [It is necessary:] and if you would say [that] it is [only] the foolish who are called children, [but] when there is no faithfulness in them they are not called children — come and hear, ‘and it says: children in whom there is no faithfulness.’ And if you would say [that] when there is no faithfulness in them they are [still] called children, [but] when they worship idolatry they are not called children — come and hear, ‘and it says: seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly.’ And if you would say [that] they are called ‘children who deal corruptly,’ [but] fit children they are not called — come and hear, ‘and it says: and it shall be, in the place where it is said to them, you are not My people, it shall be said to them, children of the living God.’”
אֲבָל רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: דִּכְשֶׁאֵין נוֹהֲגִים מִנְהַג בָּנִים אֵין קְרוּיִם ״בָּנִים״
but Rabbi Yehudah says: when they do not conduct themselves as children, they are not termed "children."

וּבִתְחִלַּת בִּנְיַן אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית, בִּתְחִלַּת הַשְּׁלִיחוּת לְהוֹצִיאָם מִמִּצְרַיִם נֶאֱמַר בְּפָרָשַׁת שְׁמוֹת: ״בְּנִי בְכֹרִי יִשְׂרָאֵל, שַׁלַּח אֶת בְּנִי וְיַעַבְדֵנִי״ (שְׁמוֹת ד:כב–כג)

And at the beginning of the formation of the Israelite nation, at the start of the mission to redeem them from Egypt, it is stated in Parashas Shemos: "Israel is My son, My firstborn; send forth My son that he may serve Me" (Shemos 4:22–23);
מְבוֹאָר שֶׁכְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל הֵם בָּנָיו יִתְבָּרַךְ, וּדְעַל כֵּן הוֹצִיאָם לִהְיוֹת לוֹ לְעַם וּלְעָבְדוֹ לְפִי שֶׁהֵם בָּנָיו
it is clear that the collective of Israel are His children, blessed be He, and that for this reason He brought them forth to be His people and serve Him because they are His children;
וְאִם אֵין קְרוּיִם ״בָּנִים״, אִם כֵּן אֵינָם בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל וְעַם ה׳

and if they are not termed "children," then they would not be included within Israel and the people of Hashem.1248Shemos 4:22-23 - “My firstborn son Israel” and the purpose of redemption: At the opening of Moshe's mission, Hashem commands him to tell Pharaoh, “Israel is My firstborn son,” followed immediately by “send My son that he may serve Me.” The verse therefore joins national sonship, liberation from Egypt, and avodah. Rav Tzadok reads this sequence as the foundation of Israel's identity as Hashem's people: the nation is redeemed for service because it is already called His son. On the plain level, however, the passage speaks about Israel collectively in confrontation with Pharaoh; applying the title to the enduring inner status of every individual is Rav Tzadok's conceptual extension.
וְנִרְאֶה דְּעַל כֵּן נֶאֱמַר קְרָא דְּ״בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם״ (דְּבָרִים י״ד:א׳) גַּבֵּי אַזְהָרַת גְּדִידָה וְקָרְחָה עַל מֵת

And it appears that for this reason the verse "You are the children of the Lord your God" (Devarim 14:1) is stated in conjunction with the prohibition against laceration and making baldness over the dead;
כִּי זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ בָּאוּמּוֹת שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם אֶלָּא הָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וּבְמוֹתָם יֵלְכוּ לַאֲבַדּוֹן עוֹלָם
for grief unto self-mutilation applies to the nations of the world who have nothing beyond this world, so that upon death they descend into everlasting destruction;
אֲבָל יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַמִּיתָה הִיא ״טוֹב מְאֹד״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה ט׳]
but for an Israelite, physical death is "very good" as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 9:5];
כִּי הִיא לְתַכְלִית טוֹב שֶׁיִּתְעַכֵּל הַזּוּהֲמָא וְיִכְלוּ הַחוֹחִים הַסּוֹבְבִים, וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַקְּדוּשָׁה יִשָּׁאֵר נָקִי מִכָּל סִיג

for it serves an ultimate good: that the physical defilement decompose, the surrounding thorns be consumed, and the holy soul-root emerge clean of all dross;1249Devarim 14:1-2; Ramban; Bereishis Rabbah 9:5 - sonship, mourning, and “death is good”: The Torah places “you are children to Hashem your God” directly before the prohibitions of gashing and making a bald spot for the dead, and then adds that Israel is a holy and chosen people. Ibn Ezra explains that children trust their father that even what they do not understand is for their good. Ramban emphasizes the enduring existence of the souls before Hashem and therefore rejects excessive mourning, while still allowing natural grief. Bereishis Rabbah records that in R' Meir's Torah, “very good” was read as “death is good,” and explains death as rest from the struggle with the evil inclination and as the cessation of wickedness. Rav Tzadok's image of the pollution and surrounding briars being consumed so that the holy root remains clean is his own purification-oriented development of this source cluster.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לְטַעַם עַל זֶה: ״דְּבָנִים אַתֶּם״ — כְּבֵן הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מֵהָאָב כֵּן אַתֶּם לֵאלֹהֵיכֶם, שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּכֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָׁה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁהִיא מִזְדַּכֵּךְ בְּמוֹתוֹ

and this is the reason stated for this: "for you are children"—just as a child is drawn from the essence of his father, so are you unto your God, possessing a supernal soul-root that is refined through death;

וּמִזֶּה גַּם כֵּן דִּכְשֶׁאֵין קְרוּיִם ״בָּנִים״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָׁה הַקַּיָּים לְעוֹלְמֵי עַד שֶׁיִּהְיֶה הַמִּיתָה לְטוֹבָתוֹ, רַק כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם דְּמִיתָתָם אֲבַדּוֹן, זֶה הוּא עֲקִירַת שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל לְגַמְרֵי מֵהֶם

and from this likewise, according to the perspective that they are not called children, it would imply that he lacks the eternal soul-root for whom death is a purification, but is like the nations whose death is utter ruin, which would constitute the complete uprooting of the name of Israel from them.
וְצָרִיךְ לוֹמַר לְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, קְרָא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר דְּ״וְהָיָה בִּמְקוֹם [אֲשֶׁר יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם לֹא עַמִּי אַתֶּם יֵאָמֵר לָהֶם] בְּנֵי אֵל חָי״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ב:א) לָא קַשְׁיָא

And one must say according to Rabbi Yehudah: the verse cited by Rabbi Meir, "and it shall come to pass that in the place where it was said unto them: 'You are not My people,' it shall be said unto them: 'You are the sons of the Living God'" (Hoshea 2:1), is not difficult;
דִּסְבִירָא לֵיהּ שֶׁתַּרְוַויְיהוּ אֱמֶת, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי לְעֵיל אַמִּשְׁנָה דְּחֵלֶק וְדִבְרֵי דּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת
for he holds that both statements are true, exactly as I wrote above regarding the Mishnah in Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 90a) and the teachings of the Dorshei Reshumos;
דַּהֲרֵי גַּם הָא דְּנֶאֱמַר ״אַתֶּם לֹא עַמִּי״ דְּנִגְזְרָה מִקּוֹדֶם, נֶאֱמַר בַּכָּתוּב דְּלֹא נִתְבַּטֵּל בַּהֹווֶה רַק בִּלְשׁוֹן עָתִיד: ״וְהָיָה״
for behold, even that decree "you are not My people" issued earlier was not annulled in the present tense, but formulated in the future tense: "and it shall come to pass";
דְּמִצַּד הַהַשָּׂגָה שֶׁבְּהִתְגַּלּוּת לֵב הַחֲכָמִים בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הֲרֵי מָנוּ אֵלּוּ שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא, וְנִשְׁנָה בַּמִּשְׁנָה סְתָם
for from the perspective of the revealed human perception of the Sages in this world, they enumerated those who forfeit their portion in the World to Come, teaching it categorically in the Mishnah;
רַק בַּגְּמָרָא גִּילּוּ הַשָּׂגַת הַדּוֹרְשֵׁי רְשׁוּמוֹת

only in the Gemara (Sanhedrin 104b) did they reveal the mystical perception of the Dorshei Reshumos,1250Hoshea 1:9 and 2:1 - “not My people” and future restoration: Hoshea first names the child Lo-Ammi and declares, “you are not My people.” The very next prophecy reverses that decree: in the place where they were told “not My people,” they will be called “children of the living God.” Kiddushin 36a treats this as R' Meir's strongest proof that even after severe estrangement the title “children” remains recoverable. Rav Tzadok reconciles the verse with R' Yehuda by distinguishing the present, revealed judgment - in which the title can disappear - from the future disclosure of the enduring root. That present/future two-level reading is Rav Tzadok's synthesis, not an explicit explanation stated by R' Yehuda.
שֶׁהַתַּלְמוּד מְגַלֶּה דְּבָרִים שֶׁסָּתְמוּ בַּמִּשְׁנָה שֶׁלֹּא רָצוּ לְפָרֵשׁ
for the Talmud unveils matters that were sealed in the Mishnah where the Tannaim chose not to be explicit,
כְּדֶרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים כ״ג סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״תַּנָּא מַסְתֵּים לַהּ סְתוֹמֵי שֶׁלֹּא יְהֵא קַלּוּת רֹאשׁ״, וּבַגְּמָרָא שָׁם פֵּירְשׁוּ הַדָּבָר

in the manner they stated [in Nedarim 23b]: "The Tanna obscurely concealed it lest people treat it with levity," whereas in the Gemara they explained the matter openly;1251Nedarim 23b - a true rule deliberately concealed from the public: The Gemara explains that the Mishnah does not state openly that a person may make an annual stipulation voiding future vows. When Rav Huna bar Chinnana wished to teach the rule publicly, Rava objected that the Tanna had concealed it so that people would not treat vows lightly. Rav Tzadok uses this as an analogy for Mishnah Sanhedrin: the Mishnah can state the severe, practical formulation, while the Gemara discloses a deeper qualification to those capable of receiving it without spiritual carelessness. Nedarim establishes the pedagogical principle of concealment; its application to the excluded figures and the World to Come is Rav Tzadok's analogy.
כִּי הַמִּשְׁנָה שֶׁהוּא הַהֲלָכוֹת בְּקִיצוּר בְּלֹא מַשָּׂא וּמַתָּן וּפִלְפּוּל נִסְדַּר לִהְיוֹת מָסוּר לַכֹּל
for the Mishnah, being the codified law in concise formulation without dialectic debate, was arranged to be transmitted to all,
וְעַל כֵּן הִסְתִּירוּ שָׁם דְּבָרִים שֶׁיּוּכְלוּ קַלֵּי הַדַּעַת לָבוֹא עַל יְדֵי זֶה לְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ
wherefore they concealed therein esoteric matters through which the shallow-minded might arrive at moral laxity;

וְכֵן כָּאן לֹא רָצוּ לְגַלּוֹת זֶה בַּמִּשְׁנָה שֶׁיֵּשׁ מַדְרֵיגָה בָּעוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁבָּהּ יֵשׁ חֵלֶק גַּם לְאֵלּוּ, דְּלֹא יָבוֹאוּ לְקַלּוּת רֹאשׁ כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל בְּבִלְעָם עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהֶחֱלִיק לָשׁוֹן:

and so here, they did not wish to reveal in the Mishnah that there exists a transcendent rung in the World to Come wherein even these outcasts have a portion, lest people stumble into levity, as occurred with Balaam through his flattering tongue.

items.h: The theme: The three levels of scholars corresponding to the three divisions of the soul and the cosmic vision of Rabbi Meir. The three categories—masters of Scripture (Mikra), masters of Mishnah (Mishnah), and masters of Talmud (Talmud)—correspond to Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, originating from the worlds of Asiyah, Yetzirah, and Beriah. From the level of Ruach in the heart, esoteric matters can be grasped only by allusion (remez); but through Neshamah and Wisdom in the brain, the hidden mysteries (mistorin) are openly perceived. Rabbi Meir was called "Meir" because he illuminated the eyes of the Sages in halachah (Eruvin 13b), grasping the primordial light of "Let there be light" (yehi or). In his Torah scroll it was written "garments of light" (kasnos or with an aleph, Bereishis Rabbah 9:5) rather than "garments of skin" (kasnos or with an ayin). He demonstrated 150 reasons to declare the impure pure and the pure impure because at the infinite source of light every created thing possesses dimensions on every side; yet the practical halachah was not fixed according to him, because earthly halachah requires the bounded conduct of this finite world.

p: וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם רָמְזוּ זֶה בַּמַּה שֶּׁלֹּא אָמְרוּ ״חוּץ״ כַּנִּזְכָּר, אֶלָּא שֶׁהִסְתִּירוּ הַדְּבָרִים שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְגַלּוֹת בַּמִּשְׁנָה בְּפֵירוּשׁ
And nevertheless they alluded to this by not stating "except," as mentioned, yet concealing those deep secrets that could not be openly stated in the Mishnah;
גַּם מִלְּבַד דְּטַעַם הַנִּזְכָּר יֵשׁ כָּאן עוֹד, כִּי דָּבָר זֶה אֵינוֹ מוּשָּׂג בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת הַלֵּב בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה רַק בְּדֶרֶךְ רֶמֶז וְרוֹשֶׁם בְּעָלְמָא
moreover, besides that pedagogical reason, there is another: this mystery cannot be grasped through the ordinary heart in this world except by way of subtle allusion and impression;
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁבַּגְּמָרָא וְכֵן בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין שָׁם] פֵּירְשׁוּ דְּבָרִים בְּהֶדְיָא, הֵם גִּילּוּ כָּל הַמִּסְטוֹרִין שֶׁלְּבַעֲלֵי תַּלְמוּד נוֹדַע הַכֹּל
and this is why in the Bavli and Yerushalmi [Sanhedrin 104b] they explained the matters explicitly, revealing all the mysteries (mistorin) so that to the masters of Talmud everything became known.
כִּידוּעַ דְּג׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת הֵם הַנִּזְכָּר בְּכַמָּה מְקוֹמוֹת: בַּעֲלֵי מִקְרָא, בַּעֲלֵי מִשְׁנָה, בַּעֲלֵי תַּלְמוּד
As is known, there are three categories mentioned in several places: masters of Scripture, masters of Mishnah, and masters of Talmud;
שֶׁהֵם נֶגֶד ג׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁבָּאָדָם שֶׁמִּגּ׳ עוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה כַּנּוֹדָע

which correspond to the three soul-levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah within man, deriving from the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah as is known;1252Bavli and Yerushalmi Sanhedrin - the explicit disclosure behind the Mishnah: The Mishnah lists three kings and four commoners as lacking a share in the World to Come. Both Talmudim then record the interpretive tradition of the dorshei reshumos: “all of them have a share in the World to Come,” deriving each Israelite figure from Tehillim 60:9-10. The Yerushalmi adds the Divine Voice protesting human certainty about this judgment and concludes that God can “make them friends” and lead them to good deeds. Rav Tzadok reads this contrast structurally: the Mishnah states the severe public formulation, while the Gemara discloses the restorative depth that the Mishnah intentionally leaves unstated.1253Scripture, Mishnah, and Talmud - nefesh, ruach, and neshamah: Ohr HaChammah on Zohar III 259b, citing the Ramak, presents this tripartite scheme explicitly: masters of Scripture correspond to the nefesh in Asiyah; masters of Mishnah to the ruach in Yetzirah; and masters of Talmud to the neshamah in Beriah. In that presentation, each lower level has less capacity to resolve contradiction, while the higher level can disclose the inward unity beneath opposed rulings. Rav Tzadok adopts this kabbalistic map as a theory of rabbinic literary form: Mishnah preserves the tension of concealment and opposition, whereas Talmud can articulate the deeper reconciliation.
וּמִצַּד מַדְרֵיגַת הָרוּחַ שֶׁבַּלֵּב אִי אֶפְשָׁר לְהָבִין וּלְהַשִּׂיג אֶלָּא בְּרֶמֶז
and from the level of Ruach within the heart it is impossible to understand except through an allusion;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מִי שֶׁזָּכָה לְמַדְרֵיגַת הַנְּשָׁמָה וְחָכְמָה שֶׁבַּמּוֹחַ שֶׁמַּשִּׂיג יוֹתֵר
unlike one who has merited the level of Neshamah and Wisdom in the brain, who perceives much more.
וּבַכָּתוּב נִתְגַּלָּה גַּם כֵּן בְּדֶרֶךְ כְּלָל דְּ״וְהָיָה בִּמְקוֹם וְגוֹמֵר״
And in Scripture it was likewise revealed in a general manner, "and it shall come to pass that in the place, etc.";
וְרַבִּי מֵאִיר בַּבָּרַיְיתָא דְּקִדּוּשִׁין פִּרְסְמוֹ גַּם כֵּן, שֶׁהוּא הִשִּׂיג כְּלָלוּת אוֹר הַגָּנוּז דְּתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
and Rabbi Meir in the Baraisa of Kiddushin publicized it as well, for he grasped the collective concealed light of the Oral Torah;
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא ״רַבִּי מֵאִיר״ עַל שֵׁם שֶׁמֵּאִיר עֵינֵי חֲכָמִים בַּהֲלָכָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּעֵירוּבִין י״ג עַמּוּד ב׳]
wherefore he was named "Rabbi Meir" because he illuminated the eyes of the Sages in halachah, as they stated [in Eruvin 13b];
כִּי הוּא הִמְשִׁיךְ הָאוֹר לְכָל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל עֵינֵי הָעֵדָה
for he channeled the supernal light to all the sages of Israel, the eyes of the congregation;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: דְּגָלוּי וְיָדוּעַ לִפְנֵי מִי שֶׁאָמַר וְהָיָה הָעוֹלָם שֶׁאֵין בְּדוֹרוֹ כְּמוֹתוֹ
and as they said there: "It is revealed and known before the One Who spoke and the world came into being that there was no one in his generation like him";
וְדָיֵיק שֶׁאָמַר ״וְהָיָה הָעוֹלָם״, כִּי הוּא הָיָה מַשִּׂיג שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָאוֹר שֶׁבִּתְחִלַּת בְּרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם בְּמַאֲמַר ״יְהִי אוֹר״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית א:ג)

and it stated with precision "the One Who spoke and the world came into being," because he attained the root of the light at the inception of the world's creation in the utterance "Let there be light" (Bereishis 1:3),
שֶׁהוּא אוֹר הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּגְנַז לַצַּדִּיקִים לֶעָתִיד לָבוֹא

which is the light of the Torah concealed for the righteous in the Future;1254R’ Meir, “who illuminates,” and the concealed primordial light: Eruvin 13b explains that R’ Meir was so called because he “illuminated the eyes of the Sages in halachah.” Chagigah 12a teaches that the first light enabled vision from one end of the world to the other, but God concealed it for the righteous in the future. Rav Tzadok joins these two passages conceptually: R’ Meir’s halachic illumination reflects a perspective rooted in the hidden light, capable of seeing beyond the fragmented appearances of the present world. This is an interpretive synthesis, not a direct identification stated by the Bavli itself.
דְּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה נִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּהִתְלַבְּשׁוּת הָאָדָם בְּכָתְנוֹת עוֹר, הַגּוּף הַמַּלְבִּישׁ לַנֶּפֶשׁ
which in this world became clothed through man's enclothing in "garments of skin" (kasnos or with an ayin, Bereishis 3:21), the physical body that garments the soul;
וּבְתוֹרָתוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי מֵאִיר הָיָה כָּתוּב ״כָּתְנוֹת אוֹר״ בְּאָלֶ״ף כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ׳]

while in the Torah scroll of Rabbi Meir it was written "garments of light" (kasnos or with an aleph), as they stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 20:12].1255Bereshis Rabbah 20:12 - “garments of light” in R’ Meir’s Torah: Bereshis Rabbah records that in R’ Meir’s Torah they found “garments of light” with an aleph in place of “garments of skin” with an ayin. The midrash does not require that R’ Meir altered the consonantal Torah scroll; later teachers often understand “his Torah” as his interpretive illumination of the verse. In Rav Tzadok’s use, the wordplay marks recovery of Adam’s pre-sin luminosity: the material garment that ordinarily conceals becomes transparent to the primordial light. This supports the se’if’s distinction between R’ Meir’s root-vision and the halachic world where concealment and opposition still operate.
וְעַל כֵּן הָיָה יָכוֹל לְהַרְאוֹת פָּנִים עַל טָמֵא טָהוֹר וְעַל טָהוֹר טָמֵא
And therefore he was able to demonstrate reasons to declare the impure pure and the pure impure (Eruvin 13b);
שֶׁזֶּהוּ מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם מִכָּל דָּבָר
for this derives from perceiving the hidden root of every single thing:
שֶׁכָּל דָּבָר מְעוֹרָב טוֹב וָרָע, וְהַנְהָגַת עוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא כְּפִי הִתְלַבְּשׁוּתָהּ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהוּא בַּעַל גְּבוּל וָסוֹף
for every created thing is an admixture of good and evil, and the governance of this world is according to its manifestation in this world, which is finite and bounded;
אֲבָל הוּא הִשִּׂיג שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָאוֹר שֶׁאֵין לוֹ סוֹף וּגְבוּל, שֶׁשָּׁם בְּכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ פָּנִים לְכָל צַד
but he grasped the primordial root of the Infinite Light, where within every single entity there are aspects pointing in every direction;
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם: שֶׁלֹּא יָכְלוּ לַעֲמוֹד עַל סוֹף דַּעְתּוֹ, שֶׁאֵין לְחָכְמָתוֹ וְדַעְתּוֹ סוֹף
and this is what they stated there: that the colleagues could not fathom the depths of his mind, because his wisdom and mind were boundless;
וְעַל כֵּן לֹא קָבְעוּ הֲלָכָה כְּמוֹתוֹ, דִּקְבִיעוּת הַהֲלָכָה הוּא הַהִילוּךְ הָרָאוּי לְהִתְנַהֲגוּת הָאָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:

and therefore the halachah was not fixed according to him, for the establishment of practical halachah is the pathway (halikhah) appropriate for human conduct in this finite world.1256Eruvin 13b - unrivaled insight without practical comprehensibility: The Bavli says that no one in R’ Meir’s generation equaled him, yet the halachah was not fixed according to him because his colleagues could not “stand at the end of his mind”: they could not determine when he was demonstrating the pure as impure or the impure as pure. The passage does not accuse him of arbitrariness; it highlights an intellectual range so great that the court could not reliably identify his final practical position. Rav Tzadok reads that range positively as perception at a root where opposing possibilities are still included, while preserving the Bavli’s reason that such perception cannot itself establish ordinary halachah.

items.h: The theme: The pupil who purified the creeping reptile with 150 reasons and the cosmic sea of the Future. In Eruvin 13b, a distinguished student in Yavneh demonstrated 150 reasons to purify a creeping reptile (sheretz). This was not hollow sophistry, for every impurity contains a concealed root in holiness without which it could not exist. When the earth is filled with knowledge as the waters cover the sea (Yeshayah 11:9), the world will become like the ocean, where all creatures are pure (Chullin 127a). King Shlomo built the Copper Sea holding 150 ritual baths (mikva'os) to tap this ultimate level. In this world, a person holding a sheretz cannot be purified even in all the waters of the world without casting the sin away; but in the Future, sins themselves will become white as snow and the dry land will return to the primordial sea where no impurity exists.

p: וְחָכְמָתוֹ שֶׁל אוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם שֶׁהָיָה מְטַהֵר הַשֶּׁרֶץ בְּק״נ טְעָמִים, אֵינוֹ חֲרִיפוּת שֶׁל הֶבֶל כְּקוּשְׁיַת תּוֹסָפוֹת שָׁם

And the wisdom of that student in Yavneh regarding whom they stated there that he could declare a creeping reptile (sheretz) pure with 150 reasons (Eruvin 13b), was not hollow dialectical sharpness as Tosafos questioned there;
דִּבְאֶמֶת אֵין שׁוּם טוּמְאָה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ טַעֲמֵי טָהֳרָה גַּם כֵּן
for in absolute truth there is no impurity that does not contain reasons for purity as well;
כִּי בְּכָל דָּבָר עַל כָּרְחֲךָ יֵשׁ אֵיזוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, דְּאִם לֹא כֵן לֹא הָיָה לוֹ מְצִיאוּת וַהֲוָיָה וְקִיּוּם כְּלָל
for within every created thing there must perforce exist some divine root in holiness, for otherwise it would have no reality, existence, or sustenance whatsoever.
וּכְשֶׁיְּתוּקַּן הָעוֹלָם שֶׁלֹּא יִהְיֶה מְצִיאוּת רַע עוֹד, יִהְיֶה הַכֹּל טָהוֹר וְלֹא יִהְיֶה שׁוּם טוּמְאָה

And when the world is rectified so that no reality of evil exists anymore, everything will be pure and there will be no impurity at all;1257Tosafos on Eruvin 13b - what could “purifying the sheretz” mean?
