Tosafos asks why producing arguments for the purity of a creature that the Torah explicitly declares impure should count as intellectual distinction. Rabbeinu Tam therefore explains the exercise more narrowly: the student sought to exclude the sheretz from the separate impurity of an animal carcass carried in the amount of an olive-bulk, not to erase the Torah’s explicit contact-impurity of the eight sheratzim. Tosafos then tests that reading against the Sifra and Ravina’s rejected inference from the snake. Rav Tzadok deliberately moves beyond this technical answer: he treats the exercise as revealing a genuine root of purity within the impure thing, while fully preserving its present halachic status.1258Eruvin 13b: “It was taught: there was a distinguished student [talmid vasik] at Yavneh who would purify the sheretz with a hundred and fifty reasons. Ravina said: I will debate and purify it — and if a snake, which kills and increases impurity, is [itself] pure, a sheretz, which does not kill and increase impurity, all the more so [should be pure]! But it is not so — [the snake] performs a mere sting-act [i.e., it causes death by injury, not by intrinsic impurity].”
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּל מַה שֶּׁבַּיָּם טָהוֹר, אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁהוּא מֵח׳ מִינֵי שְׁרָצִים הַטְּמֵאִים כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּחֻלִּין קכ״ז עַמּוּד א׳]

just as everything in the sea is pure, even though it belongs to the eight species of impure reptiles, as they stated [in Chullin 127a];1259Chullin 127a - creatures of the sea and the boundary of sheretz impurity: The sugya derives from “upon the earth” that a sea-mouse does not impart the impurity of the eight sheratzim, and it further teaches that almost every land-creature has a counterpart in the sea. Its legal point is categorical and locational: the Torah’s land-sheretz impurity does not simply transfer to the corresponding marine creature. Rav Tzadok expands that halachic contrast into an eschatological symbol: when the whole world is suffused with divine knowledge like a sea, the hidden aspect of purity will be manifest. Chullin itself does not say that present impurity will literally be annulled by immersion in seawater.
וְלֶעָתִיד: ״[כִּי] מָלְאָה הָאָרֶץ דֵּעָה [אֶת ה׳] כַּמַּיִם לַיָּם מְכַסִּים״ (יְשַׁעְיָה י״א:ט׳)
and in the Future: "For the earth shall be full of the knowledge of Hashem, as the waters cover the sea" (Yeshayah 11:9),
שֶׁיִּתְמַלֵּא הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ בְּמֵימֵי הַדַּעַת וְהַתּוֹרָה הַנִּמְשָׁלָה לְמַיִם וְיִהְיֶה כּוּלּוֹ יָם
the entire world will be filled with the waters of Divine Knowledge and the Torah (which is compared to water), becoming entirely an ocean.
וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן הַיָּם שֶׁעָשָׂה שְׁלֹמֹה בְּגֹודֶל חָכְמָתוֹ, דְּחָשַׁב גַּם כֵּן שֶׁהִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ, שֶׁיָּכוֹל לְטַהֵר הַכֹּל

And this was likewise the mystical concept of the Molten Sea made by King Shlomo in the greatness of his wisdom (I Melachim 7:23), who thought that he had attained this supreme rung wherein he could purify everything;1260Yeshayahu 11:9; Bava Kamma 82a; Eruvin 14a - knowledge, Torah-water, and Shlomo’s sea: Yeshayahu describes the future as “the earth shall be filled with knowledge of Hashem as the waters cover the sea.” Bava Kamma states the familiar interpretive rule, “water means Torah,” based on “all who thirst, go to water.” The copper “sea” built by Shlomo is described in Melachim I 7:23-26, and Eruvin calculates that it held one hundred and fifty purifying mikvaos. Rav Tzadok joins these sources symbolically: Shlomo’s vast basin embodies the aspiration to encompass every possible argument of purification. The prophetic verse speaks of universal knowledge; the claim that the world becomes “entirely sea” is Rav Tzadok’s metaphysical exposition, not a literal geographic prediction.
דְּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כָּל זְמַן שֶׁהַשֶּׁרֶץ בְּיָדוֹ, אֲפִילּוּ טָבַל בְּכָל מֵימוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם לֹא עָלְתָה לוֹ טְבִילָה
for in this world, so long as the sheretz is in his hand, even if he immerses in all the waters of the world his immersion does not avail him (Ta'anis 16a),
דְּשֶׁרֶץ אֵין לוֹ טָהֳרָה בְּמִקְוֶוה
for a creeping reptile has no purification in a ritual bath;
וְכֵן כָּל הַנּוֹגֵעַ בּוֹ, בְּעוֹדוֹ נוֹגֵעַ לֹא יָכוֹל לִיטָּהֵר
and likewise whoever touches it, while still in contact with it cannot become pure;
וַאֲפִילּוּ ״בְּכָל מֵימוֹת״, הַיְינוּ רוֹב חָכְמָה וְהַשָּׂגָה כְּ״אַחֵר״ רַבּוֹ שֶׁל רַבִּי מֵאִיר

and even "in all the waters," meaning through vast wisdom and perception like Acher the teacher of Rabbi Meir:1261Taanis 16a; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 2:3 - immersion cannot replace abandonment of sin: Rav Adda bar Ahavah compares one who confesses without turning away from the transgression to a person holding a sheretz: even immersion in all the waters of the world is ineffective until he throws it away; once he does so, forty se’ah suffice. The Rambam codifies the same image and anchors it in “one who confesses and abandons shall obtain mercy.” Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes vast Torah knowledge from teshuvah. Intellectual access to reasons of purity cannot purify a person who continues to grasp the sin; practical abandonment is indispensable in this world.
שֶׁמִּמַּה שֶּׁזָּכָה לִהְיוֹת רַבּוֹ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר מוּבָן שֶׁהָיָה בּוֹ גַּם כֵּן אוֹר גָּדוֹל שֶׁהָיָה יָכוֹל לְהָאִיר עֵינֵי רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְנִכְנַס לַפַּרְדֵּס

for from the fact that he merited to be the master of Rabbi Meir, it is understood that there was in him a tremendous light capable of illuminating the eyes of Rabbi Meir, having entered Pardes;1262Chagigah 14b-15b - Acher, the Pardes, and R’ Meir’s separation of Torah from sin: Elisha ben Avuyah is one of the four who entered the Pardes; he “cut the shoots” and became Acher. Yet the same sugya portrays him as R’ Meir’s teacher and records R’ Meir continuing to seek his return. The Gemara explains that R’ Meir could eat the fruit and discard the peel, and later sought that Acher be judged and ultimately brought to the World to Come. This is precisely Rav Tzadok’s distinction: extraordinary light and Torah may remain present, but they do not themselves erase chosen wrongdoing. The stories also resist a final equation of the sinner with his sin, since R’ Meir and R’ Yochanan continue to labor for Acher’s restoration.
וְהַכֹּל לֹא הוֹעִיל לוֹ בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְטַהֲרוֹ מִטּוּמְאַת עֲווֹנוֹתָיו, דְּצָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה וַעֲזִיבַת הַחֵטְא דַּוְוקָא
yet all of this did not avail him in this world to purify him from the defilement of his sins, for in this world one specifically requires active repentance and the complete abandonment of sin.
אֲבָל לֶעָתִיד: ״יִתַּמּוּ חַטָּאִים״, דְּהֵם עַצְמָם כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ
But in the Future: "Let sins cease," for the sins themselves will become white as snow;
שֶׁיַּחֲזוֹר הָעוֹלָם לְשָׁרְשׁוֹ כְּמוֹ שֶׁהָיָה בַּתְּחִלָּה כּוּלּוֹ מַיִם
when the universe returns to its primal root as it existed at the inception when it was entirely water;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ עִנְיַן טָהֳרַת הַמִּקְוֶוה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּסֵפֶר הַחִנּוּךְ מִצְוָה קע״ג]

which is the inner mystery of purification in a mikveh, as stated [in Sefer HaChinuch, Mitzvah 173];1263Berachos 10a; Yeshayahu 1:18; Sefer HaChinuch 173 - sins cease, whiteness, and rebirth through water: Beruriah reads “let sins cease” as referring to the sins rather than the sinners and directs R’ Meir to pray that the wrongdoers repent. Yeshayahu promises that scarlet sins can become white as snow. Sefer HaChinuch explains mikveh as an enacted return to the beginning, when the world was entirely water: the person rises as though newly created and must renew his deeds for good. Rav Tzadok combines these themes into universal future rectification. The Chinuch presents the symbolism of personal immersion; Rav Tzadok extends it from the individual to the whole world.
וּבָעוֹלָם הַזֶּה הוּא רַק בִּפְרָטֵי פְּרָטִית וּלְכָל אֶחָד כְּפִי מַה שֶּׁהוּא
and in this world this operates only in minute particularity, for each individual according to his spiritual standing;
וְלֶעָתִיד יִהְיֶה הַתִּיקּוּן בְּכָל הָעוֹלָם כּוּלּוֹ, שֶׁיָּשׁוּב הַיַּבָּשָׁה לְיָם שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ טוּמְאָה כְּלָל, וְעָדִיף מִכָּל מֵימוֹת שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה:

while in the Future the rectification will encompass the entire universe, when the dry land returns to the state of the cosmic Sea wherein no impurity exists whatsoever, surpassing all waters of this world.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים פ״ט–צ״ו

The theme: The Molten Sea of King Shlomo holding 150 ritual baths (mikva'os) and the mystery of the Fiftieth Gate of Understanding. Every matter in this world contains forty-nine facets of purity and forty-nine facets of impurity, corresponding to the seven building days of Creation multiplied by seven. The Fiftieth Gate (Sha'ar Ha-Nun), concealed in this world, restores all things to their divine source where everything is purely sacred. Moshe Rabbeinu, representing the brilliant direct light of the sun (pnei chamah), could not attain this concealed gate in this world. Rabbi Akiva and King Shlomo, however, attained perception through the reflected light of the moon (pnei levanah)—the Oral Torah—which, being less overwhelmingly blinding, permits the scholar (talmid chacham) to penetrate deeper than a prophet (Bava Batra 12a).

p: וְזֶה הָיָה כַּוָּונַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּיָּם שֶׁעָשָׂה שֶׁמַּחֲזִיק ק״נ מִקְוֵוה טָהֳרָה
And this was the intention of King Shlomo, peace be upon him, in the Molten Sea that he made (I Melachim 7:23; Eruvin 14b), which held 150 ritual baths (mikva'os) of purification;
וְיָדוּעַ דִּבְכָל דָּבָר יֵשׁ מ״ט פָּנִים טָהוֹר וְטָמֵא, שֶׁהוּא נֶגֶד ז׳ יְמֵי הַבִּנְיָן דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה כָּל אַחַת כָּלוּל מִזַּיִ״ן

and it is known that in every matter there are forty-nine aspects of purity and forty-nine aspects of impurity, corresponding to the seven building days of the cosmic structure of this world, each attribute composed of seven;
וְשַׁעַר הַנּוּ״ן הַנֶּעְלָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, הוּא מַה שֶּׁחוֹזֵר הַכֹּל לַמָּקוֹר לִהְיוֹת כּוּלּוֹ טָהוֹר
and the Fiftieth Gate (Sha'ar Ha-Nun), which is concealed in this world, is the reality wherein everything returns to the Source to become entirely pure.
וּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁהָיָה ״פְּנֵי חַמָּה״ (בָּבָא בַּתְרָא ע״ה עַמּוּד א׳) בְּהַשָּׂגַת עֶצֶם הָאוֹר הַמֵּאִיר, לֹא יָכוֹל לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹר דְּשַׁעַר הַזֶּה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה

And Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, whose visage was like the face of the sun (Bava Batra 75a) in grasping the very essence of the illuminating direct light, could not attain the light of this Fiftieth Gate in this world (Rosh Hashanah 21b);1264Eruvin 14a; Pesachim 109b - Shlomo’s Sea as 150 mikva’os: R’ Chiyya states that the copper Sea held the volume of 150 forty-se’ah ritual baths. The Bavli establishes the vessel’s capacity; it does not interpret the number 150 as three sets of the fiftieth gate. That symbolic correspondence is Rav Tzadok’s reading of the source.1265Yerushalmi Sanhedrin 4:2; Tehillim 12:7 - forty-nine faces of purity and impurity: R’ Yannai says that the Torah was not given as a rigidly cut body of rulings: an issue can be expounded through forty-nine impure and forty-nine pure aspects, derived from ‘refined sevenfold,’ seven times seven, while practical law follows the majority. Rav Tzadok maps this hermeneutic plurality onto the seven-by-seven structure of the world’s seven days. The Yerushalmi does not itself identify a fiftieth face.1266Rosh Hashanah 21b - forty-nine gates attained and the fiftieth withheld: One view states that fifty gates of understanding were created and all but one were given to Moshe, based on ‘You made him a little less than God.’ Koheles, identified with Shlomo, sought to equal Moshe and was answered that no prophet arose like Moshe. Rav Tzadok identifies the withheld gate with the future restoration in which everything returns to complete purity; that metaphysical identification is his interpretation rather than an explicit statement of the Gemara.
אֲבָל עַל רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא אָמְרוּ [בִּמְנָחוֹת כ״ט עַמּוּד ב׳ וּבְוַיִּקְרָא רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ״ב] שֶׁנִּגְלָה לוֹ מַה שֶּׁלֹּא נִגְלָה לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
but concerning Rabbi Akiva they stated [in Menachos 29b and Vayikra Rabbah 22:1] that there was revealed to him that which was not revealed to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him;
וּפֵירֵשׁ בְּ״מְגַלֵּה עֲמוּקוֹת״ שֶׁנִּגְלָה לוֹ שַׁעַר הַנּוּ״ן הַנֶּעְלָם מִמֹּשֶׁה
and the Megaleh Amukos explained that the Fiftieth Gate, which had been concealed from Moshe, was revealed to him.
וְלֹא שֶׁהָיָה מַעֲלָתוֹ גְּדוֹלָה מִמֶּנּוּ, שֶׁזֶּה אִי אֶפְשָׁר וְ״לֹא קָם [נָבִיא עוֹד בְּיִשְׂרָאֵל] כְּמֹשֶׁה״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ד:י׳)

Not that his spiritual stature was greater than Moshe's, for that is impossible, seeing that "there arose not a prophet since in Israel like unto Moses" (Devarim 34:10);1267Cf. Menachos 29b — the source R’ Tzadok cites regarding R’ Akiva: Moshe ascended on high and found the Holy One affixing crowns to the letters; he was shown R’ Akiva expounding “heaps upon heaps of halachos” upon each crown-tag — matters Moshe himself did not know — and was told, “be silent; thus it arose in thought before Me.” R’ Tzadok reads this as R’ Akiva’s grasp of the “fiftieth gate” hidden from Moshe in this world, the light of the Oral Torah that “receives from the moon.”
אֲבָל לְפִי שֶׁהַשָּׂגָתוֹ הוּא מֵאוֹר הַלְּבָנָה הַמְקַבֵּל מֵאוֹר הַחַמָּה, כִּי הוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה הַמְקַבֵּל מִתּוֹרָה שֶׁבִּכְתָב
but rather because his perception derived from the light of the moon which receives from the light of the sun, he being the root of the Oral Torah which receives from the Written Torah;
וְהִיא הַשָּׂגַת הַחָכְמָה דְּחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאָמְרוּ עַל זֶה [בָּבָא בַּתְרָא י״ב עַמּוּד א׳] דְּ״עָדִיף מִנָּבִיא״
and this is the perceptual wisdom of the Sages of Israel, concerning which they stated [in Bava Batra 12a] that "a sage is superior to a prophet";
הַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּכוֹל לְהַשִּׂיג יוֹתֵר עַל יְדֵי שֶׁהַשָּׂגָתוֹ בְּאוֹר שֶׁאֵינוֹ מַבְהִיק וּמַבְרִיק כָּל כָּךְ

meaning that he can grasp more by virtue of his perception being clothed in a light that is not so blindingly radiant.1268Bava Basra 75a - sun and moon as direct and received illumination: The elders describe Moshe’s face as the sun and Yehoshua’s as the moon, based on ‘you shall place some of your splendor upon him,’ but not all of it. The Talmudic image concerns Moshe and Yehoshua. Rav Tzadok extends its pattern of direct and reflected light to Written and Oral Torah, and therefore to R’ Akiva’s mode of attainment; the Bavli does not make that latter identification directly.
וְכֵן שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁזָּכָה לְשֶׁפַע חָכְמָה תַּתָּאָה דְּקָיְימָא בְּיָמָיו סִיהֲרָא בְּאַשְׁלָמוּתָא, שְׁלֵימוּת הָאוֹר

And likewise King Shlomo, peace be upon him, who merited the overflow of the lower wisdom (Chochmah Tata'ah), wherein in his days the moon stood in its fullness (Zohar I, 150a), in the perfection of reflected light;
בִּקֵּשׁ לִהְיוֹת כְּמֹשֶׁה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּרֹאשׁ הַשָּׁנָה כ״א סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]
sought to be like Moshe, as they stated [in Rosh Hashanah 21b];
וּלְמַאן דְּאָמַר דְּאָמַר לוֹ: ״לֹא קָם וְכוּלֵיהּ״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁבִּקֵּשׁ לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹר הַחַמָּה כְּמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
and according to the authority who holds that the Bat Kol said to him, "there arose not, etc.," it means that he sought to grasp the direct solar light like Moshe Rabbeinu;
וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה הָיָה מִמֵּילָא גָּדוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ כְּשֶׁיַּשִּׂיג הוּא שַׁעַר הַנּוּ״ן שֶׁהִשִּׂיג מִצַּד הַבְּהִירוּת מֵאוֹר הַחַמָּה, וְעַל זֶה אָמַר דְּלֹא קָם וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר

and through this he would consequently have been greater than Moshe had he grasped the Fiftieth Gate through the direct clarity of solar light, and regarding this Heaven replied that there arose not, for this is impossible;
וְאִידָךְ מַאן דְּאָמַר דְּאָמַר ״בַּמְּלָכִים קָם״
and according to the other authority who holds that Heaven replied: "among kings there arose not, [but among prophets there arose]":
הַיְינוּ מִצַּד מִדַּת הַמַּלְכוּת, פֶּה, תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, אֶפְשָׁר לְהַגִּיעַ גַּם לְהַשָּׂגָה יְתֵירָה כְּרַבִּי עֲקִיבָא:
that means: from the aspect of the attribute of Malchus, the Mouth, the Oral Torah, it is indeed possible to attain even an additional dimension of perception, like Rabbi Akiva.

items.h: The theme: Shlomo’s request to judge without witnesses and warning versus the discernment of Mashiach. King Shlomo sought to administer judicial decisions based purely on his intuitive wisdom without requiring witnesses and formal judicial warning (edim v'hasra'ah, Rosh Hashanah 21b). Heaven rebuked him because human wisdom in this world is subject to error. Absolute intuitive judgment will be realized only in the King Messiah, who is exalted above Moshe Rabbeinu and will judge not by the sight of his eyes or the hearing of his ears, but through scent alone ("and he shall scent in the fear of Hashem", Yeshayah 11:3; Sanhedrin 93b). Scent delights the soul (Berachos 43b) and links directly to the "breath of life" (nishmas chayim); one who perfects all three soul levels reaches the supernal soul of Atzilus, where no evil or error can exist.

p: וְעַל זֶה בִּקֵּשׁ לָדוּן בְּלֹא עֵדִים וְהַתְרָאָה, שֶׁהוּא דָּבָר מְבוֹרָר בְּפֹעַל
And regarding this Shlomo sought to judge cases without witnesses and formal warning (Rosh Hashanah 21b), which provide empirical verification in action;
אָכֵן הַנְּבוּאָה הוּא דָּבָר מְבוֹרָר לַנָּבִיא בִּשְׁמִיעָה מִפִּי ה׳
indeed, prophecy is verified unto the prophet through direct hearing from the mouth of Hashem;
אֲבָל הוּא בִּקֵּשׁ לָדוּן עַל פִּי הַשָּׂגַת חָכְמָתוֹ, וְאָמַר לוֹ: ״וְכָתוּב וְכוּלֵיהּ״

yet Shlomo sought to judge purely through the intellectual perception of his wisdom, wherefore a Bat Kol said to him: "And it is written: 'words of truth recorded rightly' (Koheles 12:10; Rosh Hashanah 21b)";
הַיְינוּ שֶׁאֵין חָכְמָתוֹ מְבָרֶרֶת הָאֱמֶת לַאֲמִיתּוֹ דְּאֶפְשָׁר שֶׁיִּטְעֶה

meaning that his wisdom cannot clarify absolute, infallible truth, for it is possible that he might err.1269Bava Basra 12a; Rosh Hashanah 21b - wisdom beyond prophecy, but not beyond halachic verification: Ameimar states that ‘a sage is superior to a prophet,’ after the Gemara teaches that prophecy was removed from the prophets after the Temple’s destruction but not from the sages. Rav Tzadok understands this as a subtler mode of intellectual apprehension. Yet Rosh Hashanah records that when Shlomo sought to judge matters of the heart without witnesses or warning, the heavenly response cited the Torah’s requirement of two witnesses. Extraordinary wisdom may penetrate deeply, but in this world it does not displace the evidentiary structure of halachah and remains capable of error.
וּבֵירוּר הַהַשָּׂגָה בְּחָכְמָה יִהְיֶה בְּמָשִׁיחַ, שֶׁעָלָיו אָמְרוּ בֶּאֱמֶת דְּנִשָּׂא מִמֹּשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם
And the infallible verification of perception in Wisdom will be realized in Mashiach, concerning whom they stated in truth that he is exalted above Moshe Rabbeinu (Tanchuma, Toldos 14);
וְ״לֹא לְמַרְאֵה עֵינָיו [יִשְׁפּוֹט] וְלֹא לְמִשְׁמַע אָזְנָיו [יוֹכִיחַ]״ (יְשַׁעְיָה י״א:ג׳) מֵעֵדִים יִשְׁפּוֹט, רַק ״מוֹרַח וְדָאֵין״
and "he shall not judge after the sight of his eyes, neither decide after the hearing of his ears" (Yeshayah 11:3) from witnesses, but rather "he smells and judges" (Sanhedrin 93b);
וְרֵיחַ הוּא דָּבָר שֶׁהַנְּשָׁמָה נֶהֱנֵית מִמֶּנּוּ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת מ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳]
and scent is that from which the soul derives pleasure, as they stated [in Berachos 43b];
וְהוּא מִקְרָא דְּ״נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים בְּאַפָּיו״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב:ז)
and this corresponds to the verse "the breath of life in his nostrils" (Bereishis 2:7).
וּמִי שֶׁנִּשְׁלַם בְּכָל ג׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת דְּנֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה, זוֹכֶה לְמַדְרֵיגוֹת הַדְּבֵיקוּת שֶׁמִּצַּד הַנְּשָׁמָה לַנְּשָׁמָה שֶׁבַּאֲצִילוּת
And one who is perfected across all three levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, merits the rung of cleaving that stems from the soul of the soul (Neshama le-Neshama) in the world of Atzilus;
דְּתַמָּן ״אִיהוּ וְגַרְמוֹהִי חַד״ (תִּקּוּנֵי זֹוהַר) הַכֹּל בְּיִחוּד גָּמוּר, דְּאֵין מְצִיאוּת לְשׁוּם רַע וְטָעוּת:

where "He and His causations are One" (Tikkunei Zohar, Hakdamah 3b), all in absolute unity, wherein there is no existence of any evil or error whatsoever.1270Midrash Tanchuma, Toldos 14; Tikkunei Zohar, Patach Eliyahu - Mashiach’s elevation and unity in Atzilus: Tanchuma expounds ‘Behold, My servant shall prosper; he shall be exalted and lifted up’ as referring to the King Mashiach, including the phrase ‘lifted above Moshe.’ Patach Eliyahu describes the unity of Atzilus with the formula ‘He and His life-forces are one; He and His vessels are one in them.’ Rav Tzadok joins these traditions to explain a future wisdom rooted in complete divine unity, where evil and error have no independent standing. This describes the messianic mode of revelation; it does not negate the Torah’s statement of Moshe’s unique face-to-face prophecy.1271Cf. Yeshayahu 11:3 and Sanhedrin 93b — the source for “morach ve-da’in.” The verse “va-haricho be-yiras Hashem, ve-lo le-mareh einav yishpot ve-lo le-mishma oznav yochiach” (“his delight shall be in the fear of Hashem; and he shall not judge by the sight of his eyes, nor decide by the hearing of his ears”) is expounded so that “va-haricho” reads “he shall judge by smell” — the mark, per the Gemara, by which the Mashiach is tested. R’ Tzadok ties this to Berachos 43, that scent is the one pleasure of the neshamah alone.

items.h: The theme: The Molten Sea as 150 mikva'os across the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah. Believing he had achieved the Fiftieth Gate across the three levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah, King Shlomo designed the Molten Sea to contain three times fifty (150) ritual baths. Across each of these gates within the three lower worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah (BY"A), an element of impurity still exists from which a soul must be cleansed before entering; once traversing all 150 gates, no trace of impurity remains. Shlomo placed the Sea upon twelve oxen corresponding to the twelve tribes of Israel, who bear the yoke of the Heavenly Kingdom like an ox to the yoke to purify themselves from all evil.

p: וּשְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם, שֶׁחָשַׁב שֶׁכְּבָר הִגִּיעַ לְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ, שֶׁהִשִּׂיג שַׁעַר הַנּוּ״ן בְּכָל הַג׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת דְּנֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה
And King Shlomo, peace be upon him, who thought that he had already attained this supreme rung, having grasped the Fiftieth Gate across all three levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah;
עָשָׂה הַיָּם שֶׁבּוֹ ג׳ פְּעָמִים נוּ״ן מִקְוֵוה טָהֳרָה
made the Molten Sea to contain three times fifty (150) ritual baths of purification;
שֶׁבְּכָל שְׁעָרִים אֵלּוּ עֲדַיִין יֵשׁ מְצִיאוּת לְטוּמְאָה וְרָע שֶׁצָּרִיךְ לִיטָּהֵר מִמֶּנּוּ דְּיוּכַל לִיכָּנֵס בְּאוֹתוֹ שַׁעַר

for within all these gates there still exists the reality of impurity and evil from which one must be cleansed in order to enter that gate;1272I Melachim 7:23–26; Eruvin 14a — the Sea and one hundred fifty mikvaos: Scripture describes Shlomo’s cast-metal “Sea,” ten cubits across, resting upon twelve oxen, and holding two thousand bath. Eruvin calculates its volume as one hundred fifty standard mikvaos, each of forty se’ah. These sources provide the vessel and the number 150; they do not divide the number into three groups of fifty corresponding to nefesh–ruach–neshamah or Beriah–Yetzirah–Asiyah. That threefold structure is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic reading, continuing the preceding discussion of the fiftieth gate.
וְאַחַר שֶׁעָבַר כָּל הַק״נ שְׁעָרִים שֶׁבְּג׳ עוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה, שׁוּב אֵין עוֹד מְצִיאוּת לְטוּמְאָה וְרָע
and once he traverses all 150 gates within the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, there is no longer any reality of impurity and evil.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁעֲשָׂאוֹ עַל י״ב בָּקָר נֶגֶד י״ב שִׁבְטֵי יָהּ, שֶׁהֵם כְּלַל אוּמָּה הַיִּשְׂרְאֵלִית
And this is why he fashioned it resting upon twelve oxen (I Melachim 7:25), corresponding to the twelve tribes of God who constitute the collective of the Israelite nation;
שֶׁהֵם כְּשׁוֹר לְעוֹל לְקַבֵּל עוֹל מַלְכוּתוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁהוּא הַיָּם שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה, לְטַהֵר עַצְמָם מִכָּל רָע:

who are like an ox unto the yoke to receive the yoke of His Kingdom, blessed be He, which is the supernal Sea, to purify themselves from all evil.1273II Divrei HaYamim 4:2–6 — twelve oxen and priestly purification: The parallel account again places the Sea upon twelve oxen, three facing each direction, and adds that “the Sea was for the priests to wash in.” The verses do not explicitly identify the oxen with the twelve tribes or call the vessel the “Sea above.” Rav Tzadok transforms the Temple arrangement into a national symbol: the twelve tribes bear the yoke of divine kingship, while the Sea signifies the supernal source through which Israel is purified.

items.h: The theme: The Heavenly defense of King Shlomo against the Sages who sought to exclude him from the World to Come. Although Scripture records "and Shlomo did evil in the eyes of Hashem" (I Melachim 11:6) and the Sages of the Mishnah sought to count him among those who have no portion in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 104b), a Bat Kol erupted: "Shall it be repaid from you? For you have chosen, and not I" (Iyov 34:33). Earthly Sages judge according to the revealed Torah, where reward is earned through deeds governed by free choice (bechirah). Shlomo's soul-root, however, transcended the realm of free choice, rooted in Atzilus where divine foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) reigns supreme and no evil exists. Hence at birth the prophet Nasan called him Jedidiah ("beloved of Hashem", II Shmuel 12:25), an unearned love mirroring "yet I loved Jacob."

p: וּכְבָר זָכָה הוּא לְמַדְרֵיגָה זוֹ, שֶׁאַף עַל פִּי שֶׁכָּתוּב בּוֹ ״וַיַּעַשׂ [שְׁלֹמֹה] הָרַע [בְּעֵינֵי ה׳]״ (מְלָכִים א י״א:ו׳)
And he had already attained this transcendent rung, so that even though it is written of him "And Shlomo did evil in the sight of Hashem" (I Melachim 11:6);
וּבִקְשׁוּ לִמְנוֹתוֹ בְּאוֹתָן שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
and the Sages sought to enumerate him among those who have no portion in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 104b);
יָצְתָה בַּת קוֹל: ״הַמֵּעִמְּךָ יְשַׁלְמֶנָּה כִּי [מָאַסְתָּ] כִּי אַתָּה תִבְחַר [וְלֹא אָנִי] וְגוֹמֵר״ (אִיּוֹב ל״ד:ל״ג)

a Heavenly Voice (Bat Kol) went forth and proclaimed: "Shall it be repaid from you? For you have rejected it, for you must choose and not I, etc." (Iyov 34:33);1274Cf. Sanhedrin 104b (with Iyov 34:33) — the sugya on those who “have no share in the World to Come.” When the Sages sought to include Shlomo among the three kings [Yeravam, Achav, Menasheh], a Heavenly voice went forth citing “ha-me’imcha yeshalmena ki ma’asta ki atah tivchar ve-lo ani” — “Should it be according to your mind that He requites it, that you have rejected? For you must choose, and not I.” R’ Tzadok reads the bas kol as testimony that Shlomo’s root lay above the domain of the Sages’ this-worldly judgment.

דְּגַם מִשְׁפְּטֵי עוֹלָם הַבָּא הַמּוּשָּׂגִים לְחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁדָּנוּ עֲלֵיהֶם חַכְמֵי הַמִּשְׁנָה וְאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה, הוּא הַכֹּל עַל פִּי מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּתְּנָה לְיִשְׂרָאֵל, וְ״לֹא בַשָּׁמַיִם הִוא״ (דְּבָרִים ל:יב)

for even the judgments of the World to Come perceived by the Sages of Israel in this world, as deliberated by the Sages of the Mishnah and the Men of the Great Assembly, are all evaluated according to the jurisprudence of the Torah given to Israel, which "is not in heaven" (Devarim 30:12);1275Bava Metzia 59b — “the Torah is not in Heaven” and earthly halachic authority: In the oven of Achnai dispute, R’ Yehoshua rejects even a Heavenly voice because the Torah was already given at Sinai and practical halachah follows the majority. The sugya addresses the authority to decide halachah after revelation; it does not directly define the metaphysics of reward in the World to Come. Rav Tzadok extends its principle to the Sages’ Torah-based judgments concerning reward and punishment, while distinguishing Shlomo’s deeper soul-root from that judicial plane.
אֲבָל זֶהוּ בְּשִׁילּוּם הַשָּׂכָר שֶׁמִּצַּד הַמַּעֲשִׂים דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּמִצְוֹת הַתּוֹרָה
yet this earthly jurisdiction applies strictly to the repayment of reward derived from the deeds of this world in the commandments of the Torah,
שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַכֹּל עַל פִּי מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁנִּמְסְרָה לְחַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
which is entirely governed by the jurisprudence of the Torah committed into the hands of the Sages of Israel in this world.
אֲבָל מַעֲלַת שְׁלֹמֹה הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם הָיָה מִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ נִשְׁמָתוֹ שֶׁדָּבוּק בּוֹ יִתְבָּרַךְ
But the unique elevation of King Shlomo, peace be upon him, derived from the intrinsic root of his soul which was cleaved unto Him, blessed be He;
דְּעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא מִיָּד בְּלֵידָתוֹ עַל פִּי הַנָּבִיא ״יְדִידְיָהּ״ (שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ב:כ״ה), דַּה׳ אֲהֵבוֹ טֶרֶם הִגִּיעַ לְשׁוּם מַעֲשֶׂה בִּבְחִירָתוֹ
wherefore he was named immediately at birth by the prophet Nasan "Jedidiah" (II Shmuel 12:25), for Hashem loved him before he had reached any deed through his free choice,
דְּהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַטּוֹב הַנֶּאֱהָב, כְּעִנְיַן ״וָאֹהַב אֶת יַעֲקֹב״ (מַלְאָכִי א:ב) בְּלִי שׁוּם טַעַם, גַּם בִּהְיוֹתָם אַחִים יַחַד בַּבֶּטֶן שָׁוִים כְּאֶחָד

he being the beloved root of goodness, akin to "yet I loved Jacob" (Malachi 1:2) without any causal reason, even when they were brothers together in the womb equal as one.1276II Shmuel 12:24–25; Malachi 1:2–3 — Yedidyah and love preceding deed: At Shlomo’s birth Scripture states, “Hashem loved him,” and records that Nasan the prophet called him Yedidyah, “beloved of Hashem.” Malachi likewise places Yaakov and Esav side by side as brothers and nevertheless declares, “I loved Yaakov.” Rav Tzadok reads these verses as indicating a love grounded in the root of the soul before the person has acted through free choice. The verses themselves state the love; the contrast between root-love and earned reward is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive formulation.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר ״הַמֵּעִמְּךָ וְגוֹמֵר״: שֶׁבְּמַדְרֵיגַת עוֹלָם הַבָּא שֶׁלּוֹ אֵינוֹ ״מֵעִמְּךָ״ מִצַּד מִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁעִמְּךָ
And this is what the Bat Kol stated: "Shall it be from you?": for on his level of the World to Come, it is not "from you" according to the earthly jurisprudence of the Torah in your hands;
כִּי מַדְרֵיגָתוֹ עֶלְיוֹנָה לְמַעְלָה מֵהַבְּחִירָה
because his spiritual plane is exalted far above the domain of free choice;
כִּידוּעַ בְּיִשּׁוּב עִנְיַן הַיְּדִיעָה וְהַבְּחִירָה, דְּאֵינָם בְּמָקוֹם אֶחָד
as is known in the reconciliation of Foreknowledge (Yedi'ah) and Free Choice (Bechirah), that they do not dwell in the same spiritual domain:
וּבַאֲצִילוּת שֶׁשָּׁם הַיְּדִיעָה אֵין מָקוֹם לִבְחִירָה, וּבִבְרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה שֶׁשָּׁם הַבְּחִירָה אֵין מָקוֹם לִידִיעָה:
in Atzilus where Foreknowledge reigns there is no room for Free Choice, whereas in Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah where Free Choice operates there is no room for the revelation of Foreknowledge.

items.h: The theme: The transmission of the Molten Sea to Babylon and the birth of Mashiach on Tisha B'Av. Nebuchadnezzar carried the Molten Sea to Babylon (Yirmiyah 52:17), where the Oral Torah was established by the craftsmen, smiths, and Men of the Great Assembly, culminating in the sealing of the Talmud Bavli. The perfection of the Oral Torah shone precisely after the destruction of the First and Second Temples, for on Tisha B'Av the soul of Mashiach is born (Eichah Rabbah 1:51). When the enemies entered the Sanctuary, they found the Cherubim embracing one another (Yoma 54b), showing that even at the nadir of exile, Israel's cleaving to the Living God remains unbreakable.

p: וְזֶהוּ מַעֲלַת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לְנַתֵּק, שֶׁהֵם ״חֵלֶק ה׳״ (דְּבָרִים ל״ב:ט׳) וְשָׁרְשָׁם מֵהָאֲצִילוּת, דְּשָׁם אֵין מְצִיאוּת רַע וּבְחִירָה כְּלָל

And this is the indestructible stature of Israel which can never be severed: that they are "the portion of Hashem" (Devarim 32:9), their root deriving from Atzilus, where there is no existence of evil or free choice whatsoever;1277Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 5:5; Devarim 32:9; Tikkunei Zohar, Patach Eliyahu — knowledge, choice, and Israel’s root: Rambam teaches that God and His knowledge are one and that human understanding cannot grasp how foreknowledge coexists with freedom; nevertheless, human deeds remain in the person’s hands and are judged as good or evil. “For Hashem’s portion is His people; Yaakov is the lot of His inheritance” supplies Rav Tzadok’s phrase “the portion of Hashem,” while Patach Eliyahu describes the unity of the Divine light with the sefirotic order. Rav Tzadok’s placement of knowledge in Atzilus and choice in Beriah–Yetzirah–Asiyah is a kabbalistic model of those truths, not a denial of practical human responsibility.
וּלְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל יֵשׁ רַק שׁוֹרֶשׁ נֶעְלָם, וְהוּא הָיָה כּוּלּוֹ דָּבוּק שָׁם
and while for every Jew there exists this concealed root, King Shlomo was entirely cleaved there;
וְעַל כֵּן אָמַר ״כִּי אַתָּה תִבְחַר וְגוֹמֵר״, דְּשָׁם אֵין מָקוֹם לִבְחִירָה דִּידְכוּ כְּלָל
and therefore the Bat Kol said "for you must choose, etc.," for in that supernal realm your human choice has no bearing at all.
וּנְבוּכַדְנֶצַּר הוֹלִיךְ הַיָּם לְבָבֶל, דְּשָׁם נִתְיַיסֵּד אַחַר כָּךְ הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה
And Nebuchadnezzar carried the Molten Sea to Babylon (Yirmiyah 52:17), for there the Oral Torah was subsequently established,
בַּתְּחִלָּה עַל יְדֵי הֶחָרָשׁ וְהַמַּסְגֵּר וְאַנְשֵׁי כְּנֶסֶת הַגְּדוֹלָה
initially through the craftsmen and smiths (charash u-masger, II Melachim 24:14) and the Men of the Great Assembly;
וְנִסְתַּיֵּים אַחַר כָּךְ בְּסוֹף הָאָמוֹרָאִים בַּחֲתִימַת הַתַּלְמוּד בַּבְלִי שֶׁהוּא כּוֹלֵל כָּל חָכְמַת הַתּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה כּוּלָּהּ

and concluded subsequently at the end of the Amoraim with the sealing of the Talmud Bavli, which encompasses the entirety of the wisdom of the Oral Torah;1278II Melachim 25:13–16; Yirmiyahu 52:17–20 — the bronze Sea carried to Bavel: The biblical accounts state that the Kasdim broke the bronze pillars, bases, and Sea of the Temple and carried their bronze to Bavel; they also identify the Sea as one of the vessels made by Shlomo. Strictly speaking, Scripture describes the bronze of the dismantled Sea being transported, not the intact basin itself. Rav Tzadok reads that physical transfer symbolically: the Temple’s “Sea,” developed in the preceding se’if as the source of purification and Torah illumination, is transplanted into the Babylonian exile where Torah she-be’al peh will be developed.1279II Melachim 24:14–16; Gittin 88a; Avos 1:1 — the charash ve-hamasger and the Men of the Great Assembly: The exile of Yehoyachin included “the craftsman and the smith.” Gittin identifies these titles with the thousand leading Torah scholars: when they opened a matter all others became as though deaf, and once they closed a matter no one could reopen it. The Gemara calls their earlier exile a divine kindness, because they remained in Bavel to guide the later exiles. Avos places the Men of the Great Assembly in the chain of transmission from Moshe through the prophets. Rav Tzadok joins these two stages into the initial institutional foundation of the Oral Torah in exile.1280Bava Metzia 86a — Ravina and Rav Ashi as the end of hora’ah: The Gemara pairs “Rabbi and R’ Nasan — the end of the Mishnah” with “Rav Ashi and Ravina — the end of hora’ah,” conventionally marking the close of the Amoraic redaction of the Babylonian Talmud. The source establishes the historical closing point; Rav Tzadok’s further description of the Bavli as encompassing the entirety of the wisdom of Torah she-be’al peh expresses its comprehensive spiritual role rather than a verbatim claim of the sugya.
וְשָׁם נִתְגַּלָּה הָאוֹר יָתֵר, כִּי שְׁלֵימוּת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה נִתְגַּלָּה יוֹתֵר אַחַר הַחֻרְבָּן א׳ וּב׳
and there the light was revealed all the more, for the perfection of the Oral Torah was revealed primarily after the First and Second Destructions;
דְּעַל זֶה הָיָה חֻרְבָּן א׳ וּב׳: לִהְיוֹת נִבְנֶה אַחַר כָּךְ בְּיֶתֶר שְׂאֵת, דְּ״גָּדוֹל יִהְיֶה כְּבוֹד הַבַּיִת הַזֶּה הָאַחֲרוֹן [מִן הָרִאשׁוֹן]״ (חַגַּי ב:ט) וּבִנְיָן הַקַּיָּים לָעַד

for toward this end the Destructions occurred: to be rebuilt subsequently with greater glory, wherein "the glory of this latter house shall be greater than of the former" (Chaggai 2:9) as an edifice enduring forever.1281Chaggai 2:9; Bava Basra 3a–b — “greater shall be the glory of the latter House”: Chaggai promises that the glory of the latter House will exceed that of the first. The Bavli applies the verse to the Second Temple and records whether its superiority lay in the building’s greater dimensions or in its longer duration, concluding that both were true. Rav Tzadok reads this historical increase as a pattern: destruction makes possible a later revelation of greater stature, ultimately culminating in the permanent future building. That final extension to the eternal Third Temple is his theological application of the verse.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּמִדְרַשׁ אֵיכָה א:נא וּבַיְרוּשַׁלְמִי בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ב׳ הֲלָכָה ד׳] דִּבְתִשְׁעָה בְּאָב נוֹלַד מָשִׁיחַ
And therefore they stated [in Eichah Rabbah 1:51 and Yerushalmi Berachos 2:4] that on the Ninth of Av Mashiach was born,
כִּי עַל זֶה הָיָה הַחֻרְבָּן: לְהוֹלִיד עַל יְדֵי זֶה נִשְׁמַת מָשִׁיחַ

for for this purpose the Destruction took place: to give birth through it to the soul of Mashiach;1282Yerushalmi Berachos 2:4:12; Eichah Rabbah 1:51 — Mashiach’s birth at the moment of destruction: Both sources relate the tradition of a plowman whose ox first signals that the Temple has been destroyed and then signals that the redeemer has been born; the child is called Menachem. The Midrash adds the formulation that just as the Temple was destroyed upon his arrival, so it will be rebuilt upon his arrival, and R’ Avun connects the fall of “Lebanon” immediately to the shoot from Yishai in Yeshayah 10:34–11:1. Rav Tzadok draws out the inner principle: the descent itself gives birth to the soul-force of redemption.
וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא נ״ד עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּמָצְאוּ אָז כְּרוּבִים מְעוֹרִים זֶה בָּזֶה
and therefore they stated [in Yoma 54b] that the invading enemies found the Cherubim entwined with one another,
שֶׁהוּא תַּכְלִית הַדְּבֵיקוּת דִּכְנֶסֶת יִשְׂרָאֵל בֵּאלֹהִים חַיִּים, שֶׁמִּזֶּה נִצְמַח הִתְגַּלּוּת שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַקְּדוּשָׁה שֶׁיְּבוֹרַר בְּבִיאַת בֶּן דָּוִד בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ אָמֵן

which represents the ultimate cleaving of the Congregation of Israel unto the Living God, whence sprouts the revelation of the holy root to be clarified at the coming of the Son of David swiftly in our days, Amen;1283Yoma 54b: “At the time when Israel would ascend for the festival, they would roll back the curtain and show them the Keruvim intertwined with one another [me’urin zeh ba-zeh],” saying, “see the love of the Omnipresent for you.”
שֶׁגַּם בִּהְיוֹתָם בְּתַכְלִית הַיְרִידָה שֶׁאֵין לְמַטָּה וְעַד לֶעָפָר, לֹא נִיתְּקוּ מִשָּׁרְשָׁם שֶׁבִּקְדֻשָּׁה כְּלוּם:
that even when they are in the ultimate descent down to the dust, they have not severed from their holy root in any way.

items.h: The theme: The distinguished scholar in Yavneh and the purification of the creeping reptile through 150 reasons. At the destruction of the Second Temple, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asked Vespasian for Yavneh and its sages (Gittin 56b). Yavneh derives from the root of building (binyan), for these scholars were engaged in the spiritual construction of the Third Temple. The eminent student who purified the creeping reptile (sheretz) with 150 reasons (Eruvin 13b) tapped into the light of the entwined Cherubim revealed at the destruction. These 150 reasons correspond to the 150 gates across the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, rectifying all levels of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah until sin is completely eliminated.

p: וְזֶהוּ גַּם כֵּן עִנְיַן אוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד שֶׁהָיָה בְּיַבְנֶה שֶׁהוּא בְּעֵת הַחֻרְבָּן, שֶׁאָז הָיָה כָּל חָכְמַת תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה שָׁם
And this is likewise the inner meaning of that student who lived in Yavneh at the era of the Destruction, when the entirety of the wisdom of the Oral Torah was gathered there;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּהַנִּיזָּקִין, גִּיטִּין נ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּרַבִּי יוֹחָנָן בֶּן זַכַּאי בִּקֵּשׁ מֵאַסְפַּסְיָאנוּס: ״תֵּן לִי יַבְנֶה וַחֲכָמֶיהָ״

as they related [in Gittin 56b] that Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai requested of Vespasian: "Give me Yavneh and its sages";1284Eruvin 13b: “It was taught: there was a distinguished student [talmid vasik] at Yavneh who would purify the sheretz with a hundred and fifty reasons. Ravina said: I will debate and purify it — and if a snake, which kills and increases impurity, is [itself] pure, a sheretz, which does not kill and increase impurity, all the more so [should be pure]! But it is not so — [the snake] performs a mere sting-act [i.e., it causes death by injury, not by intrinsic impurity].”1285Gittin 56b - “Yavneh and its Sages” as a preserved center of Torah: Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai asks Vespasian to grant him Yavneh and its Sages, the dynasty of Rabban Gamliel, and physicians for R’ Tzadok. The sugya also records both the criticism that he should have asked that Jerusalem itself be spared and the defense that a larger request might have been refused, leaving no rescue at all. Rav Tzadok reads the granted remnant positively: the center of Torah she-be’al peh preserved at Yavneh becomes the seed of reconstruction after the Churban. The wordplay between Yavneh and the root b-n-h, “to build,” is Rav Tzadok’s interpretive development, not an explanation stated by the Gemara.
וְעַל שֵׁם זֶה נִקְרָא ״יַבְנֶה״, שֶׁהֵם הָעוֹסְקִים בְּבִנְיָינוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם וּבַיִת הַשְּׁלִישִׁי שֶׁיִּבָּנֶה בִּמְהֵרָה בְיָמֵינוּ, שֶׁלְּתַכְלִית זֶה הָיָה הַחֻרְבָּן

and on this account it was named "Yavneh" [from the root banah, to build], for they were engaged in the rebuilding of the universe and the Third Temple that will be built speedily in our days, for which ultimate purpose the Destruction occurred.1286Berachos 64a - Torah scholars as the world’s builders: The Bavli teaches that Torah scholars increase peace in the world and expounds Yeshayah 54:13: “Do not read banayikh, your children, but bonayikh, your builders.” The immediate teaching is that scholars build peace for their generation. Rav Tzadok extends that image to the sages of Yavneh as builders of the world and of the future Temple: their preservation and development of the Oral Torah is itself part of the rebuilding that emerges from destruction.
וְאוֹתוֹ תַּלְמִיד שֶׁהָיָה הַוָּותִיק שֶׁבָּהֶם, זָכָה לְהַשִּׂיג אוֹתוֹ אוֹר הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִדְּבֵיקוּת הַגָּמוּר דִּכְרוּבִים מְעוֹרִים שֶׁהָיָה בִּשְׁעַת הַחֻרְבָּן

And that student who was the most eminent among them merited to attain that light drawn from the complete cleaving of the entwined Cherubim at the hour of the Destruction;1287Yoma 54b - the intertwined keruvim at the moment of destruction: Reish Lakish states that when the nations entered the Sanctuary they saw the keruvim intertwined with one another. The Gemara reports the embrace and the nations’ mockery, but does not explain why such a sign of closeness appeared at the moment of catastrophe. Rav Tzadok resolves that paradox mystically: the Churban contains an inward point of complete attachment, and the light drawn from that attachment gives birth to the force of future redemption.
שֶׁהוּא לֵידַת הַמָּשִׁיחַ הַמְטַהֵר וּמְזַכֵּךְ הַכֹּל, שֶׁ״יְבֻקַּשׁ עֲוֹן יִשְׂרָאֵל וְאֵינֶנּוּ״ (יִרְמְיָה נ:כ)

which is the birth of the Messiah who purifies and refines all, when "the iniquity of Israel shall be sought for, and there shall be none" (Yirmiyah 50:20);1288Yirmiyahu 50:20 - “the iniquity of Israel shall be sought, and it shall not be”: The verse places this promise in the future restoration of Israel and Yehudah and concludes, “for I will pardon those whom I leave as a remnant.” On the level of peshat, the absence of sin is grounded in divine forgiveness. Rav Tzadok reads the prophecy more inwardly: the light of Mashiach purifies and refines the entire root so completely that the sin can no longer be found. This is his theological expansion of the prophetic promise.
וְזֶהוּ טָהֳרַת הַשֶּׁרֶץ בְּק״נ טְעָמִים, שֶׁהוּא הַק״נ הַשְּׁעָרִים שֶׁשְּׁלֵימוּת נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁלּוֹ בְּעוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה:

and this is the purification of the sheretz with 150 reasons, corresponding to the 150 gates of the perfection of his Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah across the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah.1289Eruvin 13b; Ohr HaChammah on Zohar I 62a - 150 reasons, 153, and the three soul-levels: The Bavli’s text says that the distinguished student at Yavneh could purify the sheretz with one hundred and fifty reasons. Rav Tzadok’s text here speaks of one hundred and fifty-three and then identifies one hundred and fifty gates with the completion of nefesh, ruach, and neshamah in Asiyah, Yetzirah, and Beriah. Ohr HaChammah states the standard correspondence explicitly: neshamah in Beriah, ruach in Yetzirah, and nefesh in Asiyah. The move from the Gemara’s 150 to 153 is therefore Rav Tzadok’s symbolic construction; the natural reading is the 150 gates together with the three named soul-levels.

items.h: The theme: Ravina's a fortiori argument from the Primordial Serpent and the ultimate purity of Creation. Ravina, the sealer of the Talmud Bavli, sought to purify the sheretz through an a fortiori argument from the Serpent: if the Serpent who brought death and impurity is pure, how much more so a sheretz (Eruvin 13b)! The Serpent—the root of Samael—acts without free choice like an inanimate thorn (ma'aseh kotz), functioning as an axe in the hand of the hewer (Yeshayah 10:15) to fulfill the will of the King like the harlot in the Zohar (Terumah 163a). In the Future, the yetzer hara will be slaughtered, its defilement purged, and it too will remain sacred unto our God (Zechariah 9:7). Then it will become clear that all Israel's past actions were sovereignly directed from the six days of Creation, making all sins turn white as snow.

p: וְרָבִינָא שֶׁהָיָה סוֹף הוֹרָאָה בְּבָבֶל וּמֵחוֹתְמֵי הַתַּלְמוּד וְתוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, הִשִּׂיג גַּם כֵּן שֶׁמֶץ וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ בָּזֶה
And Ravina, who represented the end of halachic instruction in Babylonia and was among the sealers of the Talmud and the Oral Torah (Bava Metzia 86a), attained a trace and root in this as well;
וְאָמַר שָׁם: ״אֲנִי אָדוּן וַאֲטַהֲרֶנּוּ, קַל וָחֹמֶר מִנָּחָשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ״ (עֵרוּבִין י״ג עַמּוּד ב׳)

and he stated there: "I will debate and purify it by an a fortiori argument from the serpent, etc." (Eruvin 13b);1290Eruvin 13b: “It was taught: there was a distinguished student [talmid vasik] at Yavneh who would purify the sheretz with a hundred and fifty reasons. Ravina said: I will debate and purify it — and if a snake, which kills and increases impurity, is [itself] pure, a sheretz, which does not kill and increase impurity, all the more so [should be pure]! But it is not so — [the snake] performs a mere sting-act [i.e., it causes death by injury, not by intrinsic impurity].”1291Bava Metzia 86a - Rav Ashi and Ravina as the “end of hora’ah”: The Bavli states: “Rabbi and Rabbi Nasan are the end of the Mishnah; Rav Ashi and Ravina are the end of hora’ah.” The phrase marks the close of the Amoraic period and the authoritative formation of the Babylonian Talmud. Rav Tzadok singles out Ravina because the rejected kal vachomer itself was preserved within that sealed Oral Torah. His claim is not that every proposed argument is practical halachah, but that its inclusion can preserve a true conceptual root even when the final ruling rejects it.
רָצָה לוֹמַר דְּנָחָשׁ הַקַּדְמוֹנִי שֶׁהֵבִיא הַמִּיתָה לָעוֹלָם וְהִרְבָּה כָּל עִנְיַן הַטּוּמְאָה בָּעוֹלָם, הוּא עַצְמוֹ טָהוֹר
meaning that the Primordial Serpent, who brought death to the world and multiplied all defilement, is himself pure!
כִּידוּעַ דְּהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַסַּמֶּ״ךְ־מֵ״ם שֶׁיִּהְיֶה מַלְאַךְ קְדוּשָׁה לֶעָתִיד בִּזְבִיחַת הַיֵּצֶר
As is known that he is the root of Samael, who will become an angel of holiness in the Future upon the slaughtering of the yetzer hara (Sukkah 52a);
שֶׁ״יוּסַר דָּמָיו מִפִּיו וְשִׁקֻּצָיו מִבֵּין שִׁנָּיו וְנִשְׁאַר גַּם הוּא לֵאלֹהֵינוּ״ (זְכַרְיָה ט:ז)

wherein "I will take away his blood out of his mouth, and his detestable things from between his teeth, and he too shall be a remnant for our God" (Zechariah 9:7);1292Zechariah 9:7 - a purified remnant incorporated into holiness: In its prophetic context, the verse speaks about the Philistine cities: God removes blood and abominations from their mouths, and the surviving remnant becomes attached to God and incorporated into Yehudah. Rav Tzadok applies this pattern beyond the peshat to Samael and the primordial serpent: what presently functions as accusation and impurity will be stripped of its corrupt expression, leaving a force redirected toward holiness. The identification with Samael is therefore a mystical application, not the plain subject of the verse.
כִּי גַּם הוּא בְּהַסָּתוֹתָיו וְקִטְרוּגָיו עוֹשֶׂה רְצוֹן קוֹנוֹ דִּלְכָךְ נוֹצַר, כִּמְשַׁל הַזּוֹנָה [בְּזֹוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ פָּרָשַׁת תְּרוּמָה קס״ג עַמּוּד א׳]

for he too, through his incitements and accusations, fulfills the will of his Creator for which he was fashioned, as in the parable of the harlot [in Zohar, Terumah 163a];1293Zohar II, Terumah 163a - the king, his son, and the harlot sent to test him: The Zohar compares the evil inclination to a harlot whom a king commands to entice his beloved son in order to test the son’s loyalty. She must carry out the assignment, yet the king’s desire is that the son resist her, and her deepest success lies in his refusal. Rav Tzadok uses the parable to distinguish the seducing power’s assigned function from the human being’s moral choice: the tempter serves the divine test, while the person remains responsible to overcome it.
וּסְתָמָא דִּגְמָרָא דָּחֵי: ״דְּהוּא מַעֲשֵׂה קוֹץ בְּעָלְמָא עָבֵיד״
and the anonymous voice of the Gemara rejected this: "he merely performs the action of a thorn";
שֶׁאֵינוֹ בַּעַל בְּחִירָה כְּאָדָם הַחוֹטֵא בִּבְחִירָתוֹ
for he is not a creature endowed with free choice like a human being who sins through his choice;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן הוּא מֵהָעֶלְיוֹנִים שֶׁאֵין לוֹ בְּחִירָה וְאֵין עוֹשֶׂה בִּבְחִירָתוֹ כְּלָל, רַק שֶׁלְּכָךְ נִבְרָא וְנִשְׁתַּלַּח
whereas the Serpent belongs to the supernal agents who possess no free will and act without volition, having been created and dispatched solely for this purpose;
וְזֶהוּ מַעֲשֵׂה קוֹץ שֶׁנּוֹקֵב עַל יְדֵי הָאָדָם הַנּוֹקֵב בּוֹ, וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁנֶּאֱמַר [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה י״ט]: ״אַתָּה עֲשִׂיתוֹ רַע״

and this is the action of a thorn which pricks only when an individual pushes against it, matching what is stated [in Bereishis Rabbah 19:1]: "You [Man] made him evil."1294Midrash Tanchuma, Bereishis 7:2 - “You made it evil”: The extant Midrash Tanchuma asks why the evil inclination was created and answers that the person “made it evil”: a child does not sin, and when the person matures he can either direct or corrupt the inclination. The Midrash compares this task to sweetening bitter lupines through repeated preparation and concludes that the inclination is delivered into human hands to master. Rav Tzadok applies that teaching to the serpent’s role, while the Midrash itself emphasizes human responsibility and the possibility of transforming desire rather than blaming creation.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם נִסְדְּרוּ דִּבְרֵי רָבִינָא בַּתַּלְמוּד
And nevertheless, the words of Ravina were preserved in the holy Talmud;
וְיָדוּעַ דַּאֲפִילּוּ הַסָּלְקָא דַּעְתָּךְ דִּגְמָרָא וְהַהֲוָה אָמֵינָא הַנִּדְחֵית הִיא אֱמֶת גַּם כֵּן
and it is known that even the initial hypothesis (hava amina) of the Gemara that is subsequently rejected is likewise true;
מִצַּד דְּדָבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ לֹא נִזְכַּר בַּתַּלְמוּד שֶׁהוּא תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת, וְדָבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֱמֶת אֵינוֹ תּוֹרָה וְאֵין לְהַזְכִּירוֹ בְּדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה
because an untruth is never recorded in the Talmud which is the Torah of Truth, and a thing that is not true is not Torah and has no place in the words of Torah;

וּכְמוֹ שֶׁכָּתַבְתִּי בְּמָקוֹם אַחֵר רְאָיָה מִמַּה שֶּׁאִיתָא בַּמִּדְרָשׁ [רַבָּה פָּרָשַׁת וַיְחִי פָּרָשָׁה ק׳] לְעִנְיַן לְשַׁנּוֹת מִפְּנֵי הַשָּׁלוֹם, דְּהַכְּתוּבִים דִּבְּרוּ דִּבְרֵי בְּדַאי מִפְּנֵי הַשָּׁלוֹם מִקְּרָא דְּ״אָבִיךָ צִוָּה לִפְנֵי מוֹתוֹ וְגוֹמֵר״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית נ:טז)

as I wrote elsewhere, bringing proof from the Midrash [Bereishis Rabbah 100:8] regarding altering the truth for the sake of peace: that the verses recorded fabricated words for peace from "Your father commanded before he died, etc." (Bereishis 50:16);
וַהֲרֵי שָׁם הַכָּתוּב אֵינוֹ מְסַפֵּר שֶׁקֶר, דַּהֲרֵי הֵם אָמְרוּ לוֹמַר כֵּן לוֹ
yet Scripture itself was not recording a falsehood, for the brothers indeed said those words to Yosef;
רַק דְּאֵין לְהַזְכִּיר בַּתּוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא תּוֹרַת אֱמֶת דְּבַר שֶׁל שֶׁקֶר שֶׁהִגִּיד אֵיזֶה אָדָם גַּם כֵּן, אִם לֹא לְלַמְּדֵנוּ דְּמוּתָּר לְשַׁקֵּר כְּהַאי גַּוְונָא וְאֵין זֶה נֶחְשָׁב לְשֶׁקֶר

but rather, the Torah would never record even a falsehood spoken by another person unless to teach that it is permitted to alter the truth in such circumstances, so that it is not accounted a lie;1295Devarim Rabbah 5:15; Yerushalmi Peah 1:1:42 - altering words for the sake of peace: These sources state that Scripture records words spoken for peace in the brothers’ message, “Your father commanded before his death,” although no such command is found. The printed citation here to Bereishis Rabbah 100:9 does not match the extant section, which discusses Yosef’s consolation of his brothers; the explicit formulation appears in Devarim Rabbah and the Yerushalmi, with parallels in Midrash Tanchuma. Rav Tzadok’s inference is that Torah records the statement only because its permitted, peace-making function is itself true Torah.
וְהָכִי נַמֵּי בַּתַּלְמוּד שֶׁהִיא תּוֹרָה שֶׁבְּעַל פֶּה, וַדַּאי אֵין לְהַזְכִּיר דָּבָר שֶׁאֵינוֹ אֱמֶת אַף שֶׁדְּחָאוּהוּ
and so too in the Talmud, which is the Oral Torah, it would never record something that is untrue even when rejected.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ ״לָא הִיא״, הַיְינוּ דְּוַדַּאי כֵּיוָן דְּהַתּוֹרָה טִמְּאַתּוּ עַל כֵּן יֵשׁ טַעַם לִדְחוֹת כָּל ק״נ טַעֲמֵי הַהֶיתֵּר שֶׁלּוֹ

And perforce, when the Gemara said "this is not so," it meant: in this world, because the Torah explicitly declared it impure, there exists a valid halachic ground to push aside all 150 arguments of purity;
אֲבָל לֶעָתִיד, כְּשֶׁיְּבוֹעַר רוּחַ הַטּוּמְאָה מִן הָאָרֶץ, יִשָּׁאֲרוּ טַעֲמֵי הַטָּהֳרָה שֶׁלּוֹ לְבַדָּם
but in the Future, when the spirit of impurity is purged from the earth (Zechariah 13:2), its 150 reasons for purity will stand alone!

וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ וִיסוֹד כָּל אוֹתָם הַטְּעָמִים הוּא הַטַּעַם שֶׁגִּילָּה רָבִינָא: דְּכָל הַטּוּמְאוֹת נִמְשָׁכִים מִזּוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ וּמַשְׁכָּא דְּחִוְיָא שֶׁבּוֹ נִתְלַבְּשׁוּ גּוּפוֹת בְּנֵי אָדָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה בְּכָתְנוֹת הָעוֹר הַגּוּפָנִי הַמָּלֵא זוּהֲמָא

And the fundamental root of all those reasons is the premise revealed by Ravina: all impurities derive from the defilement of the Serpent and the "skin of the snake" (mashka d'chivya, Zohar I, 28b) wherewith human bodies in this world were enclothed in corporeal garments of skin filled with defilement;
וְאִם הַנָּחָשׁ עַצְמוֹ טָהוֹר לְפִי שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה רַק מַעֲשֵׂה קוֹץ וְהוּא כְּגַרְזֶן בְּיַד הַחוֹצֵב
and if the Serpent himself is intrinsically pure because he acts merely like a thorn, functioning as an axe in the hand of the hewer (Yeshayah 10:15);

לֶעָתִיד יִתְגַּלֶּה כִּי גַּם כָּל מַעֲשֵׂינוּ הֵמָּה רַק כְּגַרְזֶן בְּיַד הַחוֹצֵב שֶׁהֵם סְדוּרִים וּבָאִים מִשֵּׁשֶׁת יְמֵי בְּרֵאשִׁית, וְעַל יְדֵי זֶה ״כַּשֶּׁלֶג יַלְבִּינוּ״ (יְשַׁעְיָה א:יח):

in the Future it will be revealed that all our deeds likewise were merely like an axe in the hand of the hewer, ordered from the six days of Creation, wherefore all sins "shall be made as white as snow" (Yeshayah 1:18).1296Zechariah 13:2; Genesis 3:21; Isaiah 10:15 - impurity, garments of skin, and the axe in the hewer’s hand: Zechariah promises that God will remove idolatry, false prophecy, and the “spirit of impurity” from the land. Genesis describes the post-sin clothing as “garments of skin,” while Isaiah compares Assyria to an axe that cannot boast over the one who wields it. Rav Tzadok joins these images into an eschatological teaching: when the serpent’s pollution is removed, embodied history will be seen within divine providence and purified “as snow.” Isaiah’s own context still condemns the axe for arrogance, so the metaphor of instrumentality does not cancel present human accountability; Rav Tzadok is describing the future disclosure and rectification of the root.

items.h: The theme: The confession of Achan and the indestructible covenant of the Jewish soul. When the transcendent root of Israel is unveiled, it becomes evident that even the outcasts are termed "children of God" and possess a portion in the World to Come. The dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah concerns whether we evaluate an individual by his temporary fallen state or by his ultimate spiritual destination. When Achan transgressed all five books of the Torah, Hashem declared to Yehoshua: "Israel has sinned" (Yehoshua 7:11)—even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite (Sanhedrin 44a). Because Hashem knew that Achan would confess before his execution, his sin was temporary, and his confession retroactively reaffirmed his unbroken share in the World to Come.

p: וְדָבָר זֶה הוּא כְּשֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה אוֹתוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל בִּמְקוֹר מַחְצַבָּם שֶׁנֶּעְלַם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
And this truth will shine forth when that essential root of the holiness of Israel in their primal rock-hewn source—concealed in this world—is revealed;
שֶׁאֵינוֹ נִגְלָה אֶלָּא לְאוֹתָם שֶׁזָּכוּ לְהִתְלַבֵּשׁ בְּכָתְנוֹת אוֹר תַּחַת עוֹר דְּחִוְיָא כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
which is revealed solely unto those who merited to be enclothed in "garments of light" (kasnos or) rather than the skin of the snake, like Rabbi Meir;
וּסְתָם מִשְׁנָה כְּוָותֵיהּ, וְגַם סְתָם מִשְׁנָה [דְּרֵישׁ פֶּרֶק חֵלֶק, סַנְהֶדְרִין צ׳ עַמּוּד א׳] לֹא פָּלֵיג עָלָיו

and an anonymous Mishnah accords with him (Eruvin 13b), and the anonymous opening of Perek Chelek (Sanhedrin 90a) does not dispute him;1297Bereshit Rabbah 20:12; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:56 - garments of light and serpent-skin: Bereshit Rabbah records that in R’ Meir’s Torah they found “garments of light” in place of the verse’s “garments of skin.” In Dover Tzedek, Rav Tzadok explains the body as the limiting garment or vessel associated in the Zohar with the serpent’s skin, yet immediately returns to R’ Meir’s “garments of light” to show that the same garment can become transparent to its inner light. The present se’if applies that earlier teaching to the hidden root of Jewish holiness: R’ Meir perceives the light within the obscuring garment, not a different Torah text or a denial of embodied limitation.
דְּאַף הֵם נִקְרָאִים ״בָּנִים״ וְיֵשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק, דְּדָא וְדָא אֱמֶת כָּל אֶחָד בִּשְׁעָתוֹ

for even those sinners are called "children" and possess an ultimate portion, both realities being true, each in its appointed time.1298Sanhedrin 86a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - R’ Meir, the anonymous Mishnah, and the enduring Jewish root: The Bavli identifies the anonymous Mishnah with R’ Meir’s school. Rav Tzadok’s parallel in Peri Tzadik explains the Exodus “tidings of children” as a promise that even wicked descendants will never be expelled from Israel; he cites Achan, the excluded kings and commoners, and the view of the dorshei reshumos that all return to the World to Come except Bilaam. This closely parallels the se’if’s distinction between the Mishnah’s revealed judgment in its proper time and the deeper root disclosed at the end. It does not erase the Mishnah’s warnings or present consequences; it places them within an ultimate covenantal horizon.
וּפְלוּגְתַּת רַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה בִּקְרִיאַת שְׁמָם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה: אִי אָזְלִינַן בָּתַר מֵעִיקָּרָא אוֹ בָּתַר בַּסּוֹף

And the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah concerns their legal designation in this world: whether we judge according to the initial temporary state or according to the ultimate end;1299Kiddushin 36a: “It was taught: ‘you are children to Hashem your God’ — at the time you conduct yourselves in the manner of children, you are called children; [if] you do not conduct yourselves in the manner of children, you are not called children — the words of R’ Yehuda. R’ Meir says: either way you are called children, as it says (Yirmeyah 4): ‘they are foolish children,’ and it says (Devarim 32): ‘children in whom there is no faithfulness,’ and it says (Yeshayah 1): ‘seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly,’ and it says (Hoshea 2): ‘and it shall be, in the place where it is said to them, you are not My people, it shall be said to them, children of the living God.’ What is [the point of each] ‘and it says’? [It is necessary:] and if you would say [that] it is [only] the foolish who are called children, [but] when there is no faithfulness in them they are not called children — come and hear, ‘and it says: children in whom there is no faithfulness.’ And if you would say [that] when there is no faithfulness in them they are [still] called children, [but] when they worship idolatry they are not called children — come and hear, ‘and it says: seed of evildoers, children who deal corruptly.’ And if you would say [that] they are called ‘children who deal corruptly,’ [but] fit children they are not called — come and hear, ‘and it says: and it shall be, in the place where it is said to them, you are not My people, it shall be said to them, children of the living God.’”
וְהַסּוֹבְרִים דְּמוּמָר כְּגוֹי, סְבִירָא לְהוּ דִּבְרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה הֲלָכָה כְּרַבִּי יְהוּדָה דְּאֵין נִקְרָאִים בָּנִים

and those Geonim who maintain that an apostate is considered like a gentile hold that in the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah the halachah follows Rabbi Yehudah, that they are not called children;
וְאִם כֵּן הֵם ״לֹא עַמִּי״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר ״בִּמְקוֹם וְגוֹמֵר״ וְ״קְרָאוֹ וְגוֹמֵר״, שֶׁהֵם ב׳ הֲפָכִים

and if so, they are "not My people," for "children" and "My people" are inseparable counterparts, so that those who are not His children are likewise not His people and depart from the collective of Israel.
וּמֵהָא דְּעָכָן אֵין רְאָיָה, אַף דְּעָבַר עַל ה׳ חוּמְשֵׁי תוֹרָה

And from the case of Achan there is no counter-proof to their view, even though he transgressed all five books of the Torah;1300Cf. Hoshea 2:1 — “Ve-hayah bimkom asher ye’amer lahem lo ami atem, ye’amer lahem benei Kel chai” (“And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, You are not My people, it shall be said to them, Children of the living God”). This is the scriptural hinge of the whole discussion: the same nation moves between “not My people” and “children of the living God,” which R’ Tzadok reads as the two poles — origin and end — over which R’ Meir and R’ Yehuda divide.
שֶׁהֲרֵי מְפוֹרָשׁ בַּמִּשְׁנָה [סַנְהֶדְרִין מ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּהוּא נִתְוַודָּה וְיֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
for it is explicit in the Mishnah [Sanhedrin 43b] that he confessed and acquired a portion in the World to Come;
וּמֵאַחַר שֶׁשָּׁב וְנִתְוַודָּה הֲרֵי חָזַר לִכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל בְּעוֹדוֹ חַי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, וְאִגַּלַּאי מִלְּתָא לְמַפְרֵעַ דְּלֹא נִפְקַע מִינֵּיהּ
and since he repented and confessed, he returned to the collective of Israel while still alive in this world, revealing retroactively that his Jewish status was never severed!
וְאַף דְּהַשְׁתָּא הוּא דְּשָׁב, בִּתְשׁוּבָה הוּא מְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם לִהְיוֹת הֶעָוֹן מִתְכַּפֵּר וּכְאִלּוּ לֹא חָטָא

And although he repented only at the end, through repentance he rectifies the past so that the iniquity is atoned and it is as though he never sinned;1301Sanhedrin 43b-44a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - Achan’s confession and “although he sinned, he is Israel”: The Mishnah teaches that confession grants a condemned person a share in the World to Come and proves this from Achan: “Today you are troubled,” but not in the World to Come. The Gemara then derives from “Israel has sinned” that even after sin he remains Israel, like a myrtle among thorns. Peri Tzadik explicitly joins these two teachings to show that even extreme sin cannot remove the covenantal name and that correction remains possible. Rav Tzadok’s language of retroactive disclosure concerns the continuity of identity revealed through teshuvah; it does not mean that the earlier sin, punishment, or responsibility never occurred.
וְאַף דְּעַתָּה עֲדַיִין בְּרִשְׁעוֹ וְנֶעֶנְשׁוּ יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יָדוֹ, מִכָּל מָקוֹם לֹא שַׁיָּיךְ לוֹמַר דְּנֶעֱקַר שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל בָּזֶה
and even though at the moment of the decree he was still in his wickedness and Israel suffered defeat on his account, it is inappropriate to say that the name of Israel was uprooted from him;
דִּקְמֵי שְׁמַיָּא גַּלְיָא דְּסוֹפוֹ לָשׁוּב בְּחַיָּיו, וְחֶטְאוֹ וְעָנְשׁוֹ רַק לְשָׁעָה
for before Heaven it was revealed that he would ultimately repent during his lifetime, and his sin and punishment were only temporary.
וְאַף דִּקְרָא דְּ״חָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל״ (יְהוֹשֻׁעַ ז:יא) נֶאֱמַר קוֹדֶם שֶׁשָּׁב וַעֲדַיִין הַבְּחִירָה בְּיָדוֹ שֶׁמָּא לֹא יָשׁוּב
And even though the verse "Israel has sinned" (Yehoshua 7:11) was stated before he repented, when free choice was still in his hands that he might not repent;
וְאַף דְּהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא יוֹדֵעַ עֲתִידוֹת, מִכָּל מָקוֹם ״צַדִּיק וְרָשָׁע לָא קָאָמַר״ (נִדָּה ט״ז עַמּוּד ב׳)

and although the Holy One, blessed be He, knows all future events, nevertheless "whether one will be righteous or wicked He does not decree" (Niddah 16b);1302Niddah 16b; Resisei Layla 54:3 - foreknowledge, free choice, and Heaven’s role in teshuvah: Niddah teaches that the angel announces strength, wisdom, and wealth, but does not pronounce “righteous or wicked,” because everything is in Heaven’s hands except fear of Heaven. In Resisei Layla, Rav Tzadok develops the tension more fully: creation and divine knowledge encompass the eventual outcome, yet moral choice remains the person’s; even the awakening of a baal teshuvah comes from God, who nevertheless credits the opening to the human being. This is the closest internal parallel to the se’if’s answer that Heaven knew Achan would repent freely even though prophetic disclosure made that repentance certain.
וְאֵיךְ אָמַר לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ שֶׁהוּא עֲדַיִין בִּכְלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, וְהַיְינוּ שֶׁיָּשׁוּב, וּמִשֶּׁגִּילָּה זֶה לַנָּבִיא אִי אֶפְשָׁר עוֹד שֶׁלֹּא יָשׁוּב וְאֵינוֹ עוֹד שָׁב בִּבְחִירָתוֹ

and how could He tell Yehoshua that he remains included within Israel—which presumes he will repent—seeing that once He revealed this to the prophet it became impossible for him not to repent, thereby nullifying his free choice?
יֵשׁ לוֹמַר: מַה בְּכָךְ דְּהָיָה מוּכְרָח לָשׁוּב, מִכָּל מָקוֹם קְמֵי שְׁמַיָּא גַּלְיָא דְּגַם בִּבְחִירָתוֹ בְּלֹא הֶכְרֵחַ הָיָה שָׁב
One can say: what does it matter that he was ultimately compelled to repent? Before Heaven it was known that even by his own uncompelled choice he would have repented!
וְהָא דְּגִילָּה לִיהוֹשֻׁעַ זֶה וְשֶׁיִּהְיֶה מוּכְרָח, יֵשׁ לוֹמַר מִשּׁוּם דְּהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ לֹא רָצָה לְגַלּוֹת לוֹ מִי חָטָא, רַק שֶׁיִּפּוֹל גּוֹרָל כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [שָׁם מ״ג עַמּוּד ב׳]
And that He revealed this to Yehoshua so that it became fixed, was because the Blessed Name did not wish to tell him directly who had sinned, but rather that a lottery should be cast (Sanhedrin 43b);
וְעַל יְדֵי הַגּוֹרָל לְבַד לֹא הָיוּ שׁוֹמְעִין לוֹ בְּנֵי שִׁבְטוֹ לְהָרְגוֹ
and through the lottery alone the members of his tribe (Yehudah) would not have permitted Yehoshua to execute him;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ שָׁם דְּאָמַר לוֹ עָכָן: ״בַּגּוֹרָל אַתָּה בָּא עָלַי וְכוּלֵיהּ״
as they stated there that Achan challenged him: "Do you come upon me with a mere lottery? If a lottery were cast between you and Elazar the Kohen Gadol, one of you would be caught!";
וְלֹא נֶהֱרַג אֶלָּא אַחַר שֶׁהוֹדָה בְּעַצְמוֹ, וּמִי יֵימַר דְּיוֹדֶה וּמַה יּוֹעִיל בְּגוֹרָלוֹ
and he was not executed until he confessed of his own accord, and who would guarantee that he would confess, so what would the lottery have availed?
עַל זֶה הִבְטִיחוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ: ״אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁחָטָא יִשְׂרָאֵל הוּא״, הַיְינוּ שֶׁסּוֹפוֹ לָשׁוּב וּלְהִתְוַודּוֹת כְּשֶׁיִּתְגַּלֶּה עַל יְדֵי הַגּוֹרָל:

Toward this the Blessed Name assured Yehoshua: "Even though he sinned, he remains an Israelite"—meaning that in the end he will certainly repent and confess when identified by the lottery.1303Sanhedrin 43b; Resisei Layla 54:3 - the lot, confession, and an awakening that does not cancel responsibility: When Yehoshua asked who sinned, God refused to act as an informer and directed him to cast lots. Achan challenged the evidentiary force of the lot; Yehoshua pleaded that he not discredit the lots, and Ravina says Yehoshua persuaded him verbally until he confessed. The narrative therefore distinguishes heavenly exposure from Achan’s own admission. Resisei Layla supplies Rav Tzadok’s broader framework: God arouses thoughts of repentance and “opens” the way, while the act is still attributed to the person. The se’if reads God’s assurance in that same register - certainty from Heaven together with accountable confession below.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים צ״ז–ק״ב

The theme: Analyzing the divine declaration regarding Achan ("Israel has sinned", Yehoshua 7:11) and the nature of mutual responsibility (arevut). Superficially, one might deduce that an apostate remains termed an Israelite only if he ultimately repents, as Achan did. However, R' Tzadok explains that Hashem told Yehoshua "Israel has sinned" for a different reason: to explain why the entire nation suffered military defeat at Ai on account of one man. Had Achan completely severed himself from Israel, he would have possessed the status of a gentile, and his crime would not have brought collective guilt upon the community. This mirrors the prophet Hoshea's plea: "Exchange them for another nation" (Pesachim 87a)—meaning not that Hashem should replace Israel entirely, but that He should sever the habitual sinners into a separate nation so that the righteous would not suffer for the wicked ("together with the thorn the cabbage is struck", Bava Kamma 92a). By declaring "Israel has sinned," Hashem informed Yehoshua that Achan remained an integral member of the nation, binding all Israel as guarantors for him.

p: וּלְפִי זֶה יִהְיֶה אַדְּרַבָּא מִזֶּה רְאָיָה דְּלֹא נִקְרָא ״יִשְׂרָאֵל״ אֶלָּא כְּשֶׁשָּׁב אַחַר כָּךְ
And according to this, on the contrary, from this there would be proof that he is termed an "Israelite" only when he subsequently repents,
דְּאִם לֹא כֵן לְאֵיזֶה צֹרֶךְ אָמַר לוֹ זֶה כָּאן גַּבֵּי עָכָן
for otherwise, for what purpose did Hashem state this to Yehoshua here regarding Achan?
וּמִיהוּ יֵשׁ לוֹמַר בָּזֶה, דְּאָמַר לוֹ כֵּן מִטַּעַם אַחֵר לְעִנְיַן מַה שֶּׁנֶּעֶנְשׁוּ כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל עַל יָדוֹ

However, one can explain this matter by saying that He told him so for a different reason: concerning why all Israel were punished on his account (at the battle of Ai);1304Sanhedrin 44a; Shevuot 39a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8 - Israel-status and communal responsibility: Sanhedrin derives from “Israel has sinned” that even after Achan’s sin he is still called Israel. Shevuot derives from “they shall stumble one over another” that all Israel are guarantors for one another. Rav Tzadok explains in Yisrael Kedoshim that the souls of Israel are rooted together in the letters of Torah and that the bond established at Sinai cannot be severed entirely. The se’if therefore reads Achan’s continued name “Israel” not only as a statement about his private identity, but as the legal-spiritual basis for the nation’s continuing arvus toward him.
דְּאִלּוּ יָצָא מִכְּלַל יִשְׂרָאֵל, הֲרֵי אֵינוֹ עוֹד מִכְּלַל הָאוּמָּה רַק כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם
for had Achan departed from the collective of Israel, behold he would no longer be part of the nation but like all the gentiles,
וְאֵין לוֹ חִיבּוּר עִמָּהֶם אֶלָּא עִם הַגּוֹיִם, וְלָמָּה יֵעָנְשׁוּ הֵם עַל יָדוֹ
having no connection with them but rather with the gentiles, so why should they be punished on his account?
וּכְפִי הַנִּרְאֶה זֶה הָיָה כַּוָּונַת הוֹשֵׁעַ שֶׁאָמַר ״הַחֲלִיפֵם בְּאוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת״
And apparently this was the intention of Hoshea when he said, "Exchange them for another nation" (Pesachim 87a);
וּבְוַדַּאי אֵין רָצָה לוֹמַר דֶּרֶךְ חֲלִיפִין שֶׁיִּקַּח אוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת לְחֶלְקוֹ תְּמוּרָתָם

and certainly he did not mean by way of actual exchange that Hashem should take another nation as His portion in their stead,1305Pesachim 87a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - Hoshea’s proposal and the son who cannot be exchanged: Pesachim relates that when God told Hoshea that His children had sinned, Hoshea answered that they should be exchanged for another nation. God taught him through his own wife and children that one does not simply send away those bound to him as children. In Peri Tzadik, Rav Tzadok interprets the Exodus “tidings of children” as the promise that even a wicked child born into Israel cannot remove himself from the nation’s covenantal identity. The present se’if reads Hoshea’s proposal narrowly: not the replacement of Israel’s chosen root, but the imagined removal of sinners from the collective so that the worthy would no longer bear responsibility for them.
דְּחַס וְשָׁלוֹם שֶׁיַּעֲלֶה עַל דַּעְתָּם כֵּן, שֶׁיִּהְיֶה אוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת רְאוּיָה לִיכָּנֵס לִקְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל וְלִהְיוֹת בִּמְקוֹמָם
for God forbid that it should enter their minds that another nation could ever be worthy of entering the holiness of Israel and standing in their place,
וּכְבָר בְּמַתַּן תּוֹרָה הֶחֱזִירָהּ עַל כָּל אוּמָּה וְלָשׁוֹן וְלֹא קִבְּלוּהָ, שֶׁאֵין לָהֶם שַׁיָּיכוּת עִמָּהּ רַק יִשְׂרָאֵל

seeing that already at the Giving of the Torah He offered it to every nation and tongue and they refused to accept it (Avodah Zarah 2b), having no affinity with it, which belongs solely to Israel;1306Avodah Zarah 2b; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8 - the Torah offered to the nations and Israel’s irreversible bond: Avodah Zarah teaches that the Holy One brought the Torah to every nation and language, but they did not accept it until Israel accepted it. Rav Tzadok adds in Yisrael Kedoshim that from Sinai onward the inner connection between Israel and Torah can no longer be completely interrupted, because Israel’s soul-roots are themselves included in Torah. Thus the se’if’s statement that no other nation can “take Israel’s place” is not a denial that individuals from the nations may convert; it concerns the unique historical-covenantal identity of Knesses Yisrael as a whole.
וְעַל כָּרְחֲךָ דְּכַוָּונָתוֹ רַק עַל הַחוֹטְאִים שֶׁיַּעֲבִירֵם מֵאוּמַּת יִשְׂרָאֵל לְאוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת
and perforce his intent referred solely to the sinners: that Hashem should transfer them out of the nation of Israel into another nation.
[וְנִתְקַיְּימָה גְּזֵירָתוֹ בַּעֲשֶׂרֶת הַשְּׁבָטִים שֶׁנִּטְמְעוּ בֵּין הָעַמִּים, וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ (בִּיבָמוֹת י״ז עַמּוּד א׳): ״לֹא זָזוּ מִשָּׁם עַד שֶׁעֲשָׂאוּם גּוֹיִם גְּמוּרִים״

[And his decree was fulfilled in the Ten Tribes who assimilated among the nations, as they stated [in Yevamos 17a]: "They did not move from there until they rendered them complete gentiles";1307Yevamos 17a: Of “the lost ones assimilated among the nations” — “they did not move from there until [Hashem] declared them not [His people],” reckoning them as gentiles for their assimilation.
אֶלָּא שֶׁהוּא קָאֵי אַחוֹטְאִים עַצְמָם וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנִּגְזַר בַּתְּחִלָּה שֶׁיִּקָּרְאוּ ״לֹא עַמִּי״, אֲבָל שָׁם קָאֵי אַזַּרְעָם כִּדְמַיְיתֵי מִקְּרָא דְּ״כִי בָנִים זָרִים יָלָדוּ״ (הוֹשֵׁעַ ה:ז)

except that Hoshea spoke of the sinners themselves, as originally decreed that they be called "not My people," whereas the Talmud in Yevamos refers to their offspring, as it cites from the verse "for they have begotten strange children" (Hoshea 5:7);
וְשָׁם [בְּהוֹשֵׁעַ ה׳] פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י עַל פָּסוּק זֶה: לְפִי שֶׁנָּשׂאוּ גּוֹיוֹת דִּוְלָדָהּ כְּמוֹתָהּ
and there [on Hoshea 5:7] Rashi explains on this verse: because they married gentile women whose offspring possesses her gentile status;
וְהֵן הֵם גַּם כֵּן דִּבְרֵי הַלִּישָׁנָא קַמָּא דִּשְׁמוּאֵל שָׁם, וּשְׁנֵיהֶם לְדָבָר אֶחָד כִּיוְּנוּ רַק שֶׁאָמַר כָּל אֶחָד אַקְּרָא אַחֵר]

and these are likewise the words of the first formulation of Shmuel there, both intending the identical principle, each master anchoring it upon a different verse];1308Yevamos 17a; Kiddushin 68b; Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, The Egyptian Exile 1:3 - the Ten Tribes, maternal lineage, and holiness from birth: Yevamos first explains that a child of a Jewish father and a non-Jewish mother is “her son,” not his Jewish son, and then records the formulation that the assimilated descendants of the Ten Tribes were treated as full gentiles, citing “they begot strange children.” Kiddushin derives the same rule of maternal status. In Ohr Zarua LaTzadik, Rav Tzadok contrasts Israel’s holiness from the womb with the nations’ lack of that inherited covenantal status. The se’if therefore distinguishes the original sinners, whose personal Jewish root is under discussion, from later offspring born to non-Jewish mothers, whose halachic status follows their mothers.

וְכַוָּונָתוֹ הָיָה לְטוֹבָה: שֶׁיִּשָּׁאֲרוּ הַכְּשֵׁרִים לְבַד, וְלֹא יֵעָנְשׁוּ בִּשְׁבִיל הַחוֹטְאִים שֶׁאֵינָם עוֹד מִכְּלַל אֲגֻדָּתָם, לִהְיוֹת ״בַּהֲדֵי הוּצָא לָקֵי כְּרָבָא״ (בָּבָא קַמָּא צ״ב עַמּוּד א׳)

and Hoshea's intent was for the good: that the upright alone should remain and not be punished on account of the sinners who would no longer be part of their collective body, avoiding "together with the thorn the cabbage is struck" (Bava Kamma 92a);1309Bava Kamma 92a: The folk-adage “along with the thornbush the cabbage is smitten [bahadei hutza lakei kruba]” — the innocent suffers alongside the guilty. R’ Tzadok applies it to the “trace” that reaches even the worthy.

וְאַף כָּאן, הֲגַם דְּלֹא נִטְמַע בְּאוּמָּה אַחֶרֶת, אִי לָאו דְּשֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלָיו, כֵּיוָן דְּנִפְקַע מִמֶּנּוּ שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל יָצָא מִכְּלַל אֲגֻדָּתָם וַחֲבוּרָתָם וְנִפְקַע עַרְבוּתָם בַּעֲדוֹ

so too here, even though Achan had not assimilated into another nation, were it not that the name of Israel remained upon him, once the name of Israel were removed from him he would have departed from their collective and their mutual responsibility (arevut) for him would have ceased;
עַל כֵּן אָמַר לוֹ שֶׁעֲדַיִין ״יִשְׂרָאֵל״ הוּא, וְכָל יִשְׂרָאֵל עֲרֵיבִים בַּעֲדוֹ דְּהוּא עֲדַיִין בֶּן אוּמָּתָם:

therefore Hashem said to Yehoshua that he is still an "Israelite," and all Israel are guarantors for him, for he remains a son of their nation.1310Bava Kamma 92a; Resisei Layla 40:1; Divrei Soferim 10:1 - the cabbage struck with the thornbush and the unity of Knesses Yisrael: Bava Kamma preserves the proverb that together with the thornbush the cabbage is struck: the innocent can suffer through association with the guilty.
