Rav Tzadok writes in Resisei Layla that every generation forms one complete human configuration and that even sinners retain a hidden point within Israel’s collective heart. In Divrei Soferim he likewise describes Knesses Yisrael across its generations as one corporate entity. The se’if uses that unity to explain both sides of arvus: the sinner’s deed can affect the community, and the community cannot disclaim him while the name Israel still rests upon him.

items.h: The theme: The enduring root of holiness in all Jewish sinners and converts versus the nations. Even if one does not repent during his lifetime, he ultimately justifies the divine judgment upon his soul at death. In Eruvin 19a, the sinners of Israel justify their judgment in Gehinnom, confessing: "You have judged rightly, acquitted rightly, and condemned rightly," whereas the sinners of the nations continuously sin even at the very doorway of Gehinnom. During life, the yetzer may overpower a Jew's mind, heart, and limbs, imprisoning his holy soul-root; upon death, when the soul is freed from the body and the yetzer, it recognizes the truth and weeps in bitter remorse. Because a Jew's soul is rooted in the Living God, repentance cleanses past iniquity by restoring the soul to its source; for gentiles whose root is in evil, repentance driven by fear of punishment cannot effect retroactive purification.

p: וְאַכַּתִּי לָא יָדְעִינַן: אִי מִשּׁוּם דְּיָשׁוּב לְבַסּוֹף הוּא וְדַוְוקָא עָלָיו נֶאֱמַר זֶה, אוֹ דְּגַם כָּל פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל כֵּן
And still we would not know: is it because he would ultimately repent and specifically concerning him was this stated, or are all sinners of Israel likewise in this category?
וּבִפְלוּגְתָּא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר וְרַבִּי יְהוּדָה, וַאֲנַן קַיְימָא לָן כְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
And this depends on the dispute of Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehudah, and we hold in accordance with Rabbi Meir;
דִּסְתָמָא דְּבָרַיְיתָא וּדְגַמְרָא [יְבָמוֹת מ״ז סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳] שֶׁהֵבִיאוּ, קָאֵי הָכִי גַּם בְּגֵר שֶׁחָזַר לְסוּרוֹ

for the anonymous Baraisa and Gemara [in Yevamos 47b] that they cited establishes this even regarding a convert who reverted to his corrupt ways;1311Yevamos 47b; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - a convert who reverts remains within Israel: Yevamos rules that once a convert has immersed and emerged, he is a Jew in every respect; even if he later reverts to gentile conduct, he is called an apostate Jew and his kiddushin remain valid. In Peri Tzadik, Rav Tzadok explains the Exodus promise of children as assurance that even a wicked child born into Israel cannot remove himself from the covenantal nation and will ultimately have a repair. That Peri Tzadik passage addresses native-born Israel; the present se’if extends the same principle of an inseverable Israel-status to a valid convert on the basis of the convert’s Sinai-root.
דְּגַם נַפְשׁוֹת הַגֵּרִים הָיוּ בְּמַעֲמַד הַר סִינַי וּפָסְקָה זוּהֲמָתָן כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת קמ״ו רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]
for the souls of converts were likewise present at Mount Sinai and their defilement ceased, as they stated [in Shabbos 146a].
וְעַל כֵּן יֵשׁ גַּם בָּהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁלֹּא יָכוֹל לִינָּתֵק, וּמִצַּד שׁוֹרֶשׁ זֶה שֵׁם יִשְׂרָאֵל עָלָיו דִּקְדוּשָׁיו קְדוּשִׁין

Therefore there exists within them as well the root of the holiness of Israel which can never be severed, and on account of this root the name of Israel remains upon him, so that his marriage is legally binding;1312Shabbos 146a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8 - the convert’s presence at Sinai and the enduring reshimah: Shabbos teaches that although future converts were not physically present at Sinai, their mazal was present, as they are included in the covenant with “one who is not here with us today.” Rav Tzadok writes in Yisrael Kedoshim that from Matan Torah onward the contamination ceased from Israel in a manner that can no longer be wholly severed; even when the revealed light departs through sin, a reshimah of holiness remains and preserves the name Israel. The se’if applies this not only to legal status but to the convert’s inner spiritual root.
וַאֲפִילּוּ לֹא יָשׁוּב בְּחַיָּיו, סוֹפוֹ לָשׁוּב בְּמוֹתוֹ
and even if he does not repent during his lifetime, he will ultimately repent at his death;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּעֵירוּבִין שָׁם] דְּפוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל מַצְדִּיקִים עֲלֵיהֶם הַדִּין בְּגֵיהִנָּם וְאוֹמְרִים: ״יָפֶה דַּנְתָּ וְכוּלֵיהּ״
as it is taught [in Eruvin 19a] that the sinners of Israel justify the divine judgment upon themselves in Gehinnom, declaring: "You have judged rightly, etc.";
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן פּוֹשְׁעֵי אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם דְּפָשְׁעֵי וְאָזְלֵי, וַאֲפִילּוּ עַל פִּתְחוֹ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם אֵין חוֹזְרִים

unlike the sinners of the nations of the world who sin continuously, and even at the very doorway of Gehinnom do not turn back.1313Eruvin 19a; Resisei Layla 44:1 - accepting the judgment of Gehinnom and the hidden Jewish heart: Eruvin distinguishes the sinners of Israel, who weep and acknowledge that God judged properly, from the sinners of the nations, who continue rebelling even at the entrance to Gehinnom. In Resisei Layla, Rav Tzadok explains that even a Jew who has multiplied sins without limit retains a depth of heart attached to God, though it may be concealed beneath the revealed personality. The se’if reads the confession in Gehinnom as the unveiling of that hidden point once the domination of the inclination has ended.
אֲבָל דָּבָר זֶה הוּא מִצַּד הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַקָּדוֹשׁ
But this reality stems from the holy soul-root:

שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁבְּחַיָּיו גָּבַר הַיֵּצֶר לִכְבּוֹשׁ כָּל חַדְרֵי מוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ וְאֵבָרָיו, וּלְהִתְגַּבֵּר נֶגֶד אוֹתוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָׁה עַד שֶׁנִּשְׁאַר טָמוּן וְחָבוּשׁ כִּבְבֵית הָאֲסוּרִים טָמִיר וְנֶעְלָם

for even though during his lifetime the yetzer overpowered him to conquer all the chambers of his brain, heart, and limbs, prevailing against that root of holiness until it remained buried and bound as in a prison, hidden and concealed;

אַחַר מוֹתוֹ, שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה חָפְשִׁי מֵהַשְּׂאוֹר שֶׁבָּעִיסָה וְיֵצֶר הַמֵּסִית, שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁבִּקְדֻשָּׁה מַכִּיר הָאֱמֶת, וּבוֹכֶה וּמִתְחָרֵט עַל מַה שֶּׁהִנִּיחַ לַיֵּצֶר לְהִתְפַּשֵּׁט בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה וְלִהְיוֹת גְּבַר אוֹיֵב

after his death, when he is freed from the "yeast in the dough" and the inciting yetzer, the holy soul-root recognizes the truth, weeping and regretting having allowed the yetzer to expand in this world and act as a hostile enemy;1314Berachos 17a; Resisei Layla 54:3 - the “leaven in the dough” and Divine help after entrapment: Berachos records Israel’s prayer: our true will is to do God’s will, but the “leaven in the dough,” the evil inclination, and the subjugation of kingdoms obstruct us. Rav Tzadok explains in Resisei Layla that after a person has become trapped in the inclination, he cannot awaken complete return by his own strength; God must first arouse and assist him from the hidden depth of the heart. The present se’if’s account of the soul after death is a conceptual application of that structure: when the obstructing power falls away, the concealed holy will can recognize the truth.
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן בְּאוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם דְּשָׁרְשָׁם בָּרָע, וְעַל כֵּן לֹא מְהַנֵּי לְהוּ תְּשׁוּבָה לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם [כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל סִימָן א׳]
unlike the nations of the world whose root is in evil, wherefore repentance does not avail for them to rectify the past [as mentioned above, Siman 1];
כִּי כָּל כֹּחַ הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַמּוֹעִיל לְכַלּוֹת עָוֹן וּלְהָתֵם פֶּשַׁע הַקּוֹדֵם הוּא עַל הֲשָׁבָתוֹ וַחֲזָרָתוֹ אֶל שָׁרְשׁוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ
for the entire power of repentance that avails to consume iniquity and bring past sin to an end operates through restoring and returning the soul to its holy root,
וּכְשֶׁהוּא מֵאִיר בְּלִבּוֹ וְגוּפוֹ מִמֵּילָא נִדְחֶה כָּל הַחֹשֶׁךְ וְאֵינֶנּוּ

and when that root radiates within his heart and body, all the darkness is automatically dispelled and is no more;1315Yoma 86b; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - repentance repairs the past by reawakening the root: Yoma teaches that repentance can recast intentional sins as inadvertent transgressions, or even as merits when the return is from love. Rav Tzadok’s parallel discussions explain the mechanism in terms of Israel’s surviving reshimah and eventual return to an indestructible covenantal root. The se’if therefore portrays repentance not merely as the cancellation of punishment, but as the reappearance of the holy root whose light expels the darkness that had covered it. Its concluding contrast concerns this distinctive root-based transformation of the past.
אֲבָל הַגּוֹיִם שֶׁשָּׁרְשָׁם בָּרָע, אַף שֶׁשָּׁבִים וּמִתְחָרְטִים מִיִּרְאַת הָעֹונֶשׁ, אֵין מְצִיאוּת לְתִיקּוּן הַקּוֹדֵם בָּהֶם:
but the gentiles whose root is in evil, even when they repent and express regret out of fear of punishment, there is no possibility of retroactive rectification within them.

items.h: The theme: The locking of the gates of repentance and the secret tunnel carved beneath the Throne (machtores ba-rakia). Why were the gates of repentance locked before sinners like Acher (Chagigah 15a) and King Menasheh (Sanhedrin 103a), and why did ministering angels close the windows of Heaven to block Menasheh's prayer? When an individual sins so extensively that in outward deed he appears entirely like a gentile, the ministering angels and the Attribute of Judgment—operating within the lower worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah (olamos ha-perud)—recognize only his outward corruption and demand his rejection. Only Hashem, reaching from the transcendent realm of Atzilus, extends His hand beneath the wings of the Chayos through a hidden celestial breach (machtores), beaming supernatural light into the inner recesses of the heart to awaken repentance.

p: וְזֶה טַעַם גַּם כֵּן שֶׁמָּצִינוּ פְּעָמִים שֶׁנִּנְעֲלוּ שַׁעֲרֵי תְּשׁוּבָה גַּם בִּפְנֵי פּוֹשְׁעֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
And this is likewise the reason why we find times when the gates of repentance were locked even before the sinners of Israel;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״הַשְׁמֵן לֵב הָעָם הַזֶּה [וְאָזְנָיו הַכְבֵּד וְעֵינָיו הָשַׁע] פֶּן יִרְאֶה [בְעֵינָיו וּבְאָזְנָיו יִשְׁמָע]... וָשָׁב [וְרָפָא לוֹ]״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ו:י)

as it is said: "Make the heart of this people fat, and make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes... and understand with their heart, and return, and be healed" (Yeshayah 6:10);1316Yeshayahu 6:10; Rambam, Hilchos Teshuvah 6:3; Tzidkas HaTzadik §39 - repentance withheld as a consequence of chosen sin: Rambam cites “make the heart of this people fat” to establish that a person may first multiply sins freely and thereby incur a later punishment in which the opportunity to repent is withheld. The hardening is therefore not the cause of the original wrongdoing, but its judicial consequence. Tzidkas HaTzadik adds that even apparent heavenly assistance cannot by itself prove that a path is good; the ultimate remedy is prayer and Divine mercy, which can transform even a damaged root. Rav Tzadok’s present analysis goes further than Rambam’s legal formulation by locating an indestructible hidden good point through which mercy can eventually reopen return.
וְכֵן אָמְרוּ בְּ״אַחֵר״ [בְּחֲגִיגָה ט״ו עַמּוּד א׳] וּבִמְנַשֶּׁה [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ק״ג עַמּוּד א׳] דְּמִדַּת הַדִּין עִכְּבָה לְקַבְּלוֹ
and so they related regarding Acher [in Chagigah 15a] and Menasheh [in Sanhedrin 103a], that the Attribute of Judgment hindered his acceptance;
וְהוּצְרַךְ לְקַבְּלוֹ בִּתְשׁוּבָה דֶּרֶךְ מַחְתֶּרֶת בָּרָקִיעַ

and Hashem had to receive him in repentance through a secret underground tunnel (machtores) carved beneath the heavens;1317Chagigah 15a: The account of “Acher” (Elisha ben Avuya) — the bas kol that called “Return, wayward sons — except for Acher,” and R’ Meir’s [later] drawing him near; the paradigm of the great one who fell yet whose Torah endured.1318Sanhedrin 103a (and Perek Chelek): On Menasheh — “whoever says Menasheh has no share in the World to Come weakens the hands of penitents,” for the Holy One “burrowed a tunnel” to receive him in teshuvah against the Attribute of Justice.
וּבַמִּדְרָשׁ אָמְרוּ, דְּמַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת הָיוּ סוֹתְמִין חַלּוֹנוֹת הָרָקִיעַ
and in the Midrash (Devarim Rabbah 2:20) they stated that the ministering angels were closing the windows of the firmament;
וּבִפְסָחִים [קי״ט עַמּוּד א׳]: דְּיָדוֹ שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא פְּרוּסָה תַּחַת כַּנְפֵי הַחַיּוֹת לְקַבֵּל בַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה מִפְּנֵי מִדַּת הַדִּין הַמְקַטְרֶגֶת שֶׁלֹּא לְקַבְּלָם

and in Pesachim [119a]: that the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, is outstretched beneath the wings of the celestial Chayos to receive penitents on account of the Attribute of Judgment that prosecutes against accepting them.1319Pesachim 119a; Resisei Layla 54:3 - the Divine hand beneath the wings of the Chayos: Pesachim reads the singular “His hand” beneath the wings of the Chayos as the hand of the Holy One spread out to receive penitents from the claim of the Attribute of Justice. The image places Divine acceptance beneath, and therefore beyond, the angels’ ordinary field of judgment. In Resisei Layla, Rav Tzadok similarly explains that once a person has become trapped by the inclination, the first awakening of repentance must itself come from Heaven; God arouses the heart and then attributes the opening to the person. The “tunnel” is thus not an evasion of teshuvah, but the concealed source that makes teshuvah possible.
וַהֲרֵי אֵין לְךָ דָּבָר שֶׁעוֹמֵד בִּפְנֵי הַתְּשׁוּבָה, דְּמִשְׁפַּט הַתּוֹרָה לְקַבֵּל שָׁבִים
And behold, nothing stands in the way of repentance, for the statutory law of the Torah dictates that penitents must be received;
וּתְשׁוּבָה קָדְמָה לִבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּפְסָחִים נ״ד עַמּוּד א׳], וְאֵיךְ יְקַטְרֵגוּ

and repentance preceded the creation of the world as taught [in Pesachim 54a], so how could the angels prosecute?1320Pesachim 54a: “Seven things were created before the world: Torah, teshuvah, Gan Eden, Gehinnom, the Throne of Glory, the Beis HaMikdash, and the name of Mashiach” — teshuvah preceding Creation, the root of the whole work.
אֲבָל זֶהוּ בְּאוֹתָם שֶׁהִרְבּוּ לִפְשׁוֹעַ בְּכָל מִינֵי רָע שֶׁבְּכֹחַ בְּחִירָתָם
But this applies to those who multiplied transgressions in every manner of evil within the capacity of their free choice;
בְּאֹפֶן שֶׁמִּצַּד מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם הֲרֵי הֵם כְּכָל הַגּוֹיִם וְנִקְרָאִים בְּשֵׁם ״לֹא עַמִּי״
in such a manner that from the perspective of their deeds they are like all the gentiles and are designated "not My people";
וְלֹא נִשְׁאַר בָּהֶם אֶלָּא אוֹתוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ טוֹב הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁשָּׁם אֵין מְצִיאוּת רָע, וְאֵין יַד וְכֹחַ הַבְּחִירָה מַגַּעַת לְשָׁם
and there remains within them only that concealed good root where no evil exists, and where the hand and power of human free choice cannot reach;
וּמִדַּת הַדִּין הוּא בִּמְקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ מְצִיאוּת רָע דְּעַל זֶה שַׁיָּיךְ דִּין וּמִשְׁפָּט
and the Attribute of Judgment operates strictly in the domain where evil exists, for upon that alone do law and judgment apply.
וְכֵן מְצִיאוּת מַלְאֲכֵי הַשָּׁרֵת הוּא רַק בְּג׳ עוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה, שֶׁמַּתְחִיל עָלְמִין דְּפֵירוּדָא וְיֵשׁ מְצִיאוּת לָרָע

And likewise the existence of the ministering angels is confined to the three lower worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah, where the realms of separation (almin d'peruda) begin and evil possesses reality;
וְכֵן מִדַּת הַבַּת קוֹל שֶׁהִשְׁמִיעָה לְ״אַחֵר״: ״שׁוּבוּ וְכוּלֵיהּ חוּץ מֵאַחֵר״
and likewise the measure of the Heavenly Voice that proclaimed to Acher: "Return, backsliding children, except for Acher";
וְשָׁם אֵין הַכָּרָה לְאוֹתוֹ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּעְלָם שֶׁהוּא מִמָּקוֹם גָּבוֹהַּ יוֹתֵר
and in those lower worlds there is no perception of that concealed root which originates from a far higher source;
וְעַל כֵּן הֵם אֶצְלָם בִּכְלַל גּוֹיִם שֶׁאֵין לְקַבֵּל בִּתְשׁוּבָה

wherefore in the eyes of the angels such sinners are classified as gentiles who are not accepted in retroactive repentance;1321Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8; Resisei Layla 40:1 - the hidden Jewish root beyond the revealed worlds of separation: Yisrael Kedoshim teaches that after Matan Torah, even when the revealed light of holiness departs through sin, a reshimah remains that cannot be uprooted and still bears the name Israel. Resisei Layla describes the depth of every Jewish heart as a point attached to Hashem even when the person’s revealed deeds weaken its power. These passages clarify the present distinction: angelic judgment apprehends the revealed realm in which good and evil separate, whereas the higher covenantal root remains concealed from that judgment. Rav Tzadok uses this hidden point not to minimize accountability, but to explain why final exclusion is never the last word.
וְאִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לַחֲזוֹר לְשָׁרְשׁוֹ בְּכֹחַ תְּשׁוּבָתוֹ, אֶלָּא עַל יְדֵי פְּשִׁיטַת יַד הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא דֶּרֶךְ מַחְתֶּרֶת וְהֶעְלֵם לְהָאִיר לוֹ מֵאוֹתוֹ הָאוֹר הַנֶּעְלָם

and it is impossible for such a person to return to his root through the power of his own repentance alone, except through the outstretching of the hand of the Holy One, blessed be He, through a secret tunnel and concealment to illuminate him from that hidden light;
שֶׁאֵין יָכוֹל לְהָאִיר לוֹ מִצַּד הַהִתְגַּלּוּת, שֶׁכְּבָר כּוּלּוֹ רַע מִצַּד הִתְגַּלּוּת כָּל מַעֲשָׂיו וְכֹחוֹתָיו וּמַחְשְׁבוֹת מוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ
which cannot shine upon him through revealed channels, since outwardly he is entirely evil in the manifestation of all his deeds, faculties, and thoughts;
רַק דֶּרֶךְ הֶעְלֵם לְמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, שֶׁאִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עוֹזֵר, אֵין יָכוֹל לַיֵּצֶר הָרָע אַף קוֹדֶם שֶׁחָטָא, וְכָל שֶׁכֵּן אַחַר שֶׁחָטָא

but only in concealment into the depths of the heart, for were the Holy One, blessed be He, not to assist him, one could not overcome the yetzer hara even prior to sinning (Kiddushin 30b), and all the more so after sinning.
אִלְמָלֵא הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא שֶׁפּוֹתֵחַ שַׁעַר לַדּוֹפְקֵי בִּתְשׁוּבָה, לֹא יָכוֹל כְּלָל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר נֶגֶד הַיֵּצֶר וְלָשׁוּב בֶּאֱמֶת
Were the Holy One, blessed be He, not opening a gate for those who knock in repentance, one could never prevail against the yetzer and repent in truth;
רַק ״הַבָּא לִיטָּהֵר מְסַיְּיעִין אוֹתוֹ״ (שַׁבָּת ק״ד עַמּוּד א׳), וְיֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ שְׁעָרִים גְּדוֹלִים וְיֵשׁ דֶּרֶךְ פְּתָחִים וְחַלּוֹנוֹת, הַכֹּל כְּפִי עִנְיַן חֲטָאִים וְטִמְטוּם לִבּוֹ

only that "he who comes to purify himself is assisted" (Shabbos 104a), sometimes through great gates and sometimes through narrow apertures and windows, all according to the nature of his sins and the insensitivity of his heart;

וְכָל זְמַן שֶׁנִּשְׁאָר עֲדַיִין פֶּתַח קָטָן אֲפִילּוּ כְּחֻדָּהּ שֶׁל מַחַט מְפוּלָּשׁ מֵעֵבֶר לְעֵבֶר מִן ״לֵב חָכָם לִימִינוֹ״ (קֹהֶלֶת י:ב) דְּעָיֵיל בַּהּ לְהִתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב, הוּא מִתְרַחֵב וְהוֹלֵךְ כְּפִתְחוֹ שֶׁל אוּלָם

and as long as there still remains a tiny opening even like the eye of a needle perforated from side to side from the "wise heart at his right" (Koheles 10:2) through which he enters to awaken repentance, it expands continuously until it is like the entrance of the Ulam (Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2);1322Shabbos 104a; Sukkah 52b; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 5:2; Tzidkas HaTzadik §152; Resisei Layla 54:3 - assistance, the needle-point opening, and the Ulam: Chazal teach both that one who comes to purify himself is assisted and that without the Holy One’s help a person cannot overcome the evil inclination. Shir HaShirim Rabbah adds: open for Me an opening like the point of a needle and I will open for you an entrance like that of the Ulam. Tzidkas HaTzadik explains that even the smallest genuine fear of Heaven from below can become a vessel for a corresponding influx of wisdom from above. Resisei Layla stresses that after sin has tightened the inclination’s hold, Heaven must first awaken the return. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes an ordinary small opening, which assistance can widen gradually, from a fully sealed heart, which requires a concealed supernal illumination before any revealed opening exists.
אֲבָל אֵלּוּ שֶׁכְּבָר קִלְקְלוּ בְּמַחֲשָׁבָה, דִּבּוּר וּמַעֲשֶׂה הָרָעִים כָּל חֶלְקֵי נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה עַד שֶׁנֶּאֱטַם וְנִטַמְטַם הַלֵּב לְגַמְרֵי
but those who have already corrupted through evil thought, speech, and deed all aspects of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah until the heart is entirely sealed and hardened;
אִם עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִין וְכַיּוֹצֵא בּוֹ מִתְעוֹרֵר לָשׁוּב, אִי אֶפְשָׁר לוֹ לָשׁוּב לְשָׁרְשׁוֹ הַטּוֹב אֶלָּא מִצַּד הִתְעוֹרְרוּת רַחֲמֵי שָׁמַיִם הַמְרוּבִּים
if through tribulations and the like such a person awakens to repent, he cannot return to his good root except through the awakening of abundant heavenly mercies:
לְהָאִיר לוֹ וְלִפְשׁוֹט יָדוֹ לְהוֹצִיאוֹ מֵהָאֲפֵלָה בְּהֶאָרַת אוֹר עֶלְיוֹן לְמַעֲמַקֵּי הַלֵּב, שֶׁלֹּא בְּהַדְרָגָה דֶּרֶךְ פְּתָחִים בְּהִתְגַּלּוּת מוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ

to illuminate him and stretch forth His hand to extract him from the darkness through the radiance of supernal light into the depths of the heart, bypassing gradual progression through the revealed doors of his brain and heart;
וּמִשָּׁם יִתְפַּשֵּׁט הָאוֹר וְיָבוֹא גַּם לְהִתְגַּלּוּת לִבּוֹ, שֶׁיּוּכַל לְהִתְגַּבֵּר וּלְהִתְקוֹמֵם נֶגֶד הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע מַה שֶּׁלֹּא הָיָה יָכוֹל מִקּוֹדֶם
and from there the light expands and penetrates into the revealed consciousness of his heart, enabling him to overcome and rise up against the yetzer hara as he was unable to do previously;
וּלְגָרְשׁוֹ מִמַּלְכוּתוֹ וְשָׁלְטָנְתוֹ בְּכָל חַדְרֵי לִבּוֹ, וְיָשׁוּב לִהְיוֹת לֵב טָהוֹר, וְזֶהוּ כְּמַאן דְּאָמַר: מְנַשֶּׁה יֵשׁ לוֹ חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא:

expelling the yetzer from its dominion over all the chambers of his heart, returning to a pure heart; and this represents the view of the authority who holds that King Menasheh possesses a portion in the World to Come (Sanhedrin 103a).1323Tehillim 51:12; Tzidkas HaTzadik §39; Peri Tzadik, Bo 4; Takanas HaShavin 15:48 and 15:54 - “create for me a pure heart”: David asks not merely that his existing heart be cleaned, but “create for me a pure heart.” Rav Tzadok repeatedly emphasizes that beriah denotes a new creation from nothing: prayer and abundant mercy can reach where ordinary correction cannot and can transform the damaged root itself. Peri Tzadik connects David’s plea specifically with purification from the taint attached to the sin, while earlier sections of this siman linked the same verse with removal of the heart of stone and renewed life after teshuvah. The close of this se’if follows that internal chain: hidden light enters the sealed depth, spreads into the revealed faculties, dislodges the inclination’s dominion, and produces a genuinely renewed heart.

items.h: The theme: The dispute regarding Menasheh's portion in the World to Come. The anonymous Mishnah rules that Menasheh has no share in the World to Come, despite II Divrei HaYamim (33:12–16) recording that he repented, removed the foreign gods, sacrificed peace-offerings, and commanded Yehudah to serve Hashem. This Tanna held that Menasheh repented merely out of terror of physical torture inside the bronze cauldron, and not out of love that purifies the heart. Repentance from fear of punishment avails even for gentiles (like Nineveh) to rescind impending physical destruction; hence Menasheh was restored to his earthly kingdom, but not to the World to Come. Entry into the World to Come—the world of Binah—requires repentance from love (teshuvah me-ahavah), awakening the fatherly compassion of Hashem for His son ("You are the children of the Lord your God", Devarim 14:1) to restore the soul to its source.

p: וּסְתָם מִשְׁנָה דְּאֵין לוֹ, אַף דִּמְפוֹרָשׁ [בְּדִבְרֵי הַיָּמִים ב ל״ג:י״ב–ט״ז] שֶׁשָּׁב וְהֵסִיר אֱלֹהֵי הַנֵּכָר וְזָבַח לַה׳ וְאָמַר לִיהוּדָה לַעֲבוֹד לַה׳

And the anonymous Mishnah (Sanhedrin 90a) which rules that Menasheh has no share, even though it is explicit in Scripture [II Divrei HaYamim 33:12–16] that he repented, removed the foreign gods, sacrificed unto Hashem, and commanded Yehudah to serve Hashem;
סְבִירָא לֵיהּ דְּשָׁב רַק מִיִּרְאַת הָעֹונֶשׁ, וְלֹא שֶׁנִּטְהַר לִבּוֹ לָשׁוּב לִקְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא צוּר לְבָבוֹ

holds that he repented solely out of fear of physical punishment, and not that his heart was purified to return to the holiness of Israel wherein the Holy One, blessed be He, is the rock of his heart;

וְעַל כֵּן הוּשַׁב רַק לְמַלְכוּתוֹ, שֶׁזֶּה מוֹעִיל גַּם בַּגּוֹיִם כִּתְשׁוּבַת אַנְשֵׁי נִינְוֵה שֶׁהוֹעִיל לָהֶם לְבַטֵּל הַגְּזֵירָה כֵּיוָן דִּבְאוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה הָיוּ צַדִּיקִים, וְלֹא לְתַקֵּן הַקּוֹדֵם

wherefore he was restored merely to his earthly throne, which type of repentance avails even for gentiles, like the repentance of the people of Nineveh which availed them to annul the decreed destruction because at that moment they acted righteously, but not to retroactively rectify the past;1324II Divrei HaYamim 33:10-17; Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2; Sanhedrin 103a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - Menasheh’s repentance and the dispute over the World to Come: Scripture records that distress brought Menasheh to humility and prayer; Hashem restored him to Jerusalem, after which he removed the foreign gods, rebuilt the altar, and commanded Yehudah to serve Hashem. R’ Yehudah therefore grants him a share in the World to Come, while the Sages answer that he was restored to his kingdom but not to life in the World to Come. Sanhedrin also preserves R’ Yochanan’s opposing warning that denying Menasheh’s share weakens penitents, and reports thirty-three years of repentance. Rav Tzadok is therefore explaining the strict anonymous Mishnah on its own terms, not erasing the competing rabbinic tradition. Peri Tzadik similarly cites the later teaching that the listed Jewish sinners ultimately return because Israel’s root cannot be permanently displaced.1325Yonah 3:8-10; Taanis 16a; Yoma 86b; Tzidkat HaTzadik §132 - Nineveh, fear, and repair of the past: Yonah says that God saw the people’s deeds, that they turned from their evil way, and therefore did not execute the threatened calamity. Taanis stresses that the decisive factor was changed conduct rather than sackcloth or fasting. This establishes rescue from the decree and uprightness from that point forward. Yoma distinguishes a return from fear, which reduces deliberate sins to inadvertent ones, from a return from love, which can transform them into merits. Tzidkat HaTzadik distinguishes ordinary lower return from an upper return that reaches the root of the soul. Rav Tzadok uses that distinction here to explain why Nineveh can model cancellation of punishment without yet proving the deeper Israelite repair of what preceded it.
וְלֹא סְבִירָא לֵיהּ שֶׁנֶּחְתַּר לוֹ חֲתִירָה וּפְתִיחַת אוֹר
and this Tanna does not accept that a mystical tunnel was carved out for him with an illumination of supernal light;
וּכְבָר נֶעֱקַר מִמֶּנּוּ כָּל קְדֻשַּׁת יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁבְּחֶלְקֵי נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ, נְשָׁמָה שֶׁלּוֹ הַמִּתְפַּשְּׁטִים בְּמוֹחוֹ וְלִבּוֹ וְאֵבָרָיו

holding that there had already been uprooted from him all the manifest holiness of Israel across the faculties of his Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah that expand throughout his brain, heart, and limbs.1326Sanhedrin 103a; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:8; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1 - the tunnel and the surviving Jewish root: Sanhedrin interprets the unusual wording of Menasheh’s answered prayer to mean that Hashem made a concealed opening in Heaven to receive him against the protest of the Attribute of Justice. The anonymous Mishnah, as Rav Tzadok presents it here, does not recognize that opening as restoring his share in the World to Come. Elsewhere, however, Rav Tzadok teaches that after Sinai a reshimah of holiness remains even when the revealed light departs, so that the name Israel cannot be uprooted; Peri Tzadik likewise treats the enduring holiness of Jewish descent as the reason that even deeply wicked children are not finally rejected. This note marks the dialectic: the se’if formulates the Mishnah’s strict view, while Rav Tzadok’s broader writings preserve the hidden root that later teachings disclose.
וּלְזֶה צָרִיךְ תְּשׁוּבָה מֵאַהֲבָה שֶׁהוּא בָּא מֵהִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר שֶׁבְּשָׁרְשׁוֹ דְּ״בָּנִים אַתֶּם לַה׳ אֱלֹהֵיכֶם״ (דְּבָרִים י״ד:א׳)

And for such retroactive rectification one requires repentance from love, which issues from the revelation of the light within his root whereof it is said: "You are the children of the Lord your God" (Devarim 14:1);
שֶׁמִּתְעוֹרֵר הָאַהֲבָה דְּרַחֲמֵי הָאָב עַל הַבֵּן, וּ״כַמַּיִם הַפָּנִים לַפָּנִים״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ״ז:י״ט), וּבָזֶה שָׁב לִמְקוֹרוֹ וְנִתְקַן הַקּוֹדֵם

awakening the love of a father's compassion for his son, and "as in water face answers to face" (Mishlei 27:19), whereby he returns to his Source and the past is fully rectified;1327Devarim 14:1; Kiddushin 36a; Mishlei 27:19; Yoma 86b; Resisei Layla §41 - sonship, reflected love, and teshuvah from love: The Torah calls Israel children of Hashem, and R’ Meir teaches that even when they act corruptly they are still called children. “As water reflects face to face, so the heart of man to man” supplies the image of reciprocal awakening: the revealed bond of the child arouses paternal mercy, and that mercy awakens the child’s return. Yoma identifies teshuvah from love as the level at which deliberate sins become merits rather than merely losing their severity. Resisei Layla describes Israel’s distinctive power as repairing what came before until deliberate sins are transformed into merits. Rav Tzadok therefore links love, enduring sonship, return to the source, and actual rectification of the past.
אֲבָל תְּשׁוּבָה מִיִּרְאַת הָעֹונֶשׁ הוּא גַּם בַּגּוֹיִם, וְעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ דִּלְחֵלֶק עוֹלָם הַבָּא לֹא הֱשִׁיבוֹ
but repentance out of fear of punishment operates even among the gentiles, wherefore the Sages stated that to a portion in the World to Come Hashem did not restore him,
לְהַחְזִירוֹ לִהְיוֹת בִּכְלַל כָּל יִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁיֵּשׁ לָהֶם חֵלֶק לָעוֹלָם הַבָּא
so as to reinstate him within the collective of all Israel who possess a portion in the World to Come;
דְּעוֹלָם הַבָּא הוּא עוֹלַם הַבִּינָה שֶׁמִּשָּׁם הַתְּשׁוּבָה הַגְּמוּרָה בַּהֲשָׁבָה לַמָּקוֹר וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ עַל יְדֵי הַבִּינָה שֶׁבַּלֵּב דְּ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ו:י):

for the World to Come is the realm of Binah, whence originates consummate repentance through returning to the Source and Root via Understanding in the heart: "his heart shall understand, and he shall return" (Yeshayah 6:10).1328Yeshayahu 6:10; Megillah 17b; Berachos 17a; Dover Tzedek 3:15; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech §10; Tzidkat HaTzadik §132 - Binah, the heart, and complete return: Yeshayahu joins three stages: the heart understands, the person returns, and healing follows. Megillah uses that sequence to explain why the blessing of repentance follows the blessing of understanding in the Amidah. Berachos describes the World to Come as a nonphysical state of delight in the radiance of the Shechinah. Rav Tzadok develops these sources kabbalistically: Dover Tzedek links the World to Come and the inward heart; Peri Tzadik identifies the upper Shabbos with Binah and upper teshuvah; and Tzidkat HaTzadik describes upper return as reaching the root beyond the heart’s ordinary mixture of good and evil. The identification of the World to Come with Binah is therefore Rav Tzadok’s mystical synthesis of the prophetic and rabbinic sequence, not an explicit statement of the Gemara itself.

items.h: The theme: The primordial repentance that preceded Creation and the name "Adam." Chazal derive that repentance preceded Creation from Tehillim 90:2–3: "Before the mountains were brought forth... You say: Return, you children of men (bnei adam)." Israel alone is designated with the title "Adam" ("you are called Adam", Yevamos 61a), whereas the nations are termed "the sons of Noach." Adam was formed by Hashem's own hands, infused with the "breath of life" from the Source of Life—the root of Israel's souls drawn from the letters of the Torah. The nations issued from the defilement cast into Chavah by the Serpent; the yetzer hara entered Israel's hearts through eating from the Tree of Knowledge. Because Adam had no human parents conceived in lust, his holy root was directly revealed; hence Hashem opened for him an entrance to repentance (v'atah pen yishlach yado). When Hashem calls "Return, backsliding children," it is a gentle whisper (amirah bi-lechishu) awakening the inner spark of the Divine Image (demus k'mar'eh adam) upon the Throne of Glory—the form of Yaakov Avinu, the root of Israel.

p: וְזֶהוּ הַתְּשׁוּבָה שֶׁקָּדְמָה לִבְרִיאַת הָעוֹלָם, דְּיָלְפִינַן מִקְּרָא דְּ״בְּטֶרֶם [הָרִים יֻלָּדוּ] וְגוֹמֵר, תָּשֵׁב אֱנוֹשׁ עַד דַּכָּא וַתֹּאמֶר שׁוּבוּ בְנֵי אָדָם״ (תְּהִלִּים צ:ב–ג)

And this is the repentance that preceded the creation of the world (Pesachim 54a), which we derive from the verse: "Before the mountains were brought forth... You turn man to contrition, and say: Return, you children of men" (Tehillim 90:2–3);
וְ״אַתֶּם קְרוּיִם ׳אָדָם׳״ (יְבָמוֹת ס״א עַמּוּד א׳)

and "you are called 'Adam'" (Yevamos 61a);1329Cf. Yevamos 61a — “atem keruyim adam, ve-ein umos ha-olam keruyim adam” (“you [Israel] are called Adam, but the nations of the world are not called Adam”). This is the linchpin R’ Tzadok draws on: “shuvu benei adam” (Tehillim 90:3) addresses those “called Adam,” tracing to the first man’s soul-of-life from the Source of life — the root by which the call to repentance reaches Israel from before creation.
דְּהָאוּמּוֹת נִקְרָאִים ״בְּנֵי נֹחַ״ וְלֹא ״בְּנֵי אָדָם״, שֶׁלֹּא נִתְיַיחֲסוּ אַחַר אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁהוּא יְצִיר כַּפָּיו יִתְבָּרַךְ שֶׁנָּפַח בּוֹ נִשְׁמַת חַיִּים מִמְּקוֹר הַחַיִּים

for the nations of the world are termed "the sons of Noach" and not "the sons of Adam," not being genealogically credited after Adam HaRishon who was the direct handiwork of the Blessed Name, Who breathed into him the breath of life from the Source of Life;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנְּשָׁמוֹת דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל שֶׁהוּא מֵאוֹתִיּוֹת הַתּוֹרָה, שֶׁהִיא חַיֵּי עוֹלָם וְעֵץ הַחַיִּים שֶׁהָיָה מוּכָן אָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן לֶאֱכוֹל מִמֶּנּוּ לִחְיוֹת לְעוֹלָם

which is the root of the souls of Israel, originating from the letters of the Torah, which is eternal life and the Tree of Life from which Adam HaRishon was prepared to eat and live forever;1330Bereishis 2:7; Mishlei 3:18; Yisrael Kedoshim 8:1, 10:8; Resisei Layla 41:1; Peri Tzadik, Shavuos 20:1 — divine breath, Torah, and the Tree of Life: The Torah states that Hashem breathed into Adam a “soul of life,” while Mishlei calls Torah a “Tree of Life.” Rav Tzadok repeatedly joins these images without identifying them simplistically: the divine breath is the source of the soul’s life, Torah is the revealed form of eternal life, and Israel possesses an inherited root capable of receiving that life. Yisrael Kedoshim develops the unity of the Holy One, Torah, and Israel; Resisei Layla applies “one who blows, blows from within” to the soul’s inward derivation from its Source; and Peri Tzadik identifies Torah engraved upon the heart with the Tree of Life and freedom from the yetzer and death. Thus the linkage here between Israel’s souls, the letters of Torah, and Adam’s intended immortality is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis of the verses and kabbalistic tradition, not the literal wording of Bereishis 2:7 alone.
אֶלָּא שֶׁגָּרַם הַחֵטְא דְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, וּמִזּוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ שֶׁהֵטִיל בְּחַוָּה יָצָא שׁוֹרֶשׁ נַפְשׁוֹת אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם

except that the sin brought about by the Serpent's instigation intervened, and from the defilement that the Serpent cast into Chavah (Shabbos 146a) issued the soul-root of the nations of the world;1331Shabbos 146a; Yevamos 103b; Peri Tzadik, Ki Seitzei §6 — serpent-contamination and the nations’ root: The Bavli states that the serpent cast contamination into Chavah, that Israel’s contamination ceased through standing at Sinai, and that the nations did not undergo that Sinai purification; it immediately includes converts by teaching that their mazal stood at Sinai. Peri Tzadik describes the opposing national root as bound to the serpent’s contamination. Rav Tzadok goes further in this se’if by presenting the emergence of the nations’ soul-root from that contamination and by explaining how sin can draw its uncircumcised quality over an Israelite. That genealogy is his kabbalistic synthesis of the Aggadah, not an explicit biological statement of the Gemara, and it does not erase the Bavli’s express inclusion of converts within the Sinai covenant.
וּמֵאֲכִילַת עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע בָּא שְׁלִיטַת הַיֵּצֶר הָרָע בְּלִבְּבוֹת בְּנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
while from eating of the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil came the dominion of the yetzer hara within the hearts of the Children of Israel.
וּלְפִי שֶׁהוּא בָּא מֵהַסָּתַת הַנָּחָשׁ, עַל כֵּן יָכוֹל לְהַמְשִׁיךְ עָלָיו עַל יְדֵי זֶה גַּם כֵּן מִזּוּהֲמַת הַנָּחָשׁ וְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַגּוֹיִם עֲרֵלִים

And because the yetzer hara originated from the incitement of the Serpent, an Israelite through sin can draw upon himself as well from the defilement of the Serpent and the root of the uncircumcised gentiles;
דְּעַל כֵּן אָמְרוּ [בְּסַנְהֶדְרִין ל״ח עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּאָדָם הָרִאשׁוֹן מָשׁוּךְ בְּעָרְלָתוֹ הָיָה
wherefore they stated [in Sanhedrin 38b] that Adam HaRishon had his foreskin drawn;
וְרַק דֶּרֶךְ הַמְשָׁכָה לְמַרְאִית הָעַיִן דְּלָא מַבְשְׁקַר מִצַּד הַשָּׂגַת הָאָדָם שֶׁיִּרְאֶה לַעֵינַיִם וּכְפִי הַהִתְגַּלּוּת

but this was merely an external extension to outward appearances so that he was unrecognized from the perspective of human sight that looks on the surface and according to manifest conduct;1332Sanhedrin 38b; Zohar, Bereishis 43:434; Peri Tzadik, Tzav §7; Resisei Layla 58:3 — Adam’s “drawn foreskin” as covenantal concealment: Sanhedrin records R’ Yitzchak’s teaching that Adam was “one who drew his foreskin,” deriving it from “like Adam, they transgressed the covenant.” The Zohar interprets the rupture spiritually as separation from the holy covenant and attachment to the serpent’s counsel. Peri Tzadik explains that Adam was originally created circumcised and upright, but the sin drew an orlah over that holiness; Resisei Layla likewise connects the Tree-of-Knowledge mixture with the blemish of the covenant. Rav Tzadok’s qualification here — that the uncircumcised condition is the revealed appearance perceived by human eyes, while the holy root remains — is therefore his interpretive synthesis. The Gemara itself states the covenantal transgression but does not formulate this inner-versus-outer distinction.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם פָּתַח לוֹ הַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ פֶּתַח לִתְשׁוּבָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרֵאשִׁית רַבָּה פָּרָשָׁה כ״א] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְעַתָּה פֶּן וְגוֹמֵר״
and nevertheless the Blessed Name opened for him an entrance to repentance, as they expounded [in Bereishis Rabbah 21:6] on the verse "And now, lest, etc." (Bereishis 3:22);
כִּי שָׁרְשׁוֹ מִקְּדוּשָׁה הָיָה גַּם כֵּן גָּלוּי עֲדַיִין, מֵאַחַר שֶׁלֹּא הָיָה לוֹ חֵלֶק מֵאָב וָאֵם שֶׁהוּא בְּעָווֹן וְחֵטְא, רַק חֵלֶק שָׁמַיִם לְבַד

for his holy root was still openly evident, seeing that he had no physical portion from a human father and mother conceived in iniquity and sin, but solely the divine portion of Heaven alone.1333Bereishis Rabbah 21:6; Takanas HaShavin 15:45–46; Machshavos Charutz 20:13 — the opening of teshuvah after Adam’s sin: Bereishis Rabbah reads “And now, lest he put forth his hand” as Hashem opening an entrance of repentance for Adam: “and now” signifies teshuvah, but Adam answered with “lest,” understood there as refusal. Earlier in this siman, Rav Tzadok explains that Adam’s repentance was genuine yet did not restore unrestricted access to the Tree of Life or annul the mortality introduced by the serpent. Machshavos Charutz similarly places the completion of that primordial repair in the later unfolding through David and Mashiach. The present se’if adds the reason an opening remained available: Adam’s created root was still visibly from Heaven alone, without the inherited admixture that accompanies ordinary human generation. The Midrash supplies the offered opening; the analysis of the surviving holy root and the incomplete bodily repair is Rav Tzadok’s own synthesis.
וְגַם בִּבְנֵי אָדָם נֶאֱמַר ״וַתֹּאמֶר שׁוּבוּ״, שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ מְעוֹרְרָם לָשׁוּב עַל יְדֵי הַבַּת קוֹל: ״שׁוּבוּ בָנִים שׁוֹבָבִים״ (יִרְמְיָה ג:יד)
And regarding the sons of Adam it is likewise said: "and You say: Return," for the Blessed Name arouses them to repent through the Heavenly Voice: "Return, O backsliding children" (Yirmiyah 3:14);
שֶׁהוּא אֲמִירָה בִּלְחִישׁוּ בְּהִתְעוֹרְרוּת בַּלֵּב מִצַּד מַה שֶּׁהֵם ״בְּנֵי אָדָם״

which is an utterance whispered in internal arousal within the heart from the fact that they are "the children of Adam";1334Yirmiyahu 3:22; Chagigah 15a — the bas kol and the inward summons to return: Yirmiyahu calls, “Return, O wayward children.” Chagigah records a bas kol using that verse in the exceptional case of Acher, adding “except Acher”; the continuation nevertheless preserves R’ Meir’s repeated demand that Acher return and the teaching that even a Torah scholar who has broken has a remedy. Rav Tzadok’s statement here is broader and inward: the ordinary divine call reaches “sons of Adam” as a quiet stirring within the heart. That interiorized whisper is his theological explanation of how the heavenly summons is experienced; it is not the Bavli’s literal description of every thought of repentance. Its force in this se’if rests on the enduring Adamic holiness that makes the heart receptive to the call.
שֶׁיֵּשׁ בָּהֶם שׁוֹרֶשׁ קְדוּשָׁה דְּאָדָם שֶׁנִּבְרָא בְּצַלְמֵנוּ כִּדְמוּתֵנוּ
who possess the holy soul-root of Adam who was created in the Divine Image and Likeness (Bereishis 1:26);
שֶׁהוּא הַדְּמוּת שֶׁעַל הַכִּסֵּא כְּמַרְאֵה אָדָם, וְהוּא צוּרַת יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שׁוֹרֶשׁ יִשְׂרָאֵל:

which is the likeness upon the Throne resembling the appearance of a Man (Yechezkel 1:26), being the visage of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, the root of Israel.1335R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech §10): “The ‘upper Shabbos,’ which is binah — ‘upper teshuvah’ — and [before it] the yetzer departs.” Exactly the se’if: the teshuvah that preceded the creation of the world, which is binah, “before the mountains were born.”1336Bereishis 1:26; Yechezkel 1:26; Chullin 91b; Resisei Layla §§28, 41; Peri Tzadik, Nasso §15; Takanas HaShavin 12:7 — Yaakov’s image and Israel’s collective root: Bereishis describes humanity as created in the divine image, and Yechezkel sees upon the Throne “a likeness as the appearance of a man.” Chullin teaches that the angels ascended to gaze at Yaakov’s image above and descended to compare it with Yaakov below; Rashi on Bereishis 28:12 identifies the upper image as engraved on the Throne of Glory. Rav Tzadok develops this into a doctrine of Israel’s common soul-root: Resisei Layla treats Yaakov’s complete form as including the soul-roots of Israel, Peri Tzadik identifies Yaakov with the restored beauty and truth of Adam, and Takanas HaShavin 12:7 describes the generations of Israel as articulations of that single spiritual stature. The Gemara supplies Yaakov’s upper image; its identification with the enduring inner root through which every “son of Adam” can be recalled to teshuvah is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.

items.h: The theme: The anatomical and spiritual symbolism of the letters of Adam (א-ד-ם) and the governance of bodily desires. In Sotah 5a, Chazal formulate the acronym of Adam as: Efer (ashes), Dam (blood), and Marah (gallbladder/bile), encased within Basar (flesh), Boshah (shame), and Seruchah (corruption). The liver (kaved) is filled with blood, housing the animal soul (Nefesh), the source of anger (ka'as); the gallbladder (marah) secretes a drop to cool the liver's fury, preserving the body from being consumed by wrath. Overeating for physical pleasure inflames this bile, giving rise to all bodily and psychic illnesses ("a full stomach breeds all evil sorts", Berachos 32a). In contrast, the Torah path of eating morning bread with salt and measured water (pas b'melach u-mayim bim'surah, Avos 6:4) purifies the blood and sustains the soul, maintaining the liver in health and subduing the fire of lust and wrath.

p: וּשְׁלֹשָׁה אוֹתִיּוֹת ״אָדָם״ נֶגֶד חֶלְקֵי נֶפֶשׁ, רוּחַ וְנִשְׁמָה שֶׁמִּגּ׳ עוֹלָמוֹת בְּרִיאָה, יְצִירָה, עֲשִׂיָּה שֶׁמֵּעוֹלַם הַכִּסֵּא וּלְמַטָּה
And the three letters of Adam
(א-ד-ם)
correspond to the three soul divisions of Nefesh, Ruach, and Neshamah deriving from the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah which extend from the World of the Throne downward;
וּמִשְׁכָּנָם בְּמוֹחַ וְלֵב וְכָבֵד כִּידוּעַ
their physical dwellings residing in the brain (Mo'ach - Neshamah), heart (Lev - Ruach), and liver (Kaved - Nefesh), as is known.
וּבְסוֹטָה [ה׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]: ״אָדָם״ — אֵפֶר, דָּם, מָרָה; ״בָּשָׂר״ — בּוּשָׁה, סְרוּחָה וְכוּלֵיהּ

And in Sotah [5a]: "Adam" is an acronym for Efer (ashes), Dam (blood), Marah (bile/gallbladder); "Basar" (flesh) is an acronym for Boshah (shame), Seruchah (corruption), etc.;1337Ibn Ezra on Shemos 23:25; Nefesh HaChayim I:14; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 1:6 — brain, heart, and liver: Ibn Ezra locates the intellectual neshamah in the brain, ruach and the life of the person in the heart, and the appetitive nefesh in the liver. Nefesh HaChayim explains that nefesh is clothed in the blood and therefore has its primary bodily dwelling in the liver, while the circulation of blood animates the organs of action. Rav Tzadok uses the same anatomy in Peri Tzadik: Yaakov corresponds to the brain, Torah, and neshamah; Yitzchak to the heart, prayer, and ruach; and Avraham to the liver, blood, nefesh, and bodily action. The sources establish the traditional brain–heart–liver map. Rav Tzadok’s further correspondence here between the letters of “Adam,” the three soul-levels, and the worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, and Asiyah is his kabbalistic synthesis.1338Sotah 5a — “Adam” and “basar” as reminders of mortality: R’ Yochanan reads aleph-dalet-mem as efer, dam, marah — ash, blood, and gall — and beis-sin-reish as busha, seruchah, rimah — shame, decay, and worm. The teaching appears in the Gemara’s discussion of humility and the rejection of arrogance: the physical person is fragile and destined to decomposition. The Bavli supplies this moral mnemonic. Rav Tzadok then employs its three elements within his account of embodied vitality, especially the roles of blood and gall; that physiological and soul-structural application is his interpretation, not the Gemara’s explicit formulation.
וּבָשָׂר הוּא הַגּוּף שֶׁנִּקְרָא ״בְּשַׂר אָדָם״, וְהוּא כְּלִי מָלֵא בּוּשָׁה וּכְלִמָּה
and flesh is the physical body termed "the flesh of man," which is a vessel filled with shame and disgrace;
וְאָדָם הוּא עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת שֶׁהוּא מֵהַנֶּפֶשׁ הַמִּתְפַּשֵּׁט וּמִתְלַבֵּשׁ בַּגּוּף

and "Adam" embodies the essential vitality which derives from the Nefesh expanding and enclothing within the body.1339Vayikra 17:11, 14; Nefesh HaChayim I:14; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 1:6 — blood as the vehicle of nefesh: The Torah states that “the nefesh of the flesh is in the blood” and that the blood of a creature is identified with its nefesh. Nefesh HaChayim explains this as the nefesh’s clothing itself in the blood, whose movement gives life and power of action to the limbs; because the liver is filled with blood, it is described as the nefesh’s principal bodily dwelling. Peri Tzadik similarly links the liver and blood with nefesh and practical action. The verses themselves identify blood as bearing creaturely life; the localization of nefesh in the liver and its spreading through the body articulate the received interpretive tradition used by Rav Tzadok here.
וְהַכָּבֵד עִיקָּרוֹ הַכְּזַיִת בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק אֵלּוּ טְרֵפוֹת, חֻלִּין מ״ו עַמּוּד א׳]: ״עֲרוֹקָאִי, כְּזַיִת שֶׁאָמְרוּ בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה״

And the liver's vital essence is the olive's bulk (k'zayis) situated at the place of the gallbladder, as they stated [in Chullin 46a]: "My Aramean masters, the k'zayis of liver required to preserve life is at the gallbladder";

וְעַיֵּין בִּכְרֵתִי וּפְלֵתִי [רֵישׁ סִימָן מ״א], וּמַה שֶּׁכָּתַב ״מַמָּשׁ כָּל חוֹלִי וּמַחֲלָה מִמָּרָה״, הָיָה לוֹ לוֹמַר זֶה מֵהַגְּמָרָא [בָּבָא מְצִיעָא ק״ז עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״כָּל חוֹלִי — זוֹ מָרָה, מַחֲלָה — זוֹ מָרָה וְכוּלֵיהּ״

and see in the Kresi U'Plesi [Yoreh De'ah 41:1], and what he wrote that literally all sickness and illness stem from bile, he should have cited this from the Gemara [Bava Metzia 107b]: "'all sickness'—this is the bile; 'disease'—this is the bile, etc.";1340Chullin 46a: “A certain military troop (‘the ruler’s army’) came to Pumbedisa; Rabbah and Rav Yosef fled. R’ Zeira met them (Tosafos: ‘he did not need to flee, for his father was a tax-collector for the king’) and said to them: Fugitives! (fleeing ones — learn this law from me:) the olive’s-bulk that [the Sages] said [must remain of the liver for it to be kosher applies] specifically when it is in the place of the gall.” And in the Kreisi u-Pleisi on Yoreh De’ah, siman 41:1, he brings these words in parentheses: “And in a homily I said, by way of wit: In the Gemara, ‘this troop that came to Pumbedisa — Rabbah and Rav Yosef fled from it; R’ Zeira met them and said to them: Fugitives! the olive’s-bulk that they said [must be] in the place of the gall — so we learned.’ For what has this matter to do with their actually fleeing the king? But the matter, according to its plain sense, is that we require an olive’s-bulk in the place of the gall because there the vitality of the body depends. And although there is nothing more [bitter] than the gall — and literally every illness and disease depends on the gall, and the Satan, when he wished to afflict Iyov with plagues and diseases, poured the gall into his body, as it is written: ‘he pours out my gall to the ground’ [Iyov 16:13] — nonetheless so it is: in the place of His judgment, there is His work for good; in the place of evil, there the good always is; and so His wisdom is in the good of Creation; and Moshe is buried opposite Pe’or; and so all of them, this corresponding to that. Now, they wished to flee not on account of the tax, as the Tosafos wrote, but rather they did not wish to study Torah in the place of the king’s decree and Israel’s distress, and it was hard for them to study Torah there. R’ Zeira told them that one should not do so. And such is the measure, as they said: from the day the Temple was destroyed it was decreed to study Torah amid pain and confusion and pressure; and the proof is the olive’s-bulk that they said, upon which the vitality depends — the liver — is in the place of the gall; and it is easy to understand.”
וּמַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ: ״כּוּלָּן פַּת שַׁחֲרִית בְּמֶלַח וְקִיתוֹן שֶׁל מַיִם מְבַטֵּל״
and what they stated: "all eighty-three illnesses are nullified by eating morning bread with salt and a flagon of water";
הוּא אֲכִילָה כְּדַרְכָּהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה: ״פַּת בְּמֶלַח [תֹּאכֵל] וּמַיִם בִּמְשׂוּרָה [תִּשְׁתֶּה]״ (אָבוֹת ו:ד), לְהַבְרוֹת גּוּפוֹ וּלְקִיּוּם חַיּוּתוֹ לְבַד

refers to eating according to the disciplined way of the Torah: "bread with salt you shall eat, and water by measure you shall drink" (Avos 6:4), consumed solely to invigorate the body and sustain its life,1341Bava Metzia 107b; Avos 6:4; Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat 1:2 — measured eating for life: Bava Metzia identifies “sickness” with the gall bladder, teaches that eighty-three illnesses depend upon it, and says that morning bread with salt and water counteracts them; the passage then connects this regimen with prayer and the promise that Hashem will remove illness. Avos describes the Torah’s way as bread with salt and water in measure. Rav Tzadok reads these sources ethically: eating is created to sustain holy life, and the tzaddik “eats to the satisfaction of his nefesh” only to preserve life, without making bodily desire the purpose. The medical statements belong to the Gemara; their interpretation as Torah-measured eating directed solely toward vitality is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
לֹא לְמַלֹּאות תַּאֲוָתוֹ שֶׁמִּזֶּה בָּאִים כָּל הַחוֹלָאִים, בֵּין בַּגּוּף בֵּין בַּנֶּפֶשׁ
and not to satisfy physical lust, from which arise all sicknesses both in body and in soul,
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת ל״ב עַמּוּד א׳]: ״מְלָא כְּרֵיסֵי זַנֵּי בִישֵׁי״
as they stated [in Berachos 32a]: "A stomach full of food breeds all evil sorts";
וּמִזֶּה בָּא הַתְחָלַת כָּל הַחֲטָאִים וְהַסָּתַת הַיֵּצֶר, וְשֶׁגָּרַם מִיתָה לָעוֹלָם עַל יְדֵי תַּאֲוַת אֲכִילָה

and from this comes the inception of all sins and the incitement of the yetzer, which brought mortality to the world through the lust for eating (the fruit of the Tree of Knowledge).1342Bereishis 3:6; Berachos 32a; Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 7:1; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:77; Takanas HaShavin 15:44–46 — eating-desire as the root of sin: The primordial temptation begins when Chavah sees that the tree is “good for eating.” Berachos warns that after one “fills his belly,” evil kinds of conduct arise, expounding the sequence “they were filled…their heart was exalted; therefore they forgot Me.” Peri Tzadik states explicitly that the serpent’s first introduction of bodily pleasure was through eating and calls the blemish of eating the root of the corruption; Dover Tzedek likewise connects Adam’s death with desire and contrasts it with the life rooted in Torah. Earlier in this siman, Rav Tzadok traced the first human transgression from desire into the later powers of sin. Chazal identify the danger of satiation and the Torah narrates the first eating; the claim that uncontrolled eating-desire is the beginning of the entire sinful process is Rav Tzadok’s synthetic reading.
וְהוּא בָּא מִכֹּחַ הַנֶּפֶשׁ, דְּעִינּוּי אֲכִילָה נִקְרָא ״עִינּוּי נֶפֶשׁ״, וְנֶאֱמַר: ״תְּעַנּוּ אֶת נַפְשֹׁתֵיכֶם״ (וַיִּקְרָא ט״ז:כ״ט)
And this derives from the power of the Nefesh, for fasting from food is called "afflicting the soul (inuy nefesh)," as it is said: "you shall afflict your souls" (Vayikra 16:29);
וְ״נֶפֶשׁ יְתֵירָה״ דְּשַׁבָּת פֵּירֵשׁ רַשִׁ״י [בְּבֵיצָה ט״ז עַמּוּד א׳]: לֵב רָחָב לֶאֱכוֹל יוֹתֵר
and the "additional soul (neshamah yeseirah / nefesh yeseirah)" of Shabbos, Rashi explains [in Beitzah 16a]: an expansive heart to eat more;
כִּי בָּזֶה מִתְקַיֵּים הַנֶּפֶשׁ בַּגּוּף, שֶׁמִּתְהַוֶּוה מִמֶּנּוּ הַדָּם הוּא הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַשּׁוֹכֵן בַּכָּבֵד דְּכוּלּוֹ דָּם
for through food the Nefesh is sustained in the body, generating the blood which is the Nefesh (Devarim 12:23) dwelling in the liver which is entirely blood;
וּמִמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ הַכַּעַס, וּמָרָה זוֹרֶקֶת טִיפָּה וּמְנִיחַתּוֹ
and from the liver is drawn the fire of anger (ka'as), whereupon the gallbladder casts a droplet of cooling fluid and calms it (Berachos 61b);
וּמִזֶּה הוּא כָּל חַיּוּת הַגּוּף וְקִיּוּם הַכָּבֵד, שֶׁלּוּלֵי כֵן הָיָה נִשְׂרָף וְנִכְלָה בְּאֵשׁ הַכָּעַס:

and through this balance operates the entire physical vitality of the body and the preservation of the liver, which otherwise would be burned and consumed in the raging fire of wrath.1343R’ Tzadok — parallel (Machshavos Charutz §6): “Atzilus, Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah, and in the secret of the four letters [of the Name].” Exactly the se’if: the three letters of “Adam” correspond to nefesh, ruach, neshamah — the three worlds of Beriah, Yetzirah, Asiyah.1344Beitzah 16a and Rashi; Berachos 61b; Zohar, Pinchas 69:413; Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 7:1 and Miketz 6:1 — Shabbos eating and the liver–gall balance: Beitzah teaches that Hashem grants an additional soul on Shabbos, and Rashi explains it as breadth of heart for rest and joy, enabling a person to eat and drink without revulsion. Berachos states that the liver becomes angry and the gall casts a drop into it and calms it; the Zohar expands the image, describing the gall’s heat and its danger to the liver and body. Peri Tzadik presents the Shabbos meal as a repair of the primordial blemish of eating: bodily enjoyment can enter holiness, while the higher intention is to delight the additional soul, treated as a sacred guest. Rav Tzadok’s chain here — food becoming blood, nefesh dwelling in the liver, anger arising there, and gall preserving the body — combines these teachings. The Bavli does not itself state that the additional soul is generated by eating.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ק״ג–ק״ד

The theme: Anger and lust as opposing yet parallel impure shells (kelipos) of Esav and Yishmael, representing murder and illicit relations. These two drives were originally implanted by the Creator into man's soul solely for the preservation of life and propagation of the species, rooted in the divine soul-root through the cooling drop of bile that checks the liver's fury. However, an excess of bile breeds bodily illness, demonstrating that even bitter traits must be tempered. This divine paradox—sweetening the bitter with the bitter—was demonstrated to Moshe Rabbeinu at Marah right after the Exodus as preparation for receiving the Torah, teaching that the spiritual sweetness of Torah arises precisely through overcoming the bitterness of worldly trials and bodily passions.

p: וְיָדוּעַ דְּכַעַס וְתַאֲוָה הֵם ב׳ הֲפָכִים, שֵׁהֵם ב׳ קְלִיפּוֹת קָשׁוֹת דְּעֵשָׂו וְיִשְׁמָעֵאל, שֶׁהוּא רְצִיחָה וְנִיאוּף, דְּגַם הוּא נִקְרָא בִּלְשׁוֹן אֲכִילָה: ״אָכְלָה וּמָחֲתָה פִּיהָ״ (מִשְׁלֵי ל:כ) בִּלְשׁוֹן נְקִיָּה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּכְתוּבּוֹת י״ד עַמּוּד א׳]

And it is known that anger and lust are two opposites, representing the two harsh husks of Esav and Yishmael, which are murder and illicit relations; for lust is likewise designated by the term of eating: "She eats, and wipes her mouth" (Mishlei 30:20) in euphemistic language as they stated [in Kesubos 14a].1345Mishlei 30:20; Kesuvos 65b; Peri Tzadik, Miketz 6:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:44–46 — “eating” as a euphemism for sexual desire: Kesuvos discusses the phrase that a wife “eats with” her husband: Rav Ashi interprets it as marital relations, and the Gemara calls “eating” a refined euphemism, citing the adulterous woman who “eats and wipes her mouth.” Peri Tzadik connects the two appetites more deeply: the serpent’s first enticement was through eating, and the later sexual contamination is likewise described by the language of eating. Earlier in this siman, Rav Tzadok traces the primordial eating-desire into the subsequent powers of sin. The verse and Gemara establish the euphemism; the identification of eating and sexual desire as two expressions of one bodily appetite is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
וּב׳ תַּאֲוֹת אֵלּוּ הֵם מַה שֶׁהַשֵּׁם יִתְבָּרַךְ קְבָעָם בְּנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם לְצֹרֶךְ קִיּוּם הַחַיּוּת וְקִיּוּם הַמֵּין, לֹא לְשׁוּם הֲנָאָה גּוּפָנִית
And these two desires are what the Blessed Name implanted within the soul of man solely for the necessity of sustaining life and preserving the species, and not for any physical bodily gratification.
וְזֶהוּ מִשּׁוֹרֶשׁ הַנֶּפֶשׁ חַיָּה שֶׁבָּאָדָם שַׁבִּקְדֻשָּׁה, עַל יְדֵי טִיפַּת מָרָה הַמַּשְׁכֶּחַת כַּעַס הַכָּבֵד

And this derives from the root of the living soul in man in holiness, through the droplet of bile that appeases and checks the fury of the liver.1346Cf. Bereishis Rabbah 9:7 — “ve-hinneh tov me’od — this is the evil inclination [yetzer ha-ra].” R’ Nachman expounds that were it not for the yetzer, no man would build a house, marry, beget children, or engage in commerce. This grounds R’ Tzadok’s point that the very drives of anger and desire were “very good” as implanted for sustaining life and perpetuating the species — evil only in their misuse.
אֲבָל כְּשֶׁמּוֹסִיף עַל טִיפָה וּמִתְקָרֵר יוֹתֵר מִזֶּה, נִמְשָׁךְ תַּאֲוָה יְתֵירָה וּבָאִים כָּל הַמַּחֲלוֹת, וְעַל כֵּן נִקְרָא שְׁמָהּ ״מָרָה״

But when one adds beyond the measure of the droplet and cools excessively, excessive lust is drawn forth and all illnesses ensue; wherefore its name is marah [bitterness].1347Berachos 61b; Bava Metzia 107b; Zohar, Pinchas 69:413; Peri Tzadik, Korach 10:1 — the liver, gall, anger, and desire: Berachos states that “the liver becomes angry” and the gall casts a drop into it and calms it. Bava Metzia says that eighty-three illnesses depend upon the gall bladder, while the Zohar describes the gall as arousing heat in the liver’s channels and threatening to burn the body. Peri Tzadik identifies the nefesh’s dwelling in the liver and associates its anger with Esav, while the heart’s appetite is associated with Yishmael; it adds that the “leaven” of desire is beneficial only in a small measure when redirected to Torah. Rav Tzadok’s further claim here — that excessive cooling by gall produces surplus desire and illness — is his interpretive physiology, not the Bavli’s literal wording.
וְהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מַמְתִּיק אֶת הַמַּר בַּמַּר, כִּי כָּל קִיּוּם הַחַיּוּת הוּא עַל יְדֵי זֶה הַמָּר
And the Holy One, blessed be He, sweetens the bitter with the bitter, for the entire sustenance of life is upheld precisely through this bitter element.

וְהֶרְאָה זֶה הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם מִיָּד בְּיְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם בְּהַכָּנָה לְקַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה, כִּי הֵם חַיֵּינוּ, וְנִתָּן עַל יְדֵי יִסּוּרִים הַקּוֹדְמִים דִּיְצִיאַת מִצְרַיִם דַּ״וְיַמְרֲרוּ אֶת חַיֵּיהֶם״ (שְׁמוֹת א:יד)

And this the Holy One, blessed be He, demonstrated to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, immediately upon the Exodus from Egypt as a preparation for receiving the Torah, for "they are our life" (Devarim 30:20), bestowed through the preceding afflictions of the Exodus where "they made their lives bitter" (Shemos 1:14).1348Shemos 15:23–25; Midrash Tanchuma, Beshalach 24:2; Bereishis Rabbah 77:1; Yisrael Kedoshim 7:24 — sweetening the bitter with bitter: At Marah, the Torah relates that the waters were bitter, Hashem showed Moshe a tree, and the waters became sweet. Midrash Tanchuma records that the tree itself was bitter and explains that Hashem heals with the very medium through which He strikes; Bereishis Rabbah formulates the principle that the Holy One “sweetens the bitter with bitter.” In Yisrael Kedoshim, Rav Tzadok applies this principle to judgment and suffering: when unrestricted kindness would strengthen evil, the repair can come through the disciplined bitterness of din itself. The Midrash supplies the paradox of a bitter cure; the present identification of gall, Egyptian suffering, and Torah preparation as one pattern is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם מִירּוּר חַיִּים בְּגּוּף וּבְנֶפֶשׁ, שֶׁנִּשְׁקְעוּ בְּטוּמְאַת מִצְרַיִם שֶׁעִקָּרָהּ בְּתַאֲווֹת וְהֵם שׁוֹטְפֵי זִמָּה
For they experienced the bitterness of life in body and soul, having been submerged in the defilement of Egypt whose core lies in physical lusts, being flooded with depravity.
וּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל, הַגַּם שְׁגָּדְרוּ עַצְמָם בַּעֲרָיוֹת, בְּקִבְרוֹת הַתַּאֲוָה שֶׁנִּתְאַוּוּ לְבָשָׂר נֶאֱמַר: ״זָכַרְנוּ אֶת הַדָּגָה אֲשֶׁר נֹאכַל בְּמִצְרַיִם [חִנָּם]״ (בְּמִדְבָּר יא:ה)

And the Children of Israel—although they walled themselves off from illicit relations—at the graves of lust where they lusted for flesh, it was said: "We remember the fish, which we did eat in Egypt for nought" (Bamidbar 11:5).1349Vayikra Rabbah 32:5; Bamidbar 11:4–6; Peri Tzadik, Tu BiShvat 1:2 — guarded sexuality and residual Egyptian desire: Vayikra Rabbah teaches that Israel restrained themselves from sexual immorality in Egypt and were redeemed in that merit. Yet at Kivros HaTa’avah the people cried for meat and remembered the fish eaten in Egypt. Peri Tzadik describes the Egyptian exile as a purification of souls rooted in the generation of the Flood, whose corruption was desire, and presents the repair of eating-desire as the tzaddik’s eating only to sustain the nefesh. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes between Israel’s actual guarding of forbidden relations and a residual Egyptian appetite that resurfaced through food. That distinction is his reading of the juxtaposed sources, not an explicit statement of the Midrash.
וְעַל כֵּן נִצְטַוּוּ בְּאֲכִילַת מַצָּה, שֶׁהוּא צִמְצוּם תַּאֲוָה בְּיוֹתֵר
And therefore they were commanded regarding the eating of matzah, which represents the extreme constriction of physical appetite;
דְּשְׂאוֹר מִיּוּטוֹ יָפֶה, וְכֵן יֵצֶר הָרָע נִקְרָא ״טוֹב מְאֹד״ כַּאֲשֶׁר מִשְׁתַּמְּשִׁים בּוֹ רַק כְּפִי הַצֹּרֶךְ לְהַכְנִיס אֶל הַקֹּדֶשׁ
for a small measure of leaven is fine, and likewise the yetzer hara is termed "very good" (Bereishis Rabbah 9:7) when employed strictly as necessary to channel energy into holiness;
וְכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ] דְּצָרִיךְ לְחַמִידוּ דְּאוֹרַיְיתָא
and as they stated [in the Holy Zohar] that one requires a passionate appetite for the Torah (chamidu d'oraysa).
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא סט עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּכֶשְׁכָּבְשׁוֹהוּ לֹא אִשְׁתַּכַּח בִּיעָתָא בַּת יוֹמָא
And they stated [in Yoma 69b] that when they captured the yetzer hara of idolatry, a fresh egg could not be found throughout the land;
כִּי גַּם מַה שֶּׁמּוּכְרָח לְקִיּוּם הַמֵּין אֵינוֹ אֶלָּא מִצַּד הַיֵּצֶר, שֶׁעַל זֶה הָיָה בַּבְּרִיאָה ״וְהִנֵּה טוֹב מְאֹד״
for even that which is strictly necessary for the perpetuation of the species derives entirely from the yetzer, regarding which it was declared at Creation "and behold, it was very good."

items.h: The theme: The sanctity of Shabbos and the transition from Marah to the ultimate joy of the World to Come. Just as the bitterness of life in Egypt and Marah paved the way for receiving the Torah, so too the physical hardships and spiritual bitterness of the six days of work are sweetened by the holy delight of Shabbos—a foretaste of the World to Come. The bitter elements of existence, when refined, transform earthly labor into spiritual elevation, echoing the principle that for the righteous, suffering precedes eternal tranquility.

p: וּבַמָּרָה נִצְטַוּוּ עַל הַשַּׁבָּת, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק רַבִּי עֲקִיבָא, שַׁבָּת קי״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]

And at Marah they were commanded concerning the Shabbos (Shabbos 87b), as they stated [in Perek Rabi Akiva, Shabbos 118b];1350Berachos 34a; Yoma 69b; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 1:4 and 4:1; Machshavos Charutz 9:9 — matzah, leaven, and redirected desire: Berachos teaches that leaven is harmful in abundance but beneficial in a small measure. Yoma shows why the sexual inclination cannot simply be destroyed: when it was imprisoned, no fresh egg could be found, and the Sages concluded that the world could not continue without it. Peri Tzadik explains that Pesach first requires the complete removal of leaven as a corrective extreme, while Shavuos later brings chametz when desire has been redirected into “desire for Torah”; Machshavos Charutz similarly links chametz’s rising quality with the yetzer and explains why it must be eliminated at the initial Exodus from evil. The formulation of matzah as “constriction of desire” is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis of these teachings.
כִּידוּעַ דְּבַשַּׁבָּת הַתַּעֲנוּג מִצְוָה, דְּכָל הַתַּאֲווֹת הֵם אָז בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

for it is known that on Shabbos indulgence is a mitzvah, since all physical desires are then elevated into holiness.1351Shabbos 87b; Yeshayahu 58:13; Rambam, Hilchos Shabbos 30:7; Peri Tzadik, Vayeshev 7:1 and Miketz 6:1 — Shabbos pleasure as a holy repair: Shabbos teaches that Israel was commanded concerning Shabbos at Marah. Yeshayahu calls Shabbos “a delight,” and the Rambam defines its delight through food and drink prepared according to one’s means. Peri Tzadik presents the Shabbos meal as a repair of the primordial blemish of eating: bodily enjoyment can enter holiness, and the higher intention is to delight the additional soul as a sacred guest. Rav Tzadok’s statement that the desires are then “in holiness” does not mean that every appetite is automatically sanctified; it describes desire directed through the mitzvah and measure of oneg Shabbos.
וְזֶהוּ הַמַּר שֶׁהִמְתִּיק אֶת הַמַּר, שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַמְּרִירוּת דְּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה זוֹכִין לְעוֹלָם שֶׁכֻּלּוֹ טוֹב וְעֹונֶג
And this is the bitter element that sweetened the bitter: that through the bitterness of this world one merits the World that is entirely good and delightful;
וְכֵן ו׳ יְמֵי הַמַּעֲשֶׂה וְשַׁבָּת שֶׁהוּא מֵעֵין עוֹלָם הַבָּא
and likewise the six days of action and Shabbos which is a foretaste of the World to Come;
כִּי צַדִּיקִים תְּחִלָּתָן יִסּוּרִין וְסוֹפָן שַׁלְוָה:

for the righteous experience afflictions at their inception and tranquility at their end.1352R’ Tzadok — parallel (Kometz HaMincha §40): “Murder and adultery, which are Esav and Yishmael; but Yaakov — his bed was whole [mitaso sheleimah].” Exactly the se’if: anger and desire are two opposites — the hard shells of Esav and Yishmael, murder and adultery.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ק״ה–ק״ח

The theme: The consolation of the Sages who fled persecution and the necessity of cessation in Torah study (bitulah shel Torah zehu yisudah). In Chullin 46a, the Sage addressed his disciples as "my Aramean colleagues" (aroka'i, those who fled), comforting them when they were forced to flee persecutors and disrupt public Torah study. Just as the broken Tablets were placed in the holy Ark (Menachos 99a), temporary disruption or forgetting of learning serves to arouse deeper exertion and yearning ("happy is the man whom You chastise, O Hashem, and teach out of Your law", Tehillim 94:12). This embodies sweetening the bitter with the bitter: at the Red Sea, Israel experienced an overwhelming, unearned illumination (or gadol) where a simple handmaid saw what the prophet Yechezkel did not see, leading to the Song of the Sea (Az Yashir). Having gathered all holy sparks through the spoils of the Sea (bizzas ha-yam), they believed they had already arrived at the final goal of receiving the Torah, requiring Moshe to compel them onward (vayasa Moshe).

p: וְיֵשׁ לוֹמַר זֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לְהוּ ״עֲרוֹקָאִי״
And one can say that this is what he said to them: "my fleeing colleagues" (aroka'i, Chullin 46a);
לְפִי שֶׁנִּצְטַעֲרוּ עַל שֶׁהוּצְרְכוּ לִבְרוֹחַ מֵחֲמַת הַמֵּצִיק וּלְבַטֵּל תַּלְמוּד תּוֹרָה דְּרַבִּים מֵהַתַּלְמִידִים
because they grieved over having been forced to flee on account of the oppressor, thereby disrupting the public Torah study of many disciples;
וְאָמַר לָהֶם לְדַבֵּר אֶל לִבָּם, דִּפְעָמִים דְּבִיטּוּלָהּ שֶׁל תּוֹרָה זֶהוּ יְסוּדָהּ

and he spoke to their hearts that at times the suspension of Torah study is its very foundation,1353Chullin 46a: “A certain military troop (‘the ruler’s army’) came to Pumbedisa; Rabbah and Rav Yosef fled. R’ Zeira met them (Tosafos: ‘he did not need to flee, for his father was a tax-collector for the king’) and said to them: Fugitives! (fleeing ones — learn this law from me:) the olive’s-bulk that [the Sages] said [must remain of the liver for it to be kosher applies] specifically when it is in the place of the gall.” And in the Kreisi u-Pleisi on Yoreh De’ah, siman 41:1, he brings these words in parentheses: “And in a homily I said, by way of wit: In the Gemara, ‘this troop that came to Pumbedisa — Rabbah and Rav Yosef fled from it; R’ Zeira met them and said to them: Fugitives! the olive’s-bulk that they said [must be] in the place of the gall — so we learned.’ For what has this matter to do with their actually fleeing the king? But the matter, according to its plain sense, is that we require an olive’s-bulk in the place of the gall because there the vitality of the body depends. And although there is nothing more [bitter] than the gall — and literally every illness and disease depends on the gall, and the Satan, when he wished to afflict Iyov with plagues and diseases, poured the gall into his body, as it is written: ‘he pours out my gall to the ground’ [Iyov 16:13] — nonetheless so it is: in the place of His judgment, there is His work for good; in the place of evil, there the good always is; and so His wisdom is in the good of Creation; and Moshe is buried opposite Pe’or; and so all of them, this corresponding to that. Now, they wished to flee not on account of the tax, as the Tosafos wrote, but rather they did not wish to study Torah in the place of the king’s decree and Israel’s distress, and it was hard for them to study Torah there. R’ Zeira told them that one should not do so. And such is the measure, as they said: from the day the Temple was destroyed it was decreed to study Torah amid pain and confusion and pressure; and the proof is the olive’s-bulk that they said, upon which the vitality depends — the liver — is in the place of the gall; and it is easy to understand.”
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּמְנָחוֹת צ״ט רֵישׁ עַמּוּד ב׳] מִשְּׁבִירַת לוּחוֹת
as they stated [in Menachos 99b] from the breaking of the first Tablets;
וְשָׁם [סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] דְּזֶהוּ שִׁכְחַת תַּלְמוּד

and there [end of 99a] that this applies likewise to the accidental forgetting of one's learning;1354Menachos 99b; Peri Tzadik, Ki Teitzei 11:2 — breaking that becomes Torah’s foundation: Menachos derives “the nullification of Torah is its foundation” from Hashem’s approval of Moshe’s breaking the Tablets; the same passage expressly excludes forgetting caused by circumstances beyond one’s control. Peri Tzadik explains that the shattered Tablets became the beginning of Torah shebe’al peh: the second Tablets brought an expanded gift of halachah, midrash, and aggadah, so apparent loss opened a deeper form of acquisition. Rav Tzadok applies that structure to Rabbah and Rav Yosef’s forced flight. Their interruption was not voluntary neglect; under oppression, the broken continuity itself could become the basis for renewed strength and a broader transmission of Torah. The Bavli states the principle and the exemption for compulsion; its application to the displacement of a Torah community is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis.
אֲבָל עַל יְדֵי זֶה מִתְעוֹרֵר לְהוֹסִיף חַיִל בַּתּוֹרָה
for through this disruption one is aroused to redouble his strength in the Torah;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּבְרָכוֹת ה׳ סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳] מִקְּרָא דְּ״[אַשְׁרֵי הַגֶּבֶר אֲשֶׁר] תְּיַסְּרֶנּוּ יָּהּ וּמִתּוֹרָתְךָ תְלַמְּדֶנּוּ״ (תְּהִלִּים צ״ד:י״ב)
and as they expounded [in Berachos 5a] from the verse: "Happy is the man whom You chasten, O Lord, and teach him out of Your law" (Tehillim 94:12);
וְהַגַּם דִּבְהַיִּסּוּרִין יֵשׁ בִּיטּוּל תּוֹרָה, זֶהוּ הַמְתָּקַת הַמַּר בַּמַּר
and although tribulations involve the cessation of Torah study, this constitutes sweetening the bitter with the bitter,
שֶׁגִּילָּה לְמֹשֶׁה רַבֵּינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם בַּמַּסָּע הָרִאשׁוֹן שֶׁאַחַר קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה

which Hashem revealed to Moshe Rabbeinu, peace be upon him, at the first journey after receiving the initial laws at Marah;1355Tehillim 94:12; Berachos 5a; Peri Tzadik, Miketz 4:1; Yisrael Kedoshim 7:24; Divrei Chalomot §22 — affliction that teaches: Berachos reads “whom You chasten, O Kah, and teach from Your Torah” as directing suffering toward renewed Torah, and teaches that Torah itself is among the precious gifts acquired through suffering. Peri Tzadik describes Yosef’s pit and the exiles as painful preparations whose purpose becomes visible only afterward; Yisrael Kedoshim and Divrei Chalomot formulate the corresponding rule that Hashem may “sweeten the bitter with bitter,” using the constriction itself as the instrument of repair. The Gemara does not say that every interruption of study is automatically beneficial. Rav Tzadok’s claim here is more specific: when unavoidable suffering cancels Torah temporarily, it can awaken a stronger return to Torah and thereby disclose the instruction hidden within the pain.
שֶׁהָיָה לָהֶם הִתְגַּלּוּת אוֹר גָּדוֹל, דְּרָאֲתָה שִׁפְחָה מַה שֶּׁלֹּא רָאָה יְחֶזְקֵאל (מְכִילְתָּא בְּשַׁלַּח ג׳)
for at the Sea they had an overwhelming revelation of light, where a handmaid saw what the prophet Yechezkel did not see (Mechilta, Beshalach 3);
שֶׁזָּכוּ לוֹמַר שִׁירָה דְּ״אָז יָשִׁיר״
meriting to chant the song of Az Yashir (Shemos 15:1);
דְּהוּא דּוּגְמַת וְאֶפְשָׁר עוֹד יוֹתֵר מִשִּׁירַת הַאֲזִינוּ שֶׁכּוֹלֶלֶת כָּל הַתּוֹרָה

which is comparable to, and perhaps even greater than, the song of Ha'azinu which encompasses the entire Torah,1356Shemos 15:1–2; Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Shirah, on Shemos 15:2; Sanhedrin 21b; Peri Tzadik, Beshalach 6:1 — the Sea’s revelation and Torah-song: The Mekhilta reads “This is my God” as direct recognition: even a maidservant at the Sea perceived what the later prophets did not. Sanhedrin derives the mitzvah of writing an entire Torah scroll from “write for yourselves this song,” showing how Ha’azinu can stand as the Torah’s comprehensive “song.” Peri Tzadik links the Sea’s disclosure, the words “This is my God,” and Israel’s song to the completion of a spiritual clarification begun in Egypt. The primary sources establish the exceptional vision at the Sea and Ha’azinu’s relation to the whole Torah. Rav Tzadok’s further comparison — that Az Yashir is analogous to, and perhaps greater than, Ha’azinu — is his own assessment of the Sea’s all-embracing revelation.
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ מִקְּרָא דְּ״כִתְבוּ לָכֶם אֶת הַשִּׁירָה [הַזֹּאת]״ (דְּבָרִים ל״א:י״ט) עַל מִצְוַת כְּתִיבַת סֵפֶר תּוֹרָה (נְדָרִים ל״ח עַמּוּד א׳)
as they expounded the verse "Now therefore write ye this song" (Devarim 31:19) regarding the positive commandment of writing a complete Sefer Torah (Nedarim 38a).
וְעַל זֶה רָמְזוּ: גְּדוֹלָה הָיְתָה בִּזַּת הַיָּם וְכוּלֵיהּ (בְּרָכוֹת ט׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
And regarding this they alluded: "Greater was the plunder at the Sea than the plunder in Egypt, etc." (Berachos 9b);
דְּמִצְרַיִם עֲשָׂאוּהָ ״כִּמְצוּלָה שֶׁאֵין בּוֹ דָּגִים״
for Egypt they rendered "like a seabed without fish" (Berachos 9b),
שֶׁרוֹמֵז עַל קְלִיטַת כָּל הַנִּיצוֹצוֹת קְדוֹשׁוֹת שֶׁהָיוּ שָׁם

which alludes to the harvesting and extraction of all the holy sparks that were embedded there;1357Berachos 9b; Rashi to Shemos 15:22; Shir HaShirim Rabbah 1:11; Peri Tzadik, Beshalach 6:1 and Pesach 39:1 — the greater plunder of the Sea: Berachos explains “they emptied Egypt” as leaving it like a trap without grain or a deep pool without fish. Chazal and Rashi add that the plunder gathered at the Sea exceeded the wealth taken from Egypt. Peri Tzadik resolves the apparent contradiction by distinguishing material property from its spiritual content: the “great wealth” promised to Avraham was chiefly the Torah-wisdom and holiness held captive in Egypt, and the Sea completed that extraction. Thus the Gemara and Midrash speak literally about emptied wealth and greater sea-spoil; the language of absorbing “holy sparks” is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic interpretation of what that transfer accomplished.
וְהָיָה דֶּרֶךְ בִּזַּת מִלְחָמָה, אַף שֶׁהֵם הִשְׁאִילוּ מֵעַצְמָם
and this occurred by way of the spoils of war, even though the Egyptians lent them of their own accord;
מַה שֶּׁנִּשְׁאַר בְּיָדָם אַחַר כָּךְ, בְּעַל כָּרְחָךְ הִיא בִּזָּה, דְּהֵם נָתְנוּ רַק דֶּרֶךְ שְׁאֵלָה
while what remained in Israel's hands subsequently was perforce plunder, for the Egyptians had given it merely as a temporary loan;
כִּידוּעַ דְּכָל חַיּוּתָם מֵאוֹתוֹ נִיצוֹצִין קַדִּישִׁין, דְּ״אַתָּה מְחַיֶּה אֶת כֻּלָּם״ (נְחֶמְיָה ט:ו)

as is known that their entire vitality derived from those holy sparks, for "You preserve them all" (Nechemyah 9:6);1358Shemos 3:21–22, 11:2, 12:35–36; Berachos 9b; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 39:1 — borrowed vessels and recovered holiness: The Torah repeatedly describes Israel requesting silver, gold, and garments, and Berachos explains that the Egyptians supplied them “against their will,” whether that refers to Egyptian reluctance or Israel’s reluctance to carry the load.
