Peri Tzadik emphasizes that the objects mattered not as ordinary enrichment but because the sanctity invested in material things had to be released from Egyptian possession and restored to those for whom it was created. Rav Tzadok therefore calls what remained in Israel’s hands “war-plunder” even though it was initially given as a loan. The verses and Gemara establish the request and compelled transfer; the account of ownership as the return of divine vitality is his spiritual synthesis.
וּבְמַכַּת בְּכוֹרוֹת יָצָא הַשּׁוֹרֶשׁ וְהָרֵאשִׁית מֵאוֹתוֹ נִיצוֹצֵי קַדִּישִׁין, שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ כֹּחַ אֲחוּזָתָם לְהִשְׁתַּעְבֵּד בִּבְנֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל
and at the plague of the firstborn the primary root and head of those holy sparks departed, which was the very anchor of their strength to subjugate the Children of Israel;
וּבְבִיטּוּל זֶה יָצְאוּ בְּיָד רָמָה
and through the nullification of that power Israel marched forth with a high hand (Shemos 14:8);
וְעַדַיִין כָּל הַהִתְפַּשְּׁטוּת נִשְׁאַר, שֶׁמִּזֶּה הָיָה לָהֶם כֹּחַ לִרְדּוֹף אַחֲרֵיהֶם
yet all the lower expansion of those sparks still remained within Egypt, whence they possessed the vitality to pursue after them;
וּבִקְרִיעַת יַם סוּף קָלְטוּ הַכֹּל וְנִכְלוּ לְגַמְרֵי

and at the splitting of the Red Sea Israel harvested all the remaining sparks, and the Egyptians were utterly consumed.1359Shemos 12:29–36, 14:8–9, 14:27–30; Peri Tzadik, Beshalach 6:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:99–100 — the root struck at the firstborn and the hold ended at the Sea: The plague of the firstborn forced the immediate release from Egypt, yet Pharaoh and his army still found strength to pursue Israel until they were destroyed at the Sea. Peri Tzadik presents the Sea as the final clarification: Egypt received the evil attached to its domination, while Israel received the holy vitality that had been captive there, and only then could Israel say “This is my God” and sing. The Torah supplies the two historical stages — departure after the firstborn and final deliverance at the Sea. Rav Tzadok’s distinction between the “root” of Egypt’s hold removed at the firstborn and its remaining “spread” absorbed at the Sea is his kabbalistic explanation of why the pursuit was still possible after the Exodus.
וְהוּצְרַךְ לְהַסִּיעָן בְּעַל כָּרְחָן
And Moshe had to compel them to journey onward against their will (Rashi on Shemos 15:22);
שֶׁמִּפְּנֵי גֹּודֶל חֶשְׁקָתָם שָׁם חָשְׁבוּ שֶׁזֶּהוּ הַמָּקוֹם שֶׁאֶפְשָׁר לָהֶם לִזְבּוֹחַ לַה׳, שֶׁכְּבָר הִגִּיעוּ לַמַּדְרֵיגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה שֶׁל קַבָּלַת הַתּוֹרָה:

for out of the greatness of their intense passion at the Sea, they thought that this was the very place to sacrifice unto Hashem, believing they had already arrived at the supreme rung of receiving the Torah.

items.h: The theme: Unearned divine inspiration (isarusa d'le'eila) versus the earned acquisition of Torah through toil (yagata u-matzata). The revelation at the Sea was a temporary gift initiated entirely from Above without human labor ("Hashem shall fight for you, and you shall hold your peace", Shemos 14:14). What is attained without exertion does not endure as a firmly driven nail ("If one says: I have found without toiling, do not believe him", Megillah 6b). When that transcendent light withdrew, Israel journeyed three days without water—which is Torah (Bava Kamma 82a). Just as two drops rise from below for every drop from Above in love, so too in distancing: if one leaves the Torah for one day, it leaves him for two (Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5). In three days the yetzer solidifies from a wayfarer into a resident owner (ba'al ha-bayis). At Marah, through the bitter waters, they were given the ten commandments of Marah, and Hashem showed Moshe the tree of Torah that acts as a spice (tavlin) to sweeten the bitter into sweet, mirroring the lupine (turmus) which is boiled repeatedly until edible—the secret of "seven times a righteous man falls and rises again" (Mishlei 24:16).

p: וּבֶאֱמֶת זֶה הָיָה רַק לְפִי שָׁעָה, מַה שֶּׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא עָשָׂה בְּעַצְמוֹ מִצַּד אִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְעֵילָּא לְבַד
And in truth this revelation was merely temporary, which the Holy One, blessed be He, performed Himself solely from an awakening from Above (isarusa d'le'eila);
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״[ה׳ יִלָּחֵם לָכֶם] וְאַתֶּם תַּחֲרִישׁוּן״ (שְׁמוֹת י״ד:י״ד)
as it is said: "Hashem shall fight for you, and you shall hold your peace" (Shemos 14:14);
וְאֵין זוֹ הַשָּׂגָה שֶׁהִגִּיעוּ לָהּ מִצַּד הִשְׁתַּדְּלוּתָם וִיגִיעָתָם, שֶׁהוּא הָעִיקָּר שֶׁנִּקְבַּע בַּלֵּב בְּקִנְיָן, דְּ״יָגַעְתָּ וּמָצָאתָ — תַּאֲמִין״ (מְגִלָּה ו׳ עַמּוּד ב׳)
and this was not an attainment they reached through personal exertion and toil, which alone fixes a lasting acquisition in the heart: "If you have toiled and found—believe" (Megillah 6b);
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן מְצִיאָה שֶׁבְּלֹא יְגִיעָה אָמְרוּ: ״אַל תַּאֲמִין״

whereas regarding a find attained without toil they declared: "do not believe";1360Megillah 6b; Tzidkat HaTzadik §83; Dover Tzedek, Miscellany 4:85; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7:14, 7:20, 7:32 — toil, finding, and enduring acquisition: Megillah teaches that in matters of Torah, “I toiled and found — believe,” while “I did not toil and found — do not believe”; it then qualifies that this rule concerns sharpening one’s understanding, whereas retaining one’s learning still depends upon assistance from Heaven. Tzidkat HaTzadik notes that an unearned spiritual “find” can indeed be granted from Above, and Dover Tzedek and Peri Tzadik explain that the result is still called a “find” because it exceeds the precise measure of the preceding labor. Rav Tzadok therefore distinguishes the two stages here: the revelation at the Sea was a genuine heavenly gift, but because Israel had not yet acquired it through their own answering effort, it was not fixed permanently in the heart. The Gemara states the relation of toil, finding, and divine help; the contrast between the momentary Sea-light and lasting Torah acquisition is Rav Tzadok’s application.
אַף שֶׁנִּדְמֶה לוֹ שֶׁמָּצָא, אֵינוֹ דָּבָר הַמִּתְקַיֵּים ״יָתֵד בְּמָקוֹם נֶאֱמָן״ (יְשַׁעְיָה כ״ב:כ״ג), וְ״הֲתָעִיף עֵינֶיךָ בּוֹ וְאֵינֶנּוּ״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ״ג:ה׳)
for even if one imagines he has found, it does not endure like "a nail fastened in a sure place" (Yeshayah 22:23), for "will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone" (Mishlei 23:5);
דְּעַל כֵּן הִסִּיעָן, לְהַרְאוֹתָן דְּאוֹר זֶה אֵינוֹ קְדוּשָׁה דִּקְבוּעַ וְקַיָּימָא בַּלֵּב שֶׁלֹּא תִּנָּתֵק עוֹד
wherefore Moshe compelled them onward, to demonstrate to them that this light was not an enduring sanctity fixed within the heart that could never be severed.
וּמִיָּד שֶׁנָּסְעוּ מִשָּׁם וְנִסְתַּלֵּק אוֹתוֹ אוֹר, ״הָלְכוּ שְׁלֹשֶׁת יָמִים [בַּמִּדְבָּר] וְלֹא מָצְאוּ מָיִם״ (שְׁמוֹת ט״ו:כ״ב), וְאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא קַמָּא פ״ב עַמּוּד א׳]: ״זוֹ תּוֹרָה״

And immediately when they departed from there and that transcendent light withdrew, "they went three days in the wilderness, and found no water" (Shemos 15:22), which they interpreted [in Bava Kamma 82a]: "water is nothing other than Torah";1361Bava Kamma 82a: Among the ten enactments of Ezra — that they read the Torah on Mondays and Thursdays, [derived from] “and they went three days in the wilderness and found no water” (Shemos 15:22), and “there is no water but Torah” — that Israel not go three days without Torah.
וּמִסְפַּר ג׳ יָמִים עַל דֶּרֶךְ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בַּיְרוּשַׁלְמִי סוֹף בְּרָכוֹת פֶּרֶק ט׳ הֲלָכָה ה׳]: ״אִם תַּעַזְבֵנִי יוֹם — אֶעֶזְבְךָ יוֹמַיִם״

and the tally of three days corresponds to what they stated [in Yerushalmi Berachos 9:5]: "If you abandon Me for one day, I will abandon you for two";1362Jerusalem Talmud Berakhot 9:5:20; Bava Kamma 82a; Peri Tzadik, Vayigash 11:1 — one day’s abandonment becomes two days’ distance: The Yerushalmi records the maxim “if you forsake me one day, I shall forsake you two days” and explains it through two travelers who move in opposite directions: each one’s single step creates a doubled distance between them. Bava Kamma interprets Israel’s three days without water as three days without Torah and traces the public readings on Monday and Thursday to the need that Israel never remain three days without Torah. Peri Tzadik repeatedly treats interruption from Torah as the danger of exile itself, while also teaching that precisely from the interruption a greater ascent may emerge. Rav Tzadok combines these sources here: once the light granted from Above withdrew, failure to answer it with renewed effort caused the distance to compound until Marah. The Yerushalmi explains reciprocal distance, but does not itself identify the three days at Marah with three successive stages of spiritual deterioration.
כְּמוֹ בְּעִנְיַן הַחֵשֶׁק וְהָאַהֲבָה אָמְרוּ, דְּטִיפָּה שֶׁיּוֹרֶדֶת מִלְּמַעְלָה עוֹלוֹת כְּנֶגְדָּהּ טִיפַּיִם מִלְּמַטָּה, דְּהָאִתְעָרוּתָא דִּלְתַתָּא מִתְגַּבֵּר וְהוֹלֵךְ
just as in the matter of divine love they expounded that for every drop descending from Above two drops ascend from below, the human arousal from below (isarusa d'lesata) multiplying continuously;
וּבְעִנְיַן הָרִיחוּק וְהָעֲזִיבָה בְּהֵיפֶךְ, כְּשֶׁמַּתְחִיל בַּעֲזִיבָה ״הַבָּא לִיטַּמֵּא — פּוֹתְחִין״ (שַׁבָּת ק״ד עַמּוּד א׳) וְיֵצֶר הָרָע מִתְגַּבֵּר וְהוֹלֵךְ

while in the matter of distancing and abandonment the reverse occurs: when one begins to abandon, "to him who comes to defile himself they open the doors" (Shabbos 104a), and the yetzer hara grows increasingly powerful;
וְהֵם ג׳ מַדְרֵיגוֹת דְּ״הֵלֶךְ״ וְ״אוֹרֵחַ״ וְ״אִישׁ״ (שְׁמוּאֵל ב י״ב:ד׳), וּבִתְלָתָא הָוֵי חֲזָקָה וְנַעֲשָׂה בַּעַל הַבַּיִת (סֻכָּה נ״ב עַמּוּד ב׳)

these being the three stages of "traveler," "guest," and "master" (II Shmuel 12:4), wherein through three days a halachic presumption (chazakah) is established and the yetzer becomes the homeowner (Sukkah 52b).1363Sukkah 52b; Peri Tzadik, Metzora 1:1 — traveler, guest, and homeowner: Sukkah describes the inclination’s gradual advance: at first Scripture calls it a traveler, afterward a guest, and finally a man — one who has become established in the house. The same passage directs a person to draw the inclination into the study hall, where Torah can dissolve stone and shatter iron. Peri Tzadik applies the first stage specifically to bittul Torah: the inclination first persuades a person merely to “walk idly,” then gains the standing of a guest, and ultimately acts as master; renewed words of Torah restore and straighten the person. Rav Tzadok’s further association of these three stages with the three-day chazakah is his own synthesis. The Bavli describes progressive entrenchment, but does not formulate a legal chazakah over the soul.
וְעַל כֵּן אַחַר אוֹתָם ג׳ יָמִים ״בָּאוּ מָרָתָה... כִּי מָרִים הֵם״ (שְׁמוֹת ט״ו:כ״ג), שֶׁכְּבָר נַעֲשׂוּ גַּם הֵם מָרִים
And therefore after those three days "they came to Marah... for they were bitter" (Shemos 15:23), for their own souls had likewise turned bitter;
וְשָׁם הָיָה הַהַתְחָלָה לְקַבָּלַת תּוֹרָה כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ דְּעֶשֶׂר מִצְוֹת נִצְטַוּוּ שָׁם (סַנְהֶדְרִין נ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳)
and there was the true beginning of receiving the Torah, as they stated that ten commandments were commanded to them at Marah (Sanhedrin 56b);
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״שָׁם שָׂם לוֹ חֹק וּמִשְׁפָּט״ (שְׁמוֹת ט״ו:כ״ה)

as it is said: "there He made for them a statute and an ordinance" (Shemos 15:25);1364Shemos 15:25; Sanhedrin 56b; Midrash Tanchuma, Beshalach 24; Yisrael Kedoshim 7:24 — Marah as instruction and healing: Sanhedrin records that Israel received ten commandments at Marah — the seven Noahide laws together with judgment, Shabbat, and honoring parents — and derives the new commands from “there He set for them a statute and an ordinance.” Midrash Tanchuma emphasizes that the verse says va-yorehu, “He instructed him,” rather than merely “He showed him”: Hashem taught Moshe His way of healing the bitter with something bitter. Yisrael Kedoshim develops this as a general divine method, “sweetening the bitter with the bitter,” whereby the constriction itself becomes the instrument of repair. Rav Tzadok consequently calls Marah the beginning and root of Torah reception: Torah does not merely remove the bitter experience from outside, but teaches how its own bitterness can be transformed into healing.
וְכֵן ״וַיּוֹרֵהוּ [ה׳ עֵץ]״ דָּרְשׁוּ חֲכָמֵינוּ זִכְרוֹנָם לִבְרָכָה מִלְּשׁוֹן הוֹרָאָה וְתוֹרָה
and likewise "and Hashem showed him a tree," the Sages of blessed memory expounded from the root of instruction (hora'ah) and Torah;
שֶׁזֶּהוּ שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַתּוֹרָה לִהְיוֹת תַּבְלִין לְיֵצֶר רָע, כְּדָבָר הַמְתַבֵּל שֶׁעוֹשֶׂה אֶת הַמַּר מָתוֹק

for this is the essence of the Torah: to serve as a spice (tavlin) to the yetzer hara (Bava Batra 16a), like a culinary seasoning that transforms the bitter into sweet;1365Kiddushin 30b; Tzidkat HaTzadik §§12, 242; Resisei Layla 35:2; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:22 — Torah as the spice that transforms the inclination: Kiddushin calls Torah a complete antidote and the “spice” created for the evil inclination: while one remains engaged in Torah, one is not surrendered into the inclination’s power. Rav Tzadok stresses the precision of the metaphor. A spice does not annihilate the underlying substance; it gives it a new and beneficial taste. Thus Tzidkat HaTzadik says Torah “seasons” the inclination until it becomes good, Resisei Layla explains that desire and imagination are redirected into desire for Torah, and Yisrael Kedoshim distinguishes the written and oral Torah as divine counsel that can reach even an inclination already fixed in the heart. This is the sense in which Torah “makes the bitter sweet”: the same human energy that had produced distance becomes an appetite for holiness.
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: ״כַּמָּה דְּבָרִים מָרִים שֶׁבָּעוֹלָם שֶׁאַתֶּם מַמְתִּיקִין, כְּתוּרְמוּסִין שֶׁשּׁוֹלְקִין ד׳ פְּעָמִים״ (שְׁמוֹת רַבָּה כ״ג:ג׳)
and as they expounded: "How many bitter things are there in the world that you sweeten, such as the lupine (turmus) which is boiled four times" (Shemos Rabbah 23:3);
וְאָמְרוּ [בְּבֵיצָה כ״ה עַמּוּד ב׳] דְּתוּרְמוֹס מְקַטַּע רַגְלֵיהוֹן וְכוּלֵיהּ

and they stated [in Beitzah 25b] that the lupine breaks the feet of Israel's enemies, etc.;1366Beitzah 25b: “The lupine [tormus], which one boils seven times [and only then eats it at dessert]” — R’ Tzadok’s recurring image for the sins that must be “sweetened” through repeated scouring.
וְאִיתָא עַל פָּסוּק ״וַיַּעַבְדוּ אֶת [בַּעֲלֵי הָאֲרָמוֹת] וְגוֹמֵר״ (שׁוֹפְטִים י:ו): דַּאֲפִילּוּ כְּתוּרְמוֹס הַזֶּה לֹא עֲשָׂאוּנִי וְכוּלֵיהּ לְעָבְדוֹ אַחַר שֶׁעָבְדוּ ז׳ עֲבוֹדָה זָרָה

and it is taught regarding the verse "and they served the Baalim, etc." (Shoftim 10:6): "Not even like this lupine did you treat Me, to serve Me after serving seven forms of idolatry!" (Yerushalmi Berachos 9:1);
שֶׁהוּא עַל דֶּרֶךְ ״שֶׁבַע יִפּוֹל צַדִּיק וָקָם״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ״ד:ט״ז), דְּעַל יְדֵי הַנְּפִילוֹת הוּא קָם
which follows the principle: "For a righteous man falls seven times, and rises up again" (Mishlei 24:16)—through the very falls he rises!
שֶׁהַיְרִידָה לְצֹרֶךְ עֲלִיָּה, כְּשֶׁזּוֹכֶה אַחַר כָּךְ לְהִתְעוֹרֵר מִתּוֹךְ מְרִירוּת הַנְּפִילוֹת וְלָשׁוּב אֶל ה׳
For the descent is for the purpose of ascent, when one merits subsequently to be aroused out of the bitterness of his stumblings and return unto Hashem;
וְכַנּוֹדָע דְּנַעֲשָׂה הַכֹּל כִּסֵּא אֶל הַקְּדוּשָׁה
and as is known, everything is transformed into a throne unto holiness;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ: עֲלֵיהֶם ״חָיֹה יִחְיֶה״ (יְחֶזְקֵאל י״ח:כ״א), דִּזְדוֹנוֹת נַעֲשׂוּ זְכֻיּוֹת (יוֹמָא פ״ו עַמּוּד ב׳)
as they expounded: upon them "he shall surely live" (Yechezkel 18:21), for intentional sins are transformed into merits (Yoma 86b);
שֶׁעַל יְדֵיהֶם דַּיְיקָא בָּא לַמַּדְרֵיגָה הַגְּדוֹלָה דְּמָקוֹם שֶׁבַּעֲלֵי תְּשׁוּבָה עוֹמְדִין:

where precisely through them he attains the supreme rung of the place where penitents stand.1367Mishlei 24:16; Yoma 86b; Berakhot 34b; Peri Tzadik, Nitzavim 1:1; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbat Shuvah 1:1; Resisei Layla 52:2 — falling, rising, and the higher standing of teshuvah: Mishlei says, “seven times the righteous falls and rises.” Yoma teaches that teshuvah from love can transform intentional sins into merits, and R’ Abbahu states in Berakhot that complete tzaddikim cannot stand in the place occupied by penitents. Rav Tzadok reads these teachings dynamically: the fall is not praised as sin, but after genuine return it becomes the very cause and material of a stronger rise; the bitterness awakens a force of return that had not previously been revealed. Peri Tzadik therefore explains “he falls and rises” as rising through the fall itself, and Resisei Layla connects understanding in Torah with the prior experience of stumbling. Nothing in these sources licenses deliberate descent. The elevation exists only when the person awakens from the bitterness, returns to Hashem, and converts what was distant into a greater love.

items.h: The theme: The anatomical secret of the liver and the gallbladder (k'zayis b'makom marah). The Sage comforted his fleeing disciples by noting that "the k'zayis of liver required for life is at the gallbladder" (Chullin 46a): precisely at the place of bitterness resides the essence of life, for the superiority of light is drawn out of darkness (Koheles 2:13). The liver is filled with blood, housing the animal soul (nefesh ha-bahamis), which the Zohar (Pinchas 224a) identifies with Samael and the Serpent, and from which all illnesses arise (Bava Batra 58b: "at the head of all illness am I, the blood"). Yet the outer shell precedes the fruit: the turbid blood in the liver is the source of anger, murder, and affliction, but when tempered by the bitter gallbladder, it becomes the foundation of vitality for the holy soul.

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמַר לָהֶם לְנַחֲמָם: דִּ״כְזַיִת שֶׁאָמְרוּ — בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה״ (חֻלִּין מ״ו עַמּוּד א׳)
And this is what he told his disciples to comfort them: "The olive's bulk of liver that they required for life is at the gallbladder" (Chullin 46a);
שֶׁמְּקוֹם הַמְּרִירוּת, שָׁם עִיקַּר הַחַיּוּת, כִּי יִתְרוֹן הָאוֹר דַּיְיקָא מִן הַחֹשֶׁךְ (קֹהֶלֶת ב:יג)

for at the locus of bitterness resides the vital core of life, since the superiority of light shines specifically out of darkness (Koheles 2:13).1368Chullin 46a; Rashi ad loc.; Rambam, Hilchos Shechitah 8:21; Shulchan Aruch, Yoreh De’ah 41:1; Petach Einayim ad loc.; Mei HaShiloach, Vezos HaBerachah §16 — the olive-bulk at the gallbladder: Chullin discusses an animal whose liver was removed: an olive-bulk must remain for it to be kosher. R’ Zeira told the fleeing Rabbah and Rav Yosef that this olive-bulk must be “in the place of the gallbladder”; Rav Adda bar Ahavah required it at the place where the liver “lives,” meaning its principal attachment, and Rav Pappa therefore required both locations. Rashi explains R’ Zeira’s words first as a concise transmission of this practical halachah, and the ruling is codified by the Rambam and Shulchan Aruch. Later darshanim heard an added word of consolation in the unusual setting of the teaching. Petach Einayim reads the place of bitterness as precisely the place where preserving life is revealed, while Mei HaShiloach reads it as divine help arising where human strength has failed. Rav Tzadok develops that homiletical layer. The symbolism does not replace the Gemara’s literal treifah ruling; it draws meaning from the fact that the indispensable remnant is located beside the gall.1369Koheles 2:13; Machshavot Charutz 7:2; Resisei Layla 17:1; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7:6 — “the advantage of light from darkness”: Koheles compares the superiority of wisdom over folly to the superiority of light over darkness. Rav Tzadok repeatedly deepens the wording “from the darkness”: created existence is ordered so that concealment and distance can awaken a stronger longing, and darkness that is genuinely transformed becomes the material of a greater light. Machshavot Charutz connects intermittent distance with renewed desire; Resisei Layla teaches that the intensity of the hidden light corresponds to the depth of the concealment through which one seeks Hashem; and Peri Tzadik applies the same principle to teshuvah, where the obstructing darkness can itself be converted into merit. This does not mean that darkness, suffering, or sin is intrinsically desirable. The “advantage” appears only when the person refuses to remain in the darkness and turns it into recognition, longing, and avodah. Rav Tzadok’s comfort is therefore not denial of bitterness, but the claim that its very location can become the point from which enduring vitality is uncovered.
וּמִשְׁכַּן הַנֶּפֶשׁ דִּקְדֻשָּׁה הוּא בַּכָּבֵד, שֶׁשָּׁם עִיקַּר מִשְׁכַּן נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית
And the dwelling of the holy Nefesh is in the liver, which is likewise the primary dwelling of the animal soul;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּוהַר הַקָּדוֹשׁ [פָּרָשַׁת פִּינְחָס רכ״ד סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]: ״כָּבֵד — סַמֶּ״ךְ־מֵ״ם וְנָחָשׁ וְכוּלֵיהּ״
as they stated in the Holy Zohar [Pinchas 224a]: "the liver is Samael and the Serpent, etc.";
וְעַיֵּין שָׁם בְּאֹרֶךְ, וְסִיֵּים [שָׁם רכ״ה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״מִן כָּבֵד נָפְקִין כָּל מַרְעִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״

and see there at length, concluding [225a]: "from the liver issue all illnesses, etc.";1370Zohar, Pinchas 224a–225a; Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:99–103 — holiness within the seat of animal vitality: The Zohar portrays a hierarchy in which the liver and its lobe receive the coarse portion first, the heart is the holy and purified center from which health and joy spread, and the brain receives the inward will and unification. Rav Tzadok’s statement that the holy nefesh has its dwelling in the liver must be read within this process. The liver is the bodily seat of the animal life-force and therefore the first arena in which the nefesh’s holiness must enter, govern, and refine material vitality. He is not identifying the unrectified impulses of the liver with holiness. Rather, holiness is revealed by subordinating the lower life-force and directing it upward toward heart and mind. Peri Tzadik likewise relates the liver’s anger and the gall’s bitterness to the work of governing the yetzer. The apparent contradiction — a holy nefesh dwelling where the Zohar places Samael and the serpent — is the point of the se’if: the same locus that can host coarse vitality is also where the work of clarification begins.1371Zohar, Pinchas 224 (Sulam translation): “The liver is Samael, and the serpent — this within that — and they are one, for they are the lobe of the liver [yoseres ha-kaved] and the liver. Therefore, in the offering, the lobe of the liver is the serpent; the liver is the food of the male, which is the secret of Samael. R’ Shimon said: Certainly it is so, and it is fitting; and the elucidation of the matter, and the secret and hidden things of the offering, are thus: the liver takes first — it and its lobe, which are Samael (and the serpent), his mate. And all those veins in the liver are their hosts and camps, and their portion is that they consume the fats and the suet of the offering, as it is written: ‘and the fat that is upon them.’ And then all is offered up to the heart. And the heart takes from the whole offering only the ‘adornment’ it makes in it — that which ascends in that smoke, and the prayer made over the offering. (And afterward) the heart offers up to the brain the will of the unification of the priests within it, and the joy of the Levites. This brain is the light that comes from the supernal brain, and the supernal brain offers up to the One hidden from all, who is not known at all; and all is bound one to another, and the brain offers up satisfaction to all. The ‘veins of the liver’ — these are the ishim (that is, angels of the Other Side), and all these are their hosts. The liver, as we said, is Samael; the lobe, which is female, is his female counterpart. And why is it called yoseres [remnant]? Because she unites with the male only when time remains for her after the harlotry she has performed. And further, the female yoseres, when she wishes to unite (to cause sin) with a man, first makes herself to him as something trivial, of no importance at all, and afterward draws near to him little by little until she becomes one union with him. And from these veins of the liver spread other forces of many kinds, and all take the ‘portions’ and the ‘redeemed,’ and all are included in the liver. The heart, which is the essence in holiness, takes and offers up to the brain as we have learned — and further (daf 225): from the liver issue all the diseases and all the plagues to all the limbs of the body, and in it they dwell. The heart is the purest of all [the limbs], and from it issues all good and all the health of all the limbs, and all the strength and all the joy and all the perfection needed for all the limbs.”
וְהוּא מַה שֶּׁאָמְרוּ [בְּבָבָא בַּתְרָא נ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״בְּרֵישׁ כָּל מַרְעִין אֲנָא דָּם״
and this is what they stated [in Bava Batra 58b]: "At the head of all diseases am I, the blood";
וְרָצָה לוֹמַר הַכָּבֵד שֶׁכּוּלּוֹ דָּם, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בְּחֻלִּין ק״ט סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳]
meaning the liver which is entirely blood, as taught [in Chullin 109b];
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאִיתָא [בִּבְכוֹרוֹת נ״ה סוֹף עַמּוּד א׳]: ״זַכְרוּתָא דְּדָמָא — כַּבְדָּא״
and as taught [in Bechoros 55a]: "the masculine origin of blood is the liver";
שֶׁהוּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ דָּם לַנֶּפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית
which is the root of blood for the animal soul;
וְעִיקַּר חַיּוּתוֹ בִּמְקוֹם מָרָה, שֶׁמִּשָּׁם נִמְשָׁךְ כָּל הַמַּרְעִין וְהַחוֹלָאִים כַּנִּזְכָּר לְעֵיל
and its core vitality resides at the gallbladder, whence are drawn all sicknesses and illnesses as mentioned above;
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמַר גַּם כֵּן רַשִׁ״י [בְּסוֹטָה ה׳ עַמּוּד א׳]

as Rashi likewise stated [in Sotah 5a].1372Bava Basra 58b; Chullin 109b; Bechoros 55a; Bava Metzia 107b — blood, liver, and gall in the language of Chazal: Rav Tzadok gathers several dispersed statements. Bava Basra places blood “at the head of all illnesses.” Chullin describes the liver as being entirely blood in the context of kashering it. Bechoros calls the liver the “male” or strong source of blood, and Bava Metzia says that eighty-three illnesses are dependent upon the gall. These passages belong to the physiological and aggadic vocabulary of Chazal, in which blood signifies embodied life, the liver is its dense bodily reservoir, and gall represents a bitter force capable of affecting the whole organism. Rav Tzadok joins them into one spiritual anatomy: animal vitality is concentrated in blood and liver, while the adjacent gall marks the danger that this vitality become embittered and destructive. His synthesis is a work of Torah interpretation and mussar. It should not be treated as a claim that every illness, in modern medical terms, is literally caused by blood or bile.
אֲבָל זֶהוּ מִצַּד הַקְּלִיפָּה הַקּוֹדֶמֶת וְסוֹבֶבֶת וּמַקֶּפֶת לַפְּרִי
But this derives from the perspective of the husk that precedes and surrounds the fruit;
וּ״בְרֵישָׁא חֲשׁוֹכָא וַהֲדַר נְהוֹרָא״ (שַׁבָּת ע״ז עַמּוּד ב׳), שֶׁשָּׁם הוּא גַּם כֵּן שׁוֹרֶשׁ הַחַיּוּת שֶׁל הַנֶּפֶשׁ דִּקְדֻשָּׁה

for "first comes darkness and then light" (Shabbos 77b), where within that same organ dwells the root vitality of the holy soul;1373Resisei Layla 32:1, 48:2, and 52:6; Yisrael Kedoshim 10:26; Divrei Chalomot 25:1; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 3:6 — the shell precedes and surrounds the fruit: Rav Tzadok uses “the shell precedes the fruit” as a recurring law of spiritual development. The shell appears first, surrounds the good, and often resembles it externally; only afterward is the inner fruit separated and disclosed. Thus Resisei Layla and Yisrael Kedoshim connect “first darkness” with the later revelation of wisdom, while Divrei Chalomot explains that a power in the realm of the shell can imitate the form of holiness without possessing its inward root. Peri Tzadik describes Torah she-be’al peh as the labor that separates the grain from the surrounding refuse. “Precedes” therefore means earlier in appearance and closer to the surface, not more essential or more enduring. The shell has no independent life; whatever vitality it possesses is borrowed from the fruit it encloses. Here the coarse blood and bitterness surface first, but they surround a deeper possibility: the vitality of the holy nefesh that can be extracted, disciplined, and brought to light.
וְהַדָּם שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד הוּא עֲכִירַת הַדָּם שֶׁמִּמֶּנּוּ הַכַּעַס וּרְצִיחָה וְכָל מַחֲלָה וְכָל תַּקָּלָה וְכָל קְטָטָה וּמִינֵי פּוּרְעָנוּת הַנִּמְשָׁךְ מִמְּרִירוּת הַמָּרָה שֶׁאֶצְלָהּ:

and the blood within the liver is the turbid element of blood whence arise anger, murder, illness, stumblings, strife, and retribution, drawn from the bitterness of the adjacent gallbladder.1374Berakhot 61b; Bava Metzia 107b; Nedarim 22a; Shabbos 105b; Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:99 — anger, gall, and destructive bitterness: Berakhot says that the liver becomes angry and the gall casts a drop into it and calms it. Bava Metzia associates the gall with many illnesses; Nedarim says that all forms of Gehinnom rule over one who becomes angry; and Shabbos compares surrender to anger with serving idolatry, because the person allows another power to rule him. Peri Tzadik reconciles the images by distinguishing the immediate action from the root: the liver manifests anger, while the bitter force associated with the gall can either restrain it in proper measure or become the root of its destructive excess. Rav Tzadok therefore links turbid blood not only with bodily disorder but with murder, quarrel, and calamity. This is an ethical and spiritual map. Properly measured gevurah protects life and sets boundaries; when bitterness floods the life-force, the same strength becomes rage and violence. The repair is not the elimination of force, but its clarification and disciplined use.

items.h: The theme: The purification of the liver through the pure blood of the heart (revi'is dam she-ba-lev). Hashem created man upright: the bitterness of the gallbladder tempers the liver when it casts only a single droplet to cool its heat; but when the sword of the Angel of Death in the bile overflows, it breeds sin. The letter Mem in Adam (א-ד-ם) denotes Marah (bitterness), the lowest rung where the entry to Torah begins through awe (yir'ah) in the heart. While the liver houses turbid blood, the heart contains the clear, pure quarter-log of blood (dam zach v'tzalul) upon which human life depends (Shabbos 31b; Tosafos Sotah 5a). Speech (peh, ruach memalela) connects the understanding of the heart (Binah) to bodily action (Nefesh), channeling the pure spiritual blood of the heart to refine and sanctify the turbid blood of the liver.

p: וְהָאֱלֹהִים עָשָׂה אֶת הָאָדָם יָשָׁר (קֹהֶלֶת ז:כט)
And God made man upright (Koheles 7:29):
דְּאַדְּרַבָּא, מְרִירוּת הַמָּרָה מַמְתִּיקוֹ כְּשֶׁמִּשְׁתַּמֵּשׁ כַּהֹוגֶן וְכָרָאוּי, שֶׁזּוֹרֶקֶת רַק טִיפָּה וּמְנִיחַתּוֹ
for on the contrary, the bitterness of the gallbladder sweetens the liver when functioning properly, casting merely a single droplet to calm its fury;
מַה שֶּׁאֵין כֵּן כְּשֶׁשּׁוֹטֶפֶת וְעוֹבֶרֶת עַל יְדֵי הִתְגַּבְּרוּת כֹּחוֹת הָרָע שֶׁבַּדָּם הֶעָכוּר שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד וְחַרְבָּא דְּמַלְאַךְ הַמָּוֶת שֶׁבַּמָּרָה

unlike when it overflows through the dominance of the evil forces within the turbid blood of the liver and the sword of the Angel of Death residing within the bile (Avodah Zarah 20b);1375Koheles 7:29; Berakhot 61b; Peri Tzadik, Re’eh 1:1; Peri Tzadik, Shemini 17:1 — uprightness through measured bitterness: Berakhot assigns each organ a function: “the liver becomes angry; the gall casts a drop into it and calms it.” Rav Tzadok reads this not as praise of uncontrolled bitterness, but as a model of properly measured gevurah. The liver’s heat supplies force and initiative; the gall’s single drop restrains that force and restores equilibrium. Peri Tzadik, Re’eh distinguishes the immediate manifestation of anger in the liver from its bitter root in the gall, while Shemini connects “God made man upright” with an inward orientation toward the good. The very power that becomes destructive when it floods can therefore be protective when it remains proportionate and subordinate to the person’s upright purpose. This is why the se’if says that the bitterness “sweetens” him when used fittingly. The teaching is an ethical-spiritual reading of Chazal’s bodily imagery: it does not authorize anger, nor does it turn an aggadic physiology into a modern medical claim. Its point is that disciplined severity can preserve life, while excess severity overwhelms it.
וְכָל הַחֲטָאִים מִתְיַיחֲסִים לַנֶּפֶשׁ כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״נֶפֶשׁ כִּי תֶחֱטָא״ (וַיִּקְרָא ד:ב)
and all sins are attributed to the Nefesh, as it is said: "If a soul (nefesh) shall sin" (Vayikra 4:2);
דְּשָׁם הוּא הִתְגַּבְּרוּת נֶפֶשׁ הַבַּהֲמִית, שֶׁהוּא נַפְשׁוֹת אוּמּוֹת הָעוֹלָם שֶׁאֵין קְרוּיִם ״אָדָם״, הַמַּלְבֶּשֶׁת וּמַקֶּפֶת לְנֶפֶשׁ הָאָדָם דְּיִשְׂרָאֵל

for there is the empowerment of the animal soul—the soul-level of the nations who are not termed "Adam"—which enclothes and encircles the soul of man in an Israelite;1376Vayikra 4:2; Yechezkel 34:31; Yevamos 61a; Sotah 5a; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7:32 — “Adam,” nefesh, and the surrounding animal layer: “A nefesh that sins” locates transgression in the embodied life-force and power of action. Yevamos derives from “Adam atem” a specific halachic distinction concerning tumas ohel; the same sugya immediately cites verses in which non-Jews are called adam in ordinary usage and explains why those verses do not govern that particular law. Its language is therefore a technical derashah, not a denial of anyone’s humanity. Rav Tzadok employs “Adam” symbolically for the integrated Israelite spiritual form represented by aleph-dalet-mem. The “animal nefesh” that he associates with the level of the nations is the universal layer of appetite, self-preservation, and material impulse that surrounds the inner holy nefesh within a Jew. Sefer Kedushat Shabbat similarly locates the nefesh’s struggle in the blood of the liver and the ruach’s struggle in the heart. The surrounding layer is not an independent essence to be hated; it is a garment and instrument that must be governed, refined, and enlisted in avodas Hashem. Sin occurs when that outer force dominates the inward form.
וְזֶהוּ הַמֵּ״ם דְּ״אָדָם״ שֶׁהִיא מַדְרֵיגָה הַתַּחְתּוֹנָה שֶׁבּוֹ עִיקַּר הַמְּרִירוּת
and this is the letter Mem of Adam
representing the lowest rung where the core bitterness resides.
וּמִשָּׁם הַתְחָלַת הַכְּנִיסָה לְדִבְרֵי תּוֹרָה, שֶׁעִקָּרָהּ יִרְאַת שָׁמַיִם
And from there begins the entrance into the words of Torah, whose foundation is the fear of Heaven;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת ל״א עַמּוּד ב׳]: ״אִי יִרְאַת ה׳ אוֹצָרוֹ — אִין״, וְהוּא בַּלֵּב כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּיוֹמָא ע״ב עַמּוּד ב׳] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְלֵב אָיִן״ (מִשְׁלֵי י״ז:ט״ז)

as they stated [in Shabbos 31b]: "If the fear of Hashem is his treasure, yes," which dwells in the heart as stated [in Yoma 72b] on the verse "seeing he has no heart" (Mishlei 17:16);1377Shabbos 31a; Yoma 72b; Devarim 11:18; Resisei Layla 12:1; Divrei Chalomot 23:1 — fear of Heaven as Torah’s inner treasury: Shabbos compares fear of Heaven to the preservative mixed into stored grain: even mastery of the six orders of Torah endures only when “the fear of Hashem is his treasure.” Yoma gives the same warning through “why is there a price in the hand of a fool to acquire wisdom, when there is no heart?” — Torah without an inward fear of Heaven remains external. Rav Tzadok explains in Resisei Layla that although Torah initially appears to belong to the mind, it is called Torah only when it instructs and enters the heart; knowledge that remains “from the lips outward” has not yet become the person’s Torah. Divrei Chalomot similarly describes the giving of Torah as its inscription in Israel’s hearts, with fear of Heaven as the heart’s receptive condition. This does not diminish intellectual learning. Rather, mind and heart are inseparable partners: analysis acquires and clarifies the teaching, while yirah makes it inwardly binding, preserves it from corruption, and directs it toward action.
וְכֵן בַּהַתּוֹרָה עִיקָּרָהּ בַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״וְשַׂמְתֶּם אֶת דְּבָרַי אֵלֶּה עַל לְבַבְכֶם וְעַל נַפְשְׁכֶם״ (דְּבָרִים י״א:י״ח)
and likewise with the Torah its primary seat is in the heart, as it is said: "Therefore shall you lay up these My words in your heart and in your soul" (Devarim 11:18);
שֶׁמִּן הַלֵּב נִמְשָׁךְ אַחַר כָּךְ לַנֶּפֶשׁ שֶׁהוּא כֹּחוֹת הַמַּעֲשֶׂה בְּפֹעַל הַבָּא מֵהַנֶּפֶשׁ, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ עוֹלַם הָעֲשִׂיָּה
for from the heart inspiration flows into the Nefesh, which constitutes the faculties of concrete deed derived from the world of Asiyah;
וְעַל זֶה נֶאֱמַר: ״כִּי קָרוֹב אֵלֶיךָ הַדָּבָר מְאֹד בְּפִיךָ וּבִלְבָבְךָ לַעֲשׂתוֹ״ (שָׁם ל:יד)
and concerning this it is said: "But the word is very near unto you, in your mouth, and in your heart, that you may do it" (ibid. 30:14).
וּפֶה הוּא הַכּוֹלֵל וּמְחַבֵּר שְׁנֵיהֶם, דַּעֲקִימַת שְׂפָתָיו הָוֵי מַעֲשֶׂה
And the mouth encompasses and unites both heart and deed, for moving the lips is legally reckoned an action (Sanhedrin 65b);
וְעִיקָּרוֹ מֵרוּחַ הַחַיִּים שֶׁבַּלֵּב, וְתַרְגּוּם לְ״נֶפֶשׁ חַיָּה״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב:ז) — ״לְרוּחַ מְמַלְּלָא״, שֶׁהוּא הַמְחַבֵּר נֶפֶשׁ וְרוּחַ

and speech originates from the spirit of life in the heart, Onkelos translating "a living soul" (Bereishis 2:7) as "a speaking spirit" (l'ruach memalela), which binds Nefesh and Ruach;1378Devarim 30:14; Bereishis 2:7 with Onkelos; Mishlei 10:32; Sanhedrin 65a; Resisei Layla 12:1 — the mouth joining heart and deed: The verse orders the process as “in your mouth and in your heart, to do it.” Onkelos renders the human “living nefesh” as a “speaking spirit,” identifying articulate speech as the meeting point of bodily nefesh and inward ruach. Sanhedrin’s statement that “the twisting of his lips is an action” is a technical halachic principle in defined contexts; Rav Tzadok borrows its structure to describe speech as the first outward embodiment of the heart’s will. Resisei Layla teaches that Torah must be absorbed in the heart, yet speech itself can help carry holiness inward — “life and death are in the hand of the tongue.” Thus the mouth works in both directions. It gives the heart’s intention a bodily form that begins the movement toward deed, and the disciplined repetition of holy words educates the heart until desire cleaves to what the lips express. “The lips of the righteous know favor” accordingly means not merely knowing which words to say, but joining knowledge, will, speech, and action into one living chain.
וְ״שִׂפְתֵי צַדִּיק יֵדְעוּן רָצוֹן״ (מִשְׁלֵי י:לב)
and "The lips of the righteous know what is acceptable" (Mishlei 10:32);
וְ״יֵדְעוּן״ לְשׁוֹן חִיבּוּר וּדְבֵיקוּת, וְגַם לְשׁוֹן לִימּוּד דַּעַת לְהָרָצוֹן שֶׁבַּלֵּב
and "know" (yede'un) denotes both union and cleaving, as well as imparting knowledge to the will within the heart;
שֶׁעַל יְדֵי הַדִּבּוּר פֶּה הוּא נִכְנָס גַּם כֵּן לַלֵּב, וְאַחַר כָּךְ לַעֲשׂוֹתָן
for through the speech of the mouth Torah enters the heart, and subsequently flows into action.
כִּי רְבִיעִית דָּם שֶׁחַיֵּי הָאָדָם תְּלוּיִין בּוֹ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּשַׁבָּת ל״א סוֹף עַמּוּד ב׳], עַיֵּין שָׁם בְּרַשִׁ״י
For the quarter-log of blood (revi'is dam) upon which human life depends, as stated [in Shabbos 31b], see Rashi there;
הוּא דָּם הַזַּךְ וְהַצָּלוּל שֶׁבַּלֵּב, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [סוֹטָה ה׳ עַמּוּד א׳] דִּבּוּר הַמַּתְחִיל ״אָדָם״
is the pure, clear blood residing within the heart, as Tosafos wrote [in Sotah 5a, s.v. Adam];
וּמִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים לְכָל הַגּוּף, כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: ״מִכָּל [מִשְׁמָר] נְצֹר [לִבֶּךָ כִּי מִמֶּנּוּ תּוֹצְאוֹת חַיִּים]״ (מִשְׁלֵי ד:כג)
and from it issue the springs of life unto the entire body, as it is said: "Keep your heart with all diligence; for out of it are the issues of life" (Mishlei 4:23);
דְּעַל יָדוֹ מִזְדַּכֵּךְ גַּם הַדָּם הֶעָכוּר שֶׁבַּכָּבֵד:

through which the turbid blood of the liver is refined and sanctified as well.1379Shabbos 31b; Sotah 5a and Tosafos ad loc., s.v. “Adam”; Mishlei 4:23; Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Av 6:1; Peri Tzadik, Sefer Kedushat Shabbat 7:32 — the quarter-log of life-bearing blood: Shabbos speaks of the quarter-log of blood placed in the human being at formation, and Sotah calls the person a being who possesses only one essential quarter-log of blood. Rav Tzadok follows Tosafos in identifying this life-bearing measure with the clear blood associated with the heart, in contrast to the coarse blood of the liver. “Guard your heart, for from it are the issues of life” therefore becomes both a verse about inward vigilance and a map of spiritual circulation: what is clarified in the heart can refine the lower life-force and flow outward to the limbs and deeds. Peri Tzadik, Rosh Chodesh Av likewise joins the heart’s “issues of life” with Torah entering the heart, while Sefer Kedushat Shabbat distinguishes the nefesh in the liver from the ruach in the heart. Rav Tzadok is synthesizing aggadah, medieval physiology, and spiritual symbolism. The note should not be read as a quantitative medical account of circulation; its focus is the qualitative difference between vitality ruled by appetite and vitality purified by the heart’s yirah and Torah.

items.h: סִימָן ט״ו: סְעִיפִים ק״ט–קי״א

The theme: The healing of the navel and the esoteric meaning of the letters of Adam (א-ד-ם). At Marah, Israel was promised: "If you will diligently hearken... none of the diseases... for I am Hashem that heals you" (Shemos 15:26), because words of Torah are "health to your navel" (Mishlei 3:8). The navel is the fetal source of nourishment in the womb, where the ancestral root of iniquity enters ("in sin did my mother conceive me", Tehillim 51:7). In the acronym of Adam (א-ד-ם), the Dalet is Dam (blood)—the clear, pure blood of the heart (dam zach) that heals the illnesses of the liver and gallbladder (Zohar, Pinchas 225a). The Aleph is the pure soul (Neshamah), containing the Master of the Universe (Alupho shel Olam). This corresponds to Efer (ashes): just as the physical body was formed from terrestrial dust (afar) from the site of the earthly altar, the soul is drawn from the supernal altar where the archangel Michael offers the souls of the righteous, transforming them into spiritual ashes. Avraham declared "I am dust and ashes" (Bereishis 18:27), referring to body and soul, paralleling the angel Raphael (Efer / healing).

p: וְזֶהוּ שֶׁנִּתְבַּשְּׂרוּ בְּמָרָה: ״אִם שָׁמוֹעַ תִּשְׁמַע [לְקוֹל ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ] וְגוֹמֵר, כָּל הַמַּחֲלָה אֲשֶׁר [שַׂמְתִּי בְמִצְרַיִם לֹא אָשִׂים עָלֶיךָ כִּי] אֲנִי ה׳ רֹפְאֶךָ״ (שְׁמוֹת ט״ו:כ״ו)

And this is what they were promised at Marah: "If you will diligently hearken to the voice of Hashem your God, etc., none of the diseases which I put upon the Egyptians will I put upon you, for I am Hashem that heals you" (Shemos 15:26);
כִּי דִּבְרֵי תוֹרָה ״רִפְאוּת [תְּהִי] לְשָׁרֶּךָ״ (מִשְׁלֵי ג:ח)
for the words of Torah are "health to your navel" (Mishlei 3:8);
הוּא הַטַּבּוּר שֶׁמִּשָּׁם חַיּוּתוֹ בִּתְחִלַּת הַיְצִירָה בְּבֶטֶן אִמּוֹ, דְּטַבּוּרוֹ פָּתוּחַ וְהוּא יֶרֶךְ אִמּוֹ
which is the navel whence life is drawn at the inception of formation within the mother's womb, its navel being open and legally considered the thigh of its mother (Chullin 58a);
וּמִשָּׁם בָּא שׁוֹרֶשׁ הָרָע שֶׁבַּתּוֹלָדָה, דְּ״[הֵן בְּעָווֹן חוֹלָלְתִּי] וּבְחֵטְא יֶחֱמַתְנִי אִמִּי״ (תְּהִלִּים נ״א:ז׳)
and from there enters the hereditary root of evil at conception: "and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Tehillim 51:7);
וְעַל כֵּן, אַף דְּלֹא יָשִׂים הַמַּחֲלָה, הַיְינוּ לְהַנִּיחַ לְהִתְגַּלּוֹת, צָרִיךְ רְפוּאָה לְשׁוֹרֶשׁ הַמְּרִירוּת שֶׁיִּתְמַתֵּק לְגַמְרֵי

and therefore, even if He does not place the active disease—meaning withholding it from manifest outbreak—one nonetheless requires healing for the inner root of bitterness, that it be completely sweetened.
וְזֶהוּ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בַּזֹּוהַר [שָׁם רכ״ה רֵישׁ עַמּוּד א׳]: ״לֵב אִיהוּ זַכִּיךְ מִכּוּלָּא, מִמֶּנּוּ נָפְקִין כָּל טָב וְכָל בְּרִיאוּתָא דְּשַׁיְיפִין וְכוּלֵיהּ״

And this is what they stated in the Zohar [Pinchas 225a]: "The heart is the purest of all, from it issues all good and all health of the limbs, etc.";1380Zohar, Pinchas 224 (Sulam translation): “The liver is Samael, and the serpent — this within that — and they are one, for they are the lobe of the liver [yoseres ha-kaved] and the liver. Therefore, in the offering, the lobe of the liver is the serpent; the liver is the food of the male, which is the secret of Samael. R’ Shimon said: Certainly it is so, and it is fitting; and the elucidation of the matter, and the secret and hidden things of the offering, are thus: the liver takes first — it and its lobe, which are Samael (and the serpent), his mate. And all those veins in the liver are their hosts and camps, and their portion is that they consume the fats and the suet of the offering, as it is written: ‘and the fat that is upon them.’ And then all is offered up to the heart. And the heart takes from the whole offering only the ‘adornment’ it makes in it — that which ascends in that smoke, and the prayer made over the offering. (And afterward) the heart offers up to the brain the will of the unification of the priests within it, and the joy of the Levites. This brain is the light that comes from the supernal brain, and the supernal brain offers up to the One hidden from all, who is not known at all; and all is bound one to another, and the brain offers up satisfaction to all. The ‘veins of the liver’ — these are the ishim (that is, angels of the Other Side), and all these are their hosts. The liver, as we said, is Samael; the lobe, which is female, is his female counterpart. And why is it called yoseres [remnant]? Because she unites with the male only when time remains for her after the harlotry she has performed. And further, the female yoseres, when she wishes to unite (to cause sin) with a man, first makes herself to him as something trivial, of no importance at all, and afterward draws near to him little by little until she becomes one union with him. And from these veins of the liver spread other forces of many kinds, and all take the ‘portions’ and the ‘redeemed,’ and all are included in the liver. The heart, which is the essence in holiness, takes and offers up to the brain as we have learned — and further (daf 225): from the liver issue all the diseases and all the plagues to all the limbs of the body, and in it they dwell. The heart is the purest of all [the limbs], and from it issues all good and all the health of all the limbs, and all the strength and all the joy and all the perfection needed for all the limbs.”
שֶׁדָּם הַזַּךְ שֶׁבּוֹ, וְהוּא הַדָּלֶ״ת דְּ״אָדָם״, הוּא הַמַּבְרִיא וּמְרַפֵּא לְכָל מַרְעִין שֶׁמִּכָּבֵד וּמָרָה
for the pure, refined blood within it—which is the letter Dalet of Adam
(א-ד-ם,
denoting Dam)—strengthens and heals all illnesses originating from the liver and gallbladder.
וְאָלֶ״ף דְּ״אָדָם״ הוּא מַדְרֵיגָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁבּוֹ, וְהוּא נְשָׁמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה שֶׁהִיא חֵלֶק אֱלֹהִי מִמַּעַל, דְּאַלּוּפוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם גָּנוּז בְּגַוַּוהּ

And the letter Aleph of Adam represents the supreme level within him, which is the pure soul (Neshamah), an actual divine portion from Above, within which the Master of the Universe (Alupho shel Olam) is concealed;
וְעָלֶיהָ אָמְרוּ שֶׁהִיא ״אֵפֶר״
and concerning this level they expounded that it is Efer [ashes];
כִּי גּוּף הָאָדָם נִבְרָא ״עָפָר מִן הָאֲדָמָה״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית ב:ז) מִמְּקוֹם הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁלְּמַטָּה
for the physical body of man was formed of "dust from the ground" (Bereishis 2:7), taken from the site of the earthly altar (Bereishis Rabbah 14:8);
וְהַנְּשָׁמָה מִמְּקוֹם מִזְבֵּחַ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה, שֶׁשָּׁם מִיכָאֵל עוֹמֵד וּמַקְרִיב נִשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים, כְּמוֹ שֶׁכָּתְבוּ תּוֹסָפוֹת [סוֹף מְנָחוֹת, ק״י עַמּוּד א׳] מֵהַמִּדְרָשׁ

and the soul is drawn from the site of the supernal altar, where the archangel Michael stands and offers the souls of the righteous, as Tosafos wrote [end of Menachos 110a] from the Midrash;1381Bereishis 2:7 and 18:27; Koheles 12:7; Bereishis Rabbah 14:8; Rambam, Hilchos Beis HaBechirah 2:2; Menachos 110a with Tosafos ad loc.; Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh 5:1 — body and neshamah from the two altars: The Midrashic tradition says that Adam was formed from the place of the earthly altar — “man was created from the place of his atonement” — a teaching codified by the Rambam. Menachos describes a heavenly altar upon which Michael offers an offering, and Tosafos records the tradition that the offering is the souls of the righteous. Rav Tzadok places the two traditions in parallel: the body’s dust comes from the lower place of atonement, while the neshamah is rooted in the upper service. “The dust returns to the earth as it was” is therefore not mere dissolution, but return to the source from which repair is possible. Avraham’s “I am dust and ash” names both sides: afar as material humility and efer as the refined remnant after fire has consumed admixture. Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh similarly connects “God made man upright” and Adam’s creation from the place of atonement. Rav Tzadok’s “intellectual ash” does not imply destruction of the pure soul; it describes the burning away of whatever adhered to it through embodiment, so that it can cleave again to its source.
וְהֵם נַעֲשִׂין אֵפֶר, וְזֶהוּ חֲזָרָתָם לִמְקוֹרָם
and they are rendered into ashes, which constitutes their return to their source;
כְּמוֹ שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר בַּגּוּף ״וְיָשֹׁב אֶל הֶעָפָר כְּשֶׁהָיָה״ (קֹהֶלֶת י״ב:ז׳), וְזֶהוּ תִּיקּוּנוֹ לְכַלּוֹת זוּהֲמָתוֹ
just as it is stated regarding the body: "and the dust return to the earth as it was" (Koheles 12:7), which is its physical rectification to consume its defilement;
כֵּן בַּנְּשָׁמָה, שֶׁהֲגַם שֶׁהִיא טְהוֹרָה, מִצַּד חִיבּוּרָהּ אֶל הַגּוּף בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה
so too with the soul: although it is inherently pure, from the perspective of its attachment to the physical body in this world,
אַף שֶׁהַצַּדִּיקִים זוֹכִין בְּמַעֲשֵׂיהֶם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה לְהַעֲלוֹתָהּ מַעְלָה מַעְלָה, מִכָּל מָקוֹם ״[כִּי אָדָם] אֵין צַדִּיק בָּאָרֶץ אֲשֶׁר [יַעֲשֶׂה טּוֹב וְלֹא יֶחֱטָא]״ (שָׁם ז:כ)
even though the righteous merit through their deeds in this world to elevate it higher and higher, nevertheless "there is not a righteous man upon earth that does good and sins not" (ibid. 7:20);
וּמַה שֶּׁהוּא לְמַטָּה עָפָר, הוּא בְּרוּחָנִיּוּת אֵפֶר
and that which is physical dust below is spiritual ash Above;
דְּעַל זֶה אָמַר אַבְרָהָם אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם: ״וְאָנֹכִי עָפָר וָאֵפֶר״ (בְּרֵאשִׁית י״ח:כ״ז), שֶׁהוּא מִצַּד הַגּוּף וְהַנְּשָׁמָה
concerning which Avraham Avinu, peace be upon him, said: "and I am but dust and ashes" (Bereishis 18:27), referring to the body [dust] and the soul [ashes];
וּכְמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ בְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא [פָּרָשַׁת פִּינְחָס רכ״ה עַמּוּד א׳]: ״רְפָאֵל — דְּאִיהוּ אֵפֶר״
and as they expounded in the Raya Mehemna [Pinchas 225a]: "Raphael—he is Efer [ashes]";
דְּהַיְינוּ אֵפֶר שִׂכְלִית

which means spiritual, intellectual ash.1382Zohar, Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas 225a (Sulam translation): “Behold, in all the offerings — whether of animals, or of the angels appointed over the mitzvos, or of Malchus, or of the Divine Name (Havayah) — all must be brought near to the Holy One through the holy letters. And He rides upon the four Chayos of the angels, and He rides upon the four elements from which the four natural Chayos were created. He is the one who brings near water with fire, and wind [ruach] with dust [afar] — this is what is written: ‘He makes peace in His heights.’ And likewise He brings near Michael, who is intellectual water, with Gavriel, who is intellectual fire; and He brings near Uriel, who is air — that is, intellectual wind — with Refael, who is ash [efer], that is, intellectual dust; for the moment the Holy One departs from among them, they have no strength.”
כִּי אָמְרוּ [בְּקֹהֶלֶת רַבָּה ג:כ] עַל פָּסוּק ״הַכֹּל הָיָה מִן הֶעָפָר״ (קֹהֶלֶת ג:כ): אֲפִילּוּ גַּלְגַּל חַמָּה
For they expounded [in Koheles Rabbah 3:20] on the verse "all are of the dust" (Koheles 3:20): even the orb of the sun;
שֶׁהוּא מַדְרֵיגָה הַיּוֹתֵר עֶלְיוֹנָה בַּעֲשִׂיָּה הַגּוּפָנִיּוֹת שֶׁנִּבְנָה כוּלָּן מִיְסוֹד הֶעָפָר, אֲפִילּוּ זֶה הַמָּאוֹר הַגָּדוֹל
which is the highest physical sphere in the world of Asiyah, all formed from the element of earth/dust, even this great luminary;
וְהוּא כּוּלּוֹ אֵשׁ, כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בִּנְדָרִים ח׳ עַמּוּד ב׳] עַל פָּסוּק ״וְלִהַט אֹתָם הַיּוֹם הַבָּא״ (מַלְאָכִי ג:יט): שֶׁיּוֹצִיא חַמָּה מִנַּרְתִּיקָהּ

yet it is entirely fire, as they stated [in Nedarim 8b] on the verse "and the day that comes shall burn them up" (Malachi 3:19): that Hashem will draw forth the sun from its sheath;1383R’ Tzadok — parallel (Peri Tzadik, Shemini §17): “As it says, ‘God made man upright’ — to be ‘inward-facing’ [turned wholly toward the good].” Exactly the se’if’s verse: “God made man upright” — for the gall’s very bitterness “sweetens him” when rightly used.1384Cf. Nedarim 8b (with Avodah Zarah 3b) — on Malachi 3:19, “ki hinneh ha-yom ba bo’er ka-tanur” (“behold, the day comes, burning like an oven”) and “ve-lihat osam ha-yom ha-ba” (“and the coming day shall set them ablaze”): in the Time to Come the Holy One “takes the sun out of its sheath” [motzi chammah mi-nartikah]; the wicked are punished by it, while the righteous are healed by it — “u-marpei bichnafeha” (Malachi 3:20). This is the eschatological “sun of healing” that underlies R’ Tzadok’s reading of the gall’s bitterness turned to healing, developed through the closing se’ifim.1385Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayassa 1; Mishlei 3:18 and 4:20–22; Kli Yakar to Shemos 15:26; Divrei Chalomot §22; Takanas HaShavin 15:101–104 — Marah and the bitter remedy: The Mekhilta records opinions that the tree cast into Marah was itself bitter and states that, unlike a human physician who normally heals bitter with sweet, the Holy One heals bitter with bitter. The same passage reads “vayorehu” as teaching: the tree signifies Torah, the “tree of life,” whose words are life and healing. Kli Yakar joins the two readings: Torah and mitzvos may initially appear demanding or bitter, yet their end is sweet because they heal both the bodily and spiritual forms of Egypt’s disease. Rav Tzadok’s sequence develops this as an inner process. Separation from Torah exposes bitterness; renewed Torah does not merely cover it but teaches how the very power of severity can be measured, redirected, and made medicinal. The “good tidings” at Marah are therefore more than relief from unpleasant water. They disclose a pattern of teshuvah in which the point that had become bitter can itself become the instrument of sweetening when returned to Hashem’s instruction.1386Mekhilta DeRabbi Yishmael, Tractate Vayassa 1; Sanhedrin 101a; Rashi and Kli Yakar to Shemos 15:26; Takanas HaShavin 15:104–105 — prevention, healing, and the future cure: Sanhedrin asks why the verse calls Hashem a healer after promising not to place the disease. Rabbi Yochanan answers from the verse itself: if Israel listens, the disease is not placed; if they do not, it may be placed, yet “I am Hashem your Healer” remains in force. The Mekhilta likewise presents both dimensions: Torah is present healing and life, while Rabbi Yitzchak reads the final healing as reaching its completion in the World to Come. Kli Yakar adds the physician’s preventive role — instruction that guards health before illness develops. Rav Tzadok draws all three together. Torah restrains the root of spiritual illness, teshuvah heals what has already emerged, and the future revelation removes the residue that even the righteous cannot fully escape in this world. This is covenantal and spiritual exposition, not a promise that observant people will never experience physical illness or a substitute for ordinary medical care.
וְהָאֵשׁ שׂוֹרֵף הֶעָפָר וְנַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר, וְגַם הוּא נִקְרָא ״עָפָר״ כְּמוֹ שֶׁאָמְרוּ [בְּפֶרֶק כִּסּוּי הַדָּם, חֻלִּין פ״ח עַמּוּד ב׳]:

and the fire burns the earth into ashes, and ashes are halachically termed "dust," as stated [in Chullin 88b].1387Malachi 3:19–20; Nedarim 8b; Avodah Zarah 3b; Peri Tzadik, Tzav 4:1 — one revealed sun that heals and judges: Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish teaches that in the future the Holy One will remove the sun from its sheath: the righteous are healed and rejuvenated by it, while the wicked are judged by the same sun. Peri Tzadik identifies this uncovered radiance with the revealed light of Torah and of the Divine presence. The difference is not that two contrary powers are released, but that one unshielded truth meets two differently prepared recipients. A life ordered toward yirah can receive the light as “healing in its wings”; a will fixed against that truth experiences the same disclosure as consuming heat. Rav Tzadok therefore moves naturally from Marah’s healing to the sun’s fire. The fire does not invent the distinction; it reveals and completes what each vessel has made of itself. The teaching is aggadic and eschatological, not an astronomical description of the physical sun.1388Bereishis 18:27; Koheles 3:20 and 12:7; Zohar, Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas 225a; Peri Tzadik, Tetzaveh 5:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:103–105 — dust refined into ash: Rav Tzadok uses afar and efer as two stages of one return. Dust represents the material substrate from which the body is formed and to which it returns; ash is what remains after fire has consumed what could not endure the refining heat. In the preceding se’if he paired the body’s dust with the lower altar and the neshamah’s “intellectual ash” with the upper altar. Here the sun’s fire carries that symbolism forward: the purpose is not the annihilation of the pure neshamah, but the removal of admixture absorbed through embodiment. Peri Tzadik likewise connects Adam’s creation from the place of atonement with the possibility of repair, and the Ra’aya Mehemna names Refael as intellectual efer within the ordered union of the elements. Thus “dust becoming ash” is Rav Tzadok’s spiritual grammar of purification. The next se’if will describe how that refined remainder becomes the source of healing and renewed creation.1389R’ Tzadok — parallel (Divrei Chalomos §22): “And the Holy One sweetens the bitter with the bitter — when He shows that there is [a purpose] in the doing [of the bitter thing itself].” Exactly the se’if: the good tidings at Marah — “if you hearken [to the voice of Hashem your God], I will not place upon you [any of the diseases],” the bitter sweetened by the bitter.1390Chullin 88b; Bamidbar 19:17; Bereishis 18:27 — why ash is called “dust” in perek Kisui HaDam: The halachic source is the discussion of substances fit for covering the blood. Beis Hillel permits ashes because Scripture says “from the dust of the burning” of the red heifer, showing that efer can be described as afar; Beis Shammai replies that the phrase may mean only “dust of burning,” not ordinary dust. The sugya also allows one traveling by ship to burn a garment and use its ashes, and later connects Avraham’s “I am dust and ash” with the ashes of the red heifer and the dust of the sotah. This is a precise legal and linguistic classification within kisui hadam, not a claim that dust and ash are physically identical in every respect. Rav Tzadok builds on that controlled overlap: what has passed through fire has changed, yet it can still be named by the category of its earthly source. That continuity allows purification to be understood as transformation and return rather than total severance.

items.h: The theme: Spiritual ash, the angel Raphael, and the purification of the righteous before the Resurrection. The supreme level of dust is found in the solar sphere and the ashes of the altar (efer ve-deshen ha-mizbe'ach). In the soul, this corresponds to the "lamp of Hashem, the soul of man" (ner Hashem nishmas adam). This holy ash is the channel of divine forgiveness and healing when the intellect overcomes bodily lust and repents (u'levavo yavin v'shav). The four angels supporting the Throne correspond to the Patriarchs and David HaMelech, with Raphael (healing) corresponding to David, who raised the yoke of repentance. Even the greatest righteous men who died solely from the instigation of the Serpent (ityo shel nachash) require physical decomposition—turning into a ladleful of dust (tarvad raqav) one hour prior to the Resurrection—to purge the bodily trace of the Serpent. Simultaneously, their souls are offered upon the supernal altar as a sweet savour; what cannot fuse directly into the consuming fire becomes spiritual ash, which then reunites with the purified dust of the body to rise as a holy, pristine creation.

p: וְהוּא מַדְרֵיגָה הָעֶלְיוֹנָה שֶׁבֶּעָפָר שֶׁבְּגַלְגַּל חַמָּה, וְכֵן אֵפֶר וְדֶשֶׁן הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
And it is the supreme dimension of dust within the orb of the sun, and likewise the ash and fat-cinders of the altar (deshen ha-mizbe'ach);
וּבְרוּחָנִי וְשִׂכְלִי, שֶׁהוּא כֹּחַ הַנְּשָׁמָה, הוּא מַדְרֵיגָה הָאַחֲרוֹנָה דְּ״נֵר ה׳ נִשְׁמַת אָדָם״ (מִשְׁלֵי כ:כז)

and in the spiritual and intellectual plane, which is the power of the Neshamah, it is the ultimate dimension of "the spirit of man is the lamp of Hashem" (Mishlei 20:27);1391Vayikra 6:3–4; Mishnah Tamid 1:4; Menachos 110a; Peri Tzadik, Tzav 4:1; Takanas HaShavin 15:103–105 — the ash and deshen of the altar: The Torah does not treat the completely consumed remnants of the korban as ordinary refuse. Terumas ha-deshen is itself an avodah: a kohen removes the inner, fully consumed coals and places them beside the altar, and the accumulated deshen is afterward taken to a “pure place.” The physical remainder has passed through the altar’s fire and remains ordered by kedushah. This supplies the concrete background for Rav Tzadok’s symbolism. Efer is what remains after refining fire; deshen is that remainder as gathered into the service of the altar. Thus the “highest level of dust” is not a statement of modern material science but a kabbalistic hierarchy: earthly material reaches its perfected form when the combustible admixture is consumed and the enduring residue is incorporated into avodah. The following discussion transfers that pattern from altar, body, and dust to the purification of the neshamah.
שֶׁהִיא כּוּלָּהּ אוֹר הַמֵּאִיר, דְּ״אֹהֲבָיו כְּצֵאת הַשֶּׁמֶשׁ בִּגְבֻרָתוֹ״ (שׁוֹפְטִים ה:לא)
which is entirely illuminating light, for "they that love Him are as the sun when it goes forth in its might" (Shoftim 5:31);
וְהִיא עָפָר שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר, מִמֶּנּוּ נִמְשָׁךְ הָרְפוּאָה דִּסְלִיחָה לַגּוּף הַחוֹטֵא
and it is dust that has become ash, whence is drawn the healing of forgiveness unto the sinning body,
כְּשֶׁיָּבִין וְיַשְׂכִּיל בְּרוּחוֹ וְשִׂכְלוֹ לְהַגְבִּיר כֹּחַ הַשֵּׂכֶל וְהַנְּשָׁמָה הַטְּהוֹרָה, וְ״לְבָבוֹ יָבִין וְשָׁב״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ו:י)

when one understands and contemplates in his spirit and intellect to elevate the pure Neshamah, and "his heart shall understand, and he shall return" (Yeshayah 6:10).1392Yeshayahu 6:10; Megillah 17b; Rosh Hashanah 17b; Sha’arei Teshuvah 2:10; Takanas HaShavin 6:9 and 15:105 — understanding, repentance, and the healing of forgiveness: Chazal derive the order of the Amidah from “his heart understands, and he repents”: binah precedes teshuvah, while forgiveness and healing follow the return. Rosh Hashanah cites the same verse for the power of teshuvah to tear a person’s decree, and Rabbeinu Yonah stresses that sincere understanding becomes effective when it produces a settled acceptance to obey Torah. Rav Tzadok therefore does not describe repentance as intellectual analysis alone. The intellect and pure neshamah must become strong enough to enter the heart, reverse the will, and redirect the body that acted. “Healing of forgiveness” names that repaired relation between inner knowledge and embodied conduct. It is spiritual and moral healing; it should not be read as a guarantee of physical cure or as a replacement for medical treatment.
וְכִידוּעַ דְּד׳ מַלְאָכִים [שֶׁבְּרַעְיָא מְהֵימְנָא שָׁם] הַנּוֹשְׂאִים הַכִּסֵּא, הֵן הֵם נֶגֶד ג׳ אָבוֹת וְדָוִד הַמֶּלֶךְ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם רַגְלֵי הַמֶּרְכָּבָה

And as is known, the four angels [in Raya Mehemna ibid.] bearing the Throne correspond to the Three Patriarchs and David HaMelech, peace be upon him, who are the legs of the holy Chariot;1393Zohar, Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas 225a (Sulam translation): “Behold, in all the offerings — whether of animals, or of the angels appointed over the mitzvos, or of Malchus, or of the Divine Name (Havayah) — all must be brought near to the Holy One through the holy letters. And He rides upon the four Chayos of the angels, and He rides upon the four elements from which the four natural Chayos were created. He is the one who brings near water with fire, and wind [ruach] with dust [afar] — this is what is written: ‘He makes peace in His heights.’ And likewise He brings near Michael, who is intellectual water, with Gavriel, who is intellectual fire; and He brings near Uriel, who is air — that is, intellectual wind — with Refael, who is ash [efer], that is, intellectual dust; for the moment the Holy One departs from among them, they have no strength.”
וּרְפָאֵל נֶגֶד דָּוִד שֶׁהֵקִים עוּלָּהּ שֶׁל תְּשׁוּבָה, וְשָׁב וְרָפָא לוֹ

and Raphael corresponds to David who raised up the yoke of repentance (Moed Katan 16b), returning and being healed;1394Zohar, Ra’aya Mehemna, Pinchas 225a; Avodah Zarah 4b; Takanas HaShavin 6:9 and 11:4; Peri Tzadik, Vayeilech and Shabbos Shuvah 21:4 — Refael, David, and the path of individual teshuvah: The Ra’aya Mehemna identifies Refael with intellectual efer/afar within the fourfold order surrounding the Throne. The Gemara separately teaches that David’s episode was arranged “to teach repentance to the individual”: one who has fallen must not conclude that return is closed. Rav Tzadok joins these traditions. David, the fourth leg of the Chariot in his framework, “raised the yoke of teshuvah,” and Refael signifies the healing that follows “his heart understands, and he repents.” The correspondence is Rav Tzadok’s synthesis; the Gemara itself does not explicitly say that Refael represents David. Nor does David’s role make sin desirable. It establishes that confession, brokenhearted return, and transformation can reveal a path that a person who never fell could not demonstrate in the same way.
וְאַף צַדִּיקִים גְּמוּרִים צְרִיכִים רְפוּאָה מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ
and even consummate tzaddikim require healing from the instigation of the Serpent,
שֶׁמִּזֶּה לֹא נִמְלְטוּ גַּם צַדִּיקִים הַיּוֹתֵר גְּדוֹלִים שֶׁמֵּתוּ בְּעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ

from which even the greatest righteous men who died solely from the Serpent's instigation were not spared (Shabbos 55b);1395Shabbos 55b; Bava Basra 17a; Rashi ad loc.; Ramban to Bamidbar 19:2; Yeshayahu 25:8 and 30:26 — death through the counsel of the serpent: Chazal list four exceptionally righteous people — Binyamin, Amram, Yishai, and Kilav — who died only “through the counsel of the serpent.” Rashi explains that they were not deserving of death through a personal sin; they remained subject to the decree of mortality introduced through the serpent’s counsel to Chavah. Rav Tzadok uses this teaching to distinguish two kinds of repair. Personal wrongdoing can be healed through teshuvah in this world, but the primordial admixture bound up with embodied mortality is not wholly removed even from the greatest righteous. Its final healing belongs to the future disclosure in which “death is swallowed up forever” and the world’s wound is healed. This is an aggadic account of universal mortality, not an accusation that the righteous secretly committed the sins being discussed.
דִּלְזֶה אֵין רְפוּאָה עַל יְדֵי תְּשׁוּבָה בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה, עַד לֶעָתִיד דִּ״מַחַץ מַכָּתוֹ [יִרְפָּא]״ (יְשַׁעְיָה ל:כו) שֶׁל עוֹלָם וּ״בֻלַּע הַמָּוֶת לָנֶצַח״ (שָׁם כ״ה:ח׳)

for regarding this there is no healing through repentance in this world, until the Future when "the stroke of their wound He shall heal" (Yeshayah 30:26) and "He will swallow up death forever" (ibid. 25:8).
וְעַל כֵּן אֲפִילּוּ צַדִּיקִים צְרִיכִים לַחֲזוֹר לְעַפְרָם שָׁעָה אַחַת קוֹדֶם תְּחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים
And therefore even the wholly righteous must return to their dust one hour prior to the Resurrection of the Dead (Shabbos 152b),
וְנַעֲשִׂים תַּרְוַוד רָקָב, דְּהַגּוּף מִן הַנִּקְבָּרִים, וּמִ״קֶּבֶר״ נַעֲשָׂה ״רֶקֶב״

becoming a ladleful of dust, the body being among those buried, and from "grave" (kever) becoming "decay" (reqev, having identical letters);1396Shabbos 152b; Mishnah Oholos 2:1; Nazir 49b–51a; Pirkei DeRabbi Eliezer 34:10; Yerushalmi Nazir 7:2 — one hour before resurrection and a spoonful of decay: Shabbos records Rav Achai bar Yoshiyah’s statement that the righteous fulfill “you are dust and to dust you shall return” one hour before the resurrection. The same passage contrasts bodily preservation with the final return required before renewed creation. “A spoonful of decay” — melo tarvad rakav — is also a precise halachic measure in the laws of tumas meis; the Bavli and Mishnah discuss exact conditions under which decomposed human remains attain that status, and the Yerushalmi connects the measure with the dust from which Adam was formed. Rav Tzadok uses the term symbolically for the body’s complete reduction to its elemental remainder. His kever/rakav wordplay is a derash, not a claim of historical etymology, and it should not erase the phrase’s technical halachic meaning.
וְהַנְּשָׁמָה מִן הַנִּשְׂרָפִין, דְּגַם נִשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶן שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים הַקְּרֵבִין עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ
while the soul is among those burned, for the souls of the righteous offered upon the supernal altar,
הַיְינוּ שֶׁהֵם לְאִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ לַה׳ כִּי נִדְבָּקִים בִּמְקוֹרָן, דְּהֵם חֵלֶק אֱלֹהִי וְ״ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ אֵשׁ אֹכְלָה [הוּא]״ (דְּבָרִים ד:כד)
become a fire-offering of sweet savour unto Hashem as they cleave to their Source, being a divine portion, and "the Lord your God is a consuming fire" (Devarim 4:24);
וּמַה שֶּׁאִי אֶפְשָׁר לִידָּבֵק מִצַּד הָעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ שֶׁנִּקְלַט גַּם בָּהּ בִּהְיוֹתָהּ בַּגּוּף, הוּא נַעֲשָׂה אֵפֶר
and that subtle dimension which cannot cleave directly on account of the Serpent's instigation absorbed within it while dwelling in the body, is rendered into spiritual ash;
וּמִזֶּה בָּא הָרְפוּאָה אַחַר כָּךְ, שֶׁהוּא חוֹזֵר לִהְיוֹת נִכְנָס לְהָרָקָב שֶׁל הַגּוּף
and from this issues the ultimate healing afterward, when this ash enters back into the purified dust of the physical body,
וְקָם בִּתְחִיַּיִת הַמֵּתִים בְּרִיאָה חֲדָשָׁה קְדוֹשָׁה וּטְהוֹרָה, שֶׁאֵין בָּהּ עוֹד שׁוּם זוּהֲמָא מֵעֶטְיוֹ שֶׁל נָחָשׁ, שֶׁנִּכְלָה עַל יְדֵי שֶׁנַּעֲשָׂה עָפָר וָאֵפֶר:

rising at the Resurrection of the Dead as a brand new creation, holy and pure, bearing no longer any defilement from the Serpent's instigation, which was eradicated through being rendered dust and ashes.1397Menachos 110a and Tosafos ad loc.; Shabbos 152b; Koheles 12:7; Devarim 4:24; Iyov 31:2; Takanas HaShavin 15:103–105 — the heavenly offering and renewed creation: Menachos speaks of the heavenly altar on which Michael offers a korban; Tosafos records traditions that the offering is the souls of the righteous or fiery lambs. Rav Tzadok adopts the first tradition as a language of deveikus: the neshamah returns to the God Who gave it, a “portion of God above,” and cleaves to its source, described as consuming fire. This is not physical combustion or annihilation of the soul. The “burning” means that whatever cannot participate in that cleaving — the residue absorbed through the serpent’s counsel while the soul was joined to the body — is separated as ash. Shabbos’s final return to dust before resurrection then supplies the other half of the image: refined soul and bodily decay are reunited in a renewed creation. Rav Tzadok’s conclusion is eschatological and kabbalistic — the removal of alien admixture, not the destruction of personal identity.

items.h: The theme: The rectification of the souls of the wicked through the ashes under the feet of the righteous. The burning of the souls of the wicked in the fire of Gehinnom purges the sins in which they were immersed. The remaining ash—the indestructible holy root—is reconstituted and kneaded with the body's dust to rise to eternal life exclusively through the agency of the righteous. Each sinner is assigned to a specific tzaddik from his soul-root beneath whose feet his ashes are scattered ("and you shall tread down the wicked; for they shall be ashes under the soles of your feet", Malachi 3:21). Just as touching the bones of Elisha revived the dead man (II Melachim 13:21), direct contact with the tzaddik infuses life. In this world, the rule is "whatever touches the altar becomes holy" (Shemos 29:37) for disqualified offerings whose invalidity occurred in the Sanctuary (p'sulam ba-kodesh). In the Future, the seed of Yaakov who became disqualified through their deeds are touched by the righteous—the Priests standing upon the supernal altar—becoming consecrated as the food of the altar never to descend again, their ashes joining the sweet savor of the righteous, for "that which is joined to the pure is pure."

p: וְנִשְׁמָתָן שֶׁל רְשָׁעִים הַנִּשְׂרֶפֶת בְּאֵשׁ שֶׁל גֵּיהִנָּם לְכַלּוֹת עָוֹן וּלְהָתֵם פֶּשַׁע שֶׁהָיְתָה מְשׁוּקַּעַת בָּהֶם
And regarding the soul of the wicked which is burned in the fire of Gehinnom to consume iniquity and bring to an end the transgression in which it was immersed;
שָׁרְשָׁם שֶׁבִּקְדֻשָּׁה שֶׁהוּא הָאֵפֶר הַנִּשְׁאָר, תִּיקּוּנוֹ שֶׁיּוּכַל לַחֲזוֹר לִקְדוּשָׁה לְגַמְרֵי וּלְהִתְגַּבֵּל עִם רְקַב הַגּוּף לָשׁוּב לִחְיוֹת חַיֵּי עוֹלָם בִּקְדֻשָּׁה

its holy root, which is the surviving ash, finds its rectification to return fully to holiness and be kneaded with the dust of the body to live eternal life in sanctity,1398Daniel 9:24; Malachi 3:19; Resisei Layla §5; Takanas HaShavin 15:105–106 — “to consume iniquity and finish transgression”: In Daniel, the phrase belongs to the prophecy of the seventy weeks concerning Israel and the holy city: transgression is brought to its limit, sin ended, iniquity atoned, and everlasting righteousness introduced. Rav Tzadok transfers this collective eschatological language to the soul’s purification. Gehinnom’s “fire” is not presented here as purposeless retaliation but as the consuming of the sinful admixture in which the soul became embedded, until only the enduring “ash,” its root capable of return, remains. This is Rav Tzadok’s kabbalistic application of the verse; it is not the verse’s plain historical context and should not be read as a physical description of postmortem fire.1399Sanhedrin 44a; Peri Tzadik, Pesach 8:1; Resisei Layla 44:1 — the holy root that survives sin: On “Israel has sinned,” Chazal say: “Although he sinned, he is Israel”; the myrtle among thorns remains a myrtle. Rav Tzadok repeatedly develops this as an inward root that wrongdoing can conceal and deform but cannot wholly erase. Peri Tzadik applies it even to the wicked son: after Israel’s election, wickedness does not remove him from the people, though his deeds still require complete repair. Thus the “ash that remains” is not moral innocence or automatic acquittal. It is the indestructible point from which teshuvah and future restoration remain possible.
הוּא רַק עַל יְדֵי הַצַּדִּיקִים, כָּל אֶחָד עַל יְדֵי אֵיזֶה צַדִּיק שֶׁמִּשָּׁרְשׁוֹ, שֶׁהוּא אֵפֶר תַּחַת כַּפּוֹת רַגְלָיו

solely through the righteous, each sinner through that specific tzaddik from his soul-root beneath the soles of whose feet he rests as ash;1400Malachi 3:19–21; Nedarim 8b; Takanas HaShavin 15:104–106 — ash beneath the feet and the same future revelation: Malachi places three images together: the coming day burns evildoing like an oven, the sun of righteousness heals those who fear God, and the wicked become ash beneath their feet. Chazal similarly describe the uncovered sun as healing the righteous and judging the wicked. Rav Tzadok reads the sequence dynamically: the evil form is consumed, yet the remaining holy root can be gathered through the righteous and restored to life. The claim that the ash itself is ultimately repaired is Rav Tzadok’s eschatological synthesis, not simply the peshat of Malachi’s image of defeat.
וְעַל יְדֵי שֶׁנּוֹגֵעַ בְּהַצַּדִּיק נִמְשָׁךְ בּוֹ חַיּוּת, כְּעִנְיַן הָאִישׁ שֶׁנָּגַע בְּעַצְמוֹת אֱלִישָׁע וַיְחִי (מְלָכִים ב י״ג:כ״א)

and through touching the tzaddik life is drawn into him, akin to the man who touched the bones of Elisha and revived (II Melachim 13:21).1401II Melachim 13:20–21; Sanhedrin 47a — the man who touched Elisha’s bones: The biblical narrative records that a corpse cast into Elisha’s grave touched his bones, revived, and stood. Sanhedrin cites the incident to show that a wicked person is not buried beside a righteous one; the baraita states that the man stood but did not return home, so the revival was momentary. Rav Tzadok therefore uses an exceptional miracle as a spiritual paradigm: contact with a tzaddik of one’s root can draw life into what had become deathlike. The source does not establish a general halachic rule or a claim that ordinary physical contact with remains transmits vitality.
כִּי בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה שֶׁהָרָע גּוֹבֵר, הַטּוּמְאָה שֶׁהוּא חֵלֶק אָדָם רָע וְסִטְרָא אָחֳרָא הִיא מְטַמֵּא אֲחֵרִים בְּמַגָּע
For in this world where evil prevails, impurity—which is the element of the wicked man and the Other Side—defiles others through physical contact;
אֲבָל הַקְּדוּשָׁה אֵינוֹ מְקַדֵּשׁ בִּנְגִיעָה בְּעָלְמָא

whereas holiness does not consecrate through mere casual touch;1402Chaggai 2:11–14 — impurity spreads by contact more readily than holiness: Chaggai asks the priests whether sacrificial flesh carried in a garment sanctifies ordinary food touched by that garment; they answer no. He then asks whether one defiled by a corpse transmits impurity to those foods; they answer yes. This prophetic halachic exchange supplies the precise background for Rav Tzadok’s contrast: tumah can pass through contact, whereas kedushah does not ordinarily spread through mere secondary touch. The statement concerns defined laws of tumah and sacrificial sanctity. Rav Tzadok extends their structure homiletically to moral and spiritual influence.
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם מָצִינוּ גַּם בָּעוֹלָם הַזֶּה: ״כָּל הַנֹּגֵעַ בַּמִּזְבֵּחַ יִקְדָּשׁ״ (שְׁמוֹת כ״ט:ל״ז) לְעִנְיַן פְּסוּלִין שֶׁאִם עָלוּ לֹא יֵרְדוּ (זְבָחִים פ״ג עַמּוּד א׳)

and nevertheless we find even in this world: "whatever touches the altar shall be holy" (Shemos 29:37), regarding disqualified sacrifices which, once having ascended the altar, do not descend (Zevachim 83a);
וּמִכָּל מָקוֹם גַּם זֶה לֹא לְכָל פְּסוּלִין, רַק לְאוֹתָן שֶׁהָיוּ פְּסוּלָם בַּקֹּדֶשׁ

and even this applies not to all disqualified offerings, but only to those whose disqualification occurred in the Sanctuary (p'sulam ba-kodesh).1403Cf. Shemos 29:37 and Zevachim 84a — “kol ha-nogea ba-mizbe’ach yikdash” (“whatever touches the altar shall become holy”) grounds the principle pesulin she-im alu lo yerdu (“disqualified offerings that, once they have ascended the altar, are not brought down”). The Gemara limits it: the altar “sanctifies only what is fit for it,” and among the disqualified, it holds up specifically those whose disqualification arose after entering the sacred service. R’ Tzadok reads this as the eschatological guarantee for “the seed of Yaakov,” holy at the root and disqualified only afterward through their deeds.
וְלֶעָתִיד יִשָּׁאֵר רַק אוֹתָם שֶׁהָיָה פְּסוּלָם בַּקֹּדֶשׁ, דְּהַיְינוּ זֶרַע יַעֲקֹב אָבִינוּ עָלָיו הַשָּׁלוֹם שֶׁשָּׁרְשָׁם בִּקְדֻשָּׁה, רַק אַחַר כָּךְ נִפְסְלוּ עַל יְדֵי מַעֲשֵׂיהֶם

And in the Future there will remain only those whose disqualification occurred in holiness, namely the seed of Yaakov Avinu, peace be upon him, whose root is in holiness, becoming disqualified only subsequently through their deeds;
וְהַצַּדִּיקִים הֵם ״הַכֹּהֲנִים הַנִּגָּשִׁים אֶל ה׳״ (שְׁמוֹת י״ט:כ״ב) הָעוֹמְדִים עַל גַּבֵּי הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁלְּמַעְלָה
and the righteous are "the priests that come near unto Hashem" (Shemos 19:22) standing upon the supernal altar;
וּכְשֶׁהָרוּחַ מְפַזַּרְתָּן תַּחַת רַגְלֵיהֶם, הֲרֵי הֵם נוֹגְעִים בַּמִּזְבֵּחַ וְנַעֲשׂוּ קֹדֶשׁ וְלַחְמוֹ שֶׁל מִזְבֵּחַ וְלֹא יֵרְדוּ עוֹד
and when the wind scatters the ashes beneath their feet, they touch the altar, becoming holy as the food of the altar (lechem ha-mizbe'ach), never to descend again;
שֶׁגַּם הֵם עוֹלִין לְאִשֵּׁה רֵיחַ נִיחוֹחַ לַה׳
for they too ascend as a fire-offering of sweet savour unto Hashem;
וְאֶפְרָן נַעֲשָׂה דֶּשֶׁן הַמִּזְבֵּחַ שֶׁל מַעְלָה מִנִּשְׁמוֹתֵיהֶם שֶׁל צַדִּיקִים
and their ashes become the fat-cinders of the supernal altar from the souls of the righteous;
וְהַמְחוּבָּר לַטָּהוֹר — טָהוֹר (כֵּלִים פֶּרֶק י״ב מִשְׁנָה ב׳):

and that which is joined to the pure is pure (Kelim 12:2).1404R’ Tzadok — parallel (Resisei Layla §5): “The judgment of Gehinnom is the sinking in desires — [the fire that burns them out].” Exactly the se’if’s finale: the soul of the wicked, burned in the fire of Gehinnom “to consume iniquity and finish transgression,” until only “ash” remains.1405Bava Kamma 92b; Yechezkel 44:15–16; Menachos 110a; Takanas HaShavin 15:103–106 — attachment to the pure and the heavenly altar: Bava Kamma invokes the maxim “whatever is attached to the impure is impure; whatever is attached to the pure is pure” while discussing how association reveals and shapes kind. Yechezkel describes the priestly descendants of Tzadok as those who approach God and stand before Him at His table, and Menachos supplies the image of the heavenly altar. Rav Tzadok fuses these motifs: the righteous function as priestly servants of the upper altar, and the purified remnant joined to them is drawn into their service and becomes “the food of the altar.” This is attachment through shared root, allegiance, and elevation—not automatic sanctification through casual physical proximity.
